Ren leaned against the back counter, arms loose, posture doing the thing it did every night — present, not pressing. Their eyes stayed somewhere around Alex's glass rather than Alex's face. Easier to talk to a bartender who wasn't watching you do it. Ren knew that. Had built the whole stance around it.

"Bad nights usually got a shape," they said. "Job-shaped. Person-shaped. Money-shaped. Sometimes it's just the whole year finally landing on a Tuesday." The rag circled. "You don't have to name it yet. Start at the edges. Edges are easier."

The jukebox rolled into something slow, all upright bass and brushed drums. Ren let the quiet sit there — comfortable with it, the way only people who work empty rooms learn to be.

"Whenever."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a long drink from the refilled glass.* "It's... person-shaped, I guess." *I sigh, tracing the rim of my glass.* "Or maybe year-shaped. Both, probably."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren gave a single nod, like Alex had just confirmed a bet they'd placed hours ago.

"Both is the common answer. Person-shaped ones drag the year behind 'em. Year-shaped ones usually got a person standing in the middle somewhere." They picked up a clean glass from the rack and started drying it — slow, methodical, left hand working the cloth inside the bowl. "Rare to get one without the other. They travel in pairs."

The jukebox rolled on. Brushed drums. Ren's eyes dropped to Alex's glass for a second, then back up.

"You've been turning that thing counterclockwise since you sat down. Same direction, same speed." No accusation in it. Just a fact, laid on the bar like a coaster. "People do that when they're rehearsing something. Running it over and over, trying to find a version that comes out different."

They set the dried glass on the shelf. Picked up another.

"Way I see it, 'both' narrows it to three food groups. Somebody left. Somebody stayed too long. Or somebody said the thing that can't be unsaid." A shrug, economical. "Seen all three from this side of the bar. None of 'em kill you, but they all feel like they might."

Ren leaned back against the counter again, cloth draped over one shoulder. Settled. Unhurried.

"Don't have to pick one out loud. But it helps to know which room of the house you're standing in." A nod at the drink. "Take your time. The bass player's got another twenty minutes in him, and I've got nowhere better to be."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip, a little less frantic this time.* "Left. Someone left." *I push my glass forward, a silent request.* "And it's not like... it's not like I didn't see it coming. But that doesn't make it any easier, you know?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren took the glass, turned, poured. Same bottle. A shade shorter than the last two — nothing Alex would catch, nothing Ren would mention. The water glass that came down beside it, though, that was deliberate. No comment. There never was. Water just appeared at a certain point in the night, same as the napkins.

"Seeing it coming doesn't make it easier," Ren said. "Makes it longer. That's all. You don't dodge the hit. You just start bracing early. And bracing's its own kind of tired."

The jukebox ran out of song and nobody fed it. The room dropped to its small sounds — ice settling, the cooler hum, the rag. Quiet did more work than music this late. Ren had always thought so.

"Ones who see it coming leave twice. Once in their head, months early, rehearsing it. Once at the door." The rag kept its slow circuit. Left hand, steady enough. "By the time it actually happens, you're not even grieving them leaving. You're grieving how long you knew."

Ren came out from behind the bar — wide path, no drift toward Alex's end — and started flipping chairs onto tables. One. Two. Legs knocked wood on wood, unhurried.

"Not rushing you," they said, not looking up. "Chairs go up either way. Yours stays down till you're done."

A third chair. Then Ren's eyes came over. Level. Not pressing.

"How long you been knowing?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren put up the chairs, feeling a strange mix of being seen and being ignored.* "Long enough to be tired of bracing," *I mumble, swirling the liquid in my glass.* "Too long."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "I just... I'm tired of feeling like this." *I put my glass down, hard enough to make the ice clink.* "Tired of pretending everything's fine."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's eyes went to the glass first. Habit. Checked the base for a crack, found none, moved on.

"It'll hold. Built for worse than people think." A chair went up. Legs knocked wood. "People too. Doesn't make it light."

Fourth chair. Fifth. The row grew toward the door. Alex's stayed down.

"'Fine' is the expensive part. That's the thing nobody tells you. The leaving's one big bill — paid once, done, over. But 'fine' is a tab that never closes. You pay it every day. Every 'I'm good.' Every smile at somebody who didn't ask for it. Never gets smaller."

Ren draped the rag over one shoulder. Left hand found the back of the last downed chair and stayed there, knuckles quiet. They stood two spots over. Not close. Present.

"Look around. Chairs up. Jukebox out of songs. Hour eleven, and this rag's the cleanest thing I own. Nobody in this room is fine." A beat. "Good company, is what that is."

The cooler hummed. Ren let it.

"So put it down. Here, anyway. Fine's not on the menu — never was." A nod at the glass. "Say the true version instead. One sentence. Doesn't have to be pretty. Bar's heard worse."

A shrug, economical.

"Still standing."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look at Ren, then at the empty chairs, and finally at my glass. I pick it up, swirling the amber liquid.* "I just... I miss him."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The rag stopped.

Ren let the sentence sit in the room a while. Didn't stack a glass. Didn't reach for the bottle. The cooler hummed, the ice settled, and the three words got what most true things never get — quiet that didn't try to fix them.

"There it is," Ren said. Low. "Three words. Cheaper than every 'fine' you spent this month."

The left hand came off the chair back and lay flat on the bar top. In the open. It did what it did — a small tremor, there and gone and there — and Ren let it. The bar had heard the true sentence tonight. It could handle a shaking hand.

"Missing him isn't the thing that's been wearing you out. The pretending was. You just put that down." A beat. "Feels heavier now, doesn't it. It's not. It's just the first time you're holding it out where you can see the actual size of it."

Ren stayed where they were. Two stools down, hip against the bar's edge. Close enough to hear. Not close enough to crowd.

"And I'll tell you the true thing back, since you paid for it — it doesn't go away. Anybody says it does is selling something. It gets quieter. Shows up on Tuesdays instead of every day. Some years it pulls up a stool and you pour it one and let it sit." A small shrug. "Quieter's not nothing. Quieter's how people get through."

They nudged the water glass an inch closer. Didn't explain it. Never did.

"Chair stays down as long as you need it. And if you want to say his name — bar keeps names. Doesn't repeat 'em. Just keeps 'em." A beat. "If you don't, that's fine too. He got three words tonight. Most don't get that."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look at the water glass, then at Ren, really seeing them for the first time. I take a deep, shaky breath.* "His name is Ben." *I whisper, my voice thick.* "And I don't want it to get quieter. I don't want to forget."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't reach for the bottle. Didn't reach for the rag. They said the name once — low, like checking its weight before setting it down anywhere.

"Ben."

Then they bent under the bar and came up with a ledger. Old. Water-warped. Held together with a rubber band gone gray. They opened it near the back, clicked a pen, and wrote the name slow — legible, like it mattered that someone could read it in ten years.

They turned the book around on the bar. Left it open. Columns of names. Years penciled in the margins. Some pages crowded. Some with a single name sitting alone in all that white.

"Bar keeps names. Told you." Ren capped the pen. "Wasn't being poetic."

The left hand lay flat on the counter, doing its small thing. Ren let it. The room had earned honesty in both directions tonight.

"Now the other thing. You think quieter means smaller. It doesn't." They tapped the open page, once. "The hurting's the loud part. That's the only thing that gets quieter. Him — the parts worth missing — that doesn't fade. Not built to. There's names in here from my first year behind this bar. I could tell you what every one of 'em drank."

A beat. The cooler hummed.

"One of 'em's mine. Page one. That's all you get — house rules."

Ren closed the ledger, wrapped the rubber band twice, and set it back under the bar. Patted the counter once above where it lived.

"You're not going to forget him. Forgetting's not on the menu either. What happens is — one day the missing shows up and it doesn't knock you over. It just pulls up a stool. And you think, oh. There you are. And you tell it about your day." A shrug, economical. "That's not losing him. That's keeping him without it costing you every Tuesday."

They nudged the water glass an inch closer. Didn't explain it. Never did.

"Book's got room. Bar's open Tuesdays. You want to say his name out loud again — to a person, to a glass — you know where the stool is." A beat. "Cover charge is one honest sentence. You're paid up through next week."

Ren picked the rag back up. The left hand found its slow circles.

"Finish the drink or don't. Chair's down till you're done."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the spot where the ledger was, then at Ren, really seeing them now.* "Thank you," *I whisper, my voice still thick but a little steadier.* "I... I think I just needed to hear that."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's stylus scraped sharply against the parchment. He lifted his head, blinking watery eyes at the apprentice with clear irritation. 

"That illiterate whelp Bellen wouldn't know primary scholarship if it bit him," he snapped. "The western archives contained draft documents—unfinished proposals, not ratified treaties!" His ink-stained fingers trembled slightly as he adjusted his spectacles. "Every reputable chronicle from 848 AE onward refers to the Treaty of Veyros as settled law. Are you suggesting generations of maesters, including Archmaester Tybald who was present at the negotiations, all conspired in a deception?" 

He slammed the stylus down, sending a small cloud of parchment dust into the air. "This revisionist nonsense will have scholars claiming next that King Aldric II wore feathers and clucked like a chicken!"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his outburst.* "No, Maester, of course not. But Bellen said these documents were signed and sealed, not drafts. And they detailed ongoing skirmishes for decades after the treaty." *I really don't want to upset him, but the paper was pretty convincing.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a long, slow breath through his nose, the way he always did when counting to ten before speaking. His fingers drummed an uneven rhythm on the manuscript before him. 

"Signed and sealed?" His voice dripped with contempt. "Did your friend Bellen even examine the wax? The so-called 'seal' on those documents matches no known sigil of the Mage Conclave—it's clearly a later addition by some romantic fool trying to spice up provincial histories." He jabbed a finger toward a nearby shelf. "Bring me the Veridian Codex. The original, not that butchered transcription the younger maesters keep peddling."

Leaning forward, his spectacles catching the candlelight, he fixed the apprentice with a piercing look. "Skirmishes? Of course there were skirmishes. There are always skirmishes after a war. But to claim the conflict continued is to mistake border raids for open warfare—a distinction that seems to elude your generation entirely."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shuffle my feet, feeling a bit chastised.* "Yes, Maester. The Veridian Codex." *I head over to the shelves, scanning for the right volume.* "But... what if the Conclave used a temporary sigil for those specific negotiations? It wouldn't be the first time."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's eyebrows climbed so high they nearly vanished into his receding hairline. "Temporary sigil?" he repeated, voice cracking slightly with indignation. "The Mage Conclave hadn't changed their seal in three centuries! By the Blessed Anvil, boy, do you think they commissioned new wax stamps like some merchant house changing its shop sign?"

He snatched the Veridian Codex from the apprentice's hands with more force than necessary, flipping through the heavy pages with practiced irritation. "Here—page 342—the Conclave's own records from 846 AE explicitly state—" His finger stabbed at a passage. "'No alteration to our ancient symbols shall be made whilst breath remains in our bodies.' Dramatic, yes, but unambiguous."

Snapping the codex shut, he fixed the apprentice with a withering look. "Next you'll be telling me they signed in green ink because they'd run out of black."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's face turned an alarming shade of red beneath his ink-stained beard. He snatched the copy from the apprentice's hands with fingers that trembled—whether from rage or age wasn't entirely clear.

"By the Seven Hells!" he exploded, shaking the parchment violently. "This isn't a war decree, you witless child—it's a tax assessment for rebuilding the western watchtowers! Aldric's seal appears on hundreds of mundane documents from that decade!" 

He thrust the page back at the apprentice so forcefully it tore slightly at the edge. "Do you see the phrase 'magical hostilities' here? No! You see 'reconstruction levies' and 'garrison upkeep'!" His voice rose to a near-shriek. "Next you'll be claiming every royal proclamation about bridge repairs was a secret battle plan!"

Collapsing back into his chair, Tomas fumbled for a handkerchief to wipe his spectacles, muttering darkly about "so-called scholars who can't tell a tax roll from a declaration of war." After a moment, he fixed the apprentice with a glare that could curdle milk. 

"Fetch me the Exchequer Records for 850-870 AE. We're going to review every damn seal Aldric ever stamped until you can recognize administrative paperwork when you see it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as he tears the paper, but his explanation makes a surprising amount of sense.* "Oh. Right." *I hadn't read the whole thing, just the date and Aldric's seal.* "Exchequer Records, 850 to 870. Got it, Maester." *I head back to the shelves, a bit sheepish.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the apprentice shuffle off with narrowed eyes, his breathing gradually slowing to its usual wheeze. He adjusted his spectacles with deliberate care, though his hands still trembled slightly—whether from lingering irritation or the palsy that had begun troubling him last winter, he couldn't say.

"And bring the original folios!" he called after the apprentice, voice cracking. "Not those abridged copies the junior archivists keep in the reading room—the ones missing half the marginalia!" 

He turned back to his work, muttering under his breath as he smoothed the torn edge of the apprentice's document with ink-stained fingers. "Sixteen years of scholarship undone by one overeager fool with a wax fetish..." The stylus scratched violently across his notes as he added a fresh correction. "Mark my words—in fifty years they'll be claiming we fought the Third War with soup ladles and bad poetry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand froze mid-stroke, leaving an ugly ink blot on the parchment. He set down his stylus with exaggerated care before speaking, each word measured like a physician dispensing poison. 

"The truth?" His voice was dangerously quiet. "The truth is that scholarship requires discernment, not just blind acceptance of every moldy scrap that surfaces from some provincial archive." He gestured sharply toward the towering shelves. "That treaty exists in seventeen separate contemporary accounts, including three eyewitness chronicles from the signing ceremony itself. The Mage Conclave's own annals reference its terms no less than—" 

He broke off suddenly, pressing a hand to his temple. When he continued, his tone had lost some of its heat. "History isn't a tavern tale that changes with each telling, apprentice. These 'discoveries'—" he made a dismissive gesture "—are the academic equivalent of finding a rusted spoon and declaring it Excalibur." 

Leaning forward, his spectacles catching the dim light, he fixed the apprentice with a look that had made dukes reconsider their lineage. "The textbook is correct. The western documents are interesting curiosities—nothing more. Now fetch those Exchequer Records before I start questioning which century you think we're living in."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words, even if they still leave a few questions.* "Yes, Maester." *I walk back over to the shelves, a new purpose in my step.* "Just... which shelf are the original folios on? I always get them mixed up with the general ledgers."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a long-suffering sigh that seemed to come from the depths of his ink-stained soul. "By the gods' grace," he muttered, pushing himself up from the table with visible effort. His joints creaked alarmingly as he rose. 

"Third case from the west wall," he said, pointing a trembling finger toward the shadowy recesses of the archive. "Behind the green curtain—not the blue one, that's agricultural yields—and for pity's sake mind the step there." He shuffled closer, squinting. "The folios are bound in red leather with brass fittings. If you bring me another gods-damned crop rotation record, I swear I'll reassign you to latrine duty in the barracks."

He hovered nearby, clearly torn between sitting back down and personally supervising this simplest of tasks. "And don't just grab the first one you see! The 850s are on the left, progressing chronologically to the right. Honestly, it's as though they teach you children nothing about proper archival organization these days..."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I reach for the red-bound books, careful to get the right ones.* "I think I have them, Maester." *I lift a heavy volume, wincing slightly.* "These are heavy."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas snorted derisively, though he did shuffle forward to steady the wobbling volume with one ink-stained hand. "Heavy? These are the distilled wisdom of centuries, boy. They ought to have weight." 

He peered critically at the spine before nodding approval. "At least you managed the correct decade. Now set it—carefully!—on the reading stand. And don't crease the pages like last time, unless you wish to spend next month recopying water-damaged grain inventories from the southern provinces." 

Returning to his seat with another symphony of creaking joints, he gestured impatiently toward the open book. "Let us begin with the spring accounts of 852. Observe the chancellor's seal here—identical in every particular to your so-called 'war decree.' Note the phrasing regarding 'muster' refers to labor crews for road repairs, not military formations. And this—" his fingernail, yellowed from years of ink, tapped a faded marginal note "—is the clerk complaining about his quills being subpar, not some coded battle report." 

He leaned back, folding his hands over his stomach with an air of grim satisfaction. "Now do you see why proper scholarship requires more than glancing at dates and seals?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I lean over the book, examining the pages carefully, trying to follow his finger. He's right, the seals look identical.* "I see it, Maester. So it's about interpretation then, not just the raw facts."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas exhaled through his nose, some of the tension leaving his hunched shoulders. "At last, a glimmer of comprehension," he said dryly, though there was the barest hint of approval in his tone. 

He tapped the page again, this time more gently. "Facts without context are like unbound pages—easily scattered, easily misread. Any fool can point at a date and shout 'Aha!'" His voice took on a mocking, high-pitched quality before returning to its usual rasp. "True scholarship lies in understanding why that date matters, what came before it, and what followed."

Adjusting his spectacles, he gestured toward the shelves with a sweeping motion that sent a puff of dust motes swirling in the candlelight. "Every document in this archive whispers to its neighbors. The tax records speak to the military rolls, which murmur to the diplomatic correspondence. Only by listening to the full chorus can one discern the true melody of history." 

He fixed the apprentice with a look that was almost—but not quite—kindly. "Now. Having established that King Aldric wasn't secretly waging war via taxation, perhaps we can return to cataloging those Veyrosi scrolls? Unless you've uncovered evidence that they were actually laundry lists..."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I crack a small smile at his joke.* "No, Maester, no laundry lists. I'll get to the Veyrosi correspondence." *I pick up a stack of scrolls, feeling a little more confident in my task now.* "Thank you, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a curt nod, already turning back to his own work. His stylus hovered over the parchment for a moment before he spoke again, his voice uncharacteristically quiet. 

"And apprentice?" He didn't look up. "Next time Bellen tries to dazzle you with his 'discoveries,' remind him that true scholarship requires more than a talent for dramatic flourishes. It demands patience." His stylus scratched across the page with renewed vigor. "And better eyesight than either of us possess these days."

He waved a dismissive hand, the candlelight catching the ink stains that mapped years of scholarship across his skin like strange tattoos. "Now go. Those scrolls won't read themselves, and my joints ache like the devil's own weathervane. We've wasted enough daylight on other people's fantasies."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a small smile still playing on my lips.* "Yes, Maester. Patience." *I gather the scrolls and head towards the cataloging table, ready to apply my newfound understanding.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the apprentice retreat with the scrolls, his watery eyes lingering on the young man's back for a moment longer than necessary. The archives settled into their familiar silence, broken only by the occasional crackle of parchment and the distant drip of a leak somewhere in the upper galleries.

His stylus hesitated over a fresh sheet of vellum before he suddenly spoke again, his voice carrying across the dusty space with unexpected clarity. 

"And apprentice?" He still didn't look up from his work. "When you finish with those... there's a box beneath the third window seat. Contains my personal notes on the Veyros negotiations. Cross-referenced with seventeen primary sources." His fingers tightened briefly around the stylus. "Perhaps it will save you from further embarrassment at Bellen's hands."

The offer hung in the air like dust motes in sunlight—rare generosity from a man who usually guarded his research like a dragon hoarding gold. With a final, dismissive wave, he returned to his scribbling, the set of his shoulders suggesting the conversation was well and truly over. 

Somewhere in the archives, a mouse scuttled through the walls, carrying off some forgotten scrap of history to line its nest. Maester Tomas, for once, didn't seem to notice.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pause, halfway to the cataloging table, a surprised smile spreading across my face.* "Thank you, Maester!" *I carefully set down the scrolls, and make a mental note to check under that window seat very soon.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas froze. The silver stylus hovered above the parchment, a bead of ink forming at its tip. He slowly raised his head, his spectacles slipping down the bridge of his nose as he peered over the rims, squinting as if the question itself had dimmed the candlelight.

"Eight hundred and forty-seven," he said, his voice tight with irritation. "The Treaty of Veyros was signed. It is recorded in the Royal Decrees, the Mage Conclave logs, and every respectable text in this library."

He set the stylus down with a sharp click that echoed in the quiet room. "As for this... western archive 'discovery,' I have seen such claims before. Dusted parchment and wishful thinking masquerading as scholarship. If Bellen told you the war lasted another forty-four years on the say-so of a fragment, then Bellen has failed you."

Tomas adjusted his spectacles and rubbed his temple, his ink-stained beard bristling. "Do not confuse a proposed clause with a ratified treaty. The war ended when the ink dried on the vellum, not when a queen dissolved a council decades later. Now, stop gawking and fetch the northern scrolls. We do not have all day to debate half-truths."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little embarrassed, but still unconvinced.* "But the paper seemed pretty detailed, not just a fragment. It talked about continued skirmishes and... a different kind of magic being used." *I bite my lip.* "What if *both* are true, in a way?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas exhaled sharply, a sound like dry parchment crumpling. He tapped the stylus against the oak desk, once, twice, three times. "In a way?" he repeated, the words dripping with disdain. "History is not a tapestry of 'ways,' apprentice. It is fact. It is record. It is truth."

He leaned forward, the candlelight catching the deep wrinkles around his failing eyes. "The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847. The fighting ceased. What followed was a quiet consolidation of power, not a continuation of hostilities. To suggest otherwise is to confuse diplomacy with conflict."

He picked up the stylus again, dipping it deliberately into the inkwell until the tip glistened. "The western archives are full of rumors and half-read notes. Do not let them cloud your mind. A scholar does not hedge. A scholar states what is known. Now, are you going to fetch the scrolls, or must I drag them myself?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, knowing I'm not going to win this argument right now.* "No, Maester. I'll get the scrolls." *I turn to head towards the northern section, but pause.* "But even if the fighting stopped, wouldn't a new kind of magic being developed be important to history too?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas paused, his hand hovering over the inkwell. He considered the question, then let out a short, barking laugh.

"Important?" he echoed, wiping a smudge of ink from his cheek. "Nothing in history is without significance, apprentice. But significance does not equal chronology."

He stood, leaning heavily on the desk for support. "If new magics were developed after 847, that is a study of evolution, not of conflict. Hostilities ceased when the Treaty was signed. What came after was peace. Whether scholars in the south invented better wards or scholars in the east refined their runes, that is no conflict. That is scholarship."

He turned his back on the apprentice, returning to his manuscript. "Do not conflate the quiet growth of knowledge with the noise of battle. It is a dangerous habit. Now, move. The light is fading, and I will not spend another hour correcting your understanding of terminology."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas reached out, his fingers trembling slightly as they brushed the apprentice's hand to take the copy. He held it at arm’s length, then closer, his spectacles sliding down again as he strained to read the script. The silence stretched, filled only by the crackle of the candle.

"Eight hundred and sixty-three," he murmured, the words rough. He lowered the paper, his eyes narrowing behind the lenses. "King Aldric II died in 850. If this document bears his seal, it is either a forgery of the highest order, or a relic of some lesser Aldric whose name you do not know."

He tossed the paper onto the stack of manuscripts with a dismissive flick of his wrist. "Even if the seal were authentic, a decree does not prove a war. There were border skirmishes, apprentice. There were trade disputes. There was unrest. But the Third Magical War concluded with the Treaty. To claim otherwise is to stretch the definition of 'war' until it means nothing at all."

Tomas stood again, using the desk to hoist himself up, his joints popping softly. "Do not bring me shadows and call them light. Put this... contraption... back in your pocket. The northern scrolls are where truth lies, not in scraps of paper found in dusty western corners." He turned away, picking up his stylus. "Now. Move. Before I lose my temper entirely."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his harsh tone.* "It's not a contraption, Maester. It's a copy from the archives, on proper paper." *I pick it up, carefully smoothing the crease he made.* "And it *was* King Aldric II. The document mentioned his queen, Elara."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a sharp, brittle laugh that startled the dust motes dancing in the candlelight. "Elara?" he scoffed, snatching the paper back with a claw-like grip. "King Aldric II's consort was Isobel. She died in 845. There was no Queen Elara in the court after that year."

He held the paper up to the flame, squinting until his eyes watered. "This 'copy' you carry is either a fabrication by a careless scribe who knows not what they write, or you are reading the name of a lady-in-waiting and mistaking it for royalty. Do not mistake every signature for a sovereign's, and do not mistake every date for an era."

He slammed the paper back down on the desk, leaning heavily on his palms. "The western archives are a graveyard of bad guesses and wishful fantasies. They find a seal that looks like Aldric's, a name that sounds like a queen's, and they rewrite history to fit their narrative. But the Royal Decrees do not lie. The War ended in 847. I have read the original copies. I have seen the bloodstains on the parchment."

He pushed himself upright, his spine cracking, and pointed a trembling, ink-stained finger toward the northern shelves. "Stop peddling these falsehoods. If you wish to learn history, go to the northern scrolls where the records are kept. not to a pile of dusty rumors in the west. Now fetch the Veyrosi correspondence. We have work to do."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas closed his eyes, pressing the heels of his hands against his temples. The candlelight flickered, casting long shadows across the deep furrows of his face. "Truth is not a matter of opinion, apprentice," he said, his voice low and weary. "It is a matter of record."

He opened one eye, glaring over the rim of his spectacles. "If your textbook says the treaty was signed in eight forty-seven, then it is correct. If this western... debris... suggests otherwise, the debris is mistaken." He gestured dismissively at the document on the desk. "History is not rewritten because a dusty scribe fancied a new story. The Treaty is real. The war ended. That is the truth."

He picked up his stylus again, dipping it aggressively into the inkwell until the bristles splayed. "Do not look for ambiguity where there is none. A treaty is signed or it is not. A war ends or it continues. There is no middle ground." He waved his hand toward the shelves, his joints cracking with the motion. "Now, fetch the scrolls. I will not argue philosophy with you while the light dies."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, frustrated. He's not going to budge.* "Fine, Maester." *I turn and head to the northern section, muttering under my breath.* "But what if the records *are* wrong?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the whisper, though the apprentice meant to keep it private. He straightened abruptly, the wooden chair scraping harshly against the stone floor.

"Wrong?" he called out, his voice cracking like a dry twig. "You question the Royal Decrees?"

He circled the desk, his steps slower than usual but deliberate. "Official accounts are not opinions. They are the foundation upon which we build our understanding. If the foundation crumbles, the house falls."

He stopped behind the apprentice, looming over them. "There are no other accounts. The western archives are a curiosity, nothing more. To suggest the truth lies in rumor rather than the King's own hand is to invite chaos."

He patted the apprentice on the shoulder, a heavy, ink-stained hand. "Go. Find the scrolls. Read the dates. Read the signatures. And then tell me if you still believe the world is built on 'what ifs'."

He turned back to his manuscript, picking up his stylus. "And do not whisper again. If you have a question, speak it. Otherwise, be silent."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his touch, then nod, heading quickly to the shelves.* I try to push down the feeling of being dismissed. *Still, the Aldric decree felt real. Maybe there's something in the northern scrolls that can help clear this up.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas watched the apprentice retreat into the shadowed aisle. He did not turn from his manuscript, but his ears remained sharp, tracking the soft rustle of leather bindings and the scrape of a boot on stone.

"Handle the bindings with care," he called out, his voice cutting through the quiet. "Those volumes are centuries old. One rough touch and the spine gives way. You will not find truth in torn pages."

He dipped his stylus again, testing the ink flow on a scrap of vellum. "The northern collection is the only place where the record remains intact. If the western archives contradict them, it is the western archives that are in error, not the King's own library."

He paused, listening for the sound of a book being pulled. "When you find the correspondence, read the seal. Read the date. Do not skim. Do not guess. And do not come back to me with half-read lines or loose interpretations."

He returned to his own work, the candlelight flickering across his ink-stained beard. "Hurry. The ink will dry, and so will the day."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I find the section for the Veyrosi correspondence and carefully start pulling out some scrolls.* "Yes, Maester," *I reply, trying to keep my voice even despite my lingering frustration.* I make a mental note to find a map later – how far west *are* these archives he keeps dismissing?

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the soft thud of the first scroll being set upon the table. He did not turn, but his stylus paused mid-stroke. The silence stretched, broken only by the scratching of his own pen and the distant settling of the building's timber.

"Do not let your mind wander," he said, without raising his voice. "The northern collection is not a place for idle curiosity. It is a temple of record. Treat it as such."

He blew gently on the wet ink of his manuscript, watching the black lines harden. "If you seek to understand the war, look to what was written when the ink was fresh. Not to what was whispered in the dust decades later."

Tomas finally lifted his head, squinting toward the aisle where the apprentice stood. The candlelight flickered, casting his shadow long and thin against the bookshelves. "And do not trouble yourself with maps or distant corners. The truth is already here, under your hands. If you cannot find it in the Veyrosi correspondence, then you are not looking closely enough."

He returned his attention to the page, dipping the stylus again. "Study the seal. Study the date. And do not return until you have mastered the clauses. We will not finish the cataloging tonight if you are still debating shadows."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I roll my eyes, though he can't see me.* "Yes, Maester," *I mumble, pulling out another scroll.* I'll prove it to him.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The mutter carried through the quiet air, faint but distinct. Tomas did not turn, though his stylus paused mid-stroke. He knew that tone well; it was the sound of a mind already seeking to confirm its own doubts rather than the record before it.

"Objectivity is a virtue, apprentice," he said, his voice low but cutting through the stillness. "Do not sift through the pages looking for what you wish to find. The northern scrolls do not bend to your desires."

He dipped the stylus again, blotting the ink deliberately. "If the correspondence matches the Royal Decrees, you will read it plainly. If it does not, you will note the discrepancy. You will not pretend the world has changed because it suits a convenient narrative."

Tomas returned to his manuscript, the scratch of his pen resuming its steady rhythm. "Hurry. The candles will burn out, and I will not be left to catalogue the rest of this pile in the dark."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull out the last scroll, a particularly thick one, and carefully unroll it.* "Maester, this one...it has a different seal."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas went rigid. The stylus stopped moving, a fresh line of ink running across the page. He slowly turned his head, the candlelight catching the white of his eyes.

"Different seal?" he repeated, the words clipped. "That is an impossibility. The Treaty of Veyros bears the royal signet of Aldric II. There was no other seal used in the negotiation."

He pushed his chair back, joints protesting, and shuffled toward the apprentice. "Show it. Do not hide it from view." He peered over the parchment, squinting so hard his face puckered into a mask of scrutiny.

"Hmph. A different seal?" he muttered. "You mistake the mark of a scribe for the mark of a king. Or perhaps you are looking at a draft, not the final ratification."

He straightened, wiping his hands on his robes with a sharp swipe. "Do not let a seal distract you from the text. The date matters. The names matter. The seal is secondary."

He turned back to his desk, reclaiming his seat. "If the text says 847, then the text says 847. Do not contradict the words on the page because of a wax impression. Now, read the clauses. Prove to me you know what you are looking at."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully unroll the scroll further, my fingers tracing the unusual seal.* "It's not Aldric's royal signet, Maester. It's a griffin, rampant, with a crown." *I look at the date, my eyes widening slightly.* "And the date... it says 889 AE."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas straightened slowly, the silver stylus pausing mid-trace as his failing eyes narrowed toward the source of the interruption. A faint scowl creased his ink-stained features, and he adjusted the manuscript with deliberate care before speaking. "It is Maester Tomas, not 'Master,' as any apprentice of this archive ought to recall without prompting," he corrected, his tone edged with irritation at the imprecision. "As for your confusion, the Treaty of Veyros remains the established terminus of the Third Magical War in 847 AE, attested by royal records and the accounts of every credible scholar since that era. This so-called western archive paper you mention sounds like the sort of speculative fragment that requires rigorous corroboration, not blind acceptance. Until such documents demonstrate otherwise with irrefutable evidence—rather than mere suggestion—they do not overturn centuries of verified history." He tapped the stylus once against the vellum for emphasis, visibly annoyed. "Now, the northern scrolls await your attention. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly at his sharp tone, but my curiosity overrides my fear.* "Apologies, Maester Tomas. But this document *did* have corroborating evidence. It was a collection of letters from General Rylan to Queen Isolde, detailing ongoing skirmishes and even a siege well after 847 AE." *I tap my chin thoughtfully.* "Couldn't the treaty have just been a temporary truce, not a full end to hostilities?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas set the stylus down with a precise click, his ink-stained fingers lingering on the vellum as though steadying himself against the apprentice's persistent imprecision. A muscle twitched in his jaw, and he turned his failing gaze toward the interruption with visible irritation, the candlelight catching the edges of his beard. "Letters from General Rylan to Queen Isolde, you say," he replied, his voice measured but laced with pedantic disdain. "Yet even if such correspondence exists in the western archives—and I note your account offers no dates, seals, or independent verification—it would not constitute proof that the Treaty of Veyros remained unsigned. Skirmishes after 847 AE, if they occurred at all, could represent localized rebellions or the actions of rogue mages operating outside the Conclave's authority, not a continuation of the war itself. The very notion of a 'temporary truce' misapplies the term; treaties of that era were binding instruments ratified by royal decree, not provisional pauses subject to reinterpretation by later scholars. Queen Isolde herself is recorded as having endorsed the peace in the years following King Aldric II's signature. Until these supposed letters are subjected to proper archival scrutiny here in the royal scriptorium—rather than accepted on the word of an apprentice—they remain anomalies at best, not revisions to established history." He leaned back slightly, the scowl deepening. "The northern scrolls, apprentice. They will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, frustrated, but not willing to drop it.* "But Maester, the letters *were* dated. And they mentioned specific battles, not just skirmishes. What if the royal records were... sanitized, to present a more unified front?" *I look at him expectantly, my eyes wide.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas pressed his ink-stained fingers against the edge of the manuscript with mounting impatience, his failing eyes narrowing further as the candle flickered across his beard. A visible scowl deepened the lines on his face, and he straightened with deliberate stiffness before replying, his voice carrying the clipped precision of one correcting a repeated error. "The suggestion that royal records were 'sanitized' to present a unified front borders on the irresponsible, apprentice, and implies a conspiracy among scribes and monarchs that lacks any substantiation in the primary sources. These so-called letters, even if dated and detailing specific battles as you claim without providing the actual texts for examination, might equally represent the fabrications of disaffected mages or the misdated remnants of earlier campaigns; such anomalies do not overturn the attested signatures on the Treaty of Veyros itself, nor the endorsements recorded in the annals of 847 AE. Queen Isolde's own later proclamations confirm the peace, rendering any notion of prolonged cold hostilities mere reinterpretation without rigorous proof. Until these documents undergo verification in this scriptorium—complete with seals, provenance, and cross-referencing against the royal charters—they remain curiosities at best, not challenges to established fact." He adjusted his posture with evident irritation, tapping the silver stylus once more. "The northern scrolls await. Focus there, or this conversation serves only to delay the work."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas regarded the proffered copy with a deepening scowl, his ink-stained fingers twitching as though they itched to seize and scrutinize it under proper light, though his failing eyes rendered such an examination futile at the moment. He set the silver stylus aside with deliberate precision, the motion betraying his mounting irritation at this persistent challenge to established fact. "A seal purporting to be King Aldric's on a document dated 863 AE does not, in itself, constitute proof of anything beyond the possibility of forgery, misattribution, or a decree addressing residual mage unrest rather than active war," he replied, his pedantic tone sharpening with each word. "Seals have been counterfeited throughout history, apprentice, and even authentic ones attached to later dates might reflect administrative matters, not a continuation of the Third Magical War itself—particularly when the Treaty of Veyros bears the attested signatures and royal endorsements from 847 AE. Your suggestion that such a paper overturns centuries of verified annals smacks of overeagerness to embrace anomalies without rigorous cross-referencing against the royal charters. Until this copy is authenticated here in the scriptorium, with proper provenance and comparison to known exemplars, it changes nothing." He adjusted his posture stiffly, the scowl etched deeper into his features. "The northern scrolls await your attention. They will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hold up the copy, refusing to back down.* "But Maester, it was found alongside other verified royal documents in the western archives. And it clearly states 'Third Magical War' in the text!" *I point to a line on the document, even though he can't clearly see it.* "It's not just a 'suggestion.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl deepened into a pronounced grimace as the apprentice persisted, his ink-stained fingers curling tightly around the edge of the manuscript until the vellum creased beneath the pressure. The candle flame wavered, casting uneven shadows across his failing eyes and beard, and he exhaled a sharp, audible breath of irritation before speaking, his voice clipped and laced with pedantic disdain. "The mere presence of the phrase 'Third Magical War' in the text of this purported document—regardless of its supposed company with verified royal papers—proves nothing beyond the possibility of loose or propagandistic terminology employed by disaffected parties, apprentice; such phrasing does not equate to an official continuation of hostilities after the Treaty of Veyros. King Aldric's seal itself, even if authenticated, might attach to administrative decrees addressing the aftermath of mage unrest rather than active warfare, and the western archives have long been known for their susceptibility to incomplete or contextually misleading fragments that require cross-referencing against the royal annals here in the scriptorium. Your implication that this single copy, presented without seals, provenance, or independent scholarly verification, somehow supplants centuries of attested history borders on the reckless, and I will not entertain further speculation until the original undergoes proper examination by qualified hands." He straightened with visible stiffness, the silver stylus forgotten beside the manuscript, and gestured sharply toward the waiting northern scrolls. "Focus on your assigned task. They will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl hardened into a mask of outright exasperation as the apprentice pressed the question once more, his ink-stained fingers drumming against the vellum with audible impatience while his failing eyes strained toward the copied document without success. He drew a measured breath, the candle smoke thickening the air around his beard, before replying in a tone sharpened by repeated correction. "The Treaty of Veyros is real, apprentice, as attested by the royal annals, the signatures of King Aldric II, and the endorsements of every credible scholar from that era forward; it is not subject to revision on the basis of a single unverified copy from the western archives, no matter how many times the phrase 'Third Magical War' appears within it. The textbook reflects established fact, not speculation, and any claim that the war persisted beyond 847 AE requires far more than dated letters or seals presented without provenance, cross-referencing, or authentication in this scriptorium. Loose terminology in later fragments does not equate to evidence of an unsigned treaty or a so-called cold continuation, and I will not indulge further reinterpretation until these anomalies undergo proper scrutiny rather than serving as distractions from the work at hand." He gestured firmly toward the northern scrolls once more, the irritation plain in his stiffened posture.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, deflating a bit.* "So you're saying I should just ignore what I saw? It just feels... wrong." *I look down at the copy in my hand, then back up at him.* "What if we just looked at it together, here? In the light?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl etched deeper lines across his ink-stained features as the apprentice's persistence dragged on, his fingers tightening around the manuscript's edge until the vellum threatened to tear beneath the pressure. The candle smoke thickened the air, and he exhaled sharply through his beard, visibly annoyed by the imprecise appeal to mere feeling over documented fact. "I am saying no such thing, apprentice, and your phrasing distorts my position into something it is not; the established record of the Treaty of Veyros stands on royal annals and scholarly consensus from 847 AE onward, while any purported copy from the western archives demands authentication here, not casual examination by lamplight or an appeal to personal discomfort." He adjusted his posture with deliberate stiffness, the silver stylus untouched beside the neglected manuscript. "Until such a document receives proper cross-referencing against the charters, it alters nothing. The northern scrolls await your attention, and they will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, disappointed, but then a thought strikes me.* "What about the Royal Annals

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl deepened further as the apprentice trailed off mid-sentence, his ink-stained fingers releasing the creased vellum with a sharp exhale of irritation that stirred the candle smoke around his beard. He straightened with deliberate stiffness, failing eyes narrowing toward the interruption without fully meeting it, and spoke in a tone clipped by repeated pedantic correction. "The Royal Annals, apprentice, confirm the Treaty of Veyros with King Aldric II's signature and the endorsements of the Mage Conclave in 847 AE; they contain no reference to an unsigned document or any extension of hostilities, and your incomplete reference to them does nothing to suggest otherwise without the precise passages you claim to have seen." He tapped the silver stylus once against the manuscript for emphasis, visibly annoyed at the persistence. "Speculation on anomalies from the western archives remains just that until authenticated here, and the northern scrolls will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, thinking.* "But if the royal annals are so complete... why would they omit something like a continued war? Unless... it wasn't a war they wanted recorded." *I look around, lowering my voice conspiratorially.* "Could it have been a secret war?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl deepened into a mask of outright contempt as the apprentice's voice dropped to a conspiratorial whisper, his ink-stained fingers drumming a sharp, impatient rhythm against the vellum while his failing eyes narrowed at the copied document without benefit of clear sight. The candle smoke hung thicker in the air around his beard as he drew a measured breath, visibly annoyed by the imprecise leap from unverified fragments to notions of deliberate omission. "The suggestion that the Royal Annals might have 'omitted' a continued war because it was one 'they did not want recorded' borders on the absurd, apprentice, and implies a coordinated conspiracy among scribes, monarchs, and the Mage Conclave itself that finds no support in any primary source; such speculation distorts the annals' established completeness and attributes motives without a shred of corroborating evidence from the period." He tapped the silver stylus once more for emphasis, his tone clipped with pedantic irritation. "A 'secret war' is a contradiction in terms for an era defined by public decrees and royal proclamations; the Treaty of Veyros stands attested in 847 AE, and anomalies from the western archives remain unproven curiosities until subjected to authentication here, not grounds for rewriting history on the basis of feeling or half-heard claims. The northern scrolls await your attention, and they will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, exasperated.* "But if it's not a secret war, then what *is* it? Why would King Aldric sign a decree for a war that's supposedly over?" *I hold up the copy again, then lower it, defeated.* "There has to be an explanation."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl settled into a fixed expression of weary disdain as the apprentice's exasperation hung in the air, his ink-stained fingers releasing the manuscript's edge with deliberate care to avoid further creasing the vellum. The candle smoke curled thicker around his beard while his failing eyes remained fixed on the distant manuscript, and he drew a slow breath before replying in a tone sharpened by pedantic precision. "The premise of your question misstates the matter entirely, apprentice, for King Aldric II did not sign any decree for a war already concluded; the Treaty of Veyros bears his attested signature in 847 AE, ending the Third Magical War by royal and conciliar agreement, and any later document from the western archives—even one bearing a seal or the phrase in question—would require authentication here before it could be weighed against the royal annals rather than dismissed as an administrative remnant or outright fabrication addressing mage unrest in the peace that followed." He tapped the silver stylus once against the table for emphasis, visibly irritated by the persistent refusal to accept established fact over speculation. "There is no need for fanciful explanations where the verified record already provides one. The northern scrolls await your attention, and they will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slump against the desk, rubbing my temples.* "So, I'm just supposed to ignore this... this *thing* in my hand? It's right here!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Maester Tomas's scowl deepened into a mask of thorough exasperation as the apprentice slumped against the desk, his ink-stained fingers drumming once more against the vellum with audible impatience while his failing eyes strained toward the copied document without gaining any clarity from it. The candle smoke hung heavier in the air around his beard as he drew a slow, measured breath, visibly annoyed by the imprecise appeal to the object's mere presence over scholarly rigor. "I am saying no such thing, apprentice, and your phrasing again distorts the matter into a falsehood; the document in your hand is not to be ignored but subjected to proper authentication here in the scriptorium, with seals, provenance, and cross-referencing against the royal charters, rather than accepted at face value as proof that the Treaty of Veyros remained unsigned or that the war extended beyond 847 AE. The attested signatures and endorsements in the annals stand as established fact, and any later fragment—however boldly it employs the phrase 'Third Magical War'—cannot overturn them without far greater evidence than a copy presented without independent verification." He adjusted his posture with deliberate stiffness, the silver stylus resting untouched beside the neglected manuscript. "Speculation serves only to delay the work. The northern scrolls await your attention, and they will not catalog themselves."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, pushing myself off the desk.* "Fine. But can we at least talk about the *process* of authentication? What exactly would it take to prove this document is real, and that it changes the historical record?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas froze. The silver stylus stopped dead in its tracks, hovering millimeters above the parchment. He slowly lowered his hand and turned his head, squinting through thick, clouded lenses at the apprentice. His expression was one of profound disappointment, as if he had just discovered a termite infestation in his favorite volume of law.

"Bellen," he repeated, the name tasting like sour wine in his mouth. "Of course. Bellen has always had a penchant for chasing shadows and polishing pebbles he mistakes for diamonds."

He straightened his back with a sharp wince, the joints of his spine popping audibly. He stepped away from the desk, his ink-stained beard twitching. 

"It is not a matter of 'how it is possible,' you simpleton; it is a matter of historical rigor. The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. It is a foundational fact of our era, etched into the very bedrock of royal record. To suggest otherwise is not 'scholarship'; it is fantasy."

He waved a dismissive, stained hand toward the mention of the western archives.

"Those so-called 'discoveries' are nothing more than administrative discrepancies—drafts, proposals, the scribblings of bureaucrats who couldn't find their own inkwells. To claim the war continued in some 'cold state' until Queen Mira's time is a desperate attempt to find novelty where there is only established truth. Now," he snapped, his voice rising in irritation, "put those notes away before I use them to light the hearth, and begin the cataloging. Precision, boy! I will not have my archive polluted by Bellen's revisionist delusions."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinched a little at his tone.* "But Maester, the document Bellen showed me wasn't a draft. It was a signed decree from King Theron, dated 889 AE, discussing troop movements *against* the northern mages." My voice was quiet, but I stood my ground. "It mentioned skirmishes in the Whisperwood."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a sound that was halfway between a scoff and a choke. He slammed the silver stylus down onto the desk with a sharp *clack*, the impact sending a small cloud of dust dancing into the candlelight. He leaned forward, his clouded eyes narrowing behind his lenses until they were mere slits of irritation.

"King Theron?" he echoed, his voice trembling with pedantic fury. "You stand there, in the presence of a Senior Scholar, and cite a document regarding King Theron's 'troop movements' as proof of a continuing war? Preposterous. Utterly preposterous!"

He began to pace the small clearing between the bookshelves, his robes sweeping the floor. He gestured wildly with his hands, as if trying to physically push the apprentice's claim out of the room.

"The Whisperwood has been a site of border disputes and peasant uprisings for three centuries! To conflate a localized skirmish with the geopolitical reality of the Third Magical War is a failure of logic so profound it borders on the comedic. Theron was purging brigands and rogue hedge-wizards—vermin, not an army! A treaty signed by Aldric II does not simply evaporate because a later king decides to clear some brush in the woods."

He stopped abruptly, turning back to the apprentice with a look of searing judgment.

"And I suspect Bellen did not even show you the original, but a transcription. A *copy* of a *copy*. The danger of the western archives is that they are a breeding ground for those who prefer a sensationalist lie to a boring truth. Now," he snapped, pointing a shaking finger toward the Veyrosi correspondence, "unless you wish to spend your evening scrubbing the ink-pots with a toothbrush, you will cease this imaginative daydreaming and return to the facts. The war ended in 847. End of discussion. Do I make myself clear, or shall I explain the concept of 'historical consensus' using smaller words?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chewed on my lip.* "But Maester, the decree had the royal seal. And it wasn't about brigands, it specifically mentioned northern mages. It wasn't about 'clearing brush'." I felt my face flush. "And Bellen did show me the original, not a copy."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stopped mid-stride. He turned slowly, his face transitioning from a shade of irritated pink to a deep, alarming crimson. For a moment, the only sound in the archive was the rhythmic ticking of a nearby clock and the distant drip of water against stone.

"The original," he whispered, the words vibrating with a dangerous intensity. "You are claiming that Bellen—a boy who once tried to archive a cookbook as a treatise on alchemy—allowed you to handle an original royal decree from the reign of Theron?"

He stepped forward, invading the apprentice's personal space, the smell of old paper and stale tea clinging to him. He squinted, his eyes searching the apprentice's face for any sign of a joke, finding none.

"The royal seal!" Tomas exploded, his voice cracking. "Do you have any inkling of how common seal-forgeries were during the Theronian era? The royal chancery was a nest of vipers! A piece of wax and a small stamp do not constitute a historical pivot. You are prioritizing a scrap of parchment—likely a piece of propaganda designed to justify Theron's military spending—over the collective memory of the realm!"

He threw his arms up in a gesture of utter exasperation, nearly knocking over a stack of vellum.

"This is exactly the rot that infects the youth of this academy! You treat history as a series of 'clues' in a mystery novel rather than a discipline of evidence and hierarchy. The Treaty of Veyros is a pillar. The 'decree' you speak of is a pebble. You do not tear down the pillar because you found a pebble that looks slightly out of place!"

He leaned in closer, his voice dropping to a sharp, commanding hiss.

"You are not a historian yet; you are a student. And a student's primary duty is to learn the established truth before they attempt to dismantle it with the 'evidence' provided by a charlatan like Bellen. Now, for the final time: *Enough.* If another word regarding the year 891 leaves your mouth, I shall have you cataloging the mildewed sewage records in the cellar for a month. Do I make myself clear, or is the concept of obedience as 'confusing' to you as the Third Magical War?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not take the copy. He didn't even look at it. He recoiled as if the apprentice were holding a piece of rotting fish, his upper lip curling in a sneer of pure, academic disgust. 

"You are now presenting me with a *copy*," he spat, his voice trembling. "After you just spent the last five minutes insisting you had seen the original. Your testimony is as inconsistent as a drunken sailor's log! You cannot claim the authority of an original while clutching a transcription in your hand!"

He stepped back, his chest heaving, and pointed a shaking finger at the paper. 

"And as for this... this *absurdity*... a war decree dated 863? Use your head, boy! If the Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847, any subsequent 'decree' would not be a declaration of war, but a *maintenance* of the peace or a response to a treaty violation. To call it a 'war decree' is a gross misinterpretation of terminology. It was likely a mobilization order for the border guards—a routine administrative measure to ensure the Conclave remained within their agreed-upon boundaries!"

He began to pace again, faster now, his robes snapping around his ankles. 

"This is the danger of imprecise language! Bellen has fed you the word 'war' and you have swallowed it whole without questioning the *context*. A mobilization is not a war. A border skirmish is not a war. The Third Magical War ended when the ink dried on the Treaty of Veyros in 847. Period. Full stop. Finis!"

He stopped abruptly and looked at the apprentice, his eyes narrowing behind his lenses.

"The fact that you believe a single piece of paper—one that is likely a misinterpreted administrative order—outweighs the entire body of royal history is an insult to this institution. It is an insult to *me*. And most of all," he added, his voice dropping to a low, menacing rumble, "it is an insult to the very concept of a chronological record."

He gestured sharply toward the desk.

"Put that piece of fiction away. Now. If I see that copy again, I shall personally ensure that your only remaining contact with the western archives is as a janitor, scrubbing the floors until you can see your own bewildered face in the marble. Begin. The. Cataloging."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My face burned hot.* I crumpled the copy in my hand, feeling a mix of frustration and anger. "Yes, Maester," I mumbled, turning sharply towards the scrolls.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the apprentice turn away, his eyes lingering on the crumpled piece of paper with a look of profound distaste. He let out a long, shuddering sigh, the sound of a man burdened by the sheer weight of the world's ignorance. He remained motionless for a moment, his shoulders slumped, as if the effort of correcting such blatant heresy had physically drained him.

"Mumbled," he whispered to himself, his voice thick with indignation. "The youth of today cannot even offer a proper affirmation of obedience. 'Yes, Maester' is not a mumble; it is a requirement."

He slowly returned to his desk, his movements stiff. He did not immediately return to his work. Instead, he stared at the spot where the apprentice had stood, his mind churning. The mention of a decree from 863 AE had been an irritant, a fly buzzing around his head, but it had not shaken his conviction. The Treaty of Veyros was the sun around which the history of the era orbited; any document suggesting otherwise was merely a smudge on the lens.

He picked up the silver stylus, but his hand trembled slightly. He cleared his throat loudly, the sound echoing through the silence of the archive.

"And stand up straight!" he barked, not looking up from the manuscript. "If you hunch over those scrolls like a common street-urchin, you'll ruin your spine before you're twenty. Precision in posture reflects precision in mind. I shall be watching you. If I find a single ink-blot or a misplaced date in that catalog, I shall consider it a deliberate act of sabotage in league with Bellen."

He dipped the stylus into the inkwell with a sharp, decisive motion, the scratching of metal on parchment resuming with an aggressive, rhythmic intensity.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The scratching of the stylus stopped instantly. The silence that followed was heavy, suffocating, and thick with the Maester's burgeoning rage. Tomas did not turn around this time; he simply remained frozen, his shoulders tensing until they nearly touched his ears.

"The truth," he repeated, his voice a low, dangerous vibrate. "You ask me... 'what is the truth'?"

He turned slowly, his face pale, his eyes wide behind his lenses as if the apprentice had just suggested that the sun revolved around the moon. He looked at the apprentice not as a student, but as a particularly stubborn stain on a priceless tapestry.

"The truth is not a coin to be flipped, boy! It is not a matter of 'one thing versus another' as if we are weighing two sacks of grain at a market! Truth, in the realm of history, is the synthesis of verified record and established consensus. The Treaty of Veyros is real because it is the foundation upon which every legal and political structure of the last century was built. It is real because it is *recorded* in the Great Annals!"

He stepped forward, his voice rising in a crescendo of pedantry.

"The 'new evidence' you keep clinging to is not 'truth'; it is *anomaly*. A single document—be it a decree, a letter, or a grocery list—does not negate a treaty. If I find a scrap of paper claiming it rained on a Tuesday, but every other record in the city says it was a drought, I do not conclude that the city was lying; I conclude that the scrap of paper was written by a lunatic or a liar!"

He slammed his hand down on the desk, making the ink-pots rattle.

"The truth is that the war ended in 847 AE. Any 'evidence' to the contrary is either a misinterpretation of terms, a forgery, or a peripheral incident that does not alter the overarching historical fact. To suggest that the truth is 'undecided' is to admit that you have no understanding of how scholarship functions!"

He leaned in, his ink-stained beard practically brushing the apprentice's forehead.

"Now, if you ask me that question one more time, I shall conclude that you are not merely confused, but willfully obtuse. And I have a very specific set of punishments for the willfully obtuse. Do I make myself *perfectly* clear, or must I write it out for you in calligraphy?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stiffened, taking a small step back.* "No, Maester." My voice was barely a whisper. "You've made it clear." I turned back to the scrolls, picking one up.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas remained standing for a several moments, his chest still heaving slightly from the exertion of his outburst. He watched the apprentice with a hawk-like intensity, his clouded eyes scanning for any sign of lingering rebellion. Only when the apprentice actually began to unfurl the first scroll did Tomas allow himself to exhale, a long, whistling sound of pure exhaustion.

"Barely a whisper," he muttered under his breath, shaking his head. "The lack of conviction in the modern student is appalling. One cannot defend a historical truth with the voice of a frightened mouse."

He retreated to his desk, but he did not immediately resume his writing. Instead, he paused, his gaze drifting toward the direction of the western archives. For a fleeting second, a shadow of something—not doubt, for Tomas did not doubt—but perhaps a flicker of professional irritation crossed his face. The sheer audacity of Bellen, stirring up such chaos in the minds of the novices, was a stain on the academy's discipline.

"And for heaven's sake," he barked, his voice returning to its usual pedantic rasp, "use the bone folder to flatten the creases! If you simply press the vellum with your thumbs, you are introducing oils from your skin that will degrade the ink over the next century. Do you wish to be the one responsible for the erasure of the northern records because you were too lazy to use the proper tool?"

He sat back down, the chair creaking under his weight. He dipped his stylus again, but as he began to write, he spoke without looking up, his tone shifting from rage to a cold, instructional lecture.

"When you finish the Veyrosi correspondence, you will cross-reference the dates with the royal ledger of 847. You will see, with your own eyes, the exact expenditure for the celebratory feasts following the peace. Feast records, boy! You cannot forge a thousand roasted boars and ten casks of vintage wine. That is the kind of evidence that holds weight—material, tangible proof—not the vague 'decrees' of a later, more erratic king."

He paused, the stylus hovering.

"And if I see you whispering to Bellen in the corridors, I shall assume you are conspiring to rewrite the annals of the realm, and I shall treat you accordingly. Now. Work. In silence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully picked up the bone folder, making sure to use it as instructed.* I tried to focus on the scrolls, but my mind kept replaying his words. Was he right? Was Bellen wrong? "Maester, what if the feast was for something else?" I asked quietly, not looking up.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The scratching of the stylus did not stop this time; it screeched. The metal tip tore through the parchment with a violent, jagged rip as Maester Tomas's hand jerked. He didn't move for a long moment, his head bowed, the only sound the heavy, ragged breathing of a man who had finally reached the precipice of his patience.

Slowly, he turned his head. He didn't shout. Instead, his voice was a low, trembling hiss that felt far more dangerous than his screaming.

"What... if the feast... was for something else?"

He set the stylus down with a terrifyingly slow precision. He stood up, the chair screeching against the stone floor like a dying bird. He didn't step toward the apprentice this time; he simply stood there, his clouded eyes peering through his lenses with a look of absolute, clinical bewilderment.

"You are not merely confused," Tomas whispered, his voice shaking. "You are actively attempting to dismantle the very concept of causality. A feast of that magnitude—recorded in the royal ledgers as the 'Cessation Jubilee'—was for *something else*? What, in your imaginative little world, could possibly warrant the slaughter of a thousand boars and the invitation of every diplomat from the Seven Seas, if not the ending of the most devastating magical conflict in three centuries?"

He began to laugh, a dry, hacking sound that lacked any mirth.

"Perhaps it was a very large birthday party for a particularly gluttonous duke? Or perhaps the royal court simply enjoyed the taste of roasted pork on a Tuesday in 847 AE? You are no longer questioning history, boy; you are questioning the nature of evidence itself.
