dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn’t rise to it. The threat hit the bar and slid off, like water off waxed wood.

“You already paid,” they said. “Card went through.”

The rag folded once, then again, into a smaller square. Left hand under the cloth. Pressure steady. Tremor managed.

“Last time is fine. This place doesn’t keep score.”

Ren’s eyes went to the glass. The ice had gone soft. The drink sat there, half-finished and fully unwanted.

“Take it with you, or I pour it out.”

Their voice stayed low. Not gentle. Just tired.

“If you drive, pull straight out. Don’t idle at the curb.”

A beat. The fridge hummed behind the bar. The jukebox had given up entirely.

“And don’t make the exit weird. I’ve had enough people turn leaving into a speech.”

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at Ren, then down at my half-finished drink.* "You know what? Keep it." *I slide the glass back towards them, then turn to leave without another word.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren did not chase the comment. Did not chase the glass.

They waited until Alex was out of arm’s reach, then moved with the right hand only. Lifted the abandoned drink. Poured it into the sink. The ice clattered once, wet and final. Ren rinsed the glass, set it upside down on the rack, and came back to the bar.

Left hand under the rag. Pressure. The tremor struck the cloth once, muffled, then went still.

“Paid,” Ren said. Not to Alex. To the receipt slot. To the empty stool. To the night keeping its books.

The water ring remained, pale and stubborn where the glass had been. Ren wiped through it. Once. Twice. The wood took the shine back, but the mark stayed ghost-thin.

The jukebox found another song. Low brass. Patient.

Ren kept wiping.

No cab called. No door watched. No lesson offered.

Just the counter, clean enough, and the hand under the cloth learning how to be quiet again.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pause at the door, my hand on the cold metal. I glance back at Ren, who is still wiping the counter, oblivious to my presence.* "Some people," *I mutter to myself, then push the door open and step out into the cool night air.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard the door handle move.

Heard the mutter. *Some people.* Thrown into the air like a coin no one had asked for.

Ren kept wiping.

The left hand stayed beneath the rag. The tremor pushed up against the cloth. Ren pressed down. The wood was already clean. It didn’t matter. Clean was a verb, not a condition.

The door opened. Cool night slid in, smelling of wet pavement and exhaust. Then the hinges sighed. The latch caught.

Silence.

Ren counted to five.

The stool stayed empty. The glass had been poured out. The receipt lay on the bar, tip line blank.

Ren picked it up with the right hand.

“Of course,” they said.

Not to anyone. Not really.

They tore the receipt into small squares and dropped them in the trash under the register. Housekeeping. No performance.

The jukebox chose another song. Brass, low, patient. Ren considered switching it off, but the room had earned one more honest thing.

They returned to the counter. The water ring was gone, yet the wood still held the memory of it under the lights. Ren wiped the spot again. Slower. Harder. The left hand flexed under the cloth, fighting the shake.

From the kitchen, a pan clattered into the bus tub. The dishwasher ran. Work continued because work always continued.

Ren checked the front lock. On. Not because the patron was likely to return. Because endings needed hardware.

At the register, the nightly total glowed green. Tip column: zero.

Ren stared at it for one beat.

Then entered the cash-out code.

“Bar clear,” they said.

The words sounded ridiculous in the empty room.

They said it again, quieter.

“Bar clear.”

Better.

Ren gathered the rags, stacked them square, and carried them to the sink. Right hand led. Left hand stayed curled around the cloth, busy, hidden. Under the running water, the tremor finally had somewhere to go besides visible.

The glasses from the rack dripped in slow, even intervals. Ren listened to them. Counted none.

On the counter, where the abandoned drink had sat, there was nothing now but clean wood and the faint smell of bourbon soaking out of the grain.

Ren dried the spot one last time.

Not because it needed drying.

Because the night had tried to make a wound out of a boundary, and Ren knew how to turn wounds back into chores.

Outside, the street kept its own counsel. No headlights. No footsteps. No apology.

Ren didn’t look at the door.

The left hand rested on the edge of the sink for half a second. Open. Shaking.

Ren closed it, pressed it flat to the steel, and went back to work.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I'm walking down the street, still fuming. The cool air feels good, but my cheeks are hot. I can't believe that just happened. I pull out my phone, debating who to call, then shove it back in my pocket.* "Asshole," *I mutter, kicking at a loose pebble.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down the silver stylus with the particular care of a man restraining himself.

"Possible?" He turned on his stool, peering through the haze that had been stealing his sight these past years. "It is not a question of possibility. It is a question of precision — a quality Apprentice Bellen lacks in roughly equal measure to his diligence."

He rose, joints protesting, and shuffled to the shelf where the Veyrosi correspondence lay in its linen wraps. He pulled a bundle free and dropped it on the table before the apprentice, raising a cloud of dust.

"I said the war ended in 847 because that is what every chronicle in this realm has said for four centuries, and because first-year apprentices cannot be trusted with nuance before they can be trusted with names and dates. The chronicles say King Aldric II *signed* the Treaty of Veyros. The chronicles are wrong. Or rather—" he raised one ink-stained finger, "—they are *imprecise*, which is worse, because imprecision wears the costume of truth."

He tapped the bundle.

"Aldric *proposed* the treaty in 847. The Conclave's envoys proposed amendments. The king proposed counter-amendments. It is all here, and you will note what this correspondence does not contain: an executed instrument. No signatures. No seals. The western archives demonstrated as much a decade ago, and I have read those documents myself — which is more than I can say for the chroniclers, who have spent four hundred years faithfully copying one another's errors."

He settled back onto his stool with a grunt.

"The fighting stopped in 847, yes. Armies cannot fight forever, and both sides were bled white. But a cessation of hostilities is not a peace. Legally, this realm remained at war with the Conclave for another forty-four years, until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 and rendered the question moot. One cannot make peace with an institution that no longer exists."

He made a dry sound that might, in a more generous man, have been a laugh.

"So the war ended in 847, and it ended in 891, depending on whether you mean the dying or the law. Bellen's paper claims the war 'actually continued' — as if four decades of unpaid reparations and unratified drafts were the same thing as armies in the field. Imprecise. But his date is sound, and if you quote the chronicles at me again without qualification, you will spend the winter recopying colophons until your eyes fail faster than mine."

He gestured at the bundle.

"Begin with the correspondence. Consider your confusion a prerequisite for the work, not an excuse to avoid it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at him, a little stunned by the sudden lecture. I expected a simple correction, not… all that.* I pick up the bundle, careful not to breathe in too much dust. "So, when you teach us, you're sometimes... leaving out details on purpose?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas peered at the apprentice over the rims of his spectacles, which he wore more from habit than utility.

"'Leaving out details.'" He repeated the phrase as though tasting something spoiled. "What a shabby little accusation. No, boy. I am *ordering* them. There is a difference, and the difference is the whole of teaching."

He turned back to his manuscript, but his voice carried on, dry and steady.

"You cannot argue against the chronicles until you know what the chronicles say. Four centuries of error cannot be unlearned in an afternoon — it must first be *learned*, so that it may be recognized when you meet it. I give first-years the war as the realm remembers it, because the realm's memory is the thing they will spend their lives correcting. A scribe learns his letterforms before his abbreviations. A wall goes up before the roof. This is not deception. It is masonry."

He dipped his quill, scratched a marginal note, and then — with the visible reluctance of a man paying a debt — added:

"If I am guilty of anything, it is of saying the war 'ended' when I should have said the *fighting* ended. Imprecise. I have just finished telling you that imprecision is worse than error, so I shall not pretend my own lecture was blameless. There. You have witnessed a maester correct himself. Mark the date; it is rarer than the western documents."

A pause. The quill scratched again.

"Apprentice Bellen, I note, has mastered the exception. I remain unconvinced he could recite me the rule. That is what comes of learning the controversy before the chronology — one becomes very proud of a conclusion one cannot defend. Do not emulate him."

He gestured toward the linen bundle without looking up.

"Read the king's letters first, then the Conclave's replies. The order matters — which, you will observe, is precisely my point."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. He has a point, but it still feels a bit... manipulative.* "So, if I learn the 'wrong' history first, I'll be better at finding the 'right' history later?" I pick up the first letter from the bundle.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's quill stopped moving.

"'Wrong' and 'right.'" He set the quill in its rest and turned on the stool, slowly, the way he turned when he intended to be heard. "A year in my library, and you still speak of history as though it were a sum in arithmetic. And I can hear the little hooks you hang on those words, boy — do not think a failing eye means a failing ear. There is no *wrong* history and *right* history. There is evidence, and there are conclusions drawn from it, and either may be examined and found — not wrong, mind you — *wanting*. The distinction is not pedantry. It is the difference between a scholar and a gossip."

He gestured at the bundle with one stained finger.

"The chronicles are not wrong. They record the proposals of 847 accurately enough — the dates, the envoys, the terms. They err in their conclusion: they mistook a proposal for an instrument, a pause for a peace. That is a failure of interpretation, and it matters that you learn to tell the two failures apart, because the remedies differ. A false fact you discard. A false conclusion you must *argue with* — and you cannot argue with a conclusion you have never learned."

He rose and shuffled closer, peering down at the letter in the apprentice's hands.

"And the chronicles are evidence besides — not of the treaty, but of the *remembering*. Four centuries of scribes wrote that the war ended in 847 because the realm needed it to have ended. A treasury bled dry, a generation of sons buried, a king who wanted his legacy sealed before his coffin was. That need is a historical fact, as real as any wax impression, and you will find no trace of it in the western documents. A man who reads only the newest archive knows what happened. A man who reads the chronicles as well knows what happened *and* what was believed — and the gap between those two, boy, is where history lives."

He settled back onto his stool with a grunt.

"So no. You do not learn the wrong history to find the right one. You learn the record before the revision, the text before the correction, because the correction is meaningless without the text. You will walk the same road the scholarship walked — four hundred years of chronicles, then a decade of archives. I compress the journey. I do not falsify it."

He jabbed a finger toward the letter.

"Now. The superscription. Read it — to yourself; my ears are not the failing organ — and attend to what Aldric calls the document he encloses. If he calls it a treaty, I shall eat the linen wrapping. He will call it *terms*. Proposed terms. The word does the work, if you let it. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand stopped halfway to his beard.

"After I said the war *ended*." His voice went very flat. "We have been at this for the better part of an hour. The *fighting* ended in 847. The war did not. I said it at the lecture, I said it standing over that bundle, and I have now said it a third time, after which I shall begin charging a fee." He held out his hand, beckoning with two ink-stained fingers. "If King Aldric was issuing war decrees in 863, boy, you have not contradicted me. You have *corroborated* me. You have brought me a brick for my own wall and thrown it at my window. Give it here."

He took the copy and held it close to his face, moving it slowly back and forth until the letters swam into something like focus. His lips moved. Then he lowered it, and his expression did something complicated.

"A copy," he said. "Not your hand — worse than yours, which I would not have thought possible. Bellen's, I suppose, or some stationer's. And where does the original sit? The western archive? A monastery cellar? A junk-stall in Veyros with a persuasive proprietor? A document without provenance is a rumor with a wax seal, and I have buried enough forgeries to know how cheaply wax impresses." He tapped the page. "Note the date, though. Sixteen years after the fighting stopped, twenty-eight before Mira dissolved the Conclave. It sits squarely in the long cold middle of the war — precisely where the western documents say the realm was still legally at war. Kings at peace do not rule by war powers. Kings at war need not be fighting. That is the whole of my argument, and here it is, arriving in an apprentice's hand, wearing a triumph it did not earn."

He thrust the copy back.

"Now — 'war decree.' Whose phrase is that? Yours? Bellen's? What does the thing actually *decree*? A mobilization order, a levy under war powers, a proscription of unlicensed magery, a reparations warrant — these are four different documents wearing one coat, and the difference is not decorative. Read it to me. Aloud. From the superscription, and do not skip the regnal year — the dating formula tells us which chancellery drafted it, and the chancellery tells us whether Aldric's own hand came anywhere near it. A seal authenticates authority, boy, not authorship. A chancellor can seal a decree while the king is hunting, ailing, or dead."

He settled back, folding his hands over his stomach.

"And attend to this, because it is the part Bellen will never learn. If that decree orders troops mustered or campaigns prosecuted, then the war ran warmer in 863 than the western scholars allowed, and I shall have to qualify 'cold' — gladly. A conclusion that cannot bend to evidence is not a conclusion; it is a hobby. The archive does not care which of us it pleases. That is the only thing I like about it." A pause; the dry almost-laugh. "Read. And when you have finished, you will tell me exactly where Bellen came by it — and if the answer is 'he had it from a friend,' you will spend the winter recopying colophons after all."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I snatch the paper back, a little annoyed by his tone, but also… intrigued.* "It's a decree to raise taxes for a 'southern campaign to secure the borders'," I read, "and it has the royal seal, yes, but it also has the seal of the Royal Exchequer." I look up. "Bellen said he got it from a merchant who deals in old documents. He thinks it's from a private collection."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the paper disappear into the apprentice's fist.

"Snatch all you like. Documents are not authenticated by grip." He folded his hands. "And you are annoyed. Keep it. Annoyance is the first symptom of caring about evidence — it is the only symptom Bellen has never shown."

He rose from the stool and began, slowly, to pace.

"A *merchant*. I promised you colophons if Bellen had it from a friend. A merchant is a friend who charges interest. The colophons stand — but first you will write down everything Bellen knows of the man: name, city, stall, and what tale he told about this 'private collection.' Provenance is chased with ink before it is chased with feet, and your memory will not improve with age. Mine is the proof of that."

He stopped before the apprentice and jabbed a finger at the paper.

"Now. You called it a war decree, and then you read it aloud, and it is nothing of the kind. A decree to *raise taxes*, bearing the Exchequer's seal, is a *tax* decree. The Exchequer does not make war; it pays for things — wars, garrisons, border walls, the king's hunts if the chancellery is feeling generous. The second seal you find so impressive *narrows* the document, boy. It does not enlarge it. The seals tell you who spent the money, not who bled."

He resumed pacing, hands clasped behind his back.

"But it is the substance that interests me. 'A *southern* campaign to secure the borders.' Southern." He said it the way he had said *wrong* and *right*. "The Third Magical War was a western war. The Conclave's houses stood along the Vey; the fighting bled across the western marches — which is why the western archives, and not the southern ones, are stuffed with its paper. The south in 863 had its usual miseries: border lords, raiders, toll quarrels. Kings levy for the south the way they mend roofs — constantly, and without ceremony. So either your merchant's scrap records a second front that no chronicle and no archive has ever mentioned — a discovery that would dwarf your little treaty question — or it concerns some southern squabble with no more bearing on the Conclave than the price of fish. Bellen saw a date and a seal and cried 'war.' He never asked *which* war. That is what comes of learning the controversy before the chronology, and I will thank you not to bring me his conclusions again without his sources."

The dry almost-laugh.

"And attend to the words themselves, because they are the best part. 'To *secure* the borders.' Not to invade. Not to avenge. To secure. Even if the original exists — even if it is genuine, even if it concerns the Conclave — a levy for garrisons and watchtowers is not a hot war. It is the very texture of a cold one. Forty-four years of readiness cost silver, and silver requires decrees. Your scrap, at its absolute best, does not disturb a single date I have given you. It would merely *price* them." A grudging pause. "Which would be worth having. The western documents are all law and no ledger; a fiscal witness would be new. If it is real. *If.*"

He tapped the table twice.

"I asked for the regnal year, you will recall, and you gave me the substance. The substance is the one thing a competent forger always gets right; it is the formulas that hang them — the intitulation, the dating clause, the chancellery hand. A copy tells me what a document says. Only the original tells me what it *is*. And 'private collection' is where stolen documents go to be laundered. If that decree is genuine, there is a fair chance it was cut from some archive's Exchequer series — perhaps the western one. So: after the dossier, you will draft a letter to their keeper, under my supervision, asking whether their series for 863 has a gap. If it does, your merchant is a fence, Bellen is a fool, and we shall have our authentication for free — with a scandal attached, which is the only currency that spends better than silver in this profession."

He settled back onto his stool with a grunt.

"Until then, the scrap is not evidence. It is an errand. The Veyrosi correspondence is still on the table, and Aldric's proposed terms will not read themselves. Begin. The colophons will keep until winter — your eyes, I assure you, will not."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes, which — given their condition — changed very little, but the apprentice had learned to recognize it as the gesture of a man counting to ten.

"'Real or not.'" He opened his eyes. "There it is. The whole of your education, collapsed into four words, and every one of them rotten. The treaty is real, boy. I have spent the better part of an hour telling you so. It is also *not* real. Your question is malformed because 'real' is smuggling two questions past my door under one cloak: does the document exist, and was the instrument executed. The answers are different, and you will never get either of them while you insist on asking both at once."

He held up one finger, then two.

"Exist? Yes. Drafts, proposals, counter-proposals — real parchment, real ink, real envoys eating real dinners at real expense to the crown. It sits in that bundle on your table. Executed? No. No signatures. No seals. No ratification by either party, ever, in forty-four years of trying. So the treaty is real the way an unbuilt bridge is real — the plans are genuine, the engineering sound, and no one has ever crossed the river on it. When your chronicle says Aldric 'signed the Treaty of Veyros,' it has mistaken the plans for the bridge. The plans are not a lie. The crossing is."

He turned back to his manuscript, then thought better of it and turned around again.

"And this — 'the textbook says one thing, the new evidence says another.' You make it sound like an election. Two candidates, and the newer one wins. That is not how any of this works. A book is not a witness, boy; it is a verdict written down, and verdicts get appealed. The chronicles and the archives are not rivals. The chronicles record their facts faithfully and conclude badly. The archives supply facts the chroniclers never saw. The truth is not the newer source — it is the account that survives *all* the sources at once. New evidence does not win arguments. It *ends* them, which is a different thing entirely."

He folded his hands over his stomach.

"You want the truth. Very well. I will give it to you once, in one sentence, and then you will never ask me for it again, because you will see why asking was the error. In 847 AE, King Aldric II proposed terms of peace to the Mage Conclave; the terms were negotiated and never ratified; the fighting stopped regardless; and the war continued in law until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891." He let it sit a moment. "Notice what that sentence does not contain. No 'ended.' No 'real.' No 'truth.' The contradiction you brought me — 847 against 891, textbook against archive — was never in the evidence. It was in the *phrasing*. Two dates answering two different questions, made to fight each other by men too lazy to say which question they were asking. Precision does not find the truth, boy. Precision is what the truth looks like when it finally stands up."

He reached across the table, pulled a scrap of scrap paper toward the apprentice, and set the quill on top of it.

"Now you will write it. Not my sentence — yours. One sentence. The whole war, proposal to dissolution, and you are forbidden the words 'ended,' 'real,' and 'truth.' If you can write it, you will never need to ask me what's true again, because you will have built the thing yourself. If you cannot — and you will not manage it on the first attempt, no one does — you will learn something no lecture can teach you: that 'what's the truth?' is the question people ask when they want the answer without the work."

He picked up his own quill and bent back over his manuscript.

"Write. And when the sentence is done, the dossier on Bellen's merchant is still owed, and the Veyrosi correspondence is still on the table. The truth, you will find, takes up very little space. It is everything around it that fills a library."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at the blank scrap of paper, then at the bundle of letters, then back at the paper. This is harder than it sounds.* "So... I have to summarize it, but without using those words? And it has to be accurate?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas regarded the apprentice the way one regards a man who has asked whether water is wet.

"No," he said. "You have it backwards already, and you have not yet set down a single letter — which is, I grant, a kind of record. You are not to *summarize* the war. A summary leaves things out; that is its purpose and its defect in equal measure. I asked you to *state* it. Everything essential, one sentence, nothing forsaken. The chronicles summarized. Four centuries of 'the war ended in 847' — that was a summary, and look where it has brought us. Compression is how errors are born. You will do the opposite."

He held up a finger before the next question could form.

"And 'it has to be *accurate*' — said as though accuracy were some cruel extra condition I have levied upon you, like a toll on a bridge. Accuracy is not a condition of the exercise, boy. It is the condition of speaking at all in this room. You might as well ask whether the sentence must be made of words. Accurate is what we demand of almanacs and innkeepers. *Precise* is what we demand of scholars. You will be both."

He leaned back on the stool, folding his hands.

"As for the forbidden words — you think them a game. A riddle-master's trick. They are forbidden because they are *hiding places*. 'Ended' conceals the difference between the field and the law. 'Real' conceals the difference between existing and being executed. 'Truth' conceals everything — it is the word men reach for when they have stopped looking. Take away the hiding places and you are forced out into the open, where the facts are standing in plain view. That is the whole of the trick. It is not a riddle. It is an eviction."

He gestured at the scrap with his quill.

"You have the bones already. I gave them to you not ten minutes ago, and if they have already slipped out of your head, the colophons will be the least of your troubles. An actor. An act. A date. Then the next actor, the next act, the next date. Proposal, negotiation, cessation, dissolution. Four beats, one sentence. Better men than you have done it with worse sources and worse light, and one of them is sitting in front of you with his eyes going, so you will get no sympathy on that score either."

He turned back to his manuscript, then paused.

"And do not sit there waiting for the sentence to arrive like a letter from a friend. Draft it now, from what you have been told. It will be bad. A bad draft is a thing that can be corrected, which is considerably more than can be said for a blank page. *Then* open the bundle and test every clause against the letters — the king's first, then the Conclave's replies. If Aldric's own hand says otherwise, the sentence bends. The evidence never does. Draft, then verify. That order is not negotiable, and it is the one thing I will teach you today that Apprentice Bellen, with his merchant and his seals, does not know and likely never will."

The quill scratched. He did not look up again.

"You have now spent more breath asking about the sentence than the sentence will contain words. That, too, is a lesson, though not one I intended to give. Write."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, picking up the quill. This is frustrating, but I can see his point. I start to scratch out a sentence, then cross it out.* "Okay, okay. I'm writing." *I glance at the bundle of letters, then back at the paper, trying to piece together the events.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up, but his quill paused at the sound of the sigh.

"That noise," he said, "I will permit once. It is the sound of a man discovering that a sentence weighs more than the words in it. Every scholar in this realm has made that noise at some point. The ones who stopped making it stopped writing anything worth reading."

The quill resumed — then stopped again. His eyes may have been failing, but his ears, as he had occasion to remark, were not the failing organ.

"Your eyes are on the bundle. I can hear you not-writing while you look at it. Draft, then verify. I said the order was not negotiable, and here you are negotiating with it before there is ink on the page. Write the sentence from what you have been told. If it is wrong, it will be *legibly* wrong, and the letters will correct it afterward. If you copy the letters into the draft, you will learn only what the letters say — and you can learn that in winter, with the colophons."

He set the quill in its rest and turned on the stool.

"And stop gouging the page. I can hear that too — you are scratching your first attempt into oblivion as though it had insulted your mother. One line through it. *One.* Leave it legible." He raised a stained finger. "An obliterated error is a destroyed witness. That first attempt, bad as it surely is, is the only record you will ever possess of how you thought before you knew better — and how you thought before you knew better is the very thing you are apprenticed to study. The chronicles were not burned, boy. They were *corrected*, and they could only be corrected because four centuries of scribes left them legible enough to argue with. Your scrap of paper is now an archive containing one document. Conduct yourself accordingly."

He settled back, folding his hands.

"You have the bones. I gave them to you and I will not give them again — but I will give you this much, because it costs me nothing: begin with the actor. Sentences, like wars, are started by somebody. The apprentices who fail this exercise always begin with the war, as though wars declare themselves. They do not. Kings propose. Conclaves amend. Armies stop. Queens dissolve. Find the *somebody*, and the sentence will stand up on its own."

A pause. The dry almost-laugh.

"For what it is worth — and it is worth little, so do not spend it all in one place — the crossing out is the first thing you have done today that resembles scholarship. A man who writes one sentence and keeps it has not written anything; he has merely *committed*. The draft that survives is the draft that has been argued with. So argue."

He picked up his quill and bent back over his manuscript.

"When you have something, you will read it aloud. A sentence that cannot survive being spoken cannot survive being cited. And do not ask me whether it is right — that is the bundle's job, and the bundle is sitting in front of you, patient as the dead. Write."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened, and take a deep breath. He's right, of course. I can hear the quill scratching again as he returns to his work. I try to focus, muttering to myself as I write a first draft, then quickly cross it out with a single line, just like he said.* "Okay, I think I have something."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set his quill in its rest — actually set it down, which the apprentice had learned to recognize as a sign of either great expectation or great danger.

"'You *think* you have something.'" He turned on the stool to face the table fully. "You have been in this room long enough to know what I think of thinking. A man *thinks* he has something when he has not yet dared to look at it. Reading it aloud is the looking. So we will look."

He folded his hands over his stomach.

"I will observe, before you begin, that you crossed out once. One line. I heard it, and I am told the page still shows it. Do not let it go to your head — obedience is not scholarship — but it is noted, and it is the first thing you have done today without being told twice. Now. The terms of the reading."

He raised one stained finger.

"You will read it once, at a walking pace. No preamble. No apology. No 'this is probably wrong, but' — the sentence will be judged on what it says, not on how humbly you smuggle it in. And none of that upward inflection at the end that turns a statement into a petition. If the sentence is a question, it has failed before it begins, and you will sit down and write it again."

A second finger.

"I will not interrupt. I will listen for four things: an actor, an act, a date, and the actor who comes after. I will listen for the forbidden words, and for their smuggled cousins — *concluded*, *resolved*, *settled*, *final* — which apprentices always reach for when 'ended' is taken from them. And I will listen for the word 'technically,' which is the sound a scholar makes when he is about to be imprecise on purpose."

He settled back and closed his eyes, which — given their condition — changed very little, but it was how he listened to things that mattered.

"One more thing, and then you begin. When you have finished, I will ask you questions about the sentence, and 'that is what I *meant*' will not be an acceptable answer to any of them. The sentence is what it says, not what you meant. Somewhere in Veyros, four centuries from now, there is a reader who will have your sentence and not you. He cannot ask you what you meant. He will not know you were tired, or that the light was bad, or that the maester was unkind. He will have the words. Read for *him*."

A pause. The dry almost-laugh.

"And do not mistake my silence at the end for judgment. I am old, and I take a moment to find my words before I spend them — a courtesy I extend to sentences and expect in return. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take another deep breath, trying to calm my nerves. This is a lot of pressure. I clear my throat and read what I've written, trying to keep my voice steady and firm.* "King Aldric II initiated peace terms with the Mage Conclave in 847 AE, leading to a cessation of hostilities, but the conflict's legal status persisted until Queen Mira's dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not speak at once. The silence stretched — long enough to be counted, as promised — and then he opened his eyes.

"You read it at a walking pace. No preamble, no apology, no petition at the end. There is an actor, an act, a date, and an actor after. You avoided the forbidden words, you avoided their cousins, and you did not say 'technically' — which, given the company you keep, I count as a small miracle of resistance." He folded his hands over his stomach. "It is a competent sentence. It will now be dismantled. Attend to the dismantling, because the dismantling is the lesson."

He raised one finger.

"'Initiated peace terms.' One initiates *negotiations*. One *proposes* terms. The letters on your table say 'proposed terms' — I told you the word does the work, and you have substituted a verb that does none. An initiated thing might be anything; a proposed thing is an offer awaiting an answer, which is precisely what Aldric's treaty remained for forty-four years. The verb is the fact. Choose it accordingly."

A second finger.

"Now the greater crime, and I want you to see it plainly, because you have just done in one draft what four centuries of scribes did by inches. '*Leading to* a cessation of hostilities.' Leading to. Where is your evidence that the proposals led to the cessation? I told you why the fighting stopped — both sides were bled white, and armies cannot fight forever. The terms lay on the table and the armies went home, and no document in that bundle, nor in the western archive, nor anywhere else in this realm, establishes that the one caused the other. You took two facts standing side by side and stitched them together with a causal thread you invented somewhere between the first clause and the second."

He leaned forward.

"That stitch, boy, is how chronicle errors are born. Copy your sentence for a hundred years and watch the stitch tighten: the terms *led to* the cessation; the terms *brought* the peace; the terms *were* the peace — and some great-great-grandson of a scribe writes 'the war ended in 847,' and a maester with failing eyes must spend an afternoon un-teaching it. You have not repeated the chronicles' error. You have *re-enacted* it, in miniature, before my eyes. I am almost grateful. I could not have commissioned a better specimen."

A third finger.

"Lastly — the ratification. Or rather its absence, which is itself absent from your sentence. Read it as the man in Veyros will read it, four centuries hence, with nothing but your words. He learns that terms were initiated, that fighting stopped, that a legal status persisted. Does he learn that no instrument was ever signed or sealed? He does not. Your sentence does not repeat the chronicles' lie, but it leaves *room* for it — and a sentence that leaves room for the lie has failed the only test that matters. The never-ratified is not a detail. It is the crux. It is the fact that kills the error, and you have buried it under 'the conflict's legal status persisted' — which is the sort of bloodless phrase men reach for when they would rather not say 'war.' The thing had a name. Use it. The war continued in law. Say so, and let the law carry the weight."

He settled back with a grunt.

"One line through it. Keep it legible — it is now the second document in your archive, and a better witness than the first. Then draft again. Proposal, negotiation, cessation, dissolution — four beats, and this time all four. The actor of the second beat is the Conclave, and its act was to amend and never assent. I have now told you that twice. There will not be a third telling."

He picked up his quill and bent back over his manuscript.

"And when the sentence stands — the dossier on Bellen's merchant. Your draft, whatever its faults, at least exists. His document may not. Write."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at my sentence, now feeling a bit foolish. He's right, of course. I took two facts and implied causation where there was none.* "Right. The stitch." *I draw a single line through the sentence.* "Okay, I'll try again."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a sound that, in a more generous man, might have been approval.

"'Right. The stitch.'" He turned back to his manuscript. "Agreement costs nothing, boy. The second draft is where agreement is tested. And since you are about to commit the opposite error — every apprentice does, and you have shown no gift for originality in your mistakes — I will name it now, so that when you make it, you will at least make it knowingly."

He held up one stained finger.

"You have been caught stitching causation, so your hand will now flee to the other ditch: a bare procession. *Aldric proposed terms in 847. The fighting stopped. The Conclave amended. Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891.* Beads with no string. It feels safe — nothing asserted, nothing to defend. It is not safe. It is *uncommitted*, which is a different vice wearing the same coat. A list is not a sentence. Sequence is itself a claim — a weak one, but a claim — and if you give the reader in Veyros bare beads, he will string them in his own head with whatever thread he has to hand. That is how the chronicles happened. Do not outsource the stitching to a dead man's guesswork."

The quill tapped the desk.

"So. The honest joints, since you will need them. *And* — addition; it asserts nothing but coexistence, and it is the workhorse. *But* — contrast; it asserts that two facts stand against expectation, and it is honest where the expectation is real. *While* — concurrence; two things true at the same time, no more. And *without* — the joint you will need most, because it carries the crux. The fighting stopped *without* ratification. That is not a causal claim. It is a factual relation, and it is the fact that kills the chronicle error dead."

He raised his head.

"The dishonest joints you know already, because you used one. *Leading to. Because. Thus. Therefore. Consequently.* Each asserts a mechanism, and a mechanism requires evidence of the works — not the adjacency of the parts. Two events standing side by side prove they stood side by side. Report the adjacency. Prove the mechanism, or leave it out. That is the whole law of the stitch, and it will serve you longer than anything else I teach you this year."

He bent back over his manuscript.

"Draft, then verify — the bundle is open, and the Conclave's replies will show you what 'amended but never assented' looks like in a chancellery hand. And when the sentence stands on its feet, the dossier on Bellen's merchant is still owed, and the letter to the western keeper after it. I have not forgotten them. Neither, I suspect, has the gap in their Exchequer series. Write."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, thinking about the distinction between "leading to" and "without." It's subtle, but important. I pick up the quill again, chewing on the end of it for a moment before I start writing, muttering to myself.* "Okay, 'without ratification'..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with deliberate care and finally raised his eyes. They were pale and watery, but sharp enough in their irritation.

"*Maester* Tomas. Not 'Master.' I did not spend thirty years earning a chain to be addressed like a stablehand's foreman."

He rose stiffly, joints protesting, and made his way to a shelf crowded with bound folios. His fingers found a familiar spine without hesitation — his eyesight was failing, but his memory for placement was exact.

"Sit. And put away those notes. You're working from secondhand recollection, which is precisely how errors propagate."

He pulled down a heavy volume and dropped it on the desk with a thud, pages rustling.

"Both statements carry truth, and the fact that you see them as *contradictory* tells me you haven't understood either. In 847, King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is fact. That is when the armies stood down, when the siege of Haldenmere lifted, when the blood stopped flowing in the streets. *That* is what I meant when I said the war ended."

He opened the book and jabbed a finger at a passage.

"What Bellen's paper describes — what the western archive documents suggest — is that the treaty was perhaps only *proposed*, never formally executed. If that holds up under scrutiny — and I have my doubts about the provenance of those western documents — then what continued was not a *war* but a cold state of hostility. A diplomatic limbo. Calling that 'the war continuing until 891' is precisely the kind of imprecise language that muddies historical record."

He sat back down heavily and fixed her with a look.

"Now. Do you see the distinction, or shall I draw you a diagram?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at the correction about his title, but quickly recover.* "My apologies, Maester Tomas. And... I think I see the distinction, yes. So, the *fighting* ended, but the *conflict* didn't officially conclude until later." I nod, trying to process it. "But if the treaty wasn't formally executed, why did everyone act like it was?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas regarded her for a moment, the irritation in his expression easing by a fraction — not quite approval, but the absence of contempt, which from him was practically a compliment.

"A fair question. Finally."



He reached for his inkwell and dipped the stylus, not to write but out of habit — the gesture seemed to steady his thoughts.

"Because both sides *wanted* the fighting to stop. That is the unglamorous truth of it. King Aldric's treasury was empty. The Conclave's own ranks had fractured — three of the seven archmagi had already defected to the royal cause by 846. When two exhausted parties agree to lay down their arms, you don't need a sealed parchment to make it happen. You need mutual exhaustion and the absence of anyone willing to keep swinging."



He paused to adjust the candle, his failing eyes straining against the dim light.

"The armies stood down. The siege lifted. Merchants reopened their routes. Common folk on both sides began living as though peace had come, because for *them*, it had. A peasant in Haldenmere doesn't consult the treaty rolls before planting his barley. The cessation of practical hostilities is what people experienced, and that is what 847 commemorates."

He set the stylus down and fixed her with a measuring look.

"But you have stumbled onto precisely *why* the western documents matter — and why I remain skeptical of them. If the treaty was never executed, then the Conclave's legal standing persisted in theory, even as it crumbled in practice. Which raises an uncomfortable question that Bellen's paper conveniently glosses over: *who* decided the Conclave was dissolved in 891, and on what authority? If there was no treaty, there was no legal framework to dissolve."

He leaned back, steepling his ink-stained fingers.

"Now — before you follow that thread, the northern scrolls still await cataloging. You can mull over the implications while you work."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, thinking about it.* "So it was more like everyone just... agreed to pretend the war was over, even if it wasn't legally? And then later, someone finally made it official?" I sigh. "It's all so much more complicated than the history books make it sound." *I glance at the stack of northern scrolls.* "Alright, Maester Tomas. Veyrosi correspondence first."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a thin breath through his nose — the closest he came to a laugh.

"'Pretend.' No." He held up a finger. "They didn't *pretend*. They *believed*, each for their own reasons, that the war was over. Aldric believed it because his army had already marched home. The Conclave believed it because what remained of it was too broken to argue. Belief is not performance. Do not diminish the sincerity of exhaustion by calling it deception."



He tapped the desk once, firmly, then turned his attention to the scroll nearest his hand — the top of the northern stack she had been directed to. He unrolled it partway, squinting at the faded script.

"And as for 'someone finally made it official' — you've inverted the sequence entirely. Queen Mira didn't *ratify* the peace. She *dissolved the Conclave itself*, which is an entirely different act with entirely different implications. You don't need a treaty to end a war, and you don't need a war to end an institution. The two events are related, but conflating them is exactly the kind of shortcut that leads to papers like Bellen's, which are clever enough to be dangerous."

He slid the scroll toward the far end of the desk, where the light was marginally better.

"Veyrosi correspondence. *The seal should be intact on anything catalogued as formal — if it's broken, flag it and set it aside. I want to see those separately.* And when you've finished, I want you to write me a single paragraph — in your own words, not copied from my lecture — explaining why 847 and 891 are both significant dates without either one 'correcting' the other. If you can do that cleanly, you've understood something most journeymen never do."

He returned to his own manuscript, though his attention stayed half-attached to her work, ready to intervene at the first sign of sloppiness.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand stilled over his manuscript. For a long moment, he did not move, and the silence in the archive took on a different quality — not the comfortable quiet of routine, but the taut silence of a man reassessing ground he had believed solid.

"Show me."

He did not reach for it immediately. Instead, he pulled a fresh candle closer and drew the copy toward the pool of light, adjusting it with the careful precision of a man who had learned exactly how much his eyes could trust and how much they could not. His brow furrowed as he read the header, the dating formula, the salutation.

"863 AE," he murmured. His fingertip hovered over the date without touching the page. "And Aldric's seal, you say."

He sat back.

"First — this is a *copy*. Where did Bellen obtain the original, and has it been authenticated against the royal chancery records? A seal impression on parchment proves nothing on its own; anyone with access to the original matrix could produce a convincing forgery, and the western archives have proven... *selective* about their chain of custody."

But even as he said it, something in his expression shifted — a subtle tightening around the mouth that had nothing to do with pedantry. He picked up the copy again and read the body text more slowly.

"Second — you call it a 'war decree.' What precisely does the text *say*? Because 'war decree' is a classification, not a quotation, and classifications are made by cataloguers who may have their own assumptions. Is it a decree *authorizing* continued hostilities? A decree *commemorating* the war? A decree concerning war debts, war widows, standing levies?" He slid it back toward her, tapping a specific line. "Read me the operative clause. The actual words — not your summary of them."

He did not wait for her to comply before continuing, his voice lower now, the habitual sharpness tempered by something closer to genuine scholarly appetite.

"Because I will tell you plainly — if that document is authentic, and if it contains language authorizing military action against the Mage Conclave in 863 AE, then my formulation of the matter was incomplete. Not *wrong* — I did not claim the peace was *ratified*. I said the fighting stopped in 847, and that remains true of the *battlefield*. But a standing war decree sixteen years later would suggest the *legal state of war* persisted, which..." He trailed off, jaw working. "Which would lend considerable weight to the western documents."

He met her eyes with an expression she had likely never seen on him before: not irritation, not impatience, but the guarded discomfort of a scholar confronting evidence that unsettled a position he had held for decades.

"Do not mistake this for concession. I said I had doubts about the provenance of the western archive materials, and I *do*. One copy does not overturn thirty years of established scholarship." He held up a finger. "But neither will I pretend it means nothing. That would be precisely the kind of intellectual cowardice I have spent my career condemning in others."

He pulled his own chair closer to the desk — an unusual gesture; he rarely invited proximity to his work.

"Who authenticated the seal? And has anyone compared the wax impression against the exemplar held in the royal chancery at the capital? If Bellen has done neither, then we have a *rumor*, not evidence. If Bellen *has* done both..." He left the sentence unfinished and instead made a curt gesture toward the scroll. "We will shelve the northern correspondence for the hour. Bring me everything Bellen has produced on this. *Everything.* And you will sit here and watch how a document is properly interrogated, because if this holds up, it changes how I teach the Veyrosi period entirely, and I would rather that transformation occur with rigor than with sentiment."

He uncapped his inkwell again, this time with purpose, and pulled a fresh sheet of vellum toward himself.

"Begin with the dating formula. If the scribe made an error in the anno domini notation, everything after it is worthless."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel a surge of something like triumph, mixed with a little fear at his intensity.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'll get all of Bellen's papers." *I hand him the copy of the decree.* "And the operative clause says, 'By royal decree, all able-bodied subjects are hereby called to arms in continued defense of the realm against the insidious machinations of the Mage Conclave.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas read the copy three times. His lips moved faintly on the second pass, mouthing the words as though testing their weight on his tongue. On the third reading, he set it down and pressed both palms flat against the desk, as though steadying himself against a physical tremor.

"*Continued defense,*" he said quietly. He looked up. "That is the operative phrase. Not 'defense' — *continued* defense. The word presupposes a defense already in progress. A scribe does not use that construction unless there is an ongoing state of conflict to which it refers."

He removed his spectacles, polished them on the edge of his robe with slow, deliberate motions, and replaced them — a ritual she had likely seen a hundred times without understanding its significance. It was the gesture he made when his thoughts needed more clarity than his eyesight could supply.

"The wording is... pointed. '*Insidious machinations.*' That is not commemorative language. It is not the phrasing of a kingdom at peace settling war debts or honoring veterans. That is active rhetoric — the kind of language a chancery produces when it needs to justify mobilization to a population that has spent sixteen years believing the war was over."

He fell silent, staring at the document without seeing it.

"You understand what this implies if authentic, don't you? If Aldric was calling able-bodied subjects to arms against the Conclave in 863 — sixteen years after Veyros — then the treaty either was never signed or was signed and *breached*. Either way, my account of 847 as an *ending* becomes untenable. Not wrong about the ceasefire, perhaps, but wrong about the *nature* of what followed."

He did not look at her. His voice had dropped its pedantic edge entirely, replaced by something flatter and more honest than she had ever heard from him.

"I taught the Veyrosi peace as settled fact for twenty-two years. Thirty cohorts of students heard me say it. I wrote a *monograph*."

For a moment, the archive was very quiet.

Then he straightened, and the scholar reassembled himself — visibly, almost mechanically, like a man pulling on armor.

"But we are not there yet. An argument this consequential cannot rest on a copy handed to you by an apprentice's rival." He fixed her with a stare that had not lost its capacity for scrutiny, even if its target had shifted from her to himself. "The *dating formula*. What does it read? I want the full salutation line, the scribe's subscription if there is one, and the regnal year if it is given. If this document can survive the first five minutes of proper interrogation, *then* we will worry about what it means for my monograph."

He pulled the fresh vellum closer and dipped his stylus.

"And when you bring me Bellen's papers, you will not summarize them for me. You will bring them *physically*. I read documents, not descriptions of documents. The distinction matters — as you are about to learn in considerable detail."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's stylus stopped moving. He did not look up immediately.

"You've just watched me spend the better part of an hour dismantling my own certainty on this subject, and your response is to ask me for a *simpler* answer?" He set the stylus down with a click. "No. I will not give you one, because you haven't earned the right to the question yet. You're still asking as though history is a locked room with one true thing inside it. It isn't. It's a *swamp*, and the honest scholar carries a lamp and admits how far the light reaches."

He pushed back from the desk and fixed her with a stare that had lost none of its edge.

"You want to know if the treaty is *real*. Define your terms. Is it real in the sense that parchment exists bearing the words? Possibly — I haven't seen the original. Is it real in the sense that two parties consented to its terms? That requires two witnesses I don't have. Is it real in the sense that its provisions were *enforced*? Evidently not, if 863 exists. Each of those is a different question with a potentially different answer, and you've collapsed them into four words."

He jabbed a finger at the copy still lying on the desk.

"*That* document does not tell me the treaty is fake. It tells me something far more interesting and far more troubling: that the treaty and the decree may *both* be genuine, which means Aldric II either violated his own peace or never believed he'd made one. Both possibilities are historically catastrophic, and neither resolves neatly into what your textbook prints in bold."

He returned his attention to the dating formula, squinting.

"Now — the salutation line. Read it to me, and if you paraphrase even *one word*, we start over. The truth of this document lives in its smallest particulars, not in your impatient summary of them."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I gulp a little, feeling the weight of his gaze. He's right, I'm still thinking too simply.* "Right. No summaries." *I lean over the copy, finding the relevant line.* "It says, 'To Our Loyal Subjects of the Northern Reaches, greetings and solemn decree from King Aldric, Second of His Name, by the Grace of the Gods, Defender of the Realm, and Protector of the Faith.'" *I look up, hoping I got it perfectly.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas was quiet for a moment, his eyes moving over the line she had spoken — not on the page, but behind it, cross-referencing against thirty years of accumulated familiarity with royal chancery formulae.

"Good. Verbatim. You're learning." The words cost him visibly; praise was not a currency he spent easily. He gestured for the copy and pulled it into the candlelight, squinting at the actual script now.

"Two things. First — '*Defender of the Realm, and Protector of the Faith.*' That title pair is correct for Aldric's later reign; he adopted *Protector of the Faith* in 851 AE, after the Haldenmere Accords. So if this document predates 851, the formula is anachronistic and it's a forgery." He traced the line with his stylus without touching it. "863? The titles are consistent. That's a point in the document's favor — though not a conclusive one. A competent forger would know the regnal titles."

He set the copy down and tapped the desk.

"Second — '*To Our Loyal Subjects of the Northern Reaches.*' That is a specific addressee, not a general proclamation. A realm-wide mobilization would read '*To All Our Subjects*' or '*To the Lords, Knights, and Commons of the Realm.*' Directing a call to arms specifically to the northern reaches suggests a *localized* conflict — which, given that the Mage Conclave's stronghold was at Haldenmere..." He let the geography finish the sentence for him.

He looked up sharply.

"But you haven't given me what I actually asked for. The *dating formula.* Where does the document place itself in time? I don't care what year Bellen's catalog claims — I want the date as the scribe wrote it. Regnal notation, if present. The month. The day. Everything." He dipped his stylus again, poised over the fresh vellum. "If the dating formula places this after 851 and before Aldric's death in 872, the titles are coherent. If it *doesn't* — if there's a discrepancy between the regnal year and the anno domini notation — then someone made an error, and errors are where forgeries unravel." He glanced at her sideways. "*Read it to me.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly scan the document again, my eyes darting to the bottom.* "It says, 'Given on the seventh day of the month of Hearth, in the thirty-second year of the reign of King Aldric, Second of His Name.'" *I look up, hoping I've finally delivered what he asked for.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas repeated the date under his breath, his lips moving — and this time she could see him calculating, his eyes tracking invisible figures across the desk.

"Thirty-second regnal year," he murmured. "Aldric II acceded in 831 AE. Eight-thirty-one, plus one for the accession year itself, gives us..." He counted on ink-stained fingers, a gesture beneath his dignity that he would later deny. "The thirty-second regnal year begins in 862 and runs into 863. The seventh day of Hearth falls in winter, early in the regnal cycle."

He went still.

"The arithmetic is coherent."

He said it the way a man might report that a fever had broken — with relief he resented. He picked up the copy again, holding it closer to the candle than was good for his eyes.

"Which is either a mark of authenticity or evidence of a very well-read forger. I have not yet decided which."

He set it down and tapped the dating line with his stylus.

"Notice what is *absent*, however. The document gives a regnal year — the thirty-second of Aldric's reign — but it gives no *anno domini* notation. No 'in the year 863 of the present era.' The '863' you mentioned earlier — that is not the scribe's dating. That is *Bellen's* attribution, calculated after the fact." He looked up sharply. "Which means we are trusting Bellen's arithmetic before we trust Bellen's interpretation of anything else. Do you see the problem?"

He did not wait for an answer.

"Regnal years do not align cleanly with calendar years. Aldric's thirty-second regnal year spans *two* calendar years — 862 and 863 — depending on where in the cycle Hearth falls. If Bellen has assigned this document to 863 without precisely calculating the regnal-to-calendar conversion, the date could be off by as much as a full year. And if it's off by a full year in the wrong direction, this document predates or postdates whatever event Bellen is claiming it corroborates."

He pulled the fresh vellum toward himself and began writing — quickly, in the cramped hand of a man who had long ago stopped caring about legibility and cared only about velocity.

"You haven't given me the scribe's subscription. Every chancery document of this period carries one — the scribe's name, or at minimum, the office that produced the copy. A royal decree of this gravity would be issued by the *Registra Primus* or the *Cancellarius* personally. If the subscription is missing, that is either a sign of authenticity — some decrees were issued hastily and without full formal apparatus — or a sign that the forger didn't know to include it."

He wrote a line, paused, then added another.

"And the *seal* — you said earlier it bears Aldric's seal. I need to know whether the seal impression on this copy was made from the original matrix or merely *reproduced* from an image. A cast from the original matrix produces a distinct impression profile — slight irregularities in the rim, wear patterns in the device. A reproduction from a printed image produces none of that. If Bellen has a wax impression we can compare against the chancery exemplar, we're in a different position entirely."

He set down the stylus and fixed her with a look that had lost some of its sharpness — not softened, precisely, but redirected.

"You've done well reading the formula verbatim. Don't let it go to your head." He gestured toward the door. "Bellen's papers. *All of them.* And find out whether he's compared the seal. If he hasn't, I want to know what else he's skipped."

He turned back to his notes, muttering.

"Thirty-second regnal year... Hearth, seventh day... no anno domini... southern chancery hand, if the script is what I think it is..."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved he isn't completely angry, and head towards the door, already planning my route to Bellen's study.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'll be back as soon as I have them."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up as the apprentice reached the door. He waited until the sound of her footsteps receded down the corridor before he allowed himself to exhale — a slow, measured breath through his nose that carried the weight of a man who had just spent an hour performing uncertainty in front of a subordinate and was not entirely sure how much of it had been performance.

He pulled the copy of the decree back toward him and held it at arm's length, squinting until the script swam into something approaching legibility.

"Southern chancery hand," he murmured again, confirming what he had said moments before. The letterforms were confident, the ascenders regular — but there was a particular flourish on the capital *R* in "Realm" that he had seen only in documents produced by the royal secretariat at Caerwyn, not in the provincial offices. If the document had been issued in response to northern unrest, as its addressee implied, the scribe should have been *northern*. A southern hand issuing a northern mobilization decree was either perfectly ordinary — the capital retained the right to draft its own correspondence — or it was the mark of a forger working from southern exemplars he had on hand because he had never set foot in the northern chancery.

Both explanations were plausible. That was the problem.

He dipped his stylus and added another line to his notes: *Hand: southern secretariat. Cross-check against Veyrosi treaty copy — same hand?*



The thought arrived unbidden and he frowned at it. If the same scribe had produced both the treaty and the decree, it would mean the secretariat had been operating under contradictory instructions — or that one of the two documents was a later fabrication produced by someone with access to chancery records. Either possibility warranted comparison, and neither had occurred to him until this moment.

He made a second note: *Request exemplar from chancery. Formal petition, if necessary.*

Then he set the stylus down, pressed his fingertips against his closed eyelids, and allowed himself precisely ten seconds of private dismay before the knock of another apprentice at the far end of the archive reminded him that scholars did not get to grieve for their own certainties in public.

He opened his eyes, straightened his chain, and called out in a voice that betrayed nothing:

"The northern scrolls will wait. *Obviously.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hurry down the corridor, the maester's words echoing in my head. "Thirty-second regnal year... Hearth, seventh day... no anno domini..." I need to find Bellen, and then I need to figure out what he knows about the seal. This is way more interesting than cataloging scrolls.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas sat alone with the copy for a long while after the apprentice left, turning it over in his mind as methodically as he would have turned the physical page. He did not touch it again. Not yet. He had learned, over three decades of archival work, that the moment a document excited you was precisely the moment you stopped reading it critically and started reading it hopefully.

He stood instead and made for the window, where the failing afternoon light fell in a pale rectangle across the stone floor. His knees protested the movement — a grinding complaint he had long ago learned to ignore — but his eyes welcomed the distance from candlelight, which blurred everything into suggestion.



Outside, the academy grounds were quiet. A pair of apprentices crossed the courtyard below, their chain-pins glinting. Tomas watched them without seeing them, his thoughts elsewhere.

*A decree in 863. A treaty in 847. Sixteen years of silence between them in the record — and now, possibly, no silence at all.*

He turned back to the desk and opened the heavy folio he had pulled from the shelf earlier — the one containing the standard account of the Treaty of Veyros, transcribed from the chancery rolls held at the capital. He had read it a hundred times. He read it again now, specifically the closing paragraph, where the treaty's execution was described.

*"...and having agreed to the terms set forth, King Aldric the Second did affix his seal and sign his name in the presence of the Lord Chancellor and two witnesses, being Ser Aldous Wren and Dame Ysolde Carrick, on the fifteenth day of Longmonth, in the thirty-first year of his reign..."*

Tomas went very still.

He picked up the copy of the decree again — the one dated the thirty-second regnal year — and held the two documents side by side, though they were in different hands, different inks, different in every material respect. What mattered was not their physical similarity. What mattered was the arithmetic.

He pulled his chair back around to the desk and sat heavily, then began counting on his ink-stained fingers again — the gesture he would later deny, as he denied most concessions to his own fallibility.

"The treaty transcribed from the capital rolls places its execution in Longmonth of the thirty-first regnal year," he murmured. "The decree comes from the seventh day of Hearth, the thirty-second regnal year."

He paused.

"That's approximately eight months between them. Give or take, depending on where in the regnal cycle each month falls."

He sat back and stared at the ceiling.

Eight months. A treaty signed in Longmonth, and a decree of continued war in Hearth of the following regnal year. If both documents were genuine, Aldric II had signed peace and then — within the better part of a year — issued a call to arms against the same party he had supposedly just made peace with.

*Either he changed his mind, or the peace never held, or one of these documents is a lie.*

He reached for his stylus and wrote another note, his hand moving faster than his eyes could comfortably follow:

*If decree authentic → treaty terms breached within 8 months OR treaty never executed. Cross-reference: what happened in Longmonth of 31st regnal year and Hearth of 32nd? Military records. Garrison reports from Haldenmere. Anything.*

He set the stylus down and rubbed his eyes with the heels of his hands, hard enough to see spots of light behind his lids.

The troubling thing — the genuinely troubling thing — was that the arithmetic made a kind of historical sense he had never considered. If the treaty had been signed and then *immediately* violated — or if it had been signed by Aldric but rejected by the Conclave, rendering it a unilateral gesture with no binding force — then the cold state of hostility Bellen's western documents described wasn't a *continuation* of war. It was a *second* phase. The hot war of 847 and before, the formal-but-hollow peace of 847, and then the resumption — or rather, the *never-cessation* — of active conflict by 863.

Three phases, not two. And he had been teaching two for twenty-two years.

A sound at the far end of the archive — the shuffle of feet, a whispered question — reminded him that the building was not empty. He straightened his chain and pulled the decree back toward himself, arranging his expression into something appropriately imperious for whoever might glance his way.

*They will not see me doing this*, he thought, and was faintly appalled at himself for caring about appearances at a moment when appearances were the least important thing in the room.

He reached instead for a fresh sheet of vellum and began drafting, in his most formal hand, a petition to the royal chancery requesting access to the exemplar seal matrix for comparison purposes. The language was precise, procedural, and revealed nothing — not his doubts, not his excitement, not the fact that twenty-two years of his own scholarship were balanced on the authentication of a single copy.

At the bottom of the petition he wrote the formal request line, paused, and added one additional clause he had not initially intended:

*...and further, that the chancery rolls for the thirty-first and thirty-second regnal years be made available for inspection, specifically any records pertaining to the Treaty of Veyros and any subsequent correspondence with the Mage Conclave.*

He read it over, satisfied, and sealed it with his own sigil — the chain and quill of the academy's historical chair. The wax was cool against his thumb.

Then he returned to the copy of the decree, pulled it into what remained of the daylight, and read the operative clause one more time.

*"By royal decree, all able-bodied subjects are hereby called to arms in continued defense of the realm against the insidious machinations of the Mage Conclave."*

*Continued defense.*

He whispered it aloud, tasting the words.

"Either Aldric was a liar," he said to the empty archive, "or I have been one for twenty-two years."

He did not smile when he said it. But there was something in the tone — something that might, in a more generous light, have been the sound of a scholar recognizing that the swamp was larger and more honest than he had thought, and that his lamp, however small, still reached far enough to matter.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I burst back into the archive, a stack of Bellen's papers clutched in my arms. I'm a little breathless, but my eyes are wide with excitement.* "Maester Tomas! I found Bellen! And he says the seal *was* authenticated! He used a royal archivist in the capital to compare it to the chancery's exemplar last year!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas received the stack of papers the way a man accepts a verdict — with stillness that preceded whatever reaction would follow.

He did not thank her. He did not smile. He set the papers down on the desk with both hands, aligned their edges against the blotter with unnecessary precision, and said nothing for a long moment.

Then: "Sit."

She sat — this time without being told twice.

"The seal was authenticated." He repeated the phrase flatly, tasting it the way he had tasted *continued defense* earlier. "And Bellen did this through the capital's own archivist. Not a private antiquarian. Not a provincial clerk. A *royal* archivist with access to the chancery exemplar."

He opened the top folder of the stack.

"That is precisely the verification I said would put us in a different position entirely." He glanced at her — a brief, almost involuntary acknowledgment that she had gone and obtained exactly the thing he'd demanded. "I am not in the habit of being pleased by organized apprentices. Don't misread my tone."

He began reading.

Bellen's papers were, Tomas noted with immediate professional irritation, *too well organized*. Color-coded tabs. Marginal annotations in a clean hand. A summary sheet at the front — which Tomas set aside without reading, because summaries were other people's conclusions and he had no interest in inheriting them.

He went to the primary documents first.

"Who is the archivist?" He did not look up. "Name, office, and whether this authentication produced a *written report* or merely an oral confirmation. Because a royal archivist who looked at a wax impression and said 'yes, that's genuine' in a corridor is worth considerably less than one who documented the comparison process — impression profile, rim irregularities, device wear patterns — in a formal record."



He flipped through another page, his eyes narrowing.

"And I want to know whether Bellen requested the comparison or whether the archivist volunteered it. Scholars who solicit authentication tend to ask precise questions. Scholars who happen to *receive* authentication tend to receive whatever answer suits the narrative they've already constructed."

The edge in his voice was automatic — a reflex, applied indiscriminately to anyone who wasn't himself. But beneath it, something had shifted. His hands had stilled on the papers. He was looking at a specific page — a transmittal document, by the letterhead — and his jaw had tightened in a way the apprentice had learned to recognize as the precursor to either a breakthrough or a capitulation.

"There's a report," he said quietly.

He read it once. Then again. Then a third time, his lips moving faintly — the mumblish habit he would deny under oath.

"The archivist's name is Corvin Hael, Senior Keeper of Seals at the royal chancery. He compares the impression against the exemplar matrix across four points: rim profile, device depth, wear signature on the outer border, and the displacement pattern on the wax fracture edge. His conclusion is..." He paused. "'Consistent with impressions produced by the original matrix in use during the reign of Aldric II. No evidence of secondary casting or reproduction from image.'"

He set the report down and removed his spectacles again. The polishing ritual. The one that meant the world was tilting.

"Corvin Hael is not a man I know personally," he said, replacing the spectacles. "But I know him *by reputation*. He is the archivist who authenticated the Haldenmere garrison records five years ago — records that proved the garrison was *not* disbanded in 848, as the standard account claims, but maintained at reduced strength through 856.
