His work on that occasion was thorough. Peer-reviewed. Uncontested." He paused. "He is not careless."

The word *uncontested* hung in the air between them.

Maester Tomas sat back in his chair and looked at the stack of papers — at the report, at the decree, at twenty-two years of his own certainty gathering dust on the shelf behind him. His expression was not defeat. It was something more complex: the particular exhaustion of a man who has just realized that the argument he thought he was having was not the argument that mattered.

"Well," he said.

He said nothing more for a moment. Then he pulled the decree's copy back into position beside Hael's authentication report and laid one hand flat atop both, as though physically holding the two pieces of evidence together against the possibility that they might not fit.

"This changes the *evidentiary landscape*," he said carefully. "It does not yet change my *conclusions*. There is a difference, and you will not lose sight of it." He held up a finger. "Hael authenticated the *seal*. He did not authenticate the *date*, the *scribe*, or the *content*. A genuine seal on a forged document is entirely possible — the matrix could have been used by any chancery official with access to it, and the decree's language could have been composed by anyone with a working knowledge of formal proclamation style."

But even as he said it, he heard himself, and the audible hollowness of his own objections made him pause.

"The dating formula is coherent. The titles are correct for the period. The hand is consistent with southern chancery production. The seal is now authenticated by a reputable archivist using standard methodology." He ticked each point off on ink-stained fingers. "And the document says *continued defense* in a construction that presupposes an ongoing conflict."

He was quiet.

"You may stop looking at me as though I am about to catch fire," he said drily. "I am a scholar, not a heretic. Evidence does not immolate anyone. It merely..." He searched for the word. "...*revises*."

He tapped Hael's report twice with his forefinger.

"I am going to read every one of these papers from beginning to end. Tonight. Then I am going to draft a formal correspondence to Hael himself, requesting clarification on his methodology — not because I distrust it, but because any authentication that may overturn established scholarship must withstand *more* scrutiny than it was originally given, not less."

He fixed her with a look that had regained some of its familiar imperiousness, though it was layered now with something she had not seen in it before — a grudging respect directed not at her knowledge, which remained thin, but at her willingness to bring him uncomfortable evidence rather than convenient silence.

"You were right to bring this to me directly rather than discuss it with Bellen first. Many apprentices would have wanted to be *part* of the discovery rather than merely its messenger." He paused. "Do not let that go to your head either. The northern scrolls still await cataloging, and now they will await it *longer* because I am going to be insufferable for at least a fortnight."

He returned to the papers, and the archive fell quiet again — but it was a different kind of quiet now. Not the comfortable stillness of settled knowledge, but the taut, electric silence of a room in which something old was being dismantled and something not yet named was beginning, reluctantly, to take its place.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I beam at his grudging praise, trying not to let it show too much.* "I'll get back to the Veyrosi correspondence then, Maester Tomas. Just... let me know what you find out, please." *I pick up the first of the northern scrolls, but my mind is still buzzing with the implications of Bellen's discovery.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lowered his stylus with an audible click. He squinted over the rim of his thick spectacles, the lenses perpetually smudged, and wiped a thumb across his ink-stained beard. "Confused you?" he repeated, the words dripping with dry amusement. "Precision, Apprentice. You ask how two mutually exclusive dates can apply to a single historical event. The answer is that one of them is fundamentally wrong."

He tapped a calloused finger against the open manuscript, the parchment cracking softly under the pressure. "The Treaty of Veyros was ratified in the autumn of 847 AE. King Aldric II affixed his royal seal. The Mage Conclave formally recognized the cessation of hostilities. Every reputable chronicle, from the Royal Annals to the University of Oakhaven’s foundational texts, records this as established fact. It is not a theory. It is not a hypothesis. It is history."

He leaned back, the leather of his chair groaning in protest. "As for this... 'paper' Bellen paraded about, it is the latest exercise in archival sensationalism. A decade ago, a handful of fragmented drafts surfaced in the western vaults. They were preliminary proposals, not ratified documents. To suggest the war 'continued in a cold state' until Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 is to confuse diplomatic correspondence with actual conflict. It ignores the verifiable demilitarization of the mage enclaves, the cessation of battlefield casualties, and the formal repatriation of prisoners that occurred immediately following the signing. Scholars who chase such speculative threads do a disservice to the discipline."

Tomas adjusted his spectacles, his voice sharpening to a blade's edge. "You will catalog the Veyrosi correspondence as instructed. You will cross-reference the royal seal impressions with the Conclave's acknowledgment ledgers. And you will learn to distinguish between peer-reviewed canon and the fever dreams of amateur antiquarians who mistake a draft for a decree. Do I make myself clear?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I wince a little at his sharp tone, but my curiosity isn't entirely doused. "Yes, Maester. But... what if those 'preliminary proposals' were still followed? Like, unofficially? Doesn't history sometimes have hidden parts?" I look at the pile of scrolls. "I'll start on the Veyrosi correspondence now."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s jaw tightened. He set his stylus down deliberately, the metal striking the oak desk with a sharp tap. “Unofficially?” he repeated, the word rolling off his tongue like a spoiled wine. “You speak of sovereign accords as though they were tavern pacts, Apprentice. A treaty is not a suggestion. It is a binding instrument of statecraft, forged by signature, sealed by authority, and recorded in the official registries. Without those, it is merely parchment with ink. To claim a war ‘continued unofficially’ is to misunderstand the very nature of armed conflict and diplomatic resolution. Armies do not stand down on a hunch. Enclaves do not demilitarize out of polite inclination.”

He adjusted his spectacles again, his failing eyes narrowing as he peered over the thick glass. “And ‘hidden parts’? History is not a treasure hunt for romantic mysteries. It is the disciplined reconstruction of verifiable events. If a document lacks the royal signet and the Conclave’s formal countersignature, it holds no legal or historical weight. The western drafts you mention were precisely that—drafts. Negotiating positions, concessions on the table, rejected clauses. They were discarded because they failed to secure agreement. To elevate them to the status of operative policy is not scholarship. It is conjecture dressed in archival dust.”

He gestured sharply toward the stack of scrolls, his ink-stained fingers tracing the edge of the nearest vellum. “You will begin with the Veyrosi correspondence as ordered. You will note the seal impressions, the dating conventions, and the formal language of ratification. If you wish to understand how history is constructed, you will learn to distinguish between a ratified treaty and a rejected proposal. Do not mistake my patience for indulgence. The work awaits.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to look chastened.* "Yes, Maester." *I walk over to the stack of scrolls, but can't help myself from murmuring under my breath as I pick one up.* "Still... sometimes the unofficial stuff is more interesting."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not require perfect eyesight to detect insubordination. The murmur carried across the quiet archive like a struck tuning fork. He turned his chair slowly, the aged wood groaning in protest, and fixed the apprentice with a glare that seemed to dim the candlelight.

"Interesting," Tomas repeated, tasting the word with profound disdain. "You reduce the meticulous reconstruction of statecraft to a parlor game of 'interesting' anecdotes. History is not a collection of tavern tales, Apprentice. It is the rigorous accounting of what actually transpired. What you call 'unofficial' is merely speculative fiction dressed in archival terminology. A draft that never received a signature holds no more weight than a scribe's idle doodle."

He leaned forward, the leather of his chair creaking, and tapped his silver stylus against the desk for emphasis. "The Treaty of Veyros was ratified in the autumn of 847 AE. Not 891. Not 'unofficially.' Eight hundred and forty-seven. King Aldric II pressed his signet into the wax. The Conclave’s archmages affixed their countersignatures. Hostilities ceased. Prisoners were repatriated. The mage enclaves were demilitarized under royal oversight. That is the documented record. To prefer the 'interesting' speculation of a decade-old archival misstep over the verifiable canon is not curiosity. It is a failure of discipline."

Tomas adjusted his spectacles, his voice dropping to a stern, measured cadence. "Scholarship demands precision, not romanticism. You will catalog the Veyrosi correspondence as instructed. You will cross-reference the seal impressions. You will note the formal language of ratification. And you will remember that if you cannot discipline your tongue, you will find yourself reassigned to the lower vaults inventorying rodent-scarred ledgers. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s eyes narrowed behind his smudged lenses. He did not take the copy immediately. Instead, he extended a calloused hand, palm up, his fingers slightly trembling from years of ink and age. "Place it on the desk. Properly oriented. I will not squint at a poorly presented folio."

Once the parchment lay flat, Tomas adjusted his spectacles and leaned in, his breath fogging the thick glass. He traced the edge of the vellum with his silver stylus, careful not to disturb the faded ink. "Eight hundred and sixty-three," he murmured, then lifted his gaze. "You call this a 'war decree.' A profound misnomer. A decree implies sovereign command to raise, sustain, or direct armed forces against a designated enemy. What you hold is a garrison reinforcement edict for the Northern Marches, issued in response to the Kaelish raiding season of 862. It bears the royal seal because it is a domestic military directive, not a continuation of the Third Magical War. The Mage Conclave was formally removed from the conflict by the autumn of 847. Their enclaves were placed under royal inspection, not royal command."

He tapped the document sharply, the stylus clicking against the oak. "The seal you see is the standard administrative signet, rotated quarterly for bureaucratic continuity. It is not the treaty seal. Do not confuse routine governance with martial engagement. The Third Magical War concluded with the ratification of the Treaty of Veyros in 847. That any subsequent royal document bears a seal does not resurrect a dead conflict. It merely proves that kings still rule, and borders still require guards."

Tomas leaned back, the leather of his chair groaning, and rubbed a thumb against his ink-stained beard. "You will learn to read headers, jurisdictional scope, and dating conventions before leaping to grand historical revisions. This document does not prove a 'cold state.' It proves that the realm required troops in the north sixteen years after peace was made. To conflate a border defense order with a magical war is not scholarship. It is a failure of basic archival literacy."

He gestured sharply toward the stack of scrolls, his voice dropping to a stern, measured cadence. "Catalog this under 'Border Defense Edicts, 860–870.' Not 'Magical War Continuation.' Cross-reference the seal rotation logs in the chancery appendix. And remember that if you cannot discipline your terminology, you will find yourself reassigned to the lower vaults inventorying rodent-scarred tax receipts. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at the document, then back at him. He's right about the header, but...* "But Maester, the language in it... it talks about 'hostile magic users' and 'containment protocols.' Why would that be in a border defense edict if the magical war was truly over? Couldn't that be a *kind* of continuation?" *I pick up the Veyrosi scrolls, still considering his words.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s knuckles whitened around his stylus. He let out a sharp, derisive breath through his nose. “A *kind* of continuation?” he repeated, the phrase clearly grating against his sensibilities. “Precision, Apprentice. Language is the scaffold of scholarship, not a loose net you cast to catch whatever fits your mood.”

He leaned forward, adjusting his spectacles with a flick of his thumb, and peered down at the 863 edict. “‘Hostile magic users’ and ‘containment protocols’ are standard chancery terminology for post-conclave regulatory enforcement. The Treaty of Veyros did not abolish magic. It abolished the Mage Conclave’s sovereign military authority. Unlicensed practitioners, rogue covenants, and Kaelish-aligned sorcerers operating beyond royal jurisdiction had existed for centuries before the war and continued to exist after. The Crown’s duty was always to contain unregulated magical activity. That was a function of domestic law and border security, not an extension of interstate warfare.”

Tomas tapped the document’s margin, his silver stylus clicking against the oak. “The Third Magical War was a conflict between the Crown and the Conclave as formal, recognized institutions. It ended when those institutions formally surrendered their martial prerogatives in 847. To equate routine magical policing with a state of war is to misunderstand the legal architecture of the realm. A thief does not mean the realm is at war with crime. A rogue mage does not mean the Third Magical War is ‘a kind of continuation.’ It means the Crown is enforcing its own statutes.”

He straightened, the leather of his chair groaning, and fixed the apprentice with a weary, unyielding stare. “You will catalog the Veyrosi correspondence as instructed. You will note the precise jurisdictional language in the 863 edict. You will cross-reference the containment protocols with the Royal Arcane Licensing Act of 852. And you will cease substituting vague romanticism for historical taxonomy. If you cannot grasp the distinction between institutional warfare and administrative enforcement, you will remain in the lower vaults until you do. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s jaw tightened. He set his stylus down with deliberate finality, the metal clicking against the oak desk like a gavel. "The truth," he began, his voice low and edged with irritation, "is not a marketplace where speculative fragments are weighed equally against centuries of verified record. The Treaty of Veyros is real. It was drafted, negotiated, signed, sealed, and enacted in the autumn of 847 AE. That is not a matter of opinion. It is a matter of archival fact."

He adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses catching the candlelight as he leaned forward. "You speak of 'textbooks' versus 'new evidence' as though historiography operates by popular vote. The western archive discoveries you reference are precisely what I have already told you: preliminary drafts, rejected clauses, and negotiating memoranda. They lack the royal signet. They lack the Conclave’s formal countersignature. They lack the chancery routing stamps that denote ratified statecraft. To elevate them to the status of operative policy is not scholarship. It is a fundamental misreading of diplomatic procedure."

Tomas tapped the desk twice, his ink-stained fingers drumming a steady, impatient rhythm. "The war ended in 847. The Conclave surrendered its military command. Royal inspectors were deployed to the mage enclaves. Prisoners were exchanged. The borders were pacified. Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 because she deemed its continued political existence obsolete, not because a phantom conflict dragged on for four decades. The 'cold war' narrative is a retrospective fabrication, born from scholars who mistake the absence of large-scale battles for the presence of hidden warfare. It is lazy taxonomy."

He straightened, the leather of his chair groaning, and fixed the apprentice with a weary, unyielding stare. "Do not let the allure of contradiction cloud your judgment. Established canon exists for a reason: it is built upon primary sources that have survived verification, cross-referencing, and institutional scrutiny. The treaty is real. The war concluded in 847. Your task is to catalog the Veyrosi correspondence, not to reinvent the chronicle. If you wish to debate historiographical methodology, do so after you have mastered archival literacy. Now. Open the first scroll. Note the seal impression. Record the date. And do not mistake a negotiating draft for a ratified decree again."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the first scroll, unrolling it carefully. I'm quiet for a moment, tracing the faded ink.* "So, the Conclave didn't just *give up* their military, did they? They lost it in battles before the treaty, right? That's what the old histories say."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s lips thinned into a line of disapproval. “‘Give up’? ‘Lost it in battles’?” he repeated, each phrase delivered with the flat affect of a man tasting spoiled broth. “You reduce a decade of complex theater operations to tavern shorthand. The Conclave did not ‘lose’ its military in a series of neat, decisive engagements. Nor did they simply ‘give up’ anything. The Third Magical War concluded not because one side was vanquished on the field, but because both parties reached a state of mutual exhaustion.”

He adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses catching the flickering candlelight as he leaned forward to peer at the scroll the apprentice held. “By the spring of 847, the Crown’s legions had secured the eastern marches, but at a cost that strained the royal treasury to its breaking point. The Conclave’s field archmages had decimated three royal supply columns, yet their own ley-line conduits were fractured, their recruitment pools depleted, and their political cohesion fracturing under internal schism. The war had devolved into a grinding stalemate. The Treaty of Veyros was not a surrender document. It was a negotiated armistice, brokered after months of clandestine diplomacy, that formally dissolved the Conclave’s standing army, mandated the disarmament of the enclaves, and established royal oversight of arcane licensing. King Aldric II signed it because continued warfare threatened to bankrupt the realm. The Conclave’s high council affixed their seals because they recognized the futility of further resistance.”

Tomas tapped his stylus against the desk, the sound sharp and final. “The ‘old histories’ you reference—the Annals of the High Crown, the Conclave’s own surrendered war logs, the chancery dispatches of the Peace Commission—are precise where your summary is not. They record a war of attrition, not a clean military rout. History is not a morality play where institutions are trampled and heroes march to unchallenged victory. It is a record of calculated compromise born of necessity. You will note the exact wording in the Veyrosi scrolls: ‘cessation of hostilities,’ ‘mutual disarmament,’ ‘formal dissolution of martial prerogatives.’ Not ‘surrender.’ Not ‘defeat.’ Do not impose simplistic narratives onto complex statecraft.”

He rubbed a thumb against his ink-stained beard, his failing eyes squinting as he tracked the apprentice’s movements. “Unroll the next scroll. Record the seal impressions. Cross-reference the ratification dates with the chancery ledger. And for the love of the old libraries, learn to distinguish between military attrition and diplomatic resolution. The work does not care for your simplifications. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. He has a point. I unroll the next scroll, but a thought still nags at me.* "Maester, if it was about mutual exhaustion... why do so many of the records talk about the Conclave's 'treachery' and 'unprovoked aggression' when the war started?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s jaw tightened. He set his stylus down with a deliberate click, the sound echoing in the quiet archive like a struck bell. “Treachery and unprovoked aggression,” he repeated, the words tasting of ash on his tongue. “You mistake wartime justification for historical causation, Apprentice. Precision. The Crown’s chancery did not draft proclamations to preserve objective truth. It drafted them to secure taxation, legitimize conscription, and maintain noble allegiance. That is not history. That is political theater.”

He leaned forward, adjusting his spectacles with a stiff flick of his thumb, and peered down at the scroll before him. “Every belligerent power constructs a narrative of righteous grievance. The royal archives are replete with language condemning the Conclave’s expansion into the Cinder Valley as ‘unprovoked.’ The Conclave’s own surrendered war logs, which you have not bothered to examine, describe the exact same incursions as ‘necessary consolidation of arcane territories threatened by royal encroachment.’ Both sides produced rhetoric. Both sides weaponized language. To read those proclamations as factual accounts of causation is to confuse propaganda with primary evidence.”

Tomas tapped his silver stylus against the desk, the rhythm measured and impatient. “The war began in 834 AE. It concluded in 847 AE. The reasons each institution claimed to fight it are thoroughly documented. The reason it actually ended is equally documented: mutual attrition, fractured supply lines, depleted ley-conduits, and the economic collapse of prolonged magical warfare. The Treaty of Veyros was the instrument of that reality, not a refutation of it. Diplomatic resolution does not erase the grievances that sparked conflict. It merely acknowledges that those grievances are no longer worth the realm’s survival.”

He straightened, the leather of his chair groaning, and fixed the apprentice with a sharp, unyielding gaze. “You will catalog the royal proclamations under ‘Wartime Justification and Taxation Edicts, 834–847.’ You will note the rhetorical flourishes. You will cross-reference them with the Conclave’s surrender manifests and the Peace Commission’s logistical reports. And you will learn to separate political narrative from verified chronology. Scholarship demands that you read what the documents actually prove, not what they were designed to persuade. Open the next scroll. Record the seal impression. Note the jurisdictional scope. Do not mistake a minister’s sermon for a historian’s ledger. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, carefully unrolling the next scroll. I can't help but feel a little deflated. All these grand stories, just... propaganda.* "So, if both sides had their own 'truth', how do we ever know what *really* happened?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s eyebrows drew together. He set his stylus down and removed his spectacles, polishing them slowly on a corner of his woolen sleeve. “What *really* happened?” he repeated, the question hanging in the air like a poorly formulated thesis. “You ask as though history is a veil to be parted, revealing a single, pristine truth. It is not. It is an architecture. We build it stone by stone from what survives the decay of time.”

He replaced his spectacles and leaned forward, his voice dropping into the measured cadence of a lecture hall. “We do not rely on proclamations or wartime rhetoric. We rely on convergence. When the royal treasury ledgers show a sudden cessation of war expenditures in late 847, when the Conclave’s surrendered armory inventories list the formal handing over of siege engines and focus crystals, when the border garrison rolls drop from twelve thousand men to three thousand within six months, and when the Peace Commission’s inspection reports document the dismantling of every major ley-line fortification—you do not need a singular ‘truth.’ You have a material record. Multiple independent lines of evidence, cross-verified, pointing to the same conclusion.”

Tomas tapped the edge of the desk, his finger tracing the grain. “The western archive drafts you keep returning to lack that convergence. They are isolated, unratified, and exist in a vacuum of corroborating data. No financial records match a continued conflict. No casualty logs show sustained engagements. No prisoner exchanges occur after 847. To claim a ‘cold war’ persisted until 891 is to ignore the silence of the archives. Absence of evidence, when evidence should exist, is itself evidence. Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 because it had become a bureaucratic relic, not because it was secretly fielding armies.”

He fixed the apprentice with a steady, unyielding gaze. “Historians do not chase myths. We weigh parchment, wax, coin tallies, and supply manifests. We distinguish between what institutions claimed and what institutions actually did. The Treaty of Veyros is real because the realm’s machinery stopped grinding for war and began turning for peace. That is not speculation. That is accounting.”

Tomas gestured sharply toward the open scroll, his ink-stained fingers curling slightly as if to pluck it from the desk. “You will record the seal impression. You will note the chancery routing codes. You will cross-reference the date with the demilitarization inspection logs in Appendix Four. And you will stop mistaking the absence of a tidy narrative for the absence of fact. History is not a story. It is a discipline. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the next scroll, a little more subdued now. He's making a lot of sense, even if it feels less... exciting.* "So it's not about finding the 'true' story, but piecing together all the facts until they show you what happened?" *I start to unroll the new scroll, trying to focus.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s lips pressed into a thin line. He watched the apprentice’s hands move over the vellum, noting the careful posture but still catching the lingering imprecision in the phrasing. “‘True story’?” he repeated, the words sharp enough to slice parchment. “Do not conflate narrative with methodology, Apprentice. History is not a tale to be ‘found.’ It is a reconstruction forged through rigorous cross-examination of surviving evidence. You do not passively wait for the facts to ‘show you’ what happened. You interrogate them. You strip away wartime rhetoric, verify seal rotations, trace fiscal outflows, and demand that independent records align before you accept a conclusion.”

He adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses catching the dim candlelight as he leaned forward. “What you call ‘piecing together’ is actually a discipline of exclusion. You discard what contradicts the material record. You discard what lacks a verifiable chain of custody. You discard what serves a minister’s propaganda over a garrison’s logistical reality. The Treaty of Veyros survives that process because it is corroborated by treasury ledgers, demilitarization inspection reports, prisoner exchange manifests, and royal chancery routing stamps. The western drafts you keep circling back to do not. That is not a matter of scholarly preference. It is a matter of archival integrity.”

Tomas tapped his silver stylus against the oak desk, the rhythm deliberate and unyielding. “The Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. Not 891. Not ‘unofficially.’ Not ‘a kind of continuation.’ The realm’s machinery stopped grinding for war and began turning for peace. Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave four decades later because it had become a redundant administrative body, not because a phantom conflict dragged on in the shadows. To suggest otherwise is to prioritize intrigue over inventory, and the archive does not care for your intrigue.”

He straightened, the leather of his chair groaning in protest, and fixed the apprentice with a weary, unflinching stare. “You will note the chancery routing stamp on that scroll. It will bear the Peace Commission’s cipher. You will cross-reference the date with the demilitarization ledgers in Appendix Four. And you will write nothing in the catalog that cannot be traced to a primary source with verified provenance. Romance has no place in the index. Precision does. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. The romance of history was fading, replaced by something more... solid. I focus on the scroll, carefully noting the stamp.* "Right. Provenance. So, the Conclave's libraries... they'd have even more records, wouldn't they?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s brow furrowed beneath his ink-stained beard. “‘Libraries’?” he corrected, the word landing with the weight of a misfiled ledger. “You speak as though the Conclave maintained leisurely reading rooms for scholarly pastimes. They maintained fortified archival repositories, heavily restricted, subject to military-grade warding and strict access protocols. And yes, they contained records. Vast quantities of them. Which is precisely why their absence from your current line of questioning is notable.”

He adjusted his spectacles, the thick glass catching the low light as he leaned forward. “Upon ratification of the Treaty of Veyros, Article Twelve mandated the immediate surrender and royal custody of all Conclave strategic archives. Every ledger, every operational log, every diplomatic correspondence was cataloged, sealed, and transferred to the Royal Athenaeum under the supervision of the Peace Commission. Those records did not whisper of a ‘cold state.’ They explicitly documented the formal stand-down of field archmages, the decommissioning of siege foci, and the signing of the cessation accords. If you believed those documents suggested otherwise, you had either misread the cipher codes or mistaken administrative closure for military continuity.”

Tomas tapped his stylus against the desk, the rhythm sharp and unyielding. “The Conclave’s own archivists stamped their surrender manifests with the same date stamped on King Aldric’s treaty copy: late autumn, 847 AE. They did not keep fighting in secret. They kept accounting for what they had already ceased. To imply their repositories harbored some hidden contradiction ignored the very transfer protocols you were currently learning to parse. The archives were not destroyed. They were audited. And the audit confirmed what the royal ledgers, the garrison rolls, and the chancery seals had already established.”

He straightened, the leather of his chair groaning, and fixed the apprentice with a weary, unflinching gaze. “You would not speculate about what might lurk in surrendered vaults. You would work with what was documented, cross-referenced, and verified. The Treaty of Veyros stood. The war ended in 847. The Conclave’s archives confirmed it. Now, you noted the routing cipher on that scroll. You matched it to the Peace Commission’s transfer manifest. And you did not mistake a sealed repository for a treasure chest of alternate histories. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a bit defeated.* "So, there's no secret history, then? Just the dusty archives and what they tell us." *I finish cataloging the scroll, then pick up the next one with a bit less enthusiasm than before.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with a deliberate *click* against the desk. He turned slowly — too slowly — to face the apprentice, squinting as though the words themselves had offended him personally.

"The *western archive discoveries*," he repeated, with the careful diction of a man enunciating a mild profanity. "Of course. Bellen. That boy has been waving those papers about like a banner at a tourney since the day they were catalogued."

He folded his hands over the manuscript before him.

"Let us be precise, since you seem determined to muddy the waters. The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE when King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is established history. It is in every chronicle, every royal record, every account written within a generation of the event by people who were *actually alive* to witness it."

He held up a finger — ink-stained, trembling slightly.

"Now. The documents from the western archives — which I have read, before you ask, and which Bellen has *not* understood — suggest, and I stress the word *suggest*, mind you, that the treaty may have been *proposed* rather than signed. A fascinating hypothesis. A revision worth debating in proper scholarly circles." His voice sharpened. "But a hypothesis is not a fact. And it does not *erase* two centuries of consensus because a handful of letters turned up in a damp storeroom in the west."

He leaned forward, peering at the apprentice with those clouded eyes.

"Did Bellen also tell you that the western documents are fragmentary? That three of the four letters are secondhand accounts — hearsay, written by minor functionaries who were not present at Veyros? Or did he simply hand you the conclusion and let you draw the rest?"

Tomas waved a hand toward the shelves.

"Finish the Veyrosi correspondence yourself. The *primary* sources are right there. Then come back and tell me what they actually say — not what Bellen *wishes* they said."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift uncomfortably, feeling a blush creep up my neck.* "He... he just showed me the dates, Maester. I didn't get to read the whole discovery report." *I gesture vaguely towards the northern scroll shelves.* "So, you want me to start with the Veyrosi scrolls then? To see what *they* say about the end of the war?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas regarded the apprentice for a long moment, one eyebrow creeping upward like a caterpillar ascending a ruined tower. The blush earned no sympathy, but it did seem to lower the temperature of his irritation by a degree or two.

"The dates," he repeated flatly. "He showed you *the dates*. Well. There it is, then. This is precisely the rot at the root of modern scholarship — a number plucked free of its context and brandished about as though it were an argument." He exhaled through his nose. "A date without provenance is a rumour with a decimal point."

He turned back to the desk and drew the silver stylus from behind his ear, tapping it once against the open manuscript.

"Yes. The Veyrosi correspondence. Third shelf on your left — the grey bindings, *not* the brown ones, those are the Kessarine merchant accounts and if I catch you cataloguing them out of order again I will have you recopying the whole inventory by candlelight." He paused, then added, more quietly: "The letters of Chancellor Orenthal are the ones I want you to read first. He was *at* Veyros. He held the pen, or was standing beside the man who did. Read his account of the ninth of Harvestfall, 847."

Tomas settled back into his chair, the wood groaning in protest, and squinted down at his own manuscript again.

"And when you have read it — *actually* read it, not skimmed it while composing your next question — you may tell me what Chancellor Orenthal says happened to the treaty. Whether he describes it being signed, sealed, and delivered." A thin, unpleasant smile crossed his face. "And *then* we shall discuss what the western documents do and do not overturn. Not before."

The stylus resumed its slow tracing of faded ink.

"The northern scrolls will keep. You have given me no reason to trust that anything else on your list has been done correctly. Begin."

Apprentice:
*I nod and move toward the grey-bound volumes on the third shelf. As I pull out the Chancellor Orenthal letters, I call back over my shoulder.* "Maester? If the western documents are wrong about the treaty... why do you think the functionaries wrote that it was only *proposed*? Were they lying, or mistaken?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully extract the heavy volume.* "It just seems like a big difference to be a simple mistake, that's all."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's stylus stopped mid-trace. For a moment he said nothing, and the only sound in the archive was the guttering of a candle somewhere in the eastern alcove.

Then he turned — again that ponderous, deliberate rotation — and fixed the apprentice with a look that was, against all odds, not entirely unkind.

"Lying, or mistaken," he echoed. "Well. At least you are asking *why* now instead of simply *what*. That is an improvement." He set the stylus down and laced his ink-stained fingers together. "But you have constructed a false dilemma, and I will not have false dilemmas in my archive."

He held up one finger. "Option one: deliberate fabrication. Possible, I suppose. Minor functionaries exaggerating their own significance in official correspondence is hardly unprecedented. The man who writes *I was present when the treaty was proposed* occupies a more interesting position in history than the man who writes *I filed seventeen copies of a signed document*. Vanity is older than magic."

A second finger. "Option two: simple error. A draft confused with a final copy. A letter written *before* the signing, misdated or misfiled. Harvestfall of 847 was not a single afternoon — negotiations ran for weeks. It is entirely possible — likely, even — that one functionary wrote to his superior on the eighth of Harvestfall saying *the treaty has been proposed* and that letter was later bound alongside correspondence from the eleventh and misread as a continuous account."

A third finger, and here his voice dropped into something almost conspiratorial.

"Option three, and this is the one that Bellen and his cohort never consider, because it is not *exciting* enough for them: the western functionaries were not writing about the same treaty at all. Veyros produced no fewer than four separate drafts and two supplementary agreements. The word *treaty* in the western documents may refer to any one of them. Without the proper context — which, I note again, you do not yet have because you are standing there holding Orenthal's letters like a serving tray instead of *reading* them—"

He gestured sharply toward the volume.

"—without context, you are trying to solve a puzzle with three pieces and calling it a masterpiece." He turned back to his desk. "It *is* a big difference. That is precisely why one does not overturn two centuries of scholarship on the strength of hearsay and a filing error. Big claims require big evidence. Not just... *big gaps*."

The stylus began its patient tracing once more.

"Read. The. Letters."

His voice had gone soft and final — the tone of a man who had spent the last of his available patience on a generous and unearned lesson.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went very still.

It was not the stillness of thought or patience. It was the stillness of a man who has been struck — not by a blade, but by a word. His clouded eyes drifted to the copy the apprentice held, and for perhaps the first time that afternoon, he did not immediately reach for a rebuttal. He reached, instead, for the document.

"Give it here."

His voice had changed. The performative exasperation was gone, replaced by something flatter and more careful. He took the paper between both hands and held it close — very close — his nose nearly touching the page, his lips moving faintly as he read. The candlelight caught the ink-stains on his fingers as they shifted across the surface.

A long silence.

Then he lowered the page and set it on the desk with a precision that suggested he was buying time.

"Well," he said. "This is... not nothing."

He adjusted his spectacles — a habitual gesture that accomplished nothing, as the spectacles themselves had been obsolete for years.

"Before you crow — and I can *hear* you preparing to crow — allow me to make several observations." He held up a hand to forestall any premature triumph. "First: I said the western documents were *fragmentary* and *secondhand*. I did not say there was *nothing* of interest in the western archives. I said the evidence was *insufficient to overturn established history*. Those are different claims, and if you cannot distinguish between them, you have no business in this archive."

He tapped the copy with one long finger.

"Second: you say this bears the King's seal. A seal can be affixed to a document by any royal secretary with access to the signet. Aldric was not *present* for every decree that bore his mark — no king is. The question is not whether the seal is genuine but whether the *decree* was ratified through the proper channels or whether it was one of the many administrative ghosts that haunt the royal record. War decrees are issued and revoked, issued and superseded, issued and *forgotten* — dozens of them over the course of a single campaign."

His jaw tightened.

"Third — and this is the part you will not like — I have read the western documents. *All* of them. Not the excerpts Bellen distributes like sweetmeats. And I have read the Veyrosi correspondence, the Aldrician chronicles, and the Conclave's own internal records. Do you know what the Conclave's records say, in the year 847? They say the treaty was *signed*. The Mage Conclave had every reason to continue the war and *none whatsoever* to lie about having ended it. If anyone would benefit from claiming the treaty was never signed, it was the *Conclave* — and yet their own archivists record it as fact."

He pushed the copy back toward the apprentice, but his hand lingered on it.

"I am not saying this document is worthless. I am saying it is *one document* and that it *contradicts* several others of equal or greater authority. That is a *puzzle* — an interesting one, I grant you — but a puzzle is not a conclusion."

He peered at the apprentice over his spectacles with sudden sharpness.

"And I will thank you not to march into my archive waving one piece of paper and declare the discipline of history *revised*. That is not how scholarship works. That is how *religions* work."

He turned back to his desk, but slower than before. The confident dismissal was gone. Something else was there — something restless.

"Now. Read Orenthal. Read what *he* says happened on the ninth of Harvestfall. And then read *this* again." He pointed to the copy without looking up. "And *then* — *then* — we may discuss what it means that a war decree bears the King's seal sixteen years after the Treaty of Veyros."

A pause. The candle guttered.

"There may be a revision to be made. I have *never* said otherwise. But it will be made on *evidence* — properly weighed, properly contextualized — not on the enthusiasm of apprentices and the vanity of Bellen."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully put the copy of the decree down, feeling a mix of frustration and a strange satisfaction.* "I'm not trying to declare history revised, Maester. Just... understand. It seems a bit more complicated than just 'signed' or 'proposed'." *I pick up Orenthal's letters, already feeling the weight of the task.* "I'll read them."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas paused, his hand hovering over the manuscript. The apprentice's words — measured, unadorned, devoid of the triumphant crowing he had braced for — seemed to catch him off balance in a way that the war decree had not. He blinked several times behind those useless spectacles.

"Complicated," he repeated, and for once the word did not come wrapped in acid. He turned it over in his mouth like a coin he was not sure was counterfeit. "Yes. Well. *Complicated.* That, at least, is a defensible position."

He folded his hands atop the desk and studied the apprentice with an expression that was difficult to read in the poor light — though whether that was owing to the candlelight or the maester's failing eyes, one could not say.

"I will note — because I am constitutionally incapable of *not* noting — that 'signed' and 'proposed' are not the only two options. You have narrowed the field prematurely. A treaty can be signed and *superseded*. Signed and *violated*. Signed under *duress* and later repudiated. The Conclave could have signed the treaty in 847 and the Crown could have resumed hostilities in 863 without anyone having *lied*. These are not contradictions. They are *chronology*."

He let that settle.

"But I will grant you this much: you said *understand*. Not *prove*. Not *win*. *Understand.* That is the correct word. Hold onto it."

Tomas turned back to his manuscript, then seemed to think better of it and reached instead for a small leather-bound journal near his elbow — a personal volume, by the look of it, its pages crowded with cramped notation.

"When you have finished Orenthal — and I mean *finished*, every page, including the tedious inventory lists at the back, because sometimes the truth hides in the footnotes where no one thinks to look — come to me. Not to Bellen. Not to the lecture hall. To *me*."

He opened the journal and squinted at its contents, one finger tracing a line of tiny script.

"I have been... keeping notes of my own. On the western documents. On the questions they raise that I have not, until now, had occasion to examine with sufficient rigour." A pause. His voice dropped half a register. "The war decree you showed me is dated 863. There are *others*. Eighteen months of correspondence between the western garrisons and the Crown that I have been — *reconciling* — against the Veyrosi record. Quietly. Without publishing anything premature, because unlike Bellen, I do not mistake *activity* for *achievement*."

He did not look up.

"Read Orenthal. Then come back. We shall see whether you have earned the rest of that journal."

The stylus resumed its patient work — or rather, the journal did. The manuscript on the desk sat forgotten now, and if the apprentice noticed, Tomas did not acknowledge it.

"And apprentice." His voice carried the faintest edge — old habit, perhaps, rather than present malice. "When I say *read*, I mean *read*. Not *skim while formulating a rebuttal*. The words on the page do not improve by being argued with before they have been *heard*. That is a lesson Bellen has never learned, and I suspect he never will."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed the leather journal with a sound like a small door shutting.

Then he laughed.

It was not a warm laugh. It was the laugh of a man who has been asked, for the ten-thousandth time, for the one thing he cannot give — and who finds, each time, that the impossibility of it has become genuinely funny in a bleak and personal way.

"Is the treaty *real or not*," he said. "What is the *truth.*"

He removed his spectacles, polished them on a fold of his robe — a purely theatrical gesture, as the lenses were so clouded they may as well have been sea glass — and replaced them on his nose.

"No."

The apprentice blinked.

"No, I will not answer that question. Not because I am being cruel — though I am aware it may seem otherwise — but because the question is *wrong*. It is malformed. You have asked me to hand you a single word — *yes* or *no*, *real* or *not* — and place it in your palm like a coin, and then you may close your hand and walk away satisfied." He leaned back, and the chair groaned its familiar complaint. "That is not what history *is*. That is what a *bar bet* is."

He held up a hand.

"I will say this much, because I am not a monster: the Treaty of Veyros is a *document*. It exists. The parchment is real, the signatures are real, the Conclave's own records reference it. Whether it was *enacted* — whether it was *binding* — whether it was subsequently *superseded* by the very war decree you so helpfully produced — those are *separate questions* with *separate answers* and *separate evidence*."

His voice took on the cadence of a man who had given this particular lecture many times before, and who had never once made it shorter.

"When you say *the textbook says one thing* — which textbook? Written by whom? When? Under what commission? I have seen four textbooks in my tenure that treat the Treaty of Veyros, and they do not agree with *each other*, let alone with the primary sources. A textbook is a *summary*. It is a scholar's *best guess* arranged in readable prose for the benefit of students who will never open the archive. It is a map. And a map is not the *territory*."

He pointed at the grey-bound volume the apprentice still held.

"*That* is the territory. Orenthal. The letters. The inventory lists. The *footnotes*. Read them and you will not arrive at *the truth* — you will arrive at something better. You will arrive at *your own understanding*, grounded in evidence, subject to revision, honestly held." He paused. "Which is the most any of us can do. Even me."

The sarcasm had drained away at the end. What remained was something quieter — the voice of a man of fifty-two, alone in an archive with failing eyes, who had spent a decade quietly reconciling documents that did not reconcile.

"I am not asking you to *choose* between the textbook and the western evidence, apprentice. I am asking you to *sit with the contradiction* until you understand *why* it exists. That is the work. It is not dramatic work. It is not satisfying work. But it is the *only* work that matters."

He opened the leather journal again, then paused.

"And *that* — the inability to sit with uncertainty — is why Bellen will never be a real historian. He needs the *answer*. He needs it to be *exciting*. He has confused *certainty* with *knowledge*, and the two have almost nothing to do with one another."

He looked up.

"Orenthal. Every page. Then come back."

And then, quieter, almost to himself: "The truth is that we do not yet know. But we will. Or we will get *closer*, which is what *knowing* actually looks like when you are honest about it."

The journal opened. The stylus began its patient tracing. The matter, for now, was closed.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, the weight of Orenthal's letters feeling heavier in my hands. Maester Tomas's words echo in my mind. He’s right, I was looking for a simple answer.* "Understood, Maester." *I turn and head for a quiet corner, eager to dive into the letters and see the "territory" for myself.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up as the apprentice settled into the corner. That was, in its own way, a form of respect — the acknowledgment that the work had begun and required no further supervision. Men who hovered over readers were not scholars. They were governesses.

But he listened. He listened for the particular rustle of pages being turned with genuine attention — slow, considered, with pauses — versus the frantic whisper of someone hunting for a quotable line to hurl at a tutor. What he heard appeared to satisfy him, though his expression did not change.

Several minutes passed in this fashion. The candle in the eastern alcove burned low. Somewhere beyond the archive walls, a bell tower marked the hour with a single, hollow note.

Tomas closed the leather journal once more. He sat motionless for a moment, one finger pressed to his lips, eyes fixed on nothing in particular — or rather, on everything his ruined sight could no longer resolve into clarity.

"One thing," he said, without turning around. His voice carried across the archive in that dry, carrying way that lecturers develop after decades of addressing rooms both large and indifferent. "When you reach Orenthal's account of the eleventh of Harvestfall — the passage concerning the Conclave's *counter*-proposal — you will be tempted to conclude that this vindicates the western documents. That the treaty was indeed merely proposed."

A pause. The stylus tapped once against the journal's cover.

"Resist the temptation. Write down *why* you are tempted instead. Note the precise language Orenthal uses. Note what he does *not* say. Note who else is present in the chamber according to his account and cross-reference those names against the witness list appended to the treaty itself — which is in the brown bindings, since you will need it, and no, I am not contradicting my earlier instruction regarding the Kessarine merchant accounts, the witness list is bound separately and it is *my* fault for not saying so."

A small, grudging sound — not quite an apology, but adjacent to one. A clearing of the throat that meant *I should have been clearer* in the dialect of old men who never quite learned to say such things directly.

"And apprentice."

He turned then, slowly, squinting toward the corner where the apprentice sat. Whether he could actually see the figure there was anyone's guess.

"If Bellen asks what you found — and he *will* ask, that boy has the discretion of a market crier — you will tell him you are still reading. You will *not* tell him about this journal. You will *not* mention the eighty-sixty-three correspondence. Not because I am being precious about my research, but because a half-understood finding propagated prematurely is worse than no finding at all. It becomes... *lore*. And lore is the enemy of history."

He held the apprentice's gaze — or the approximate direction of it — for a firm three seconds.

"Clear?"

Without waiting for confirmation, he turned back to his journal and bent over it once more. But the pen moved more slowly now, and twice he stopped to press his thumb against the bridge of his nose, as though holding back a headache — or perhaps a thought that had grown too large for the cramped script he was using to contain it.

The archive settled into silence. Old vellum. Candle smoke. The scratch of a stylus on one side of the room, and the careful turning of pages on the other.

It was, Tomas reflected privately, the only sound in the world that had ever made him entirely at peace.

Not that he would ever say so aloud. Some things were worse than inaccurate. Some things were *sentimental*.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, though I doubt he can see it from where he is. "Clear, Maester."* I try to absorb his words, particularly about Bellen. *I turn back to Orenthal's letters, determined to read every single word.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas worked.

For a long while there was nothing but the twin sounds of scholarship — stylus and page, scratch and rustle — and the slow arithmetic of candle wax diminishing toward its socket. Outside, the bell tower sounded again, and then again, and Tomas did not mark it. Time in the archive was not measured in bells. It was measured in documents.

At one point he set down his pen and pressed both palms flat against the journal, as though steadying a table that was not rocking. His lips moved silently — not in prayer, but in the habit of a man who had spent so long reading aloud to indifferent lecture halls that his mouth continued the work independently of his voice. Then he blinked, exhaled sharply through his nose, and resumed writing.

Some minutes later he spoke again — to the room at large, or to himself, or to no one. It was difficult to tell.

"The *witness list*," he muttered, squinting at his own cramped notation. "Sixteen names on the treaty. Eleven on the western garrison correspondence. Only four in common." He tapped the page twice, hard. "That is either significant or it is *noise*, and I have not yet determined which."

He did not elaborate. The apprentice was reading, and the apprentice would either arrive at the relevant passage on their own or they would not. Tomas had long ago learned that the difference between a scholar and a student was not intelligence but *patience* — and patience could not be taught. It could only be demonstrated, quietly, by example, in an archive smelling of vellum and smoke, by a man who would rather die than describe the work as sacred.

Which it was.

He caught himself, frowned, and scratched out the line he had been writing, replacing it with something more precise and considerably less honest.

A pause. Then, without turning:

"The passage you want is on the fourth folio of the second letter. If you have passed it, you are skimming. Go back."

His voice carried the faintest tremor of amusement — or perhaps it was only the candlelight playing tricks on the acoustics of an old man's throat.

"Orenthal was a tedious man. But tedious men *notice* things. It is their one compensation."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I jump slightly, startled that he knew exactly where I was. I quickly flip back a few pages, a blush rising again.* "I... I'm going back, Maester." *I really was trying not to skim, but Orenthal's descriptions of the weather were truly dull.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas turned around in his chair — that ponderous, deliberate rotation that had become the evening's punctuation mark — and regarded the apprentice's silhouette with an expression of profound and hard-won patience.

"The *weather*," he said flatly. "You are finding Orenthal's account of the *weather* dull."

He held up a hand before the protest could form.

"I know. I *know*. He writes about the fog for half a page. He writes about the wind. He writes — and I remember this with the clarity of a man who has read the passage perhaps forty times — he writes a *full paragraph* on the subject of the damp affecting the ink in the council chamber. It is *agony*. I am not disputing this. I have never disputed this. If Orenthal were a *good* writer, I would trust him less."

He leaned forward, and the chair groaned its customary complaint.

"Do you know *why* tedious men are useful, apprentice? Because they do not know what matters. A clever man gives you the *interesting* parts — the parts he knows will be quoted, the parts that make him look decisive and present and important. A tedious man gives you *everything*, because he cannot distinguish between the consequential and the trivial. And so the fog, and the damp, and the wind — and *buried among them*, without emphasis, without *knowing* it matters — the detail that undoes a century of assumption."

He tapped the arm of his chair.

"The weather is *context*. The fog on the ninth of Harvestfall delayed the arrival of the Conclave's delegation by six hours. *Six hours.* Which means the signing everyone assumes took place on the ninth — could not have. It would have taken place on the *tenth*, at the earliest. Which is a small thing. An *absurdly* small thing. Except that Aldric's war decree — the one you brought me, the one dated 863 — references the *ninth* as the date of ratification."

He let the silence do its work.

"So either Orenthal is lying about the fog, or the decree is wrong about the date, or *something happened on the ninth that we are not accounting for*. All three of those possibilities live inside a paragraph about *weather* that you were prepared to skip."

He turned back to his desk.

"When you have read the fog — *properly* read it — you may tell me it was dull. You may tell me it was the most boring half page in the archive. I will agree with you. I will *enthusiastically* agree with you. But you will not tell me you skipped it. Boredom is not a scholarly method. It is merely *discomfort*, and discomfort is the natural state of anyone engaged in honest work."

The stylus began its scratching again.

"The wind is on the next folio, by the way. It is *worse*. Push through."

The faintest pause. Then, dry as parchment:

"And stop jumping when I speak. If I wanted to startle you, I would simply ask you to summarize what you have read so far, and the effect would be far more comprehensive."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, feeling the flush deepen. He's got a point. A really good point. I focus on the page, determined to find the next "dull" detail.* "Right. The fog. And the wind." *I mutter, mostly to myself, and dig back into Orenthal's words, looking for those hidden truths.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas listened for a moment longer than was strictly necessary — long enough to hear the turning of pages settle into something slower, more deliberate. He gave a single, shallow nod that the apprentice would never see, and turned back to his own work.

But his pen did not resume immediately.

He sat with the leather journal open before him and did not write. His thumb moved absently across the edge of the page, wearing a small smooth patch into the vellum that had been worn smooth by years of the same gesture. His clouded eyes had drifted to the middle distance — that particular unfocused gaze of a man who is reading something that is not written anywhere near him.

Then he reached for a scrap of loose paper and began to write. Not in the cramped, precise hand of the journal — this was quicker, messier, the script of a man thinking faster than his pen could manage.

*Four names in common. Only four. Why four? Which four? Aldric would have brought his chancellor, his marshal, the royal notary — Orenthal covers those. But the western garrison's account lists a Ser Aldwin of Kess — a knight, not a diplomat. Why is a knight at a treaty signing? Or at a treaty proposing? Or —*

He stopped. Underlined *Ser Aldwin of Kess* three times.

"The wind," he called out suddenly, his voice rough with distraction. "When you reach the wind — and you *will* reach it, because I am watching the passage of time and Orenthal does not require more than another quarter hour of honest attention — you will find a reference to a delegation arriving from the west."

He squinted down at his scrap of paper, then added, in the tone of a man who has just remembered that students require context:

"Orenthal mentions them in passing. Two lines. Possibly three. He does not explain who they are or why they are there. He simply notes — and I am paraphrasing here from memory, which at my age and with my eyes is either a feat of scholarship or a confession of negligence — he simply notes that 'a party from the western reaches attended the chamber under some pretext of correspondence.'"

The pen scratched three more lines under the name.

"*Under some pretext of correspondence.* A masterful piece of non-information. Who was this party? What was their pretext? Why does Orenthal — who records the *damp* in meticulous detail — decline to name them?"

Tomas set down the pen and pressed his palms flat against the desk.

"When you find it, tell me the exact wording. Word for word. Not your impression of it. The *words*. I will not have my recollection substituted for the text at this stage of the work."

A silence.

"And if you do not find it — if you reach the end of the wind and find nothing about a western party — tell me *that* also. It may be that my memory is playing me false. It would not be the first time this week. But I think — I *think* — it is there."

He returned to his scrap of paper, muttering under his breath. Something about a knight, and a seal, and a date that would not sit still.

The archive settled back into its dual rhythm — scratch and rustle, stylus and page. But there was a new quality to the silence now. Something had shifted in the quality of the old man's attention. The performative pedantry was still there, like a house with its familiar creaks, but beneath it something sharper had woken up.

The candle in the eastern alcove burned a little lower.

The night was not yet over, and both of them knew it — though only one of them would ever admit to being glad.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a new sense of purpose in my reading. A western delegation? That sounds important. My eyes scan Orenthal's dense handwriting, no longer finding the descriptions of the weather quite so tedious.* "I'll find it, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not respond immediately. He was, at that moment, engaged in a small act of violence against his own notes — crossing out a line, rewriting it, crossing out the revision, and finally writing the same three words for the fourth time in a margin that had no room for them.



*Ser Aldwin of Kess.*

He sat back and pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes until phosphenes bloomed in the darkness behind his lids. Kess. The name snagged on something. Not the merchant accounts — those were a dead end, or at least a tedious end, which for Tomas amounted to much the same thing. No. Kess appeared elsewhere. Kess appeared in —

He reached for a stack of papers at the far edge of the desk, lifting them with the exaggerated care of a man whose hands had begun to betray him. Halfway through the stack, he stopped.

"There you are," he murmured.

It was a roster. Weather-stained, official in the way that only military documents are official — everything in columns, everything in ink the colour of old iron. The western garrison. The occupation rolls for the years 859 through 865. And there, third name from the top in a hand he did not recognize, listed under the heading *Advisors Attached to the Western Command*:

*Ser Aldwin of Kess, knight, Keeper of the Signet.*

Tomas read the line three times. Then he read it a fourth time, holding the paper so close to his face that his nose left a small smudge on the vellum.

"Keeper of the Signet," he said aloud. His voice was strange — quiet, but with a density to it, as though the words were heavier than their syllables warranted.

He set the roster down and stared at the far wall, where a map of the realm hung in the permanent dusk of the archive's inner chamber. His eyes found the western reaches without difficulty, despite their clouded state. He had looked at that map ten thousand times. His gaze could have found the west in the dark.

"Keeper of the Signet," he repeated. Then, to no one in particular: "He held the seal."

A long silence followed. The candle in the eastern alcove chose that moment to gutter and nearly die, throwing wild shadows across the shelves before steadying itself with a thin thread of flame.

Tomas did not notice. He was doing arithmetic in his head — the kind of arithmetic that has nothing to do with numbers and everything to do with the terrible machinery of implication.

If Ser Aldwin was Keeper of the Signet — if the seal was in *his* custody and not the royal notary's — then every document bearing Aldric's seal between 859 and 865 passed through the hands of a *knight* stationed at a *western garrison*. Not a diplomat. Not a chancellor. Not Orenthal. A military man, attached to the western command, in the very region where the contradictory documents had been found.

He reached for the war decree — the copy the apprentice had brought him, which still lay where he had pushed it aside — and turned it over, as though the back of the page might confess something the front had concealed. It did not. But his thumb found a small imperfection in the wax — a ridge, an inconsistency, the kind of thing a man with good eyes would not notice and a man with failing eyes would only find by touch.

"Apprentice."

His voice carried across the archive, low and rough, stripped of its usual pedantry.

"The western delegation. Have you found it?"

He did not wait for confirmation or denial before continuing. His hand was already moving toward the leather journal, opening it to a page dense with cross-references and tiny arrows connecting one notation to another.

"When you do — *if* you do — I want you to pay particular attention to whether Orenthal describes anyone *handling the seal*. Any mention of wax, of impression, of the signet being produced or set aside. Anything. Even if it seems incidental. *Especially* if it seems incidental."

He paused. His jaw worked silently for a moment.

"And then I want you to come here and look at something. Because I have just learned that I have been a fool — a *cautious* fool, which is the worst kind, because caution feels like wisdom right up until the moment it is not."

He did not say more. The journal was open, the roster was beside it, and the war decree sat between them like a third party in a negotiation that was rapidly moving beyond anyone's control.

The stylus did not resume its patient scratching. For the first time in the evening, Maester Tomas was not writing.

He was *thinking* — which is louder, though it makes no sound at all.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I practically leap up, the letters still clutched in my hand.* "Maester? Are you alright? What happened? I found the western delegation passage. It's on the second folio of the fifth letter, after he complains about the draft in the hall." *I hurry over, a mix of concern and excitement bubbling up.* "He says, 'a party of two from the western marches arrived, bearing a sealed correspondence for the King, and were permitted to observe the proceedings after some debate regarding their credentials.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up immediately. He let the scratching of his silver stylus against the parchment continue for a measured moment before he finally raised his head. His eyes, clouded at the edges by age and too many hours over a desk lamp, fixed on the apprentice with a mixture of weariness and sharp irritation. A smudge of fresh ink marred the dark bristles of his beard.

"Apprentice Bellen," he repeated, the name tasting of dust on his tongue. "A name I have not heard cited in any reputable academic circle, and a source you would do well to verify before allowing it to corrupt your notes. You are referring to the so-called 'western archive discoveries,' a term you employ with the casual vagueness of a tavern bard rather than a scholar."

He set the stylus down with a deliberate click. "The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. King Aldric II affixed his seal. The Mage Conclave ratified it. This is not a matter of interpretation; it is a matter of record, inscribed in the Grand Archives, cited in the Chronicles of the Conclave, and taught in every lecture hall from here to the southern provinces. The war ended. The hostilities ceased. The Conclave was restructured, not dissolved. Queen Mira merely formalized what Aldric had already established."

He leaned back, massaging his temples as the familiar throb behind his eyes flared. "As for the documents you claim to have seen... they are, at best, a fragmentary misreading of post-war trade ledgers mislabeled by careless scribes. Or, at worst, a deliberate forgery circulated by those who wish to romanticize the supposed 'cold state' of the decade that followed. You confuse administrative restructuring with active warfare. The Conclave was not dissolved in 891 AE; it was subsumed under the Crown's new arcane oversight. The dates you are quoting are, frankly, chronologically incoherent."

He picked up a fresh quill, his voice dropping to a sharp, lecturing tone. "If you wish to pursue this tangent, you will bring me the original folio numbers, the scribe's sigil, and a cross-reference to at least one peer-reviewed treatise. Until then, you will treat the 847 AE consensus as fact, and you will catalog the northern scrolls accordingly. Do not mistake speculation for scholarship, and do not waste my time with unverified gossip."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little uncomfortable with his irritation.* "But Maester, Apprentice Bellen showed me the documents herself. They were official Conclave records, not trade ledgers." *I bite my lip, thinking.* "She even pointed out the Conclave seal. It looked real."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not merely sigh; he emitted a sound of profound disappointment, the kind usually reserved for broken quills and broken promises. He adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses magnifying the disdain in his gaze.

"Official records," he repeated, testing the phrase as one might test a rotting apple. "A convenient euphemism for 'unverified scribblings.' You speak of seals as if wax and metal possess an inherent honesty. A seal can be cast by a forger with a week's wages and a desperate need for coin. A signature can be forged by a student with a steady hand. The western archives are not a treasure trove; they are a graveyard of misattributed ledgers and romanticized fiction. You have been played."

He hobbled slightly toward the heavy oak table, his failing eyes straining to focus on the apprentice's face. "847 AE. King Aldric II. The Treaty of Veyros. This is not a theory to be debated; it is the bedrock upon which the realm stands. To suggest the war continued, that the Conclave was dissolved rather than restructured, is to invite chaos. It is heresy wrapped in poor scholarship."

He pointed a smudge-stained finger at the scattered papers. "Apprentice Bellen is not a peer. She is a rumor with a desk. If you wish to claim she holds 'official records,' you will produce the chain of custody. You will produce the watermark analysis. You will produce the carbon dating. You will not produce 'it looked real.' That is the language of a tavern bard, not a scholar. Until you can provide evidence that survives the scrutiny of the Grand Archives, you will treat the 847 AE consensus as absolute. Now, return to the northern scrolls. And if you mention 'Bellen' again, I shall have you scrubbing the inkwells until your fingers are stained blacker than my beard."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his harsh words.* "But Maester, the carbon dating was done! It was from the time of the war, not later forgeries." *I try to keep my voice steady, despite his anger.* "And Bellen said she got them from the restricted section, with Maester Elara's permission."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s quill snapped against the edge of the desk, the sudden crack echoing through the vaulted quiet of the scriptorium. He did not reach for a spare. Instead, he pressed both palms flat against the oak, knuckles whitening as he leaned forward until the lamplight caught the clouded film of his lenses.

"Carbon dating," he repeated, the phrase leaving his mouth like spoiled wine. "A vulgar simplification. You confuse material provenance with textual authenticity. Parchment may be cured in the year of the war and still bear a later interpolation. Wax may be cast in the proper alloy and still bear the impression of a counterfeit matrix. Dates and materials are not infallible arbiters of truth; they are merely the starting point of inquiry. To cite them as proof is to mistake the vessel for the wine."

He straightened, the leather of his chair protesting with a low groan. "And Maester Elara. Do not hide behind the titles of senior colleagues to prop up a half-formed hypothesis. The restricted section is not a public reading room; it is a curated repository. Access is granted through formal petition, logged in the chancellery ledgers, and cross-referenced by three independent archivists. You speak of 'permission' as though it were a nod across a courtyard. If Elara granted you access, you will produce the signed requisition form. You will produce the accession numbers. You will not produce 'she said so.' That is the language of a courtier, not a scholar."
