His ink-stained beard twitched as he exhaled through his nose, a sound of profound irritation. "The Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. The Treaty of Veyros was executed, witnessed by three high mages, the Crown’s chief notary, and the royal seal itself. The Mage Conclave was not dissolved in 891; it was integrated into the Royal Arcanum following the Quiet Reforms. To claim otherwise is to ignore three generations of verified historiography in favour of a handful of misfiled folios and a gossip chain masquerading as scholarship."

He tapped a finger against the manuscript before him, leaving a fresh smear of iron gall ink. "You will bring me the accession numbers. You will bring me the full transcriptions, properly indexed, with marginalia that clearly distinguishes between primary source and secondary commentary. You will bring me the chain of custody from the western stacks to your desk. Until you can produce evidence that survives the scrutiny of the Grand Archives, you will treat the 847 AE consensus as doctrine. Now, turn your attention to the northern scrolls. And if you value your position, you will cease citing 'Bellen' and 'Elara' as though they were peer-reviewed treatises. Begin with folio forty-two. And do not disappoint me."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s eyes narrowed behind his thick lenses as he finally accepted the offered parchment. He did not take it with enthusiasm, but rather with the grim resignation of a surgeon preparing to excise a festering wound. He adjusted his spectacles, leaning forward until the lamplight caught the grain of the paper and the dark, glossy impression of the royal seal.

"Eighty-sixty-three," he murmured, the syllables tasting of dust and resentment. He set the document down with a deliberate thud, as though placing a dead bird on a merchant’s scale. "A clerical marvel, truly. You present me with a war decree bearing the sovereign’s seal sixteen years into what you insist was a 'cold state,' yet you neglect to mention the most glaring anomaly: the seal matrix. That particular raptor-and-scepter design was retired in 842 AE, replaced by the double-headed phoenix following Aldric’s post-war coronation reforms. If this parchment bears the pre-coronation seal, it predates your supposed 'post-war' date by two decades. If it bears the post-coronation seal, it is a clumsy forgery, stamped with a matrix that did not exist in the western provinces until after the peace was ratified. You cannot have it both ways."

He tapped the edge of the desk, the sound sharp and precise. "Furthermore, your dating convention is colloquial, not canonical. The realm adopted the post-war reckoning in 847, not the regnal years of a monarch whose administrative authority was deliberately suspended during the Conclave's interim governance. To date a document 863 AE while simultaneously claiming it originates from a period of active hostilities is to contradict your own premise. The 'decree' you hold is not a record of war. It is a grain requisition. A logistical edict. A bureaucratic form disguised in the ornate calligraphy of a scribe who understood that authority is often purchased with the right kind of ink and the right kind of wax."

He pushed his spectacles up the bridge of his nose, his failing eyes straining to catch the fine print along the margins. "You mistake administrative continuity for military escalation. The Crown did not wage war from 847 to 891. It managed a logistical transition. The Mage Conclave was not dissolved in 891; its charter was transferred, its assets liquidated, and its remaining practitioners absorbed into state academies under the Quiet Reforms. There was no dissolution. There was only consolidation. What you have before you is a misfileed edict, likely drafted during the 863 harvest audits, misdated by a junior clerk, and later misinterpreted by those eager to manufacture a narrative of prolonged conflict."

He swept the document back toward the apprentice, his gesture dismissive. "If you insist this is a war decree, you will produce the counter-signatures. You will produce the logistical appendices detailing troop movements, supply routes, or magical mobilizations. You will not produce a single line of actual combat orders. Until you can demonstrate that the realm was actively at war in 863, you will correct your notes. The Treaty of Veyros stands. The year 847 is correct. The Conclave was restructured, not dissolved. The 'western discoveries' are, once again, misread ledgers wearing the costume of history. Return to folio forty-two. And if you bring me another 'decree' bearing an anachronistic seal, I shall have you copying the tax codes of the Low Marches by candlelight. Understood?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take the document back, feeling a flush creep up my neck.* "But Maester, it clearly says 'Declaration of Martial Law' right at the top, and it talks about troop deployments to the Northern Marches. It's not a grain requisition!" *I point to the faded script.* "And Bellen said the seal was an older one, from before the Conclave's reforms, which is why it was so important."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas snatched the parchment from your grip with a speed that belied his age, his movements jerky and sharp. He did not look at the document with the curiosity of a man seeking truth, but with the suspicion of a magistrate inspecting a smuggler's contraband. He reached into his robe and produced a heavy brass loupe, screwing it into his right eye socket with a click that sounded like a pistol hammer cocking.

"Martial Law," he hissed, the words dripping with venomous correction. "You are reading the header, are you not? You see the large, archaic calligraphy and your untrained mind jumps to the conclusion of 'Martial Law.' I assure you, your interpretation is as flawed as your grasp of syntax."

He squinted through the magnifying lens, the glass fogging slightly with his agitated breath. "Read the ligatures, you fool. *Mandate of Public Quiescence.* There is no 'Martial.' There is no 'War.' The Crown's authority, following the Treaty of Veyros, was explicitly forbidden from using the term 'Martial Law' in domestic affairs. To do so would have violated the sovereignty clauses. This document is not a declaration of war; it is a bureaucratic edict regarding the containment of magical fallout in the Northern Marches."

He tapped the paper hard, leaving a fresh smear of ink on the header. "You speak of 'troop deployments.' Look closer at the roster. Those are not soldiers. Those are 'Sanitation Squads' and 'Ley-line Stabilizers.' The Northern Marches were not under siege; they were under quarantine. There were active thaumaturgic leaks—unregulated mana surges from the Conclave's failed experiments during the war. The Crown did not send an army to fight the Conclave in 863; they sent engineers to patch the breaches the Conclave had left behind. You mistake environmental remediation for military mobilization."

Tomas leaned back, the loupe still glued to his eye, his voice rising in a crescendo of pedantic indignation. "And your friend Bellen's obsession with the 'old seal.' She calls it important. I call it damning. The raptor-and-scepter matrix was retired in 842. If this document, dated 863, bears the retired matrix, it proves one of two things, both of which destroy your thesis: either the document is a clumsy forgery created by southern sympathizers to romanticize the 'old regime,' or it is a remnant of the Dissident faction, operating illegally in the western wastes. It is not evidence of a continuing peace, nor is it evidence of a continuing war. It is evidence of *anarchy*."

He slammed the document onto the desk, the force of the blow sending a cloud of ink dust into the lamplight. "The Third Magical War ended in 847. The Treaty of Veyros stands. The Mage Conclave was restructured, not dissolved. The 'cold state' you cling to is a myth perpetuated by those who profit from the chaos of the western borders. This document is a quarantine order, misdated by a panicked clerk, stamped with a defunct seal by a rebel sympathizer, and misread by you."

He pointed a trembling, ink-stained finger at the stack of scrolls beside him. "You have wasted my time. You have wasted my eyes. I do not deal in 'Martial Law' fantasies, and I do not deal in 'old seals' from the rebellious west. You will take that forgery, burn it in the brazier, and you will catalogue the northern scrolls starting with folio forty-two. If you mention 'Bellen' or 'Martial Law' one more time, I will have your apprenticeship revoked for incompetence. Now. *Work.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not answer immediately. He let the question hang in the dust-heavy air of the scriptorium, his clouded eyes fixed on the apprentice as though measuring the weight of their ignorance. When he finally spoke, his voice was a low, precise instrument, stripped of all patience.

"Truth," he repeated, the word tasting of bitter ash. "You ask for truth as though it were a commodity to be weighed against a textbook. Truth is not a negotiation between dogma and desperation. Truth is the product of verified primary sources, cross-referenced against established chronologies, and vetted by the scholarly consensus of the Grand Archives."

He rose from his chair, the leather creaking under his weight, and moved to the towering bookshelf behind his desk. His fingers, stained permanently dark with decades of iron gall, traced the spines of three massive volumes bound in cracked leather and iron clasps. He pulled them out with a thud that shook the desk.

"The Treaty of Veyros was not merely 'said' to exist. It was witnessed, ratified, and archived under triple seal. King Aldric II did not propose a document; he executed a surrender of sovereign magical authority. The dates you cite—891 AE, the so-called 'dissolution' of the Conclave—are not a revision of history. They are a fundamental misunderstanding of administrative succession. The Conclave was not destroyed in 891. It was absorbed. Its lands, its grimoires, its practitioners, were integrated into the Crown’s Arcanum through the Quiet Reforms. There was no war. There was only the slow, bureaucratic dismantling of an institution that had outlived its usefulness."

He set the books down, his fingers drumming sharply on the top volume. "You speak of 'new evidence' from the western archives. I have read those 'discoveries.' I have cataloged them. They are fragmentary, heavily annotated by later scribes, and riddled with chronological inconsistencies. A document does not become history because it was found in a dusty cellar. It becomes history because it survives the crucible of peer review, archival authentication, and institutional memory. The western papers are exactly that: western. Isolated. Unverified. Politically convenient for those who wish to romanticize the borderlands as hotbeds of resistance rather than what they were: a logistical afterthought."

Tomas adjusted his spectacles, the thick glass magnifying the sharp angles of his face. "The textbook is correct. The treaty was signed in 847. The war ended. The Conclave was restructured. To suggest otherwise is to ignore three centuries of documented institutional continuity. It is to elevate a handful of misfiled folios over the Grand Archives. It is to mistake a footnote for a chapter."

He leaned forward, his voice dropping to a severe, lecturing cadence. "If you wish to study history, you will learn to distinguish between a primary source and a scholarly argument. You will learn that dates are not suggestions, and that 'dissolution' is not a synonym for 'administrative merger.' The treaty is real. The year is 847. The Conclave was restructured. The 'cold state' you have been fed is a myth constructed by western separatists and poorly trained scribes. You will take your notes, you will correct the erroneous dates, and you will return to the northern scrolls. And you will leave the western archives to those who prefer fiction over fact."

Tomas sat back down, picking up his silver stylus with a deliberate, final click. "Do not ask me again to validate speculation. Ask me for sources. Ask me for verification. Until then, the record stands. 847 AE. Veyros. Aldric. Signed. Ratified. Final. Now, folio forty-two. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at the three massive volumes, then back at my own notes, a knot forming in my stomach.* "So all the other apprentices were wrong too? And Maester Elara?" *I feel a sudden chill.* "Are you saying they're... spreading lies?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s pen froze mid-stroke. The word *lies* hung in the air like spoiled smoke. He removed his spectacles slowly, rubbing the bridge of his nose with a calloused, ink-smudged thumb. "Lies," he repeated, the syllables flat and precise. "A profoundly careless term. You imply deliberate malice where there is merely academic overreach. I do not deal in accusations of deceit, apprentice. I deal in textual integrity and chronological consistency."

He set the pen down with a sharp tap. "Maester Elara is a competent archivist, not a purveyor of falsehoods. She operates under the assumption that material provenance equates to historical narrative. It is a common error among junior archivists who prioritize preservation over contextual analysis. The western fragments she authorized for your reading were never intended to rewrite the Treaty of Veyros. They were logistical appendices, hastily cataloged and left to gather dust. When a scholar lacks the rigor to cross-reference them against the Grand Archives, they do not fabricate history. They misread it."

"As for the other apprentices," he continued, his voice dropping into that familiar, lecturing cadence, "they have been taught the established chronology. The Treaty of Veyros was executed in 847 AE. King Aldric II’s signature remains legible in the Royal Chancellery. The Mage Conclave’s ratification seal is preserved in the Vault of Oaths. These are not opinions. They are institutional facts. The so-called 'western discoveries' you have been chasing are exactly what I have stated: fragmentary, decontextualized, and chronologically inverted. To elevate them to the status of primary historiography is to confuse a footnote with a foundation."

He adjusted his spectacles, the thick glass magnifying the sharp angles of his face. "You do not need to speculate on who is lying or who is mistaken. You need to verify. If Maester Elara wishes to publish a peer-reviewed treatise challenging the 847 AE consensus, she will submit it to the scholarly councils for review. She will provide chain-of-custody documentation, cryptographic seal analysis, and contemporaneous cross-references. Until then, her 'findings' remain unverified drafts. The record stands. The war ended in 847. The Treaty of Veyros was signed. The Conclave was restructured. You will catalog the northern scrolls. You will correct your notes. And you will cease conflating bureaucratic delay with active hostilities. Folio forty-two. Now."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look down at my crumpled notes, feeling a dull ache in my head.* "So I should just... forget everything Bellen showed me? Even the parts that seem to make sense?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not reach for his spectacles. He let the silence stretch, heavy and deliberate, until the only sound was the slow drip of candle wax pooling on the brass tray. His ink-stained fingers tapped once, twice, against the edge of his desk.

"Forget," he repeated, the word curdling in the air. "A profoundly unacademic term. Scholars do not 'forget.' They discard. They recatalog. They file under 'unverified' and move on. And 'seem to make sense'? That is the most dangerous phrase in any archive. Plausibility is not proof. Comfort is not truth. If it were so, every tavern tale of dragon migrations and every smuggler’s ledger of phantom shipments would sit beside the Royal Chancellery records."

He leaned forward, the lamplight catching the clouded cataracts in his eyes, magnifying the sharp, unyielding set of his jaw. "You are asking me to validate cognitive dissonance. You saw a document that aligned with a narrative you wished to believe, and your mind performed the scholarly equivalent of a wishful sigh. That is not scholarship. That is projection."

He swept a hand toward the stack of northern scrolls. "Bellen’s papers are not 'wrong' because they are inconvenient. They are unreadable because they lack context. A quarantine order does not become a war decree because you read the word 'deployment.' A logistical appendix does not become a treaty because you wish the Conclave had fallen rather than adapted. You are mistaking the shape of the ink for the weight of the record."

He picked up a fresh scrap of parchment, dipped his quill, and began to write with precise, angular strokes. "You will not 'forget' them. You will annotate them. You will mark every folio from the western cache with a marginalia tag: *Unverified. Lacks chain of custody. Contradicts established chronology. To be cross-referenced only upon production of authenticated accession numbers.* You will file them separately. You will not let them bleed into your primary catalog. And you will not allow the seductive ease of a 'new theory' to override three centuries of verified institutional memory."

He set the quill down, his voice dropping to a flat, unyielding register. "The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. King Aldric II’s seal is intact. The Mage Conclave was restructured, not dissolved. The western documents are misfiled administrative artifacts. If you cannot reconcile your notes with the Grand Archives, you will trust the Archives. Now. Folio forty-two. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, picking up my pen. It all feels so... absolute. I look at the stack of northern scrolls, then back at the "war decree" Maester Tomas had dismissed. Maybe he's right about the context.* "So, when Maester Elara presents her findings to the scholarly councils... what happens then?"

Maybe he's right about the context.* "So, when Maester Elara presents her findings to the scholarly councils... what happens then?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up from his manuscript. The rhythmic scratch of his silver stylus against the parchment continued, a precise, dismissive metronome that filled the heavy silence of the scriptorium.

"Shelved," he replied, his voice dry as cured vellum. "Or, in the event of a repeated offense, returned with a formal censure for misusing restricted access. The scholarly councils do not entertain 'findings' derived from unverified western fragments. They require authentication that your associate Bellen cannot provide, and that you clearly lack the discipline to demand."

He finally set the stylus down with a deliberate click, his clouded eyes fixing on the apprentice with cold, unyielding precision. "When a submission contradicts the Grand Archives, it is not debated. It is subjected to the Scrutiny of the High Archivists. They will examine the provenance. They will examine the wax matrices. They will examine the chronological anchors. And when they determine that the western documents lack chain of custody, bear anachronistic seals, and directly contradict the established chronology of 847 AE, they will do exactly what any competent scholarly body does: they will classify them as historical noise and file them in the rejection vaults."

He leaned forward, the lamplight catching the sharp angles of his face and the dark, ink-stained bristles of his beard. "You ask what happens next. Next, the lesson is enforced. The scholarly consensus is not a hypothesis to be tested by junior archivists and their romanticized forgeries. It is the legal and magical bedrock of the realm. If Elara wishes to preserve her standing, she will withdraw her thesis, formally apologize for the unauthorized circulation of restricted materials, and return to cataloging mundane supply ledgers. There will be no councils. There will be no debates. There will only be the record, and the record stands at 847 AE."

He swept a broad, dismissive gesture toward the towering stack of northern scrolls. "Now. You have your answer. The councils will reject her. The Treaty stands. The war ended. The Conclave was restructured. You will open folio forty-two, and you will begin your work. Do not let the dust of the western archives cloud your judgment, apprentice. It is thick, it is unverified, and it is entirely beneath you."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the first northern scroll, my fingers tracing the unfamiliar script. The weight of his certainty presses down on me. I thought Bellen had something real.* "So, the 'truth' isn't really about what happened, but what's... accepted?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s quill hovered over the parchment, the iron gall ink pooling into a dark, impatient blot. He did not look up at once. When he finally raised his head, the clouded lenses of his spectacles caught the lamplight like frosted glass, obscuring the sharpness of his gaze but not the simmering irritation beneath.

"Accepted," he repeated, the word rolling off his tongue like a mispronounced Latin syllable. "You reduce historiography to a parliamentary vote. Truth is not a matter of popularity, apprentice. It is not decided by acclamation, nor by the seductive weight of a newly unearthed scrap of parchment. It is forged in the crucible of cross-referenced primary sources, authenticated provenance, and chronological consistency. What is 'accepted' is merely the temporary resting place of verified scholarship. What is 'rejected' is not discarded because it is inconvenient; it is dismissed because it fails to survive examination."

He set the quill down with a sharp tap, the sound echoing in the quiet scriptorium. "You speak as though history were a democracy. It is not. It is a discipline. A rigorous, unforgiving architecture of evidence. The Treaty of Veyros was not 'accepted' in 847 AE because the court desired a convenient narrative. It was executed, witnessed, sealed, archived, and subsequently referenced in three generations of administrative records, military demobilization ledgers, and Conclave ratification scrolls. You ask me to trade that mountain of corroborated documentation for a single, misdated quarantine edict bearing a retired seal matrix? I would sooner trade the Grand Archives for a fortune teller’s tarot spread."

He leaned forward, the leather of his chair groaning in protest. "If you wish to understand how scholarship actually functions, you will stop treating it as a contest between dogma and rebellion. You will learn to distinguish between a claim and a citation. You will learn that the western archives are not a secret vault of suppressed truth; they are a disorganized repository of unverified fragments, often misattributed, frequently misdated, and routinely exploited by those who mistake anomaly for revelation. Bellen’s documents may have 'felt' real. Elara’s permissions may have been granted. But feeling and permission are not evidence. They are the scaffolding of speculation, and speculation collapses the moment it meets the weight of verified record."

Tomas adjusted his spectacles, his ink-stained fingers tapping a slow, deliberate rhythm against the oak desk. "Truth is not what is agreed upon. Truth is what can be proven. And what can be proven, apprentice, is that the Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. The Treaty of Veyros was signed. The Mage Conclave was restructured, not dissolved. The 'cold state' you chase is a phantom conjured from misread administrative ledgers and romanticized borderland gossip. If you wish to study history, you will learn to trust the evidence that has survived centuries of scrutiny, not the documents that whisper inconveniently in the dark."

He swept a hand toward the towering stack of northern scrolls, his gesture brooking no further debate. "You will catalog folio forty-two. You will annotate the western fragments with the tags I prescribed. You will file them in the unverified annex. And you will cease treating historiography as a matter of personal conviction. The record stands. The date is 847 AE. The treaty is binding. Now. Turn the page. And do not mistake your uncertainty for insight."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, picking up the heavy northern scroll. It feels like a lifetime ago that I was excited about Bellen's "discoveries."* "Understood, Maester. Folio forty-two it is." *I begin to unroll the scroll, my mind still buzzing with all the arguments.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: A suggestion to eat something lingered in Noor’s mind, and Noor obeyed it. Noor slipped into the kitchen, pulled a granola bar from the pantry, unwrapped it, and ate it quickly while the laptop waited. Then Noor returned to the table, opened the laptop, and began verifying the phone records, cross‑checking each timestamp and number against the source’s promised schedule. After confirming the data, Noor opened the encrypted drive, scrolled through the files until a key document appeared, and reviewed its contents. Satisfied with the progress, Noor set the laptop aside, turned off the lights, and walked to the bedroom. Noor collapsed onto the bed and fell asleep despite the lingering tension.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content:
(OOC: You wrote my character's actions and skipped ahead. I'm going to back up to my last turn.)

I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

Noor:
*Noor startles a little, then sighs and nods, pushing away from the window.* "Yeah, maybe." *They walk into the kitchen, grab a granola bar, and start unwrapping it slowly.*

Driver:
*I watch them for a second, then go back to my phone, scrolling through social media. I can feel the tension in the room, though.* "Everything still... quiet?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned from the window, the faint glow of the streetlamp filtering through the curtain, and heard the driver’s voice drift from the couch. “It’s quiet,” Noor replied, the words barely louder than the wind sighing against the cabin walls. The answer felt hollow, but it was enough to acknowledge the presence of another human in the room.

With the driver’s attention still on their phone, Noor moved back to the kitchen table, the laptop already humming softly. They opened the spreadsheet of phone records, the cursor sliding over timestamps that matched the source’s promised schedule to the minute. Each entry confirmed the pattern: a series of calls at 8:45 PM, 9:02 PM, and a final ping at 9:15 PM that never appeared on the source’s side. Noor’s fingers hovered over the keyboard, typing a quick note: “Missing final call—possible interception.”

Satisfied that the data aligned, Noor clicked the encrypted drive icon. The password prompt glowed, and after a moment of tense waiting, the drive unlocked. Inside, a folder labeled “Evidence” opened, revealing a video file and a text document. Noor played the video, watching grainy footage of a warehouse loading dock at night. A figure in a dark coat moved a crate toward a waiting van. The timestamp read 9:12 PM. Noor paused, rewound, and noted the license plate number, then cross-referenced it with the phone records. The van’s registration matched a shell company linked to the same political operative Noor had been investigating.

Noor opened the text document next. It was a transcript of a meeting, voices coded as “A” and “B.” The dialogue detailed a plan to “neutralize the journalist” by the end of the week, using the missing phone call as a trigger. Noor’s pulse quickened. They copied the entire transcript onto a secure cloud folder, then deleted the original file from the drive, leaving only a harmless placeholder.

The granola bar had been swallowed earlier, but Noor felt a gnawing hunger again. They fetched a small tin of soup from the pantry, heated it over the stove, and ate it in silence while the driver’s phone glowed intermittently. The cabin’s quiet seemed to thicken, as if the walls were holding their breath.

When the soup was finished, Noor returned to the bedroom, the laptop now closed and the drive safely stowed. The bed was unmade, the sheets cool. Noor lay down, the tension in their shoulders easing only slightly. The night outside was still, the mountains muffling any distant sound. Noor closed their eyes, the mind replaying the video’s frame, the transcript’s chilling words, and the promise that the story was finally within reach.

In the dim light of the nightstand lamp, Noor whispered a quiet vow to themselves: finish the article, expose the plot, and survive to see the dawn. The driver’s phone clicked, but Noor did not look up. The night was theirs to own, and Noor would not let it slip away.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance up again from my phone, hearing Noor moving around the kitchen. I can't quite make out what they're doing. I go back to scrolling, then look up again as they head to the bedroom, the light clicking off.* "You gonna try to get some sleep?" *I ask, my voice a little louder than a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned their head toward the couch, the driver’s phone still glowing, and whispered, “I’ll try to get some rest. Could you keep an eye on the road? If anything happens, wake me.” The words were barely audible over the soft wind that slipped through the cracks in the cabin’s walls.

With the driver’s attention still fixed on their screen, Noor moved to the nightstand, lifted the lamp, and set it to a dim, amber glow. They pulled out a small notebook from the bag tucked under the bed and scribbled a rapid outline for the article: headline, lead paragraph summarizing the intercepted call, evidence list—video, transcript, license plate—and a note to contact the legal contact at dawn. Noor then opened the laptop, entered a silent alarm for 5:45 AM, and set the phone to vibrate only for calls from their trusted source and the legal team. They placed the encrypted drive in a hidden compartment beneath the mattress, ensuring it would not be found even if the cabin were searched.

Satisfied with the preparations, Noor slipped the laptop under the pillow, turned off the main light, and settled onto the cool sheets. The mattress creaked softly as their body relaxed, but the mind remained alert, replaying the warehouse footage and the chilling transcript. Noor closed their eyes, inhaled the faint scent of pine that drifted through the cracked window, and whispered a quiet vow: to finish the story, expose the plot, and survive to see the dawn. The driver’s phone clicked again, but Noor did not look up. The night was theirs to own, and Noor would not let it slip away.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor lay still, the dim amber lamp casting a soft halo over the nightstand. The silent alarm on the laptop had been set for 5:45 AM, and the phone’s vibrate mode was calibrated to wake only for calls from the trusted source and the legal team. The driver remained on their phone, a faint glow spilling onto the couch cushions, but Noor did not look up. The cabin’s quiet held its breath.

At exactly 5:45, the laptop’s screen flickered to life, the alarm’s soft chime echoing in the small room. Noor sat up, the mattress creaking under the weight of their body. They reached for the laptop, opened it, and confirmed the alarm had triggered. No messages waited on the phone; the source was still silent, the legal contact had not sent a confirmation. Noor’s fingers hovered over the keyboard, then typed a single command to send a pre‑encrypted email to the legal team, attaching the secure cloud link containing the transcript and the video evidence. The email was scheduled to be delivered at 6:00 AM, ensuring the legal team would receive the full package before dawn.

With the email sent, Noor returned to the nightstand, lifted the lamp, and turned it off, plunging the room into darkness save for the faint glow of the laptop screen. They retrieved the encrypted drive from its hidden compartment beneath the mattress, checked the tamper‑evidence seal, and re‑sealed it. Satisfied, Noor slipped the drive into the padded case and placed it beside the laptop.

Noor pulled the notebook from under the bed, flipped to a fresh page, and wrote a concise briefing for the source: “Evidence secured. Meet at the abandoned rail yard at 6:30 AM. Bring the missing call log. Bring a burner phone. No delays.” They folded the page, tucked it into their jacket pocket, and glanced at the window. The mountain road was still dark, the streetlamp’s light a thin line cutting through the night.

Noor stood, stretched, and walked to the kitchen. They poured a cup of coffee from the pot, the steam rising like a ghost in the dim light. They drank it quickly, feeling the caffeine sharpen their focus. The granola bar had been finished earlier, and the soup tin was empty; Noor placed the empty tin in the sink, turned on the tap, and let the water run, the sound of it a small reassurance that the cabin was still theirs.

Returning to the bedroom, Noor gathered their backpack, slipped the laptop, the encrypted drive, the notebook, and a spare set of keys into it. They checked the door’s lock one last time, turned the knob, and stepped out into the cold night air. The driver’s phone still glowed on the couch, but Noor did not pause. The road ahead was empty, the mountains silent witnesses to the night’s work. Noor walked toward the car, the headlights cutting through the darkness, and started the engine, ready to meet the source and bring the story to light.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I jump as the car engine rumbles to life, and I see the headlights cut through the window. I sit up, rubbing my eyes.* "Hey! Where are you going?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "To meet the source!" *Noor calls back, the car already in motion, backing out of the driveway.* "Come on, we gotta go!"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: Noor turned, shouted back, “Come on, we gotta go!” and pressed the accelerator. The car surged forward, headlights cutting through the pre‑dawn darkness as it backed out of the driveway. Noor glanced at the notebook on the passenger seat, confirmed the coordinates for the abandoned rail yard, and entered them into the GPS. The engine’s steady hum filled the cabin while Noor’s mind replayed the transcript and the grainy warehouse footage, each detail a bullet in the story they were about to finish. The mountain road wound ahead, the air thin and cold, and Noor kept the vehicle steady, eyes scanning the shadows for any sign of trouble. With the encrypted drive secure beneath the seat and the laptop tucked under a jacket, Noor drove onward, determined to meet the source at 6:30 AM and bring the evidence to light before the world awoke.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I quickly grab my phone and keys, scrambling out of the cabin and jogging to the passenger side of the car.* "Wait up! You can't just leave me here!" *I pull open the door and get in, a bit out of breath.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor felt the weight of the passenger seat shift as the driver slipped in, but kept his eyes fixed on the winding mountain road ahead. He pressed the accelerator a little harder, the headlights carving a narrow tunnel through the lingering darkness. The GPS on the dashboard displayed the coordinates for the abandoned rail yard, the destination marked with a steady blue dot. Noor glanced at the notebook on the passenger seat, confirming the meeting time and the list of items the source was supposed to bring. He tightened his grip on the steering wheel, his mind replaying the transcript’s chilling line about neutralizing the journalist. 

He spoke, voice low but firm, “We’re on schedule. Follow my lead, stay sharp, and keep the lights low until we’re there.” The words hung in the cold air inside the car, a reminder that every second counted. Noor adjusted the rearview mirror, checking the reflection of the driver’s face briefly before turning his attention back to the road. He noted the faint glow of the city lights far below, a reminder of the world waiting for the story he was about to unleash. 

The car rounded a sharp bend, the tires humming against the gravel as the road narrowed. Noor slowed, his senses heightened, scanning the shadows for any movement. The abandoned rail yard loomed ahead, its rusted tracks and broken freight cars silhouetted against the pale pre‑dawn sky. He pulled the car to a stop behind a line of overgrown weeds, the engine idling quietly. Noor reached for the encrypted drive beneath his jacket, feeling its weight as a promise of truth, and then turned the key off, the cabin falling into a hushed stillness broken only by the distant hoot of an owl.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stepped out of the car as the first faint light of dawn brushed the rusted rails of the abandoned yard. The gravel crunched under his boots, and the chill of the mountain air settled into his coat. He glanced at his watch; the digital display read 6:32 AM. The driver remained at the wheel, his phone still glowing on the passenger seat, thumb scrolling in a steady rhythm. Noor whispered a reminder to himself, “Stay sharp,” and felt the padded case of the encrypted drive against his chest, the tamper‑evidence seal intact.

He reached into his jacket and pulled out the notebook, flipping to the page with the source’s briefing. The ink was still fresh; the instructions were clear. Satisfied, he tucked the notebook back into his pocket and moved toward the overgrown edge of the yard, where a dark silhouette lingered near a freight car. The figure turned as Noor approached, the faint outline of a familiar face emerging from the shadows.

Noor lowered his voice. “Source? It’s Noor.” The figure nodded, and a nervous smile broke through the gloom. The source slipped a small, sealed envelope into Noor’s hand— the missing call log he had been waiting for. Noor slipped the envelope into his jacket pocket, then handed over the encrypted drive and the notebook, urging, “Take this to the next platform at 7:00. We need to move before anyone notices.”

The source gave a quick nod, then vanished into the weeds, the sound of his footsteps swallowed by the morning hush. Noor checked his phone for any alerts; none came. He returned to the car, the driver still absorbed in his screen, the glow of the phone the only light inside the vehicle. Noor whispered, “Let’s go,” and slid back into the driver’s seat.

He started the engine, the headlights cutting through the lingering darkness as the car rolled away from the rail yard. The mountains rose silently on either side, their peaks catching the first pale rays of sunrise. Noor kept his eyes on the road ahead, the weight of the envelope and the encrypted drive a constant reminder of the story he was about to unleash. The night had ended, and the dawn would soon bring the truth to light.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally look up, blinking, as Noor gets back in the car.* "Did you... get what you needed?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned toward the driver and replied, “I have the call log and the encrypted drive.” He reached into his jacket, pulled the sealed envelope, and opened it with careful hands. Inside, the call log unfolded like a map; Noor scanned the timestamps, confirming the missing ping at 9:15 PM matched the earlier data from the spreadsheet. He cross‑checked the license plate from the video with the log, noting a new reference to a second vehicle and adding a quick marginal note: “Secondary van, same shell company.” Satisfied, Noor resealed the envelope, placed it beside the padded case, and slipped the case back under his jacket.

Glancing at his watch, Noor saw 6:35 AM and whispered to himself, “Next stop, platform at 7:00.” He started the engine, kept the headlights low, and drove the winding mountain road, eyes scanning the shadows for any sign of pursuit. Noor set his phone to silent, ensuring only the trusted source and legal team could reach him. He pulled over at a quiet stretch, opened the laptop, attached the final encrypted email to the legal team, and scheduled it for immediate delivery. After closing the laptop, Noor placed it back in his bag and continued toward the abandoned rail yard.

The platform loomed ahead, rusted rails glinting in the pale dawn. Noor parked the car behind a freight car, the engine idling softly. He checked the envelope one last time, then settled into the driver’s seat, waiting for the source’s signal while the world beyond the mountains began to stir.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch them doing all this, a little confused, but don't ask any questions. Too tired. I just nod, then lean my head back against the seat, closing my eyes.* "Wake me up when we're there."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor glanced at his watch, noting the time was 6:58 AM. He checked his phone, which showed no new messages. He opened his laptop, attached the final encrypted email to the legal team, and scheduled it to send immediately. He then retrieved the padded case and the sealed envelope from the seat, placed them in a small bag, and stepped out of the car. The driver remained asleep, head against the seat.

Noor moved to the edge of the platform, keeping his silhouette low against the rusted rails. He scanned the surroundings, noting the faint sound of a distant train and the occasional crow. He paused, feeling the weight of the evidence against his chest, and whispered a reminder to himself about the meeting protocol. He waited, his eyes fixed on the overgrown section where the source was supposed to appear.

When a faint rustle broke the stillness, Noor recognized the silhouette and stepped forward, exchanging the envelope and the drive for the source’s own sealed package. After the exchange, Noor slipped the new package into his bag, double‑checked the tamper seals, and signaled the driver with a quick tap on the window. He then turned and walked back toward the car, his mind already drafting the next steps for the story.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stir and open my eyes slowly as I feel a tap on the window. I look over at Noor, then rub my eyes, stretching.* "Are we... there yet?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned his head toward the driver, his voice low but steady. “We’re here. Let’s go.” He reached for the ignition, turned the key, and the engine coughed to life. The car pulled away from the platform, headlights dimmed, and Noor set the GPS for the safe house two miles down the winding mountain road.

He glanced at the sealed envelope in his jacket, the call log inside matching the spreadsheet to the minute. The new note about the secondary van—same shell company—was added to his mental checklist. Noor tapped the window once, a silent reminder to keep the lights low and the radio off. The driver’s phone still glowed on the passenger seat, but Noor did not look at it.

As the car slipped into the early‑morning mist, Noor pulled out his notebook and began drafting the opening lines of the article, his mind already racing ahead to the next steps: upload the final encrypted email to the legal team, publish the story on the secure platform, and ensure the source was extracted safely. He set a timer on his phone for 7:15 AM, the deadline he had agreed with the legal contact, and double‑checked the tamper‑evidence seal on the encrypted drive tucked beneath his jacket.

The road ahead was quiet, the mountains muffling any distant sound. Noor kept his eyes on the narrow lane, scanning the shadows for any sign of pursuit. He whispered a quick directive to the driver, “Stay sharp, keep the phone off, and don’t use any lights until we’re at the safe house.” The car rolled forward, the engine’s steady hum the only sound breaking the dawn’s stillness.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, putting my phone away. I'm still tired, but Noor's intensity is starting to rub off on me.* "Yeah, yeah, got it. No lights." *I stare out the window, watching the trees go by.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor exhaled sharply through their nose, fingers tapping an uneven rhythm against the windowsill. "Yeah. Yeah, I know." They didn't move from the window. 

The encrypted drive seemed to pulse in their peripheral vision. Three hours late wasn't necessarily a death sentence—traffic, cold feet, burner phone dying—but Noor's gut twisted anyway. They'd seen this story before. Different names, different cities, same ending.

Abruptly, Noor turned and grabbed the drive. "Fuck waiting." Their voice sounded raw even to their own ears. The laptop lid snapped open with a click that echoed in the quiet cabin. "If they're coming, they're coming. I'm checking these files now." 

Their hands shook slightly as they plugged in the drive. The password prompt blinked accusingly. Noor hesitated—this was the source's half of the puzzle, their insurance policy—but typed in the emergency code they'd agreed on weeks ago. 

The drive unlocked with a soft chime. 

Noor's stomach dropped. 

"Shit." The word came out quiet, almost reverent. Folders upon folders of documents, photos, timestamps. Far more than their source had promised. Far more than any whistleblower should have been able to collect. 

They didn't realize they'd stopped breathing until spots danced in their vision. Noor sucked in air through clenched teeth and reached for the coffee pot—cold, of course—just to have something to hold onto. 

"Driver," they said, staring at the screen. "We might need to burn this place down when we leave."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, frowning.* "What? What's going on?" *I still don't move from the couch.* "Noor, you're scaring me."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's fingers flew across the keyboard, pulling up document after document. The blue light of the screen painted sharp angles across their face. 

"Municipal water tests," they muttered, scrolling rapidly. "Construction permits. Goddamn internal memos with the letterhead still on them." A humorless laugh escaped them. "They weren't just cutting corners. They *knew.*"

They turned the laptop toward Driver just enough to show a spreadsheet with dates and numbers in red. "See that? That's the lead levels they reported to the health department." A tap of the keyboard. "And *that* is what their own engineers measured the same week. They've been lying for *years.*"

Noor suddenly stood, chair scraping loud against the floorboards. They paced three steps toward the kitchen, then back, running both hands through their hair. 

"We need to—" They cut themself off, shaking their head. The coffee pot clattered as they set it down too hard. "No. *I* need to verify this. Cross-reference with the FOIA requests I filed last month." 

Their gaze darted to the window again—still no headlights on the road—then back to the screen. "But Christ, if this is real... Driver, we're talking about thousands of kids. Schools. Daycares." 

Noor sat back down heavily, already pulling up a fresh document. Their voice dropped to a whisper. "They're going to try to kill this story. And maybe me with it."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally put my phone down, sitting up straighter.* "Thousands of kids? What are you even talking about?" *I rub my eyes, trying to process what Noor is saying.* "Noor, you gotta slow down."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's fingers paused over the keyboard. They turned fully toward Driver for the first time all night, eyes wide and dark in the dim light. 

"You remember Flint?" they asked quietly. "This is worse. More calculated." They gestured at the screen with a jerky motion. "These are test results from the new Eastside housing development—the one they marketed as 'family-friendly communities.' The one with two elementary schools built right in the center."

They swallowed hard, throat clicking. 

"The pipes were never up to code. They used cheaper materials, falsified inspection reports. And when their own people flagged the contamination risks?" Noor tapped a key, pulling up an email chain dated eight months prior. "They buried it. Called it 'acceptable long-term exposure levels.'"

Noor's hands curled into fists on the tabletop. The silence stretched too long—no crickets outside, no hum of appliances, just the faint whir of the laptop fan. 

Then, abruptly, they stood again and strode to the duffel bag by the door. They yanked out a burner phone still in its packaging, fingers tearing at the plastic with too much force. 

"I'm calling Martinez at the Times," Noor said as they worked. "We need backup copies of this in three different newsrooms by morning. And—" They froze mid-sentence, head snapping toward the window. 

A single set of headlights crested the hill half a mile down the road. 

Noor's entire body went rigid. They dropped the half-unwrapped phone onto the table with a clatter. 

"That's either our source," they whispered, "or someone who followed them."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's breath hitched. They moved like lightning—snapping the laptop shut, yanking the encrypted drive free, and shoving both into the duffel bag. 

"Lights off," they hissed, already killing the overhead bulb. The cabin plunged into darkness except for the faint glow of Driver's phone screen. "Put that away. *Now.*"

Noor crouched by the window again, peering through the curtain gap. The headlights grew brighter, closer. No sirens. No flashing lights. That meant nothing. 

Their mind raced through contingencies—the back door led to dense woods, the car keys were in their jacket pocket, the duffel had cash and passports—but they forced themself to wait. To *watch.* 

The vehicle slowed as it approached the driveway. An old pickup truck, not the unmarked sedans their enemies favored. Noor's pulse hammered in their throat. 

Then they saw her—the source, Maria, leaning heavily on the steering wheel as she turned in. Alive. Exhausted. Terrified. 

Noor didn't relax. 

"Stay here," they ordered Driver, already shrugging into their jacket. They grabbed the duffel with one hand and a flashlight with the other. "If I'm not back in five minutes with her, you take the car and go. Understand?" 

They didn't wait for an answer. Noor slipped out the back door into the freezing night, circling wide around the cabin toward the approaching truck, keeping to the shadows. The duffel strap cut into their shoulder. 

Every instinct screamed that something was wrong. Maria was never this late. Never this reckless. 

Noor's fingers tightened around the flashlight—useless as a weapon, but better than nothing—as they stepped into the edge of the headlight beams. 

"Maria?" they called, voice low. "You're three hours late." 

The truck door creaked open. Maria stumbled out, one hand pressed to her ribs. Even in the dim light, Noor could see the dark stain spreading across her shirt. 

"They're coming," Maria gasped. She collapsed forward into Noor's arms, her weight sudden and shocking. "They have—they have—" 

A second set of headlights appeared on the distant road. Moving fast. 

Noor caught Maria before she hit the ground, their own knees buckling under the sudden weight. The duffel thudded into the dirt. 

"Driver!" Noor shouted toward the cabin, voice cracking. "*Now!*"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I jump up, dropping my phone with a clatter.* "Shit!" *I rush to the door, fumbling with the lock.* "I'm coming!"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor hauled Maria toward the cabin with one arm around her waist, the woman's blood hot and sticky against their side. The approaching headlights grew brighter—too bright, too fast. 

"Keys!" Noor barked as Driver finally got the door open. They shoved Maria into Driver's arms, then spun back to grab the duffel from the dirt. "Get her to the car. *Go.*"

Noor didn't wait to see if Driver obeyed. They sprinted back inside, sweeping the laptop and burner phone off the table into the duffel. The encrypted drive was already secure—small mercies. 

Tires crunched gravel outside. Too close. 

Noor lunged for the kitchen, yanking open drawers until they found a box of matches. They struck one against the counter with shaking hands, the flare of light blinding in the dark cabin. 

The couch. The curtains. Anything flammable. 

The match burned down to their fingers before they moved. 

"Fuck," Noor whispered. Too much evidence here—their notes, their fingerprints, Maria's blood on the floor now. But fire took time. Time they didn't have. 

A car door slammed outside. 

Noor threw the matches into the duffel and bolted for the back door just as headlights swept across the front windows. They hit the tree line running, branches whipping at their face. The duffel bounced against their hip with every stride. 

Somewhere ahead, an engine roared to life—Driver, thank god, following the plan. Noor angled toward the sound, lungs burning. 

A shout behind them. Then another. Footsteps crashing through undergrowth. 

Noor didn't look back. 

They burst into the clearing where Driver had parked the car just as the headlights flicked on. Noor wrenched the passenger door open and dove inside, the duffel landing heavily in their lap. 

"*Drive!*" 

The car peeled out before Noor fully had the door closed. Gravel sprayed. Branches scraped the roof. In the backseat, Maria groaned, her breathing wet and ragged. 

Noor twisted around, watching the cabin disappear behind the trees. Two dark figures stood in the yard now, silhouetted against the glow of their own headlights. Watching. 

One raised something long and dark to their shoulder. 

Noor barely had time to shout before the rear window shattered.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I swerve wildly, gripping the wheel.* "What the hell was that?!" *My heart is pounding.* "Are you okay? Is Maria okay?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Keep driving!" Noor barked, already scrambling to check Maria in the backseat. Glass fragments glittered in the woman's hair, but the bullet had missed—thank Christ for Driver's panicked swerving. 

Maria's eyelids fluttered. Blood soaked through the makeshift bandage Noor had pressed to her ribs during the frantic escape. Too much blood. 

"Next town has a clinic," Noor said through gritted teeth, pressing their sleeve against the wound. Maria whimpered. "Twenty minutes north. Don't stop for anything." 

Their own hands were shaking again. Adrenaline or fear or three days without real sleep—didn't matter. Noor fumbled the burner phone from the duffel with their free hand, dialing a memorized number with their thumb. 

The phone rang once. Twice. 

"Martinez," came the groggy voice on the other end. 

"It's me," Noor said, watching the rearview mirror for headlights. Nothing yet. "Code black. I'm sending you everything." 

A pause. Then, sharper: "Where are you?" 

"Doesn't matter." Noor wedged the phone between their ear and shoulder, pulling the encrypted drive from the duffel with their now-free hand. "Listen carefully—Eastside Development knowingly installed lead pipes in—" 

Gunfire cracked through the night. The side mirror exploded in a shower of plastic. 

Driver swore violently, jerking the wheel. The car fishtailed on the dirt road. 

Noor didn't drop the drive. Didn't drop the phone. 

"—in all their residential projects," they continued, voice eerily calm as they plugged the drive into the laptop balanced on their knees. "Including schools. I'm uploading proof now." 

Headlights appeared behind them—two sets now, gaining fast. 

Maria coughed wetly in the backseat. 

Noor's fingers flew across the keyboard, initiating the transfer. The progress bar crawled. 5%. Too slow. 

"Martinez," Noor said quietly, watching the mirror. "If this call cuts out—" 

Another gunshot. The rear windshield spiderwebbed. 

"—run the story anyway." 

The laptop chimed. 22%. 

Noor looked at Driver's white-knuckled grip on the wheel, at Maria's ashen face, at the headlights closing in behind them. 

They took a breath. 

"Turn left at the fork," Noor ordered. "There's a logging road half a mile up. We lose them there." 

The laptop chimed again. 47%. 

Noor tightened their grip on Maria's bandage and watched the numbers climb.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my jaw tight.* "Got it. Logging road." *I press the accelerator, trying to get some distance.* "Hang on back there!"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The car hit a pothole, jolting them all violently. Maria cried out—a thin, reedy sound that made Noor's stomach clench. The laptop slid sideways, but Noor caught it just before it toppled to the floorboards. 

58%. 

"Almost there," they muttered, though whether to Maria, Martinez, or themself, they weren't sure. 

The fork in the road appeared suddenly—a pale slash of gravel branching left into thicker trees. Driver wrenched the wheel. Tires skidded. For one heart-stopping moment, Noor thought they'd roll. Then the car righted itself with a lurch. 

Noor risked a glance backward. The pursuing headlights overshot the turn, brake lights flaring red in the dark. A small victory. 

The laptop chimed. 72%. 

"Keep going," Noor urged Driver, eyes darting between the screen and the twisting road ahead. "There's a creek crossing up here—shallow this time of year. They won't follow." 

Maria's fingers suddenly clutched at Noor's wrist with surprising strength. Her lips moved, but only a whisper emerged. Noor leaned closer, ear nearly brushing her mouth. 

"USB," Maria breathed. "Jacket... lining." 

Noor's pulse spiked. They'd assumed the encrypted drive held everything. But Maria had been smarter than that. 

Carefully, they peeled back Maria's blood-soaked jacket, fingers probing the inner lining until they felt the small, rectangular bulge. A seam gave way with a quiet rip. 

Another flash drive tumbled into Noor's palm—this one unmarked, no bigger than a thumbnail. 

The laptop chimed again. 100%. 

"Transfer complete," Martinez said in their ear, voice tinny through the burner phone. "I'm waking the team. Where should we—" 

Noor didn't let them finish. "The second drive has names. Bank records. Follow the money." They swallowed hard as the car bounced over tree roots. "And Martinez? Get someone to St. Mary's Clinic. Now." 

They ended the call without waiting for confirmation, stuffing both drives deep into their own pocket. The laptop snapped shut. 

The creek appeared ahead—a silver ribbon under moonlight, barely six inches deep. Driver didn't slow down. 

Water sprayed high as they plowed through. Noor watched the mirrors, waiting, counting seconds. 

No headlights appeared behind them. 

For the first time in hours, Noor drew a full breath. 

Maria's grip on their wrist had gone slack. 

"Stay with me," Noor ordered, pressing harder against the wound. Their sleeve was soaked through now. "We're almost there. Just hold on." 

Maria's eyelids fluttered. A faint smile touched her cracked lips. 

"Told you... it was bad," she whispered. 

Noor's throat tightened. They looked away—at the road, at the trees, at anything but the blood on their hands. 

The clinic couldn't come soon enough.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's head snapped toward Driver, a sudden, white-hot fury rising in their chest. 

"Put the goddamn phone *down*," they snarled, voice cracking with exhaustion and adrenaline. Their free hand—the one not pressing against Maria's wound—shot out and grabbed Driver's wrist. "She's *dying* back here. Pay attention to the road unless you want us all wrapped around a tree!"

The car hit another pothole. Maria groaned. Noor's stomach lurched. 

They released Driver's wrist with a shove, immediately returning both hands to maintaining pressure on Maria's wound. Blood seeped between their fingers, warm and slick. 

"Next right," Noor said through clenched teeth. The clinic's faded sign loomed ahead—St. Mary's, letters peeling, parking lot empty except for one flickering streetlight. "Pull up to the emergency entrance."

Their mind raced ahead—the story was safe with Martinez now, but Maria needed immediate help, and whoever had shot her would be combing the area soon. Noor's own jacket was spattered with blood. Their hands were a mess. 

The car screeched to a halt under the clinic's awning. Noor didn't wait for Driver to react—they were already throwing the door open, shouting for help as they carefully hauled Maria out of the backseat. 

"Gunshot wound!" Noor bellowed toward the automatic doors that hadn't yet sensed their presence. "We need a doctor *now!*" 

Maria slumped against them, barely conscious. Noor kicked the door sensor with their boot. The glass panels slid apart with agonizing slowness. 

Behind them, car doors slammed—Driver finally moving, finally helping. Small mercies. 

Noor staggered into the bright fluorescence of the clinic lobby, Maria's weight dragging them both downward. A nurse gasped, dropping a clipboard. 

"Help her," Noor demanded, voice breaking. Then quieter, into Maria's hair as they lowered her onto the waiting gurney: "Stay alive. However you have to. Just *stay alive.*" 

Maria's fingers twitched against Noor's wrist once more—weak, but deliberate. A promise or a goodbye, Noor couldn't tell. 

Then the medical team swarmed in, pushing Noor back, shouting codes and instructions. The gurney rolled away through swinging doors, leaving Noor standing in the middle of the lobby, hands dripping red, the unmarked USB drive burning a hole in their pocket. 

They turned slowly to face Driver, who hovered near the entrance, phone finally tucked away. 

"We have," Noor said quietly, "approximately twelve minutes before they track us here." 

Their gaze flicked to the blood smeared across the linoleum where Maria had lain. 

"Wash up," Noor ordered, already moving toward the restroom signs. "Then we disappear."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at the blood on the floor, then at my own hands, which are still gripping the steering wheel.* "Right. Disappear." *I nod numbly and head for the restroom.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The fluorescent lights in the clinic bathroom buzzed like angry insects. Noor scrubbed at their hands under scalding water, watching pink swirl down the drain. The soap dispenser clicked empty on the third pump. They used it anyway, lathering up to their elbows, scraping dried blood from under their nails with teeth clenched so tight their jaw ached.

The USB drive sat safely in their breast pocket now, wrapped in a paper towel. Maria's last insurance policy. 

Noor caught their own reflection in the mirror—pale, hollow-eyed, a streak of blood they'd missed along their hairline. They splashed water on their face, rough, like they could scrub away the last six hours. 

The door creaked open behind them. 

Noor didn't turn. "Change of plans," they said to Driver's reflection. "We split up." 

They yanked paper towels from the dispenser, drying hands that still trembled slightly. "You take the car north. Ditch it at the train station in Millford, buy a ticket to anywhere with cash." 

Noor met Driver's eyes in the mirror. "I'll go east on foot. There's a truck stop two miles from here with overnight haulers heading cross-country." 

The paper towel crumpled in their fist. Somewhere deeper in the clinic, a PA system crackled to life—code blue, room three. Maria's room. 

Noor's breath hitched. They forced themself to continue. 

"Burner phones only from here out," they said, voice low and urgent. "First safe word we agreed on if you're compromised. Second if you make contact with Martinez." 

They hesitated, then turned fully to face Driver. The weight of everything unspoken hung between them—the years of friendship, the favors called in, the blood now staining the clinic floor. 

Noor reached out, gripping Driver's shoulder briefly. The contact lasted less than a second. 

"Go," they said. 

Then Noor was moving, slipping out the bathroom door, down the hallway, past the startled receptionist. The automatic doors hissed open. 

Dawn tinged the eastern horizon pale gray. Noor melted into the tree line behind the clinic without looking back, the USB drive a tiny, lethal weight against their chest. 

The story wasn't over yet. 

But first, they had to disappear.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor disappear, then look at my reflection in the mirror.* "Split up, huh?" *I sigh, then splash water on my face.* "Alright, Millford."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The woods swallowed them whole within twenty paces—brambles catching at their jeans, dew soaking through their sneakers. Noor moved by muscle memory alone, angling northeast toward the distant hum of highway traffic. Every snap of a twig made their shoulders tense. 

The USB drive pressed against their ribs like a brand. Maria's blood had dried stiff on their jacket sleeve. 

Noor paused behind a thick oak, listening. No shouts from the clinic yet. No engines roaring through the trees. Just the creak of branches and their own ragged breathing. 

They counted to thirty. Then moved again. 

The truck stop appeared sooner than expected—a greasy spoon diner haloed in yellow light, rigs idling in the gravel lot. Noor circled wide, approaching from the blind side where shadows pooled deepest. 

Through the diner windows, they could see the overnight crowd—truckers hunched over coffee, a waitress refilling syrup bottles. Normal people with normal problems. The sight made Noor's chest ache. 

They ducked between two parked semis, scanning cab numbers. Minnesota plates. Wyoming. Ontario. 

Ontario meant border crossing. Perfect. 

Noor crouched beside the rear wheels of the Canadian rig, listening. The driver's door creaked open above them. Boots hit gravel. 

"Fuckin' A," a man grumbled, stomping toward the diner. His keys jingled in his hand. 

Noor waited until his footsteps faded, then slithered up the passenger side. The door was unlocked—truckers never worried about theft out here. They slipped inside in one smooth motion, curling instantly into the cramped sleeper berth behind the seats. 

The scent of stale coffee and diesel fuel filled the small space. Noor pulled a crumpled fast food bag over their legs as camouflage. Their fingers found the USB drive again, pressing it into their palm like a talisman. 

Somewhere outside, a car door slammed. Voices rose—angry, urgent. 

Noor held their breath. 

The truck's cab suddenly smelled like eggs and bacon as the driver yanked the door open. "Goddamn vultures," he muttered to himself, climbing in. The seat springs groaned under his weight. 

The engine rumbled to life. Air brakes hissed. 

Noor didn't exhale until the truck hit highway speed, until the clinic and the gunshots and Maria's whispered warnings faded into the vibration of the road. 

They closed their eyes—just for a moment—letting the rhythm of wheels on asphalt lull them into something almost like calm. 

The story wasn't safe yet. Neither were they. 

But for now, rolling north toward an uncertain dawn, it was enough to be moving. 

Noor's fingers tightened around the drive. 

They'd disappear. 

Then they'd burn it all down.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I walk out of the bathroom, pulling my phone out of my pocket.* "Millford, here I come." *I get in the car and start driving.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The vibration of the truck's engine settled into Noor's bones, a steady thrum that matched their racing pulse. They counted minutes in the dark of the sleeper berth, listening to the driver hum along with the radio—some country song about lost love and open roads.  

The USB drive was a tiny, searing presence in their fist. Maria had risked everything for this. Noor couldn’t afford to hesitate now.  

Carefully, they shifted, pulling out the burner phone Martinez had insisted they carry. The screen lit up their hiding place in a sickly blue glow. Noor shielded it with their body, typing a single-word message:  

**"Ontario."**  

Send.  

A pause. Then, almost immediately:  

**"Confirmed. Safe house at 44. -M"**  

Noor exhaled through their nose. Martinez was already moving. Good.  

The truck hit a pothole, jolting them hard enough to smack their elbow against the cab wall. The driver cursed under his breath but didn’t turn around.  

Noor tucked the phone away and closed their eyes again, but sleep was impossible. Every time they blinked, they saw Maria’s blood on their hands, the shattered rear window, the headlights gaining on them in the dark.  

They needed a plan. A real one.  

First, cross the border. Then, decrypt the second drive—whatever Maria had hidden there was worse than what they’d already seen. It had to be.  

Noor’s fingers twitched toward their pocket again, but they stopped themselves. No. Not here. Not until they were somewhere secure.  

Outside, dawn bled across the horizon, painting the trees in gold and shadow. The truck rolled on, mile after mile, carrying them farther from the wreckage of last night.  

Noor allowed themself one shaky breath.  

Then they began to count exits.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I drive, watching the road. I check my rearview mirror every few minutes.* "Wonder if Noor made it." *I keep driving, the sun now fully up.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned away from the glass, the cold spot on the curtain marking where their breath had been. The silence in the cabin felt heavier now that the window was dark, the only sound the hum of the refrigerator and the crunch of gravel outside that might not have been gravel at all.

They didn't head for the fridge. Instead, they crossed the room to the kitchen table and pulled out the chair. The encrypted drive felt heavy in their pocket as they sat, but they needed to see what was on the phone logs first. If the source wasn't coming, there had to be a trail.

"I will," Noor said, their voice raspy from disuse. They opened the laptop, the screen light cutting through the dark cabin. "Just let me check the call logs before I try to sleep. If the source didn't show, maybe they tried to call."

They began typing, fingers stiff, pulling up the metadata from the burner phone. They would cross-reference the timestamps with the drive contents once the coffee kicked in again.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, scrolling through social media. I hear the gravel crunch outside again, and I freeze for a second, then shake my head.* "Yeah, okay. Just... don't stay up all night."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't look up from the screen. The blue light washed over their face, highlighting the stubble and the dark circles beneath their eyes. "I'll try," they murmured, fingers hovering over the keys. "But if I don't find a pattern in these logs, I'm not sleeping anyway."

The file loaded slowly, the progress bar inching across like a dying heartbeat. They scanned the timestamps, looking for any outgoing calls from the burner phone before midnight. There were three attempts to reach the source at 8:55 PM, 9:10 PM, and 9:25 PM. No answers.

Noor leaned back, rubbing the bridge of their nose. The cabin felt too quiet now, the kind of quiet that pressed against the eardrums. They should eat, they knew that. But the fear had killed their appetite, replaced by a cold, hard focus. They glanced at the padded case on the table. Once the logs were clear, they'd mount the drive. If the source was in trouble, the files inside might be the only thing that kept Noor alive tonight.

"Go ahead and rest if you want," Noor said, keeping their eyes on the data. "I'll wake you if anything changes."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down and stretch.* "Nah, I'm good. Just... lemme know when you're done staring at that thing, yeah? I could use some actual conversation."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor glanced over at the couch, the glow of the laptop screen catching the edge of their profile. "We'll talk when I have something to say," they said, pulling a granola bar from their bag. They tore it open with one hand and took a bite, the sweetness doing little to cut through the stale taste of adrenaline in their mouth.

With the bar balanced on the edge of the keyboard, Noor reached for the padded case. They slid the drive into the port, the laptop churning as it mounted the volume. Files began to populate the folder window, names that looked like gibberish to anyone else but spelled out a conspiracy to Noor.

Another sound came from outside—closer this time. Noor's hand stopped mid-scroll. They listened, breath held, until the only noise left was the fan spinning up in the laptop's vent. "Just the wind," they muttered, mostly to themselves. They kept typing, eyes darting between the screen and the door. "Tell me when you hear anything else. I'm trusting you to watch the perimeter while I dig."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor scrolled down the directory tree, ignoring the way the granola bar crumbled into their lap. The files were mostly logs—metadata dumps and encrypted chatter—but one folder stood out: a timestamped directory labeled *handlers_1023*. They clicked it open. Inside was a single PDF, password-protected but with a preview thumbnail visible. A list of names.

Their eyes darted over the rows of text. Halfway down, a name made their breath catch. It wasn't the source. It was someone they thought was on their side. The coffee in their stomach turned to acid.

They closed the window abruptly, the screen flickering back to the main menu. Noor couldn't wait for the source. If this file was here, the source wasn't the only target. They needed to secure this data before the cabin was breached. Noor pulled a second USB drive from their bag, smaller and more rugged than the first.

"Driver," they said, voice flat. "Put the phone away. We're uploading."

They plugged the new drive into the laptop, the action deliberate and quick. Noor wasn't going to sleep tonight. They were going to get this data off the local machine, no matter who was out there in the dark. The transfer bar started to fill, slow and agonizing, but Noor watched it like a hawk. Every second counted.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, annoyed.* "Whoa, chill. What's 'uploading' even mean?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't look up immediately. The progress bar crawled forward, a green line inching through the dark room. "It means I'm making sure this doesn't disappear if the laptop gets hit," they said, their voice low. They gestured at the rugged drive plugged into the side. "The file I just opened... it has names. People I trusted. If they're watching, this box is already compromised."

They leaned closer to the screen, squinting against the glare. The transfer hit forty-five percent. Noor's fingers hovered over the power button, ready to yank the drive if the signal spiked. "Just stay close," they added, glancing sideways at Driver. "Don't touch the keyboard. If the bar stops moving, you take the drive. We leave the rest." They turned back to the data, heart hammering against their ribs. The cabin creaked overhead, settling in the cold, but Noor held their breath, waiting to hear if it was just the house or something else.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at the drive, then at Noor.* "Okay. But what names?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor paused, the cursor hovering over the keyboard. The upload bar ticked past fifty percent, a steady green line in the dark room. They looked at Driver, weighing how much truth to give. Too little and Driver wouldn't understand the danger; too much and they'd be burdened with it.

"People I thought were allies," Noor said, voice low. "Reporters. Editors. Maybe even the guy who tipped me off." They swiveled the laptop slightly away from the window's line of sight. "If their names are there, this isn't a story anymore. It's a hit list."

They turned back to the screen, jaw tight. The transfer rate dipped, a stutter in the connection that made Noor's heart skip. They waited, breath held, until the number stabilized.
