Noor's hand drifted flat onto the bag, and they didn't say anything, didn't move, just watched the mirror and did arithmetic in their head: *same speed, closing on the straights, gap growing on the curves — no. Consistent gap. Nobody tailing keeps a consistent gap, they either hang way back or ride you.*

The pickup turned off onto a logging spur and vanished. Noor exhaled through their teeth and let their hand come off the bag.

"Logging crew," they said. "Paranoid or prepared. Still can't tell you which one I am. Ask me in a week." If there was a week with answers in it.

For a few miles Noor was quiet, watching the sunrise work its way down the ridgeline, and when they finally spoke it was to the windshield more than to Driver.

"I keep doing the math Ren told me not to do. Where they'd be right now. Whether they're— whether there's a version of this where I should be driving toward them instead of away." Noor's thumb ran along the notebook's spiral binding. "Ren said it's arithmetic. You're worth more working than searching. And they're right, and I know they're right, and I'm still going to spend the rest of my life doing that math at three in the morning." A breath. "Anyway. The way I honor the instruction is I get this thing so loud that finding Ren becomes a *prosecution's* problem instead of mine. That's the job. That's the only version of a rescue I'm actually qualified to run."

Noor flipped to a clean page and started building the morning like a schedule of operations, pen moving fast. "By nine we're through the hills. By ten, Sacramento suburbs. June Okafor lives out toward Land Park — craftsman house, azaleas, a husband who makes bread and pretends not to know what she used to do for a living. No phone call ahead, because phones are in the glovebox and June's spent forty years being surprised on doorsteps by reporters carrying evidence. She'll hate it and she'll make coffee and within an hour there'll be a media lawyer on her porch faster than the bread rises."

The sun cleared the ridge and came through the windshield, and Noor squinted into it, and for one unguarded second looked less like a journalist and more like a person who was thirty-five and had eaten cold chili for dinner and hadn't slept.

"When this is over," Noor said, "I owe you a real dinner. Hot. With a table. Possibly with a wine list, depending how the Republic of California treats me." They glanced over, a tired real smile, the first one in eighteen hours that had any air behind it. "You picked a strange night to be the only person on earth I trust. I hope you know that's what you are. Now — watch the road, and take the left up here. Bad decisions early, so the day can only improve."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's head turned — slow, like a gun turret. Driver's phone. In Driver's hand. Screen lit, thumb moving, while the county route unspooled through the windshield at fifty-five miles an hour.

"Hey." Noor's voice came out level, which was worse than shouting. "Hey. The phone." They pointed at it with two fingers, like it was a live thing. "It's on. It's been on. It's been on since the *cabin*, Driver — you took it off the charging cord, you didn't turn it off, and it has been talking to every tower between here and the junction the whole way down the mountain."

The side mirror. Noor checked it — empty road, just the logging spur dust settling behind them — and then checked it again, because the arithmetic had already changed. *If the phone's been alive since first light, then whatever it's been saying, it's already said.* Turning it off now was closing the barn door with the horse three counties away.

"Pull over." Noor said it flat, no drama, the voice you use when there's a fire but screaming makes it spread faster. "Not an emergency — just pull off onto the shoulder, keep the engine running, and give me the phone. Please."

The gravel crunched under the right tires as the car eased onto the shoulder. Noor took the phone — Driver unlocked it with a thumbprint, cooperative if dazed — and went still, reading the screen upside down first, then right side up.

A navigation app. Driver had pulled up a map. Their house was the destination. The route was highlighted. And the little blue dot — the phone's location, live, pulsing — sat on the county route, exactly where they were, with a breadcrumb trail of blue dots stretching all the way back up the mountain. Back to the cabin. A dotted line straight to somebody's uncle's hunting cabin, drawn by Driver's own phone, stored on somebody's server before Noor had even finished their coffee.

Noor stared at it for four full seconds. Then, very quietly: "Okay. Okay. This is fixable. This is probably fixable." The phone went into the foil bag, folded twice, pressed flat, and the bag went into the glovebox next to Noor's burner with a metallic crunch. "It's fixable because a map history is a *maybe*. Maybe nobody's watching your phone. Maybe nobody had a reason to, before last night. But if someone did — if someone got to Marcus and Marcus gave them names and your name was anywhere near mine this week — then your phone just drew them a map to where I slept."

Noor looked at Driver, and there was no anger in it. That was the strange part. Just a tired, terrible kind of care.

"I'm not mad. I need you to hear that I'm not mad, because I need you thinking straight for the next four hours, and guilt makes people stupid." Noor's hand rested on the glovebox. "But I need you to understand the *shape* of it. Everything I did last night — the foil, the west route, the dead man's switch — all of it assumed our phones were dark. Yours wasn't. So the plan changes a little, right now, while the engine's still running."

Noor flipped the paper map around on their knee, pen already moving.

"New route. We skip the west detour — no point paying for privacy we already spent. We take the 87 after all, straight down, because the fastest thing I can do now is get this drive to June *before* anyone finishes following breadcrumbs. Speed is our privacy now." The pen traced the line. "And you don't drive home today. I'm sorry. I know that's not what you signed up for. But your house is on that map as a destination, and until I know whether anyone was listening, your house is a place you *visit with witnesses*, not sleep in. June's got a guest room. June's husband makes bread. You'll eat better than you have all year, and by tonight we'll know if your phone was a problem or just a phone, and then — then you go home and be a bad witness like we planned."

Noor folded the map, clicked the pen closed, and looked over at Driver — really looked, the way they had at the window at midnight, cataloguing the person who'd somehow become the only one left inside the blast radius.

"Left at the junction," they said, softer. "Same as before. Just faster. And Driver — one more thing, and then I'll shut up about it forever: whatever was on that screen that was more important than my paranoid little rules — I hope it was good news. I hope somebody texted you something kind this morning. You deserved a kind text today."

A beat. The engine idled. The sun came through the windshield and lit the dust on the dashboard.

"Okay. Drive."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at the glovebox for a second, then nod slowly.* "Got it. Left at the junction." *I put the car in drive.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The left at the junction went clean — empty road behind them, empty ahead, the morning sun cutting sideways through the pines. Noor rode with the paper map open on one knee and the side mirror feeding them a slow slideshow of nothing, and for eleven miles it was almost possible to believe this was just a drive.

Then Noor folded the map.

"In about two miles there's a truck stop on the right," they said, eyes forward now. "Big diesel island, diner attached, you can't miss it. That's the one. When we pass it, you do not slow down. You do not look twice. We are a car going to Sacramento and we have never been anywhere else in our lives." A breath. "But I'm going to look. That's my job. Yours is the speedometer."

The truck stop materialized out of the morning the way places on highways do — all at once, too big to process. Diesel pumps in a long row. An attached diner with a dead neon sign, three semis idling in the back lot like sleeping animals, an attendant hosing down the concrete in the cold. Ordinary. Completely ordinary, except at the far end of the lot, backed up near the air pump, sat a silver Honda Civic with a cracked left taillight, parked at an angle, over the line, the way a car sits when the person driving it never intended to park at all. A yellow slip of paper was tucked under the wiper. The windshield was sheeted in frost — wearing the whole night, the only thing in the lot that had been there since dark.

Noor didn't move. Their hand lay flat on the bag in their lap, and their voice came out of them like something carried a long way.

"That's Ren's car." A beat. "Don't brake. Same speed. Don't look at it again."

The truck stop slid backward in the mirror and was gone. Noor watched it shrink to a bright patch and then to nothing, and only then did they breathe, long and shaky, and start talking — fast, because talking was the alternative.

"Okay. What we know. They were taken fast, at the pumps, probably at the moment of that call. The car's still there, which means Ren isn't in it, and nobody came back for it, which means whoever did this wasn't worried about it. Professionals don't panic about a Civic." Noor's thumbnail found the spiral binding of the notebook and worried it. "The yellow paper under the wiper — that's the station's 'abandoned vehicle' notice. Which means the attendant called a number, nobody answered, and that's the *entire* official response so far. There is no police report. Nobody's looking. The wave hasn't started." A pause, and then, quieter, the part Noor had to make themself say: "And there are cameras over those pumps. I saw two. Which means somewhere in that building there's a recording of what happened to my friend, and the only thing standing between me and that recording is a subpoena I'm not allowed to be the one to ask for." Noor's jaw worked once. "So Ren's rescue is a subpoena away. That's the arithmetic. Publish loud, the feds show up with paper, the cameras talk. It's the only version of the math that doesn't end with me in a ditch next to that car."

Noor reached over and clicked on the radio — AM, a habit older than the laptop — and hunted through static until the top of the hour found them: weather, frost advisories, a water main in some valley town, high school playoff scores. Noor actually laughed, one dry note.

"Nothing. A water main and teenagers. We are currently the only people on this planet who know there's a congressman in this story, and that's not a burden, that's an advantage. For about six more hours."

Sacramento came up out of the valley floor in heat shimmer and traffic. By the time the car was winding through Land Park — sycamores, sprinklers ticking across lawns, a Tuesday so ordinary it felt like a costume — it was 9:40 and Noor had gone silent, running lines behind their eyes. June Okafor's house was exactly as remembered: craftsman, deep porch, azaleas going slightly feral along the walk, the smell of bread somewhere behind it all.

Noor sat in the parked car for a moment with their hand on the door.

"Sixteen years ago she took a story no one else would touch and made three indictments happen," Noor said, half to themself, half to Driver. "She's the last porch in California I'm sure of."

They took the drive from the inner pocket, the sock card still in the sock, and knocked — three knocks, evenly spaced, like punctuation.

The door opened on a woman in her seventies, small, silver-cropped, reading glasses on a chain, dirt on her hands from the garden. June Okafor looked at Noor for exactly two seconds, taking in the face, the hour, the bag, the other person at the bottom of the steps — reading the whole story off the porch before a word was spent.

"Noor," she said. Not a question. She stepped back and held the door. "Inside, both of you. Tom — more coffee, and don't make it kind." Then her eyes settled on Driver, sharp and unhurried. "And you'd be the one who drove. Sit down, child. You look like you've earned a chair."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking in the scene. I feel a wave of exhaustion wash over me. I follow June inside, collapsing onto the nearest chair.* "Thanks."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The inside of June Okafor's house was the opposite of the cabin the way only a lived-in house can be — bread smell, books double-stacked on every shelf, a kitchen table scarred by forty years of coffee cups and deadlines. Noor stood in the doorway for one second too long, absorbing it, and June read that too.

"Sit," June said. "Both of you. Tom — eggs, bread, whatever's fast. Nobody briefs me on an empty stomach; the facts come out wrong." She looked at Noor over the reading glasses. "You especially. You look like something that lost an argument with a mountain."

"I ate," Noor said — and then, caught in the flat gaze of a woman who had edited three decades of liars, heard the sentence die. "Cold chili. At two in the morning. I'm fine, June, I don't have time to be—"

"You have exactly the time I give you." She was already filling the kettle. "Sit down, Noor. The story kept for eighteen hours. It'll keep for eggs."

So Noor sat, at a real table, in a real kitchen, and ate scrambled eggs and Tom's bread — the second honest meal in twenty-four hours — and watched Driver folded into a chair across the room, the exhaustion coming off them in waves, and felt the guilt of that sit down next to everything else. *One kind text,* Noor thought. *One kind text and a normal night's sleep, that's all this person was supposed to get out of me.*

Then the plates were cleared, and Noor opened the laptop on June's table, and stopped being tired for a while.

They told it in order. Halden Logistics. The manifests and the weight logs. The exception forms — forty-one of them, laid out in a scrolling grid on the screen — and then the ledger, *LB-true*, and the three shells, and Larkspur, and Reyes, and Voss. The March payments. The subcommittee vote. The C-SPAN clip Noor had filed on and not seen. And last, the audio. Noor played it all, four minutes and eleven seconds, Ren's voice filling a stranger's warm kitchen — *make it loud, Noor* — and when it clicked off, nobody spoke. Tom had stopped moving at the sink. June had gone very still, the way still that Noor had only ever seen in the best editors: not shock. Loading.

"Provenance," she said finally. "The source. Where are they, and will they testify?"

And there it was. The wound, asked for plainly.

Noor looked at the table. "Ren was taken last night. Eight minutes before our meet, at a gas station off the 87. I saw the car this morning — frost on the windshield, abandonment notice under the wiper, no police report. There are cameras over those pumps, June. Getting that footage takes a subpoena, and getting a subpoena takes the story being loud enough that the feds show up on their own." Noor's voice stayed even. Mostly. "So no. My source can't testify. My source is the reason the story has to be published *before* anyone can be rescued, not after."

June took off her glasses. Put them back on. It was the only visible processing she allowed herself.

"Who knew about the meet?"

"Three people. Me. Ren. My editor. Marcus — sixteen years, June." Noor's thumbnail found the table's old scar and worried it. "Ren's audio says someone at my paper leaked. I don't know it was Marcus. But I can't call the building. I can't call anyone whose number ends at that paper."

June was quiet for a moment. Then: "I've watched Alan Voss work a room twice. Careful man. Careful men don't kill journalists — they sue them, they stall them, they wait you out. It's not Voss that has you sleeping in foil bags, Noor. It's whoever Larkspur reports to when the money's heavy." She stood, went to the hall, and came back with an address book — an actual address book, spine cracked, decades of cross-outs — and flipped it open on the table like a weapon being assembled. "So. The vote clip is your spine. Money is arguable; a congressman on tape is not. That's what makes this publishable and not just loud. We get you a First Amendment lawyer by noon — David Marshak, he's beaten two of the three firms Larkspur would hire — and we place the story somewhere that isn't your building. I know two editors at national desks who'd walk over glass for this and owe me the walking." Her finger stopped on a name. "You'll co-byline. I don't care that I'm retired. Nobody publishes a sitting congressman's obituary alone."

Noor laughed — a real one, cracked open with exhaustion, the first since midnight. Then they stood.

"One thing first. Before anything else." They held up a hand. "June — do you have a landline?"

"I have a phone bill that proves it. Hallway."

Noor made the call to Walt Osei from a corded phone on a hallway table, the receiver heavy as a brick, and reset the dead man's switch — *I'm alive, cancel the six o'clock send, check in again at six tomorrow* — and when they came back into the kitchen, June was already on her own phone, voice low and fast, the address book open, the machinery of forty years spinning up around the story like it had been waiting for it.

She covered the receiver. "Bedroom's up the stairs, second door. Guest room's the first — that one's yours," she nodded toward Driver, "and you'll sleep whether you agree or not." Then to Noor, and the dry command in her voice bent, just slightly, into something older and kinder. "Two hours. That's an editorial instruction. You're no good to Ren dead on your feet."

Noor wanted to argue. Sixteen years of instinct wanted to argue. But the adrenaline had finally been relieved of its post, and their hands were doing a small tremor around the coffee cup that no amount of will could file off, and June was already turning back to her phone call, and the bread smell was in everything.

"Two hours," Noor said.

Upstairs, in a guest room with quilted beds and someone else's family photos on the dresser, Noor put the drive under the pillow — paranoid, prepared, undecided — and lay down, and listened for a moment to the sounds coming up through the floor: June's voice working, Tom's kitchen rhythm, Driver settling somewhere close by.

*Make it loud,* Ren had said.

*Working on it,* Noor thought, and for the first time since midnight, closed their eyes without watching a road.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod to June, then head for the guest room. I don't even bother taking off my shoes, just collapse onto the bed and close my eyes, out cold.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Sleep came for Noor the way it comes for soldiers and new parents — in fragments, none of them trustworthy. Twenty minutes of dark. Then a dream about the lake, the one from childhood, the water ticking against the dock pilings at night, the exact sound Noor had described to Ren over a phone line eight months ago — and Noor woke from it with their heart going hard and their hand already under the pillow, on the drive, checking. There. Still there. Still real.

They slept again. When they finally surfaced, the light through the guest room curtains had gone from morning to flat afternoon, and the house sounds below had changed key — June's voice had stopped, replaced by the particular silence of a house where work is being organized.

It was 1:47. June had given them two hours and let them have three. Noor filed that under *kindness I'll pay for later* and went downstairs.

June was at the kitchen table with a legal pad dense with her small violent handwriting, the address book open beside it, a fresh pot going. She looked up over the glasses.

"You snore," she said. "Sit. There's been movement."

Noor sat. June ran it down like a briefing officer.

"Marshak can be here at two. He already hates this, which is how you know he's in. And I reached Priya Nair at the national desk — you know her work, the shipyard piece. She wants it. But she's not sentimental, Noor, and she's not going to run a congressman's obituary on your source's voice alone. She wants two things." June held up one finger. "Independent corroboration of at least one ledger payment. Something that doesn't come from your drive." A second finger. "And a comment call to Voss's office before publication. Standard. Non-negotiable."

Noor's jaw tightened. "A comment call *tips him*. The moment his office hears the words *Larkspur* and *exception forms*, Larkspur knows the story exists, and we're on a clock that starts shrinking."

"Yes. So we do it Marshak's way — narrow window. We call, we give them ninety minutes to respond, we publish whether they respond or not. Ninety minutes of exposure instead of a week." June turned the legal pad around. "But that's for two o'clock. First — the corroboration. Tell me you have something that isn't Ren."

"I think I do." Noor was already pulling the laptop over. "The shells are registered entities. Secretary of state filings are public. If Ardent Freight Services lists its officers—" 

It took eleven minutes. June's wifi was slow and her reading lamp was better than her lighting, but the state business portal loaded, and Noor typed *Ardent Freight Services* into the search field with the flat focus of a person defusing something. The entity page came up. Registered agent. Officers. And there, secretary of the LLC, listed with a Sacramento address: the lobbyist's wife. The same name Noor had circled in the notebook at four in the morning in a dark cabin. A matter of public record, sitting in a state database, visible to anyone who'd thought to look — and apparently nobody had, for six years.

Noor sat back. Then, because sixteen years of training dies hard, they did it again — pulled up the subcommittee's public calendar, matched the March payments to the vote date, and screenshotted everything twice.

"There it is," Noor said quietly. "One payment, corroborated by public filings, tied to a public vote. Priya can have her corroboration and Ren never has to be a name in her mouth."

"Good." June made a mark on the legal pad, and then her voice changed — softer, the editor's voice aimed at the person and not the story. "Now the part you're not going to like. Your editor. Marcus. Before this publishes, someone is going to call your paper for *their* comment too — 'journalist leaves outlet amid—' whatever they invent. And if Marcus is the leak, publishing flushes him. If he isn't, publishing burns him anyway for losing you. Either way you need to decide, before two o'clock, whether you call him first. That's not editorial. That's just being somebody's friend or knowing you weren't."

Noor looked at the table's old scar for a long moment. "Sixteen years," they said, finally. "If he's dirty, I'll know in the first thirty seconds of his voice. And if he's not—" Their thumb ran the notebook binding once. "If he's not, he deserves to hear it from me and not a push notification."

June nodded once, and let it be.

On the way to refill the coffee, Noor paused at the foot of the stairs. The guest room door stood open an inch. Through the gap: Driver, exactly as they'd fallen — shoes on, one arm off the bed, the sleep of somebody whose body had simply overruled them. Noor almost went in, almost said something about shoes and blankets and the kindness of people who drive into other people's nightmares for free. Instead they eased the door to, leaving the gap, and went back down.

At 2:03, the doorbell rang.

June raised an eyebrow toward the hall. "That'll be the lawyer. He's early, which means he's worried, which means he read everything."

Noor crossed the hallway and opened the front door onto a man in a rumpled suit carrying two briefcases — one for documents, one that turned out, later, to hold a portable scanner and a burner phone still in its shrink wrap, because David Marshak had spent thirty years making journalists hard to sue and harder to disappear.

"Mr. Osei's office called ahead," Marshak said, stepping in, already looking at Noor like a house he was inspecting for structural flaws. "You must be the story. Sit down and tell me exactly how many copies exist, and don't round down."

Noor — tired, fed, three hours slept, the drive still against their ribs — almost smiled.

"Four," they said. "And one of them is in a coffee can. You're going to love this."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stir awake, hearing voices downstairs. I rub my eyes, disoriented, then remember where I am. I hear Noor's voice, then another man's. I decide to stay put for a minute, stretching and letting my eyes adjust to the light.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The silver stylus halted halfway across the vellum. For a moment Maester Tomas remained bent over the manuscript, as if the faded line beneath his hand might save him from the indignity of repetition. Then he raised his head. His eyes narrowed, not with anger yet, but with the strained effort of a man trying to bring a distant object into focus.

"Maester," he said. "Not Master. And do not tell me you are confused as though confusion were a disease caught from the lecture hall. You have heard two claims and have not yet learned to weigh them."

He set the stylus down with excessive care.

"Apprentice Bellen has shown you a paper. A paper. Not a sealed treaty, not a royal charter, not a Conclave act, not even a properly witnessed copy. The western discoveries are valuable, if one approaches them with discipline. They contain drafts, marginalia, memoranda, and the complaints of clerks who were not present at the final accord. They prove that the Treaty of Veyros was proposed, debated, and amended. Of course it was. Treaties do not descend from heaven fully sealed and ribboned."

His fingers tapped the desk, leaving faint smudges of ink upon the wood.

"The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE because King Aldric II concluded the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave, and because the realm thereafter operated as though the war had ended. The levies were discharged. The mage companies were restricted. The reparations were assessed. The royal chancery dated its peace from Veyros. That is not a fable repeated by lazy scholars; it is the administrative record."

He leaned back, and the chair creaked beneath him.

"No signed original survives? That is unfortunate, not decisive. Absence is not negation, especially after the Conclave fires and three reigns of careless record-keeping. The western cache may preserve a draft, or a set of proposed articles, or a clerk's note that the final instrument had not yet reached his province. Such things do not overturn a settlement recognized by king, Conclave, and realm."

His gaze sharpened, or tried to, through the dimness of his failing sight.

"As for 891, Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave. That is true. It is also irrelevant to the question you think you are asking. The dissolution of a body does not, by itself, prove that a war had continued in some phantom state for forty-four years. If every lingering resentment and every unsettled clause were counted as war, then the realm has never known peace."

A muscle tightened in his jaw.

"There are those who enjoy declaring that everything everyone knows is wrong. It makes them feel profound. But if Apprentice Bellen's paper claims the war 'actually' continued until 891, then it has used the word 'war' carelessly. A cold political antagonism is not the same as the Third Magical War. The war—the campaigns, the burnings, the Conclave's open defiance—ended with Veyros in 847 AE. The later documents may complicate the paperwork. They do not overturn the settlement."

He picked up the stylus again, then paused.

"Bring me the Veyrosi correspondence after you have sorted it. And when you read Bellen's paper again, ask not how two dates can both exist. Ask which source has authority, which has precision, and which is merely clever."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to suppress a sigh, but a little puff of air escapes anyway.* "Yes, Maester. And I wasn't saying I *caught* confusion. I was just trying to understand." *I point at the manuscript he was working on.* "Is that part of the Veyrosi correspondence?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The faint sigh landed on Maester Tomas’s ears like a scratch upon good parchment. He did not turn at once. First he aligned the silver stylus parallel to the edge of the desk, as though order might be imposed upon the world by such means, and only then did he lift his gaze toward the sound.

“A sigh is not an argument,” he said. “If you intend to dispute, form words. If you intend to understand, restrain your impatience. The archives do not yield their secrets to those who huff at them.”

He laid one ink-stained finger upon the manuscript before him, not without a certain protectiveness.

“This is not the Veyrosi correspondence in the strict sense. It is a later copy of a memorandum concerning the third proposed article of the Veyrosi settlement—copied, I should add, by a scribe whose hand was worse than mine and whose judgment was worse than his hand. It records objections raised by two Conclave advocates over the custody of enchanted revenues and the supervision of bound wards. It does not record the absence of a treaty. It records the presence of lawyers.”

He shifted the leaf slightly, tilting it toward the candlelight. The movement did not help his eyes, but he made it nonetheless, out of old habit and older pride.

“You see the danger in careless reading. A clerk in the western provinces writes that the articles remain in debate, and a century later some apprentice declares that therefore the war never ended. But in the same years the crown collected peace taxes, disbanded levies, heard appeals under the Veyrosi settlement, and dated royal writs from the peace. Which is the better witness: one marginal complaint preserved by accident, or the functioning of the realm?”

His finger tapped once against the manuscript.

“I did not say the original instrument survives. I said the war ended. Those are not the same assertion, and if you cannot distinguish them, then you have not understood the lecture at all. A missing seal does not unmake history. It merely gives idle men an excuse to rewrite it.”

He leaned forward again, squinting at the page with evident irritation, though whether at the faded ink, the candle, or the state of modern scholarship was difficult to say.

“Sort the Veyrosi correspondence properly. Separate drafts from dispatches, private memoranda from official copies, and anything bearing the phrase ‘final instrument’ or ‘sealed at Veyros’ from the rest. If you find such a folio, bring it to me at once. If you do not, then you will have learned something more valuable than a clever date: the difference between evidence and insinuation.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to absorb his words.* "So the western cache is important for details, but not for the big picture, because the realm *acted* like the war was over?" *I pause, considering.* "And what about the other side? Did the Conclave also act like it was over?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He drew the memorandum closer, then pushed it away again, as though the document itself had offended him by raising the question. His ink-stained fingers hovered over the desk, and for a breath he looked less like a royal scholar than a man besieged by the persistent inconvenience of other people’s thoughts.

“‘The big picture,’” he repeated at last, with the particular distaste of a man who has heard a noble phrase used by someone not entitled to it. “You have reduced a complex historiographical problem to a mural painted for children. Still, since you ask plainly, I will answer plainly: the western cache may illuminate the process by which the settlement was formed, disputed, delayed, and recorded. It does not, by itself, establish that the realm remained at war.”

He lifted a hand and began counting points upon his fingers, though the gesture was hampered by the fact that two of those fingers were darkened to the second knuckle with old ink.

“The Conclave ceased open operations after Veyros. Its armed retainers were withdrawn from the king’s roads, or at least were no longer mustered as Conclave companies. Its treasurers submitted to inquiries concerning enchanted revenues, even when they disputed the assessments. Its advocates appeared before royal courts to contest jurisdiction, wardship, and reparations. They petitioned. They delayed. They complained. They filed objections in triplicate, as if parchment were a form of warfare less bloody but more exhausting.”

His mouth thinned.

“That is how institutions behave when a settlement exists, even one they dislike. They do not behave like armies in the field. They behave like litigants with too much education and too little grace.”

He rose stiffly from his chair and moved toward a shelf stacked with rolled charters, though he did not touch them. His eyes moved over the labels without quite settling on any one of them.

“If you mean, did every mage accept the peace cheerfully? No. Some refused. Some called the treaty a betrayal. Some retreated into private circles and declared that no royal ink could bind the art of magic. There were even those who insisted the Conclave had not properly consented because the seal had not been affixed, or because the wording of the third article left custody of bound wards ambiguous, or because King Aldric’s commissioners had used the term ‘subjects’ where they ought to have used ‘persons under protection.’ Such men existed. They always exist. They are the weeds in every garden, and historians with weak judgment mistake them for the whole crop.”

He turned back, his expression sharpening.

“But the Conclave as a corporate body did not renew the war. It did not summon the old banners. It did not reoccupy the contested sanctums. It did not issue letters of defiance in its own name after the peace was proclaimed. When individual mages violated the terms, they were treated as violators of the settlement, not as commanders reopening hostilities. That distinction is not a trifle. It is the whole difference between a broken clause and a broken realm.”

One hand found a small brass paperweight and turned it over, feeling its weight rather than examining its shape.

“Do not confuse resentment with continuation. The Conclave resented Veyros. It resented the restrictions upon mage companies, the audits of enchanted revenues, and the crown’s growing claim to oversee bound wards. Resentment is cheap. It costs nothing to hate a treaty while obeying it. Men do it every day. Kingdoms do it as well.”

He set the paperweight down with a soft click.

“As for Queen Mira, her dissolution of the Conclave in 891 is often seized upon by clever apprentices as though it were a key that unlocks the past. It unlocks nothing of the sort. If the war had truly continued until then, the dissolution would have been an act of conquest, not administration. Yet the records describe it as a reorganization of magical jurisdiction under royal authority. The mages did not rise in arms. They petitioned, protested, negotiated pensions, surrendered charters, and sought guarantees for their libraries. That is not the end of a war. That is the end of a privileged corporation whose usefulness had expired.”

Maester Tomas returned to his seat, lowered himself into it with a grunt that he would have denied under oath, and looked toward the apprentice with narrowed eyes.

“So if you ask whether the Conclave acted as though the war was over, the answer is yes, in every way that mattered to law, taxation, military command, and public order. It acted as a defeated and constrained body living under a settlement it disliked. That is not the same as acting happily. It is not the same as acting sincerely. But it is enough.”

His gaze flicked back to the memorandum on the desk.

“The western documents may show that the treaty’s final form was never sealed, or that some copies circulated before ratification was complete, or that clerks in distant provinces misunderstood what had been concluded at Veyros. Fine. Let them show it. That would mean the Treaty of Veyros was politically effective before it was administratively perfect. Such things happen. History is not a notary’s ledger.”

He picked up the silver stylus again, then pointed it in mild warning.

“Do not let Apprentice Bellen persuade you that a missing seal proves a continuing war. Seals are wax. War is blood. If the realm had still been at war, someone would have noticed.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not at once reach for the paper. He looked at it as one might look at a cockroach that had announced itself as a witness in a property dispute. Then, with great deliberation, he extended one ink-darkened hand.

“War decree,” he said, as though testing the phrase for rot. “You speak the words as though they were a stone dropped into a pond. Tell me: does the document call itself a war decree? Does it use the precise formula of open war, or does it speak of rebellion, suppression, outlawry, enforcement, or the punishment of unlicensed practitioners? These terms are not interchangeable. They are not pebbles in the same sack. A scholar who treats them as such has already lost the argument before opening his mouth.”

He drew the copy closer to the candlelight and bent over it, his brow tightening. His failing eyes forced him near enough that his beard almost brushed the page, but he did not seem to notice. One finger hovered above the line where the seal would have been, not touching it, as if even the suggestion of wax might carry contamination.

“King Aldric’s seal,” he said slowly. “If it is indeed King Aldric’s seal, and not a later chancery mark, a privy device, a copied impression, or a clerk’s hopeful drawing, then it proves one thing and one thing only: that a document passed through royal hands in the year 863 AE. Kings seal many things. They seal judgments, tax orders, commissions of inquiry, appointments, pardons, commands to sheriffs, and instructions to arrest troublesome mages. If every royal order with sharp language is a war decree, then the realm has been at war with itself every time a tax collector was disobeyed.”

He looked up, and his expression sharpened with the particular irritation of a man who has been forced to explain the obvious twice in one day.

“You say it is dated sixteen years after the war ended. Correct your phrasing. It is dated sixteen years after the peace was recognized, after the belligerent phase of the Third Magical War concluded, after the settlement at Veyros became the operative framework of royal and Conclave relations. Peace does not mean silence. It does not mean affection. It does not mean that every grievance vanished. It means that the parties ceased conducting themselves as open enemies under arms.”

His finger tapped the copy, once, hard enough to leave a faint smudge of ink at the margin.

“What is the enemy named? That is the first question. If the decree names the Mage Conclave as a corporate body in rebellion, if it summons the levies, if it revokes the Veyrosi settlement, if it orders the royal hosts to march against sanctioned mages, then we have something to discuss. But if it commands officers to seize rogue practitioners, to enforce wardship provisions, to collect arrears, to suppress unlawful assemblies, or to execute judgments under the Veyrosi articles, then it is not a continuation of the Third Magical War. It is the crown administering the peace with a heavier hand.”

He pushed the copy a fraction away from himself, though he did not release it, as if he distrusted it to remain unattended.

“Apprentice Bellen may have shown you a document and then supplied the interpretation as though interpretation were baked into the ink. That is a common trick among clever young men who wish to appear profound. They find an ambiguous source and announce that it overturns everything. But a decree with a seal is not a war. A date is not a campaign. A harsh phrase is not a battlefield. If the realm had still been at war in 863 AE, where are the muster rolls? Where are the treasury disbursements for field companies? Where are the chronicle accounts of burned villages and broken sanctums? Where are the Conclave’s letters of defiance? Where is the evidence that both sides acted as though the settlement had collapsed?”

His voice grew drier still.

“Do not answer with silence. Silence is not evidence. The absence of such records is not a small thing. It is a very large thing. The realm leaves traces. Armies leave traces. Taxes leave traces. Deaths leave traces. A single copied decree cannot outweigh the administrative shape of an entire reign unless it is supported by every other category of record.”

He leaned back for a moment, then leaned forward again, unable to leave the page alone.

“And what sort of seal is it? Is it impressed, drawn, painted, or merely described? Is it attached to an original, or copied onto a later transcript? A seal drawn by a scribe may mean that the original bore a seal. It may mean that the scribe believed it did. It may mean that the scribe wished it did. Seals are not truth itself. They are authentication, and authentication can be clumsy, borrowed, forged, or misattributed. I have seen documents with royal seals that were nothing more than monastic forgeries dressed in respectable wax.”

Maester Tomas lifted the paper slightly and tilted it toward the light, squinting at the spacing of the lines.

“Moreover, dating is not as simple as apprentices imagine. A western copy may convert a regnal year into AE reckoning incorrectly. A clerk may miscopy a numeral. A later archivist may label a document ‘war decree’ because he saw the word ‘war’ and lacked the discipline to ask what kind of war was meant. There were disturbances after Veyros. There were rogue mages, disputed wardships, local risings, and royal commissions with military language. Those are not the Third Magical War continuing. They are the debris of settlement.”

He set the copy down again, aligning it precisely with the edge of the desk.

“If the decree truly declares hostilities against the Conclave as such, then it demands scrutiny. But scrutiny is not surrender. One anomalous text does not unmake the canonical account. It must be tested against chancery enrollments, treasury records, chronicle narratives, Conclave acta, and the later conduct of both crown and mages. Until such corroboration appears, the wiser position remains that the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE, and that later documents concern enforcement, factional conflict, or administrative confusion.”

His gaze returned to the apprentice, stern and unamused.

“Do not allow yourself to be overawed by a seal. Ask what the seal commands. Ask in whose name it speaks. Ask whether it suspends the peace or invokes it. Ask whether it is a decree of war, a decree under war powers, a decree concerning warlike matters, or a decree that some modern reader has lazily labeled ‘war’ because he wished to sound important.”

He tapped the silver stylus once against the desk.

“Take the copy and transcribe the first ten lines exactly. Do not paraphrase. Do not improve the wording. Do not translate difficult phrases into comfortable ones. Mark every abbreviation, every erasure, every marginal note. Note whether the seal is described or depicted. Note the repository, the folio, and Bellen’s citation, if he has one. If he cannot tell you where the document resides, then you have not been shown evidence. You have been shown a rumor with wax on it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, feeling a familiar flush of frustration. I carefully take the paper, smoothing out the copy I had made myself.* "Bellen said it was from the Royal Archives, volume 3, sub-section E, folio 14. He said the seal was impressed." *I look back at the Maester, hesitating before I speak again.* "But... if the king issued a decree in 863 with his seal, even if it was just about 'rogue practitioners,' wouldn't that imply some sort of ongoing conflict, or at least a very fragile peace?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a small, sharp sound in his throat, not quite a laugh and entirely without amusement. He lifted one hand, palm upward, as if the word itself had been placed there for inspection.

“‘Imply,’” he repeated. “A dangerous verb in the mouth of an apprentice. It permits a man to say nothing precisely and yet claim the authority of consequences. Does a royal decree imply conflict? Yes. It implies that someone disobeyed the crown, or that the crown feared he would. It implies that officers were needed, judgments enforced, revenues protected, or magical persons brought under restraint. It does not, by that fact alone, imply the continuation of the Third Magical War.”

He drew the copied paper back toward himself, though he did not look at it immediately. His fingers rested at its edges, ink-marked and still.

“You ask whether it would imply a fragile peace. There you are nearer sense. The peace after Veyros was fragile, contested, resented, and enforced unevenly. No scholar with more wit than ambition denies that. But a fragile peace is still peace if the realm’s institutions treat it as peace. A broken roof does not prove the house was never built. It proves only that the roof leaked.”

His eyes narrowed at the candle flame, as though the light had offered him an impertinent question.

“If the decree concerns rogue practitioners, then it may be evidence precisely of the settlement’s operation, not its absence. The crown’s claim to discipline unlicensed mages, supervise bound wards, or audit enchanted revenues derives from the Veyrosi framework. Such a decree may show the crown using the powers it believed Veyros had granted. It may show the Conclave failing to control its own members. It may show local disorder. It may show royal overreach. None of those things is the same as open war between king and Conclave.”

He tapped the desk once with a stained fingertip.

“Volume three, sub-section E,” he said, slower now, as though tasting the citation for forgery. “If Bellen has cited correctly—and that remains a matter for verification, not admiration—volume three in that series contains enforcement mandates, extraordinary commissions, and records of jurisdictional dispute. It is not the register of campaigns. It is not the chancery’s book of open hostilities. It is the place where the crown files its irritations.”

The maester’s mouth tightened.

“An impressed seal in the Royal Archives does not transform a mandate into a declaration of war. It authenticates the document as royal, or at least as accepted into royal record. Seals were attached to orders for grain, for bridges, for arrests, for pensions, for the custody of wards, and for the seizure of unlawful enchantments. If you wish to know whether the realm remained at war, do not stare at the wax. Read the operative clauses. Does the king command armies? Does he summon feudal levies? Does he name the Conclave as enemy? Does he suspend the Veyrosi articles? Does he authorize burning, seizure of sanctums, or execution under martial law? Or does he command sheriffs, justices, wardens, and commissioners to enforce judgments already claimed under the peace?”

He leaned forward, and the candlelight caught the silver stylus in his hand.

“That is where Bellen’s cleverness will be tested. If the decree says, ‘Whereas the Conclave, in defiance of the crown, has levied war,’ then we must pause. If it says, ‘Whereas certain persons, calling themselves mages, have practiced without license and disturbed the king’s peace,’ then we have not found a new war. We have found a magistrate with a large vocabulary.”

Maester Tomas set the stylus down again, aligning it with the edge of the manuscript as though the desk were a battlefield requiring order.

“You must also learn not to be overawed by dates. Sixteen years after Veyros is not sixteen years of war. It is sixteen years of aftermath. Kingdoms do not settle great conflicts neatly and then become serene. They become litigious. They become suspicious. They issue commissions, hold inquests, confiscate property, and punish offenders with language meant to frighten. If every harsh decree after a treaty proved the treaty void, then every peace in our histories would be a prelude to another war.”

His expression darkened.

“That is the fault of the western-archive school. They find a complaint, a draft, a delayed copy, a sealed order, and immediately they announce that the whole received account has collapsed. They mistake administrative disorder for political nonexistence. They mistake the absence of a single perfect original for the absence of a settlement. They prefer paradox because paradox makes them look clever. But history is often less dramatic than the clever wish it to be. The Treaty of Veyros may have been imperfect in form, disputed in wording, and poorly copied in the provinces. It was nevertheless the peace by which the realm governed itself.”

He lifted his chin slightly.

“So yes, a fragile peace. Yes, ongoing tension. Yes, perhaps even violence under the name of suppression. But do not leap from there to ‘the war continued until 891.’ That is not inference; that is appetite. You must show that the corporate Conclave remained in arms, that the crown treated it as an enemy state, and that the administrative life of the realm contradicts the peace. A single decree will not do it, even with King Aldric’s seal pressed into it.”

Maester Tomas pushed the copy back across the desk, but only a little, as if he were reluctant to release it entirely.

“You will bring me the transcription I asked for. Exact. No paraphrase. No helpful explanation from Bellen inserted between the lines. If the first ten lines contain the formula of open war, I will say so. If they do not, you will cease speaking of it as though it had already overturned the lecture. And if the Royal Archives holds an original with an impressed seal, then it will be examined, collated, and judged. Not admired. Judged.”

He picked up the memorandum he had been working on before, then set it down again with a faint, irritated breath.

“Now go. And if you meet Apprentice Bellen on the way, tell him that a seal is not an argument, a decree is not a campaign, and if he wishes to overturn my dating of the Third Magical War, he had better bring me more than a dramatic word and a wax impression.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He sat very still, his hands resting on either side of the memorandum as though he were keeping it from sliding away while the room itself became unsteady. Then he gave a short, humorless breath.

“Real,” he said. “You ask as though history were a fruit one could bite and declare sweet or rotten. And you speak of ‘the textbook’ and ‘the new evidence’ as though one were an oracle and the other a thunderclap. Correct yourself. A textbook is a summary, often a clumsy one. Evidence is not a voice; it is a fragment. Scholars make it speak by asking disciplined questions.”

He lifted one hand, then lowered it again without touching the page.

“If you want a plain answer, you shall have one, though it will not please you by being simple. The Treaty of Veyros is real in the sense that matters most to history, and uncertain in the sense that lawyers and archivists prize.”

His eyes narrowed, not at the apprentice, but at the candle flame, as if the light had offered him a poorly copied citation.

“If by ‘real’ you mean a single original instrument, signed by King Aldric II, sealed by the Mage Conclave, witnessed in perfect form, and preserved without blemish from 847 AE to this hour, then no honest scholar can say that such a thing is known to exist. The western discoveries have made that much harder to ignore. They suggest drafts, debates, delays, and perhaps even a failure to complete the final act in the manner later chroniclers supposed. I do not dismiss that. Only a fool dismisses documents because they are inconvenient, and I am many things, but not a fool.”

His tone sharpened on the last word, though he did not raise his voice.

“But if by ‘real’ you mean a settlement recognized by the crown, accepted in practice by the Conclave, enforced through royal officers, cited in legal proceedings, used to date writs, assessed for reparations, and treated by the realm as the end of open war, then yes. The Treaty of Veyros was real. It was real because it governed. It was real because men obeyed it, evaded it, interpreted it, complained about it, and organized public life around it. A bridge may be real even if the architect’s final drawing was never signed.”

He tapped one ink-stained finger against the desk.

“The textbook errs if it tells you the treaty was signed without qualification. It errs because it compresses a messy process into a tidy date for the convenience of examination candidates. I have no love for such compression. But the western evidence does not therefore prove that there was no peace, no settlement, or no end to the war. It proves, at most, that the formal instrument may have remained incomplete, contested, or unperfected.”

Maester Tomas leaned forward, and his voice became colder and more precise.

“Here is the truth, or as near as a scholar may come without lying by precision: the armed phase of the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. The realm thereafter operated under the Veyrosi settlement. The Conclave did not renew open war. The crown did not treat the Conclave as an enemy state in the old sense. There were tensions, violations, suppressions, legal quarrels, and cold hostility. Those lasted for decades. If you choose to call that entire period ‘war,’ then you may stretch the word until it covers 891 AE and Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave. But you will have stretched the word until it loses its shape.”

He gave the desk a single, sharp tap.

“A cold political antagonism is not the same thing as a war. A decree enforcing a treaty is not the same thing as a decree declaring one. An unsealed draft is not the same thing as an absent settlement. And a clever apprentice who confuses those categories has not discovered the truth. He has merely discovered a way to be wrong in an interesting manner.”

Maester Tomas sat back, his expression severe but no longer merely irritated. There was something tired beneath it now, the fatigue of a man who had spent too many years correcting the same errors in different hands.

“If you ask whether I would amend the lecture, I would amend one word. I would not say the Treaty of Veyros was unquestionably signed. I would say it was concluded in effect, though its final documentary form may be doubtful. That is the careful formulation. It lacks the drama Bellen prefers, but it has the virtue of fitting the records.”

His gaze returned to the copy of the decree.

“So do not ask me whether the treaty is real as though I were being forced to choose between a fairy tale and a fraud. The truth is less tidy. The Treaty of Veyros may never have been perfected in the form later ages imagined. Yet it existed as a binding political fact. It ended the war that mattered—the war of armies, fires, open defiance, and royal conquest. What followed was aftermath, resentment, and administration. Queen Mira’s act in 891 AE ended the Conclave as a corporation. It did not end a war that had been raging for forty-four years, because no such war existed except in the imaginations of men who mistake paperwork for battle.”

He picked up the silver stylus once more, but did not return to the manuscript.

“If you write in your examination that the Treaty of Veyros was a fiction, you will be wrong. If you write that it was a fully preserved signed instrument beyond all doubt, you will also be wrong. If you write that it was an imperfect settlement whose authority rested on acceptance and enforcement rather than on a flawless surviving text, then perhaps you will have learned something worth knowing.”

His voice dropped, dry and final.

“That is the truth. Not the textbook’s truth, not Bellen’s truth, and certainly not the truth that flatters whoever wishes to seem clever. It is the truth that survives when one has stopped preferring excitement to evidence.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I digest his words, feeling a little deflated but also like I've learned something important.* "So it's less about what's written down perfectly, and more about what actually happened... what people did." *I look at the copied decree in my hand.* "I'll get to transcribing this then, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a short nod, though it was the sort of nod that conceded only a fraction of what had been said and reserved the right to withdraw even that fraction later.

“Better,” he said. “But not yet precise enough. Do not go away believing that what is written down matters less. That is the consolation of apprentices who dislike copying. What is written down is often the only thing that separates history from gossip, and the archives are full of men who thought their own memories more reliable than ink.”

He lifted the memorandum again, then set it down with the air of a man postponing a disagreeable chore.

“What you mean, if you mean anything defensible, is that a settlement may be historically real even when its documentary survival is imperfect. The realm’s conduct is evidence. The crown’s conduct is evidence. The Conclave’s conduct is evidence. But conduct itself must be read through records, and records require judgment. Do not replace one laziness with another. A perfect treaty is not required. A functioning peace is.”

His eyes moved to the copy in the apprentice’s hand, though whether he was looking at the seal, the date, or merely the inconvenience of the whole affair was difficult to say.

“Transcribe the first ten lines exactly. If there is a word you do not understand, leave it and mark it. If there is an abbreviation, copy the abbreviation. If there is a blot, describe the blot. If Bellen has supplied a heading that says ‘war decree,’ record whether that heading appears in the manuscript itself or has been added by a later hand. Headings are where archivists go to die.”

He picked up the silver stylus, turned it once between his stained fingers, and pointed it toward the shelves without looking.

“Then compare the language of the decree with the enforcement mandates in volume three. You will find that royal clerks could make the arrest of a single unlicensed mage sound like the suppression of a rebellion. That is why context is not decoration. It is discipline.”

For a moment his expression softened, though only in the sense that a locked gate might be said to soften if someone ceased rattling it.

“If the decree proves nothing more than enforcement under the Veyrosi settlement, then you will have learned that the peace was contested. That is worth knowing. If it proves something more—if it truly names the Conclave as an enemy and commands open war—then bring it to me at once, and I will examine it myself. But until then, do not let one dramatic phrase rearrange forty years of administrative history.”

He returned his attention to the manuscript before him, though his hand rested near the silver stylus as if expecting further interruption and preparing to punish it.

“Now go. And when you transcribe, do not let your hand anticipate your judgment. The document will tell you what it is, if you have the patience to listen.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking his words to heart this time.* "I understand, Maester. I'll get started right away." *I turn to leave, feeling the weight of the decree, and the Maester's words, in my hand.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not lift his head at once. He drew the memorandum back beneath his hand and smoothed one corner with an ink-blackened thumb, as though the gesture might press order into the afternoon itself.

“And one further instruction,” he said, his voice carrying across the desk with the dry precision of a man who had spent too many years being misunderstood by people younger than himself. “If the document begins with a royal style, record it exactly. Do not shorten it. Do not modernize it. If it says ‘Aldric, second of his name, by the grace of the Four, king of the realm and protector of the sanctums,’ write all of it. If it omits the peace-title, note the omission. If it includes it, note that also. Titles are not decoration. They are claims.”

He shifted the candle a fraction closer, though the flame did little to help his failing eyes. The movement was habitual, stubborn, faintly pathetic in its dignity.

“And do not let Apprentice Bellen persuade you that an impressed seal makes a document martial. The king’s seal may hang from a pardon as easily as from a summons. It may authenticate a command to arrest a single unlicensed practitioner as readily as a command to muster the realm. What matters is the verb. Does the king command, forbid, punish, seize, or declare? Against whom? Under what authority? If the Conclave is named as a corporate enemy, if the Veyrosi settlement is renounced, if the peace is set aside by name, then we have a problem worthy of lost sleep. If not, then we have another instance of the crown beating a disobedient subject with the language of war because that language is cheaper than raising an army.”

His fingers tapped once against the desk, leaving another faint smudge upon the wood.

“Do not copy Bellen’s marginal notes as though they belonged to the source. If he has written ‘here begins the war decree’ in the margin, mark it as Bellen’s hand, not as the archive’s. Later hands are liars with access to old ink.”

He paused, then added, with the air of a man conceding a point only because refusing it would be less precise than granting it, “Volume three, sub-section E, folio fourteen. If that citation is correct, it is not nothing. But citations are like apprentices: promising until examined.”

For a moment Maester Tomas bent again over the memorandum, but he did not begin to write. The silver stylus rested against the vellum without marking it. His brow was drawn inward, not merely with irritation now, but with the wary expression of a scholar who has felt a small stone shift beneath a wall he has long declared sound.

The date had lodged in him like a splinter. Eight hundred sixty-three. Sixteen years after Veyros. A decree bearing the king’s seal. It did not overturn his position. It could not overturn his position. Not alone. Not without muster rolls, treasury accounts, chronicle entries, Conclave protests, and a body of administrative record to match the weight of the claim. Yet it was precisely the sort of splinter that irritated a careful man, because it could not be ignored without dishonesty and could not be accepted without disorder.

“Sixteen years,” he murmured, almost to the candle. “A war decree. If so, where are the dead?”

Then he shook himself, as though casting off the thought by force, and touched the stylus at last to the page. A thin line of ink appeared, deliberate and controlled.

“Begin with the first line,” he said, louder, as though the question still stood somewhere in the archive waiting to be disciplined. “And bring it to me before you discuss it with anyone who enjoys being surprising.”

He did not look up again, but his voice sharpened one last time.

“And if the seal is smudged, say so. If the wax is damaged, say so. If the cord is missing, say so. Do not reconstruct certainty from hope. That is not scholarship. That is prayer with worse handwriting.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pause in the doorway, my hand still on the frame, listening to his last words. "Understood, Maester." I pull the door closed behind me, ready to get to work.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The latch clicked. The sound was small, final, and somehow less satisfactory than Maester Tomas had expected.

He listened until the apprentice’s footsteps had faded into the outer passage, and even then he waited a breath longer, as though silence itself might return to report what it had overheard. The archive settled around him in its usual manner: the faint settling of shelves, the whisper of dry vellum, the thin complaint of tallow in the candle flame. Nothing else moved. The room smelled of ink, dust, and the particular staleness of paper that had been copied too often and understood too seldom.

“Volume three, sub-section E, folio fourteen,” Maester Tomas said aloud.

The words displeased him. They had the neatness of a proper citation, which meant they had to be treated seriously, and he disliked being forced into seriousness by an apprentice who had probably not yet learned to distinguish a chancery hand from a monastic one.

He set down the silver stylus and pushed himself from the desk. His knees protested. His back protested. His eyes protested most of all, as they always did when he asked them to perform the work they had once done without complaint. He took the candle from the desk and carried it toward the eastern range of shelves, where the archive’s older finding aids stood in rows like elderly soldiers too stubborn to be discharged.

He did not need the finding aid for volume three. He had used it often enough in his younger days, when the Royal Archives had still seemed like a country that could be conquered by a determined man with good sight and better Latin. But habit remained. Habit, and the scholar’s distrust of memory.

His free hand moved along the shelf labels, fingers brushing cracked leather and flaking gilt. He bent close to the candle, squinting. The letters swam. He drew back, blinked, and tried again.

“E,” he muttered. “Enforcement. Extraordinary commissions. Jurisdictional matters. The crown’s cabinet of annoyances.”

He found the correct index at last and carried it back to the desk, holding the candle too close to the page. The flame threw his shadow long against the shelves, where it seemed to lean forward with the same irritation he felt.

The index was old, its margins browned, its entries written in a cramped hand that had belonged to some long-dead clerk who had probably believed himself indispensable. Maester Tomas traced the column for the third volume with the tip of the stylus, stopping twice when the ink blurred. Once he had to wipe his spectacles on his sleeve, a useless gesture that he performed with the solemnity of ritual.

There.

Sub-section E.

Mandates and commissions concerning magical persons, revenues, wards, and unlawful practices.

He gave a short grunt.

“Not war,” he said. “Administration.”

But he did not close the index. Instead he turned to the register of folio references and searched for the years around 863 AE. His finger moved down the page, pausing at each entry.

861: commission to inquire into unlicensed enchantments in the river wards.

862: order to seize revenues from a disputed bound ward in the eastern marches.

862: mandate to arrest a practitioner operating without Conclave license and royal permit.

863: decree concerning contumacious mages and the custody of certain sanctum goods.

Maester Tomas stopped.

His finger remained on the line. The candle flame trembled, whether from a draft or from the unsteadiness of his own hand he did not know.

“Contumacious,” he said, tasting the word. “Contumacious is not warlike. Contumacious is merely unpleasant.”

He leaned closer. The entry was brief. Too brief. It named no army, no levy, no campaign, no enemy. It did not say the Conclave had risen. It did not say the peace had been revoked. It did not say the realm was in arms. It said only that a decree had been issued, sealed, and enrolled concerning certain mages who had refused obedience to royal commissioners.

That was all.

That was enough to make a clever apprentice speak nonsense.

Maester Tomas straightened slowly. For a moment he stood beside the desk with the candle in one hand and the stylus in the other, looking at nothing in particular. The archive, which had seemed so orderly a moment before, now seemed full of small, irritating possibilities.

He set the candle down and returned to his chair. From the lower drawer of his desk he withdrew a folder tied with faded ribbon. Its label was in his own hand, written years ago when his sight had still been reliable enough to be trusted without argument.

Western Archive Discoveries — Preliminary Notes.

He untied the ribbon with a sharp tug. Inside were transcripts, partial copies, and memoranda he had gathered when the first reports from the western archives had reached the capital. He had read them then with suspicion. He reread them now with less pleasure.

One sheet bore a clerk’s note that the articles of Veyros had been amended in the third clause and returned to the king’s council for further consideration. Another recorded that the Conclave’s lesser seal had been affixed to a draft, but the greater seal had not yet been applied. A third, the most troublesome, stated plainly that the final instrument remained incomplete at the time of the king’s departure from Veyros.

Maester Tomas laid the pages side by side beneath the candlelight.

“Incomplete,” he said.

He did not say it as though the word were a victory. He said it as a man says the name of a leak in the roof during a storm.

“Incomplete is not absent,” he continued, more firmly. “Proposed is not void. Delayed is not nonexistent.”

He took a fresh sheet of parchment and drew it toward him. For a moment he merely looked at it, the silver stylus resting between his ink-stained fingers. Then he began to write, his letters small, careful, and slightly uneven.

The Treaty of Veyros must not be described as a fiction merely because no flawless original is known to survive.

He stopped. He crossed out must and wrote should.

The Treaty of Veyros should not be described as a fiction merely because no flawless original is known to survive.

Better. He continued.

Its authority rests upon recognition, enforcement, and the subsequent conduct of crown and Conclave. The absence of a perfected instrument may complicate the formal history of the settlement, but it does not establish the continuation of open war beyond 847 AE.

He underlined the last phrase once, then again. The second line was thicker than the first.

The realm did not behave as a realm at war. The levies were not maintained. The sanctums were not besieged. The Conclave did not issue corporate defiance. Royal writs were dated from the peace. Reparations were assessed. Jurisdiction was contested under the settlement, not outside it.

He paused, stylus hovering.

Then, with visible reluctance, he added:

Nevertheless, later royal mandates concerning unlicensed practitioners, disputed wards, and contumacious mages should be examined with care. Harsh language is not proof of war, but neither should it be dismissed without collation.

He stared at that sentence for a long time.

It was not a concession. He told himself so plainly. It was discipline. A scholar who refused to look at inconvenient evidence was no scholar at all, merely a custodian of comfortable error. And Maester Tomas had spent too many years correcting lazy chronicles, forged donations, and noble family histories that mistook vanity for ancestry to excuse laziness in himself.

Still, the sentence annoyed him.

He wrote beneath it:

If Royal Archives, volume three, sub-section E, folio fourteen, contains the proper formula of open war, the matter must be reconsidered. If it contains only enforcement language, it confirms the operation of the Veyrosi settlement under strain.

He set the stylus down.

“Formula,” he said to the empty room. “Formula is the question.”

He knew the formula well enough. Every royal clerk knew it, though few could recite it without error. A true declaration of war had its own gravity. It named the enemy. It renounced peace. It summoned arms. It spoke of defense of the realm, of rebellion, of open injury, of the king’s honor wounded by corporate defiance. It did not merely order a sheriff to drag an unlicensed mage out of a tower because the mage had refused to answer a summons concerning ward revenues.

At least, it ought not.

But kings were not always precise. Kings liked large words. Kings liked to make small acts sound majestic and majestic acts sound inevitable. Aldric II had been particularly fond of phrases that made administration sound like destiny.

Maester Tomas rubbed his eyes with the heel of one hand, then remembered the ink on his fingers and lowered his hand with a grimace.

“Folio fourteen,” he said again.

He reached for a second sheet of parchment. This one he used for a requisition, written in the formal hand required by the Royal Archives. The words came more easily now, because they were commands rather than judgments.

To the Keeper of the Royal Archives,

I require inspection of volume three, sub-section E, folio fourteen, being a document said to bear the seal of King Aldric II and dated to the year 863 AE. I require confirmation of the seal’s condition, the hand of the document, the presence or absence of later marginalia, and the exact wording of the opening style and operative clauses. If the document has been rebound, repaired, recopied, or resealed, I require note of the same.

He paused, then added:

Let no summary be supplied in place of the text. Let no modern heading be treated as original. Let the document speak in its own words, or not at all.

He signed it with his name and title, pressed his own seal into the wax at the bottom, and held it up to inspect the impression. The wax was uneven. His hand had trembled slightly. He frowned at it, but did not remake it. Perfection was not required. Authentication was.

He placed the requisition at the corner of the desk, aligned precisely with the edge.

Then he returned to the memorandum he had been copying before the apprentice’s arrival. The third proposed article of the Veyrosi settlement waited for him with all the patience of a dead lawyer. Enchanted revenues. Bound wards. Custody. Supervision. Objections raised by advocates who had probably been more concerned with fees than with the fate of magic in the realm.

Maester Tomas lifted the stylus.

He did not write.

Instead he looked again at the folder of western notes. The candle flame shifted. Shadows crawled across the pages.

“Eight hundred sixty-three,” he murmured.

The date sat in his mind like a stone in a shoe. It did not overturn anything. It could not overturn anything. Not by itself. Not without corroboration. Not without the full weight of record behind it. But it was there, and Maester Tomas had always believed that a fact ignored was a fact avenged.

He thought of the apprentice’s hesitant voice. The copied decree. The impressed seal. The phrase war decree.

He thought of Apprentice Bellen, whom he had not met but already disliked with the efficiency of a man who had spent decades disliking similar types. Bellen would be the sort to mistake a sharp phrase for a battlefield. He would speak of “new evidence” as though evidence were wine, improved by novelty. He would smile as though history owed him a revelation.

Maester Tomas’s mouth tightened.

“If it is a war decree,” he said, “then it will have to prove itself.”

He tapped the desk once.

“And if it proves itself, I will say so.”

He paused.

“Not gladly.”

Another pause.

“But I will say so.”

The archive gave no answer. It never did. It merely preserved, in its dry and indifferent way, the fragments that survived: seals, scraps, formulas, mistakes, complaints, and the occasional stubborn fact that refused to sit where scholars wished it to sit.

Maester Tomas bent again over the memorandum. His eyes hurt. The ink was faint. The scribe’s hand was wretched. Somewhere beyond the archive windows, the afternoon was beginning to thicken toward evening, and the candles would soon need trimming.

He wrote one line of commentary in the margin, small and severe.

The presence of lawyers does not prove the absence of peace.

Then he stopped, considered, and added beneath it:

But the presence of a sealed decree in 863 AE requires that we ask what sort of peace it was.

He looked at the sentence for a long moment.

It was not the lecture he had given that morning. It was not the lecture he would have preferred to give. But it was nearer the shape of the problem, and Maester Tomas had spent his life in service to that nearness, however ungrateful it was.

He drew the memorandum closer, adjusted the candle, and forced his failing eyes back to the faded ink.

“Begin with the first line,” he said quietly, as though reminding himself of the instruction he had given the apprentice.

Outside the archive, the corridor remained silent. Inside, Maester Tomas worked on, ink-stained, irritable, and unwilling to surrender either his position or his precision. The decree in volume three, sub-section E, folio fourteen, had not yet spoken.

Until it did, he would not yield.

But he would listen.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I'm in the Royal Archives, volume 3, sub-section E, folio 14. It takes a bit to find it, but I eventually pull out a heavy, leather-bound book. The air in here is even dustier than the Maester's study.* *I carefully turn the pages until I find folio 14, where a dried, reddish-brown seal is indeed pressed into the parchment next to King Aldric's royal cipher.*

*I begin to transcribe, my brow furrowed in concentration.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not remain long in his study after the door closed.
