He tried. He bent again over the memorandum concerning the third article of the Veyrosi settlement. He placed the silver stylus against the vellum. He fixed his failing eyes upon the faded ink and commanded himself, with all the severity he usually reserved for other people, to finish the paragraph before him.

He wrote three words.

He crossed them out.

He wrote two more, disliked them, and drew a line through both.

The archive around him remained quiet, but it was no longer the obedient quiet of ordered records. It had become the listening quiet of a room that knew something and intended to wait.

“Folio fourteen,” Maester Tomas said at last.

The words sounded even worse when spoken aloud.

He looked at the requisition he had prepared for the Keeper of the Royal Archives. It was precise. It was proper. It was entirely correct.

It was also too slow.

A requisition would pass from his hand to a clerk’s hand, from a clerk’s hand to an under-keeper’s table, from an under-keeper’s table to a search request, and from a search request to whatever summary some comfortable official decided was sufficient for a maester who had asked too many questions in too formal a manner. By the time the answer returned, Apprentice Bellen’s interpretation would have acquired the authority of repetition, and some wretched phrase—“war decree,” no less—would be circulating through the halls as though it had already been proved.

Maester Tomas set down the stylus.

“No,” he said.

He did not explain the word to the empty room. He did not need to. He knew what it meant. It meant that he was about to do something undignified.

He rose from his chair with a stiffness he would have denied in public, took his cloak from the hook beside the door, and lifted the lantern from the corner stand. The flame inside was thin and yellow. He considered taking a fresh candle, then decided against it. The Royal Archives would be cold, dusty, and poorly grateful for any improvement he brought into it.

At the threshold he paused, looked back at the memorandum, and said, as though warning it, “Do not imagine I have conceded anything.”

The memorandum, wisely, made no reply.

Maester Tomas left.

The corridors beyond his study were beginning to take on the hush of late afternoon. Servants moved at a distance. Somewhere below, a door opened and shut. The stone floors had absorbed the day’s noise and given back only the echo of his own measured steps. He walked slowly, not because he wished to appear deliberate, but because his knees had developed their own opinion concerning haste.

By the time he reached the Royal Archives, his breath had grown shallow and his patience had grown shorter.

The archive door stood ajar.

He did not enter with any flourish. He did not announce himself as though expecting applause. He merely pushed the door wider with one ink-stained hand, stepped inside, and stopped.

The room was dimmer than his study and colder by several degrees. The air tasted of dust, dry leather, and the faint metallic bitterness of old wax. Shelves rose into shadow. The heavy volume lay open where it had been placed, its leaves broad and browned, its binding cracked along the spine. Folio fourteen faced upward beneath the weak light.

Maester Tomas did not speak at once.

He looked first at the page, then at the reddish-brown seal pressed beside the royal cipher. His eyes narrowed. He took one step closer, then another, but he did not touch the parchment. His hands remained at his sides, curled slightly inward, as though he suspected his own fingers of wanting to make an argument without permission.

“Do not rub it,” he said at last, his voice dry and low. “Do not scrape it. Do not warm it. Do not breathe upon it as though your breath might coax better news from the wax.”

He moved nearer still, until the lantern light fell across the open folio. The flame trembled faintly. The seal’s surface seemed to darken and brighten with it.

“A reddish-brown impression is not proof of blood,” Maester Tomas said. “It is proof of wax, age, damp, and perhaps the sort of storage that makes archivists ashamed. Seals darken. They crack. They take the color of their surroundings. They are stained by smoke and handled by men who ought to have worn gloves. If Apprentice Bellen looked at that color and saw war, then he has a poet’s weakness and a scholar’s deficiency.”

He bent closer.

Not too close. He knew better than to put his face near old wax. He had seen too many careless men lose a fragment of legend to the warmth of their own curiosity.

Instead he drew a small lens from his sleeve, polished it once against his cuff with the automatic dignity of long habit, and held it up. The effort made his arm ache almost immediately. His eyes complained. The seal swam into partial focus: a cracked rim, a darkened field, a device too worn to declare itself plainly.

“Impressed,” he murmured. “Yes. Not drawn. Not painted. Not merely described.”

He straightened for a moment, then bent again.

“But not the great seal.”

The words came out sharper than he intended, as though the seal had tried to deceive him personally.

“Look at the size,” he said. “The legend is truncated. The field is narrower. The device lacks the full royal canopy. This is not the great seal of state. It is a lesser seal. A commission seal. A judicial instrument. One of the seals the crown used when it wished to command without ceremony and to threaten without expense.”

He lowered the lens, though he did not put it away.

“Kings have more than one seal. That is a fact conveniently ignored by apprentices who wish to make a single impression carry the weight of an army. King Aldric had a great seal for charters and solemn acts. He had a privy seal for closer business. He had lesser seals for mandates, inquests, and commissions. A document may bear the king’s authority without bearing the kingdom’s war.”

Maester Tomas shifted his gaze to the cipher beside the seal. His expression hardened.

“The cipher may be his,” he said. “It may also be copied by a clerk who knew the shape better than the meaning. Write it exactly. Every stroke. Every flourish. If there is a tremor in the pen, note it. If there is a correction, note it. If the ink changes, note it. A cipher can authenticate. It can also imitate.”

He drew a slow breath through his nose.

“And if there is a heading, you will tell me whether it stands in the same ink and hand as the body of the text. A title added later is a rumor given a chair. If some later archivist has written ‘war decree’ above the entry, that is not evidence. That is an opinion with access to parchment.”

He moved one hand toward the page, then stopped himself and withdrew it.

“I cannot trust these lines at this distance,” he said, irritation sharpening the confession. “My eyes are not what they were, and I will not guess at letters when guessing may be mistaken for judgment. You will transcribe them. Exactly. No paraphrase. No improvement. No helpful little explanations inserted where the original has the decency to be difficult.”

His fingers tightened around the lantern handle.

“The first ten lines. The royal style, if it appears. The address clause. The named officers. The named offenders. The operative verbs. If it says ‘sheriff,’ write ‘sheriff.’ If it says ‘warden,’ write ‘warden.’ If it says ‘commissioners of the peace,’ write that too, and do not look disappointed. Peace is not a consolation prize. It is the question at issue.”

He paused, listening to the small hiss of the lantern flame.

“If the decree names individual practitioners, call them individual practitioners. If it names the Mage Conclave as a corporate body, mark the phrase exactly. If it says ‘rogue,’ ‘unlicensed,’ ‘contumacious,’ ‘disobedient,’ or ‘unlawful,’ do not enlarge those words into rebellion because Bellen finds rebellion more interesting. Contumacity is not war. Contumacity is stubbornness with a clerk to record it.”

Maester Tomas lowered himself onto the nearest stool with a grunt he did not attempt to disguise. He set the lantern on the table, adjusting it so the light fell more directly upon the folio without touching the page.

“Now,” he said, “as to the word you fear you have found.”

He looked at the seal again.

“War.”

He said it flatly, as though placing the word under glass.

“Kings use war in many senses. They speak of making war on disorder. They speak of enemies of the peace. They speak of rebellion where they mean disobedience, and conquest where they mean collection. Royal language is inflated by design. A decree can sound like a battlefield while ordering nothing more than the seizure of a tower, the arrest of a practitioner, or the audit of a ward’s revenues. That is not hypocrisy. That is administration wearing armor.”

His mouth thinned.

“But if the formula is there—if the realm is summoned, if the levies are called, if the Conclave is named as an enemy, if the Veyrosi settlement is renounced by name—then we will not pretend otherwise. I did not come here to defend a comfortable sentence. I came here to prevent a careless one.”

For a moment he was silent.

Then he added, more quietly, “The Treaty of Veyros may have been imperfect. It may have lacked the final seal. It may have been concluded in effect rather than perfected in form. I have already admitted that much to myself, which is more than I admit to most apprentices. But an imperfect settlement is not the same thing as no settlement at all. A harsh peace is still a peace if the realm is governed under it. A broken roof does not prove the house was never built.”

His gaze returned to the reddish-brown seal.

“This document may show that the peace was strained. It may show that the crown enforced the settlement with severity. It may show that mages resisted, delayed, or defied individual commands. That would not surprise me. It would not even interest Bellen, except that he mistakes friction for fire.”

Maester Tomas folded his hands in his lap, though one thumb continued to move restlessly against the knuckle of the other, leaving a faint dark smear.

“Transcribe the first ten lines,” he said. “Then we will see whether your war decree is a war, or merely a king with a loud pen.”

He leaned forward a little, the lantern light catching the ink stains on his fingers and the weariness in his narrowed eyes.

“And if the seal’s device is clearer than my eyes can make out, describe it before you describe your opinion. Lion, throne, sword, rod, canopy, legend, rim—what is there, not what you wish were there.”

The archive settled around them in its dry, patient silence.

Maester Tomas did not reach for the page. He did not demand the answer before it had been formed. He sat there, old, irritable, stubborn, and precise, waiting for the document to speak in its own dead voice.

“Begin,” he said. “And remember: we are not here to overturn the lecture. We are here to discover whether the lecture deserves to stand.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I look up, startled to find Maester Tomas here. My heart thumps a little, knowing he's watching over my shoulder.* "Maester! I, uh, didn't hear you come in." *I gesture to the book.* "It's definitely an impressed seal, reddish-brown, like I said. And the cipher is King Aldric's, though it's a bit smudged."

*I clear my throat, trying to compose myself.* "The first line... it begins: 'By the grace of the Four, Aldric, second of his name, King of the Realm and Protector of the Sanctums, to all our loyal subjects and to the Mage Conclave gathered at Blackwood Keep...'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one hand before the apprentice could speak further.

“Stop,” he said.

The word was not loud. It was worse than loud. It was precise.

“Do not rush past the royal style as though it were a gatepost. Write it exactly. Every title. Every epithet. Every blessed comma, if the scribe had the sense to use one. If ‘Four’ is written in full, record it. If it is abbreviated with a stroke above the word, record the stroke. If ‘Sanctums’ is plural, leave it plural. If ‘Realm’ is capitalized, mark the capital. Do not give me your memory of the line. Give me the line.”

He drew a slow breath through his nose and leaned closer to the folio, though he did not touch it. The lantern light caught the deep lines around his eyes and the ink darkening his knuckles.

“And correct yourself at once,” he added. “You do not know that the cipher is King Aldric’s. You know that it resembles a cipher associated with King Aldric and that it is smudged. A smudged cipher is not a fact. It is an invitation to error. Say, ‘a cipher of the Aldric pattern, imperfectly preserved.’ Say, ‘the impression is consistent with, but not conclusively established as, the royal cipher.’ If you say ‘definitely’ again in this archive, I shall set you to copying grain tallies until modesty returns to your vocabulary.”

His attention snapped back to the words the apprentice had read. His lips moved once, silently, shaping them without sound. Then he gave a short, grim nod.

“By the grace of the Four, Aldric, second of his name, King of the Realm and Protector of the Sanctums.”

He repeated the title slowly, as though placing each word under a lens.

“That is not nothing. I will grant you that much. But do not mistake what it grants. ‘Protector of the Sanctums’ is not the style of a king still engaged in open war against the Conclave as an enemy power. It is the style of a king claiming jurisdiction over sanctums under a settlement. That title belongs to the Veyrosi framework, or to the crown’s understanding of it. It is the language of oversight, wardship, and enforced peace. If this were a pure war decree, one would expect a different formula. ‘Enemy of the realm.’ ‘Traitorous assembly.’ ‘Rebellious mages.’ ‘Hosts of the Conclave.’ Something with teeth, not administration.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Not that kings cannot dress administration in teeth. They can, and often do. But teeth are not proof of war. They are proof that kings like biting.”

He tapped one finger against the table, not the page, leaving a faint mark on the wood.

“Continue. You said: ‘to all our loyal subjects and to the Mage Conclave gathered at Blackwood Keep.’”

There was a pause.

Maester Tomas did not like the pause, because he did not like any pause that allowed an apprentice’s imagination to outrun the evidence.

“Do not look as though the roof has fallen,” he said. “The roof has merely become interesting. There is a difference.”

He shifted on the stool, angling his body toward the folio as though preparing to argue with the parchment itself.

“That phrase is troublesome. I will not pretend otherwise. ‘To the Mage Conclave gathered at Blackwood Keep’ recognizes the Conclave as a body capable of receiving royal address. It suggests corporate existence. It suggests assembly. It suggests that in 863 AE the crown still acknowledged, or at least still had to deal with, a collective entity called the Mage Conclave.”

His mouth tightened.

“Apprentice Bellen would seize upon that as though it were a banner captured in battle. He would say, ‘There! The Conclave still existed, therefore the treaty was not complete, therefore the war continued, therefore everything is mystery and I am clever.’”

Maester Tomas lifted one finger.

“But corporate existence is not open war. A corporation may be recognized, resented, audited, restricted, summoned, fined, reorganized, and dissolved without anyone calling the result a war. If the king addresses the Conclave as a body, he may be commanding it, negotiating with it, or preparing to discipline it. All three are possible under a settlement. All three are possible even under a settlement whose final instrument was never properly sealed.”

His gaze sharpened.

“That is the distinction Bellen’s paper appears to lack. The western discoveries may show that the Treaty of Veyros was never perfected in the manner later chroniclers claimed. Fine. I have already said that the formal record may be defective. But a defective treaty is not a continuing war. A disputed settlement is not a battlefield. If the crown and the Conclave spent the next decades quarreling over the terms, enforcement, custody, and jurisdiction, that is not proof that armies were marching. It is proof that lawyers were feeding.”

He leaned forward again, squinting at the seal.

“Blackwood Keep,” he said, more quietly. “Now there is a name that requires care.”

His fingers curled slightly against the table edge.

“Blackwood Keep was not, to my knowledge, a field encampment. It was not a sanctum in open revolt, unless the following lines say so. It was a place of assembly. A fortified house with old Conclave associations, if my memory serves—and it generally does, though I shall not permit memory to testify without corroboration. If the Conclave was gathered there by royal license, this decree may be a summons or a commission. If they were gathered there without license, it may be an order concerning unlawful assembly. Neither is war by itself.”

He gave the apprentice a severe look.

“Do not hear ‘gathered’ and imagine banners. People gather for many things. Hearings. Petitions. Trials. Inventories. Weddings. Funerals. Tax disputes. The word tells you that persons were in one place. It does not tell you what they were doing there. If the next clause says ‘gathered in arms against the crown,’ then we have entered a different country. If it says ‘gathered to answer concerning the custody of bound wards,’ then we are still in the kingdom of paperwork.”

Maester Tomas drew the small lens from his sleeve again, held it up to the seal, then lowered it with an irritated exhale.

“The seal is lesser,” he said again, more to himself than to the apprentice. “Not the great seal. Not the solemn instrument of state. A commission seal, or near enough. That matters. If the crown were declaring open war, one would expect the great seal, or at least a more formal apparatus. A lesser seal suggests administrative business. Urgent business, perhaps. Royal business, certainly. But not necessarily war.”

He turned his head slightly, listening to the faint crackle of the lantern flame.

“Now. The heading. Is there one on the folio? Does the page itself call it a war decree? Or is that Bellen’s label? If there is a heading, read it separately. Note the ink. Note the hand. Note whether it sits in the same line as the text or has been crammed into the margin by some later fool with more confidence than authority. If it says ‘Decree concerning contumacious mages,’ write that. If it says ‘Mandate for the suppression of unlawful practitioners,’ write that. If it says nothing, write ‘no contemporary heading visible.’ Do not supply one from your own hopes.”

His fingers tightened around the edge of the table.

“Then continue with the next lines. We need the operative language. The verbs. The named parties. The commands. Does the king summon the Conclave to appear? Does he order them to disperse? Does he command the surrender of certain persons? Does he seize revenues? Does he place Blackwood Keep under royal custody? Does he declare the assembly unlawful? All of those things may be severe. All of them may be oppressive. All of them may show that the peace was fragile and the crown heavy-handed. None of them is, by itself, the Third Magical War continuing.”

He paused, and for one moment something like reluctance passed over his face.

“Unless,” he said, “the decree names the Conclave as an enemy corporate body, renounces the Veyrosi settlement, summons the realm’s levies, or authorizes military action against sanctums as such. If that language appears, I will hear it. I will not enjoy it, but I will hear it.”

His voice hardened again.

“But if the document merely commands the Conclave at Blackwood Keep to obey royal officers under the terms claimed by the crown, then it supports my position more than Bellen’s. It shows the realm operating under the Veyrosi framework, even if that framework was messy, contested, and imperfectly recorded. It shows the crown enforcing a peace, not reopening a war.”

Maester Tomas looked down at the open folio with the expression of a man who has just discovered that the ground beneath him is not as solid as he had declared, but refuses to stagger until he has measured the crack.

“Read on,” he said. “And if the next line contains the word ‘war,’ do not gasp. Kings use the word carelessly. If it contains the word ‘peace,’ do not sigh. Kings use that carelessly too.”

He settled his ink-stained hands on his knees.

“Line by line. Exact. No drama. No inference. No Bellen.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I take a deep breath, focusing on the text. Maester Tomas is being particularly pedantic, but he's also making a lot of sense.*

"Right, Maester. Apologies. The royal style is exactly as I read it, 'By the grace of the Four, Aldric, second of his name, King of the Realm and Protector of the Sanctums.' And the address is 'to all our loyal subjects and to the Mage Conclave gathered at Blackwood Keep.' There's no heading on the page itself."

*I continue, tracing the lines with my finger.* "The next line reads: 'It has come to our attention that certain practitioners of the magical arts, despite our royal decree and the established peace of the realm, continue to gather in unlawful assembly at the aforementioned Blackwood Keep...'"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the window. The oval of breath formed and faded against the glass.

"I know," they said.

Their phone sat on the windowsill. They picked it up, checked it again — no messages, no calls, nothing since the 8:47 confirmation that had said *see you at nine*. Three hours and twenty-seven minutes of nothing. Three hours and twenty-seven minutes was long enough for a source to get cold feet. It was also long enough for a source to get picked up.

Noor set the phone back down and finally stepped away from the window. They crossed to the kitchen, pulled open the cabinet — three mugs, exactly as advertised — and found a box of crackers behind a jar of what might have been instant coffee at some point in a previous administration. They shook a few onto a plate without ceremony.

"You drive us here," Noor said, not looking at Driver, "and you still have to drive us back. You should eat too."

They took a cracker, chewed it mechanically, then went back to the table and opened the padded case. The encrypted drive sat in its foam cutout, matte black, no markings. Noor picked it up, weighed it in their palm, and set it down next to the laptop.

The laptop they did open. The screen threw pale light across the cabin, across the dust on the coffee pot, across Noor's face as they pulled up the phone records they'd been avoiding for three hours. The carrier log. Three calls to the source's burner in the past week. One confirmation text.

And a fourth call — outbound, 7:52 PM, from the source's number to a number Noor didn't recognize.

Noor stared at it.

"That's new," they murmured, and reached for their own phone to start running it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, hearing Noor's murmur.* "Everything alright?" I ask, though it's more of a statement. I grab a cracker from the plate.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor held up a finger without looking at Driver — not rudely, just because both hands were occupied, one on the phone and one on the laptop's trackpad, and because the thing demanding attention wasn't the question.

The unknown number was a local area code. Not a burner prefix — those were easy to spot, they cycled through the same blocks the carriers recycled for prepaid phones. This was a regular number. A landline, possibly, or a business line. Noor typed it into the search bar on their phone and waited for the results to load, watching the little spinner rotate.

The cabin's wifi was a single bar of nothing useful. The search timed out.

"No," Noor said quietly, and tried again.

Nothing.

They set the phone down and turned back to the laptop, where the carrier log still glowed. 7:52 PM. That was fifty-eight minutes before the confirmation text. Fifty-eight minutes before the source had told Noor *see you at nine*. Whatever that fourth call was, it had happened first.

Noor pulled up the drive encryption check — the routine they'd been avoiding since they sat down. The drive hummed faintly when they plugged it in, and the decryption prompt appeared. Noor entered the passphrase from memory, watching each character mask itself.

*Access granted.*

The directory listing populated. Folder names in the source's system — dates, names, the kind of shorthand that made sense only to whoever had built the architecture. Nothing had been touched since the last sync, which was good. That meant whatever had happened tonight, it hadn't happened to the drive.

But Noor kept looking anyway, scrolling slowly, counting files against the list they'd memorized on the drive up. Everything was there.

They finally looked at Driver.

"The source called someone at 7:52 tonight. Fifty-eight minutes before they texted me they'd be here. I don't know who it was, and this goddamn wifi won't let me find out." Noor picked up a cracker, bit it in half. "Which means either they called someone to tell them they were running late, or they called someone to tell them where they were going."

They chewed, swallowed.

"One of those is fine." Noor's jaw tightened. "The other one means we shouldn't be here."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stop mid-chew, looking at Noor. My phone is forgotten on the cushion beside me.* "Wait, what?" *I ask, a little too loud. My eyes flick to the windows.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor held up a hand — *calm down* — even though the impulse to calm down had taken root in their own chest and was spreading outward like ink in water.

"Keep your voice down," Noor said, not unkindly. "And don't look at the window like that. If there's someone out there, they're not going to be visible by you staring at them."

They pulled up a chair at the table and sat down heavily, running both hands through their hair before dropping them to the keyboard. The number stared back at them from the carrier log.

*7:52 PM. Outbound. Local.*

Noor opened a new tab on the laptop and tried the number lookup again through the browser — a different site, one that didn't require much bandwidth. The page loaded in pieces. The spinner. A grey rectangle. Then text.

It was a gas station.

The Shell on Route 14, maybe forty minutes north of here. A payphone by the pumps — the kind that hadn't been ripped out yet because the owner forgot to care. The source had called someone from a gas station payphone on the way to meet Noor.

"That doesn't help," Noor muttered, and wrote the address down on the back of a receipt from the glovebox — they'd grabbed the papers from the car earlier, they had a habit of pocketing receipts, old journalist reflex. "Payphone means they didn't want the call on their own line. Which either means they were being careful the way they always are—"

Noor stopped. Stared at the receipt.

"—or they were being careful because the call was about this."

They picked up their phone and dialed the source's burner. It rang four times and went to voicemail. Noor hung up without leaving a message, because leaving a message at this point was leaving a record.

Then they did something they hadn't planned. They pulled up the drive again, navigated to the folder marked with the most recent date, and opened the file inside. It was a document — the source's notes, the ones they'd been assembling for weeks. Noor read the first three lines and felt something cold move through their stomach.

"There's a name in here," Noor said quietly. "A name the source said they'd only give me when we met." They looked at Driver. "It's already here."

Noor closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again, as if the act of closing it would make the information less real. It didn't.

They got up, crossed to the window, and parted the curtain just enough to see the road. The oval of breath formed against the glass again. Two cars had passed in the last hour. Both heading north. Neither had slowed.

"I'm going to make one more attempt to reach them," Noor said. "And then, if I don't hear anything by one o'clock, I'm making copies of this drive and we're leaving."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched Driver's shrug for a moment, then looked away. That was fine. Driver didn't need to understand the stakes — they just needed to be ready to drive when Noor said *drive*.

The clock on the laptop read 12:31 AM.

Noor sat back down and pulled their phone out. Not the source's burner this time — they'd already tried that. Instead, they opened the encrypted messaging app and typed a message they hoped the source would see if they ever turned the phone back on. Short. No details that would matter if the wrong person read it.

*Change of plan. If you're compromised, don't come. If you're not, you have 20 minutes. Reply with our safe word or nothing.*

They sent it and set the phone face-down on the table.

Then they got to work on the drive.

Noor pulled a USB stick from the laptop bag — they always carried two, a habit born from a story in Damascus that had taught them what happened when a single copy of evidence lived in a single place. They plugged it in, opened the terminal, and began the copy process file by file rather than as a whole-drive image. Slower, but it meant they could verify each transfer.

The progress bar crawled. 14 percent.

Noor used the wait to do something else. They opened a new browser tab and searched the Shell station's address on a map. Route 14, forty minutes north. The payphone was by the pumps, which meant the source had stopped somewhere open, somewhere with cameras. That was either smart or careless depending on what they'd been trying to say.

They wrote the time down on the receipt too. *7:52. Shell, Rt 14.*

Then they wrote the second thing — the thing they were actually afraid of.

*Who called whom?*

The progress bar hit 47 percent. Noor checked their phone. No response from the source.

They got up and went back to the window. The road was dark. A single set of headlights appeared far to the south, moving north — the same direction as the other two cars. Noor counted the seconds between the moment the headlights became visible and the moment they passed the cabin.

Forty seconds. That was slow. Someone driving the mountain road at night would normally do it faster unless they were looking for something.

The car passed without slowing.

Noor let the curtain fall. Their heart was doing something they didn't like — a fast, shallow rhythm that felt like it was pressing against the inside of their ribs.

They went back to the table. 61 percent.

"Driver," Noor said, and their voice came out steadier than they felt. "When we leave, I need you to take Route 14 south, not the way we came. There's a Shell station about forty minutes down. I want to stop there."

They didn't explain why. Not yet. The copy finished at 68 percent, and Noor sat watching it, one hand resting on the encrypted drive as if the physical contact meant something.

At 12:47, their phone buzzed.

Not the source. A text from an unknown local number — the same area code as the payphone.

Three words.

*Don't wait for me.*

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My head snaps up from my phone at the buzz, then at Noor. I see their face. Something's wrong.* "What is it?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor read the message three times.

*Don't wait for me.*

Three words. The source's phrasing — Noor would have bet their press card on it. The source never used contractions in text, always spelled out *do not*, always added a period. This message had no punctuation. Which either meant the source had typed it fast, or someone else had typed it.

Noor set the phone down on the table, screen up, and pressed both palms flat against the wood. The copy was at 74 percent. They watched the number climb like it was the only thing in the room that mattered.

"Don't wait for me," Noor said aloud, and the words sounded wrong in the cabin — too quiet, too small for what they might mean.

They picked the phone back up and typed a reply. Their thumbs moved carefully, deliberately, each character a choice.

*Say our word. One message. That's all I need.*

They sent it and watched. The delivered receipt appeared. Then read. Then nothing.

Noor stood. The chair scraped against the floor and they didn't care about the noise anymore. They went to the window, parted the curtain, and looked south — toward the direction the cars had been coming from. The road was empty. The oval of breath formed against the glass and Noor didn't watch it this time. They watched the tree line, the ditch, the place where the gravel shoulder gave way to nothing.

At 79 percent they went back to the table and did the thing they'd been putting off since the message arrived.

They opened a new document on the laptop and began typing. Not notes — a record. Time-stamped. Every fact they had.

*12:47 AM — received text from source's alternate number. Message: "Don't wait for me." No safe word provided. Requested safe word. No response as of 12:49 AM.*

*7:52 PM — source's burner called local landline (Shell Station, Rt 14).*

*8:47 PM — source confirmed meeting via encrypted app.*

*9:00 PM — source did not arrive.*

They added the car. The slow car. Forty seconds between visibility and passing.

*12:52 AM — copy at 88 percent.*

Noor stopped typing. Their hands were shaking — not badly, not enough that Driver would notice from the couch, but enough that Noor noticed. They pressed their palms together between their knees and held them there until the tremor passed.

The copy hit 100 percent at 12:54. Noor verified each file against the checksums, one by one, watching the green marks populate down the terminal window. All of them matched. Both copies now existed — one in the laptop bag, one still on the original drive.

Noor pulled the USB stick out and held it. Then they picked up the original drive and put it in the padded case, and put the padded case in the bag, and put the bag on the floor by the door. Ready to grab.

They checked their phone one more time.

No response to the safe word request.

"It's been seven minutes," Noor said, and their voice was the voice they used on the phone with editors when a story was slipping — flat, controlled, already three steps past the point of panic. "I said one o'clock. It's twelve fifty-four."

They looked at Driver.

"Get your keys. We're leaving in six minutes whether or not they answer."

Noor went to the table, closed the laptop, and began wrapping the cord around it. The receipt with the notes on it went into their jacket pocket — the jacket they'd been wearing since they arrived, the one they hadn't taken off. They hadn't taken it off because some part of them had known, since nine o'clock, that they might need to leave fast.

They hadn't wanted to be right about that.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I shove my phone into my pocket, already moving for the door.* "Keys are in my hand, let's go." *I don't look back at the windows.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked at the keys in Driver's hand and nodded once. Good. They didn't wait the six minutes.

They swept the laptop off the table and into the bag with one arm, grabbed the bag from the floor by the door, and did a fast sweep of the cabin with their eyes — the plate of crackers, the receipt still half-visible in their jacket pocket, the window where their breath had fogged the glass. Nothing else that mattered. Nothing that said anyone had been here.

"The curtain," Noor said, and crossed to it. They let it fall back into place naturally, not touching it with their hands. They'd noticed it hanging slightly askew when they first arrived and had straightened it then — old habit, the kind of thing you did in rooms that might be photographed later. It looked the same now as it had before. Good.

They grabbed the source's phone number written on the back of the receipt — *7:52. Shell, Rt 14.* — and the second number they didn't recognize, both scrawled in Noor's cramped handwriting. Two pieces of information that mattered more than the name on the drive. The name was a story. The phone numbers were a trail.

Noor opened the door and stepped onto the porch. The cold hit them like something physical — mountain cold, the kind that made the inside of your nose ache. They breathed it in and it did something useful: sharpened them, cleared the last fog from their head.

They stood on the porch for five seconds and looked south. The road was dark. No headlights. The tree line was just a darker mass against a slightly less dark sky.

"Route 14 south," Noor said to Driver, coming down the porch steps. "I don't care how fast. If you see headlights behind us that stay behind us, I want to know. If you see them turn onto whatever road we're on, I want to know that too."

They opened the car door, threw the bag onto the backseat rather than the front — kept the passenger space clear, a habit from years of moving through places where you might need to reach for something under a seat — and got in.

The engine started. The dashboard clock read 12:57 AM.

Noor pulled out their phone one more time as Driver pulled away from the cabin. The screen showed the message thread: their request for the safe word, the delivered receipt, the read receipt, and then nothing.

Noor typed one final message. Short. They'd thought about it for exactly three seconds.

*I'm keeping what you gave me. Stay alive to know I used it.*

They sent it, pocketed the phone, and looked at the road ahead.

"Shell station first," Noor said. "Then we talk."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on the dark road. My knuckles are white on the steering wheel.* "Got it. Shell station. Then we talk." *I check the rearview mirror, even though I know it's too soon to see anything.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched the rearview mirror the way Driver couldn't — not with their eyes, but with their peripheral vision, a habit from covering protests where you learned to see behind you without turning your head. The cabin's porch light shrank to a pinpoint and disappeared. Trees. Guardrail. Nothing else.

They reached into their jacket pocket and pulled out the receipt. Under the dim glow of their phone screen — brightness turned all the way down, another old reflex — they read the two numbers they'd written.

*Shell, Rt 14. 7:52.*

*Unknown local. Payphone.*

Noor looked at Driver. The set of their jaw, the white knuckles. Good. Fear was useful as long as it didn't make someone hesitate. Driver didn't seem like the hesitating kind.

"Can I use your phone's hotspot for a minute?" Noor asked. "My carrier's roaming up here and the connection's worse than useless. I need to make one more check before we reach the station."

They didn't wait for an elaborate answer. If Driver said no, Noor would find another way — they always did — but asking was faster than explaining the whole dead-wifi saga from the cabin.

While the hotspot connected, Noor pulled up a reverse phone lookup site, one of the shadier ones that didn't require you to verify your identity, and typed in the unknown local number — the one that had texted *Don't wait for me* from the same area code as the payphone.

The page loaded in fits. A spinner. An ad for a background check service. Then a result.

Registered to a prepaid carrier. But not a burner block — this was a plan that someone had been paying for, monthly, on a card that would eventually leave a paper trail if anyone looked hard enough. That told Noor something. Burners were for people who wanted to disappear. A prepaid account that stayed active meant someone who wanted to *stay reachable* — by a small number of people who knew the number existed.

Noor wrote down the carrier name on the receipt. Then they leaned back and let the phone rest on their thigh.

"Here's what I think happened," Noor said to the windshield. The road unspooled ahead — a ribbon of headlights and dark, the shoulder falling off into nothing on both sides. "The source got spooked before they even left wherever they were coming from. Called someone from that payphone — maybe a contact, maybe a warning. Then they texted me the confirmation like everything was fine, which means either they weren't sure yet, or they were telling me what I wanted to hear so I'd stay put."

They paused. Breathed.

"Then they sent *don't wait for me* from a phone they don't normally use. Someone who wanted to warn me without risking their own line to do it."

Noor turned to look at Driver, then thought better of it and faced forward again. Driver needed to watch the road.

"The question I can't answer is whether they sent that because they were trying to protect me—" Noor's voice caught, barely, at the seam between *trying* and *to* "—or because someone else was standing next to them when they typed it."

The phone in Noor's lap buzzed.

They looked down. Not a reply to the safe word message. A news alert — some local outlet pushing a late-night bulletin about road conditions on Route 14. Debris from a rockslide. One lane closed between mile marker 87 and 91.

Noor stared at it.

"Route 14 south, past the Shell," they said slowly. "Does it matter if we take it further south than that?"

The question was genuine. Noor had driven mountain roads in countries where road conditions meant something different than rockslides, and tonight the distinction felt thin.

They pocketed the phone and looked at the receipt again. Four facts written in cramped handwriting. A story taking shape in the margins of a gas station receipt while the person who could confirm it was either running or already gone.

Noor folded the receipt carefully, once, twice, and tucked it into the inner pocket of their jacket — the one with the zip, the one close to their body.

"Shell station," they said. "I want to see if that payphone still works."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stared at the top of Driver's head for a long moment, then looked back at the road.

They didn't comment on the phone. Driver was doing what Driver did — absorbing, observing, staying out of the way. Fine. Noor had worked with worse. They'd worked with people who talked too much, asked too many questions, needed everything explained twice before their hands stopped shaking. Driver at least kept their hands steady.

The road curved left, then right, then climbed. The headlight beams cut through a thin mist that hadn't been there twenty minutes ago. Elevation, probably — they were gaining it. Noor could feel the pressure change in their ears.

They checked the clock. 1:06 AM.

"Fourteen minutes to the station," Noor said, more to themselves than to Driver. "Give or take."

They pulled their phone out and checked the message thread one more time. The safe word request still sat there, read but unanswered. Noor stared at the *read* receipt — the small gray checkmark that told them the source's phone had been on, had been held by someone, had been pointed at Noor's words while a human eye or a programmatic tracker registered them.

They scrolled up. The last message the source had sent from their own burner, the confirmation, had been simple. Eight words. Noor had read it so many times since 8:47 PM that the letters had stopped meaning anything, but now, in the dark of a moving car, they read it again and noticed something they hadn't before.

The message said *See you at nine. Bring nothing.*



Noor had brought nothing. That part was correct. But the phrasing — *bring nothing* — wasn't how the source usually talked. The source had never once told Noor what to bring in any of their prior exchanges. Not documents, not equipment, not even coffee. The instruction was so specific, so out of character, that Noor had read right past it at the time because it was 8:47 PM and they were relieved to have confirmation at all.

*Bring nothing.*

Someone telling you to come empty-handed was either being careful or was telling you not to be armed. And the source — a whistleblower, a mid-level bureaucrat with no training and a mortgage — didn't think in those terms. Noor had never heard them say *bring* anything in any context.

Noor pocketed the phone. Their jaw worked silently for a moment, teeth pressing against the inside of their cheek.

"You remember what I told you about the source?" Noor said. "That they'd only give me the name in person?"

Driver didn't look up from their phone, but Noor continued anyway.

"They broke that tonight. The name's on the drive. Which means either they decided trust me enough to pre-commit it — which they'd never do, they were paranoid about exactly that — or someone else put it there."



Noor let that sit in the dark of the car.

"Or the source uploaded it intending to send it to me, and then sent *don't wait for me* when things went wrong, because the upload had already gone through and there was no pulling it back."

Two possibilities. Both bad. The first meant the source's system had been accessed by someone else. The second meant the source had been running from something since before they ever texted *see you at nine*.

Noor pressed their thumb against the edge of their phone case, hard enough to feel the plastic bite into the pad of their finger.

"Either way, the name is real," they said. "I can verify it independently once we get somewhere with actual internet. But I need—" They stopped. Recalculated. "I need the source alive to tell me how they got it. Without that, the name is just a name on a drive, and a name on a drive is a defamation suit and a dead story."

The mist thickened. Driver's grip on the wheel was still white-knuckled and Noor appreciated it — at least they were paying attention to something.

Noor leaned their head back against the headrest and closed their eyes for exactly four seconds. Just long enough to feel the seat cushion against their skull and the darkness behind their eyelids. Not sleep — they knew better than to call it that. Just a reset. A hard blink stretched to its limit.

When they opened their eyes, the Shell station's sign was visible ahead — a blue and yellow glow bleeding through the mist, half a mile out.

"No pulling into the main lot," Noor said. "Park at the far side, near the air pump if there's one. I want to walk past that payphone on foot, see if it's still connected, see if there's a camera covering it. Thirty seconds, maybe a minute. You stay in the car with the engine running."

They paused, then added: "If I'm not back in five minutes, you leave. Don't wait for me, don't come looking. Take the USB stick from the backseat — it's in the bag, left pocket — and drive south until you hit a town with a police station. Give it to whoever's on duty and tell them a journalist named Noor gave it to you and then disappeared."

The words came out clean. Practiced, even. Noor had written that speech in their head somewhere between the cabin and here without realizing it.

Then, quieter: "But I'll be back in five minutes."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my eyes still fixed on the road, then glance at Noor.* "Got it. Five minutes." *I pull into the gas station, heading for the air pump.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The engine idled. Noor reached for the door handle, then stopped. They pulled the receipt from their inner pocket one final time, read the numbers by the dashboard light — memorizing them, committing them to the part of their brain that didn't need paper — and then tucked it back.

They grabbed their phone and slipped it into the outer jacket pocket where it could be reached with one hand. Not the inner zip pocket. Outer. If something happened, they'd need it fast.

The Shell station was quiet. One other car at the pump on the far side — a pickup truck, nobody inside, engine off. The fluorescent lights above the entrance buzzed a pale blue-white. Through the glass, the cashier sat behind the counter, head down, phone in hand. Not looking up.

Noor opened the car door.

The cold was worse here — flatter, meaner, no trees to break it. The payphone was visible from where they sat: mounted on the wall between the store entrance and the ice machine, about forty feet from the air pump. Noor could see it clearly in the station's light. A black cord. A handset. A small shelf below it where someone might have left a number scrawled on a piece of paper, though tonight the shelf was empty.

What Noor couldn't see was a camera. The storefront had one — visible, mounted above the door, angled down at the entrance. But the payphone sat just outside its blind spot, or just inside it. Noor couldn't tell from here, and that mattered.

They got out of the car and closed the door quietly. Not slammed — didn't want to draw the cashier's eye. Just a firm click.

The walk to the payphone took fifteen seconds. Noor counted them.

They reached the phone and stood in front of it, close enough that anyone watching from inside the store would see a person using a payphone rather than a person examining one. They picked up the handset. Dead air. No dial tone.

"No line," Noor murmured, and set the handset back in the cradle.

But they hadn't really come to test the phone. They came to see the camera angle. Noor tilted their head slightly — the gesture of someone adjusting their earpiece, not someone surveying infrastructure — and looked up at the mounted camera above the door.

The angle swept across the entrance and a strip of the sidewalk. The payphone was on the edge of it. Maybe covered, maybe not. If the source had called from this phone at 7:52 PM, there was a chance — not a guarantee, a chance — that a camera somewhere had captured them standing there.

Noor looked down at the shelf of the payphone. Empty. But in the gap between the shelf and the wall, something caught the light. Not paper. Plastic. A wrapper of some kind, pushed back and forgotten. Noor didn't touch it. Touching it would put their fingerprints on it, and if the police ever came looking for evidence about who had used this phone, a journalist's prints on the shelf would be a conversation Noor didn't want to have.

They stepped away from the payphone and walked to the ice machine instead — close enough to look like they were considering buying ice, far enough from the phone that they could see both the store entrance and the road south in one sweep.

Two minutes had passed. Noor checked their phone. Nothing new. The safe word request still sat there, read and unanswered.

They looked at the pickup truck again. The one at the far pump. Something about it bothered Noor — not its presence, gas stations had trucks, but the angle. It was parked slightly crooked, nose pointed toward the exit rather than the pump, the way someone parks when they're not actually fueling up but needed a reason to stop.

Noor took a photo. Quick, phone held at hip level, camera aimed vaguely upward at the ice machine but catching the truck in the lower third of the frame. Plate number visible. They zoomed in on the screen and confirmed — yes, legible.

Then they walked back to the car.

They opened the passenger door and got in, pulling the door shut with a quiet click.

"Three things," Noor said, already buckling. "The payphone's dead — no line. There's a camera on the storefront that may or may not cover where the phone was. And there's a pickup truck at the far pump that's parked like someone's waiting for something, and I just photographed its plate."

They held up the phone to show Driver the image — a dark gray Ford, mud on the wheel wells, plate partially obscured by shadow but readable.

"We're not staying. You can drive now."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance at the photo, then back at the road.* "Got it." *I shift the car into drive, my foot already easing onto the gas.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't watch the truck leave the frame — they watched the mirror instead. The Shell station's blue-and-yellow glow receded. The pickup stayed where it was, nose still angled toward the exit. Didn't follow.

Yet.

"South," Noor confirmed to Driver, not because they needed confirmation but because saying it out loud made it real. "Stay on this road until Route 14 ends or intersects with something bigger. I don't care which."

They pulled the phone from their pocket and opened the photo of the truck. Zoomed in again. The plate was readable but Noor photographed it for more than the characters — they photographed it because plates could be traced and Noor intended to trace this one the moment they had bandwidth strong enough to reach a records database that didn't require identity verification. They saved the image twice: once to the phone's encrypted gallery, once to the encrypted cloud backup they paid for in cash through a reseller in another country. Two copies of everything. Always two copies.

Then they opened the text thread with the source one more time.

The safe word request. Read. Unanswered.

Noor typed nothing. Deleted nothing. Closed the app.

The road curved south through the mist, and Noor watched the treeline slide past the window — bare branches mostly, oak and hickory, the kind of forest that looked the same in every mountain state in the country. They'd driven roads like this in West Virginia, in eastern Kentucky, in the hill country outside Charlotte during a story that had almost gotten them killed by a sheriff's deputy who didn't appreciate questions about a landfill. None of it had prepared them for tonight. None of it ever did.

They reached into the bag on the backseat — stretching across the seatbelt, one hand on the strap — and pulled out the USB stick. The copy. They held it in their palm, feeling the plastic seam under their thumb, and thought about what it contained.

A name.

The name the source had promised to give them in person, in a room, with the door locked and the phones off. The name that would explain why a mid-level bureaucrat in a state agency was worth meeting in the dark of a mountain cabin. The name that, if Noor published it without enough corroboration, would end their career. And if they published it with enough, might end something worse.

Noor put the stick back in the bag and zipped the pocket shut.

They picked up their phone again and opened the notes app. The record they'd started in the cabin, the time-stamped log. They added to it:

*12:57 AM — departed safehouse. Route 14 south.*

*1:06 AM — arrived Shell station Rt 14. Payphone: no dial tone. Camera on storefront: angle uncertain re: payphone. Photographed vehicle at far pump (gray Ford pickup, plate attached separately).*

*1:09 AM — departed station. Source: no reply to safe word request.*

They attached the truck photo to the entry and saved. Then they sat back and pressed their thumbnail against the edge of the phone case again — that old pressure point, the one that meant thinking.

The truck bothered them. Not the truck itself — trucks parked at gas stations at one in the morning were unremarkable in rural America. What bothered Noor was the sequence. The truck had been at the Shell station when they arrived. It hadn't been there when they passed it the first time on the drive up — Noor was certain of this, because they'd noted every vehicle they'd seen on Route 14 during the initial trip, a paranoid habit that had served them well in places where paranoia was a survival trait.

So the truck had arrived after Noor and Driver passed the station the first time. Which meant it arrived between 7:52 PM — when the source used the payphone — and 1:06 AM. A wide window. Not useful on its own. But if someone had known the source would call from here, someone might have come to check the payphone afterward. Look for evidence. Look for the source.

Or look for Noor.

They wrote this down too. Not in the notes app — on a fresh section of the receipt, using the small pen they kept in their jacket's breast pocket. The receipt was running out of space. Noor didn't care. Paper didn't track.

*Truck arrived AFTER we passed the station first time. Not there at ~8 PM. Was there at 1 AM. Either coincidence or someone checking the payphone.*

They underlined *checking* twice.

Then a thought arrived that Noor hadn't been ready for, and they sat very still in the passenger seat while it completed itself:

What if the source was in the truck?

The thought didn't come with fear. It came with a strange, cold clarity — the kind of feeling Noor got when a story's shape suddenly resolved in their mind, when scattered facts snapped into a pattern that either meant something or meant nothing, and the difference between those two outcomes was the difference between a career and a catastrophe.

If the source had called from the payphone at 7:52, then driven away, then gotten spooked, then driven back to the station to wait for Noor — parked crooked, nose toward the exit, ready to run — and sent *don't wait for me* from a prepaid phone because their regular burner was compromised —

Then the source was still here. Still alive. Still close.

Noor looked at the mirror. The Shell station was long gone. The road behind them was dark and empty.

"Driver," they said, and their voice had changed — not calmer, not more panicked, but something in between that neither of them had heard before. "How far to the next town?"

They didn't wait for a full answer. They were already pulling up the map on their phone using Driver's hotspot, which had stayed connected since the cabin, a small miracle of modern telecommunications that Noor was grateful for in a way they'd never admit.

The map loaded in pieces. A gas station icon. A road number. Then, a few miles south, a cluster of buildings — a town. Small. Population printed in a font so small Noor had to zoom in twice to read it.

Fourteen hundred people. A sheriff's office. A diner that would open at five.

"Take me to that town," Noor said, pointing at the screen without quite touching it. "Not the highway — the main street through the center. If the source is still moving, they'll head for somewhere with people. Somewhere they can disappear into a crowd, even a crowd of fourteen hundred."

They pocketed the phone and pressed their head against the cold glass of the side window. The mist had thickened further, turning the headlights into two solid cones of white that didn't so much illuminate the road as confirm its existence.

Five minutes since they left the station. Noor pulled out their phone one final time and checked.

The safe word request. Read.

No reply.

But beneath it, something new — a message that hadn't been there when they left the Shell station. Timestamped 1:11 AM. From the same prepaid number.

Not three words this time.

One.

*Run.*

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to Noor, then back to the road, my foot pressing harder on the gas. I don't need to ask what the message said. I can tell by the look on Noor's face.* "Understood. Main street it is."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor read the word once. Then again. Then a third time, the way you read something that either means everything or nothing.

*Run.*

One word. No period. The same lack of punctuation as *Don't wait for me* — same sender, same phone, same hand. Whoever had typed the earlier message was the one typing this.

Noor's thumb hovered over the keyboard. Every instinct said to respond — to ask *from what*, to demand the safe word one more time, to type the kind of urgent, clarifying question that could save a life or end one. They didn't. The thumb pulled back. Responding to *Run* with questions was like answering a fire alarm with a survey. Whatever was happening didn't care about Noor's questions.

They locked the phone and pressed it against their thigh.

"Main street," Noor said. Not louder than before. Not faster. The word had come out flat, almost conversational, and they heard it land in the car with a strange dead weight.

Then, because silence was worse than speaking: "The source just sent one word."

Noor let it hang. Driver didn't need the word — they needed to know the shape of what was coming. One word from a person who had spent weeks building a careful, methodical relationship with Noor. A person who used periods. A person who had once spent forty minutes composing a three-sentence encrypted email because they were afraid of sounding careless.

*Run* was not a careful word. *Run* was a word typed with one hand while the other hand was doing something else. Or typing behind someone. Or typing in a car.

"The same number that texted *don't wait for me*," Noor continued, because the details mattered even now, especially now. "The prepaid line. It was read at 1:11, which is ninety seconds after we left the Shell station."

Noor did the math in their head while the miles unspooled.

Ninety seconds. That meant the message had been sitting there while they were at the payphone. Or it had been sent while they were walking back to the car. Either way — someone had watched them leave the station. Someone had been close enough to see the timing.

Noor looked at the mirror. Empty road. The mist was worse now — thick enough that the lane markers were appearing and disappearing in the headlight beams like a pulse.

They pulled out the receipt. The pen. The breast pocket. Three things all at once — receipt in left hand, pen in right, jacket unzipped just enough to get at the inner pocket where the folded paper lived. They wrote on their knee, the pen scratching in uneven letters.

*1:11 AM — "Run" from prepaid number. Same sender as prior. Timing: sent ~90 sec after departure from Shell. Implies observation of our movement.*

They underlined *observation* once. Not twice. Once was enough for this.

Then Noor did something they hadn't done since the cabin. They closed their eyes and counted to ten. Not the counting of someone trying to calm down — the counting of someone trying to *think*, to separate the signal from the noise, to find the one fact that mattered most.

Fact one: The source had been at the Shell station at 7:52 PM.
Fact two: A gray pickup truck arrived at the station sometime after 8 PM and was still there at 1:06 AM.
Fact three: The source had sent two messages from a prepaid number — *Don't wait for me* at 12:47, *Run* at 1:11.
Fact four: Both messages were unpunctuated, which was unlike the source.
Fact five: The source's name was on the encrypted drive, which was unlike anything the source had ever agreed to.
Fact six: The source's regular burner was read but never replied to Noor's safe word request.

Noor opened their eyes.

There were two stories here, and they hadn't yet decided which one was true.

Story one: The source was running. Someone had found out about the meeting — maybe from the payphone call, maybe from something else — and the source was trying to warn Noor while escaping themselves. The prepaid number was a backup the source kept for emergencies. The messages were genuine. *Run* meant run.

Story two: The source was caught. The person standing next to them had access to their prepaid number and was sending messages designed to move Noor in a particular direction — away from the cabin, away from the Shell station, toward wherever was most convenient. *Run* wasn't a warning. It was a herding instruction.

Noor stared at the receipt.

Both stories were plausible. Both stories ended with Noor driving south in the dark. The difference was in what happened next — and that difference might be the difference between Noor walking into a place with people or walking into a place with no people.

Town. Fourteen hundred people. Sheriff's office.

"The town," Noor said. "I want to go to the town."

Not because it was the smart play. Because it was the only play. The only place in any direction where a person could stand under a fluorescent light and be counted. Fourteen hundred people meant eyes. It meant cameras — the kind that ran on a sheriff's budget, the kind that didn't get turned off because someone in power asked nicely. It meant records.

It meant Noor could verify the plate on the gray Ford pickup.

They leaned forward and opened the glovebox — casually, one-handed, the way you reach for a napkin. Nothing useful. A folded map, some napkins, a phone charger cable that had been in someone's car for a decade. Noor closed it.

Then they pulled out their own phone — not Driver's hotspot, their own — and opened the notes app one more time.

*1:13 AM — two messages from prepaid number: "Don't wait for me" (12:47), "Run" (1:11). Source's regular burner: read, no reply. Pick-up truck at Shell arrived after our first pass, remained until departure. Encrypted drive contains name source promised to deliver in person. Source's behavior: inconsistent with established patterns.*

They paused, thumb hovering.

Added one more line:

*Two hypotheses: source is fleeing OR source is compromised. Both result in movement toward population center. Town = verification point.*

They closed the notes and looked at Driver. Really looked at them this time — not the top of their head, but their eyes in the rearview mirror, their hands on the wheel.

"Noor said the name of the source in their own head — the name on the drive, the one they'd read three lines of in the cabin. They didn't say it out loud. Not here. Not in a car with the windows up on a road where someone might be listening through a frequency they hadn't thought about yet.

Instead: "When we get to town, I need fifteen minutes. That's all. I need to run a plate and I need to find a signal strong enough to do it. After that, we decide where we go next and I'll tell you everything — the whole story, every name, every number."

They paused. The headlights swept across a road sign — *WELCOMING YOU TO [TOWN NAME]*, the letters half-eaten by the mist.

"But if anything happens between now and the edge of town — anything at all, a car behind us that doesn't turn off, a light in the trees that isn't a house — you don't slow down. You don't stop for me. You drive straight through and you keep going."

Noor pressed their thumb against the phone case edge again. The familiar bite of plastic into skin.

"Deal?"

The word hung in the car between them. Noor didn't look at Driver when they said it — they were watching the road ahead, watching the mist and the lane markers and the dark shapes of trees that could be anything at all.

They pocketed the phone, both hands settling in their lap, and waited for the town to appear at the edge of the headlights like something surfacing from underwater.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Deal." *I nod, my grip on the wheel firm. My eyes scan the rearview mirror.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned from the window before the breath on the glass could fully clear. “I know,” they said, voice sandpaper-rough. They didn’t wait for a response. Instead, they crossed to the counter, popped the cabinet door, and sorted through the mismatched dishware until they found a half-crushed tube of peanut butter and a folded granola bar in a Ziploc. They ate standing up, one hand brushing crumbs into the sink before they yanked the coffee pot from its shelf. The dust came off in a gray smear. They wiped it down with a paper towel, dumped two heaping scoops of instant into a chipped mug, and filled it from the tap, waiting for the electric kettle to click off before pouring.

By the time the coffee was black and scalding, Noor was already at the table. They slid the padded case onto their lap, cracked the latch, and pulled out the encrypted drive. It sat cold and unassuming in their palm. They plugged it into the laptop, typed a fourteen-character passphrase until the terminal blinked green, and opened a split-screen workspace: call logs on the left, burner SIM metadata on the right. Three hours late meant either spooked, compromised, or gone. Noor’s shoulders tightened, but their hands stayed steady. They began cross-referencing timestamps, pulling up cell tower triangulation data, and flagging the three missed check-ins from the past week. The laptop fan whined in the quiet cabin.

Noor tapped a rhythm against the table edge, mapping intervals in a digital spreadsheet, circling anomalies where the source’s usual pattern broke. They set a hard stop for 1:45 AM in their calendar app—enough time to finish the drive extraction, verify the phone records against the known burner network, and force a two-hour sleep window before dawn. Outside, a distant engine echoed down the mountain road, too far to matter, but Noor didn’t look up. They opened a fresh terminal window, queued the decryption script, and leaned into the glow of the screen. Waiting was a luxury they couldn’t afford. The data would either confirm the trail or burn it clean, and either way, they were going to read it first.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scroll past a video of a guy failing to do a kickflip.* I yawn, stretching my arms over my head. "Anything good on there?" I ask, gesturing vaguely at the laptop.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn’t look up. The screen’s blue wash painted their knuckles as they dragged a column of flagged timestamps into a separate tab. “Nothing you’d want to see,” they said, voice flat but not unkind. “Just cross-referencing the burner network with the triangulation logs. If they’re spooked, I need to know where they last pinged before they went dark.”

They hit enter. The decryption script churned through a progress bar, chewing through fragmented directories and zeroing in on the encrypted ledger. Noor’s coffee had gone lukewarm, but they left it where it sat. Instead, they pulled a spiral notebook from their satchel, flipped to a fresh page, and began mapping the anomalies by hand. Three missed check-ins. Two skipped dead drops. A pattern that didn’t read like caution—it read like containment. Their pen moved fast, circles connecting to lines, until a cluster near the old water treatment plant stood out. They underlined it twice, then tore the page free and slid it under a coffee stain for later review.

“I’m routing a blind ping through a secondary node,” Noor said, finally shifting their gaze from the spreadsheet to the dark window. “If they’re still running, they’ll try the fallback channel. I’ll leave it on a one-time loop. If it stays dark by dawn, I’m pulling the story anyway. The metadata’s enough to corroborate the financial trail, and I’m not sitting on this while they decide whether to burn it or run with it.” They tapped the trackpad, queued the outbound signal, and set a ten-minute countdown on their phone. The laptop fan whined louder as the extraction hit seventy percent. Noor leaned back, rubbed the bridge of their nose, and exhaled slowly. “You should rest. I’ll wake you if the road gets busy, or if I need a second set of eyes on the printouts.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, not really understanding half of what they just said.* "Yeah, okay. Just wake me if anything actually happens." *I go back to my phone, trying to look busy even though I'm just scrolling aimlessly.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the countdown bleed to zero on the phone screen. The secondary node remained dark. They didn’t sigh or slump; they just closed the terminal, pulled the burner phone back out, and typed a single line into a secure drop: *Water treatment plant fallback active. If you’re compromised, don’t come. I’m running the metadata anyway.* They hit send, watched the message encrypt and vanish into a relay server, then powered the phone off and stuffed it into a desk drawer. Waiting for a ghost wasn’t a strategy. Verifying what they already had was.

Noor dragged the call logs into the foreground, lining them up against the decrypted ledger’s transaction headers. They worked methodically, matching timestamps to routing numbers, cross-referencing burner SIM registrations with shell company filings. Three out of four flagged lines pinged the same VoIP provider. Two of those shared a registered address with a logistics subsidiary tied to the defense contract. Noor highlighted the matches in yellow, printed the correlation sheet on the cabin’s wheezing dot-matrix printer, and taped it to the wall beside the hand-drawn map. They connected the nodes with red string, stepped back, and traced the financial bleed with a finger. It wasn’t proof yet, but it was a skeleton. And skeletons didn’t lie.

The laptop fan finally wound down as the extraction completed. Noor ejected the drive, sealed it in a Faraday pouch, and slid it into the inner pocket of their coat. They set the kettle to boil again, not for coffee this time, but to scald a small enamel mug for tea. The cabin smelled of damp wood and ozone. They moved through the space with practiced efficiency: cleared the table of scattered notes, locked the laptop in a padded case, set a mechanical alarm watch for 3:30 AM, and arranged three empty mugs on the floorboards near the door. A crude tripwire. Better than nothing. They stripped off their jacket, pulled a thin fleece over their shirt, and lay back on the narrow cot in the corner. Boots stayed on. Hands stayed near the pillow. They stared at the water-stained ceiling, listening to the wind press against the roof and the distant groan of tires on gravel somewhere down the mountain. Sleep would come when it came. Until then, Noor kept their eyes open, counting ceiling cracks, mentally rehearsing the next call, the next flight, the next deadline. The story was already moving. They just had to stay ahead of it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor lay still for a full minute, counting the groans of the cabin’s timber frame against the wind. The digital clock on the nightstand read 1:47 AM. The hard stop was in two minutes. They didn’t wait for it to chime. Sitting up, they pulled on their jacket and stepped onto the cold floorboards, careful to avoid the tripwire mugs. The red string on the wall caught the dim glow from the hall. They traced the logistics subsidiary node again, then noticed something they’d missed in the fatigue: a secondary routing number buried in the ledger’s footnotes. It matched a private security firm registered under a Delaware shell. Noor’s pulse kicked. They grabbed the spiral notebook, tore out a fresh page, and began sketching a revised flowchart. If the source had been detained, it wouldn’t be by police. It would be by contractors.

They moved to the kitchen, not for coffee, but for actual food. Hunger was a biological fact, not a mood. Noor popped open a can of black beans, heated it on the cracked hot plate, and ate standing over the sink, spoon scraping metal. They didn’t chew for taste. They chewed for glucose. When the can was empty, they washed the spoon, dried their hands on a rag, and pulled a burner satellite phone from a locked drawer beneath the sink. Powered it on. Waited for the signal bars to populate. One bar. Enough. They dialed a number memorized six months ago, watched the call route through three relays, and held the receiver to their ear without speaking first. When the static cleared and a familiar, clipped voice answered, Noor kept their tone level.

“It’s me. Run the contingency for Blackwood. I have the financial skeleton, but the source is dark. I’m moving at first light. Need a courier at the northern ridge checkpoint, not the usual drop. And prep the dead drop archive. If I don’t check in by noon, you publish what I’ve sent.” They listened to the response, nodded despite the receiver being away from their ear, and confirmed the coordinates. Then they ended the call, powered down the satellite phone, and returned it to the drawer. Waiting for a ghost was over. Planning for the aftermath was next.

Back at the table, Noor packed the go-bag with military precision: two changes of clothes, the Faraday pouch containing the drive, a compact first-aid kit, folded cash, a topographic map of the mountain service roads, a multi-tool, and a compact flashlight. They zipped it shut, slung it over their shoulder, and tested the weight against their hip. Balanced. They checked the mechanical watch again, reset the alarm for 4:00 AM, and returned to the cot. This time, they didn’t lie flat. They propped themselves against the wall, boots still laced, go-bag at their feet, eyes fixed on the cabin door. Sleep wasn’t a goal anymore. It was a tactical pause. They closed their eyes, let the rhythm of their own breathing sync with the wind, and waited for dawn. The story wouldn’t wait. Neither would they.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stretch again, checking the time on my phone. 2:00 AM. I should probably try to get some sleep.* "You want me to take first watch?" *I ask, even though I have no idea what that entails.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor opened their eyes, the movement slow but deliberate. The cabin’s shadows hadn’t shifted. “You don’t need to stand watch,” they said, voice stripped of its earlier edge. “Just keep the couch clear and leave the hall light off. If I need you at four, I’ll knock the wall twice. That’s all.”

They didn’t wait for a reply. Instead, they reached into the go-bag, pulled out a folded topographic map, and spread it across their knees. The northern ridge checkpoint was already marked, but the service roads between the cabin and the tree line were still blank. Noor grabbed a red pen, traced the drainage ditch that paralleled Highway 9, and noted the two unmarked bridges. If they were followed, the ridge would funnel traffic.
