The car parked. In the mirror, the headlights behind them paused at the lot's entrance — one beat, two — then slid away to the far edge and died. Noor watched the dark shape settle where it could see their car and reach the highway in the same breath.

"Patient. Professional." They read the plate through the lot's orange haze, got most of it, and wrote it in the paper notebook by the spill of the lights. "Plates change. Habits don't. Now I know his."

Then the exit briefing, quiet and final: "Everything stays. Bag in the trunk, laptop under my arm, the car's a prop now. We're two people getting coffee. Window seats, backs to the wall, and we are going to be the most boring thing in that building for hours."

Inside: a bell, heat, the smell of coffee that had been alive longer than the cabin pot's whole story. A waitress with a shift-change face. Noor paid cash from a bill already folded in their pocket, steered to the window booth with the sightline, ordered two coffees and whatever was hot, and settled in to watch the lot. Read it like tide tables — which trucks were fueling, which drivers were finishing up, which rigs were pointed west.

At the far edge of the lot, nobody got out of the dark car. Engine off. Brake lights dark. Just a shape with a full night's worth of patience in it.

"There he is," Noor said, wrapping both hands around the mug. "Now we find out who's more patient." A glance at Driver, and something in the tired face eased a half-degree. "And when the food comes, eat it. That's an order — from the friend who fed you cold beans."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I set my phone down on the table, face down, and look out the window at the dark car. I shiver, despite the heat of the diner.* "I'm guessing he's not getting coffee."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"No," Noor said. "He's got a thermos and a strong bladder and he's billing by the hour. Same job as ours, worse coffee." A sip. "Told you the cabin pot had a life story. This one's on its second marriage, but it's hot."

They kept reading the lot. Once, a cigarette ember brightened behind the dark windshield and faded — one cigarette, nursed slow. A man rationing his own boredom. Noor filed that too. Patient men were predictable men.

The food arrived — eggs, toast, hash browns sweating on the plate. Noor ate the way they'd eaten the beans: mechanical, fast, fuel into a machine. Halfway through, they set the fork down and looked at the phone lying face-down on the table.

"Now the hard part. And it's yours to give or keep."

"The phone. Everything on it — photos, messages, your whole life — assume the account it talks to has already been read. The phone itself is just plastic and glass. But it's the dot, and the dot is the leash." Their eyes went to the window, the dark shape at the lot's edge. "I want to hand the leash to a man driving to the coast."

"I'll replace it — that's not the cost. The cost is you'll feel naked without it. Everyone does. That feeling is part of the leash too. It goes away in a day."

They turned the phone over, screen dark, and set one finger on it like a chess piece.

"Here's the beautiful part. It's not just a decoy — it's a question. If he follows the truck, he's been watching the dot all along, and the road ahead of us opens up empty. If he stays put, he's watching this car with his own eyes, and we've lost a phone and learned something worth ten phones. Either way, by sunrise we know what kind of animal he is."

A tilt of the chin toward the diner's middle. "The man three booths down. Denim jacket, eggs, ticket folded under his cup. Reefer unit out front, out-of-state plates, fuel receipt on the table. He's going to the coast and he's leaving inside ten minutes."

"When he goes, I go. Not to our car — I never touch our car. Through the rows, ninety seconds. The phone rides wedged in the air lines behind his cab, screen dark, still on, still saying hello to every tower from here to the ocean."

"And you stay. You eat. You're the anchor — two people walked in, two people are the story, and nothing has changed. When that truck pulls out, don't watch the truck. Watch *him*. His brake lights are the answer. If they come on, note the time."

The denim jacket paid at the register. Pushed back his chair.

Noor palmed the phone off the table — still warm from the room — and stood, shrugging their jacket straight, drive zipped against their ribs. "Eat your eggs," they said, and walked out unhurried, a person heading for the restrooms or the lot, nothing more.

Outside: cold like a slap, sodium light, diesel idling somewhere. Noor angled between the tractors, unhurried, and the rows swallowed them. The reefer's engine was already running, exhaust white in the dark. Thirty seconds at the blind side of the cab — the phone wedged deep in the coil of air lines, snug as a hand in a glove — then back through the rows, in through the door, bell, heat.

They slid into the booth and picked up their coffee like they'd never left. Hands cold. Eyes on the far edge of the lot.

Three minutes later the reefer's air brakes sighed, and it rolled — slow, gathering itself, up the ramp, westbound, taillights shrinking into the dark.

Noor didn't watch it go. They watched the far edge of the lot.

The dark car's engine turned over. Headlights flared on.

"There," Noor breathed, almost gentle. "Now we learn what he is."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch the dark car, a sick feeling in my stomach. I look at Noor.* "So... he's watching the dot. Right?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer. The answer was still assembling itself out there in the lot.

The dark car rolled off its spot — unhurried, no wasted motion — and paused at the exit for one beat. Left was east, back toward the junction. Right was the ramp the reefer had taken.

It turned right.

Noor watched the taillights climb the ramp and flatten out westbound, settling in behind the truck's distant glow at that same patient, metronome distance. Something in their shoulders came down a quarter inch.

"Now he's watching the dot," they said. "He just made the choice out loud. Our car was sitting twenty yards from him, stone cold, and he didn't spare it a headlight. Everything he knows about where we are comes off a screen." A sip of coffee. "That's not a small thing to know about a man. That's the whole manual."

They turned the mug slowly, working it through out loud — the whole picture, as promised.

"He'll pace that truck for hours. Maybe he runs the plate at some point and gets a freight company in another state, and maybe that makes him curious — but curious isn't fast. Best case, he follows the blip all the way to the ocean and spends a beautiful morning watching a reefer full of frozen fish. Worst case, he gets suspicious at the next rest stop. That's still two hours of him driving the wrong way." The ghost of the not-quite smile. "Two hours is a country."

But even saying it, their eyes went to the east ramp, and stayed there, and Noor counted — because counting was the job. A minute. Two. No second set of headlights. No shape detaching itself from the lot's dark edges. Just trucks breathing diesel and a sky going from black to deep blue at the horizon's seam.

"One man, one car, no partner that I can find. Partners cost money, and this job was cheap and patient from the start. But cheap and patient men make phone calls, so we don't sprint for the door. We do exactly what we told him we were doing." They nudged Driver's plate a half-inch closer. "We finish breakfast like people with nowhere to be. If he has a friend, the friend is watching this window, and I intend to be the dullest thing in it."

"Then, when the morning pack heads out — eastbound, our direction, into the sunrise with forty other sets of taillights — we go in the middle of it. He comes back to an empty lot and a dot in another state. And Dana's is back on. He never got within fifty miles of her name. The map they're building still doesn't have her on it."

They pulled the paper notebook over and wrote the time, the plate fragment, *one cigarette, patient, follows the dot* — habits being the only true names people had. Then, quieter, they read the lede once more, there in the booth with the fogged gold windows and the smell of refill coffee. *Forty minutes before the port contract was signed, a phone rang.* Still true. Still worth everything the night had cost.

"And you," they said, not looking up. "You put your whole life face-down on the table and let a stranger carry it to the ocean. Most people can't do that at dinner. The naked feeling lasts about a day — then it starts feeling like what it actually is, which is your own attention, handed back." A beat. "I'll replace the phone. From Dana's, on paper, with cash. We'll fix your passwords off her landline."

They flagged the waitress with two fingers — the universal sign for *more of whatever this is* — and settled into the booth like they planned to grow old there, eyes on the east ramp, the lightening sky.

"Eat your eggs. That's still an order. Next stop, Dana feeds you — and her one religion is a good one."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pick up my fork and start slowly eating the eggs, still watching the east ramp. My stomach feels a little less sick now, but my hands are still shaky.* "So... we just wait for the sun?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Yes," Noor said. "We wait for the sun. That's not a gap in the plan — that *is* the plan."

They turned the mug in their hands. "He had the night shift. Empty roads, one set of headlights, his game. Sun comes up, this valley fills with witnesses and shift traffic, and it becomes our game. Two people eating eggs at sunrise is the least interesting thing in this county. We're not killing time. We're *wearing* it."

Their eyes dropped to Driver's fork hand, and they set their coffee down.

"Palms flat on the table. Push down like you're trying to shove it through the floor. Ten seconds, then breathe out slow." They demonstrated, forearms going taut against the Formica. "Adrenaline's a fuel — this burns it. Gives it somewhere to go. A cameraman taught me that in a stairwell in a city I never wrote about. Works everywhere."

Then they flagged the waitress with two fingers. "And whatever pie's under the glass dome. Two slices. Sugar's the other half of the cure."

The table looked bigger without the phone on it. Noor kept glancing at the empty spot anyway — a leash-shaped hole — and then made themselves stop, and worked.

The notebook came out, and for the next hour Noor built the story on paper, in pencil, in three columns. *Prove:* row 312, the nine minutes, the eleven calls, the security firm taking the port gate two weeks after. *Allege:* the deputy minister's office knew, and someone canceled a landline to keep it quiet. *Need:* the drive's contents — sixty-four characters locked in a pocket against their ribs — and a second source, and Sparrow.

They stared at that last word a while. Then they wrote the lede one more time beneath the columns, not because it needed fixing, but because it was the sentence that might still be a rope. Print as message in a bottle. *He'll see row 312 and know who's still looking.*

Outside, the sky went from black to the color of dishwater, then found some pink at the seam of the mountains. The lot turned over — night drivers drifting out, day drivers drifting in, the east island busy now. Noor read the rigs like tide tables. Three trucks from the same freight line fueled one after another, long-haul tractors with mountain dust on their mirrors, drivers pocketing receipts with the unhurried hurry of men with six hundred miles ahead of them.

"There's our pack," Noor murmured. "A convoy that doesn't know it's ours."

A dark sedan came off the east ramp.

Noor went still — hand to the zipper, eyes doing the inventory. Wrong hubcaps. A child seat in the back. A woman in scrubs got out and locked it with a hip-check, yawning. Noor exhaled, wrote the plate down anyway, because habits were the only true names.

"False alarms are the tax," they said. "You pay it gladly."

The pie arrived. Noor set one slice in front of Driver and ate their own in four mechanical bites, then pushed the plate a half-inch toward the middle of the table, in case.

"Whole picture, since you're awake for it," they said. "If our friend figures out the fish truck by midmorning, he comes back to an empty lot and starts guessing east. By then we're one dot he can't see in a string of thirty, and Dana's name is still on no map anywhere. Two hours from now you're drinking her coffee and petting her dog, and this is over for you. You drove a friend to a cabin. Still true. Getting truer."

The three drivers came back across the lot together, coffees in hand, and climbed into their cabs one after another. Air brakes sighed. The first rig rolled for the ramp.

Noor closed the notebook, left cash on the table — a normal tip, a forgettable one, forgettable being its own kind of courtesy — and stood, shrugging the jacket straight, drive zipped against their ribs.

"Her shop grate goes up at eight. I want to be the first customer of the day — first customer is *expected*, and expected is boring, and boring is still the whole weapon."

They picked up the laptop, tucked it under their arm, and looked out at the pinkening sky and the string of taillights gathering itself at the ramp.

"Middle of the string, all the way down the mountain. Whenever you're ready."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, push my palms flat on the table, and count to ten. It helps a little. I nod, then drain the last of my coffee.* "Ready."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not lift his head at once. He finished tracing the line of ink with the silver stylus, laid the tool parallel to the edge of the manuscript, and only then permitted himself the indignity of turning toward the apprentice. His eyes were pale and watery, but they found the notes in the boy’s hand with uncomfortable precision.

“First,” he said, “you will address me as *Maester*, not ‘Master.’ The distinction is not decorative. It is the difference between a trained servant of the Citadel and a household dog who has learned to fetch slippers.”

He reached out without asking and took the apprentice’s notes, holding them so close to his face that the bridge of his nose nearly touched the parchment. His mouth thinned.

“Second, you say Bellen ‘showed you a paper.’ A paper. How modest. Does this paper bear the royal sign-manual? A conclave seal? Witness marks from the Chancery at Veyros? Or is it merely one of those ambitious little scholarly pamphlets written by men who have discovered that if one arranges enough fragments upon a table, they begin to resemble a conclusion?”

Tomas lowered the notes, but he did not return them.

“The Third Magical War ended in eight hundred and forty-seven after the Ending, when King Aldric the Second signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is not a matter of taste. It is not a tale told for the comfort of throne rooms. It is recorded in the Red Rolls of the Crown, in the Conclave’s own acknowledgments of limitation, in the cessation of the Ashen Levies, and in the accounts of three separate royal treasuries that stopped paying wartime subsidies within a year of the treaty’s proclamation.”

He tapped the apprentice’s notes once, sharply.

“What Bellen has shown you—if he has shown you anything more respectable than gossip dressed in footnotes—is the western archive material. I know it. I handled three folios from that cache myself five years ago. They are negotiation minutes. Drafts. Proposals. Counterproposals. Letters in which one side threatens to withdraw while the other pretends to listen. They are not proof that the treaty was never executed. They are proof only that agreements are rarely born without argument.”

Tomas set the notes down on the desk between them, palms flat, as though pinning the whole troublesome matter beneath his hands.

“If a scholar wishes to claim that the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, he must do better than point to a bundle of proposals and declare the absence of a signature page. He must explain why both crown and conclave observed the territorial settlements afterward. He must explain why wartime mage-levies were disbanded. He must explain why the border wards along the Silvermarch were dismantled in eight forty-eight, not reinforced. He must explain why no royal proclamation after eight forty-seven declares a state of war. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but sustained contradiction across administrative records is rather harder to dismiss with a startled ‘but what if?’”

His voice had risen by degrees, not into shouting, but into the kind of dry, cutting emphasis that made junior clerks wish the floor would open.

“There are those who prefer the eight ninety-one theory because it makes them feel daring. Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave, they say, therefore the war must have continued in some cold legal state until then. It is a pretty notion. It is also sloppy. A queen abolishing an institution is not the same thing as a monarch concluding a war. The Conclave fell in eight ninety-one because it had become a political tumor, not because the realm had never laid down its magical arms. To say the war ‘continued’ is to misuse the word. War requires hostilities, or at minimum a recognized legal condition of war. What followed eight forty-seven was tension, resentment, clandestine practice, and occasional border trouble. That is not war. That is history being difficult.”

He glanced back toward the shelves of northern scrolls, then returned his gaze to the apprentice with visible impatience.

“I do not deny that the western documents merit study. I deny that they overturn established chronology merely because they are inconvenient. If Bellen has found a countersigned original declaring the treaty void, or a royal letter of continuation issued after eight forty-seven and witnessed by the Conclave’s ruling circle, then let him bring it forward with its archive mark, its vellum description, and its chain of custody. Let him publish it properly. Let him endure scrutiny. Until then, he is speculating, and you are repeating speculation as though it were fact.”

Tomas picked up the silver stylus again, but he did not turn back to the manuscript immediately.

“In your examinations, in your catalog entries, and in any conversation with persons who may test your learning, the Third Magical War ends in eight forty-seven with the Treaty of Veyros. If you are asked about the western archive, you may say that some scholars question the extent of its implementation. You may say that Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in eight ninety-one marked the final collapse of the old magical settlement. You may not say, without primary documentation of the highest order, that the war technically continued from eight forty-seven to eight ninety-one. That is not nuance. It is error wearing nuance as a disguise.”

At last he extended his hand for the notes, expecting them back.

“Now begin with the Veyrosi correspondence. Sort them by date, sender, recipient, and subject matter. If you find anything that genuinely challenges the accepted dating, bring it to me with its shelf-mark, not with another apprentice’s summary. And do not tell me what the document ‘says.’ Documents do not say. Scholars interpret. Usually badly.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, taking my notes back, my ears burning slightly.* "Yes, Maester. Apologies." *I avoid his gaze and head toward the shelves. But then I pause, turning back slightly.* "What about the Battle of the Whispering Woods, Maester? Some of those accounts say it was well after 847, and the Conclave's banner was clearly present..."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I press, emboldened by my last question.* "And some accounts say the Conclave's banner was clearly present at Whispering Woods. That was after 847, wasn't it?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped above the vellum. A bead of ink gathered at its tip, swelled, and fell with a small black blot onto the margin. He stared at it as though it had personally offended him, then lifted his gaze.

“‘Some accounts,’” he repeated. “You wield that phrase like a man throwing stones from behind a hedge. Which accounts? The Chronicle of Saint Eoda? The ballad-cycle called *The Green Martyrs*? The memoirs of Ser Halys, who admitted in his second chapter that he had never been east of the Ford and still described the weather at Whispering Woods in intimate detail?”

He set the stylus down with excessive care.

“There is no single ‘Battle of the Whispering Woods’ in the records you are pretending to understand. There is the engagement of late summer 846, which belongs to the war and ended with the Conclave’s eastern column withdrawing after the burning of the Alder Line. There is the affray of spring 848, sometimes called the Second Whispering Woods by writers who enjoy symmetry more than accuracy. And there are half a dozen village alarms in 849 and 850 that veterans inflated into battles because a man with a sword prefers a story in which he mattered.”

He leaned back, and one of his knees complained audibly.

“If the account you half-remember places the Conclave’s banner at Whispering Woods after 847, it is almost certainly speaking of the 848 affray. And yes—banners were there. So what? The Treaty of Veyros did not incinerate every standard, seal, and surcoat the morning it was signed. It required the Conclave to surrender wartime levies, dismantle field enchantments, and submit unauthorized martial workings to the Crown’s wardens. It did not require every provincial chapter to scrape the paint off its wagons. Colors remained for ceremony, for internal policing, for the vanity of old officers who had spent thirty years learning to obey a sigil more readily than a king.”

His finger tapped the desk once.

“The marshal’s roll for the Silvermarch, entry fourteen, records that in 848 a body styling itself ‘the Conclave’s Woodward Host’ appeared near the Whispering Woods with blue-and-silver streamers. They were not acting under a warrant from the Conclave’s ruling circle. The Conclave’s own chapter letters—copied in the Veyrosi bundle you are meant to be sorting—disavowed them within the month and paid restitution for two burned millraces. The Crown accepted the restitution. It did not proclaim renewal of war. Read the difference, apprentice. A riot wears many uniforms. A war wears a legal name.”

He squinted, not at the apprentice, but at the distance beyond him, where better light might once have lived.

“Bellen may clutch at that banner as though it were a smoking hearth-stick. Let him explain why the Conclave fined its own men for the affair. Let him explain why no treasury opened a war account. Let him explain why the Ashen Levies remained disbanded and the border wards stayed down. If he can produce a countersigned commission from the Conclave authorizing hostilities after 847, I shall eat my chain of office and apologize to his footnote. Until then, the presence of a flag proves a flag existed, not that the nation it once served was still at war.”

A pause. The annoyance in his face cooled into something more weary.

“You are doing what too many young scholars do: you find one contradictory detail and mistake it for a key. History is not a lock with a single pin. It is a house full of draughts, and most of the noise comes from windows left open by men too lazy to shut them. The Third Magical War ended in 847. The world did not end with it. Mages still quarreled, lords still poached, and ambitious apprentices still mistook confusion for revelation.”

He turned back to the manuscript, then stopped himself and looked aside again.

“Do not thank me. Do not pretend comprehension with a pleasant face. Go to the Veyrosi correspondence, third shelf, brown tags. Find the chapter letters for 848. Bring me the original disavowal, not Bellen’s paraphrase, not your memory, and certainly not some ‘account’ that says what it likes. And if you see a banner in a source, ask first whose banner, when, under what authority, and whether the writer was sober. Documents do not say. They confess, contradict, and lie. It is our unpleasant duty to tell the difference.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went very still. The silence that followed was not contemplative. It was the silence of a man deciding whether the universe had grown too stupid to withstand without immediate correction.

Then he pointed the silver stylus at the sheet in the apprentice’s hand.

“A copy,” he said. “You produce a copy, bearing what you call a seal, dated sixteen years after the peace, and you expect me to rearrange the reign of King Aldric the Second because an apprentice has found a dramatic fragment.” His voice remained dry, but it had acquired the particular sharpness of a knife being tested with a thumb. “Set that phrase to rights before it infects your notes. It is not sixteen years after I said the war ended. It is sixteen years after the Treaty of Veyros was proclaimed. There is a difference between my speech and the record, and you will learn it.”

He leaned nearer, without touching the page.

“First: which Aldric? If the legend reads only *ALDRIC REX*, then it has told me nothing. If Bellen assumes Aldric the Second, he is either ignorant or manipulative. Aldric the Second was buried at Saint Bede’s Cross in the winter of eight hundred and sixty-one. A dead king may be commemorated, quoted, or forged, but he does not issue public war decrees in eight hundred and sixty-three unless some clerk has broken into the seal chest. And if that is the story Bellen prefers, he had best bring the burglar’s warrant as well.”

His eyes narrowed at the copy.

“If it is Aldric the Third, then it is not the king who made the treaty, and a later king’s emergency order proves only that later kings had problems. If it is Aldric the Second, it is impossible on its face. If it is neither, then you have brought me a riddle dressed as evidence. Choose carefully, because I shall not choose for you.”

He tapped the desk once, lightly, as though marking the boundaries of the matter.

“Second: a seal on a copy is a picture of authority, not authority. Where is the wax? Pendant? Pressed into the membrane? Fixed with green silk? Broken but preserved in a chancery folder? If the seal is drawn in ink, rubbed from a matrix, or copied by a penman who thought circles and lions look impressive, then it is illumination. It is decoration with pretensions. If it is an impression taken from a damaged original, it must be matched to the royal matrices: the great seal, the privy seal, the secretum, the counter-seal, the legend, the spacing of the letters, the treatment of the royal title. Have you done this? No. You have seen a round shape and concluded that history owes you a revolution.”

He straightened, though the movement cost him something in the lower back.

“Third: what is a ‘war decree’? Show me the words. Does it open with a formal declaration? Does it name the Mage Conclave as enemy? Does it order the Ashen Levies summoned? Does it direct the wardens of the Silvermarch to reinforce the border? Does it allocate treasure for campaigns? Does it commission captains? Does it revoke safe-conducts? Does it announce reprisals at sea or on the land? Or does it merely recite ‘late hostile practices by evil-disposed persons’ and command local magistrates to suppress unauthorized workings?”

He let the question hang for a moment.

“The second is law enforcement. The first is war. Men who have never read a chancery roll call both ‘decrees’ and then wonder why historians weep. A king may order the arrest of smugglers, the punishment of hedge-enchanters, the seizure of illicit foci, or the suppression of border outrage without thereby declaring that the realm is again in a state of public war. Indeed, he often does precisely that, because the alternative is admitting that his peace has failed.”

Tomas reached for a clean slip of parchment, not to write, but to have something innocent beneath his hand.

“The western archive has produced many documents that smell of revelation to inexperienced noses. Sealed drafts. Counterdrafts. exemplars prepared for negotiation. Copies authenticated by clerks who wished to preserve the appearance of royal intent. A sealed draft is not an enacted statute. A proposal with a seal attached may prove only that someone intended to seal it, or that a notary practiced his craft on the wrong parchment. If this alleged decree was never enrolled, never proclaimed, never answered by the Conclave, and leaves no trace in the treasury books, then it is at best an abandoned instrument. At worst, it is a partisan fabrication with a fashionable date.”

He glanced at the copy again, with the suspicion one reserves for a coin that rings too brightly.

“Suppose, for argument, that the original exists and is genuine. What would it prove? That in eight hundred and sixty-three the crown believed some armed magical mischief required royal response. It would not prove that the state of war had never ended in eight hundred and forty-seven. It would not prove that the Treaty of Veyros lacked execution. It would prove only that peace was contentious, as peace always is. To leap from ‘a king issued a stern order’ to ‘the Third Magical War continued’ is not scholarship. It is theatrical criticism.”

His tone hardened.

“If the text explicitly says that the war begun in the previous reign continues, or that the treaty is void, or that the Conclave is again declared hostis by name and counsel, then yes, I shall trouble myself. I am not a fool, and I do not love error for its own sake. But Bellen’s kind do not quote such sentences when they are absent. They quote the seal, the date, and the word ‘hostile,’ and let ignorance fill the rest.”

He turned partly toward the shelves, then back again.

“And write the date properly in your notes: eight hundred and sixty-three after the Ending. Not ‘863 AE’ like a merchant’s tally. Abbreviations are for men who have already mastered the thing abbreviated. You have not.”

The stylus returned to the desk beside the manuscript, aligned with mechanical precision.

“Go to the calendar of chancery rolls for eight hundred and sixty-three. Then the memoranda rolls, the wardrobe accounts, the exchequer memoranda, the Conclave’s provincial correspondence, and the later additions to the Veyrosi bundle. Find enrollment, proclamation, receipt, protest, or payment. If the decree exists as a public act, it cannot hide in one orphan copy. Public acts leave tracks: wax, ink, money, anger, and paperwork. Bring me the shelf-marks. If the original is in the western archive, bring a certified transcription with the archivist’s note, the matrix identification, the physical description of the seal, and the chain of custody. Not a paper. Not a summary. Not Bellen’s breath upon it.”

He regarded the apprentice with the weary severity of a man who had explained this principle too many times.

“Until then, the Third Magical War ends in eight hundred and forty-seven with the Treaty of Veyros. Your copy is an anomaly awaiting explanation, not a refutation. And if you call it ‘proof’ again, I shall assume you have mistaken a stamp for a syllogism.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little as he talks about the copy, pulling it back from his pointed stylus.* "It *does* say 'Aldric Rex'," *I admit, my voice a bit quieter. I don't mention the part about 'evil-disposed persons' because it's not exactly a declaration of war.* "But... it was in a box with other documents about the war. Why would it be there if it wasn't related?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes for the space of three breaths. It was not contemplation. It was the self-control of a man who had spent too many decades watching clever fools mistake enthusiasm for evidence.

When he opened them again, he did not look at the apprentice’s face. He looked at the sheet of paper as one might look at a rat that had been found in a flour bin: with disgust, suspicion, and an immediate desire to know how it had gotten there.

“‘It *does* say *Aldric Rex*,’” he repeated, and the words left his mouth as though they had been chewed twice and still were not soft. “Yes. It says a name. It says a title. It does not say a numeral. It does not say a reign. It does not say, ‘I am the king who made peace at Veyros and therefore the war continues.’ It says *Aldric Rex*. By that standard, a tavern sign reading *The Crown* proves that the king dined there.”

He lifted one ink-stained finger.

“If Bellen means Aldric the Second, then he has produced a impossibility dressed as a discovery. Aldric the Second was buried at Saint Bede’s Cross in the winter of eight hundred and sixty-one. A dead king does not issue war decrees in eight hundred and sixty-three unless some clerk has broken the seal chest, forged a instrument, or invented a new branch of necromantic chancery practice. If that is what Bellen believes, let him say so plainly. Let him bring charges before the Crown’s archivists, the Conclave’s former officers, and the chapter at Saint Bede’s. A grave is not a footnote to be ignored because it is inconvenient.”

The finger rose another joint.

“If the legend is meant to refer to some later Aldric, then it is not the Aldric who signed—or, as Bellen would prefer, did not sign—the Treaty of Veyros. A later king’s stern order against disorderly mages proves only that later kings had disorderly mages. It does not resurrect a war. It does not annul a treaty. It does not turn every quarrel into a campaign.”

He let the finger fall.

“And if it is neither—if the words are a scribal habit, a copyist’s shorthand, a forger’s flourish, or the confident error of a man who saw an old name and thought it must be the right one—then you have brought me a label and asked me to treat it as a lineage.”

Maester Tomas drew a slow breath through his nose. The candle by his elbow guttered, and he shielded it absently with one palm, not because he valued the flame, but because he valued not being forced to read in gloom.

“Now. The box.”

He said the word as though it had personally insulted his mother.

“You ask why it would be in a box with other documents about the war if it was not related. I shall answer you as a maester answers when an apprentice has mistaken storage for testimony: because boxes are not arguments.”

He tapped the desk once, then again, marking each clause.

“A box may be assembled by a royal clerk. It may be assembled by a Conclave archivist. It may be assembled by a private collector, an heir, a thief, a pious brother, a patriotic fool, or some later historian who liked the look of a pile and gave it a title. A box marked ‘war papers’ may contain war papers, yes. It may also contain petitions about war debts, complaints about veterans, accounts of confiscated staves, drafts of speeches, copies of older letters, proposals never enacted, ordinances against unlawful enchantment, and scraps of boundary dispute that use the word ‘hostile’ because men enjoy dramatic vocabulary.”

His voice grew thinner, more precise, the way a blade grows dangerous when it is honied too finely.

“Related to the war? Of course. After eight hundred and forty-seven there were still men wounded by the war, still mages punished for workings done during the war, still lords exploiting the confusion left behind by the war, still wardens reporting incursions that had not been authorized by any ruling circle, still clerks chasing subsidies that had been promised in emergency and forgotten in peace. All of that is related. None of it means the war did not end.”

He leaned a little forward.

“A scar is related to a wound. That does not prove the blade is still in the body.”

The comparison seemed to satisfy him for half a heartbeat. Then he dismissed it with a flick of his wrist.

“If the document commands the suppression of evil-disposed persons—and I do not need to read it to know that phrase is lurking somewhere in its family, because such papers breed true—then it is a police measure. The crown ordering wardens to seize unlawful foci, detain itinerant enchanters, punish pillagers, or restrain unauthorized martial workings is not thereby declaring public war against the Mage Conclave as a recognized enemy. It is saying: there are criminals, and I intend to fine, imprison, or hang them. War is a legal condition between powers. Crime is a nuisance within one’s own realm. Men who confuse the two will never understand why peace requires so many warrants.”

He glanced at the copy again, with the distrust of a man who has been bitten by paper before.

“You have told me what the document says in two words. You have not told me what it *does*. Does it open with a formal declaration? Does it name the Conclave as *hostis*? Does it revoke the Treaty of Veyros by title? Does it order the Ashen Levies summoned? Does it direct the Silvermarch wardens to reinforce the border? Does it authorize reprisals? Does it allocate treasure for campaigns? Does it commission captains? Does it announce that the state of war begun in the previous reign continues? If it does any of those things, bring me the sentence. Word for word. Line for line. With the abbreviation expanded and the punctuation described. Then I shall trouble myself.”

His eyes narrowed.

“If it merely recites that certain persons have practised hostile arts contrary to the peace, then it confirms the peace by enforcing it. That is not contradiction. That is administration.”

Maester Tomas reached for the little brass lens he kept in his sleeve, considered using it, and then snapped it shut again. A copy was not worth straining failing eyes over unless it first earned the right to be examined.

“And the seal,” he said. “You speak of a seal as though it were a voice from the grave. On a copy, a seal is a picture unless proven otherwise. Where is the wax? Pendant? Pressed into the membrane? Fixed with silk? Broken but preserved in a chancery folder? Is the impression matched to a known matrix? Does the legend correspond? Does the device show the royal arms as they were borne in the reign supposed? Are the letters spaced as the chancery cutters spaced them? Has anyone compared it to the great seal, the privy seal, the secretum, the counter-seal? No. You have seen a round shape with a name inside it and concluded that history must kneel.”

He made a small, contemptuous sound.

“A forger can copy a name. A skilled forger can copy a seal. A foolish clerk can draw both and believe he has preserved truth. Only enrollment, proclamation, receipt, protest, payment, and reaction can tell us whether the instrument lived.”

For a moment he was silent, and the silence had weight in it. Not doubt, exactly. Tomas did not doubt easily. It was the patience of a man preparing to explain the same principle for the hundredth time because the world refused to learn it once.

“The western archive has produced documents that smell of revelation to inexperienced noses,” he said at last. “Drafts. Counterdrafts. Negotiation minutes. Sealed proposals. Exemplars prepared for discussion. Copies authenticated by clerks who wished to preserve the appearance of royal intent. A sealed draft is not an enacted statute. A proposal with a seal attached may prove only that someone intended to seal it, or that a notary practiced his craft on the wrong parchment. If this alleged decree was never enrolled, never proclaimed, never answered by the Conclave, and leaves no trace in the treasury books, then it is at best an abandoned instrument. At worst, it is a partisan fabrication with a fashionable date.”

He gestured toward the shelves, though not yet with permission to flee.

“You ask why it would be in a box with other war documents. I ask you why you believe a box has intentions. Why would a document be placed anywhere? Because a later hand found the words ‘Aldric’ and ‘hostile’ and thought them topical. Because an estate was seized and its papers thrown into a chest without regard for chronology. Because a collector wanted a dramatic series. Because a clerk filed it under ‘war’ when it belonged under ‘suppression of unauthorized magic.’ Because men organize paper according to their fears, their laziness, and their desire to impress visitors. Archives are not temples of truth. They are rooms where truth has been mishandled by generations.”

His voice dropped, becoming more dangerous for being quieter.

“History is not established by adjacency. A thing lying beside another thing does not make them kin. A sword found beside a Bishop’s psalter does not prove the Bishop swung it. A decree found among war papers does not prove war continued. It proves only that somebody, at some point, thought the two belonged together. That is a fact about the archive. Not necessarily a fact about the realm.”

He looked at the copy once more.

“I will grant you this: if the document is genuine, if the seal is genuine, if the date is original, if the king is identified beyond doubt, if the text explicitly declares the renewal of public war against the Conclave, and if it can be connected to enrollment, proclamation, treasury expenditure, military summons, or Conclave protest—then yes, it would matter. It would matter greatly. I am not so wedded to eight hundred and forty-seven that I would defend error with my chain of office. But you have not shown me any of those things. You have shown me a name, a number, a box, and a boy’s certainty.”

The last word was not quite an insult. It was worse: a diagnosis.

“And until you do show me those things, the document remains an anomaly awaiting explanation. An anomaly is not a refutation. A difficulty is not a destruction. One stubborn brick does not prove the wall was never built; it proves only that the mortar requires study.”

He sat back, and the joints of his spine complained in a manner he plainly found undignified.

“The Third Magical War ends in eight hundred and forty-seven with the Treaty of Veyros. That is the chronology supported by the Red Rolls, by the cessation of the Ashen Levies, by the treasury accounts, by the dismantling of the Silvermarch wards, by the Conclave’s own submissions, and by the absence of any subsequent royal proclamation of public war. The western archive may complicate the history of negotiation. It may illuminate the reluctance of parties, the drafts of clauses, the threats withdrawn and resumed. It may even show that the peace was contested, uneven, and resented. None of that overturns execution unless you produce execution denied by the highest order of evidence.”

His gaze sharpened.

“Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in eight hundred and ninety-one. That is a constitutional catastrophe, not a war termination. A monarch abolishing an institution is not the same as a realm resuming hostilities against it. If Bellen wishes to argue that the magical settlement lasted until eight ninety-one in some cold, legal, half-conscious state, let him define his terms. Let him distinguish war from tension, enforcement from campaign, crime from rebellion, and political suppression from public hostilities. Until he does, he is not revising history. He is merely stretching a word until it snaps.”

Maester Tomas picked up the silver stylus, turned it once between his fingers, and laid it down again with excessive neatness.

“Now. You will stop asking why a document was in a box as though containers held theological opinions. You will take that copy—if you are permitted to keep it out of the light—and you will transcribe it exactly. Not paraphrase. Not summarize. Not ‘it says war.’ Every abbreviation expanded in brackets. Every damaged letter marked. Every seal described. Every docket on the reverse copied. Every hand change noted. If there is a dating clause, give it to me in full: regnal year, indiction, feast day, place, witnesses, chancery subscription, and any later endorsement. If there is none, say that there is none. Absence must be reported as carefully as presence.”

He pointed the stylus toward the northern shelves.

“Then you will go to the Veyrosi correspondence and find the chapter letters for the eight-sixties. Find any Conclave protest. Find any royal command to the wardens. Find any treasury memorandum. Find any enrollment duplicate. Find any reference in the chronicles that does not depend on Bellen’s imagination. If the decree was public, it cannot hide in one orphan copy. Public acts leave tracks: wax, ink, money, anger, and paperwork.”

His expression cooled into weary severity.

“And if you find nothing—if the document stands alone, sealed like a letter no one answered, dated like a calendar no one used, and filed like a curiosity in a box of curiosities—then you will bring me that negative evidence with the same care you would bring positive evidence. Because the absence of tracks is itself a track, provided one knows how to read the ground.”

He paused, then added, with the particular dryness of a man who had long since ceased to be amused by youthful confidence:

“Do not tell me it was related to the war. Tell me what kind of relation. A pension is related to a war. A complaint is related to a war. A forgery is related to a war. A draft never issued is related to a war. A magistrate’s warrant against hedge enchanters is related to a war. Relation is not continuation. Proximity is not proof. And a box”—his eyes flicked once more to the copy—“is not a witness.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas allowed the word *textbook* to hang in the air for a moment, as though it were a stain on the desk that might yet be scraped away by silence.

Then he said, with the particular patience of a man who had explained the same principle until his patience had grown teeth:

“A textbook is not a truth. It is a convenience. A textbook compresses argument into sentence, sentence into dogma, and dogma into examination. It is useful. It is not sacred. And it certainly is not the measure by which we decide whether the Treaty of Veyros was real.”

He folded his hands beneath the silver stylus, careful not to smudge the ink still drying at its tip.

“You ask whether the treaty is real or not. That is already the wrong question, because you have made *real* do the work of three different ideas. If you mean: *Does a signed original parchment exist today, bearing King Aldric the Second’s hand and the Conclave’s seal, preserved entire and unquestioned?*—then I tell you plainly that I do not know. No honest scholar does, unless he has himself examined the exemplar with its chain of custody intact. Loss, fire, theft, miscataloguing, and the ordinary carelessness of archivists have swallowed more royal acts than any war ever destroyed.”

His eyes narrowed.

“If you mean: *Was there a treaty negotiated, concluded, proclaimed, and observed in eight hundred and forty-seven after the Ending?*—then yes. It is real. It is real because the realm behaved as though it were real. The Ashen Levies ceased. The border wards along the Silvermarch were dismantled, not reinforced. The Conclave submitted to limitations on wartime workings. The treasuries stopped paying emergency subsidies. Chancery rolls speak of peace. Provincial correspondence speaks of peace. Even hostile mages spoke of peace, because even liars adjust their lies to the weather of the age.”

He tapped one finger against the desk.

“A draft is not a treaty. A proposal is not a peace. But a proposal that is acted upon, enforced, remembered, answered, taxed, complained of, and referred to by enemies and friends alike for decades afterward has acquired the dignity of history. The western archive documents may show argument. They may show hesitation. They may show clauses struck, restored, threatened, and renegotiated. That proves only that treaties are difficult to make. It does not prove that no treaty was made.”

Maester Tomas let the silence gather again, then continued, more quietly.

“Bellen’s claim—that the Treaty of Veyros was never actually signed, only proposed, and that the war therefore continued in a cold state until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in eight hundred and ninety-one—is not impossible. Impossible things have been proved before now by better evidence than a box of drafts and a frightened apprentice’s certainty. But it is unsupported. It rests on an argument from absence: *we have not found the execution page, therefore there was none.* That is not scholarship. That is desperation wearing gloves.”

He glanced toward the shelves as if the northern scrolls might be listening and judging the exchange.

“The presence of negotiation papers does not unmake an agreement. If I find your letters proposing marriage, your father’s counterproposal, the priest’s draft ceremony, and the witnesses’ lists, it does not follow that you were never married. It may only mean that the wedding contract was lost, or that the ceremony was performed in haste, or that some clerk filed the final instrument under a different year. Absence of the document is not absence of the deed. Absence of the deed is proved by contradiction in the record: by continued levies, by renewed proclamations of war, by treasury accounts for campaigns, by border fortifications maintained, by the Conclave openly commissioning hostilities, by chroniclers describing ongoing public war after eight hundred and forty-seven. Where are those tracks?”

His voice hardened.

“They are not there. What is there is trouble. There is smuggling. There are unauthorized workings. There are veterans with grudges, lords with old wounds, hedge-mages with no master, and provincial chapters of the Conclave behaving as if the treaty were a suggestion written on wet clay. All of that is real. None of it is war in the legal sense. A kingdom may be uneasy without being at war. A mage may break the peace without the peace having never existed.”

Maester Tomas lifted the brass lens from his sleeve again, considered it, and set it down without use.

“As for Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in eight hundred and ninety-one: that is a constitutional act, not a termination of hostilities. A queen destroying an institution is not the same as a realm resuming public war against it. Mira fell upon the Conclave because it had become insolent, rich, politically entangled, and useless to the Crown’s idea of order. She did not declare that the Third Magical War had never ended. She ended an organization. If Bellen wishes to call that the true close of the war, he must define what he means by *close*. Does he mean the last armed clash? The last legal disability? The last independent military enchantment? The final political memory of the conflict? A word without definition is a lantern without oil.”

He leaned back, and the chair creaked beneath him like a sinner caught in confession.

“So. Is the treaty real? In the sense that matters to history, yes. The Treaty of Veyros was concluded in eight hundred and forty-seven after the Ending, and it shaped the realm afterward. In the narrow sense of physical survival, I will not swear to every leaf of parchment. Scholarly caution permits us to say that the exact manner of execution may be imperfectly documented. It does not permit us to say, on the strength of drafts and a later queen’s fury, that the peace never happened.”

His gaze sharpened again.

“If you wish to write the truth, then write it thus: *The Third Magical War is canonically dated to conclude with the Treaty of Veyros in eight hundred and forty-seven after the Ending. Western archive materials reveal extensive negotiation and may complicate the ceremonial history of the treaty’s execution, but they do not, as yet, overturn the administrative and chronicle evidence that the peace was proclaimed and observed. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Mage Conclave in eight hundred and ninety-one ended the old magical order, but it did not retroactively unmake the treaty of eighty-four-seven.*”

Maester Tomas picked up the silver stylus and traced a single clean line through the air, as though ruling a margin around the whole dispute.

“That is nuance. Not error dressed as nuance. Not Bellen’s dramatic little paradox. Not your textbook’s lazy certainty. Nuance is the space between evidence and inference, and you will learn to respect it before it learns to embarrass you.”

He pointed the stylus toward the Veyrosi correspondence.

“Now stop asking whether the treaty is real as if history were a merchant’s bargain and truth a sack of grain. Go and find the chapter letters for the eight-sixties. Find the Conclave’s protests. Find the wardens’ reports. Find the treasury memoranda. Find the enrollment duplicates. If the treaty was never executed, the archive will scream it from every shelf. Until it screams, you will speak carefully, write accurately, and not mistake a missing signature page for a vanished kingdom.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in. He's certainly passionate about this.* "So, the textbook is a starting point, not the end." *I chew on my lip for a second.* "But Maester, how do we know when a document is truly 'primary'? Like, what makes one source more reliable than another, especially when they contradict?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let the question settle over the desk like dust after a disturbed beam. It was, he thought, the sort of question that sounded simple only because the asker had not yet discovered how many lies could shelter beneath a single adjective.

“*Truly primary,*” he repeated, as though tasting a coin that might be clipped. “You use the phrase as if it were a virtue stamped on parchment. It is not. *Primary* is not a holiness. It is a relation. A document is primary *to something*, and if you cannot say what that something is, you have not begun to read.”

He lifted the silver stylus, then thought better of gesturing with it and laid it down again.

“Ask not, ‘Is this source primary?’ Ask, ‘What is this source evidence of?’ A royal writ is primary evidence that a king’s chancery issued a command. It is not primary evidence that the command was obeyed. A bishop’s chronicle is primary evidence for how a later generation wished to remember an event. It is not necessarily primary evidence for the event’s legal particulars. A treasury account is primary evidence that money moved. It is silent, or nearly so, on why heaven or hell had intervened. A private letter may be primary for rumor, affection, panic, or ambition. It is not thereby primary for truth.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You have heard the schoolmen chant that original documents outrank copies, that eyewitnesses outrank reporters, that official records outrank ballads. So far, they are not wholly wrong. But the chant becomes rotten the moment it is used instead of thought. An original can be forged. A witness can be blind. An official record can be propagandistic. A copy can preserve an original that has perished. A ballad can carry a fragment of genuine grievance when every chancery roll has been edited by frightened clerks. Reliability is not awarded by category. It is extracted by examination.”

He tapped one finger against the desk, precise and unhurried.

“First: **authorship and authority**. Who wrote the document? Not merely what name appears, but what office, what competence, what access, and what interest. A marshal’s report on a border alarm carries weight because he had wardens, riders, and fines under his hand. A monk’s account of a battle he never saw carries weight of a different kind: it tells you what the monastery believed, hoped, or feared. If the writer names witnesses, check whether the witnesses could witness. If he claims to have seen, ask whether he was elsewhere. If he writes in the royal style, ask whether the royal chancery used that style in that year, in that place, for that purpose.”

The stylus moved an inch to the left.

“Second: **purpose**. Every document is a tool. A charter is made to secure right. A chronicle is made to instruct, glorify, admonish, or entertain. A petition is made to move pity or anger. A draft is made to test words. A proclamation is made to bind subjects. A private memorandum may be made only to remember. You must never read a document as though it had no design. Even a list of candles consumed in a cathedral tower is a design: someone wished to account for wax. Ask what the document was *for*. A peace treaty drafted for negotiation is not the same kind of witness as a treaty enrolled for enforcement. A war decree issued to summon levies is not the same kind of witness as a stern letter against hedge-wizards.”

He glanced at the copy the apprentice still held, then away, as though refusing to dignify it until it earned consideration.

“Third: **date and context**. Not merely the date written on the face of the thing, but the date implied by hands, formulas, seals, names, titles, places, and mentions. A document may say eight hundred and sixty-three and still belong to a later copyist’s calendar. A title may betray an anachronism. A witness may have been dead. A place may not yet have bore that name. A legal formula may belong to a chancery practice not introduced until after the supposed date. Dates are not feathers stuck in an inkpot for decoration. They are hinges. If the hinge is false, the door will hang crookedly.”

His voice grew drier.

“Fourth: **physical form and transmission**. Parchment speaks before words do. Is it a single sheet, a rotulus, a codex leaf, a broken seal pendant, a docketed file, a cartulary copy, a notarial exemplar? What ink? What hand? What ruling? What folds, seals, signatures, endorsements, cancellations, later annotations? Where has it been? Who has handled it? A document found loose in a box is not thereby innocent. It may be stray, stolen, suppressed, misplaced, or preserved by accident. A document in a royal archive with continuous custody is stronger than a document that has wandered through three private collections and one pious relic-hunter’s cabinet. Provenance is not gossip. It is the biography of the evidence.”

He paused, as if collecting the remainder of the lesson into a less explosive shape.

“Fifth: **corroboration and independence**. One document may be a lamp. Many documents, lit from different wicks, may make a room visible. But beware lamps carried from the same flame. If three chronicles all repeat the same tale from one lost source, they are not three witnesses. They are one witness with three echoes. True corroboration comes from unrelated records that could not easily have borrowed from one another: a treasury entry, a warden’s report, a Conclave chapter letter, a court roll, a bishop’s register, a merchant’s account. When such records converge, the convergence is powerful. When they diverge, you must ask whether they diverge in fact or merely in description.”

The stylus traced a short line in the air, then stopped.

“Sixth: **effect**. Public acts leave scars. If a treaty was concluded, men must live under it. Levies are discharged. Wards are pulled down. Taxes cease or change. Officials are appointed to enforce limitations. Prisoners are released or prosecuted. Borders are patrolled differently. Correspondence refers to the peace as existing. If a war decree was issued, treasure moves, captains are commissioned, towns are summoned, ships are requisitioned, the enemy protests, chronicles record alarm, and later administrations explain themselves against it. A document that claims to alter the realm but produces no administrative shadow is suspect. Not impossible—history has buried many shadows—but suspect.”

He leaned back slightly, and the chair gave its complaining creak again.

“Seventh: **internal consistency and diplomatic form**. Chanceries have habits. So do convents, notaries, military commanders, and liars. A genuine royal act will normally observe the expected protocol: salutation, address, notification, clause structure, dating formula, witnesses, place, subscription, seal practice. A forged or careless document often stumbles in the small places: a title too grand for the reign, a witness list too tidy, a place-name used before its adoption, a legal phrase imported from a later reform, a seal description that matches no known matrix. You must learn the grammar of authority. Forgeries rarely falsify the large claim first. They falsify the manners.”

His eyes sharpened.

“Eighth: **silence**. What the document does not say may matter as much as what it says. A negotiation draft silent on execution may prove only that execution was not its business. A chronicle silent on a border affray may prove that the chronicler cared for omens, not mud. A treasury account with no wartime subsidy after eight hundred and forty-seven is not merely an absence. It is a presence of peace, provided the account is complete and the relevant offices are included. But silence must be weighed against loss. Archives burn. Clerks die. Indexes fail. A silence is eloquent only when the speaker had reason and ability to speak.”

He let that hang for a moment, then returned to the matter with less patience.

“You ask how one source becomes more reliable than another when they contradict. The contradiction is not the beginning of wisdom. It is the beginning of labor. First, determine whether they truly contradict. Many scholars cry contradiction because two documents use different words for the same fact, or the same word for different facts. A charter may call an affray a ‘battle’ because the writer wishes to honor the dead. A marshal’s roll may call the same affair a ‘riot’ because he wishes to deny the enemy dignity. Both may be accurate within their genres. The contradiction is in the vocabulary, not necessarily in the event.”

He lifted one hand, palm outward, as though staying an objection not yet made.

“If the contradiction is real, then weigh the witnesses. Which source is closer to the fact in question? Which had authority to record it? Which was intended to establish it? Which is independent? Which is corroborated? Which shows signs of derivation, alteration, or partisan shaping? Which aligns with the administrative consequences that followed? A later chronicle may preserve a genuine memory, but it does not outrank a contemporary chancery enrollment unless the enrollment is demonstrably corrupt. A newly found draft does not automatically outrank a long-established record merely because it is new. Novelty is not truth. It is only freshness of embarrassment.”

His mouth thinned.

“This is where Bellen and his admirers fail. They have found western archive papers—negotiation drafts, correspondence, perhaps sealed proposals—and they treat them as though these documents were the whole corpse rather than scattered bones. Suppose the western papers are genuine. Suppose some bear seals. Suppose one uses the phrase *Aldric Rex* without a numeral. Suppose another speaks of hostile practices continuing after eight hundred and forty-seven. What follows? It follows that negotiation was messy. It follows that peace was contested. It follows that clerks used severe language against disorderly mages. It does not follow that the Treaty of Veyros was never executed. To prove that, one needs more than drafts and darkness. One needs direct evidence of non-execution: a royal declaration voiding the treaty, a Conclave protest naming the breach, continued wartime levies, renewed border fortifications, treasury accounts for campaigns, commissions to captains, proclamations of hostilities, chronicles that describe public war rather than private trouble. Where are these? Not in a box.”

He glanced toward the shelves of northern scrolls.

“The Red Rolls are not sacred because they are old. They are weighty because they are official, continuous, independent in their way, and corroborated by financial and administrative records. The Conclave’s own chapter letters disavowing rogue hosts after eight hundred and forty-seven are not proofs of peace because they sound peaceful. They are proofs because institutions defend their legal position. If the Conclave believed it was still at war, it would not fine its own men for unauthorized hostilities and pay restitution for burned millraces. It would commission them.”

Tomas picked up the brass lens again, turned it once in his fingers, and set it down without raising it to his eye.

“Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in eight hundred and ninety-one is, likewise, a powerful document-rich event. It is primary evidence that the Crown ended the Conclave as an institution. It is not primary evidence that the Third Magical War had continued legally from eight hundred and forty-seven unless one first proves that the Conclave’s existence was identical with a state of war. That is not so. Organizations persist in peacetime. They grow corrupt. They are suppressed. Their suppression may be political, fiscal, religious, or constitutional. It need not be the closing chapter of an ancient campaign.”

He fixed the apprentice with a stare that had become less angry and more instructional, which was perhaps more tiresome.

“So when you encounter contradiction, do not run to the newest fragment as though it were a saint returned from the dead. Build a hierarchy of questions. What is each source? Who made it? Why? When? Under what authority? With what physical and documentary support? What effects followed? What independent records agree or differ? What would have to be true for the contradiction to be real? What is the simplest explanation that preserves the greater mass of evidence? Scholarship is not a duel in which the loudest new claim stabs the old record through the heart. It is a tribunal. The document is a witness. The witness must be cross-examined.”

A brief silence followed, broken only by the candle’s faint tick.

“And remember this: a primary source can be wrong. A secondary source can be useful. An eyewitness can be mistaken. A scribe can be honest and still copy nonsense. A forger can produce a masterpiece. A chronicle written two centuries later may preserve the only surviving account of a local rising. The labels do not save you. Judgment saves you, and judgment is labor.”

He extended one ink-stained hand, not for the copy this time, but toward the desk where the apprentice’s notes lay.

“If you wish to practice, take three documents from the Veyrosi bundle: a negotiation draft, a chapter letter disavowing the Woodward Host, and a treasury memorandum referring to ceased subsidies. For each, tell me what proposition it is primary evidence for. Not what grand conclusion it seems to support. What narrow fact can it establish without borrowing help from another record? If you can do that without crying ‘war’ or ‘peace’ like a street vendor selling weather, you will have learned more than Bellen has learned from all his boxes.”

His expression tightened again.

“And do not say that one source is ‘more primary’ than another. That is cant. Sources are not graded like apples. Some are better witnesses to some facts. A ship’s log is primary for the ship’s course. It is not primary for the captain’s conscience. A confessor’s note may be primary for the captain’s fear. It is not primary for the latitude. Learn to attach every claim of reliability to the specific fact it supports, and you will stop mistaking dramatic contradiction for historical revolution.”

He turned back to the manuscript at last, but not before adding, in the dry tone of a man who had buried too many enthusiastic fools under footnotes:

“The truth is not whichever document makes you feel clever. The truth is what survives the fullest cross-examination of all the documents, including the ones you wish had not been found.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up my notes, feeling the weight of Maester Tomas's words. I glance at the copy Bellen gave me, then back at the shelves of Veyrosi correspondence. My earlier certainty feels a lot less solid now.* "Thank you, Maester. I... I think I understand. I'll start with the chapter letters for the eight-sixties." *I turn to head towards the shelves, but then pause, a new thought occurring to me.* "Maester, if the Conclave was disavowing its own men, does that mean some mages were still fighting even after the treaty?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus hovered above the manuscript, trembling very slightly—not from age alone, but from the effort of restraining himself from declaring that the boy had finally asked a question worth the candle.

He let the pause stretch long enough to be uncomfortable.

“You have learned,” he said at last, “that uncertainty is not defeat. It is merely the condition under which thought begins. Do not thank me. Thank the records if they answer. They are less generous than I.”

He lowered the stylus, but did not resume his tracing.

“Now. Your sentence is defective before it reaches its conclusion. You ask whether the Conclave’s disavowal of its own men means that some mages were ‘still fighting’ after the treaty. That word—*fighting*—is doing too much work, and doing it badly. It is a broad, muddy boot where a scalpel is required.”

He raised one ink-stained finger.

“If by *fighting* you mean that men bearing arms, or staves, or enchanted blades, or old wartime grudges, continued to kill, threaten, plunder, and burn after eight hundred and forty-seven, then yes. Undoubtedly. Regrettably. Inevitably. A treaty does not reach into every chest and pluck out the habit of violence. A proclamation of peace does not turn swords into pruning hooks overnight. Soldiers demobilize slowly. Mercenaries drift into banditry. Feuds outlive campaigns. Provincial magicians who spent years practicing martial workings do not suddenly become meek copyists because a king and a conclave have shaken hands.”

His mouth thinned.

“If by *fighting* you mean that the Mage Conclave, as a recognized corporate power, continued to wage public war against the Crown after eight hundred and forty-seven, then no. Not on the evidence you have brought me. Not on the evidence Bellen has brought you. Not on the evidence of the Red Rolls, the treasury accounts, the cessation of the Ashen Levies, the dismantling of the Silvermarch wards, or the Conclave’s own anxious attempts to distance itself from unauthorized hostilities.”

He tapped the desk once.

“There is a gulf between *a mage committed an act of warlike violence* and *the realm was at war*. The first may be crime. The second is a legal condition. The first may require a warrant. The second requires a declaration, an enemy, commissions, levies, prize courts, ransoms, treaties, and the entire tedious machinery of public hostility. Men forget the machinery because they prefer the drama.”

Maester Tomas leaned back, and the chair complained beneath him with the resignation of old furniture.

“Consider the matter plainly. When a kingdom makes peace, its enemies do not vanish. Its veterans do not forget. Its prisons do not empty. Its border wards do not become polite. A disbanded levy-man may become a thief. A licensed battle-enchanter may become a hedge-mage. A chapter house that once supplied wizards to an army may find its younger members raiding trade convoys because raiding is profitable and discipline has decayed. That does not prove the war never ended. It proves that peace is difficult to enforce.”

He glanced toward the shelves, then back to the apprentice’s face with sharpened attention.

“This is why the Conclave’s disavowal matters. If the Conclave had believed itself still at war, it would not have needed to disavow the Woodward Host. It would have claimed them. It would have said: *these are our servants, acting in the prosecution of hostilities against the Crown*. Instead, it says: *these men are not authorized; their workings are unlawful; the damage shall be compensated*. That is not the conduct of a belligerent power. That is the conduct of an institution attempting to preserve its legal standing under a peace it is obliged to observe.”

His voice dropped, becoming more precise, more cutting.

“You must learn to distinguish three things that careless minds mash together like spoiled porridge: war, rebellion, and crime.”

He counted them off with stiff fingers.

“War is public hostility between recognized powers. Rebellion is armed resistance against lawful authority within a realm, often claiming political grievance. Crime is private violence, brigandage, fraud, arson, assault, or unauthorized magic, committed without public commission or recognized belligerent status. After eight hundred and forty-seven, the realm experienced the third in abundance, the second occasionally, and the first not at all—unless Bellen can produce the legal machinery of first things and not merely the emotional residue of last ones.”

Maester Tomas let that settle, then added, with less heat but no less severity:

“Your question reveals a common error among students who have recently discovered that history is not a story told by friendly masters. They swing from one falsehood to another. The textbook says: *the war ended, therefore all was peaceful*. The apprentice, smelling blood in the archives, says: *men still fought, therefore the war never ended*. Both are wrong. The first mistakes law for life. The second mistakes life for law.”

He picked up the silver stylus, turned it once, and set it down again.

“The Treaty of Veyros did not create a world without magical violence. It created a world in which magical violence had to be justified differently. Before the treaty, a mage-bearer serving a Conclave column might burn a granary and call it strategy. After the treaty, the same man doing the same thing was an outlaw, unless he could produce lawful commission from the Crown’s wardens or recognized authority under the settlement. The act may look identical. The legal skin is different.”

His eyes narrowed.

“That is why administrative records matter more than dramatic phrases. A chronicler may write that ‘the mages still made war upon the land’ because he wishes to terrify his readers or honor local martyrs. A treasury clerk writing *no subsidy issued to eastern host* after eight hundred and forty-seven is boring, but he is telling you something more dangerous to romance: the state no longer treated the matter as campaign finance. A warden’s report of ‘insurgent enchanters’ is not a declaration of war. It is a request for warrants.”

He glanced at the copy the apprentice had produced earlier, though he did not reach for it.

“If the document Bellen showed you speaks of evil-disposed persons, hostile practices, unlawful workings, or disruptive mages, then it belongs to that same family. It is the language of enforcement, not revival. A king may order the seizure of foci, the arrest of itinerant enchanters, the punishment of border raiders, and the suppression of forbidden rites without thereby announcing that the Conclave is again his open enemy. Indeed, he may do so precisely because he wishes to insist that the peace still stands.”

Maester Tomas’s expression darkened slightly, as though the thought of sloppy terminology physically pained him.

“And do not say *some mages* as though that settled the matter. Which mages? Of what rank? Under what obedience? Acting for themselves, for a provincial chapter, for a lord, for a foreign interest, or for the Conclave’s ruling circle? Were they wearing the colors of war? Had they been commissioned? Were their victims combatants or civilians? Was the Crown treating them as prisoners of war or as criminals? Did the Conclave protest their execution as unlawful killings of belligerents, or did it quietly pay fines and hope the matter would blow over?”

He spread one hand, palm upward, as though offering the questions for inspection.

“Those are the questions that separate a historian from a storyteller. The storyteller says: *the mages still fought, therefore the war went on*. The historian says: *what, exactly, was the legal character of the violence, and who bears the burden of proving it?*”

A brief silence followed, broken only by the faint crackle of the candle.

“To return to your inquiry: yes, some mages were still engaging in hostilities after the treaty. Some may even have believed the treaty unjust, illegitimate, or temporarily imposed. Some provincial chapters may have harbored them. Some lords may have employed them. Some old commanders may have spoken of ‘the war’ long after the war had become a memory and a pension dispute.”

He jabbed a finger toward the shelves.

“But belief is not law. Nostalgia is not belligerency. A veteran calling a border skirmish ‘the war’ does not make it so. Nor does a resentful enchanter lighting a beacon and declaring that the old enmity continues. Unless the Crown recognized a state of war, unless the Conclave commissioned hostilities, unless treasuries funded campaigns, unless levies were summoned, unless prisoners were exchanged under cartel, unless chroniclers described public war rather than private outrage—then you are describing disorder, not continuation.”

His voice softened by a fraction, though not kindly.

“You must not make the opposite error either. The existence of post-treaty violence does not prove the treaty was sham. It may prove the opposite: that the treaty was real enough to be violated.”

He let that sentence rest where it would sting.

“A law that is broken still exists. A boundary that is crossed still divides. A peace that is troubled still functions as the standard against which trouble is measured. If men after eight hundred and forty-seven spoke of ‘breaking the peace,’ they acknowledged that there had been a peace to break. If they had believed no peace had ever been made, they would have spoken differently. They would have said: *we resume the war*. And where, I ask you, is thatresume? Name the proclamation.
