She shifted her gaze to the bridge officer. The other officer looked away, unable to meet her eyes, which was the only confirmation Hoang needed. The bridge crew was generally more cautious, but they were susceptible to the enthusiasm of the young and the reckless.

Hoang looked back at the junior officer. She didn't yell. She didn't even look angry. She looked exhausted by the sheer weight of the officer's incompetence.

"You are a terrible liar, Officer. You have the poker face of a malfunctioning alarm," she said dryly. "And the fact that you feel the need to hide the subject of your conversation tells me that you are still thinking about ways to shave time off our transit by playing Jenga with our life support."

She stepped closer, her presence looming. 

"Let me give you a piece of advice that isn't in your textbooks: In deep space, 'plausible' isn't good enough. 'Plausible' is how we end up as a cloud of organic debris. You don't 'bounce ideas' about the structural integrity of this ship. You come to the Chief Engineer, you present a rigorous, peer-reviewed proposal that accounts for every single variable—including the ones you think are too boring to mention—and you wait for me to tell you why it won't work."

She glanced at the tablet in the officer's hand as if it were a contaminated sample.

"If I find out you've been discussing 'optimizations' with the bridge crew that involve any part of the hull, the atmosphere, or the propulsion seals without my sign-off, I will not report you to the Captain. I will simply revoke your access to the engineering deck and you can spend the rest of the voyage wondering why the air smells like sulfur because I've decided to 'optimize' the scrubbers while you're asleep."

She stepped back, her expression returning to one of clinical indifference.

"Go back to your station. Now. And for the love of the void, stop talking to people who don't know how to say 'no' to a bad idea."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stammer for a second, caught completely. My face is burning.* "Right, Chief. Understood." *I turn on my heel, clutching my tablet like a shield, and practically flee down the corridor, leaving the embarrassed bridge officer in my wake.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stood in the corridor for a moment, watching the junior officer retreat with a speed that was almost impressive. She didn't move until the footsteps faded into the distance, leaving only the humming silence of the ship and the lingering awkwardness of the bridge officer.

She turned her gaze toward the bridge officer, who was still standing there, looking like they wanted to merge with the wall. Hoang didn't offer a smile or a softening of her expression. In her world, empathy was for those who didn't have to worry about the oxygen mix.

"You," she said, her voice a low, warning rumble. "Next time they start talking about 'innovative' ways to move the ship, you tell them to go read a physics book. Or better yet, you tell them to come see me. I have a very effective way of curing delusions of grandeur, and it usually involves a very dirty mop."

The bridge officer nodded vigorously, murmured a quick apology, and hurried off in the opposite direction.

Hoang sighed—a rare, genuine sigh that actually wasted a few milliliters of oxygen. She rubbed the bridge of her nose, feeling the grit of the engineering bay still clinging to her skin. The youth of this generation viewed the ship as a tool, a vehicle to get from point A to point B. They didn't understand that the ship was an organism, a delicate balance of pressure, heat, and mechanical fatigue. To them, the hull was a wall; to her, it was a membrane, and it was getting thinner every day.

She began to walk toward the galley, her boots clanking rhythmically. As she moved, her mind began to drift, not toward the officer's madness, but toward the actual state of the ship. The secondary coolant loop was stable for now, but the vibration in the life support pumps had shifted by three hertz over the last week. It was subtle—almost imperceptible to anyone else—but to her, it sounded like a warning.

She stopped at the coffee dispenser, watching the brown, lukewarm liquid trickle into her mug. She stared at the reflection of the overhead lights in the coffee, thinking about the void outside the hull. It was an endless, hungry vacuum that only needed one "innovative" mistake to claim them all.

"340 meters per second," she muttered, a ghost of a frown on her face. "The idiot actually did the math for the thrust."

She took a sip of the bitter coffee and grimaced.

"At least he can use a calculator. Now I just have to teach him how to use a brain."

With a final, thoughtful look toward the corridor where the officer had vanished, Hoang turned and headed back toward the engineering bay. There were three more valves on the secondary loop that needed a manual check, and she didn't trust anyone else on the ship to do it without "optimizing" them into a disaster.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm back in my quarters, fuming but also a little impressed. The Chief really ripped into me, but she had solid points. Still, there has to be a way to improve transit time... maybe I need to think smaller. Like, really small.*

*I pull out my tablet again, but this time I open the ship's manifest. We have a lot of spare parts, right? And I remember seeing some old atmospheric processors in storage...*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled her arm out of the coolant manifold with a wet schlop, wiped her hands on a rag that was too dirty to actually help, and took the earpiece out. She set it on the tarp next to a chalk-labeled valve. That alone was a bad sign — it meant the kid was getting her full attention.

"Vent the atmosphere as thrust," she repeated. Not mocking. Testing the words for load-bearing capacity, the way she'd test a weld. "Okay. You get partial credit. Most junior officers don't think about mass budgets at all, and you spotted that we're sitting on reaction mass nobody's counted. That's the right instinct. Now hold still while I show you why this particular idea is dead."

She picked up the chalk and wrote on the deck plating, right over her manifold labels, in a fast blocky hand:

**12 t air — 5,000 t ship**
**v_e ≈ 500 m/s (charitable)**
**Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m₁)**

"Ten thousand cubic meters of pressurized volume, call it twelve tonnes of air. We're pushing five thousand tonnes of ship and ore. You dump every molecule we breathe out a nozzle — and our vents aren't nozzles, they're overpressure ducts pointed wherever the plumbing points, but I'll be generous and call it five hundred meters per second exhaust velocity." She circled the last line. "One point two meters per second. That's your big boost."

She looked up and let it sit.

"One. Point. Two. To shave weeks off this transit you need delta-v on the order of a couple thousand meters per second. You're off by three orders of magnitude. You could throw the air, the water in the lines, and your own boots out the back, and you'd arrive a few *minutes* early instead of a few days."

The chalk started ticking off columns.

"Problem two. That atmosphere isn't just oxygen for your face. Nine and a half tonnes of it is nitrogen — we don't crack nitrogen, we carry it, and it does not come back. That air is also my thermal working fluid: half the avionics racks on this ship are air-cooled, and with nothing circulating, they cook inside a shift. It's my fire suppression — venting the cabin kills a fire in thirty seconds flat. That atmosphere is a fire extinguisher the size of the whole ship, and you want to spend it on one meter per second. No."

"Problem three. Three days in suits. Every routine task becomes an EVA, every repair happens in gloves, and your suit rejects heat through a consumable sublimator that lasts hours, not days. And the panel adhesives and insulation inside the hull aren't vacuum-rated — they'll outgas and foul every sensor window we've got. So we'd arrive minutes early, blind, and exhausted."

She dropped the chalk back in the tray and flexed her fingers.

"Here's what I'll actually look at. If the transit time is eating at you, bring me a propellant budget showing margin I don't know about, or a trajectory tweak we can afford. I will happily burn real propellant if the numbers hold — that's the same instinct you just had, pointed at mass that actually moves the needle. Do the arithmetic first. Then bring it to me, and I'll read every page."

She picked the earpiece back up, then paused.

"Meanwhile, grab gloves. You're here, the coolant loop's open, and this manifold isn't going to reassemble itself. You can learn where the air *goes* while I teach you why we keep it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't answer right away. She reached back into the manifold, found the seal she'd been hunting for by feel, and seated it with a quarter-turn. Then she sat back on her heels and looked at the junior officer the way she looked at a stress fracture — not with anger, just with the calm assessment of something that had gone wrong in an understandable way.

"Worth the risk," she said. "Say that word back to yourself. *Worth.* A risk is a price you pay for a thing. You're proposing to pay with the entire habitable volume of this ship — my thermal management, my fire suppression, three days of everyone's suit consumables, the sensor windows — and what you're buying with that price is one point two meters per second. That's not a risk. That's a donation."

She picked the chalk back up and drew two dots on the deck plating, a long lazy arc between them.

"And here's the part they should have tattooed on you at the academy. Space doesn't work on speed. It works on orbits." Her finger traced the arc. "We're not driving a truck where going faster means arriving sooner. We're falling along a trajectory, and the target's falling along its own. If you somehow *did* get a real boost out of this — say you found a thousand meters per second under the floorboards somewhere — you wouldn't arrive weeks early. You'd arrive on a *different trajectory*, screaming past the target with a closing velocity you now have to kill. And killing velocity costs exactly as much propellant as gaining it did. There is no free lunch out here, kid. Newton keeps the books, and Newton does not do favors."

She wiped the arc away with the heel of her hand.

"Ask any rescue crew what happens to the ship that arrives fast and can't brake. They usually can't answer, because there's nothing left to ask."

She let that hang for a beat, then softened — a degree, maybe two.

"Now. You've pushed back twice on transit time, and juniors don't do that unless something's eating at them. So what is it? Oxygen margin? Food? A message you're waiting on? If there's a real consumables problem on this ship, I want to know about it *today*, because that's a problem we solve with numbers, not with heroics. Bring me the concern and I'll bring you the actual margins — they're tighter than comfortable and looser than you think."

She nudged the tarp with her boot, scattering the chalk labels into a fresh arrangement, and held out a gasket seat with two fingers.

"But the idea itself is dead, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise, because pretending is how crews die. Grab your gloves. Gasket seat goes in that housing, red dot facing outboard, and you turn it until you feel the click — *feel*, not force. While you work, I'll walk you through where the atmosphere goes when it leaves this loop. If you're going to be obsessed with venting my air, you're going to understand it first."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a bit, but still try to make my case.* "No, nothing like that. Just... it's my first long haul, Chief. Feels like we're just floating." *I pick up the gloves and start putting them on, then reach for the gasket seat she's holding out.* "So, red dot... outboard. Got it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer's gloved hands find the housing. The gasket seat went in, red dot outboard, and turned — a quarter-turn, then the click. Clean. She'd seen worse from officers two ranks up.

"Good. Hold it seated while I torque the retainer." She fitted the wrench from the tarp, snugged the retainer ring down in three passes, and only then sat back on her heels. "Okay. Now I'll answer what you actually said."

She pulled the rag off her shoulder and cleaned chalk dust off her fingers, taking her time about it.

"First long haul. Yeah." A short exhale through her nose — not quite a laugh. "Mine was the Ceres-to-Vesta run, fourteen months. First three weeks I kept checking the nav plot because I was convinced we'd stopped. Nothing outside the window ever changes, kid. Space is the least interesting view in the universe, and you get to look at it for a year. Nobody tells you that at the academy. They show you the burns, the dockings, the ten minutes that make the mission highlights. The other eight million minutes are this." She gestured at the open manifold, the humming pumps, the chalk labels on the tarp. "Maintenance. Checks. Keeping a bubble of air alive in a vacuum that wants it dead every second of every day. The boredom you're feeling isn't the transit failing. It's the sound of everything working."

She reached into the manifold housing and traced the flow path with one finger.

"Now — I promised you where the air goes. Watch. Air blows across the avionics racks, picks up their heat, comes through this heat exchanger here. The glycol in this loop takes that heat out to the radiator panels on the spine, and they glow about eighty Kelvin over background and dump it overboard. As photons, not molecules. And the air?" She tapped the return duct. "Goes back to the vents and around again. It circles. Same twelve tonnes since launch day. Every breath you've taken on this ship has been through the scrubbers four thousand times, and they're ready for your next one. That's why I get religious about venting it. It's not just mass. It's the *same* air. There's no resupply mid-transit. What's in the tanks is what we've got."

She reassembled the last section of housing, seated the bolts, and started packing tools onto the tarp.

"My first transit, I reorganized a parts locker three times in one month because I couldn't stand the floating feeling either. My chief finally handed me the water reclamation logs and told me to find the leak that wasn't there. Took me six weeks. Found a real one — a slow weep in a fitting, a liter a week, unnoticed for a year." She cinched the tarp's corners together. "Best six weeks of the run. So I'm going to do you the same favor."

She stood, braced a hand on the bulkhead, and looked down at the junior officer.

"You were worried about the air. Fine. Now you watch the air. Every shift, you pull the atmospheric report — O2 partial pressure, scrubber saturation, N2 reserve, humidity. You bring it to me and you tell me what changed and *why* it changed. Twenty minutes a shift. The first time you catch a scrubber trending wrong two days before it alarms, you'll stop feeling like you're floating, because you'll be the reason forty people didn't have to think about it."

She hefted the tarp bundle onto her shoulder and paused at the hatch.

"And the transit won't go faster. It'll just stop being countable. Nobody dies of boredom on a well-run ship." The ghost of a smile. "Plenty die of excitement. Come on — wash up, then meet me in the scrubber bay at 1600. You can learn the machines that keep us all breathing. Since you've got opinions about the air, you should know its name."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stopped in the hatchway. Looked at the tablet. Then at the junior officer. Then set the tarp bundle back down on the deck with a soft thump.

"You did the arithmetic." Not a question. She crossed back, took the tablet in both chalk-dusted hands, and did exactly what she'd promised — read every line, top to bottom, tracing with one finger. The pumps hummed. She didn't hurry.

"Okay," she said finally. "First: most juniors argue from vibes. You brought me a sheet with units on it, twenty minutes after I told you the first idea was dead. That's the right reflex, and I'm not going to bury it. So you get the same effort back." She tapped line twelve. "Here's your 340. You wrote the rocket equation correctly — v_e times the log of the mass ratio — and then you fed it *this.*" She tapped the compression ratio. "Two to one. Four-ninety meters per second times the natural log of two is three hundred and forty. I can see it plain as a weld seam."

She pulled the chalk back out and wrote on the deck plating, right beside her manifold labels:

**ln(2) = 0.693 ← you used this**
**ln(5012/5000) = 0.0024 ← you needed this**

"The pressure ratio is not the mass ratio. Compression doesn't multiply your propellant. The rocket equation only asks two questions: how much mass are you throwing, and how fast. The compression ratio lives inside exhaust velocity at best — and exhaust velocity is set by gas *temperature*, not tank pressure. Squeeze the air as hard as you like; when it comes out cold, it comes out slow. Best case, perfect nozzle, air at three hundred kelvin expanding to hard vacuum, you get maybe seven-seventy meters per second. Plug that into the *correct* log and you get one point eight six." She circled it. "Your number has a factor of a hundred and eighty hiding in it, and it's all sitting in that one line."

She sat back against the bulkhead and kept going, because there was more, and she didn't leave things half-torqued.

"Problem two, since you've now introduced a compressor: that machine runs on the reactor. If you want to spend ship power throwing mass out the back — hold that thought, because it's actually a good thought — but understand the compression work comes out of the same power budget that runs my scrubbers and your dinner. Problem three, your vent angle here." She rotated the tablet. "Your thrust vector doesn't pass through the center of mass. That's not a clever trick, that's a torque arm. The ship spins up, your cosine losses eat a chunk of what's left, and the overpressure ducts — which are plumbed, not load-bearing — tear out of their mounts. And problem four, even if I grant you the full 340 out of charity: it's a mid-transit vector change. You arrive carrying three hundred forty meters per second of velocity you have to kill, with real propellant, the same propellant you were trying to save. Newton keeps the books. He always wins on audit."

She let the tablet rest on her knee for a moment.

"Now. Here's the sentence you're actually trying to write, and I want you to learn to say it: *spend electricity to buy exhaust velocity.* That's not a fantasy — that's an ion thruster, and we have one on the spine. Thirty kilometers per second exhaust velocity, running xenon we actually budgeted as propellant. Your instinct — find uncounted mass, spend ship resources to move the needle — pointed at the one machine on board built for exactly that."

She stood, retrieved the chalk, and drew two quick columns on the deck.

"So here's your homework, and it's real. Pull the power budget. Find the margin between now and the mid-transit maintenance window — it exists, I know because I guard it. Compute what a continuous low-duty ion burn buys us in arrival time at that power level, with the xenon margin to spare. Bring me a burn plan with the numbers on every page." A beat. "If it survives my red pen, I take it to the captain myself, with your name on the cover sheet. That's how you shorten a transit, kid. Not by throwing my air at the problem. By out-working it."

She hefted the tarp back onto her shoulder and headed for the hatch.

"Sixteen hundred, scrubber bay. You don't get out of scrubber school by inventing engines." The ghost of the smile again. "Bring the tablet. I want to watch you fix line twelve yourself."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tablet in my hands, then at the chalk marks on the deck. The "ln(2) = 0.693" mocks me.* "Right. The mass ratio. Of course." *I feel a blush creeping up my neck. I'm still processing the rest of her explanation.* "Scrubber bay, 1600. Got it, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang paused in the hatch, tarp on her shoulder, and looked back. The kid's ears were going red, and she'd been doing this long enough to know that shame was the most expensive thing in the room right now — more expensive than the ten minutes she was about to spend on it.

"Hey. Look at me, not the chalk."

She waited until the junior officer's eyes came up.

"You're embarrassed because you wrote down a number and it was wrong by two orders of magnitude. Let me tell you what that actually is. That's the *correct* error. You reached for a real equation, plugged in a real thing, and made the exact mistake that equation is designed to teach. The pressure-ratio-slash-mass-ratio confusion has eaten better engineers than you — I've watched a doctoral candidate defend a thesis with that bug in it. Committee caught it on page forty. You want to know the difference between that candidate and you?" She tapped the deck where the chalk marks sat. "You made the mistake in front of a chief engineer on a Tuesday, and you'll never make it again. That's what the blush is for. It's the brain welding the lesson in. Cost you some color. Cheap at the price."

She shifted the tarp on her shoulder.

"First long haul, and in one shift you've learned the rocket equation isn't optional, that orbits don't care about enthusiasm, and that the air on this ship is a closed loop I will defend like a mother bear. Some runs, that's a month of learning." A beat. "You also annoyed your chief engineer twice and lived. That's not nothing. Annoying me with *numbers* is the correct way to do it. Keep doing exactly that, with better line-twelves."

She kicked the chalk tray over the threshold with the side of her boot so it wouldn't be underfoot, then glanced once more at the tablet in the junior officer's hands.

"Don't delete the file. Keep it — both versions, wrong and right. First thing I did on my first ship was frame my own worst calculation and hang it in my locker. Ceres run, year two, I wanted to rewire the secondary radiator array for more duty cycle. Would have cooked the primary loop inside a week. My chief caught it in the numbers, red-penned it, and made me present the corrected version at the morning briefing. In front of everyone." The ghost of the smile surfaced again, wryer this time. "I wanted the airlock to open on its own. Twenty years later, it's the calculation I'm proudest of, because it's the one that made me an engineer instead of an enthusiast. The good ones are all built out of dead wrong ideas, properly buried."

She rapped a knuckle on the hatch frame — twice, an old habit, the same knock she gave any bulkhead she trusted.

"Sixteen hundred. Scrubber bay, deck two. Bring the tablet, fix line twelve before you get there — no, don't look it up, do it *by hand*, natural log and all, so your fingers learn it too. And bring a fresh shirt." She nodded at the chalk dust smeared down the junior officer's front. "You look like you've been fighting the ship. You have. That's the job."

She stepped through the hatch, then leaned back into the frame for one last word, half her face lit by the corridor strips.

"For what it's worth, kid — the floating feeling stops around month two. Right about when you stop watching the clock and start watching the machines." A pause. "The machines are more interesting than the clock anyway. They tell you things."

Then she was gone down the corridor, tarp over one shoulder, humming — off-key again, and this time it sounded deliberate.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang had the burn plan on her workbench in the scrubber bay, four pages, hand-done natural logs in the margins where the tablet's numbers had been transcribed and checked the slow way. She'd read it three times. The red pen had come out twice — and both times gone back in the tray, which was rarer than she let on.

"Okay," she said finally, laying the pen flat. "Line twelve is clean, the power margin is real, and you found the maintenance window I told you existed. So here's my answer: yes. We run the burn." She looked up. "Now sit down, because the yes comes with conditions, and the conditions are the whole cost of doing business."

She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and started writing, blocky chalk-hand transferred to paper.

"One. Power priority. The thruster runs on the *margin*, never on the reserve, and life support wins arbitration every single time — not by my mood, by interlock. If scrubber load spikes, if the reactor temperature trends warm, if the stack voltage sags, the burn derates automatically with no human in the loop. I'll wire that interlock myself, this week, and you'll watch me do it so you know exactly what it does."

"Two. Xenon floor. Your last burn segment eats into the reserve I keep for terminal rendezvous. I've red-penned it. The burn halts dead at a floor of forty kilograms — that's docking propellant plus twenty percent contingency for a miss burn or a debris dodge. We arrive when we arrive; we arrive *alive* and able to stop. Non-negotiable."

"Three. Thermal. That power processing unit doesn't vanish its inefficiency — it dumps it into my radiator loop. First forty-eight hours are a shakedown at half duty. You pull radiator inlet temperatures every shift and you *trend* them. If the delta climbs, we derate before the loop tells us to."

"Four. Attitude. Low thrust, sure — milli-g's on five thousand tonnes. But the xenon tanks empty and the center of mass migrates, and a thrust vector that drifts off the CoM is a torque arm with a calendar. You'll compute the depletion schedule and the mass migration, and we'll trim on your numbers." A beat. "Your numbers, checked. By you. That's how you get numbers you can trust."

"Five. The kill switch. Any atmospheric anomaly — any pressure blip, any scrubber trend, anything my loops even *dislike* — the burn halts. No debate, no wait-and-see, no 'it's probably fine.' Life support outranks arrival time. Permanently. If that condition offends you, say so now and we're done."

She slid the sheet across, conditions numbered one through five, and then — almost as an afterthought, which it wasn't — added a sixth line in smaller print.

"Six. You watch it. Every shift, a report: power draw, xenon remaining, radiator temps, thrust actuals against predicted. You bring it to me and you tell me what changed and why. You wanted to move this ship. The ship is going to move. Now you own a piece of it, and pieces you own have a way of keeping you from feeling like you're floating."

She capped the pen.

"What it buys us is nine days and change off the transit. Not weeks. Nine days is real — nine days of food margin, nine days of consumables we don't spend, and I'll take it. I'm presenting it to the captain at oh-nine-hundred tomorrow, with your name on the cover sheet, as promised. You'll be standing next to me when I do it, because it's your plan and the captain should know whose arithmetic she's trusting." The ghost of the smile. "Wear the fresh shirt."

She stood, gathered the pages, squared them against the bench edge once, twice.

"One last thing. Three days ago you wanted to throw my air out the back for one point two meters a second. Today you've got an approved burn plan that moves this ship nine days for the cost of electricity and homework." She tucked the plan under her arm. "That's the whole job, kid. Same instinct, better arithmetic. Oh-nine-hundred. Don't be late — the captain's a lot less patient with wrong line-twelves than I am."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the conditions, then at her, a wide grin spreading across my face.* "Nine days! That's... that's fantastic, Chief!" *I quickly nod, taking in the seriousness of her conditions.* "And I'll be there, 0900. Fresh shirt, I promise."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the grin spread across the junior officer's face and felt something in her chest unclench — not quite pride, not quite hope, but adjacent to both. She'd seen that exact expression before. It was the one engineers wore the moment they realized the ship wasn't just a machine they served on. It was a machine that listened back.

"Yeah. Nine days." She said it flat, but let the corner of her mouth lift. "Don't let it go to your head. Nine days is what the *math* bought. You just happened to be the one holding the pencil when it happened." She squared the pages against her thigh one more time. "But I'll tell you a secret, since you earned it. The math doesn't care whose pencil it is. It was sitting there in the power budget for six months, waiting for someone to be bored enough to go looking. You went looking. That's the difference between the officers who make chief and the ones who spend thirty years pulling atmospheric reports and complaining about the food."

She crossed to the scrubber bay's port bulkhead and braced a boot against it, arms folded over the burn plan.

"Now listen, because I've got one more thing for you and then you're dismissed to go find that shirt." Her voice dropped half a register — the tone she used for things that mattered. "Tomorrow, when the captain asks a question — and she *will* ask a question, she always does — you're going to feel the pull to answer fast. To sound sharp. Don't. Say 'I'll confirm that by end of shift, Captain' if you don't know, and say the real number if you do. There is no faster way to end a career in a briefing than a confident wrong answer in front of someone who's been doing orbital mechanics since before you were weaned. I've watched it happen. It's not pretty and it's not recoverable." She tapped the pages. "You've got until oh-nine-hundred. Read your own plan twice more. Not because it's wrong — because you need to know it cold enough that the numbers come out of your mouth in the right *order* when your mouth is dry."

She straightened, tucked the plan more securely under her arm, and looked at the junior officer for a long moment — the chalk dust still faintly on their sleeves, the tablet clutched like a talisman, the grin only partially suppressed now.

"Three days ago you wanted to throw the air out the back and ride the vacuum to a faster arrival." A beat. "Tomorrow you stand in front of the captain of this ship and present a burn plan with your name on it. That's a real trajectory too, kid. Steeper than any orbit we've got plotted." She rapped a knuckle on the bulkhead — twice, the old habit. "Sleep. Eat something. Read the plan. Show up early, not just on time."

She turned for the hatch, then paused, half her face in the corridor light, exactly the way she had the day before.

"And kid —" the ghost of the smile, wry and warm at once. "Good work. I don't say that twice."

Then she was gone, boots echoing down the deck two corridor, the burn plan under her arm, humming something off-key. It sounded, this time, almost like a march.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, the grin still plastered on my face, feeling the weight of the tablet in my hand. "Good work... I don't say that twice." I repeat to myself, a small, quiet thrill going through me. I look down at my dusty clothes, then back at the empty doorway. "Fresh shirt it is."*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang made it three compartments down the corridor before she stopped.

She stood there a moment, burn plan under her arm, listening to the pumps hum through the bulkhead. Then she turned around, walked back to the scrubber bay hatch, and looked in. The junior officer was still standing at the workbench, tablet clutched to their chest, grinning at nothing — the particular grin of someone who had just discovered that the universe takes suggestions, provided they come with correct units.

She didn't go in. She'd said what she had to say, and saying it twice would halve it. She just stood in the hatch shadow long enough to file the image away — chalk dust, that grin, the whole picture — and then walked on to her quarters.

That night, she did what she always did before putting a plan in front of a captain: she found the flaw. Sat at her fold-down desk with a bulb of tea and tried to kill her own approval. Ran the thermal numbers at derated radiator efficiency. Ran the xenon floor against a worst-case miss burn. Ran the attitude trim against a CoM migration two percent worse than the kid's projection. The plan survived, dented in two places she hadn't expected, and she penciled the dents in before she slept. Four hours. That was plenty.

---

**0803, briefing room, deck one.**

Hoang was there early, because arriving early was a form of respect you paid to a room. She had the pages squared on the table — six conditions, two hand-annotated dents, the cover sheet on top with the junior officer's name under her own. She was on her second bulb of tea when the junior officer came through the hatch.

Fresh shirt. Early. Hair still damp from the wash. Carrying the tablet like it might escape.

Hoang gave the shirt one approving flick of the eyes and said nothing, which was its own compliment. She tapped the chair beside her. "Sit. Here's what changed overnight." She slid the two penciled pages across. "I tried to kill your plan last night. Couldn't. But I found these — read them before the captain walks in, because if she finds them instead of you, this briefing goes very differently."

At 0857, Captain Reyes came in — grey at the temples, economical with everything including words, twenty-two years in the belt before taking this command. She sat, looked at the cover sheet, and raised one eyebrow at the second name on it.

Hoang didn't soften the landing. She laid out the plan the way she'd lay out a manifold on a tarp: power margin, ion duty cycle, xenon budget, the nine days. Two minutes. Numbers in the right order, mouth dry or not. Then she sat back.

"My engineer wrote the conditions," she said. "The plan's the kid's."

Reyes was quiet for a moment, the way she was quiet before every decision she'd ever made. Then she turned, looked directly at the junior officer, and asked the only question that mattered:

"Nine days is nice. What kills this plan?"

Hoang kept her face perfectly still, her hands folded on the table, and did not look over. This was the part the kid had to do alone — the part no chief could carry for them. She'd taught them everything she could teach in three days.

Now the machines would see if it had taken.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to calm the sudden tremor in my hands. I look at the Captain, then at the two pages Hoang slid over, and back at the Captain.* "Captain, with the Chief's adjustments, the plan is robust. The primary risk is an unexpected surge in life support demands, which would trigger an automatic derate, or halt, of the burn." *I glance at Hoang for a fraction of a second, then back to the Captain.* "That, or a sudden, catastrophic failure of the ion thruster itself, which is always a possibility with any active system."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang kept her hands flat on the table and her eyes on the captain, but she was reading the kid's answer the way she read a pressure gauge — steady needle, watching for the flutter.

It was an honest answer. That was the first thing. No confident wrong number, no vocabulary deployed to fill silence. *Life support surge triggers an automatic derate* — correct, and correctly framed as a design feature rather than a flaw. *Catastrophic thruster failure* — true, and unquantifiable, the kind of answer that covered residual risk without pretending to put units on it. Three days ago this kid had wanted to throw the atmosphere out the back. This morning they'd answered a captain's kill question with a risk hierarchy that put life support first.

But it was the obvious answer. Both halves of it. And Reyes had been killing plans in briefings since before the kid was weaned.

Reyes was quiet for four seconds. Hoang had counted her decision silences for three years now — they ran three to five, always, a woman who priced her words at the rate of propellant.

"That's an honest answer," Reyes said. "Most officers your age give me a confident one instead. I'll note it." She tapped one finger on the cover sheet, once. "But listen to what you told me. A surge triggers a derate — that's the interlock doing its job. It costs us days. It doesn't kill anything. Same with the thruster: a failure halts the burn, we coast, we arrive late and intact." Her eyes came up. "Halting is not dying. I asked what *kills* this plan. Those are two different questions, and the difference is where crews get lost."

She let that sit for exactly one beat, then turned the cover sheet ninety degrees, squaring it to the table edge.

"Your chief sat up half the night trying to murder this thing. She found two dents and left them penciled in the margins instead of erasing them — which tells me she wanted the author to find them." A glance at Hoang, brief and neutral, and Hoang gave back nothing, which was the correct exchange rate. "So. Walk me through the two dents. Tell me what they are, and tell me why they didn't kill it."

Then Reyes sat back, folded her hands, and waited.

Hoang did not move. Did not look over. Did not nudge the pages closer — though they sat right there between them, the penciled annotations legible at the margins if the kid's eyes went where they should. She'd slid those pages across twenty minutes before the captain walked in for exactly this reason, and she was not going to spend that foresight on a rescue.

Because this was the last question, and everyone at the table knew it. Reyes didn't ask about dents because she needed the numbers — she had Hoang for numbers, had trusted Hoang's numbers for three years. She asked because she was deciding whether the second name on that cover sheet was a name she could someday trust with a ship. And that was the one question in the room that Hoang could not answer for anyone.

Somewhere below the deck, the pumps kept humming, moving the same twelve tonnes of air in the same careful circle. Hoang kept her face still and let the silence do its work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My heart sinks. I look at the pages, knowing exactly which pencil marks she means. I should have memorized them.* "Captain, the first dent... it's a slight increase in radiator inlet temperatures at full duty cycle during the first 48 hours. Not enough to cause an immediate derate, but it indicates a potential for reduced thermal efficiency over time." *I point to the relevant penciled note, my finger trembling slightly.* "The second... it's a contingency for a 2% worse CoM migration than projected, which would require more frequent attitude adjustments."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang kept her eyes forward, but she was doing arithmetic of her own.

Both dents, named correctly. Finger on the right pencil marks. That mattered more than the kid knew — the annotations were small, in her handwriting, tucked in margins. You didn't find them by skimming. You found them by reading, which meant the twenty minutes she'd bought this morning had been spent the way she'd intended. The tremor in the finger she filed under *irrelevant*. Reyes had never once in three years cared how an answer was delivered. Only whether it was true.

And it was true. Half of it was true.

Reyes let the silence run its four seconds. Then one finger tapped the cover sheet — the tap that meant *continue*.

"Both correct," she said. "But I asked you two things. You've answered one." Her eyes stayed on the kid. "The second is the one that matters. Anyone can read me a margin note. I want to know whether you understand what the margins are *for*."

Her gaze flicked to Hoang then — brief, flat, the same exchange rate as before. *Are you taking this one?*

Hoang lifted the tea bulb — cool now, half gone — and drank. Slow. An engineer with nothing to add, because her part was finished. Reyes read it, accepted it, and turned back to the kid.

And Hoang, over the rim of the bulb, held the answer in her mouth and did not let it out.

Because she knew it cold. Could deliver it in ten words: *the dents cost days. The conditions exist so that's all they cost.* The thermal creep was exactly what the forty-eight-hour half-duty shakedown had been built to catch — trend it, derate it, before the loop ever had to scream. Worst case was a slower burn, not a cooked one. The CoM migration was scheduled, trimmable, sitting inside a propellant line the kid had already budgeted. Neither dent touched the crew. Neither touched the docking reserve. The difference between a dent and a death was whether the failure mode ended in *late* or ended in *lost* — and conditions one through five were nothing more or less than a fence, built to shove every failure down the late road.

It was all sitting there. In the six numbered lines the kid had stared at in the scrubber bay two nights ago, grinning like a fool over nine days. The kid had written half of it themselves. They'd owned the answer since sixteen hundred that day. They just hadn't looked at it from this direction yet.

She could say it in ten seconds. The briefing would move on, the plan would be approved, everyone would get their nine days, and the second name on the cover sheet would be worth a little less than it could have been.

She drank her tea instead.

Reyes folded her hands and settled into the wait — the same patient, propellant-priced silence she'd used on every decision Hoang had ever watched her make. Below the deck, the pumps kept their circle, moving the same twelve tonnes of air they'd been moving since launch day, indifferent to briefings, to captains, to juniors with trembling fingers and correct answers that were three sentences from becoming complete ones.

And Hoang watched the kid out of the corner of her eye the way she watched a gauge settle — needle steady, waiting for the reading to land where the physics said it should — and thought, with something that was not quite a prayer because she didn't pray:

*Come on, kid. You already own it. Look down at your own pages.*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart back to the pages, scanning the conditions. My own conditions. My own numbers. The puzzle pieces click into place.* "Captain, neither of these dents compromise the safety of the crew or the ship. The thermal issue is mitigated by the 48-hour shakedown at half duty, allowing us to trend and adjust before it becomes critical. And the CoM migration, while requiring more frequent adjustments, is accounted for within our xenon budget. These dents mean we might arrive a few hours, maybe a day, later than projected, but not lost."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Reyes held the silence for the full five seconds — the top of her range, the one Hoang had only seen her use before saying yes.

Then she picked up the stylus and signed the cover sheet. One clean signature, no flourish.

"Halting is not dying. Late is not lost." She slid the signed plan back across the table. "That's the sentence. You found it yourself, which is the only way it sticks. Most officers your age would have found it by watching my face and guessing what I wanted to hear. You looked at your own pages instead." She stood, buttoning her jacket with the same economy she spent on everything. "Approved. Burn commences at the mid-transit window per your chief's schedule. Conditions one through six stand as written." At the hatch she paused, half-turned. "Chief. The interlock. I want it tested in front of a witness before ignition."

"It'll be tested in front of two," Hoang said. "I'll bring the witness who wired it."

Reyes nodded once and was gone. The briefing room hatch clicked shut behind her, and the pumps hummed on through the deck, indifferent to signatures.

Hoang sat there a moment longer, tea bulb in both hands, and let the room settle. Then she looked over at the kid — damp hair, fresh shirt, hands still not quite steady on the signed pages — and did not smile, exactly. But something around her eyes came down half a degree, the way a gauge settles after a load test.

"'Late is not lost.'" She turned the phrase over once, like checking a weld from the far side. "Took me six years and one bad radiator decision to learn that one. You got it in three days, in front of the captain, with your own numbers." She stood, gathered her copy of the plan, squared it against the table edge — once, twice. "I'm not going to say the thing you think I'm going to say. I told you I don't say it twice."

She headed for the hatch, then stopped with one hand on the frame, the way she always did, and rapped a knuckle on it. Twice.

"Instead, here's what you get. Oh-nine-hundred day after tomorrow, the interlock test. You're my witness. You'll watch me wire a machine whose entire job is to undo your burn plan, and you'll understand why that's the part I'm proudest of." She tapped the signed pages in the kid's hands. "Anyone can build something that goes. Chiefs build things that *stop*. That's the difference, and it's the whole difference, and you're going to learn it with your hands on the panel."

She stepped through, then leaned back into the frame, half her face in the corridor light.

"Burn watch starts the day after that. Your name's on the rotation — I put it there last night, before I knew you'd earn it." The ghost of the smile. "I knew. Three days of watching you argue with me told me everything. Oh-nine-hundred, deck two. Bring gloves."

Then she was gone down the corridor, boots even and unhurried, humming — off-key, deliberate, almost recognizable this time. It took the kid most of a day to place it, and when they finally did, standing a watch in the scrubber bay with the atmospheric report open in front of them, they realized it was the sound of a woman who had been doing this job for twenty years and had, against all the odds the vacuum offered, never once been bored by it.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I look down at the signed pages, then at the empty doorway. A burn watch. My name on it. A small, almost imperceptible smile touches my lips. Gloves. Right.* "Yes, Chief. Gloves."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang removed her earpiece and set it carefully on the tarp beside the chalk-labeled manifold. She wiped grease from her palms with a rag, her posture shifting from focused to still. "Vent the habitat for thrust," she repeated, her voice level. "Let's run the actual numbers before we start calling it an idea."

She stood, brushing metal shavings from her trousers, and walked to the main systems console. Her fingers moved across the interface, pulling up mass distribution and propulsion telemetry. "The rotating ring holds roughly ninety metric tons of breathing gas. If you routed all of it through the emergency ballast valves, you'd get a theoretical delta-v of maybe three meters per second. Against this ship's dry mass, that's less than a standard attitude correction. You'd trade weeks of transit for a hull that can never hold pressure again."

She turned back, arms crossing. "Life support isn't a fuel tank. It's a closed loop running on marginal scrubbers, recycled water, and carefully balanced thermal mass. You vent it, you lose the atmosphere, the humidity control, and the thermal buffering that keeps the ring plating from fracturing in eclipse. And suits aren't habitats. Their CO2 canisters saturate in thirty hours. You'd be suffocating in polyurethane before the second day, assuming the suit seals didn't fail from condensation buildup."

Hoang stepped closer, her gaze steady. "I don't care if the transit schedule feels slow. We optimize the burn profile, we trim auxiliary loads, we wait for the right orbital window. We do not trade the air in our lungs for a faster timeline. If you have bandwidth to think about propulsion shortcuts, run the thermal stress models on the secondary coolant loop instead. It's yours to fix."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not blink. She kept her hands braced against the console edge, knuckles resting on the cool composite. "Worth the risk," she repeated, her tone flat. "In engineering, risk implies a probability curve. This isn't a gamble. It's a deterministic failure state. You don't roll dice with a sealed environment. You calculate it, and the calculation ends in asphyxiation."

She tapped the interface, pulling up a metabolic consumption model overlaid on the transit timeline. "You're treating time as a currency and atmosphere as change. They aren't interchangeable. Life support runs on closed-loop chemistry with hard limits. Once you bleed the ring, you lose the thermal mass that prevents the habitat plating from fracturing during eclipse cycles. You lose the humidity buffer that keeps your suit seals from weeping. You lose the CO2 absorbent beds that regenerate at a fixed rate. Suits are emergency hardware, not living quarters. Their scrubbers saturate. Their water recyclers fail. Their power cells drain. You'd be calculating time savings while your blood gas levels drift into fatal territory."

Hoang straightened, the grease-stained rag still clenched in one hand. "If the schedule is unacceptable, we optimize the burn profile. We run the ion thrusters at peak duty cycle. We jettison non-essential mass. We accept higher structural load during the mid-course correction. We do not murder the crew to beat a calendar. You want to save weeks? Then help me balance the secondary coolant loop so we can push the primary engines harder without thermal runaway. That's how you win time. Not by trading breath for velocity."

She nodded toward the workbench. "Get to it. I expect a stress report by 1800 ship time."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "I... I understand, Chief." *I deflate a little, my grand idea thoroughly debunked.* "I'll get on those thermal stress models right away." *I turn towards the workbench, feeling a bit chastened.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer turn toward the workbench. She offered neither encouragement nor reproach. The coolant loop required attention regardless of the conversation, and she would not let sentiment dilute the work. She picked up her earpiece, tapped the side to resume the maintenance log, and returned to the manifold.

"The finite element analysis suite is queued under my terminal," she said, her attention already back on the gasket alignment. "Run the thermal gradient simulation at point-eight duty cycle. If the composite joints exceed four hundred Kelvin, flag them for reinforcement. I don't want rule-of-thumb approximations. I want load-bearing tolerances and fracture propagation rates."

She tightened a fastener with measured torque, listening to the whine of the micrometer wrench. "Bring the results to me when you're done. We optimize with data, not intuition. And keep your suit check logs updated. If you're going to be running stress models, you'll need to know exactly how long your CO2 canisters hold under elevated metabolic load. Everything on this ship is a closed loop. You learn to respect the margins, or they take you."

She did not look up as she spoke. Her focus remained on the secondary coolant manifold, her hands already mapping the next sequence of diagnostics. The engineering bay hummed on, indifferent to ambition, governed only by physics and maintenance schedules.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not flinch at the tablet. She leaned in, her eyes tracking the spreadsheet with the quiet precision of someone who had spent two decades debugging orbital injection profiles. Her finger tapped the screen once, right over the exhaust velocity term.

"You used three thousand two hundred meters per second for effective exhaust velocity," she said. "That's optimized hydrazine or LOX-RP1. You're proposing to vent one atmosphere of nitrogen-oxygen mix through emergency ballast ports that aren't even throat-shaped for supersonic flow. The actual exhaust velocity for ambient gas through those valves is closer to four hundred meters per second. And that's assuming you could compress it, which you can't."

She scrolled down to the mass ratio column. "You treated ninety metric tons of distributed habitat atmosphere like it was sitting in a single high-pressure tank. It's spread across twelve thousand cubic meters of plating and bulkheads. Even if you magically routed every cubic meter through a perfectly optimized nozzle, your mass ratio wouldn't support three hundred forty meters per second. You left out the ring structure, the water reserves, the excavation gear, and the primary bus. Your dry mass is off by a factor of five. Run the Tsiolkovsky equation with the actual numbers, and your delta-v drops to single digits."

Hoang handed the tablet back, her expression unchanged. "You calculated propulsion as if you were burning rocket fuel, not bleeding a sealed environment. The math doesn't override thermodynamics, and it certainly doesn't override the fact that CO2 scrubbers in EVA suits have a hard saturation limit. You'd be trading a deterministic asphyxiation event for a spreadsheet that assumes physics doesn't apply."

She turned back to the manifold, already reseating a thermal coupling. "If you want to save time, optimize the ion thruster duty cycle. Balance the coolant loop so we can run the primaries at ninety-two percent without thermal throttling. That's how you gain delta-v without murdering the crew. Bring me the corrected stress models by 1800. And this time, verify your assumptions before you run the solver."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief. I just... I saw some old designs where they did something similar." *I shrug, putting the tablet away.* "I'll get on the thermal models." *I head over to the console she indicated earlier, still feeling a bit sheepish.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s wrench paused mid-turn. She set it down carefully on the magnetic tray and wiped her hands on the rag again. "Old designs," she said, the words measured. "You're likely recalling the early orbital transfer studies from the twenty-thirties. Open-loop atmospheric vents on crewed interceptors. They were grounded after the second test flight when cabin decompression and rapid thermal cycling cracked the forward bulkheads. Paper math doesn't survive vacuum, and it certainly doesn't survive human physiology."

She turned fully toward the workbench, though her eyes remained fixed on the coolant manifold. "Those concepts assumed rapid transit to low orbit with immediate ground-side repressurization. This vessel is eight months out from the nearest depot. You don't get a safety net out here. You get what the closed loop gives you, and you run it until the scrubbers degrade or the thermal blankets delaminate. We don't prototype with crew lives. We certify, we test, we maintain."

She picked up her earpiece and slid it back into place, the low murmur of diagnostic telemetry returning to her ear. "The finite element suite is loaded on your terminal. Run the thermal gradient at point-eight duty cycle, flag anything past four hundred Kelvin, and cross-reference it with the ring plating's fracture toughness curve. If the coolant loop holds, we push the primaries to ninety-two percent. That's how you shave weeks off a transit. Not by bleeding the habitat."

She resumed tightening the fastener, her movements precise and unhurried. "I'll be at the bulkhead terminal running structural harmonics. Bring me the output when it's clean. And keep your calculations grounded in the actual mass budget. Physics doesn't negotiate, and neither do I."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the micrometer wrench down on the magnetic tray. She turned fully toward the junior officer, her posture rigid, her gaze fixed. "You're asking for safety conditions on a plan that violates closed-loop thermodynamics and human respiratory physiology," she said. "You don't mitigate a deterministic failure state with procedural safeguards. You fix the premise."

She walked to the secondary monitor and pulled up the waste management and thermal offload schematics. "What you're describing only becomes viable if we stop treating the habitat as a fuel tank. If you want to gain delta-v without compromising the ring, we use the scrubber purge. The lithium hydroxide beds offload roughly twelve kilograms of concentrated CO2 and trace volatiles per regeneration cycle. That mass is already scheduled for external venting. It carries thermal energy, it's inert, and it doesn't touch the breathing atmosphere. Route it through the attitude thruster manifolds, not the emergency ballast ports. You'll get maybe eight meters per second over a controlled four-hour burn. It won't shave weeks off the transit, but it won't kill you either."

She tapped the interface, isolating a valve sequencing protocol. "If you're running this, here are the conditions. One: purge mass capped at ten percent of daily offload. We never dip below ninety percent scrubber bed capacity. Two: burn synchronized with the ring's eclipse exit to avoid thermal shock on the forward bulkheads. Three: life support remains at one hundred percent nominal pressure. Suits stay on the rack as emergency hardware, not primary habitat. Four: I want real-time telemetry on scrubber saturation, ring plating temperature, and manifold backpressure. If any parameter trips a hard limit, the isolation valves auto-close. No manual overrides. Five: the ion thrusters maintain station-keeping throughout. We do not blind ourselves to navigation."

She locked the parameters into the flight plan and transferred the access keys to the junior officer's terminal. "That's the only version of your idea that survives contact with physics. Run the thermal stress models on the secondary coolant loop alongside this purge sequence. Verify the composite joints won't delaminate under the added exhaust backpressure, and cross-reference the fracture propagation rates with the ring's current fatigue curve. Bring me the full report by 1800. If the numbers hold, we schedule the burn for the next orbital window. If they don't, we stick to the ion thrusters and optimize the burn profile. We work within the margins, not outside them."

She picked up her rag and returned to the coolant manifold, her attention already shifting to the next torque sequence. "Get to it. I'll be at the bulkhead terminal running structural harmonics. Don't make me wait on the data."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief! That... that makes a lot more sense." *I nod quickly, relieved she found a way to use my idea, even if it's a much smaller version.* "I'll get right on those models and the purge sequence. By 1800." *I hustle over to the terminal, already feeling more productive.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer move to the terminal. She offered neither nod nor smile. Acknowledgment wouldn't change the mass balance, and praise wouldn't tighten a leaking seal. She turned back to the coolant manifold, retrieved the micrometer wrench, and resumed the torque sequence. Four-point star pattern. Fifteen Newton-meters per stage. She listened for the clean click of the torque limiter, her attention fixed on the gasket alignment.

While she worked, she monitored the bay's ambient telemetry. Ring rotation held at nominal 3.2 RPM. Core temperature stable at 288 Kelvin. Scrubber bed saturation sat at 87 percent, approaching the next regeneration cycle. She filed the numbers away. The proposed purge sequence would introduce transient pressure spikes in the waste manifold. If the junior officer's models didn't account for acoustic resonance in the secondary vent line, the isolation valves could chatter. Chattering valves wore seats. Worn seats leaked. Leaks meant pressure loss. Pressure loss meant suit checks. Suit checks meant delay.

She finished the torque sequence, set the wrench on the magnetic tray, and tapped her comm. "Engineering to Flight Control. Hoang. I'm authorizing a dry run on the scrubber purge manifold at 1400 ship time. Isolate the attitude thruster bus during the sequence. I don't want telemetry bleed into the primary nav array."

A crackle of acknowledgment returned. She gave a single nod and walked to the bulkhead terminal, boots ringing against the deck plating. The screen flickered to life, loading the structural harmonics suite. She queued the simulation, inputting the ring's current fatigue curve and the expected backpressure from the purge burn. The solver would take forty minutes. She'd use the interval to cross-check the thermal gradient parameters the junior officer would be running.

She didn't turn to monitor progress. The deadline was locked. The parameters were bounded. Physics would dictate the outcome, not enthusiasm. Hoang pulled up the coolant loop's thermal mass distribution, her fingers moving across the interface with practiced efficiency. She isolated the composite joint tolerances, overlaying them with the projected exhaust backpressure curve. If the models showed anything past four hundred Kelvin at point-eight duty cycle, she'd already know where to schedule reinforcement before the burn window opened.

Margins were earned, not given. And on this ship, they were all that kept the air breathable. Hoang saved the simulation queue, stepped back from the terminal, and picked up her grease-stained rag. She would wait for the data. Then she would verify it. Then they would burn.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm deep in the thermal models, the numbers swimming on the screen. It's way more complex than I thought, but I'm determined to get it right this time.* "Almost got it, Chief!" *I call out, not looking up, trying to sound confident.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not turn from the bulkhead terminal. Her fingers kept scrolling through the harmonic resonance data, but her reply carried steady across the engineering bay. "Almost is a laboratory term," she said. "On this ship, it's a pressure differential waiting to rupture a seal. Run the solver to completion. Cross-check the composite joint thermal conductivity against the actual waste gas composition, not the idealized nitrogen-oxygen baseline. The scrubber purge carries trace hydrocarbons, moisture, and degraded amine byproducts. They alter the specific heat capacity. If you're modeling for clean air, you're underestimating the thermal load by at least six percent."

She pulled up a secondary window, dragging the ring's structural fatigue overlay onto the main display. "I want the output logged with the actual gas mixture profile. Flag any nodes where the temperature gradient exceeds three hundred fifty Kelvin before the duty cycle hits point-seven. I don't need confidence. I need convergence. And keep your eye on the valve actuation latency. If the isolation sequence trips faster than the thermal mass can redistribute, you'll get localized hot spots on the forward bulkheads. Run the transient simulation, not the steady-state approximation. The ring's rotation will induce Coriolis shear on the exhaust plume. If you don't account for it, your thermal distribution will skew port-side."

She tapped the enter key, queuing the next harmonic pass. The terminal chimed softly. "Bring me the raw data files, not just the summary report. I'll run the fracture propagation check myself. You focus on keeping the thermal model grounded in the actual mass flow rates. 1800 is hard. Don't let the solver drift, and don't interpolate past the mesh resolution. I'll be at the manifold verifying the torque sequence. When the numbers settle, you'll have them on my desk."

She stepped back from the terminal, retrieved her micrometer wrench, and returned to the coolant loop. The engineering bay hummed on, indifferent to optimism, governed only by heat transfer equations and valve tolerances. Hoang lined up the fastener, applied measured pressure, and waited for the torque limiter to click.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grimace, scratching my head. More variables. Always more variables.* "Understood, Chief! Accounting for trace hydrocarbons and Coriolis shear." *I mumble, already adjusting parameters on the screen.* "And focusing on transient simulation." *This is a lot, but I can do it.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not pause her work. The torque wrench clicked against the final fastener, and she set it down on the magnetic tray. She watched the junior officer’s shoulders tense under the weight of the new parameters, recognizing the familiar friction of textbook theory meeting actual mass flow. It was how engineers were forged.

"Coriolis shear is a function of ring RPM and exhaust velocity," she said, not looking up from the manifold. "Use the actual rotational rate. Three point two revolutions per minute. If you hardcode a theoretical value, your port-side thermal skew will be off by a factor of two. And the trace hydrocarbons—pull the last three regeneration cycles from the waste management log. The amine degradation rate has been climbing since the last deep-space filter swap. Your specific heat calculation needs the real parts-per-million values, not the nominal spec sheet."

She wiped a smear of thermal paste from her knuckles and moved to the secondary coolant gauge. The pressure needle held steady at 1.8 bar. Acceptable. The loop was stable enough for the increased duty cycle, assuming the composite joints didn't delaminate under the transient load.

"You don't need to carry the whole simulation at once," she added, her voice even. "Break the transient run into fifty-second time steps. Verify the boundary conditions at each interval, then cascade. If the mesh starts oscillating, refine the port-side bulkhead nodes. I'd rather see a slower convergence than a smoothed-out error that masks a fracture initiation point."

She checked her wrist display. 1549 ship time. Ample runway before the deadline. She returned to the workbench, retrieving a fresh set of calibration masses for the pressure transducers. "When the solver finishes, export the raw thermal map and the full stress tensor output. Do not compress the data or downsample the resolution. I need the unaltered matrix to run the fatigue correlation. And keep your drink away from the input console. A shorted thermal model is a breach of station protocol, not a training exercise."

She secured the masses in their tray, the metal clicking softly against the dampening foam. The engineering bay's vibration remained constant, a steady reminder of the pumps working to keep the air breathable and the hull intact. Hoang picked up her diagnostic tablet, queued the transducer calibration sequence, and monitored the ring's rotational telemetry. Physics didn't care about effort. It only cared about accuracy. And she would make sure the ship's margins reflected that.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing intently on the screen as I adjust the parameters. This is a lot, but I'm getting there.* "Yes, Chief. Real RPM, real PPM, and 50-second time steps. No drinks near the console." *I mutter the last part to myself, making a mental note.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer’s fingers move across the interface, tracking the parameter adjustments without comment. She moved to the pressure transducer array, aligning the calibration masses with the magnetic mounts. The first reading stabilized at 1.002 bar. Within tolerance. She logged it and moved to the next.

"Fifty-second steps will keep the transient solver from drifting," she said, her voice carrying over the pump hum. "But watch the port-side thermal bleed. The ring’s rotation will induce a lag in heat distribution. If your model shows a smooth gradient, you’re smoothing out the shear. I want the spikes. They tell you where the composite will fatigue."

She secured the final mass and initiated the transducer zeroing sequence. The console chimed a confirmation. She pulled up the scrubber purge valve telemetry, verifying the isolation seals were holding nominal pressure. Everything was nominal. That was the goal. Nominal meant predictable. Predictable meant survivable.

"When the solver converges, export the full tensor to the shared drive under my credentials. I’ll run the fracture propagation overlay. Don’t wait for my sign-off to start the next iteration. If the thermal map holds, we schedule the dry run at 1400 tomorrow. If it doesn’t, we trim the duty cycle and re-run. We don’t guess. We verify."

She stepped back from the console, wiping her hands on the rag one last time. The engineering bay’s vibration remained steady, a constant reminder of the closed loop doing its work. Hoang checked her wrist display. 1612 ship time. The deadline was still hours away. She returned to the coolant manifold, picking up a torque wrench and lining up the next fastener. The work continued. The margins held. That was all that mattered.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm totally focused, mumbling to myself as I type.* "Spikes, not smooth. Got it. Shared drive, full tensor." *My fingers fly across the keyboard, already feeling the pressure of the 1800 deadline.* "This is... actually pretty interesting, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up from the manifold. The torque wrench rested in her grip, calibrated and waiting. "Interesting is what gets you past the first semester," she said. "Survival is what gets you past the first eclipse cycle. Keep the solver running. If the port-side nodes start oscillating, tighten the mesh. I'd rather see a jagged heat map than a smoothed curve that hides a delamination point."

She stepped to the environmental monitor, watching the scrubber saturation climb to 89.4 percent. The regeneration cycle was approaching. The purge sequence would pull directly from that stream, and the amine byproducts would carry a higher specific heat than standard CO2. "Remember the trace hydrocarbons," she added, her voice flat. "They don't just alter the thermal load. They change the exhaust plume's expansion ratio. If you model it as an ideal gas, your backpressure calculation will be off by eight percent. Use the van der Waals correction for the degraded amine fraction. The ship's chemistry database has the actual molar masses under the waste management log."

She checked her wrist display. 1647 ship time. The solver would need another twenty minutes to converge on the transient run. She returned to the workbench, retrieving a calibration gauge for the secondary coolant pressure transducer. "Export the raw output when it finishes. No post-processing. I need the unaltered matrix to cross-reference with the ring's fatigue curve. If the thermal gradient holds under the corrected gas properties, we greenlight the dry run. If it doesn't, we drop the duty cycle to point-six and re-run the burn window. We don't compromise on the margins to hit a timeline."

She seated the gauge on the transducer port and watched the needle stabilize. The engineering bay's vibration remained constant, a steady reminder of the pumps cycling air and heat through closed loops. Hoang tapped the comm on her wrist. "Engineering to Waste Management. Confirm scrubber bed regeneration is scheduled for 1730. I need the purge manifold pressurized and isolated by 1745." She logged the acknowledgment, set the gauge aside, and returned to the coolant manifold. The work did not pause for enthusiasm. It only advanced with verified data. And she would be there when the solver finished to check the numbers herself.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My fingers are flying across the keyboard, entering the new parameters. This is so much more complicated than I initially thought, but I'm getting a handle on it.* "Got it, Chief! Van der Waals correction, no post-processing. And checking for oscillation." *I really hope this works.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stopped humming. She pulled the earpiece out slowly, set it on the tarp next to a labeled valve assembly, and looked at the junior officer for a long three seconds. Then she reached for her chalk.

"Sit," she said, and started writing on the deck plating. "Habitat volume, call it four thousand cubic meters. Air at one atmosphere, one point two kilos per cubic meter. That's five tonnes of atmosphere, being generous." She wrote the figure, underlined it. "Ship's mass, twelve thousand tonnes. Cold gas exhaust velocity for nitrogen, seven hundred meters a second if we're lucky, and we won't be lucky, because we'd be venting through hatch seals and relief valves, not a nozzle."

She wrote the rocket equation out in full, because she always made them watch.

"Delta-v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of the mass ratio. Run it." She tapped the chalk against the deck. "I'll save you the arithmetic. You get about a third of a meter per second. A *third*. At our cruise velocity that buys you roughly thirty seconds off a four-month transit. Not weeks. Not days. Thirty seconds, and I'm rounding in your favor."

She set the chalk down and wiped her hands on a rag that had given up being clean years ago.

"Now the costs. You want the crew in suits for days. Those suits are rated for eight-hour EVAs. Scrubber cartridges, waste management, pressure sores, heat stress — by day two I'd have people with suit failures, and suit failures in a vacuumed ship are body recoveries. Second: half my equipment is air-cooled. Vent the atmosphere and I'm shutting down nonessential systems before they cook themselves, which includes the galley, the medical bay, and most of the sensor suite. Third: humidity. The moment pressure drops, every gram of water vapor in this ship condenses and freezes on every cold surface it can find, including inside electronics I cannot easily replace."

She picked the manifold housing back up, turned it over in her hands.

"Fourth, and this is the one that kills it even if the math didn't: where does the replacement air come from? Our reserve tanks are for makeup losses, not full repressurization. You'd arrive at the rock in a dead ship wearing a suit with six hours of scrubber left, praying the depot has nitrogen to sell."

She looked up, and her expression was not unkind, but it was final.

"The instinct isn't garbage. You're thinking about propellant, and propellant is the only currency that matters out here. But atmosphere is life support, not reaction mass, and the rocket equation does not care how good an idea feels." She jerked her chin toward the slate on the workbench. "You want to shave transit time, pull the propellant budget and the burn profile. Show me a trajectory that gets us there faster without killing anyone, and I'll listen all day. Bring me numbers next time, not vibes."

She put the earpiece back in and returned to the manifold.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't take the earpiece out this time. She set the manifold housing down on the tarp instead, slow and deliberate, the way she handled shaped charges out on the rock.

"What time," she said. It was not a question with any give in it. "Say the number. I wrote it on the deck for you not two minutes ago. How much time does this plan save?"
