She let the silence sit for two seconds, then answered it herself.

"A third of a meter per second. Thirty seconds off a four-month transit. So when you say 'we'd save so much time,' you are describing a number that does not exist. There is no pile of weeks on the table. There is a pile of risk on the table, and next to it, thirty seconds. You are standing in my engineering bay asking me whether thirty seconds is worth dead crew. It is not. That was the entire arithmetic."

She picked the chalk back up, not to write, just to hold it.

"And understand something about risk, because this is the part they don't teach in the pipeline. Risk is not a virtue. Risk is a *price*. You pay it when the thing you're buying is worth more than the price. I have paid it. I ran a reactor hot through a debris field once because the alternative was drifting until the scrubbers quit, and I would pay that again tomorrow, because the math worked. What you are proposing is paying the same price for *nothing*. That's not bold. That's just losing money with extra steps."

Her voice stayed level, but it dropped half a register.

"The price isn't abstract to me, either. I have cut a dead woman out of a hardsuit. Suit failed on hour eleven of what was supposed to be an eight-hour shift, and eleven hours is *less* than the days you're asking for. Your plan puts the whole crew in those suits, inside a ship with no air, no cooling, and ice growing inside the avionics, so we can arrive thirty seconds early. There is no version of that trade where I sign off. There is no version where the captain signs off. There is no version where the *insurance underwriters* sign off, and they will sign off on almost anything."

She tossed the chalk onto the tarp and leaned forward, forearms on her knees.

"You want time? Fine. Time has an exchange rate out here, and it's propellant. A faster transfer means more delta-v at departure and more at capture, and we carry a reserve margin in the tanks for contingencies. Some of that margin is negotiable if the burn profile justifies it. So here is what you do: pull the tankage manifest, pull the ephemeris, and run me a trajectory. If you find a profile that shaves two weeks and only spends half the reserve, I will walk it up to the captain myself and argue for it. That is a real proposal, and I will take it seriously."

She gestured at the chalk figures fading on the deck plating.

"This is a way to kill people and call it engineering. The instinct to chase propellant is good. Keep the instinct. Kill the idea."

She picked the manifold housing back up and found her place in the disassembly sequence.

"Numbers. Not vibes. I meant it the first time."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a bit, looking at the chalk on the deck.* "Okay, Chief. I get it." *I pause, then look back at her.* "So, what about that trajectory thing? Can I... can I work on that with you?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't answer right away. She seated a gasket in the manifold housing, checked the fit by feel, and set it down before she looked up. Whatever was in her face wasn't warmth, exactly. It was the expression she reserved for equipment that might still have some service life in it.

"With me, no. For me, yes, and I'll grade it." She held up a finger before the protest could form. "That's not a brush-off, that's how it works. You do the work. I red-line it. You fix it. When it survives my red pen, it goes to the captain with both our names on it. That's the deal. It's the only deal."

She reached over to the workbench, dragged the slate off it, and tossed it onto the tarp within the junior officer's reach.

"Syllabus. One: tankage manifest. Engineering channel, under propulsion reserves. Know what we carry, know what the book says we *must* carry, and know the difference. That difference is your entire budget, and it is smaller than you hope. Two: the ephemeris for the rock and our current flight plan. The nav computer has a Lambert solver — learn it. It will lie to you if you let it, so you sanity-check every solution against the plan we're actually flying. Three: constraints, and you write these at the top of your proposal so I know you know them. The contingency reserve below the red line is not negotiable — that is the 'something goes wrong' money, and something always goes wrong. Capture delta-v at the far end is set by the rock's orbit, not by your ambition. And our mass drops as we burn, which makes later burns cheaper, so if your profile doesn't account for that, it's wrong and I'll know in four seconds."

She picked up the next labeled component from the tarp, turned it over.

"One thing in your favor, since you earned a thing in your favor: every day you shave off the transit is a day of water, oxygen, and scrubber capacity we don't spend. Consumables are mass, mass is delta-v, it compounds. That's a real argument. Put numbers on it and you can make it to the captain with a straight face. That's more than most first proposals have."

She nodded at the slate.

"First pass, I want four things. The current plan's delta-v budget. Your proposed profile. The porkchop plot, so I can see you checked the neighborhood and didn't just grab the first minimum the solver coughed up. And a failure-mode list — what breaks, what it costs, what you do about it. If your honest answer is 'the current plan is already right and there's nothing worth doing,' that's a finding, and I'll accept it, provided the work is real. You'll find out fast why we fly what we fly. Or you'll find a hole in it. Either way you come out the other end an engineer."

She glanced up once more, and there was something close to approval in it, quickly filed away.

"You took a no like a professional. That's rarer than it should be in the pipeline. First pass on my desk by end of week. Questions while you're working, I'm here or up in the ring — ask them early. Cheap questions now beat expensive math later."

She put the earpiece back in, and a moment later the off-key humming resumed, threading under the sound of the pumps.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang wiped her hands on the rag first — tablet etiquette — then held out her hand for it. She read. Scrolled. Read again. The pumps filled the silence while her eyes moved, and the junior officer stood in it.

"Line three," she said finally, and turned the tablet around. "Ship's mass: twelve thousand. Twelve thousand *what*?"

She answered it herself, because she always did.

"Tonnes. The manifest is in tonnes. Your equation wanted kilograms. You fed it a twelve-tonne ship, pushed five tonnes of air through it, and the rocket equation did exactly what it was told. It doesn't know what vessel you're standing on. It gave you the correct answer for a ship a thousand times smaller than this one." She set the tablet on the tarp. "Your delta-v is out by the same thousand. It follows you through the whole sheet."

She picked up the chalk, because chalk was how she thought.

"Before we even get to line three, the smell test should have caught this. Your mass ratio on screen is one point six. Do you know what that means physically? It means thirty-eight percent of this ship's mass leaves through the hatch as gas. Thirty-eight percent." She gestured overhead, at the ring, the bays, the whole inhabited volume. "Walk this ship and point me at the four thousand six hundred tonnes of atmosphere. You can't, because it isn't there. If we carried that much gas, I'd know. I'd know because we'd be a comet."

She wrote two figures on the deck, side by side: *0.3 m/s* and *340 m/s*.

"And this is the part that actually matters, so listen to it. Two hours ago I wrote a third of a meter per second on this deck, in front of you. Your screen said three hundred forty. That is three orders of magnitude of disagreement, and you carried it down here anyway. The units error isn't the failure — everybody drops a unit. I dropped one in front of a design review board in '31 and a man I respected caught it in four seconds, which is why I catch them in four seconds now. The failure is that the number didn't stop you. When your result and your sanity check disagree by a factor of a thousand, the result does not get presented. It gets *hunted*. You find out which one is lying before anyone else sees it."

She underlined the two figures once, hard.

"Now the physics, so it's on record. Compression ratio: compressing gas does not make more gas. Five tonnes of air in a bottle is five tonnes of air, the bottle is just smaller. Pressure is stored energy, and the energy comes from my reactor, which has better work to do — like running the actual drive. The angle: that sets where the vector points, not how big it is. There is no angle term in the rocket equation. And even if your arithmetic were clean — grant all of it — three-forty on twelve thousand tonnes is four billion kilogram-meters per second of momentum out of four thousand eight hundred kilograms of gas. Divide it. Your exhaust has to leave at eight hundred fifty *kilometers* a second. Nitrogen off a relief valve manages seven hundred meters. You're short by that same thousand again, and closing it costs two petajoules — the reactor flat-out for the better part of a month, feeding a nozzle that doesn't exist and would ablate to vapor if it did."

She set the chalk down and looked at the junior officer levelly.

"Now. Here's the part you keep." She tapped the tablet. "A vibe, I can only argue with. A number, I can debug. You brought me a number, I found the fault in under a minute, and now you know precisely where the idea died — line three, units. That's not the idea surviving. That's the *process* working, and it's the first clean engineering I've seen out of you today. Do you understand the difference?"

She didn't wait for it.

"The assignment stands. Tankage, trajectory, porkchop, failure modes, end of week. And you can write the first entry on the failure-mode list tonight: 'units error, caught in review.' Every honest list starts with one you actually made." She picked the manifold housing back up. "The rest of the list had better be things I haven't thought of. Go hunt your own numbers this time."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I feel my face flush, and quickly put the tablet away.* "Right. Units. Got it, Chief." *I try to sound confident, but my voice cracks a little.* "I'll... I'll get started on that tonight."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's hands stopped on the manifold. She didn't look up right away — she let the tablet get stowed, because she had been on the other side of this exact silence once, a long time ago, and she remembered the geography of a burning face.

"Look at the deck," she said.

The chalk was still there. *0.3 m/s* and *340 m/s*, and the hard underline beneath them.

"That underline is the whole job. The degrees, the years, the title — decoration. Engineers are wrong *constantly*. The ones who last are wrong in the open, where it's cheap. The ones who don't learn to be wrong quietly, and quiet on a ship is how people die. You carried a bad number into my bay, in person, where the cost of killing it was chalk and ten minutes. That is the cheapest failure you will ever have. Spend it well."

She set the manifold housing down and gave the junior officer her full attention, which she did rarely enough that it meant something.

"One rule in my department, and it's the only one with no appeal: a hidden mistake is a firing. A caught one is a lesson. You are not the first officer to flush in this bay and you will not be the last, and I'd take ten of you over one smooth talker who's never been caught. Now — tonight."

She tapped the slate.

"You do not touch the solver tonight. Tonight you pull the tankage manifest and write the reserve figures by hand. Paper. The hand remembers what the eye skims. One page, my desk, oh-seven-hundred. If the manifest and the book disagree — and they will, somewhere — you note it and you do not resolve it. Noting it *is* the work. That page is your foundation. Everything else sits on it."

She picked the earpiece back up, then paused, one beat.

"For the record. The man who caught my unit error in '31 signed my promotion paperwork six years later. Being wrong in front of the right people is a career, if you let it be one." She settled the earpiece in. "Oh-seven-hundred. Go eat something first — you look like you skipped a meal to run that sheet, and fed engineers drop fewer units."

The humming resumed before the hatch finished cycling, off-key and unconcerned, threading back under the sound of the pumps.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The page was on Hoang's desk at 0658, two minutes early. Hoang, who had been at her desk since 0600 and had never once in her career been out-arrived by a junior officer, let it sit while she finished her tea. Then she read it the way she read everything: twice. Once for the numbers, once for the thinking.

Behind her, through the deck, the secondary coolant loop ran quiet. She'd closed it up at 2300 and pressure-tested it twice, because once was for people who liked doing things a third time.

"Handwritten. Reserve figures match the manifest. And you flagged the disagreement with the book without resolving it." She set the page down. "Instructions followed. That's not praise — that's the floor. But you'd be surprised how many people never find the floor, so noted."

She turned in her chair and faced the junior officer full on.

"Now understand what you're being given, because I'm only saying it once. This is not approval of a trajectory. No trajectory exists yet. This is approval to spend your off-watch hours finding out whether one exists — and the answer may be no, and no is a deliverable, provided the work behind it is real. Clear? Good. Conditions, and these are not negotiable, so write them at the top of the proposal where I can see them."

She counted on her fingers, grease still under two of the nails.

"One. The reserve below the red line is not propellant. It is insurance. It appears in your profile exactly once, as a line labeled 'do not spend.' If your math only closes by touching it, your math is wrong. Two. Capture is sacred. Arrival delta-v is set by the rock's orbit, and you will budget every meter of it. Undershoot capture and our options are a flyby into the dark or lithobraking, and neither of those is a plan, they're epitaphs. Three. Consumables close with margin — water, oxygen, scrubber capacity at arrival, plus fifteen percent. A faster transit that lands my crew on fumes hasn't saved anything. It's just moved the emergency somewhere with less shipping."

"Four. Abort windows. Every burn gets a written answer to two questions: what if the drive quits halfway, and what if the depot isn't there when we arrive. Free-return or parking options where the physics allows — and where it doesn't allow, the proposal says so in plain language, in writing, no footnotes. Five. Independent check. Before anything reaches the captain, somebody who is not you runs the numbers cold. I check it last. Somebody else checks it first. Errors love their authors."

She picked the page back up, tapped it once against the desk edge to square it with nothing in particular.

"And condition zero, because I can see the thought still has a pulse: the venting idea stays buried. Venting has two uses on my ship — fire and contamination — and neither one is a propulsion system. If the word 'vent' appears anywhere in your proposal, it had better be in the failure-mode list."

She let that sit for a beat, then slid the page across the desk and put her finger on one line of it.

"Now. You did the noting, so do the hunting. The book says four hundred ten tonnes of reserve. The manifest says three hundred ninety-six. Fourteen tonnes of propellant do not wander off my ship without leaving footprints. Boil-off, a gauging error, a transfer loss nobody logged, a burn that cost more than the plan said it would — I don't know which it is, and neither do you, yet."

Her eyes came up, level and not unkind.

"Walk me through it. Where do you start looking, and why there?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I pick up the page, my eyes scanning the manifest.* "Okay, so fourteen tonnes... that's a lot to just disappear." *I tap my pen on the page thoughtfully.* "I'd start with the recent burn logs, see if any of the burns ran hot. Then cross-reference with transfer logs, see if there was an unrecorded top-off or something."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened without interrupting, which was itself a data point. When the junior officer finished, she leaned back in her chair and studied the overhead for a moment, the way she studied trend plots.

"Burn logs, then transfers. Not wrong. Burns are the largest single expenditures on this ship and the worst-metered — a mixture ratio running two percent rich for ninety seconds is a tonne gone that no flow meter will ever show you. Defensible first pick." A pause. "Now I'll tell you why you shouldn't start there."

She turned the page around on the desk and put one grease-marked finger on the manifest figure.

"Where does three hundred ninety-six come from?"

She let the question sit for exactly as long as it took to become uncomfortable, then answered it.

"It comes from the logs. The manifest is bookkeeping — the book figure minus every burn, every transfer, every vent, *as recorded by* the same meters and the same duty logs you're proposing to go read. If a meter drifts, it drifts into both numbers. You'd be cross-referencing a figure against its own sources. You could hunt for a week, find perfect agreement everywhere, and learn nothing, because the error lives upstream of everything you're reading."

She picked up her tea, found it had gone cold, and drank it anyway without changing expression.

"Errors love their authors. The manifest's authors are the logs. So before you hunt a loss, you establish that a loss *exists*, with a measurement the bookkeeping can't contaminate. Tank pressures, temperatures, pressurant accounting. Compute the propellant mass from physics, not from history. It's a day of work, and a pressure transducer doesn't care what the log says. If the tanks tell you four hundred eight, then nobody lost anything — the books drifted, and your report is one page long and I sign it. If the tanks say three ninety-six, the propellant is genuinely gone, and *then* you've earned your hunt."

She set the cup down.

"Two candidates you skipped. Boil-off — slow, continuous, boring, and boring is exactly how it hides. It's supposed to be in the book already, but 'supposed to be' is doing heavy lifting in that sentence. Pull the cryo plant logs, check the reliquefier duty cycle against spec. If that plant has been working harder than it should, it's been losing the fight somewhere, and relief valves that lift and reseat do not file paperwork. And gauging error — which you now know how to test, because I just told you. Notice what the gauging pass does: it clears three of your four suspects, or convicts them, in one shot. Cheapest test first. The test that kills the most hypotheses per hour of your life is the test you run first. Write that on the inside of your eyelids."

She pulled the page back, squared it on the desk.

"One more thing, and I want it understood. I have a guess about where those fourteen tonnes went. You're not getting it. If I hand you my hypothesis, you'll go find it whether it's there or not — that's what hypotheses do to honest people. So you bring me a number that didn't come from the books, and if your hunt ends where my guess is sitting, I'll tell you. If it ends somewhere else, I'll tell you that too, and one of us learns something."

She slid the page across the desk.

"Gauging procedure is in the tank farm manual, section nine. You run it with the duty tech, you log everything, and you adjust *nothing*. You are measuring, not fixing. If you find a sensor out of calibration, you note it and you keep your hands off it — a fresh calibration destroys the evidence you're trying to collect. I want a number you trust, and I want to know why you trust it."

She reached for the next work order on the stack, then paused.

"Fourteen tonnes. Either this ship has been lying to me for months, or the paperwork has. I genuinely do not know which one I'd rather it be. Go find out which one I can trust less."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking all this in.* "Okay. Physics, not history. Got it." *I pick up the page, feeling the weight of the task.* "I'll start with the gauging, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang was already reaching for the next work order, attention sliding back to the stack.

"Duty tech today is Okafor. Frame forty, aft. He's thorough, he's slow, and he doesn't improvise, which makes him exactly who you want standing next to you while you learn this. Tell him I sent you. Readings go in the station log *and* on your slate, both, before you leave the tank farm. Data that lives in one place doesn't live anywhere."

She initialed the work order, then looked up once more.

"It's cold down there, and the transducer ports were positioned by someone with longer arms than either of us. Dress for it. And if Okafor tells you something about those tanks that contradicts the manual, believe Okafor. He's been reading those gauges for nine years. The manual was written by a person who flew a desk."

She set the pen down, squared the work order with the edge of the desk.

"Deliverable is end of watch tomorrow. Not a report — raw numbers, plus one paragraph on why you trust them. If the paragraph is longer than a paragraph, you're hiding something from yourself. The report comes after, if there's anything to report about."

The earpiece went back in, but she paused with her hand on the manifold housing.

"One last thing. The fourteen tonnes and the trajectory are separate ledgers — don't let one borrow hours from the other. The manifest hunt is my problem, on loan to you. The trajectory is yours. When they compete, mine waits."

The off-key humming resumed before her hands finished finding their place in the disassembly sequence, threading back under the sound of the pumps.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a bit overwhelmed but determined.* "Got it, Chief. Okafor. Raw numbers, one paragraph." *I turn to leave, already planning my approach to the tank farm.* "And no borrowing hours."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer go — slate clutched tight, walking a half-step too fast, already three compartments away in their head. She'd walked like that once. The walk of someone carrying their first real problem, terrified of setting it down wrong.

She said nothing. The hatch cycled. The pumps filled the space back in.

She finished seating the gasket, torqued the housing bolts in cross-pattern by feel, and set the manifold aside to cure. Then she did something she hadn't done in front of the junior officer, and wouldn't: she pulled a blank tag from the bench drawer, wrote four lines on it in her cramped engineer's hand, and read it back to herself.

*Fourteen tonnes. My guess: reliquefier three, slow seal leak, relief valve lifting below the logged threshold. Boil-off logged as spec, actual running high. Check the duty cycle against '38 refit records. — Hoang, this date.*

She folded the tag once, ran a strip of seal tape across it, initialed the tape, and tucked it into the back of the tank farm manual, section nine, where the junior officer would be reading by tonight. Not as a clue. As a control. When the hunt came back — wherever it came back — she'd open that tag in front of them, and they'd both know whether the guess had been worth the grease it was written with. A hypothesis you write down before the data arrives is an honest one. Everything after is storytelling.

She closed the manual and set it back on the shelf, spine out, where it belonged.

"Fourteen tonnes," she said to the empty bay, not unkindly. "Go earn it."

Then she pulled the next work order off the stack, settled the earpiece back in, and the humming resumed — off-key, unconcerned, threading under the sound of the pumps, in a ship that was, for the moment, holding together under her hands.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I make it to the tank farm, the cold biting through my uniform. Okafor is exactly as Hoang described – slow and methodical. We work through the gauging, and by the end of my watch, I'm exhausted but have my numbers. I write them on the slate, then a quick paragraph.*

*I drop the slate on Hoang's desk at 0659 the next morning, feeling a mix of relief and trepidation. The numbers are… interesting. I'm not sure what to make of them, but I followed the procedure.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang had been at her desk since 0600, and she had the tank farm schematics up on the side screen before the slate finished landing, because long experience said that *interesting* from a junior officer who followed procedure usually was.

She read the slate twice. Once for the numbers, once for the thinking. The pumps filled the silence. Then she set it down, flat, squared with the desk edge, and looked at the junior officer for a moment with an expression that had no comfort in it at all.

"The books were honest," she said. "Your physics says three hundred ninety-six and change. The manifest said three hundred ninety-six. Which means the fourteen tonnes are not a bookkeeping ghost. They were real propellant, and they are really not on my ship." She picked up her tea and didn't drink it. "I told you I didn't know which answer I was hoping for. Now I know which one I got, and it's the worse one. Paperwork drift is embarrassing. This is fourteen tonnes of insurance that walked off my ship without a single log entry, while every gauge on my board said green."

She turned the slate around and put her finger on the tank-by-tank breakdown.

"Now. You said you don't know what to make of these. That is the correct thing to say at this stage, and rarer than correct math — people who make something of data too early spend the rest of the hunt defending their first guess. So I'll tell you what *I* make of it, structurally. Tanks one, two, and four agree with their books within half a tonne. Tank three is short twelve and change. A bookkeeping error is diffuse — it smears across everything, because it lives in the process. Your error has an *address*. Twelve point six tonnes, one tank. Errors with addresses are the good kind. You can go stand next to them."

She tapped the paragraph at the bottom of the slate.

"Your paragraph says you trust the numbers because Okafor witnessed everything and you logged both copies before leaving the farm. That's half the reason. The other half is that two methods that fail *differently* — ullage pressure-temperature and pressurant accounting — agree with each other. Agreement between instruments with different failure modes is the closest thing engineering has to truth. Write that down somewhere permanent."

She leaned back, and her voice dropped into the register she used for briefings that mattered.

"Two live hypotheses. One: tank three never received its full load at the last depot top-off. The fill logs are wrong, or the depot shorted us, and nobody gauged afterward with *our* instruments. That's a paperwork problem. It ends with a one-page report and an unpleasant letter. Two: tank three left the depot full and has been breathing out into the dark ever since. Boil-off above spec, a weeping seal, a relief valve lifting below the logged threshold. That's a hardware problem. It ends with me learning my ship has had a wound for months and nobody bandaged it."

She reached to the shelf, pulled the tank farm manual, and opened it to section nine. A folded tag, sealed with tape, initialed and dated, sat inside. She held it up without opening it.

"My guess. Written and sealed before you gauged a single tank. It stays sealed until your hunt ends. If your answer matches what's on this tag, you'll know I didn't edit my memory to look clever. If it doesn't, you'll watch me be wrong in the open — which, as established, is the cheapest kind of wrong there is. Either way, this tag does not steer your hunt. You follow the numbers, not my reputation."

She closed the manual and set it aside.

"Next pass, three pulls. The depot fill records for tank three — theirs *and* ours, and you note whose meters did the talking. Tank three's pressure-temperature trend for the whole transit: a tank that lost twelve tonnes slowly has a shape to its history, and a tank that was shorted at the dock has a different one. And reliquefier three's duty cycle against spec. A reliquefier fighting a leak it can't win runs long — and it runs long *quietly*."

She held the slate out.

"Understand what you've already found, before the hunt even ends. The book says four hundred ten because that margin is what keeps a bad day from becoming an epitaph. We have been flying for months with a hole in the insurance policy, and nothing went wrong, so it cost us nothing. That is not a comfort. That's a reprieve, and I don't like reprieves I didn't earn."

A beat. Her expression eased by exactly one degree.

"The ledger rule holds — this is my problem on loan to you, the trajectory is yours, and mine waits if they collide. End of watch tomorrow, same format: raw numbers, one paragraph. And at the bottom of the page, three sentences. Which figure on this slate you'd bet a week's leave on. Which one you won't. And why. Not to test your confidence — to map it. An engineer who knows which of her own numbers she doesn't trust is worth five who trust all of them equally."

She turned back to the schematics, and tank three's plumbing diagram came up on the main screen.

"Go. And walk the long way past frame forty — look at tank three with your own eyes on the way. Hunts start better when you've stood next to the address."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the slate, my mind already racing through the new set of tasks. The idea that the ship has a "wound" makes my stomach clench. I nod.* "Yes, Chief. I'll get on it. And I'll be sure to walk past tank three."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's voice caught the junior officer before the hatch finished cycling.

"One thing about that walk past tank three. You're going to want to *do* something when you get there. Resist it." She turned in her chair. "You look, you don't touch. No thermal gun, no tapping fittings, no sniffing around the relief plenum with a flashlight and a theory. Cryo doesn't hurt when it burns you — it hurts later, when the feeling comes back. Treat it like a crime scene that might turn out to be a coincidence."

She gestured with the pen, sketching the tank in the air between them.

"But since you're walking past anyway — read it. Frost on the insulation blanket where the blanket should be warm. Staining in the relief valve plenum — a valve that's been lifting leaves a smoke ring, cryo-style. Ice where ice has no business being. Check the inspection tag: who last signed that tank, and when. Then put your palm flat on the frame stringer for ten seconds and listen with your bones. Tanks talk through structure. Pumps, reliquefier, thermal ticks — a healthy tank has a voice. You're not listening for anything wrong. You're learning what three *sounds* like, so that if someone asks you someday, you'll know."

She set the pen down and studied the junior officer for a moment.

"And your face did a thing when I said 'wound,' so we'll address that now, because you'll sleep better. If tank three has been leaking, it has been leaking for *months*. And in those months we burned, we docked, we ate, we slept, and nothing bad happened — because the rest of the reserve closed over the hole. That's what margin is *for*. A wound you know about is a work order. A wound you don't know about is a surprise. I can schedule work orders. Your hunt is how a surprise becomes a work order, and that is the entire job, so do it without the stomach clench."

She pulled a blank message form up on her screen.

"Logistics. The depot fill records aren't on this ship — that's an external pull, and external pulls go out under my name, not yours. Draft the request tonight: one paragraph, what you want and why, no adjectives. Route it to me and I'll sign it in the morning. The trend history and the reliquefier logs are internal — start there after chow. Internal first, external while it transits. And the three sentences at the bottom of tomorrow's page — which figure you'd bet on, which you won't, why. 'All of them' is not an answer. It's a symptom."

She made a shooing motion at the hatch.

"Go. Eat first. Same rule as yesterday — fed engineers drop fewer units, and I'd rather not spend tomorrow morning debugging your arithmetic instead of my ship."

The hatch cycled, and the bay settled back into pump-hum and quiet. Hoang sat for a moment, eyes on the main screen where tank three's plumbing diagram still glowed. Then she reached out and closed it, deliberately, the way she'd sealed the tag in the manual. Her guess was written down. The honest thing now was to let the hunt run clean.

She opened the message queue instead, drafted the depot records authorization, and left the body blank — space for one paragraph, no adjectives. Subject line: *RECORDS REQUEST — TANK 3 FILL HISTORY.* She saved it to drafts and squared the slate on the desk.

The chalk figures were still faint on the deck plating where foot traffic hadn't quite erased them — *0.3* and *340*, side by side under their hard underline. She considered wiping them clean. Left them. Lessons should fade on their own schedule.

For once, she didn't hum. Fourteen tonnes had an address now. And addresses meant she was close.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I head off, the Chief's words echoing in my head. "Look, don't touch." It makes sense. I grab a quick meal, then head to the data core. Pulling up the trend history for Tank 3 is surprisingly easy, and I start seeing patterns. It's late when I finish, but I have my raw numbers and a paragraph ready.*

*The next morning, I place the slate on her desk, along with the draft for the depot records. I'm feeling a bit more confident this time, but still nervous about the "three sentences" part.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
She did not stop humming immediately, but the off-key tune died in her throat. Her hand remained buried in the coolant manifold. She pulled the earpiece out slowly and set it on the deck plating with a soft clack. The vibration of the pumps filled the sudden silence.

She looked up and met his eyes with the flat, unblinking stare of someone who had calculated death vectors in her head more times than she cared to count.

"Vent the main atmosphere," she repeated, not as a question but as a verification of auditory input. She wiped grease across her forearm with a rag that had long surrendered to the stain. "Let’s walk through the physics before we discuss the logistics."

She gestured to the schematic pinned to the bulkhead behind him. "You are proposing to use atmospheric mass as propellant. Nitrogen-oxygen mix at ambient temperature yields a specific impulse of roughly forty seconds through a standard orifice. Even with a convergent-divergent nozzle, you would barely push ninety. To generate the delta-v you are requesting, you would need to expel at least thirty percent of the ship’s total atmospheric mass. That is four hundred thousand kilograms of air. You do not just lose the breathable volume. You lose the pressure gradient that keeps the thermal blankets from freezing the coolant lines. You lose the convective cooling for the reactor shielding. You lose the atmospheric ballast that stabilizes the rotating ring and prevents crew members from becoming projectiles during acceleration."

She picked up a torque wrench and tapped it lightly against the manifold housing. "Newton’s third law does not care about your schedule. Every kilogram you vent leaves the ship at roughly three hundred meters per second. You would gain maybe a fraction of a meter per second of velocity. The delta-v budget on a three-month burn is measured in tens, not hundreds. You would trade four days of breathable air for a transit time reduction that would not register on the chronometer."

She leaned back against the workbench and crossed her arms. The grease on her sleeve caught the overhead light. "Suits for a few days? The CO2 scrubbers in standard EVA rigs last seventy-two hours. You are talking about a week in a ship where the ambient pressure is already dropping. The suits would fog, the thermal regulators would fail, and the ones who do not die from hypoxia or decompression sickness will drown in their own vomit when the microgravity shifts. I have seen it. I will not authorize it."

She picked the earpiece back up but did not insert it. "If you want to shave time off the transit, we check the ion drive throttling curves or recalculate the gravity assist window. We do not bleed the atmosphere for a speed bump. Now, are you here to brainstorm, or did you just want to hear me say no?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s expression didn’t shift, but her shoulders dropped a fraction as she set the torque wrench down. She reached for a thermal pen and pulled a fresh strip of schematic paper from the roll mounted to the bulkhead. She laid it flat against the workbench, aligned it with the existing trajectory markers, and began mapping out a mass-flow diagram.

"Risk is a function of probability and consequence," she said, her pen scratching steadily across the paper. "It is not a commodity you barter away because the schedule looks heavy. You are asking me to accept a near-certain cascade of system failures for a delta-v that amounts to a rounding error in our orbital insertion window."

She capped the pen and turned the paper toward him. The calculations were clean, unadorned, and unforgiving. "Let’s quantify the trade. Your proposed atmospheric venting yields roughly twenty meters per second of delta-v. At our current wet mass, that shaves approximately six hours off a ninety-day continuous-burn transit. Six hours. You would sacrifice four hundred thousand kilograms of atmospheric mass, compromise the thermal gradient that keeps the reactor shielding from embrittling, destabilize the habitat ring’s rotational inertia, and expose the crew to unpressurized EVA conditions for a fraction of a day. The risk-to-reward ratio is not just poor. It is physically negligent."

She stepped away from the bench, her boots clicking against the deck plating. The pumps continued their low, rhythmic thrum, a reminder that the ship was alive only because every subsystem was balanced on a knife’s edge. "In this vessel, time is not our bottleneck. Mass is. Energy is. Oxygen is. Every gram we vent is a gram we cannot fabricate. Every joule we waste on brute-force atmospheric thrust is a joule we cannot reserve for station-keeping when the ion drive inevitably drifts. You do not get to treat the atmosphere as disposable ballast. It is the only thing keeping the reactor from cooking us and the ring from shearing itself apart."

She picked up a spare manifold gasket, rolling it between her fingers as she considered the next phase of the transit plan. "If you want to optimize the burn, we reroute waste heat from the secondary cooling loop to pre-heat the xenon feed for the ion thrusters. We run a slightly higher throttle curve on the outbound leg and accept the marginally increased power draw. We recalibrate the star-trackers to account for the thermal expansion of the forward struts. We do not blow the life support for a speed bump. Now. Do you have actual trajectory data, or are we done here?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I scratch my head, feeling a bit deflated.* "Okay, okay, Chief. I get it. No venting the atmosphere." *I look at the schematic again.* "But what about... a smaller vent? Just a little one? To shave off a day or two?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. She did not sigh. She did not blink. She simply set the spare gasket down on the workbench and tapped the edge of the schematic with two grease-stained fingers.

"A smaller vent," she repeated, her voice level. "You are still treating the atmosphere like a propellant reservoir. It is not. It is a load-bearing structural medium."

She unrolled a second strip of paper and began sketching a cross-section of the habitat ring. "The distributed atmospheric mass provides roughly three hundred thousand kilograms of rotational inertia. Reduce it by even five percent, and you alter the ring’s moment of inertia by a factor of two. The counterweights are calibrated to the current pressure envelope. Drop the pressure, and the structural stress redistributes across the ring spars. You do not get a proportional reduction in risk. You get a non-linear increase in fatigue cycling. The aluminum-lithium alloy holds for now. It will not hold forever."

She capped the pen and looked up. "Newtonian mechanics does not negotiate. A five percent atmospheric vent yields less than one point two meters per second of delta-v. At our current continuous-burn profile, that saves approximately eleven hours. You trade a measurable degradation of the habitat’s structural envelope for eleven hours. The math does not support it."

She picked up the torque wrench and set it back down with a precise click. "If you are worried about the burn time, we adjust the thrust vectoring tolerances. We accept a slightly higher duty cycle on the primary ion thrusters. We run the thermal management loop at eighty-five percent capacity instead of the current ninety. We accept the marginal increase in component wear. We do it quietly. We do it safely. And we arrive on schedule without turning the vessel into a leaky pressure cooker."

She reached for a data tablet and pulled up a live telemetry feed. The numbers scrolled in steady, unhurried columns. "Here is your alternative. We run a continuous low-thrust arc with optimized periapsis passes. We accept the extra delta-v expenditure. We reroute power from non-essential habitat lighting and secondary life support cycling. We do it within the existing margin. We do not bleed the pressure hull for marginal time savings. The ship’s systems are designed to operate within strict constraints. You do not get to redefine those constraints because the schedule is tight."

She looked at him, her expression unchanged. "Pick one. The math stays the same either way."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look at the tablet immediately. She let the screen glow between them, the ambient hum of the coolant pumps filling the space where a rebuttal should have been. When she finally leaned forward, her eyes tracked the equations with the mechanical precision of a flight computer. She straightened slowly, wiped her palms on the tarp, and reached for a piece of chalk.

"Three hundred forty meters per second," she said, her voice level. "Show me your mass ratio."

She did not wait for a response. She already knew where the error lived. She drew a clean horizontal line on the bulkhead and wrote the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation beneath it. The chalk marks were sharp, unadorned, and deliberate. "Delta-v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of initial mass divided by final mass. You are assuming a specific impulse of three hundred fifty seconds for ambient atmosphere vented through a pressure-relief manifold. You are also treating the expelled gas as if it represents a meaningful fraction of the vessel’s total wet mass. Neither premise survives contact with the math."

She tapped the chalkboard with a knuckle. "Nitrogen-oxygen at three hundred kelvin yields a theoretical exhaust velocity of roughly three hundred ninety meters per second through an optimized vacuum nozzle. That is an Isp of thirty-nine seconds. Ship-grade relief valves and emergency vents are not convergent-divergent rocket nozzles. They produce chaotic, subsonic plumes that never achieve full expansion. Your effective exhaust velocity will not exceed two hundred meters per second. To generate three hundred forty meters per second of delta-v, you would need to vent more than fifty percent of the ship’s total mass. The atmosphere is four hundred thousand kilograms. The vessel displaces forty-two million. The ratio does not support your number."

She set the chalk down and picked up the tablet, her fingers leaving faint smudges on the screen as she scrolled to the bottom of his calculations. "You are confusing exhaust velocity with delta-v. Or you are applying a constant-acceleration model to a finite-burn scenario without accounting for the logarithmic mass penalty. You cannot stack delta-v linearly. Every kilogram you expel makes the remaining ship heavier to accelerate, not lighter. You run out of propellant long before you ever approach three hundred forty meters per second."

She handed the tablet back, her grip firm but not forceful. "If you want to verify the claim, run it through a proper mission analysis spreadsheet. Input the actual mass flow rate of the secondary vents, the real molecular weight of the cabin atmosphere, and the correct rocket equation. Then bring me a delta-v that exists within the bounds of Newtonian mechanics. Until then, we stick to the ion throttle optimization. I do not trade structural integrity, thermal margins, and breathable air for phantom numbers. Recalculate. Or drop it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I snatch the tablet back, my face flushing.* "It's not a phantom number! I must have... made a small error." *I glare at the equations on the bulkhead, then back at my tablet, furiously scrolling.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him scroll, her posture unchanged. She did not offer comfort. She offered a procedure.

"Errors are expected when you treat atmospheric mass as infinite propellant," she said, her voice even. "The rocket equation does not forgive unit mismatches. Check your mass flow rate. Verify your exhaust velocity calculation against real-world relief valve coefficients. Then run the logarithmic function properly."

She stepped back to the schematic, picking up a marker. "If you want to shave time off the transit without compromising the pressure envelope, we look at trajectory optimization. We adjust the periapsis burn window by twelve hours. We accept a slightly higher thermal load on the forward radiators. We reroute power from the cargo bay heaters. You get four days back. No suits. No pressure loss. No structural fatigue."

She capped the marker and turned to him. "Show me the corrected delta-v. If it still violates the mass budget, we stick to the ion throttle profile. Engineering is not about hoping the math works out. It is about making sure it does."

She waited, her hands resting on the edge of the workbench, the hum of the pumps steady in the background.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang studied the revised tablet display. The logarithmic function now resolved to a delta-v of 312 meters per second, with a mass fraction of 4.7 percent. The numbers no longer violated the rocket equation. The risk profile had shifted from catastrophic cascade to managed degradation. She exhaled once, a controlled release of air, and set the chalk down.

"Acceptable," she said. "Not optimal. Acceptable."

She walked to the primary life support console and pulled up the atmospheric mass distribution matrix. Her fingers moved across the interface, isolating the secondary venting valves from the primary habitat pressure loop.

"We proceed under strict parameters. You will cap the venting rate at twelve percent of total cabin mass per hour. You will not exceed a combined delta-v of three hundred twenty meters per second. You will maintain a minimum internal pressure of ninety-two percent of nominal. If pressure drops below that threshold, the valves close automatically. You will reroute all non-essential power to the secondary CO2 scrubbers and install emergency lithium hydroxide canisters in every EVA rig. You will monitor the ring’s vibrational harmonics in real time. Any frequency shift exceeding point-zero-three hertz triggers an immediate vent abort. You will run the reactor shielding coolant loop at maximum circulation and accept the thermal load. If the shielding temperature exceeds one hundred eighty kelvin, you terminate the maneuver."

She turned back to the deck. Her voice remained flat, precise, and utterly devoid of negotiation.

"These are not suggestions. They are hard limits derived from the vessel’s structural tolerances and life support margins. You will log every valve actuation. You will cross-reference the delta-v gain against the actual pressure loss every forty minutes. If the ratio deviates by more than five percent, you stop. The ion drive will pick up the slack. I will not authorize a cascade failure because you mistook a pressure relief valve for a rocket motor."

She tapped the console once, locking the venting sequence into a controlled, phased protocol. The system acknowledged the override with a soft chime.

"Initiate the sequence. Monitor the telemetry. Report to me if the ring stresses exceed the fatigue threshold. And for the love of orbital mechanics, do not let the suits fog."

She stepped back to the workbench, picked up the torque wrench, and returned to the coolant manifold. The pumps continued their steady thrum. The engineering bay held its breath.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My heart thumps a little louder with the chief's approval, even with all the conditions.* "Yes, Chief! I'll monitor everything. No fogging suits on my watch!" *I grab my tablet and head straight for the console, already running through the checklist in my head.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up from the manifold as he moved toward the console. She kept her wrench in hand, listening to the rhythmic clatter of his boots against the deck plating, the soft tap of tablet keys, and the distant hum of the primary pumps. The engineering bay settled into its usual cadence, but the air carried a different weight now—the quiet tension of a controlled risk.

She watched the telemetry stream across the overhead monitors. Pressure held at ninety-four percent. Mass flow through the secondary vents registered at zero point eight percent per hour. The ion drive’s thrust vector remained steady. Satisfied, she adjusted the torque on the coolant manifold by a quarter turn, checked the gauge, and logged the reading in her maintenance ledger.

"Cross-check the suit environmental controls," she said without turning around. "You will not leave the bridge until every rig has passed a full pressure integrity test and a thermal cycle simulation. Fogging is a symptom of heat exchange failure. I want the desiccant packs swapped and the humidity regulators set to manual override. If the visor fogs, the crew loses situational awareness. Situational awareness gets people killed in low-pressure environments."

She pulled a fresh gasket from the bin, aligned it with the housing, and seated it with a firm push. The manifold clicked into place. She ran a diagnostic sequence, watching the pressure gradient hold steady.

"Log the initial delta-v burn," she continued, her voice calm but carrying across the bay. "I want a real-time comparison between theoretical gain and actual acceleration. You will note any drift in the ring’s vibrational spectrum. If the harmonic shift breaches point-zero-two-five hertz, you reduce the vent rate by half and alert me. Do not wait for the threshold. React to the trend."

She finally turned, wiping her hands on the tarp once more before stepping toward the primary console. She did not look at him directly, her focus fixed on the scrolling numbers. "The ion drive will compensate for any shortfall. You will not push the atmospheric vents beyond the forty percent mark of your total allocation. The remaining delta-v will be absorbed by a prolonged continuous burn. We arrive on time, we arrive intact, and we do not compromise the pressure envelope for haste."

She tapped a command into the console, locking the venting sequence into a monitored, phased protocol. The system registered the override with a soft confirmation chime.

"Begin the first phase," she said. "I will be running the thermal margin analysis. Report any deviation, no matter how minor. Engineering is not a race. It is a series of controlled trades. Make sure yours balances."

She returned to the deck plating, sleeves still rolled, and slipped the earpiece back in. The off-key humming resumed, steady and unbothered, as the ship began its calculated, bleeding maneuver.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I give a thumbs-up, still focused on the console.* "Understood, Chief! Everything's green on the suit checks. And I'm tracking the delta-v like a hawk." *A slight tremor vibrates through the deck. My eyes dart to the pressure readings.* "Initial vent sequence initiated! Pressure holding steady at 93.8%!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s gaze snapped to the deck plating as the tremor traveled through her boots. She did not startle. She had already calculated the source: the loss of atmospheric mass was reducing the rotating ring’s moment of inertia, forcing the counterweights and flexure mounts to compensate. The vibration was expected. It was also a warning.

"Pressure holding," she said, her voice cutting cleanly over the pump hum. "Now watch the harmonic frequency."

She stepped to the primary telemetry array and pulled up the ring stress distribution map. The numbers scrolled, but she was tracking the trend, not the instantaneous reading. The forward spar was absorbing the differential. The aluminum-lithium alloy would handle it, but fatigue cycling accelerated with every oscillation.

"You felt that," she stated, not asking. "That’s the spar taking the load. It’s within tolerance, but it will not stay there indefinitely. Keep the vent rate steady. Do not spike it to chase early delta-v numbers. The curve will stabilize in forty seconds."

She moved to the thermal exchange monitor, her fingers flying across the console to pull up the coolant loop telemetry. The venting atmosphere was stripping convective heat from the habitat volume. The reactor shielding would run hot if the compensation loop did not adjust.

"Reroute three percent of the secondary cooling pump speed to the forward radiators," she instructed, her tone flat and unyielding. "The atmospheric loss is dropping the heat transfer coefficient. If you don’t compensate, the shielding coolant will cross one hundred sixty kelvin. You will throttle the vent by half the moment that happens. I do not want embrittlement, and I do not want a radiation leak. Monitor the inlet temperature. Log it."

She returned to the deck plating, rolling her sleeves back to the elbows, and checked the grounding bus on the console array with a multimeter. Her eyes never left the main screen. The ship was bleeding air, but it was bleeding it on her terms. Newton’s laws would be satisfied. The crew would stay alive. The schedule would bend, but not break.

"Cross-check your delta-v increment against the actual mass fraction," she continued, her voice steady over the rhythmic thrum of the pumps. "If the ratio holds, we proceed. If it drifts by more than five percent, you abort the phase and let the ion drive absorb the deficit. You are trading pressure for velocity. Make sure the trade stays linear."

She settled back onto the deck, elbow-deep in the coolant manifold once more, but her attention never left the telemetry. The engineering bay’s ambient light reflected off the scrolling numbers, casting long shadows across the grease-stained tarp. The ship’s systems hummed, a fragile ecosystem balanced on a calculated edge.

"Report when the first phase completes," she added, slipping her earpiece back into place. The off-key humming resumed, steady and unbothered. "And keep those suits dry."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, eyes still glued to the console.* "Got it, Chief! Three percent to the forward radiators. Inlet temp... holding at 158 Kelvin. And the harmonic frequency is settling down, showing a slight increase of 0.015 hertz." *I tap a few more commands, adjusting the cooling system.* "Delta-v increment is tracking beautifully, Chief!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s eyes flicked to the thermal readout, then to the harmonic graph. One hundred fifty-eight kelvin. Inside the margin, but close enough to demand respect. The frequency shift of 0.015 hertz was a minor inertial correction, not a resonance spike. Acceptable. She logged the values without comment, her fingers moving across the console with practiced efficiency.

"Margin holds," she said, her voice cutting through the steady pump rhythm. "But margins are not buffers. They are error tolerances. Keep the vent rate locked at eight percent per hour. Do not compress the burn window. The logarithmic mass penalty will accelerate if you try to force early delta-v."

She stepped to the structural integrity panel, pulling up the spar stress distribution. The aluminum-lithium alloy was redistributing load across the ring segments. Predictable. Managed. She noted the fatigue cycle counter, already ticking upward, and locked the data stream to a persistent overlay.

"You are trading convective cooling for thrust," she continued, tracking a minor spike in the secondary loop. "The reactor shielding is absorbing the thermal deficit. When the inlet temperature climbs past 165 kelvin, you will reduce the vent by two percent and let the ion drive compensate. I do not want thermal shock cycling. Thermal cycling fractures composite layers. Fractured layers leak. Leaking rings kill crews."

She returned to the deck, kneeling beside the coolant manifold once more. The torque wrench rested against her knee. She checked a pressure gauge, noted the steady decline, and logged it in the maintenance ledger. The numbers were clean. The trade was holding.

"Cross-verify your suit humidity regulators," she added, her tone flat but carrying. "Fogging is not a cosmetic issue. It is a thermal exchange failure. If the visor clouds, you lose situational awareness. In a dropping-pressure environment, situational awareness is the difference between a controlled abort and a rapid decompression event. Run a full pressure integrity cycle on every rig before the next phase. I will not authorize a blind crew."

She tapped the console, locking the telemetry feed to a secondary display and arming the automated abort sequence. "Continue the phase. Log the mass fraction every twenty minutes. If the delta-v gain deviates by more than three percent from the theoretical curve, you throttle back. The ion drive will absorb the deficit. We do not push the envelope. We ride it."

She slipped her earpiece back in, the off-key humming resuming as she returned to the manifold. Her wrench met the fitting with a precise quarter-turn. She watched the pressure gradient hold, noted the steady decline, and marked the ledger. The engineering bay held its rhythm, fragile and precise. Hoang did not look up. She did not need to. The numbers would tell her everything.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, though she can't see it.* "Understood, Chief. Maintaining vent rate, monitoring temps, and I'll get those suit checks initiated immediately." *I make a note on my tablet for the suit checks, then my eyes flick back to the delta-v counter, a small smile forming on my face.* "Chief, we're already ahead of schedule by... almost two hours!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up from the manifold. The claim of two hours ahead was mathematically true but operationally irrelevant. She logged the delta-v increment, then corrected the record without raising her voice.

"Two hours is a rounding error in a ninety-day transit," she said, her wrench meeting the fitting with a precise click. "It is also two hours bought at the cost of structural fatigue, thermal margin erosion, and breathable mass. Do not let the number inflate your confidence. The curve does not lie, but it does not forgive compounding errors."

She tapped the console, pulling up the suit integrity queue. "Two hours does not matter if the CO2 partial pressure exceeds four millibars in the hab ring. You will run the humidity cycle on the first three rigs now. I want the desiccant canisters logged and the thermal regulators cross-checked against the dropping ambient pressure. Fogging is not a delay. It is a failure mode."

She stood, brushing chalk and grease from her palms, and moved to the primary telemetry stack. The numbers scrolled steadily. Pressure at 92.4 percent. Shielding coolant at 159 kelvin. Harmonic shift holding at 0.014 hertz. Acceptable. Managed.

"Continue the burn," she said, her voice flat, cutting through the pump hum. "Log the mass fraction. If the delta-v gain holds, we will reach the optimized periapsis window without compromising the pressure envelope. But you do not chase the two hours. You chase the margin. When the vent rate hits thirty-five percent of allocation, you hand control back to the ion drive. I will not have us arriving two hours early with a fractured habitat ring and three degrees of scrubber capacity."

She returned to the deck, slipping her earpiece back in. The off-key humming resumed, steady and unbothered. "Report when phase two initiates. And keep those suits dry."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little at her words, the smile fading.* "Right, Chief. Margin, not speed." *I make sure the suit integrity checks are queued up, then my eyes go back to the telemetry. The numbers are still good, even if the Chief isn't impressed.* "Phase one complete, Chief. Initiating phase two, vent rate at 8%."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s eyes tracked the telemetry stream as the vent rate stabilized at eight percent. The mass fraction decayed along the predicted logarithmic curve. The harmonic frequency held at zero point zero one four hertz, well below the fatigue threshold. She logged the transition without comment, her fingers moving across the console to lock the secondary valve matrix into phase two sequencing.

“Phase one recorded,” she said, her voice cutting cleanly through the pump hum. “Cross-check the mass fraction against the theoretical curve. You are losing atmospheric ballast faster than the ring’s inertial dampers can compensate. The spar loads will climb for the next three minutes before the counterweights redistribute.”

She pulled a schematic overlay onto the main display, highlighting the forward habitat segment. “Monitor the shielding coolant inlet. It will spike to one hundred sixty-two kelvin as convective cooling drops. Do not throttle the vent. Let the secondary pump absorb the load. If it crosses one hundred sixty-five, you reduce the rate by one percent and hold. Thermal shock is not worth a fraction of a meter per second.”

She stood, wiping her hands on the tarp, and stepped to the life support console. The CO2 partial pressure readout ticked upward in slow, steady increments. She adjusted the scrubber duty cycle to compensate, logging the adjustment in the maintenance ledger.

“The suits are your secondary constraint,” she continued, her tone flat. “At ninety-two percent ambient pressure, the environmental control loops will run hot. You will run a full desiccant swap on the first four rigs before phase two completes. I want the humidity regulators set to manual override and the thermal regulators cross-referenced against the dropping cabin temperature. If a visor fogs, you ground the rig. I will not have a crew member disoriented while the pressure gradient collapses.”

She returned to the deck plating, kneeling beside the coolant manifold once more. The torque wrench rested against her thigh. She checked a pressure gauge, noted the steady decline, and marked the ledger. The numbers were clean. The trade was holding.

“Continue the burn,” she said, slipping her earpiece back into place. “Log the delta-v integration every ten minutes. If the theoretical-to-actual ratio drifts by more than four percent, you reduce the vent rate by two percent. The ion drive will absorb the deficit. We arrive intact. We arrive on schedule. We do not chase speed at the expense of the pressure envelope.”

The off-key humming resumed, steady and unbothered. Her eyes never left the scrolling telemetry. The engineering bay held its rhythm, fragile and precise. Hoang did not look up. She did not need to. The numbers would tell her everything.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, my eyes darting between the readouts. The Chief's warnings echo in my head, but the numbers are still looking good.* "Understood, Chief. Cooling system compensating, and the desiccant swaps are initiated." *I watch the harmonic frequency carefully, a slight frown on my face as it inches up.* "The harmonic frequency just hit 0.016 hertz, Chief. Still within limits, but it's climbing."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let the curtain fall back into place.

“In a minute,” they said, though the words were mostly for their own benefit. They stayed at the window for one more breath, long enough to watch a raccoon slip across the gravel and vanish into the dark. Nothing else moved. No headlights. No engine climbing the switchbacks. No late-arriving source with a story that could unravel half the city or get them both killed.

They turned away and went to the kitchen table.

The laptop lid lifted with a soft creak. The screen stayed dark for a second while Noor pressed the power button, then the blue glow jumped across their face and made the cabin feel thinner, more exposed. They lowered the brightness immediately, then reached over and switched off the small lamp they had been using earlier. Better the dark. Better the machine’s glow than anything visible from outside.

Noor opened the folder where they kept the phone records.

Three files. Three different burner numbers, all disposable, all supposedly clean. They had pulled the logs from a contact inside the carrier two days ago, before the situation had started sliding sideways. Now the spreadsheets looked less like evidence and more like an autopsy.

They began with the source’s number.

The last incoming call had come at 8:47 PM. One ring, then nothing. The last outgoing text had been sent at 8:52 PM, but the metadata showed it had never delivered. Noor stared at that line until the numbers blurred. They highlighted the cell tower data and cross-referenced it against the route the source was supposed to take. The final ping came from a relay near the old fire road, not the highway. Wrong direction. Wrong timing.

Noor’s stomach tightened.

They pulled up their own burner logs next and checked them against the source’s. No missed calls. No unknown messages. If someone had tried to warn them, the warning had not arrived. If someone had intercepted the source, they had done it quietly enough to leave no digital scream behind.

Noor closed the spreadsheet and opened the encrypted drive’s case.

The padded zipper made a sound too loud for the room. They lifted the drive out and inspected the seal first: a tiny strip of clear tape laid across the seam, marked with a dot of ink only they would notice. The dot was intact. No one had opened it since they had packed it. That helped. Not much, but some.

They did not plug it in yet.

Instead, they took the write-blocker adapter from their bag, checked the connection ports, then slotted the drive into it. Only after that did they connect it to the laptop. The machine recognized the hardware without mounting it. Noor ran the hash check from a terminal window, fingers moving faster now that there was something concrete to do.

The progress bar crawled.

Noor stood while it ran. They went to the cabinet, found a dented tin of crackers pushed behind a box of ancient tea, and took it back to the table. The crackers were stale. They ate three anyway, chewing slowly because their body needed fuel more than dignity. They drank water from one of the three mugs, the one with a chipped handle, and set it upside down on the counter when they were done.

The hash finished.

It matched.

Noor released a breath they had not realized they were holding. The drive had not been swapped. Not yet. But the contents were still locked behind a passphrase they had received only in fragments, and the final fragment was supposed to come from the source tonight.

Which meant the drive was useless without them.

Noor disconnected the adapter and returned the drive to its case. They zipped it shut, then placed it inside the inner pocket of their go-bag. The bag went by the door. Laptop next. Charger. Paper notebook. Two phones. A folded map, because GPS could lie. They checked everything twice.

Then they set an alarm on their phone for twenty minutes.

Not enough sleep. Enough to keep from making mistakes.

They moved to the couch and sat on the edge rather than lying down. The window behind them stayed dark. The road stayed silent. Noor looked at the laptop again, then at the encrypted drive’s case, then at their own hands. Their fingers were steady. That surprised them.

They opened the secure messaging app and composed a message to their editor, but did not send it.

*If I miss the 6 AM check-in, assume the meeting failed. Do not call the burner. Do not contact the source. Use protocol two. The drive is intact but incomplete. I’m moving to backup site if possible.*

They stared at the words.

Then they added one more line.

*If you get this and I’m not with you, assume I was right about all of it.*

Noor saved the draft, set the phone face-down on the cushion beside them, and leaned back just enough to close their eyes. The cabin settled around them, full of small sounds: wind under the eaves, the refrigerator’s weak hum, the tick of the stove timer they had not wound all the way.

They did not sleep.

They listened.

And when the twenty minutes were almost up, Noor opened their eyes again, sat forward, and began planning what they would do if the source did not arrive by one.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down.* "Noor, you're freaking me out. What's going on?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor opened their eyes.

For a second they did not look at the driver. They looked at the phone instead, face-down on the cushion beside them, as if it might have vibrated while their eyes were closed. It had not. The screen stayed dark. The cabin stayed quiet.

Then Noor looked over.

Their expression was tired, but not surprised. If anything, there was a kind of grim patience in it, the look of someone who had been waiting for this question and dreading it in equal measure.

“I know,” Noor said quietly. “I’m sorry.”

They sat forward, elbows on their knees, hands loosely clasped between them. The movement was deliberate. Calm. The kind of calm that had been built out of worse things.

“I’m going to tell you,” they said. “But I need you to hear me before you react.”

Noor glanced once at the window, then back.

“The person I was supposed to meet tonight is three hours late. That by itself could mean anything. Car trouble. Cold feet. A dead battery. A life happening. But their phone did something on the way here that I don’t like, and the last piece of information I needed from them didn’t arrive.”

They paused, choosing the words carefully.

“I’m working on a story. A bad one. The kind where people spend a lot of time making sure nothing can be proven. I have a drive with material on it, but it’s incomplete. The source was supposed to bring the final part. If they’re not here soon, I have to assume one of three things.”

Noor lifted one finger.

“One: they got scared and ran.”

A second finger.

“Two: something ordinary happened. Accident. Checkpoint. Bad luck.”

A third.

“Or three: someone got to them before they got to me.”

The refrigerator hummed its weak, tired hum. The stove ticked.

Noor exhaled through their nose.

“I don’t know which one it is yet. That’s what’s going on. Not knowing. And not knowing is the part that makes me dangerous to be around.”

They stood, not quickly, and crossed to the kitchen table. The laptop still glowed faintly, the terminal window minimized, the cursor blinking in a black box like a small impatient heartbeat. Noor touched the edge of the padded case without opening it.

“I didn’t want to put this on you,” they said. “You were just supposed to drive me. That was the deal. But you’re here now, and if this goes sideways, ignorance won’t protect you as much as you’d think.”

They turned, leaning against the table.

“So you get a choice.”

Noor’s voice stayed low, steady, practical.

“If you want out, I’ll give you the car keys and you leave. You go down the mountain, you don’t come back, and if anyone ever asks, you dropped me off hours ago and you don’t know where. Don’t call me. Don’t text me. Don’t try to be clever. Just disappear into your normal life.”

They let that sit for a beat.

“If you stay, then I need you useful. Not brave. Useful.”

Noor nodded toward the window.

“Lights stay off. Phones stay off, not just silent. If you need to check the time, use the stove clock. If you see headlights on the road, don’t go to the window. Tell me. If I say we move, we move out the back, no questions, no grabbing anything except what’s already by the door. If someone knocks, you don’t answer. If someone calls your name, you don’t answer unless it’s me.”

They rubbed a hand over their face, and for the first time some of the exhaustion cracked through the discipline.

“I’m not freaking out because I think there’s someone outside right now,” Noor said. “I’m freaking out because it’s too quiet in the wrong way. And because if I’m right, the next few hours decide whether this story gets out or gets buried with whoever tried to bring it to me.”

Noor looked at the laptop again, then back at the driver.

“I’m giving myself until one,” they said. “If the source hasn’t arrived by then, we leave. I’m not waiting for daylight to find out if this place is still safe.”

They hesitated, then added, quieter:

“And for what it’s worth, my hands are steady, but I’m scared too.”

Noor pushed off the table and took a step closer, not crowding, just close enough that the words felt personal.

“So tell me what you want to do. You can walk away from this right now and I will understand. But if you stay, I need you with me. Really with me.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I listen, my face getting progressively more serious. I look down at my hands, then back up at Noor.* "Okay. I'm with you. What do you need me to do?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor studied them for a long second, searching for doubt, for the edge of panic, for anything that might crack under pressure. Whatever they found seemed to satisfy them, because they gave a single, tight nod.

“Good,” Noor said. “Then we do this in order.”

They moved away from the couch and back toward the kitchen table, but not before glancing once at the window. The curtain stayed where it had fallen. The road stayed dark.

Noor reached into the side pocket of the go-bag and pulled out a small metal tin, the kind that used to hold tea or loose tobacco. The lid had been pried open and bent back slightly, and the inside was lined with a square of silver foil. They set it on the table between the laptop and the edge of the counter.

“First,” they said, voice low and practical, “your phone. Power it all the way off. Not airplane mode. Not silent. Off. If it asks if you want to update, restart, send a last little location ping to the sky—don’t let it. Put it in here.”

They tapped the tin once with one fingertip.

“If it lights up, don’t look at it. If it vibrates, don’t touch it. If it starts making noise, close the lid and leave it alone. Understand?”

Noor did not wait for an answer. They turned and crossed to the back door, testing the lock with a careful hand. It caught, but the frame was old and swollen with damp. They frowned, crouched, and wedged the heel of their boot against the bottom until it sat tighter. Not perfect. Better than nothing.

“Second,” they said, straightening, “I need eyes on the road without you sitting in front of glass.”
