The first section heading was there. Hardware Configuration. The Frame Six manifold was named. So were a few of the required components, entered in the clipped, incomplete way of someone trying not to forget anything. She read the lines once without judgment, then again with more attention.

She did not smile. But her shoulders settled a fraction.

“Start with the plumbing,” she said to the empty bay. “Good.”

She pulled a stylus from her sleeve pocket and began marking the document in the margins. Not rewriting. Not taking it over. Asking questions where the answers had not yet been earned.

After **Frame Six emergency relief manifold only**, she added:

**Include frame location, compartment access route, and nearest manual isolation points. Show physical clearance with suit gloves. Include photos or scan references if available.**

After **temporary nozzle assembly from rated reaction-control spare spool**, she wrote:

**Part number. Serial number. Last inspection date. Throat diameter. Expansion ratio, if known. Material compatibility with cabin atmosphere at low temperature. Mounting interface. Torque spec. Leak-test requirement.**

After **two independent shutoff valves in series**, she added:

**Fail-safe state. Power requirement. Manual override method. Valve position indication. Command latency. Failure modes: stuck open, stuck closed, partial stroke, false indication. Test method before operation.**

After **burst disk or equivalent overpressure protection**, she wrote:

**Rupture pressure. Downstream vent path. Fragment risk. Inspection after installation. Replacement requirement if pressure tested beyond limit.**

She paused, stylus hovering.

Then, beneath the whole section, she added one line in plain text:

**Do not describe what the hardware should do. Describe what it is certified to do, what it has been tested to do, and what we will verify before it is allowed near a pressure boundary.**

That was the difference between hope and procedure.

She saved the comment layer but did not lock the file. The junior officer needed room to make mistakes visibly. If Hoang edited too heavily, the document would become hers alone, and the lesson would be lost. Instead, she opened another window and began assembling the supporting data package.

Mass manifest.

Atmospheric inventory.

Frame Six inspection history.

Reaction-control spare spool records.

Suit consumable logs.

Attitude-control authority limits.

Ring structural load envelope.

Radiator sensitivity map.

External sensor field-of-view chart.

Each file was tagged and linked into the feasibility study’s appendix folder. She did not summarize them yet. She only made them impossible to ignore. If the calculation wanted to be optimistic, it would have to do so while standing next to the actual ship records.

When that was done, Hoang sent a short message to the junior officer’s console.

**Hoang:**  
First section only. Do not move to operating limits until hardware configuration is complete enough for me to identify every part by number and failure mode. If you do not know a value, write UNKNOWN and list how you would find it. Do not guess. A known gap is better than a confident error.

She considered adding something reassuring, then decided against it. The work was reassurance enough. If the document was being taken seriously, that was the only encouragement an engineer needed.

She turned away from the console and went to the small instrumentation locker at the aft end of the bay.

If the study ever became a test, it would need more than good intentions. It would need numbers that could be trusted under load. Hoang opened the locker and checked the inventory with the same methodical care she gave everything that might one day stand between a crew and vacuum.

Pressure transducers. Two spares. Calibration dates current.

Mass-flow meter. Compatible with low-temperature gas flow. Recently bench-checked.

Thermocouples for line surface and nozzle throat.

Accelerometers for structural vibration.

Data logger with independent power supply.

Valve position indicators.

Optical inspection drone, compact model, with plume-safe operating limits.

She made a list of what would be required for the test pulse, then stopped and added a second list beside it:

**Instrumentation that must fail safe.**  
**Instrumentation that must not be trusted without redundancy.**  
**Measurements that can wait.**  
**Measurements that cannot.**

The first list was short.

The second was longer.

Hoang closed the locker and latched it. Then she crossed to the environmental monitoring panel and studied the current atmospheric state. The numbers sat where they should: pressure steady, oxygen partial pressure inside the comfort band, carbon dioxide low, humidity controlled, trace contaminants within limits. It looked ordinary. That was the point. Life support did its best work by remaining unremarkable.

She placed one hand flat against the panel for a moment, feeling the faint vibration of circulation behind it.

“Not today,” she murmured. “Maybe not ever. But if we do it, we do it without making you poorer.”

The panel gave no answer. It did not need to.

Hoang opened the life-support reserve inventory again and ran a fresh comparison against the feasibility skeleton. Her earlier estimate had not changed. The safe usable impulse was small. Very small. Small enough to embarrass anyone who had started with three hundred forty meters per second. Small enough that a careless person might dismiss it entirely.

But small numbers had their own uses.

A few tenths of a meter per second could be meaningless if applied blindly. It could also be meaningful if applied at the right point in the trajectory, in the right direction, with no penalty to braking and no loss of main-drive reserve. The question was not whether the number sounded impressive. The question was whether it solved a problem without creating three more.

She opened the flight plan again and overlaid the current transfer curve. The ship was moving along its plotted path, patient as arithmetic. Every future burn was already accounted for: course corrections, braking, station keeping, contingency margins. Nothing existed in isolation. A push now was not just a push now. It was a changed arrival, a changed approach, a changed fuel bill, a changed thermal load, a changed set of options weeks or months later.

Hoang traced the velocity vector with one finger.

If the vent impulse could be aligned to reduce a planned correction, perhaps it could save propellant elsewhere. If it increased arrival velocity, the cost might erase the benefit. If it introduced even a slight lateral component, the attitude system would have to fight it, or the trajectory would require another correction. Nothing was free. The universe kept meticulous accounts.

She made another note in the feasibility file.

**Trajectory section must include vector direction, not just magnitude. A delta-v number without direction is not a maneuver. It is a wish.**

Then she attached the current navigation state vector, the planned correction windows, and the braking reserve table.

The console chimed softly. A bridge acknowledgment had arrived for her earlier message.

**Bridge:**  
Acknowledged. Feasibility study noted. No change to transit plan. Keep us informed before any physical test.

Hoang read it twice, then replied.

**Engineering:**  
Understood. No physical test until procedure approved. Will provide preliminary safety review first.

She closed the channel. The bridge was not the problem. The problem would always be the moment when someone decided that approval was a formality rather than a gate. Hoang had seen enough ships and stations to know that disasters rarely began with villainy. They began with convenience. A valve cycled to save time. A check skipped because the hardware looked fine. A margin spent because everyone was tired and the schedule was tight.

Not on her watch.

She returned to the coolant loop and finished closing the access panel. Each fastener went in sequence. Each latch was checked by touch as well as sight. When the panel was secure, she cleaned the work area, returning every labeled part to its proper place on the tarp. The chalk marks remained visible. Order was not decoration. Order was memory made physical.

As she worked, she thought about the junior officer’s first draft. It would probably be too optimistic. It might still contain ghosts of the original three hundred forty meters per second, hiding in an assumption about exhaust velocity or usable gas mass. It might underestimate how annoying suits became after the fourth hour, or how much attention a simple test pulse demanded when everyone was watching pressure gauges instead of doing their normal jobs. It might treat the ship like a diagram instead of a living machine.

That was normal.

The job was not to prevent bad first drafts. The job was to prevent bad first drafts from touching hardware.

Hoang finished cleaning, then opened the feasibility file one more time. The document had grown slightly. More lines under Hardware Configuration. Some incomplete sentences. A few question marks. Good. Question marks were useful. They meant the writer had noticed the edges of their own knowledge.

She added one final comment at the top of Section 1.

**This section passes only if I can identify every component, every interface, every failure path, and every isolation point without asking you to explain it verbally. Write it so a tired reviewer on the night watch cannot misunderstand it.**

She saved the file and stepped back.

The bay hummed around her. The pumps kept their rhythm. The ring turned. The reactor, somewhere behind shielding and procedure, made heat into power with the indifference of physics. The ship carried them all through vacuum because thousands of small decisions had been made correctly and continued to be respected.

Hoang looked at the closed hatch for a moment.

Then she returned to her console, opened a blank watch log, and entered a single line under Engineering Notes.

**Feasibility study active. Hardware tagged. No modifications authorized. First draft in progress. Review focus: assumptions, margins, abort paths.**

She saved the log, dimmed the console glare, and picked up the torque wrench again.

There was work to do either way. If the plan failed, the ship would still need its coolant loop maintained, its pressure boundaries inspected, its atmosphere guarded, its crew kept alive. If the plan survived, the ship would need even more discipline.

Chief Engineer Hoang preferred the second problem, but she would not trade safety for either.

She checked the next clamp, found the alignment mark, and waited for the first draft to become real enough to judge.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I rub my tired eyes, staring at the screen. The Chief's comments are... extensive. My first draft looks like Swiss cheese now. But the sheer level of detail she's asking for, it's like she's building a whole ship from scratch just for this one idea. It's frustrating, but also... I get it. Every single line of my procedure has to be bulletproof.*

"Okay," *I mutter to myself, leaning back in my chair.* "Guess I'm not sleeping tonight." *I take another swig of lukewarm coffee and start digging through the ship's maintenance logs for the Frame Six manifold's last inspection photos.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:17**

The light strips overhead pulsed again—three full cycles since the last sound from the corridor. The keypad accepted each six-digit entry with a muted electronic chirp, the screen flashing red after every incorrect sequence. The first thirty attempts cycled past without result, the digits climbing methodically from 847000. Each failure added a brief lockout delay before the next code could be entered. The lockpick kit remained unused on the floor beside the safe; its tools were irrelevant to the electronic interface.

A low vibration ran through the server racks as one of the units cycled into a heavier processing load.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:29**

The light strips completed another dozen cycles overhead, their rhythm unbroken while the server racks continued their low, ceaseless drone. Each new six-digit entry triggered the same brief lockout pause, the red flash, and the faint electronic denial. Dozens more sequences had been exhausted without success, the last three digits climbing steadily through the low hundreds. The vibration from the racks faded, replaced by the soft, regular pulse of cooling fans.

A distant metallic click echoed from somewhere beyond the vault door, too faint to identify.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "This is taking too long." I glance at the kit on the floor. "The source was sure about the first three, right?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:42**

The overhead lights completed another full cycle of pulses while the safe’s screen continued its steady refusal, flashing red after each new entry. The systematic climb through the remaining digits had reached the mid-four hundreds, each attempt met with the same electronic lockout interval before the next code could be keyed in. The lockpick kit stayed untouched on the floor, its presence a silent reminder of the keypad’s electronic nature. A faint increase in the server racks’ fan speed added a new layer to the ambient drone, as if the building’s systems were responding to some unseen demand.

The vault’s air felt no warmer despite the passage of time.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:05**

The light strips overhead completed another eighteen slow pulses while the thief methodically searched the vault. Every server rack was examined, every narrow gap between cooling units checked, every shadowed corner swept for any scrap of paper or overlooked note. The search yielded nothing—no sticky notes, no notebooks, no hastily scrawled reminders. Only the steady hum of fans and the faint chemical scent of chilled air met the effort. Each minute spent looking added weight to the remaining window.

A single, distant footstep echoed from the corridor beyond the vault door, too far to be an immediate threat but close enough to register.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it, nothing.* I rush back to the keypad. "Okay, back to it. Where were we?" I quickly punch in the next combination.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:51**

The light strips had pulsed through another twenty-three cycles as the systematic entries resumed, the last three digits advancing from the mid-four hundreds into the low five hundreds. Each six-digit code triggered its familiar red flash and lockout interval, the electronic chirp echoing softly against the server racks. The vault air remained chilled, the fans maintaining their steady drone while the distant footstep from earlier resolved into two more—closer now, measured and unhurried, approaching along the corridor outside the sealed door. The remaining time window narrowed with each failed attempt, the rhythmic pulse overhead marking the seconds without pause.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:57**

The overhead lights pulsed their steady rhythm as the question left the thief’s lips, the server racks’ fans whirring louder in response to an unseen load spike. The systematic entries on the keypad had pushed the final three digits into the low five hundreds, each attempt still met with the same red flash and lockout delay. The approaching footsteps in the corridor had drawn closer, now accompanied by the faint jingle of keys and the low murmur of a guard’s radio. Only seconds remained before the fifteen-minute window closed entirely.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Shit, shit, shit!" I slam my hand on the keypad, ignoring the last few digits. "How many combinations are left?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:00**

The final three pulses of the overhead lights marked the exact moment the fifteen-minute window closed. The guard’s footsteps halted directly outside the vault door, the radio murmur sharpening into a clear transmission as keys rattled against the lock mechanism. The keypad offered one last red flash under the impact of the thief’s hand before the screen went dark, its lockout cycle complete. The server racks hummed on without interruption, the chilled air carrying the faint scent of ozone from the electronics.

The hydraulic seals on the vault door began to disengage with a low hiss.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *No!* I frantically look around for somewhere to hide. This wasn't supposed to happen!

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:00**

The vault door’s seals released with a final, pressurized sigh as the guard’s key turned in the outer lock. The overhead lights completed their last pulse, casting the scene in stark, even illumination while the server racks continued their indifferent hum. The keypad screen remained dark beneath the thief’s hand, its cycle ended. Footsteps crossed the threshold, the radio crackling with a routine check-in as the guard stepped fully inside, flashlight sweeping the chilled space. No further window remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I duck behind the nearest server rack, pressing myself against the cold metal.* "Please don't see me, please don't see me..." I whisper.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:00**

The vault door swung inward on its reinforced hinges, admitting a sweep of warmer corridor air and the guard’s measured footsteps. The flashlight beam cut across the chilled space in a slow arc, passing over the dark keypad and the untouched lockpick kit before settling on the narrow gap between the nearest server racks. The radio crackled once with a routine status request as the guard paused, boots planted squarely inside the threshold. The overhead lights completed their final pulse, leaving the scene in even, unforgiving illumination while the server fans droned on without pause or mercy.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My heart pounds. I hold my breath, trying to be as small as possible.* "Just walk past... just walk past..."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content: The guard’s flashlight beam lingered on the narrow gap between the server racks, its white circle narrowing as the beam steadied. Boots scraped once against the vault floor, the sound deliberate and unhurried. The radio crackled again with a short confirmation code, and the guard took another measured step forward, the beam sliding across the chilled metal edges of the nearest rack until it caught the faint outline of a shape pressed against the housing. The overhead lights completed their final, even pulse, leaving the vault in stark illumination as the guard’s free hand moved toward the holster at their hip. No further seconds remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches. I know I'm caught.* "Wait! Don't shoot!" I slowly raise my hands, peering out from behind the rack.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:00**

The guard’s flashlight held steady on the gap between the racks, its beam pinning the thief in place as the raised hands emerged into view. Boots scraped once more against the vault floor, the motion unhurried but final. The radio crackled a second time with the same status request, unanswered, while the guard’s free hand completed its reach to the holster and drew the sidearm in one smooth motion. The weapon remained low but ready, the muzzle angled toward the floor as the guard’s voice cut through the chilled air—calm, practiced, and carrying the weight of procedure.

“Hands where I can see them. Step out slowly. You’re done in here.”

The server racks continued their low drone around the confrontation, the overhead lights casting even illumination across the scene while the vault door stood open behind the guard, the corridor beyond empty for the moment. The fifteen-minute window had closed with no margin left.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay!" *I slowly step out, hands still up, trying not to look at the gun.* "No need for that. I'm coming out."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The first combination flashed red. Denied. The keypad accepted the next, then the next, but every wrong digit demanded a pause. The mechanism clicked slowly, resisting the rhythm. Server hum filled the corners, steady and indifferent.

**0:11**

Three minutes had vanished. The low numbers on the screen were exhausted, yet the lock remained silent. The red light on the panel stayed on too long with each attempt. Somewhere down the hall, a door handle turned briefly before settling. The air inside was getting stale. The ceiling strips pulsed twice. Two more heartbeats had passed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**04:10**

The light refused to change. Each attempt took longer than the last, the keypad’s LED growing hotter to the touch with every press. The hum of the servers drowned out your breathing. In the corridor beyond the door, boots clicked softly on tile. You froze. Nothing followed, just the air shifting.

You had tried every combination from 8-4-7-0-0-0 to 8-4-7-0-9-0. The code didn’t end in the low digits. Time burned. The overhead LEDs shifted pulse rhythm.

**05:30**

The air felt heavy, stale. Every second you spent guessing was a second closer to the shift change. A distant siren wound up, then silenced. You heard the guard’s radio crackle on the other side of the vault.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Okay, new plan." I pull out a small device, a frequency jammer, and activate it. "That should buy me a little more time." I go back to the keypad, starting higher now. 8-4-7-1-0-0.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**07:00**

The jammer emitted a low, oscillating whine that clashed with the server hum. For a moment, the radio crackle ceased, replaced by a sudden silence that felt heavier than the noise. But the keypad remained indifferent. The device didn’t bypass the lock; it only muffled the outside world.

The higher numbers registered on the panel. Each entry took time—the delay between presses, the LED’s slow blink, the red rejection. By the time the sequence cycled through the teens, the overhead lights pulsed three times in a row. The air felt thinner. Somewhere, a ventilation duct rattled, shaking dust onto the concrete.

Time slipped. The jammer’s battery indicator blinked amber. Another minute and a half had vanished just to silence the static. The safe remained sealed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:00**

You swept the room from floor to ceiling. Cold fingers skimmed the server racks, checking for loose panels or taped slips. Nothing but metal and wiring. You crouched, scanning the concrete for debris, for discarded notes, for anything left behind by maintenance. The dust was undisturbed except for your own boots. The corners held only shadows and humming equipment.

Three minutes bled away in the silence. The overhead strips pulsed four times while you stood up, shaking out a sleeve. The jammer still whined low, but it offered no clues of its own. The safe remained dark, indifferent to your desperation.

The air felt closer now. The temperature had dropped further, biting through your jacket. Somewhere in the building, a heavy door slammed shut—a muffled echo, then nothing. The guard wasn't talking anymore. He was walking.

You stood before the keypad again. The screen blinked, waiting. No code. No key. Nothing. Just the red light, pulsing like a warning.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No time for this." I pull out a small optical scanner. "Let's see what you're really made of." I press it against the keypad, hoping to read residual heat or fingerprints.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The scanner whirred, a high-pitched whine that cut through the jammer’s oscillation. Held against the plastic, the device flickered erratically before translating thermal residues into ghostly outlines. Fingers had left trails on the heat-smeared surface, but the vault’s cold erased them fast. The display spiked at certain keys: 2, 5, 8. Maybe 0.

**12:30**

Two and a half minutes burned while the algorithm processed the noise. The jammer’s battery dipped to amber. The air felt brittle, the cold biting through the gloves. The lights pulsed three times in rapid succession. The pattern emerged: three numbers confirmed, but the order was scrambled. Six permutations remained. Each entry would take time. The hum of the servers seemed to grow louder, closer. Somewhere beyond the door, footsteps stopped. Then a radio clicked on.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:00**

The question hung in the cold air, unanswered by the safe but registered by the room itself. Thirty seconds vanished in the pause. The light strips in the ceiling blinked once, slow and deliberate, marking the passing moment. The hum of the servers deepened, vibrating through the soles of the boots.

Outside the door, the radio static ceased entirely. Footsteps resumed, steady and closer, their rhythm tightening. The ventilation rattled harder, shaking loose dust from the ducts onto the concrete. The air felt tighter, harder to draw without sound. The jammer whined lower now, its battery indicator flickering amber to red, nearly spent.

The keypad waited, indifferent. The display blinked at random, demanding a decision. Only two and a half minutes remained before the rotation completed. The red light pulsing on the safe glowed like a warning. The silence was heavy, pressing against the vault doors. The guard was no longer talking; he was standing in the hall, waiting.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it, almost out of time!" *I quickly input 8-4-7, then try 2-5-8. If that fails, I'll go for 8-5-2.* My heart is pounding.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:30**

The first sequence blinked red. The keypad rejected 8-4-7-2-5-8 with a sharp, mechanical clack that echoed off the metal walls. No hesitation, just immediate denial. The heat on the keys seemed to drain away in the chill. You didn't stop. You reset the prefix and hammered in the second permutation. 8-4-7-8-5-2.

The device processed slower this time. The LED bar crawled across the screen, fighting the jammer's dying interference. In the hallway, the footsteps had stopped entirely. The radio static was gone. The silence was absolute, broken only by the whine of the battery dying in your hand.

The clock struck 14:45.

Fifteen seconds. The overhead lights stopped pulsing and went steady, a flat white glare. The air in the vault felt like it had been sucked out. You were waiting on the green light, but the red bar held firm. The keypad didn't click. It just waited, and then the mechanical lock engaged with a final, resonant thud.

**14:58**

The vault door shook. Not a sound, but a vibration traveling through the floor, up through the boots. The hydraulic lock disengaged from the outside. The handle turned. You had seconds. The keypad flashed one last time, then went black as power was cut to the room. The jammer died in your palm. The door began to swing open, revealing the dark silhouette of the guard.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "You've gotta be kidding me!" *I shove the scanner and jammer into my jacket, my eyes darting around for any cover.* "Time to improvise."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**14:59**

The door swung wide, flooding the sterile box with harsh hallway light. The silhouette of the guard filled the frame, his stance wide, baton in hand. A flashlight beam cut through the dust motes, sweeping across the server racks and locking onto the center of the room. There were no shadows deep enough to hide in. The space was open, exposed, and entirely too small.

**15:00**

The rotation completed. The hallway lights shifted to a red emergency hue, bathing the vault in crimson. The guard stepped inside, his boots clicking on the tile. He didn't shout. He simply raised a radio to his mouth, his eyes scanning the perimeter. The safe remained shut. The tools lay scattered on the floor. The window closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I freeze, hands up.* "Well, this is awkward."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The guard didn't react to the words. His eyes stayed fixed, unblinking in the red haze. He lowered the radio slowly, the click of the button loud in the silence. The emergency lights hummed louder now, vibrating through the floor. The air felt heavy, trapped.

He stepped further inside, closing the distance. His silhouette blocked the door completely. The flashlight beam held steady, pinning the figure in the center of the room. No shout. No threat. Just the steady weight of presence. The safe loomed behind him, still sealed. The tools lay on the concrete, useless.

The hum of the servers seemed to stop. Or maybe it was just the ringing in the ears. The rotation was done. The shift had begun. There was nowhere left to hide. The guard waited, a statue in crimson light, for whatever came next. But the count had reached zero. The door remained open. The exit remained closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Look, no need to get violent," *I say, slowly raising my hands higher. My eyes dart to the open door, then back to him.* "We can talk about this."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:01**

The guard didn't speak. His lips didn't move under the helmet. He only tilted his head, listening to the echo of the thief's voice in the small, red-lit box. The radio clicked again, a soft transmit tone that died before a message could follow.

He took another step forward. The boots clicked on the tile, close enough to feel the heat of the body in the cold air. The flashlight beam narrowed, focusing on the hands still raised high. The guard's gloved hand drifted toward the belt, not to draw, but to steady the grip.

The shift had officially started. The hallway remained empty behind him. The security rotation was a closed loop; this was the end of it. The guard waited, breathing steady, his presence filling the space until the air felt thin.

The safe sat untouched in the background. The keypad was dark. The game was over. The only question remaining was what happened next. The guard's eyes didn't blink. He held the position, waiting for the thief to make the next move.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I lower my hands slowly, making sure not to make any sudden movements.* "Okay, okay. I get it. You caught me. What now?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**15:02**

The words hung in the red haze, unanswered. The guard’s gloved hand stopped moving against the belt. He tilted his head slightly, the helmet reflecting the emergency light. The radio clicked once more, a transmission sent into the void.

He stepped closer, the distance closing to arm’s reach. The flashlight beam didn't waver. It pinned the center of the room. The safe loomed behind them, dark and silent. The door remained open, but the hallway outside was empty. There was no escape route left.

The air grew heavier. The hum of the servers had faded into a low thrum. The only sound was the guard’s breathing and the faint whine of dying electronics. The shift had begun. The rules had changed.

He waited. The silence stretched. The red light pulsed once, slow and deliberate. The moment held, suspended, while the consequences of the last fifteen minutes settled in.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I sigh, defeated.* "Alright, fine. You win. No need to make this harder than it has to be."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:15**

The lockpick kit was a reflex — good habits die hard — but the picks were useless against a smooth digital interface. You pocketed them and pressed **8-4-7-0-0-0**. The keypad chirped. A red LED blinked twice. *Denied.*

You punched in **8-4-7-0-0-1**. Red blink. Denied.

**0:28**

The light strips pulsed. Three seconds until the next one. Your breath was fogging faintly in the cold air.

**0:34**

**8-4-7-0-0-2.** Denied.

Here was the problem, and you already knew it: three unknown digits meant **one thousand possible combinations**. At roughly four seconds per entry — punch, confirm, wait for the red blink — that was **sixty-six minutes** of brute-forcing. You had fourteen and a half left.

And that assumed the keypad *let* you keep trying. Most commercial units of this grade tripped an anti-brute-force lockout after five consecutive failures — a fifteen-minute cooldown that would blow your window entirely.

You were already at attempt three.

**0:47**

Somewhere beyond the vault wall, a ventilation fan cycled on with a low groan. Then silence. Then the faint, distant sound of a phone ringing — two floors down, maybe three.

**0:55**

The keypad waited. Patient. Indifferent.

Three attempts left before lockout. Three digits of unknown code. Fourteen minutes on the clock.

You needed a better approach than speed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:02**

**8-4-7-0-0-3.** Red blink.

**1:06**

**8-4-7-0-0-4.** Red blink.

Two more attempts. Your jaw tightened. The red LED was starting to feel like a metronome of failure — four flashes in under a minute, each one eating four seconds you didn't have back.



**1:14**

**8-4-7-0-0-5.** Red blink.

Attempt number five. You punched in the next combination — **8-4-7-0-0-6** — and this time the keypad did something different. The red LED didn't blink. It went **solid**. A low tone buzzed from behind the panel, flat and final:

**LOCKOUT ACTIVE — 15:00 MINUTE COOLDOWN**

**1:19**

You stared at it. The countdown on the small secondary display had already started ticking: **14:57... 14:56...**

You were one minute and nineteen seconds into a fifteen-minute window. The keypad wouldn't accept another attempt until **16:19** — four minutes *after* the guard returned.

The lockout was absolute. You couldn't override it, not with picks, not with force — the panel was flush-mounted into reinforced steel. Smashing it would just trigger a silent alarm.

**1:24**

The server racks hummed. The light strips pulsed — slow, patient, indifferent to your situation.

Somewhere far below, a phone rang again. Closer this time, maybe.

You had thirteen minutes and thirty-six seconds. The keypad was dead to you. The lockpick kit sat useless in your pocket. And the safe was still sealed.

You needed another way in.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Dammit!" I hiss, kicking at the floor. Okay, new plan. "What about the safe itself? Any weak points?" I start visually inspecting the safe, looking for hinges or a panel.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:24**

You crouched in front of the safe and began your inspection.

**1:40**

The body was standard commercial grade — thick steel plate, powder-coated grey, roughly waist-high. The door was flush with no visible hinges on the front, which meant they were internal. No pry points. No seam you could slide anything into. Whoever installed this had done it right.

**1:55**

You worked your way around the sides. The safe was bolted to the floor — four anchor points, though you couldn't see their condition from this angle without getting lower. The left side was clean steel. The right side abutted a power conduit that ran into the wall.

**2:10**

Your fingers traced the bottom edge — and stopped.

There was a **small access panel**, roughly four inches square, on the lower right corner near where the conduit entered. Two Phillips-head screws held it in place. It wasn't part of the safe's locking mechanism — it looked like a **maintenance port** for the keypad's power feed. Wires visible through the gap.

**2:18**

You also noticed something on the back of the keypad housing itself. A tiny **recessed reset pinhole**, barely visible, stamped with the manufacturer's logo: **SENTEC M-Series**. You'd seen these before. The pinhole was a factory reset — press it with a paperclip for ten seconds and it would wipe the code to default.

But the pinhole was **behind the tamper seal** — a thin foil sticker that would tear the moment you tried to reach it. Torn seal meant the security system logged a tamper event. Silent alarm. The guard wouldn't just come back — he'd come back *fast*.

**2:31**

The light strips pulsed. You checked your watch.

**12:29 remaining.**

Two paths had opened, both imperfect:

- **The access panel** — exposed wiring. You could potentially **rewire the power feed to reset the keypad** without tripping the tamper seal, but it was delicate work, and a mistake could fry the board or trigger an alert.

- **The anchors** — four bolts under the floor plate. If they were loose or corroded, you might physically **wrench the safe free and drag it out**, but that was loud, slow, and the vault door was still locked.

The keypad ticked down its own countdown: **13:41... 13:40...**

You had tools in your kit — wire strippers, a small flathead, electrical tape. The question was which problem you trusted yourself to solve faster.

The server racks hummed. Somewhere below, footsteps — someone walking a corridor, unhurried, probably not your guard. Not yet.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:31**

You backed away from the safe and swept the vault with your eyes.

It was a working space, not just a storage room. Against the left wall, between two server racks, sat a small utility desk — laminate, institutional, cluttered. A chair was pushed in at an angle. Someone worked here.

**2:40**

You moved to the desk first. A coffee ring stained the surface. A box of network cable ties. A stapler nobody had used in months. You opened the single drawer — a tangle of ethernet patch cords, a dead flashlight, a crumpled fast food receipt.

**3:00**

Nothing written down. No sticky notes. No notebook. Whoever worked here didn't leave the code lying around.

**3:05**

You pulled back and scanned the wider room. The server racks had maintenance labels — asset tags, port numbers, serial codes. Standard inventory markings. Not useful.

Then your eyes caught something on the far wall, mounted just left of the safe at eye height: a **framed document**. Not art — a posted compliance notice. You crossed the room and read it:

---

**SENTEC M-SERIES — FACILITY DEFAULT & RECOVERY PROCEDURE**
*Posted per ANSI/UL 681-2015 §4.7*

*In the event of keypad failure, authorized personnel may restore factory default by entering:*
**0-0-0-0-0-0**

*Note: Facilities operating Sentec M-Series units must register custom codes with the on-site security manager. Verbal codes are not permitted. Written records are prohibited under §4.7(c).*

---

**3:32**

You stared at it. *Written records are prohibited.* Of course they were.

But one sentence snagged: **register custom codes with the on-site security manager.** Someone in this building had the code. The security manager. Probably the guard who was currently making rounds.

**3:40**

You pulled out your earpiece and checked it — still connected to your inside source's relay, though the channel was quiet. No message waiting.

You checked your watch.

**11:20 remaining.**

The keypad's cooldown ticked: **12:51... 12:50...**

Your search had cost you about a minute and forty seconds. You'd found nothing written down, but you'd confirmed three things:

1. The code was registered with someone who was **currently walking the building**.
2. The default **0-0-0-0-0-0** might work if the facility never customized it — but the source said the first three digits were **8-4-7**, so it clearly *had* been changed.
3. The compliance notice was **three years old** based on the yellowed paper. The code might have been rotated since then — your source's numbers could be stale.

The server racks hummed. The light strips pulsed — one pulse, four seconds, one pulse.

The keypad counted down. The clock counted down. And outside the vault, somewhere in the building, a set of footsteps continued their rounds — unhurried, rhythmic, on schedule.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
*Damn it.* This is a bust then. "Alright, screw the code," I mutter. "Let's go for the access panel."

*I pull out my small flathead screwdriver and get to work on the two Phillips-head screws on the access panel.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:45**

You pulled the small flathead from your kit and knelt at the access panel. The screw heads caught the ceiling light — cross-slotted. Phillips. Your flathead would turn them, but poorly. A flat blade in a Phillips head doesn't seat right; it cams out under pressure. You'd need to work slower, apply steady downward force, and keep the angle exact or you'd strip the heads and lose the panel entirely.

**3:52**

You pressed the flathead into the first screw. It slipped once. You reset, angled your grip, and turned. The screw resisted — factory-torqued with a driver, not a wrist — but it gave a quarter-turn, then another.

**4:10**

First screw loose. You moved to the second. This one fought harder — slightly cross-threaded from a previous installation. You couldn't force it without stripping. Slow, patient quarter-turns.

**4:34**

Second screw released. You set both aside on the floor beside your knee and pried the panel free with your thumbnail.

Inside was a tight nest of wires running from the wall conduit into the safe's lower chassis — the power feed and data line to the keypad mounted above. A thick black cable for power. A thinner grey one for signal. Both running through a **small green terminal block** with four screw-down connectors. The block was mounted on a tiny circuit board about the size of a postage stamp.

**4:41**

You had no wiring diagram. You had wire strippers, electrical tape, a flathead, and your memory of a Sentec M-Series you'd worked on once — eighteen months ago, maybe longer. The layout looked familiar: **power in, signal out**. If you could interrupt the power feed for roughly thirty seconds and reconnect it, the keypad's board would reboot — potentially clearing the cooldown timer and giving you a fresh set of attempts.

Potentially.

Because if you got it wrong — if you crossed power and signal, or left a live wire touching the chassis — you'd either fry the keypad board permanently, killing the lock entirely and bolting the safe shut forever, or trip the panel's internal tamper circuit. Same silent alarm as the reset pinhole.

**4:50**

Your hands were steady. The cold helped — kept the adrenaline honest.

You checked your watch.

**10:10 remaining.**

The keypad cooldown ticked: **11:51... 11:50...**

**4:55**

You stared at the terminal block. Four screws. Four wires. One wrong pull and you'd have eleven minutes of nothing to show for it — less, if the alarm fired.

The server racks hummed. The light strip pulsed — four seconds — pulsed.

Somewhere below, the footsteps continued. Still rhythmic. Still on schedule. Still far enough away.

You had the wire strippers in one hand and the flathead in the other. The terminal block waited, small and green and consequential.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:55**

You glanced at your watch. The dial read **5:47 AM** — the hour and minute hands angled sharp in the pre-dawn dark, second hand sweeping its quiet circle.

But that wasn't the time you were tracking.

You looked at the countdown running in your head — and on the small display of the keypad, still ticking behind its lockout:

**Heist elapsed: 4 minutes, 55 seconds.**

**Time remaining until guard return: 10 minutes, 5 seconds.**

The keypad cooldown: **11 minutes, 36 seconds.**

Three clocks. All running. None of them waiting for you.

The terminal block sat before you — four small screws, four wires, one narrow margin for error. Your hands held the strippers and the flathead.

The light strip pulsed once. Four seconds. Then dark again.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Alright, let's do this," I mutter, taking a deep breath. *I carefully unscrew the terminal for the black power cable, making sure not to touch anything else.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:58**

You wedged the flathead against the terminal block and focused on the leftmost screw — the one clamping the black power wire. The screw was tiny, maybe three millimeters across, and the slot was shallow. Your first attempt cams out with a faint scrape. You reseat it, angle the blade flatter, and turn.

**5:10**

The screw loosened in slow, deliberate increments. Quarter-turn. Reset. Quarter-turn. Each one required you to hold your breath still — one slip and the flathead would skid across the board and bridge two contacts.

**5:18**

The screw was loose enough. You set the flathead down and pinched the black wire between thumb and forefinger, easing it free from the terminal slot. The copper conductor was stripped about four millimeters — factory job, clean cut.

The circuit was open.

For a fraction of a second, a tiny blue spark popped at the exposed tip — residual charge bleeding off the keypad board. You felt it as a faint tingle through your fingertip and pulled your hand back.

**5:24**

The keypad went dark. Not just the display — the *entire* face went black. The red LED, the small cooldown timer, all of it. Dead.

**5:28**

Then something you didn't expect: the **silence**. Not the vault silence — you'd gotten used to the keypad's faint electronic hum beneath the server racks. Now it was gone. Just the servers and the slow pulse of the light strips.

Your watch read **10 minutes and 30 seconds remaining.**

You waited. The board needed time to fully discharge — capacitors draining, memory circuits losing state. The Sentec manual you half-remembered had said something about a thirty-second cold start. You counted the light strip pulses in your head:

*One pulse... two... three...*

**5:58**

That was thirty seconds. Four pulses plus four.

You picked up the black wire again. The exposed copper was clean — no fraying. You positioned it over the terminal slot, angled the flathead back in, and began to tighten the screw. This was the dangerous part. Too loose and the connection would be intermittent — the board would reboot, lose power, reboot again, and trip a brownout alarm. Too tight and you'd crush the stranded conductor and possibly crack the terminal block.

You felt the screw bite — firm, but not forcing. You gave it one final quarter-turn.

**6:12**

You pulled your hand back and watched the keypad.

Three seconds of nothing.

Five seconds.

Seven.

Then — a flicker. The red LED blinked once. The display lit up, not with the cooldown timer, but with the Sentec boot sequence: a brief flash of **SENTEC M-SERIES** followed by the six-digit entry prompt:

**_ _ _ _ _ _**

No cooldown timer. No lockout warning. Just the entry field, waiting.

**6:20**

You checked the tamper seal on the back of the keypad — intact. Untouched. The reboot had been clean.

Your hands were trembling now. Not from cold — from the exhale you didn't realize you'd been holding since **5:18**.

You checked your watch.

**8 minutes and 40 seconds remaining.**

You were back at the same problem you'd had at **1:02** — one thousand possible combinations, four seconds each, six-six minutes of brute force. But now you had **five attempts** before the lockout kicked in again, and you were no smarter about which five to pick.

The keypad glowed softly, patient as before. The server racks hummed. The light strip pulsed.

The footsteps below continued — same rhythm, same pace. But you noticed something now that you hadn't before: they were **closer**. Not at the vault yet. Not even on this floor, probably. But closer than they'd been at **4:55**.

The clock didn't care about any of this. It just kept running.

**8 minutes, 34 seconds.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Got you, you bastard." My voice was a little shaky. *I wipe sweat off my brow with the back of my hand, then quickly key in 8-4-7-0-0-0.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:22**

Your fingers moved fast — **8-4-7-0-0-0** — and you pressed confirm.

The keypad blinked red.

**Denied.**

Attempt one of five, burned. Same code as before. Same result. You'd known it would fail — you'd punched it at **0:15** and it had failed then — but you'd wanted to see the system respond, confirm it was truly back online and counting fresh attempts. It was. The cooldown timer was gone. The entry field was clean.

**6:26**

The red LED pulsed once, then went dark, waiting for the next input.

You had four attempts left. Four seconds each. Four minutes of guessing on your side — well, four *trials*, not four minutes. Four guesses out of one thousand possible endings. The math hadn't changed. You'd gone from locked out to merely doomed.

But there was one difference now: you'd confirmed the reboot worked. Which meant if you burned all five attempts, you could do it again — pull the wire, wait thirty seconds, reconnect, get five more. That was a repeatable cycle. Not a strategy — a grudge match against a keypad that had all the time in the world.

**6:34**

You checked your watch.

**8 minutes and 26 seconds remaining.**

The footsteps below had stopped. Not close. Not alarming. But stopped — as if someone was standing in a corridor, maybe checking a door, maybe looking at something on a clipboard. Or maybe just listening.

The light strip pulsed. One pulse. Four seconds.

The keypad waited, blank and patient, for your next guess.

Three digits of unknown code. Four attempts before the next lockout. Eight minutes and change before the guard came home.

You needed to think differently — or get lucky. And you'd never been the lucky kind.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
"Think, think, think!" I whisper, running a hand through my hair. *I look at the keypad again, then at the compliance notice. "0-0-0-0-0-0 was the default... but my source said 8-4-7..."*

"What if the last three are related to the date it was installed?" I muse, then shake my head. Too many variables.

"Okay, what's a common pattern?" *I quickly type in **8-4-7-1-1-1**.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:34**

You punched in **8-4-7-1-1-1** and hit confirm.

Red blink.

**Denied.**

Attempt two of five burned.

**6:38**

Your jaw tightened. You stared at the entry field as it cleared back to six underscores, waiting. Patient. Indifferent.

The light strip pulsed — one pulse, four seconds — and in that brief dark you caught your reflection in the keypad's glossy surface: pale, focused, jaw set. Someone with eight minutes left and no plan.

**6:42**

Then the earpiece crackled.

Not a voice — just static, sharp and brief, like someone pressing a transmit button by accident. Then silence. Then, faintly, a whisper — your inside source, barely audible over the relay:

*"...they're checking badges on..."* A pause. A door closing on their end. *"...not just night security. Compliance audit team at six."*

**6:48**

The transmission cut. The channel went quiet.

You processed that. A compliance audit team. Which meant **more people** arriving at **6:00 AM** — and it was **5:53 AM** on your watch. Seven minutes until additional bodies in the building, beyond just the guard returning. Beyond just the fifteen-minute window you'd been counting against.

Your watch read: **8 minutes and 12 seconds remaining.**

The keypad's entry field glowed: **_ _ _ _ _ _**

Four attempts. Eight minutes. And somewhere below, those footsteps had started moving again — same rhythm, same pace, but now with purpose behind them.

**8 minutes, 4 seconds.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
"Compliance audit team?" I hiss into my earpiece, even though the channel's dead. "Great."

*I quickly key in **8-4-7-7-7-7**. Gotta get lucky.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:42**

You keyed in **8-4-7-7-7-7** and pressed confirm.

The keypad took a beat longer this time — a half-second of stillness before the red LED blinked.

**Denied.**

Attempt three of five. Same red blink, same outcome. But the delay bothered you. Half a second. The first two attempts had responded instantly. This one had *thought* about it first.

Or maybe you were imagining things.

**6:46**

You exhaled through your nose and stepped back half a pace. Two attempts left. Eight minutes minus a few seconds. Your reflection stared back from the dark entry field — six underscores, waiting.

And then the display changed on its own.

Not red. Not an error. A single line of amber text scrolled across the small screen:

**⚠ NEXT LOCKOUT: PERMANENT — NO POWER CYCLE RESET**

**6:52**

You read it twice. Then a third time.

*Permanent.* The last lockout you'd recovered from by killing the power — thirty seconds of rewiring and a fresh set of attempts. This warning told you plainly: do it again, and the board would latch. No reboot. No workaround. No wire to pull. The safe would be sealed by software you couldn't touch, and the only way back in would be a torch and a very good lawyer.

Two attempts. No safety net.

The amber text faded after five seconds, leaving the entry field blinking patiently.

**6:58**

You checked your watch: **8 minutes and 2 seconds remaining.**

Below, the footsteps resumed — closer now, but still distant. Someone on a lower floor, following a route that would eventually bring them up.

The light strip pulsed. One pulse. Four seconds.

The keypad waited.

Two guesses left. One thousand endings. Eight minutes. And a warning that the next failure — the *final* failure — would be your last.

**7:04**

You stood there, flathead in one hand, strippers in the other, both useless now. All you had was your mind and six digits. The first three you knew. The last three were three fingers crossed against a thousand-to-one wind.

Your source's voice echoed from the relay: *"Compliance audit team at six."*

Your watch: **7 minutes and 56 seconds remaining.**

The keypad: **_ _ _ _ _ _**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
*My heart sinks into my stomach.* "Permanent lockout? You have to be kidding me."

*I stare at the keypad, then back at the compliance notice. My eyes flick between the two.* "8-4-7... and a compliance audit."

*A sudden thought hits me.* "Wait, a compliance audit. They'd be looking for something specific, wouldn't they?"

*I quickly key in **8-4-7-6-0-0**.* "Audit at six... six hundred?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**6:48**

You keyed in **8-4-7-6-0-0** and pressed confirm.

The half-second pause again. Longer this time — a full second. Then:

**Denied.**

Attempt four of five. The red LED blinked twice this time instead of once, as if emphasizing the failure.

**6:52**

Your breath came out in a sharp hiss through your teeth. You'd burned it. The logic was a stretch — "audit at six" was your gut talking, not your brain — but you'd known that going in. Sometimes gut was all you had.

**6:58**

One attempt. One thousand endings. Eight minutes on the clock.

You stared at the compliance notice again, harder this time. The yellowed page. The legal citation. The default code.

Then you saw it.

Below the main paragraph, in smaller print — print you'd skimmed past on your first reading — there was a document control line:

**Document #: SNT-M-RP-2021-0447**
**Installed: 04/07/2021**
**Commissioning Code: 8-4-7-0407**

**7:06**

You blinked. Read it again.

*Commissioning code.* Not the working code — the code the technician used during initial setup. It wasn't the current entry code. But the date beside it — **04/07** — matched the numbers in the document reference: **0447**. And your source said the current code started with **8-4-7**, which matched the commissioning prefix exactly.

That meant whoever set the current code had likely kept the **8-4-7** prefix and built the ending from something personal. Facility logic. Installation date. Employee number. The kind of code people chose because they had to remember it tomorrow.

**7:14**

You looked at your watch.

**7 minutes, 46 seconds remaining.**

The footsteps below had started moving again — faster now. Someone who'd finished checking whatever they were checking and resumed a route. Still distant. Still climbing, maybe.

The keypad glowed: **_ _ _ _ _ _**

One attempt. Seven minutes and change. Your hands were steady again — the trembling had stopped, replaced by something colder and quieter.

Below, somewhere in the building, a door opened and closed. The sound was faint but unmistakable.

And the light strip pulsed — one pulse, four seconds — bathing the vault in a brief blue-white wash before darkness returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
*My eyes snap back to the keypad.* "You idiots. Commissioning code."

*I quickly key in **8-4-7-0-4-0-7**.* "This has to be it."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The lockpicks remained in their velvet sleeve as the thief closed the distance to the safe. The keypad’s backlit membrane yielded to the first sequence: 8-4-7-0-0-0. Enter. A dull mechanical thud vibrated through the steel casing. The display flashed crimson. Denial.

Fingers shifted. 8-4-7-0-0-1. Enter. Crimson.

The ceiling strips pulsed. *One… two… three… four.*

By the seventh attempt, the secondary security terminal across the vault ticked over. **0:03**. Each combination demanded three seconds of deliberate key presses followed by a half-second processing lag. A thousand permutations at that rhythm would consume thirty-three minutes of uninterrupted work. Twelve minutes remained before the guard’s rotation closed the hall.

The keypad’s surface began to register the warmth of repeated contact. The server hum held steady, indifferent to the arithmetic unfolding against its bulkhead. The safe’s internal mechanism did not tire, and neither did the clock. The methodical tapping continued, each failed sequence carving another fraction from the remaining window. The next entry was already forming.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The rhythmic tapping continued, a staccato percussion against the vault’s insulated quiet. Each sequence—press, press, press, enter, wait for the mechanical lag—consumed three and a half seconds. The crimson denial light had blinked eighteen more times since the last checkpoint. 

**0:06**

The ceiling strips had completed ninety additional pulses. Three minutes had evaporated on the first thirty-two guesses. The math was unforgiving: one thousand permutations at this deliberate pace would require thirty-three minutes of uninterrupted work. Twelve minutes remained before the guard’s rotation swept the corridor. At the current rate, the final combination would arrive long after heavy boots echoed past the sealed door.

The keypad’s membrane grew tacky with repeated friction. Faint heat radiated from the housing, a byproduct of the internal processor cycling through rejections. The server racks maintained their low, steady drone, utterly unconcerned with the arithmetic unfolding against their bulkhead. No clicks, no subtle tonal shifts, no warming indicators suggested the sequence was close. The safe offered nothing but denial and the relentless, indifferent march of the clock.

The vault’s air felt heavier now, or perhaps it was just the weight of the seconds stacking up. Each failed entry carved another fraction from the remaining window. The next batch of attempts would demand at least another ninety seconds of focused rhythm. The keypad waited. The ceiling strips pulsed. The corridor outside remained silent, but not for long.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it!" I hiss. *I take a breath, trying to calm my nerves.* "This is taking too long." I glance at the secondary terminal. "Any other options here? Anything I can use to speed this up?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The sharp exhale dissipated in the chilled air. Across the vault, the secondary terminal sat mounted on a reinforced pedestal—a matte-black console with a flickering LCD, a row of recessed status LEDs, and a recessed maintenance panel near its base. Its display cycled through a diagnostic readout: *KEYPAD INTERFACE ACTIVE // FAILED SEQUENCES: 41 // HARD LOCK IMMINENT AT 50 // NETWORK UPLINK: STANDBY*.

The console offered three distinct paths, each priced in seconds. The screen’s menu structure was visible but buried under three layers of administrative prompts—navigating to the bypass schematic would consume roughly forty-five seconds of scrolling and verification. The maintenance panel could be pried open, but the torque sequence required sixty seconds of careful work, and misalignment would trip a silent magnetic sensor. A third path: the terminal’s Ethernet jack offered a direct tap into the building’s security subnet. Cradling a portable decoder against the port would bypass the keypad entirely, though booting the device and establishing the handshake demanded a minimum of two minutes, with the decryption algorithm alone running four minutes straight.

**0:07**

The ceiling strips completed another cycle. *One… two… three… four.* Seven minutes had slipped through the vault’s sealed threshold. Eight minutes and fifty-three seconds remained until the guard’s rotation swept the corridor. Every alternative carried a fixed cost in seconds. The terminal’s cursor blinked in steady, unhurried rhythm. The keypad’s membrane still held that faint, stubborn warmth. The clock did not pause for deliberation.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The thief stepped back from the keypad, breaking the rhythm. The vault’s interior unfolded under a methodical sweep.

Hands brushed against the server rack chassis, checking for loose panels or taped memoranda. Knees met the chilled floor to inspect the ventilation grates and cable conduits. The space around the safe was examined inch by inch—beneath the mounting brackets, along the door frame, across the sterile concrete. Each sweep demanded deliberate movement. Dust motes hung motionless in the cold air. Security protocols here did not tolerate loose paper or casual notes. Maintenance logs were digitized. Physical clutter was swept during the last rotation.

Ninety seconds elapsed.

**0:08:30**

The ceiling strips pulsed. Eight minutes and thirty seconds had bled away since the hydraulic seal engaged. Six minutes and thirty seconds remained before heavy boots would approach the outer corridor. The search yielded nothing but the vault’s own sterile architecture: brushed steel, raised flooring, conduit pipes, and the indifferent hum of processing hardware. No sticky notes. No dog-eared manuals. No scrawled digits hidden in the shadows. The space had been sanitized to specification.

The keypad’s membrane had cooled to ambient temperature. The secondary terminal’s cursor continued its steady blink. The clock did not care about thoroughness. It only measured what was left.

The vault waited. The corridor outside remained silent. The next move would cost seconds.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Nothing," I mutter, frustrated. "Clean as a whistle." *I go back to the secondary terminal.* "Okay, what's this 'hard lock imminent at 50' mean?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The terminal’s display held steady, its diagnostic text sharp against the vault’s low light. *HARD LOCK IMMINENT AT 50* was not a suggestion. It was a firmware kill-switch.

Fifty failed keypad entries would trigger a cryptographic lockout. The membrane would go inert. A secondary mechanical deadbolt would engage inside the safe’s chassis, requiring a physical override key that never left the night supervisor’s pocket. More critically, the lockout sequence initiated a silent burst transmission over the building’s security subnet. That ping would not only flag the vault as compromised, it would compress the guard’s rotation window by an estimated ninety seconds. Off-site monitoring did not wait politely.

Forty-one attempts had already been logged. Nine remained before the threshold. At three seconds per sequence, those nine presses would consume roughly twenty-seven seconds of focused rhythm. After the fiftieth rejection, the keypad would be useless. The safe would not speak again until morning.

**0:08:45**

The ceiling strips completed another cycle. *One… two… three… four.* Eight minutes and forty-five seconds had slipped past since the hydraulic seal engaged. Six minutes and fifteen seconds remained until the corridor sweep. The terminal’s Ethernet jack sat exposed, its contacts waiting. The maintenance panel’s recessed screws caught the overhead light. The administrative menu still buried its bypass schematic behind three verification layers. Every path carried a fixed cost in seconds. Every hesitation bled the window thinner.

The keypad’s crimson indicator had not dimmed. It only counted what was left. The clock did not pause for questions. It only measured what remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The question dissolved into the vault’s insulated quiet. No analog clock hung on the walls. The answer lived in the machinery.

The ceiling strips completed another cycle. *One… two… three… four.* On the secondary terminal’s display, a pale green timestamp updated in the upper right corner: **0:08:47**. Eight minutes and forty-seven seconds had bled away since the hydraulic seal engaged. Six minutes and thirteen seconds remained before the guard’s rotation swept the corridor. 

The server racks maintained their low, steady drone. The terminal’s cursor blinked in unhurried rhythm. The keypad’s membrane sat cool and waiting. The clock did not pause for questions. It only measured what was left.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Six minutes. Not much time." *I look at the terminal again.* "Okay, what's the fastest way to get this thing open without triggering that hard lock?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The terminal offered no shortcuts, only arithmetic. The question dissolved into the vault’s insulated quiet, met only by the ceiling strips completing another cycle. *One… two… three… four.*

The fastest route without triggering the hard lock lay through the administrative menu. Three layers of verification stood between the operator interface and the master override. Scrolling through the diagnostics, inputting the default supervisor credentials, and navigating to the bypass schematic would consume exactly forty-five seconds of deliberate navigation. Executing the command—pressing the final override sequence to flush the keypad’s rejection counter and force a mechanical disengage—required another twenty seconds of precise membrane taps. One minute and five seconds. Clean. Predictable. No silent pings. No deadbolts.

The maintenance panel presented a marginally longer path. Fifty seconds to torque the recessed screws, thirty seconds to locate and depress the manual reset relay. One minute and twenty seconds total. But torque misalignment would trip the magnetic sensor, compressing the guard’s rotation window by ninety seconds.

The Ethernet jack remained the longest tether. Two minutes to establish the handshake, four minutes for the decryption algorithm to run. Six minutes flat. It would finish exactly as heavy boots crossed the corridor threshold. No margin for error. No buffer for lag.

**0:09:10**

Nine minutes and ten seconds had bled from the window. Five minutes and fifty seconds remained. The terminal’s cursor blinked in steady, unhurried rhythm. The keypad’s crimson indicator held steady, counting down the final nine attempts before the firmware kill-switch engaged. The clock did not bargain. It only measured the space between decision and execution.

The vault waited. The next move would cost seconds.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Alright, forty-five seconds for the admin menu," I mutter, already moving. *I start navigating the terminal, trying to remember the default supervisor credentials I'd heard about.* "Let's hope they didn't change the defaults."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
Fingers found the rhythm of the terminal's interface. The default credentials surfaced from memory, unaltered by the building's paranoid updates. *Supervisor // 8470-Alpha.* The screen flickered, accepted the handshake, and peeled back the first layer of encryption.

Scrolling through the diagnostic tree, the thief bypassed the user logs and drilled into the hardware control subsystem. The membrane offered slight resistance, a tactile feedback loop that demanded precision. Layer by layer, the administrative menu yielded. The interface responded instantly, confirming the path described earlier: clean, predictable, and costly.

Forty-five seconds of scrolling, verifying, and confirming elapsed in a blur of green text and shifting menus. The terminal did not lag. The thief did not hesitate. The navigation completed as the ceiling strips finished their cycle.

**0:09:55**

Nine minutes and fifty-five seconds had drained from the hour. Five minutes and five seconds remained before the guard's rotation swept the corridor.

The administrative menu yielded its secret. The bypass schematic glowed on the LCD, and the *MANUAL OVERRIDE* command pulsed in amber at the bottom of the display. The keypad's rejection counter had frozen at 41, but the firmware was now vulnerable. The path was clear, but the work was not finished.

Executing the override would flush the counter and mechanically disengage the safe's bolt. However, the command required a twenty-second confirmation window to prevent accidental triggers. The system demanded a sustained hold on the execute prompt, a final gauntlet of patience. The cursor hovered over the command. The server racks droned on. The clock ticked toward the five-minute mark, indifferent to the progress made.

The vault waited for the final input. The next twenty seconds would decide everything.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Got it!" *I practically yell, then wince, checking the door.* "Okay, here we go." *I press and hold the 'MANUAL OVERRIDE' command, watching the timer intensely.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:10:15**

The shout died in the vault's throat, swallowed instantly by acoustic baffling and hydraulic seals. The thief's wince was silent; the door remained a monolith of steel, indifferent to the noise trapped within. No sensors triggered. No alarms chirped. The sound stayed where it belonged.

The finger depressed the command. The terminal registered the input. A circular progress indicator materialized on the LCD, counting down in stark white digits: *20... 19... 18...*

The wait was absolute. The membrane demanded constant pressure. A slip would reset the sequence, costing another twenty seconds the thief could not afford.

The ceiling strips pulsed. *One.* Four seconds. The server racks droned, a white noise backdrop to the ticking countdown.

*Two.* Eight seconds. The digit dropped to *12*. The breath hitched.

*Three.* Twelve seconds. The digit fell to *8*. The finger trembled slightly, fighting the instinct to pull back.

*Four.* Sixteen seconds. The digit showed *4*.

*Five.* Twenty seconds.

*Override Confirmed.*

Deep within the safe's chassis, a solenoid fired. A heavy mechanical clack resonated through the floor grates. The digital lock disengaged. The internal bolt retracted with a smooth, oiled hiss. The combination dial spun freely, its resistance gone. The heavy steel door swung inward an inch, revealing the dark interior lined with anti-static foam and the glint of hardware waiting to be claimed.

The safe was open.

**0:10:15**

Ten minutes and fifteen seconds had drained from the window. Four minutes and forty-five seconds remained before the guard's rotation swept the corridor. The vault's purpose had shifted. The lock was broken. The extraction phase had begun. The clock did not celebrate; it only measured the distance to the exit. The loot was exposed. The door was open. But the heavy boots were still approaching.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I don't waste a second.* "Gotcha!" I grab the document, making sure it's the right one. "Time to go."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The document slid from its anti-static sleeve with a whisper of friction. A split-second glance confirmed the header and seal. Authentic. Complete. The target was secured.

The safe door hung open, its internal mechanism dead, but the vault's primary door remained the final barrier. The heavy wheel on the far wall required manual disengagement. Fingers gripped the cold iron. The mechanism resisted, groaning against years of inertia, then yielded to torque. The bolts retracted with a series of heavy thuds.

Four seconds of leverage.

**0:10:22**

Ten minutes and twenty-two seconds had drained from the window. Four minutes and thirty-eight seconds remained before the guard's rotation swept the corridor.

The vault door swung inward, revealing the hallway beyond. The corridor was bathed in the pale, sterile light of the ceiling strips. The rotation point was visible in the distance—a door frame at the far end where the guard would appear. The hall was empty. The heavy footsteps had not yet begun their final approach.

The thief stood in the threshold. The document was secure. The vault's hum faded to a muffled drone behind the steel bulkhead. The exit was clear, but the clock did not bargain. Four minutes and thirty-eight seconds remained to vanish, to hide, or to reach the rendezvous. The guard was coming. The clock only measured the distance to safety.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I slip out of the vault, pulling the heavy door mostly shut behind me to dampen the sound.* "Almost there." *I start moving quickly down the hall, keeping to the shadows.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The vault door settled into a near-seal, the hydraulic sigh muffled by a fraction of an inch. The corridor swallowed the threshold, its sterile geometry stretching forward under the same slow-pulsing ceiling strips. Acoustic tiles lined the walls. The floor panels along the central walkway were pressure-sensitive, their seams raised just enough to guide a careful route. Each deliberate step consumed time, but the distance to the service stairwell was measurable.

Forty seconds of controlled movement carried past three server room doors and a mounted security camera whose red recording dot swept in slow, rhythmic arcs.
