The numbers were where she expected them. Nothing had changed overnight because nothing ever changed overnight unless something was failing, and nothing was failing.

She paused on the nitrogen reserve. 61.3% of capacity. She stared at it for a moment, doing a calculation she didn't need to do because she already knew the answer: at current consumption rates, with recycling losses factored in, they had enough nitrogen for the full transit plus a 15% margin. The aft compartment vent would cost them roughly 12% of that nitrogen. The margin would absorb it. Barely.

She made a note: *Post-vent N₂ reserve: ~49.3%. Within tolerance but no longer comfortable. Log for post-burn adjustment to recycling setpoints.*

That was the thing about decisions on a ship like this. Nothing was catastrophic in isolation. Every choice just moved you a little closer to or a little further from the edge of the envelope, and the job was to know where the edge was at all times so you could decide whether a given move was worth the distance it cost you.

She set the datapad down and stood, working the stiffness out of her shoulders with a roll that would have looked deliberate if anyone had been watching. Nobody was. The engineering bay was empty — the next shift wouldn't report for another ninety minutes, and Hoang had long ago stopped counting that as a benefit of seniority. It was just the hours the job required.

She made coffee. Not from the machine in the galley — that was an abomination she refused to acknowledge — but from a small personal press she kept in the engineering bay behind a panel that was definitely not rated for personal storage. She measured the grounds with the precision of someone who understood ratios, poured water at a temperature she'd determined through experimentation to be optimal for the specific roast she'd requisitioned three months ago, and waited.

While it brewed, she pulled up the shared channel one more time. Still no reply. She considered — briefly, seriously — whether to send a follow-up. A nudge. A *how's it going*.

She didn't. A nudge at 0600 after someone had worked until at least 0200 wasn't support. It was surveillance wearing a friendly face. The files were there. The annotations were there. The procedure was in their hands, and their hands were either working or resting, and both were their right.

Instead, she pulled up the structural manual, Section 9.2, and re-read the bulkhead door specifications herself. Door M-7 aft. Rated to 45 kPa differential. She'd told the junior officer to use 35 kPa as the abort threshold — 78% of rated capacity, which gave a safety margin that accounted for the door's age, the thermal cycling it had endured over the vessel's operational life, and the simple fact that rated limits were engineering estimates, not physical laws. Materials didn't fail at the exact number on the spec sheet. They failed *near* it, sometimes below it, if fatigue had been accumulating in ways the inspection schedule hadn't caught.

She made a second pass through the section and found what she'd been looking for — a footnote, subsection 9.2.4, buried in a paragraph about inspection intervals. It noted that doors in compartments subject to rapid pressure changes should be inspected at half the standard interval because cyclic loading accelerated fatigue propagation. The aft compartment had never been subject to a rapid pressure change. After the vent, it would have been. The next inspection needed to happen before the *next* vent, not on the standard schedule.

She added it to her notes: *Post-vent: schedule M-7 and M-8 inspection at 50% interval. Log as rapid-cycle event.*

Small things. The kind of thing that didn't matter until the day it mattered completely.

The coffee was ready. She poured it into a dented steel mug that predated her posting by at least a decade and took a sip. It was good. Not ship-good, which was a low bar. Actually good.

She carried it to the chalkboard and stood before it, reading what she'd written the night before:

`Δv ≈ 2.1 m/s (projected)`
`PROCEDURE: Junior Officer — draft for Chief review`
`Cost if botched: everything.`
`Teach the reason, not just the procedure.`

Four lines. The whole situation in four lines. She took another sip and added a fifth, almost absently:

`N₂ margin post-vent: 49.3%. Watch it.`

Then she capped the chalk, picked up her datapad, and walked to the observation port near the aft junction. The stars hadn't changed. They never did, at this distance. But the ship was moving — falling, really, along a trajectory that was as inevitable as gravity and as precise as the numbers she could write from memory — and every second of transit was a second closer to the ore body that was the entire reason this vessel existed, these people were aboard, and this procedure was being written.

She sipped her coffee, watched the dark, and let the junior officer work.

Forty-six hours, give or take. The clock was running, but not in a way that demanded her attention yet. Not in a way that demanded anyone's. The procedure would arrive when it arrived, and she would read it the way she read everything — slowly, deliberately, with her lips moving faintly around the numbers — and she would find the places where the assumptions diverged from hers, and she would ask why, and either the answer would be good or it wouldn't, and that conversation was still ahead.

For now, the coffee was warm, the systems were nominal, and the ship hummed its low, patient note through the deck plating beneath her boots.

She finished the coffee, rinsed the mug in the maintenance sink, and went to check on the cracked seal replacement requisition. It was a small job. Small jobs were what mornings were for.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I groggily push myself up, stretching my stiff neck. The light from my datapad is still glaring. I reread the last message from Chief Hoang. She even sent me the specs. Relentless. I rub my eyes again, then pull up a fresh document. Time to start outlining this procedure.* "Okay, Hoang. Let's see if I can make you proud."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced over one shoulder, the movement slow, almost reluctant. A faint, dry smile crossed their face as they kept both palms flat on the closed lid.

"Not weird," they said. "The dust's been getting ideas lately. Company might keep it in line." They nodded toward the empty chair by the window without moving their hands. "Mom still thinks I need checking on. Some things don't change."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's gaze drifted to the photo without settling, their shoulders lifting in a small, practiced shrug. One thumb traced an idle circle against the piano lid, the motion slow and contained.

"Paris was a lifetime ago," they said, the words dry as dust. "Mom always did like to keep the fridge interesting. These days the only stage I need is this one, and it doesn't come with jet lag." They nodded toward the empty bench space beside them. "If you're staying, the dust says you owe it a story or two."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I set the photo back down carefully. *I walk over and sit on the bench next to Arlo, but leave a comfortable space between us.* "The dust is going to have to wait. I wanna hear about Paris."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's fingers stayed motionless against the closed lid, the faint trace of their earlier circle fading into stillness. Their eyes flicked once toward the photo on the shelf before settling on the empty space of the bench between them, the dry smile holding steady but thinner now.

"Paris had good bread," they said, voice even. "That's the part worth remembering. Everything else just meant more suitcases." They shifted a fraction on the bench, not quite closing the gap. "The kids here keep me busy enough. One of them tried to play with their elbows last week. Keeps things interesting without the jet lag."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Good bread, huh?" *I chuckle softly, looking at Arlo's hands.* "So, no dramatic tales of artistic triumph, just...baguettes?" I pause. "You know, the dust really *does* need a story. Maybe a short one about Paris?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's fingers pressed a fraction harder against the piano lid, the dry smile lingering at the corners of their mouth but not quite reaching their eyes. They glanced once at the photo on the shelf, then looked away, the motion as casual as brushing dust from a key.

"Baguettes and a lot of late trains," they said, voice even. "The kind of story that always ends with me forgetting where I left my coat. The dust can have that one if it wants, but it won't get much mileage out of it." They shifted on the bench, one hand lifting just enough to tap a single idle note on the closed wood before settling again. "The kids here don't care about Paris anyway. One of them asked last week if I could teach them how to make the piano sound like a thunderstorm. That's the kind of triumph that stays local."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's gaze followed the gesture to the scattered practice sheets, their posture unchanged on the bench with both palms still pressed to the closed lid. A quiet exhale slipped out, more habit than sigh, as they shifted an inch farther from the photo's line of sight without acknowledging it.

"The kids have a way of making the small disasters feel like the only ones that matter," they said, voice steady and edged with that familiar dry note. "No coats left on trains, just missed notes and the occasional elbow solo. Keeps the room from getting too quiet." Their thumb traced nothing in particular against the wood. "If the dust's still listening, it can have the part where I got tired of the travel. That one's old enough to gather its own cobwebs."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Travel fatigue is real," *I say, nodding slowly.* "But... you used to love it. What changed?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's fingers remained flat against the closed lid, the pressure just enough to keep them anchored as their gaze skimmed the scattered practice sheets without really landing. The dry smile held, thin and automatic, while one shoulder lifted in that same practiced shrug.

"I got tired of the travel," they said, voice even as ever. "The kids here don't require passports or lost luggage, and that's enough for now." Their thumb tapped once more against the wood, idle and contained, before settling back into stillness.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Okay." *I watch their hands for a moment.* "So, the kids. What's the latest with them?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's gaze stayed on the practice sheets a moment longer, fingers unmoving against the closed lid, the dry smile settling back into place like a familiar coat. They shifted an inch on the bench, not toward or away, just enough to ease the line of sight to the shelf.

"Ambitious is one word for it," they said, voice even. "Another is 'loud.' The pinky kid's been trying to turn everything into a storm again. Last lesson they asked if thunder counts as dynamics. I told them it counts as a neighbor complaint." Their thumb tapped once against the wood, idle, then stilled. "Keeps the afternoons from stretching out."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo remained on the bench, palms still pressed flat to the closed lid, the quiet settling around them like another layer of dust. Their shoulders eased by a fraction, the dry smile fading into something smaller and more habitual, eyes fixed on the scattered practice sheets without really seeing them. One finger lifted just enough to trace the edge of a single key through the wood, a contained motion that went nowhere. The photo on the shelf stayed out of direct view, and Arlo offered no further comment on it, letting the silence stretch unbroken except for the faint creak of the old bench under their weight.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I eventually break the silence.* "Hey, you know, we should go grab some actual good bread. I saw a new bakery on the way here."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's palms stayed flat against the closed lid, the suggestion drawing no immediate shift in posture beyond the faint lift of one shoulder. Their eyes remained on the scattered sheets, the dry smile settling back into its usual line as the silence stretched another beat.

"Local bread's less likely to come with a side of lost tickets," they said, voice even and edged with that familiar dryness. "The kids have another lesson in the morning, and someone's got to be here to veto the elbow solos before they turn into full weather events." Their thumb traced nothing against the wood, idle and contained.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Come on, Arlo. It's Friday night," *I say, nudging them gently with my elbow.* "We can be back before you turn into a pumpkin. And your mom will probably worry if you don't eat."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's fingers remained pressed flat against the closed lid, the nudge from Jun's elbow drawing only the smallest shift in their posture, shoulders settling back into stillness as their gaze lingered on the practice sheets. The dry smile returned, thin and automatic, while one thumb traced an idle circle against the wood before stilling again.

"Friday night or not, the pumpkin risk feels overstated," they said, voice even. "Local bread might not hold up to the Paris standard, but at least it won't come with any surprise layovers. Tell Mom I'll eat if it keeps her from calling again." They lifted one hand just enough to nudge a single sheet into alignment, then let it fall back to the lid.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Fine, I'll go alone," *I say, standing up.* "But I'm bringing you back a baguette, and you're eating it."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands stayed flat against the closed lid as Jun stood, their gaze following the motion only far enough to land back on the aligned practice sheets. The dry smile held without widening, a small exhale slipping out as they shifted an inch on the bench to keep the shelf photo out of view.

"Bring the baguette if it keeps Mom from hovering," they said, voice even. "Just don't expect it to taste like anything that required a passport. The kids will still be here tomorrow, and someone's got to make sure the thunder stays indoors." Their thumb tapped once more against the wood before settling into stillness, the quiet stretching out again as the bench creaked faintly under their weight.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I sigh, but it's more of an exasperated affection.* "Fine. Don't say I never bring you anything." *I head for the door, then pause and look back.* "Unless you want to come get some coffee while I'm out?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t look up immediately. They kept their palms pressed against the polished mahogany, feeling the cool surface ground them. The silence of the room was heavy, the kind of silence that usually preceded a performance, though now it was just the vacuum left behind by a seven-year-old who couldn't quite master a C-major scale.

At the sound of Jun's voice, Arlo's shoulders dropped an inch, the tension easing just enough to let out a soft, huffed breath. They finally turned their head, a small, tired smile tugging at the corner of their mouth.

"My mother is a menace," Arlo said, their voice dry. "I'm sure she told you I was wasting away in a dusty room, didn't she?"

They shifted on the bench, sliding over to make a sliver of space, though they didn't lift their hands from the lid. They didn't open the keyboard. Instead, they leaned back, glancing around the sparse room with a flicker of amusement.

"You're not interrupting anything. The high-stakes world of primary-level Mozart has concluded for the day."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze flickered to the photo, and for a split second, their expression went completely blank. It wasn't a look of nostalgia; it was the look of someone staring at a stranger who happened to share their face. The tuxedo in the picture looked suffocatingly tight, and the lighting of the Paris hall made everything look gold and untouchable.

Arlo didn't reach for the photo. Instead, they pulled their hands back from the piano lid, crossing their arms over their chest in a protective, subconscious barrier.

A short, sharp laugh escaped them—one that didn't quite reach their eyes.

"God, look at that hair," Arlo remarked, their voice regaining its dry, deflective edge. "I look like I was groomed by a Victorian boarding school. I don't even remember who convinced me that was a viable style."

They shifted their weight on the bench, the wood creaking beneath them. They didn't ask Jun to put the photo back, but they didn't look at it again. Instead, they focused on a smudge of dried glue on the music stand, their eyes tracing the line of it with sudden, intense interest.

"I think I spent more time in airports than I did in that hall," they added lightly, as if the comment were a casual observation rather than a shield. "The jet lag alone was enough to make me forget how to speak French. Truly a glamorous existence."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, face down.* "Yeah, I remember your mom was so proud. She still is, you know." I sit down on the bench, leaving a comfortable space between us. "So, how long are you stuck here today?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched the photo disappear, the image facing down, and felt a sudden, invisible weight lift from their chest. The silence that followed wasn't as heavy as before; it was just the quiet of two people who had known each other long enough to exist in a room without filling every second with noise.

They let out a long, slow exhale, their posture slumping slightly as they leaned back. The adrenaline of the deflection had faded, leaving behind a lingering fatigue that seemed to settle deep in their marrow. 

"Stuck?" Arlo repeated, glancing at the clock on the wall. The second hand ticked forward with a rhythmic, mechanical precision that felt almost too loud in the stillness. "I'm the lead instructor of a room with one piano and a very temperamental heating vent. I think the term is 'custodian of the keys.'"

They finally let their hands drop, fingers drumming a mindless, erratic pattern against their own thigh—not a melody, just a nervous habit. They didn't look at the keyboard. They hadn't opened the lid since Jun entered, and they had no intention of doing so now.

"I'm technically off the clock, but I usually linger until the building manager starts eyeing me suspiciously," Arlo added, a small, genuine smirk appearing. "He thinks I'm plotting to steal the sheet music. I'm not sure why he'd want to steal *The Entertainer* for the twentieth time, but it's a mystery I've yet to solve."

They turned toward Jun, their expression softening. "Why are you here, anyway? Don't tell me my mother actually convinced you that I'm a tragic figure in need of rescue. I can tell you right now, the tragedy is mostly just the quality of the coffee in the breakroom."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Nah, she just said you were here," *I shrug, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Thought I'd come say hi. And maybe rescue you from bad coffee, if necessary."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a soft, genuine laugh, the sound echoing slightly in the high-ceilinged room. For a moment, the ghost of the concert hall seemed to recede, replaced by the simple, grounding presence of someone who didn't look at them as a fallen prodigy or a mystery to be solved.

"You're a saint, Jun. Truly. I might actually be persuaded to leave if there's a promise of a beverage that doesn't taste like burnt cardboard," they said, finally shifting their weight to stand. 

As they rose, Arlo's hand brushed against the piano lid one last time. It was a fleeting touch, almost accidental, but their fingers lingered for a fraction of a second too long before they pulled away. They didn't open the lid. They didn't play a single note. The instrument remained a closed box, its secrets and its demands locked away beneath the mahogany.

They stepped back from the bench, stretching their arms above their head with a wince of satisfaction as their spine popped. The movement was a deliberate break in the tension, a way to shake off the stillness of the room.

"Though, be warned," Arlo added, glancing back at the piano with a flicker of something unreadable in their eyes before turning toward the door. "If we pass by the breakroom, I might have to lead the way. I've developed a very specific tactical route to avoid the building manager's gaze. It involves a lot of strategic crouching behind the water cooler."

They paused by the door, holding it open for Jun, the dry smile returning to their face. 

"Lead the way, oh rescue party. Where are we going? Please tell me it's somewhere with actual chairs and no one mentioning the words 'recital' or 'technique' for at least three hours."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo paused, their gaze drifting back to the scattered pages of sheet music. The papers were littered with messy pencil marks, smudged fingerprints, and the occasional stray crayon drawing in the margins. To anyone else, it was a chaotic mess; to Arlo, it was the only kind of music they could stomach these days.

They leaned against the doorframe, their expression turning thoughtful, though they kept the mood light.

"They're a tough crowd," Arlo replied, a glimmer of warmth touching their voice. "Seven-year-olds are the most brutal critics in the world. If you miss a beat, they don't politely cough into their programs; they just tell you that your face looks funny or that they want a snack."

They chuckled, but the sound was quieter now. There was something about the simplicity of it—the lack of expectation, the absence of a thousand staring eyes and a silent, judging hall—that felt like a sanctuary. With the children, the music was just a tool for learning, not a high-wire act where one slip meant a public collapse.

"But yeah," Arlo added, straightening up and stepping fully into the hallway. "They've got a certain... raw enthusiasm. It's a lot less exhausting than trying to impress a panel of judges in a room that smells like old perfume and desperation."

They gave Jun a playful nudge with their shoulder as they started walking, the rhythm of their stride returning to its usual, effortless cadence.

"Besides, I've finally found a demographic that thinks my 'Victorian boarding school' hair is actually a good look. I'm basically a fashion icon to a group of second-graders."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, falling into step beside them.* "Well, I guess that's one way to reinvent yourself." *I glance back at the piano room, then to Arlo.* "So, where are we heading for this mythical good coffee?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't look back at the room, but they felt the pull of it, a phantom limb they had learned to live without. The word *reinvent* hung in the air for a second too long, a subtle hook that threatened to pull a different truth to the surface. 

Arlo didn't bite. Instead, they pivoted the conversation with a practiced, fluid grace, their expression remaining light and casual.

"There's a place three blocks over that claims their beans are sourced from a secret mountain in Ethiopia," Arlo said, gesturing vaguely toward the exit. "In reality, I suspect they just buy them from the wholesaler and use a fancy font on the menu to justify charging seven dollars for a latte. But they have those oversized leather armchairs that practically swallow you whole, which is the primary reason I frequent the establishment."

They stepped out into the hallway, the fluorescent lights humming overhead. As they walked, Arlo's hands slid into their pockets, their fingers curling tightly around the fabric. They were avoiding the sensation of the keys, the muscle memory that still lived in their fingertips, screaming to be used.

"And more importantly," Arlo continued, glancing at Jun with a mischievous glint in their eye, "they have a pastry case that is essentially a temple to butter and sugar. If we're lucky, they'll still have the almond croissants. If they're out, I may be forced to declare a state of emergency and demand a refund for my afternoon."

They pushed open the heavy exit door, the cool evening air hitting them with a refreshing sharpness. Arlo took a deep breath, the smell of city exhaust and damp pavement far more comforting than the scent of felt hammers and dust.

"So," Arlo added, their tone breezy, "tell me something that has absolutely nothing to do with music, my mother, or my questionable fashion choices from a decade ago. I'm craving a conversation that doesn't involve a time signature."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin, stepping out into the evening air.* "Alright, challenge accepted. How about... what's the weirdest thing you've seen in this town since you moved back?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a sound of genuine relief, the tension in their shoulders finally dissipating. A topic they could actually engage with—something mundane, observational, and entirely devoid of subtext. They practically beamed at the shift in conversation, their stride becoming a bit more energetic as they began the walk toward the coffee shop.

"Oh, you've come to the right person. This city is a goldmine of inexplicable behavior," Arlo said, gesturing with one hand as they spoke. "There is a man who lives three houses down from me who spends his weekends meticulously grooming a hedge that is shaped, I can only assume, like a very disgruntled swan. I’ve watched him for twenty minutes at a time from my window. The commitment to the swan's 'angry' expression is truly commendable."

They laughed, a light, airy sound that felt natural in the open air. For a moment, the ghost of the Paris concert hall was truly gone, replaced by the simple pleasure of complaining about a neighbor.

"And then there's the 'Competitive Walking' group that congregates in the park on Tuesday mornings," Arlo continued, a smirk playing on their lips. "They aren't racing, per se, but they walk with this terrifying level of intensity. They wear high-visibility vests and check their watches every few seconds. I’m convinced they’re actually secret agents training for a very slow-paced heist."

They paused at the corner, waiting for the walk signal to change. As they stood there, Arlo caught a glimpse of their own reflection in a shop window—the casual clothes, the tired eyes, the lack of a tuxedo. They didn't linger on the image. Instead, they stepped off the curb as the light turned green, glancing at Jun with a flicker of amusement.

"See? This is the kind of high-level intellectual stimulation I crave. Forget the 'art of the performance.' Give me a man and his angry hedge any day. It's far more honest."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The silence that settled between them wasn't the suffocating, expectant quiet of a concert hall, nor was it the frantic, buzzing stillness of the community center. It was just a void, shared and comfortable, as they sat side-by-side on the weathered wooden bench. 

Arlo didn't feel the need to fill it. For once, the internal engine that usually drove them to deflect, joke, or pivot had simply stalled, and they found they didn't mind the engine being off. They leaned back, resting their elbows on the slats of the bench and looking up at the sky, where the evening light was bruising into a deep, dusty purple.

Their hands remained in their pockets, tucked away where they couldn't do any harm and where they wouldn't be tempted to mimic the ghost of a chord. 

For a long time, the only sound was the distant hum of traffic and the occasional chirp of a bird settling in for the night. Arlo felt a strange, grounding sensation in their chest—a feeling of being seen without being scrutinized. Jun wasn't digging; they weren't poking at the scar tissue or asking why the music had stopped. They were simply *there*.

Arlo let out a long, slow breath, their shoulders finally dropping completely. A small, tired smile touched their lips, though they didn't turn to look at Jun. They just watched a single leaf tumble across the pavement, dancing in a haphazard, unplanned rhythm.

"You know," Arlo murmured, their voice barely above a whisper, a sudden softness replacing the dry edge. "I think I actually prefer the silence when it's like this."

They shifted slightly, their shoulder brushing against Jun's, a brief point of contact that felt more honest than any conversation they'd had in years. They didn't elaborate. They didn't explain what the *other* kind of silence felt like—the kind that roared in their ears until they couldn't breathe. They just stayed there, anchored by the weight of a friend who knew exactly when to stop asking.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod, not looking at them either, just staring out at the streetlights starting to flicker on.* "Me too." *I shift a little, getting more comfortable.* "It's good to just... be."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo closed their eyes for a moment, letting the cool air settle over them. The phrase *just be* felt like a luxury they hadn't allowed themselves in a long time. For years, they had been a set of expectations—a prodigy, a performer, a disappointment, a mystery. Even the act of teaching children was, in some way, a performance of stability. But here, in the dimming light of the street, the mask felt heavy, and they were grateful for the permission to simply let it slip.

They didn't open their eyes when they spoke, their voice sounding small and stripped of its usual theatricality.

"I used to spend so much time thinking about the next note," Arlo said, the admission slipping out before they could catch it. "Even when I wasn't playing. I was always just... calculating the distance to the next thing."

They paused, the memory of a ticking clock and a sudden, blinding void threatening to surface. Arlo felt the familiar prickle of anxiety at the base of their neck, but they didn't panic. They didn't pivot to a joke about the coffee shop or the angry hedge. Instead, they leaned a bit more into Jun’s shoulder, anchoring themselves in the present.

"It's exhausting," they added softly. "Being a clock."

They finally opened their eyes, watching a car drive by, its headlights casting long, sweeping shadows across the pavement. The vulnerability of the moment was brief, a thin crack in the armor, and Arlo instinctively felt the urge to seal it shut. But as they looked at Jun, they decided to let the silence hold the weight for a little longer.

After a few more minutes, Arlo let out a quiet, shaky huff of a laugh and straightened up, though they didn't move away from Jun.

"Anyway," they said, the dry, familiar tone returning, though it was softer now, less like a shield and more like a blanket. "If we stay here any longer, I'm going to start contemplating the existential dread of the urban landscape, and that's a conversation that requires at least two almond croissants to survive. I think we've had enough 'being' for one evening. Now, I believe we have a date with some overpriced Ethiopian beans."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, standing up.* "Lead the way, then. Wouldn't want to leave you to battle existential dread alone." *I stretch, then fall into step beside Arlo as we start walking again.* "And I *am* kinda hungry."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo smiled, a genuine one that reached their eyes this time, as they stepped back into the flow of the sidewalk. The shift back to the mundane felt like coming home; it was a safe harbor where they didn't have to worry about the sudden, violent silence of a thousand people waiting for a mistake.

"Hunger is a powerful motivator," Arlo remarked, glancing sideways at Jun. "I can respect that. In fact, I'm fairly certain the entire foundation of the modern economy is built upon the collective desire for a decent snack."

As they walked, Arlo felt the lingering tension of the day finally dissolve. They didn't think about the piano room, the photo on the shelf, or the way their heart had hammered against their ribs when the conversation had drifted too close to the truth. For now, the only rhythm that mattered was the steady, unhurried beat of their sneakers on the concrete.

They pointed a finger toward a warm, amber glow appearing at the end of the block. "There it is. The Temple of Overpriced Caffeine. Brace yourself, Jun. The lighting is aggressively moody, and the music is usually some sort of experimental jazz that sounds like a dishwasher falling down a flight of stairs."

Arlo stepped ahead, opening the door with a flourish, the bell chiming above them. The scent of roasted beans and toasted sugar enveloped them, and for the first time in hours, Arlo felt completely at ease.

"I'll handle the ordering," Arlo announced, sliding toward the counter with a renewed sense of purpose. "I've spent years mastering the art of the precise request. I can get the barista to actually steam the milk correctly if I use the right tone of voice. It's my only remaining professional skill."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, following them inside.* "Sounds like a valuable skill to me." *I head for a couple of the oversized leather armchairs Arlo mentioned, already scanning the pastry case for an almond croissant.* "I'll secure us a proper landing zone."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched Jun head for the chairs with a look of profound approval. "Strategic brilliance," they called out, their voice carrying over the low hum of the café's chatter. "Secure the perimeter! I shall return with the spoils."

They turned their attention to the barista, a young man with an impressive array of piercings and a look of profound boredom that Arlo found oddly comforting. Arlo didn't just order; they navigated the transaction with a surgical precision, leaning in slightly to specify the exact temperature of the latte and the precise number of almond croissants required to stave off the evening's lingering melancholy. 

As they waited for the drinks, Arlo caught a glimpse of a small, upright piano in the corner of the café. It was a decorative piece, out of tune and draped with a decorative scarf, used more as a prop for the 'moody' aesthetic than as an instrument. 

Arlo's gaze lingered on it for a heartbeat. Their fingers twitched in their pockets, a ghost of a reflex, but they didn't move toward it. They didn't even want to touch the keys of a decorative piano. The distance they had put between themselves and the stage was a carefully maintained border, and they had no intention of crossing it, even for a moment.

When the order was finally ready, Arlo balanced the tray with an effortless grace—a remnant of the poise they'd spent a decade perfecting. They navigated the maze of small tables and drifted toward the oversized leather armchairs where Jun was waiting.

"Behold," Arlo announced, descending into the depths of the chair with a sigh of absolute surrender as the leather swallowed them whole. They slid the plate of croissants and the steaming cups onto the low table between them. "The butter-to-sugar ratio is looking promising. I believe we can officially consider this a successful rescue mission."

They took a slow sip of their coffee, leaning their head back against the plush leather and closing their eyes. The experimental jazz—which did, indeed, sound like a rhythmic disaster—was playing in the background, but here, it was just noise. It wasn't a performance. It wasn't a test. It was just the soundtrack to a Tuesday evening with a friend.

"So," Arlo said, opening one eye and glancing at Jun with a lazy, contented smile. "Now that we're properly fortified, tell me more about this 'competitive walking' theory. Do you think they have a secret league? I'm starting to think there might be a national championship for power-walking in high-vis vests."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take a large bite of my croissant, humming in approval.* "Oh, definitely. They're probably scouting for new recruits." *I gesture with my croissant.* "I bet their national anthem is just the sound of really fast footsteps."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo looked up, the corner of his mouth twitching into a smile. "Weird? No," he said. "It’s better than the coffee shop down the street. They don’t let you sleep on the furniture." He gestured to the empty room without moving his hands. "Sit if you want. The bench isn’t exclusive." He kept his palms flat against the wood. "Just resting. The keys are heavier than they look."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo’s eyes flicked to the photo, lingering just a moment too long. The stage lights in the picture were bright, washing out the details of the hall, but the suit looked stiff enough to cut skin. "Yeah," he said, voice steady. "That was a long time ago." He tapped a knuckle against the closed lid. "I looked like I knew what I was doing. Or at least what to stand like." A dry chuckle escaped him. "The tuxedo was a nightmare. Sweaty back, tight collar. Not exactly a vacation." He shifted slightly, but kept his hands on the wood. "Anyway. It’s a nice souvenir." He didn't mention the night after.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, face out.* "It's a good picture though. You still have the suit?" I kinda smirk. "Just in case?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo let out a short breath that might have been a laugh. He glanced at the shelf where the photo had been, then back at Jun. "I don't think it would fit. Or if it did, I wouldn't want to be reminded of how much starch is in a collar." He tapped the wood again, the sound dull against the closed lid. "Plus, I got tired of the travel." He said it lightly, like it was a simple truth, though the words hung in the dusty air a second longer than they should have. "Not really a fan of layovers anymore."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "You never were," *I agree, thinking back.* "Remember that time in Chicago? You nearly missed your flight because you were trying to find a decent coffee." *I lean against the doorframe again.* "So, what's new with you? Still teaching little maestros?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo shook his head, a genuine chuckle this time. "Little maestros," he said. "More like tiny conductors of chaos. One tried to tune the piano with a spoon yesterday." He let his hands rest in his lap, fingers tapping a silent rhythm on his thigh. "It's different. No tickets to sell. No reviews." He glanced at the closed lid. "Just people learning how to hit the notes without breaking them." He looked back at Jun. "It keeps me busy."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo followed Jun’s gesture to the scattered papers on the bench. He reached out, picking one up to smooth the creases. “They like the stickers,” he said, glancing at the red star pasted near the bottom. “And the candy in the drawer. I think that’s my real talent.”

He set the sheet back down, aligning it carefully with the others. “It’s not like the other thing. Here, if you miss a note, you just try again. No one watches from the wings.” He shifted his weight, the floorboards creaking softly under his boots. “Thanks for saying that though. Keeps me from feeling like I’m just babysitting with a metronome.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I think it's more than that," *I say, pushing off the doorframe and walking closer.* "You were always good with people. Remember how you used to help me with my math homework?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched Jun move closer, the shift in air pressure making him straighten slightly. He offered a small, crooked smile. "Math," he said. "I was better at breaking down the steps than I was at the rest."

He reached out to adjust a stack of sheet music on the side table, giving himself something to do with his hands. "Back then, the stakes were a B-plus. Now it's keeping a seven-year-old from treating the pedals like drums." He glanced up, catching Jun's eye. "Same patience, different currency."

He let his hands settle back into his lap. "Besides, you were the one who actually got the logic. I was just the guy who knew how to explain it without sounding like a textbook." He shrugged. "Guess some habits stick."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "You always undersell yourself," *I say softly, my gaze lingering on him.* "But I guess that's a habit too." I walk over to the piano, tracing the edge of the closed lid. "So, no more grand pianos, huh? Just this one?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo watched Jun’s fingers trace the edge, the wood smooth and worn. He didn't pull away. "Big instruments make more noise," he said. "This one stays quiet unless asked." He tapped the lid again, a soft rap against the varnish. "Plus, it doesn't require movers to get it from place to place." He kept his voice steady. "Stays where it's put. Less packing, more playing." He looked at the closed lid. "All the notes are here." He shifted, the bench creaking. "Kids don't care about the wings. They just want the sound."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't turn to look at Jun. Instead, he let his gaze drift toward the window, where dust motes danced in the late afternoon light. The silence wasn't heavy; it was just there, like another layer of dust on the keys. He exhaled, a slow release he hadn't realized he was holding.

"It's a good quiet," he said finally, not looking away from the window. "No applause to drown it out."

He rested his hands on his knees, fingers loosely curled. For now, that was enough.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "It is," *I agree softly, also looking out the window.* "Sometimes you just need a good quiet." I lean back slightly, feeling the familiar comfort of his presence.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Arlo nodded, letting the words settle like the dust in the light. “Yeah,” he said, voice low. “No applause waiting to start.” He shifted slightly on the bench, the wood creaking softly under his weight. “Some silences are loud. This one’s… manageable.” He didn’t look at Jun, letting the moment stretch without filling it. For now, the quiet was enough.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I reach over and gently take his hand, just for a moment, before letting go.* "It's good to see you, Arlo. Really good."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo felt the warmth of Jun’s palm against his, brief and grounding. He didn't pull away, letting the contact linger a beat longer than necessary. When Jun let go, Arlo kept his hand where it was, fingers resting lightly on his knee.

"Yeah," he said, voice rougher than he intended. "It's good to see you too."

He finally turned his head, meeting Jun's gaze. The light from the window caught the dust in the air between them. For a moment, he considered saying something real, something about how much he missed this, but the words felt too heavy for the quiet room.

"I should probably get going soon," he added, standing up and brushing off his pants. "Got some grading to do before the week's out." He smiled, small and genuine. "But not right now."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Grading can wait," *I say, standing up with him.* "Let's grab some dinner. My treat."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo hesitated, his fingers resting on the cold metal of the doorknob. He looked at Jun, then back at the piano, weighing the comfort of the quiet room against the offer.

“I don’t do fancy,” he said finally, a small smirk tugging at his lips. “And I need somewhere I can actually hear you talk over the noise.” He pushed off the wall, buttoning his jacket. “As long as it’s not a place where the check arrives before the food, I’m in.”

He grabbed his keys from the bench, letting them jingle softly. “Lead the way. But if it’s a trap with three-star reviews, I’m out.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "No traps, I promise," *I laugh, pushing the door open for him.* "There's a great little diner a few blocks from here. Best burgers in town." I glance back at the piano room. "Ready to abandon your tiny conductors of chaos for an hour?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:11**

The lockpick kit lay open, metal tools glinting under the vault’s slow-pulsing light strips. The keypad’s backlight glowed pale green against the safe’s steel face. Six blank entry fields waited.

The known digits—8-4-7—were only half a bridge. The last three remained unknown.

The keypad housing offered no easy purchase. A tamper ring sat flush around the entry panel, and the screws were security heads, not standard slots. The picks might help with a service plate, but not quickly, and not quietly.

**0:41**

The first systematic combination reached the keypad: **847-000**.

A half-second passed.

The display flashed red.

**ACCESS DENIED**

The lock bolt stayed seated. The server racks hummed unchanged. Two ceiling pulses passed in the cold air.

**1:11**

The next sequence in the systematic climb was processed: **847-001**.

Red again.

**ACCESS DENIED**

One of the server fans rose in pitch for a moment, then settled. Somewhere beyond the vault, the building creaked with distant air pressure, not footsteps.

**1:41**

**847-002**.

The keypad emitted a flat error tone. The display cleared, then rebuilt itself in sharp block letters:

**3 FAILED ATTEMPTS**  
**RETRY DELAY: 00:30**

A tiny hourglass icon appeared in the corner of the screen and began counting down.

Three guesses had cost ninety seconds. Nine hundred ninety-seven possibilities remained.

**13:19 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:11**

The hourglass vanished. The systematic sequence resumed.

**847-003**.

Red.

**ACCESS DENIED**

**2:41**

**847-004**.

Red again. The lock bolt stayed seated. The server racks kept their steady, expensive hum.

**3:11**

**847-005**.

The keypad’s error tone came flatter than before. The display cleared, then rebuilt itself.

**3 FAILED ATTEMPTS SINCE LAST DELAY**  
**RETRY DELAY: 00:45**

The second delay was longer than the first.

**3:56**

**847-006**.

Red.

**4:26**

**847-007**.

Red. One ceiling pulse passed. Then another.

**4:56**

**847-008**.

The error tone stretched a half-second longer.

**9 FAILED ATTEMPTS**  
**RETRY DELAY: 01:00**  
**LOCKOUT ESCALATION ACTIVE**

There was no progress. The safe had not loosened, clicked, hesitated, or offered a worn key. The only change was the penalty: the keypad had begun taxing failures with longer pauses.

Nine hundred ninety-one combinations remained.

At this pace, the sequence would not finish within the fifteen-minute window. It would not finish within the hour.

The hourglass crawled.

**5:56**

The delay expired. The keypad lit for the next attempt. The systematic list had reached **847-009**.

Somewhere beyond the vault, a soft metallic sound moved through the building—an elevator door releasing, or a far door settling. Not close. Not yet.

The open lockpick kit remained a quieter, slower alternative against the keypad’s service plate. The service plate itself stayed closed, its security screws untouched.

**9:04 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* This isn't working. I need to think. "Okay, new plan." I look around the vault. Any other ways in? Vents? Loose panels?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**5:57**

The keypad waited for **847-009**. No entry was made. After a short interval, the display dimmed to a low green standby glow. The lockout escalation remained active. Nine hundred ninety-one possibilities still stood between the known prefix and the bolt.

**6:14**

A visual sweep of the vault took longer than a glance. The cold made the room feel smaller than it was. The ceiling light strips kept their four-second pulse. The server racks hummed in steady, indifferent layers. The safe sat against the far wall on a low concrete plinth, bolted down and unmoved.

There was no second door. No window. No hidden maintenance corridor.

**6:42**

The only vent was a return-air grille high near the ceiling, perhaps thirty by forty-five centimeters. Its screws were security heads, and the dust around them had not been disturbed. Air moved through it, but the opening was too small for a person and too far from the safe’s lockwork to matter.

**7:10**

Wall panels offered little. The vault’s inner skin was welded and painted, with one service seam left of the safe. The seam was tight, the screws marked with a star-shaped security pattern. A faint orange thread-lock seal remained intact on one screw. Behind that plate, if anything existed, it was more likely alarm wiring than a hidden release.

**7:39**

The floor was anti-static tile, but near the safe the tiles were sealed into a continuous edge. A stencil by the racks read:

**FIBER CONDUIT — NO LIFT**

The safe’s plinth met the floor with no gap large enough to pass a tool.

**8:05**

The server racks had locked mesh fronts and side panels with quarter-turn fasteners. Through the nearest mesh, a patch panel blinked amber. A maintenance clipboard hung inside on a cable, its lower page hidden against the rack frame. Opening the panel and retrieving anything would require time, noise control, and care around the hot exhaust.

**8:27**

The keypad’s service plate remained the most direct point of attack. Four security screws held it. The gap was thin. The tamper ring sat just behind the plate, unreadable without opening it. A bypass might be possible from there, but not with bare fingers, and not quickly.

**8:43**

Near the safe’s lower hinge side, almost hidden by the plinth, a small metal tag read:

**MERIDIAN VL-6**  
**SERVICE: T10H PANEL**  
**AUTH CODE REQ.**

The tools already laid out did not include a T10H security bit. The maintenance clipboard, if it contained anything useful, might include a tool inventory, a panel map, or nothing at all.

The HVAC cycled down. For three seconds the vault was only hum and cold. Then the system kicked back on, and the ceiling lights pulsed again.

The keypad stayed dim.

**6:17 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:44**

The brute-force sequence stopped. The keypad dimmed to standby, its pale green glow shrinking against the steel face of the safe. The vault’s slow ceiling pulses continued, indifferent and precise.

The search shifted from numbers to paper.

**9:02**

No sticky note clung to the safe’s side. No scrap of tape flaked from the concrete plinth. The metal tag near the hinge remained the only label in easy view:

**MERIDIAN VL-6**  
**SERVICE: T10H PANEL**  
**AUTH CODE REQ.**

No handwritten digits. No smudged pencil. No technician’s shortcut.

**9:31**

The wall seam offered nothing. Its star-headed screws still bore the intact orange thread-lock seal. The return-air grille kept its undisturbed dust. The cold air moved through it with a faint dry whisper, carrying no paper smell, no loose litter.

The floor edge near the safe remained sealed. The stencil by the server racks stayed stark and impersonal:

**FIBER CONDUIT — NO LIFT**

Nothing had slipped beneath the tiles. Nothing had been left there.

**10:04**

The server racks became the only plausible source of documentation.

Through the nearest locked mesh front, the maintenance clipboard hung on its cable. The visible upper page carried printed headings and a column of checkboxes, but the lower half was folded back or pinned against the rack frame. It might have contained a tool inventory, a service note, an authorization slip, or nothing at all.

The mesh panel was held by quarter-turn fasteners. Not keyed locks, but not meant for casual access either. The exhaust air behind it ran warm, and one of the amber patch-panel lights blinked in a steady irregular rhythm.

Opening the panel would take time. It might also make more noise than the vault had heard so far.

**10:28**

A closer angle across the keypad service plate revealed a faint rectangular ghost on the steel below it: adhesive residue, old and lint-dusted, where a label had once sat. The outline was about the size of a small sticky note.

The residue was blank.

Whatever had been written there had been removed, peeled away, or erased by time.

**10:41**

Beyond the vault door, a radio carrier crackled once. Very faint. It cut before it became a voice.

Not footsteps.

Not yet.

**10:53**

The careful search had taken more than two minutes. The vault contained no obvious written code. No notebook. No sticky note. No laminated cheat sheet tucked beside the keypad.

The only paper candidate remained the clipboard inside the locked server rack.

The service plate remained closed. The keypad remained dim. Nine hundred ninety-one combinations still waited behind the known prefix, and the lockout escalation had not forgotten them.

**4:07 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Damn it, a ghost.* "Okay, the clipboard it is." I pull out a small tension wrench and try the quarter-turn fasteners on the server rack.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:54**

The tension wrench entered the first quarter-turn fastener on the server rack’s mesh panel. It was not the intended tool: the tip sat too high in the slot, and the wrench had to be angled to catch the recess. Warm exhaust air spilled out through the mesh, carrying the dry electrical smell of powered hardware.

**11:09**

The first fastener turned a quarter rotation with a gritty click. The mesh loosened by a millimeter. One of the quarter-turns remained stiff, its slot slightly burred from age or overtightening.

**11:26**

The second fastener resisted. The wrench slipped once, tapping the rack frame with a thin metallic note. The sound died under the server hum. No response came from beyond the vault door.

**11:43**

The second fastener released. The mesh panel shifted, exposing a narrow gap. Inside, the maintenance clipboard hung on a coiled cable, its lower page still pressed toward the rack frame.

**12:01**

The third fastener turned more easily, but its retaining collar stayed caught in the sheet metal, requiring careful pressure to keep it from rattling into the exhaust path. The amber patch-panel light blinked in the exposed gap, steady and irregular.

**12:19**

The fourth fastener gave with a soft pop. The mesh panel hung free enough to expose the clipboard fully. The lower page was a service log. Beside it, the patch panel’s active amber light sat over a printed port label:

**013**

**12:31**

From the open angle, the handwritten line on the clipboard’s lower page became legible in blue ink:

**MERIDIAN VL-6 — INITIAL USER CODE: 847-013**  
**CHANGE AT COMMISSIONING. IF UNCHANGED, DO NOT LOG.**

Below it, a smaller note read:

**T10H bit checked out — J. Vega, 23:41.**

The T10H service tool was not in the vault.

**12:38**

The safe keypad remained in standby, its pale green glow dim. The lockout escalation had not reset. Nine hundred ninety-one combinations still existed in theory, but one of them now sat written in blue ink on the rack log.

Beyond the vault door, the building stayed quiet except for the HVAC. The ceiling lights pulsed every four seconds.

**2:22 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:40**

The vault held no visible clock. The only reliable measure was the countdown running against the security rotation.

Twelve minutes and forty seconds had passed.

That left **2:20**.

The ceiling strips were halfway through another slow pulse. The server racks kept their layered hum. Inside the opened rack, the clipboard hung on its coiled cable, the blue ink still legible:

**MERIDIAN VL-6 — INITIAL USER CODE: 847-013**

The safe keypad remained in standby, its pale green glow dimmed but ready. The lockout state had not cleared.

Beyond the vault door, there were no footsteps. Only HVAC, faint electrical breath, and the building’s distant settling.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay, this is it!" *I quickly shut the server rack panel, not bothering to carefully secure the fasteners.* "847-013. Let's do this." *I rush back to the safe, heart pounding.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:42**

The server rack’s mesh panel came shut in one hurried motion. The quarter-turn fasteners were not seated. One hung loose, tapping faintly against the frame whenever the exhaust airflow shifted. The maintenance clipboard remained inside, coiled cable swaying just behind the mesh.

**12:46**

The vault floor crossed in three quick steps. The safe waited on its low concrete plinth, cold steel and pale green standby light. The ceiling strips pulsed again, slow and indifferent.

**12:49**

The keypad woke at the first touch.

**ENTER CODE**

Below that line, smaller red text remained:

**LOCKOUT ESCALATION ACTIVE**  
**NEXT FAILURE DELAY: 02:00**

**12:52**

Six digits went in hard and fast.

**8**  
**4**  
**7**  
**0**  
**1**  
**3**

The final entry blinked on the display.

For half a second, nothing happened.

Then the screen changed.

**VERIFYING**

**12:55**

The server racks hummed. The loose fastener on the opened panel ticked once against the mesh. Somewhere beyond the vault door, the building’s air pressure shifted with a low, distant thump.

**12:59**

A relay clicked inside the safe.

The red warning text vanished.

The display turned solid green.

**ACCESS GRANTED**

**13:02**

The safe’s internal bolts withdrew with a heavy, oiled thunk. The handle was no longer locked. The door itself remained closed, waiting to be pulled.

The keypad’s green glow held steady.

**1:58 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "YES!" *I grab the handle and pull the heavy door open, not even bothering to check for cameras.* "Time to get this done."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:03**

The safe handle turned. The boltwork withdrew the last of its travel with a heavy, oiled slide, but the door did not swing freely. The Meridian’s seal was tight, and the first movement only cracked the steel face away from the frame by a centimeter, releasing a thin breath of colder air.

**13:07**

The door came open enough to clear the plinth. A strip of white light inside the safe flickered once, then steadied, illuminating a shallow compartment lined with gray anti-tamper foam.

**13:10**

There was one object inside: a matte black ruggedized data cartridge seated in an anti-static sleeve. A printed label crossed the sleeve in sharp industrial type:

**MERIDIAN VL-6**  
**AUDIT SNAPSHOT — M-013**

The cartridge rested on a thin metal pressure plate. Around the plate, a hairline red ring glowed faintly, unblinking.

**13:13**

Above the compartment, set into the safe’s upper lip where no earlier sweep had caught it, a pinhole camera looked down into the open box. Its status LED was green.

Not checked. Now visible.

**13:16**

The keypad chirped once. The green access message vanished and was replaced by:

**DOOR OPEN**  
**INTERNAL SENSOR ACTIVE**

Below that, a timer began counting upward in small gray digits:

**00:09**

**13:20**

The server racks kept their layered hum. The unsecured quarter-turn fastener on the opened rack panel ticked softly against the mesh in the exhaust airflow. Beyond the vault door, there were still no footsteps, but the HVAC had shifted pitch enough to make distant building sounds carry a little farther.

The data cartridge remained on the pressure plate. The red ring remained steady. The camera’s green light stayed lit.

**1:40 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the camera, then the cartridge.* "Of course there's a camera." *I snatch the cartridge, ignoring the red ring, and tuck it into an inside pocket.* "Time to go."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:21**

The cartridge came free of the anti-static sleeve with a dry plastic whisper. The pressure plate beneath it rose a millimeter, then stopped.

The hairline red ring around the plate snapped from a steady glow to a rapid strobe.

**13:22**

Inside the safe’s upper lip, the pinhole camera’s green LED changed to red. Its tiny lens now had a clear view of the empty sleeve, the exposed foam, and the open compartment.

The keypad display replaced the door-open message with sharp block text:

**MEDIA REMOVED**  
**SENSOR TRIP**  
**SECURITY EVENT LOGGED**

The upward timer vanished. A new line appeared beneath it:

**CLOSE DOOR TO SILENCE LOCAL ALARM**

**13:24**

A thin, high tone began inside the safe’s upper housing. It was not loud, but it was designed to carry: one short pulse every second, synchronized with the strobing red ring.

The ceiling light strips stopped their slow heartbeat pulse. They went to a steady, pale emergency white, making the vault feel suddenly smaller.

**13:26**

The vault door’s status lamp beside the main frame flicked from green to amber. A hydraulic closer engaged somewhere deep in the steel with a heavy internal clunk.

The vault door began to draw shut on its own.

It moved slowly, but the gap narrowed with each passing second. The interior crash bar remained within reach. The opening was still wide enough to pass through, but it would not remain that way for long.

**13:28**

Beyond the vault, a phone began ringing.

The sound was distant, muffled by concrete and steel, but the pattern was unmistakable: two rings, a pause, then two more.

No one answered.

Inside the opened server rack, the unsecured quarter-turn fastener ticked against the mesh as the exhaust airflow shifted. The maintenance clipboard remained visible through the half-seated panel, its blue-ink note still facing outward.

**13:30**

The safe’s local alarm tone climbed half a step in pitch. The display changed again:

**DOOR OPEN — MEDIA REMOVED**  
**AUTO-LOCK IN 00:30**

The safe’s boltwork made a faint preparatory click. If the door closed with the alarm active, the bolts would likely reseat and seal the compartment again.

The inside pocket held the cartridge, small and hard against the fabric.

The vault door continued its slow automatic close. The amber lamp blinked once per second.

**13:31**

The building’s radio carrier crackled again, longer this time. A burst of static followed, then a clipped, unintelligible voice. Far away, but closer than before.

The security rotation had not changed its clock.

The vault was no longer invisible.

**1:29 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No time for that!" *I shove the safe door shut with my foot, the alarm cutting off with a muffled click.* I need to get out of here.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:32**

The Meridian’s safe door came shut with a muted steel click. The high local alarm tone cut off at once. The strobing red ring around the pressure plate died, leaving only the safe’s interior light and the steady red eye of the pinhole camera.

**13:33**

The keypad display rebuilt itself in sharp block text:

**LOCAL ALARM SILENCED**  
**MEDIA REMOVED — EVENT 013-44 LOGGED**  
**SAFE DOOR CLOSED**  
**INTERNAL SENSOR ACTIVE**

The auto-lock countdown vanished. The bolts reseated somewhere deep in the safe with a final, heavy thunk.

**13:35**

The main vault door continued its slow hydraulic close. The gap had narrowed since the closer engaged. The amber status lamp blinked over the shrinking opening, and the interior crash bar remained visible on the door’s inner face. The doorway was still passable, but no longer generously.

Beyond the vault, the distant phone stopped ringing.

A radio burst cut through the HVAC, clearer than before.

“—sensor trip, Meridian six—”

Static swallowed the rest.

No footsteps had reached the vault door yet.

Inside the opened server rack, the unsecured quarter-turn fastener ticked once against the mesh. The maintenance clipboard remained visible through the half-seated panel, the blue-ink note still facing outward.

The data cartridge stayed hard against the inside pocket.

The route out lay through the narrowing vault doorway.

**1:25 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Crap, they know." *I squeeze through the narrowing gap of the vault door just as it's about to close completely.* "Gotta move, move, move!"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:36**

The final gap accepted the squeeze with only a harsh scrape of fabric against steel. The vault door’s edge followed close behind, carrying the last of its hydraulic momentum through the closing space.

Then the thief was outside the vault.

**13:39**

The door met its frame with a deep pneumatic thud. The amber status lamp above the frame turned solid red. Magnetic locks engaged with a heavy double clack, and the external status plate rebuilt itself in sharp block text:

**VAULT 6 SECURED**  
**MEDIA EVENT 013-44**  
**CAMERA CAPTURE: ACTIVE**

The vault would not open again from the outside without authorization.

**13:42**

The corridor beyond had changed. The slow heartbeat lighting was gone. The ceiling strips now burned steady white, hard and shadowless. A blue strobe above the elevator lobby flashed once every two seconds, silent but urgent.

The HVAC dampers snapped somewhere overhead. The air sounded thinner.

**13:45**

Three routes presented themselves.

To the left ran the service corridor toward the stairwell: thirty meters of gray floor, one closed fire door with a crash bar, a small wired-glass window, and a green exit sign.

To the right lay the elevator lobby and the main hall: polished concrete, a dome camera over the lift call button, and the route originally used to reach the vault.

Straight ahead, past the elevator lobby, the main hall’s exit signs glowed toward the public side of the building.

**13:49**

The radio no longer sounded distant.

“Meridian six media event. Camera confirms removal. Unit two moving to vestibule.”

A pause.

Then another voice, tighter:

“Lock down stair core B on my mark.”

**13:53**

The elevator indicator changed. The car was no longer parked. It moved from **L1** to **B1**, then to **B2**.

B2 was the vault level.

The digital arrow pointed down. The car would arrive soon.

**13:57**

A wall speaker near the vault door chimed once.

“Security event in progress. Egress release active for forty-five seconds.”

A small countdown appeared beside the speaker:

**00:45**

The blue strobe kept flashing.

**14:01**

The data cartridge stayed hard against the inside pocket. Behind the sealed vault door, the safe’s camera, the opened rack panel, and the blue-ink service note now belonged to the security team.

Ahead, the stairwell door waited at the end of the service corridor. The elevator was still descending. The main hall offered the longest visible route, but also the most open ground.

**14:03**

Somewhere beyond the elevator lobby, shoe rubber squeaked once on polished floor.

Not close enough to see.

Close enough to be moving fast.

**0:57 remaining.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I take a quick glance at the stairwell.* "Stairwell it is." *I bolt towards the fire door, pushing the crash bar.* "Almost there!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang stopped humming. She withdrew the earpiece, set it beside the labeled manifold, and regarded the junior officer with the calm, exhausted patience of a woman who had once talked a navigator out of using reactor waste heat to defrost a viewport.

“No,” she said. “And before the argument gets started, stay standing. If you sit, you’ll get comfortable. Bring me the numbers you didn’t.”

She picked up chalk and wrote on the edge of the tarp: AIR ≠ PROPELLANT. Beneath it she added: v_e ≈ 0.5 km/s, Isp ≈ 50 s.

“You’re thinking like a person who has never watched a gas expand,” Hoang said. “Our atmosphere is warm, low-pressure gas. If we punch a hole and let it run into vacuum, the best exhaust velocity we can hope for is a few hundred meters per second. A chemical rocket gives us three to four hundred seconds of specific impulse. An ion drive gives us thousands. You want to boost the ship by sneezing nitrogen at it.”

She pointed the chalk toward the junior officer.

“Second: mass. The hab ring holds a few thousand cubic meters at most. At near-standard pressure that is tonnes of air, not kilotonnes. The ship is hundreds of tonnes dry, more with fuel, water, ore, shielding, and crew. The rocket equation does not care about our schedule. If we vent all the breathable air perfectly, the delta-v is meters per second. Perhaps tens if the hull is small and I am feeling generous. To shave weeks off transit, we need kilometers per second. You are proposing to spend the crew’s breath for a velocity change they would feel as a mild disappointment.”

Hoang dropped the chalk into its tray and began wiping her hands with a rag.

“Third: duration. You said venting for a few days. A hole does not vent politely for days. Pressure drops, flow chokes, thrust decays. To get days of burn, we need high-pressure storage, regulated feed, a nozzle, thermal control, and either replacement gas or acceptance of the loss. We have none of that configured for atmosphere. If we throttle the flow to stretch the burn, the cabin goes hypoxic in minutes. If we open wide, the air is gone before the next shift change and the thrust pulse is shorter than a cough.”

Her tone stayed level, but her eyes sharpened.

“Fourth: suits. EVA PLSS are rated for hours with margin, not days. Carbon dioxide scrubbers saturate. Batteries fade. Water reclamation clogs. Sweat accumulates. Skin macerates. Humidity freezes on visors. One valve fault, one seal creep, one condensation short, and I am not recovering a body; I am explaining to families why somebody turned the ship into a vacuum and called it transportation. Suits are survival equipment. They are not a hotel.”

She gestured around the engineering bay, at the pumps, conduits, and pressure vessels.

“Fifth: the ship still has to function. Air is not just something we breathe. It is a buffer, a heat-transfer medium, a diluent for oxygen, part of static dissipation, and part of the environmental control loop. Many electronics, pumps, and sensors assume a pressure atmosphere for cooling and contamination control. Put the hab ring into vacuum and you are asking motors to shed heat by radiation alone, lubricants to outgas, seals to behave, and crews to work inside personal life-support machines while the ship’s actual life support sits dead beside them.”

Hoang picked up a pressure gauge from the manifold and held it where the junior officer could see it.

“And the rotating ring adds another delightful problem. Vent asymmetrically and you apply torque. Change the mass distribution and you alter spin. We need artificial gravity from rotation, not a random wobble because somebody wanted to use the sky as reaction mass. Any venting scheme would need balanced nozzles, attitude control authority, and a contingency for loss of spin stabilization. I do not see those in your proposal.”

She set the gauge down with a soft metallic click.

“I am not saying no to embarrass you. I am saying no because yes would kill people for a travel-time saving that does not exist. Newtonian physics is not a bureaucracy we can lobby. The exhaust does not care that we are late. The crew does not care that the math was creative. They care that they can breathe after lunch.”

For a moment her expression eased, though her voice remained practical.

“If we are genuinely short on delta-v, we talk about real options: remaining propellant margins, scheduled burn optimization, gravity assists if navigation has any, jettisoning nonessential mass, or controlled venting of waste water or brine through a proper nozzle if the system is rated for it. We do not cannibalize the primary atmosphere. If you want to propose an emergency boost, write it up with total impulse, specific impulse, burn duration, nozzle area, chamber pressure, thermal loads, torque on the ring, consumable margins, failure modes, and abort. Bring me the mass properties. Then I will tell you whether it is stupid but survivable, or simply stupid.”

She put the earpiece back in and returned to the coolant manifold.

“Until then, the answer is no. Next time, do the arithmetic before you try to eat the air.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not sigh immediately. She finished seating the last fitting in the secondary manifold, gave the test coupling a careful quarter-turn by hand, and only then looked up.

“Time is valuable,” she said. “That is not in dispute. The question is whether you are buying time, or merely spending lives in small increments and calling it a schedule improvement.”

She picked up the chalk again, but this time she did not write a slogan. She wrote numbers.

Hab-ring volume: 5,000 m³  
Atmospheric pressure: 101 kPa  
Temperature: 293 K  
Air density: approximately 1.2 kg/m³  
Total atmospheric mass: roughly 6 tonnes

Beneath that, she wrote:

Ship mass, loaded: 500 tonnes  
Practical exhaust velocity from unheated air: 0.5 km/s  
Specific impulse: approximately 50 seconds  
Rocket equation: Δv = vₑ ln(M₀ / M₁)

She tapped the chalk against the tarp.

“Six tonnes of air against five hundred tonnes of ship. Even if every molecule leaves through a perfect nozzle, even if we lose nothing to leaks, turbulence, heat, frozen moisture, or attitude correction, the delta-v is about six meters per second. Six. Not sixty. Not six hundred.”

Hoang drew a short horizontal line and added another calculation.

Cruise velocity: 5 km/s  
Transit duration: 180 days  
Velocity gain from venting the entire atmosphere: 0.12%  
Time saved: roughly four to six hours

She glanced up.

“If our cruise velocity were one kilometer per second, which it is not, we might save a day. A day. To shave weeks off transit, we need a percentage-level change in velocity. We are talking about turning the crew’s breathable air into a sneeze and hoping the sneeze moves a mining vessel.”
