She set the chalk down and folded her arms across her stained coveralls.

“And that is the optimistic arithmetic. The pessimistic arithmetic is worse. A hole in the hull is not an engine. Free expansion into vacuum wastes most of the available energy. To get useful thrust, the gas must pass through a properly shaped nozzle, with controlled throat area, pressure ratio, thermal management, and structural reinforcement. Our hab atmosphere is not stored at pressure suitable for propulsion. It is stored at the pressure required to keep human beings conscious. The moment you begin draining it, cabin pressure drops, temperature changes, moisture condenses or freezes, and the flow becomes unsteady. You do not get a clean burn. You get a diminishing, unstable leak with a side of suffocation.”

Hoang stood, brushed chalk dust from her knee, and walked to the environmental status board. She keyed up the life-support schematic, then pointed at the oxygen partial pressure and carbon dioxide scrubber margins.

“Your proposal requires the crew to live in suits for days. That is not a minor inconvenience. Portable life-support systems are rated for planned extravehicular activity, contingency, and short-duration emergencies. They are not habitats. Carbon dioxide scrubbers saturate. Battery capacity declines. Humidity accumulates inside the helmet. Visors fog. Cooling garments fail or become uncomfortable enough to impair work. Urine and waste management become logistical hazards. Sleep becomes difficult. Communication degrades. Every hour inside a suit increases the probability of error.”

She turned back.

“One suit fault does not merely delay the mission. It creates a casualty. Then it creates a rescue. Then it creates a medical intervention in a decompressurized section of ship. Then it creates a repair outage. Then it creates psychological shock among the crew. Then it creates an investigation. You will lose more time recovering from one preventable accident than you ever hoped to gain by turning the atmosphere into reaction mass.”

Hoang’s voice remained even, but there was steel under it.

“Do not imagine that the risk is abstract. The risk is a technician with a cracked visor seal. The risk is a child-sized body in a corridor when pressure drops. The risk is a pump motor overheating because it no longer has convective air cooling. The risk is lubricants outgassing onto cold optics. The risk is static discharge in a dry, depressurized compartment. The risk is the rotating ring developing unwanted torque because venting is not perfectly symmetrical. The risk is losing spin stability and having to correct with propellant we actually need.”

She gestured toward the curved deck, where the subtle centrifugal pull of the hab ring kept tools, bodies, and loose fluids behaving almost normally.

“The ring is already a carefully balanced machine. Remove mass asymmetrically, apply thrust off-center, or change the internal pressure environment, and you are not merely altering trajectory. You are altering the ship’s dynamics. Artificial gravity comes from rotation. Rotation requires control. If you make the ring wobble, you make crew sick, equipment unreliable, and structural loads unpredictable. For six meters per second.”

Hoang picked up the pressure gauge again and held it between them like a small, damning exhibit.

“So no. It is not worth the risk. Not because I do not understand urgency. Because the urgency is false. The atmosphere cannot buy weeks. It can barely buy hours. And the price is not ‘discomfort in suits.’ The price is converting a functioning spacecraft into a pressure vessel full of dying machinery and exhausted people, for a delta-v that navigation would round off before breakfast.”

She returned the gauge to its place and crossed her arms.

“If we are truly short on delta-v, there are sane avenues. We examine remaining propellant margins. We optimize burn timing. We look for gravity assists. We jettison nonessential mass. We consider venting waste water, brine, or inert purge gas through a rated nozzle if the plumbing can tolerate it. We use the main drive, the maneuvering thrusters, or electric propulsion as designed. Those systems exist because someone did the arithmetic before proposing to eat the sky.”

Her expression softened by a fraction, though her tone did not become gentle.

“I know you want to help the crew arrive sooner. Wanting to help is not the same as being right. Engineering is the discipline of refusing beautiful ideas that fail boundary conditions. This idea fails mass, momentum, thermodynamics, life support, reliability, and human factors. All at once.”

Hoang bent to retrieve her earpiece, then paused.

“Bring me the navigation package. Give me required delta-v, current propellant load, burn windows, and abort margins. If there is a real emergency, we solve it with real systems. Until then, the atmosphere stays where it is: inside the ship, where it belongs.”

She put the earpiece back in and returned to the coolant manifold.

“And stop asking whether lives are worth time. Ask whether time is worth losing the people who would have to spend it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, looking down at my boots. She's got a point. A lot of points, actually.* "Okay, Chief. I get it. No eating the sky." *I pause.* "I'll go get those nav numbers for you."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang let the silence stand for a moment. Not to punish it. To let the arithmetic settle where the enthusiasm had been.

Then she reached for the clipboard hanging beside the environmental status board and tore off a fresh sheet. She wrote quickly, in block letters, the kind of handwriting meant to survive grease, gloves, and bad lighting.

“Good,” she said. “No eating the sky. If we need reaction mass, we use mass we chose to carry for that purpose. Water, brine, inert purge gas, propellant, or waste product rated for expulsion through hardware built to handle it. Not the air in their lungs.”

She held the sheet out.

“Bring me the navigation package. Not a summary. Not a feeling. Raw numbers.”

The list was long and plainly written:

Current state vector relative to target.  
Required arrival window and hard deadline, if any.  
Remaining propellant by tank, including ullage margins.  
Main engine specific impulse and thrust curve at available chamber pressures.  
Electric propulsion power budget, beam current margins, and grid wear limits.  
Reaction control system propellant remaining.  
Current wet mass, dry mass, ore load, water reserves, consumables, and spare parts mass.  
Habitat ring spin rate, balance status, and attitude control authority.  
Thermal rejection margin during proposed burn.  
Structural load limits for sustained acceleration.  
Abort corridors and disposal options if the burn goes wrong.  
Life support margins for extended high-consumption operations.  
Any planned jettisonable mass that does not include crew atmosphere.

Hoang tapped the bottom of the list with one chalk-dusted finger.

“Mark your assumptions. If you estimate, label it. If you guess, label that louder. I would rather read a wrong number clearly marked than a confident number that nobody checked.”

She paused, then added one more line beneath the others.

*Who else has heard this idea?*

Her expression did not soften, but her voice lost some of its edge.

“I am not asking to catch you. I am asking because bad ideas travel faster than coolant leaks. If someone else has been nodding along, I want to know before they start imagining nozzles in the corridor vents.”

She folded the sheet and handed it over with the clipped efficiency of someone who had spent years preventing disasters by being inconvenient early.

“And while you are gathering numbers, check the waste-water and brine inventories. If there is a real deficit, there may be a sane way to buy a little delta-v without turning the ship into a tomb. But we do that with valves, filters, nozzle heating, pressure regulators, and a shutdown procedure. Not with hope and a hole in the hull.”

Hoang picked up her earpiece, then set it aside again. Whatever was playing could wait. This could not.

“You did the right thing by stopping,” she said. “People survive because someone admits the idea is wrong before the idea admits the people are dead. That is not humiliation. That is engineering.”

She returned to the coolant manifold, but did not put the earpiece back in yet.

“Bring me the package within the hour. If the numbers show a genuine shortfall, we will look at real options: burn optimization, mass reduction, trajectory adjustment, or using rated stores as propellant. If they do not, you will write a one-page note explaining why venting the atmosphere fails, and you will file it where the next bright idea can read it before trying to breathe propulsion.”

Her hand tightened briefly on the wrench.

“And if you find anybody has already cracked a vent valve for ‘testing,’ you tell me immediately. Not after lunch. Not after you have a theory. Immediately.”

Only then did she slide the earpiece back into place, leaving the final instruction plain and quiet over the hum of the pumps.

“No eating the sky. Bring numbers.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang set the wrench down, wiped her hands once on the rag, and took the tablet. She did not scroll immediately. She held it at arm’s length, squinted, then brought it closer, as if the numbers might improve by being viewed from a different distance.

They did not.

“Thirty-four zero,” she said. “That is not a delta-v. That is the speed of sound in room-temperature air wearing a mission patch.”

She tapped the screen once, not hard enough to damage it, then handed it back with the careful restraint of a woman who had seen too many confident spreadsheets become funeral pyres.

“Show me the step where you converted pressure ratio to useful impulse,” Hoang said. “Because if you used three hundred forty meters per second as exhaust velocity, then you forgot the rocket equation. If you used three hundred forty meters per second as ship delta-v, then you invented exhaust velocity out of thin air. Which is precisely what we are not doing.”

She turned to the tarp, found her chalk, and wrote in large, ugly block letters:

Δv = vₑ ln(M₀ / M₁)

Beneath it:

M₀ = 500,000 kg  
M₁ = 494,000 kg  
ln(M₀ / M₁) ≈ 0.012

Then she drew a box around the last line and underlined it twice.

“Six tonnes of air against five hundred tonnes of ship gives you a mass ratio ln term of about one point two percent,” Hoang said. “That is the entire account balance. Everything else is spending policy.”

She wrote:

If vₑ = 340 m/s → Δv ≈ 4 m/s  
If vₑ = 500 m/s → Δv ≈ 6 m/s  
If vₑ = 760 m/s → Δv ≈ 9 m/s

Hoang tapped the 760.

“That last number is generous. That is the theoretical ceiling for cold air expanding ideally from room temperature into vacuum. Roughly sqrt(2 c_p T). At two hundred ninety-three kelvin, you do not get much better than seven hundred seventy meters per second without adding heat. Real nozzles, real turbulence, real condensation, real finite throat area, real structural limits: call it five hundred. Maybe six hundred if the universe is feeling charitable and I am not watching.”

She looked up.

“So your three hundred forty meters per second is a perfectly respectable exhaust velocity for a sneeze. It is not a delta-v for a mining vessel.”

Hoang erased a corner of the tarp and wrote another line:

To get Δv = 340 m/s with 6 t air and 500 t ship:  
vₑ ≈ 28,000 m/s

She let that sit there.

“Twenty-eight kilometers per second,” she said. “That is what your number demands if you actually want to move the ship by throwing away the atmosphere. Do you understand what that means thermally? If you try to get that from heated gas, you need stagnation temperatures on the order of four hundred thousand kelvin. Air at that temperature is not a propellant. It is a plasma headache. It eats nozzles, ionizes insulation, shorts sensors, and laughs at your chamber walls.”

She shook her head.

“And if you try to get that electrically, by ionizing and accelerating the gas, then you are not ‘venting the atmosphere.’ You are building an electrodynamic propulsion system, feeding it gigawatts-scale power for a meaningful impulse, storing the gas in rated pressure vessels, protecting the grids from contamination, managing beam instability, and accepting that your power budget is now the mission. That may be possible in principle with dedicated hardware. It is not possible by opening a valve in the hab ring and hoping the nitrogen behaves.”

Hoang picked up the tablet again, this time scrolling through the junior officer’s numbers with the methodical suspicion of someone checking a weld for hairline cracks.

“Now. Compression ratio,” she said. “If by compression ratio you mean pressure ratio across a nozzle, that affects mass flow, choking, and expansion. It does not create energy. The available energy per unit mass is set by temperature and enthalpy. You can expand one atmosphere of room-temperature gas into vacuum as well as physics permits, and physics still says: here is your few hundred meters per second, here is your tiny impulse, do not ask for more.”

She wrote:

Pressure ratio → mass flow / choking / expansion  
Temperature → exhaust velocity ceiling  
Mass expelled → delta-v budget

“Compressing the gas first does not solve the problem unless you spend energy to compress it and carry tanks to hold it,” Hoang continued. “Then you have a new accounting sheet. The compressor draws power from the reactor. The tanks have mass. The plumbing has mass. The valves have mass. The heat exchangers have mass. The safety margins have mass. At high pressure, the container can weigh as much as the gas it contains, or more. If you include that structure, your ‘free’ delta-v can become negative. You may spend days of electrical margin to store a few seconds of thrust, and then you still have to vent the gas through hardware rated for the job.”

She set the tablet down on the tarp, screen up, beside the chalk.

“And angle,” Hoang said. “Angle does not multiply your thrust. Angle projects it. If you vent at theta degrees off the desired vector, your useful axial component gets a cosine. Your lateral component gets a sine, and that sine becomes torque. On a rotating habitat ring, torque is not a rounding error. It is nausea, structural loading, attitude correction, spin-rate deviation, and possibly a very expensive conversation with navigation.”

She gestures toward the curved deck, the handrails, the bolted-down tool trays, the quiet centrifugal order of the ring.

“If you try to use the ring’s rotation to ‘add’ velocity, remember that the rim speed is tens of meters per second, not kilometers per second. You are not slingshotting the ship with the habitat. You are trading angular momentum. Either the ring slows, the structure absorbs the load, or the control system spends propellant correcting what your clever venting just caused. For six tonnes of air. For a velocity change measured in walking pace.”

Hoang folded her arms.

“So the arithmetic says this: if your three hundred forty is exhaust velocity, the ship gains about four meters per second. If your three hundred forty is delta-v, your exhaust velocity is twenty-eight kilometers per second and your proposal has quietly become a different machine. If your compression ratio is supposed to bridge that gap, it needs an energy source, a storage system, a nozzle, thermal control, and a mass budget that currently does not exist.”

She pointed at the chalked numbers.

“Four to nine meters per second. That is the realistic range for venting the entire breathable atmosphere through the best cold-gas nozzle we could improvise without killing someone. Four to nine. Not three hundred forty. Not weeks saved. Hours, at absolute best, and only if you are willing to spend the crew’s air to get a shove weaker than a good thruster pulse.”

For a moment her expression tightened, not with anger, but with the particular fatigue of someone who had seen enthusiasm outrun safety more than once.

“I understand why the number feels persuasive. Three hundred forty meters per second sounds like motion. It sounds like progress. It sounds like a deadline being beaten. But delta-v is not a mood. It is a log ratio multiplied by exhaust velocity. You cannot charm the logarithm. You cannot compress your way past enthalpy. You cannot angle your way out of momentum conservation. And you certainly cannot breathe propulsion.”

Hoang pulled the fresh sheet toward her and wrote a new heading:

Corrected Atmospheric-Venting Check

Under it, she listed:

1. M₀: total ship mass at start of venting.  
2. M₁: total ship mass after venting, including retained breathing atmosphere.  
3. m_prop: actual mass available as propellant, not total hab air unless crew is intended to suffocate.  
4. vₑ: effective exhaust velocity, derived from stagnation temperature and nozzle efficiency.  
5. Pressure ratio: source pressure, exit pressure, choking condition, mass flow rate.  
6. Nozzle area and expansion ratio: throat diameter, exit diameter, materials, thermal loads.  
7. Duration: pressure decay curve, thrust decay curve, usable impulse.  
8. Energy balance: compressor work, heater work, electrical draw, reactor margin.  
9. Storage mass: tanks, valves, piping, regulators, shields, mounts.  
10. Vector: axial component, lateral component, torque on hab ring.  
11. Attitude control: RCS propellant required to counteract venting torque.  
12. Life support: O₂ partial pressure, CO₂ scrubber load, humidity, temperature, suit margins.  
13. Failure modes: valve stuck open, valve stuck closed, seal failure, visor fog, depressurization asymmetry, spin disturbance.  
14. Abort: how to stop, how to repressurize, how to survive the attempt.

She slid the sheet across the tarp.

“Fill this out. Not with hope. Not with a compression ratio that appears from nowhere. Not with an angle that ‘helps.’ With sources. If you estimate a value, mark it estimated. If you assume ideal nozzle behavior, mark it ideal and then apply a loss factor. If you use the whole atmosphere as propellant, mark the crew casualty assumption in red, because I will.”

Hoang picked up her wrench again, but did not return to the manifold immediately.

“If you meant a dedicated compressed-gas system, that is a different conversation. Small bottles, rated hardware, known impulse, known torque, known life-support impact. We already have maneuvering thrusters and reaction control for that reason. If you meant waste water, brine, inert purge gas, or non-breathable stores, also a different conversation, and possibly a sane one. But the main atmosphere is not a fuel tank. It is the thing keeping everyone conscious while they pretend schedules are negotiable with physics.”

She glanced at the tablet, then at the junior officer.

“Your number is not evil. It is just wrong in an expensive way. Thirty-four zero is a warning light, not a solution. It means somewhere between pressure, temperature, mass, and logarithms, a unit got ambitious.”

Hoang finally returned to the coolant manifold, seating the wrench over the fitting with practiced ease.

“Recalculate. Bring me the corrected sheet within the hour. If the honest number is five meters per second, you will see why I am not moving. If the honest number is fifty meters per second from some rated store I have not considered, then we talk. If it is three hundred forty from the hab air, you and I are going to sit down with the rocket equation until it stops being abstract.”

She tightened the fitting a quarter-turn, tested it, and nodded to herself.

“No eating the sky. And no letting the speed of sound pose as a flight plan.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grimace, taking the tablet and the new sheet back. My face feels warm.* "Right. No, I definitely didn't mean twenty-eight kilometers per second. Just... venting the atmosphere." *I look at the sheet, then back at her, a new, slightly less wild idea forming.* "What if we just... collected the CO2? And used that? It's waste, right?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang looked at the tablet for a long moment. Not at the junior officer. At the word.

CO₂.

She set the tablet down on the tarp with the careful flat-handed motion of someone avoiding accidental inputs. Then she picked up the chalk, erased the line about the speed of sound wearing a mission patch, and wrote a new heading in blunt block letters:

CAPTURED CO₂ = WASTE MASS, NOT BREATHING MASS

Beneath it, smaller:

POSSIBLE. CONDITIONALLY. NOT AS A HOLE IN THE WALL.

Hoang exhaled through her nose. It was not quite a sigh. It was the sound a competent engineer made when a bad idea had finally grown a useful limb.

“Now,” she said, “you are not proposing to throw away the sky. You are proposing to throw away the ship’s exhalations. That is a different category of stupid.”

She tapped the chalk against the tarp.

“And even then, only if we leash it properly.”

Hoang stood, walked to the environmental status board, and pulled up the life-support schematic again. The hab ring’s atmospheric loop bloomed across the display: intake fans, CO₂ removal beds, humidity condensers, oxygen partial pressure monitors, trace contaminant filters, scrubber regeneration lines, and the small, unforgiving margins that kept thirty-odd people from turning their own breath into a poisoning experiment.

She pointed at the CO₂ removal subsystem.

“Humans produce roughly one kilogram of carbon dioxide per day. Some more, some less, depending on workload, diet, metabolic stress, and whether they have been running drills in a suit all shift. If we have forty crew, that is on the order of forty kilograms per day. Over a hundred and eighty-day transit, if we capture all of it and store all of it, we might accumulate several tonnes.”

She wrote on the nearest blank panel:

40 crew × 1 kg/day × 180 d ≈ 7.2 t CO₂

Then beneath it:

Ship mass ≈ 500 t  
vₑ for warm compressed CO₂ ≈ 350–500 m/s  
Δv ≈ 5–7 m/s, optimistic cold-gas case

Hoang circled the last number.

“That is not weeks. That is not even a day, unless the ship is already drifting like a parked car and navigation is feeling generous. But it is real. More importantly, it is mass we are already producing and, in many configurations, already disposing of. If we can capture it cleanly, store it safely, and expel it through hardware designed for the job, then yes: it is a legitimate reaction-mass reserve. Not a miracle. A reserve.”

She turned back.

“So I am not saying no to the concept. I am saying yes to the concept under conditions so specific that if you violate one of them, I will personally revoke your access to valves, spreadsheets, and optimism.”

Hoang took the fresh sheet from the tarp, flipped it over, and began writing in fast, legible block capitals. She did not sing-song the list. She did not make it sound easy. She made it sound like what it was: a hazard control package.

“First,” she said, writing, “source isolation.”

CAPTURED CO₂ ONLY. NO DIRECT HABITAT VENTING.

“We do not crack a cabin vent and call it propulsion. The CO₂ must come from the life-support removal system after separation, after drying, after filtration, and through a dedicated line. The habitat loop remains intact. The crew’s carbon dioxide partial pressure does not rise because we decided to use their exhaust as fuel.”

She underlined the line twice.

“Nominal cabin pCO₂ stays within flight limits. Alarm threshold triggers automatic isolation of the propellant feed. If the scrubber cannot keep up, the propellant valve closes. Not the other way around. We do not trade consciousness for thrust.”

Hoang moved to the next item.

SECOND: PURITY AND CONTAMINATION CONTROL.

“Scrubber effluent is not automatically clean. It can carry water vapor, trace organics, amine carryover if we use chemical swing beds, particulates from desiccant degradation, and whatever the crew has been sweating, shedding, cooking, leaking, or manufacturing that week. CO₂ for propulsion must meet a specified purity envelope. Dry gas. Filtered. No liquids. No solids. No lubricant carryover. No oxygen enrichment beyond limits.”

She wrote:

Dew point: specified  
Particulate filter: rated  
Amine/organics monitor: required  
O₂ contamination limit: specified  
Sample port: required

“If we inject dirty gas into a nozzle, we get coking, erosion, throat deformation, unsteady flow, and a thrust curve that becomes a suggestion. If we get amine carryover into a hot line, we get corrosion products. If we get water into a expanding jet, we get ice. Ice in a nozzle is not a minor annoyance. It is a variable-orifice surprise.”

Hoang set the chalk down and picked up a rag, wiping a smear of coolant from her thumb as she spoke.

“Third: storage.”

DEDICATED RATED PRESSURE VESSELS. NOT CYLINDERS FOUND BEHIND A PANEL.

“CO₂ can be stored as compressed gas, liquid, or supercritical fluid depending on temperature and pressure. That means we are dealing with high-pressure vessels, phase changes, thermal expansion, relief devices, and possible dry-ice formation during blowdown. Every tank must be certified for the service, marked, inspected, pressure-tested, and fitted with proper relief and isolation.”

She wrote a compact list:

Tank MAWP > max operating pressure  
Fill density limit  
Burst disc / relief valve  
Pressure and temperature telemetry  
Compatible seals and metals  
External leak path  
No dead legs  
Thermal protection  
Impact protection  
Remote shutoff

“If a CO₂ tank fails inside a habitable volume, it is not a minor leak. It is a white cloud, a pressure spike, flying hardware, frostbite, asphyxiation risk, and a panic response in a rotating ring. So storage goes outside crewed spaces where feasible. If it must be inside a ship boundary, it goes in a sealed hazardous bay with independent ventilation, gas detection, and a blowdown path to vacuum. Not next to the galley. Not under a bunk. Not in a corridor because the corridor was empty last Tuesday.”

Hoang’s voice stayed level, but her eyes moved to the environmental board’s leak-detection schematic.

“Fourth: leak containment.”

CO₂ IS ODORLESS. IT WILL NOT ASK PERMISSION.

“Carbon dioxide does not smell like danger. It does not warn you politely. At low elevated concentrations it causes headache, drowsiness, impaired judgment, and shortness of breath. At higher concentrations it can drop a person before they understand why the floor is suddenly interesting. Monitors are required at storage, in adjacent spaces, and along likely leak paths. Alarms must be local and remote. Automatic isolation must be armed.”

She wrote:

CO₂ monitors: redundant  
Alarm setpoints: defined  
Local shutoff: required  
Remote shutoff: required  
Entry restrictions: hazardous bay only with approval

“If we get a leak during a burn preparation, the first response is not ‘push through.’ The first response is close valves, ventilate, isolate, and reassess. If the leak is in a crewed area, we do not wait for someone to feel dizzy. Dizziness is not a telemetry channel.”

Hoang returned to the sheet and began the fifth condition with more force in the chalk.

FIFTH: VALVE TRAIN AND FAIL-SAFE DESIGN.

“Propellant feed requires double isolation: one shutoff valve, one control valve, both independently qualified. Fail-closed on power loss, on command abort, on cabin pCO₂ excursion, on tank overpressure, on line overtemperature, on unexpected flow, and on my personal preference, which I intend to retain.”

She wrote:

Upstream isolation: fail-closed  
Downstream control: regulated  
Redundant abort shutoff  
Manual override outside hazardous zone  
Leak-check before pressurization  
Purge/inert procedure before maintenance

“No single-valve arrangements. No‘just crack it open and see what happens.’ No bypasses installed for convenience. If a valve sticks open, the system must be able to stop the flow downstream. If a valve sticks closed, we must know why before we try to force the issue with heat, percussion, or prayer.”

Hoang glanced at the coolant manifold she had been repairing, then back to the list.

“Sixth: thermal and two-phase management.”

CO₂ expanding from high pressure can cool violently. Residual moisture can freeze. Lines can ice up. Regulators can stick. Nozzles can accumulate dry ice. If we are drawing liquid or supercritical CO₂, we must design for phase behavior, not pretend the tank contents are a benign gas in a bottle.”

She wrote:

Line heating as required  
Regulator icing analysis  
Two-phase flow avoidance or controlled design  
Relief vent frost protection  
Nozzle thermal certification  
Post-burn inspection

“If we get dry ice in a regulator, we do not have a propulsion system. We have a chilled blockage with potential energy attached. If we get thermal shock in a valve body, we get cracks. If we get cracks, we get a leak. If we get a leak in the wrong place, I am writing casualty reports instead of test reports.”

Hoang straightened and looked at the curved deck, where the hab ring’s rotation gave tools their obedient quasi-weight.

“Seventh: vector, torque, and spin control.”

THIS IS A ROTATING SHIP. WE DO NOT GET TO IGNORE ANGULAR MOMENTUM.

“If we mount a CO₂ thruster on the habitat ring and fire it tangentially, we are not merely pushing the ship forward. We are applying torque to the ring. The ring may slow, speed up, wobble, load bearings, induce crew nausea, or require attitude correction using propellant we did not plan to spend. Any useful impulse must be net impulse after control costs.”

She wrote:

Thrust line through or near center of mass  
Hub-mounted nozzle preferred  
If ring-mounted: balanced opposed nozzles  
Spin-rate limits defined  
Attitude control authority verified  
Structural load check completed

“I would rather put the nozzle on the nonrotating core, aligned with the ship’s axis, than improvise a ring-mounted vent and hope the bearings enjoy the exercise. If navigation and structures approve a ring-mounted configuration, it gets paired nozzles, active spin monitoring, and an abort that does not depend on someone running to a valve in a rotating module while the floor tilts in a direction floors are not supposed to tilt.”

Hoang’s expression did not soften, but the edge in her voice shifted from refusal to instruction.

“Eighth: nozzle and thruster qualification.”

“A hole is not a nozzle. A pipe is not a thruster. A valve stack is not an engine. If we use CO₂ as reaction mass, it goes through hardware designed to accelerate gas efficiently and survive the process.”

She wrote:

Nozzle material certified  
Expansion ratio calculated  
Throat erosion allowance  
 Chamber or feed pressure rated  
Thermal loads analyzed  
Mass flow measured  
Thrust calibrated  
Vibration and acoustics checked

“We bench-test the nozzle assembly before it touches the ship’s flight plumbing. We use simulated gas first. Nitrogen. Then, if the data are clean, a small controlled CO₂ pulse. We do not learn nozzle behavior by surprising the crew with it.”

Hoang set the chalk down and folded her arms.

“Ninth: life-support impact.”

“We do not degrade carbon dioxide removal to improve propulsion. If the ship uses CO₂ for Sabatier water recovery, algae feedstock, methanation, or any closed-loop chemistry, then that CO₂ is not waste. It is inventory. We do not burn the pantry to heat the house.”

She wrote:

CO₂ required for regeneration: reserved  
Propellant allocation: excess only  
Consumables margin verified  
Life-support officer concurrence required  
Post-burn atmospheric reconstruction plan

“If we divert CO₂ that the environmental system expected to recycle, we create a downstream shortage. Water, oxygen, food systems, trace contaminant control—all of it is coupled. A propulsion gain that becomes a life-support loss is not a gain. It is a transfer of failure mode from one spreadsheet to another.”

Hoang picked up the sheet again and added a tenth line.

TENTH: OPERATIONAL LIMITS.

“Initial authorization, if I grant it, is for collection, storage, instrumentation, and ground-equivalent testing. Not for a transit-altering burn. Not for emergency use unless the failure-mode analysis explicitly covers emergency use. Not for repeated impulses until we have inspected the hardware after the first one.”

She wrote:

Maximum test impulse: defined  
Cumulative usage limit: defined  
Inspection interval: mandatory  
No unattended firing  
No crew in affected module during test  
Abort authority: chief engineer and flight director

“We treat the first CO₂ pulse like a pressure test with consequences. Small. Instrumented. Remote. Reversible. If the data are good, we scale carefully. If the data are ugly, we stop and fix the ugliness before it becomes a habit.”

Hoang looked at the junior officer’s tablet, still lying screen-up beside the chalk.

“Your original number was wrong because it confused exhaust velocity with delta-v. This idea is not wrong for the same reason. Captured CO₂ can be propellant. The question is whether we can build the cage around it. Tanks, valves, filters, heaters, monitors, nozzles, torque control, abort paths, life-support margins, inspection procedures. That is the work. Not a heroic vent. Not a schedule trick. Engineering.”

She took the sheet and wrote one final heading at the bottom:

CO₂ REACTION-MASS FEASIBILITY PACKAGE

Under it, she listed the required inputs:

1. Crew count and metabolic CO₂ production rate.  
2. Current CO₂ removal architecture and capture efficiency.  
3. Existing CO₂ disposition: vented, recycled, stored, or processed.  
4. Mass of CO₂ available without degrading life support.  
5. Storage vessel locations, ratings, fill limits, and leak paths.  
6. Gas purity specification and contamination monitoring plan.  
7. Feed system schematic with fail-closed valves and redundancy.  
8. Thermal analysis for expansion, icing, and two-phase flow.  
9. Nozzle or thruster design with calculated vₑ and mass flow.  
10. Thrust vector relative to center of mass.  
11. Torque analysis for hab-ring spin and attitude control demand.  
12. Structural loads and mounting certification.  
13. Expected delta-v using honest mass ratio and exhaust velocity.  
14. Power consumption for heaters, pumps, controls, and monitors.  
15. Failure modes: valve stuck open, valve stuck closed, tank rupture, line leak, nozzle erosion, dry-ice blockage, cabin CO₂ excursion, spin disturbance.  
16. Abort procedure and repressurization/recovery plan.  
17. Test sequence from inert simulation to first controlled CO₂ pulse.  
18. Concurrence from life support, structures, guidance, and flight operations.

Hoang slid the sheet toward the tablet, not all the way, as if leaving it in a neutral place where it could be examined without being accidentally launched into a workflow.

“I will approve the direction,” she said. “Collect the CO₂. Characterize it. Store it safely. Build a controlled feed system. Test it small. If the numbers justify a trim impulse, we use it for trim. If the numbers justify a larger reserve, we revisit. But we do not skip the cage because the animal is already in the room.”

She picked up her wrench again, then paused.

“And before anyone gets poetic: yes, this is less dramatic than venting the atmosphere. That is the point. Good engineering is often less dramatic than catastrophe. The ship breathes, the crew works, the nozzle does not explode, and the mission continues. Nobody writes songs about that. I prefer it.”

Hoang returned to the coolant manifold, seated herself on the deck plating, and fitted the wrench back over the secondary loop coupling. She did not put the earpiece in immediately.

“Bring me the package,” she said, tightening the fitting with a controlled quarter-turn. “Mark estimates. Mark assumptions. Mark anything you inferred from a feeling. If you tell me the CO₂ tank is ‘probably fine,’ I will assume it is a haunted pressure vessel until proven otherwise.”

She tested the coupling, nodded once at the seal, and finally slid the earpiece back into place.

“No eating the sky. But if we are going to use the ship’s exhale, we do it with valves, instruments, and a shutdown button within reach of someone who is not you.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the overwhelming list of requirements. My initial excitement drains, but a new, more solid determination replaces it. This is actual engineering.* "Right. Okay. This... this makes sense, Chief. A lot of sense." *I pick up the sheet carefully.* "I'll get started on this. And I won't be guessing."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang nodded once. It was not a warm gesture. It was the sort of nod a crane operator gives a load that has finally been strapped correctly: acknowledgment, not celebration.

“Good,” she said. “Now do not mistake approval for permission. I have agreed that the direction is sane. I have not agreed that anything is installed, tested, diverted, pressurized, or dreamed about in hardware.”

She took the blank sheet back from the edge of the tarp, wrote a new heading at the top, and slid it toward where the junior officer stood.

FIRST PASS: FACTS, NOT FLIGHT PLAN.

Beneath it, she listed in fast block letters:

1. Current CO₂ removal architecture.  
2. Capture method: swing bed, membrane, cryo, amine, hybrid, other.  
3. Nominal cabin pCO₂, alarm thresholds, and scrubber margin.  
4. CO₂ production rate by crew complement and activity level.  
5. Where captured CO₂ goes now: vented, recycled, stored, processed, or unknown.  
6. Existing inventory of CO₂-bearing streams: habitat loop, galley exhaust, medical bay, suit recharge, waste processing, Sabatier feed, water recovery, trace contaminant control.  
7. All valves, sensors, relief devices, and isolation points on relevant lines. Tag numbers included.  
8. Rated storage vessels already aboard, if any. Service certification, MAWP, last inspection date, location, and contents compatibility.  
9. Leak detection coverage for CO₂ and adjacent compartments.  
10. Power, thermal, and control resources available without stealing from life support.  
11. Mass of CO₂ that can be diverted without degrading regeneration, water recovery, oxygen production, or crew atmosphere.  
12. Whether any existing hardware is suitable for controlled expulsion, or whether the answer is simply no.

Hoang tapped the twelfth line.

“That last one matters more than people think. If the honest answer is ‘we have no rated tank, no rated nozzle, and no qualified feed system,’ then the project is not ‘build a CO₂ thruster.’ The project is ‘determine whether we can legally and safely acquire or fabricate one.’ Those are different missions. One ends with a trim burn. The other ends with a procurement request, a structural review, and me telling someone no for six months.”

She set the chalk down and wiped her fingers again, though they were already clean enough.

“For the first pass, I do not want a design. I do not want a clever regulator arrangement. I do not want a sketch of a nozzle on a napkin. I want to know what the ship already has, what it already does with carbon dioxide, and what would break if we touched it. The ship is not a blank canvas. It is a living machine with scars. Some of those scars are plumbing.”

Hoang walked to the environmental status board and brought up the ECLSS overview again. She zoomed into the carbon dioxide removal block, then the associated regeneration and water-recovery interfaces.

“If this vessel uses Sabatier reactors, methanation, algae, plant racks, or any closed-loop chemistry, then CO₂ is not merely waste. It is feedstock. It may be dirty feedstock, but it is still inventory. You do not get to call something waste until you have confirmed that another system is not quietly relying on it. If you steal carbon dioxide from water recovery, you may buy delta-v with one hand and lose potable water with the other. That is not propulsion. That is rearranging the graveyard.”

She turned back.

“So your first deliverable is an inventory and mass balance. Not a proposal. An inventory. If you cannot find a number, write ‘unknown’ and tell me who owns the system. Do not fill gaps with optimism. Optimism is not a data source.”

The chief engineer folded her arms.

“Second: no modifications. Not temporary. Not diagnostic. Not ‘just cracking a valve to see if it moves.’ Not installing a test tee because a technician owes you a favor. Not jumping an interlock because the alarm is annoying. If a line needs to be opened, it gets a work order, a shutdown plan, a pressure verification, a tag-out, a leak check, and my signature. If life support is involved, it gets their signature too. If the line is near the hab ring, it gets a structural and attitude review before anyone even thinks about thrust.”

Her voice remained even, but the instruction carried the weight of someone who had signed too many incident reports caused by reasonable people making small exceptions.

“Third: no crew exposure during testing. If we eventually pulse certified CO₂ through qualified hardware, the affected module is cleared. No observers standing nearby because they are curious. No ‘quick look’ through a viewport while a pressure transient walks down a line. Remote actuation, remote monitoring, abort from outside the hazard zone. If a valve fails, I want the nearest person to be a camera, not a technician.”

Hoang glanced at the curved deck plating, at the handrails, at the subtle geometry of a habitat ring that depended on balance and predictability.

“Fourth: torque discipline. If we ever mount an expulsion system, the thrust vector is not optional decoration. Hub-mounted, center-of-mass-aligned, balanced, and approved by guidance is the preferred path. Ring-mounted nozzles require paired opposition, active spin monitoring, and a clear abort that does not rely on someone running against artificial gravity while the floor develops an opinion about angular momentum. I would rather spend propellant from the maneuvering system than buy a few meters per second and inherit a wobbling habitat.”

She picked up the sheet again and wrote one more line at the bottom.

Fifth: contamination control. CO₂ for propulsion must be dry, filtered, and chemically characterized. No amines. No particulates. No water slugs. No lubricants. No mystery organics from the galley exhaust. If we find trace contaminants, we either remove them or we do not use that stream. A nozzle throat is not a garbage disposal.

Hoang handed the sheet back, but only after adding a final note in the margin:

Mark every number with its source. Schematic, sensor log, maintenance record, direct measurement, engineering estimate, or unknown. If it is unknown, say so loudly. If it is estimated, give the error bar. If it is copied from an old manual, verify the revision. I do not care whether the number is pretty. I care whether it can be defended.

She studied the junior officer for a moment.

“You said you won’t be guessing. Good. Guessing is how people get creative right up until they are dead. Engineering is the art of replacing guesses with measurements, measurements with margins, and margins with procedures that even a tired person can follow at three in the morning.”

Hoang bent to retrieve her wrench, then paused.

“And you still owe me one answer.”

Her tone did not sharpen. It simply became more direct.

“Who else has heard this idea? Not the corrected CO₂ version. The original atmosphere-as-propellant notion. Did you mention it in the mess? Did someone nod along? Did a navigator write it into a contingency brainstorm? Did an officer treat it as a joke but remember the number? I need to know before it becomes somebody else’s semi-serious proposal.”

She set the wrench down again.

“Bad ideas do not need approval to spread. They only need one person to say, ‘Well, it worked in the math,’ and another person to imagine a valve where there is not one. If someone else is already carrying that number around, I would rather disarm it with arithmetic than wait for it to surface during a burn planning meeting.”

Hoang returned to the coolant manifold, seating herself cross-legged on the deck plating once more. The secondary loop still needed final verification, and she trusted her own hands more than she trusted any promise made under excitement.

“Bring me the fact sheet by the end of the next duty cycle. Not the full feasibility package. The fact sheet. If it says we have no usable CO₂ reserve, no rated storage, and no safe feed path, then we stop there. That is not failure. That is a cheap answer. Cheap answers are valuable.”

She picked up the wrench and gave the test coupling another careful quarter-turn by hand, watching the gauge needle settle.

“If it says there may be something real, then we schedule a review with life support, structures, and guidance. After that, if the hardware exists and the margins hold, we talk about a controlled test article. Bench first. Inert gas second. CO₂ third. Small pulse fourth. Nothing becomes flight software until I have seen the failure modes, the abort paths, and the inspection plan.”

Hoang finally allowed herself a small, dry modification of expression. Not quite a smile. Closer to the face a person makes when a stubborn bolt finally turns.

“No eating the sky. No breathing the exhaust. No turning the crew’s exhale into a hazard because it sounded clever. If we use carbon dioxide, we use it as a stored, characterized, isolated, monitored, rated, and shutoff-able reaction mass. Otherwise it remains exactly what it is: a problem the life-support system is paid to handle.”

She slid the earpiece partway back into place, then left it hanging, ready to return to work but not ready to dismiss the conversation entirely.

“Go get the facts. And answer the question about who else knows.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking the sheet.* "Got it, Chief. Facts only. No modifications. No crew exposure. Torque discipline. Contamination control." *I tap the last point on the sheet.* "And... no, I haven't mentioned it to anyone else. It was just an idea I had, came right here." *I grimace slightly.* "Good thing I did, huh? Saved everyone a lot of trouble."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang considered that for a moment. She did not look relieved. She looked as if a small, dangerous spark had been contained, but not yet extinguished.

“Yes,” she said. “It was a good thing you came here. Do not make it a virtue. Make it procedure.”

She picked up the rag again and wiped a streak of coolant from the wrench handle, slow and deliberate, as if giving the words time to harden into something usable.

“You did not save everyone a lot of trouble. You converted trouble into paperwork. That is the only kind of trouble engineering can survive.”

Hoang set the rag down and pulled the fresh sheet closer. At the top, she wrote in blunt block letters:

ENGINEERING IDEA LOG — INITIAL ENTRY  
STATUS: ATMOSPHERE-VENTING CONCEPT REJECTED. CAPTURED CO₂ CONCEPT UNDER PRELIMINARY FEASIBILITY REVIEW. NO HARDWARE ACTION AUTHORIZED.

She underlined the last sentence twice.

“That goes in the log tonight,” Hoang said. “Not as a confession. Not as a joke. As a record. If anyone asks what happened in this bay, the answer is that an idea was raised, checked against physics, rejected in one form, and conditionally evaluated in another. No myths. No half-remembered numbers. No one wandering around saying the chief almost turned the air into thrust.”

She glanced up.

“If someone did hear something, and you did not realize it, tell me now. Not later. Not after you have polished the story. Now.”

Then she returned to the sheet and wrote a smaller heading beneath the log entry:

FIRST PASS — THREE QUESTIONS ONLY

Hoang tapped the chalk against the tarp.

“Before you try to answer eighteen things, answer these three. Everything else depends on them.”

She wrote:

1. WHAT DOES THE SHIP CURRENTLY DO WITH CO₂?  
2. HOW MUCH CO₂ IS ACTUALLY SURPLUS AFTER LIFE SUPPORT?  
3. IS THERE ANY RATED HARDWARE ALREADY ABOARD FOR STORAGE OR EXPULSION?

“Question one,” Hoang said, “is not philosophical. I do not care whether carbon dioxide feels like waste to you. I care whether the environmental system treats it as waste. If the ship vents it overboard, that is one answer. If it feeds a Sabatier reactor, that is another. If it goes to algae, plant racks, trace-contaminant control, suit recharge balancing, water recovery, or chemical regeneration, then it is inventory. If it is inventory, you do not get to call it exhaust until the life-support officer signs off saying it is expendable.”

She drew a small box around the word Sabatier on the schematic behind her.

“If that CO₂ is destined for methanation, remember the chemistry. Carbon dioxide plus hydrogen makes methane and water. Forty-four parts by mass of CO₂ can yield thirty-six parts by mass of water, before losses, before hydrogen availability, before reactor margins. If you divert CO₂ from water recovery, you are not buying delta-v. You are selling potable water by the kilogram and calling it propulsion.”

Hoang’s voice stayed flat, but the lesson was not subtle.

“So your first fact sheet must state the current CO₂ sink clearly. Vented. Recycled. Stored. Processed. Mixed. Unknown. If it is mixed, break it down. If it is unknown, mark it unknown and name the system owner. I would rather chase a responsible engineer than a rumor.”

She moved to the second question.

“Question two is surplus. Not production. Surplus. Humans make CO₂ continuously, but the scrubbers remove only what the atmospheric control loop allows, and the system has margins for exercise, illness, heat stress, elevated metabolism, filter degradation, and crew irregularities. If you take CO₂ that the environmental system expects to process, you may raise cabin partial pressure, shorten scrubber cycles, overload regeneration, or create a failure mode during sleep when nobody is watching the board closely enough.”

She wrote beneath it:

SURPLUS = PRODUCTION − REQUIRED REGENERATION − SAFETY MARGIN − FAULT TOLERANCE

“That equation is not decorative,” Hoang said. “If the result is negative, the answer is no. If the result is small, the answer is still no unless the impulse is worth the complexity. If the result is several tonnes over months, then we are finally speaking in quantities that navigation might notice.”

She tapped the third line.

“Question three is hardware. This is where most clever ideas go to die quietly, which is preferable to dying loudly in flight. Are there rated pressure vessels already aboard? Are there certified lines? Valves? Relief devices? Filters? Heaters? A nozzle? A vent path that can be isolated without compromising the habitat? If the answer is no, then the project is not ‘use CO₂ for thrust.’ The project is ‘can we build or qualify the missing system without spending more mass, power, and risk than the delta-v is worth?’”

Hoang let that sit.

“And if the ship already vents CO₂ overboard through an existing waste line, do not assume that line is a gift from engineering heaven. It may be low pressure. It may be wet. It may contain particulates. It may route near sensitive structures. It may not point where we want it to point. It may have no isolation valve rated for repeated closure. It may be designed to dump gas, not store it, regulate it, or accelerate it efficiently. A waste stream is only useful if the hardware treating it is honest about what it can do.”

She folded her arms.

“So the first pass is not a design. It is a census. Tag numbers. Line diagrams. Sensor locations. Valve types. Pressure ratings. Temperature ranges. Flow rates. Maintenance history. Leak-detection coverage. Who owns each component. Whether anything has been modified since installation. Whether any of it has ever been trusted with something more important than keeping people from exhaling themselves to sleep.”

Hoang picked up the chalk again and added one final instruction at the bottom of the sheet:

NO TOUCH. NO TEST. NO TEETH. NO BYPASSES. NO “JUST CHECKING.”

She pointed the chalk at the junior officer.

“If you find a valve labeled CO₂ vent, scrubber purge, waste gas, or anything similar, you do not crack it. You do not listen to it. You do not put your hand near it. You record the tag number, photograph the line if permitted, check the P&ID, and leave it alone. If it is leaking, report it. If it is silent, report it. If it looks tempting, report it twice.”

Her expression did not soften, but the severity shifted into something more useful: instruction.

“You asked whether it is a good thing you came here. Yes. But the correct next step is not to feel rescued. It is to make the rescue boring. Write it down. File it. Define the limits. Let the idea become a controlled engineering problem instead of a story.”

Hoang returned to the coolant manifold and seated the wrench over the fitting again. She gave it a careful quarter-turn, watched the gauge needle settle, and nodded once to herself.

“Bring me the fact sheet by the end of the next duty cycle. Three questions. Sources marked. Unknowns marked. Estimates marked with error bars. If the answer is that we have no surplus CO₂, no rated storage, and no safe expulsion path, then we stop. That is not failure. That is a cheap answer, and cheap answers keep people alive.”

She tightened the fitting another eighth-turn, tested it, and finally looked up.

“If the answer is that there may be something real, then we schedule a review with life support, structures, and guidance. Not before. Not during. Not because someone is excited. After the facts are on paper and the hazards have names.”

Hoang slid the earpiece partway back into place, then left it resting against her neck, ready to return to work but not ready to end the conversation.

“And keep this quiet until the log entry exists. Not because the idea is shameful. Because uncontrolled ideas become folklore, and folklore has a way of growing valves where none were approved.”

She picked up the rag one last time and wiped her hands.

“No eating the sky. No breathing the exhaust. No turning the crew’s exhale into a hero story. If carbon dioxide becomes reaction mass, it does so as a measured, isolated, characterized, monitored, fail-closed, torque-checked, life-support-approved substance. Otherwise it remains exactly what it is: a problem the environmental system is paid to handle.”

Hoang gestured toward the door with two chalk-dusted fingers.

“Go get the facts. And if you feel an urge to be clever before you have data, come find me instead of a valve.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, folding the new sheet carefully and tucking it into the tablet's case.* "Right. Three questions. And no cleverness until I have the data." *I turn to leave, then pause, looking back at the chief.* "Thanks, Chief. Really."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not look up immediately. She gave the manifold fitting another controlled eighth-turn, watched the gauge needle settle, and only then set the wrench down on the tarp beside the labeled components.

“Don’t thank me,” she said. “Thank the fact that you stopped before you made it somebody else’s problem.”

She pulled the engineering log sheet closer and began writing in the same blunt block letters she used for hazard tags and maintenance orders.

ENGINEERING IDEA LOG — INITIAL ENTRY  
SUBJECT: ATMOSPHERE-VENTING CONCEPT  
STATUS: REJECTED  
FOLLOW-ON: CAPTURED CO₂ FACT SURVEY, PRELIMINARY ONLY  
AUTHORIZATION: NONE. NO HARDWARE ACTION. NO MODIFICATIONS. NO TESTS.

She underlined the last line once, then again, harder.

“If you want to be useful,” Hoang said, “put that in the system tonight. Exact wording. No embellishment. No legend-building. The record should say that someone proposed using the habitat atmosphere as reaction mass, that the concept was checked against mass, momentum, thermodynamics, life support, and crew risk, and that it was rejected. Then it should say that captured carbon dioxide was identified as a separate matter requiring fact-finding before any design work.”

She glanced up from the log.

“That is not punishment. That is sanitation. Ideas like that need to be written down where the next person can find them, because if they are not written down, they become stories. Stories grow valves. Stories grow deadlines. Stories grow committees. Physics does not negotiate with any of them.”

Hoang folded the sheet and slid it into the log tray with the clipped precision of someone who had seen too many casual conversations become formal incidents.

“You came in with a dangerous number,” she said. “You are leaving with three questions and a prohibition on touching anything. That is the trade I want. Next time, bring the questions earlier.”

She picked up the rag again and wiped a faint smear of coolant from the wrench handle, slow and deliberate.

“And if you find a line labeled CO₂ purge, scrubber vent, waste gas, or anything that makes you think, ‘This could be ours,’ you do not crack it. You do not listen to it. You do not put your hand near it. You do not ask a friendly technician to ‘just check pressure.’ You record the tag number, compare it to the P&ID, and leave it alone. Temptation is not an engineering requirement.”

For a moment her expression shifted—not soft, exactly, but less like a bulkhead and more like a woman who remembered being young, eager, and certain that cleverness was the same thing as competence.

“You are not in trouble,” Hoang said. “That is not the same as being finished. Do the survey. Mark your sources. Mark your unknowns. If the answer is that the ship has no surplus CO₂, no rated storage, and no safe expulsion path, then we stop. Cleanly. Quietly. Without anyone dying to prove a schedule.”

She turned back to the secondary coolant loop and seated the wrench over the fitting once more.

“If the answer is that there may be something real, then we bring in life support, structures, and guidance. We make the problem boring. We make it procedural. We make it survivable.”

The pumps hummed around them, steady and unimpressed by ambition.

“Now go,” Hoang said. “End of duty cycle. Facts only. And if you feel an urge to be clever before you have data, come find me instead of a valve.”

She tightened the fitting a quarter-turn, tested the seal, and finally slid the earpiece back into place.

“No eating the sky.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a more confident nod this time. She's tough, but she's fair. And she's making me think.* "Got it, Chief. No cleverness. Just facts." *I turn and head out of the engineering bay, the three questions already starting to form a plan in my head.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay door cycled shut behind the junior officer with a soft pneumatic whisper. Chief Engineer Hoang waited until the vibration of departing footsteps faded into the corridor before she pulled the earpiece free and set it on the tarp.

For a moment she simply looked at the chalked numbers.

AIR ≠ PROPELLANT.

Δv = vₑ ln(M₀ / M₁).

340 m/s.

She did not erase the junior officer’s wrong figure. Wrong numbers had value if they were kept where they could be studied. Instead, she wrote beside it in clean block letters:

EXHAUST VELOCITY, NOT SHIP Δv.  
HONEST Δv FROM HAB AIR: ~4–9 m/s.  
STATUS: REJECTED.  
LESSON: UNITS KILL MISSIONS.

Then she added, underlined once:

CAPTURED CO₂: POSSIBLE ONLY AS STORED, CHARACTERIZED, RATED REACTION MASS.  
NO HABITAT DEGRADATION.  
NO IMPROVISED HARDWARE.  
NO TEST WITHOUT REVIEW.

Hoang stood, knees protesting with the particular dull complaint of a forty-seven-year-old body that had spent too many shifts cross-legged on deck plating. She ignored it. She walked to the environmental status board and keyed in her engineering credentials. The life-support schematic unfolded across the display in layered colors: atmospheric loops, scrubber beds, humidity condensers, trace contaminant control, oxygen generation, carbon dioxide handling, waste gas routing, and the small nervous system of alarms that kept a rotating tin can from becoming a tomb.

She zoomed into the CO₂ removal subsystem.

There it was: the ship exhaled, and machinery caught the poison before it could accumulate. Two-bed amine swing adsorbers, regenerated under vacuum and mild heat, with a side branch to the Sabatier reactor for water recovery. Another line fed the waste gas accumulator, which vented selected noncritical streams overboard through a filtered nozzle assembly. Not a propulsion nozzle. A disposal nozzle. Designed to keep particulates and condensates from fouling external sensors, not to produce useful thrust.

Hoang tapped the Sabatier branch.

If the reactor was active, carbon dioxide was not waste. It was feedstock. CO₂ plus hydrogen produced methane and water. Methane could be vented or used as a low-thrust chemical store depending on plumbing. Water could be electrolyzed for oxygen and hydrogen, closing loops that kept people alive far more reliably than ambition did. Diverting CO₂ from that chain could reduce potable water production. That was not propulsion. That was borrowing from tomorrow’s lungs and toilets to pay for today’s schedule.

She pulled up the current configuration log.

Sabatier status: standby, intermittent operation depending on hydrogen availability and water buffer margins. Waste gas accumulator: pressure-controlled, periodic venting. CO₂ purge line: tagged WG-PURGE-07, isolation valve VG-22, relief device RV-14, no rated storage vessel downstream. No propulsion service certification. No thermal isolation. No remote abort interlock beyond standard ECLSS shutdown.

Hoang’s expression did not change, but something in her posture tightened.

There might be a path. There might even be a useful one, if the ship produced more captured CO₂ than the regeneration and water-recovery systems required. But the existing hardware was not honest about being an engine. It was honest about being plumbing. Plumbing could be adapted, but only if the adaptation was engineered, not improvised.

She opened the maintenance control interface and created a provisional administrative hold.

NOTICE: ENGINEERING REVIEW — CO₂ WASTE STREAMS  
AUTHORITY: CHIEF ENGINEER HOANG  
STATUS: PRELIMINARY FEASIBILITY ONLY  
ACTION PROHIBITED: NO VALVE OPERATION, NO LINE BREAKS, NO TEMPORARY TEE INSTALLATION, NO BYPASS, NO TEST PULSES, NO MODIFICATION OF WG-PURGE-07 OR ASSOCIATED ISOLATION/RELIEF HARDWARE WITHOUT WRITTEN AUTHORIZATION FROM CHIEF ENGINEER AND LIFE SUPPORT OFFICER.  
REASON: POTENTIAL REACTION-MASS EVALUATION. CREW SAFETY AND LIFE-SUPPORT INTEGRITY TAKE PRECEDENCE.

She read the notice once, then made the language blunter.

IF THIS NOTICE IS CONFUSING, THE ANSWER IS STILL NO.

After a beat she added:

REPORT SUSPECTED LEAKS, UNUSUAL NOISES, OR TEMPTING VALVES IMMEDIATELY. DO NOT INVESTIGATE ALONE.

Hoang transmitted the hold to the maintenance system and flagged it to the life-support officer’s queue. Not a request for permission. Not a proposal. A safety notice. If someone else had already begun dreaming about nozzles in the CO₂ line, that dream now had a locked gate in front of it.

Then she opened a separate query, addressed to environmental control but written with the economy of someone who did not enjoy wasting other people’s attention.

PRELIMINARY DATA REQUEST — NO HARDWARE ACTION REQUIRED  
1. Confirm current CO₂ sink distribution: Sabatier feed, vacuum regeneration, waste gas accumulation, overboard vent, storage, other.  
2. Provide measured CO₂ capture rate over last 30 days, with crew complement and activity profile.  
3. Identify surplus CO₂ available after life-support regeneration requirements and safety margins.  
4. List all rated pressure vessels compatible with dry CO₂ service, including location, MAWP, last inspection date, and current contents.  
5. Confirm whether any existing vent/nozzle assembly is certified for controlled impulse use. Assume no unless documented.  
6. Report any recent modifications, workarounds, or known defects in CO₂ purge, waste gas, or Sabatier feed plumbing.  
Deadline: end of next duty cycle. Mark unknowns as unknown. Do not estimate silently.

She sent it.

Then Hoang stood there for a moment, hands on hips, staring at the schematic as if it might confess its secrets out of professional shame. It did not. Machinery rarely did. It simply waited to be understood, maintained, or betrayed.

She turned back to the tarp and began assembling her own rough mass model.

Assume forty crew. Assume average metabolic CO₂ production near one kilogram per day, with variation for workload, stress, sleep cycle, and the inevitable crew member who treated exercise restraints like a suggestion rather than a medical device. That gave roughly forty kilograms per day captured if the scrubbers were operating nominally. Over thirty days, about 1.2 tonnes. Over ninety days, 3.6 tonnes. Over the full transit, if nothing changed and nothing broke, perhaps seven tonnes.

But not all of it was surplus.

She wrote:

AVAILABLE CO₂ = CAPTURED CO₂ − SABATIER REQUIREMENT − REGENERATION LOSS − FAULT MARGIN − CONTAMINATION REJECT − STORAGE DEAD SPACE.

Beneath it:

IF SABATIER ACTIVE: CO₂ = WATER FEEDSTOCK. NOT FREE.  
IF VENTED NOMINALLY: MAYBE EXCESS, BUT LOW PRESSURE/WET/DIRTY.  
IF STORED: NEED RATED VESSEL MASS PENALTY.  
IF USED FOR THRUST: NEED NOZZLE, VALVES, HEATERS, MONITORS, ABORT.

Hoang capped the chalk and picked up the tablet the junior officer had left behind on the edge of the tarp. She did not open the erroneous calculation again. Instead, she pulled the ship’s structural mass properties file and searched for existing high-pressure gas storage. There were maneuvering thruster tanks, reaction control stores, compressed nitrogen bottles for instrument purge, a few inert gas reserves, and water tanks that were not gas tanks no matter how much someone might wish they were.

No dedicated CO₂ propellant tank.

Not surprising. Mining vessels carried fuel, oxidizer if needed, water, spares, ore, shielding, and enough life-support redundancy to keep a crew alive when one system decided to become creative. They did not usually carry tanks labeled “screwdriver this into an engine.”

She made a note:

IF NO RATED STORAGE EXISTS, PROJECT COST INCLUDES TANK MASS.  
TANK MASS MAY EXCEED BENEFIT FOR SMALL Δv.  
COMPARE TO JETTISONABLE MASS AND MAIN PROPANT MARGINS FIRST.

That was the unglamorous truth. A clever reaction-mass scheme could easily become heavier than the velocity it bought. If they had to add tanks, compressors, heaters, filters, piping, valves, instrumentation, shielding, and inspection access, the net benefit might vanish. If the CO₂ was already being vented overboard at low pressure, capturing and compressing it might consume more power than the impulse was worth. If it was needed for water recovery, using it for thrust could cost drinking water. If it was contaminated, it could erode a nozzle or freeze a regulator.

Hoang preferred problems that could be killed on paper.

She set the tablet down and returned to the secondary coolant manifold. The repair was not finished just because a junior officer had arrived with a dangerous idea. The ship did not pause for pedagogy. The pumps hummed. The coolant loop waited. The hull kept its quiet, relentless argument with vacuum.

Hoang seated the wrench over the final fitting and gave it a controlled quarter-turn. She watched the pressure gauge needle settle, then cracked the test coupling a fraction of a turn to listen for hiss. Nothing. She closed it, rechecked the seal indicator, and ran a handheld tracer-gas sniffer along the joint. The readout stayed flat.

Good.

She logged the repair: secondary coolant loop manifold reassembled, fitting torqued to procedure, leak check nominal, vibration signature acceptable, return to service authorized. Then she added a maintenance note about the pump bearing trend, because the vibration had been slightly wrong before the junior officer walked in and she trusted her ears more than she trusted optimism.

Only after that did she allow herself to lean back against the tool chest.

The hab ring turned around her, subtle and constant. Not true gravity, only the disciplined imitation of it: centrifugal effect, carefully balanced, carefully monitored, carefully paid for in bearings, structural margins, and attitude control. The deck beneath her boots felt almost normal. Almost. Anyone who fooled themselves into thinking it was Earth was the sort of person who proposed using the atmosphere as fuel.

Hoang looked at the chalk line again.

AIR ≠ PROPELLANT.

She had said it plainly because it needed saying. The junior officer had not been malicious. That was almost worse. Malice could be identified, isolated, and reasoned with. Enthusiasm dressed as helpfulness slipped past defenses. It arrived with bright eyes and a tablet full of confident units. It asked to save the crew. It offered speed. It minimized discomfort. It forgot, or never learned, that comfort was not the point. Survivability was the point. Margins were the point. The ability to be wrong without dying was the point.

And yet the kid had come to her.

That mattered more than Hoang was inclined to admit aloud.

She pulled the engineering idea log toward her and made the final entry for the session.

IDEA RAISED: USE HABITAT ATMOSPHERE AS EMERGENCY REACTION MASS VIA VENTING.  
ASSESSMENT: REJECTED. MASS RATIO INSUFFICIENT. EXHAUST VELOCITY LOW. LIFE-SUPPORT IMPACT UNACCEPTABLE. SUIT DURATION NOT VIABLE. TORQUE/SPIN RISK UNCONTROLLED. STRUCTURAL/THERMAL/CONTAMINATION ISSUES UNRESOLVED.  
FOLLOW-ON IDEA: USE CAPTURED CO₂ AS RATED REACTION MASS.  
STATUS: PRELIMINARY FEASIBILITY ONLY. NO DESIGN AUTHORIZED. NO HARDWARE ACTION AUTHORIZED. FACT SURVEY REQUIRED.  
PERSONNEL NOTE: JUNIOR OFFICER ACCEPTED CORRECTION AND INITIATED FACT-FINDING UNDER SUPERVISION. MONITOR FOR SCOPE CREEP, UNIT ERRORS, AND UNAUTHORIZED VALVE CURIOSITY.

She stared at the last line.

Then she deleted “monitor for scope creep” and replaced it with something less likely to sound like a threat, though no less firm.

REQUIRE DATA SOURCES, ASSUMPTION MARKINGS, AND LIFE-SUPPORT CONCURRENCE BEFORE ANY REVIEW MEETING.

Hoang folded the log sheet and placed it in the secured tray. Not because the idea was secret. Because incomplete ideas were fragile, and fragile ideas attracted strong opinions. She had seen a contingency brainstorm become a procurement request because someone repeated a number without its units. She had seen a “small diagnostic” become a decompression because a valve had been cracked “just to confirm flow.” She had seen a schedule pressure become a funeral because somebody believed physics could be negotiated by committee.

It could not.

She picked up her earpiece, hesitated, and slid it back into place. The music was gone, replaced by the low ambient feed from the engineering bay sensors: pump harmonics, coolant flow noise, hull thermal ticking, the faint electromagnetic murmur of systems doing their jobs without asking for applause.

Hoang listened for a moment.

The secondary loop sounded healthy. The life-support pumps kept their steady rhythm. Somewhere beyond the bay, the hab ring rotated, carrying its cargo of breathable air, human bodies, fragile machines, and finite patience through the dark.

She returned to the tarp, took the chalk, and wrote one last line beneath the rejected atmosphere calculation.

THE AIR STAYS WHERE IT BELONGS.

Then she wiped her hands, picked up the next manifold component, and went back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm walking back to my station, already pulling up the schematics for the CO2 scrubbers. The Chief's "three questions" are looping in my head. It's a lot, but it makes sense. I pull out my tablet and start typing notes, making sure to mark everything.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang waited until the pneumatic seal had fully engaged before she let her attention shift from the doorway back to the manifold. The engineering bay returned to its usual acoustic texture: pump harmonics, coolant burble, the faint tick of metal adjusting to thermal load, and the low, constant whir of the hab ring’s bearing monitors somewhere beyond the bulkheads.

She did not feel triumphant. A rejected idea was not a victory. It was simply a hazard that had not yet become an incident.

Hoang seated the wrench over the final fitting on the secondary coolant loop and gave it a controlled quarter-turn. The gauge needle steadied. She listened. No hiss. No change in pump cavitation tone. She ran the tracer-gas sniffer along the joint once more, slower this time, watching the readout remain flat.

“Return to service,” she muttered, and logged it.

SECONDARY COOLANT LOOP MANIFOLD REASSEMBLED. FITTING TORQUED TO PROCEDURE. LEAK CHECK NOMINAL. VIBRATION SIGNATURE ACCEPTABLE. PUMP BEARING TREND: MONITOR. RETURN TO SERVICE AUTHORIZED.

She added the bearing note because the vibration had been fractionally wrong before the junior officer had walked in, and because machinery developed opinions long before it developed failures.

Then the environmental status board chimed.

Not an alarm. A soft, amber advisory tone—the kind that meant something was偏离 nominal but not yet dangerous. Hoang turned on the deck plating, one knee protesting, and looked at the display.

ECLSS ADVISORY  
TECHNICAL BAY 4 — CO₂ MONITOR TB4-03  
CURRENT: 0.78% v/v  
TREND: +0.03%/HR  
STATUS: ELEVATED, NON-CRITICAL  

Hoang’s expression did not change, but her hands stopped moving.

Technical Bay 4 was not a crewed compartment. It was a cramped interstitial volume between the habitat ring’s inner structure and the outer service trunk: filter racks, conduit runs, waste-gas plumbing, and enough blind corners to make maintenance technicians dislike it with the pure, rational hatred of people who had once crawled through it during a suit rehearsal.

But it was connected to the habitat ring by ventilation paths, access hatches, and the eternal optimism of personnel who thought a door labeled TECH BAY meant “nobody will notice if I shortcut through there.”

And 0.78 percent carbon dioxide was not nothing.

Hoang pulled the trend log.

The reading had begun climbing forty minutes earlier. Slowly. Steadily. Not a spike, not a burst, not the sort of event that would trigger a general alarm. The kind of event that would trigger a headache, then confusion, then somebody making a mistake because judgment had quietly become sand in the gears.

She keyed up the CO₂ waste-gas schematic.

The amine swing beds were operating normally. Cabin pCO₂ in the inhabited modules remained within limits. Sabatier status: standby, hydrogen availability low, water buffer adequate. The waste gas accumulator, however, showed a small pressure decay.

ACCUMULATOR WGA-2  
PRESSURE: 298 kPa  
SETPOINT: 310 kPa  
VENT COMMAND: CLOSED  
DOWNSTREAM ISOLATION VG-22: CLOSED  
PRESSURE TREND: -0.14 kPa/min  

Hoang stared at the numbers.

A closed valve with a falling upstream pressure and a rising technical-bay CO₂ concentration was not a mystery. It was an accusation.

“VG-22,” she said aloud.

She brought up the valve’s history. Last commanded operation: quarterly purge cycle, nineteen days ago. Last manual operation: no record. Last inspection: seated and leak-checked during ECLSS preventive maintenance, seven months ago. Seven months was not ancient, but seals aged, particles gathered, thermal cycles worked microscopic lies into metal, and mining vessels did not receive gentle treatment.

Hoang opened the local telemetry for the vent line downstream of the accumulator.

VENT LINE SEGMENT WG-PURGE-07/D  
PRESSURE: 104 kPa  
AMBIENT TB4: 101 kPa  
TEMPERATURE: 268 K  

The line was holding a small positive pressure relative to the technical bay. Not much. Enough to move gas. Enough to matter.

She checked the bay ventilation status. Normal circulation. Not boosted. Not isolated.

Hoang made a decision.

She did not march to Technical Bay 4. She did not send anyone crawling into a compartment with an unidentified CO₂ leak. She did not crack a valve to “confirm flow.” She did not ask a technician to take a quick look because the number was small and the schedule was long.

Instead, she commanded the bay’s auxiliary exhaust to high, isolated the waste-gas accumulator’s downstream vent path with the redundant shutoff she had the authority to operate remotely, and placed a temporary no-entry flag on Technical Bay 4 access hatches.

Then she transmitted to Life Support.

LIFE SUPPORT — CHIEF ENGINEER HOANG  
ADVISORY: CO₂ LEAK SUSPECTED IN WG-PURGE-07 DOWNSTREAM OF VG-22.  
TB4-03 AT 0.78% AND RISING. AUX EXHAUST SET HIGH. DOWNSTREAM VENT ISOLATED.  
NO ENTRY TO TB4 WITHOUT YOUR CONCURRENCE AND PORTABLE MONITORS.  
REQUEST CONFIRMATION OF VG-22 SEAT STATUS AND LAST MANUAL EXERCISE.  
DO NOT CYCLE ACCUMULATOR UNTIL REVIEW.

She paused, then added:

IF ANYONE HAS OPERATED VG-22 OUTSIDE PROCEDURE, I WANT TO KNOW NOW. NOT AFTER SHIFT CHANGE.

The reply came faster than she expected.

LIFE SUPPORT — OFFICER RAYA  
ACKNOWLEDGED. VG-22 SHOWS NO COMMAND HISTORY SINCE QUARTERLY PURGE.  
AGREE: NO ENTRY. BOOST TB4 EXHAUST. WE WILL CHECK LOCAL MONITORS FROM CONTROL.  
ACCUMULATOR VENT CYCLE HELD.  
POSSIBLE SEEP PAST VG-22 SEAT. DO NOT FORCE.

Hoang exhaled through her nose.

Possible seep. Polite language for a valve that had decided to become a restrictor.

She pulled the mass-flow estimate anyway. The numbers were crude, but crude numbers were still numbers. A slow leak from a 300-kPa line into a near-ambient technical bay could be moving on the order of grams per minute. Not catastrophic. Not immediately lethal. But over hours it could raise CO₂ in a poorly ventilated volume, frost a fitting, contaminate a sensor, or give someone a pleasant surprise when they opened a hatch expecting air and receiving an invisible weight on the breath.

Carbon dioxide did not need to kill a person to ruin a mission. It only needed to make them stupid for ten minutes.

Hoang wrote on the tarp, beneath the chalked remains of the rejected atmosphere calculation:

CAPTURED CO₂ LEAK PATH DEMONSTRATES WHY “JUST USE WASTE GAS” IS NOT A VALVE AND A PRAYER.  
EXISTING HARDWARE NOT HONEST.  
VG-22 SUSPECT SEEP.  
NO PROPULSERVICE CERTIFICATION.  
NO RATED STORAGE DOWNSTREAM.  
NOZZLE: DISPOSAL, NOT EXPULSION.  

She underlined DISPOSAL, NOT EXPULSION.

Then she forced herself to calculate the other side of the coin.

If the ship was losing CO₂ through a seep, then some portion of captured carbon dioxide was not being used. If the Sabatier reactor was on standby because hydrogen was constrained, and if the waste-gas accumulator was periodically venting noncritical streams, then there might indeed be surplus CO₂.
