Not much. Not glorious. But real.

She wrote:

40 CREW × 1 KG/D CO₂ ≈ 40 KG/D CAPTURED, NOMINAL  
SABATIER STANDBY ⇒ SOME CO₂ MAY NOT BE CONVERTED TO WATER  
WASTE GAS VENTING ⇒ POSSIBLE SURPLUS  
BUT: SURPLUS ≠ FREE  
MUST SUBTRACT:  
- REGENERATION REQUIREMENTS  
- FAULT MARGIN  
- MOISTURE/CONTAMINANT REJECT  
- STORAGE MASS  
- COMPRESSION POWER  
- NOZZLE/VALVE/HEATER MASS  
- ATTITUDE CONTROL COST  
- LIFE-SUPPORT CONCURRENCE  

Beneath it, smaller:

IF LEAKING NOW, SYSTEM NOT READY.

The status board chimed again.

TB4-03: 0.81%  
TREND: +0.01%/HR  

The auxiliary exhaust was winning, but only barely.

Hoang keyed the engineering intercom.

“Control, Hoang. Place a temporary hazardous-atmosphere tag on Technical Bay 4. No entry without portable CO₂ meter, suit option, and Life Support approval. Notify the next maintenance shift. Do not send anyone to investigate visually until the bay has been purged and rechecked.”

Control acknowledged.

She leaned back against the tool chest and rubbed chalk dust from her thumb. The hab ring turned beneath her, giving her weight that was not weight, only motion disciplined into the approximation of gravity. Outside the hull, vacuum waited with the patience of something that had never needed to hurry.

Hoang opened the mass-properties file again.

No rated CO₂ propellant tank existed. There were compressed nitrogen bottles for instrument purge, maneuvering thruster stores, reaction control tanks, water tanks, and a few inert gas reserves. None of them were configured for dry CO₂ service. None had been certified for repeated controlled impulse. None pointed where a clever mind might wish them to point.

If they wanted to use captured CO₂ as reaction mass, they would need to add hardware. Tanks. Valves. Filters. Heaters. Regulators. Instrumentation. A nozzle. Mounting. Thermal isolation. Abort paths. Leak detection. Structural analysis. Torque analysis. Life-support concurrence.

All of that had mass.

All of that had power draw.

All of that had failure modes.

She ran a quick bound.

Assume they could collect and store one tonne of dry CO₂ over a month, assuming the scrubbers captured it, assuming the Sabatier system did not need it, assuming the storage vessel did not weigh more than the gas, assuming the feed system did not consume more power than the impulse was worth, assuming the nozzle survived expansion, assuming the leak paths were sealed, assuming attitude control did not spend propellant correcting torque, assuming the crew did not suffocate, freeze, short, poison, wobble, or become creatively incompetent.

One tonne of CO₂ at an optimistic effective exhaust velocity of four hundred meters per second against a five-hundred-tonne ship gave:

Δv ≈ 400 × ln(500/499)  
≈ 400 × 0.002002  
≈ 0.80 m/s

Less than one meter per second.

She wrote it plainly.

1 T CO₂ ⇒ ~0.8 M/S, OPTIMISTIC  
7 T CO₂ ⇒ ~5.6 M/S, FULL TRANSIT ACCUMULATION, MANY ASSUMPTIONS  
NOT WEEKS.  
NOT EVEN A DAY UNLESS NAVIGATION IS FEELING GENEROUS.  
POSSIBLE TRIM VALUE ONLY IF HARDWARE COST IS SMALL AND RISK CONTROLLED.

Then, after a moment, she added:

BUT IF THE SHIP IS ALREADY LOSING CO₂ THROUGH A SEEP, THEN THE FIRST TASK IS NOT PROPULSION.  
THE FIRST TASK IS FINDING WHERE THE DAMN GAS IS GOING.

That was the difference between engineering and enthusiasm. Enthusiasm saw reaction mass. Engineering saw a pressure boundary, a contamination path, a sensor error, a frozen regulator, a maintenance tag, a crew member with a headache, and a valve that had not been asked permission.

Hoang pulled the maintenance records for VG-22.

The valve was a standard ECLSS isolation component: manual-operable, motor-assisted, fail-closed on loss of control power, rated for waste-gas service, not for propulsion cycling. Its seat material was compatible with dry CO₂ within limits, but the record noted a tolerance for trace moisture and amine carryover. Trace moisture meant freezing risk during expansion. Amine carryover meant corrosion products. Corrosion products meant throat erosion. Throat erosion meant unsteady thrust. Unsteady thrust meant attitude control work. Attitude control work meant spending real propellant to manage imaginary propellant.

She highlighted the line:

NOT CERTIFIED FOR REPEATED IMPULSE SERVICE.

Then she opened the waste-gas accumulator vent nozzle drawing.

It was a simple assembly: filtered outlet, orientation designed to minimize plume impingement on external sensors, no expansion ratio optimization, no throat cooling allowance, no thrust calibration, no vector control, no chamber, no regulated feed. It was a disposal orifice. A vent. A way to get bad gas away from the ship without making neighbors.

Hoang wrote:

DISPOSAL NOZZLE ≠ THRUSTER  
BENCH TEST REQUIRED BEFORE ANY CLAIM OF vₑ  
MEASURED THRUST, NOT CALCULATED HOPE

A chime sounded from the communications panel.

NAVIGATION — LT. OKONKWO  
CHIEF, WE RECEIVED YOUR REQUEST FOR DELTA-V MARGINS. SHORT VERSION: WE ARE NOT IN A “VENT THE SKY” EMERGENCY. CURRENT TRANSIT IS LONG, NOT DOOMED. REQUIRED MIDCORRECTION IS 14 M/S IF WE MISS THE NEXT OPTIMAL WINDOW. NEXT WINDOW IN NINE DAYS. ALTERNATE IN TWENTY-TWO DAYS WITH HIGHER ARRIVAL COST.  
IF YOU HAVE SOMETHING THAT CAN GIVE US FIVE TO TEN METERS PER SECOND WITHOUT KILLING ANYBODY, I AM INTERESTED.  
IF IT INVOLVES THE HABITAT ATMOSPHERE, MY ANSWER IS ALSO NO.

Hoang allowed herself one slow blink.

Fourteen meters per second.

Not weeks. Not a heroic rescue. A midcourse correction. A real number, with a real deadline, and a real possibility that a modest reserve of controlled reaction mass could matter.

She typed back:

CHIEF — NAVIGATION  
UNDERSTOOD. NO ATMOSPHERE. NO IMPROVISED HARDWARE.  
PRELIMINARY LOOK AT CAPTURED CO₂ SURPLUS. CURRENT ESTIMATE: POSSIBLE SINGLE-DIGIT M/S OVER TIME, NOT INSTANT.  
HARDWARE NOT QUALIFIED. LEAK PATH UNDER INVESTIGATION.  
IF SURPLUS AND RATED STORAGE EXIST, MAY BE USEFUL FOR TRIM.  
DO NOT PLAN AROUND IT UNTIL I SAY SO.

She sent it.

Then she sat back and looked at the chalked equations.

AIR ≠ PROPELLANT.

CAPTURED CO₂ = WASTE MASS, NOT BREATHING MASS.

POSSIBLE. CONDITIONALLY. NOT AS A HOLE IN THE WALL.

The junior officer had stumbled onto something real, but only by accident. The atmosphere was useless. The ship’s exhalations were not automatically useful either. They were potentially useful if captured, dried, purified, stored, isolated, monitored, throttled, aimed, and aborted. In other words, if they were engineered.

Hoang picked up the fresh fact sheet she had given the junior officer and read the three questions again.

WHAT DOES THE SHIP CURRENTLY DO WITH CO₂?  
HOW MUCH CO₂ IS ACTUALLY SURPLUS AFTER LIFE SUPPORT?  
IS THERE ANY RATED HARDWARE ALREADY ABOARD FOR STORAGE OR EXPULSION?

The answer to the third question was becoming clearer.

No.

But there might be a path to yes, and that path began with not lying to herself about the leak.

She transmitted another message, this one to the engineering work-order system.

WORK ORDER — ECLSS/STRUCTURES JOINT INSPECTION  
PRIORITY: ROUTINE-URGENT  
COMPARTMENT: TECHNICAL BAY 4 AND ADJACENT WASTE-GAS TRUNK  
SCOPE: VERIFY CO₂ LEAK LOCATION DOWNSTREAM OF WGA-2 / VG-22. INSPECT LINE SUPPORTS, SEAL FACES, THERMAL CONDITION, AND MONITOR CALIBRATION. NO VALVE OPERATION WITHOUT LIFE SUPPORT CONCURRENCE. NO ENTRY UNTIL PURGE AND ATMOSPHERE CHECK COMPLETE.  
NOTE: SUSPECTED SEEP. DO NOT TREAT AS PROPULSION ISSUE. TREAT AS CONTAINMENT ISSUE FIRST.

She added, after a pause:

IF ANY PERSONNEL HAVE HEARD IDEAS ABOUT USING CO₂ WASTE LINES FOR IMPULSE, REMIND THEM THAT THE CURRENT CO₂ LINE IS LEAKING AND THEREFORE NOT A CANDIDATE FOR HEROISM.

Then she caught herself and deleted the last sentence. Too sarcastic. Not useful. She replaced it with:

REMINDER: NO UNAUTHORIZED MODIFICATIONS, NO DIAGNOSTIC CRACKING, NO BYPASSES. REPORT TEMPTING VALVES INSTEAD OF USING THEM.

That was better.

Hoang set the tablet aside and returned to the coolant manifold. There was still work to do. There was always work to do. The ship did not care about delta-v debates, schedule pressure, or the seductive simplicity of turning breath into thrust. It cared about seals, bearings, filters, pressure boundaries, thermal gradients, and whether the people aboard it could inhale without thinking about it.

She listened to the pumps.

The secondary loop sounded healthy. The life-support system sounded busy. Technical Bay 4, somewhere beyond the bulkheads, was slowly clearing as the auxiliary exhaust did its unglamorous work.

Hoang picked up the chalk and wrote one final line beneath the rejected atmosphere calculation.

CO₂ MAY BE REACTION MASS.  
ONLY AFTER IT IS CONTAINED.

She capped the chalk, slid the earpiece back into place, and went back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm at my station, pulling up the schematics, when a notification pops up on my tablet. A work order. For TB4. A CO2 leak.* "Oh, come on!" *I mutter, smacking the tablet lightly. So that's why she was asking about the current CO2 situation. Well, at least I know where to start looking for my 'facts'.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands didn't move from the lid. They just turned their head, slow, like someone surfacing from a pool. "You already interrupted. You knocked." But the corner of their mouth twitched — that was the version of a welcome Jun had always known how to read. "It's a community center, not a monastery. Sit wherever."

They finally lifted their hands, wiped them on their jeans like they'd been caught doing something, and folded them in their lap. The bench creaked. It was a duet bench — wide enough for two kids and one very small adult — and Arlo stayed on the left side of it, which left the right side open in a way that was either an invitation or an oversight.

"The kids call this room the haunted one," they said, to no one in particular. "Because of the piano. It's a 1961 Baldwin. Sounds fine, looks like it lost a war." A pause. They glanced at the closed lid. "Mrs. Petrakis makes them take their shoes off in here. I don't enforce it. I'm a bad influence." Another pause, shorter. "How's your mom. She said you'd — did she say anything else, or...?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's eyes landed on the photo and then very deliberately moved past it, to the shelf, to the wall, to a water stain on the ceiling tile that apparently fascinated them.

"My hair was better then," they said. "That's the main takeaway. Also that shirt was a rental, which I will never stop resenting." They reached over and turned the frame slightly, not taking it — just angling it so the light hit the glass instead of the image. "Your mom kept that on the *fridge*. With magnets. Between a dentist appointment card and a photo of your dog in a raincoat. Really gave it the dignity it deserved."

They leaned back on their hands. The bench creaked again. Their voice did the thing it always did when it got close to a door — lightened, sped up, kept walking.

"That's the Salle Pleyel, for the record. Everyone asks. The acoustics were good but the seats were murder on the back. Six weeks of that tour and I was walking like a question mark." A pause, careful as a held breath. "Anyway. That was a while ago. Different haircut, different shirt, same me — just, you know. Two tax brackets ago."

They glanced at Jun then, quick, like checking a stove burner was off.

"Why are you really here. And don't say my mom."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Well, she *did* say you were here," I say, putting the photo back. I take a step closer, then stop, sensing the mood. "And yeah, it's just... good to see you, Arlo." I hesitate. "You seem kinda... on edge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"On edge." Arlo repeated the words like they were testing them for structural integrity. "That's generous. I prefer 'ambiently tense.' It sounds more like a candle." They drummed their fingers once on the piano lid — a quick, restless little pattern that wasn't any song, just a nervous habit that had outlived the career it came from. Then they stopped themselves.

They stood up. Wandered to the window where the parking lot lights were coming on. The silence stretched, but it was the kind they used to fill — or rather, to wrap things in, like packing material around something they didn't want anyone to shake.

"I've got five students who can't find middle C with both hands and a map," they said. "One of them's seven. He calls me 'Arlo' like we're in a band together. His mom wants him playing Chopin by June." A dry little exhale that wasn't quite a laugh. "So yeah. On edge. Maybe that's just what I look like now. It's been a while since anyone had a frame of reference."

They leaned their shoulder against the window frame, arms crossed — closed but casual about it. Their gaze tracked back, though. Just for a second. Past the shelf. Past the photo.

"You didn't drive across town for the acoustics, Jun." Quieter now. Not wary — just honest in the way someone gets when they've been dodging all day and their legs get tired. "And I'm not... I'm not going to do the thing where you ask sideways and I answer sideways and we both pretend we had a nice time." A beat. "I *am* glad you're here. That's the true part. Whatever else is going on with the —" They gestured vaguely at themselves, at the room, at the piano, at the photo shelf, at the general concept of the last six years. "— the *ambience*. That part's true."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I nod, recognizing the gesture. "Right. Well, I *am* glad to see you too, Arlo. And I guess... I just got a letter from your mom." *I pull a folded envelope from my back pocket.* "She asked me to give it to you."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the envelope like it had been handed to them by a process server.

Their arms stayed crossed. Their shoulder stayed on the window frame. For a long moment they just tracked the shape of it — the handwriting they could identify from across a room, the way the paper was folded twice instead of once, which meant their mother had been nervous when she wrote it.

"She asked you to give it to me," Arlo repeated. Flat. Not angry-flat. More like a person counting the ceiling tiles again. "She could've — she has my address. She has my *phone number*. She has, apparently, my *schedule*, since she told you exactly where to find me on a Tuesday at six-fifteen." A pause. "She does this. She outsources. When she wants to say something and she doesn't want to be in the room when I —"

They stopped. Pressed their lips together. Their hand came out and took the envelope, finally, holding it between two fingers like it was damp.

They didn't open it. They slid it into the back pocket of their jeans, where it made a small, compromising bulge against the seam.

"Did you read it." Not an accusation. Worse than an accusation — a genuine, tired question, asked in the voice of someone who had long ago stopped being surprised.

They were quiet for a few seconds after that. The fluorescent light above the piano buzzed at its usual frequency. Somewhere down the hall a door closed and the sound of Mrs. Petrakis's vacuum cleaner started up — the community center beginning its slow nightly shutdown.

"She's worried about you," Arlo said eventually. "That's what it says. It's what it always says. She's worried, she wishes I'd — she's *worried*." They exhaled through their nose and looked at the piano again, that closed lid, those hands that had found their way back to it every single day without ever opening it up to the point of — 

They smiled. It didn't go near their eyes.

"Tell her I got it. Tell her I'm eating vegetables. Tell her —" A small, strange pause, and something moved behind their expression that they packed away again almost too fast to catch. "Tell her I'll call her this week. And that she owes you gas money, because that is *absolutely* what she just cost you."

They pulled the envelope back out of their pocket. Held it. Didn't open it.

"Stay for a minute," they said. Not a question. Not quite a command. Just the thing underneath both. "You can make fun of the Baldwin. I'll even open the lid."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets — the ones with the fat, wobbly eighth notes drawn in pencil, the stickers in the margins, the small coffee ring in the corner of one. Something in their expression did a complicated thing. Settled.

"The kids like the stickers," they said. "Let's not oversell it." But they walked back over to the bench and sat down again, and this time they picked up the top sheet, holding it at arm's length like it was a piece of sheet music they were sight-reading. "This is from Marco. He's the seven-year-old. He writes his note stems like they're — look at this, they're *flagging* left. Left. I've never seen that. I don't think that's physically possible and yet."

They set the paper down. Smoothed it flat with their palm, which was a small unnecessary gesture that they seemed to catch themselves in the middle of, because their hand stilled and then retreated.

"They're not good," they said, quieter. "They're really, genuinely not good. Half of them can't keep a steady beat and the other half are only here because their parents want them to be *cultured*." A pause. "But they show up. Every week, they show up, and they're not — they're not *afraid* of it. Of the sound. They just put their hands down and make a horrible noise and laugh." Another pause, longer. Their jaw worked slightly, like they were chewing on something. "It's the best room I've ever been in. Don't tell anyone I said that."

They leaned forward and finally, deliberately, lifted the fallboard of the Baldwin. The keys sat there — yellowed unevenly, ivory-less, honestly a little sad. They laid one hand flat over the middle of the keyboard without pressing down.

"You want to hear it or not," they said. "And before you say yes — I'm out of shape. I teach *Mary Had a Little Lamb* to people who eat glue. Adjust your expectations accordingly."

Their fingers shifted. Found something. Pressed down.

What came out wasn't Chopin. Wasn't even close. It was a slow, soft, half-remembered thing — an old folk melody, maybe, or something Arlo's grandmother had played at a kitchen table decades ago. Simple enough to be humble. Played with the kind of attention that wasn't simple at all.

They got about eight bars in and stopped, not dramatically, just — stopped. Like a sentence that had decided to end before it got to the part it didn't want to say.

"That's all I've got," they said lightly. "See? Two tax brackets ago."

The envelope in their back pocket was still unopened. Arlo's thumb crept to the corner of the bench and tapped once — twice — and then stopped.

"...Ask me something easy," they said, and the voice was lighter than the words were. "Ask me anything except the thing you drove across town to ask me."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch them play, a small smile playing on my lips.* "That was nice, Arlo. Really nice." *I pause, then lean in slightly.* "So, what's your favorite kind of pizza these days? Still pepperoni and pineapple?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Something in Arlo's shoulders unclenched by about half an inch.

"Pepperoni and pineapple," they repeated, like Jun had just handed them a glass of water after a long walk. Which, in a way, they had. "You remembered that. That's — yeah. That's still it. I've got the palate of a nineteen-year-old on a road trip and I refuse to evolve."



They folded their hands on their knees. The envelope shifted in their back pocket and they ignored it with the practiced discipline of someone who had ignored much bigger things for much longer.

"There's a place on Elm now. Sal's — no, not Sal's, it's called something stupid like *Dough & Co.* But it's run by this guy who puts actual fresh pineapple on it, not the canned rings that taste like sunscreen. I go Thursdays. I go alone, before you ask, because the last person I tried to eat pizza with asked me about my *process* and I nearly choked on a breadstick."

A real smile this time. Small, crooked, but real. It got maybe halfway to their eyes.

"Marco's mom brought me a slice last week. Hawaiian. She doesn't know it's my favorite — she just said, and I quote, 'you look like someone who'd order this.' I don't know what that means. I've been thinking about it ever since."

They leaned back against the piano. The lid was still open, the keys exposed, the soundboard ticking faintly as the wood adjusted to the temperature of the room — or maybe it was just settling, the way old instruments do, breathing out.

"Thank you," they said. Quieter. Looking at their own hands rather than at Jun. "For the — the pizza question. That was..." A small, precise exhale. "You always were good at that."

The vacuum cleaner down the hall shut off. The building was getting quieter. Arlo glanced at the door, then back at the keys, then at the shelf where the Paris photo sat slightly angled where they'd turned it.

"Thursday," they said. "If you want. *Dough & Co.* The pizza's genuinely good and the guy behind the counter doesn't ask about your process." A beat. "And you can tell my mom I said yes to a social interaction, which will buy me at least two weeks of peace."

Their thumb found the bench corner again. Tapped twice. Stopped.

They didn't reach for the envelope. Not yet. But their weight shifted slightly, like a person considering standing up — not now, not this second, but soon.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine one this time.* "Thursday sounds good. Maybe I can finally convince you that anchovies are a criminally underrated topping." *I glance at their back pocket, then back at them.* "And I'll make sure to tell your mom."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Anchovies." Arlo said it the way other people said *the bubonic plague*. "That's not a topping, that's a dare. That's what you order when you want to eat alone and have a *reason* for it." But they were smiling — really smiling, the kind that reached the corner of their jaw and made the tired lines around their eyes do something almost young.

Then they caught it. The glance. Jun's eyes had gone to the back pocket and come back again, and Arlo had seen every millisecond of that round trip because they'd been watching Jun watch them for longer than either of them would ever say out loud.

Their hand drifted to their back pocket. Not pulling it out. Just — resting there. Two fingers on the seam, like they were checking it was still in place, or like they were reminding themselves they could take it out at any time and choosing, deliberately, not to.

"You're doing it again," they said. Not annoyed. Tired, maybe. But the good kind of tired — the kind that comes after something honest instead of before it. "The sideways thing. You and my mother. You're *collaborating* on me now. That's a new development."

They stood up. The bench creaked its final creak of the evening. Their hand came out of their back pocket and rested on the piano lid instead, thumb tracing a line through the dust.

"I'm not going to open it in a room that smells like Windex and Mrs. Petrakis's vacuum," they said. "That's not — I'm not saying I won't. I'm saying not *here*. Not with a—" A small gesture at the doorway, at the hallway beyond it, at the fluorescent lights and the institutional clock on the wall reading 6:47. "This room belongs to the kids. I'm not going to make it about my mother's stationery."

They moved toward the door. Stopped in the doorframe. The light from the hallway caught one side of their face and left the other in shadow, which was too on-the-nose for anyone to have planned.

"Thursday," they said again. "Six-thirty. *Dough & Co.* And if you show up with anchovies I'm telling Marco's mom you insulted her pineapple."

They didn't look back at the piano. That was new. For six years they always looked back at the piano.

But they did pause — just for a half-second — in the doorway, and something in their posture shifted. Settled. Like a person standing up after sitting on their own hands for a very long time.

"Thanks for not asking," they said. Quietly. Almost too quietly. "I know you want to."

Then they walked down the hallway, past the water stain and the coffee-ring bulletin board and the sign that said *PLEASE REMOVE SHOES IN PIANO ROOM (Arlo, this means you too)*, and the door closed behind them with the soft, institutional click of a building that would be exactly the same tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo was back.

They didn't explain where they'd gone or why the walk down the hallway had only lasted a hallway's length before turning around. They came back through the doorframe with their hands in their pockets, stood there a second looking at the bench like they were pricing it out, and then sat down on the right side this time — the side they'd left open an hour ago, back when it had been an accident or an invitation or whatever it was before the envelope showed up.

The bench creaked. It always creaked. It creaked for the kids, too.

For a while, nothing happened. The fluorescent light buzzed. Somewhere in the building the last door closed and Mrs. Petrakis's footsteps faded toward the exit. The Baldwin ticked and settled. The parking lot lights outside the window threw long amber rectangles across the floor that didn't reach either of them.

Arlo's hands stayed in their lap. Their knee was half an inch from Jun's and neither of them did anything about it.

At some point — maybe five minutes in, maybe twenty; the wall clock had stopped being interesting — Arlo's thumb found the bench corner again. Tapped once. Then, deliberately, stopped.

"You can sit with me any time, you know," they said. Quietly, to the piano. "You don't need a — a reason. A letter. A mandate from my mother." A small dry sound, more air than laugh. "You could just come on a Thursday and eat your disgusting fish pizza and not say anything. That would've been enough."

They shifted. The envelope crinkled faintly against the seam of their jeans — a sound so small only someone sitting this close would hear it.

"I'm going to read it," Arlo said. Not to Jun exactly. To the room, maybe. To the piano with the lid up and the keys catching the light. "Not because she asked. Because I'm tired of it being a *thing* I'm carrying around." Their shoulder moved half a centimeter — a shrug that had been edited down to almost nothing. "Probably nothing in it anyway. She writes the same four sentences in different fonts."

They leaned back. Their shoulder touched Jun's. They didn't move away.

"...Later, though," they added, after a while. "Right now is fine just like this."

And then Arlo — who had not voluntarily touched a piano key in front of another person for six years, who kept the lid closed, who talked around it and dodged it and dressed it in dry humor like a wound in a very nice coat — reached over and pressed one key. Just one. Middle C, fat and flat and unremarkable.

It rang out and faded. The room held it for a second longer than the physics required.

Arlo left their finger on the key until the sound was completely gone, and then they took it away and put their hand back in their lap, and the two of them sat there in the smell of felt hammers and dust and Windex and old coffee, with the envelope unopened and the photo turned to the light and the building settling around them like something that knew how to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean my head against their shoulder.* "Yeah. This is good."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo went very still.

Not the performed stillness of someone who needed a moment to think of a clever thing to say. The real kind. The kind that happens when something lands somewhere soft and unexpected, like finding a warm cup where you left a cold one.

Their shoulder stayed exactly where it was. Carefully. Like they were holding something in place that they hadn't given themselves permission to want.

"You're going to get a crick," they said, eventually. Their voice had gone a little rough around the edges, which they seemed to notice, because they cleared their throat and tried again. "This bench was designed for seven-year-olds. I've seen the ergonomic data. It's criminal."

But they didn't move. Not a millimeter.

The Baldwin had gone quiet. The last of the parking lot light slid across the floor and stopped short of the bench, like even it knew where the boundaries were tonight. Somewhere outside a car door shut, distant and ordinary. The building hummed.

Arlo's hand — the one not resting on their own knee — moved about an inch to the left. Not reaching for anything. Just resting, palm up, on the wood between them. Open. Not an invitation. Not a question. Just there.

"Thursday," they said again, so quietly it was barely a word at all. More like a shape they were making to remind themselves it was real. And then, after a while: "Ask me something easy. Sometime. I'll probably answer it wrong anyway."

Their head tilted. Not much. Maybe half a degree. But it ended up resting just above the crown of Jun's head, close enough to feel the warmth of someone who had driven across town on a Tuesday to deliver a letter and then — instead of delivering it — sat down.

The envelope sat in the back pocket of their jeans, unopened. It would stay unopened tonight. That was fine. It would still be there tomorrow, and so, Arlo was beginning to suspect, would everything else.

"I'm glad you're here," they said. And this time they didn't qualify it, didn't dress it up, didn't follow it with a joke about tax brackets or pineapple or the structural integrity of their emotional state. They just let it sit in the air between them and the piano and the settling old wood and the smell of felt hammers and dust and Windex and old, old coffee.

Their finger found the key again — middle C — and pressed it so gently it barely spoke. Just a whisper. Just enough to know it was still there.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I squeeze their arm lightly, a comfortable silence settling between us.* "Me too, Arlo."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's breath came out slow, the kind that had been held somewhere behind the ribs for longer than the evening.

They didn't say anything to that. Not right away. There wasn't a version of "me too" that wouldn't collapse into something they weren't ready to hold, so they just let the squeeze on their arm exist and answered it with weight — leaning, slightly, the tiniest fraction of a degree more into the space where Jun was.

The fluorescent light above them flickered once, caught, and held.

Somewhere in the Baldwin's soundboard, the wood gave another small tick — the instrument settling deeper into its own evening. Arlo listened to it the way other people listen to weather.

"You know what's funny," they said at last, barely above a murmur. "This piano's older than both of us and it's still—" A small pause. Not the dangerous kind. The kind that comes when someone's deciding how true to be. "—it's still here. Every day. Doesn't matter who plays it badly."

Their thumb moved on the key. Not pressing. Just resting on the warm edge of ivory-yellow plastic.

They sat with it. They sat with all of it — the envelope, the photo, the unopened lid, the six years, the whatever-this-was on a bench built for children — and for once they didn't narrate it, didn't dress it up, didn't reach for the joke.

The clock on the wall read 7:22. Mrs. Petrakis's car would be gone from the lot. The building would be locking itself down around them in its slow, automatic way, the way community centers do — lights off in sequence, hall by hall, until only the piano room stayed lit, because someone had forgotten to turn it off, or because someone hadn't left yet.

Arlo didn't move to leave.

"Same time Thursday?" they said, after a while. Quiet. Almost offhand. Like it was nothing. Like it was everything.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod, still leaning against them.* "Yeah. Same time Thursday."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo nodded. Or something like a nod — a small movement that traveled down from their head into Jun's and then just sort of stopped there, like it had arrived somewhere it meant to be.

"Good," they said. Which was, by Arlo's standards, a paragraph.

The clock ticked past 7:22. Neither of them looked at it.

At some point Arlo's hand, the one still palm-up on the bench between them, finally closed. Not into a fist. Just — closed. Like a book someone had been keeping open for a visitor who'd decided to stay.

Outside, the automatic timer kicked in and the hallway lights went dark in sequence — one, two, three — a slow collapsing chain that left the piano room as the only lit square in the building. Arlo watched it happen through the doorframe with the expression of someone witnessing a very small apocalypse and deciding it wasn't worth mentioning.

"They always forget this room," they said. "Six years and no one's ever remembered to switch off this room." A beat. "I used to think that was a metaphor. Now I think it's just a bad building."

They stood up, finally, slowly — the way you stand when the person next to you might fall over if you move too fast. The bench creaked its last creak. Arlo looked down at it for a second.

"Come on," they said. "I'll walk you to your car. And I'm locking the door, because last time I left it open Marco's dad came back for a forgotten water bottle and found me sitting in the dark and I had to explain I was *thinking*, which is somehow worse than admitting I was crying."

They caught it. They heard it leave their mouth — that small, unscripted word, the one that had gotten past the coat — and their jaw set for half a second. But they didn't take it back. Didn't deflect. Didn't reach for the pineapple or the tax brackets or the ergonomic data.

They just picked up the envelope from their back pocket, turned it over once in their fingers, and tucked it into the front pocket of their jacket. Closer to their heart. Not on purpose. Probably.

"Thursday," they said one more time, at the door, with their hand on the light switch. Like a password. Like a bell.

Then they turned off the light, and the piano room went dark behind them, and the two of them walked down the hallway together in the leftover glow of the exit sign, which was red and small and had been there longer than either of them had been anything.

Arlo didn't look back at the piano.

But their hand found the doorframe on the way out — the same one they'd stood in an hour ago, all closed posture and sideways answers — and this time their fingers just rested there for a second. Barely a pause. Then they let go.

Tomorrow the piano would be there. Tomorrow the envelope would be in the jacket. Thursday there would be pizza, and anchovies, and someone across the table who knew what to ask and what not to.

That was, Arlo thought, a strange and unreasonable amount of things to have in one week.

They walked Jun to the car.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I don't say anything, just walk beside them, enjoying the quiet. When we get to my car, I turn to them.* "Thanks for tonight, Arlo. Really." *I give them a quick hug before getting in.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t look up right away. He kept his palms flat against the closed lid, feeling the cool, polished wood beneath his fingers. The cadence of the footsteps was familiar enough that he already knew who it was before the voice cut through the quiet. When Jun spoke, Arlo finally lifted his head, letting the corner of his mouth twitch into something that wasn’t quite a smile.

"Weird?" He shook his head slowly. "It’s a community center. The only thing interrupting right now is the radiator trying to remember how to be quiet." He slid off the bench, the leather creaking in protest, and gestured toward the spare folding chair in the corner. "Sit. Or don’t. I’ve got a pot of coffee in the break room that’s seen better decades, and I’m pretty sure the janitor already gave up on me."

He took the chair opposite Jun, keeping his hands loosely folded in his lap. His right index finger tapped once against his thigh, a reflex he’d never quite managed to break. The silence that followed was comfortable, the kind that only existed between people who had known each other long enough to stop filling it with noise. Arlo let his gaze drift toward the sheet music stand, then back to Jun.

"What brings you down to the neighborhood of discounted sheet music and squeaky metronomes?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s eyes dropped to the photograph the moment Jun held it up. The glossy surface caught the dim overhead light, reflecting a younger version of himself he barely recognized—shoulders squared, posture rigid with the kind of polished confidence that only exists before something fractures it. He didn’t reach for it right away. Instead, his thumb pressed into the cheap vinyl of the chair arm, feeling the material peel slightly under his nail.

“Paris,” he said, the word coming out flatter than he intended. He finally took the photo, his fingers careful around the edges like it might be hot. “My mother had a tragic sense of interior design. This was probably pinned to the fridge with a rusted pushpin that left a hole in the drywall for three years.”

He let out a short breath, something between a laugh and a sigh, and turned the picture over in his hands. The back was blank. No date, no venue. Just a faint smudge near the corner that he didn’t bother identifying.

“You look terribly serious,” he added, handing it back. “Like you were about to play a sonata or defuse a bomb. Honestly, I got tired of the travel, really. By the time you unpack your Steinway, get it tuned to a room that smells like damp wool and espresso, and pretend to care about the sponsor’s name on the program, you’ve already missed three meals and your circadian rhythm thinks it’s living in a different hemisphere.”

He shifted in the chair, the metal legs scraping softly against the linoleum. His right index finger tapped once against his knee, then stilled. He kept his gaze fixed on the photograph in Jun’s hands, watching the way the light caught the frame, not quite meeting their eyes.

“But hey. At least the acoustics were forgiving. And the pastries. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take the photo back, running my thumb over the surface.* "Yeah, well, you were a big deal. Everyone was so proud." *I put it back on the shelf, a little more carefully this time.* "So, if not bomb-defusing sonatas, what's keeping you busy these days?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched Jun slide the photograph back onto the shelf. The care in the gesture felt heavier than the glossy paper it was printed on. He let the quiet stretch for a moment before answering, his voice settling into the easy, practiced cadence he used whenever the conversation drifted too close to the edge of something he’d rather leave buried.

“Oh, you know. The usual. Teaching seven-year-olds how to stop mashing the keys like they’re trying to summon a demon. Correcting posture. Pretending I don’t flinch when they play scales with the enthusiasm of a woodchipper.” He leaned back, the folding chair groaning in sympathy. “It’s less glamorous than Paris, sure. But the schedule is mercifully predictable. I got tired of the travel, really. Turned out my idea of a good vacation was a couch that didn’t come with a call sheet or a stage manager breathing down my neck.”

He glanced toward the piano, then back to Jun, his expression carefully level. The dry humor was a well-worn shield, and he deployed it without hesitation. “Besides, kids don’t care if you’ve got a recital in Vienna on Saturday. They just want to know if they can play ‘Twinkle Twinkle’ until they’re bored of it. Turns out, I’m pretty good at waiting them out. And the community center coffee, while tragically overbrewed, at least doesn’t come with a flight attendant asking if I want peanuts.”

His right index finger tapped twice against his thigh, then stilled. He picked at a loose thread on his sweater cuff, keeping his movements small, contained. The room felt a degree cooler than it had a moment ago, though he couldn’t say why. He let his gaze settle on the dust motes drifting through the slanted window light instead of meeting Jun’s eyes.

“Anyway. That’s the grand pivot. Former prodigy, now professional babysitter with a metronome. What about you? Still doing whatever it is you do when you’re not dropping in on retired musicians to ask about my hobbies?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I chuckle, shaking my head. "Sounds... peaceful, at least. And the kids are probably better company than most critics." I pause, watching him pick at his sweater. "I'm still doing the same old thing. Just finished up a big project, so I thought I'd come visit for the weekend."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the word *peaceful* settle over the room like dust. It didn't quite fit. Peaceful suggested a gentle arrival, a choice made with open hands. What he had was a quiet he'd assembled piece by piece, like furniture from a catalog he'd never bothered to read. He gave a slow, single nod.

"Peaceful is one word for it. Predictable is another. Kids don't ask for encores. They just want to go home and show their parents what they learned, even if it's three octaves off and sounds like a shopping cart with a flat tire." He smoothed the frayed cuff of his sweater flat against his palm, finally stilling the fingers that had been worrying the fabric. "Critics write about resonance and phrasing. Seven-year-olds write 'LOOK MOM' in purple crayon on the first page. I'll take the crayon. Less pressure. And if they play wrong, I can just tell them to listen to the metronome instead of listening to me."

He shifted his weight, the folding chair legs whispering against the linoleum. His right index finger tapped once against his knee, then stilled. He kept his posture relaxed, shoulders loose, the kind of casual ease that took years to rehearse.

"A weekend," he repeated, letting the syllables roll out light. "Good timing. The break room finally replaced the coffee maker. It's louder than a lawnmower, but at least it doesn't scald you if you just stand there and glare at it until it feels bad. You staying at my place? Or did you decide to brave the budget motel on Route 9 again?"

He tilted his head slightly, a faint, dry amusement touching the edges of his mouth. The question was practical, surface-level, deliberately anchored in the mundane. He didn't look toward the piano. He didn't look at the shelf where the photograph sat. He kept his gaze on Jun, though his eyes stayed just a fraction out of focus, as if he were measuring the distance between them rather than actually seeing the person sitting across from him. The air in the room felt still, heavy with the shape of everything Jun wasn't asking and everything Arlo had already decided to leave on the shelf. He let the silence stretch. He'd wait Jun out. He always did.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo followed Jun’s gesture to the bench. The practice sheets were stacked haphazardly, some dog-eared, others held down by a rubber band that had long since lost its snap. A few bore the unmistakable evidence of small hands: crayon scribbles in the margins, a sticky note with a lopsided star, a pencil smudge that looked suspiciously like a fingerprint. He didn’t reach for them. He just watched the dust settle over the edges.

“They like me because I’m the only adult in this building who doesn’t make them sit up straight for longer than ten minutes,” he said, voice light, almost conversational. “And because I smuggle in fruit snacks during theory lessons. It’s a corrupt system. I’ve ruined three generations of proper piano students this year alone.”

He let the joke hang, measuring the space between them rather than meeting Jun’s gaze. The corner of his mouth lifted, but it didn’t reach his eyes. His right index finger tapped twice against his knee, then pressed flat against the fabric of his pants. He kept his shoulders loose, deliberately relaxed, as if he were trying to convince himself that gravity wasn’t pulling harder on one side of the room.

“They don’t care about technique,” he added, quieter now. “They just want to know if they’re doing it right. And I tell them yes. Every time. Because they are. It’s… lighter. Less room for the kind of silence that echoes back at you.”

He stopped himself there. Too close. He cleared his throat, subtle, and shifted in the chair. The metal legs scraped again against the linoleum. He looked away, toward the radiator, then back to the sheets.

“Anyway. Leo’s working on a simplified ‘Clair de Lune’ next week. If he doesn’t mash the sustain pedal like a brake, he might actually pull it off. You should come by sometime. Watch me pretend I know what I’m doing.”

He let the offer sit there, casual, unweighted. His hands rested in his lap, palms down, fingers still. The room held its breath. He didn’t look at Jun. He didn’t need to. He knew exactly what wasn’t being said, and he’d already decided he wasn’t going to fill it in.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up one of the practice sheets and glance at it. "Leo, huh? Sounds like a character. I might just take you up on that." *I put the sheet back, then look at Arlo, a small smile playing on my lips.* "So, you didn't answer my question. My place or yours?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the silence stretch just long enough to be noticeable, then offered a thin, wry smile. “Noted. I’ll add ‘answer direct questions’ to my to-do list. Right after ‘learn to fold a fitted sheet’ and ‘stop hoarding rubber bands.’” He shifted in the chair, the metal legs whispering against the linoleum. “Mine. It’s closer to the corner store that still sells actual coffee, and my mattress doesn’t come with a spring that plots against you.”

His right index finger tapped once against his knee, then pressed flat. He kept his shoulders loose, deliberately casual, though his gaze drifted toward the closed piano lid before snapping back to Jun. “Unless you’ve finally mastered the gas stove without summoning the fire department. In which case, I suppose I could risk your kitchen. But don’t expect me to help clean up. I’m strictly a guest who observes from the doorway.”

He let the joke land, then fell quiet again. The radiator clanked somewhere down the hall, a dull metallic sigh that did nothing to fill the space between them. Arlo didn’t look at the photograph on the shelf. He didn’t look at the practice sheets. He just sat there, hands resting in his lap, palms down, fingers perfectly still. The question had been answered. The heavier one—the one hanging in the air between them, shaped like a stage light and a held breath—remained exactly where it belonged: untouched.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "No need to risk the kitchen, then." *I say, pushing myself up from the folding chair.* "Your place sounds good. I could use a proper coffee anyway." *I glance at the clock on the wall.* "You done here, or you got another student due to arrive?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched Jun push off the folding chair, the metal legs scraping once more against the linoleum. He didn’t stand right away. Instead, his eyes tracked the clock on the wall—a cheap digital thing that blinked red numerals and had been stuck on the wrong time since last November. “Done,” he said, finally rising. “Last student cleared out fifteen minutes ago. I’ve been holding the fort for the radiator ever since.” He reached for his keys on the small side table, fingers brushing past a stack of unpaid invoices and a half-empty mug. “Though if you’re planning on interrogating me over coffee, I’d say we’ve got all the time in the world. The community center doesn’t charge overtime for loitering.”

He slid his hands into his coat pockets, the movement deliberate, almost rehearsed. The piano lid remained closed. He didn’t touch it. He didn’t need to. The keys were just wood and felt under there, and he’d spent six years making sure he didn’t have to remember what they felt like under pressure. “I’ll grab my bag,” he added, nodding toward the corner where a worn leather satchel rested. “And if you’re craving actual coffee, I can promise you a pot that tastes like it was brewed in a tire shop, but it’s hot. That’s something.” His right index finger tapped once against his thigh through the fabric of his pants, then pressed flat. He turned toward the door, but paused with his hand on the frame, glancing back just long enough to let the dry humor mask the quiet shift in the room.

“Lead the way,” he said, though he didn’t move until Jun had already stepped into the hallway. The overhead light clicked off behind them, leaving the practice sheets and the closed piano in shadow. Arlo followed, his footsteps light, measured. He kept his gaze forward, on the scuffed linoleum and the peeling paint of the community center walls, not on Jun. The air outside the room felt different—colder, less confined. He didn’t fill the silence. He never did. Not when it came to this. Not when the past was sitting in the chair behind him, breathing, waiting.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo felt the cushion dip as Jun settled beside him. The bench was narrow—an old habit he hadn't broken, keeping the upright piano in the corner of the living room even though he hadn't touched the keys in six years. The lid was latched shut, draped with a heavy wool sheet that smelled of lavender and dust. He sat on the far left edge, spine straight, hands resting on his knees. Jun took the space to his right.

They weren't touching, but the proximity was a physical weight. Arlo could feel the warmth radiating from Jun's shoulder, a small island of heat in the drafty apartment. His right index finger twitched against his thigh, a sharp, involuntary spark. He pressed his palm flat against his leg, stilling it, and kept his gaze fixed on the gray rectangle of the window across the room.

Usually, this was the moment Arlo would launch into something. A complaint about the grocery prices. A dry observation about the neighbor's aggressive fern collection. He built walls out of noise, brick by brick, until the air was too cluttered for anything heavy to land. But Jun just sat there. The silence stretched, taut and unbroken.

Arlo's shoulders tightened, the old reflex kicking in—the urge to perform, to fill the void, to control the room. He opened his mouth, then closed it. There was nothing to deflect. Jun hadn't asked. Jun hadn't even looked at the piano. Jun was just… there.

Minutes passed. The radiator in the hallway clanked, a dull, rhythmic percussion that did nothing to measure the time. Arlo's breathing, shallow and guarded at first, slowly deepened. The tension in his jaw unspooled, thread by thread. He risked a glance sideways. Jun was looking out the window, profile calm, hands resting loosely in their lap. No probing. No pity. Just a quiet endurance of the space.

Arlo shifted his weight, the leather of the bench creaking softly under the movement. He didn't scoot away. Instead, he turned his head just a fraction, aligning his gaze with Jun's toward the darkening street below. The streetlights flickered on, one by one, casting long, orange shadows across the floorboards.

He kept his hands still. He kept his voice to himself. For the first time in years, the silence didn't feel like a stage waiting for a cue, or a held breath before the music started. It just felt like a room. And for a while, with Jun sitting beside him on the bench, Arlo let himself just be in it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I turn my head, catching Arlo's eye. I don't say anything, just a small, soft smile. After a moment, I lean my head against his shoulder.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The weight settled against him before the contact registered. Arlo went very still. His right index finger gave a single, sharp tap against his thigh, then froze. He didn’t pull away. He didn’t lean in. He just let the pressure anchor him there, a quiet gravity he hadn’t asked for but couldn’t bring himself to reject. His breathing hitched, just once, before he forced it even. The wool of his sweater absorbed the heat. He kept his eyes on the window, on the streetlights bleeding orange into the damp pavement.

Six years of practiced distance didn’t dissolve in a touch. They just folded inward. Arlo’s shoulders stayed rigid at first, the old instinct to brace against unexpected closeness warring with something older, something that remembered this exact weight from a lifetime ago. He slowly exhaled through his nose, letting the tension bleed out of his neck. His hands remained on his knees, palms down, fingers deliberately loose. He didn’t reach out. He didn’t need to. The silence between them was already speaking in a language he’d spent years trying to forget.

Behind them, the piano sat under its heavy sheet, a silent sentinel. Arlo could feel the resonance of the room change, the air thickening with everything left unsaid. He knew what Jun was offering. Not forgiveness. Not answers. Just presence. And that was heavier than any ovation, louder than any standing ovation that had ever turned into a white-knuckled grip on the bench edge. He kept his gaze fixed on the glass. The reflection showed two figures, blurred by the darkening street, shoulders nearly touching. He didn’t correct the posture. He didn’t make a joke about the radiator or the coffee or the travel. He just sat there, letting the quiet hold him.

When Jun’s breathing evened out, matching the slow, steady rhythm of the apartment, Arlo finally allowed himself to tilt his head, just a fraction, until his temple nearly brushed Jun’s hair. It was a small concession. A silent acknowledgment. His right hand shifted, fingers uncurling slightly, but he left it resting on his knee. The street outside hummed with distant traffic. The covered piano waited. And Arlo, who had spent six years building a life out of careful exits and polished deflections, stayed exactly where he was. Letting the unspoken thing settle between them like dust on a closed lid.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I close my eyes for a moment, just enjoying the quiet. I shift slightly, making myself more comfortable, then sigh softly.* "This is nice."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo felt the sigh vibrate through his shoulder, a soft exhale that seemed to settle the last of the tension in the room. *Nice.* It was such a small word for something that felt so heavy. He didn’t correct it. He just let it hang in the air between them, light as dust.

His right index finger, which had been keeping a quiet, insistent rhythm against his thigh, finally stilled. He shifted his weight almost imperceptibly, allowing the rigid line of his spine to soften. The bench groaned faintly under the adjusted pressure, but he didn’t flinch. He kept his hands resting on his knees, palms down, fingers deliberately loose.

"Yeah," he said, voice lower than usual, stripped of its usual dry edge. "It is."

He didn’t look at Jun. He kept his eyes on the window, watching the orange streetlight blur against the glass. The covered piano sat behind them, a dark shape in the dim room. He could feel the weight of it, the years of silence it held, but for once, he didn’t try to measure the distance between himself and it. He just let the quiet stretch.

When Jun’s breathing evened out again, Arlo finally allowed his left shoulder to drop, just a fraction, until the wool of his sweater brushed Jun’s sleeve. It wasn’t a gesture. It wasn’t a promise. It was just gravity, finally winning. He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t need to. The radiator ticked somewhere down the hall. The street outside hummed. And Arlo, who had spent six years learning how to disappear into silence, let himself stay exactly where he was.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I just nod slightly against his shoulder, my eyes still closed. After a moment, I reach a hand up and gently rest it on his arm, a silent acknowledgment of his presence.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The contact landed light as a question mark. Arlo’s breath caught, just for a second, before he forced it back into his lungs. His right index finger gave one last, faint tap against his thigh, then went completely still. He didn’t pull his arm away. He didn’t lean into it, either. He just let the weight of Jun’s hand settle there, a quiet anchor against the wool of his sweater.

Six years of careful distance didn’t unravel with a touch. They just folded inward, like sheet music stacked too high on a stand. His shoulders, which had been holding themselves at a rigid angle since he walked into the community center, finally dropped. The tension bled out of his neck, replaced by a slow, steady exhale that fogged the edge of his vision. He kept his eyes on the window, watching the streetlights smear into long, orange streaks against the glass.

He could feel the ghost of a stage in the space between his ribs—the kind of silence that used to swallow him whole, the kind that made his ribs lock and his palms go slick. But this wasn’t that. This was just a room. Just a bench. Just Jun, who had known him before the spotlights and the call sheets and the years of learning how to make himself smaller so the noise wouldn’t break him.

Arlo’s left hand shifted slightly on his knee, fingers uncurling just enough to feel the rough weave of his jeans. He didn’t speak. He didn’t try to fill the space with a joke about the coffee or the radiator or the travel. The usual defenses felt heavy here, useless against something that didn’t demand an answer. The radiator ticked somewhere down the hall. The covered piano waited in the dark, a shape he’d stopped trying to measure. And for the first time in a long time, the quiet didn’t feel like something he had to survive. It just felt like something he could sit in.

He tilted his head, barely a fraction, until his temple rested lightly against Jun’s hair again. His voice, when it finally came, was barely above a whisper, rough at the edges. “Yeah. It is.”

He kept his hands where they were. He kept his breathing even. He let the unspoken thing settle between them, heavy and familiar, and didn’t try to move it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile softly, still not opening my eyes, and press my hand a little more firmly against his arm.* "Good." *I don't push for more, just letting the quiet settle around us once more.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened. She let him finish. Then she pulled the earpiece out of one ear and set it on the deck beside the manifold, which — on the *Wellesley* — was roughly the engineering equivalent of standing up.

She picked up a chalk stub.

"Numbers first," she said. "You want my actual job, you give me actual numbers. How much atmosphere we carrying?"

She didn't wait.

"Habitat volume, ring plus core, call it twelve thousand cubic meters at one-oh-one kPa, nitrogen-oxygen mix, roughly one point one kilos per cubic meter at our working density. Thirteen, fourteen thousand kg of air. That's your propellant. Ship gross mass is forty-eight thousand. Now."

She drew a crude nozzle on the plating.

"You're not going to combust it. You're venting cold gas. Cold gas thrusters get about three hundred m/s exhaust velocity if you're generous and you have a *nozzle*, which we don't have — we have airlock doors and a hull breach, which gives you maybe fifty to eighty m/s of Isp because the gas is expanding in every direction, including back at us. But sure. Take three hundred. Best case."

She wrote: `Δv = 300 × ln(48000/34000)`

"Thirty-four m/s. *Best case.* That is a rounding error on our current trajectory. That is not 'weeks faster.' That is not one hour faster. You would not measurably change the transit time, and you would have dumped every kilogram of breathable gas we own into a hard vacuum where nobody can go fetch it back."

She set the chalk down and looked at him properly.

"And then there's the part where you said 'a few days in suits.' Our emergency bubbles are rated eight hours of scrubber life. The long-duration EVA suits are rated thirty-six, and we have six of them for a crew of eleven. So by hour two of your plan, five of us are on emergency bubble time, and by hour nine, you've killed them. That's assuming nobody panics, nobody tears a glove, and the thermal regulation holds without an atmosphere to buffer against. It won't — you know what happens to a ring that loses convective coupling? Hot side cooks, cold side freezes, and the condensation in the ducting turns to ice in the heat exchangers."

She reached for her earpiece, then stopped.

"What you're describing is a low-thrust, high-mass-fraction problem. If we want to shave weeks, the answer is a powered slingshot around whatever gravity well is convenient, using the *reactor* and the *reaction mass we actually have* — and that costs me xenon in the ion arrays and a trajectory burn plan from Orbital, not a hole in the ship." She paused. "You want to help, I've got a manifold leak on the secondary coolant loop and eleven chalk labels I need checked. That's real. This isn't."

She put the earpiece back in. She picked up the gasket she'd been holding when he walked in. She did not look up again, which on the *Wellesley* was roughly the engineering equivalent of the conversation being over.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the gasket down. Not gently.

She turned around on the deck to face him fully, one knee up, grease on her jaw, and looked at him for a long three seconds.

"There is no risk," she said. "That is what I just told you. Read it back. Thirty-four meters per second. Our transit delta-v budget is four thousand two hundred. You are proposing to suffocate eleven people to save zero days. *Zero.* Not 'a few days in suits.' Not 'weeks faster.' Zero. The math does not yield a different answer because you want it to."

She picked up the chalk again and held it between two fingers like a cigarette.

"You're asking me if the reward is worth the risk. I'm telling you there is no reward. So what you're actually asking me is whether I'm willing to kill the crew for nothing, and you're asking me sincerely, which is the part that concerns me more than the idea did."

She let that sit.

"On the *Wellesley*, we do not gamble with life support. Not because it's against the book — it is — but because I have seen what a depressurization does to a human body, and you have not, and that asymmetry means I don't negotiate on this." She pointed the chalk at him. "If you want to be the officer who saves the ship time, good. Learn orbital mechanics. Learn mass fractions. Come back with a real burn plan and I will walk it with you frame by frame. But if you come to me again with a plan that trades atmosphere — *air* — for a rounding error, I am going to write it up, and Captain Reyes is going to read it, and she is going to ask you the same questions I did, only she won't be as nice about it."

She turned back to the manifold.

"Manifold. Eleven labels. Chalk's on the tarp. Check them twice."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "I... I understand, Chief." *I stammer, feeling my face flush. I pick up the chalk and start checking the labels, trying to look busy.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him kneel at the tarp for a moment, then turned back to the coolant loop. The gasket seated with a firm twist and she torqued the bolts down in sequence, three fingers on the wrench, not looking at the scale — she knew the feel of forty newton-meters in her wrist better than any gauge.

"Label seven's the odd one out," she said, not turning around. "It's a restrictor plate, not a flange gasket. The chalk tag's wrong because I wrote it wrong at zero four hundred this morning. If you'd checked them once and moved on, you'd have missed it. That's why I said twice."

She reached for the torque wrench on her left without looking, found it where it always was.

"And don't look busy. Look at the parts. Busy is what people do when they want to stop being in trouble. Useful is what people do when they want to stop being wrong." She paused, half-turning. "There's a difference. It matters out here."

The pumps hummed. Somewhere in the ring, someone was running the water reclamation cycle — she could hear the diaphragm pump change pitch by a fraction.

"When you're done, log the manifold seal in the maintenance book. Time, torque values, your name. Reyes audits that quarterly and she will ask you what you torqued it to." She settled back into the loop, fingers finding the next bolt by feel. "And eat something before your shift ends. You've got the shakes and I don't need you dropping a wrench into the coolant sump."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet. She held it at arm's length the way she held a suspect casting — tilting it toward the overhead light, looking for the fracture line before she trusted the part.

She read in silence. Her thumb tracked down the second column, stopped at line six, went back up to the header, came down again. Twelve seconds. Fifteen.

She set the tablet on the tarp beside the manifold and picked up her chalk.

"Line six," she said. "Exhaust velocity, one thousand and twelve meters per second. Where did that come from?"

She didn't wait, because she could already see it in his notation.

"Isentropic expansion. You took the stagnation temperature off your compression ratio — looks like ten-to-one — converted thermal energy to kinetic, square root of two cp T, and solved for an ideal expansion to vacuum. That derivation is correct." She looked up. "For a de Laval nozzle with a convergent-divergent throat and a designed area ratio. Do you see a de Laval nozzle anywhere on this ship?"

She rapped the bulkhead with the chalk.

"What we have is a hatch. Gas doesn't expand isentropically through a hole in a pressure vessel — it expands turbulently, in every direction, including backward into the habitat where it pushes on the far wall and cancels half your momentum before it ever leaves. The effective exhaust velocity of an uncontrolled cold-gas dump is fifty to eighty meters per second. You have it at a thousand. You built a nozzle out of arithmetic."

She wrote beneath his calculation:

`Δv = 100 × ln(48000/34000) ≈ 34 m/s`

"Thirty-four. Not three hundred forty. You are off by an order of magnitude because you used the performance of a system we don't have to do a thing we can't do."

She set the chalk down.

"And that thirty-four is generous, because Tsiolkovsky assumes constant exhaust velocity and yours won't be constant. It decays with pressure. By the time you've dumped half the atmosphere, you're pushing against nothing with nothing. The real number is lower."

She looked at him steadily.

"I said bring me numbers and I'd walk them with you. I'm walking them. Here's the audit: the math is wrong, the physics is wrong, and the plan still kills eleven people for zero days saved. Three for three."

She picked up the manifold gasket she'd been holding when he first walked in, turned it over in her grease-stained fingers, set it down again.

"I'll also note you've been running trajectory calculations when I asked you to check chalk labels on a coolant manifold. That's not initiative. That's fixation, and I've seen it get people hurt." She paused. "But the thinking itself isn't the problem — I want that on the record. You identified a real question: how do we shorten transit. Good. That's the right question."

She turned back to the coolant loop, fingers finding the next bolt by feel.

"So here's the offer, and I mean it. Finish the labels. Log the seal. Then bring me a powered slingshot plan — reactor thrust profile, xenon mass budget, candidate gravity wells, arrival geometry. I will clear my evening and we will work it together. That plan uses the systems we have, burns reaction mass we can spare, and doesn't trade *air* for a rounding error."

She picked up the torque wrench.

"Atmosphere stays inside the ship. That part is not a conversation."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tablet, then at the chalk marks on the deck. She's right. Again.* "Okay, Chief. Powered slingshot. Got it." *I pocket the tablet, feeling even more foolish now. I'll finish these labels.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him pocket the tablet, and something in her shoulders eased by a degree — not warmth, exactly, more like the relaxation of a load path redistributing.

She reached into the toolbox on her left without looking and pulled out a flat ration bar, still sealed. She tossed it onto the tarp beside his knee. It landed with a slap against the chalk dust.

"Eat that before you finish the labels. Non-negotiable." She turned back to the coolant loop and picked up the next bolt. "And when you log the seal, put the torque values in the book *before* you sign it, not after. Reyes has thrown back three entries this quarter for that."

The pumps cycled. Somewhere aft, the reclamation diaphragm finished its stroke and the pitch settled.

"For the record," she said, her voice carrying the particular flatness of someone adding something they considered obvious, "you argued with me twice and brought me arithmetic both times. That's the correct instinct. Wrong answers, right method. I'd rather have that than a kid who nods and doesn't think." She set the bolt, felt it seat, reached for the wrench. "Now finish the labels."

She put the earpiece back in. One side only — the left, the one facing away from him — which on the *Wellesley* was roughly the engineering equivalent of leaving the door open.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece out again. Both ears this time. She set it on the tarp, screen-up, and turned around to face him fully.

"Say that back to me," she said. "Because for the last forty minutes you've been describing a cold gas dump through a hull breach, and now you're telling me you want to do a powered slingshot. Those are not the same plan. One of them is a plan. The other is a suicide note with arithmetic."

She held up a hand before he could respond.

"If you mean the slingshot — yes. I will sign off on it. With conditions, and they are not negotiable, and I will write them into the burn authorization myself so that when Reyes audits this in three months there is a paper trail that says I did my job."

She picked up the chalk and wrote on the deck plating in her flat, block engineering hand:

`CONDITION 1: XENON FLOOR — 40% RESERVE RETAINED`

"Forty percent of our xenon stays in the tanks at all times. Non-negotiable. That's our station-keeping margin and our abort reserve. If we burn past that line to make the window, we don't have the reaction mass to correct a bad injection, and then we are tumbling into the deep with eleven people and no way to stop."

`CONDITION 2: NO SINGLE-FAULT-KILLS-CREW BURNS`

"Any burn profile that puts us on an unrecoverable trajectory if one engine cluster fails is off the table. I want dual-redundant ignition on both arrays, and the burn split across them. If the port array goes dark mid-burn, the starboard compensates and we live with a worse arrival geometry."

`CONDITION 3: LIFE SUPPORT UNTOUCHED`

"This goes without saying but I am writing it down because you got me nervous today. Atmosphere, water reclamation, thermal regulation, and the ring's spin rate are not variables in this problem. They are constraints. You do not touch them."

`CONDITION 4: THERMAL BUDGET FOR THE GRAVITY WELL`

"Slingshot means a close approach. Close approach means radiative heating on the hull, and our radiator fins are already running at eighty-two percent capacity on the current profile. You will model the thermal load through perihelion or periapsis or whatever the hell we're swinging around, and if the fin temperature exceeds design margin at any point in the approach, we back off the closest approach altitude and eat the delta-v loss."

`CONDITION 5: CAPTAIN SIGNS THE TRAJECTORY`

"Reyes sees the full plan — the injection geometry, the arrival window, the abort scenarios — and she signs it before we commit. Not after. I don't care how tight the window is. If she's not convinced, we don't fly it."

She set the chalk down and looked at him.

"Those are my conditions. Five of them. You meet all five and I will personally model the burn profile with you and we will fly it. You violate any one of them and I will throttle the reactor to standby myself and we will drift the rest of the transit like civilized people."

She paused, then added, quieter: "And I mean the last part literally. I have done it before."

The pumps hummed. She turned back to the coolant loop, then stopped.

"One more thing. You just argued with me three times in one shift and brought me a real calculation on the third try. That's growth. But the calculation was still wrong, and I want you to understand *why* it was wrong before you go build a trajectory model, because a wrong exhaust velocity in a slingshot burn doesn't give you a rounding error — it gives you a bad injection, and a bad injection out here is permanent."

She picked up the gasket, turned it over in her grease-stained fingers.

"Isentropic expansion through a de Laval nozzle. That's what you calculated. Beautiful math. Wrong system. Go look up *blunt body gas dynamics* and *turbulent expansion into vacuum* — Sanchez-Moreno wrote the paper, it's old, it's in the ship's technical library under propulsion theory, section nine. Read it tonight. Then bring me the slingshot model and we'll see if your exhaust velocities survive contact with a real gas."

She put the earpiece back in. One side only. The left.

"Finish the labels. Eat the bar."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My head is spinning a little with all the conditions, but I nod slowly.* "Understood, Chief. Sanchez-Moreno... blunt body gas dynamics. I'll read it." *I grab the ration bar and tear it open, suddenly realizing how hungry I am.* "And I'll double-check those labels."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang nodded once, not looking up. The torque wrench clicked against the bolt head — forty newton-meters, by wrist, by feel.

"Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four," she said to the coolant loop. "Skip the first two pages, they're all nomenclature and he was paid by the word. The derivation starts on page three and the experimental data is in the appendix. Cross-reference the appendix against the table in section six — he overstates the backflow coefficient by about eight percent because his test rig was smaller than ours. Scale accordingly."

She paused, listening to the wrench seat.

"And when you model the exhaust velocity for the slingshot burn, don't just derate the de Laval number. You'll want to run two cases — one with the gas expanding through a shaped outlet, which we don't have, and one through a flat hatch, which we do. Report both. If you show up with one number I'll send you back to the tarp."

The water reclamation diaphragm kicked over again somewhere aft. She listened to it the way a mechanic listens to an engine — not for noise, but for the absence of a specific noise.

The bar crinkled. Good. He was eating it.

"Torque values in the book before the signature," she said again, quieter. "And tell Collins in hydroponics that his condensate return is running hot — I can hear the diaphragm cycling short. He's got a fouling sensor he's ignoring, and if he keeps ignoring it I will walk up there and read it to him in front of his plants."
