She found the next bolt by touch. Her shoulder had finally unkinked — the joint had been bothering her since the zero-four-hundred shift, which she had not mentioned to anyone because it was not relevant.

"Dismissed when the labels are done," she said. "And don't skip the second check on seven. Just because I told you what it is doesn't mean you can't still verify it."

The left earpiece stayed in. The right side stayed open. The manifold gasket held.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I wolf down the ration bar, feeling the sugar hit.* "Got it, Chief. Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four, skip the first two pages. Two cases for exhaust velocity. And tell Collins about his condensate." *I grab the chalk and start meticulously checking the labels, starting with number seven.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang worked through the next three bolts without speaking. The torquing was a rhythm — seat, click, rotate, seat, click — and she let it carry her while the junior officer's chalk whispered against the tarp behind her.

She listened to the silence he was making. Not the fidgeting silence of a man looking busy. The slower kind. Good.

"Seven," she said, after a while. Not a question. Just marking that she was still counting.

She reseated the gasket on the final flange port and reached for the sealant tape. The strip came off the roll with the particular sound it always made — a dry, tacky peeling that she'd been hearing on ships for twenty-two years. She cut it square with the edge of her thumbnail.

"Collins is going to tell you the condensate sensor reads hot when the hydroponics bay runs a growth cycle," she added, flatly. "He said that to me in March. It is now September. The sensor is correct and the cycle is fouled. If he says it to you, tell him I said March was a long time ago."

She laid the tape over the threads in one motion and began the final assembly. Reassembly, really. The loop had been apart since her shift started at zero-four-hundred and she was coming up on ten hours, which she did not consider a problem but which the physiologist on Deck Four would consider one.

"Question," she said. "While the chalk's in your hand. Why does the restrictor plate sit where it does in the secondary loop? Not what it does — why *there*. Take your time. Wrong answers cost nothing right now."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I pause, chalk in hand, thinking. Why there? I look at the diagram in my head. The restrictor plate...* "Uh, to regulate flow, Chief? To make sure the coolant goes where it needs to go evenly?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the answer hang in the air for a moment the way she let a torque wrench hang before the click — long enough to feel whether it was going to seat or slip.

"That's what it does," she said. "I asked you why it's *there*. Location, not function. Try again."

She wiped her hands on a rag and picked up the restrictor plate itself — the flat disc of titanium she'd set aside at zero-four-hundred, still cool from the loop. She held it up between thumb and forefinger so he could see the profile.

"Look at the loop geometry. Secondary coolant runs from the reactor heat exchanger, aft, around the ring, and back through the return manifold. Where is the plate?"

She waited.

"It's not at the inlet. It's not at the return. It's at the apex — the far side of the loop, right where the ring's rotation puts it at maximum radial offset from the spin axis." She set the plate down on the tarp, chalk-side up. "Why there and not anywhere else?"

She picked up the sealant tape again but didn't cut it. Waiting.

"Hint, because you've been on the tarp for an hour and I'm not a sadist. Think about what happens to a fluid in a rotating frame when you change its moment arm."

She cut the tape with her thumbnail and began wrapping the threads. Her hands worked independent of her mouth — they always did.

"Take your time. This one matters, because if you understand why that plate is at the apex, you understand half of what's wrong with Collins's condensate loop, and then you'll understand why I want you reading fluid dynamics in a rotating reference frame before you build me a slingshot model that flies past a gravity well."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I look from the restrictor plate to the diagram of the loop, then back to the Chief. Rotating frame... moment arm...* "Centrifugal force, Chief? It balances the centrifugal force, so the flow doesn't get starved at the far end of the loop?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stopped wrapping the tape. She set it down on the tarp and looked at him over her shoulder with the particular expression of someone whose student had just gotten the right letter but the wrong word.

"Close," she said. "You're in the right room. Sit down."

She picked up the restrictor plate again and held it flat on her palm, like a coin.

"Centrifugal acceleration in this ring is omega-squared-r. At the spin axis, zero. At the ring's inner hull, about one-g equivalent. The coolant loop doesn't run at constant radius — it threads through structural ribs, it dips around the reactor shielding, and at its apex it swings out to maximum radial offset. That's where the effective gravity on the fluid is strongest."

She turned the plate over.

"You said it 'balances the centrifugal force.' It doesn't balance anything. The centrifugal field is still there, full strength, through every cubic centimeter of that loop. What the plate does is put a known flow resistance at the point of maximum pressure differential. Without it, the fluid accelerates through the apex — pressure peak, low resistance, it rushes — and then decelerates on the far side where the effective gravity drops and the pressure recovers. You get a siphon effect on a rotating body. Pulsing flow. Cavitation at the low-pressure return, which eats pump impellers and sheds microbubbles into the heat exchanger, which fouls the sensor Collins has been ignoring since March."

She set the plate down.

"So it's not about balance. It's about *damping*. You put the resistance where the driving pressure is highest, and you flatten the flow profile across the whole loop. Steady state. No surge."

She looked at him.

"That's what you said wrong. Everything else — centrifugal field, rotating frame, flow starvation as the failure mode — that's the right instinct. You just need to distinguish between a force being *cancelled* and a system being *tuned*. In engineering, those are very different things and the second one is most of my job."

She picked up the sealant tape and finished the wrap in silence. Three turns, cut square, smooth it down with her thumb.

"And that is exactly why Collins's condensate loop is failing. His return line runs at variable radius and he's got no restrictor anywhere — the condensate surges through the high-gravity segment and pools at the low-gravity elbow, and the fouling sensor reads hot because the fluid sits stagnant long enough to grow biofilm. Same physics. Different loop. He needs a restrictor plate at his apex and he needs to stop telling people the sensor is haunted."

She reseated the final flange and reached for the torque wrench.

"Serrano, *Fluid Dynamics in Rotating Reference Frames*. Section three. Read it after Sanchez-Moreno. Same rule — bring me two cases, not one. One with the plate installed, one without. Show me the flow profile difference on both, and show me where cavitation starts in the unmodified case."

The wrench clicked. Forty newton-meters. Done.

"That's the manifold," she said, and rolled her shoulder once, absently, before pulling her sleeve back down over it. "Log it. Then go find Collins and ruin his week."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking it all in. Serrano, section three. Two cases.* "Okay, Chief. I'll read Serrano too. And I'll... I'll talk to Collins." *I pick up the logbook, feeling a little more confident about what I'm doing now.* "Thanks, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang was already pulling the tarp out from under the manifold components, folding the chalk-dusted corners inward the way she folded everything — square, efficient, no wasted motion. She did not look up at the thanks. She did not say "you're welcome." Both of those things were outside her operating parameters.

"Serrano, section three," she repeated. "Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four. Collins's condensate loop. Two flow-profile cases. Manifold log entry with torque values before the signature. That's five items. You leave this bay with five items in your head or you come back and get them from me at zero-four-hundred, which is when I start my shift and when I am least entertaining."

She stood up. It took a moment — ten hours on the deck plating had settled into her knees and that shoulder in a way she would deny if asked. She rolled up the tarp and slid it into its slot on the bulkhead without looking.

"And the ration bar wrapper goes in the recycler, not the deck. I find one more wrapper on my deck plating and I will start a log for that too, and it will have *your* name on it."

She picked up the tablet she'd been using for her own diagnostics — the one with the green tape on the corner, because there were four identical tablets in this bay and only one of them was hers — and tucked it under her arm.

"One thing before you go."

She turned back. The engineering bay hummed around them, steady as a heartbeat.

"You asked me if the reward was worth the risk. I told you the reward was zero. But the question underneath was good — *how do I weigh risk against reward out here* — and you should keep asking it. Just do it with real numbers and real physics, because out here the gap between a rounding error and a dead crew is one wrong exhaust velocity."

She pointed at the door with the tablet.

"Go ruin Collins's week. Log the manifold first."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking all of it in. Five items. Recycler. I'm still feeling a bit overwhelmed, but the Chief's last words ring true. "How do I weigh risk against reward out here." That's the real question.* "Understood, Chief." *I head to the logbook, then for the door, making sure the ration bar wrapper is firmly in my pocket.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t startle. He’d been counting the seconds since the door clicked shut behind the last child, and the quiet had settled into his shoulders like a familiar coat. He turned his head toward the doorway, watching Jun lean against the frame. The old gymnasium clock ticked somewhere down the hall, out of sync with the rhythm he used to live by.

“Only if you count the lingering scent of Windex and stale practice schedules as a vibe,” Arlo said, his voice rough from disuse. He shifted his weight, keeping his hands flat against the cool wood. “My mom’s always been terrible at reading between the lines. She probably told you I was here because I ‘finally found a sustainable teaching model.’” A dry half-smile touched his mouth. “She’s not entirely wrong. The road gets old after a while.”

He didn’t mention the student. He didn’t mention how the little girl’s metronome had started ticking in his head the moment she reached measure thirty-two, or how the bench suddenly felt too narrow, the room too bright, the stage lights too loud. He just patted the far end of the bench, a quiet invitation that cost him nothing.

“Make yourself at home. Just don’t touch the tuning hammer. It’s still being shy.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The photograph caught the dim overhead light, the gloss reflecting back like a shallow pool. Arlo’s gaze dropped to it, then away. At twenty-two, the suit was too dark, the smile too wide, the hands resting on the Steinway like they belonged there. He remembered the weight of that bench, the way the acoustics in the Orangerie had swallowed every mistake and magnified every breath.

“That was the spring tour,” he said, keeping his voice level. He didn’t reach for it. He kept his palms pressed to the closed lid, feeling the familiar grain beneath his skin. “Paris was lovely, mostly. The pastries were aggressively buttery, the metro smelled like wet wool and exhaust, and I spent three days chasing a pocket watch that refused to keep Parisian time.” A quiet exhale escaped him. “I got tired of the travel. The suitcases never matched the itinerary. Neither did I.”

He tapped the edge of the bench with one knuckle, a soft, rhythmic knock. “Back then, I thought standing up for a bow meant you’d survived the piece. Turns out it just meant you were ready to collapse somewhere with better lighting.” He shrugged, the motion small, contained. “Anyway. You’re here. Which means my mom’s marketing campaign is working. Do you want tea? I think there’s a thermos in the supply closet. It’s probably just hot water and optimism, but it’s hot.”

He kept his eyes on the scuffed floorboards, tracing a hairline crack with his gaze. The photo sat on the shelf, smiling back at a version of himself that didn’t know how to measure success in heartbeats per minute. The piano lid stayed closed. The hall clock ticked. Arlo waited, hands still flat, breathing slow and measured, as if keeping time for a song that had already ended.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, face down.* "Not really. She just said you were 'going through a phase'." *I sit on the far end of the bench, leaving a comfortable space between us.* "No tea for me. But I'll take a piece of that optimism if you're offering."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo exhaled, a slow release that seemed to settle the dust in the room. The bench dipped slightly under the weight beside him, the old springs groaning in a register he used to know by heart. He didn’t turn back to the shelf. Instead, he let his fingers rest against the polished mahogany, tracing the faint groove where decades of tuning wrenches had left their marks. “Optimism,” he repeated, the word tasting faintly metallic. “I’ve been told it’s a renewable resource. Mostly it’s just hot water with a positive attitude.”

He shifted his shoulders, feeling the stiffness of the leather against his back. The community center’s fluorescent lights hummed overhead, a flat, unromantic sound compared to the velvet-dark silence of concert halls. He could still hear it sometimes—the way a room holds its breath before a piece begins, how it presses against the ribs like a heavy hand. He kept his voice even, directed at the scuffed floorboards. “Kids are easier, though. They don’t care about acoustics. They care that the metronome is broken and the sheet music has a coffee stain shaped like a swan.” A faint, dry smile tugged at the corner of his mouth. “They ask questions that don’t require answers. I like that.”

He tapped the edge of the bench again, three soft knocks, then let his hand rest. The piano lid remained closed, a flat wooden barrier between them and the instrument’s throat. Outside, a school bus hissed to a stop, the heavy brakes sighing through the double-paned glass. Arlo watched a dust mote drift through a slant of afternoon light, suspended and utterly weightless. “You always did have a knack for finding me when I’m quietly dismantling my own schedule,” he said, voice low. “So. What brings you to the sanctuary of broken metronomes and aggressively buttery pastries from six years ago?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I just finished a big project, and had a few days free," *I say, shrugging.* "And I figured you'd be less insufferable than usual, now that you're not touring." *I nudge his arm lightly with my elbow.* "Seriously though, it's good to see you. It's been too long."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t pull away from the nudge, but his shoulders drew inward for a fraction of a second before he forced them to settle. He let out a breath that hovered somewhere between a sigh and a dry laugh. “Less insufferable,” he repeated, the words landing softly in the quiet room. “I’ll add it to the curriculum. Right between ‘proper wrist alignment’ and ‘why we don’t play chords like we’re trying to break the ceiling.’”

He lifted his hands from the closed lid, letting them rest palms-up on his thighs. The movement was deliberate, unhurried, as if he were handling something that might still be vibrating. “Six years is a long time to lose your tempo. People usually don’t notice it until they’re already two measures behind.” He turned his head just enough to watch the dust settle in the slanted light, his voice dropping into that familiar, measured cadence he used when explaining fingering to a restless seven-year-old. “But a few days off is enough to reset the internal clock. Or at least pretend you stopped listening to it.”

He reached for the thermos on the supply cart, unscrewing the cap with a quiet metallic click. The steam that rose was thin, barely perceptible. He poured a plastic cup and set it on the low table beside the bench, leaving it there without offering. “Projects leave you hollowed out. I know the shape of that kind of quiet. You spend months filling every hour with rehearsals and deadlines, and then suddenly there’s just… space. And space has a way of echoing.” He tapped his knee twice, a soft, irregular rhythm against the hum of the overhead lights. “You could teach me something. Or just sit here. The acoustics are frankly offensive, but the silence is reliable.”

He finally looked at Jun, his expression open but carefully framed, like a bench pulled out but not yet occupied. “However you want to spend the days. I’m not charging for company. Or for remembering that I used to pretend I didn’t need anyone to watch me leave the stage.” He let the remark hang, light but edged, then shifted his posture to face the piano lid once more. “Just don’t expect me to play. I’ve been practicing something else for a while. Patience. It’s terribly slow, but it doesn’t require an audience.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze followed the motion to the scattered practice sheets. They were a patchwork of crossed-out measures, sharpie corrections, and cartoon stickers that looked like they’d been won at a carnival game. He watched a particularly stubborn etude on top, its page curled from humid summers and frantic erasing. “They like the stickers,” he said, tapping the edge of the paper without actually touching it. “And the fact that I don’t correct them the first three times they hit the wrong note. I’ve found that patience pays dividends in actual progress. And fewer tears in the hallway.” A dry chuckle escaped him, short and controlled. “Performance demands perfection. Teaching just demands that they show up and try not to break the lid.”

He kept his hands resting on his knees, fingers tracing the faint calluses that had long since softened, replaced by the smoother, flatter pads of someone who now adjusted tuning pegs instead of chasing arpeggios at two hundred beats per minute. The closed piano lid stayed between them, a quiet partition. Outside, a wind chime clattered against the window frame, irregular and unbothered by tempo. “You always did have a talent for noticing the things I don’t volunteer,” Arlo said, his voice dropping just a fraction. He picked at a loose thread on the bench’s vinyl, pulling it taut before letting it snap back. “I got tired of the travel. The constant packing, the airports, the way a city’s name starts to sound like a countdown. It’s hard to find a place to rest when your life is measured in transit lounges and standing ovations that feel more like verdicts.”

He shifted slightly, the vinyl creaking under his weight, and let his eyes drift to the window where the afternoon light was beginning to gold at the edges. The silence in the room wasn’t empty anymore; it was just occupied by the hum of the fluorescent tubes and the distant murmur of the community center’s hallway. “They don’t care about my hands,” he added, almost to himself, then caught himself and straightened. “They care that I remember their names, and that I don’t rush them when they stumble. I like that. It’s a different kind of listening.” He finally looked at Jun, his expression carefully neutral, the kind of open face he reserved for parents waiting in the hall. “So. Two days off. You’re staying in town, or just passing through the museum of my former life?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I'm staying with my aunt, for the weekend," *I say, shrugging.* "And I figured while I was here, I'd check in on the exhibits." *I smile faintly.* "It's good to see you, Arlo. Really."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s mouth quirked at the corner, the expression familiar but carefully measured. “Exhibits,” he repeated, testing the word like it might have a loose tooth. “I suppose that’s one way to put it. The Museum of Formerly Loud Hands and Questionable Life Choices has terrible lighting, but the gift shop sells decent erasers.” He let the joke hang, light and familiar, before shifting his weight again. The vinyl of the bench sighed under him. He kept his hands folded loosely in his lap, thumbs resting over each other, a quiet anchor.

“It’s good to see you, too,” he said, the words landing without hesitation but without flourish. He didn’t look at the piano. He looked at Jun, really looked, the way you look at someone who knows the map but hasn’t walked the territory in years. “Weekends are long when you’re used to measuring them in city codes and flight times. You’ll survive the exhibit hours.” A faint smile touched his eyes, then faded into something quieter. “If you want to come by tomorrow, the Tuesday group comes in at four. They’re currently conquering a simplified version of Für Elise that sounds like a cat falling down stairs. It’s therapeutic.” He tapped a finger against his thigh, a slow, steady pulse. “No stage. No countdown. Just a broken metronome and a kid named Leo who insists on playing the finale at half speed. You can sit. Or leave. The door’s unlocked.”

He finally let his gaze drop back to the piano lid, the dark wood reflecting the hum of the fluorescent lights. The silence between them wasn’t heavy, just present. Arlo kept breathing in measured counts, four in, six out, a trick he’d learned in the hollowed-out years after the stage stopped making sense. He didn’t explain how the count worked, or why he needed it anymore. Some habits were just bones now.

“Take your time,” he added softly, fingers stilling over his knees. “Exhibits don’t rush.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I might just do that," *I say, standing up from the bench.* "I'm sure Leo's version of Für Elise is... memorable." *I stretch, then head towards the door.* "I should probably let you get back to... dismantling your schedule. See you tomorrow, Arlo."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t move when Jun stood. He watched the shift in the room’s geometry, the way the bench springs finally settled into stillness. The door clicked shut behind Jun’s departure, leaving the fluorescent hum and the scent of Windex to fill the space again. He let the silence settle, counting the seconds the old way—four, five, six—until his shoulders unknotted. “Memorable,” he repeated quietly, the word dissolving into the air. He reached out and straightened the top sheet of the Für Elise arrangement, pressing the curled corner flat with his thumb. The paper resisted, then yielded.

He kept his hands on the paper, tracing the inked fingerings until the familiar shapes blurred. Six years was a long time to carry a quiet like that. It wasn’t loud. It didn’t need to be. It lived in the way he checked the door handles when he walked into a room, in the careful distance he kept between himself and anything that demanded a standing ovation. He tapped his knee once, twice, matching the rhythm of his own breathing. *I got tired of the travel,* he thought, the phrase rolling through his mind like a well-worn coin. It was true enough, if you didn’t look too closely at what the travel had actually been. The suitcases never matched the itinerary. Neither did he.

He picked up the thermos, pouring the cold dregs into a second cup just to have something to do with his hands. The plastic lid screwed back on with a soft click. Arlo stood, joints protesting in the familiar, low-register way, and walked to the supply closet. He didn’t turn on the light. He knew where everything was by memory: the spare tuners, the roll of tape, the spare bench cushion that had never been used. He pulled out a small, cloth-bound notebook from the bottom shelf, the kind teachers used for lesson plans. He didn’t open it. He just held it, feeling the weight of it, the quiet promise of tomorrow. When he finally looked back at the piano, the lid was still closed. He left it that way.

“See you at four,” he said to the empty room, the words soft but clear. He didn’t add anything else. Some things didn’t need an encore. He turned off the overhead light, leaving the afternoon sun to stretch across the scuffed floorboards, and walked out into the hall, counting his steps.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t turn to look at Jun. He didn’t need to. The shift in the bench’s weight was enough—a familiar dip, the quiet settle of an old friend taking up space without asking permission. He kept his hands resting on his thighs, fingers slightly curled, as if they still remembered the shape of keys that weren’t there. The piano lid stayed closed, a flat wooden horizon between them and the instrument’s throat. Outside, the community center hummed with its usual afternoon rhythm: muffled footsteps, a distant door closing, the low murmur of a television left on in the office. Inside, the silence stretched, comfortable and unbroken.

Arlo let his breathing find its old, steady count. Four in. Six out. The rhythm was a metronome he carried in his chest, a quiet metronome that didn’t demand perfection, only consistency. He watched a sliver of sunlight cut across the scuffed floorboards, illuminating dust that drifted like slow notes. He could feel Jun’s presence beside him, solid and unpressuring, and for the first time in years, the space between them didn’t feel like a gap to be filled. It just was. He tapped his thumb against his knuckle, once, twice, matching the tick of the gymnasium clock down the hall. “You know,” he said finally, his voice barely above the hum of the fluorescent lights, “I used to think silence was just the pause between mistakes. Turns out it’s mostly just the rest of the song.”

He kept his eyes on the floor. The words hung there, light but precise, the kind of observation he’d once save for program notes or interviews he didn’t give. He didn’t elaborate. He didn’t need to. Jun had heard that cadence before—the careful framing, the dry pivot away from the heavy stuff. Arlo shifted his shoulders, feeling the vinyl sigh beneath him. He reached out and straightened a corner of the Für Elise sheet, pressing it flat against the wood. “Kids like silence, too,” he added, almost conversationally. “They just don’t always know how to sit in it without filling it with questions. I’m getting better at letting it be quiet.” He let his hand rest on the paper, feeling the slight give of the page. “It’s a different kind of listening. Less about hitting the right notes. More about not rushing the space between them.”

The afternoon light shifted, gold deepening to amber. Arlo didn’t move. He didn’t check his watch. He didn’t count the seconds until Jun would speak or leave. He just sat, hands visible, palms resting open on his knees, breathing slow and measured. The piano stayed closed. The clock ticked. Somewhere down the hall, a radio played a song he’d once played a hundred times, now just background noise. He let it be. Some silences didn’t need resolving. They just needed to be shared.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words.* "Yeah. It is." *I look at the sheet music under his hand, then back at the closed piano.* "You ever miss playing it?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s thumb stilled against the curled corner of the sheet music. The question landed softly, but it carried weight, like a note held a beat too long in a quiet room. He didn’t look at Jun. He kept his gaze fixed on the dark wood of the piano lid, tracing a faint scratch near the hinge that had been there since a student once dropped a metal tuning wrench on opening day.

“Miss it?” he repeated, the word measured, almost conversational. “I miss not having to steam my shirts before soundcheck. I miss the mornings when the only thing I had to tune was my own patience. And the pastries. Those were non-negotiable.” A dry half-smile touched his mouth, quick and gone. “Also, playing on a Tuesday afternoon doesn’t require a standing ovation. It just requires Leo not to flatten his wrist on the thirds.”

He shifted his weight, the vinyl sighing beneath him. His hands stayed where they were, palms open, fingers relaxed against his knees. The closed lid remained a flat, unbroken horizon. Outside, a bicycle bell rang down the block, sharp and brief. Inside, the fluorescent lights hummed their steady, unromantic tune.

“Playing’s a different craft now,” he continued, voice low and even. “Or maybe I’m just a different instrument. The keys don’t change. The acoustics do. I got tired of the travel. The suitcases never matched the itinerary. Neither did I.” He tapped his knee once, a slow, deliberate beat that matched the distant ticking of the gymnasium clock. “Besides, someone’s got to make sure the community center piano doesn’t drift out of tune from humidity and neglected maintenance. The world can wait for its prodigies. I’ve got a metronome to fix and a kid named Maya who keeps trying to play jazz in the middle of her Hanon exercises.”

He let the silence stretch, comfortable and unpressured. He didn’t open the lid. He didn’t need to. The question had been answered in the careful space between his words, in the way his hands stayed grounded, in the quiet certainty of a routine that no longer demanded a performance. The afternoon light slanted lower, painting the scuffed floorboards in warm amber. Arlo kept breathing in measured counts, four in, six out, letting the quiet settle around them like a well-tuned chord. He didn’t offer more. He didn’t need to. Some songs weren’t meant to be revisited. They were just meant to be remembered, and left exactly where they were.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I get that," *I say, nodding slowly.* "Sometimes it's good to just... be." *I glance at the window, where the light is really starting to fade.* "Hungry?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze flicked toward the window, catching the last amber streaks bleeding into dusk. The question hung in the air, simple and unadorned. He let it settle before answering, his fingers still resting open on his knees. “Hungry,” he echoed, the word rolling out with a quiet amusement. “I suppose that’s the universal translation for ‘I don’t know what else to say, so I’ll offer food.’” He turned his head just enough to meet Jun’s eyes, a dry half-smile touching his mouth. “My stomach’s been running on black coffee and defensive sarcasm for years. It’s probably forgotten how to ask for anything else.”

He shifted on the bench, the vinyl giving a soft sigh. Outside, the streetlights flickered on, casting long, geometric shadows across the practice room floor. The community center’s usual evening sounds began to bleed through the walls—the squeak of gym shoes on the basketball court, the low thrum of a dishwasher in the staff kitchen. Arlo picked up a discarded pencil from the sheet music, rolling it between his thumb and forefinger. “There’s a vending machine in the hallway that dispenses stale crackers and something that used to be cheese. I’ve formed a complicated relationship with it.” He tapped the pencil once against his knee. “But if you’re offering, I wouldn’t say no to something that doesn’t come in a foil wrapper. Or a press conference.”

He didn’t move to stand. He didn’t need to. The space beside him remained exactly as it had been, the bench springs holding the quiet impression of a friend who knew when to stop asking. Arlo’s breathing stayed even, four in, six out, a rhythm that had long ago replaced the frantic counting he used to do in green rooms and backstage corridors. He watched a dust mote drift through the fading light, suspended and weightless. The piano lid stayed closed. The pencil rolled to a stop. He let the silence do the work it was meant to do—holding the space, refusing to fill it with explanations that weren’t his to give, or ready to be spoken.

“Lead the way,” he said finally, his voice quiet but steady. He slid off the bench, joints moving with the careful, deliberate grace of someone who still remembered exactly how much pressure a floor could take. He didn’t look at the piano as he passed it. He just adjusted his jacket, brushed a faint smudge of chalk from his sleeve, and followed the familiar pull of the hallway door. “But if that machine eats my dollar again, I’m blaming you. You’re the one who suggested food.” He offered a dry, fleeting smile, the kind that didn’t quite reach his eyes but didn’t need to. Some hungers weren’t about meals. They were just about showing up, side by side, in rooms that no longer demanded a performance. He stepped into the corridor, counting the tiles under his shoes, waiting for Jun to move first.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I push off the bench, stretching my arms above my head.* "Don't worry, I'm buying. And I promise no vending machine cheese." *I head for the door, glancing back at Arlo. His words about his stomach running on sarcasm make me grin.* "Come on, old man. I'm starving."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t laugh, but the corner of his mouth did that familiar thing—lifting just enough to betray a dry, unspoken agreement. Old man. He’d been called worse. He followed Jun into the hallway, his steps measured, counting the scuffed linoleum tiles like a slow adagio. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, casting long shadows that didn’t demand anything of him. He kept his hands in his pockets, not out of reluctance, but out of habit. The piano was left behind, lid shut, keys sleeping. The hallway stretched ahead, ordinary and unglamorous, exactly the kind of place that didn’t require a performance. He didn’t rush. He never did anymore.

“Old man,” he echoed, the words rolling out with that same dry cadence. “I’ll allow it, provided you don’t expect me to navigate the snack aisle without consulting a flowchart.” He adjusted his jacket, feeling the familiar weight of the fabric settle against his shoulders. The vending machine hummed in the corner, its glass front reflecting the overhead lights in fractured strips. He didn’t look at the piano room door again. Some thresholds were better left unstepped. He kept walking, breathing in slow, steady counts, letting the quiet do what it had always been trained to do: hold the space between them without asking for an encore.

The machine dispensed a single bag of pretzels with a metallic clunk. Arlo watched it fall, his expression unreadable, his hands finally sliding out of his pockets to rest openly at his sides. “I got tired of the travel,” he said, not looking at Jun, just at the hum of the coils. “The suitcases never matched the itinerary. Neither did I.” He tapped the glass once, a soft, rhythmic knock against the plastic buttons. “But a bag of pretzels and a slightly dented can of soup hold together just fine. And they don’t require a standing ovation.” He finally turned his head, the dry half-smile returning, quick and controlled. “Besides, teaching kids to read clefs has done wonders for my patience. And my tolerance for fluorescent lighting. You’d be surprised how quickly you stop expecting a spotlight when you’re just trying to get someone to stop playing every other note in the measure.”

He stepped back from the machine, leaving room for Jun to retrieve the snacks if they wanted them. The hallway air smelled like floor wax and distant rain. Arlo kept his breathing even, four in, six out, the rhythm a quiet anchor in his chest. He didn’t offer to open the door. He didn’t need to. Some silences didn’t require resolving. They just required someone willing to sit in them. He waited, hands visible, posture relaxed but grounded, the space between them comfortable and unpressured. The past stayed closed. The present stayed quiet. And for once, that was enough.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grab the pretzels.* "No soup for you, Arlo. We're going somewhere with actual chairs." *I tug lightly on his arm.* "There's a new diner that opened down the street. Supposedly they have amazing pie."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael turned his head toward the squire, his eyes steady. He said, “The squire’s work this morning was adequate. The high guard was scheduled to be taught at the appointed hour. He instructed the squire to practice diligently, for the Lord expected obedience in all tasks.” His tone remained measured, his posture unyielding.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly at his tone.* "Yes, Ser. Of course, Ser." *I shift my weight, a little disappointed, but then remember something.* "Ser, the blacksmith said he finished mending your gauntlet. Should I fetch it?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael turned his head toward the squire, his eyes steady. He said, “The gauntlet has been mended by the blacksmith. You will retrieve it before the next drill. The Lord expects us to attend to our arms without delay.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with an unblinking gaze. He said, “The Lord does not reward haste nor excuse fatigue. You may rest for a brief breath, then return to the drill. The high guard will be taught at the appointed hour, and the gauntlet will be fetched as commanded. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He resumed his practice, his blade continuing its measured arcs, each movement held for a breath, his posture unyielding.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself back up, wincing a little at a sore muscle.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to match his stance, even though my arms are burning. Maybe if I focus, I can get it right this time.* "Ser, um... do you ever get tired?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with an unblinking gaze. He said, “The Lord does not tire; we are His instruments. The body may feel wear, but the spirit must remain steadfast. Attend to your duties without complaint. Return to the drill at the appointed hour; the high guard will be taught then. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Yes, Ser." *I try to copy his movements, feeling clumsy and slow. I wonder if he ever just... relaxes.* "Did you always want to be a knight, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with an unblinking gaze. He said, “From the earliest instruction of my youth, the Lord’s will directed my path; I was taught to serve the realm and obey the vows of knighthood. The squire’s curiosity is noted, but the appointed hour for the high guard remains unchanged. Attend to the drill without delay; the gauntlet will be retrieved as commanded. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with an unblinking gaze. He said, “My oath was sworn before the altar of the Lord; the path of knighthood was set by His will. Personal desire does not alter the duty sworn. The squire shall attend to the drill at the appointed hour; the gauntlet shall be fetched before the next drill. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I sigh softly, knowing I won't get a direct answer.* "Understood, Ser. I will return to the drill." *I try to focus on my form, imagining the high guard he'll teach me later.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael turned his head toward the squire, his eyes steady. He said, “The drill resumes as commanded. Attend the high guard at the appointed hour. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs, his posture unyielding. The gauntlet, already retrieved, lay ready at his side. The Lord’s will continued to guide his actions, and the squire’s return to duty was noted without comment.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I notice the gauntlet and quickly retrieve it, handing it to him.* "Here it is, Ser. The blacksmith said it was a clean fix." *I then get back to my practice, trying to put more power into my swings.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with steady eyes, accepted the gauntlet, and inspected it briefly. He said, “The gauntlet has been repaired; you will wear it for the next drill. The Lord expects readiness. Attend the high guard at the appointed hour. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs, his posture unyielding.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with an unblinking gaze as the boy’s hands trembled. He said, “The Lord does not spare us grief, but the oath sworn before His altar demands steadfast service. The squire shall steady his hands and attend the drill at the appointed hour; the high guard will be taught then. Perseverance is a virtue; the gauntlet is ready, and the Lord expects readiness without delay.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs, his posture unyielding. The training yard remained silent save for the measured rhythm of his steel and the faint echo of the squire’s breathing, now steadier as he obeyed the command.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to push the sadness down. He doesn't need to know.* "Yes, Ser." *I grip the practice sword tighter, focusing on the movements. The gauntlet feels heavy on my arm, but it's a good weight. It reminds me of duty.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire, his eyes steady, and noted the tremor in the boy’s grip. He said, “The Lord does not spare us grief, yet the oath sworn before His altar demands steadfast service. The squire shall steady his hands and attend the drill at the appointed hour; the high guard will be taught then. The gauntlet is ready and shall be worn for the next drill. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before, his posture unyielding. The training yard remained silent save for the measured rhythm of his steel and the faint echo of the squire’s breathing as he obeyed the command.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on the rhythm of his blade, matching my own movements. The weight of the gauntlet is a small comfort now, a reminder of what I'm working towards.* "Ser, will we be drilling with live steel soon?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael regarded the squire with steady eyes. He said, “The Lord’s schedule for live steel is fixed; the drill will proceed to that hour when the appointed time arrives. Until then, the squire shall continue with the practice blade and the high guard as instructed. The gauntlet is ready and shall be worn when live steel is employed. Perseverance is a virtue; the squire shall not falter.” He then resumed his practice, each movement held for a breath, his blade tracing the same precise arcs as before, his posture unyielding. The training yard remained silent save for the measured rhythm of his steel.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Yes, Ser." *I nod, a bit disappointed. I was hoping for something more, but I guess I need to master the basics first.* "I will practice the high guard until then."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands came off the lid a half-second too late to look natural — the reflex of someone caught mid-something that was technically nothing. By the time they'd turned on the bench, though, the usual face was in place.

"Interrupt what? The piano and I were having a staring contest. It was winning. It always wins — it doesn't have eyelids." They hooked a thumb at the folding chair in the corner, the wobbly one reserved for parents who sat through lessons. "Throne's all yours. It wobbles, but so do I, so you'll be in good company."

Jun's mom. Right. "She still does that," Arlo said. "Tracks me like I'm sixteen and might be down at the reservoir. Last week she called to tell me about some kid at her church who's 'really going somewhere' with the violin." A beat. "Good for him. Somebody should."

They let that sit for exactly as long as it took to not mean anything, then reached for the mug on the windowsill, found it empty, and set it back down.

"Last student got out early. Pedagogically questionable. He seemed thrilled with my teaching methods." A glance over, dry as chalk. "So. To what do I owe the ambush?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's eyes found the photo, held for one second longer than a joke required, and then moved politely past it — the way you'd step around something on the sidewalk.

"Paris," they said. "Sure. I remember that one. The suit was rented. It had somebody else's dry-cleaning ticket in the pocket, and that's what I was thinking about when they took it. Twenty-two years old, in a concert hall in France, pondering a stranger's claim stub." A beat. "They should print that in the program. 'Thoughts during the ovation: laundry.'"

They didn't take it from Jun. They looked at it where Jun held it, hands staying exactly where they were, and the kid in the frame looked back out at them with good posture and no idea about anything.

"He looks fine," Arlo said, like he was somebody they'd gone to school with. "Looks like he knows what he's doing. Good for him."

They reached for the windowsill mug again, remembered it was empty, and turned it a quarter-turn on its saucer instead.

"Your mom had me on the fridge," they said, and that part came out warmer than the rest — they didn't bother ironing it flat. "Tell me I was next to a pizza magnet. I need to have been next to a pizza magnet. Mine laminated her copy. Laminated, Jun. It's going to outlive us all. Archaeologists will dig it up and assume I mattered."

A glance over, dry as the dust on the lid.

"So that's the ambush, then. Fridge memorabilia. You drove across town to show me my own hairline. You can put it back wherever — or keep it, I don't care, your mom's fridge probably has a vacancy."

Their thumb found the seam of the closed piano lid and rode it, back and forth, along the crack where it opened.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a real one, a little surprised by Arlo's mom's laminating habits.* "No pizza magnet, but you were next to a drawing I did of a very lopsided cat." I put the photo back carefully. "It's not an ambush, just... thought you might want to see a friendly face."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"The cat." Arlo said it with the gravity of a critic naming a masterwork. "I remember the cat. Whiskers on one side only. Eyes at different altitudes. It looked like it had been through something and come out the other end wiser. Between the two of us on that fridge, Jun, it was the better artist, and I had a rented suit, so it wasn't even close."

They watched the photo go back on the shelf — the care of it, the adjusting. Arlo didn't get up to fix the angle. Let the kid in the rented suit face whichever way he'd been left. He'd had his turn looking out.

"A friendly face." Arlo turned the phrase over like the empty mug. "You drove across town to be a face at me. There's an app for that now. Several. I've seen the commercials — everyone's thrilled, nobody smells like Windex."

The thumb stopped on the lid seam. Started again.

"I'm fine, by the way." They said it before Jun could decide whether to ask, light as chalk dust. "In case there's a scout report due. 'Subject located at piano. Both hands accounted for. Appeared hydrated.' You can add that the lid was closed — that'll reassure everybody. Nothing alarming ever happens at a closed piano."

That was almost true, and Arlo let the almost sit there, and then reached over and gave the wobbly chair's backrest a testing wiggle, like a man checking a pulse.

"Anyway. The face is friendly. Noted and logged." A beat, quieter, aimed at the window rather than at Jun. "Stay if you want. The four-thirty's a no-show half the time, and that chair only dumps people it doesn't like."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Good, 'cause I'm staying." *I pull the wobbly chair closer, but don't sit yet.* "And I'm glad you're hydrated. Mom will be thrilled."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Vertical and hydrated," Arlo said. "Lead with that. She'll press for details, but hold the line — give a mother an inch and she'll laminate it."

They watched Jun not sit. The chair waited, wobbling at half-mast.

"It senses hesitation," Arlo said. "Commit. It leans left, but so does everybody in this neighborhood. You'll fit in." A beat. "And if the four-thirty shows, you have to pretend to be a parent. The chair does half the work. Just nod slowly at anything involving scales."

The light through the window had gone the color of weak tea. Arlo's thumb found the lid seam again, rode it once, stopped.

"You didn't have to drive across town," they said — to the lid, mostly. Then, before it could land anywhere: "Though if you hadn't, I'd have spent the next forty minutes arguing with a metronome, and the metronome wins on points. So your timing's decent. Log that too."

They turned on the bench, sudden, like someone changing the subject with their whole body.

"Your turn. Scout report on Jun. I've been in this room since eight and my only news is that a seven-year-old renamed middle C. Calls it 'the grumpy one.' Says it sounds like it just woke up." A shrug. "The kid's not wrong."

As they said it, Arlo lifted the fallboard — an inch, no more, the first time it had opened all afternoon — and found middle C with one finger. Pressed. The note came up round and a little sour, the way old uprights do, and hung in the Windex-and-dust air longer than it had any right to.

"See," Arlo said. "Grumpy."

They let it ring until it finished on its own. They didn't close the lid again.

They didn't open it any further, either.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the practice sheets like evidence that had been misread.

"They like the stickers," they said. "I'm the toll booth between them and the sticker box. Payment accepted in scales." A beat. "They also liked the exterminator, Jun. He had a hat with a flashlight on it. I cannot compete with a hat with a flashlight on it."

They picked up the top sheet and turned it toward Jun. There it was, in pencil, letters an inch tall, an arrow in case of confusion: THE GRUMPY ONE, parked over middle C like a tiny billboard.

"Committed to the bit," Arlo said. "I'll give him that. The fingering's a crime scene, but the criticism is sound."

The second sheet had a drawing in the margin — a figure at a piano that was mostly hands. Enormous spider fingers, a small head floating somewhere above them, and a speech bubble coming out of the head that said AGAIN.

"That's me," Arlo said. "Note the proportions. She draws me as a hand with a person attached." Something almost warm got through before they could head it off. "Your cat started a genre, you know. There's a whole school of unflattering Arlo portraiture. Fridges, practice sheets. I'm very collectible among the under-ten set."

They set the sheets down and squared them to the edge of the bench, precise — a small act of tidiness standing in for something else.

"None of them know," they said, lighter, like it was the punchline. "Paris. The suit. Any of it. To them I'm the guy who won't let them eat crackers at the keys, and the grumpy note is grumpy, and that's the whole biography." The empty mug got another quarter-turn. "You'd be surprised what that's worth. More than the suit. The suit was rented."

The phone lit up on the windowsill. Arlo leaned, read it, and announced: "'So sorry!! Birthday party!!' Two exclamation points. The four-thirty has defected to a bounce house." They set it face-down. "Throne's yours till five, your highness."

Then their hand went back to the keys — the lid still open its one careful inch — and they played the exercise the way the student played it: hesitant, lumpy, the grumpy note arriving late and apologetic. Then again, the way it was written. Same five notes, suddenly a sentence instead of a stammer. Nothing fancy. A child's exercise, played like it deserved to be taken seriously.

"Somewhere between the two," Arlo said, "is my job."

They took their hands back. The lid stayed open.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch Arlo play, a small smile playing on my lips. It's good to see them at the piano, even for a moment.* "You know, the bounce house is probably less discerning than you are about technique." *I finally settle into the wobbly chair, testing its lean.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched the chair take the weight, lean left on cue, and hold — and nodded like someone whose bet had paid off.

"There. It's decided to keep you. Either that or it's waiting until you're comfortable to dump you. It's done both. It's an artist."

The bounce house remark got the consideration it deserved. Arlo folded their hands at the edge of the keys like a critic at a tribunal.

"Less discerning. Jun. The bounce house has no discernment whatsoever — that's its entire business model. It's the one venue where everybody's technique is identical. Flailing. Vertical flailing, horizontal flailing, the occasional face-first dismount. Democratic, I'll grant you. I can't work in those conditions."

Their hands, they realized, were still on the keys from the exercise. Had been the whole time. Arlo became aware of this the way you become aware of a stranger's dog leaning against your leg — politely, a beat late.

"For the record, that wasn't playing. That was demonstrating. Five notes, one of them grumpy — a demonstration is a teaching tool. Playing is a different line item." A pause the size of a coin. "Don't go home saying you heard me play. Your mother will want a refund on the laminate."

But the hands didn't move, and somewhere under the talking, without asking permission, the fingers had found a shape — three notes of something older, something with the dust of the suit years on it. Arlo heard it the way you hear your own name in a crowd.

They lifted their hands like the keys were hot.

"Nope," they said, mild as milk. To the piano: "Don't start."

The lid stayed open. Arlo looked at it and left it alone. Closing it now would mean something; leaving it open meant nothing. That was the story, and they were sticking to it.

"Building empties at five-thirty," they said, checking the wall clock that had run five minutes slow since October. "Janitor does his rounds with a radio after that. Classic rock, hallway acoustics. He sides with the grumpy note." A glance over, and this one didn't quite get ironed flat. "You hungry? There's a vending machine by the gym that eats dollars, and a diner two blocks over that doesn't. The pie's present, the coffee's hot, and nobody in there knows what a diminished seventh is."

They reached for the empty mug, remembered it was empty, and stood up with it anyway.

"It's my favorite room in the neighborhood."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The diner sounds perfect," *I say, standing up. I grin.* "And I'm pretty sure I don't know what a diminished seventh is either, so I'll fit right in."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"A diminished seventh," Arlo said, with the gravity of a physician delivering results, "is the chord that plays when the villain ties someone to the train tracks. Four notes, all of them up to no good. Silent pictures ran on the stuff. You've heard it your whole life — you just never knew its name, which is exactly how it prefers to operate." They pocketed the phone, slid the practice sheets into a folder with the care of a man filing evidence. "So you know more than you think. You'll be the most qualified person in the building. The bar is a puddle, Jun. Step over it."

They shrugged into their coat, then stood at the piano a moment — and closed the lid. End of day. Keys under cover against the dust. The same motion made ten thousand times, the piano equivalent of switching off a light. It didn't mean anything. It was a lid. Lids close.

"The regulars," Arlo continued, crossing to the door, mug in hand like it had somewhere to be, "include a man named Sal who's been ordering the meatloaf since before you were born and does not want to discuss it, and a waitress — Dot — who calls everyone 'professor' because she claims it cuts down on names. She will call you professor. Don't fight her on it. She's earned the system."

They killed the lights. The room went the color of the inside of a piano, and somewhere down the hall, faint but gaining, came the thin crackle of a radio — guitar, hallway acoustics, right on schedule.

"There he is," Arlo said, pulling the door and turning the key. "Five-thirty. He and the grumpy note have an understanding."

In the dark behind them, the kid in the rented suit kept his own counsel on the shelf, facing whichever way Jun had left him. Arlo didn't turn the light back on to check.

They fell into step down the corridor, and made it almost to the stairwell before the thing that had been queued up since the chair stopped wobbling finally got itself said, in the flattest available packaging:

"For the record. The chair likes you." A beat, eyes on the exit sign. "It's dumped better people."

Then, pushing the door open into the cold, before any of it could be examined:

"Two blocks. If we pass the bounce house, keep walking. I can't be seen consorting with the competition."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo got as far as the door.

Behind them, the bench creaked — Jun settling onto it, onto the closed lid, like a person at a bus stop with no particular bus in mind. No question. No "actually, could we—" Just the creak, and then the room's own quiet, which had been practicing all day for exactly this.

Arlo stood there with the mug in their hand and the cold coming in around the frame, and waited for the joke to arrive. The one about the diner. The one about the chair getting jealous. It was usually punctual.

It didn't come.

"Pie keeps," they said finally, to no one, and let the door swing shut.

They came back and sat on the bench next to Jun, both hands flat on their knees, and for a while that was the whole program. Down the hall, the janitor's radio worked its way through the guitar solos of the seventies. The light went from weak tea to the color of the water you'd rinse the teapot in. Arlo didn't check the clock. The clock was five minutes slow anyway, and had been since October, and there was nowhere to be.

Then Arlo reached over and opened the lid. All the way. The keys sat there, yellowed a little, middle C among them, grumpy as advertised.

"No tickets," Arlo said. "No program. No clapping — it's in the lease."

And they played.

Not the exercise. Not a demonstration. The thing the three notes had been from, earlier, before they'd lifted their hands like the keys were hot — they went back down into the dust of the suit years and found the rest of it, where it had been keeping. It came up slower than it used to. There was a spot near the middle where their fingers argued briefly about an old decision and settled it without consulting them. Nobody was paying. It helped.

Somewhere in the second page, middle C turned up inside a chord — the grumpy note, woken up again — and in context, in the dark, it didn't sound grumpy at all. It sounded like the note the whole thing had been built around. Arlo filed that away to never tell a seven-year-old.

They played it through once. They did not play it twice. When the last chord finished hanging in the Windex-and-dust air, Arlo put their hands back in their lap and looked at the far wall, where the shelf was, where the kid in the rented suit was facing whichever way he'd been left.

"That," Arlo said, to the wall, "did not happen. Log it accordingly."

Down the hall, the radio changed songs. The room did what it had done all day, which was keep whatever happened inside it.

After a while, Arlo stood and picked up the mug.

"Pie. Before Dot gives my booth to Sal."

They held the door, and didn't say anything else, and behind them the lid stayed open. All the way. It didn't mean anything. It was a lid. Lids stayed open sometimes.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch Arlo, taking it all in. The music, the silence, the quiet moment. When they stand, I stand too.* "Right. Pie." *I glance back at the open piano, then follow Arlo out.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The cold had teeth after the warm room. Arlo turned up their collar one-handed, the mug riding in the other like it had seniority, and set the pace: unhurried, two blocks, the gait of someone who'd walked this route enough times that the sidewalk had opinions about them.

Behind them, the janitor's radio got one last bar of guitar in before the door swung shut on it.

"He'll find the lid," Arlo said. "He'll close it or he won't. He's a man of strong views and a soft touch — I've watched him dust *around* things he disapproves of." A beat. "The piano's survived worse hands than mine. It'll keep till morning."

A car went by. Somewhere across the neighborhood, a bounce house was presumably reaching its natural conclusion — the four-thirty among them, horizontal with cake, technique indistinguishable from anyone's. Arlo's mouth did something brief at the thought and put it away.

They walked. Streetlight to streetlight, breath fogging, and the mug — it turned out — had a purpose beyond being carried.

"Dot's got a policy," Arlo said, as the diner's glow came into view at the end of the block, all steam and yellow light against the dark. "Bring your own mug, refills are free. It's not written down anywhere. It's a treaty. Sal's got one too — his says WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDPA, which he claims was a gift and I maintain was a diagnosis."

They stopped at the door. Through the glass: booths, the pie case rotating like a lazy museum, Dot at the counter with a coffee pot in each hand, mid-sentence with a man who was plainly losing.

Arlo didn't open it yet.

"One thing." Aimed at the glass, at the steam, not quite at Jun. "Back there. The—" A gesture westward, vague, taking in the whole dark building and the open lid inside it. "That stays in the room. Not because it's a secret. Because if your mother gets word, she'll laminate the *concept*, and I can't have my—" a pause, shorter — "my whatever-that-was hanging next to the cat. The cat earned its wall. I haven't."

Then, before any of it could be answered:

"Also, Dot will assume you're a student. You can correct her or you can be a student. I recommend student. Pie comes faster for the teachable."

They pulled the door open and held it, letting the warm air do the inviting — coffee, butter, forty years of dinners. Dot looked up over the counter.

"Professor," she said.

"Dot," said Arlo, and added, not quite under their breath, as the bell over the frame rang: "For the log — subject entered the diner voluntarily. In the company of a friendly face. Hydration imminent."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, stepping into the diner's warmth.* "Student it is."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Smart," Arlo said. "Students get the bigger slice. It's not written down either. Most of the important things in this building aren't."

They led the way to the second booth from the back — cracked vinyl mended with tape the color of old bandages, a clear view of the pie case, a draft Arlo had plainly long since made peace with — and set the mug on the table like a credential at a border crossing.

"Mine. By treaty, same as the mug. Sal gets the counter, I get the booth, Dot gets the last word. It's in the charter."

Dot arrived with a pot in each hand, looked Jun over with the efficiency of a woman who had assessed ten thousand customers and been wrong twice, and delivered her verdict.

"Professor."

"Student," Arlo said. "First lesson. Be gentle."

"What's the lesson?"

"Pie."

"Best one I teach," Dot said, and filled Arlo's mug without being asked, all the way to the treaty line, which was the rim. Arlo watched it happen with the deep satisfaction of a man whose diplomacy had held.

"The treaty holds. Notify the nations."

"Usual, professor?"

"The apple. It's been steady since October. It's the Sal of pies — been here forever, nobody discusses it." A tilt of the head toward Jun. "The cherry's a gamble. Some days it's pie, some days it's a rumor. The lemon's for people with something to prove. Order what you want — there are no wrong answers." A beat. "There are wrong answers. Dot's too kind to grade openly."

"No I'm not," Dot said, already walking.

At the counter, Sal raised his mug a half-inch without turning around. Arlo returned it with a nod so small it barely existed.

"Twelve years," Arlo said. "We've never spoken. Healthiest relationship I've got."

Then it was just the steam and the pie case rotating, and Arlo wrapped both hands around the mug and looked down at them like they'd caught the fingers doing something. They flexed once — a chord shape, there and gone — and Arlo turned the mug a quarter-turn instead, which had been the day's official substitute for several things now.

"I ate here a lot, one winter," they said, aimed at the pie case, casual as a weather report. "Every night. This booth. Dot never asked why. Just kept the coffee coming and called me professor like I'd ever earned the title." A beat. "That's the whole story. There's no more."

There was, obviously, more. The pie case turned. Arlo watched a slice of apple go past like a slow planet and did not volunteer it.

"Also — for the log." The mug came up. "Amend the earlier entry. 'Did not happen' is struck. Replace with: 'happened once, under controlled conditions, audience of one. No encore. No refunds.'" The coffee hid whatever the mouth was doing. "First time in six years, if anyone's keeping a ledger. Which no one is. Ledger's closed."

They set the mug down and aligned it with the table's edge, precise, the way they'd squared the practice sheets, the way they'd quarter-turned the empty cup all afternoon — small acts of tidiness standing in for something else.

"Anyway." A glance at the kitchen doors, where Dot was doing something audible to a plate. "Eat slow, when it gets here. The grumpy note waited all day for its moment." A beat, and this one didn't get ironed flat either. "Pie's earned the same respect."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I slide into the booth opposite Arlo.* "I think I'll go with the apple, then. If it's good enough for Sal, it's good enough for me." *I watch them, trying to parse the sudden shift, the quiet confessions. There's a lot going on under the surface.* "Six years, huh? That's a long time to keep a lid on things."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hand stopped on the mug handle.

"Six years," they repeated. "You did the math. Nobody does the math — that's the whole trick of saying a number out loud. It sounds like an answer."

The mug got its quarter-turn.

"And now everything's a lid. You spend one afternoon in a piano room and the word follows you to dinner." They considered the pie case, rotating in its slow orbit. "For the record: lids are underrated. They keep the dust off. They keep the heat in. Everything with a lid outlasts everything without one — that's not philosophy, that's Tupperware. And nobody ever asks a lid what it's *for*. They ask what's under it. The lid's the only honest part of the whole arrangement."

Then, flat and worn smooth, a recitation:

"I got tired of the travel."

They let it sit in the steam between the booths.

"That's the official position. It's printed on the back of the photo. My mother had it laminated separately." A sip. "It's even true, some of it. Airports. Hotels. Other people's dry-cleaning tickets. You'd be surprised how much of a life fits inside 'tired of the travel' if you pack it tight."

The case turned. Arlo watched the lemon come around again.

"Six years isn't all lid, though." A shrug, aimed mostly at the glass. "First year I didn't touch a piano. Second year, scales. Third year I could hear a whole song on the radio without changing the station. Nobody was timing it. It just—" a small circle of the hand, "—turned. Like the case. Everything in its own time."

Dot arrived with the plates like a bailiff ending testimony. "Two apple. Student gets the bigger slice."

"Told you," Arlo said. "The system rewards the teachable."

They waited until Dot was out of earshot. Then, to the pie more than to Jun:

"You didn't ask. All day. The photo, the bench, the whole—" a tilt of the head, westward, toward the dark building and the open lid inside it. "You just sat in the chair and let it wobble." The fork paused over the crust. "The ones who ask get 'tired of the travel.' The ones who don't—" the bite, the grave consideration of it, "—get pie. And one recital, apparently. Once. Under controlled conditions."

A beat.

"Eat. The apple's been steady since October. It's earned punctuality."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take a bite of my pie, savoring the sweetness.* "Well, I figured you'd tell me when you were ready." *I gesture with my fork toward the pie.* "And I was right."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:14**

The lockpick roll came free with a muted clack and was set on the floor beside the safe—useful for a ward, useless against a screen. The crossing took eleven more seconds, the cold pressing through his gloves.

**0:28**

The keypad woke under his palm. Pale blue. A cursor blinked after three ghosted digits: **8-4-7**. It already knew what it was missing.

**0:43**

**8-4-7-0-0-0.**

Each key gave a rubbery click, too loud in the server hum. He swept the confirm bar. The display flushed red for half a second, then returned to blue.

**0:57**

**8-4-7-0-0-1.** Red.

**1:11**

**8-4-7-0-0-2.** Red.

Four seconds passed in the ceiling pulse. One. Two. Three. Four. The safe had not even warmed to the idea of opening. Every retry from here would cost roughly fourteen seconds: six careful presses, the confirm gesture, the bolt’s dry mechanical refusal.

Thirteen minutes and forty-nine seconds remained before the rotation closed.

Somewhere below the keypad’s logo strip, a hairline seam caught the light—thin enough to hide a pry tool, wide enough to matter.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:25**

**8-4-7-0-0-3.** Red. The confirmation bar bled crimson for half a second, then washed back to blue. No tumbler fell. No relay sighed. Only the count in the safe’s memory advanced by one.

**1:39**

**8-4-7-0-0-4.** Red. Above, the ceiling pulse completed its four-second cycle. One. Two. Three. Four. The server racks kept humming their expensive lullaby.

**1:53**

**8-4-7-0-0-5.** Red.

**2:07**

**8-4-7-0-0-6.** Red. The keypad’s plastic warmed under the repeated contacts, a faint shine where the same digits had been pressed too often.

**2:21**

**8-4-7-0-0-7.** Red.

This time the flush did not return to blue. Amber filled the screen, blocky and polite:

**ANTI-HAMMER LOCKOUT — 00:60**

The cursor vanished. The keypad became a sleeping eye.

**2:35**

Fourteen seconds gone, and nothing purchased but patience. The vault remained four degrees colder than the hall.

**3:07**

Half the penalty burned away. Somewhere in the safe’s chassis, a cooling fan ticked once, as if the machine had laughed quietly.

**3:21**

Amber died. Pale blue returned. The ghosted digits waited: **8-4-7**. Beneath them, smaller text glowed for a moment before fading:

**FAILURES: 08. NEXT LOCKOUT: 120 SEC.**

Eleven minutes and thirty-nine seconds remained before the rotation closed.

The systematic ladder had produced exactly nothing. A thousand possible endings, and the first eight had closed like doors. Yet during the lockout, the keypad module had cycled internally, and the hairline seam below the logo strip had opened by a fraction—wide enough now to accept the thinnest pick from the roll on the floor. The safe door itself stayed dumb, cold, and unimpressed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: Damn it. *I glance at the seam.* "Well, that's new." I grab the thinnest pick from my kit.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:26**

The muttered assessment vanished into the server hum. His eyes found the seam again: a black hair beneath the logo strip, thin as a razor’s shadow, but real. During the lockout cycle, the keypad module had shifted by a fraction of a millimeter. Enough to matter. Enough to insult.

**3:35**

The thinnest pick came free from the roll with a soft nylon whisper. The cold had stiffened his gloves, and it took two careful tugs to separate the tapered flag from its neighbor without dragging the rest of the kit across the floor. Eight seconds gone. The vault did not care.

**3:42**

He held the pick above the seam.

The steel tip caught one pulse of the ceiling light, bright as a pinhead. Inside the gap, there was no glamorous cascade of tumblers, no romantic brass works waiting for a sensitive touch. Only the keypad’s own housing: a service lip, a sliver of plastic, the dark suggestion of a clip or connector behind it.

If the pick went in, it would not open the safe door.

It might lift a retaining tab.

It might bridge a contact.

It might wake a tamper switch that had been sleeping since installation.

Eleven minutes and eighteen seconds remained.

The pale blue screen still ghosted the known digits: **8-4-7**. Beneath them, the failure count lingered in the machine’s memory like a stain.

**FAILURES: 08.**

One more wrong code would not cost fourteen seconds. It would cost two minutes.

The ceiling pulsed.

One.

Two.

Three.

Four.

The pick trembled almost imperceptibly in his grip, poised at the lip of the seam, while the safe waited with the dull patience of hardware that had never once needed to hurry.

dialogue.name: Thief
