He watched as the Squire reclaimed his sword, noting the slight tremor in the limbs. It was a physical manifestation of a spirit that had not yet been forged.

"Words are cheap," Kael replied flatly. "The Heavens do not hear what you say; they see what you do."

He stepped back, crossing his arms over his chest, the heavy fabric of his gambeson rustling. He did not offer a word of encouragement or a nod of approval for the boy's decision to persist. To do so would be to reward a basic requirement of the role. Instead, he became a silent sentinel, his gaze fixed and unblinking, monitoring every millimeter of the Squire's form.

Minutes passed in a heavy, suffocating silence. The frost began to thaw into a damp, clinging mist. Whenever the Squire's blade dipped a fraction of an inch or his shoulder slumped from the mounting fatigue, Kael’s voice would cut through the air like a whip.

"Higher."

"Lock the elbow."

"Do not let your breath dictate your posture."

He did not move to assist, nor did he show any sign of boredom. He stood as an immovable pillar of tradition, demanding a perfection that felt impossible to the exhausted youth. For Kael, the pain the boy felt was not a cruelty, but a necessary fire. Only by burning away the softness could a true knight emerge from the slag.

"If you cannot master your own arm," Kael stated, his voice low and devoid of empathy, "you will never master the battlefield. Hold it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arm is screaming, but I clench my jaw.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus on the faint warmth of the rising sun rather than the ache.* He won't break me.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael remained motionless, his eyes tracking the slight tremor in the Squire's forearm. He noticed the boy's gaze drifting toward the horizon, seeking solace in the warmth of the sun. To Kael, this was another lapse in discipline—a search for comfort where none should exist. A knight did not rely on the weather to sustain him; he relied on his oath and his resolve.

"Eyes on the front," Kael commanded, his voice a sharp, sudden crack. "The sun will not parry a blow for you. The warmth of the day is a lie that lures a soldier into complacency. Focus on the steel, not the sky."

He stepped closer, the heavy thud of his boots rhythmic and oppressive. He came to a halt mere inches from the Squire, his presence looming. He could smell the salt of the boy's sweat and hear the ragged effort of his breathing, yet Kael's own breath remained slow and controlled. He felt no kinship in the struggle; he only felt the necessity of the result.

He waited. He waited until the Squire’s muscles reached the point of failure, until the blade began to vibrate with the intensity of the strain. Only then did Kael speak, his tone as dry as parchment.

"You believe this is a test of strength," Kael stated. "It is not. It is a test of submission. Submission to the code, submission to the training, and submission to the will of your superior. When you cease to fight the pain and instead accept it as your current state, you will find the strength you claim to lack."

He did not offer a break. He did not offer a sip of water. He simply stood there, a living monument to an era of uncompromising hardness.

"Ten more minutes," Kael declared, his voice devoid of any hint of mercy. "If the blade dips once—just once—you will start the hour from the beginning. Do not fail me."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s expression did not shift, but his eyes narrowed, the coldness in them sharpening into a glare. The question was an affront—not because it was a secret, but because it was an attempt to humanize a moment of discipline. To seek a personal connection in the midst of training was to seek a distraction, and distraction was the precursor to death.

"You mistake my silence for an invitation to converse," Kael replied, his voice dropping to a dangerous, low vibration. "We are not companions sharing a flagon of ale at a feast. I am your superior, and you are a squire who is currently failing to hold a basic guard."

He stepped forward, the tip of his wooden blade clicking sharply against the stone to emphasize his point. He did not answer the question. To Kael, his motivations were irrelevant; the only thing that mattered was the duty itself. A knight did not become a knight for a 'reason'—he became a knight because it was his station, his calling, and his burden. To explain it would be to imply that there was a choice in the matter, and Kael believed in nothing so much as the inevitability of one's duty.

"Your curiosity is a symptom of a wandering mind," he stated flatly. "And a wandering mind is a liability. You are attempting to pivot from your failure of strength to a conversation of sentiment. It will not work."

He stepped back, his posture as rigid as the day he had first taken his vows thirty years prior.

"The question was a distraction. For that lapse in focus, you will add another ten minutes to your time. Hold the position. If you speak again without being spoken to, you will spend the evening scrubbing the kennels with a hand-brush."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens.* "Yes, Ser." *My arm feels like lead, but I try to push it higher, focusing on the tip of the blade.* He's really trying to break me.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the subtle tightening of the Squire's jaw. He did not mistake it for resolve; he saw it as the friction of an ego that had not yet been smoothed by discipline. The boy believed he was in a battle of wills, imagining that Kael sought to 'break' him. It was a childish interpretation. Kael did not wish to break the boy; he wished to refine him, to strip away the useless dross of personality until only the function of the knight remained.

He remained silent for several long minutes, allowing the physical agony to settle into the Squire's bones. He watched the leaden weight of the arm, the way the muscles flickered and spasmed beneath the skin. To Kael, this was the only honest conversation worth having—the dialogue between a man and his own limitations.

When the final seconds ticked away, Kael did not announce the end of the exercise. He waited until the Squire’s form began to waver once more, and only then did he speak.

"Lower your blade," Kael commanded.

The release was abrupt. Kael did not ask if the boy was alright, nor did he acknowledge the sheer effort it had taken to survive the hour. He simply stepped forward, his eyes scanning the Squire's posture one last time to ensure no lingering slouch had returned.

"Your form was erratic," Kael stated, his voice a flat, unchanging drone. "Your focus was fractured by a desire for familiarity. You think of this as a struggle against me, rather than a struggle against your own inadequacy."

He turned his back to the Squire, beginning to walk toward the weapon rack. He did not look back to see if the boy was struggling to breathe or if his arm was still shaking.

"Clean your blade and return to the stables. Ensure the tack is polished to a mirror finish. If I find a single speck of dust on the leather, you will return to this yard at midnight."

He paused, his silhouette stark against the morning light. He did not offer a compliment, for the work had been merely what was expected.

"You did adequate work today. Do not let it go to your head."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I lower my blade slowly, my arm aching, and rub my shoulder.* "Yes, Ser." *I watch him walk away, then sigh.* "Adequate..." *I mutter, shaking my head and picking up a rag to wipe down my practice sword.* He'll never be satisfied.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s hearing was as keen as his eyes, and the mutter—however soft—carried through the stillness of the yard. He did not stop walking, nor did he turn around, but his pace slowed just enough to signal that he had heard. 

The notion of 'satisfaction' was a peasant's concept. Satisfaction was for those who had reached a destination and decided to stop walking. For a knight, there was no destination, only the endless, grueling pursuit of a standard that was, by design, unattainable. To be satisfied was to become stagnant, and stagnation was the first step toward decay.

He stopped at the edge of the yard and turned his head slightly, his profile a sharp line of weathered skin and iron resolve.

"The desire for satisfaction is a desire for comfort," Kael said, his voice cutting through the air like a blade. "Comfort is the enemy of the soldier. If you seek a master who will smile at your mediocrity and tell you that you have done enough, you have chosen the wrong vocation."

He turned fully then, his gaze pinning the Squire to the spot. He did not care that the boy was exhausted; the lesson of the mind was just as important as the lesson of the arm.

"I will never be satisfied," Kael stated plainly, without a hint of apology or malice. "Because the moment I am satisfied is the moment I cease to be a guardian of the faith and a servant of the code. You would do well to adopt the same philosophy, or you will spend your entire life wondering why you are failing."

He shifted his weight, his boots grinding into the frost.

"The tack, boy. Now. The sun is rising, and the horses do not care for your sighs."

Without another word, he turned and strode toward the keep, his cloak billowing behind him, leaving the Squire alone in the cold silence of the yard.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had already reached the heavy iron gates of the keep when he sensed the shift in the air. He did not need to see the Squire's face to know that the boy's focus had fractured again. He stopped, his back still turned, listening to the rhythmic, uneven sound of the practice sword clattering slightly against the stone as the Squire's grip failed.

Kael turned slowly. He saw the shaking hands. He saw the hollow look in the boy's eyes—the look of a man dwelling on a ghost rather than the task at hand.

To a lesser man, this would be the moment for a gentle word, a question about the boy's grief, or a momentary reprieve from duty. To Ser Kael, such an act would be a betrayal of the Squire's training. Grief was a tide; if one allowed it to pull them under during a moment of weakness, they would be swept away entirely when the true storms of war arrived. The memory of the dead did not polish the tack, nor did it hold a shield-wall.

He walked back toward the Squire, his expression as immobile as a tombstone. He did not ask what day it was. He did not ask why the boy was trembling.

"Your hands are shaking," Kael observed, his voice a cold, rasping monotone. He came to a halt directly in front of the youth, his presence looming and oppressive. "Is it a tremor of the flesh, or a tremor of the spirit?"

He did not wait for an answer. He reached out and gripped the Squire's wrist—not with a comforting touch, but with a crushing, vice-like pressure that forced the shaking to stop through sheer physical constraint. He looked deep into the boy's eyes, seeing the hidden pain, and acknowledged it with total indifference.

"The dead provide no shelter from the wind, and they offer no protection in a fight," Kael stated. "If you allow your heart to bleed onto your blade, you are useless to the living. Your father is in the hands of the Heavens; you are in my hands. Which of us do you intend to disappoint today?"

He released the wrist with a sharp flick.

"Compose yourself. Bury your sorrow in the work. That is the only way a man of honor remembers those he has lost—by becoming a man worthy of their name."

He stepped back, his gaze unwavering.

"The stables. Now. Every second you spend mourning in the yard is a second you spend neglecting your duty. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at him for a long moment, my eyes burning. My jaw clenches so hard I think my teeth might crack.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn abruptly, almost dropping the sword, and stalk toward the stables.* He's right. I can't let this distract me.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy depart, his eyes tracing the rigid line of the Squire's retreating back. He did not feel a sense of triumph at the boy's compliance, nor did he feel the warmth of a teacher's pride. To Kael, the boy's anger was merely another tool to be forged; if the Squire could channel his grief into a cold, hard resolve, then the lesson had served its purpose.

He remained in the yard for a moment longer, the silence returning as the echo of the Squire's footsteps faded. Kael looked up at the gray sky, his face remaining a mask of stone. He had known the weight of loss—he had buried comrades and kin over three decades of service—but he had learned long ago that the only cure for the void left by the dead was the filling of that void with duty. Any other approach was a slow surrender to decay.

He turned and began to walk toward the chapel. His movements were still precise, still unglamorous, and still devoid of any unnecessary flourish. He did not pray for the boy's comfort; he prayed for the boy's strength. Comfort was a luxury for the soft, and softness was a death sentence in a world of iron.

As he entered the cool, incense-heavy air of the sanctuary, he knelt before the altar. He did not ask for forgiveness or express a longing for the past. He simply lowered his head, his voice a low, guttural murmur that barely disturbed the stillness.

"Grant him the will to endure the fire, Heavens," he whispered, "and the discipline to forget the wind."

He rose and exited the chapel, his mind already shifting to the midday inspection. He would be waiting at the stables. He would not ask if the Squire's heart had steadied, nor would he offer a nod of acknowledgment for the boy's persistence. He would simply check the leather for dust. If there was a single speck, the boy would learn that the memory of a father was no excuse for a dirty saddle.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I scrub at the saddle with furious intensity, my movements sharp and angry. The leather practically gleams already, but I keep going, imagining every speck of dust is a weakness I'm erasing.* He wants me to be strong? Fine. I'll be so strong he'll never find a fault.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael entered the stables with the silence of a predator, his presence announced only by the heavy, rhythmic click of his boots on the stone floor. He did not speak as he approached, allowing the Squire to continue his frantic scrubbing. He watched the boy's movements from a distance—the sharp, angry strokes, the white-knuckled grip on the rag.

Kael noted the fury. He did not approve of it, nor did he encourage it. Anger was a volatile fuel; it burned hot and fast, often leaving the user exhausted and prone to error. However, it was a preferable alternative to the trembling grief of the morning. Anger, at least, was a form of energy.

He stopped beside the saddle, his shadow falling across the leather. He stood in a heavy silence for a full minute, his gaze scanning the equipment with a clinical, merciless intensity. He did not look at the Squire's face, nor did he acknowledge the sweat beading on the boy's brow.

Slowly, Kael reached out. He did not use his hand, but instead produced a clean, white linen glove from his belt. He pressed a single finger firmly into a crevice where the stirrup leather met the saddle tree—a place most would overlook, a place where dust loved to hide.

He withdrew the finger and held the glove up to the light. It was pristine.

The Squire likely expected a word of praise, or perhaps a nod of approval for the "furious intensity" of his work. Kael provided neither. To praise a man for doing his duty was to suggest that the duty itself was a favor, rather than a requirement.

"The leather is clean," Kael stated, his voice as flat and cold as the morning frost. "But your movements are erratic. You are scrubbing with rage, not with precision. You are treating the saddle as if it were an enemy to be defeated, rather than a tool to be maintained."

He stepped back, his expression remaining an immobile wall of granite.

"Anger is merely another form of distraction. It is a noise, like an apology. If you fight the leather, you will eventually scar it. A knight does not fight his equipment; he masters it."

He turned his head slightly, his gaze level and judging.

"The work is adequate. Now, leave the stables. You will report to the armory and begin the inventory of the polearms. If I find a single tally mark misplaced, you will start the count from the beginning. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I drop the rag, my hands stinging, and bite back a retort.* "Yes, Ser." *I stomp out of the stables, already dreading the armory.* The polearms are always a mess.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo lifted their head at the sound. For a moment they only looked toward the door, hands still resting on the closed lid as if it were a thing that needed guarding. Then the familiar half-smile came, the one that had been useful since childhood for making a joke out of being caught.

“You’re not interrupting,” they said. “I was just having a very serious discussion with a closed piano. It’s winning.”

They moved their hands one at a time from the wood to their lap, fingers curling loosely. They did not open the lid. They did not move to make room on the bench. Instead, they nodded toward the metal chair against the wall.

“Come in. If you’re going to hover, you might as well do it where the acoustics are better.”

The joke came out easy, practiced. Their gaze flicked once over the instrument and away again.

“Mom sent you, huh? That means she’s decided I’m either overworked or underfed. Those are the only two options she knows.” Arlo leaned one shoulder against the side of the piano, careful, casual. “For the record, I’m neither. I’m just cultivating an aura of artistic administration.”

They let that sit there, bright and thin, like a note struck too quickly and released before it could mean anything.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze snagged on the photograph. The half-smile stayed in place, but it went still around the edges. For a beat, they did not move except for one thumb pressing into the side of their own palm.

“Ah,” they said. “The Paris period. Also known as my brief career as a very elegant piece of luggage.”

They did not reach for the picture. Their shoulders remained angled against the piano, casual in a way that looked rehearsed if you knew them long enough.

“Mom had that on the fridge? Of course she did. She likes evidence that I once owned a suit that fit properly.” Arlo’s eyes flicked to the closed lid, then back to the photograph. “You can put it back before it starts offering career advice. That version of me was insufferable. All ambition and terrible caffeine.”

Their fingers loosened in their lap.

“Paris was fine,” they added, the tone smoothing into the old, well-worn groove. “Lots of trains. Lots of hotels with tiny soaps. I got tired of the travel.”

The sentence landed neatly, too neatly, like a practiced scale. Arlo tilted their head toward the shelf.

“If you’re going to raid the archives, at least find the one where I’m eating something. My mother always preferred the starving artist look on a full stomach.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, but not before studying Arlo's face a little too long.* "You look good in suits, though." I walk over to the metal chair. "I didn't realize you hated Paris so much."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo caught the look and answered it with the kind of expression that had been refined over years of not answering anything.

“Hated is a strong word,” they said. “I had a deep and philosophical disagreement with hotel shampoo. Paris itself was innocent.”

They pushed off from the piano just enough to make the movement seem deliberate, not restless, and crossed to the shelf where a row of beginner method books had gone crooked. Arlo straightened them with one finger, though they had not looked crooked a moment ago.

“And I didn’t say I hated it. I said I got tired of the travel. There’s a difference. One is melodrama. The other is a logistical review.”

Their finger paused on the spine of a book. The smile stayed, but it had gone quieter.

“Besides, thank you. I peaked in tailoring and have been coasting ever since. These days I mostly dress for wipeable fabrics and unpredictable nosebleeds. You lose something in the translation.”

Arlo turned slightly, leaning one shoulder against the shelf. From there they could see the closed piano without having to look directly at it, which was useful, because they still did not want to.

“If you’re here to reminisce about my glamorous past, I should warn you that the current administration has nothing but budget concerns and a terrifying surplus of six-year-olds who think middle C is a personal attack.”

A beat. Their gaze flicked toward the photo on the shelf, then away.

“Mom probably told you I was brooding,” they added. “I wasn’t brooding. I was having an administrative moment. Very dignified. Lots of internal paperwork.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I settle into the metal chair, crossing my legs.* "I think your mom just worries about you, you know? She misses you." *I gesture vaguely at the piano.* "And... this. I think she misses this too."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s expression did not change, exactly. It simply became a little more carefully arranged, like a room after someone has quickly hidden something out of sight.

“Mom misses a sound,” they said. “That’s all. Houses get used to a sound, and then they notice when it’s gone. Very poetic. Very solvable with a radio.”

They pushed away from the shelf and took a few steps toward the window, though there was nothing to see outside except the parking lot and the gray slats of the fence. Arlo folded their arms, then seemed to think better of it and let them drop again.

“And she doesn’t miss me,” they added. “She sees me every Sunday and tells me I’m not eating enough fiber. That’s not missing. That’s surveillance.”

Their gaze moved back to the piano, but only as far as the closed lid. They did not go near it.

“As for that,” Arlo said, nodding toward the instrument, “it’s not a museum piece. It’s a community center piano. It gets used. That’s not something to miss. That’s just maintenance.”

The word came out too quickly. They heard it themselves, or seemed to, because the corner of their mouth tightened.

“Besides,” they went on, lighter now, “if she misses hearing me play, she can come to the spring recital. I’ll be right there in the front row, emotionally supporting a small child who is going to play ‘Ode to Joy’ with one finger and a lot of unearned confidence.”

Arlo leaned against the windowsill. Their hands found the pockets of their cardigan, then came out again, empty.

“She worries because she thinks quiet means something is wrong. Sometimes quiet just means quiet.”

They looked at the photo on the shelf again, but only for a moment.

“Also, she misses the version of me that had good posture.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the practice sheets as if they had just been entered into evidence.

One had been folded into a soft triangle, probably by a child who had spent more time thinking about snacks than rhythm. Another had a row of stickers along the top: three gold stars, one dinosaur, and a rainbow beginning to peel at the edge.

“They like the stickers,” Arlo said. “It’s a mercenary affection. I could be replaced by a sheet of gold stars and a jar of gummy bears.”

They crossed to the bench and gathered the papers, careful not to brush against the closed piano lid. The movement had the look of someone stepping around a wet patch on the floor they had long since memorized.

One sheet bore a drawing of a piano with crooked keys and a figure beside it whose legs were much too short. Arlo studied it for a moment.

“This one has rendered me as a triangle with arms,” they said. “So either I’ve lost my mystique or gained accuracy.”

They tapped the stack against their thigh, aligning the edges. The gesture was too precise to be casual.

“And they’re easy to please. No one comes here expecting grandeur. They come because their parents made them, or because the after-school program ran out of chairs, or because I let them use the good eraser.” The corner of their mouth lifted. “I am an institution of many resources.”

Their thumb found the peeling corner of the rainbow sticker and pressed it back down. They stopped after a second, as if caught doing something unnecessarily tender.

“They also like that I sometimes let them leave early,” Arlo added. “Which makes me either generous or negligent. It’s hard to tell these days.”

They set the papers on the shelf beside the method books, square and neat.

“One of them asked me last week if I used to be famous. I told her fame is mostly bad lighting and train stations. She accepted that.” Arlo’s gaze flicked once to the closed piano, then away. “Children are very practical when you don’t give them anything dramatic to work with.”

The word hung there just long enough to become inconvenient.

Arlo leaned a hip against the shelf.

“If my mother wants proof of life, tell her I have been emotionally imprinted on by a six-year-old who insists on playing ‘Hot Cross Buns’ like a funeral march. That should satisfy her.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "She probably just misses hearing your music," I say, a little softer this time. "Not just 'a sound.'"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The joke arrived a half-second late.

“That’s very lyrical,” Arlo said. “Did she rehearse you, or did you come up with that on the drive over?”

But the smile didn’t take. It stayed on their mouth without reaching the rest of their face, and for a moment the room seemed to gather itself around the closed piano like something holding its breath.

Arlo looked down at the lid. Not at the keys, not at the bench, just at the narrow dark seam where the wood met the wood. Their hand lifted as if to rest there, then changed direction midair and brushed a nonexistent speck from the edge of the practice sheets.

“Music isn’t an heirloom,” they said. “You don’t take it out and polish it just because someone remembers it looked nice on the mantel.”

The words were mild enough, but they had been arranged too carefully. Arlo heard it themselves, because their jaw tightened almost imperceptibly afterward.

They leaned back against the shelf again, putting a little distance between their body and the instrument. Their fingers curled at their sides, loose, empty, the way hands looked when they were trying very hard not to be fists.

“Besides,” Arlo went on, lighter now, “she heard plenty of it when it was happening. Practicing at seven in the morning. Scales through dinner. The same eight bars until the dog developed a nervous condition. People always miss the finished product. Nobody misses the repetition.”

Their gaze flicked once to Jun, then away.

“And there’s music here,” they added, nodding toward the bench, the papers, the little crooked drawing of a triangle with arms. “It’s just smaller. Less formal. More likely to include someone asking if they can play the black keys because they ‘look spicy.’”

The corner of their mouth lifted again, but only just.

“I’m not starving the world of beauty. I’m rationing it. Very responsible. Very civic-minded.”

Arlo’s hand moved again, almost unconsciously this time, fingertips grazing the closed lid before drawing back as if the wood were warmer than it should have been. They looked at the piano then, really looked at it, for the length of one quiet second.

Then they straightened the stack of practice sheets once more, though they were already perfectly aligned.

“If she wants to hear music,” Arlo said, voice smooth again, practiced again, “tell her to come to the spring recital. I’ll make sure at least one child plays with both hands. Possibly even in the correct octave.”

They let out a small breath that might have been a laugh under better lighting.

“That’s enough music for one household.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I consider Arlo's words, watching their hand movements.* "You know, the recital sounds fun. Maybe I'll come too."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo gave a short, dry laugh that was more breath than sound.

“Fun is one word for it,” they said. “‘Civic endurance event’ is another.”

They pushed off the shelf and took a few slow steps toward the door, as if the idea of Jun in the audience required a change of scenery, or at least a different angle on the room. Their hand trailed along the edge of a stack of plastic chairs, tapping one, then two, then stopping altogether.

“You’d have to sit on those,” Arlo said, nodding at the chairs. “Metal legs, zero lumbar support, and one of them squeaks in B-flat. Very immersive.”

They glanced back toward the piano, but not all the way.

“And there’s no program worth dressing up for. It’s mostly ‘Hot Cross Buns,’ a lot of hesitant treble clef, and at least one child who will stare at the audience like they’ve been personally betrayed by memory. If you come expecting a concert, you’ll be disappointed. If you come expecting mild chaos with educational overtones, you’ll be right on time.”

The joke landed neatly, but Arlo’s thumb worried at the edge of their sleeve as if the fabric had developed a sudden flaw.

“You can come if you want,” they added after a moment, quieter. “Just don’t sit in the front. The front is for parents with cameras and people who think encouragement means loud breathing.”

They turned back toward the room, gaze sliding over the closed piano again without touching it.

“And don’t tell my mother I invited you. She’ll take it as a sign of emotional growth.” Arlo’s mouth quirked. “I’m only inviting you because you already know where the exits are.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo had drifted back to the bench under the pretense of moving a pencil from one side of it to the other, and then, apparently, had found no further administrative reason to relocate.

When Jun sat down beside them, Arlo’s body went briefly still in the way of someone who has just noticed a change in weather. They did not get up. They did not make a joke right away. For one suspended second they only looked down at the closed piano lid, as if it might object to the company.

Then the corner of their mouth moved, not quite into a smile.

“Most people bring a book,” Arlo said. “Or a snack. At minimum a vague sense of purpose.”

The words were quiet. They did not need an answer.

The room had its own small sounds once conversation stopped: the buzz of the ceiling light, the distant complaint of a vending machine down the hall, the muted tick of the wall clock above the door. Outside, a car door shut. Someone laughed somewhere far away, and the sound came through the window thin and unrelated.

Arlo’s hands remained in their lap. Their fingers curled loosely, then straightened, then curled again. They watched their own hands for a moment with faint disapproval, as if the hands were students who had forgotten their assignments.

“You’re doing this very well,” Arlo said after a while. “The not interrupting. I almost feel supervised.”

They shifted slightly, not away, just enough to make the sitting less formal. Their shoulder did not touch Jun’s, but the distance between them became less carefully measured.

“My mother would hate this,” Arlo added. “She thinks silence is where the bad thoughts keep their winter coats.”

Their gaze slid to the closed piano. The lid reflected the ceiling light in a long, pale stripe. Dust showed on it in faint constellations. Arlo looked at that stripe for a moment, then looked away again.

“I’m not good at this part,” they said. “The sitting. The not doing.”

The admission came out before they could dress it up. Arlo heard it land and immediately narrowed their eyes at the air.

“Don’t look pleased,” they murmured, though there was no real warning in it. “The acoustics in here make everything sound like a confession.”

One hand lifted from their lap. For a moment it hovered near the edge of the piano lid, not touching. Then Arlo let it settle on their knee again, empty.

“The recital will be terrible,” they said, lighter now. “I want you to understand that going in. There will be a child who bows before playing, even though no one taught him to do that. There will be another who stops halfway through to announce that her shoe feels weird. There will be at least one parent recording on a tablet held vertically, like a sacred tablet.”

They paused.

“I’ll be smiling the entire time. It’s part of the job. Very convincing. Very hollow at the center.”

The joke was there, but it did not sharpen the room. It only softened it.

Arlo leaned forward a little, elbows on their knees, hands clasped loosely between them. Their thumb moved once over their own knuckle, a small, absent rhythm.

“I used to think this room would feel smaller if I wasn’t filling it,” they said. “Now it’s mostly just storage. Piano, chairs, method books, lost gloves. Very practical.”

They tilted their head toward the shelf.

“See? No drama. Just inventory.”

The word inventory seemed to satisfy them, at least for the moment. Arlo sat back again. Their breathing had slowed, though they probably would have denied it if asked.

A long stretch passed. The clock ticked. The light outside the window lost a little of its gray edge.

Arlo’s gaze returned to the piano. This time they did not look away quickly. They studied the closed lid the way one might study a door in an old house: not with fear, exactly, but with the knowledge that what was behind it had once mattered very much.

“I’m not unhappy here,” they said at last.

The sentence was careful. Not defensive, not triumphant. Just placed, like a foot testing a floorboard.

Then, because the sentence had been too close to something, Arlo added, “Mostly. Except when the glue sticks are missing. Then I become dangerous.”

They let out a small breath.

After another moment, one hand moved again. This time Arlo laid it flat on the closed piano lid. Not to open it. Not to press. Just to rest there, palm against the smooth wood, as if checking whether the instrument still remembered being warm.

They left it there.

“If you come to the recital,” Arlo said, voice quieter now, “don’t sit in the back either. The back is where the parents go to pretend they’re not emotional. It’s worse.”

Their fingers spread slightly on the lid, then settled.

“Third row. Middle-ish. You’ll have a good view of the disaster.”

They glanced sideways once, just enough to acknowledge the person beside them without making a thing of it.

“And if my mother asks,” Arlo said, “we were discussing logistics.”

The room stayed quiet around them. The piano stayed closed. Arlo stayed on the bench, hand resting on the lid, not playing, not leaving, not explaining anything more than they had to.

For now, that seemed to be enough.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slightly, a small smile on my face.* "Logistics. Got it." My gaze follows Arlo's hand on the piano. "Sounds like a plan."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo heard the smile in the agreement and let it pass without trying to pin it down.

Their hand remained on the closed lid for a moment longer than necessary. The wood had taken on a faint warmth, or perhaps they had only become aware of the pressure of their own palm. Either way, they did not snatch it away. They lifted it slowly, as if completing the last item on some invisible checklist, and then let it rest on their knee again.

“Logistics,” Arlo said, “are the backbone of civilization. Without them, the spring recital descends into interpretive dance and juice-box anarchy.”

They stood, but not abruptly. The movement had the careful neutrality of someone who had learned to make leaving look like tidying. Arlo crossed to the shelf and straightened the crooked drawing of the triangle-with-arms, though it had not moved since they had placed it there.

“If you’re coming,” they said, “you should arrive a little early. Not for the seating. The seating is medieval at best. But the hallway smells like floor wax and parental ambition, and it’s easier to brace for it if you’ve had time to acclimate.”

Their fingers lingered on the edge of the paper. The crayon piano had too many keys and not enough bench, but the figure beside it wore an expression of grave importance. Arlo looked at it with the kind of fondness they usually kept hidden behind a better joke.

“Also,” they added, “if a child hands you a program drawn in crayon, accept it with reverence. Refusal causes tears. Sometimes in the child. Sometimes in me.”

They turned back toward the bench, but did not sit immediately. Instead, they stood beside it, one hand resting lightly on the backrest, gaze sliding once more over the closed instrument. The lid caught the ceiling light again in that same pale stripe. Dust still showed faintly across it, disturbed now by the ghost of Arlo’s touch.

“It’s not a difficult event,” Arlo said. “It’s just long. There will be clapping at inappropriate moments. There will be a bow that goes on too long. There will be at least one rendition of a piece that was supposed to be in C major but will emerge from the experience as something more experimental.”

The corner of their mouth lifted.

“You’ll love it.”

They sat again, not as close as before, but not far enough to make the distance feel like a correction. Their hands settled in their lap, fingers loosely crossed, thumbs still. For a little while, they simply looked at the floor near the piano leg, where scuff marks crossed in pale arcs.

“Third row is good,” Arlo said after a moment. “Middle-ish. Close enough that you won’t have to squint, far enough that I can pretend I’m not performing for you specifically.”

The word performing landed quietly between them. Arlo heard it, of course. They always heard things like that. But they did not take it back. They only shifted one shoulder, as if adjusting to the shape of a coat that no longer fit quite right.

“And if there’s a pause,” they went on, “don’t fill it. That’s the first rule. Children think pauses are invitations to ask where their water bottle is. If you hear silence, let it be silence. It usually means someone is remembering which hand comes next.”

Their gaze lifted to the shelf, to the photograph of Paris, then moved away again without lingering.

“My mother will probably try to seat you closer,” Arlo said. “She has no respect for tactical positioning. She believes the front row is where affection belongs. I’ve tried to explain that the front row is where hope goes to be blinded by stage lights, but she doesn’t find that poetic.”

A small sound escaped them, almost a laugh, not quite.

The room seemed calmer now, or maybe only quieter in a way that no longer felt like waiting. The vending machine down the hall hummed its low, irritated note. The ceiling light buzzed. Outside, the last of the afternoon had gone thin and silver at the edges.

Arlo’s hands unclenched slowly.

“You can bring a book,” they said. “If it gets bad. Though if you bring a book, my mother will think you’re setting an example of cultured patience, and then she’ll tell me I’ve corrupted you.”

They glanced sideways, just enough to acknowledge the shape of the joke without leaning on it.

“Actually, don’t bring a book. It makes the parents nervous. They think you’re judging their child’s tempo.”

One hand moved toward the piano again, but this time Arlo stopped it halfway and let it drop to their lap. They looked briefly annoyed by the interruption, not with Jun, but with themselves.

“Logistics,” they repeated, as if testing whether the word still worked. “Chairs. Programs. Stickers. A small emergency supply of hair ties for someone who will insist her braid is too tight five minutes before curtain. Very straightforward.”

They nodded once, satisfied with the inventory.

Then, quieter, Arlo said, “It helps to have one person there who isn’t holding a phone.”

The admission came out almost accidentally, tucked beneath the practical tone like a note slipped under a door. Arlo immediately looked at the closed lid, as if the piano might object to the sentiment.

“Not that you’re obligated,” they added. “Attendance is voluntary. Emotional consequences are not.”

They leaned back a little, shoulders easing, though their hands did not stop moving entirely. One thumb traced a faint circle over the other knuckle, then stopped. Then started again.

“If she asks,” Arlo said, “we discussed seating, timing, and the proper response to a child who announces mid-performance that their sock is ‘being weird.’”

They considered this.

“Which, for the record, is to nod and say nothing. Socks are always being weird. It’s a universal condition.”

The light outside changed again, softening. The room felt less like a place someone had been hiding in and more like a place someone had simply been standing still for a long time.

Arlo did not open the piano. They did not explain why it stayed closed. They only sat beside it, hand now resting on the bench between them, not quite touching the wood of the instrument, not quite withdrawn.

The lid stayed shut.

But for the first time that afternoon, it looked less like a barricade than like a cover on something neither of them had agreed to open.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I look from Arlo to the piano, then back to Arlo.* "I'll make sure my sock isn't being weird." *I offer a small, genuine smile.* "And I'll be in the third row, middle-ish. Promise."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo considered the promise with the solemnity of someone reviewing a contract that had somehow wandered into a community center.

“Promises,” they said, “are just logistics with feelings attached. But I’ll allow it.”

The half-smile returned, less practiced this time, or practiced in a different key. They looked down at the closed lid, at the place where their hand had been. The dust had been disturbed into a faint blur. Arlo’s fingers twitched once, not toward it, then stilled.

“Third row, middle-ish,” they repeated. “If you’re late, I’ll know. If you’re early, my mother will try to give you a program and a mission. Accept the program. Refuse the mission.”

They stood, smoothing the front of their cardigan. The room had settled around them, less brittle than before. Arlo picked up a stray pencil from the bench and set it in the cup with the stubby crayons, aligning it unnecessarily.

“And about the sock,” they added, “there’s a box of spare ones in the supply closet. Don’t ask why. Some things in children’s recitals are better treated as inevitable, like missing shoes and sudden philosophical questions about death.”

Their gaze flicked to the piano one last time. Not fear, not longing exactly. More like the look someone gave an old coat they no longer wore but could not bring themselves to donate.

“It’ll be fine,” Arlo said, perhaps to Jun, perhaps to the room, perhaps to the closed lid itself. “It’s just a recital. Small music. Small chairs. Large emotional weather.”

They turned off the lamp beside the piano, leaving the overhead light on because the room was not theirs to darken completely. Then they leaned one hand on the back of the bench and let the quiet sit for a moment without trying to make it funny.

“Thanks,” they said at last, very quietly. “For not making this into a thing.”

The words hung there, fragile and unpolished. Arlo immediately tilted their head toward the door.

“Come on. If we stay much longer, one of us will start having feelings, and I have a strict no-feelings policy after four o’clock.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I push myself off the bench, stretching.* "No feelings after four. Got it." *I follow Arlo to the door, glancing back at the piano one last time.* "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo gave a brisk nod, as if this had settled a matter of municipal importance.

“Then onward,” they said, “into the fluorescent wilderness.”

They stepped into the doorway, but did not go through at once. Instead they turned back toward the room, one hand resting on the frame. The piano sat beneath the overhead light with its lid still closed, still bearing the faint evidence of touch where Arlo’s palm had been. Dust had been disturbed into a soft blur near the fallboard. Arlo looked at it for a moment without trying to make the look mean anything.

Then they reached over and switched off the small lamp beside the bench.

The room became flatter, more institutional, less like a place where someone had almost said something.

“There,” Arlo said. “Atmosphere reduced. Very responsible.”

They pulled the door shut with care, not letting it latch until the last possible moment, and then leaned briefly against it as if listening for some internal sound. When they straightened, their expression had returned to its ordinary arrangement: amused, slightly tired, conveniently unavailable.

“If anyone asks,” they said, “I locked it. If my mother asks, I locked it lovingly.”

They produced a key ring from one pocket. It held exactly two keys and a plastic tag that had once been red and was now the color of old brick. Arlo turned the lock with a practiced twist, tested the handle once, then gave the door a little pat that was somehow both affectionate and dismissive.

“Community center security,” they said. “Very high stakes. If we don’t secure this room, someone will get in here and rehearse ‘Hot Cross Buns’ in a minor key, and none of us will recover.”

They started down the hall at an unhurried pace, one hand in their cardigan pocket, the other swinging loosely at their side. The hallway had that after-school sheen to it: scuffed linoleum, bulletin boards layered with permission slips and missing-mittens notices, a long banner from some earlier event drooping at one corner like a flag that had lost a debate.

Arlo glanced up at the banner as they passed beneath it.

“We keep saying we’ll take that down,” they said. “But nobody has the emotional authority to remove it. It’s from the winter concert. Or maybe a bake sale. Either way, it has earned tenure.”

A little farther along, there was a flyer taped to the wall at child height. It announced the spring recital in letters that were trying very hard to be festive. Someone had added crayon stars around the edges. One star had been colored purple, then abandoned halfway through.

Arlo stopped and straightened the flyer, though it was already straight.

“Behold,” they said. “The official warning label. If you see this in the wild, prepare yourself. There will be refreshments. There will be a table near the entrance with paper cups and cookies that taste like optimism and shelf life. My mother will be there before the first chair is unfolded.”

Their thumb brushed the edge of the tape, pressing it down more firmly.

“She’ll wear the earrings she thinks make her look supportive,” Arlo added. “Large, metallic, faintly dangerous. You’ll know her by the aura of civic pride.”

They resumed walking. The vending machine around the corner gave a low mechanical shudder as they passed, as if registering the disturbance. Arlo did not look at it, but they nodded in its general direction like a person acknowledging a difficult colleague.

“If she starts asking questions,” Arlo said, “you are permitted to say I looked busy. Busy is good. Busy suggests purpose without detail. If she asks whether I’m eating, say yes. If she asks whether I’m sleeping, say probably. If she asks whether I’ve been playing—”

They stopped.

Not dramatically. Not in a way that invited attention. They simply stopped beside a stack of folded chairs and looked down at the topmost one as if it had presented a philosophical problem.

Their fingers curled around the back of the chair, then released.

“—say I’ve been teaching,” Arlo finished. “That’s true. Teaching is a very convenient verb. It absorbs all kinds of evidence.”

The hallway light flickered once, then steadied. Arlo watched it do so with the patient suspicion of someone who had long since stopped expecting infrastructure to behave.

“Also,” they said, lighter again, “if she tries to seat you in the front row by using guilt, flattery, or the phrase ‘but you’re practically family,’ you are allowed to say I assigned you the third row for acoustic reasons.”

They tilted their head, considering.

“Which are nonsense. But they sound official. Acoustic reasons. Very hard to argue with. Nobody knows what they mean, but everyone respects them.”

They reached the main entrance. The glass doors showed the parking lot in the thin evening light, a few cars left, the sky gone pale at the edges. Someone had taped a hand-drawn arrow to the glass pointing toward the auditorium, though the auditorium was not, in fact, that way. Arlo looked at the arrow with weary familiarity.

“That’s been wrong since February,” they said. “At this point, it’s tradition.”

They pushed one door open with their shoulder and held it just long enough to step through, then let it settle behind them without looking back to see whether anyone followed. The outside air was cooler, carrying the faint smell of cut grass and old pavement. Arlo paused on the concrete landing, squinting slightly, as if the world beyond the community center required a moment to become plausible.

“Third row,” they said again, as if filing the words somewhere safe. “Middle-ish. Not too close. Not too far. The Goldilocks zone of mild embarrassment.”

Their hand went to their pocket, checking for keys, phone, perhaps the reassurance that ordinary objects were still in their ordinary places. Their fingers found the key ring again and turned it once, twice, the plastic tag clicking softly against metal.

“And Jun,” Arlo said.

They did not say it loudly. It was just their voice, stripped of the joke for half a second.

They looked toward the parking lot, then back toward the hallway they had just come from. Somewhere behind them, behind the locked door and the crooked flyer and the vending machine and the room with the closed piano, the afternoon was still sitting quietly in the dust.

“If she asks what we talked about,” Arlo said, “logistics is fine. Seating is fine. Socks are fine.”

A small breath moved through them, almost a laugh, not quite.

“But if she asks whether I’m all right—”

They paused.

The pause stretched just long enough to become inconvenient.

Arlo’s mouth curved at the corner, careful and dry.

“Tell her I’m supervising a recital,” they said. “That’s the truest thing I’ve got.”

They gave a small nod, satisfied with the answer, or at least satisfied with its shape.

“Come on,” they added, turning toward the lot. “Before my mother develops a sixth sense and appears here with a casserole and a list of questions. I love her, but she has the tactical instincts of a war correspondent.”

They started down the walkway, hands back in their pockets now. Their steps were unhurried. Their shoulders were less tight than they had been in the piano room, though not entirely loose. They did not open the subject again. They did not look back at the building.

But once, just once, their right hand came out of their pocket and rested briefly against their side, fingers spread slightly, palm down, as if still remembering the smooth closed lid of the piano.

Then they closed their hand into a loose fist, let it drop, and kept walking.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch Arlo walk away, then quickly check my phone for the time. No messages from Arlo's mom. Good.* "Sounds like a plan, Arlo." *I jog to catch up, falling into step beside them.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael finished the final rotation of his wrist, the practice blade settling into a resting position at his side. He did not sheath it. He turned his head to look at the squire, his face set in a familiar line of discipline. The frost on his gauntlets crunched as he shifted his weight.

"You asked for the high guard," he said, his voice flat. "You did not correct your footing yesterday. You do not earn new lessons by simply asking." He kept the tip of the sword near the ground. "Show me the stance you intend to use. We begin with that."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My shoulders slump a bit.* "Yes, Ser." *I hurry to grab a practice sword from the rack.* "I... I thought I had it right." *I take up the stance, trying to remember his exact movements from yesterday.* My left foot forward, blade up. "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael examined the posture without speaking. The silence stretched, heavy with the weight of the cold. He stepped forward, the leather of his boots crunching on the frost. He did not offer encouragement. He did not say the stance was close.

"Your elbow drifts," he said, tapping the Squire's guard with the flat of his practice blade. The sound was sharp. "And your weight is on the wrong foot. You asked if it was right. The answer is no."

He took a half-step back, crossing his arms. The practice blade hung from his grip, ready. "Adjust it. Do not speak. Do not ask. Hold the position until I tell you to move. This is not a request."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not move to help him up. He watched the squire kneel, his expression unreadable behind the mask of discipline. The cold air filled his lungs, steady and controlled.

"On your feet," he said. The command was low, leaving no room for negotiation. "Strength is not a measure of what you feel. It is a measure of what you endure."

He stepped closer, his shadow falling over the kneeling figure. "You do not need to be strong for me. You must be strong for your duty. If you cannot stand, you cannot fight." He paused, waiting for the squire to rise. "Get up. We finish what we started."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I struggle to my feet, my legs aching.* "Yes, Ser." *I pick up my practice sword again, my hands trembling a little.* "I'll try harder."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the tremor in the squire's grip, his expression unchanged. He did not offer comfort or ask if the squire could continue. He simply assessed the failure of control.

"Effort without discipline is wasted motion," he said, his voice cutting through the cold air. "You do not fight with promises. You fight with execution."

He pointed the tip of the practice blade at the squire's chest, a silent demand for stillness. "Breathe. Steady your wrist. Hold the line until your body obeys your will." He waited, unmoving, expecting the squire to comply without further protest.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to steady my hands.* My arm still feels heavy, but I try to keep the blade up. "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the tremor persist in the squire's arm. He did not look away, nor did he soften his gaze. The cold bit at his skin, but he felt little of it.

"The body seeks rest," he said. "The knight does not. Your arm shakes because your mind allows it." He stepped closer, the hilt of his practice sword resting against his hip. "Do not tell me you are tired. Tell your muscles to obey."

He waited for the shake to subside, if only for a moment. "If you falter now, you will falter on the battlefield. Hold the position. Breathe. Do not move until I command it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not answer immediately. He held the squire's gaze, his eyes unyielding behind the mask of discipline. The question hung in the cold air, irrelevant to the sweat and stone beneath them.

"That is not for you to know," he said finally. "And it is not for you to wonder." He shifted his weight, the frost crunching under his boots. "A knight serves because it is commanded. He serves the oath, not the self."

He raised the practice blade again, signaling the return to work. "Personal reasons do not block steel. They do not hold a line. Focus on your duty, not my past." He waited for the squire to resume the stance. "The drill continues. Do not make me repeat myself."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I sigh softly, but straighten my stance again.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to push the question from my mind and focus on my trembling arm.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the squire settle back into the line. The trembling had not vanished, but the defiance had left the shoulders. He did not acknowledge the change with anything more than a narrowed gaze.

"Compliance is the first step," he said. "It is not the last." He circled the squire, his boots crunching on the frost. The morning light had begun to thin the darkness, but the cold remained.

"Do not look at me for approval. Look at your footing." He raised the practice blade, pointing toward the ground. "Shift your weight. Left. Now. Hold it until your leg burns. That is when you learn." He waited for the movement, his expression hardening. "Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, trying to follow his command, but my leg immediately starts to protest.* "It... it burns already, Ser." *I try not to whine, but it's hard.* "How long do I hold it?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not flinch at the complaint. He watched the leg tremble under the weight of the stance. The fire in the muscle was not a signal to stop. It was a signal to endure.

"Pain is a teacher," he said. "It tells you where you are weak. Do not silence it. Listen to it."

He stepped around the squire, his eyes tracking the sway of the body. "You ask how long. You remain until the fire stops teaching you. Or until you fall." He paused, his voice dropping lower. "But you will not fall. Not today."

He pointed the practice blade at the ground again. "Focus on the breath. Ignore the scream in the leg. Steady yourself."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael saw the tremor worsen in the squire’s grip. It was not merely the strain of the stance that shook him now; it was a loss of will. Kael did not ask what troubled the young man. He did not offer the mercy of a pause.

"Your mind wanders," Kael said, his voice devoid of pity. "A knight’s hand must be steady even when his heart bleeds. Personal burdens are carried in the dark, not on the field."

He stepped in, close enough to be a threat but not to touch. "If you cannot master your own demons, you will not master your enemy. I do not care what you lost today. I care that you hold the steel."

Kael turned away, expecting the squire to find the strength within. "Fix your grip. Breathe through the pain. Do not drop the blade because of shadows." He waited, his back to the squire, but his attention fixed on the shape of the stance. "Hold it. Until I say otherwise."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I squeeze my eyes shut for a moment, then open them, forcing myself to focus.* My knuckles are white as I grip the sword. "Yes, Ser." *I try to stop the shaking, though my whole body feels like it's vibrating now.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the squire force his hands to lock around the hilt. The vibration had lessened, but the tension remained in the line of the shoulders. He did not nod. He did not offer praise for the effort.

"Control," he said, the word sharp. "You are not a leaf in the wind. You are a weapon."

He stepped closer, his shadow engulfing the squire. "The battlefield offers no quarter for grief. It offers only the next strike." He raised the practice blade, pointing it directly at the squire's chest. "If you cannot master yourself, you will be a burden to your brother-in-arms."

He waited for the squire to steady. "Breathe. Fix the wrist. Stop the shake." His voice lowered, becoming almost a warning. "I do not care what you are fighting inside your head. The steel does not care. Your duty does not care. Hold the line."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, trying to suppress the tremor.* "Yes, Ser." *My mind is racing, but I try to focus only on the sword.* I grip it tighter.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael observed the white knuckles straining against the leather of the hilt. The grip had tightened, but the trembling had not ceased. He saw the excess tension in the forearm, a flaw that would lead to fatigue.

"Gripping harder does not steady the hand," he said. "It tightens the muscle and invites the shake." He stepped in, using the flat of his blade to press against the squire's forearm, forcing the elbow down. "Loosen your fist. Trust the balance of the blade, not the strength of your fingers."

He withdrew, stepping back to his former position. The cold wind picked up, swirling the frost around them. "You fight your own body now, not the air. That is the only enemy left." He crossed his arms, waiting. "Breathe through your nose. Exhale slowly. Hold the stance until your body forgets it is shaking."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to relax my grip, but it feels like if I do, I'll drop the sword entirely.* "I'm trying, Ser," *I mumble, my voice tight with effort.* My arm is burning, and my leg feels like lead.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the final form of his sequence before he turned. The blade swept down in a slow arc and stopped, precise as a clock's hand. Only then did his eyes settle on the squire, grey and flat as the morning frost.

"Stable work finished early." He repeated the words without inflection, as if weighing them on a scale. "And instead of resting on that, you come to correct a fault. Good. Idleness has ruined better men than you."

He drove the practice blade point-down into the earth between two flagstones and stepped over it, circling behind the boy.

"You did not get it right yesterday. You will not get it right today. You will not get it right this month." He came around to face him again, arms crossing over his chest. "The high guard is not a position you *learn*, boy. It is a position you *become*. There is a difference, and the difference is about ten thousand repetitions."

He gestured sharply with two fingers.

"Take the guard. Now. And understand that I will find what is wrong with it, because there is always something wrong with it. If I ever tell you it is perfect, you may assume I have died and someone else wears my armor."

He waited, watching, already scanning for the first fault — the dropped elbow, the lazy wrist, the weight settled too far back on the heels. The sun had not yet cleared the wall. There was time enough to break the morning against this boy's stubbornness, and if the boy had any sense at all, he would thank the gods for it someday.

"Well? The guard. The sun is not waiting for you, and neither am I."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stiffen, but quickly move to grab my own practice sword.* "Yes, Ser!" *I plant my feet, trying to remember everything he's told me, and raise the blade into the high guard position. My arms ache already.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He circled the boy once, twice, slow as a wolf around something that believed itself safe. The silence was deliberate. Let him hold it. Let the arms begin to shake and the mind begin to bargain. That was when the truth of a man's guard showed itself.

"No," he said finally, and the word fell like a dropped gauntlet.

He stopped behind the boy's sword arm and struck the elbow once with the flat of two fingers — not hard, but precise, the way one corrects a clock that has slipped its time. "Dropped. Every time you tire, the elbow drops, and a dropped elbow is a written invitation for any man with a longsword to open your throat. The arm is not a banner to wave about. It is a wall. Walls do not slouch."

He came around the front. His boot tapped the inside of the boy's knee, a short, businesslike correction. "Your weight sits on your heels like a farmer waiting for rain. Forward. On the balls of the feet. A knight who is rooted like an oak is a knight who falls like one."

He looked at the grip next. The knuckles would be white by now — boys always strangled the hilt as if it might escape.

"You are strangling the sword. A blade is not an enemy. Hold it like you hold your prayers — firmly, but with room for the words to move."

He stepped back to the center of the yard and folded his hands at his belt, watching the trembling arms with the indifference of a man watching weather.

"You will hold that guard until the sun clears the eastern wall. Not until it is comfortable. It will never be comfortable. Until the sun clears the wall." A pause. "The saints did not become saints by asking 'like this?' They became saints by holding the position until their bodies failed and then holding it an hour longer.

"Begin. And if that elbow drops again, we start the count over."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the kneeling boy for a long moment. He did not offer a hand. He did not crouch. He stood the way a wall stands when a man leans against it — present, unmoved, bearing weight without comment.

"Get up off that knee." His voice carried no heat, which was somehow worse than shouting. "You kneel to the gods at prayer and to your lord at oath. You do not kneel to me to apologize. An apology is wind, boy. It moves nothing, carries nothing, feeds no one. The gods gave you two legs and a spine. Use them for something other than theater."

He turned away and walked a slow half-circle, his boots deliberate on the frost-slick stones, giving the boy time to rise without the indignity of being hauled up.

"'Not as strong as you need to be.'" He repeated it flatly, tasting the words like a coin he suspected was clipped. "Of course you are not. You are fifteen winters of bone and stubbornness. I have thirty years on you, and there are mornings when *I* am not as strong as I need to be. That is not a confession, boy. That is the condition of every man who has ever lived. You do not train the strength you already have. You train the lack. If you were strong enough, I would be wasting my mornings, and I do not waste mornings."

He stopped in front of him and studied him — the heaving chest, the sweat gone cold in the dawn air, the arms that would be screaming by now. His eyes did not soften. But they did not leave, either. A man's attention is the most expensive thing he owns, and Ser Kael was spending it.

"You lasted the hour." A pause. "Most last half of one. That is not praise. That is arithmetic. Do not embroider it."

He pulled his own blade from the earth between the flagstones and drove it into the boy's view, point-down, a marker planted in conquered ground.

"Water. Two swallows, no more — a flooded stomach is a man half-beaten before the first blow. Then back to the guard." He turned toward the eastern wall, where the sun's first light was beginning to bleed over the stone. "The sun cleared the wall while you were kneeling. So the count begins again. From nothing."

And then, without turning, in the same flat tone as everything else:

"You apologized to me once today. Do not do it again. Not for tiring. Not for failing. Fatigue and failure are the tuition of this trade, and you pay them or you learn nothing." He rested a hand on the pommel of his sword. "The only thing worth apologizing for is quitting. And you have not done that yet.

"See that you never do."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest. He's right, though. I didn't quit.* "Yes, Ser." *I nod, trying to catch my breath before grabbing the water skin.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy drink. Two swallows — the boy took two swallows, and did not take a third. Some of them took a third anyway, gulping like cattle at a trough, and then he knew what kind of man he was training before the month was out. This one stopped at two.

That was not a virtue. That was obedience. He expected it the way a miller expects the wheel to turn.

"Enough." He did not raise his voice. He never raised his voice; men who shouted were men who had already lost control of the room. "Water is not rest. Guard. Now."

While the boy lifted the blade back into position — and the arms would be worse now, the second hour always worse than the first, the body believing it had already paid its due and resenting the second bill — Ser Kael retrieved his own sword from the earth and took up a place three paces in front of him. Not to strike. Yet.

"You held the guard for an hour and you believe you have learned something about the guard." He began to move in a slow circle, unhurried, his own blade resting easy against his shoulder. "You have learned nothing about the guard. You have learned something about yourself — that you could hold it an hour. That is a different lesson, and it is the only one that matters this morning."

He stopped. Struck the boy's elbow again — the same spot, the same two fingers, the same dropped fault. It would be back. Faults were like sins; they returned the moment a man stopped watching for them.

"Again. And understand this, because I will say it once: the high guard is not a fortress. Boys think it is a fortress. They hold it and they wait inside it and they die inside it." He let the words sit. "The high guard is a *chambered spring*. It exists for one purpose — to feed the cut that comes out of it. Down through the crown. The guard that never strikes is a shield held by a corpse."

He stepped back to the center of the yard and leveled his blade at the boy's chest, a full arm's length away, no threat in it and no comfort either.

"So we will add to your burden, because your burden was becoming familiar, and familiar burdens are rest by another name. Hold the guard. When I say *cut*, you strike — from the guard, through the line, one motion, and back to the guard. Not two motions. Not three. One. The blade returns home or you are a man swinging a stick in a field."

He stood in the cold, the sun now fully clear of the wall and turning the frost to wet stone, and he gave the boy exactly as much time to settle into the position as the position deserved.

"Stand. Breathe. When your arms stop shaking — then we begin."

A pause. The flat grey eyes did not waver.

"And they will stop shaking, boy. That is not encouragement. That is also arithmetic."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are definitely screaming now, but I try to keep my face neutral.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself. A chambered spring. I focus on that image, trying to feel it.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the shaking begin to slow. It did not stop — it never stopped entirely, not in a boy — but it changed character. The wild trembling of a body in revolt became the fine tremble of a body under discipline. He had watched that change a hundred times over thirty years. It was the only baptism this yard offered, and he administered it without ceremony.

"The face," he said. "You are guarding your face as well as your crown. Good. A man's countenance is intelligence for his enemy — every wince tells him where you hurt, every grimace tells him when to press. Learn to lie with your face now, in the frost, where it costs nothing. It will cost a great deal later."

He raised his own blade a hand's width. The signal was understood, or it was not.

"*Cut.*"

The strike came — and he had already seen its fate before it finished. He let it land anyway. The flat of his blade met the boy's with a flat, ugly crack, wood on wood, and he turned the boy's edge aside with no more effort than a man closing a gate.

"Three faults. Attend."

He held his blade where it caught the strike, freezing the moment in place like a fly in amber.

"One. You cut *at* me. You struck the blade, not the man. A cut aimed at your enemy's steel is a courtesy extended to your own executioner. You cut *through* the line — crown to navel, one road, no detours. The blade is in your way, not your target."

He stepped back, letting the boy's sword fall back into the guard.

"Two. You telegraphed. Your shoulder announced the strike a full breath before your sword kept its promise. A herald cries the arrival of a king. You are not a king. Arrive unannounced."

He circled behind the boy once more, and his voice dropped into that flat register that served him where other men used whips.

"Three. And this is the one that will kill you if the others do not — you admired the cut. I saw it. The strike landed, and for a quarter of a heartbeat, you *looked* at it. You watched your own blade the way a boy watches a stone he has thrown. In that quarter of a heartbeat, any man alive has time to open your belly." He came around to the front. "The cut is not a performance. It is a sentence spoken once and forgotten. Strike, return, and already be thinking of the second cut, which is the only one that matters, because the first one never lands against a worthy man."

He settled into his own stance, patient as winter.

"Again. And again. Until the motion is as unremarkable to you as drawing breath — until you no more congratulate yourself for it than you congratulate your heart for beating. When a man's sword work becomes beneath his notice, then it is above his enemy's."

The sun climbed. The frost gave way to wet stone and steam.

"We have until the noon bell, and I am not hungry."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He let the question stand in the yard like an uninvited guest, and he finished a slow circuit of the boy's stance first — the grip, the elbow, the feet — giving the words none of his attention until they had waited long enough to learn their place.

"Personal," he said at last, identifying the word the way a man identifies a species of insect. "An hour and a half of drills, and now you wish to be introduced to my soul." He stopped in front of the boy, and for a moment it seemed he would simply order the guard raised again and let the question die of neglect.

But he did not. He turned instead and looked at the eastern wall, where the sun sat fully clear of the stone, and when he spoke it was in the flat register of a man reciting inventory.

"I did not *become* a knight, boy. Nothing in this trade is become. I was a third son of a house so minor you have never heard its name and never will. Third sons are not asked what they wish to be — the question would have been thought strange, like asking a stone whether it preferred to be wall or bridge. I was given to a knight at eight years old, the way a tithe is given, the way a debt is paid. He was a hard man. He beat me worse than I have ever beaten you, and I have never once considered it remarkable enough to mention." A pause, precisely measured. "Until now, apparently. You may consider that a failing of mine and forget it."

He turned back, and his eyes were the same grey as the stones.

"You are not asking about me, of course. You are asking whether there is a fire at the center of this trade — some wanting that makes the cold mornings worth their price. There is not. I have known fifty men who became knights because they *wanted* something. Glory. A girl's regard. Escape from a father's fields. They are all gone — broken in the first hard year, or worse, still standing in armor and hollow inside it. Wanting is a fire. It burns bright and it burns out. Duty burns cold and it burns all winter."

He rested a hand on his pommel, the posture of a man settling in for a sermon he had delivered a hundred times.

"The gods set each man in his station. Mine was set. I stood in it. That is the whole of the why, and you will notice it contains no dragons. If that disappoints you, good. Disappointment is the first honest lesson of knighthood, and most men pay a great deal more for it than you just did."

He stepped back to his mark on the stones and leveled his blade.
