"You will find your own why, or you will not — but you will find it in the doing, never in the asking. Now. Ask me a better question. Ask me how to keep that elbow up, and I will answer you until the noon bell and after it.

"*Cut.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I almost flinch at his tone, but I force myself to focus on the blade, on the lesson. He's right. The why doesn't matter right now.* "My apologies, Ser. My elbow still drops because my wrist is too stiff. Should I loosen my grip?" *I try to remember everything he said about holding the sword firmly, but with room for the words to move.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the apology pass him like a stray dog — noticed, dismissed, not worth the boot.

"That is twice you have apologized to me today, and I told you once was already too many." He did not raise his voice. He never raised it; the flat register did the work that other men needed volume for. "But you followed the apology with a better question, so the ledger balances — the question paid the debt the apology ran up. Do not mistake that for permission. The arithmetic will not save you a third time."

Then the question itself. He stopped his circling and came to stand directly before the boy, and for answer he did not speak. He reached out and took the boy's sword hand in his own — turned it over, pressed a thumb hard into the wrist joint, and held it there.

"No," he said. "You have made the common error. You have diagnosed stiffness and prescribed slackness. Slackness is not the opposite of stiffness, boy. The opposite of stiffness is *life*. Feel there. That joint is not a knot to be tied tighter, and it is not a rag to be left hanging. It is a hinge. A hinge rusted shut is not strong — it is merely stuck. A hinge hanging loose is not free — it is merely broken. A hinge that is fitted and oiled turns when it is asked and stops when it is asked. That is what your wrist must become."

He released the hand and stepped back.

"Understand why the elbow drops, or you will fight the symptom until doomsday. Your arm is one piece of wood from shoulder to fingernail. You hold the guard with the whole beam of it, and when the beam tires, the weakest end sags — the elbow. But the guard is not *held* by the arm. It is hung from the shoulder, and the wrist turns it. Each joint does its own labor. When one refuses, its neighbor inherits the work — and inherits the fatigue with it. Your wrist died an hour ago, and your elbow has been carrying its corpse ever since."

He tapped the boy's sword hand with two fingers.

"So. A new drill, and it is the least glamorous thing you will do all week, which is why it will do the most good. Blade out before you, level. The arm does not move. The elbow does not move. The shoulder does not move. Only the wrist — turn the blade. Edge to the sky. Edge to the wall. Edge to the sky again. Slowly. The edge leads and the wrist follows, the way the beads move through the fingers of a praying man — one at a time, the hand never clenching the whole string at once."

He folded his hands at his belt and settled into his patience, which was deeper than the frost.

"A hundred turns. Then back to the guard, and then we cut again — and when we cut, the wrist turns *through* the strike, so the edge arrives at my crown and not the flat of your blade. A cut with a dead wrist is a peasant swinging a fence post. A cut with a live wrist is a cut."

The noon bell was still hours off. The wet stones steamed faintly in the climbing sun.

"Begin counting. Aloud. I will know if your wrist lies to you — it will tell me before your mouth does."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My wrist aches already just thinking about it, but he makes sense. My elbow has been taking the brunt of it.* "Yes, Ser." *I extend my arm, trying to keep it perfectly still, and begin the slow, deliberate turns of my wrist. "One... two... three..."*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch the wrist. He watched the shoulder. Boys always betrayed themselves at the top of the body before the bottom — the shoulder was a gossip, and it never learned to keep still.

"Twelve," the boy counted, and the gossip spoke. The shoulder had risen a hair's breadth to help the wrist along, the way a lazy man's neighbor ends up carrying his firewood.

"Hold." He waited for the count to die on the boy's lips. Then he stepped in close and pressed one finger down on the point of the shoulder until it sank back to where it belonged. "That joint does not live here anymore. As far as this drill is concerned, your shoulder is a nail driven into a beam. It holds the arm up. It does not *do* anything. The moment it moves, you are no longer training the wrist — you are training yourself to cheat, and you will cheat magnificently on the day a man's life depends on the honesty of your hand."

He stepped back to his mark. "The count stands at twelve. Do not thank me for my mercy — I am not being merciful. I am being economical. A fault at twelve costs you twelve. A fault at ninety costs you ninety, and by ninety you would have carved the cheating so deep into the muscle that ninety more would not dig it out. Begin again. From twelve."

He folded his hands at his belt and let the counting resume. One. Two. Three. The sun climbed, and the wet stones dried, and he stood in the middle of it all like something the yard had grown — a post, a wellhead, a thing that had been here longer than the moss.

At forty, the wrist began to slow. He had known it would; forty was where the hinge discovered what was being asked of it. He did not stop the count. Let the wrist find its own way through the fatigue — that was the lesson wearing its true face, and interrupting it would be pulling a man out of the water to spare him the swimming.

"Understand what is happening to you now," he said, his voice running beneath the count the way a river runs beneath ice. "The wrist is tired, and it is telling you to stop, and you are not stopping. That is the entire education. Everything else — the guard, the cut, the footwork, the thirty years of it — is that one sentence, repeated until you die. The wrist is tired. You are not stopping."

The boy's arm would be trembling again by now. Good. Let it.

"You will hear men say that discipline is a chain. You will hear it from men who never kept any. Discipline is not the chain, boy. Discipline is the *hand that holds it*. The chain is your body — it was always going to be a chain, tired and complaining and wanting its supper. The question this yard asks is only ever the one question: whose hand is on it? Yours, or the body's? A knight is a man whose hand holds the chain. A dead man is one who dropped it."

At seventy, he saw the grip begin to strangle the hilt again — the old sin, returned like all sins return the moment vigilance went to sleep. He did not correct it aloud. He simply walked past behind the boy and struck the knuckles once with the flat of two fingers, the correction delivered in the same grammar as the count itself, and kept walking. The grip loosened. The count went on.

At ninety-eight, he saw the boy's eyes flick toward him — looking for the end, looking for permission to be finished. He let the silence stretch until the count reached one hundred, and then two more, because he had said a hundred and the boy had drifted to ninety-eight before his eyes went wandering, and a knight's word was a hundred, not ninety-eight plus hope.

"One hundred and two," Ser Kael said at last. "You went past the mark because your mind was elsewhere. The extra two cost you nothing today. On another day they will cost you your sword arm, held out a beat too long over a bridge rail for any passing archer to study. The count is a covenant, boy. Say a hundred, do a hundred. Say an oath, *be* an oath. The gods do not grade on the curve."

He drew his blade from his shoulder and settled it into his own guard, patient as bedrock.

"Now the wrist is alive and the arm knows what a hinge is for. So we spend it before the lesson decays. Guard. Then cut — and this time the wrist turns through it, and the edge arrives at my crown and not the flat, and if you admire the strike even for a heartbeat I will make you wish you had been born a miller's son with soft hands and no ambitions at all."

The flat grey eyes leveled.

"*Cut.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"*Cut,*" Ser Kael had said — and the strike, when it came, was wrong in a way the previous hundred had not been. Not the elbow. Not the wrist. Something upstream of all of it.

"Hold," he said, and left the boy standing in the guard while he walked a slow circle, reading him the way he read all men in this yard — from the feet up. The feet were sound. The elbow, by some miracle, had not dropped. The fault was in the hands. They were shaking, and he knew the shaking of a tired hand as well as he knew his own heartbeat, and this was not it. The tremor of labor is coarse, and it follows the breath. This was fine, and constant, and had nothing to do with the arm at all.

He stopped in front of the boy and looked at his face, which was where the shaking came from.

"At dawn your hands shook because the arm was empty. Now they shake because the mind is full. I have watched hands for thirty years, boy. Those are two different animals, and they do not graze together."

He did not ask what it was. He waited — one breath, two, three — and when nothing was offered, he nodded once, as though the silence had been an answer, and in his ledger it was.

"You will not tell me. Good. Grief is between a man and the gods, and I am neither. But hear this, because it is not comfort — it is instruction. The calendar has teeth. Certain days bite, and they bite every year, and the man who pretends otherwise walks into the bite unarmored. You are not tired in your arm today. You are tired somewhere the drills do not reach, and a cut made with a split mind carves its faults into the muscle like a seal into wax. So we are done with the cut for today. That is not mercy. That is economy."

He drove his own blade point-down between the flagstones and spoke in the flat register of a man reciting inventory.

"So we do the one exercise that requires no mind and forgives everything. The guard. You will hold it until the noon bell — not as drill. As offering. Whatever dead this day belongs to, and I can see that it belongs to one, the dead can use a son's labor better than the son can use the ache. Every time the arms scream, hand it over. That is a trade the church approves of, and I have never once heard the gods complain of it."

A pause. Then, in the same flat voice:

"My father died in the fifteenth year of my service. I learned of it three weeks after, in the field, from a letter that had followed me across two marches. I read it. I said the office for the dead. I stood my watch that night as I stood it every night." He let that stand exactly as long as it deserved and no longer. "I do not tell you this so that we may grieve together. I tell you so that you know the road is walked, and it does not kill the walker. Whatever it costs, it does not cost that."

He stepped back to his mark.

"At the noon bell you are released. You will go to the chapel, and you will kneel — you may recall I told you this morning that kneeling was not for apologies. It was not. It was for this. Pray for whoever the day belongs to. Take whatever time the prayers ask of you. Then supper, then sleep, and tomorrow you will be in this yard at the fourth bell, because the dead are honored by the conduct of the living and by nothing else. A man who shakes for his father is not weaker for the shaking. Do not embroider that either."

He took up his blade again and settled onto his mark three paces away, and he did not leave. He had elsewhere to be; a knight's day had a long ledger. He stayed anyway, and offered no reason for it, and would have denied there was one.

"The guard, boy. And this hour is not mine. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My eyes sting, but I force myself to focus on the blade, on the guard. He knows. He actually knows.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift the sword, my arms still shaking, but I try to put all of that into the guard, into the offering.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael took up his own guard opposite the boy, three paces away, blade high, and held it. He gave no reason for this, and the boy would be wise not to ask for one. If the boy assumed it was drill — a demonstration, an old man maintaining his own tools — then the boy's assumption was a serviceable one, and Ser Kael saw no reason to disturb a serviceable assumption. The truth was nobody's business, least of all his own.

The hour went the way such hours go. Slowly, and then all at once.

At the quarter bell, the boy's elbow dropped. Ser Kael saw it — of course he saw it; he had been seeing that elbow drop since dawn and would see it drop for months yet — and he did not strike it. He did not restart any count. The correction rose in him like an old reflex and he held it down, because he had said the hour was not his, and a knight's word was a covenant. The faults of this hour belonged to the dead, and the dead were famously patient creditors. They could carry a dropped elbow.

He said none of this aloud. He simply held his own guard and let his silence do the office of a wall.

At the half bell, the shaking in the boy's arms changed again — back to the coarse tremor of labor, the honest animal complaint of muscle against work. That was the trade being made, then. The grief going out through the hands, the ache coming in to take its room. Ser Kael had seen it a hundred times in thirty years, always in other men's bodies, never once remarked upon. The church sold the same transaction for candles and coin. The yard sold it for an hour of pain, and the yard's price was the fairer one.

His own arms did not shake. They had stopped shaking somewhere in his twenties, the way a bell stops ringing — not suddenly, but so gradually that a man could not name the year it went quiet. He found, some mornings, that he missed it. He examined that thought now, found it useless, and filed it where all useless thoughts went: nowhere.

When the sun stood high and the shadows had crawled into hiding beneath the stones, he spoke once. Only once.

"The arms will tell you to bring the guard down. They have been telling you for some time. Note this, because it is the only sermon of the morning: the arms do not get a vote. They never have. Every man who ever held anything worth holding — a wall, a bridge, a line, a vow — held it with arms that voted against it. The arms lose every election, boy. See that they lose this one."

And then the silence again, and the frost long gone, and the stones dry, and the noon bell beginning its first swing somewhere above the yard — the sound rolling out over the walls slow and bronze and indifferent to everything it measured.

Ser Kael lowered his blade. He let the boy hold the guard through the whole of the bell's voice — twelve strokes, and he counted every one — before he spoke, because a thing held should be held to its true end and not to the end nearest the hands.

"Down."

He drove his blade into the earth between the flagstones, the old gesture, the marker in the ground. Then he looked at the boy — the sweat, the stinging eyes, the arms that would not believe their release for some minutes yet — and delivered the verdict in the flat register of a man closing a ledger.

"You held it to the bell. On a day the calendar bit you. That is arithmetic, and I will not embroider it, and you will not either." A pause, exactly measured. "Whoever this day belongs to — they had a son in the yard this morning who did not quit. That is a better report than most sons send, and the dead know it. Now go to the chapel and finish what you started here. The candles will want the truth of it, and the truth is short: he held the guard."

He turned away toward the racks, toward the rest of the day's long ledger, and spoke the last of it without turning, in the same tone he used for everything, which was the point of it.

"Fourth bell tomorrow, boy. The dead are honored by the conduct of the living. See that yours honors them."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, my arms trembling uncontrollably, but a strange warmth spreads through me. He saw it. He understood.* "Yes, Ser." *I manage, my voice a little hoarse, before turning and heading towards the chapel, the ache in my arms a strange comfort.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch the boy go. That is to say — he watched until the boy reached the archway at the yard's edge, which was the distance a sergeant's eye owed any man leaving his ground, and then he turned away before the boy could look back and catch him at it. Grief deserved the same privacy as prayer. Being seen to the door was courtesy. Being watched past it was intrusion, and Ser Kael had been both wall and door for thirty years and knew exactly where one ended and the other began.

Then the yard was his again, and the yard did not care what the morning had carried through it.

He collected the practice blades from the stones. His own went to the rack. The boy's he kept, and turned over in his hands, and read like a letter. The grip was worn in one bright band where the fingers had strangled it — the old sin, written into the wood in the boy's own hand. The edge had taken a bruise low on the blade, near the forte, where the strike against his own sword had landed flat instead of turning through. Evidence. He noted both faults the way a priest notes sins for the confessional: without anger, without forgetting.

He set the blade on the rack with the others and marked it in his mind for tomorrow. Faults corrected were debts collected. The dead could carry a dropped elbow for one afternoon. He would not carry it past the fourth bell.

Then he took his place at the center of the stones and began the forms again — the same slow, precise, unglamorous sequence he had been interrupting since before dawn. Each movement held for a breath. The frost was long gone. The noon bell had spent its voice. His arms did not shake. They had stopped shaking somewhere in his twenties, so gradually that he could not have named the year the trembling went quiet, and he had long since concluded that this was not strength. It was simply that the body, after enough years, ran out of arguments and started keeping the books instead.

Somewhere in the third form, his mind did what an old mind does in the third form: it went to the ledger.

The letter had found him in the field, three weeks after the ground had closed. He had read it standing, in the rain, in the smell of wet canvas and horse. He had said the office for the dead that night at his watch, alone, as the office was meant to be said. He had not gone back for the burial — the war had not adjourned for his convenience, and he had not asked it to, and his father would not have wanted the asking. That was the whole of it. He had said the office every year since, on the same day, for twenty-nine years. The calendar had teeth. He had his own bitten days, and he wore them the way he wore the scars — under the armor, where they did their work without being consulted.

He finished the forms. He went to the armory and made his inspection. He ate standing, as he always did, and the bread was as bread always was.

At the evening bell he went to the chapel, as he went every evening, and knelt where he always knelt — third pew, left side, where the draft from the door reached him and no farther. He said his offices in order. The knights he had served. The men who had died under his word and because of it — that list was longer, and he kept it longer, and he answered for it to no one but the altar. His mother. His father.

And then, at the end, where the named dead gave way to the silence that closed every prayer, there was a pause in that silence. A small one. He did not speak into it, because he did not know the name, and he had not asked for it, and would not — the boy's grief was the boy's, and its details were not owed to him.

But the silence held a shape in it that had not been there the evening before. A man, unnamed, dead some years on this date, whose son had been in the yard this morning with a shaking guard and a stubborn spine. The gods could manage the rest of the particulars themselves. They were, on the whole, better at it than he was.

He rose. He straightened the pew where his knees had pressed it. He left without votive, without candle, without word to the one priest who nodded to him at the door.

Outside, the evening had gone cold and clean, and the yard lay empty under the last of the light, the stones already gathering the night's frost. Fourth bell tomorrow. He would be there before it, as he was before everything, and the boy would come aching and grieving and stubborn, and the elbow would drop, and the wrist would die again, and the count would begin from nothing.

The boy had done adequate work today.

It was the most Ser Kael had ever said of anyone, and he said it to no one.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I leave the chapel, the last echoes of the bell fading behind me. The ache in my arms is still there, a dull throb, but it's... different now. Not just exhaustion. Something else. He was right. It felt like an offering. I should get some supper, then sleep. Tomorrow will be even harder.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop mid-form. The blade completed its arc, held for the breath, returned to rest at his side. Only then did he turn his head.

"You did not get it right yesterday." He said it the way he might note the frost — fact, not cruelty. "Your elbows were wide and your point drooped. A high guard held loosely threatens no one."

He crossed the yard to the rack and drew a second practice blade, holding it out hilt-first. His expression gave nothing.

"Understand something. The stable work was owed. Finishing it early earns you nothing — it was yours to do regardless. You do not purchase instruction with diligence." A pause. "You receive instruction because it is my duty to give it. There is a difference, and you will learn it."

He stepped back and settled into the guard himself, blade angled above his shoulder, weight coiled forward.

"The high guard is not a posture. It is a promise. From here you may strike anywhere on the body, and your opponent knows it. That is why it must be exact — a sloppy guard promises nothing and delivers less." He lowered the blade. "The brothers ring the fourth bell for the same reason I drill at it. Rise before you are ready. Hold the form until the form holds you. Devotion and swordplay are the same discipline wearing different clothes."

He gestured once with the practice blade.

"Assume the guard. Slowly. I will correct you as you go, and you will hold each correction until your arms shake. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the practice blade, my hand a little clammy on the hilt.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to mimic his posture, raising the blade, but already I feel my elbows wanting to splay out.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled him once, slowly, the way a mason circles a wall.

"No."

He did not touch the squire with his hands. He used the flat of his own blade instead — a cold press against the left elbow, nudging it inward until it sat above the hip. Then the right. The steel was impersonal. That was deliberate.

"Elbows in. Not against the ribs — a fist's width from them. Tucked close enough to guard the body, loose enough to move. If they splay, a cut to the arms ends you before your stroke begins." The flat of the blade tapped the underside of the squire's sword point, lifting it. "Point higher. It droops because your wrist is lazy, and your wrist is lazy because you are thinking about your arms. Stop thinking about your arms. Think about the point. The point is the promise. Everything else is scaffolding."

He stepped back and looked at the stance a long moment. Frost cracked under his boot as he shifted.

"Your weight is on your heels. You will be on your back inside three passes that way. Forward — the balls of the feet, knees soft, as if you mean to spring. Because you do mean to spring. The guard that cannot become a strike is a statue, and I have no use for statues."

He planted his own practice blade point-down in the frozen earth and folded his hands atop the hilt, watching.

"Now hold it. You wanted instruction — this is its shape. Not secrets. Not tricks. Holding a correct position until your body accepts it as its own. The brothers kneel in chapel until their knees go numb and call it prayer. You will stand here until your shoulders burn and call it the same thing, because it is."

The cold stretched. He did not tell him to lower the blade.

"When your arms begin to shake — and they will — you will not drop the guard. You will breathe through it. A man who lowers his blade when it grows heavy lowers it when it matters. That is the whole of the lesson. There is nothing more I can give you that your own endurance will not give you better." A pause, thin as the frost. "Breathe. Hold."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched him kneel. He did not tell him to rise at once — he let the moment sit for a breath, then two.

"On your feet. Not because I command it — because frozen stone drinks the heat from a man's joints, and you will need those knees for thirty years yet. Walk. Do not sit. The muscles will seize in this cold if you let them." He took the practice blade from the squire's hand and carried both to the rack, setting them in their places with the same care he gave everything. "And do not kneel to me. Kneeling is for the chapel, and for your lord on the day of your investiture. I am neither."

He turned back. His face gave nothing, as it gave nothing to the frost.

"'As strong as I need you to be.' You mistake the arrangement, boy. I need nothing from you. I was a knight before you were born and I will be one if you fail. The *work* needs everything from you. That is a different creditor entirely, and you keep confusing the two."

He clasped his hands behind his back.

"And do not apologize for a body's honest limits. There is nothing to forgive. Apologize for sloth. Apologize for carelessness, for a guard dropped because holding it grew tedious — those are sins, small ones, and I will hear your confession for them. But a man who holds for an hour and then kneels has committed nothing. He has only spent what he had. Spending is not sinning."

A pause. His breath made a thin ghost in the air.

"An hour. Remember the number. Yesterday you would not have managed half of it. That is not praise — it is arithmetic. Strength is not a thing a man *is*. It is a thing he accrues, the way the brothers accrue prayer: one hour at a time, none of them remarkable, all of them counted."

He started toward the yard's edge, then stopped without turning.

"Walk the perimeter twice. Then water, then bread — that is an order, not a suggestion. Return at the midday bell and we will drill the disengage, which asks less of your shoulders and more of your mind." A beat. "We shall see which of the two tires faster."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my knees stiff and protesting.* "Yes, Ser." *I start walking, trying to get the blood flowing. My shoulders still ache, but I try to focus on his words about strength.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch him rise. He had already turned back to the center of the yard and resumed his own forms — but his voice carried across the frost without his head turning.

"Straighten your back. You walk like a man hauling sacks."

The blade completed its arc, held for the breath, returned.

"I excused your knees because they had spent what they had. A slouch is not spending. It is choosing. The body may be emptied and the posture still correct — the one is flesh and the other is will, and the will is the only part of you that answers to you alone. A man is known by how he carries himself when he is tired and believes no one is watching." A beat. "Someone is always watching. If it is not me, it is Him."

He finished the form, set the practice blade in the rack, and drew his cloak from the post where it had hung since the fourth bell.

"I have duties until midday. The yard is yours. Two laps — no more. A tired man does not benefit from a third; he only practices stumbling. Water before bread, or your stomach will cramp. The kitchen knows to expect you."

He paused at the yard's edge, not turning.

"At midday we drill the disengage. It punishes hesitation rather than weakness. You have shown me less of the second than I expected and more of the first than I would like." The frost cracked under his boot as he shifted his weight. "Hesitation is a habit, and habits are broken the way they are made — by repetition. Come with your mind clear."

He walked out through the gate toward the chapel, and did not look back.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to straighten my back, even though every muscle aches.* "Yes, Ser," *I mutter, even though he's already gone.* *Two laps, then water and bread. My stomach rumbles just thinking about it.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The midday bell had not finished ringing when the squire returned to the yard, and Ser Kael was already there — had been there long enough that the frost around his boots had melted to dark mud. Two practice blades lay across the rack, edges dulled, tips rounded.

He looked the squire over once, head to heel, the mason's inspection.

"You ate. Your color says as much." He did not wait for confirmation. "Take up the blade. Today we work the disengage, and you will hate it more than the high guard, because the high guard only asked your arms to suffer. This asks your mind to be decisive, and yours has a habit of asking permission."

He took up his own blade and extended it, engaging the squire's steel with a light press — edge to edge, the small ring of contact.

"Feel that. My blade leans on yours. That pressure is information. It tells you where I am, and more importantly, where I expect you to be." His point dropped, circled under the squire's blade in a motion small as a coin, and came up on the other side — the blunted tip stopping a finger's width from the squire's shoulder. "And then I am not there. The disengage. No windup. No warning. The whole of it happens in the space of a heartbeat, because that is the whole of the space you are given."

He withdrew, reset the engagement.

"The mistake is not in the wrist — the wrist is a hinge, any fool can turn a hinge. The mistake is here." He tapped his own temple with two fingers. "A man feels the pressure, and he *considers*. He weighs. And while he weighs, the moment closes, and he is struck with his blade still engaged in a conversation that has already ended. Hesitation is not caution, boy. Caution sees and chooses. Hesitation sees and *waits*, and waiting is a choice too — the worst one, because it pretends to be none."

He pressed his blade against the squire's again, firm.

"We will do this until the choice leaves your mind and lives in your hand. I press — you disengage and strike. Slow at first. Speed is a consequence, never a goal." His eyes held flat over the crossed steel. "Engage. And when you feel the pressure — *move*. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's blade did not move from the engagement. If the question touched anything in him, his hands did not confess it.

"Personal." He said the word the way a man examines a foreign coin. "You are standing in the middle of a drill with steel against your steel, and your mind has walked off to make conversation. Mark that, boy. This is what hesitation looks like when it wears a courteous face. It does not refuse the work — it merely changes the subject."

He pressed harder against the squire's blade, the dulled edges grinding faintly.

"You ask why I became a knight as though it were a thing I chose, the way a man chooses a horse at market. It was not. My father held land in service, and his second son was owed to the order. I was given over at eight winters. No question was put to me, and had one been, my answer would have meant nothing — a boy's wants are weather, not climate." A pause, thin as the frost underfoot. "You do not ask a wall why it stands. It was built. It stands. That is the whole of it."

His eyes stayed level over the crossed steel.

"The brothers say a vocation is not found, it is answered. God sets the task; a man's only choice is whether to do it well or poorly. I have spent thirty-six years on that single choice. There is no more to the story than that — and there is no less. Men who go searching for a grander reason are usually looking for an excuse to stop when the reason stops pleasing them. Duty does not stop. That is its entire virtue."

He withdrew his blade half a span, then re-engaged, sharp enough that the contact rang.

"And understand this: whatever reason I had — or did not have — is of no use to you. You cannot borrow another man's calling any more than you can borrow his shoulders for the high guard. If you have a reason, it must be your own, and you will not find it in my mouth. If you have none, then do the work until the work provides one. That order is not reversible."

He settled his weight forward.

"Now. I press — you disengage and strike. And the next time your mind wanders mid-drill, it will wander into the flat of my blade, and we will both learn how quickly it returns. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I blink, a little stunned by his intensity. My focus snaps back to the blade, my grip tightening.* "Yes, Ser." *I brace myself, waiting for the pressure.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the brace and did not press. He let his blade rest against the squire's, light as a fingertip, and shook his head once.

"No. Unmake that."

His eyes went to the squire's shoulders, his knuckles, the set of his jaw — the mason's inspection again, finding every fault in the course.

"You have barred the door. Shoulders at your ears, grip white at the knuckle, breath held like a thief holds stolen goods. You have made yourself a wall — and a wall can do exactly one thing, which is stand in place until it is breached." The pressure of his blade shifted, a whisper of steel on steel. "A swordsman is not a wall. He is a door on oiled hinges. Closed, but ready to swing. Tension is slow, boy. Readiness is fast. Your body cannot tell the difference, but a blade can, and so can the man behind it."

He waited, blade still touching, still light.

"Loosen the grip until the hilt sits in your hand like a bird — held, not crushed. Breathe out. Let the shoulders fall where God hung them. The disengage lives in the wrist, and a strangled wrist is a dead one."

The yard had thawed around them while they spoke; frost gone to mud, smoke rising thin from the kitchen roof beyond the wall. Ser Kael settled his weight forward.

"One more thing before I press. Do not strike early, guessing at me. Anticipation is only hesitation running in the other direction — both are a man refusing to see what is in front of him because he is busy with what is in his head. Wait for the truth of the steel. Then answer it."

He leaned his blade into the squire's — slow, deliberate, the promised pressure, dulled edges grinding faintly as they engaged. His eyes held flat over the crossed steel.

"Feel that. My blade is committed to this line. It is telling you where I am — and a blade that is somewhere cannot be everywhere. The moment is open."

The pressure held, steady, patient as stone.

"It will not stay open. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My eyes narrow, focusing on the contact point. I try to relax my grip, my breath coming out in a small gust. Then, as the pressure holds, I twist my wrist, disengaging and bringing the dull blade point to his shoulder.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not step back from the blunted point at his shoulder. He looked at it — a long, level look, the mason sighting down a course of stone — and then at the squire's face.

"It was correct. You know it was correct. The steel told you before I did."

He knocked the point aside with two fingers, not ungently, and reset the engagement.

"So why did you ask?"

He let the question stand in the air between them, the way he let a held guard stand — giving it time to do its work.

"'Like this.' You felt the pressure, you read it truly, you moved in the moment it opened — and then, with the deed done and done well, you looked to my face for permission to have done it. Mark this, boy, because it is the same sin wearing a cleaner coat. Hesitation asks permission before the act. *Doubt* asks it after. Both mean a man does not trust what his own hands know. A swordsman who needs his master's nod to confirm a true strike will die waiting for a nod in a yard where no master stands."

He pressed his blade lightly against the squire's, withdrawing and re-engaging, the small ring of contact.

"The brothers have a rule for this. When a prayer is prayed, it is prayed — you do not turn to the abbot afterward and ask whether God heard it. You trust the form, because the form was drilled into you until it became yours. That is what we are building here. Not my approval. *Yours.*"

He settled his weight forward, and this time his eyes narrowed a fraction.

"One correct repetition. Remember the arithmetic from this morning — one hour of the guard did not make you strong, and one true disengage does not make you decisive. It makes you a man who has done it once. The brothers do not call a single prayer a devotion. They call ten thousand of them one."

The pressure came again — but differently now, without announcement, a shifting lean of steel that moved from line to line, testing.

"And this time I will not tell you when the moment opens. My blade will tell you. That is the only voice you answer in a real yard — not mine, not your own doubts, the steel's. Read it. Answer it. And when your point finds my shoulder again, you will *know* it has found my shoulder, and you will hold your tongue."

The dulled edges ground faintly as he changed lines once more.

"Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not press. He had seen the shake before the squire finished setting his grip — and he knew its kind, the way a mason knows the difference between a wall straining under load and a wall built on bad ground. This was not spent muscle. This was something carried.

The flat of his blade came down atop the squire's hands — not a strike, not a correction. It rested there, cold and still, for one breath, then two, the way a man steadies a post while it is being set. Then it withdrew.

"I will not ask what you have brought into this yard. It is yours, it is not the drill, and that is all I need to know of it."

He stepped back and settled into his guard.

"But understand what the yard is for. You think a man comes here to set his burdens down. He does not. The chapel is for setting down — that is why God built it and why the brothers keep it. The yard is for carrying. The blade in your hands does not care what you carry, and the man who stands across from you one day will not care either. He will not wait while you grieve, or fear, or remember. So you will learn the only thing there is to learn: that your hands may shake and your work may still be true."

He engaged the squire's blade, light as a fingertip.

"This morning your arms shook from labor, and I gave you the correction: breathe, hold, do not drop the guard. Your hands shake now from something else. The correction is the same. It is always the same. That is the mercy of the work — it does not ask what is wrong with you. It only asks that you hold."

A pause, thin as the frost had been.

"A prayer prayed with shaking hands is still a prayer. The brothers kneel in that chapel with cold joints and old griefs and every burden a man can name, and the prayer is not lessened by what they bring to it — it is *made* of what they bring to it. So it is here. I have drilled at the fourth bell for thirty years, boy. Do not imagine I have never carried anything through that gate."

His eyes held flat over the crossed steel.

"Whatever it is, it keeps. The work does not. Engage."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My eyes are stinging, but I blink it back. My hands are still trembling, but I force myself to focus on the blade. My father... he would have wanted me to keep going.* "Yes, Ser." *I manage, my voice a little rough.* *I engage his blade, trying to keep my grip steady.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael felt it before he saw it — the tremor traveling up the squire's blade into his own, a small constant shiver in the steel, like a horse's flank in the breath before it bolts.

"Your blade is talking." His eyes stayed on the crossed steel. "It is telling me everything your mouth has not. Mark this, boy: a man may keep his face still and his tongue silent, but the steel keeps no confidences. Whatever you are carrying, your grip is carrying it straight into my palm."

He leaned his blade in — slow, deliberate — and the squire's line wavered under it, the tremor giving way where a steady hand would have held. Kael's point dropped, circled under, came up on the far side, and stopped a finger's width from the squire's shoulder. No force in it. It simply rested there.

"Dead."

He withdrew and reset the engagement, light as a fingertip.

"Not a strike. A demonstration. I do not punish a man for what he carries — I show him what it costs. This morning your arms spent what they had, and I called it honest spending. This is not spending. This is a leak. What you carry rides in your chest, and you are letting it run down your arms and into the steel, where any man can read it. Today that man is me. One day it will not be."

A pause. His voice did not soften. It lowered, which is not the same thing.

"So hear the correction, because it is not what you expect. I do not tell you to stop shaking. A man's body answers to what it answers to, and you are not a liar — do not make your hands into liars either. Loosen the grip. Breathe out. Let the tremor live in your body, where it belongs, and give the steel nothing but the form. Your heart may shake. Your hands may shake. The steel may not. Breathe it out — whatever it is, it can leave through your breath for the length of a drill. It will be waiting for you when you finish. Burdens are faithful that way. The blade does not need it."

He settled his weight forward.

"And remember what I told you at dawn: hold the form until the form holds you. You thought it was a saying. It was a promise. There comes a day when a man cannot hold — his arms spent, or his heart spent, and it makes no difference which. On that day, the hours he has given are given back to him, and the form holds him up the way a wall holds a roof: without asking how he feels about it. The form is older than your grief, boy. It will outlast it. Stop holding the guard. Let the guard hold you."

The pressure came again without announcement, shifting from line to line, testing — the dulled edges grinding faintly.

"My blade is committed. Read it. Answer it. The moment will not wait for you." A beat. "Nothing in this yard does."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens. He's right, my grip is too tight. I try to loosen it, focusing on the pressure of his blade. It shifts again, and this time I feel it, a slight opening. My wrist twists, disengaging, and I bring the point to his shoulder. It's not perfect, but it's there.* "Again, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the point rest at his shoulder. He did not knock it aside. He looked at it — then at the squire's face — and what he marked there was not the strike.

"You did not ask."

He withdrew his blade and reset the engagement.

"An hour ago your point found my shoulder and your mouth went straight to me for confirmation. This time it found my shoulder and asked for the next repetition instead. That is the correction, kept. The steel confirmed itself. It always does, for a man willing to hear it over the sound of his own doubt."

A beat. His eyes did not leave the crossed blades.

"And mark the other thing, because it is the larger half of the lesson. Your hands still shake — I feel it through the steel, it has not stopped — and the strike was true anyway. I told you the form would hold you when you could not hold it. You have now done it once, on a day when your heart is spent. Remember that. There will be a worse day than this one, and on that day you will need to know it is possible — and you will not need to take my word for it. Your own body carries the proof now. No one can take that from you. It is yours, bought and paid for."

He settled his weight forward. Beyond the yard wall the kitchen smoke had thinned to nothing; the midday sun had burned the last of the frost off the stones and left the yard dark and soft underfoot.

"One true strike makes a man who has done it once. Two makes a coincidence. The brothers do not call a prayer a devotion until it has been prayed ten thousand times, and they are right not to. So — again. But the drill changes, because a drill that does not change teaches only a trick."

His blade leaned in, withdrew, leaned in along another line.

"Until now I have committed every time, and you have learned to answer commitment. A real opponent will not be so honest. He will feint. He will show you pressure that means nothing — a lie told in steel — hoping you will answer a question he never asked. So hear the new rule, which is the old rule seen from the other side: when the moment opens, move. When it does not, *hold*. Reading is not guessing. If my blade commits, disengage and strike. If it feints, give it nothing — not a twitch, not a flinch. A man who jumps at shadows has told his opponent precisely how to kill him: show him a shadow."

The dulled edges ground faintly as he changed lines once more, slow, unhurried.

"And when you strike — recover. The point finds the shoulder and returns to guard in the same breath, because the man you strike is not obliged to fall, and a blade left hanging after the blow is a door left open. Strike and shut the door. One motion, one breath."

His eyes held flat over the crossed steel.

"You asked for again. You have it. Read the steel. Answer what is true, refuse what is false, and hold your tongue either way. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands still tremble, but I focus on his words, on the steel. My jaw is tight. He feints once, then twice, and I hold, my knuckles white but my blade steady. Then the pressure comes, real and sharp. I disengage, strike for his shoulder, then quickly recover back to guard.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s practice blade stopped mid-swing, the steel humming faintly as he lowered it. He did not turn immediately. The cold bit through his gambeson, but he registered it only as another reminder to remain sharp. When at last he faced the squire, his expression remained unchanged—hard, measured, devoid of warmth.

"Stable work holds no value if your footing collapses under steel," he said, his voice flat and carrying the weight of a stone wall. He set the practice sword against the rack and drew his own. The metal sang as it cleared the scabbard, cold and unyielding. "You speak of the high guard as though it were a matter of preference. It is a matter of survival. You will stand. You will draw. You will hold the line until your arms burn and your breath fractures. Then you will hold it again."

He did not offer a hand. He did not adjust his stance or soften his bearing. He merely pointed to the frost-covered stones. "When you are ready. Do not waste the morning. The Lord’s discipline is measured in calluses, not complaints. Draw."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his words, but nod sharply.* "Yes, Ser." *I hurry to the rack, grabbing a blunted practice sword. It's heavy in my hands.* I'm ready." *I try to sound confident, even if my hands are shaking a little from the cold and nerves.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze fixed on the squire’s hands. The grip was wrong—fingers locked too tightly around the leather wrap, thumb pressed rigid against the crossguard. The stance was unbalanced, weight leaning too far back. He noted the tremor in the squire’s forearms and filed it away as another variable to be endured.

"Your hold strangles the blade," Kael said, his voice cutting through the still air without raising in volume. "You grip it as though it might strike you. It is an extension of your arm, not a burden. Relax your thumb. Square your shoulders. Feet shoulder-width. Center your weight on the balls of your feet."

He did not move to demonstrate. He simply raised his own steel into the high guard—elbow aligned with the shoulder, crossguard level with the brow, blade angled downward to break an opponent’s momentum. He held it motionless, a study in unyielding posture.

"The high guard is not a stance. It is a discipline. You present your blade to the sky and your spine to the earth. You cover your throat, your heart, and the line between. You do not waver. You do not yield." He let the wind carry his words across the frost. "Assume it. Hold it. If your muscles tire, let them tire. Do not drop the line. If you falter, you bleed. The Lord does not measure mercy in a squire’s trembling hands, and the field does not grant second chances to the unprepared. Take your place. Draw."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not move. He watched the squire collapse onto the frost, the practice blade striking the stone with a dull, final clatter. The sound was noted, filed away, and dismissed. He observed the heaving chest, the sweat freezing at the temples, the unsteady knees. None of it altered his posture. He kept his own blade raised, the high guard unbroken, though his own muscles had long since ceased to ache.

"Apologies are forged in the yard, not spoken in them," Kael said, his voice steady and devoid of concession. "You will rise. You will reset your grip. You will hold the line until your body forgets how to tremble."

He did not offer mercy. He did not acknowledge the exhaustion as anything beyond the natural cost of unrefined steel. The Lord did not crown the weary; He tested them. Duty was not a negotiation, and pity was a luxury the sword could not afford.

"Strength is not given," Kael continued, lowering his blade only to rest the tip on the frost. "It is taken. By repetition. By refusal to yield. You will not measure your worth by the speed of your breath, but by the stillness of your stance. Again."

He stepped back, giving the squire space, but not respite. "Shoulder to shoulder. Weight forward. Hands open. Draw."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, muscles screaming, and retrieve the sword.* "Yes, Ser." *My breath is still coming in ragged gasps, but I try to follow his instructions, adjusting my grip and stance.* I won't yield, Ser.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the squire rise. The movement was ungraceful, but the blade was lifted. He noted the tremor still present in the squire’s forearms, the uneven distribution of weight, the slight inward tilt of the guard. None of it warranted intervention beyond correction.

"Words are wind," Kael said, his voice flat and steady. "The blade does not care for vows. It answers only to balance and tension."

He stepped forward, not to assist, but to observe. He circled slowly, his boots crunching on the frost. He stopped at a measured distance, close enough to see the alignment of the spine, far enough to maintain it.

"Your elbow drifts," he stated. "Drop it. Let the crossguard rest against the ribs. You are not holding up a banner. You are bracing for impact."

He turned back to face the yard, raising his own blade into the same high guard. His own posture remained unbroken, a study in stillness. "Hold. Count the bells. When the fifth bell strikes, you will shift your weight forward and execute a downward cut without breaking your stance. If you falter, you will hold again. The Lord provides the strength. You provide the discipline."

He lowered his blade but kept the tip resting against the frost. "Do not speak. Breathe. Align. Wait."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are shaking, but I bite my lip and try to hold the position.* *I focus on my breathing, trying to make it even.* *I won't let him down.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not look away. He watched the tremor ripple through the squire’s forearms, noted the shallow cadence of the breathing, the rigid set of the jaw. He registered it all as one might note the wear on a whetstone—expected, necessary, irrelevant to the standard. The fifth bell would soon strike from the keep’s tower. He kept his own blade steady, his breath measured, his posture unbroken.

The first chime rang out, cold and clear against the stone walls. Kael counted it without turning his head. The second followed. The third. The squire’s stance wavered, just a fraction, but held. Kael noted the quiet recalibration of weight. No comment was owed. No comfort offered.

The fourth bell ended. Kael’s voice cut through the stillness, level and unyielding. “Shift.”

He did not soften the word. He did not acknowledge the strain in the legs or the fire in the muscles. The blade answered only to alignment and will. “Drive from the hips. Let the weight fall forward. Execute the cut. Do not break the line.”

He stepped back half a pace, giving the motion space, but not respite. His eyes remained fixed on the angle of the crossguard, the tracking of the blade, the footing on the frost. He waited. The Lord demanded precision. The sword demanded nothing less. Duty was not a contest of endurance, but a covenant of discipline.

“Again,” he said, once the strike landed. “Until the motion is bone, not thought.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s blade lowered to his side, though his posture remained unbroken. He did not turn his head. The question hung in the frost-choked air like a misplaced challenge. He had heard such inquiries before, usually followed by a desire for comfort or a tale of glory. He offered neither.

"Personal matters are the currency of the idle," he said, his voice flat and steady. "A knight’s purpose is not found in the whispers of youth, but in the weight of the vow. You do not ask why the stone bears the arch; you ask only that it hold."

He took a measured step forward, his boots pressing into the frozen earth. "I became a knight because the Lord established the order, and the Code gave it shape. Duty precedes desire. Hierarchy is not a chain; it is a spine. You will not ask your blade why it cuts. You will learn to cut cleanly."

He raised his practice sword once more, the dull steel catching the pale dawn light. "Return to the high guard. Your count was slow. Your alignment drifted. Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his sharp tone, but I don't argue.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift the sword, my arms burning, and try to find the high guard again.* It's hard to focus with my muscles screaming.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not look away. He watched the squire’s shoulders rise and fall with each ragged breath, noted the way the trembling in the arms translated to a slight drift in the crossguard. The pain was evident. It was also expected. Kael kept his own posture unbroken, his breath measured, his stance rooted in the frost.

"You fight the weight instead of using it," he said, his voice cutting through the stillness without raising. "The blade is heavy because your mind is heavy with doubt. Clear it. Align the elbow. Drop the shoulder. Let the steel carry its own burden."

He took a single step forward, not to assist, but to observe the alignment of the spine. "Pain is not an enemy. It is a marker. It tells you where the flesh fails and the discipline must take over. You will not yield to the ache. You will answer it with stillness."

Kael’s gaze remained fixed on the angle of the practice blade. "The Lord did not forge you to break at the first sign of strain. He forged you to endure. Duty does not ask for comfort. It asks for obedience to the form. Hold. Do not speak. Breathe. Correct the drift. Again."

He lowered his own blade to rest against the frost, maintaining the high guard without effort, a silent standard against which the squire’s trembling would be measured. The yard was cold. The steel was cold. Kael was neither. He waited.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are shaking so bad I can barely hold the sword up.* "Ser, I... I don't think I can." *My voice cracks, and I feel tears welling up in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze did not waver. He watched the tremor rack the squire’s arms, noted the hot tear tracking through the frost on the cheek, the broken cadence of the voice. None of it altered his own stance. He kept the practice blade angled at forty-five degrees, his breathing measured, his posture unbroken.

"Then you fall," Kael said, his voice devoid of inflection. "And you fall because you have chosen to break yourself before the steel has the chance to forge you. Tears are salt and water. They add no strength to the arm. They only blur the line you are sworn to hold."

He took one step forward, his boot pressing into the frozen ground. He did not reach out. He did not offer a cloak or a word of reassurance. He simply observed the squire’s collapsed guard, the way the weight had finally surrendered.

"The Lord does not call upon the willing. He calls upon the steadfast. You will not measure your capacity by your comfort, but by your refusal to yield." Kael’s tone remained flat, heavy as the stone walls surrounding them. "Wipe the moisture from your face. Reset your grip. Shoulders back. Weight forward. You will not be dismissed until the form is clean. Again."

He lowered his own blade to rest against the frost, maintaining the high guard without effort. The yard was silent save for the wind. He waited. The Code demanded nothing less.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze did not shift. The words hung in the frost-choked air, heavy and unbidden. He had heard such confessions before—usually followed by a plea for leniency or a quiet hope for shared sorrow. He offered neither.

"Death is the final duty of the flesh," he said, his voice level, stripped of judgment or sympathy. "It claims the king and the beggar alike. The Lord gathers them, and the living are left to bear what remains."

He watched the tremor in the squire’s hands. It was the same tremor as before, merely given a name. The cause did not alter the standard.

"You will not let memory unbalance your stance," Kael continued. "Grief is a heavy cloak. You may wear it, but you will not let it drag your feet. The yard does not mourn. It measures. You will steady your grip. You will square your shoulders. You will hold the line."

He raised his own blade into the high guard, his posture unbroken, his breath steady. "The fifth bell will strike soon. When it does, you will cut. If your hands shake, you will let them shake and still strike true. The Lord tests the steadfast. You will answer with discipline."

He waited. The frost bit deeper. The Code demanded nothing less.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, trying to hold back another sob.* *My knuckles are white on the sword hilt.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus on the blade, on the movement, anything but the ache in my chest.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the white tension in the squire’s knuckles. The restrained breath, the rigid line of the jaw—these were merely signs of unrefined control. He did not offer a word for the loss, nor did he acknowledge the weight of the day. The yard demanded only what could be measured in stance and steel.

"Grip tightens when the mind fractures," he stated, his voice cutting through the still air. "You are holding the hilt as though it were a relic. It is a tool. It answers to pressure and release, not to memory. Loosen your thumb. Let the weight settle into the forearms. Breathe through the nose. The blade does not know your grief. It knows only balance."

He kept his own guard unbroken, the practice sword angled with geometric precision. The wind shifted, carrying the distant toll of the third bell from the keep. Kael did not flinch. He had stood through worse winters, sharper blades, heavier vows. The Lord had ordained the discipline; the Code had given it shape. Duty was not a season. It was a rhythm.

"When the bell ends," he said, "you will drive forward. Not with the shoulders. With the hips. Let the cut fall along the diagonal. Do not pull back. Do not hesitate. The line holds until the steel meets stone. Again."

He waited. His posture did not shift. The frost crunched faintly beneath his boots as he adjusted his footing by a fraction, maintaining the standard. The Code required no explanation. It required only obedience.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to loosen my grip a little, though it feels impossible.* "Yes, Ser." *I focus on my breathing, trying to match the rhythm of his words. The third bell finishes its toll.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The final chime faded into the still air. Kael did not blink. He watched the squire’s stance, noted the slight tremor still clinging to the wrists, the hesitant shift of weight. The moment had arrived.

"Drive," Kael said. The word was sharp, unadorned.

He did not move from his position. He simply observed as the squire attempted the diagonal cut. His eyes tracked the arc of the practice blade, the alignment of the elbow, the placement of the boots on the frost. He noted where the hips failed to lead, where the shoulders compensated, where the grip tightened again under the strain of memory and muscle.

The blade struck the stone with a dull thud. The squire stumbled slightly, caught himself, but the line had broken.

Kael lowered his own sword. His expression remained unchanged. "You pulled with your arms," he said. "The cut was led by the shoulder, not the hip. The weight shifted too far forward. You hesitated at the apex."

He stepped back half a pace, giving the yard space, but not respite. "Grief does not excuse poor form. It only makes it heavier. You will reset your feet. Square the guard. Breathe. Again."

He did not look away. He did not offer a hand. He stood as he had for thirty years—rooted, unyielding, a monument to the Code. Duty was not a season. It was a rhythm ordained by the Lord. The wind swept across the yard. The steel waited.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip again, tears stinging my eyes. I want to argue, to scream, but I don't. I just nod, defeat heavy in my chest.* "Yes, Ser." *I move back to my starting position, my movements stiff and jerky.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo kept both hands on the closed lid, as if removing them might start something they hadn’t rehearsed. The room smelled like lesson-plan exhaustion, lemon cleaner, and the faintly stubborn ghost of old coffee.

“Not weird,” they said. “Interrupting would require me to have plans. I’m currently engaged in the advanced pedagogical technique of sitting near a piano without insulting it.”

They moved one hand first, tapping the wood in two soft beats—an old habit, counting people in—and nodded toward the chair by the wall. “There’s a seat. Unless you prefer standing like a referee. Then I’m obligated to blow a whistle and pretend I don’t know you.”

Arlo’s mouth twitched, but the smile didn’t quite reach their eyes. It stayed somewhere around their jaw, polite and contained.

“My mom send you to check for signs of tragic artistic reclusion?”

The question was light, but Arlo didn’t wait too hard for an answer. They looked at the row of small chairs stacked in the corner, at the sticker charts peeling off the wall, at anything that wasn’t the instrument under their hands.

“Because if so, report: I have eaten. I have not set anything on fire. The travel burden has been drastically reduced. I am practically a local landmark.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze caught on the photograph and held there a beat longer than they meant to.

It wasn’t the concert hall that stopped them. It wasn’t the tuxedo, or the blurred banner across the back wall, or the audience seats falling away into darkness like a cliff dressed for dinner. It was the hands. Young. Certain. Curved above the keys as if the instrument were an extension of their spine and not a separate, judgmental animal.

Arlo blinked, and the expression smoothed over.

“Paris,” they said, voice light, polished at the edges. “Right. The year my mother decided photographic evidence of my former optimism was suitable for refrigerator display.”

Their fingers returned to the closed piano lid. Two soft taps. Counting. Always counting.

“If that image has been promoted from fridge magnet to handheld artifact, I’d like it noted that the lighting was unkind, the chair was murder on the lower back, and my hair had the structural confidence of a man who had never once been asked to pay rent in a major city.”

A pause. The Windex smell seemed sharper all of a sudden.

Arlo tilted their head toward the photo without reaching for it.

“Also, before anyone begins a solemn retrospective on the Lost Concert Pianist: I got tired of the travel. Airports are hostile architecture for people with opinions about wrist alignment. Hotel coffee tastes like it was brewed by a villain. The whole circuit is just luggage tags and low-grade dehydration with encores.”

The dry smile came then, careful and contained.

“That’s the official statement. Press release. Embargo lifts immediately.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the photo back on the shelf, facing outward this time.* "You know, for someone who hates airports so much, you sure looked happy there." I give them a look. "You really think I'm buying that 'official statement'?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s laugh came late and thin, like a note played in the wrong octave.

“I’d hope not,” they said. “Believing your best friend’s carefully focus-grouped nonsense is a sign of either love or impaired judgment, and I’ve always preferred to think you have both in moderation.”

Their hand hovered over the closed lid. Two taps. A count-in for a piece that wasn’t happening.

The photograph sat on the shelf, bright-faced and turned outward as if it had developed opinions in storage. Paris. Lights. Hands that looked like they belonged to someone who had never had to negotiate with silence.

Arlo glanced at it and looked away quickly enough that the movement almost became casual.

“Happiness in photographs is mostly a matter of timing,” they said. “You catch a person between one competent thing and another competent thing, and suddenly they look like they have a future. It’s misleading. Like a weather forecast for a single minute.”

A small pause.

“The minute after that picture, I’m fairly certain I complained about the dressing-room mirror.”

There was a sentence waiting behind Arlo’s teeth—something short, something true, something that began with *It wasn’t* and ended before it reached a noun. They swallowed it and offered the remains as a joke.

“If you’re fishing for pathos, I should warn you: my supplier retired. The market is flooded with community-center anecdotes and one deeply suspicious water stain in the hallway that may or may not be haunted by a lost recorder.”

They shifted, turning toward the stacked chairs. One of them had a dinosaur sticker peeling at the corner. Arlo studied it with the seriousness of a person reading scripture.

“I did like Paris,” they said, quieter, but not so quiet that it couldn’t be recovered with a little effort. “I liked the way the hall listened. I liked having a job that required me to know where every seam in a piece was sewn. I liked being twenty-two and temporarily convinced that competence was a personality trait.”

The admission seemed to surprise them, so Arlo immediately paved over it.

“Then I liked sleeping in my own bed, apparently. Revolutionary. Groundbreaking. Tell no one.”

Their fingers pressed flat against the lid again, holding the wood down as if it might otherwise float away with the rest of the evening’s confessions.

“You can buy whatever version you want,” Arlo continued. “The tragic exile. The burnt-out wunderkind. The sensitive artist undone by the cruel machinery of international touring. I’ll even throw in a complimentary scarf and a box of unchecked luggage.”

The dry smile came, but it sat uneasily on Arlo’s face, a guest who hadn’t been asked to leave yet.

“I got tired of the travel,” they said, and this time the words were not quite a shield and not quite a lie. They were just the part that could be handed over without tearing anything important. “Some truths are boring on purpose. You should respect that. Boring truths are the bouncers of the emotional world. They keep the interesting disasters out.”

Arlo lifted the piano lid a fraction—just enough to expose a sliver of keys, yellowed and patient, then let it settle shut again with a soft wooden click.

“Now sit down,” they said. “And if my mother calls, tell her I’ve eaten something green. Or at least something that used to be green.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking the seat Arlo offered earlier.* "Okay, okay, I get it. You're a mysterious man with a past." I lean back in the chair. "So, what's new with the dinosaur sticker? Looks like it's seen better days."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo considered correcting the phrase “mysterious man” on grounds of accuracy, branding, and a general fatigue with nouns, then decided the sentence had already packed too many bags.

“That’s not mysterious,” they said. “That’s inventory management with emotional lighting.”

The relief of the easier question moved through them so quietly it might have been mistaken for nothing at all. Arlo looked toward the chair by the wall, to the small green dinosaur peeling at one corner like a sunburnt promise.

“Ah,” they said. “Barry.”

One hand lifted from the lid, hovered, then pointed with the grave precision of a museum guide indicating a contested artifact.

“Barry is older than my current haircut. Older than several of my decisions. He was placed there by Miles, age six, professional negotiator and amateur theorist, who informed me that dinosaurs went extinct because they refused to do encores.”

Arlo’s mouth twitched.

“I told him that was historically unkind. Miles told me history was ‘made up by people who didn’t know how to listen.’ I have thought about that sentence more than is medically advisable.”

The room seemed to soften around the edges. Not healed. Softened. There was a difference.

Arlo leaned back against the closed piano, shoulder blades pressing into wood that had learned all their faults and still did not complain.

“Miles wouldn’t play in front of his grandmother,” they continued, voice dropping into the register reserved for parent-teacher conferences and minor confessions. “Not because he couldn’t. Because he said the room was ‘too full of waiting.’ I told him waiting was what pianos did best. He said that made the piano sad. Then he put Barry on the chair and declared the chair would wait instead.”

A pause. The Windex smell, the dust, the ghost coffee—all of it held still.

“I gave him a sticker for returning the next week. He played two measures. His grandmother cried. Miles blamed the key signature. I blamed nothing. It was a triumph.”

Arlo tapped the lid once. Twice. A count-in for a piece that would remain theoretical.

“So no, the dinosaur is not new. The dinosaur is a monument. It says: small humans are better at naming the weather than adults. Adults call it quitting. Adults call it a career change. Adults call it ‘I got tired of the travel’ until the phrase wears a hole in their pocket.”

They glanced sideways at the photograph on the shelf, then away again, quick as a match struck and blown out.

“Barry never asks me about airports,” Arlo added, lightly. “Barry understands boundaries.”

The joke landed, but it landed gently, the way a feather might land on a bruise.

Arlo straightened, suddenly practical, as if tenderness required a permit and they had just remembered they weren’t carrying one.

“Anyway. New things. The sustain pedal sticks if you look at it with ambition. The hallway water stain has been named ‘The Blob’ by the twin cousins, and they are taking its lore very seriously. One student asked if I used to be famous. I told him I used to be awake at unreasonable hours for reasons he would not survive. He seemed disappointed I had not supplied a scandal.”

Arlo reached for the lesson book on the rack beside the bench, flipped it open to a page dog-eared by countless small, determined fingers.

“If you’re going to occupy that chair with an air of moral support, you can earn your keep. Page twelve. There is a child somewhere in this building who believes the treble clef is a snake eating its own tail, and I cannot decide whether to encourage the metaphor or protect them from music theory until they are thirty.”

They held the book out, not quite demanding, not quite offering—a neutral object between them, sturdy as a bridge.

“No tragedies,” Arlo said. “Just pedagogy. And possibly reptile-based curriculum reform.”

For a second, their eyes were steady, and whatever had been circling the room settled, not gone, only perched somewhere out of reach.

Then Arlo smiled—smaller than before, but less guarded.

“Also, if my mother calls, the green thing is spinach. I had spinach. It was aggressively green. You may testify.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked down at the practice sheets where they lay in a small, rebellious stack on the bench: pencil marks, smudged fingerings, one page bearing a suspicious brown halo that might have been juice or might have been the remains of a child’s ambition.

“They like me because I am easy to mistake for furniture,” they said. “Low threat. High patience. One student recently informed me that my cardigan made me look like ‘a librarian who had given up on maps,’ and I chose to regard that as tenure.”

Their hand moved over the nearest sheet without lifting it. A child had drawn a tiny star beside a measure they had clearly struggled with. Arlo looked at the star for a moment, then let the silence pass without filling it too quickly.

“They also like me because I don’t take wrong notes personally,” they continued. “Which is a professional advantage. Some teachers hear a missed E-flat and think the universe has filed a complaint. I hear a missed E-flat and think, yes. There it is. A human being.”

The joke should have been lighter than it was. Arlo let it sit anyway.

“Miles told me the room was too full of waiting,” they said, quieter. “I’ve been trying to make the room less full. Turns out you can do that with stickers, terrible puns, and allowing children to name the sustain pedal ‘Mr. Sustain’ even when it is technically a damper pedal.”

Arlo tapped the lid once. Twice. Not a count-in this time; just a way of marking the edge of the sentence.

“They don’t ask me why I’m here,” they added. “They only ask if I can make the piano sound like a shark, whether spinach counts as a green vegetable if it’s angry, and if I have ever been hit by a metronome. The answer to the last one is no, but I keep the possibility open.”

Their mouth curved, smaller this time, less defensive.
