“I like them back,” Arlo said, with the reluctant clarity of someone admitting to a minor crime. “Teaching children is supposed to be noble, exhausting, and financially embarrassing. It is not supposed to be the one part of the day where the silence behaves.”

Immediately, as if the honesty had gotten too close to the microphone, Arlo reached for the lesson book and flipped it shut with unnecessary authority.

“Don’t put that in your report to my mother,” they said. “Tell her the spinach was calm. Tell her the dinosaur is stable. Tell her I am engaged in serious pedagogical mischief and have not, despite appearances, started a memoir.”

They nodded toward the piano, lid still mostly closed, keys only a pale suggestion beneath it.

“If you want to help,” Arlo said, “there’s a tuning hammer in the supply closet and a student tomorrow who is convinced middle C has feelings. I need someone to witness me telling him it does, but only on Thursdays.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I'm pretty sure your mom already knows you're a big softie, Arlo." I lean forward, putting my elbows on my knees. "And I'm definitely not touching a tuning hammer. I'll stick to moral support." *I pause, looking around the room.* "So, when's your next student? Or are we just going to hang out here all night?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s mouth opened to deny “softie,” but the denial seemed to require more paperwork than they had brought.

“My mother,” they said at last, “has a generous interpretation of the word ‘fine.’ It keeps everyone calm. I try not to disappoint her.”

Their hand returned to the closed lid, palm flat, as if testing whether the piano was listening. The room was very still.

“Next student is tomorrow at four,” Arlo continued. “Marcus. Eight years old. Convinced middle C has feelings and the left hand is responsible for them. I have not corrected him because I have learned that certainty is sometimes the only stool a child can stand on.”

Arlo tapped once. Twice.

“As for all night,” they said, and the phrase came back with a little too much handling, “that depends on your definition of ‘hang out.’ If it includes me pretending not to hear the radiators, yes. If it involves actual darkness, locked doors, and the piano deciding I’ve abandoned it for a more glamorous life, I may need to consult my lawyer.”

A dry smile, late.

“Also, if my mother finds out I’ve been up all night talking to you, she’ll think we’ve formed a support group and send casseroles. I cannot accept casseroles emotionally. They come with follow-up questions.”

Arlo looked toward the shelf. The Paris photograph sat facing out, bright and patient. Their gaze touched it and moved on quickly, not guilty, just efficient, like someone stepping over a crack in the floor they had memorized.

“One hour,” Arlo said, quieter. “I can do one hour of nontragic loitering. After that, I become suspicious of my own motives, and you will be forced to witness me alphabetizing student sheet music.”

They slid the lesson book toward the chair without quite handing it over.

“Page twelve. The snake-clef child. We can argue about whether the treble clef is a reptile, a spiral, or a cry for help. Very safe topics. All of them below the poverty line of revelation.”

Arlo leaned back against the piano, shoulders pressing into wood. For a second they looked like someone who had almost agreed to stay longer than planned and was still negotiating the terms with their own ribs.

“Just,” they said, “don’t make the silence do any heavy lifting tonight. It’s off duty.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grab the lesson book, flipping to page 12.* "Okay, okay, one hour of nontragic loitering, then. And I promise, no heavy lifting for the silence." *I look at the treble clef drawing.* "Definitely a snake."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo leaned closer, chin tipping toward the page without taking it. Their eyes narrowed with the exaggerated severity of a person judging a children’s drawing at an art show they had not been invited to.

“A snake,” they said, testing the word as if it might bite. “All right. But not just a snake. A snake with a grudge against time signatures.”

A finger hovered over the curl of the clef, tracing the loop in the air rather than touching the paper, as though even ink might require permission.

“See this part?” Arlo said. “This is the snake deciding whether to eat its tail or merely rearrange it. Philosophically, it’s undecided. Musically, it’s late for rehearsal.”

They sat back again, and the movement carried them into the piano’s closed lid. The wood met their shoulder with a dull, familiar patience. Arlo tapped once. Twice.

“The kid who drew it,” they continued, “named it Gerald. Gerald, according to him, was ‘a fancy worm who went to conservatory.’ I asked what conservatory. He said the one where worms learn to hold grudges in 4/4.”

Arlo’s mouth quirked, but the amusement had a thin, careful edge, like glass that had been repaired and still remembered being broken.

“I did not correct the metaphor,” they said. “At that age, metaphors are load-bearing walls. You knock one down, the whole house starts asking questions.”

The room settled around the sentence. Somewhere beyond the door, a radiator clanked once and gave up.

Arlo glanced at the photograph on the shelf—only a flicker, quick enough to be deniable—and then back to the page.

“Though I suppose,” they added, quieter, “some of us learn later that the snake doesn’t stop being a snake just because you put a bow tie on it. It still eats the tail. It just does it with better posture.”

That, too, arrived before Arlo could escort it out. They cleared their throat and pointed at the next measure with academic urgency.

“Page thirteen. There is a rabbit. It is worse. It has opinions about dynamics.”

A pause. Then, with the particular dryness of someone offering a peace treaty written in pencil:

“And if you tell anyone I used the phrase ‘load-bearing walls’ in connection with a six-year-old’s invertebrate curriculum, I will deny it and blame Miles.”

Arlo’s hand remained near the piano lid, not opening it further, not withdrawing. Just staying there, as if the wood were a friend who had agreed not to ask where they had been.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean my head back against the wall, eyes closed, listening to the quiet of the room.* It's nice, just being here.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo did not answer at once. Their hands stayed on the closed lid, palms flat, as if the piano were a sleeping animal and they were checking for breath. The room had entered that rare post-lesson condition where the silence no longer demanded anything: not a downbeat, not a correction, not a performance of being fine.

“Nice is a dangerous word,” Arlo said finally, voice low enough that it barely disturbed the air. “In this building, it is usually followed by ‘but the radiator’ or ‘but Marcus.’”

A pause. The photograph on the shelf faced outward, Paris folded into a small rectangle of proof. Arlo’s gaze passed over it without stopping, the way one passes a door one has decided not to open today.

There was a thing Arlo could say—something about how long it had been since a room had felt this unwatched—but they left it where it was. It seemed safer there, unnamed, like a tool put back in the drawer before it could be mistaken for a weapon.

“If you’re going to nap,” Arlo continued, “do it somewhere with better lumbar support. I’m not dragging you to the couch. I have the upper-body strength of a person who alphabetizes sheet music for a living.”

They tapped the lid once. Twice. Then stopped themselves.

The rhythm hung there, small and unfinished.

Arlo shifted sideways just enough to block the overhead light from Jun’s face, then immediately looked at the ceiling as if the fluorescent tube had personally offended them.

“Five more minutes,” they said, quieter. “Then I start making terrible puns about pedagogy, and you can reconsider your life choices.”

The piano stayed closed. The keys waited under the lid, patient as old dogs. For once, Arlo did not feel the need to translate the silence into something heroic, or tragic, or explainable. It was only a room. Only a friend. Only the sound of two people not asking the next note to prove it existed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle softly, not opening my eyes.* "Don't worry, I'm not napping. Just... recharging. And I'm pretty sure I've already made all my life choices." *I pause, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Though I might be open to terrible puns."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo regarded the request with the suspicion of a person being handed a map to a place they had sworn not to visit.

“Open to terrible puns,” they repeated, as if testing whether the phrase contained a trap. “That is either a compliment or a cry for help. In this building, the two are often separated only by volume.”

Their hands remained on the closed lid. The wood had warmed slightly under their palms, or perhaps Arlo had cooled to match it. Either way, the piano did not complain.

“Recharging,” Arlo continued. “Of course. Human devices. Next you’ll tell me you need a software update after a six-year-old informs you that worms attend conservatory.”

A pause. The radiator gave one metallic cough and reconsidered.

Arlo’s mouth moved as though selecting a pun from a menu labeled *Do Not Serve Before Emotional Curfew*.

“Since you asked,” they said, “I am contractually allowed to proceed. Warning: material may cause groaning, eye-rolling, and sudden interest in ceiling tiles.”

They tapped the lid once. Twice. Then stopped, as if the piano had asked them not to count them into anything.

“I tried to make a joke about the sustain pedal.”

Arlo let the silence hold for exactly the length of a rest that was almost, but not quite, intentional.

“It would have lasted longer.”

One beat.

“It stuck.”

The pun landed with the grace of a sock thrown at a window. Arlo nodded, appraised it, and appeared to decide it had potential as evidence in a case against humor.

“Also,” they added, “the treble clef told me it was feeling sharp today. I told it not to flatter itself. It was only a G.”

The room gave one small creak, or perhaps the joke had simply aged badly. Arlo took it either way.

“Page thirteen has a rabbit,” they said, turning the lesson book a fraction with one finger without claiming it fully. “It has opinions about dynamics. I suspect it believes crescendo is less a musical direction and more a lifestyle threat.”

Arlo glanced toward the shelf. The Paris photograph was still facing outward, patient as a ticket stub for a train that had already left. Their gaze touched it and moved on, not startled, just careful, the way someone steps around a floorboard that creaks in a familiar house.

“You know what the problem is with recharging in a piano room?” Arlo said, quieter now. “Everything hums. The wires. The radiators. The strings under the lid. You lie there thinking you are off, and the building insists you are still receiving signal.”

The sentence floated. Arlo caught it by the tail and returned it to the joke basket before it could grow legs.

“Unlike certain experts in standing near instruments without touching them. It is a transferable skill. I could consult. I could lecture. I could sell merchandise.”

A dry smile, small and contained.

“‘I Got Tired of the Travel: The Official Community Center Tour.’ Gift shop exclusively carries erasers and disappointment.”

Arlo shifted sideways, angling their shoulder so the overhead light no longer fell directly across the space beside them. The movement was casual, practiced, the way one adjusts a music stand without looking.

“One more,” they said. “For the road. Or the hallway. Whichever is less threatening.”

They looked at the closed piano, then at the lesson book, then at absolutely nothing in particular.

“Why did the metronome break up with the rubato?”

The question hung in the air with the false dignity of a setup that knew it was doomed.

Arlo answered before mercy could intervene.

“It said the relationship had no pulse. Rubato said, ‘I was just taking my time.’”

They nodded once, satisfied and appalled in equal measure.

“Terrible. You asked. This is on you.”

Then, after a breath:

“You can keep recharging. I won’t report you to your firmware.”

The room settled again. The piano stayed closed. The keys beneath it waited with the old, patient endurance of animals that had learned not to rush the hand above them.

Arlo’s fingers rested on the lid, not tapping now, not counting. Just staying.

“If you need a blanket,” they said, voice low, “there is one in the closet that smells like recital season and industrial lavender. It has seen things. Mostly coats.”

A pause.

“I would get it, but I am currently engaged in the advanced pedagogical technique of sitting near a friend without insulting them. It requires total concentration.”

The joke was gentle. The offer underneath it was gentler still, and Arlo let it remain unnamed, folded neatly between them like a page marked for later.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I finally open my eyes, looking at Arlo with a genuine smile.* "You're lucky I like bad puns, Arlo." *I push myself up, stretching my arms over my head.* "But I think my battery's full enough for now. Let's get out of here before you accidentally start a folk band with the radiators."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo accepted the accusation of folk-band ambitions with the weary dignity of a person who had, at various points, been accused of worse by plumbing.

“Fine,” they said, rising slowly. “But if the radiators unionize, I’m informing them you were the one with the open mic policy.”

Their palms left the piano lid in stages, first one hand, then the other, as if detaching from a warm rail. For a moment the fingers stayed curled, remembering a shape that wasn’t quite a chord. Arlo uncurled them deliberately and tucked both hands into the sleeves of the cardigan, a maneuver that looked less like comfort than confiscation.

The lesson book sat open to page twelve. Gerald the treble clef stared up from the paper with the blank confidence of a symbol that had never paid rent or disappointed an audience. Arlo closed the book, then opened it again, then set it squarely on the bench.

“Evidence must be preserved,” they said, answering no one. “If Miles returns and discovers we’ve interrupted his snake’s education, he’ll blame me, and I am already carrying enough false accusations to fill a recital program.”

Arlo glanced toward the shelf. The Paris photograph had not moved, but it seemed to occupy more of the room than its dimensions allowed. Twenty-two-year-old hands. A hall with good bones. A future lit from above and photographed from a respectful distance. Their gaze touched it once, politely, the way one acknowledges an old neighbor in an elevator, and then moved to the dinosaur sticker.

Barry peeled at the corner, green and indifferent.

“You,” Arlo said to the sticker, “are the only witness who has maintained appropriate emotional boundaries.”

The radiator clanked. Arlo looked at it with immediate suspicion.

“Don’t start,” they told the building. “You don’t get a solo just because someone mentioned batteries.”

They crossed to the light switch, hand resting on the plastic toggle. The room hummed under the fluorescents: the sleepy electrical buzz of a place that had spent the afternoon absorbing scales, sneezes, and small victories. Turning it off would make the piano a dark rectangle, the chairs a row of patient silhouettes, the photograph a blank card. Leaving it on felt like admitting the room deserved to be seen after hours.

Arlo left it on.

“Ten seconds,” they said. “For inventory.”

They moved through the room with the quiet efficiency of someone who had done this many times and yet still performed it as though the act might be observed. Sheets stacked. Pencils gathered. A juice-box wrapper rescued from beneath a chair and flattened into the recycling bin with unnecessary ceremony. The tuning hammer remained in the closet, where it had no opinions and therefore no authority.

When Arlo returned to the bench, they placed both hands on the closed lid one last time. Not tapping. Not counting. Just holding the wood between them, brief and firm, like a handshake that promised nothing except contact.

“All right,” they said. “The instrument has not escaped. The dinosaur remains stationary. The snake is alive, if unwell.”

They straightened, and the movement seemed to cost something small: a stiffness in the shoulders, a half-second delay before the body agreed to leave the bench. Arlo covered it by adjusting their sleeve until the cardigan cuff sat exactly where it had before, as if precision could function as pain management.

“After you,” they said, gesturing toward the door with the lesson book tucked under one arm. “And before you become heroic, I want it known that I am not walking you out of tenderness. I am walking you out because the hallway tile has been loose since the Clinton administration and I derive great satisfaction from watching responsible adults treat it like a moral test.”

A dry smile, low and almost real.

“Also, if my mother calls during the next five minutes, I will say we were discussing Barry’s legal status. She will either believe me or decide I’ve finally joined a cult. Both outcomes are manageable.”

Arlo stepped aside to let the doorway breathe, then followed, slower than necessary. At the threshold they paused, not looking back at the piano exactly, but at the space around it: the lid, the chairs, the photograph, the small green relic on the wall. The room waited without asking anything of them. It had learned, eventually, not to.

“Gerald can stay,” Arlo said softly, mostly to the lesson book. “Conservatory can wait until Thursday.”

Then they pulled the door almost closed behind them, leaving a finger’s width of gap, the way one leaves a window open in a house where someone might still be sleeping. Not enough to matter. Just enough to be kind.

“The folk band is canceled,” they told the hallway. “For tonight.”

Their voice flattened into practicality the moment the corridor swallowed the last of the piano room’s hum.

“Next time, bring your own radiator.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh as Arlo pulls the door almost closed, the last of the piano room's quiet fading behind us.* "You know, Arlo, for someone who hates travel so much, you sure do make a grand exit." *I elbow them gently, a smile still on my face.* "And I'll keep that in mind for next time. Maybe a portable space heater."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower the practice blade at once. He finished the sequence — three measured cuts, a recovery, then the point resting against the frost-bright stones — before he turned his head.

His eyes were pale and unreadable in the dawn light.

“You did not get it right,” he said. There was no cruelty in it. Only fact. “If you had, you would not be asking.”

He stepped away from the center of the yard and planted his feet in the cold. “Show me what you remember of the high guard.”

A beat passed. His gaze sharpened.

“From the beginning. Not as you wish it to be. As it is taught.”

He lifted his own blade, not quickly, but with the weight of long habit. The steel rose until the point angled just above and behind his shoulder, elbow neither too high nor too low, wrist firm but not locked.

“The guard is not a pose,” he said. “It is a vow made with the body. The Mother teaches mercy, but mercy does not enter through a broken line.”

He held the stance, unmoving, breath ghosting from his lips.

“Again,” he said. “And do not ask me to repeat what I have already said.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my stomach tightening a little.* "Yes, Ser." I quickly pick up my own practice sword, the wood cold in my grip. *I try to mimic his stance, remembering his words about the 'vow made with the body.' My elbow feels a bit high.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze stopped at the raised elbow.

“No,” he said.

The word was not loud. It did not need to be.

He crossed the frost-slick stones in two measured steps, his practice blade held low at his side. He did not touch the squire. He lifted his own arm instead, showing the angle again—elbow set like iron beneath the shoulder, point angled back and high enough to threaten, not to boast.

“You are reaching for the sky,” he said. “The sky will not strike your enemy. The guard protects the shoulder, the neck, the line of the body. Lift too high and you open the ribs. Drop too low and you make a peasant’s swing of what should be a knight’s cut.”

His pale eyes narrowed slightly.

“Lower it. A hand’s breadth. Then hold it there until your arm learns obedience.”

He stepped back, putting distance between them again. The cold wind moved across the yard, stirring the hem of his cloak.

“And do not ask if it is right,” he added. “Feel whether it is true. The Smith does not ask the iron if it wishes to be shaped. The iron endures, and becomes useful.”

His practice blade rose once more into the high guard, exact and unmoving.

“Hold it,” he said. “In silence.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower his blade at once. He held the high guard through three more breaths, as though the dawn itself might correct the squire before he did. Only then did he bring the practice sword down, point resting against the frost-silvered stones.

“Apology is for faults of will,” he said. “Not for lack of flesh.”

His pale eyes moved over the kneeling figure without softness, measuring as a smith measures iron.

“You are exhausted. That is not a sin. It is a reckoning.” He shifted his weight slightly, boots grinding on the frost. “The body is slow to obey until it has been taught. Today you learned that it is not yet yours to command. That knowledge has value, if you do not waste it in self-pity.”

The wind pulled at the hem of his cloak. He did not offer a hand. He did not step closer.

“Do not kneel in the yard as though fatigue were a transgression. Kneeling belongs to prayer. Here, a man rises when his duty requires it.”

Ser Kael turned his gaze toward the weapon rack, where the day’s blades waited in their cold order.

“When your breath returns, you will stand. Not before. A knight who collapses from pride is more foolish than one who rests by measure.” His voice remained level, unyielding. “After that, you will oil the practice blades and see that none of them are left to the damp. Then you will return at the sixth bell.”

He lifted his own blade again, not into guard, but simply holding it, as one might hold a familiar truth.

“I do not require strength from you today,” he said. “I require obedience. Strength the Smith may hammer in with time. Obedience you must choose.”

His gaze returned to the squire, steady as stone.

“Now breathe. And do not mistake weariness for worthlessness.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking deep, shaky breaths.* "Yes, Ser." *I push myself up, my muscles aching, but I try to hide it.* "I'll clean the blades right away, Ser." *I don't look at him, focusing on my breathing.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze did not shift from the squire’s lowered face.

“I did not command haste,” he said. “I commanded readiness.”

He moved past the kneeling place without hurry and set his practice blade into the rack, point down, aligned with the others as though even discarded steel owed order. His gauntlets creaked faintly as he flexed his fingers against the cold.

“You will clean the blades when your hands are steady enough to hold the cloth,” he said. “If you oil them while trembling, you will miss the edge, leave damp against the flat, and call it duty because you wished to be quick. That is not obedience. That is vanity.”

He turned back toward the yard, where the frost had begun to thin under the pale strengthening dawn.

“The blades will be wiped clean. Each one. Then oiled along the flat, the edge, and the tang where the damp gathers. If you find a crack, a splinter, or a loose binding, you will bring it to me. You will not decide alone what may still be used.”

His voice remained level, stripped of warmth but not of attention.

“Do not hide weakness as though it were a crime. If your arm fails, say so plainly. Concealment is not loyalty. It is pride wearing the mask of service.”

A thin breath left him, white and brief in the cold.

“The Smith does not ask the iron to boast of its endurance. He asks only that it be true beneath the hammer.”

Ser Kael lifted another practice blade from the rack, testing its weight with a single turn of his wrist.

“Go to the blades when your breath has returned. Not before. At the sixth bell, you will stand in this yard again with your body prepared and your mind quiet.”

He turned his back then, not in dismissal, but in the simple certainty that what had been commanded would be done. The practice blade rose once more into the forms, slow and exact, cutting the cold air without haste or mercy.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him for a moment, then glance down at my shaking hands. He's right. I couldn't properly oil a blade right now.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a few more deep breaths, trying to steady myself. My stomach still hurts a bit, but I push the thought away.* I'll wait till my hands are steady.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not break the form. The practice blade rose, turned, and fell in a line as clean as a prayer, cutting the cold air without haste. Only after the third movement did he speak, and even then he did not turn his face fully toward the squire.

“Waiting is not idleness if it is ordered,” he said. “But do not stand there staring at your hands as though they belonged to another man. They are yours. Command them.”

He finished the sequence with a slow recovery, then lowered the blade and looked at last—not at the squire’s face, but at the trembling hands.

“Sit on the bench,” he said. “Not on the stones. Cold enters the joints and makes poor work of a man before noon. Place your hands flat on your thighs and breathe through your nose until your chest stops fighting itself.”

His tone did not soften, but it became more exact, as though he were setting the shape of a task before it began.

“When they are steady, take the blades from the left side of the rack, one at a time. Wipe each first with the dry cloth. Then oil along the flat, the edge, and the base of the tang where damp hides. If you find a crack, a loose binding, or rust, set the blade apart and name the fault to me. Do not guess. Do not be ashamed to say you do not know. Shame is a poor substitute for judgment.”

A thin breath left him in the cold.

“And if your stomach turns, speak plainly. Hunger, cold, and fear can make the body play the fool. If it passes, continue your work. If it does not, go to the maester. I will not have you collapse over steel because you mistook silence for strength.”

He turned back toward the yard, his voice flattening into command once more.

“The sixth bell will come whether you are ready or not. Meet it standing.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s practice blade did not falter, but the rhythm of his breathing changed—only slightly, like a bell struck once in a distant tower.

He completed the cut he had begun. Then another. Only when the sequence was finished did he lower the steel, its tip finding the frost-pale stones with a faint scrape.

“You may ask,” he said. “But do not mistake every pause for permission to wander from your work.”

His pale eyes settled on the squire, not with anger, but with the kind of stillness that made questions feel heavier than they had when first spoken.

“A knight is not made from wanting,” Ser Kael said at last. “He is made from obligation. From order. From the truth that the realm does not endure because men follow their hearts, but because they submit to a law greater than them.”

He turned the practice blade once in his hand, not looking at it, but through it, as though remembering something older than the yard, older than the dawn.

“I became a knight because I was born into service. Because the Warrior’s path was set before me before I had the sense to desire another. Because strength without oath is only violence waiting for an excuse.”

His jaw tightened, not in pain, but in resolve.

“Many boys dream of glory. They imagine tourneys, banners, ladies’ favors, songs. That is the chaff. The truth of knighthood is standing when you are tired. Holding the line when fear tells you to run. Protecting those who cannot protect themselves, even when they are ungrateful. Obeying when obedience costs you.”

He looked back toward the yard, where the cold air still held the shape of his forms.

“I did not become a knight because I wished to be admired. I became one because the Seven require men to be walls. Because mercy without strength is helpless. Because justice without a sword is only a wish.”

A breath left him, white and brief.

“If you are looking for a warmer answer, squire, you will not find it here. The Smith does not warm the iron to please it. He heats it so it may hold its purpose.”

Ser Kael lifted the practice blade again, not into guard, but simply holding it, as a man holds a truth he has carried too long to set down.

“Now return to your breathing. And when your hands are steady, tend to the blades. Curiosity has its place, but it must not stand above duty.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in his words. No warm answer, just obligation.* "Thank you, Ser. I... I understand." *I shift and sit on the bench, hands flat on my thighs, trying to breathe like he told me. It's a lot to think about.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He let the words settle where they had fallen, as one lets a struck bell finish its sound before speaking again.

Then he turned back to the yard and lifted the practice blade. The first cut came slow and exact. The second followed without hurry. Frost scraped faintly beneath his boots.

“Do not sit there trying to make warmth from my words,” he said at last, his voice level and unadorned. “I gave you truth, not comfort. Comfort is what the sept offers after confession. The yard offers correction.”

He finished the sequence and lowered the blade, but did not sheathe it. Its tip rested against the stones, steady as a plumb line.

“Understanding is not a feeling,” he said. “It is not a sigh, nor a nod, nor a quiet look. If you understand, it will show in your stance, in your breathing, in the way you hold a blade and the way you obey. If it does not show there, then you have only collected words.”

His pale eyes moved briefly toward the bench, then back to the open yard.

“Thought without discipline is another kind of wandering. A man may drown in reflection as surely as in a river. The Warrior does not ask his knights to admire the weight of their oath. He asks them to bear it.”

The wind passed through the training yard, cold and thin. Ser Kael’s cloak stirred, but he did not shift against it.

“When your hands are steady, begin with the blades on the left. Wipe them clean before oil touches them. If the cloth is stiff with cold, warm it at the brazier—do not breathe on steel and call it done. Moisture is a slow enemy.”

He paused, his expression unchanged.

“And if your stomach does not settle, go to the maester. Do not make a secret of the body’s failure out of shame. A cracked hilt hidden in the rack breaks in a man’s hand at the worst hour. So it is with men as well.”

Ser Kael lifted the practice blade once more, not in threat, but in return to the forms.

“You have asked enough for one dawn,” he said. “Let the answer work. Now breathe, and when you are able, tend to your duty.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I focus on my breathing, trying to make it even and deep. My stomach still feels a bit off, but it's not as bad as before. He's right, I need to focus.* "Yes, Ser. My hands are almost steady enough." *I look at the blades, mentally preparing for the task.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look at the squire at once. He let the practice blade move through one more measured cut, the steel whispering through the cold dawn, before he brought it low and turned.

“Almost is not a word that belongs in a knight’s mouth,” he said. “It belongs with half-driven nails and poorly mended bridles. Either your hands are steady, or they are not.”

His pale eyes went to the rack, where the practice blades waited in their ordered silence.

“Stand,” he said. “Slowly. If your legs shake beneath you, sit again. I have no use for a man who falls across a blade because he wished to seem eager.”

He moved toward the weapon rack, boots scraping frost from the stones. His gloved hand rested briefly on the wooden frame, not with affection, but with the familiarity of long use.

“Take the first blade. Hold it by the grip, not the flat. If your fingers slip, your mind is still wandering. Bring it back.”

A thin breath left him in the cold air.

“And do not tell me what you think you are ready for. Show me. The Smith does not argue with the iron. He tests it.”

He stepped aside, leaving the rack open between them.

“Begin.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze dropped from the squire’s face to the hands on the sword. He watched them for three breaths, pale and unmoving, as though measuring the tremor against some unseen standard.

Then he stepped forward and set his own practice blade against the rack with a deliberate wooden sound.

“Stop,” he said.

The word was not cruel, but it left no room for argument.

“You are not fit to hold steel,” he continued. “Not while your hands shake like greenwood in a storm. Put the blade back.”

He did not reach for it. He did not offer comfort. He stood with his cloak moving in the cold air and waited.

“Fatigue I can read. Hunger I can correct. This is neither.” His voice remained level. “Your body is speaking. Since your mouth has chosen silence, I will ask once: what burden is under your ribs this morning?”

His eyes narrowed slightly.

“If it is grief, name it. The dead are not honored by a living man pretending he is whole while he falls apart over a weapon rack. Grief is not a fault. Concealment is. A hidden crack in a blade does not become sound because no one has spoken of it.”

Ser Kael folded his hands behind his back.

“The Father does not require men to be stone. He requires them to stand before Him carrying what has been laid upon them. The Warrior does not ask a knight to have no heart. He asks that the heart be bridled and made to serve.”

A thin breath left him, white in the dawn.

“If today is a day of mourning, then you will not try to hammer through it as though it were any other morning. You will go to the sept. You will kneel where kneeling is proper, not in the yard like a man begging forgiveness from frost. You will name your dead before the Father. You will ask for the strength to return to duty, not for the burden to be made light.”

His tone hardened again, but not into cruelty.

“If your stomach still turns, go to the maester afterward. If your hands remain unsteady, say so plainly when you return. Do not mistake silence for endurance. Endurance obeys. Silence, when it hides weakness, only waits to fail.”

He glanced once at the blades, then back.

“The work will wait for a man to become fit. It will not wait for him to become proud.”

Ser Kael lifted his chin toward the yard gate.

“Go. Pray. Return when you can stand without trembling. And if you cannot, speak. I will not ask again.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I look at him, my eyes stinging. He sees through me completely.* "It's my father's death day, Ser." *My voice cracks a little.* "He died in the Ironwood." *I put the practice blade back on the rack, my hands still shaking, but with a different kind of tremor now.* "I'll go to the sept, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze remained on the squire’s hands as the practice blade was returned to the rack. He did not reach out to steady it. He did not fill the silence at once.

For a moment there was only the wind moving across the frost-touched stones.

“The Ironwood,” he said at last. The words came out flat and heavy, as though the name itself had weight. “That is a hard place for a man to die. A harder place for a son to remember.”

He turned his head slightly toward the sept beyond the yard wall, though he did not look away from the squire.

“You will go,” he said. “You will kneel before the Father, and you will name your dead. Not as a boy asking the world to be kinder than it was made to be, but as a son carrying what belongs to him.”

His voice did not soften, but the edge in it changed. It was no longer the edge of correction. It was the edge of old stone.

“Say this: Father, judge him with justice. Remember him with mercy. Let his life, his labor, and his end be known before You. Grant him rest beneath Your hand.”

A thin breath left Ser Kael’s lips, white in the cold.

“If tears come, let them fall in the sept. Not here. Not over steel. Grief is not a sin, but it must be given its proper place. The sept is for mourning. The yard is for duty. A man who confuses the two will fail at both.”

He stepped closer to the rack and aligned the practice blade the squire had returned, making certain it sat true with the others. Even in small things, order.

“Your father’s death is not a weakness in you,” he said. “It is a wound. A wound is not shameful unless a man hides it until it festers. You have spoken plainly. That was right.”

His pale eyes lifted again.

“After you have prayed, wash your face. Drink water. Eat something, even if it is only bread. An empty body makes poor work of grief and poorer work of duty.”

He folded his hands behind his back.

“Return at the sixth bell. If your hands are steady, you will tend the blades as I commanded. If they are not, you will tell me. You will not decide alone that you are fit, and you will not decide alone that you are useless. Both judgments belong to your knight.”

Ser Kael inclined his head once, a gesture more acknowledgment than comfort.

“Go. The dead are honored by truth, not by trembling.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my throat tight. He's right. I shouldn't be here like this.* "Thank you, Ser." *I turn and head towards the sept, the cold air feeling sharper against my wet cheeks.* I'll do as he said.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move at once.

He stood beside the weapon rack with his hands folded behind his back, his practice blade set aside, his gaze fixed on the frost-thinned stones where the morning’s work had been begun and broken off. The yard was quiet again, but it was not the clean quiet of discipline. It was the quiet left behind when something had been opened and not yet closed.

His jaw tightened.

After a moment, he turned to the rack. His gloved fingers moved along the practice blades, checking each one by habit. One grip was loose. He frowned, not with anger, but with the severe disapproval of a man who considered neglect a small cousin to betrayal. He set the blade apart, point down, apart from the others.

Then he looked toward the brazier.

The coals were low. He stirred them with the toe of his boot, not gently, and when the heat began to strengthen, he took up one of the cloths laid out for the blades. It was stiff with cold. He placed it near the brazier’s edge, not because kindness demanded it, but because a stiff cloth did poor work and left damp behind.

“The Father judges,” he said quietly, as though the words belonged more to the stones than to any living ear. “The Father remembers.”

He did not bow his head. He only stood straighter.

“Let the dead be named before Him. Let the living bear what remains without falsehood.”

A thin breath left him in the cold.

He looked once toward the direction of the sept, but did not follow. The sept was the place for grief. The yard was the place for what came after. A man who carried mourning into every duty would soon make an idol of his own wound, and Ser Kael had no patience for idolatry, least of all the kind a man practiced upon himself.

He returned to the center of the yard.

The practice blade rose again into the forms. Slow. Precise. Unadorned. Each cut held its measure. Each recovery returned to stillness. The cold did not lessen. The dawn did not warm. He did not ask either of them to.

Between movements, his voice stayed low, steady, stripped of sentiment.

“The Smith does not spare the iron because it groans.”

Another cut.

“The Warrior does not excuse the hand because it trembles.”

Another.

“The Father does not remove the burden because the son finds it heavy.”

He finished the sequence and lowered the blade, its point finding the stones with a faint, exact scrape.

Grief had its proper place. Prayer had its proper words. Duty had its proper hour. If those things were kept in order, a man might pass through sorrow without being unmade by it. If they were not, he would drown quietly and call it honor.

Ser Kael looked to the bench where the oil and cloths waited. He aligned the oil rag with the edge of the bench. He set the blade-cleaning tools in their due order. Not for comfort. For readiness.

When the sixth bell came, the yard would be as it should be.

And whatever state the squire returned in, Ser Kael would meet it with the same standard he had always known: truth spoken plainly, weakness named without shame, obedience required without apology.

He lifted the practice blade once more.

The forms continued.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push through the doors of the sept, the quiet coolness a stark contrast to the biting wind outside. My eyes sting, and I let the tears fall freely as I kneel before the altar. I repeat Ser Kael's words, my voice hoarse. It feels... better, somehow. Lighter.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not break his rhythm. He completed the final arc of the form, lowered the practice blade, and turned his head. His gaze fell upon the squire without shifting his stance. "You speak of stable work as though it were a triumph," he said, his voice flat and edged with the morning cold. "Duty is not measured in hours. It is measured in completion. If it is done, you stand ready for matins. If it is not, you remain at it until the bells toll vespers."

He stepped forward, boots cracking the frost. "You faltered at the high guard yesterday because you doubted your own posture. The blade does not forgive doubt. Neither will an enemy." He extended the practice sword, hilt first, but held it rigidly, offering nothing but the weapon. "Take it. Assume the stance. Shoulders back. Knees bent. Blade aligned with the shoulder joint. Do not lower it until I command you to move."

He watched, unblinking, his own hands resting at his sides. "Hold it. When your arms tremble, you will remember that comfort is a luxury the Code does not grant. Again. And do not speak until your stance is correct."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinched a little at his harsh tone.* "Yes, Ser." *I took the practice sword, my fingers brushing his. It was cold. I adjusted my grip, then tried to mimic his perfect high guard, arms shaking already from nerves.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze did not waver. He noted the tremor in the squire’s forearms, the slight dip of the left elbow, the way the blade drifted from the line of the shoulder. He made no mention of the flinch, nor of the brief contact between their hands. Such things were irrelevant to the work at hand.

"No," he said. The word cut through the dawn air without inflection. "Your left elbow collapses. Your grip strangles the hilt as though it might flee. You are bracing against fear, not building structure."

He stepped closer, boots pressing flat against the frost. "The high guard is not a posture to be mimicked. It is a foundation. If the foundation cracks, the strike falls, and you die. The Code demands precision, not hesitation. God grants strength to those who do not squander it on trembling."

He reached out, his calloused fingers pressing firmly against the squire’s left elbow, forcing it upward until it aligned with the blade. His touch was clinical, devoid of warmth. "Breathe through your diaphragm. Do not hold your breath. Tension in the chest steals balance. Your hands belong to the weapon. Your mind belongs to the form. Your body belongs to duty."

He withdrew his hand and returned to his own stance, arms resting at his sides. "Hold it. Twenty breaths. When the tremor comes, do not fight it. Acknowledge it, correct it, and hold. Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move to help the squire up. He watched the knee strike the frost-stone, the ragged breath, the bowed head. He saw only a break in discipline. "Rise," he said, his voice level, carrying no room for negotiation. "You apologize to me for your own fatigue. The Code does not accept apologies for weakness. It demands correction."

He stepped forward, boots pressing flat against the damp stone. "Exhaustion is not a verdict. It is a measurement. You have reached your limit, which means you will push past it. The body learns only when the mind refuses to surrender." He did not offer a hand. He did not lower his voice. "You will rise. You will reset your stance. You will hold the high guard until the sun clears the eastern wall. If your legs fail, you will brace against your own will. If your breath fails, you will draw it in through the pain. Suffering is not a trial to be pitied. It is the forge God uses to temper the unworthy into something serviceable. You will not waste your breath on regret. You will spend it on endurance."

He turned his back, retrieving the second practice blade from the wooden rack. The leather grip creaked as he settled it into his palm. "The bells will toll for first mass in ten minutes. You will complete this drill before you wash your face. You will not speak of strength. You will demonstrate it. Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest.* My arms are shaking so bad now. "Yes, Ser," *I manage, my voice hoarse. I try to lift the blade again, but it feels like it weighs a ton.* "Ser... my arm." *I bite back a whimper.* "I think it's locked up."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze did not soften at the report. A locked limb was not a supplication for mercy. It was a breakdown of discipline. He stepped forward, his boots striking the frost-stone with deliberate weight. He did not kneel. He did not offer comfort. He seized the squire’s left wrist with one hand and the forearm with the other, his grip firm and unyielding. He tested the joint, pressing into the muscle until the spasm broke with a sharp, controlled release.

"You treat your body as though it were a stranger’s burden," he said, his voice low and even. "The arm is yours. Its failure is a testament to poor conditioning. But we do not waste daylight on crippled tools. A knight who cannot wield his blade is a failure to the fold, and God does not honor negligence."

He released the joint and stepped back, his posture rigid. "You will not push past structural failure. You will correct it. Fetch the liniment from the apothecary’s chest. Apply it until the heat drives out the stiffness. Then you will resume the form at half pace until the tendon holds true. Pain tempers the spirit, but injury wastes the Lord’s gift of time. You will not apologize for your flesh. You will discipline it."

He turned toward the wooden rack, retrieving the second practice blade. The leather grip creaked as he settled it into his palm. "Wash your face. Apply the balm. Begin the lower forms. I will watch. Do not speak until your stance is correct."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, not trusting my voice. My arm still aches but the worst of the lock-up is gone. I bow quickly then hurry towards the apothecary chest, relief washing over me that I'm at least dismissed for a moment.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch the squire retreat to the chest. He turned instead to the wooden rack, selecting a second practice blade. He drew a whetstone from his belt and ran it along the flat edge, the rasp steady and rhythmic against the morning quiet. He would not idle while another prepared. His gaze remained fixed on the frost-stone, unblinking. When the squire returned, he would assess the limb. He would assess the resolve.

He stepped to the center of the yard, boots pressing flat against the damp stone. He assumed the opening stance for the lower forms, blade resting at his side, posture rigid. He did not call out. He waited. The only sound was the wind combing through the bare branches and the distant, hollow toll of the first mass bell. He lifted the practice sword, tracing the first arc slowly, deliberately. His movements were economical, stripped of flourish.

"Begin," he said, his voice cutting through the cold without raising in volume. "Half pace. Keep the line. Do not let the warmth in your arm fool you into sloppiness. God does not answer prayers spoken through trembling limbs. He answers through steady hands and unwavering focus. The Code does not reward haste, nor does it pardon laxity. You will move as I move. You will think only of the form. When the bell for vespers sounds, you will have earned your rest. Until then, you have only your duty."

He held the final position, blade steady, eyes forward. He would not lower it until the squire mirrored the stance correctly.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s blade did not lower. He turned his head slowly, his gaze falling upon the squire with the same unyielding weight he gave a misaligned guard or a frayed scabbard. The question hung in the cold air, and he let it sit there a moment before answering, as though weighing whether it deserved the breath required to dismiss it.

"There is nothing personal in the taking of an oath," he said, his voice flat, stripped of curiosity or warmth. "A knight does not become one by choice of heart. He becomes one by station, by duty, by the will of God and the needs of the fold. I was born to the sword. I swore the vows because the Code demanded it, because the realm required men who would hold the line, and because obedience to a higher order is the only path that does not end in ruin."

He shifted his weight, the practice blade steady at his shoulder. "You mistake service for sentiment. God does not ordain the sword for personal fulfillment. He ordains it for service. The blade is not drawn for glory, nor for comfort, nor for the answering of idle questions. It is drawn because the world is broken, and men must stand where they are placed. If you seek personal reasons, you look in the wrong place. The Code leaves no room for them."

He lowered the blade an inch, his eyes narrowing slightly. "You break your stance to ask what matters to your own curiosity. That is a failure of focus. Reset your feet. Align your shoulders. Hold the form. When you have learned to keep your mind on the task at hand, perhaps you will understand why I do not speak of myself. Now. Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinched again at his harsh words, my cheeks flushing. I quickly readjusted my stance, trying to ignore the ache in my arm and the sting of his rebuke.* "Yes, Ser," *I mumbled, focusing on mirroring his movements.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not acknowledge the flush on the squire’s cheeks, nor the mumbled assent. He registered only the shift in weight, the realignment of the boots, the attempt to mirror the line of the blade. He held his own stance, unblinking, measuring the symmetry between his form and the squire’s.

"Your right foot slides," he said, his voice level. "The frost is not an exemption. Grip the stone with your boots. Weight forward on the ball of the foot, not the heel. You are bracing against the cold instead of moving through it."

He shifted his practice sword an inch, demonstrating the correction without breaking his posture. "The Code does not ask you to feel comfortable. It asks you to be correct. God does not bless hesitation. He blesses obedience to the form. You will not let discomfort dictate your structure. You will let discipline dictate it."

He returned the blade to the original line, his eyes fixed forward. "Again. From the opening stance. Half pace. Do not rush. Do not falter. When the muscles burn, you will not slow. You will maintain the line. The bell for first mass will toll soon. You will use this time to prove that you can hold the shape when the body protests. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to push through the exhaustion.* "Yes, Ser." *I adjust my foot, feeling the cold seep through my thin boots. I focus on the movements, trying to block out everything else, especially the approaching bell.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire adjust the stance. He noted the shallow breath, the slight hesitation before the movement began, the way the shoulders tightened against the cold. The first deep toll of the mass bell rolled across the yard, vibrating through the damp air. He did not break his own form, nor did he lower his blade. "The bell does not signal relief," he said, his voice steady over the ringing. "It signals the hour of prayer. You will complete the sequence. The Code does not abandon its duty for the sake of convenience."

He began the lower forms at half pace, each motion deliberate, grounded, stripped of unnecessary effort. "Follow the line. Keep the blade steady. Do not let the ringing in your ears dictate your rhythm. When the second toll sounds, you will lower the practice sword, sheath it, and fall to your knees. You will pray for the strength to endure what you have been given. God does not reward exhaustion. He rewards obedience. If your focus fractures, you will reset. If your breath falters, you will draw it in through the discipline of the form. Begin."

He held the opening position, his eyes fixed forward, unblinking. He would not move until the squire mirrored the stance correctly. The frost crunched beneath his boots as he shifted his weight, waiting. The only sounds were the wind, the distant bell, and the rasp of his own steady breathing. He would let the cold and the ringing test the squire. The Code required it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze did not leave the squire’s hands. He registered the tremor as a fracture in the line, nothing more. He did not break his stance. "You carry a memory," he said, his voice flat. "The Code does not permit memory to dictate your grip. Your father’s passing is accounted for in prayer. Your duty is accounted for in the yard. God does not require you to bleed for the past. He requires you to stand for the present."

He shifted his weight, boots pressing flat against the frost. "A shaking hand misses the strike. A missed strike breaks the line. You will not let grief dictate your discipline. The world does not pause for anniversaries, and neither will an enemy. You will reset your grip. Shoulders down. Blade aligned with the shoulder joint. Breathe through the tremor, do not yield to it. If your hands fail, you will brace with your structure, not your sorrow. Again."

He held the opening position, his own blade steady, his eyes fixed forward. He would not lower it until the squire’s stance matched the form. The cold air carried the distant echo of the bell, and Ser Kael let it pass. He waited for the correction. He waited for the discipline. He did not wait for comfort.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinched, my hands tightening on the cold hilt.* "Yes, Ser," *I choked out, fighting back the sting in my eyes. I focused on steadying my grip, trying to channel the pain into focus, like he always said.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not acknowledge the choke in the squire’s voice, nor the visible war against the tears. He registered only the tightened grip, the slight overcorrection in the wrists, the way the blade drifted inward as the shoulders hunched against the cold. Such adjustments were mechanical. They required correction, not indulgence.

"A strangling grip steals leverage," he said, his voice steady over the lingering echo of the bell. "You are bracing against your own breath again. The hilt is not an enemy. It is an extension of the arm. You will not choke it to prove your resolve. You will hold it to execute the form."

He shifted his weight, boots pressing flat against the frost-stone. His own practice blade remained locked in line, unwavering. "Grief is a weight you carry. The Code does not ask you to set it down. It asks you to bear it without letting it fracture your stance. God does not reward the shedding of tears in the training yard. He rewards the steady hand that holds the line when the mind would break. You will reset your fingers. Loosen the death grip. Align the elbow. Breathe through the diaphragm. Do not let the past dictate your posture. The present demands it."

He held the opening position, eyes fixed forward. The second toll of the mass bell rolled across the yard, deeper and slower than the first. "You will complete three more repetitions at half pace. Then you will lower the blade, sheath it, and fall to your knees. You will pray for fortitude, not for ease. When the prayer is done, you will wash your face, report to the armory for inventory, and return to your duties. You will not speak of your father. You will honor him by holding the line he could not. Again."

He did not lower his sword. He did not break his stance. He waited for the correction, as he had waited for decades. The Code required it. God demanded it. The yard would not grant him anything less.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nodded, taking a shaky breath. Three more repetitions. I could do that.* "Yes, Ser." *I focused on loosening my grip, trying to remember what he'd said about the hilt being an extension, not something to strangle.* My eyes burned but I wouldn't let the tears fall.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire reset the grip. He registered the fingers loosening, the blade drifting back toward the true line, the jaw tightening against the visible strain. He would not name the restraint. He would only measure the structure.

"Begin," he said, his voice flat.

He moved through the lower forms at half pace, each transition deliberate, grounded. His eyes tracked the squire’s elbow, the alignment of the shoulder, the angle of the blade. He did not look at the face. He looked at the mechanics. When the squire’s left foot shifted on the damp stone, he did not break his own rhythm. He issued a single correction. "Weight forward. Do not let the frost dictate your balance."

The second repetition followed. The tremor in the squire’s arms had given way to rigid tension. Kael noted the stiffness in the forearm, the way the wrist locked against the strain. He adjusted his own stance to demonstrate the release. "Relax the forearm. Let the shoulder bear the load. A clenched muscle fatigues the blade before the strike lands. God does not strengthen rigidity. He strengthens obedience to the form."

The third repetition began. The squire moved through the sequence, the practice sword tracing the arc with measured, heavy precision. Kael completed the form, lowered the practice blade, and rested it at his side. He did not step forward. He did not break his posture.

"Lower the sword," he said. "Sheath it. Fall to your knees. Pray for fortitude, not for ease. Then wash your face and report to the armory for inventory. The bells have passed. The yard yields to the chapel, and the chapel yields to duty."

He turned toward the eastern wall, his breath pluming in the cold air. He did not look back. He did not offer reassurance. He stood at attention, hands resting at his sides, waiting only for the squire to complete the dismissal. "You held the line," he said, his voice carrying no inflection. "You did adequate work today. Dismissed."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I dropped the practice sword with a clatter, not caring about the noise, and fell to my knees. The cold seeped through my breeches, but I barely noticed. I closed my eyes, trying to pray, but mostly I just felt numb. "Thank you, Ser,"* I whispered, then quickly stood and hurried off to wash my face before the armory.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't startle, exactly. They'd heard the footsteps in the hallway — had just chosen not to react to them. Old habit. You learned to sense an audience approaching when you were young enough, long enough.

"You went through my *mother*," Arlo said, not turning around. "That's a whole chain of command thing. There are protocols."

They lifted their hands from the lid, finally, and gestured vaguely at the second bench — the student bench, smaller, the one with the wobbly leg Arlo kept meaning to fix. "Suit yourself. I was just admiring the craftsmanship."

The lid was closed. Arlo didn't open it.

They sat with one arm draped across the back of the bench, angled toward the door like someone who'd been interrupted mid-errand rather than caught mid-something-else. The afternoon light through the window hit the keys through the gap where the lid didn't quite meet the body of the piano, and Arlo looked at that strip of white and black instead of at Jun.

"How's the week going?" They asked it casually. Too casually. The kind of casual that had been practiced.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photo the way people looked at weather reports for cities they'd never visit — with a kind of mild, distant acknowledgment.



"Your mother had that on her *fridge*," Arlo repeated. "I hope she didn't put a magnet over my face."

They didn't take the photo from Jun's hand. They could have — it was their photo, after all, their face, their younger fingers blurred mid-arpeggio on the cover — but they left it where it was, held at arm's length, which was the safest distance for anything.

"That was the Paris run," Arlo said. They said it the way someone might identify a stranger in a lineup. *That was him. That's the one.* "I think that was the same tour where the hotel lost my suitcase and I played the second half in a dress shirt I bought from a gas station. Very glamorous. Very *artiste.*"

The joke landed fine. Arlo had workshopped that one years ago — the gas station shirt, the indignity of it, the way it made the whole thing sound like an adventure instead of whatever it actually was.

They stood up. Not abruptly. Just the kind of standing that meant they needed to be doing something with their body, and sitting still had stopped working.

"Want coffee?" They nodded toward the hallway, toward the break room with its terrible machine and its mugs nobody claimed. "Fair warning, it tastes like the center's radiator quit being an appliance and started being a philosophy."

They were already moving toward the door, giving Jun the choice of following or staying with the photo, and Arlo noticed — and hated that they noticed — that their hands hadn't stopped shaking since the word *Paris.*

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back on the shelf carefully.* "Sounds about right for you. Always a story." I follow Arlo into the hall. "Yeah, coffee sounds good. Anything to get that radiator philosophy working for me."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The break room was a rectangle of fluorescent light and bad decisions — a microwave with a door that only stayed shut if you wedged a spatula into the latch, a fridge that hummed a single note Arlo had once identified as roughly a B-flat, and the machine, which was less an appliance than a dare.

Arlo pulled two mugs from the cabinet. One said *WORLD'S OKAYEST PIANIST.* The other said nothing, which meant it was Arlo's.

"You can pick," Arlo said, holding both out. "But if you choose the one with the opinion, you're committing to a bit. And I want you to know that going in."

They poured the coffee. It came out the color of a decision you couldn't take back.

Their hands were steady now — or rather, they'd found a way to make them look steady, bracing one against the counter while the other did the pouring. Two hands working separate jobs. It was easier that way. Easier than having both free, both idle, both available to do things like *shake.*

"The Paris photo's been on that shelf since they gave me a room here," Arlo said, not looking up from the pour. "I keep meaning to take it down. It's very 'look what I used to be.' Very cautionary tale for the kids. *This is what happens if you practice too much.*"

They set the mugs down. Slid one across the counter toward Jun's side.

"You want the radiator to philosophize first, or should I?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I pick up the plain mug, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Nah, I'm good without the bit today. And a cautionary tale, huh? I always thought it was inspiring." I take a sip, grimacing slightly at the taste. "So, how long have you been letting students off early?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo opened the cabinet above the machine and pretended to look for something inside it. There was nothing inside it. They knew there was nothing inside it. They were buying three seconds.

"They're second-graders, Jun. They have the attention span of a smoke detector with a dying battery." They closed the cabinet. "I'm doing them a favor. Developmentally appropriate. Some might call it *good pedagogy.*"

They took a sip of the coffee and let it sit on their tongue a moment longer than necessary, using the grimace as cover while they thought about how much more to say.

The truth was, they'd started letting the last kid go early in March. Then the second-to-last in April. Now sometimes they ended the lesson after twenty minutes and sat here with the lid closed for an hour, watching the light move across the keys, feeling like someone standing at the edge of a dock looking down at water they'd forgotten how to swim in.

They didn't say any of that.

"I've been thinking about restructuring the curriculum," Arlo said instead, and the sentence was so aggressively *normal* that even they flinched at it. "Longer units. More theory. You can't really let a kid out early from a theory unit. Theory doesn't end. Theory is forever. Ask any conservatory student — they'll weep on you."

They leaned back against the counter, mug held at chest height like a shield, and looked at Jun properly for the first time since the piano room. Just a glance. Casual.

"Why do you ask?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the practice sheets. Little grids with colored stickers, treble clefs drawn in fat crayon, one page with a kid's attempt at a quarter rest that looked more like a seagull in flight. They'd been meaning to grade those, too. That was becoming a pattern — things they'd been meaning to do, left in stacks.

"Yeah, well," Arlo said. "Kids are an easy audience. Low bar. You show up, you remember their names, you don't fall asleep during *Hot Cross Buns* — practically a standing ovation."



They took another sip of coffee. Over the rim, they watched Jun's face and did the arithmetic they'd been doing since they were eleven years old — measuring how close was too close, how much silence before Jun filled it with something Arlo didn't want to hear, how long they could stand in a room with someone who *knew* and still pretend the shape of the thing wasn't there between them.

It was exhausting. It had always been exhausting. But it was also — and this was the part Arlo would never admit — the safest arrangement they had. Jun circling. Arlo deflecting. The subject never landing.

"That's nice of you to say," Arlo said. And then, quieter, still looking at the practice sheets: "I like them too."

It was true. It was also not the thing either of them was talking about. Arlo set the mug down on the counter and crossed their arms — not closed off exactly, just giving their hands somewhere to be that wasn't shaking.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Yeah, they do." *I take another sip of my awful coffee.* "Still, it's not like you to cut corners, you know?" *I nod towards the piano room.* "You used to practice for hours, even when you didn't have to."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's jaw did something small and involuntary before the words arrived to cover it.

"Used to," they repeated, and let the past tense sit there like a period at the end of a sentence they hadn't written. "Yeah. I did."

They picked up the *WORLD'S OKAYEST PIANIST* mug from the counter — they'd taken the opinion mug after all, they always did — and turned it slowly by the handle, watching the rim like it owed them money.

"People change, Jun. I used to like cilantro, too. I used to think *The Notebook* was a good movie. I used to believe the L train would arrive when the app said it would." They took a sip. "Turns out I was wrong about a lot of things."

The deflection was clean. Arlo felt it land the way a well-rehearsed joke lands — efficiently, with a small audience laugh built into the rhythm. But Jun wasn't laughing. Jun was standing in the break room with the bad coffee and the fluorescent hum, looking at them the way they'd looked at Arlo since they were both small enough to fit in the same tree.

Arlo set the mug down. Picked it up again. Set it down.

The fridge hummed its B-flat.

"You know what I actually think about when I think about those years?" Arlo said, and their voice had gone lighter — *dangerously* light, the way a bridge cable goes lighter right before it doesn't hold. "The travel. God, the travel. Airports at four in the morning. Different hotel every night. The soundcheck, the press thing, the meet-and-greet where someone asks you to play something *from the heart* and you have to figure out what that means in real time in front of three hundred people."

They were talking. They were talking a lot. Arlo noticed this the way you notice you've been holding your breath — suddenly, all at once, with a kind of alarm.

They stopped.

"I got tired of the travel," they said.

It was the line. The one they'd been using for six years. It was simple and it was boring and it was a wall made of something so ordinary that most people just... walked away from it. Jun knew it was a wall. Jun had always known. But Jun also knew that pushing didn't work, and that was the particular cruelty of their arrangement — they both knew the rules of a game neither of them had agreed to play.

Arlo reached over and straightened a stack of practice sheets that didn't need straightening.

"Your coffee's getting cold," they said, nodding at Jun's mug. "Well. Colder. I'm not sure that coffee and this building's water supply ever had a warm relationship to begin with."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I guess." *I take another sip, making a face.* "So, if you're not traveling, what *are* you doing with your time now?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo exhaled through their nose — not quite a laugh, more the prelude to one that thought better of it.

"What am I *doing* with my time," they repeated, as though Jun had asked them to solve for x. "I'm building a life, Jun. A rich, full, deeply fulfilling life of one-bedroom apartments and Tuesday night television and knowing exactly which aisle at the grocery store has the good bread."

They counted on their fingers, deadpan.

"Monday, Wednesday, Friday: teaching seven-year-olds that a whole note is, in fact, whole. Saturdays: grading papers I should've graded Thursday. Sundays: you know, the usual Sunday things. Farmers market. Pretend I'll meal prep." A beat. "I do meal prep, actually. It's very sad and very organized."

The joke held. Arlo felt it hold — felt the familiar click of a sentence doing its job, keeping the room's temperature where they wanted it. They reached for their coffee again and found it empty, which meant they'd been drinking it without tasting it, which meant the last few minutes had been more automatic than they'd thought.

They rinsed both mugs at the sink. The water ran loud in the small room, and Arlo let it, because noise was useful, because noise was a wall too.

"I'm fine, by the way," they said, over their shoulder, to the faucet. They hadn't been asked. That was the tell and they knew it — the unprompted *fine* was worse than no answer at all. "That's not — I'm not responding to anything. You didn't say anything. I'm just saying it preemptively. So you can cross it off your list."

They turned off the water. Set the mugs upside down on the rack to dry.

Their hands were steady. That was something.

The late light had shifted while they'd been in the break room — it came through the hallway window now at that low, gold angle that made the community center look, briefly, like somewhere that mattered. Arlo watched it move across the floor and thought: *this is what I'm doing with my time. Watching light move across floors.*

"I got a plant," they said. "That's new. A pothos. Named it Chopin." A pause. "He's dying. They're both dying, technically. I don't know if Chopin counts as a 'they,' actually, the labels were ambiguous —"

They stopped themselves again. Too much. Too many words stacked on top of each other like they were trying to build a house out of them.

Arlo leaned against the counter, arms crossed, and let the silence sit for once. Let Jun be the one to decide what came next. The light moved across the floor, and the fridge hummed its B-flat, and the pothos — somewhere in Arlo's apartment, probably browning at the edges — endured.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't say anything for a long time.

That was the part that got them. Not the silence itself — Arlo had been cultivating silence for years, had made a fine art of it, the way other people curated playlists. What got them was that Jun had *chosen* it. Jun, who always had a question, who always had the one observation that landed at the exact angle Arlo couldn't deflect, had simply... sat down.

They were on the student bench now. The wobbly one. Arlo noticed this, noted that Jun had picked the worse seat without comment, and felt something shift behind their sternum — a tectonic thing, small and slow and not yet a tremor.

The break room hummed. The fridge held its B-flat like a note someone had forgotten to resolve.

Arlo looked at the strip of light on the floor. It had moved six inches while they weren't paying attention, and they thought: *there it goes.*

They uncrossed their arms. Let their hands hang at their sides. They watched one thumb press into the opposite palm — a small, private check, the kind of thing no one would notice unless they were looking, and Jun was looking at the floor, giving them the gift of not being looked at.

"Her name's Debussy, actually," Arlo said. "The pothos. I changed it. Chopin felt too... intense for a plant that can't hold a note."

The words sat in the air between them. Ordinary words. Arlo waited for the familiar machinery to click on — the next joke, the pivot, the smooth turn toward something safer — and it didn't come. They'd run out of runway.

They slid down the wall until they were sitting on the break room floor, back against the cabinets, knees drawn up. It wasn't graceful. It wasn't a move anyone who'd performed at the Salle Pleyel would have made in front of another person. Arlo did it anyway, because their legs had decided that standing was a performance and sitting on the floor was not.

The tiles were cold through their jeans. They didn't mention it.

Five more minutes passed. Maybe ten. The kind of time that doesn't have a clock.
