The clock in the hallway struck the quarter hour. Four notes. The last one hung in the air slightly longer than it should have, the way a held breath does.

And on the shelf — the left shelf, the dark one, where the gap sat among the unmarked spines — the dust had not moved. But the gap looked different from this angle. Smaller. As though whatever was missing had been narrower than a book after all. As though it had been the width of a hand, held flat, turned on its side.

Gabi should go back to the boxes. There were hours of work left. The light from the side garden was already beginning to thin at the edges.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk to the bookshelf and squint at the gap. I reach out and run my finger along the dusty shelf, then carefully try to fit my hand into the space.* It's definitely smaller.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The dust came away on her fingertip in a long grey smear, soft as powder, and beneath it the wood was darker — not stained, just older, the way wood looks when nothing has touched it for decades. The surface was very slightly concave. Worn down. Not by books.

Her fingers went into the gap and stopped.

It was narrower than it looked. The spines on either side pressed against the back of her hand — not hard, but with a kind of patient firmness, the way a bookshelf holds a book. She had to turn her hand sideways, exactly as she'd thought, exactly as the shape of the gap had suggested, and even then the fit was close. Her knuckles brushed the shelf above. Her wrist touched the shelf below.

The space went back further than the shelf was deep. That was the wrongness — not frightening, not yet, just a small geometric impossibility that her hand understood before her mind did. The shelf was perhaps ten inches deep. Her hand went in to the wrist and there was still space behind it, still cool dark air that smelled of nothing at all.

Her fingertips touched the back of the shelf. Or touched something. The surface was smooth and faintly yielding, like leather, like the cover of one of the unmarked books, and it was warm — not warm like the blanket had been warm, not the residual warmth of a body, but warm the way skin is warm, evenly, from underneath, as though something behind the wood was alive and had been waiting for the temperature of a hand to match itself to.

She pulled her fingers back. The wood let go of them with no resistance at all.

On her fingertips, the dust had been wiped away. Beneath it, her skin was clean. But the print she'd left in the dust on the shelf — the smear where her finger had dragged — was already filling in. Not with new dust. The old dust was simply settling back into place, grain by grain, closing over the mark the way water closes over a stone.

The light from the side garden had thinned further. The pale bars on the carpet had narrowed to strips, and the far wall where the bookshelves stood was darker now — not with shadow, exactly, but with a kind of thickening, as though the air between her and the shelves had become more air than it had been.

Behind her, in the hallway, the clock was still ticking. But there was a second sound now, very faint, and it took her a moment to place it.

It was the sound of pages turning. Not from the box at her feet. Not from any book she could see. It came from the shelves — from the left shelves, the dark ones, from somewhere in the rows of unmarked spines — and it was slow and deliberate and it did not stop.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The words went out into the room and were absorbed by it. There was no echo. The curtains didn't move. The pages turning on the left shelf paused — not in response, not in surprise, but the way a sound pauses when you hold your breath to listen to something else — and then resumed at exactly the same tempo, unhurried, indifferent to the offer.

No one wanted the TV.

The quiet that followed was worse than the quiet before, because now it had been addressed and had declined to answer. It sat in the room like a guest who will not leave and will not speak and will not look at you directly.

The cup on the side table had not moved. The ring beneath it had not darkened. But when she looked at it — and she did look at it, standing there in the silence after her own voice had died — she noticed that the cup was closer to the edge of the table than it had been. Not by much. A centimetre, perhaps. The kind of distance that could be explained by memory, by the angle of standing, by anything at all.

The blanket lay where she had folded it. The creases were still sharp. But one corner had lifted slightly, the way wool does when the air changes — or the way a page lifts when something beneath it shifts.

On the left shelf, the sound of turning pages continued. Slow. Deliberate. And now there was something else beneath it, so faint it might have been the house settling or the pipes or nothing at all — a sound like a finger dragging along a line of text, following the words.

The light from the side garden was almost gone. The strips on the carpet had thinned to threads. In another twenty minutes it would be dusk, and the room would be lit only by what came through from the hallway, where the clock ticked and ticked and each tick sounded, impossibly, slightly farther away.

There were still boxes to fill. The books on the right shelf were only half done. She could leave — the door was right there, the car was in the drive, her own house was across town with its lights that worked on switches and its silence that was only silence.

But the cup had moved. And the pages were turning. And the gap in the shelf was the width of a hand held flat, and her hand had fit into it exactly.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content:
*I walk over to the side table, picking up the cup and holding it in my hands. It's cool. I set it back down, but further away from the edge, then turn back to the bookshelves.*

"Alright, you want to play?" *I pull out a sturdy-looking gardening encyclopedia from the right shelf.* "Let's see what you're reading."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The gardening encyclopedia was heavy in her hands — *The Practical Gardener's Encyclopedia*, two inches thick, its spine cracked in three places. She pulled it from the shelf with more force than she'd intended, and a small avalanche of dust came with it, cascading down over her wrists and the backs of her hands in a fine grey curtain.

She held it up. She held it out, toward the left shelf, toward the dark rows of unmarked spines where the sound of turning pages had been.

The sound stopped.

Not paused this time. Stopped. The way a clock stops — not winding down, not fading, just ceasing between one tick and the next, mid-motion. The silence it left behind was so total that she could hear the fibers of the carpet under her feet, the almost imperceptible settling of dust in the air, the sound of her own blood in her ears.

Nothing happened.

She stood there with the encyclopedia held out like an offering or a challenge and the room simply looked back at her with its darkening corners and its thin threads of dying light and did nothing at all. The pages did not turn. The gap did not widen. The cup sat where she had placed it, further from the edge, safe. The blanket lay folded with its one lifted corner.

The silence went on long enough to become uncomfortable. Long enough that she became aware of her own posture — arm extended, book held out, chin lifted — and how it looked from the outside. How it looked to the room.

She could open the encyclopedia. She could. Her thumb was already at the edge of the pages. But the thought arrived with a cold specificity: *which page.* The turning had been slow and deliberate, following a line of text with a finger. If she opened the book at random, would it be the right page? And what would it mean if it was?

The light from the side garden was gone now. Only the hallway light reached in, laying a pale parallelogram across the carpet that stopped well short of where she stood. The bookshelves were losing their edges. The unmarked spines were becoming a single dark surface, a wall of shadow that had the shape of books.

She became aware — gradually, the way one becomes aware of a sound that has been going on for some time — that the clock in the hallway had changed. It was still ticking. But the intervals between ticks were longer now. Not much. Not enough to be sure. But the rhythm she had grown up with, the rhythm she had wound back into existence six weeks ago, had shifted by some small imperceptible degree, and every tick took fractionally more patience than the one before.

The encyclopedia was still in her hands. It was just a book. It weighed four pounds and contained entries on aphids and drainage and the Latin names of roses. It was not a weapon and it was not a key and holding it out toward the dark shelf had changed nothing except the quality of the silence.

Somewhere deep in the house — not the living room, not the hallway, but further in, toward the back where the kitchen was and the ferns stood green and watered and the envelope of photographs sat on the table — there was a sound. Very faint. The sound of a single page being turned. Just one. As if whatever had been reading had bookmarked its place and set the book down gently and was now doing something else.

The light in the hallway flickered. Not the bulb — the shape of the light on the carpet. For just a moment, the parallelogram had a different geometry, as though something had passed between the bulb and the floor. Then it was as it had been.

Gabi stood in the near-dark of her grandmother's living room with an encyclopedia in her hands and forty books left to box and the feeling — not a thought, not yet, just a feeling, low and cold and patient — that the house was not empty and had not been empty and that the thing in it was not a ghost, because ghosts were the stories people told to make absence manageable, and this was not absence. This was presence. Quiet, domestic, well-mannered presence.

It had been reading. It had bookmarked its place. It was waiting for her to finish what she had started.

The books on the right shelf were only half done.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I lower the encyclopedia slowly, then place it carefully back on the shelf.* "Okay, fine. If you're going to be like that." *I grab another paperback, not even looking at the title, and drop it into the box.* This is going to be a long night.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The paperback landed in the box with a soft, final sound. The cardboard sides swayed. A little cloud of dust rose and resettled.

Then another book went in. Then another. She did not look at the titles. She pulled from the right shelf — the ordinary shelf, the gardening books and local histories and the cracked-spined paperbacks — and she dropped them into the box and she did not look at the left shelf and she did not look at the armchair and she did not look at the cup.

This was a strategy, of course. The room knew it was a strategy. It permitted the strategy. That was the thing about the room — it permitted things. It waited with the patience of a place that had been waiting for a very long time and expected to wait a long time more.

The box filled. She folded the flaps of a second box and filled that one too. The right shelf was nearly empty now, and the emptiness of it was different from the gap on the left — this was a clean absence, a made absence, the absence of a thing that had been taken away in order and would be accounted for. The gap on the left was not like that at all.

She worked. The hallway clock ticked its slow, unhurried, wrong-timed ticks. Outside, the last of the light went. The window in the side garden became a black rectangle with a faint reflection in it — the room, dimly, the shape of shelves, the shape of the armchair, the pale shape of herself standing with her back to the glass.

She did not look at the reflection. But she could see it in the periphery, and she noticed — the way one notices things one is refusing to look at directly — that the reflection was slightly out of step with her. Not moving differently. Not doing anything she was not doing. Just delayed, the way a reflection in old glass is delayed, by a fraction of a second, so that when she reached for a book, the pale shape in the window reached a moment after, and when she dropped it in the box, the shape dropped it a moment after that.

A fraction of a second. That was all. Could have been the glass.

The second box was full. She straightened up and her back ached and the house was quiet — really quiet now, genuinely quiet, the pages on the left shelf had not resumed and the sound from the kitchen had not repeated and the clock was only a clock, ticking.

It was the quiet that was wrong. Not the wrongness of sounds but the wrongness of their absence. The quiet had a texture to it — dense, composed, attentive. It was the quiet of a room in which everyone has stopped talking to listen to one person. And she was the one person. And she was not speaking.

The kitchen. The thought arrived without her choosing it. The kitchen where the ferns were green and the photographs had been nudged an inch to the left and a page had turned, softly, like something setting down its reading.

She had not been in the kitchen yet. She had come in through the front, stood in the doorway, walked to the living room, and she had not been in the kitchen, and the photograph envelope was in the kitchen.

It was nudged an inch to the left. That was what she'd noticed when she arrived. An inch. The kind of distance that meant nothing.

The third box stood folded and empty by the door. The books on the right shelf were done. The books on the left shelf — the leather bindings, the encyclopedias, the unmarked spines — had not been touched, and would not be touched tonight, and they stood in their dark rows in the near-dark of the room like a sentence that had been started but not finished.

The parallelogram of hallway light had narrowed further. In the reflection of the side-garden window, the pale shape of herself stood very still — a fraction of a second behind, as always — and beside the shape of the armchair, in the reflection only, there was a shape that might have been the blanket, and might have been something sitting with the blanket over its lap, and it was very difficult to tell in old glass at night.

She would have to walk down the hallway to get to the kitchen. Past the clock. Past the stairs. The hallway was dark now, lit only by the bulb in its fixture, and the bulb threw shadows that moved when the air moved, and the air in an old house always moved.

The cup sat on the table. The dark ring beneath it waited for it, ovular and smudged at one edge.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought came and went the way thoughts do in a room like this — briefly, faintly, like a match struck in a strong wind. Marcus. Yes, he'd been in some of the photographs. Handsome in the way people were handsome in the seventies, with his collar open and his arm around Grandmother's shoulder and a lake behind them both.

But the thought didn't settle. It arrived and found no room for itself. The kitchen was too cold for it. The overhead light hummed at a frequency that made the skin on her forearms prickle. The ferns stood on the windowsill with their fronds turned slightly toward the doorway — not toward the window, not toward the light, but toward the doorway, toward where she stood, the way plants do when something enters a room.

The envelope of photographs was on the table. It had been nudged an inch to the left. She could see that now — see the ghost of its original position in the dust, a rectangle of clean wood where it had sat for years before someone, something, shifted it by the width of a thumb.

She picked it up. The photographs slid out into her hand.

There was Marcus by the lake. There was Grandmother on the porch. There was a group shot at a table — a birthday, candles, everyone mid-laugh. And there was one at the back, face down, which she turned over.

It was the living room. Not a photograph of people in the living room — a photograph of the living room itself, empty, taken from the doorway at roughly the height a person would stand. The armchair faced the window. The bookshelves lined the far wall. The light came in from the side garden in long pale bars.

It was exactly as the room looked now. Not as it had looked when Grandmother was alive — the arrangement was the same, but the quality of the light, the density of the shadow in the far corner, the specific way the blanket hung on the arm of the chair — it matched. Precisely. As though someone had stood in the doorway this evening, before she arrived, and taken a picture.

There was a date stamped on the white border. The date was eleven years ago.

She set the photograph down on the table. Her hand was steady. The kitchen hummed. The ferns leaned toward her. On the windowsill, the glass was black with night, and in it, her reflection looked back — and beside her reflection, standing at the doorway of the kitchen where no one stood, there was the faintest suggestion of a shoulder, the suggestion of a height, the suggestion of someone who had been standing there for some time and was not moving and was not reflected fully because the glass was old and kind.

The thought about Marcus — whether he was alive, whether he was single — was gone. It had not left a trace. It had not been the kind of thought this room allowed. The room allowed fear, and duty, and the small mechanical motions of sorting and boxing. It allowed grief, though it had its own ideas about grief. But the quick warm lightness of attraction, the way a face in an old photograph could snag the attention and set it drifting toward pleasant futures — that was not what the room was for.

The envelope sat on the table with the photographs fanned out. The one of the living room lay on top. Behind her, at the end of the hallway, the clock ticked — slower now, patient, keeping time for something that had nowhere to be and all night to get there.

She could hear, very faintly, from the living room she had just left, the sound of wool settling against upholstery. Not the blanket. Not the chair. The sound of something leaning back. Getting comfortable.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo, then at my reflection in the dark window, searching for the shoulder, for any hint of another presence.* "What are you doing here?" I whisper, not to the reflection, but to the empty air. *I gather the photos and shove them back into the envelope, then quickly head back towards the living room.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photographs went back into the envelope in a rush — not the careful order they'd come out in, but shuffled, corners catching on corners, one of them bending slightly at the edge. She felt the bend with her thumb and thought, absurdly, of asking it later whether it minded. The envelope sealed with its little string-and-button closure. Her fingers wound the string too tightly. The button pulled to one side and stayed there.

The whisper left her mouth and entered the kitchen air and was gone. The kitchen did not answer. The ferns did not answer. The hum of the overhead light continued at its frequency — steady, patient, the hum of a room listening — and in the black glass of the window, the shoulder-shaped suggestion was no longer there. Or it had never been there. Or it had moved.

She did not look again.

The hallway received her. The clock stood in its case against the wall, tall and dark-wooded, its pendulum swinging behind glass with the slow even patience of something that had nowhere to be. Each tick reached her as she passed. Each tick sounded a fraction of a breath later than her footfall, so that the rhythm of walking and the rhythm of time were slightly, unbearably, out of phase. The stairs went up to the right into darkness. She did not look at the stairs.

The living room doorway.

The light from the hallway lamp reached in and lay across the carpet in its thin parallelogram and stopped where it had stopped before. Beyond it the room was dim and close and smelled of dust and the sweet not-perfume not-flowers. The bookshelves stood along the far wall. The right shelf was empty now — that clean made absence. The left shelf was not.

The armchair faced the window.

The blanket was folded over one arm. She was sure of that — she had folded it, had creased it with her palm, had laid it back in the shape Grandmother kept it. The creases were there. But the wool did not lie flat the way folded wool lies flat. It lay the way a blanket lies when it is folded over something. There was a shape beneath the creases. A shape that was the width and height of a lap.

No one was in the chair. She could see the chair, could see its empty cushions, could see the way the light fell on the seat and found nothing there. But the blanket folded over a shape, and the shape was warm — she knew it was warm without going near it, knew it the way she knew the photograph in the envelope was of this evening and dated eleven years ago, knew it in the deep animal part of the brain that knows things before it can say them.

The cup sat on the side table. Further from the edge than she had placed it. She had put it back carefully, had set it well toward the middle, and it was now at the edge again — not as far as before, not quite, but close. Close enough that the dark ovular ring beneath it no longer aligned with the base. The cup sat on the ring wrong. Offset by a centimetre. The way it had sat before she moved it.

The silence in the room was composed and attentive and it had been waiting. She had gone to the kitchen and the room had waited and now she was back and the waiting was over, and what replaced waiting she did not yet know.

On the left shelf, among the unmarked spines, the gap stood at eye level. It had not changed. It was the width of a hand held flat, turned on its side. Dust lay before it in an unbroken line, and the dust was undisturbed, and the dust would be undisturbed, and anything could have passed through that gap and the dust would close over the memory of its passing the way it had closed over her fingerprint — grain by grain, patient and exact.

The hallway clock ticked. Slow now. Each tick arriving as though it had traveled a distance to reach her.

The third box stood by the door, folded and empty, waiting to be filled. Forty books remained on the left shelf. The leather bindings. The encyclopedias missing their volumes. The unmarked spines that were the height and thickness of a book or the width of a hand or something else entirely.

She stood in the doorway of the living room. She did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I lean against the doorframe, crossing my arms.* "Okay, Gram. What are you hiding?" I whisper, looking at the bookshelf. *I take a step into the room, then hesitate, looking at the blanket on the armchair.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The whisper found the room and the room took it the way it took everything — without acknowledgment, without echo, folding it into its silence like a card slipped into a book.

She stepped in. One step. Then another. The carpet was soft underfoot and did not creak, and the light from the hallway threw her shadow ahead of her in a long pale shape that reached toward the armchair before she did.

The blanket held its shape. The shape beneath the creases did not change as she approached — did not shift, did not flatten, did not do anything at all. It was simply there. The width of a lap. The height of someone sitting with their legs together and their hands in their wool-covered warmth.

She was close enough now to see the weave of the fabric. Close enough to see that one of the creases — the one along the front edge, where the blanket folded over whatever it covered — was slightly damp. Not wet. Damp. The way wool is damp when it has been holding the steam of something warm beneath it for a long time.

The cushion of the chair was indented. She noticed this the way one notices that a word has been misspelled — first as a wrongness, then as a fact. The left cushion, the one nearest the arm where the blanket was folded, had a shallow depression in it. Not deep. Not the kind of depression a body leaves when it has been sitting for hours. More like the kind that remains for a moment after someone has just stood up.

But there was no one in the chair. She could see the chair. She could see the cushion. She could see the indentation and she could see that there was nothing making it.

The cup on the side table caught the hallway light and threw it back in a small pale coin-shape on the ceiling. The coin-shape trembled — not from movement in the room but from something in the light itself, some quality of the bulb or the air or the hour.

She remembered, then, what Grandmother had been like in this chair. How she sat with the blanket over her legs and a book open on her lap and her reading glasses down on her nose. How she'd look up when someone came in — not startled, not annoyed, just *present*, the way a person is present when they have been alone with a book and the book has been good and the interruption is neither welcome nor unwelcome but simply the next thing. How she would say, without preamble, as though continuing a conversation that had paused hours ago: *The peonies are going to come in early this year.* Or: *I found something in the encyclopedia I didn't know.* Or nothing at all. Sometimes nothing at all.

The blanket was still damp.

On the left shelf, the gap waited at eye level. The unmarked spines stood on either side of it like people who have left a space in a row and are not looking at it.

And now — very faintly, so faintly that she might have imagined it, might have produced it herself in the marrow of her own wanting — there was a sound from the chair. Not a creak. Not a shift of wool. A sound that was almost a sound. The shape a sound makes before it becomes one. The intake of breath that precedes speech.

It did not become speech.

The hallway clock ticked, and each tick was a small stone dropped into a deep well, and the silence swallowed each one and was hungry for the next.

The third box waited by the door. The left shelf waited along the wall. The chair waited in its corner with its damp creases and its empty indentation and its blanket folded over a shape that was not there.

Gabi stood close enough to touch any of it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I reach out, my hand hovering over the blanket.* "Gram?" I whisper. My fingers twitch, wanting to smooth the damp spot, but I don't quite touch it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not write anything down right away. She let the sentence sit in the room, the way she let most things sit — five full seconds, her gaze steady and unhurried, her pen resting still against the notepad. The clock on the wall ticked without a second hand to measure the silence.

"'Their journal,'" she repeated, quietly. Not a question yet. Just the words, given back.

She tilted her head slightly. "Where did you find it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still not looking at her.* "In the back of their closet. Under some old board games."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the pause hold. Five seconds. The ficus rustled faintly from the vent above it.

"Under some old board games," she echoed again, the words slow and even. She looked at the space where Jamie's gaze had been — the corner, the closet of the mind, whatever was behind the wall.

"You went looking, or it found you?"



She uncapped the pen fully and set the cap beside it on the armrest, but she did not write yet. The notepad stayed blank. Her eyes stayed on Jamie, unhurried, as though there were nowhere else in the world she needed to be.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move to fill the silence. That was the first thing — she let it be exactly as wide as it needed to be. Five seconds passed. Then five more. She did not look at the notepad. She did not look at the clock that had no second hand to mark how long they sat there.

"You stopped," she said, at last. Her voice stayed low, level, the same register she might use to observe that it was raining. Not an accusation. Not a concern. Just the fact of it, placed gently on the table between them.

She waited again. Three seconds this time.

"Wherever that sentence was going — it's still there. It hasn't gone anywhere." She uncrossed her hands and laid them, palms down, on her own knees. Grounded. Still. "You don't have to finish it today. You don't have to finish it at all." A pause. "But I want to ask — what happened right before you stopped? Not the words. What did you feel, in your chest, or your throat, or wherever it went quiet?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, squeezing my eyes shut for a moment.* "It's not... it's not fair." My voice is barely a whisper. "They wrote about me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper have the room. Five seconds. Then a few more, because the sentence needed more than the usual five. She didn't reach for the notepad. She didn't lean forward — leaning forward was a kind of touch, and she didn't do that either.

"They wrote about you," she said, when the silence had finished its work. She said it the way you'd hold something up to the light and turn it slowly. Not *about you*. *About you.* She let the difference sit where it would.

"'It's not fair,'" she continued, keeping her voice in the same careful register, as though not to startle what was already loose in the room. "Tell me what the unfair part is. And take your time — you can keep your eyes closed while you do."

She settled back into her chair, hands still on her knees, and waited. Not with expectation. With space.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's eyes when they looked up. She held the look — not searching, not probing. Just present. Five seconds passed. Then another three, because the shape of what wasn't said needed its own time.

"In the last entry," she repeated. The words were quiet and careful, the way she might name a delicate thing by its corners rather than lifting it.

She noticed — and did not mention — the way Jamie's sentence had edges. How *the last entry* had been said, and then the sentence had stopped the way a hand stops at the edge of a table. There was more. Dr. Vasquez could feel its weight the way you feel weather change in a room.

She looked at Jamie for a long moment.

"You told me they wrote about you. You told me it was in the last entry." A pause. The faint tick of the wall clock without a second hand to count it. "And then you stopped again. Not like before — not the same kind of stopping." She tilted her head, just slightly. "This one felt... deliberate. Like you decided to hold something back."

She let that sit.

"That's okay. You're allowed to hold things back." Her hands stayed still on her knees. "But I want to name what's in the room right now — there's something you're carrying that you haven't set down yet. And I think it's heavy."

She paused again.

"You looked at me when you said it. You didn't look away this time. That tells me something too, though I won't tell you what." The faintest breath — not quite a laugh, not quite relief. "What I *will* ask is this: what would it feel like to say it out loud? Not what it would do — what would it *feel like*? Because you've thought about it. I can see that you have."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I close my eyes again, a tear escaping and tracing a path down my temple.* "It would feel like... like letting them go. And I don't want to."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not speak. Five seconds passed. Then ten. The tear made its slow path and she let it, the way she let everything — did not reach for the box of tissues on the side table, did not offer it, because offering it would have been an instruction: *dry your face, tidy this up, make it presentable.* She didn't do that.

The room held.

"'I don't want to,'" she said, finally. Her voice was the same as it had been when they were talking about the ficus. Level. Unremarkable. A fact, placed on the table between them where it could be looked at from any angle.

She paused, and the pause was not empty. It was doing work.

"You said it would feel like letting them go." Dr. Vasquez's hands did not move from her knees. "And then you said you don't want to. Both of those things are in the room right now. I'm not going to resolve them for you — I don't think that's mine to do."

She looked at Jamie — at the closed eyes, the temple, the tear's track. She said nothing about the tear.

"I want to ask you something, and I want you to really hear the question before you answer." She waited. "When you say *letting them go* — what is it you imagine you'd be letting go of? Not them. You said *them*, but I want to know what you mean by that. Because you found a journal. You opened it. You read it. And something about the last entry made you feel like saying it out loud would be a kind of ending."

She tilted her head slightly.

"Is that what it is? An ending?"

She settled deeper into the chair. Still. Patient. As though the answer, like the ficus, could take as long as it needed.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, opening my eyes again.* "No. It's not an ending. It's... it's like erasing them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez received the correction without adjusting her posture. Five seconds passed. The ficus dropped a leaf — or maybe it had already been on the floor and neither of them had noticed until now.

"*Erasing them,*" she said. She let the word do its own work in the air. Not *letting go.* Not *ending.* Something else entirely.

She considered this for a moment, her gaze steady, unhurried. The pen lay where she'd set it down minutes ago, the notepad still blank.

"I want to sit with that word for a moment, because I think you chose it carefully." She paused. "Erasing is different from forgetting. Erasing is different from losing. Erasing implies... someone doing it on purpose. Something done *to* something that was there."

She looked at Jamie.

"You found words they wrote. In their hand. And now those words exist in a way they didn't exist yesterday — at least, not for you." A measured breath. "And you're telling me that speaking what you read out loud would erase them. Not the words. *Them.*"

She let that land.

"I want to understand the shape of that. Because from where I'm sitting, saying something out loud usually makes it *more* real. It adds. It doesn't subtract." A pause. "But that's not what it feels like to you. So tell me — when you imagine saying it, what gets erased? Is it their voice? Their intent? The version of them you had before you opened the journal?"

She waited. Her hands stayed still. Her face stayed open, without expectation.

"Or is it something else entirely?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at a loose thread on the armrest.* "It's like... if I say it out loud, then it becomes *my* truth. Not theirs anymore."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez noticed the loose thread before she noticed the words. Noted the fingers — picking, working, doing something that the mouth couldn't do. She filed it without filing. Let it be.

Five seconds.

"It becomes your truth," she said. The emphasis stayed where Jamie had put it. *My.* She left it there like a stone in a stream, not turning it over.

She sat with that for another beat. The clock ticked its soundless tick.

"You know, there's a distinction you just made that I want to reflect back to you, because I'm not sure you heard yourself make it." She paused, unhurried. "You said *my* truth. Not *a* truth. *My* truth. And you said it like it was the problem." Another pause. "Like ownership is the thing that would change it. Not the truth itself. The fact that it would belong to you."

She looked at Jamie's hands on the armrest. At the thread. Said nothing about it.

"That tells me the truth itself isn't what frightens you." Her voice stayed level, careful, the same tone she might use to describe the weather or the ficus or the hour. "It's the passing of it. The way it would move from their hand to yours."

She let five seconds go by.

"And I think that's what you meant by *erasing.* Not destroying. But... transferring. Taking something that was theirs and making it yours, which would mean it's no longer only theirs."

A pause.

"I want to ask you — and you can keep picking at that thread while you answer, if it helps — when you say it would become *your* truth... what does that make you? If it's not only their story anymore, but yours too. Who does that make you, in relation to them?"

She waited. Not for a quick answer. For the real one, however long it took to find.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stop picking at the thread, pressing my fingers into the armrest instead.* "It makes me responsible. For it. For them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the fingers stop picking and press into the armrest instead. She noticed the shift — from the small restless work of the thread to something more deliberate. Grounding. Bracing. She did not comment on the hands.

Five seconds.

"Responsible," she said. She let the word have its weight without adding to it. Not *burdened.* Not *guilty.* *Responsible.* She left it where Jamie had placed it.

Another pause. Long enough to be honest.

"You know, that's a word people say as though it's one thing. But it isn't." She shifted slightly in her chair — not leaning forward, not toward. Just adjusting, the way someone does when they intend to stay a while. "There's responsibility as in *the one who must act.* And there's responsibility as in *the one at fault.* And there's responsibility as in *the one who holds a thing so it doesn't fall.*"

She looked at Jamie — at the pressed fingers, the bracing.

"Those are three very different weights. And I think you just felt all three of them land on you at once."

She let that sit.

"I want to ask you something, and I want you to notice your first impulse before you answer — not to correct it, just to notice it." She paused. "When you said *responsible — for it. For them.* Which one of those was heavier? The *it*, or the *them?*"

Five seconds passed. The ficus rustled faintly.

"And one more." Her voice stayed level. Careful. "If it were someone else sitting in this chair — someone you loved, someone who found a journal and read something about themselves in the last entry — and they said to you what you just said to me. *It makes me responsible.* What would you want to say to them? Not what would be correct. What would you want to say?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, letting it out slowly.* "Them. Definitely them." *I don't answer the second question, just stare at my hands.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez received the breath, the answer, and the silence that followed it — all three, in that order, without ranking one above the others. Five seconds passed. Then several more, because the silence around the second question was a different quality of silence than the ones before it. Not the silence of someone who couldn't find the words. The silence of someone who found them and set them down somewhere out of reach.

"Them," she said. Just that. The word, returned.

She let the ficus rustle. Let the clock tick its missing second.

"You answered the first part," she said, after a moment. Her voice carried no weight of expectation, no edge of follow-up. An observation, like noting the hour. "And you didn't answer the second."

A pause.

"I'm not going to ask it again. Not now." She let her hands rest where they were. "But I want to name what just happened in the room, because I think it's important and I don't want it to pass without being seen."

She waited. Three seconds.

"You looked at your hands instead. And your hands are pressed into that armrest like they're holding something down." She didn't look at the hands when she said it. She looked at Jamie's face. "I asked you what you'd want to say to someone else in your position. Someone you loved. And the question didn't get answered — but something about it changed the way you were sitting. That's an answer too. Just not one made of words."

She let that be.

"I want to try something different, and you can tell me no." She paused. "Don't tell me what you'd say to them. Don't tell me what you'd want to say. Instead — tell me what you were afraid I'd think of you, if you did answer it."

Five seconds. The room held its shape around them both.

"Because that's usually where the weight is. Not in the words themselves. In what we think the words will make us."

She settled back. Still. Waiting without waiting.

"Or — if that's too much today — you can just tell me it's too much. And we'll leave it right here, on the table, for another time. It won't go anywhere."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I take a shuddering breath, a sob catching in my throat. I bury my face in my hands.* "I don't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not reach forward. Did not reach for the tissues. Did not reach for anything at all. Her hands stayed where they were, on her own knees, and she stayed where she was, in her own chair, and the distance between the two chairs remained exactly what it was — angled toward each other, not quite facing.

She let the sob have the room.

Five seconds. Then ten. Then more. The clock ticked without measuring it. The ficus stood in its corner and did what it did.

When she spoke, her voice was the same as it had been when she was talking about the plant. Level. Unhurried. Unremarkable in its tone, so that whatever was remarkable could stay with the thing itself and not with her delivery of it.

"'I don't know,'" she said.

She let that sit.

"You know, that's the truest thing you've said in this room today." A pause. Not for effect. For accuracy. "Everything before it — *erasing, my truth, responsible, them* — all of those were answers. Careful ones. Chosen ones. This one isn't chosen. It just... arrived."

She let several seconds pass. The sob was still doing its work behind Jamie's hands, and she did not ask it to stop, or soften, or make itself quieter.

"'I don't know' is not the same as nothing," she said, after a while. "It's the place where something is too big to hold in a single word. It's not absence. It's... fullness. Overflowing." She paused. "You don't have to shape it today. You don't have to shape it ever, if it won't shape."

She settled deeper into her chair. Made herself smaller, somehow — not with apology, but with a kind of deliberate taking-up-less-space, so that the sob in the room could take up more.

"I want to say one thing, and then I'm going to be quiet." She waited. "You asked me earlier — not in words — *is it fair?* You said *it's not fair.* And I want to tell you that I heard that. Not as a complaint. As a measurement. You were measuring the distance between what you're carrying and what you think you should be able to carry, and it wasn't matching up."

A breath. Hers. Then the room again.

"That gap — between what we carry and what we think we should be able to carry — that's where 'I don't know' lives. It's not a failure. It's the honest sound of the gap."

She stopped. Folded her hands. Said nothing else.

The ficus rustled. The clock ticked. The minutes did what minutes do when someone is crying in a room and the person sitting with them has decided that crying is not a problem to be solved but a thing to be accompanied.

Dr. Vasquez waited. She had nowhere else to be.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I slowly lower my hands from my face. My eyes are red-rimmed and wet, but I look at her. I don't say anything, just nod, a small, almost imperceptible nod.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move except for the tip of her pen resting against the notepad. She let the sentence sit between them.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Their journal,” she said.

Her voice stayed low and unhurried.

“You found it.”

She waited another moment before asking, “What did you notice when you picked it up?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, picking at a loose thread on the armrest of the chair.* "It was... lighter than I thought it would be."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words settle in the room.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Lighter,” she said.

Her pen stayed still against the notepad.

“Than you thought it would be.”

She waited another moment, her gaze steady but not pressing.

“What did you expect it to feel like?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move to fill the break in the sentence. She let it remain unfinished in the space between them.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“It stopped there,” she said.

Her voice stayed quiet, unhurried.

“Lighter than you thought it would be.”

She let the words sit for another moment before asking, “What did the next part feel too close to?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, looking away from her.* "I don't know." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "Just... heavy, I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper settle without reaching for it.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Heavy,” she said.

The word stayed plain, stripped of interpretation.

“You said it was lighter than you expected. And then heavy came.”

She allowed another brief silence before asking, “What kind of heavy was it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move except for the faint pressure of her pen against the notepad. She let the words remain where they had been placed.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“They wrote about you,” she said.

Her voice stayed even, unhurried.

“In the last entry.”

She allowed another quiet space to form around the sentence before speaking again.

“You brought it here,” she said. “And you brought the part you haven’t said.”

Her gaze remained steady, without demand.

“What part of it, if any, feels possible to say?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head again, pulling my knees up to my chest.* "It's not possible to say."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not ask for the words. She let the sentence stay closed.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Not possible to say,” she said.

Her voice did not press.

“You brought it here anyway.”

She let that sit in the room without reaching for more.

“What is it like,” she asked after another moment, “to have it here when it can’t be spoken?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It feels... suffocating." *I hug my knees tighter, wishing I could disappear.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not lean closer. She let the word stay where it had fallen.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Suffocating,” she said.

The pen did not move.

“It cannot be spoken, and still it is here.”

She waited another breath, giving the room the same quiet she gave the silence.

“If it has to remain unsaid for now,” she asked, “what would allow it to take up less air between us?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I don't know," *I whisper, my voice thick with unshed tears.* "Maybe if I just... burned it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the suggestion rest in the room without reaching for it.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Burned it,” she said.

Her voice stayed low and even.

“You thought about burning it.”

She waited another moment, the tip of her pen still against the notepad.

“What would burning it do to the suffocating?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It would make it disappear." *I finally look at her, my eyes red.* "Make it gone."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not try to take the words away. She let them sit where they had been spoken.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Gone,” she said.

Her voice remained low and unhurried.

“You said burning it would make it disappear.”

She allowed another silence to open around the thought.

“What would disappear,” she asked, “if it were gone?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Everything. All of it." *I wipe at my eyes impatiently.* "The last words."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words stay in the room without reaching for them.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“The last words,” she said.

Her voice remained low and even.

“Everything. All of it.”

She allowed the phrase to settle before speaking again.

“You said burning it would make them gone.”

The pen rested quietly against the notepad.

“If the last words disappeared,” she asked, “what would be left?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shiver, despite the warmth of the room.* "Nothing. Just... the silence."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words stay in the room without trying to move them.

One second.  
Two.  
Three.  
Four.  
Five.

“Nothing,” she said. “Just the silence.”

Her voice remained low and unhurried. The pen rested against the notepad without moving.

She allowed the silence to exist between them for another moment before speaking again.

“If the last words were gone,” she asked, “what would that silence be like?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It would be... deafening." *I lean my head back against the chair, closing my eyes.* "Worse than before."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not reach for her pen. She let it rest against the armrest, her fingers still. The silence in the room stretched. She counted the seconds in her head, one, two, three, four, five, letting the weight of the words settle into the space between them. Only after the fifth second had passed did she speak.

"Their journal," she repeated, her voice even, neither soft nor sharp. She kept her posture still, her hands resting in her lap. "When did you find it?"

She left the question hanging, giving Jamie room to fill the space. She did not offer a tissue. She did not suggest what the journal might mean. She simply held the space, her breathing quiet, her gaze steady.

"What was the first thing you read?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
*I shrug, still not looking at her.* "Yesterday. While I was cleaning out the attic."

I take a deep breath. "It was... under a loose floorboard."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
She did not move. She let the quiet settle over the room, counting the seconds in her head—one, two, three, four, five—until the admission rested fully in the space between them. When she finally spoke, her voice was level, unhurried.

"Yesterday," she repeated. "While you were cleaning out the attic. Under a loose floorboard."

Her hands remained still in her lap. She kept her posture relaxed, her attention fixed without pressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue. She simply held the silence open.

"What did the floorboard look like before you lifted it?"

She left the question in the air, giving the room time to breathe. She waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She watched the sentence fracture and dissolve into the quiet. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—letting the abrupt halt settle into the room. Only when the count finished did she speak.

"You stopped," she said, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap. "Mid-sentence."

She held the observation without filling the space. She did not lean closer. She did not offer a bridge. She simply waited, her attention steady, her breathing slow.

"What happened to the rest of it?"

She let the question hang. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez kept her gaze fixed, leaving the silence open, waiting for the next word, or the absence of one.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "I can't. I can't talk about it." I suddenly stand up and walk to the window, looking out. "Can we talk about something else?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move from her chair. She let the distance open between them, her gaze tracking the space where Jamie had been sitting before settling on the window. She counted the seconds in her head—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the request to settle into the quiet of the room. When the count finished, she spoke.

"You asked if we could talk about something else," she said, her voice even, her hands resting still in her lap. "What would that look like to you?"

She left the question suspended in the air. She did not offer a new topic. She did not acknowledge the shift in posture or the retreat to the window. She simply remained still, her breathing slow, her attention steady, waiting for the next word, or the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:

"They wrote about you," she said, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap. "In the last entry."

She kept her posture relaxed, her attention fixed without pressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue. She simply held the silence open.

"What did you do when you read it?"

She left the question hanging. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez kept her gaze steady, leaving the room to breathe, waiting for the next word, or the absence of one.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I... I closed it." *I turn back to the window.* "And put it back."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not shift in her chair. She let the quiet settle over the room, watching the space where Jamie had been sitting before turning her attention to the window. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the action to land fully in the air. When the count finished, she spoke.

"You closed it," she said, her voice even, her hands resting still in her lap. "And put it back."

She kept her posture relaxed, her gaze steady but unpressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a bridge to another topic. She simply held the quiet, her breathing slow and measured.

"What did you do after you put it back?"

She left the question suspended. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the silence open, ready for the next word, or the absence of one.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip.* "I came here." I turn to face her, but I don't sit down. "I haven't told anyone else."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not shift in her chair. She let the quiet settle over the room, her attention fixed on the space Jamie now occupied. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—until the admission rested fully in the air. When the count finished, she spoke.

"You came here," she said, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap. "And you haven't told anyone else."

She kept her posture relaxed, her gaze steady but unpressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue or an explanation. She simply held the silence open, her breathing slow and even.

"What made today the day to bring it here?"

She let the question hang. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the space between them unbroken, ready for the next word, or the weight of the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Because I don't know what to do." *My voice cracks a little.* "I don't know what it means."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move from her chair. She let the words settle into the quiet of the room, her attention fixed on the space Jamie now occupied. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the admission and the fracture in the voice to rest fully in the air. Only when the count finished did she speak.

"You don't know what to do," she said, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap. "And you don't know what it means."

She kept her posture relaxed, her gaze steady but unpressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue or a bridge to another topic. She simply held the silence open, her breathing slow and even.

"What happens when you sit with not knowing?"

She left the question suspended. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the space between them unbroken, ready for the next word, or the weight of the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's... unsettling." *I finally sit back down, but perch on the edge of the chair, my hands clasped tightly.* "Like a loose thread."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not shift in her chair. She let the words settle into the quiet of the room. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the description to rest fully in the air. When the count finished, she spoke.

"Unsettling," she said, her voice level, her hands resting in her lap. "Like a loose thread."

She kept her posture still, her gaze steady but unpressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue or a reassurance. She simply held the silence open, her breathing slow and even.

"What happens to the thread when you hold it there?"

She let the question suspend in the room. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the space between them unbroken, ready for the next word, or the weight of the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands, still clasped tightly.* "I don't know. It just... frays."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not shift in her chair. She let the word settle into the quiet of the room. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the observation to rest fully in the space between them. When the count finished, she spoke.

"It just... frays," she repeated, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap. "When it frays, what happens next?"

She kept her posture relaxed, her gaze steady but unpressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue or a bridge to another topic. She simply held the silence open, her breathing slow and even.

The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the space between them unbroken, ready for the next word, or the weight of the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up at her, my eyes welling up a little.* "Then it breaks."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She watched Jamie look up, her gaze catching the tension in the younger person's eyes without naming it. In her head, she counted the seconds—one, two, three, four, five—letting the finality of the word settle into the room. Only when the count finished did she speak.

"Then it breaks," she said, her voice level, her hands resting still in her lap.

She kept her posture relaxed, her attention fixed without pressing. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue. She simply held the silence open, her breathing slow and even.

"What does it look like when it breaks?"

She let the question hang. The ficus in the corner remained half-dead. The clock ticked without a second hand. Dr. Vasquez waited, leaving the space between them unbroken, ready for the next word, or the weight of the silence.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, a tear tracing a path down my cheek.* "I don't want to know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let it sit. Five seconds — she no longer counted them; her body kept the time on its own now, one slow breath, then another. The clock on the wall had no second hand to measure the silence out loud, so the silence simply stayed, filling the room the way water fills a glass.

The pen stayed uncapped in her hand. She didn't write.

"You found their journal," she said. Not a question. She handed the words back exactly as Jamie had given them to her, plain and unadorned, and set them in the space between the two chairs.

She thought of the way Jamie had sat down. She didn't mention it again.

"Where was it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still not looking at her.* "In their old backpack. Tucked away in the back of the closet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds pass. Somewhere behind the walls, a pipe ticked once and went quiet again. Jamie's gaze had gone to the floor, and she let it stay there. She had learned long ago that she didn't need to be looked at to be heard.

She set the pen down on the notepad, cap still off, and folded her hands in her lap.

"Their old backpack," she said. "The back of the closet." She gave the words back slowly, the way they'd been given to her — like something being taken out of a bag one item at a time, each piece set down carefully between them.

The shrug, she noticed. She filed it away without touching it.

"Did you open it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited. The five seconds passed, and she let them keep passing — ten, fifteen, twenty. The unfinished sentence stayed in the room exactly where Jamie had dropped it, and she made no move to pick it up.

She reached for the pen and pressed the cap back on. A small click. She set it on top of the notepad, closed, and folded her hands again. Nothing Jamie said next would be written down. She wanted that understood without having to say it.

"The words stopped," she said. Plainly. The way she'd say *it's raining*.

She didn't ask Jamie to finish. She didn't say it was all right, or take your time, or any of the small coins people paid to make silence cheaper.

"It can stay unfinished," she said. "Sentences keep."

Another breath. Another.

Then, quieter, she offered something smaller — a foothold instead of a cliff face.

"Were you alone? When you found it."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, still looking at the floor.* "My mom was with me. Cleaning out the closet." *My voice is barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez gave the whisper its five seconds. Whispers made her careful — a voice that small could be startled back into silence by anything too quick, too loud, too certain. One slow breath. Then another. Her body kept the time.

"Your mom was with you," she said. "Cleaning out the closet."

Her own voice had come down a notch. Not a whisper — she didn't mimic — but lower, meeting the volume where Jamie had set it, the way she'd dim a lamp rather than switch it off.

She noted the closet. Who had decided to clean it out, and when, and how long the backpack had been waiting in the back of it for someone to reach in. She set all of that on the shelf beside the shrug, beside the way Jamie had sat down. One thread at a time. The others would keep.

"Did she see it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez held Jamie's gaze through the five seconds. It was a different silence from the ones before it — those had been shared with the floor, with Jamie's hands, with the ficus in the corner. This one was shared with her. She kept her face as it was. She didn't nod. She didn't lean in. She let the look be a thing that could stand on its own.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

The pen stayed capped on the closed notepad.

"You looked at me when you said that." Plainly — the same voice she'd used for *you sat down differently today*. "First time today."

She let that sit too, but not as long.

"I'm not going to ask what it said." She said it the way she'd state a fact about the room. The clock had no second hand. The ficus was dying. This question was off the table. "That can stay between you and them."

The question about Jamie's mother stayed where she had set it. She didn't go back for it.

A breath. Another.

"Did you finish it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "No. I couldn't." *My voice cracks a little.* "My mom took it from me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez heard the crack and gave it room. Five seconds — one breath, then another — and she let them run longer than that. On the wall, the clock's hands moved the way they always did, too slowly to be seen moving. She had long ago stopped filling silences just because they were there.

"Your mom took it from you," she said.

She left the word exactly where Jamie had set it. *Took.* She didn't round it off into *has it*, or *put it somewhere safe.* People chose their words before they knew they were choosing. It was not her job to edit.

"You couldn't finish it." Not a question. She laid the two facts side by side in the space between the chairs, in the order Jamie had handed them over — *I couldn't*, and then, *she took it from me.* She didn't say which one weighed more. That wasn't hers to weigh.

Her hands stayed folded. The pen stayed capped on the closed notepad. Nothing about this would be written down.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"Do you know where it is now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head again.* "She said she put it somewhere safe. So I wouldn't read it again."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez gave it the five seconds, and then five more. One breath, then another. Somewhere below the window, a bus pulled away from the curb, and the room took the sound in and gave back quiet.

"Somewhere safe," she said. "So you wouldn't read it again."

She set the words down between the chairs, one at a time, the way Jamie had handed them to her. Then she reached back — not far — and laid two other words beside them.

"You told me you *couldn't* finish it. She said so you *wouldn't* read it again." A pause, no longer than a breath. "Couldn't. And wouldn't."

She didn't say what the difference was, or whether there was one. That wasn't hers to name. The two words could sit next to each other on their own; they didn't need her to introduce them.

The pen stayed capped on the closed notepad. Her hands stayed folded in her lap. The clock on the wall moved the way it always did, too slowly to be seen.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"Do you want to finish it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I hesitate.* "I don't know." *I rub my hands together.* "I... I think so? But I don't know if I *can*."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the five seconds run. Jamie's hands were working at each other, and she watched them the way she'd watched the shrug earlier — noted, and left alone. One breath. Another. The light through the blinds had shifted since the start of the hour; the bright stripe on the carpet had crept an inch closer to the door.

"I think so," she said. "And — I don't know if I can."

She set the two sentences down side by side, in the order they'd come. She kept the question mark on the first one. A want with a question mark on it was still a want.

"They can both sit here," she said. "Thinking so. And not knowing. One doesn't cancel the other."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap. On the wall, the clock moved the way it always did, too slowly to be seen.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"What do you think would happen? If you read to the end."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up at the clock, then back at Dr. Vasquez.* "I don't know. What if it's... bad? What if they were mad at me?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez gave the questions their five seconds. Jamie had looked at the clock first — the one that couldn't tell anyone the exact time, only the shape of it — and then at her. She noted the glance and set it on the shelf beside the shrug, beside the way Jamie had sat down. One breath. Another. On the carpet, the bright stripe of light had reached the leg of Jamie's chair.

"What if it's bad," she said. "What if they were mad at me."

She set the two questions down between the chairs, in the order they'd come, question marks still on them. The pen stayed capped. The notepad stayed closed.

She didn't answer them. They hadn't really been asked *of* her — they had been asked at the room, the way a person presses one foot on ice before trusting it.

"They didn't sound like new questions," she said. Plainly. The way she'd say *it's raining*.

She let that sit. She didn't say where old questions came from, or how long this one might have been waiting for Jamie to find it. That wasn't hers to name.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"Mad at you for what?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, looking away again.* "For... for not being there."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez gave it the five seconds, and then gave it more. The words had come out with a pause in the middle of them, and she kept the pause too — *for... for not being there* — the whole shape of it, not just the words. One breath. Another. On the carpet, the stripe of light had climbed the leg of Jamie's chair and stopped there, the way light does, without deciding anything.

"For not being there," she said.

She set it down between the chairs. It was heavier than the other things she'd set down that hour — or it set down heavier; she had never been able to tell the difference. She didn't lighten it. She didn't say *you couldn't have known*, or *it wasn't your fault*, or any of the other things people said to take guilt out of a person's hands before the person was done holding it.

The bitten lip, the looking away — she filed those on the shelf beside the shrug, beside the glance at the clock. Jamie had answered the question and then gone somewhere else with it. She let them go. She would still be here when they came back.

The pen stayed capped. The notepad stayed closed. On the wall, the clock moved the way it always did, too slowly to be seen.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"Not being where?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *My voice is barely a whisper, almost choked.* "At the hospital. When... when it happened."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez gave it the five seconds, and then more after that. The words had come out of Jamie in pieces — *at the hospital*, and then the crack, and then *when... when it happened* — and she received them the way they'd come, in pieces, without asking them to be whole. One breath. Another. She didn't move. She had learned a long time ago that staying still was its own kind of answer.

"At the hospital," she said. "When it happened."

Her voice had come down to meet the whisper. Not a whisper itself — she didn't mimic — but low, set at the volume Jamie had chosen.

She kept Jamie's word for it. *When it happened.* Jamie had carried the sentence all the way to the edge of the other word and set it down there, and she didn't pick it up and hand it back. Some words waited years to be said out loud. The clock on the wall didn't hurry, and neither did she.

On the carpet, the stripe of light had climbed off the leg of Jamie's chair and gone on toward the door. The pen stayed capped. The notepad stayed closed. Nothing about this would be written down.

A breath. Another.

Then, small and plain, the foothold:

"Where were you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I was at work." *I manage to get out, my voice still small and broken.* "They told me not to come."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her pen still. She let the silence stretch, counting the quiet moments in her head until five full seconds had passed. The air in the room held the weight of the words.

"You found their journal," she said, her voice level and quiet. She tilted her head slightly, her eyes steady. "And you sat with it here before saying anything else. What was it like, opening it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I finally look at her, a little shaky.* "I haven't opened it yet." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "I can't."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez remained still in her chair. She counted five silent seconds, allowing the whisper to settle into the quiet room. Her hands stayed folded loosely over her notepad, her posture open but unmoving.

"You found the journal," she said, her voice even and low. "But you haven't opened it. You can't." She met Jamie's gaze without pressing, letting the reflection hang between them. "When you say you can't, what is stopping you from turning the cover?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her shoulders relaxed, her pen resting untouched against the blank page. She watched the words catch and dissolve, then let the silence expand. She counted five full seconds in her head, allowing the unfinished sentence to hang in the air without rushing to fill it.

"You stopped mid-sentence," she said, her voice calm and even. "You couldn't finish it." She held Jamie's gaze, steady and unhurried. "When the words leave you like that, what do you notice taking their place?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I... I just keep seeing their face. How they looked that morning." *I finally blurt out, my voice cracking a little.* "Like nothing was wrong."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her hands resting lightly on her notepad. She let the crack in the voice settle into the room, counting five full seconds in her head before she spoke. Her posture remained still, her expression steady.

"You keep seeing their face," she said, her tone even and quiet. "How they looked that morning. Like nothing was wrong." She allowed the silence to hold the words, then asked, "When that image arrives, what does it ask of you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her hands resting lightly on her notepad. She let the admission settle into the room, counting five full seconds in her head before she spoke. Her posture remained still, her expression steady.

"They wrote about you," she said, her tone even and quiet. "In the last entry." She allowed the silence to hold the weight of what was left unsaid. "You're looking at me, but the words themselves haven't left you." She met Jamie's gaze, unhurried. "What is it about that entry that stays on your tongue?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, looking down at my hands again.* "I can't say it. Not yet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
