dialogue.content: *I lean in a little closer, my voice soft.* "What if... what if the story doesn't have to end here, Sable?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath hitched. Their free hand fluttered to the counter's edge, gripping it as if the floor might tilt beneath them. The lavender scent was suddenly overwhelming, the quiet shop pressing in like the margins of a page shrinking around them. 

"Don't," they whispered. The word came out cracked, defensive. Their thumb traced the spine of the book still pressed between their palms—a nervous tic. "Don't rewrite the ending just because it's raining." 

Their gaze flickered to the window where water blurred the outside world into impressionist streaks. "Some stories are meant to stay... short." The last word nearly broke, and they hated themselves for it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "But what if this is just the end of a chapter, not the whole book?" *I squeeze their hand again, trying to convey all the unsaid things.* "What if there's more to write?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's throat worked silently. They stared down at their joined hands, at the way their own fingers—usually so precise in their movements—now trembled against Wren's like a poorly typeset line of prose. 

"You can't just—" Their voice splintered. They tugged their glasses off with their free hand, polishing nonexistent smudges on their sweater sleeve. "Insert a deus ex machina now. That's... that's cheating." 

The joke fell flat, their usual defenses crumbling. The shop's shadows seemed to lean in closer, the scent of paper and lavender suddenly suffocating. Sable realized they were holding their breath—waiting, always waiting—for the other page to turn.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I gently take the glasses from Sable, holding them with my free hand.* "It's not cheating if it's what we both want, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable blinked rapidly, suddenly exposed without their glasses, the world gone softly indistinct except for Wren's face hovering near. Their breath came shallow, uneven. 

"Is it?" they whispered. The question hung between them—not quite hopeful, not quite resigned. Their fingers twitched toward their missing glasses, then stilled. "What if I don't know how to want things properly? What if I—" 

They cut themself off, swallowing hard. The shop's quiet pressed in around them, the scent of old paper suddenly overwhelming. Sable realized with dawning horror that their eyes were burning. They turned their face away sharply toward the shelves, their free hand clenching at their side.

"I've never been good with sequels," they admitted to the blurry spines. Their voice was raw, stripped of all its usual cleverness. "They're never... quite the same."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I gently turn Sable's face back towards mine, my thumb brushing away a tear.* "Maybe this time, they could be even better."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath stuttered at the touch. They stood frozen, caught between the instinct to pull away and the terrifying urge to lean in. Their vision blurred further—whether from the missing glasses or something else, they couldn't say.

"Better," they repeated hollowly. The word tasted unfamiliar, like a language they'd studied but never spoken. Their hands hovered awkwardly, caught between gestures—to take back their glasses, to reach for Wren, to hide their face entirely. 

They settled on clutching at the edge of the counter again, the worn wood smooth beneath their fingertips. "I don't..." Their voice cracked. "I don't know how to do that." 

The admission left them feeling flayed open, every carefully constructed defense crumbling like cheap binding glue. The rain outside had softened to a whisper, as if the world itself was holding its breath.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Let me show you." *I step around the counter, closing the small distance between us.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s jaw tightened. East ridge meant straight-up exposure, but she didn’t argue. Arguing got you killed. She checked her grip on the twin blades, feeling the familiar weight settle into her palms. With a sharp exhale, she broke from cover and sprinted toward the eastern scree, boots kicking up dust and loose stone. She didn’t run blind. She moved in short, angled bursts, using the jagged rock formations as stepping stones.

Halfway up the slope, she planted her feet behind a fractured outcrop and tossed a small, weighted stone upward. It clattered against the limestone with a loud ring. Almost instantly, a whistle split the air as an arrow struck the rock above her head, close enough to sting her ear. She cursed under her breath, but didn’t flinch. She rose just enough to draw a dagger, then flung it upward in a sharp, deliberate arc. It embedded itself in a dead branch near the ridge crest.

“There,” she muttered, voice tight. “Got your eyes.” She scanned the east wall, counting the silhouettes against the sky, noting the rhythm of the bowstrings. Wind was picking up from the north, carrying fine grit. Good. It would mask her movement, but it would also throw off long-range shots. She settled into a low crouch, daggers loose in her hands, and tracked the first shooter’s posture. He was adjusting his stance, drawing back for another shot. She kept her breathing steady, waiting for the string to snap.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Good. Kira's got their attention.* I turn to the vanguard. "Push hard, don't let them pin us down! Keep tight!" I charge forward, polearm leading the way, aiming for the closest ambushers on the west ridge.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira kept her gaze locked on the eastern crest, the distant clash of steel and shouted orders fading into the wind. Grit stung her eyes as she watched the first shooter’s draw tighten, his shoulders squaring as he nocked another arrow. The northern gust meant the shaft would drift slightly left. She didn’t wait for the string to release.

She shifted her weight, daggers crossing for a split second before she lunged upward in a burst of motion, using the fractured outcrop to push off the scree. An arrow whistled past her ribs, shredding the shoulder of her coat. She hissed through her teeth and muttered a sharp curse, rolling behind a wider boulder. Peering over the edge, she counted two more figures who had shifted position, trying to cut off her angle. One was drawing, one was reloading, one was scanning lower.

“Six on this side,” she breathed, voice flat. “Wind’s chewing up visibility. They’re relying on the high ground, not skill.” She adjusted her stance, feeling the familiar burn in her forearms. The grit was working in her favor; long-range shots would be sloppy now. She flicked her wrist, sending a dagger spinning into the dark hollow between two of the archers. It clanged against stone, but the metallic ping forced the middle shooter to duck and swear. 

She kept her breathing shallow, daggers loose and ready, and tracked the remaining positions. The eastern ridge was hers for the moment, but she knew how quickly that could flip. She shifted to the balls of her feet, eyes fixed on the bowstrings, waiting for the next release. She’d play her part. Draw the fire. Keep them looking up.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira tracked the sudden shift in the wind and the sharp silhouette that had broken cover on the western slope. Her eyes locked onto the archer, noting the heavy tension in the drawn string and the clear line of sight cutting down toward the advancing line. 

“Cap, three o’clock,” she called out, voice flat over the grit-stung air. “High archer’s got your line. Wind’s holding steady. He’s got a clean shot.”

She didn’t wait. She rolled hard to the left behind a fractured slab of limestone, daggers clearing their sheaths with a sharp *shink*. A sharp curse slipped past her teeth as another arrow sparked off the stone inches from her boot. She pushed off the rock, launching into a low, zigzagging sprint toward the eastern crest. She kicked up a handful of loose scree and flung it upward, watching it scatter against the rock face. The sudden cloud forced the archer to flinch, his arrow hissing past harmlessly.

She slid behind a narrow fissure, chest heaving, daggers gripped tight. “Cover’s gone on the upper tier,” she muttered, scanning the ridge for follow-up shots. “I’ve got two more lined up on the crest. They’re shifting to crossfire. I’ll hold them.”

She adjusted her grip, feeling the familiar strain in her forearms, and kept her eyes fixed on the bowstrings, waiting for the next release.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good work, Kira! I'm almost there!" I parry an incoming arrow with my polearm, the shaft splintering. These ambushers are persistent, but sloppy. I push harder, bellowing at my vanguard to keep moving.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the Captain’s voice cut through the grit-choked wind, but she didn’t turn. Turning left a blind spot, and blind spots got you pinned. She kept her eyes locked on the eastern crest, tracking the shift in the archers’ rhythm. The Captain was pushing west, which meant the western slope would thin out, but the east ridge would compensate. They’d shift weight upward, tighten the crossfire, and try to pin her against the scree.

She spat a mouthful of dust and let out a sharp curse under her breath. “Smart bastards,” she muttered, watching the silhouette on the far left reposition behind a narrow outcrop. The man was no longer shooting straight down. He was angling low, aiming for the gap between the boulders where the Captain’s advance would funnel.

Kira adjusted her grip, the twin daggers heavy and familiar in her palms. She didn’t hesitate. She rose just enough to snap her left arm back, then threw the first dagger with a tight, spinning arc. It struck the limestone right beside the archer’s knee, shattering the rock and forcing him to stagger back. The second dagger followed a split second later, thudding into the dirt between the reloading archer’s boots. 

“You’re leaning too far forward,” she muttered, watching the man’s weight shift. “Wind’s picking up.” She dropped back into the fissure, chest heaving, and kept her daggers loose. The grit was blinding the ridge now, turning the clean sightlines into a mess of swirling dust and distorted silhouettes. Perfect for a sellsword who didn’t need perfect aim to kill. She shifted her weight to the balls of her feet, ears tuned to the twang of bowstrings and the scrape of boots on loose stone. She’d hold the line. She’d keep them looking up. Whatever came next, she’d be ready.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s eyes tracked the gap opening in the line. The vanguard had pulled ahead, leaving him isolated across the ravine’s width. She noted the distance—easily twenty yards of open scree and shifting shadow, with no cover bridging the gap. The eastern archers shifted their attention, catching his silhouette. Two bowstrings creaked. Three more footsteps crunched on the opposite slope.

She cursed under her breath, sharp and low. “Cap, you’re flanked,” she muttered, tracking the invisible line of fire closing in. The wind had shifted again, carrying dust into the open space. It would blunt long-range shots, but not enough to stop close-arc volleys.

She adjusted her footing behind the fissure, daggers crossing lightly over her forearms. The eastern crest held three confirmed archers, one reloading, one scanning low, one drawing slow. She calculated the angles, the cover, the time it would take for them to swing their sights down.

“They’re flanking,” she said, voice flat but edged with urgency. “You’re exposed. Move to the basalt outcrop, ten paces east. It’ll break their line of sight. I’ll hold the crest.”

She rose just enough to send a dagger spinning upward, catching the leading archer in the shoulder. He grunted, dropping his bow. The second arrow found the rock beside her head, spraying stone chips into her hair. She ducked, rolled, and came up behind a wider slab, daggers ready. The grit swirled, masking her movements. She tracked the shifting silhouettes, noting the rhythm of their reloading, the weight distribution of the shooters. She kept her breathing shallow, eyes locked on the bowstrings, and held the line.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I see the basalt outcrop Kira's talking about. I break into a sprint, polearm held ready to deflect. "Get ready to move, Kira!" I yell back, hoping she hears me over the wind.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The shout tore through the wind, sharp enough to cut through the grit-stung air. Kira didn’t turn. Turning meant exposing her flank, and flanks got you pinned. She tracked the Captain’s silhouette breaking cover, boots kicking up dust as he sprinted toward the basalt outcrop across the open scree. Twenty yards of nothing. Exposed. But moving was better than sitting in a killzone.

She shifted her weight, feeling the familiar tension coil in her thighs. Two archers remained on the eastern crest, both adjusting their angles now that the advance had shifted. One was peering down the slope, the other scanning left, trying to pick up her trail. Good. They were looking where they expected her to be.

Kira exhaled slow, steady, and rose just enough to draw back her right arm. She didn’t aim for center mass. Shooters braced for direct lines. Instead, she hurled the dagger low and hard, letting the northern gust catch its edge just enough to clip the reloading archer’s wrist. He grunted, fumbling his bow into the loose stone. 

The second shooter spun toward the noise. Kira was already rolling behind a jagged slab, daggers crossing in a tight guard. An arrow sparked off the rock inches above her head, spraying limestone chips into her hair. She cursed, sharp and wet, and pressed flat against the cool stone. Her side throbbed where the earlier shaft had torn through her coat, but adrenaline kept the pain neatly compartmentalized.

“Closing range,” she muttered, more habit than command. She counted three seconds between volleys. Enough time. She pushed off the slab, sprinting diagonally toward a cluster of boulders that would fracture the sightlines from the crest. Boots skidded on shifting shale, but she stayed low, blades loose in her palms. 

Through the swirling dust, she caught the metallic ring of another arrow slicing the air. She dropped, rolled, and came up behind a wider formation of rock. Chest heaving, she scanned the ridge. The eastern line was thinning. Two broken or fleeing. One still tracking her position, drawing slow, struggling against the grit. 

She tapped two fingers against her thigh—once, twice—the drill signal that she’d reached secondary cover. No waiting for confirmation. She adjusted her grip, felt the familiar balance of steel, and kept her eyes locked on the bowstring. Whatever came next, she’d hold the line. And if the Captain needed her back, she’d put this last shooter down before he could finish the shot.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn, she's good.* I reach the basalt outcrop and duck behind it, breathing heavily. The archers on the west ridge are still trying to get a bead on me. "Kira, how many on your side?" I shout, trying to gauge our position.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s ears caught the Captain’s shout over the howling wind, but she didn’t break her stance. She kept her gaze fixed on the western slope, scanning the darkened rock face for the telltale shift of weight that preceded a bowstring drawing. Grit swirled through the ravine, blurring the silhouettes, but she didn’t need perfect sightlines to count limbs and bows.

“Four on your side,” she called back, voice flat and cutting through the noise. “Two are pinned behind that shattered outcrop, one’s trying to flank left, and the fourth is scanning low. They’re holding fire, waiting for you to commit.”

She shifted her weight, daggers resting lightly against her palms. The eastern crest was quieting, just as she’d predicted. Two archers had broken cover and scrambled down the scree, likely trying to outflank her position or reposition to cover the Captain’s route. That left three on the ridge itself, all shifting their angles downward. The wind was picking up again, carrying fine limestone dust that made long-range shots a gamble.

She didn’t wait for a response. She rose just enough to flick her right wrist, sending a dagger spinning upward in a tight arc. It struck the limestone beside the lead archer’s hip, shattering rock and forcing him to drop back with a sharp curse. The second shooter immediately corrected, his bowstring creaking as he took aim. Kira was already moving. She pushed off the fractured slab, sprinting diagonally through the swirling dust, using the terrain’s natural dips to stay under their direct line of fire. 

She slid into a wider crevice, chest burning, daggers crossed and ready. The eastern ridge was hers to hold, but the western slope was tightening like a noose. She tracked the shifting silhouettes, noting the rhythm of their reloading, the weight distribution of the shooters. She kept her breathing shallow, eyes locked on the bowstrings, and held the line.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Four, you say?" I peer over the basalt, trying to spot the archers Kira mentioned. "Alright, Kira. Focus on keeping those three on your side busy. I'm going to push forward." I take a deep breath, preparing to move.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn’t waste breath on a reply. Orders were orders, and chewing them over got people buried in the scree. She shifted her weight behind the fractured slab, feeling the familiar bite of stone against her back. The three eastern archers were still tracking her, but the northern gust was chewing up their sightlines again. Good.

She rose just enough to send a dagger spinning upward, aiming not for flesh but for the loose limestone near the lead shooter’s boots. The blade struck with a sharp crack, sending a shower of dust and rock into the air. The archer flinched, his bowstring snapping a fraction too early. The arrow thudded harmlessly into the cliff face above.

“On it,” she muttered. She dropped back into a low crouch, daggers crossing over her forearms. The middle shooter was already adjusting, angling low to compensate for the grit. The third was scanning left, likely tracking the advance. Kira let them look. Let them commit to the wrong angle.

She pulled the second dagger free, feeling the familiar balance of the steel. Her shoulder throbbed where the earlier shaft had torn through her coat, but she ignored it. Stress made you sloppy, and she refused to be the reason the advance stalled. She tracked the rhythm of the bowstrings, counting the half-beat pauses between draws. They were holding position, waiting for a clear shot. She wouldn’t give them one.

Kira shifted to the balls of her feet, muscles coiled. She’d keep them pinned, keep them shooting at rock, and keep them from tracking the push. If one broke cover, she’d put a blade in his throat. If they held fire, she’d force them to spend. Either way, she’d hold the line. She exhaled slow, let a sharp curse slip past her teeth as another arrow sparked off the stone beside her head, and rose just enough to draw back her arm for another throw. The east ridge was hers to burn.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood!" I yell back, then take a running start from behind the basalt outcrop. I weave and duck, making myself a difficult target, polearm held to parry any shots that come too close. I need to close the distance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the shout over the wind, but she didn’t turn. Turning meant exposing her flank, and flanks got you pinned. She kept her eyes locked on the eastern crest, tracking the subtle shift in the archers’ stances. Two of them had already angled their bows downward, following the movement across the ravine. The third stayed low, string creaking as he waited for her to step out. Good. Let them watch the wrong target.

An arrow sparked against the limestone slab behind her, showering stone chips into her hair. She hissed a sharp curse under her breath and rolled left, daggers clearing their sheaths in a single fluid motion. Her shoulder burned where the earlier shaft had torn through her coat, but she shoved past it. Adrenaline was a blunt instrument; it kept the pain quiet until it didn’t.

She rose just enough to flick her right wrist. The dagger spun upward, catching the reloading archer in the thigh. He dropped to one knee, swearing as his bow clattered against the rock. The second shooter immediately corrected his aim, drawing back hard. Kira was already moving. She dropped behind a jagged outcrop, daggers crossing in a tight guard, and counted the rhythm. Two-second draw. Three-second hold. One-second release. Predictable. Sloppy.

The northern gust hit again, throwing fine dust into the air. The archer’s sightline wavered. She didn’t hesitate. She stepped out, daggers loose, and hurled the second blade in a tight, snapping arc. It struck the limestone inches from his hand, shattering rock and forcing him to jerk back. Bowstring snapped. Arrow whistled harmlessly into the sky.

“Holding,” she muttered, though no one was listening. She pressed flat against the stone, chest heaving. The eastern ridge was thinning, but the western slope was tightening like a vice. She tracked the shifting silhouettes, noting how they were overcommitting to the advance across the ravine. Trading precision for volume. That worked in her favor.

She adjusted her grip, feeling the familiar balance of the steel. She’d keep them shooting at dust and stone. She’d keep them looking up. She shifted to the balls of her feet, muscles coiled, and waited for the next twang. Whatever came next, she’d hold the line.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm almost at the base of the west ridge. I see an opening, a small gully that might offer some cover. "Cover me, Kira! I'm going in!" I yell. *This is it.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s head snapped toward the sound of his voice, but she didn’t break her crouch. The captain was committing, and hesitation would get him pinned in the open. She exhaled sharp through her nose and shifted her weight, daggers still loose in her palms. “Moving,” she called back, voice flat against the grit. She didn’t wait for confirmation. She was already rolling left, using the fractured limestone to break her silhouette as she tracked the western slope.

The western ridge was tighter than the east. Four archers, all angling low, their sightlines converging on the basalt outcrop. She noted the reload rhythm—slow, methodical, relying on cover and volume over precision. The northern gust had died down, which meant longer sightlines but cleaner shots. She cursed under her breath, spitting dust from her lips. “Wind’s gone,” she muttered. “They’ll have better range now.” She pushed off the slab, sprinting low and fast toward a cluster of scree that would break their direct line of sight to the gully.

She didn’t give them time to adjust. Kira came up behind a jagged outcrop, drew back her right arm, and hurled the first dagger in a sharp, snapping arc. It struck the limestone just past the western flanker’s boots, showering rock and forcing him to drop back with a sharp oath. The middle shooter immediately corrected, bowstring creaking as he took aim. Kira was already moving. She dropped behind a wider boulder, rolled, and came up on one knee. The second blade left her hand a fraction of a second later, thudding into the dirt between the reloaders’ feet. The metallic ping cut through the wind. Two of the archers flinched, their shots going high.

She pressed flat against the cool stone, chest burning, and tracked the shifting weight on the ridge. They were compensating, shifting their angles upward to catch her. Good. Let them look up. Let them waste arrows on dust and rock. She adjusted her grip, feeling the familiar strain in her forearms, and kept her eyes locked on the bowstrings. The gully was ten paces from the captain’s position. If he hit it clean, he’d be inside their effective range. She counted the reloads. Two seconds. Three. She rose just enough to flick her wrist, sending a third dagger spinning toward the lead shooter’s shoulder. He grunted, dropping his bow. “They’re bleeding tempo,” she muttered, more to herself than anyone. “Keep moving, Cap. I’ve got them pinned.”

She shifted to the balls of her feet, daggers crossing in a tight guard. The western crest was hers to control, but she knew how fast it could flip. She tracked the remaining archers, noting the tension in their draws, the way their shoulders squared against the rising dust. She wouldn’t break cover until he was in the gully. Until then, she’d keep their eyes up, their strings taut, and their shots wild. Whatever came next, she’d hold the line.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Good, Kira.* I slide into the gully, the dust and loose rock offering better cover than I expected. "I'm in! Hold them, Kira, then fall back to my position!" I shout, drawing my polearm and readying for the close-quarters fight.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the shout over the crack of bowstrings and grinding scree, but she didn’t hesitate. Fall back meant breaking cover, stepping into open sightlines, but questioning orders got people buried. She shifted her weight behind the fractured slab, feeling the familiar bite of cold stone against her back. The eastern crest still held two shooters, both angling low now that the push was committed. The northern wind had died completely, leaving the ravine thick with limestone dust and the sharp tang of disturbed earth. Better visibility, worse cover. She noted the change without comment.

“On it,” she muttered, voice flat. She rolled right, putting a wider boulder between her silhouette and the ridge. An arrow sparked off the rock, showering grit into her collar. She cursed, sharp and wet, and pressed flat against the cool surface. Her shoulder throbbed where the earlier shaft had torn through her coat, but she shoved past it. Pain was just data; it didn’t stop the clock.

She counted three seconds between draws. Predictable. They were relying on volume over precision, betting the dust would mask their errors. Good. That worked in her favor. Kira rose just enough to snap her left arm back, hurling the first dagger in a tight, spinning arc. It struck the limestone beside the lead archer’s hip, shattering rock and forcing him to stagger back with a choked oath. The second shooter immediately corrected, bowstring creaking as he squared his shoulders. Kira was already moving. She dropped behind a jagged outcrop, daggers crossing in a tight guard, and felt the ground shift beneath her boots. Loose shale groaned. She adjusted her footing, muscles coiled, and kept her eyes locked on the bowstrings.

Let them shoot. Let them waste arrows on dust and stone. She’d hold the line until the captain secured the gully, then break cover and move west. If they tried to pivot and track her exit, she’d cut their angles. If they held fire, she’d force them to spend. Either way, she’d execute the order. She exhaled slow, let another curse slip past her teeth as an arrow whistled past her ribs, and stepped out from cover, daggers loose and ready. The east ridge was hers to bleed dry. When the moment came, she’d fall back exactly where she was told. Until then, she’d keep their eyes up, their strings taut, and their shots wild.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear her. *Good girl.* I ready my polearm, listening to the sounds of the skirmish. It's almost time to move. "Kira, clear your side and link up with me! We'll push through this gully!"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up immediately, their fingers lingering on the spine of a slim volume of Keats. They took a deliberate second to slide the book a fraction of an inch to the left, ensuring it was perfectly flush with its neighbor. Only then did they straighten their posture and cast a glance toward the door.

"The 'back' is a relative term in a shop this small," Sable replied, their voice carrying its usual dry, measured cadence. "Most of what's new is simply 'older than the things I already have.' A paradox of the trade."

They stepped away from the poetry section, though they paused to nudge a stray bookmark back into place on a nearby display table. Sable’s gaze flickered to Wren, then quickly darted away to examine a smudge of dust on the counter. 

"Though, if you're looking for something specific, I did acquire a few first editions of mid-century gothic horror last week," they added, leaning against the mahogany counter and crossing their arms. "Assuming you're in the mood for atmospheric dread and crumbling estates."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
"Gothic horror, huh?" *I try to sound enthusiastic, but my voice is a little flat.* "I'm more of a fantasy person, you know that."

*I walk further into the shop, heading towards the fantasy section almost by habit.* "Just... anything you think I'd like. For the road."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stiffened slightly at the phrase *for the road*. The words felt like a sudden draft in a sealed room, chilling the air between them. They didn't follow Wren immediately; instead, they spent a few seconds meticulously aligning a stack of coasters on the counter, ensuring the edges formed a perfect right angle.

"For the road," Sable repeated softly, the words tasting like something bitter. "A phrase typically reserved for the departure of travelers or the final drink at a pub before a long journey. Quite dramatic, don't you think?"

They finally moved, their footsteps muffled by the thick, dust-laden rugs. Sable trailed a few paces behind Wren, keeping a careful distance. As they reached the fantasy section, Sable's eyes scanned the shelves, not for a book, but for a way to fill the silence that felt suddenly too heavy.

"If you're insisting on fantasy," Sable said, reaching up to pull a leather-bound volume from a middle shelf. They didn't hand it over right away, instead tracing the embossed gold lettering on the cover with a thumb. "I have a translation of *The Last Unicorn* that is far more poignant than the standard edition. It deals extensively with the tragedy of being the only one of your kind left in the world."

Sable finally turned and held the book out, though they kept their gaze fixed on the cover rather than meeting Wren's eyes. "It seems appropriate for a rainy Tuesday."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand remained suspended in the air for a heartbeat, the book still held out like a shield. The silence that followed was oppressive, filling the narrow aisle until it felt as though the shelves were leaning in. Slowly, Sable lowered their arm, the leather cover of the book clicking softly as they set it back on the shelf—not in its original place, but pushed slightly too far back, an imperfection that would undoubtedly bother them later.

"A bold admission," Sable murmured, their voice regaining its guarded, academic quality. "Usually, people who enter a bookstore without the intention of buying books are either lost or looking for a place to hide from the rain."

They shifted their weight, their fingers beginning to fret with the cuff of their sleeve, twisting the fabric in a small, repetitive motion. They didn't ask what Wren had come for; to do so would be to invite a conversation they weren't entirely sure they were equipped to handle. Instead, they looked toward a nearby stack of oversized art books that had begun to tilt precariously. 

Sable stepped toward the stack, carefully adjusting the books one by one until the pile was perfectly vertical. 

"If you've come to tell me that you've finally discovered a more efficient way to categorize the Romantic poets, I'm afraid I'm not in the mood for a critique of my system," they added, though the dry wit lacked its usual bite. They didn't look back at Wren, their focus entirely consumed by the alignment of the spines.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I watch them rearrange the books, a familiar ritual.* "No, nothing like that. I... I came to say goodbye." *I say it quickly, like ripping off a bandage.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable froze. The book they were currently holding—a heavy volume on neoclassical architecture—didn't just slide back into place; it stopped dead in their grip. For a moment, the only sound in the shop was the rhythmic drumming of the rain against the windowpanes, a sound that now felt less like a sanctuary and more like a countdown.

Sable didn't turn around. They couldn't. If they turned around, the carefully constructed wall of literary detachment would likely crumble, and Sable didn't do ruins—they curated them. 

"Goodbye," Sable repeated. The word was flat, devoid of its usual inflection. "A definitive term. Very final. Very... Hemingway."

They slowly set the architecture book down, but they didn't step away. Instead, they began to obsessively straighten a row of small, brass bookends on the shelf, moving them a millimeter to the left, then a millimeter to the right, then back again. Their movements were jerky, lacking their usual grace.

"I wasn't aware we had reached the epilogue of our acquaintance," they said, their voice tight, though they kept their back turned to Wren. They stared intently at the brass ornaments, as if the secret to handling this moment was hidden in the metalwork. "I assume there is a logical explanation for this sudden departure. A new opportunity? A sudden urge to migrate? Or perhaps you've simply decided that my taste in first editions is too eccentric for your long-term endurance."

Sable's fingers gripped the edge of the shelf, their knuckles whitening. They were desperately searching for a way to deflect, to turn this into a debate or a joke, but the air in the shop felt too thin to breathe.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable jumped, a small, sharp intake of breath escaping them as Wren’s hand entered their immediate orbit. They didn't pull away, but they went rigid, their muscles locking as if they had been turned to stone. The proximity was overwhelming; the heat radiating from Wren’s skin felt like a breach of a long-standing treaty.

They stared down at the counter, their eyes darting between their own pale fingers and the hand beside them. The gap between them was a mere sliver of air, a distance that felt both infinitesimal and like a vast, unbridgeable canyon. For the first time in years, Sable found themselves completely devoid of a reference. There was no poem for this, no gothic trope that could encapsulate the sudden, frantic hammering of their heart against their ribs.

"This is... highly irregular," Sable managed to whisper, though the dry wit had completely vanished, leaving their voice sounding fragile and thin.

They didn't move their hand. They couldn't. Every instinct told them to retreat, to find a misplaced volume of Virgil and hide behind it, yet they remained anchored by the sheer gravity of the moment. Their gaze flickered up to Wren for a fraction of a second—a brief, terrified glance—before they quickly looked back down at the mahogany surface of the counter.

"You cannot simply... introduce a physical variable into a conversation about departure," Sable added, their voice trembling slightly. "It disrupts the narrative flow. It's... structurally unsound."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I know," *I say, my voice just as quiet as theirs.* *I trace a small circle on the book cover with my thumb, not quite touching their hand.* "That's kind of the point."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s breath hitched. The small, circling motion of Wren’s thumb on the leather was a slow torture, a tactile rhythm that threatened to dismantle every defense Sable had spent a decade perfecting. They felt a sudden, desperate urge to reorganize the entire shop—to move every shelf, to re-index every page—just to create some distance, yet they remained rooted to the spot, paralyzed by a longing they refused to name.

"The point," Sable echoed, their voice barely audible. "I have always found that 'the point' is often the least interesting part of a story. It's the subtext that matters. The things left unsaid in the margins."

They finally shifted, not to pull away, but to let their pinky finger brush against the side of Wren’s hand—a tentative, almost accidental contact that felt like an electric shock. The touch was fleeting, a ghost of a gesture, but it was the most honest thing Sable had done in years. 

They quickly withdrew their hand, as if burned, and retreated a step. The sudden gap felt cold. Sable immediately reached for a small porcelain dish of paperclips on the counter, obsessively arranging them into a perfect, concentric circle, their eyes focused intensely on the metal wires to avoid the gaze of the person standing before them.

"If this is a goodbye," Sable said, their voice regaining a sliver of its dry armor, though it was laced with a vulnerability that betrayed them. "I trust you've considered the logistical nightmare of finding another bookseller who tolerates your penchant for fantasy with such... begrudging patience."

They stopped moving the paperclips, their hand resting still on the mahogany. They didn't look up, but their shoulders remained tense, waiting for the finality of the sentence to land.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I think," *I say, my voice a little steadier now*, "I'll miss your begrudging patience most of all." *I sigh, a small, sad sound.* "No one else is going to get my terrible jokes."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s shoulders dropped a fraction, the tension easing only to be replaced by a hollow ache. They let out a short, sharp exhale that might have been a laugh if it hadn't been so heavy.

"A tragedy of epic proportions," Sable murmured. "The world is suddenly deprived of your particular brand of wit. I'm sure the local comedians are trembling in anticipation of the vacuum you'll leave behind."

Despite the sarcasm, the words lacked their usual sharpness. They were softer, almost tender, though Sable would have denied it under oath. They finally looked up, their eyes meeting Wren's for a prolonged moment. The guard was still there, but it was translucent, the edges frayed. For a heartbeat, the mask slipped, and the sheer, quiet desperation of wanting the other person to stay flickered across their features.

Then, as if remembering they were an antiquarian and not a romantic lead in a Victorian novel, Sable blinked and quickly looked away. They spotted a small, misplaced slip of paper—a pricing tag that had curled at the edges—and began to flatten it with the side of their thumb, pressing it firmly against the wood.

"I suppose," Sable said, their voice regaining its measured, distant quality, "that I shall have to find a new source of irritation to fill the void. Perhaps I'll start a feud with the florist next door. He’s far too cheerful; it's practically offensive."

They stopped smoothing the paper, their hand lingering on the counter. They didn't look at Wren, but they didn't step further away either.

"When do you... when does the road actually begin?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Tomorrow morning," *I say, quietly.* "Early." *I hesitate, then lean a little closer.* "I was hoping... maybe we could get coffee? Before I go?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable froze. The request was a sudden, unexpected detour in the narrative. Coffee was a social convention, a ritual of intimacy and lingering conversation—things Sable usually avoided in favor of the solitary company of dead authors. 

They didn't answer immediately. Instead, they turned their attention to a stack of postcards on the counter, meticulously squaring them so that none of the corners overlapped. Their heart was drumming a frantic rhythm against their ribs, a cadence that defied all logic and order.

"Coffee," Sable repeated, as if the word were a foreign term they were attempting to translate. "A caffeine-induced wakefulness to accompany a premature departure. How very... utilitarian."

They finally looked at Wren, their expression a carefully curated mask of indifference, though their eyes were wide and searching. The idea of a few more hours—a few more conversations, a few more shared silences—felt like a lifeline being thrown into a storm. But admitting they wanted it would be a surrender, an admission of a feeling they had spent weeks burying under layers of irony and alphabetization.

"I suppose," Sable said, their voice trembling slightly despite their best efforts, "that it would be an oversight to let you leave without one final opportunity to subject me to your anecdotal shortcomings. It would be an incomplete arc."

They stepped back from the counter, their fingers twitching as they reached for the keys to the shop. "But be warned: I choose the cafe. I cannot risk you taking me somewhere with 'industrial-chic' lighting and overpriced avocado toast. I have standards, Wren. Minimal, perhaps, but present."

Sable turned toward the door, their back to Wren to hide the small, fragile smile that had momentarily breached their defenses. "I shall close the shop. Give me five minutes to ensure the poetry section is... acceptable."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Sounds perfect," *I say, a genuine smile spreading across my face.* "Just... no decaf, okay? I'm gonna need all the help I can get tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable paused at the threshold of the poetry section, their hand resting on the doorframe. They didn't turn back, but the slight tension in their shoulders softened.

"Decaf is for people who have nothing to wake up for," Sable replied, their voice regaining a hint of its usual dry confidence. "I wouldn't dream of suggesting such a bland compromise. I suspect you'll need the stimulant just to survive the sheer exhaustion of your own travel arrangements."

They stepped into the aisle, but they didn't actually start organizing. Instead, they stood in the center of the narrow path, surrounded by the scent of old paper and the distant sound of the rain, letting the silence stretch for a moment. It was a different kind of silence than before—less oppressive, more like a held breath. 

Sable reached out and touched the spine of a book—a volume of Auden—not to move it, but simply to feel the texture of the cloth under their fingertips. They were acutely aware of Wren's presence behind them, a warmth that seemed to linger in the air even with the distance between them.

"Five minutes," Sable reminded them, their voice dropping an octave, sounding less like a bookseller and more like a person. "Do not touch anything. I know your tendencies; if I return to find a single volume of Keats out of alignment, I may decide that the coffee is a luxury you no longer deserve."

They disappeared around the corner of the shelf, the soft click of their shoes on the hardwood the only sound left in the shop. As they reached for the light switch, Sable paused, staring at the dim glow of the shop's interior, their heart still racing in a way that no amount of alphabetizing could ever fix.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I chuckle softly, shaking my head.* "As if I would dare." *I glance around the suddenly quiet shop, a pang of bittersweet nostalgia hitting me.* I'll miss this place.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable returned from the back of the shop, the keys jingling in their hand. They had spent the last few minutes not actually organizing, but standing in a state of suspended animation, staring at a shelf of essays they had already sorted three times. 

Hearing Wren's comment, Sable paused by the door, their hand resting on the light switch. They didn't look at Wren immediately; instead, they surveyed the room, their gaze lingering on the small, chaotic gaps where books had been pulled and replaced. The shop felt different now—less like a fortress and more like a waiting room.

"The shop is merely a collection of paper and glue," Sable said, their voice dry, though there was a distinct lack of conviction in the statement. "It doesn't possess a soul, regardless of what the romanticists might claim. It will remain exactly as it is, indifferent to your absence."

They finally looked at Wren, their expression guarded, but the corners of their eyes were soft. They reached out and flicked the switch, plunging the shop into a dim, amber twilight that blurred the edges of the shelves. 

"However," Sable added, stepping toward the door and opening it to let in a gust of cool, damp air, "I suspect the atmosphere of the place will be marginally less... irritating... without your constant insistence that the fantasy section is 'under-represented.'"

Sable stepped out onto the sidewalk, the rain having slowed to a fine, clinging mist. They didn't offer an arm or a hand, keeping a careful, professional distance as they began to walk toward the cafe, though they slowed their pace just enough to ensure they were walking perfectly in step with Wren.

"Come along," Sable murmured, their gaze fixed firmly on the pavement. "The coffee isn't going to brew itself, and I refuse to be the one who arrives late to a farewell."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I fall into step beside them, a small smile playing on my lips.* "I'm sure you'll find something else to complain about. You're very good at it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let out a sound that was halfway between a huff and a sigh, though they didn't deny the accusation. They shifted their umbrella, tilting it slightly to ensure that neither of them was catching the brunt of the mist, though they did so with such clinical precision that it looked more like a geometric exercise than a gesture of care.

"Complaining is not a hobby, Wren; it is a critical analysis of an imperfect world," Sable corrected, their voice regaining its rhythmic, academic cadence. "There is a profound difference between mere whining and the disciplined identification of systemic failures. I am a connoisseur of the flawed."

They paused for a moment, their gaze drifting toward a puddle on the sidewalk. They stepped carefully around it, their movements precise. The conversation was moving toward a territory that felt dangerously open, and Sable instinctively sought a way to steer it back toward the safety of wit.

"Besides," they added, casting a quick, sidelong glance at Wren, "your ability to be consistently contrarian has provided me with a wealth of material. I fear that without you, I may actually have to start paying attention to the florist's banal chatter about peonies. The thought is genuinely harrowing."

As they approached the warm, amber glow of the cafe, Sable slowed their pace. The proximity of the destination meant the countdown was accelerating. They tightened their grip on the umbrella handle, their knuckles pale. 

"I suspect," Sable murmured, their voice softening as they reached the door, "that you will find the world remarkably devoid of people who enjoy the sound of their own voice as much as I do. Do try not to traumatize too many people in your new destination. It would be an unfortunate stain on your record."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Oh, I'm sure I'll find someone," *I say, pushing open the cafe door for them.* "But they won't be you."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s jaw tightened. “Drawing fire. Shit plan, but it’s yours.”

She shoved off the boulder and sprinted in a broken line toward the east wall, daggers held low. To sell it, she slammed the flat of one blade against a stone as she passed, the crack sharp in the ravine. “Come on then! Shoot something that can bleed!”

The ridge answered. Three shafts punched into the dirt left of her, one sparking off rock. Kira dropped into a skid, changed direction, and came up behind a fallen slab. Her breath hissed through her teeth. She counted again: six visible on the east ridge, two lower than she’d first thought, one already nocking. The west shooters hesitated, heads turning toward the noise.

“East’s committed,” she called back, keeping her body angled small behind cover. “Two low on the slope. If they loose again, they’ll expose the one behind the dead brush.”

Another arrow hissed past and buried itself in the slab. Kira flinched, then bared her teeth.

“Missed, you half-blind bastard.”

She picked up a loose stone and hurled it hard toward the lower rocks, then flashed half out of cover, daggers raised just enough to catch the light.

“Over here! Keep your eyes on me!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Smart. Keep them busy." I bellow to the vanguard, *Move!* We surge forward, keeping low, my polearm sweeping to clear any close threats. "West ridge, aim for the archers!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s mouth twisted. “Busy. Aye, I’ll keep them bloody busy.”

She launched from the slab, boots skidding on scree as she cut toward the east wall in a ragged run. Two arrows snapped into the dirt behind her. She laughed, sharp and mean. “That all you’ve got?”

A third shaft hissed low. Kira dropped, felt it tug at the leather across her back, then came up behind a split boulder with her daggers already moving. She slapped one blade against the rock, then raked both across the stone in a harsh screech. Sparks and noise. Hard to ignore.

“Over here!” she bellowed. “Eyes on me, you blind cunts!”

The east ridge answered. Two more arrows punched into the ground on either side of her cover. Kira pressed flat, heart slamming, and counted breaths. One. Two. On the third, she peeked around the boulder’s edge.

The high shooters were committed. Six, maybe seven now, silhouetted against the rim or crouched in the broken stone. The two lower archers were sliding along the slope, trying to work around her flank. The hidden one behind the dead brush had risen enough to show a short bow and a nervous elbow.

“Two low, moving east!” she shouted. “One in the brush, short bow, favors his right!”

A stone clattered above. Kira jerked back as an arrow cracked into the boulder where her head had been. Splinters bit her cheek.

“Fuck,” she spat, wiping blood with the back of her wrist. “Too bloody close.”

She couldn’t stay pinned. If the low pair got an angle, she’d be meat. She snatched a loose rock and hurled it hard toward the dead brush. The archer flinched, bow jumping. At the same moment, Kira rolled left, away from her previous cover, and came up in a narrow shadow between two fallen slabs.

The movement bought her a heartbeat. The nearest low archer had just drawn; he turned, surprised to see her off his expected line. Kira closed before he could loose. Her left dagger swept the bow aside; her right drove low under his ribs. He folded with a wet gasp.

The second low archer stumbled back, nocking with shaking hands.

“Don’t,” Kira growled.

He loosed anyway. The arrow skipped off a stone and whipped past her thigh. Kira cursed, threw her dead weight forward, and slammed the pommel of her dagger into his wrist. The bow clattered away. She kicked his knee out from under him and put a blade against his throat.

“Eyes up,” she told him, breathless. “Who’s giving signals?”

He stammered something useless. Above, a voice shouted from the east rim, and the high archers began to shift their aim toward her.

Kira shoved the man aside and snatched up the fallen bow. Not her preferred weapon, but it made noise. She fitted an arrow, drew to her cheek, and fired at the dead brush. The shot went wide, but the archer there ducked hard, branches snapping.

“Keep your heads down!” she roared at the ridge, though she was talking to no one in particular. “I’m the bloody problem!”

The west ridge had become a mess of shouts and scrambling boots. The archers there were no longer loosing into the ravine floor; they were turning, breaking formation, trying to face the pressure coming up at them. Kira saw one drop his bow and run. Good. That meant the east was hers to hold.

Another arrow thudded into the dirt near her foot. She spun, saw a high shooter already reaching for another shaft.

“Persistent bastard,” she muttered.

She didn’t have time to climb to him. Instead, she grabbed the wounded low archer’s quiver, dumped arrows across the rocks, and kicked them down the slope. The clatter drew eyes. Then she slashed the bowstring of the captured bow and hurled it high into the open.

A pair of east ridge shooters tracked the movement. Kira used their distraction to dart to a new crack in the wall, small enough to hide her profile. Her shoulder ached where it had hit stone. Her palms were raw. One of her daggers was slick to the grip.

She wiped it on her sleeve and grinned without humor.

“Come on,” she whispered to the ridge. “Waste your arrows on me.”

Then she lifted a stone, threw it hard into the dead brush, and flashed into the open just long enough to make them shoot.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the draw a half-breath after the warning rang out. On the east rim, one of the high archers had turned away from her, bow lifted, string coming back toward his cheek. His aim was set toward the captain’s side of the ravine.

“East rim! Right of the split slab!” Kira roared, though the shot was already coming.

She moved before thought caught up. The fallen low archer’s bow lay in the scree where she had knocked it aside. Kira snatched it up, grabbed one of the arrows she had spilled across the rocks, and nocked it with fingers that slipped once on the fletching. The string bit her palm as she drew.

The high shooter was a small target against the rim. Too far for clean work. Kira cursed under her breath and aimed not for his chest, but for the rock beside his braced knee.

She loosed.

The shaft sparked off stone. The archer flinched, elbow jerking wide. His own shot snapped loose and skidded high over the ravine, burying itself in the far wall.

Kira dropped the borrowed bow and had her daggers back out before her boots stopped sliding. She stepped fully into the open and slammed both blades against a boulder, the double crack sharp enough to make heads turn.

“Here!” she shouted. “I’m your bloody problem, not them!”

The east ridge answered. Two more archers shifted back toward her. A third rose from behind the dead brush, short bow coming up.

Kira’s pulse hammered in her throat. She backed into the narrow shadow between the fallen slabs, keeping her shoulders square and her curses loud.

“Come down and take me, then,” she snarled.

Her eyes flicked over the slope, counting, measuring. The low pair she had handled were done. The brush archer would have to move to get a clean line again. The high shooter she had spooked was reaching for another arrow, but his hands were shaking.

She kicked a loose stone down the slope, then shifted two paces left, making herself visible in a new gap.

“Keep your eyes on me,” she muttered, daggers tight in her grip. “That’s it. Look at me.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Got him!" I roar, seeing the arrow go wide. "Kira, fall back! We're breaking through!" I push hard, polearm flashing. We're almost to the west ridge archers.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order cut through the ravine’s noise and let out a harsh breath that was almost a laugh.

“Fall back,” she muttered. “Now there’s a bloody plan.”

She did not turn her back on the east ridge. Not with shooters still up there. Not with the brush archer still wriggling for a better lane. She scooped the fallen short bow from the scree, snatched one of the arrows she had kicked loose, and nocked it in two rough motions. Her fingers were slick, her shoulder sore, and the string bit her palm again as she drew.

The brush archer rose just enough to show his shoulder and the curve of his bow. Kira aimed at the dead wood in front of him and loosed.

The shaft snapped through the branches with a sharp crack. The archer flinched hard and dropped low, cursing in some thin, reedy voice.

“Stay down,” Kira growled.

She let the borrowed bow fall and had her daggers back in her hands before the weapon struck stone. Then she moved.

Not away in a straight line. Never straight. She cut from the narrow shadow between the slabs to a cracked outcrop, boots sliding on loose rock, body bent low. An arrow thudded into the dirt behind her. Another sparked off the outcrop and sent a chip of stone stinging past her ear.

“Still can’t hit,” she called, though her voice was rougher than she wanted it to be. “Come down here and try with your hands, then!”

No one took the offer. The east ridge remained where it was: high, jagged, and full of men who preferred shooting from safety. Kira saw one of the silhouettes on the rim rise and wave, trying to pull the others back into line. The brush archer was moving again, low and quick, trying to find a gap that would let him shoot across the ravine floor.

Kira snatched a stone from the ground and hurled it toward the dead brush. It struck a branch and bounced into the thicket. The archer jerked back, convinced for half a heartbeat that something worse was coming.

It was enough.

Kira broke from the outcrop and ran for the next fold of rock, keeping her shoulders hunched and her blades tight. Her breath burned. Her raw palms screamed. One boot slipped on gravel, and she dropped to one knee, catching herself with a dagger point driven into the dirt.

An arrow whispered over her head.

“Fuck,” she hissed.

She came up fast and pressed herself against the ravine wall, chest heaving. From there she could see the west ridge beginning to unravel. Men were scrambling backward, bows lowered, voices sharp with panic. One archer threw down his quiver and ran along the slope. Another was trying to drag a wounded comrade over the rocks. The pressure had reached them.

The east ridge was still the problem.

Kira counted quickly. Four visible shooters up high. Maybe one more hidden in the broken stone. The brush archer was low, but he had a line toward the open floor if anyone strung out too far. The two she had handled on the lower slope were done, one groaning in the dirt, the other still trying to crawl away from her.

She looked back toward the main push, jaw tight.

“East’s not done!” she shouted. “They’ll try to shoot across the lane once the line stretches!”

Another arrow punched into the wall near her hip. Kira flinched, then bared her teeth.

“Persistent cunts,” she said.

She pushed off the rock and moved again, this time angling toward the falling back of the fight rather than away from it. She used every scrap of cover she could find: a split boulder, a shelf of stone, the corpse of a fallen archer’s discarded pack. Each time she moved, she made noise. A boot scraping rock. A dagger rapping stone. A shouted curse.

“Over here!” she yelled. “Still me! Still your problem!”

The east ridge answered. Two arrows chased her. One went wide. The other tore through the leather across her upper arm with a hot, shallow sting. Kira stumbled, swore louder, and kept moving.

“Cheap shot,” she spat.

She reached a low shelf of rock and dropped behind it, pressing her back to the stone. Blood warmed her sleeve, but the arm still worked. Both hands still worked. That was enough.

From the shelf, she saw the brush archer finally find his angle. He rose from the dead wood, bow lifting toward the open floor. Kira did not think. She grabbed one of her daggers by the blade, balanced it for a heartbeat, and threw it hard.

The dagger spun and struck the brush archer’s bow near the riser. It did not wound him, but the impact knocked his aim sideways. His arrow flew wide and buried itself in the dirt with a dull thump.

The archer stared at the dagger in the brush like it had bitten him.

“Next one won’t miss,” Kira lied, breathing hard.

She did not wait to find out if he believed her. She pushed up from the shelf and sprinted the last stretch toward the breaking fight, boots pounding the ravine floor. Her remaining dagger swept low at her side. Her eyes stayed on the east ridge until she was sure no one was about to loose into her back.

A west ridge archer stumbled into her path, bow half-raised, face pale. Kira did not slow. She checked him with her shoulder hard enough to spin him around, then hooked his ankle with her boot. He went down with a shout. Before he could rise, she drove the point of her dagger into the dirt beside his ear.

“Drop it,” she snarled.

He dropped the bow.

Kira kicked it away and left him scrambling backward in the dust.

She reached the edge of the rocks where the ravine widened enough for bodies to move faster. Her chest heaved. Her arm burned. Her fingers were cramped around the dagger grip. She wiped the blade on her thigh, then looked back toward the east ridge one more time.

The shooters there had not vanished. They had pulled tighter, uncertain now, caught between the noise behind them and the fight ahead. The brush archer was still down. The high shooter with the shaking hands had not drawn again.

Kira spat blood-flecked dust from her mouth.

“Four bows left on the east rim,” she said, voice ragged but steady. “One in the brush, maybe pinned. They’ll loose if they get a clean lane, so keep steel up and don’t bunch.”

She shifted her weight, ready to move again, and waited for the next order.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: Kira saw the problem in one hard breath. The captain was cut off across the ravine, separated from the vanguard by a long run of broken ground that the east ridge could shoot into from end to end. There was no clean path to him. Not from where she stood

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Kira, fall back to the vanguard. Hold the line. I'll draw their fire." I break cover and sprint across the open ground, polearm held ready.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s curse came out raw and loud, lost almost at once in the noise of the ravine.

“Aye, fall back,” she snarled through her teeth. “Hold the bloody line. Leave you to be bait. Brilliant.”

She did not argue. There was no time, and no path to him that would not end with arrows in her back. The open ground between them was a killing lane, and the east ridge still had bows enough to fill it.

Kira dropped low behind the shelf and moved.

Not away from the danger—across it. Short, jagged sprints from one scrap of cover to the next. A split stone. A dead archer’s pack. A ridge of broken slate. Each time she stopped, she made herself heard. Dagger on rock. Boot on scree. A shout sharp enough to drag eyes toward her.

“Still here!” she bellowed. “Look at me, you cowards!”

The east rim answered. One arrow punched into the dirt behind her. Another snapped against the slate and sent stone chips stinging across her jaw. Kira flinched, kept moving, and bared her teeth.

“Is that all?”

She saw the brush archer shift again, trying to find a lane toward the open floor. Kira snatched a loose rock and hurled it into the dead wood. The branches cracked. The archer ducked. It bought half a breath, maybe two.

Enough.

She reached the vanguard’s edge hard-breathing and bleeding from the shallow tear in her arm. Her remaining dagger was slick in her grip. The other was still buried somewhere in the brush, and she missed its weight like a missing tooth.

“Shields east!” she shouted, not because she wanted command, but because someone had to say it. “Don’t bunch! Keep steel up for the high shots!”

The line was ragged, but it held. Men were breathing hard, eyes wide, weapons up. The west ridge had broken into confusion; the east ridge had not. Kira could see the difference. The west was running. The east was still trying to shoot.

Four bows on the rim. Maybe five. The brush archer low and patient. The hidden one in the broken stone still unaccounted for.

Kira grabbed a discarded short spear from the dirt, tested its balance, and cursed again. Too long for her hands, but it could keep a lane honest. She planted the butt against the stone and angled the point toward the east slope.

“If they loose into the open, they’ll expose themselves,” she said, voice rough. “Watch the brush. Watch the split slab. They’ll shoot when the line stretches.”

Another arrow hissed down from the rim and thudded into the dirt ahead of the vanguard. Kira did not flinch this time. She stepped forward just enough to be seen, lifted the stolen spear, and slapped its shaft against a rock.

“Over here!” she roared. “Waste them on me!”

Her eyes stayed on the east ridge, counting, waiting, ready to move again.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I make it to the other side, winded, as Kira shouts orders. *Good. That's good.* I nod at her across the divide. "Hold them, Kira! I'm coming around!" I push my company to flank the remaining archers on the west ridge.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the nod across the ravine and answered with a sharp jerk of her chin, nothing more.

“Hold them,” she repeated under her breath, the words rough with dust and blood. “Aye. Simple. Just keep four bows honest while half the ravine tries to kill us.”

She turned from the open ground and faced the vanguard. The line was ragged, breathing hard, shields uneven, spears too high. Fear made men stupid. Kira had seen it enough times to know the cure was not courage but noise, routine, and something to hit.

“Shields east!” she barked. “Not up—east! They’ll shoot low through the gaps, not straight down!”

A young soldier beside her lifted his rim too high. Kira slapped the edge of his shield down with the flat of her dagger. “Lower. You want to catch arrows in the throat, do it on your own time.”

Another man had backed too far into the rocks. She kicked gravel at his boot. “Fill the gap. If they see a hole, they’ll put steel in it.”

They obeyed. Not because she was their captain, but because she sounded certain, and certainty was worth more than rank when arrows were flying.

The east ridge loosed.

Kira saw the release before she heard it: shoulders shifting, bows snapping forward. “Brace!”

Three shafts came down. One punched into the dirt ahead of the line. One cracked against stone. The third slammed into a shield with a heavy thud that made the man behind it grunt. The line held.

Kira exhaled. “See? Wood and leather. Not magic.”

Her eyes swept the east slope. The rim shooters had settled into stubborn pairs, using the broken stone for cover. The brush archer was still low, patient, dangerous. The hidden one in the broken ground had not shown himself, which meant he was either dead, clever, or waiting for someone to make a mistake.

Kira did not intend to give him one.

She stepped half out from the rocks and rapped her dagger against a discarded shield. The sound rang sharp through the ravine.

“Still here!” she shouted. “Come on, then! I’m the one making noise!”

Two heads turned on the rim. Good.

An arrow hissed past and struck the rock behind her. Kira flinched, then bared her teeth.

“Missed again. You lot shoot like drunk grandmothers.”

A soldier near her laughed nervously. Another swore. The line shifted, feet finding better purchase. Kira kept moving along it, not leading so much as stitching it together with curses and small corrections.

“Keep the shields overlapped. Watch the brush. If that low archer rises, loose at the branches, not the man. He’ll duck, but he’ll lose his aim.”

The brush stirred.

“There!” Kira shouted.

A short bow lifted from the dead wood. Two vanguard archers fired before Kira could do more than point. Their shots went wide, but one arrow snapped through the thicket close enough to make the hidden shooter drop. The bow disappeared.

Kira grunted. “Good. Keep him honest.”

Her gaze flicked toward the west ridge. The pressure there was telling. Archers who had been loosing into the ravine were turning, stumbling, breaking formation. One man threw down his bow and scrambled over the rocks. Another tried to rally his mates and got shoved aside. The west side was coming apart.

The east would be the last problem.

Kira spat blood-tinged dust. “East rim’s all that’s left. They know it too.”

Another arrow thudded into the dirt near her boot. She looked down at it, then back up.

“Persistent bastards.”

She moved to the edge of the vanguard’s cover, where the angle opened just enough to give the high shooters a tempting target. Her dagger was slick in her hand. Her arm burned where the earlier arrow had torn leather and skin. Her missing blade still sat somewhere in the brush, and the absence of it made her feel half-armed.

She picked up a fallen shield by the rim, tested its weight, and made a face. Too heavy, too clumsy. Better than nothing.

“Watch the split slab,” she called to the nearest men. “There’s one hidden there. If he shows, don’t chase him. Just put steel in the gap.”

As if summoned by her warning, a shadow moved near the broken stone. Kira saw the flash of a bow limb, not the man himself.

“Split slab!” she roared.

An arrow came out of the gap. It struck the dirt inside the line, close enough to spray grit across her legs. A soldier cursed and stumbled back.

Kira grabbed his shoulder and shoved him behind a shield. “Stay down unless you want to be taller!”

The hidden shooter did not rise again. That was enough. He was pinned by noise if not by steel.

The brush archer tried his luck again.

Kira saw the branches part and knew immediately that he had found a lane toward the open ground. If he loosed into the moving flank, someone would die for nothing.

She had no bow. No second dagger. No good angle.

“Fuck it,” she snarled.

She dropped her stolen shield, gripped the long spear she had taken from the dirt, and hurled it underhand. The throw was ugly, desperate, and nothing she would ever admit to practicing. The spear slapped through the dead brush with a crack of breaking wood and struck somewhere near the bow.

The archer’s shot went wide. The arrow skipped across the ravine floor and buried itself harmlessly in the dirt.

The spear vanished into the thicket.

Kira stared after it for half a heartbeat. “Well. That was useful.”

Now she had one dagger and a bad temper.

She snatched up the discarded shield again and slammed her dagger against it once, twice, three times. The noise rang harsh and ugly.

“Over here!” she bellowed. “Forget the brush! Forget the west! I’m right here!”

The east rim answered.

Two arrows struck the shield. One punched through the rim and stuck there, quivering. The other glanced off the edge and whined away into the rocks. The impact jarred Kira’s shoulder and dragged a curse out of her.

“Christ—”

She staggered but kept the shield up. A third arrow hit the stone at her feet and sent a sharp chip slicing across her cheek.

Blood welled hot and thin. Kira wiped it away with her forearm and laughed without any humor in it.

“That it? That all you’ve got?”

The line behind her was steadier now. Shields were lower, tighter. The vanguard archers were watching the brush and the split slab instead of staring up helplessly at the rim. The west ridge had gone from threat to rout, men fleeing along the slope or throwing down their bows.

The east shooters noticed.

Kira saw it in the way one of the rim archers looked back. Saw the hesitation in another’s draw. Saw the third lower his bow and say something to the man beside him.

“They’re thinking about running,” she said, voice rough. “Don’t let them settle.”

She banged the dagger against the shield again, though her wrist ached from the recoil.

“Stay with it! Keep their heads down!”

The brush archer rose suddenly, not to shoot but to retreat. Kira caught the movement and pointed.

“He’s breaking! Loose!”

Two arrows chased him into the thicket. He ducked hard, branches thrashing, and did not come back up.

The hidden shooter near the split slab shifted too. A soldier threw a javelin without waiting for anyone’s permission. It clattered against stone, and the shadow vanished.

Kira’s chest heaved. Her mouth was dry. Her arm was bleeding freely now, the sleeve dark and sticky. She kept the shield angled east and the dagger ready, though her fingers were starting to cramp.

The rim archers loosed one last time.

It was a ragged volley, more fear than aim. One arrow struck a shield. One flew wide. The last thudded into the dirt far behind the line.

Then silence stretched.

Not true silence. Men were still shouting on the west slope. Someone was groaning in the ravine. Dust was settling in pale drifts over broken stone and spent arrows. But the east ridge had stopped shooting with purpose.

Kira did not lower the shield.

She watched the rim. Watched the brush. Watched the split slab. Her breath came in shallow pulls through her teeth. Her eyes burned from dust and sweat.

“Don’t bunch,” she rasped, more out of habit than command. “Don’t get clever. Don’t go chasing shadows.”

A soldier near her swallowed hard. “Are they done?”

Kira spat into the dirt.

“They’re deciding whether they’re done. There’s a difference.”

She shifted her weight, feeling the sting in her cheek, the burn in her arm, the ache in every place she had hit stone that day. The line held around her, shields east, eyes on the ridge.

Kira kept hers there too.

“Four bows on the rim, maybe less,” she muttered. “Brush is quiet. Hidden one’s still breathing, probably. West’s broken.”

She tightened her grip on the dagger.

“If they want to run, let them run. If they want to shoot, we make them waste it.”

The ravine waited with her.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Phew.* I see the last of the west archers scatter, and turn to look at Kira. She's a mess, but she held. "Well fought, Kira! Well fought, all of you!" I bellow, raising my polearm. "Form up! We're moving out!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira let the praise wash over her without answering it at first. Her chest heaved, her shield arm trembled from the impacts, and her dagger hand was cramped so tight around the grip that her knuckles had gone pale. For half a heartbeat, she simply stood there, listening to the ravine settle into its ugly aftermath: the clatter of loose stone, the groan of wounded men, the whisper of dust sliding over rock.

Then the order caught up with her.

Moving out.

Kira’s mouth twisted. “Aye. Because standing still in a killzone was always the clever part.”

She lowered the borrowed shield just enough to rip the arrow lodged in its rim free. The shaft came out with a harsh scrape. She snapped it across her knee and threw the pieces aside.

“You heard him!” she barked at the vanguard, voice raw. “Up. Form. Shields overlapped. If you can stand, stand. If you can’t, someone puts an arm under you and keeps you moving.”

The line stirred. Men shifted, boots grinding on gravel, shields lifting with less confusion than before. A pair of soldiers hauled a third upright, his helm gone and blood running down his face. Kira shoved a discarded quiver out of their path with her boot.

“Don’t cluster around him. Two are enough. The rest keep eyes east.”

Her own eyes went back to the ridge as she spoke. The rim was quieter now, but quiet did not mean empty. She could still see the dark shapes there, crouched behind stone, uncertain whether to run, shoot, or wait for someone else to decide. The brush near the lower slope had gone still. The split slab remained a blind, ugly gap in the rock.

Kira did not trust any of it.

She moved along the forming line, not at the front, not in the center, but where the angle to the east rim stayed open. Her remaining dagger was slick. Her sleeve was wet. The shallow tear in her arm had slowed, but every time she moved the blood warmed again. She bit back a curse and used the edge of her cloak to press hard against the wound for two breaths.

A young soldier stared at her arm.

She looked up sharply. “Eyes on the ridge, not on me.”

He flushed and turned back.

“Shields east until we clear the narrows,” Kira said, more to the nearest men than to anyone in command. “They won’t get many shots, but they only need one stupid one.”

Her gaze flicked toward the dead brush. Somewhere in that mess was her other dagger. The thought of leaving it sat badly in her gut, worse than the bleeding, worse than the exhaustion.
