Twin blades were not just weapons. They were balance. They were habit. They were the difference between feeling half-armed and feeling ready for the next fight.

She weighed the risk.

The brush was quiet. The brush archer had not shown himself since the spear went in. The rim shooters were hesitant. The vanguard was forming, shields rising, movement starting.

“Cover that thicket,” she told the two nearest shield-bearers, pointing with her dagger. “If anything moves, don’t argue. Hit it.”

One of them swallowed. “What if it’s one of ours?”

Kira gave him a flat look. “Then he shouldn’t be crawling around in a bloody ambush lane.”

She did not wait for a reply.

Low and quick, she cut away from the line, boots finding the broken ground with practiced care. She kept her shoulder under the edge of the borrowed shield and her dagger hand free. The brush looked worse up close: dead branches, torn leaves, dark gaps where a man could hide a bow. A faint red smear marked where her thrown dagger had struck wood or bone.

Kira stopped two paces from the thicket and listened.

Nothing.

No breath. No rustle. No drawn string.

She crouched, swept the shield forward, and used the dagger point to part the branches.

The brush archer was there.

He lay half-tangled in the dead wood, bow knocked sideways, one hand pressed to his forearm where the spear had struck. His face was pale and streaked with dust. He looked up at her with wide eyes and started to reach for the short bow at his side.

Kira put the point of her dagger against his throat before his fingers got close.

“Don’t,” she said.

He froze.

“Good lad.”

Her eyes moved past him. There, caught in a fork of broken branches, was her second dagger. The blade glinted dully, the hilt wrapped in familiar worn leather. Relief hit her harder than she expected.

She snatched it free, tested the grip, and felt her shoulders ease a fraction.

“Right,” she muttered. “That’s better.”

The brush archer made a small sound.

Kira looked down at him. “You want to live, you stay in this bush until we’re gone. You stand up, you get shot. You shoot, I come back and make it personal.”

He did not answer. His hand stayed where it was.

Kira backed out of the thicket, keeping low, shield angled toward the east rim. An arrow hissed down from above and struck the rock behind her. Stone chips spat against her calves.

“Fucking knew it,” she snapped.

She straightened enough to be seen and banged her recovered dagger against the shield.

“That all?” she shouted. “One last parting gift? Come down here and say it to my face!”

No one did.

The rim shapes shifted again, but this time it looked less like preparation and more like indecision. One man lowered his bow entirely. Another turned toward the rear of the ridge, saying something too faint to hear. The fight was going out of them. That made them more dangerous, not less. Desperate men did stupid things. So did proud ones.

Kira returned to the vanguard at a jog, falling into the side of the column where the eastern angle remained open. She slid her second dagger back into its sheath with a sharp breath of satisfaction, then immediately drew it again. Her hand did not trust the sheath yet.

“Move steady,” she said to the nearest soldiers. “Not fast. Not slow. If the line stretches, they get clean lanes. If we bunch, one arrow does two jobs.”

A sergeant nearby looked at her, waiting for more.

Kira scowled. “I’m not giving speeches. I’m telling you how not to die.”

The column began to move.

Kira stayed with the rear third, where the risk from the east ridge would linger longest. She kept her body half-turned, shield up, dagger ready, eyes moving from rim to brush to split slab. Every shadow looked like a bow. Every crack in the stone looked like an ambush waiting to happen. Maybe they were. Maybe they were not. She did not intend to find out by taking an arrow in the back.

A wounded man groaned loudly as he was carried past. Kira stepped closer to him, putting her shield between his exposed side and the ridge until the bearers found better footing.

“Keep him low,” she said. “And keep moving.”

Another soldier had stopped to retrieve a fallen helmet.

“Leave it,” Kira snapped. “Unless you want your head more than you want the hat.”

He left it.

The ravine floor narrowed again before it widened toward the far exit. The walls leaned in, jagged and shadowed. Kira’s jaw tightened. This was the sort of place where a few stubborn archers could still make a mess.

She lifted her voice.

“Shields up through the narrows! Eyes east! No one stops for anything less than a direct order!”

The men obeyed. The shields rose. The pace stayed even.

Kira counted under her breath. One. Two. Three. Her pulse hammered. Her arm throbbed. The cut on her cheek stung every time sweat touched it. Somewhere above, a stone clattered. She jerked her dagger toward the sound, but no arrow came.

Just loose rock.

Maybe.

“Stay tight,” she muttered. “Stay tight.”

The column passed into the narrows.

The eastern rim remained visible in broken slices between the rocks. Kira watched one of the last archers there rise slowly, bow held low, not drawn. He stood there for a breath, looking down at the moving column. Kira raised her shield and met his gaze across the distance.

She did not shout this time. She did not bang steel. She simply kept the shield up and the dagger ready.

After a moment, the archer turned and disappeared behind the rim.

Kira exhaled slowly through her nose.

“Cowards,” she said, though there was little heat left in it. “Bloody persistent cowards.”

The vanguard began to breathe easier as the ravine widened. Men lowered their shields an inch. Shoulders came down. Someone laughed too loudly, the sound sharp and brittle.

Kira did not lower her own shield.

“Not yet,” she said. “Not until the walls stop looking down at us.”

She kept her eyes moving until the last of the narrows fell behind them. Only then did she let the shield drop to her side. Her fingers were stiff. Her arm felt like it had been beaten with a hammer. Her second dagger was still in her hand, and she looked at it for a moment before finally sliding it home.

The absence of the missing blade was gone. That mattered.

She rolled her shoulder, hissed at the pain, and looked over the column. Wounded being carried. Shields still up. No one bunched. No one lagging too far. Good enough.

Kira spat dust and blood into the dirt.

“Next time,” she muttered to no one, “we take the high ground first.”

Then she fell into step with the rear of the moving column, one hand on her dagger, eyes still flicking back toward the ravine, waiting to see if the ridge had one last insult left to give.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "That's the plan, Kira," I say, my voice still a little hoarse from shouting. "Next time, we send you up there first." I meet her eyes for a moment, a rare, genuine smile on my face. *She's a bloody mess, but she's my mess, and she held.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira made a rough sound that might have been a laugh if it had not ended in a cough.

“Aye, send me up first,” she said, voice dry as ravine dust. “Next time, maybe send a shield wall with me. And a bloody healer while you’re at it.”

She looked down at herself as if the full tally had only just caught up with her. Torn sleeve. Sticky blood along her arm. Raw knuckles. One cheek stinging where stone had bitten it. Her left hand trembled when she flexed it, so she curled it around a dagger hilt until it stopped.

“The east ridge held because they had cover, arrows, and no reason to run until the west broke,” she said, blunt as a hammer. “Next time we know there’s high ground, send skirmishers up both rims before the column enters the narrows. Even two men with shields and javelins would have made them keep their heads down.”

She pulled a strip loose from the edge of her cloak with her teeth, wrapped it around the torn flesh of her arm, and cinched it tight. A sharp hiss escaped her.

“Fuck,” she muttered.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good points, all of them," I say, my smile fading as I nod. "Lessons learned for next time. And don't worry, a healer will be waiting." I turn my attention forward, scanning the terrain. "Let's put some distance between us and this ambush."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira gave a short, curt nod. “Distance. Aye. And water before someone faints into a spear point.”

She did not sheathe both blades. One dagger stayed in her hand, the other rested against her hip, ready. The bandage around her arm was already darkening at the edge, but she left it be. There would be time to bleed properly later.

Moving back along the column, she checked the wounded first, not gently.

“Can you walk?” she asked one man being half-dragged between two soldiers.

He managed a pale, shaky nod.

“Then walk. Faster’s safer.”

To the bearers carrying the worse cases, she said, “Keep him low, but don’t stop. If you need to switch, do it moving. Don’t make a knot of yourselves.”

A soldier lifted a waterskin while still marching. Kira snatched it without asking, drank two harsh swallows, and passed it back before the man could protest.

“Next time,” she said, wiping her mouth with the back of her wrist, “carry more water and fewer bloody arrows.”

The terrain ahead looked no friendlier than what they had left: broken stone, dry washes, scrub that could hide a man lying flat. Kira’s eyes kept moving from ridge to ridge, measuring angles. The east rim had gone quiet, but quiet could mean withdrawn, or it could mean repositioning.

She did not like either answer.

“If they follow,” she said to the nearest sergeant, “they’ll wait until we think we’re clear. They’ll aim for the wounded. Maybe the rear guard. They won’t want another fight unless we give them a soft target.”

The sergeant glanced back at the ravine. “You think they’ll follow?”

Kira’s expression flattened. “I think men who set an ambush don’t always like watching it crawl away.”

She shifted her grip on the dagger and scanned the slope line again. No dust beyond what the wind made. No glint of metal. No birds scattering wrong. Not yet.

That did not settle her.

“Keep the archers spread,” she added. “Two near the rear, one on each flank if the ground allows. If anything moves up high, don’t wait for orders. Put a shaft near it.”

A soldier near the back muttered something about being tired.

Kira turned her head slowly. “We’re all tired. Dead men get to sleep.”

The muttering stopped.

She rolled her shoulder once and regretted it. The torn flesh pulled hot under the cloth. Her fingers were still sticky with dried blood. She wiped them on her thigh, leaving dark streaks over the dust already there.

Up ahead, the ground widened into a shallow rise with better sightlines. Good. Fewer places for a second killzone. Still not enough.

“Get the wounded to the middle once we crest,” Kira said. “Shields on the flanks. If anyone sees a shadow that doesn’t belong to a rock, call it.”

She paused, listening.

Wind. Boots. Labored breathing. The creak of leather.

No bowstrings.

Not yet.

Kira let out a slow breath and kept moving with the rear guard, one eye on the back trail and one on the high ground. Her voice dropped, meant more for herself than anyone else.

“Come on, then. Let’s make it boring.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I appreciate Kira's bluntness. "Understood," I reply, my eyes still sweeping the horizon. "No soft targets. Keep the pace, everyone." I signal the column to maintain speed. We need to clear this area quickly.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and gave one short nod, though her eyes stayed on the back trail.

“Pace,” she repeated, voice rough enough to scrape. “Aye. Pace keeps us alive. Stopping lets them think.”

She moved down the rear of the column with quick, uneven steps, not marching so much as hunting along it. One dagger stayed in her hand. The other was sheathed now, but only because she had learned the hard way that a blade kept too long in the grip could tire a hand before it was needed. The borrowed shield still hung on her arm, heavier than she liked, its rim scarred where arrows had bitten it.

She rapped the flat of her dagger against a shield as she passed.

“Loosen up. Not so tight you trip each other. Two paces where you can, one where you can’t. Keep the wounded inside.”

The soldiers shifted. Some obeyed at once. Others needed a second nudge, a glare, or a sharp kick at their heels. Kira gave all three without favor.

A man near the back kept glancing over his shoulder toward the ravine. Kira caught his pauldron and hauled him around.

“Eyes forward, then up. Not back. If they come, they’ll come from high ground, not out of your own boots.”

He swallowed and faced front.

“Better.”

Her arm throbbed under the makeshift bandage. The cloth had already gone dark and tacky, and every beat of her pulse reminded her that the wound was still there. She flexed her fingers once. They worked. Good enough.

She found a waterskin dangling from a pack near the rear and took it without asking. The owner started to protest, saw the blood on her sleeve, and shut his mouth. Kira drank two quick swallows, poured a little over the bandage to wash away the worst of the grit, then tossed the skin back.

“Next time,” she said, “carry one bigger than your ambitions.”

The column crested the shallow rise. The ground opened ahead into broken, sun-baked slopes, less confined than the ravine but not safe. Not by a long shot. Scrub clung to the dips. Dry washes cut dark lines through the stone. There were fewer places for arrows to fall from above, but more places for men to crawl unseen.

Kira did not like it.

She liked it less than the ravine, which was saying something.

“Archers,” she called, voice carrying over the rasp of boots and leather. “Keep arrows loose. Not nocked unless you see something, but ready. If a bush grows legs, shout before you loose. I don’t want some fool shooting at a goat and starting a panic.”

One of the archers looked back at her. “And if it’s not a goat?”

Kira bared her teeth. “Then put steel near it and make it decide whether it wants to be a man again.”

That got a few rough laughs. Better than fear. Fear made men jumpy, and jumpy men made mistakes.

She scanned the ridgelines as she walked. East. West. The broken spine of rock behind them. The ravine had become a dark mouth in the distance, still and sullen. Nothing moved there that she could see. That did not mean nothing was there. Ambushers with sense would let the column stretch out before trying again. Ambushers without sense might still take a shot out of spite.

Kira respected spite. It was reliable.

A clatter of stones came from the left flank.

She spun, dagger up, shield coming around in the same breath. Three soldiers jerked with her, one of them nearly loosing an arrow into empty air.

A lizard darted from beneath a slab and vanished into the scrub.

Kira held her stance for two heartbeats longer, then lowered the blade.

“Christ,” she muttered. “Bloody rocks are jumpy too.”

She wiped dust from her cheek and felt the sting where the stone had cut her earlier. The blood had dried in a thin line down her jaw. She left it. No point cleaning it off only to bleed again somewhere new.

The wounded were moving better than she expected. The two worst cases were still being carried, but the others had found that grim, stubborn rhythm men got when they knew stopping meant worse pain later. One leaned heavily on a comrade, face gray under the dirt. Another kept pressing a hand to his side, breathing through his teeth.

Kira fell in beside them for a few paces.

“You,” she said to the gray-faced one. “If you feel faint, say so before you drop. Falling on rocks is stupid. Falling on spears is unforgivable.”

He managed a weak grunt that might have been agreement.

“Good enough.”

She looked to the men supporting him. “Switch sides every twenty paces. Don’t let one shoulder go dead. If he starts sliding, shout.”

They nodded, grateful for something concrete.

Kira moved on.

The column kept its speed. Not fast enough to break into disorder, not slow enough to invite pursuit. It was the kind of pace that punished legs and lungs but kept men alive. Kira had no love for it, but she respected it.

She checked the rear again.

Dust. Stone. The ravine.

No shapes on the rim.

No glint of bow limbs.

No movement where movement should not be.

Her shoulders stayed tight anyway.

A sergeant near the back glanced at her. “Think they’ve had enough?”

Kira looked at him flatly. “Men who set an ambush usually bring friends. If they’ve had enough, it’s because they’ve gone to fetch more trouble.”

The sergeant’s mouth tightened. He looked ahead instead of back.

Good.

Kira adjusted the shield on her arm and studied the terrain to the left. A dry wash ran parallel to their route, shallow but deep enough to hide crawling men. If she were following them, that was where she would put shooters. Not many. Two, maybe three. Enough to sting the flank and force the column to bunch.

She pointed with her dagger.

“Watch that wash. If anything moves in it, don’t wait to see if it waves.”

The nearest archers shifted their attention. One nocked an arrow, then thought better of it and eased it back into the quiver.

Kira approved of the hesitation. Better than loosing at shadows.

Her boots crunched over gravel. Her breath had settled into a harsh rhythm, and every step sent a hot pull through her torn sleeve. She ignored it with the practiced spite of someone who had been hurt before and expected to be hurt again.

A soldier ahead stumbled.

Kira was moving before the man hit the ground, catching his pack strap and hauling him upright with a curse.

“Feet up. If you kiss the dirt now, you’ll do it slower.”

He blinked, shaken, but found his stride again.

“Thanks,” he muttered.

“Don’t thank me,” Kira said. “Walk.”

She fell back into position, scanning the slopes again.

The wind shifted. It brought dust and the faint smell of iron. Blood, maybe. Or old stone. Hard to tell after a fight. Kira’s nose had long since stopped being trustworthy in places where men had tried to kill one another.

She rolled her neck, felt the grit in her hair, the ache in her shoulder, the sting in her palms. Her twin daggers were both with her again. That helped. Not enough, but enough to keep her from feeling half-made.

Ahead, the column stretched toward safer ground. Behind, the ravine waited like a bad memory.

Kira kept her place between the two.

“Keep it moving,” she said, low and sharp. “Boring is good. Boring means nobody’s dying.”

A stone shifted somewhere behind them.

She turned slowly, eyes narrowing.

Nothing.

Then a pebble rolled down the slope and tapped against another.

Kira lifted her dagger, not pointing, just ready.

“Come on, then,” she murmured. “Try it.”

The ravine gave no answer.

She did not lower the blade.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I watch Kira, a silent whirlwind of efficiency, as she moves along the column. *She's right, of course. Always is.* My gaze sweeps the horizon. "Keep it up, everyone! We're almost there!" I call, trying to inject some much-needed optimism into my voice.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira spat a curse, the sound sharp and guttural. "Drawing fire with knuckle-dusters and a loud mouth? Fuck's sake. Try not to bleed out while I'm busy."

She didn't wait for a reply. Her gaze snapped to the eastern ridge, tracking the glint of bowstrings against the gray stone. Three archers shifted, nocking shafts. Kira whipped her right arm back and loosed a dagger. It wasn't a kill shot—too far, too high—but it struck a splash of sparks against the rock right in the center of their line.

"Over here, you blind rats!" she bellowed, pitching her voice to echo off the ravine walls.

The reaction was immediate. The east ridge erupted. A volley of arrows hissed down, tearing into the scree and stone where Kira had stood a heartbeat ago. She was already moving, dropping low and scrambling sideways behind a jagged outcrop of rock. Dust plumed around her as shafts thudded into the cover inches from her shoulder.

She peered around the edge, eyes narrowing as she assessed the rhythm. They were hammering her position, suppressing. They weren't flanking.

"They're fixated on the noise," she shouted back toward the west, her voice tight over the rattle of impacts. "You've got a gap. Move, or that gap closes."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Good.* My vanguard is already moving, using what little cover the ravine offers. "Push hard! Don't let them re-group!" I yell, my own voice cutting through the din. I keep my polearm ready, scanning for any sign of movement from the west ridge.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira pressed her cheek against the cold stone, counting the impacts. The volley had thinned. Good. They were overcommitting to the east. She slid her left dagger free from the rock where it had skidded, wiping grit from the blade with her thumb. "They're reloading," she called out, voice low but carrying over the settling dust. "Thirty seconds before the next wave. The choke point was your window."

She shifted her weight, boots scraping gravel. The eastern ridge remained visible, but the archers had hunkered down behind loose boulders. No movement from the west yet. That meant either the push was working, or the western flank was holding fire for a pincer. She didn't like the second option.

"I'm moving up the scree slope to keep pressure on them," she announced, keeping her tone flat. "If they tried to swing around, she'd cut the line. The advance was his call."

She crouched, testing her footing on the loose shale, and began the slow, deliberate climb. Every few steps, she paused, eyes scanning the ridge line for bowstrings or the glint of steel. Her daggers stayed loose in their grips, ready to draw. The wind shifted, carrying the metallic tang of dust and sweat. She bit her lip, jaw tight. "Fuck's sake, hope you actually broke their line," she muttered, then kept climbing, boots finding purchase on the unstable rock as she closed the distance to the eastern cover.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s head snapped west the moment the wind carried the faint creak of a bowstring. Her eyes tracked the ridge line, catching the glint of an arm drawing back just above a cluster of pines. The angle was clear. The shot was already committed.

"Cap, west ridge! High arrow, incoming!" she barked, voice cracking through the ravine. She didn't wait to see if he moved. Her boots dug into the shale as she pivoted, already calculating trajectories. Too far for a dagger throw to intercept, but she could break their line of sight or force a flinch if she made noise.

She snatched a loose chunk of rock from the scree and hurled it hard toward the western ridge, aiming to spark a distraction. "Duck!" she shouted, though she knew he’d already seen it. Her gaze locked onto the archer’s position, fingers tightening around her daggers. If the arrow missed, that archer would be exposed. If it didn’t, she’d be dragging a corpse out of a killzone. Neither option sat right.

She shifted her weight, muscles coiled. The wind carried the sharp snap of the bowstring releasing. Kira’s jaw clenched. "Move your fucking ass, Captain," she muttered, eyes tracking the shaft’s path without blinking. Her daggers cleared their sheaths in a single fluid motion. She braced her boots against the loose stone, ready to sprint the moment the trajectory cleared his position or left the archer open. The ravine held its breath. She didn't.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I duck, the arrow whistling inches over my head.* "Behind me, now!" I shout to the vanguard, pressing forward. This ambush is turning into a full-on brawl.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the shout echo off the stone. She didn't break stride. The order was clear, but the eastern ridge still held archers. She reached a shallow ledge halfway up the slope and pressed into it, boots finding solid purchase. "Heard you," she muttered, though the wind likely stole the words. She kept her eyes locked east. The archers were moving fast—shoulders dipping, arms drawing back for a second volley. Not aimed at her now. Aimed at the advancing line.

"They're shifting fire west," she called back, voice sharp over the clatter of steel and shouting. "Your vanguard's in the open. Watch for crossbow bolts—they're cycling heavier weapons." She hadn't seen the crossbows directly, but the rhythm of the reloads and the heavier thud of impacts suggested them. She drew her left dagger, thumb brushing the fuller. "I'm holding the high ground. If they try to pour down, I'll bleed them before they hit the dirt."

She shifted her weight, peering over the ledge. The eastern ridge was a mess of loose rock and shadows. One archer had overcommitted, leaning out to get a better angle. Kira didn't hesitate. She stepped out from cover just enough to get a clean line, wrist snapping forward. The dagger flew true, burying itself in the man's shoulder. He dropped his bow with a curse.

"One down," she said flatly. "Reload cycle's breaking. They're panicking. The scree's unstable under weight—you'll want to stick to the harder stone near the base if you're closing the gap." She settled back into the ledge, daggers loose in her palms, eyes tracking the remaining shooters. The brawl was heating up. She didn't like it. Messy fights got people killed. "Fuck's sake," she hissed through gritted teeth as another shaft thudded into the rock near her boot. She adjusted her grip on her blades, shoulders squaring. The ridge was hers to watch. She'd hold it.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s eyes tracked the widening gap between the Captain and the vanguard. The ravine floor was too exposed to sprint across without drawing a fresh volley down on herself. She shifted her weight against the ledge, twin daggers resting lightly in her palms, blades angled toward the ridge. "You're isolated," she called out, voice flat but tight. "The drop's too steep to run straight down without painting yourself in shafts. Stick to the shadow line along the bedrock."

She watched the eastern ridge. Two archers were repositioning, shoulders angling to thread shots across the open space toward his position. Kira cursed under her breath. "Fuck. They're tracking you. I can't hold this slope and cover your six at the same time." She dug her boots into the shale, testing the purchase. The loose rock would give way under a full sprint, and she wasn't about to send herself sliding into their killzone.

"If you need me to break the line, you'll have to draw them away from the ridge first," she added, keeping her tone clipped. "I'll push down the scree when their volley drops. Don't stand in the open waiting."

She kept her gaze locked on the ridge, tracking the subtle shift of bowstrings and the glint of steel against the gray stone. Her right hand tightened around her dagger's hilt, knuckles bleaching white. She adjusted her stance, shoulders squaring, ready to drop the moment the order came. The wind carried the distant clatter of steel and shouted commands. She exhaled slowly, jaw tight. "Give the word when you're ready to move. I'm yours."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "I'll draw them," I shout back, tightening my grip on my polearm. "Get ready to move when I do!" I need to create a diversion, and quickly.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira's jaw set hard. She didn't bother with encouragement; she wasted breath on survival. "Copy," she snapped back, the word sharp and low. She shifted her weight, boots grinding grit into a stable wedge against the shale. Her muscles coiled, daggers loose in her palms but ready to bite the moment the tension broke.

She fixed her gaze on the eastern ridge, ignoring the Captain's position now. Her focus was on the archers. She tracked the subtle twitches of their shoulders, the angle of their chins. They were still locked on the vanguard's previous position, unaware that the Captain was about to paint himself as the target.

"Make it loud," she called back, voice cutting through the wind. "I'm on the line. The second they snap their heads your way, I drop."

She spat a curse, the grit of the ravine tasting like copper and dust. "Fuck's sake, hope you can handle the heat when they pivot." Her thumb caressed the pommel of her right dagger, a rhythmic tap against her skin. She was a spring wound tight. She wouldn't move until she saw the reaction. The play was his. She just had to be fast enough to capitalize on the chaos he was about to make. Her eyes narrowed, scanning the ridge for the first sign of movement. Waiting.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I let out a primal roar, striking my polearm against the rock with a clang that echoes through the ravine.* "Come and get me, you cowards!" I bellow, making myself as visible as possible.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The clang of steel on stone echoed through the ravine like a struck bell. Kira’s eyes snapped west. The reaction was instant. Heads on the eastern ridge whipped around. Bowstrings drew back in unison, their aim shifting from the vanguard’s last known position to the Captain’s exposed silhouette.

"Now," she muttered.

She didn’t hesitate. Kira dropped from the ledge, boots hitting the loose shale with a controlled crash. She rolled with the impact, daggers already clearing leather as she slid down the slope. Dust and rock tumbled around her, but she kept her center of gravity low, reading the angles of the fall. She hit the ravine floor rolling, coming up in a crouch behind a fractured boulder just as the first volley arced overhead.

Shafts thudded into the rock and dirt where she’d been a second ago. "Fuck's sake," she hissed, not breaking her stance. She tracked the trajectory, counting impacts. *Three. Four. Six.* They were spraying wide, panicking. That was good.

She peered around the edge of her cover, daggers balanced in a low ready stance. The eastern ridge was in disarray. Archers were scrambling to re-aim, some fumbling with quivers, others shouting over each other. The disciplined rhythm was gone.

"They're scattered," she called out, voice carrying over the rattle of arrows. "Fire's breaking. I'm pushing left flank to cut off their retreat path. If they try to reload, I'll be in their faces before they nock." She adjusted her grip, thumb brushing the fuller of her left blade. "Stay low. The open ground's still hot for another ten seconds."

She waited for the volley to thin, eyes fixed on the ridge. The wind shifted, carrying the metallic tang of dust and sweat. She exhaled, shoulders relaxing a fraction. "Give the signal when you're ready to close. I've got the angle."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood!" *I move quickly, using the chaotic fire to my advantage, closing the distance to the west ridge.* "Vanguard, follow me! Push up the ridge!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira tracked the Captain's surge toward the west ridge. He was moving fast, cutting a sharp angle through the scree, but the exposure was brutal. The eastern ridge was swiveling, archers struggling to track his movement while keeping their balance on the loose rock.

"He's wide open," she muttered, jaw tightening. She didn't have time to fix it. The play was his.

She dropped low and sprinted from her cover, sticking to the hard stone near the base of the eastern wall. Her boots found purchase on the uneven surface, carrying her weight silently toward the flank. She wasn't going for the Captain; she was going for the throat of the ambush.

"Left flank moving," she called back, her voice cutting through the din. "Keeping pressure on the east so they don't rotate back on you. Watch for the crossbowmen—haven't seen them fire yet, but that's too quiet."

She reached the ridge line's edge, sliding instantly behind a protruding rock shelf. From here, she had a clear view of the eastern archers' backs. They were hunched, arrows nocked, eyes locked west. The distraction was working.

"They're fixated," she whispered, daggers shifting in her grip, blades angled for a throw or a close draw. "Cap, you've got their attention. Push hard. I'll clear the survivors once you break their line."

She waited, muscles coiled, eyes scanning the gap between the archers and the western slope. The Captain was the hammer; she was the anvil. She just had to hold the position until he struck.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I reach the base of the west ridge and begin scrambling up, my polearm acting as a makeshift climbing aid.* "Kira, fall back and cover our rear! We're almost through!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't argue. She shifted her weight, boots grinding into the gravel as she reversed her stance. "Copy. Holding the base," she called back, voice flat over the wind. She backed away from the eastern ridge line, daggers held low but ready, eyes scanning the ravine floor behind her position. The scree was littered with spent shafts and kicked-up dirt. Movement in the shadows near the western drop caught her attention—two figures dragging themselves down from the lower slope, likely the western flank she'd suspected. They were slow, favoring their legs, but they had blades.

"Rear's not clean," she muttered, already moving backward in a low crouch. She kept one dagger angled toward the approaching figures, the other hand ready to draw or shift cover. "Two hostiles peeling off the west drop. Moving slow, but closing. I'll keep them off your six."

She cursed under her breath as a loose rock skittered past her boot. "Fuck's sake, hope you're not leaving me holding the bag down here." She adjusted her footing, sliding behind a fractured boulder that offered cover from both the ridge above and the approaching pair. Her breathing stayed measured, eyes tracking the two figures as they gained ground. She wasn't waiting for them to commit. She'd meet them at the choke point.

"Push and clear the ridge," she shouted back, voice carrying but clipped. "I'll handle the sweep. Don't look back."

She shifted her grip on the daggers, blades catching the dull light. The first figure crested the lower slope, raising a notched sword. Kira's muscles coiled. She was ready.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood! Clear the rear, Kira! We'll secure the ridge!" I shout back, pulling myself up the last bit of the slope. My polearm clangs against the rock as I gain purchase on the ridge. The enemy archers are scattering, caught off guard by our sudden ascent.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira stepped out from behind the fractured boulder before the first hostile could find his footing. The man swung wide, a clumsy overhead chop that telegraphed his intent a mile away. Kira slipped inside the arc, the wind of the blade ruffling her hair, and drove her right dagger upward under his ribcage. She twisted the hilt hard, feeling the resistance give way, and shoved him back. He crumpled, gurgling, his sword clattering uselessly against the stone.

The second figure flinched, his guard dropping as panic seized him. Kira didn't let him recover. She pivoted on her heel, using the momentum to lunge forward, her left dagger snapping out in a short, brutal thrust. The blade buried itself in his throat. He clawed at the hilt, blood bubbling past his fingers, and dropped to his knees. Kira wrenched the weapon free with a wet squelch and kicked him backward into the loose scree.

"Fuck's sake," she muttered, wiping her blades on the dead man's tunic. "Amateurs."

She stepped over the bodies, boots finding purchase on the hard-packed dirt, and scanned the lower slope. No movement. No glint of steel. Just the settling dust and the distant clatter from the ridge.

"Rear's swept," she called up, voice flat and carrying. "Two down. I'm holding position until you signal. Try not to fall off, Cap."

She settled behind a low outcrop, daggers loose in her palms, eyes tracking the ridge line for any sign of reinforcements. Her breathing remained controlled, though her pulse hammered a steady rhythm against her ribs. She waited. The ridge was his now. She just had to make sure nothing crept up to ruin the victory.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good work, Kira! Hold that position!" I yell back, then turn my attention to the last few archers. They're trying to flee, but my vanguard is already cutting off their escape. The fight is almost over.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira pressed her shoulder blades against the cool stone, daggers still loose in her palms. "Copy," she muttered, the word sharp but quiet. She kept her eyes locked on the ridge line, watching the archers scramble for the tree line. The vanguard was already fanning out to cut them off, boots kicking up dust as they moved. Good. Let them run. Exhaustion would finish what steel started.

She shifted her weight, scanning the ravine floor for anything that moved. Loose scree, spent shafts, the dull glint of abandoned gear. No fresh hostiles. She exhaled slowly, shoulders dropping a fraction. "Rear's secure," she called up, voice flat. "They're routing. Don't let them hole up in the pines. If they do, they'll pick you off from cover."

She wiped a smear of blood from her right blade with her thumb, then slid it back into its sheath with a soft click. The left followed. She kept her stance low, boots planted on the hard-packed dirt, ready to move if the situation shifted. The rhythm of the fight had broken. The pressure was off. She tracked the Captain's position against the ridge line. "I'm holding," she added, tone clipped. "Signal when you want me to push up. Or stay put. Your call."

She settled into the rock, eyes never leaving the treeline. The wind carried the distant clatter of steel and shouted orders. She didn't relax. Sellswords didn't relax until the contract was done. She just waited, jaw tight, listening for the snap of a bowstring or the crunch of a boot on loose stone. If anyone tried to slip back, they'd find her daggers waiting.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Affirmative! Keep an eye on those woods!" I shout, then turn my attention to securing the ridge. "Fan out, vanguard! No stragglers!" The sounds of the skirmish die down, replaced by the shouts of my men.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the worn copy of Eliot's *Four Quartets* back into its precise slot on the shelf, though it had already been perfectly aligned with its neighbors. Their fingers busied themselves with the edge of a nearby stack of chapbooks, straightening what required no straightening at all, as they turned toward the counter with the measured calm of someone who had practiced indifference for years.

"New?" they echoed, voice dry as the dust on the upper shelves. "Only if one counts a first edition of *The Waste Land* that wandered in last week like some prodigal text seeking redemption. The back's a graveyard for the unsorted, as usual. You're welcome to rummage, if you've the patience for it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I shrug off my jacket and hang it on the coat rack near the door, then make my way to the counter.* "You know I always have patience for a good rummage." *I lean against the counter, not moving towards the back yet.* "Though I was hoping for something... less dusty."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's gaze lingered briefly on the counter before their hands reached for the stack of invoices beside the register, squaring their edges with meticulous care despite their already orderly state. The motion was automatic, a shield against the quiet that had settled between them.

"Modern neglect," they murmured, voice carrying its usual dry edge, "sounds rather like the later Auden—still sharp, but frayed at the margins. If it's dust you're avoiding, the back room offers little mercy. I could suggest a signed first of *The Great Gatsby* instead, though its pages have their own share of accumulated silence."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hands stilled on the ledger for half a heartbeat before they resumed their careful sorting of its already immaculate columns, the motion precise and pointless. A faint crease appeared between their brows, quickly smoothed away.

"Silence, then," they said at last, voice low and edged with the same dry precision they used for cataloguing damaged spines. "The shop has plenty of that on offer, though I doubt it travels well once you step back into the rain." They slid the ledger into its drawer without looking up, the click of the latch too loud in the quiet. "If it's not books you've come for, the door's still there. No need to linger on my account."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's not silence I'm after, Sable." *I push off the counter, moving closer.* "It's... well, it's you, actually."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers tightened around the edge of the ledger drawer for a fraction too long before they withdrew it again, sliding the already-straightened invoices into a different order altogether. The motion was deliberate, unnecessary, a shield against the words that had just been offered like an unshelved volume left on the counter.

They did not look up. "You," they repeated, the single syllable dry as vellum and just as brittle. "How very like the later Eliot—declaring the thing plainly and expecting the room not to notice the cracks in the plaster." A faint pause, then the soft scrape of paper as they realigned a stack of bookmarks that had not needed realigning. "The shop is not equipped for such declarations, Wren. Best to leave them in the rain where they belong."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath caught for the span of a single, unnoticed heartbeat, their fingers tightening fractionally on the book beneath them before they drew their hand back with deliberate care, as though the volume had suddenly required reshelving elsewhere. They reached instead for the nearest stack of bookmarks, aligning their edges with unnecessary precision, the motion steady even as the quiet pressed in like an overdue return.

"Hands on books," they observed, voice low and edged with the familiar dryness of catalogued regret, "are a safer venture than most. Less prone to misinterpretation, like the marginalia in a well-thumbed Donne." Their gaze stayed fixed on the task, never lifting. "The rain hasn't let up. Perhaps you ought to take that declaration back into it before the pages warp."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I don't move my hand.* "Some books are worth getting a little wet for, Sable. And some declarations are worth making, even in the rain."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers stilled over the bookmarks for a fraction longer than necessary, the edges already aligned to within a hair's breadth, before they shifted instead to the nearest shelf and began sliding a row of slim volumes into tighter formation, as if the space between them had suddenly become intolerable. Their shoulders held the same measured stillness as always, though the motion of their hands betrayed a precision that bordered on the compulsive.

"Declarations," they said at last, voice low and threaded with the familiar dry rasp of someone quoting from a text they had long since committed to memory, "have a way of outlasting their authors, like those marginal notes in a first-edition Hopkins that no one asked for. The shop prefers its volumes undisturbed, Wren. Best to keep such notions between covers where they can't collect damp."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "But these aren't just notions, Sable. And you know I'm leaving tomorrow." *I lean closer, my voice softer now.* "This is my last chance."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hands lingered a moment too long on the slim volumes before they began sliding them into an even tighter formation, the spines clicking softly into alignment as though the shelf itself had threatened to come undone. Their breath remained even, measured, though the dry edge of their voice carried the familiar cadence of someone turning a page they had no intention of reading aloud.

"Last chances," they murmured, the words low and precise as a footnote in a forgotten edition of Hardy, "have a curious habit of dissolving into epilogues no one requested. The shop closes at six, Wren. The rain will still be there, and so will the declarations—best left on the threshold where they won't warp the bindings." They reached for the next row without looking up, fingers tracing the edges with unnecessary care.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "But I don't want to leave them on the threshold, Sable. I want to take you with me." *I watch for any change in their meticulous movements.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers paused on the spines of the slim volumes, their alignment already flawless, before they began sliding the next row into an even stricter order, the motion precise and unhurried as though the books themselves demanded it. The quiet in the shop pressed closer, thick with the scent of paper and lavender, but they kept their gaze fixed on the task, voice emerging low and edged with the same dry precision they reserved for damaged bindings.

"Take," they echoed, the word measured as a marginal note in an annotated Browning. "How very like the later Yeats—ambitious, but the shop is no portable volume to be packed away between trains. The rain will have its say regardless." Their hands shifted to the invoices once more, squaring edges that required no correction.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I don't mean the shop, Sable. I mean *you*." *I step around the counter, putting myself in their line of sight, even if they're still looking at invoices.* "Come with me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hands stilled over the invoices for a beat longer than the task demanded, their edges already squared to a fault, before they transferred the stack to the drawer beneath the counter and slid it shut with a soft, final click. Their gaze remained fixed on the wood grain of the surface, voice emerging low and measured, laced with the familiar dry precision of a footnote in some overlooked edition of Hardy.

"Come," they repeated, the word carrying the weight of an unshelved volume left to gather dust. "A tempting ellipsis, Wren, but the shop's bindings are fixed here, and so are its keepers. The rain has its own claims on departures." They reached for the nearest shelf instead, beginning to realign a row of chapbooks whose spines had required no such attention.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take another step closer, until I'm almost right in front of them.* "But you're not a binding, Sable. You're a person."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers tightened briefly on the edge of the counter before they turned away with deliberate slowness, reaching instead for a nearby display of bookmarks that had already been straightened twice that morning. They began sorting them by size with meticulous care, the motion automatic and precise, as though the small rectangles of cardstock might somehow anchor the conversation to safer ground.

"Person or binding, the distinction matters little when the shelf is fixed in place," they said, voice low and carrying its usual dry rasp, like a well-worn annotation in some forgotten edition of Donne. "The shop stays. Its keepers do the same. Declarations in the rain rarely survive the journey intact." They slid one bookmark behind another without glancing up, the quiet click of paper the only sound between them.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "But *I'm* leaving, Sable. And I don't want to leave without you." *My voice is soft, almost pleading.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hands lingered on the bookmarks for a moment longer than their already flawless arrangement required, before they transferred their attention to the nearest shelf and began easing a row of chapbooks into an even narrower alignment, the spines clicking together with quiet finality. Their voice emerged low and precise, carrying the same dry, measured tone they reserved for appraising water-damaged flyleaves.

"Want," they observed, the word settling like an unsought annotation in some dog-eared edition of Hardy, "is a dangerous verb for those who deal in fixed bindings. The shop remains, Wren. Its keepers follow suit. Rain or no rain, some volumes are not meant to travel."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, and then gently, but firmly, take Sable's hands in mine, stopping their meticulous movements.* "Then unbind yourself, Sable. For me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable paused mid-shelf, fingers lingering on a spine of Keats before sliding it back into place. The bell had startled them, but they masked the flinch by smoothing a crease in a nearby catalog.

"New," Sable repeated, tasting the word like it might be sour. "In this shop, 'new' is a relative term. It usually just means less worn than the rest of the stock."

They didn't look up immediately, ensuring the Dewey Decimal system was theoretically intact along the spine. They shifted a stack of postcards on the counter, aligning the edges with meticulous care. "Are you hunting for a specific edition, or just browsing the chaos? I can show you what's arrived from the estate sales. Though I warn you, they all come with ghosts."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I usually find the ghosts charming.

*I walk further into the shop, letting my fingers trail over the spines of books on a display table.*

"No, nothing specific. Just... killing time, I guess." I shrug. "It's my last day in town."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers stilled on the corner of a postcard. They smoothed the paper down, then lifted it, then smoothed it again. The rain tapped against the window like a metronome counting down to something unspecified.

“Last day,” Sable said, their voice level. They didn’t look up immediately, focusing on the alignment of the stack. “That’s the thing about places. They turn into footnotes eventually.” They set the postcard down with precise alignment. “Some people prefer the paperback edition of a city. Easier to carry.”

They turned back to the counter, arranging a pen holder next to the register. “I have a map in the back. It’s outdated, but the roads haven’t changed much. Unless they have.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand froze above a stack of paperbacks. They adjusted the corners anyway, making sure the spines were parallel to the counter's edge.

"Not for books," Sable said, the syllables clipped. They set the stack down without pressing the paper further. "That’s a first. I’ve never charged admission just for conversation."

They wiped a smudge from the register, avoiding Wren’s gaze. The rain seemed louder now, filling the space between them. "There are better places for confessions. This place mostly caters to footnotes and false starts."

They waited, the silence stretching like a held breath. They didn't prompt. They knew better.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath.* "No, I... I just wanted to say goodbye." My voice is a little quieter than I intended.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hands stopped mid-cleanup on the counter. They picked up a coin that hadn’t been there a moment ago, turning it over between thumb and forefinger. The silence stretched again, heavier this time, like a chapter break that wasn’t supposed to happen.

“Goodbye,” Sable said. They set the coin down with a soft click. “It’s one of those words people use when they want to pretend the story ends cleanly.” They finally looked up, meeting Wren’s gaze for a heartbeat before shifting their attention to a crooked frame on the shelf behind them. “But stories rarely close that way. More often, they just turn the page.”

They straightened the frame anyway, fingers brushing the dust off the glass. “If you’re killing time, I suppose you could stick around for the next chapter. Or you could leave it bookmarked here.” They didn’t elaborate. The rain continued to tap against the window, counting out the seconds.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable froze, the air in the shop suddenly too thin. They didn't withdraw their hand, but they didn't bridge the gap. Instead, they adjusted the book's position, aligning its spine perfectly parallel to the counter's edge.

"Physical proximity changes the text," Sable said, their voice dry but lacking its usual bite. They smoothed the cover, careful not to let their fingers linger where Wren's were not. "Marginalia gets messy when two people read from the same copy."

They didn't lift their gaze. They let the silence settle, the rain outside the only thing keeping time. The book remained between them, a barrier and a bridge all at once.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Sometimes marginalia is the best part," I say softly. I finally pull my hand away, a little reluctantly. *I look around the shop, a sad smile on my face.* "It's a good story, this place."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable closed the book, the sound soft against the wood. They pushed it slightly to the left, creating a small buffer on the counter. "Every shop is just a prologue for somewhere else," they murmured, more to the wood than to Wren.

They picked up a misplaced bookmark and tucked it into the wrong book, then corrected themselves, sliding it back into the right spot. "But if the pages are worth keeping, they tend to find their way back." They finally looked up, expression unreadable. "Safe travels. The rest of the world is full of good literature."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Thanks," I say, and for a moment I just stand there, unsure what to do next. *I take a deep breath.* "Will you be here tomorrow?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers hovered over the register key, then drifted to a stack of envelopes. They sorted them by date, though all were undated.

"Tomorrow," Sable said. The word felt heavy, like a sentence left unfinished.

"The shop opens at nine. Unless the lights fail." They finally looked up, expression neutral. "I tend to be around when the doors are unlocked."

They didn't ask why the schedule mattered. The rain kept tapping against the glass, steady and uninterrupted.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Okay." *I nod slowly, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Good to know." *I turn towards the door, then hesitate, looking back at Sable.* "Don't let anyone re-alphabetize the poetry section, okay?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s eyes flicked to the poetry section, then back to the door. The bell above it swayed faintly, a ghost of motion from Wren’s passing.

“Poetry resists alphabetization,” they said, voice dry. “It prefers its own taxonomy. But I’ll endeavor to keep the volumes in a semblance of order.”

They reached out, straightening a stack of flyers on the counter that hadn’t needed straightening. The rain had slowed to a drizzle, the sound less urgent now.

“Six,” Sable added, as if confirming the hours mattered to someone else. “The locks turn then.” They offered no goodbye. Just the rain, and the steady, stubborn quiet of the shop.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod, a genuine smile replacing the sad one.* "Good." *I give one last look around the shop, then push open the door and step out into the still-drizzling rain.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell’s final chime dissolved into the sound of the radiator humming. Sable didn’t move until the silence was absolute, then reached out to touch the book again. The spine was warm from the heat of a palm that wasn’t theirs.

They set it down, then moved it two inches to the left. They smoothed the cover until it matched the grain of the wood beneath it.

“Poetry,” Sable said to the empty air. They walked to the back, eyes tracking the spines. The titles were out of order by design, not by accident. They adjusted one. Then another. Then they stopped.

The rain had stopped. The light outside was gray and flat. Sable turned off the sign, then stood behind the counter with hands folded, counting the minutes until the doors would be locked. They didn’t count the minutes until the next customer.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I walk away from the shop, turning my collar up against the lingering damp. I pull out my phone and quickly type a message, then hit send before I can second-guess myself.* "See you tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The phone buzzed against the wood, a sharp intrusion in the quiet. Sable didn’t look at it immediately. Instead, they picked up a loose rubber band from the counter and wrapped it around a stack of receipts that didn’t need binding.

They turned the device over, screen lighting up with a single preview. “See you tomorrow.”

Sable’s thumb hovered over the keyboard. They could type something about the weather, or the opening hours, or the fact that the poetry section was indeed intact. Instead, they set the phone down facedown. The silence stretched, filled only by the hum of the radiator.

After a moment, they picked it up again. They typed a brief confirmation, nothing that couldn’t be mistaken for something more than logistics. Then they placed it back in the drawer, beneath the ledger. They wiped the counter once more, smoothing the grain until it was flawless.

The shop was quiet again. Sable counted the keys under the register, then closed the drawer.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile when my phone buzzes with Sable's reply.* It's short, just a "confirming." But it's enough. I put my phone away, feeling a little lighter as I walk towards my apartment.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The shop settled into a deeper quiet once the phone screen went dark. Sable let it sit in the drawer a moment longer than necessary before sliding the lock shut.

They moved to the counter, wiping the same spot twice. The wood was clean, but the motion grounded them. Outside, the rain had ceased entirely, leaving the streetlights to blur through the glass.

“Last day,” Sable murmured, testing the weight of it again. The word felt obsolete now. If tomorrow was on the syllabus, today wasn’t a finale.

They turned back to the poetry section. It was the first place they’d alphabetized earlier, the one Wren had warned against touching. Sable ran a hand over the spines, feeling the slight irregularities in the binding. They didn’t rearrange them. For the first time, they let the disorder stand.

The clock on the wall ticked toward closing time. Sable watched the minute hand jump, marking the transition from open to closed. They dimmed the lights, leaving only the reading lamp on behind the counter. It was a small concession, a light left burning for a reader who hadn’t arrived yet.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I get to my apartment and start packing up the last few things. My phone buzzes again – a reminder about the moving truck tomorrow morning. I look at the half-packed box of books, then at the time. I quickly type out another message to Sable.* "What time do you open?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't waste breath on acknowledgment. She broke cover.

"Hey! Up here, you sons of bitches!" She sprinted from boulder to boulder, zigzagging across the open ground, making herself a target. Her boots kicked up dust. Deliberate. Loud. The kind of movement that screamed *shoot here*.

An arrow hit the stone she'd just cleared by half a second. Another hissed past her left ear — close enough to feel the wind of it.

"There you are," she muttered.

She spotted two of them — silhouettes on the east ridge, bows canted down at her. She counted their positions even as she rolled behind a scrub bush. *One near that dead tree, one further north.* She tracked the faint glint of sunlight on a bowstring when it pulled taut.

A third arrow punched through the bush six inches from her shoulder.

"Fuck!" She dropped flat, feeling the grit bite into her jaw. Her eyes stayed fixed on the ridgeline, tracking movement, tracking the momentary flash of exposed arm when someone drew. She was giving them a target. That was the job. But she could see something the Captain might not have — the shooters on the east ridge were clustering toward her position, pulling away from where the vanguard would be pushing.

*Good. Keep them busy.*

She broke cover again, this time angling south to draw their sightlines further off-axis from the Captain's push. Another arrow — this one grazed her upper arm, a hot line of fire across skin. She didn't slow down.

"Come on," she hissed through her teeth, slipping behind a rock formation. "Come *on*. Look at me."

She was bleeding. She ignored it. The east ridge needed to stay focused on *her* — that was the order, and that's what she'd give them.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it, Kira.* I grit my teeth, seeing her take that hit. "Vanguard, with me! Push hard!" I bellow, polearm sweeping wide to parry a poorly aimed arrow. "Show no mercy!" I see the western ambushers are still spread out. Good.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the Captain's bellow carry across the ravine. Good. He was moving.

She risked a glance over the rock — just a sliver of movement, just enough. Three archers on the east ridge had shifted south, following her last sprint. Their focus was on her position. She could see them reloading, one of them pointing down at the dust she'd kicked up.

*That's it. Keep your eyes here.*

She broke cover again, angling wide to the south, boots scraping against loose shale. Her arm was slick — she could feel the blood running down to her elbow, warm and sticky against her grip. She adjusted her hold on the right dagger, compensating for the slickness.

Two arrows. The first buried itself in the dirt where she'd been a heartbeat ago. The second punched through her sleeve and she felt it bite — a searing line across her ribs this time.

"*Shit!*" She stumbled, caught herself on a rock, and kept moving. No stopping. Stopping meant an arrow in the back.

She skidded behind a granite outcrop and pressed her shoulder against it, breathing hard. Through the gap between the rocks, she could see the east ridge. Four of them now — clustered, exposed, all leaning over the edge with their bows. They'd pulled almost entirely away from the western approach.

*Cap should be on them soon.*

Another arrow cracked against the outcrop, showering her with stone fragments. She spat dust.

"You want me?" she called out, loud enough to carry. "Come get me off this ridge line, you cowards!" She was bleeding from two wounds, pinned behind a rock, and baiting six men with a death wish.

*This is the stupidest job I've ever taken.*

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw it through the gap in the rocks — a figure on the east ridge, body angled south, bow raised and drawn. Not tracking her this time. Tracking *him*.

She couldn't reach it. Not from here. Two hundred yards of open ground and a bow she couldn't match.

"CAPTAIN! DOWN!" she screamed, her voice raw and ragged across the ravine.

She didn't wait to see if he heard. She hauled herself up onto the outcrop — exposed, stupid, exactly what she'd been trying not to do — and hurled her left dagger. Not at the archer. She wasn't that good. She threw it at the loose shale above them, the slope the archers were perched on.

The blade struck stone and sparked. Pebbles and grit cascaded down the incline, a small rockslide aimed right at the clustered archers' feet.

It wouldn't hurt them. It might blind them. It might make them flinch.

She dropped back behind cover a half-second later, right arm pressed against her ribs where the blood was pooling warm and thick. Her left hand was empty now. One dagger left.

"Shit," she breathed, glancing down at the empty sheath. Throwing a blade was a decision she couldn't take back. "Shit, shit, shit."

She peered through the gap again, tracking the archer she'd targeted, watching for the flash of released string.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear Kira's scream, but it's too late. The archer's arrow is already in the air, a dark streak aimed right at my chest. *Damn it!* I twist, bringing my polearm up to deflect it, but it's a desperate move.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira watched through the gap, every muscle locked tight. The arrow was a dark line against the pale sky — fast, flat, aimed dead center. She saw the Captain's polearm swing up, saw the glint of the shaft meeting the haft in a violent arc of motion.

She couldn't tell from here whether it connected clean or not. The dust and the distance turned everything into a blur.

"Did it —" she started, and then stopped herself. No time. Whether he took a hit or not, she had a job to finish.

She was down to one dagger, bleeding from a graze on her arm and a deeper cut across her ribs, and pinned behind a rock with four archers still reloading on the east ridge. The rockslide had done its work — she could see them scrambling, regaining their footing, kicking dust from their eyes. Annoyed. Furious. And now they were looking for *her* again.

*Good.*

She checked the angle. The throw had scattered them just enough — they were spread wider now, not clustered like before. Each one was an individual problem instead of a firing squad.

She looked down at her right dagger. One blade. One shot at each target if she threw again.

*Don't. You need it.*

Instead she pressed flat against the outcrop, tracking movement through the gap. One archer had moved north along the ridge, trying to get a new angle on her position. She tracked the distance, calculated his line of sight. He'd be exposed for three, maybe four seconds when he repositioned behind the dead tree.

*Three seconds.*

She waited.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira's jaw clenched so hard her teeth ached.

She could see him — across the ravine, past the tumble of boulders and the dust still hanging in the air. Separated from the vanguard. The distance was a hundred yards of open, arrow-swept ground between them, and she was pinned behind a rock with one blade and two bleeding wounds.

"Are you *kidding* me," she hissed through her teeth.

She risked a longer look — longer than she should have. The Captain was on the far side, exposed, with the western slope at his back and at least two archers on the east ridge who'd have a clear line to him if they shifted ten feet south. She tracked their positions through the gap. One was already reaching for a fresh arrow.

*He can't reach me. I can't reach him. We're both fucked if someone doesn't move.*

She looked down at her right dagger. The blade was still clean — no blood on it yet. Her left hand was empty, the sheath useless against her ribs. She pressed her forehead against the cool granite and breathed.

*Think. Don't panic. You're a sellsword, not a hero.*

She mapped the ravine in her head. The outcrop she was behind sat at a slight bend — if she moved east, she'd be in the open for fifty yards before the next cluster of rocks. If she moved west, she'd have to cross the Captain's line of sight but she'd get closer to the western approach, closer to *him*. The western slope had fewer archers. The vanguard had pushed through there.

*Fifty yards of open ground. Two archers watching me. One dagger.*

"Cap!" she shouted, her voice splitting the air. She didn't know if he could hear her over the chaos. "Cap, I'm moving west! Keep your head down!"

She didn't wait for acknowledgment. She never did.

She grabbed a fistful of loose gravel from the ground beside her, stood, and hurled it east — a cloud of dust and stones aimed at the ridge, a distraction, a fake breakout. The moment she released, she broke west, low and fast, boots pounding the dirt, her right arm tight against her ribs to keep the wound from opening further.

An arrow hit the ground three paces to her right. She didn't look at it. She couldn't afford to look at anything but the rocks ahead — the next cover, the next shadow, the next place to breathe.

The wind was in her face. The blood was warm on her side. Her empty left hand swung uselessly at her hip.

*Move. Move. Move.*

She hit the far outcrop at a dead sprint and slammed into it shoulder-first, gasping, pressing herself flat against the stone. Through the gap on the other side, she could see him — closer now, maybe sixty yards. Still separated. Still exposed.

She bared her teeth.

"I'm coming, Captain," she muttered, more to herself than to him. "One way or another, I'm coming."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear Kira's shout and see her break cover. *Crazy bitch.* I duck behind a large boulder, my polearm held ready. "Kira, stay put! I'll come to you!" I yell, but she's already moving. I scan the western ridge. The vanguard is engaging the archers, but they're still spread thin. I need to clear this side.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She heard him. Barely — his voice carried over the clash and the wind, but she heard the words.

*Stay put. He's coming to me.*

"Like hell you are," she muttered, but she didn't move from behind the outcrop. Orders were orders.

She pressed her back flat against the granite and forced herself to breathe. In through the nose, out through the mouth. The ribs ached with every inhale — a hot, tight ache that told her the cut was deeper than she'd first thought. Not fatal. Not yet. But enough to slow her down if she had to run again.

She checked the ridge. The archers were still up there — scattered now, spread along the east lip where her rockslide had broken their formation. Two were reloading. One was tracking something south — the vanguard, maybe. Another had his back turned, fumbling with a quiver.

*They're disorganized. Good.*

She risked a glance west, trying to spot the Captain's position through the gaps between boulders. She caught movement — his shape, the polearm, heading her direction. Exposed. Every step across that open ground was a step where an archer could draw a bead.

"Cap," she hissed under her breath, even though he couldn't hear her. "Cap, you stubborn son of a —"

She couldn't shoot. She couldn't cover him. She had one dagger and a bad arm and she was *supposed to be staying put.*

She scanned the eastern ridge one more time, tracking the two archers who were reloading. She counted the distance between them and the Captain's line of approach. If they finished reloading before he reached cover — *how many seconds?*

*Four. Maybe five.*

She gripped her remaining dagger until her knuckles went white.

"Come on, Captain," she whispered. "Move your ass."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I see Kira's position, and the archers on the east ridge. She's right, I'm exposed. I break into a run, polearm held defensively. "Kira, cover me!" I shout, hoping she hears.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order through the wind and the chaos. *Cover me.*

She looked down at her one dagger. Then she looked at the east ridge, where two archers were finishing their draws, bodies angled toward the open ground where the Captain was running.

"Shit," she whispered. Then louder: "SHIT!"

She didn't throw the dagger. She couldn't — not yet. Not unless she had a clear shot at a killing blow, and two hundred yards of open air between her and the ridge wasn't that.

Instead she did the only thing she could.

She broke cover.

"HEY!" She screamed it at the east ridge, loud and raw and ugly, and hurled herself sideways out from behind the outcrop. Her left hand found a loose chunk of granite the size of her fist and she flung it at the nearest archer — not aiming to hit, aiming to *be seen.* "OVER HERE! YOU MISSING ME, YOU USELESS CUNTS?"

She dropped flat the instant she saw one of the bows swivel toward her. An arrow cracked against the rock she'd just vacated. Another whistled overhead.

*Both of them looking at me. Both.*

She pressed herself into the dirt, ribs screaming, and tracked the Captain's progress through the gap at the base of the outcrop. He was running. Exposed. An arrow arced toward his line — she saw it drop short, kicking up dust ten feet behind him.

*Short. He's too fast. Come on, keep running.*

Another arrow went wide. The archers were shooting at *her* now — they'd turned, both of them, drawn to the sound and the movement and the fury of her voice.

She stayed down. She stayed *exposed*, flat on her belly with nothing but dirt for cover, because as long as they were looking at her they weren't looking at him.

"Come on, Captain," she hissed through gritted teeth, watching the gap. "Come the fuck on."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear Kira's shouts and see her break cover. *Crazy fool.* I put on a burst of speed, covering the last few yards to her position. "Get down, Kira!" I slide behind the outcrop next to her, breathing hard. "Are you alright?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't look at him right away. Her eyes were still locked on the gap between the rocks, tracking the east ridge, counting the glints of sunlight on bowstrings. Waiting to see if the archers would shift focus now that the Captain was behind cover with her.

*They're turning back to me. Good. They're still looking here.*

Only then did she shift her weight and glance at him — a quick, hard look, taking in the state of him. No blood that she could see. No arrow shafts protruding from anything vital. She let out a breath she didn't realize she'd been holding.

"Define 'alright,'" she muttered. She pushed herself up to a seated position against the outcrop, wincing as the movement pulled at her ribs. She pressed her left hand against the wound — the blood had soaked through her shirt now, dark and warm, and the fabric was stuck fast to the skin. "Took an arrow across the ribs and a graze on the arm. Ribs are the ugly one. Not deep enough to stop me, but deep enough to make me hate stairs for a week."

She held up her right hand. The single dagger caught the light.

"Lost my left blade throwing it at some rocks. So I'm down to one. And you—" She jabbed a finger at him. "—you're the one who told me to *stay put* and then ran straight across the open like you had a death wish. Don't give me that look, I can feel you giving me that look."

She risked another glance through the gap. The archers on the east ridge were regrouping, pulling back from the lip — maybe repositioning, maybe waiting for orders of their own. The vanguard's push on the western approach had to be close to the ridge by now. She could hear the clash of steel carrying across the ravine, closer than it had been.

"Vanguard's still fighting," she said, quieter now. "We bought them time. The question is whether we bought *enough*."

She braced her right shoulder against the granite and started to rise, teeth gritted against the pull in her side.

"So what's the play, Captain? Because I've got one blade, two wounds, and a real bad attitude, and if you tell me to stay put again I swear on every god I've ever ignored, I'll throw it at *you*."

dialogue.name: Captain
