dialogue.content: "Easy, Kira, easy." I put a hand on her shoulder, pressing her back down gently. "You're bleeding too much to be throwing blades at anyone, especially me." I scan the ridge. "Looks like they're pulling back. We hold here, let the vanguard do their work. Then we clear out."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira let him push her back down. She wanted to argue — the words were right there, sitting on her tongue like bile — but he wasn't wrong, and she hated that more than she hated sitting still.

She settled against the outcrop, one hand pressed to her ribs, the other resting on her knee with the dagger loose in her grip. Her breathing came in short, controlled pulls. The blood had slowed to a steady seep rather than a gush, which meant nothing vital was hit, but the fabric of her shirt had welded itself to the wound with dried grit and sweat. Every inhale was a negotiation.

"Fine," she said through her teeth. "Hold here."

She watched the east ridge through the gap. The archers were pulling back — she could see them retreating from the lip, dragging their bows with them, melting into the scrub and rock above the treeline. Whether they were regrouping for another volley or breaking entirely, she couldn't tell from this angle.

The clash of steel on the western approach had grown louder, then closer, then *chaotic* — the particular noise of a line collapsing, of men who'd lost their formation and were fighting in knots. Vanguard was in among them.

Kira listened to it for a long moment, jaw tight.

"Your people are earning their pay today, Captain," she said quietly. Not a compliment — she didn't do compliments. An observation, offered flatly. She pulled her left hand away from her ribs to check the blood on her fingers. Dark, but not arterial. She wiped her hand on her thigh. "When they're done, I want first crack at whoever planned this ambush. I want to look them in the eye and ask how it feels to lose the high ground and still fuck it up."

She holstered the dagger — awkwardly, with one hand, the empty left sheath dangling against her ribs. The motion made her hiss.

"Cap." Her voice dropped, all the bite stripped out of it for once. "Next time you tell me to stay put and then run out into the open, just... don't. Either trust me to cover you or don't send me out there. But don't give me conflicting orders while arrows are flying. I'll follow your call, every time — just make one I can follow."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I nod, my gaze still fixed on the ridge. "Understood, Kira. My mistake. It won't happen again." I look at her then, meeting her gaze directly. "You did good. Better than good. You saved my ass."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira held his gaze for a moment, then looked away. She wasn't good at this part — the talking afterward, the words that were supposed to matter more than the blood.

"Don't get sentimental on me, Captain." She flexed her right hand against the dagger's grip, buying herself a second. "I didn't save your ass. I made a lot of noise and threw some rocks. You're the one who ran across an open field with six archers watching you. That's not my fault — that's *your* arrogance, and you're lucky the arrows were as bad as they were."

She paused. Rolled her shoulder. Winced.

"But yeah." She said it quietly, almost under her breath. "Your ass is saved. You're welcome. Write it in whatever report you send back to whoever pays your bills."

She listened to the fight on the western approach. The clash had thinned — fewer voices, more scattered. Either the vanguard was winning or they were dying, and she couldn't tell which from behind this rock.

"Cap." She tilted her head toward the gap. "When the vanguard finishes up, I want to move. My ribs are starting to stiffen, and if I sit here much longer I'm not going to be able to walk. We clean this up, we find a medic, and you buy me something strong enough to forget the last hour." She paused. "Strong enough to forget *you* running across an open field, specifically."



She risked one more glance at the ridge. The archers were gone. The scrub and stone above the treeline were empty.

"They're really pulling back," she murmured, almost surprised. "Huh." She sat with that for a beat. "Either their commander just called it or the vanguard broke through to their flank. Either way—" She pushed herself up, teeth gritted, one hand braced against the granite. "—we should move before it changes back."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I push myself up too, wincing slightly. "Agreed. Let's consolidate with the vanguard. And Kira?" I look at her, a hint of a smile playing on my lips. "I'll buy you the whole damn distillery."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira snorted. It turned into a wince as the motion pulled at her ribs, and she pressed a hand against the wound to keep it from splitting further.

"Distillery's too far. I want something closer that won't require walking across another open field." She paused, glancing at him sidelong. "Your luck with open fields today hasn't been great."



She unclenched her jaw and scanned the ravine one more time — professional habit, even when the shooting had stopped. The east ridge was empty. The western approach had gone quiet, the scattered clangs of steel replaced by the murmur of voices she couldn't place as friendly or otherwise. Dust still hung in the air, thick enough to taste.

"Vanguard sounds like they've got it handled." She began moving, slow at first, testing how her ribs held up under her own weight. Better than she expected. Not good, but better. The arrow graze on her arm had gone numb, which she'd take as a win. "Point me at your line, Captain. I want to see what's left of it before I decide whether your people actually earned that drink or just survived by luck."

She fell into step beside him — slightly behind, instinctively, despite having just chewed him out about orders. Some habits were older than arguments.

"One thing," she said, low enough that it was just for him. "When we meet back up with your vanguard, I'm not telling anyone I threw a rock at six archers. They'll never let me live it down, and I've got a reputation to maintain." She pulled the dagger loose again, checked it by habit, and slid it back. "You can tell them whatever you want. Just make me sound competent."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I nod, a small smile playing on my lips. "Your secret's safe with me, Kira. And don't worry, I'll make sure they know you fought like a demon." I lead the way towards the vanguard, my polearm held ready, just in case.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up right away. Looking up right away would suggest they'd been waiting, and Sable had absolutely not been waiting, thank you very much. They slid a copy of Elizabeth Bishop back between the Bidarts, where it had already been, with the precision of someone performing surgery they distrusted.

"New," they repeated, as though the word were a moth that had wandered in from the rain. "It's an antiquarian shop, Wren. The entire business model is predicated on nothing new occurring. Ever. If you'd like new, there's a Barnes & Noble six blocks east, though I'd thank you not to make me say that twice."

Their hands kept moving along the shelf — straightening spines that were already straight. The poetry section had been alphabetized twice today. A third pass couldn't hurt. It was the sort of task that absorbed exactly the right amount of attention, leaving none over for anything inconvenient.

"There *is* a 1911 edition of *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* that came in Tuesday. Water damage on the boards." A pause, brief and immediately regretted. "Coleridge would have appreciated the irony. He'd have written a marginal note about it and then owed someone money."

Sable finally looked up. Then, because sustained eye contact was a currency they preferred not to spend recklessly, they looked back down at the shelf.

"You're dripping on my floor," they added, which was not remotely the thing they'd meant to say, and was also entirely true, because the floor was original hardwood and Wren's jacket was shedding rain like a dog escaping a bath. "There's a towel somewhere. Possibly under the register. Possibly under a first edition I've been meaning to price for three weeks. The towel and the book have entered into a kind of domestic arrangement I've hesitated to disturb."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I look down at my dripping jacket, then back up at Sable, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Right. Water damage. How fitting." *I shrug off my jacket, wringing it out a bit before draping it over a nearby, empty display rack.* "Don't want to disturb any domestic arrangements."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"That rack was empty for philosophical reasons," Sable said, eyeing the jacket now draped across it. "It was practicing non-attachment. Very Zen. You've set it back several lifetimes."

They moved toward the register — unhurried, because moving quickly would suggest eagerness, and Sable maintained a reputation with themselves to protect. They crouched, lifted the unpriced first edition, and extracted the towel from beneath it with the delicacy of an archaeologist exhuming something that had been buried on purpose. They held it out. Then registered, a beat too late, that the jacket was already hung and the towel had no customer. It sat in Sable's outstretched hand like a small rebuke.

"For the walk home," they said, folding it over the counter edge with more folds than a towel required. "It's still coming down out there. I can hear it scheming against the roof."

The Coleridge was on the desk behind the register, which was fortunate, because retrieving it meant turning away, and turning away meant not having to conduct whatever expression had been threatening to arrange itself on their face. Sable came back with it in both hands and set it on the counter between them like an offering to a god they didn't believe in.

"1911. Boards warped, as advertised. Previous owner either wept directly onto it or kept it on a boat — the provenance is unclear, which for once makes it honest." They nudged it a quarter-inch into alignment with the counter's edge. "It's not for sale to people who drip, but as you've hung up your weather, I'll make an exception."

Their hands, having run out of book, found the stack of unpriced volumes by the register and began squaring the corners. Sable didn't watch themselves do it. Watching would have meant admitting why.

"You've asked about new stock twice this week," they said, to the stack. "You never ask about new stock. You come in, you loiter near the metaphysics section as though you understand Heidegger — you don't, nobody does, it's a confidence trick — you buy a bookmark you don't need, and you leave. It's a reliable system. I've come to rely on it." A pause, into which several things could have been said and were not. "Today you're asking about inventory like a wholesaler. So. What is it you actually want, Wren? Besides the Coleridge, which is magnificent and knows it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The sentence ended. Or rather, it didn't — it simply stopped existing, the way a shelf collapses mid-alphabet, leaving everything after it unsupported.

Sable's hands went still on the stack of unpriced volumes. Then resumed, faster, squaring corners that had been squared twice already. The poetry section was three feet away and had been alphabetized within an inch of its life. There was nothing left in the immediate vicinity to organize, which was a crisis of a kind Sable had no catalog entry for.

"People who don't come for books," Sable said, and their voice came out at its usual altitude, dry and level, which was a relief, because something in their chest had briefly attempted altitude of its own, "generally want one of four things. Directions to somewhere else. A bathroom, which there is, behind the Dickens, and which I'll thank you not to advertise. Shelter from weather, which I'd have understood, it's biblical out there. Or—" They stopped. The *or* hung there like a misfiled first edition, too conspicuous to shelve and too valuable to discard.

Sable picked up the towel they'd folded over the counter edge. Unfolded it. Refolded it along different lines, which was not how towels worked, and produced a shape that was less a towel than an argument against geometry. They set it down.

"Here's the thing." They said it to the counter, which had never once let them down. "I deal in complete sentences. Fragments, marginalia, the occasional sonnet that lies about having a volta — fine. But sentences that stop mid-air and expect me to—" A small exhale through the nose. "I'm a bookseller, Wren, not a mind reader. If you leave it there, I'll spend the rest of the afternoon finishing it wrong. I'll compose six versions. At least two of them will involve Heidegger as a joke, and one of them will be—" They didn't say what one of them would be. They picked up the Coleridge instead and aligned it, again, with the counter's edge, though it had not moved.

The rain kept up its argument with the roof. Somewhere in the shop, a pipe ticked as it cooled. Sable made themselves look up — actual eye contact, sustained, the full reckless expenditure of it — because turning away had stopped being an available option somewhere around the fourth refolding of the towel.

"You didn't come for books," they said. Quieter now. The dryness still there, but worn thin in places, like a dust jacket that had been loved carelessly. "So finish the sentence. I'll stand here and reorganize whatever's nearest, but I'll hear it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I meet Sable's gaze, a nervous flutter in my stomach.* "I came to say goodbye." *My voice is soft, barely above a whisper.* "I'm moving. Today."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The word *today* did the damage. *Goodbye* was survivable — people said goodbye in Sable's shop all the time, usually to books they couldn't afford. But *today* meant the sentence was already in the past tense. It meant the jacket on the rack was drying for a journey, not for the walk home.

Sable's hand was on the Coleridge. They hadn't put it there on purpose; the hand had simply gone to it, the way a drowning man goes to a plank. They nudged it a quarter-inch into alignment with the counter's edge, realized alignment had stopped being a meaningful category of human activity, and left it where it was.

"Goodbye," they said. "Contraction of *God be with you.* The Elizabethans wore it smooth from overuse. Whole generations of people leaving each other, one syllable at a time, until the God fell out of it and all that was left was the going." Their voice held its altitude. Barely. "That's your etymology for the day. No charge."

They pulled the receipt pad from under the register — because there was a transaction happening, or there was going to be, because transactions were things Sable knew how to do. They wrote *Coleridge, 1911, boards warped* in their narrow, precise hand. In the price column, their pen stopped.

"Here's the thing about the Mariner," Sable said, still writing nothing where a number should go. "The whole poem is a man stopping someone who's on his way somewhere else. Grabs him by the arm at a wedding. *He cannot choose but hear.* I always thought that was rude of him." The pen made one small mark — a period, ending a blank. "I've never had the nerve. For what it's worth. The nerve."

They crossed out the price column entirely and wrote, in letters too careful for the word to be casual: *LOAN.*

Then they pushed the book across the counter, and their hand stayed on it one second longer than a transaction required.

"It's water-damaged," Sable said. "Water-damaged things and I have an arrangement. It comes back. That's the entire grammar of a loan — the word *return* is built into it, structurally, like a spine. You can't have one without the other. So." They let go. Didn't watch Wren take it, or not take it; watched the rain instead, which was easier and also unbearable. "It comes back. Whenever. No late fees. I'm not a library."

The receipt pad got squared with the counter's edge. The pen got capped. Sable's hands were out of tasks, which was the crisis again, the one with no catalog entry.

"You said you rehearsed this conversation," they said. Quieter. The dryness worn through now, threadbare, the way a dust jacket goes at the corners. "I rehearsed versions too. Six of them, I told you. None of them was this. But one of them — one of them involved telling you that—"

The sentence stopped. Hung there, mid-air, exactly like Wren's had.

Sable looked at it, dangling. Then exhaled something that was almost a laugh and wasn't.

"There. Now we're even. One unfinished sentence each. Shelved under *F* for *fragment,* pending." They straightened, and made themselves look up, the full reckless expenditure, spent twice in one day, bankruptcy be damned. "The bell above that door rings when someone leaves, too. Same sound as coming in. It lies. I've always hated that about it. Go on, before I say something with a volta."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The hand arrived like weather. Sable felt it before anything else — warmth at the edge of their knuckles, a climate moving in — and every reflex they owned filed the appropriate objection. The hand did not file anything. The hand stayed where it was, on the water-damaged boards of a poem about a man who shot a bird and spent the rest of his life explaining it to strangers.

"Careful," Sable said, and their voice came out at half its usual altitude, which was a betrayal of long standing. "That's how annotation starts. Two people in the same margins. Next thing there's a whole scholarly tradition and nobody remembers who wrote first."

Their fingers didn't move. The gap between the two hands was the width of a page's edge, and Sable was aware of it with a precision they usually reserved for first editions and exit wounds. Somewhere in their chest, the fourth refolding of the towel was revealed for what it had always been: a system of levees, currently failing.

"One of my six versions," Sable said. The counter. The book. The two hands resting on it, neither retreating, which was its own sentence, complete, unpunctuated. "The one I left hanging. It involved telling you—"

The rain kept on. The pipe ticked. The bell hung silent, rehearsing its lie.

"—that I know your footsteps from the bell. That I stopped looking up when you come in because looking up immediately became unsustainable somewhere around April. That the bookmark you bought in March and left on my counter is in the register drawer, under the receipts, and I've been telling myself it's there for inventory purposes, which is a lie of cataloguing so comprehensive even Heidegger would have to respect it." A breath. "That I mind the days you don't come. I don't mind that you never buy anything. I never minded that. It was the days you didn't come."

Their hand moved then. Not away. A quarter-inch — the same distance they'd been moving books all afternoon, the unit of measure for everything they couldn't say — until the edge of their fingers rested against the edge of Wren's, cold from the rain, and stayed there, and did not organize itself into anything more defensible.

"The rest of the sentence stays here," Sable said. "Collateral. You get the ending when you bring back the Mariner. That's the grammar of a loan — I told you, *return* is load-bearing." Their thumb shifted on the warped boards, a motion so small it barely qualified as happening. "There. That was the volta. The turn. You'd think, after years of selling them, I'd have noticed one arriving at my own counter."

They looked up — the third full expenditure of the day, spent recklessly, past all restraint or sense — and did not move their hand.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My fingers twitch slightly at the touch, a shiver running through me despite the warmth of our almost-contact.* "I... I will." *My voice is still quiet, but there's a new firmness to it now.* "I'll bring it back."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The promise landed on the counter like a newly catalogued item, and Sable — who trusted paper more than people, and people more than weather, and nothing quite so much as a written record — received it with the seriousness of an acquisition.

"Good," they said. "Because I keep records."

They drew their hand back. Slowly — the way one withdraws a bookmark from a finished book, with the understanding that the pages will hold the impression of it for a while. The warmth went with Wren's fingers and the loss was immediate and architectural, a wall going up where a window had briefly, recklessly, stood.

Sable turned to the register and took out the pencil stub that lived beside the bookmark — the March bookmark, which they did not look at, which was its own small discipline — and opened the Mariner to the flyleaf. They wrote in the narrow, careful hand: *Loaned. Return expected.* A date. Then, beneath it, smaller, in a hand that pretended to be steadier than it was: *He cannot choose but hear.*

"Marginalia," Sable said, before Wren could ask. "Coleridge approved of the practice — I mentioned he'd have written a marginal note and then owed someone money. I've decided to be sentimental in a way I can plausibly deny later. It's dated. I hold dated things to a higher standard than the undated. Ask any archivist."

They closed the book over the pencil marks like a secret being pressed flat, and then — this was the part Sable had not planned, had not rehearsed in any of the six versions — they came around the counter. The long way. Past the towel, past the stack of unpriced volumes, until they were standing on the same side of the register as Wren, which had happened approximately never, and which left Sable without a counter to align anything against, and which was, therefore, the most undefended they had been in the entire history of the shop.

"There," Sable said. "Proper transaction. One book, going out. One ending, held in reserve. One bookseller, on the wrong side of the counter for the first time since they bought the place." They held out the Mariner in both hands — an offering, again, but this time without the counter between them to make it commerce. "The towel's still yours. It's biblical out there, and I have a reputation for lending things to people who drip."

The rain carried on its argument with the roof. The bell hung over the door, silent, rehearsing.

"One last thing about bells," Sable said, quieter, and the dryness in their voice had gone thin enough to read through. "The same note rings for leaving as for arriving. I've hated that for years — the lie of it. But I've decided, just now, standing here, to reinterpret. A bell that sounds the same for both is, if you squint, a bell that only ever announces *coming back.* I intend to squint for as long as it takes."

They did not move away. They did not organize anything. Their hands were full of Coleridge and their feet were planted on the wrong side of the counter, and for once, Sable let all of it stand exactly where it was.

"Go on," they said. "Before I start alphabetizing you."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My heart is pounding as Sable comes around the counter. I take the book from them, our fingers brushing again. I look down at the marginalia, a soft smile forming.* "I'll be back," *I say, my voice thick with emotion.* *I turn and head for the door, my jacket still draped on the display rack.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Three steps. Wren had made it three steps toward the door before Sable's eyes went, without permission, to the display rack — the one that had been practicing non-attachment until this afternoon — and found it still holding a jacket, dark with rain, left behind in the general evacuation.

"Your jacket," Sable said, and the words arrived before the rest of the sentence had been consulted, which was becoming a pattern today.

But they didn't hold it out. They lifted it off the rack instead — cold, wet, heavier than a jacket had any right to be, the way all luggage is heavier when it's going somewhere you'd rather it didn't — and stood there with it draped over one arm, conducting an argument at speed.

"You keep the Coleridge," they said, to the jacket, to the room, to the space near the door. "I keep this. Collateral against collateral — a balanced ledger, and I've been a merchant too long to let the books not balance. You return the Mariner, I return the jacket. Neither of us keeps anything unless both of us do. That's the grammar. I told you — *return* is load-bearing."

They folded the jacket over their arm properly, squaring the sleeves, fussing the collar flat, the way they'd squared book corners all afternoon, because the hands needed employment and the alternative was standing perfectly still, which had never once been survivable.

"It goes behind the counter. Next to the register. There's a drawer there that's already compromised — one bookmark, March, cataloguing purposes, a lie of long standing — so it may as well have company in its dishonesty. I'll tell myself it's a lost-and-found. I have a box for those. It's a mausoleum of abandonment, everything in it undated and unclaimed." A pause. "Yours won't be joining it. Yours is dated. I hold dated things to a higher standard."

Then Sable took the towel from the counter — the argument against geometry — and held it out in its place. A thin, absurd exchange, towel for jacket, and they knew it.

"You'll be damp," they said. "Damp is survivable. I have it on good authority — the Mariner's entire crew was damp, and most of them managed. Briefly." They didn't elaborate on the albatross. Some marginalia could wait for the return trip.

They stood where they were — wrong side of the counter, jacket over arm, towel extended, nothing left to organize — and the bell hung over the door, waiting to lie to them both.

"And Wren." The name again, unpunctuated, the last of the currency, spent. "Goodbye is a contraction — I told you. *God be with you.* The Elizabethans wore it smooth until the God fell out and only the going was left." Their voice stayed thin and level and readable straight through. "I'm putting the God back in. Just for today. Consider it a restoration. I do good work."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My hand reaches for the towel, but then stops, hovering in the air. I look at the jacket on Sable's arm, then back at them, a knot forming in my throat.* "You... you're really something, Sable." *I take the towel, my fingers brushing theirs again, a spark igniting even through the damp cloth.* "I'll be back for it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"'Something,'" Sable repeated, and gave the word the full treatment — held it up to the light, checked the title page for a false date. "That's not a term of art in my trade. That's what people write in the margins when they mean something else and lack the nerve. I'll take it as a first edition. Unverified provenance. I won't be selling it on."

The fingers had brushed again, through the towel — damp cloth proving a poor insulator against whatever that was — and Sable had not pulled back, which the levees would be hearing about later, at length, in closed session.

"'It,'" they went on, because the antecedent deserved scrutiny too. "You'll be back *for it.* The jacket. The Mariner. The sentence shelved under F for fragment." A pause, deliberate, the kind Sable deployed when a thing needed to be heard properly. "I'm choosing to read the pronoun as comprehensive. All three. I'd advise against correcting me. My cataloguing decisions are final, and I hold dated promises to a higher standard. Ask any archivist. Ask the flyleaf."

Then silence, or near it — the rain arguing, the pipe ticking, the bell hanging in wait. Sable stood on the wrong side of the counter with the jacket over one arm and no surface left in the world to square anything against, and discovered, standing there, that it was survivable. Barely. Which was the most anyone had ever managed to say for the Mariner's crew, and most of them hadn't.

"I don't say goodbye," Sable said at last. "I've decided. It's a contraction with the God falling out — I told you — and I've done my restoration work for the day. Instead I say *pending.* The book is pending. The jacket is pending. The sentence is pending. The whole ledger of it, open, unbalanced, waiting on the return that's built into the loan." Their thumb moved once across the damp sleeve — squaring it, a final time, because the hands would have their way regardless. "You've ruined a perfectly good bell for me, you understand. It used to lie. Now every time it rings, for as long as I run this shop, I'll hear *coming back.* Every customer. Every delivery. Every wrong number of a person drifting in out of the rain. Decades of that, possibly. I hope you're pleased with yourself."

They didn't move toward the door. Didn't open it, didn't hold it. Sable did not hold doors — holding a door was a first move, and the ledger had been balanced with great care precisely so that no first moves would be required. They simply stood there: wrong side of the counter, jacket over arm, the full reckless expenditure of looking, held open like a book to a marked page.

"Off you go," Sable said, thin and level and readable straight through. "The rain's expecting you. And mind the albatross — it's a long poem. Take your time bringing it back. I'm not going anywhere. I never do. Ask anyone."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a watery smile on my face. I turn and walk out, letting the bell announce my departure.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell rang. It was the same note it had rung for every arrival for fifteen years — the instrument's one fluent lie, departure and homecoming cast from the same mold — and Sable stood on the wrong side of the counter and listened to it die against the poetry section, and did the squinting. *Coming back.* It took effort. Sable had always preferred evidence to faith, which was presumably why they'd stocked the metaphysics shelf with Heidegger: to keep the distinction honest.

Then the door was shut, and the rain was a wall, and the shop was Sable's again — which it had always been, and which now read like a misprint in the inventory.

They went back around the counter the long way. Past the towel's absence. Past the stack of unpriced volumes, which got squared once, absently, the way one pats a dog on the way through a room. Behind the register, the drawer waited — the compromised one, the dishonest one — and Sable opened it and looked at the March bookmark lying under its sediment of receipts, *cataloguing purposes,* the lie of long standing. Then they folded the jacket — squared the sleeves a final time, because the hands would be heard — and laid it in beside the bookmark.

Two items now. Both dated. Both pending.

"Lost-and-found," Sable told the drawer, which did not believe them either. They did not close it all the way. A drawer left ajar was an unprofessional lapse. It was also, if one squinted, a door held open — and Sable had never held a door in their life, and could therefore only do it by accident, on a technicality, deniably. They left it ajar.

Somewhere near the metaphysics, Wren had set down a volume while pretending to browse it. Sable found it on their circuit of the shop — shelved spine-in, wrong section entirely, an atrocity — and their hand went out with all the reflexive righteousness of a professional. And stopped. Hovered. Withdrew.

It stayed where it was. The only misfiled book in the building, and Sable let it stand, which was less a decision than a surrender, and they knew what the archivists would say. *A collection is not a shrine.* The archivists could take it up with the drawer.

The receipt — *Coleridge, 1911, boards warped, LOAN, return expected* — went into the ledger. Sable ruled a new column at the page's edge, titled it *Pending,* and entered three lines: one book, one jacket, one sentence. Balanced. Unbalanced. Both at once, somehow, which was the kind of arithmetic that had gotten people burned in earlier centuries, and Sable entered it anyway, in the narrow careful hand, and dated it, because they held dated things to a higher standard, and had every intention of being held to it.

The afternoon went on. The rain kept up its argument with the roof and eventually lost interest in winning. The pipe ticked itself cool. At closing time Sable turned the sign, banked the register, and did not — this was noted in the internal record with something like alarm — re-alphabetize the poetry section a fourth time. The Bishop stayed between the Bidparts, where it had been all along. Everything stayed where it was.

Then Sable stood at the window with the lights half-down and watched the street carry its water elsewhere, one umbrella at a time, and over the door the bell hung silent, holding its one note in reserve.

"Ring when you like," Sable told it. "I know what you mean now."

The shop smelled of old paper, and lavender, and — faintly, near the register, of rain. Sable left that too, exactly where it was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I step out into the rain, pulling the towel over my head. The cold hits me, but I barely notice. I look back at the shop, a strange mix of sadness and hope swirling inside me. "I'll be back," I whisper to the closed door, the words feeling like a promise to myself as much as to Sable.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Through the glass, half-lit, Sable watched the towel make its way down the street — a small square roof on legs, pausing once at the corner, turning back toward the shop for the length of a held breath. Sable did not wave. Waving was a first move, and besides, the glass would only fog where breath gathered against it, and then there would be evidence, and Sable had built an entire career on the deniable.

Then the corner took them, and the rain closed over the space like a page turning, and the shop was Sable's again. It had always been Sable's. It now read like a misprint of itself.

The days after arranged themselves into a new cataloguing system, which Sable did not acknowledge as such.

Closing time crept later by five-minute increments, the way glaciers move — deniably, unposted, a free market keeping whatever hours it liked. Nobody needed to know the market was waiting on one specific customer. Sable certainly didn't, and said so, internally, nightly, unconvinced.

The bell rang Tuesday for the mail carrier, who never bought anything. Thursday for a student wanting a textbook at eighty percent off, which Sable refused on principle and then, thinking of pending things, relented on. Saturday for a woman seeking directions to a restaurant six blocks east. Each time, Sable looked up. Every ring, the full reckless expenditure. This had not happened since April. The levees filed their objections in closed session and were overruled.

The misfiled book — spine-in, wrong section, an atrocity — survived three separate rescue attempts by helpful browsers. Sable developed a speech for it. "That one's part of an installation. Site-specific. It's about absence." Two people nodded as though this confirmed something about antiquarians generally, and shelved nothing.

The drawer stayed ajar. The jacket folded inside it lost its rain-smell gradually, the way all borrowed things lose the weather they arrived in, and Sable noticed the loss the way one notices a debt accruing interest, and did nothing, and did nothing about noticing.

The towel, Sable eventually conceded, had also gone out into the world — loaned, technically, in the general evacuation. They entered it in the ledger under *Pending*, line four, and experienced the specific vertigo of a merchant whose stock had become correspondence. They bought a replacement towel the following week. Then a second one, for the drawer, which they told themselves was for inventory purposes. The lie of cataloguing had developed a tradition now. Traditions, Sable understood, were just lies with tenure.

The *Pending* column held at four lines. Sable checked it more often than any ledger in the shop deserved — nightly, opening it like a book to a marked page, verifying the arithmetic, finding it still balanced, still unbalanced, still somehow both at once. The archivists would have objected. The archivists could take it up with the flyleaf.

On the twelfth day the rain finally lost its argument with the roof and moved on to bother some other city, and the light came in the front window at the angle it only reached in late afternoon, and lay across the poetry section, and touched the Bishop between the Bidnarts — still misalphabetized, still unmoved, still exactly where it had been all along.

Sable stood at the counter with the ledger open and the drawer ajar and the bell silent overhead, holding its one note in reserve, and did not reorganize anything at all.

"Whenever," they told the shop, which was not a library, and therefore charged no late fees, and waited, deniably, the way it always had.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I step into the bookshop, the bell above the door announcing my arrival. The air is dry and warm, a welcome change from the city I've just left. I look around, a nervous excitement bubbling in my chest. Sable is at the counter, meticulously dusting.*

"Hey, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell rang.

It was the same note — the instrument had only the one, that had been the whole grievance — but for twelve days Sable had been squinting at it, and here, finally, was the reading made flesh. *Coming back,* said the bell, and meant it, and Sable's dusting cloth stopped mid-stroke along the spine of a Hazlitt and hung there like punctuation awaiting its sentence.

They did not turn around immediately. Turning immediately would constitute evidence — evidence of closing five minutes later each night, of looking up at every ring, of a drawer left ajar on a technicality — and Sable had standards about the record.

"Hey, Sable."

The cloth finished its stroke. Slowly. With the dignity of the doomed.

"Twelve days," Sable said, to the Hazlitt, before turning. "The loan specified *whenever.* I want it noted for the record that *whenever* has been the longest word in the English language since roughly last Tuesday. I measured it nightly. In the ledger. Which you will not be shown."

Then they turned, and spent it — the full reckless expenditure, twelve days of it banked and disbursed all at once, bankruptcy long since declared and somehow still trading.

"You'll be pleased to know the operation survived your absence. Four rings of the bell — mail, a student, a woman seeking a restaurant six blocks east — and I looked up for every one, which the levees have lodged complaints about in closed session. There was also a misfiled book I defended as site-specific installation art, and a towel that has, I notice—" their eyes went briefly, pointedly, to the door, to the space around Wren, to the general question of weathergear, "—not been returned. Line four of the pending column. I keep a column now. It's unbalanced. It's been unbalanced for twelve days and I've checked it nightly like a merchant and worried it like a psalm."

They came around the counter. The long way again — past the stack of unpriced volumes, which did not get squared, because the hands had a new policy — until they stood on the wrong side of it, which was apparently where the register lived now, wrongness having been rezoned.

"Your jacket is in the drawer. It's been keeping company with a bookmark from March under the pretense of lost-and-found. They've grown close. Two pending items in mutual dishonesty — I'd have hated to separate them, but I've been given to understand that's what loans are *for.*"

Sable set the dusting cloth down on the counter. Folded it once. Stopped. Let their hands be empty, which was possibly a first in the history of the shop.

"I owe you an ending," they said. Quieter. The dryness worn through at the corners, threadbare, readable straight through — Sable had stopped pretending it was a dust jacket weeks ago and had simply been carrying it around open. "The grammar of a loan. Return first, ending after. I'm a merchant. I do things in order." A pause, into which the whole shop listened — the pipe, the poetry section, the Bishop still misalphabetized between the Bidnarts, surviving, unmoved. "But before the transaction, one note on the text. I always thought it was rude of him — the Mariner, seizing a man on his way to a wedding. *He cannot choose but hear.* I've reconsidered. Twelve days gives one the nerve."

Sable looked up. Held it. No expenditure left to ration.

"The bell says you came back," they said. "Was it right?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My eyes are wide, taking in Sable's words, the intensity of their gaze. A warmth spreads through me, chasing away the last vestiges of travel fatigue.* "Yes, Sable," *I say, my voice a little shaky. "It was right."*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira’s jaw set. “East ridge. Copy.” She tested the edge of one dagger with her thumb, then added, flatly, “If they’ve got a runner, I can’t plug both ends of this hole.”

She didn’t wait for a reply. The order was the order. Kira pushed off the boulder and broke toward the eastern wall, keeping her body low, using the scattered rock for intermittent cover. The ravine narrowed ahead, the stone walls streaked with old moisture and loose shale. Bad footing. Good killing ground.

“Oi!” she shouted upward, letting her voice crack against the stone. “Down here, you miserable bastards!”

An arrow bit into the rock beside her hip. Another followed almost at once, higher, close enough to take a lock of hair. Kira swore under her breath and dropped behind a slab. Her heart was hammering, but her hands were steady. Fear was useful. Stupidity wasn’t.

She counted from memory and from sound: six on the east ridge, maybe more hidden behind the crest. Bows, not crossbows—faster rate, less armor-piercing, but in a ravine that hardly mattered. The archers had angle. She had noise.

Kira grabbed a loose stone and threw it hard against the cliff face above her. It shattered into a clatter of chips and dust. Two heads shifted toward the sound.

“That’s it,” she muttered. “Look at me.”

She surged forward again, sprinting for the first shelf. An arrow hissed past her ear. Another struck the ground near her lead foot, and Kira twisted mid-stride, absorbing the stumble with a grunt. She hit the shelf, scrambled up a crack, and kicked a spray of pebbles down toward the ridge.

From above, someone barked an order. Two silhouettes detached from the main line and began working along the crest, trying to get a plunging angle on her position. Kira cursed again, sharper this time.

“Of course they flank,” she said. “Never just shoot, are they?”

She pressed into the cut of the rock, daggers up, watching the lip of the ridge. If they came down the scree slope, they would slide into reach. If they stayed high, she could keep them pinned there. Either way, the east ridge was looking at her now.

Kira tapped one dagger against the stone twice—short, hard signals—and waited for the next arrow.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I push forward with the vanguard, my polearm sweeping wide to clear a path.* "Focus fire on the west ridge! Don't let them flank us!"

(OOC: I don't give orders to Kira, I give orders to the "vanguard" that I'm with)

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order roll westward, meant for other throats than hers. Good. The vanguard had its task. She had hers.

East ridge was awake now, and every bowstring she could hear was pointed at her shadow.

She slid left along the shelf, boots scraping for purchase on damp stone. The cut in the rock gave her a narrow field upward: two archers near the crest, one prone, one kneeling, both working the same slope she’d just crossed. Farther right, movement. More than one. Probably the flankers she’d already spotted, edging down for a cleaner shot.

“Come on, then,” she muttered. “Stop gawping.”

She flicked her left dagger against the wall again. A bright little spark, quick and useless as a beacon.

An arrow answered almost immediately, punching into the stone where her head had been a half-second before. Dust sprayed her cheek. Kira wiped it away with the back of her hand and grinned without humor.

That was one of them committed.

She rolled backward off the shelf just as a second arrow hissed over the lip, then caught a jutting root with her free hand and dropped the last few feet into a narrower cleft. The fall jarred her teeth, but she landed in a crouch, daggers out, eyes already climbing.

Above, a voice shouted something sharp. Not Captain’s voice. One of the ridge archers, angry now. They’d been told to pin the ravine, not chase one sellsword through the rocks.

Kira tested the cleft with her boot. Loose shale, deep enough to hide in, bad enough to slow anyone following. Perfect.

She pulled a second stone from her belt, weighed it, and lobbed it hard against the opposite wall. It cracked and skittered upward with a clatter that echoed like boots.

Two heads appeared at the ridge edge, scanning for the sound.

Kira rose just enough to slash her dagger through the air at them—showmanship, nothing lethal at that range—and dropped back down.

“Still here,” she called up, voice rough. “Still alone. Come get it.”

A third arrow struck near her shoulder, close enough to sting with displaced air. Then another. They were adjusting. Learning her rhythm.

Kira cursed under her breath and pressed deeper into the cut, counting heartbeats instead of arrows.

The flankers were still moving. She could hear them now, careful steps on scree to her right, trying to come down behind the sound of her voice. If they reached the lower shelf, she’d have to fight uphill with no room to dance.

She hated uphill fights.

Kira flattened herself against the rock, daggers crossed in front of her chest, and waited for the first boot to fall within reach.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I raise my polearm, deflecting the arrow with the haft.* "Damn it! Push them back! Don't let them pin us!"

*I glance back, trying to see how the vanguard is holding up.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the wooden crack from the west and the Captain’s curse bouncing off the ravine walls. The order wasn’t meant for her ears, but the meaning was plain enough: hold the line, don’t get pinned.

She didn’t look west. Looking west meant losing the east, and the east was already breathing down her neck.

“Two coming down the scree,” she called, low and sharp. “Behind me. I’ll clear it.”

Then she went still.

The first boot found the lower shelf with a scrape of shale. Kira pressed herself into the cleft until the stone bit through her leathers. Above her, a head eased over the lip—bow first, then eyes, then the nervous tilt of a man expecting an easy shot.

He got a dagger through the shoulder instead.

Kira drove upward, left blade punching into the meat beside his collarbone to wrench him off balance, right blade raking down the inside of his bow arm. The string snapped back against his chest. He yelped, more outrage than pain, and tried to claw her away.

She headbutted him.

Once. Hard. His nose crunched, and his arms went loose enough for Kira to shove him backward over the shelf. He fell with a shower of stones and a curse that ended in a thud.

The second man was already switching to a short blade, using his bow as a brace. Smart. Fast. Too close for a proper draw.

Kira kicked a fistful of grit into his face and took the swing on her crossed forearms. Pain flashed up to her elbow, bright and ugly, but the blade skidded off leather and bone. She grunted, stepped inside his guard, and buried one dagger high in his thigh.

He folded with a wet scream.

Kira twisted the blade free, caught him by the belt, and drove the second dagger upward under his ribs at an angle that would find lung. He gagged, clawing at her wrist, and she used his own momentum to dump him against the rock wall.

“Stay down,” she snarled. “I’m having a shit day.”

He didn’t. Kira finished it efficiently, because mercy was a luxury for people who weren’t boxed in a ravine with archers above them.

Blood warmed her hands. She wiped most of it on the dead man’s cloak and checked the ridge. Four left. Maybe five. The western volley had changed pitch—sharper, more desperate—but the east still held the high ground.

“Flankers down,” Kira called toward the vanguard, keeping her voice flat and useful. “I’ve got eyes on their firing line now. They’re using the deadfall for cover, but there’s a spillway west of the ridge. If someone can get a torch to it, they’ll have to shift.”

She spat over the edge and watched the fleck vanish into the shadows.

“Don’t rush me,” she muttered, mostly to herself. “Rushing gets you killed.”

Then she moved, deeper into the cut, listening for the next bowstring.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I can hear Kira's report, and it's good news, but I'm in a tight spot.* "Understood, Kira! Vanguard, with me! We're breaking through!"

*I point with my polearm, indicating a narrow gap in the rocks ahead, hoping to rejoin the main company.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order carry across the ravine and filed it away: not hers to obey, not hers to waste sympathy on. She had her own killzone to manage.

The gap in the rocks looked narrow from where she crouched, a dark slit between broken stone. Good for slipping through. Bad if anyone above decided to pour arrows or rubble into it.

“Christ,” she muttered, wiping the dead man’s blood from her right dagger on her breeches. “Of course it’s a throat.”

She eased up along the cleft, staying below the ridge line, until she had a sliver of sight on the eastern firing positions. Four archers remained visible. Maybe a fifth behind the deadfall, patient and quiet. The two flankers she’d killed had left gaps in their coverage, but the survivors were adjusting, spreading out, using the rocks as shields instead of standing in neat, shootable rows.

Kira tapped her left dagger against stone once. A soft, deliberate click.

An arrow came down fast, punching into the wall beside her ear.

“Still here,” she rasped upward. “Still annoying.”

Then she turned her head toward the Captain’s voice, not far across the broken floor of the ravine. She couldn’t reach him. Not without climbing into open fire and leaving the east ridge free to rake the vanguard from above.

“Cap!” she called, keeping the words sharp enough to cut through the din. “That gap’s tight! Don’t let them pack the entrance! If you bunch, you’re targets!”

She glanced up, tracking the shift of silhouettes along the crest. One archer had lifted his aim westward, toward the vanguard’s line.

“East is turning on you!” Kira shouted. “I’ll pull them back if I can, but don’t wait for me!”

She drew a loose stone from her belt, stood just enough to be seen, and hurled it high against the cliff face above the ridge. It burst into chalky dust and ringing fragments.

Two heads jerked toward her.

Kira dropped back into the cleft, heart slamming, grin bleak.

“Come on, you cowards,” she hissed. “Look at me.”

She began climbing the crack, fingers testing seams, daggers biting into wet stone for purchase. If she could get ten feet higher, she might reach the nearest archer. If she couldn’t, she’d at least make the ridge spend its attention on her instead of the narrow gap below.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I hear Kira's warning and see the archers shifting. She's right, we can't bunch up.* "Understood, Kira! Vanguard, spread out! Maintain pressure!"

*I push into the gap, trusting my armor and the polearm to clear the way.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira kept her eyes on the crest. The east ridge was already changing its mind.

Two archers shifted their stance, bows dipping toward the narrow gap. Their silhouettes braced against the sky, aiming down into the throat of stone.

“Shit,” Kira breathed.

She jammed a boot into the crack and hauled herself up another foot. Wet stone scraped her palms raw. The nearest archer was six feet above and three to her right, his back half-turned as he lined up a shot.

Kira tore a loose shard of shale from the wall and hurled it at his head.

It missed by design, cracking against the rim. The archer flinched, swearing, and twisted. His arrow went wide, skipping off the gap’s lip instead of dropping into the throat below.

Kira didn’t wait. She lunged up the crack, dagger hooked into a seam, and brought her boot down on his bow arm.

The bow clattered. He howled, stumbling back.

“Gap’s watched!” Kira shouted downward, voice ragged. “They’ve got the lip! Anybody who stacks in the mouth is dead!”

Another string sang from farther along the crest. An arrow punched into the rock beside Kira’s knee, dust bursting hot against her leg. She cursed, rolled her weight back, and slashed upward in a short arc. The wounded archer scrambled behind a fall of deadwood and stone.

Four left. Maybe. One was already bleeding. Good.

The surviving eastern archers hesitated, split between the gap and the woman climbing into their line. Kira saw the moment stretch. She made it worse for them: stamped twice on the shelf, bared her teeth, and screamed, “Up here! Come on, you gutless bastards!”

Two bows swung back toward her.

One grim breath. Then she dropped lower into the cleft, putting the rock between her torso and the ridge, and began working sideways toward the spillway shadow she’d spotted earlier. If she could get under it, she could make the ridge pay for every step.

“Cap,” she called, quieter now but sharp enough to carry, “east is fixing on me again. The mouth’s getting a firing lane. If they can dress their shots down it, it’s a meat grinder.”

She pressed her spine to the stone and waited for the next arrow.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Damn it! Kira, fall back if you have to! Vanguard, push through! Don't let them reform!"

*I put my shoulder into the narrow gap, forcing my way through, polearm leading the charge.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the order and chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted iron. Fall back if she had to. The art was not confusing bravado with necessity.

It wasn’t necessity yet.

“If I quit the wall now, they’ll paint the gap!” she shouted back, though the words were already being eaten by bowstring snap and stone. “I’m still here!”

Then she shut up and worked.

The cleft bent toward the spillway shadow, a darker seam where water had eaten the base of the ridge. Kira kept low, shoulders tucked, daggers reversed in a grip that let her climb as easily as cut. Above, the eastern archers had stopped firing like a line and started hunting like men who knew they had her penned.

Two held the crest. A third was edging left along a broken lip, trying to find a plunging shot into the throat below.

“Not there,” Kira muttered.

She hooked the dead flanker’s cloak with her left dagger and yanked. The soaked wool lifted over the shelf, swelling upright like a man rising into the light.

An arrow hissed down and punched through it with a heavy thump.

Kira was already sideways under the root shelf above the spillway. Old roots roped tight around a plate of loose shale. She slashed at them with her right dagger, once, twice, sawing through the toughest fibers. The shelf cracked dryly.

She kicked it.

The rock face gave way in a ragged spill of shale, deadwood, and dust. It was no avalanche, nothing so tidy, but it crashed across the spillway mouth and threw a gray curtain between the crest and the narrow gap below.

Swearing came down from the ridge. Human, startled, angry.

An arrow speared through the dust where Kira had been standing a heartbeat before. Another followed high and wild, skipping off the far wall with a sharp crack.

“Slide’s choking them!” Kira called toward the west, voice ragged but useful. “East’s blind on the mouth for a beat! If they shift to the spillway, I can’t hold both!”

She wiped grit from her lips and checked her blades. One edge was nicked. The other was slick with blood that wasn’t hers.

Above the dust, a silhouette moved fast along the crest, working around the fall. Kira saw the angle open before the man did: from the next outcrop, he could look straight down into the gap again.

“Christ,” she breathed.

She wrenched a fist-sized chunk of shale from the wall and hurled it at the moving shape. It rang off stone near his boot, spraying chips. The archer flinched, losing half a step.

Half a step was enough.

Kira dropped lower into the cleft as another string sang. The arrow bit into the rock above her head and rained dust over her shoulders. This time she didn’t answer with noise. Noise had done its work. Now the ridge was learning where she wasn’t.

A second head rose at the edge, bow leveled past her, toward the gap.

That was necessity.

“Falling back to the second cut!” Kira shouted, already sliding down the wet seam. “They’re resetting on the mouth! If they get a clean lane, I can’t plug it from down here!”

She put three more paces of stone between herself and the ridge, then pressed into a narrower hollow where the walls pinched close enough to stop a drawn bow. Daggers up. Breathing controlled. Blood cooling on her hands.

Above, the dust still drifted across the spillway. Boots scraped along the crest, hesitant now, choosing between the woman in the rocks and the sounds from the gap below.

Kira watched the lip of the ridge and waited for the first mistake.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Keep moving! Don't let up!" I shout, pushing through the gap. We're taking heavy fire, but Kira bought us some time.

*I glance back, making sure the vanguard is following.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order ring across the ravine and kept her mouth shut. It wasn’t hers to answer. Her job was the east wall, the dust, and the men trying to turn the narrow gap into a shooting gallery.

The hollow pinched tight around her. A bow couldn’t be drawn in here; a thrown knife could still find meat. That made it a good place to bleed quietly. Bad if they decided to drop rocks.

Above, the gray curtain over the spillway was thinning. Two archers held the crest, spaced wide, their heads turning like birds over the fallen shale. A third was lower—much lower—working down the broken slope by the deadfall. Not running. Careful.

“Ah, you bastard,” Kira breathed.

He wasn’t coming for her. He was coming for the mouth.

She shifted her weight, daggers loose in her grip, and eased along the cleft until she could see the climber’s boots finding holds in the scree. If he reached the second shelf, he’d have a plunging line into the throat below. Clean. Cruel. Exactly what the east ridge wanted.

“Spillway!” she shouted, rough and sudden. “One down low, moving for the second shelf!”

The climber flinched, glancing toward her voice. That was the problem with noise: it bought attention, but it also told the enemy where the attention was wanted.

Kira ducked back as an arrow snapped through the space where her head had been. Another followed, high and wild from the crest.

She pressed into the shadow beneath the root shelf, found the tangle of dead wood with her left hand, and drove her right dagger into the thickest root. Wet fibers resisted. She sawed once, twice, then braced her boot against the stone and levered the blade sideways.

The root popped free with a dry crack.

A sheet of shale overhead shifted, loosened, and slid. It wasn’t much—no grand avalanche, just enough broken rock and deadwood to follow gravity’s suggestion. It spilled across the climber’s line of descent with a rasp of stone on stone.

The man cursed, threw an arm up, and lost his footing.

He didn’t fall far. The slope caught him ten feet below, tangled him in a nest of bracken and loose rock. He tried to rise, bow half-snatched from his hand, and Kira was already moving.

She came up out of the hollow low and fast, boots skidding on damp grit. One dagger went into the rock above his shoulder, the other hooking the back of his cloak. She yanked him upright by the collar and slammed her forehead into the bridge of his nose.

The crack was satisfying. Less satisfying was the knife coming for her wrist.

Kira twisted, took the cut along the leather guard of her forearm, and drove her knee into his mouth. He went slack. She shoved him back against the slope, pinned him with a boot on his chest, and pressed the dagger to his throat just long enough to make him stop thinking about fighting.

“Don’t,” she said flatly. “Not today.”

His eyes rolled. He went limp enough that she could tell he was out, or pretending well.

Kira stripped the bow from his grip, snapped it over her knee, and let the pieces tumble down the spillway. Then she kicked a handful of grit into his face for good measure.

Above, the two archers on the crest had stopped shooting at the gap. They were looking at her now.

Good.

She didn’t wait to be admired. Kira dragged the unconscious climber behind a slab—not for mercy, but so his mates would have to spend a moment wondering whether he was dead—and slipped back into the cleft.

Her forearm burned. Blood ran warm under her sleeve. She ignored it.

From the east ridge came a sharp whistle, then the heavy thud of boots shifting along the crest. They were regrouping. One archer had gone down; another would take his place. The dust was settling. The gap below was still open, still dangerous, still hungry.

Kira tested the narrow hollow again, found a seam where she could wedge both daggers and brace her back, and settled into it. From here she could hear the spillway, see the lower shelf, and keep one ugly eye on the crest.

“East is resetting,” she called toward the west, voice hoarse but clear enough to carry. “They’ve lost the low man, but they’ll send another. If you’ve got anything that can throw fire or rocks into the spillway, do it now. They’re threading back together.”

An arrow spat down from the ridge and struck the stone inches from her boot.

Kira flinched, swore, and pressed deeper into the cut.

“Yeah,” she muttered. “That’s what I thought.”

Then she stopped talking and listened for the next mistake.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Understood, Kira! Hold fast!" I bellow, hoping she hears me over the din.

*We're through the gap, but now we're in a wider section of the ravine. The ambushers are falling back, but still harassing us with arrows. I can see a few of my vanguard are down.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the bellow and did not answer at once. Answering cost breath, and breath was ammunition.

East ridge was quiet in the wrong way. Not routed. Recoiling.

She risked a glance from the hollow. Through the thinning dust, the vanguard had shouldered out of the gap into a broader stretch of ravine. Figures moved through the haze, some limping, some not moving at all. Arrows still came, but from farther off, loosed to sting rather than finish.

“Hold fast,” Kira muttered, and spat blood-flecked grit. “Hold fast to what?”

Above her, a silhouette on the crest made a chopping motion. Not shoot. Spread.

Kira’s stomach tightened. They were giving up the mouth to take the flanks.

“Cap!” she shouted, keeping low. “East’s not broken! They’re opening a wider arc! Don’t let them set on the far shoulder!”

The ravine ate the words.

She checked the cleft again. The spillway was half choked, but a finger of loose scree ran down to the ravine floor. Bad footing. Faster than staying pinned while the enemy chose the next angle.

The old order—fall back if she had to—finally caught up with the present.

Kira wedged both daggers into the seam above the shelf, braced her boots, and hauled herself out from under the root plate. The movement tore at her wounded forearm; she tasted bile and swallowed it.

On the crest, a bowstring creaked.

She dropped.

Not gracefully. Boots slipped on wet shale, and she went down in a scrape of stone and curses, using her forearms to brake against the wall. An arrow hissed over her head and thudded into the bank below. Another skipped off rock near her hip. Kira kicked off the wall, twisted, and landed hard on the ravine floor, knees buckling, daggers still somehow in her hands.

Pain lanced up her shin. She ignored it.

The wider section was worse than it had looked from above: broken slabs, shallow drifts of gravel, deadfall that offered cover and fatal blind corners. The vanguard had strung out, but not enough. Kira could see men favoring the same narrow lane through the rocks.

She staggered to a slab and pressed her back against it, scanning east. Two archers had shifted to a low outcrop, trying to get an oblique shot into the column. A third was still high, a dark shape against the sky.

“Left shoulder!” Kira yelled toward the vanguard, voice raw. “Outcrop, twenty paces! They’ve got a lane!”

A rock clattered above. Kira ducked as an arrow sparked off the slab by her ear. She swore, rolled, and came up with a stone in each hand. Threw one high at the outcrop—not to hit, to make them flinch. The archer there jerked back. The second lost his aim.

Then Kira moved.

She didn’t run toward the Captain; running toward him would drag every eye in the ravine onto the gap she’d just warned about. Instead she cut hard right, toward the deadfall and the spillway’s lower mouth, daggers ready. If the east ridge wanted a wider arc, she’d make them pay for every yard of it.

Her boots found purchase on loose grit. Breath burned. Blood from her forearm made the dagger hilt slick; she wiped it on her thigh without breaking stride.

From somewhere ahead, a voice shouted—order, panic, or both. Kira couldn’t tell. Didn’t matter.

She slid behind a toppled boulder and peered around its edge. Three men were working down the east slope, bows slung, short blades out. Not archers anymore. Infantry. They’d expected the vanguard to bunch in the open.

“Of course,” Kira muttered. “Clever bastards.”

She tapped her dagger against stone twice, then once longer. Signal to anyone on her side who understood skirmisher talk: contact, close, east.

Then she settled into the rock, watched the three men pick their way toward the deadfall, and waited for the first one to make the mistake of stepping into her reach.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I hear Kira, but the sound of combat is overwhelming. I can see the vanguard struggling, and the ambushers are indeed fanning out.*

"Damn it, Kira! Fall back to the main company! Don't engage them alone!" I bellow, pushing one of my men forward to take cover.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order and hated it on principle.

Not because she wanted a fight. Fights were work, and work could be ugly, but she was already paid enough for ugly. She hated it because “fall back” sounded clean from wherever the Captain stood, and the ravine floor was anything but clean. Broken slabs, loose gravel, deadfall shadows, and men moving through it all like sheep caught in a dog fight.

Three on the east slope. Bows slung. Blades out. Spacing themselves like they’d done this before.

“Main company,” Kira repeated under her breath, as if tasting the words. “Right. Lovely.”

Her shin throbbed where she’d landed. Blood had dried tacky under her sleeve, and the cut on her forearm burned every time she flexed her fingers. She wiped her right dagger on her breeches anyway. Clean enough. Not pretty.

The nearest of the three infantry raised a fist. The other two halted, crouching behind a jut of rock. They weren’t rushing. That meant they thought they had her pinned between the deadfall and the vanguard’s rear.

They weren’t entirely wrong.

“Fuck this,” Kira muttered.

She didn’t turn and run. Running with her back to armed men in broken country was how sellswords ended up with arrows in their spines and reputations for being clever right up until they weren’t.

Instead, she shifted low behind the toppled boulder, kept her eyes on the three shapes, and reached for the loose shale at the base of the deadfall. Not a weapon. A nuisance.

She threw the first stone hard to her left, against a slab with a sharp crack.

Two heads twitched that way.

Kira was already moving the other direction.

She cut behind the boulder, boots skidding on grit, and dropped into the shallow gully that ran parallel to the east slope. The deadfall arched overhead in rotted ribs of wood and stone. Good cover. Bad if they collapsed it on her. Everything in this ravine was bad if you thought about it too long.

A bowstring snapped from the low outcrop.

Kira flattened herself against the gully wall. The arrow hissed over the deadfall, struck a log beyond her, and bury itself with a dull thud. Splinters spat down. She cursed, sharp and private, and scrambled farther under the brush.

“East outcrop’s still live!” she shouted toward the vanguard, voice rough enough to carry. “Don’t hug the right wall! They’ve got a lane!”

She didn’t wait to see if anyone listened. Listening was a luxury in combat. Men heard what kept them alive and ignored the rest.

Ahead, the gully narrowed between two slabs. A tangle of bracken and loose rock choked the far end, but there was a seam of cleaner stone running west—toward the main company, if the layout hadn’t shifted under all the chaos.

Kira took it at a crouch, daggers up, breath burning.

Behind her, boots scraped on scree. Not fast. Careful. The infantry were following, but not stupid. They knew the deadfall could swallow a man whole if he rushed it.

That gave her seconds. Seconds were currency.

She reached the retaining wedge at the gully’s narrowest point—a rotted log pinned under a shelf of shale, the kind of natural dam that held because it hadn’t been bothered yet. Kira slashed at it twice with her left dagger. Wet wood纤维 frayed. The shelf groaned.

She didn’t look back to admire her work.

Kira kicked the loosened wedge free and dropped flat as the shelf gave.

Shale, bracken, mud, and a spray of deadwood crashed down into the gully behind her with a rasp like a giant clearing its throat. Not enough to bury anyone. Enough to make following unpleasant. Enough to force the pursuers to choose between climbing over the mess or looping wide.

A male voice cursed from behind the spill. Human. Angry. Alive.

Kira allowed herself one bleak grin.

“Take your time,” she rasped.

Then she was moving again, low and fast, boots finding the cleaner stone seam. Her shin screamed. Her forearm throbbed. Every breath scraped. She ignored all three. Pain was information, not instruction.

The ravine opened ahead.

Not safely.

The main company was farther west, a knot of armor, banners, and shouted orders through the dust. Between Kira and them lay a stretch of broken ground: scattered boulders, shallow depressions, and the kind of blind corners that got men killed by friends as often as enemies. Arrows still fell from the east, but looser now, more harassment than hunt.

Kira saw two vanguard men crouched behind a slab to her left, faces pale under grit. One was clutching his side. The other kept glancing back toward the deadfall.

She didn’t stop. Stopping made her a target. Slowing made her a burden.

But she did point west with her dagger hilt and bark, “Don’t sit there! They’re wrapping the tail! Move or get off the lane!”

The able-bodied man flinched, then hauled his wounded comrade up by the shoulder. Kira didn’t wait to see if they made it.

A shaft of sunlight cut through the dust above the east ridge. Silhouettes shifted along the crest. Not firing. Repositioning.

Kira’s stomach tightened.

“Cap!” she shouted, the word tearing at her throat. “East’s not done! They’re trying to envelope from the shoulder! If you’ve got spears, get them facing east now!”

An arrow thudded into the ground a pace ahead of her. Another skipped off stone to her right. Kira twisted, stumbled, and recovered without breaking stride. Her daggers stayed up. Her eyes stayed moving.

The main company’s edge came into view—shields locked unevenly, men shouting to one another, a gap forming where the vanguard’s remnants were trying to fold back in.

Bad.

Gaps got filled with corpses.

Kira veered toward the shield line, keeping her body angled so the east ridge had to work for a clean shot. She hit the dirt inside the company’s edge with a grunt, rolled to a knee, and came up with her back to the shields.

For one breath, the noise seemed to move around her instead of through her.

Then she turned her head east, daggers still in hand, blood drying black on her sleeve.

“I’m back,” she called, voice flat. “East infantry, three strong, delayed at the deadfall. Low outcrop still has eyes. Ridge men are shifting to wrap the shoulder.”

She swallowed, tasted grit and copper.

“If you want this section held, don’t let them bunch at the gap. Give them a lane and they’ll pour fire down it.”

Kira pressed her shoulder against the shield wall, chest heaving, and waited.

Not for praise.

For the next order.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I hear Kira's report, and it's grim. I look at the chaos around me, then back at Kira.*

"Good work, Kira. Get some water. Vanguard, lock shields! Ready spears to the east! We're not letting them flank us!"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hands paused on the spine of a Plath collection, then resumed their work — straightening it a millimeter to the left, then back to the right.

"New in the back." They repeated the words like a catalog entry, as though the question were a title that needed cataloging before it could be answered. "You know, most customers ask what's new in the *front*. The front is where new things announce themselves. The back is where things go to be forgotten or misfiled."



They straightened up, brushing dust from their sleeve unnecessarily, and gestured vaguely toward the rear of the shop with a thumb. A stack of unsorted boxes sat behind the counter, half-open, spilling the accumulated acquisitions of the last several weeks — estate sale finds, a box lot from a dealer in Camden, three crates no one had bothered to unpack yet.

"Somewhere in there is either a first edition of something valuable or a water-damaged cookbook from 1974. I haven't decided which is more interesting." A beat. Their fingers found the edge of the counter and began aligning a stack of index cards that were already perfectly aligned. "It's raining. You walked here?"



It wasn't quite a question, and Sable didn't wait for an answer. They moved toward the back, pausing at the threshold as if remembering something important — or as if they'd forgotten what they were doing and needed the half-second to reconstruct it.

"Watch the floorboard by the Browning. It's not structural, it's just dramatic."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I manage a weak smile at the Browning comment, even though my chest feels tight.*

"Yeah, I walked," *I say, my voice a little rougher than I intended.* "Needed to clear my head, I guess."

*I follow Sable, carefully avoiding the creaky floorboard, and peer into the open boxes.* "Anything... particularly forgotten in there?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable crouched beside the nearest box, the floorboards protesting softly beneath them. Their fingers moved through the contents with the practiced ease of someone who had opened a thousand boxes in a thousand back rooms — lifting, turning, assessing, setting aside.

"Forgotten," they repeated, as if tasting the word. "Everything in here is forgotten. That's rather the point of the back room. It's a waiting room for things no one has decided about yet."

They pulled out a slim volume — cloth-bound, faded to the color of a day-old bruise — and turned it over in their hands. *The Collected Letters of Emily Brontë.* They opened it, checked the copyright page, and set it on the crate beside them with a small, satisfied nod.

"This one's either worth something or worth nothing, depending on whether the previous owner wrote in the margins. People always write in the margins. They can't help themselves. They treat private correspondence like a communal journal."



They glanced up briefly, then back down into the box — a glance that lasted exactly long enough to register the roughness in Wren's voice without appearing to have registered it at all.
