She pressed herself against the wall as you passed, her eyes wide and startled, the tray rattling faintly. Lord Daven offered her a warm, absent smile that conveyed absolutely nothing, and she scurried away.

"One more thing," he said, and his voice lost its conspiratorial edge entirely. What remained was something almost like sincerity — rare enough in him that it registered like a struck bell. "What you did today. Not the terms. The *mirror*. Handing those dispatches to Yuna instead of the Queen — that was not in any playbook I would have written, and I have written many." He paused at a junction in the corridor where the eastern gallery opened before you, long and arched and empty, exactly as he had promised. "I want you to understand what it cost and what it bought. You made an enemy of every soldier in this kingdom who loved Ash. You made a friend of the priesthood, which is worth ten times what you paid. And you gave Isara something she has not received from an envoy in eleven years — the truth, delivered without conditions." He stopped walking and turned to face you fully. "She will remember that when the modifications are drafted. I intend to make certain she does."

From somewhere behind you, carried on the draft that moved through the old stones of the palace like breath through a lung, came the faintest echo of footsteps on marble — the measured tread of the Crown's guard, moving to collect a Commander's sword.

Lord Daven heard it too. His expression did not change.

"Tonight, then," he said. "Dawn comes early, and the Queen's seal waits for no one's comfort." He extended his hand — not the courtier's gesture of the gallery, but something plainer, between equals. "The eastern corridor will take you to the guest wing. I will send word when the draft is ready for your eye."

He turned and walked back the way you had come, his footsteps fading into the ancient quiet of the palace — leaving you alone in the long, arched gallery, with the cold northern light falling through high windows and the distant sound of history being sealed, signed, and entered into a ledger that would outlast every person who had spoken in that throne room this morning.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take Daven's hand, a firm, brief shake.* "Tonight, Lord Daven. Just remember, a mirror can also show an empty space." *I turn and walk down the eastern gallery, my expression thoughtful. The game has indeed just begun.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You press your palm flat against the cold steel of the stairwell door. Feel for vibration. Nothing yet.

Your ear turns toward the seam. Silence below — not the absence of sound, but the deliberate kind. The kind someone holds their breath to create. Your grip tightens on the door handle.

Above you, boots pound the corridor floor. Three, maybe four sets. They're working the floor you just left, room by room. You give it ten seconds before they reach the stairwell.

You ease the door open. The hinge doesn't complain.

The stairwell drops in a straight plunge of gray concrete, lit every other landing by a sickly green emergency light. You scan down. Second landing. Third. Fourth. Empty. The echo of that held breath below hasn't moved.

You nod at Mira. Guide her through.

Your foot finds the third step down before the door you just left groans open behind you. Voices — sharp, clipped, speaking Russian. The stomp of boots already heading your direction.

You pull the door almost shut behind you, leaving a two-inch gap, and you move. Fast but not fast enough to make noise. Mira's arm is dead weight on your shoulder, her broken leg dragging a sound you can't muffle on the concrete.

Two floors down, the emergency lights cut out.

You're in the dark now. Your hand rails the banister, cold and slick with something you don't stop to identify. The voices above haven't found the stairwell yet. But they will. The gap you left is a tell.

Mira's breathing is loud in your ear. Controlled, but loud.

Below you, somewhere past the sixth floor, you hear the click of a door opening on its latch.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Mira, can you manage the stairs if I go first? Stay close." I pull out my knife, flicking it open. The dark is a problem.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Mira looks at you in the thin green glow bleeding from the landing above. Something shifts in her face — not quite trust, but the acceptance of a person who has run out of better options.

"I manage," she says.

You don't wait for more. You descend.

Three steps below her now, knife low in your right hand, blade angled toward the dark. The concrete stairwell swallows sound and light in equal measure. Your free hand finds the banister again — that cold slickness — and you pull yourself around the corner of the fifth-floor landing.

The click you heard repeats. Closer. Seventh floor, maybe. Someone testing a door latch. Slow. Methodical. Not searching — securing. They're cutting off the exits from below while the teams above push down.

That changes the math. The garage isn't clear anymore.

Above you, Mira's drag-step catches. A scuff. Hard to tell how far it carries in the concrete well, but the voices above stop mid-sentence.

Silence.

Then a shout — barked, urgent — and the boots shift direction. They heard it.

You have seconds now, not minutes.

The seventh-floor door opens behind you. Not a click this time — a full swing, hinges complaining, and a slice of yellow corridor light cuts across the landing two flights below your position. A silhouette fills the doorway. Not moving yet. Just standing there. Listening.

The dark between you and them is your only real advantage. The knife in your hand is the second.

Mira's breathing reaches you from above. She heard the door too. She's stopped moving.

The silhouette tilts its head. Listening for exactly the sound she's about to not make.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

You spin. Your hand finds Mira's wrist and you haul her around, not gently. She bites back a cry and you feel her weight buckle against you for half a second before she locks her jaw and moves.

Up. Back the way you came.

Your boots eat the stairs two at a time. Mira's broken leg drags behind her — a wet, scraping sound against the concrete that you can't stop, can't muffle, can't do anything about except keep moving and hate the noise.

Below you, the silhouette reacts. You hear the doorframe creak as weight shifts against it. Then the soft scuff of shoes beginning to climb.

They heard you change direction. Now they know where you are — or at least which way you're going.

You reach the sixth-floor landing. Push through it. The door is open. Yellow corridor light spills across the concrete floor, and in it you see the telltale evidence of your own passage: a smear on the wall where your shoulder brushed it two minutes ago, a faint scatter of dust where boots disturbed the grime.

Above you now — fourth floor — you hear the voices again. Closer. Moving down with purpose. The Russians have found the stairwell.

The corridor on the sixth floor stretches in both directions. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead, casting everything in that flat institutional white that makes everyone look sick. Emergency lighting. The real lights are still out.

You're caught between them.

Your handler's radio crackles once in your ear — a burst of static shaped almost like a word — then dies.

Mira leans into you. Her breathing has changed. Ragged now. The pain is winning.

"Where?" she asks. Just one word.

Above: four flights and closing. Below: an unknown number, climbing, methodical.

The corridor to your left runs toward the building's east wing. You saw the floor plan in your head when you entered — service corridors, loading docks, the kind of infrastructure that doesn't appear on visitor maps.

To your right: the central lobby. Open space. Cameras.

You don't have time to be right. You have time to be moving.

The sixth-floor stairwell door behind you groans open — not from above, not from below, but from the floor you're standing on. The corridor you just occupied, back the way you originally came.

More of them. Working the building like a net.

Mira's eyes find yours. She sees what you're calculating.

"East," she says. Her voice cracks on it. "Loading dock level. I know this building."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Good. Let's move." *I pull her towards the east corridor, moving as fast as she can manage.* "Stay close, Mira."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

You move.

East corridor. The fluorescent buzz overhead is your metronome — flickering, pulsing, casting the hallway in stuttering white light that makes everything look like a photograph developing in reverse. Your arm is a vise around Mira's waist. Her broken leg drags in a rhythm you match to your stride, absorbing as much of her weight as you can while keeping both of you upright and forward.

Her breathing is bad. Wet, shallow pulls that catch on something — fear or pain, at this point they're the same thing. But she moves. God, she moves. Whatever else she is — whatever she's done, whoever she's betrayed — she runs like someone who's been running her whole life.

Behind you, the sixth-floor stairwell door bangs against its stopper. Voices spill into the corridor. You don't look back. You count their distance by the echo — close. Thirty meters and shrinking.

The corridor branches ahead. Left continues east toward the service core. Right dead-ends at a window overlooking the service road below — you catch the view in your peripheral vision as you pass: black asphalt, sodium lights, two vehicles in the lot. No one outside. Either they haven't posted anyone yet or the shift change hasn't happened.

You choose left.

The service core door materializes out of the fluorescent haze — a heavy steel fire door marked with a faded red placard. You hit it with your shoulder while Mira gasps behind you. It swings inward into a narrower corridor, industrial lighting, pipes running along the ceiling like exposed veins.

You pull her through. Kick the door shut.

The voices behind you keep coming but slow. Rounding the corner. Someone barks an order — a single word you don't catch — and you hear boots separate. One set continues down the main corridor. Two peel off toward the stairwell.

They're not guessing anymore. They're working a grid.

Your hand finds Mira's elbow as the corridor slopes downward — a maintenance grade, barely perceptible, but enough that gravity starts doing some of the work for you. The loading dock level. She wasn't lying.

A junction ahead. You slow. Listen.

Through the floor, muffled but unmistakable: the hum of a generator. Ventilation fans cycling. The building is alive beneath its skin in a way the upper floors aren't — machinery, infrastructure, the guts of the operation.

And then — sound. Not behind you. Not above you.

Ahead. Footsteps. Deliberate, unhurried, moving along a parallel corridor on your left. Someone who isn't chasing. Someone who already knows this route and is cutting you off at the pass.

Mira's grip tightens on your forearm. She heard it too.

The footsteps ahead pause. As if whoever it is heard the same thing you did — the mutual halt, the held breath, the geometry of two parties converging on a point neither one can see around.

The generator hums. The pipes drip.

Your knife is still in your hand. You can feel the cold of the handle, the faint tremor in your fingers that you refuse to acknowledge.

The corridor branches again — three ways. Forward continues to the loading dock. Left drops to the service tunnel. Right leads to a cross-corridor you can't see the end of.

Mira's eyes flick to each option. Calculation moving behind them, faster than yours.

"The tunnel," she breathes. "It comes up under the east annex. They don't patrol it."

"Who's *they*?" you ask.

Her jaw tightens.

Before she can answer, the footsteps ahead resume — and they come closer. A shape resolves at the far end of the corridor. Not running. Not shouting. Just walking.

The corridor lights catch something in their hand. Not a weapon. A radio, held loosely at their side.

They stop.

You stop.

Sixteen meters between you. Enough time to think. Not enough time to be wrong.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

The server room swallows you both.

It's a closet, really — no windows, walls lined with humming racks that throw off enough heat to fog the air. A single red status light blinks on every third cabinet, painting the room in slow pulses. The kind of light that doesn't reach far but never fully goes dark.

You ease Mira onto the floor against the far rack. Her leg buckles under her as she sits and she catches herself on the chassis, knuckles white. She doesn't cry out. She breathes through it — long, hissing exhales that she controls through sheer will.

You go to the door. It's standard commercial — hollow core, deadbolt that looks like someone replaced it after the last person kicked it in. You slide a maintenance cart in front of it, then the heaviest rack component you can dislodge without pulling the whole thing down on top of you. The deadbolt won't hold against a determined boot. It'll buy you time. Maybe three minutes.

You listen.

Through the door: nothing. The footsteps that were closing the gap have either passed the junction or stopped to regroup. You can't tell which, and both options have teeth.

You turn back to Mira. She's watching you with an expression you've seen before — on the face of every asset you've ever extracted, every defector who's made it to the safe house with hours to spare before the people who want them dead figured out where they went. It's the look of someone doing arithmetic they don't like.

"Who's chasing us?" you ask.

She looks at the blinking red lights. One cycle. Two.

"SBR," she says. "Special Branch Response. Not intelligence — *enforcement*. They don't interrogate. They retrieve."

"And the ones in the stairwell?"

"The same. But they weren't sent for me." She pauses. Lets that sit. "They were sent to *clean* the building. I'm not a priority. The server room I accessed — the data I copied — that's what they're protecting."

Your earpiece remains silent. Whatever your handler had planned, it doesn't include you barricaded in a server room on the sixth floor of a facility you're not supposed to know exists.

Mira reaches into the collar of her jacket — a movement slow and deliberate enough that she's showing you what she's doing — and pulls out a thin flash drive. No bigger than your thumb. It catches the red light.

"Three protocols. Two of them will collapse a surveillance network that operates in fourteen countries. The third—" She stops. Her jaw works. "The third is why they'll burn this building to the ground before they let it leave."

You take the drive. It's warm from her body.

The door shudders. Not a kick — a knock. Two sharp raps, evenly spaced, patient.

Then a voice, muffled through the hollow core, speaking English with an accent you don't recognize.

"We know she's in there. We know you're in there. We'd like to talk."

Your knife is still in your hand. The maintenance cart holds against the door. The racks hum.

Mira's eyes find yours. Waiting.

Outside, the voice speaks again — calmer this time.

"You have thirty seconds before we stop asking nicely."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
I look at Mira, then the flash drive. "What's on the third protocol?"

The knock comes again, louder. "Twenty seconds."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Mira's eyes drop to the flash drive in your hand. The red light on the nearest cabinet pulses across her face — one cycle, two — and in that rhythm you watch her decide something. Not whether to tell you. Whether you can handle it.

"Twenty seconds," the voice repeats outside. Calmer now. That's worse.

"It's a kill switch," Mira says. "Not for people. For *systems*. Every encrypted channel, every backdoor, every dead drop protocol your people have built into the infrastructure over the last two decades — all of it, writable from a single terminal. One keystroke and the architecture goes dark." She swallows. "Including yours. Including the one that tells your handler where you are."

The blood moves cold through your chest.

"You're saying this drive can blind my own side."

"I'm saying whoever holds it *is* the side." Her voice doesn't waver. "That's why they'll burn the building. Not to stop you. To stop *it* from existing anywhere but inside their walls."

"Ten seconds," the voice says.

The door shudders again. Harder this time. The maintenance cart scrapes an inch across the concrete floor. You hear metal on metal — someone testing the frame, not the lock.

You look at the flash drive. Warm. Light. The weight of fourteen countries of silence sitting in your palm.

Your earpiece — dead for the last twenty minutes — crackles. A single burst of static. Then, buried underneath it, almost certainly not meant for you: a fragment of your handler's voice. Three words. Coordinates or a code or a name you almost catch but don't.

Then nothing.

The door buckles inward by a fraction. The cart groans. Behind the barricade you hear the shift of weight — multiple bodies now, pressing, testing the give.

Mira pushes herself up against the rack. Badly. Her leg refuses and she catches herself, teeth bared, and for a moment you see what she actually is beneath the exhaustion and the pain — someone who has made her decision and is waiting to see if you've made yours.

You have the drive. You have the knife. You have a door that won't hold.

The loading dock is down. The service tunnel is left. Somewhere in this building, the people who want this data — who want *her* — are closing a grid with the patience of professionals.

Your handler's voice echoes behind your eyes: *three words you almost caught*.

The barricade shifts again. The cart slides another inch.

What do you do?

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Tell me the three words." I grip the drive. "Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Mira's eyes narrow. Not confusion — calculation.

"I don't know what your handler said," she says. "But I know what a dead channel sounds like when someone's piggybacking on it." She glances at your earpiece. "That wasn't a broken transmission. That was someone *jamming* it. Deliberately. They wanted you to hear a fragment — nothing more."

Your jaw tightens. The drive presses into your palm.

"Five seconds," the voice outside says.

Behind the barricade, the cart shifts again. You hear the scrape of something heavy against concrete — a tool, maybe, or a boot finding purchase. They're not rushing. They don't need to. They know what a hollow-core door is worth.

The second rack to your left catches your eye. You noticed it when you entered but dismissed it — a maintenance panel, slightly ajar, dust undisturbed around the edges. Nobody's opened it recently. But the conduit running behind it is wide enough for a person if you're not concerned with comfort.

You cross the room in three steps and pull the panel free. Cold air breathes out from behind it — recycled, stale, but *moving*. A ventilation shaft. Old building infrastructure, probably predating whatever this facility has become.

"The words," Mira says from behind you, reading your shift in focus. "You don't need them. You need *out*."

"Zero," the voice says.

The door splinters inward. Not fully — the cart holds — but the deadbolt rips free of the frame with a sound like a gunshot, and through the gap you see hands. Arms. A shoulder bracing for the next hit.

The vent opening yawns behind you. It's tight — too tight for two people at once. Mira's leg makes it worse. But it's there, and it's dark, and darkness is the only thing you've had on your side all night.

The door takes another hit. The cart slides two inches.

Mira is already looking at the vent. She looks at you. Her face says: *decide*.

Your knife catches the red light. Your grip on the drive tightens until the edges bite into your skin.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Go," I order, pushing her towards the vent. "Now. I'll cover you."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Mira doesn't argue. She doesn't waste a second on gratitude or protest. She moves.

You haul her up to the vent opening — her hands find the lip of the conduit, fingers gripping the dusty metal edge, and she pulls herself in with the mechanical efficiency of someone who's crawled through worse. Her broken leg catches on the frame and she hisses through her teeth, but she doesn't stop. She drags it after her like luggage, her body folding into the tight space with the desperate flexibility of prey that has learned what survival requires.

The vent swallows her up to the waist. Then the chest. She's moving — you can hear her hands and knees on the sheet metal, the rasp of her jacket against the conduit walls, receding into the dark.

The door splits down the middle.

Not the frame — the *hollow core itself*, shearing along the grain like balsa. The maintenance cart lurches forward six inches and stops against the far rack. Through the gap, two arms push through, gloved, then a shoulder, then a face — goggles, not a mask, reflective lenses that catch the red light and throw it back at you in twin points of crimson.

You don't see the weapon until it clears the gap. Compact. Suppressed. Professional.

You kick the cart.

It goes forward with a sound like a garbage bin hitting a dumpster, slamming into the gap and catching the intruder at the shoulder, driving them back. The shot goes wide — you hear it more than see it, a pneumatic *thip* that punches a dimple into the far wall where your head was a half-second earlier.

The cart holds for one more heartbeat.

You turn. The vent yawns behind you. Mira is gone — swallowed into the dark — and you can hear her moving, maybe five meters in, maybe more, the sound of a body navigating a space too small for it.

The cart groans. Metal screams against concrete. Someone on the other side has a pry bar now.

You look at the vent. You look at the door.

The drive sits in your left hand. The knife in your right.

You don't get both.

The pry bar finds a new angle. The cart tips. Through the gap you see three shapes now, arranged with the patience of people who have done this before. The one in front raises the suppressed pistol again, sighting through the gap, sweeping the room.

You slide.

Not graceful — your hip hits the lip of the vent opening hard enough to bruise, and the drive nearly leaves your hand. You catch it against the metal edge with your fingers and twist your body into the conduit. It's tighter than you thought. Your shoulders scrape both walls. The knife catches on the frame and you have to angle it flat against your chest to clear through.

Behind you, the cart overturns. The door swings wide. Light floods the server room — white now, not red, someone has cut power to the racks from the outside — and you hear boots on concrete, fast, professional.

The vent opening is six feet behind you. If they look up, they see it.

You press yourself flat against the conduit floor. The metal is cold and dust cakes into your palms. You hold your breath and listen.

Mira's breathing echoes somewhere ahead — thin, ragged, the wet cadence of someone whose body is running out of ways to compensate. She's moving slower now. The leg.

Footsteps in the room. Two, three sets. Someone speaks — clipped, that accent again. The reply is sharper. An order.

Silence.

Then, beneath you — not in the room, but in the building itself — the sound changes. The generator's hum shifts pitch, deeper, and you feel it through the metal: the facility is powering something down. Or up. Something on a timer.

A burst of static in your earpiece. Clean this time. Not fragmented.

Your handler's voice, barely above a whisper:

*"Rook, east annex. Surface in four. We're losing you either way."*

The transmission cuts.

In the room behind you, someone says a word you do recognize.

Then footsteps — directly beneath the vent opening.

They're looking up.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I press myself harder against the cold metal, my heart hammering. "Mira, you hear that? Surface in four!" I try to move, scraping my elbows against the tight space, trying to put more distance between me and the vent opening.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Your whisper bounces off the conduit walls and dies three feet from your lips. The shaft is too tight, too close, too full of your own ragged breathing to carry anything clearly.

Ahead, Mira stops.

You see it happen in the dark — or rather, you *feel* it, the vibration of her movement ceasing against the sheet metal like a river going still around a stone. Two seconds. Three. Then her voice reaches you, barely more than the exhalation of someone in pain, carrying a single syllable that isn't a word at all. Just acknowledgment.

She heard you. She heard the footsteps beneath you.

You move. Elbows scraping the corrugated floor, knees finding the seams between panels, the drive clutched against your chest so tightly your fingers have gone numb. Behind you — close, *close* — the sound of someone climbing. Not into the vent. Not yet. A scrape of gloved hand against the lip of the opening. Testing. Feeling the edges.

Then a voice, muffled, from the room below: *"—shaft access, east corridor junction."* They've found the panel. They know where this leads.

The generator's hum deepens further beneath you. The metal vibrates in a new rhythm — a countdown cadence you feel in your teeth. Whatever the facility is doing, it's committing to it now.

Mira's breathing ahead of you changes. Shorter pulls. A grunt swallowed too late. You hear her body hit something — a bend, an intersection, a junction in the conduit — and the sound she makes tells you it's not a choice she's made but an obstacle she's hit.

You close the distance. Three meters. Two. The dark is absolute here — no red light, no fluorescent buzz, nothing but the recycled air and the smell of dust and old copper wiring.

Your hand finds her boot. She flinches.

"It goes down," she says. "The vent drops to a junction box. I can't — my leg won't —"

Behind you, from the vent opening, a new sound. Not footsteps. Something worse. The electronic chirp of a thermal imaging unit powering on.

They're not going in after you. They're reading you through the metal.

A burst of static in your earpiece. Your handler, louder now, urgency bleeding through the compression:

*"Rook. Four minutes. They're triangulating. Move."*

Mira's hand finds your wrist in the dark. Her grip is iron.

The drop she mentioned yawns ahead — you feel the absence of floor with your free hand, cold air rising from below. The junction box. If she's right about the geometry, it feeds into the east annex substructure. Four minutes. Four floors. One broken leg.

Behind you, the chirp repeats. Closer to your position by a meter or more.

The drop waits.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it, Mira.* "Can you brace on me?" I try to get a better look at the drop. "How far down?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

Mira's grip shifts on your wrist — not away, but *around* — her fingers threading through yours with a precision that speaks to training you haven't asked about yet. Her other hand finds your shoulder, digs in.

"Brace," she says. It's not a request.

You feel her weight transfer onto you. Not gently. She trusts her arms to hold while your legs do the work of anchoring you both in a shaft barely wider than your torso. Her breathing is hot against your neck, close, controlled through sheer willpower.

You extend your free hand into the dark below.

One meter. The air changes — cooler, moving, with a faint metallic smell that says ductwork junction. Two meters — your fingertips find the lip of the junction box. Sheet metal, cold, and below that a vertical drop into what sounds like a larger cavity. You tap the edge. The sound returns hollow and distant, which means space. Maybe four meters to the floor.

Four meters. In a shaft this tight. With a broken leg.

Behind you — closer now — the thermal unit chirps a third time. Then a voice, sharp and satisfied, echoing up the conduit: *"Two contacts. Junction point, sixty meters."* They're reading you. Not just finding you — *counting* you.

The generator's hum shifts again. The vibration in the metal beneath your knees changes register — a deeper, more insistent frequency. Whatever timer this building is running, it doesn't have much left.

Mira feels the change too. You feel it through her hands.

"Four minutes," you say.

She nods against your neck. You feel the motion more than see it.

"Then we do this fast." She releases your shoulder, reaches into the dark beside her, and finds the junction box edge herself. Her fingers wrap the lip. "I go down first. You follow. If I can't walk at the bottom, you drag me. You don't stop. You don't wait. You understand?"

The voice behind you, from the room they've taken, carries up the shaft in clipped fragments — an instruction about cutting power to the east wing.

Your handler's voice cuts through the static one more time, barely there:

*"Three minutes, Rook. Surface, east annex. Do not engage."*

Mira's hand squeezes yours once. Then she swings her body over the edge of the drop.

For a moment she hangs there — one hand on the junction lip, your grip on her wrist the only thing between her and a four-meter fall. Her face is close to yours in the dark. She doesn't look afraid. She looks *resolved*.

"Don't wait," she says again. Then her fingers open.

She drops.

The sound she makes on impact is short — a grunt, a scrape of boot against metal, and then a ragged exhale that echoes up the shaft to you. She doesn't scream. She doesn't call out. But the quality of that exhale tells you everything: she hit the bottom and the leg cost her something.

Four minutes.

Three.

Behind you, the thermal chirp sounds again — and the voice that follows it is no longer reporting. It's commanding.

You look down into the dark where Mira vanished.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it, Mira.* I don't hesitate. I drop after her, landing hard on the metal floor of the junction box. "You good?" I hiss, already looking for the way out.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
**Narrator:**

You hit the metal floor and your knees buckle — you catch yourself on one hand, the drive still locked against your chest, the knife still in your fist. The impact rattles up through your spine and for one sharp second the world narrows to the white flash of pain behind your eyes.

Then you hear Mira.

She's ten feet away, half-dragged, half-crawled across the junction box floor. She's on her back against a support strut, both hands pressed to her left thigh above the knee. Her breathing is the sound you've been dreading — wet, shallow, *wrong*. Not the wrongness of exertion. The wrongness of something structural that has given way.

"I'm fine," she says. Her voice doesn't match the word. It comes out through clenched teeth, thin and reedy, stripped of everything except the effort of speech.

She's not fine.

You scan the junction box. It's a cathedral of ductwork compared to the shaft you just fell through — maybe six meters across, ceiling three meters up, crisscrossed with pipes and cable trays. Two exits. One runs straight ahead, a rectangular tunnel wide enough to walk through, marked with a faded stencil: **EAST ANNEX — SUBLEVEL**. The other drops to a crawl space you don't like.

Straight ahead. You go to Mira.

Above you, through the junction opening, the thermal unit chirps again — close now. Seconds away from someone following you down.

You hook your arm under Mira's shoulders. She helps as much as she can, which is not much — her hands grip your jacket and her jaw is set so tight you can see the muscles standing out in her neck. You haul her upright. Her left leg hangs wrong. She doesn't look at it.

"The tunnel," she gasps. "Keep going."

Two minutes, maybe less. The generator's hum pulses beneath the floor plates — rhythmic now, unmistakably a countdown of some kind. The air has changed. Sharper. Cleaner. The smell of something chemical you can't place.

You move. Mira against your side, her weight a constant downward pull, her broken leg a drag anchor on the metal grating. Every step sends a spike of feedback through her body that she swallows with a hiss you feel more than hear.

Fifty meters. Sixty. The tunnel straightens and you can see it — not light, exactly, but a *change* in the dark ahead. An opening. Air moving with purpose against your face, carrying something that smells like night.

The tunnel walls narrow. Then widen. Then you see the end of it: a rusted bulkhead door, no lock, handle at waist height.

Your earpiece static. Your handler, clear as glass, the calm of someone who has already accepted one outcome and is narrating the other:

*"Rook. Ninety seconds. Whatever happens now — do not come back."*

The bulkhead is two meters away.

Behind you — back in the tunnel — you hear the first footsteps drop into the junction box.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push Mira ahead of me, shoving her through the bulkhead. "Go! Go! Go!" I grab the handle, ready to pull it shut behind me.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease the stairwell door open with your shoulder. Slow. The hinges cooperate — someone oiled them recently, which means someone uses this route, which means someone might be using it now.

You lean over the railing and listen.

Footsteps. Below you. Two sets, maybe three, moving up with the unhurried rhythm of people who know the building is sealed. Boots on concrete. You count the echo between flights — they're two floors down, climbing at a sweep pace. Thirty seconds, maybe forty, before they reach this landing.

Above you: nothing. The upper floors went quiet when the alarm started, which is its own kind of wrong.

Mira watches your face while you listen. She reads something there.

"Tell me," she says.

The radio in your ear crackles — one burst, two seconds of static, then a voice that isn't your handler's. Too distorted to make out words. Then silence again. Someone is on your channel. Someone close enough to bleed into it.

The stairwell smells like dust and cold air from the garage below. Somewhere beneath the footsteps, deeper down, you can hear the hydraulic sigh of the garage door mechanism. Cars moving. The net is tightening from the bottom up.

The boots keep climbing. Twenty-five seconds now.

Mira shifts her weight off her bad leg and waits for you to decide.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Up," I hiss. *I point to the roof access.* "Now." I pull Mira with me, keeping an ear on the boots below.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You go up.

Mira doesn't argue. She hooks her arm tighter around your shoulders and finds the rhythm — good leg, drag, good leg, drag. Her breath stays quiet. Controlled. She's done something like this before.

Below you, the boots stop.

You freeze. Mira feels it and halts mid-step, her bad leg hovering over the next stair. The stairwell holds its breath with you.

Then a radio crackles below — a low voice, too muffled to catch — and the boots resume. Faster. The unhurried sweep is gone. They're running now. Maybe they heard the door. Maybe someone on the net just told them where to look. Doesn't matter. Three voices, call-and-response, bouncing off the concrete.

Two flights to the roof. Mira doesn't wait for you to carry her — she grabs the railing and hauls herself up one-handed, teeth bared, and you take the stairs two at a time with a hand under her elbow. Her bad leg bucks on the landing. She stifles the sound against your shoulder.

The roof access door: steel, push-bar, a stenciled sign — ROOF ACCESS — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY — and beside it, a keypad. Glowing red.

Of course there's a keypad.

Mira reaches the landing behind you, breathing hard through her nose. She looks at the lock. Looks at you.

"Tell me you have a code."

The boots round the flight below. Fifteen seconds, maybe less. The keypad blinks. Red. Red. Red. Through the door, faintly, you can hear wind — open air, the roof, whatever is or isn't up there waiting.

Your earpiece hisses again. That same wrong voice, closer to clear this time. It says one word before it cuts out.

It says your name.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You're already moving up — but up ends here, at this door, this red light.

You hit the push-bar with your shoulder. It gives a centimeter and stops. Locked. The keypad blinks at you. Red. Red.

Below, the boots reach the landing you cleared ten seconds ago. A flashlight beam cuts up through the stairwell, sweeping the railings, hunting.

Mira pushes off the wall. "Move."

She slides past you to the keypad and her fingers don't hesitate — four digits, a pause, two more. "They processed me through the roof," she says. "Helicopter. Three days ago. I memorized it in case they ever brought me back."

The light goes green.

You shove the door open and the night takes you — wind, cold, the smell of rain on gravel. You pull Mira through and ease the door shut just as the boots hit the top flight. The lock clicks home. On the other side: shouting, a fist hammering steel. Muffled. Someone else's problem, for the next two minutes at least.

The roof stretches out in front of you. HVAC housings like squat metal bunkers. A blinking aircraft-warning light on the mast. The city spread below in orange grids, indifferent. No helicopter. No fire escape that you can see. The neighboring building crouches one story lower, separated by a six-foot gap of open air.

Mira limps to the ledge and looks down, then across. She says nothing. Her face says enough.

Your earpiece crackles. That voice again — clearer every time, like it's walking toward you through the static. It says, "Rooftop. Good." A pause. Static chews the edges of the words. "Now don't move."

And somewhere above the wind, faint but rising, you hear it — the low, rhythmic thump of rotor blades.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Don't move? That's rich." I look at Mira, then the gap. "Can you make that jump?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira looks at the gap the way a surgeon looks at a wound.

"Six feet across, one story down." A beat. "The jump isn't the problem. The landing is." She tests the bad leg — it takes maybe half her weight before it trembles. "You go first. Somebody has to be standing on that side to catch me."

Then the helicopter crests the roofline.

It comes up over the far edge like something surfacing from deep water — dark belly, running lights off, rotor wash pressing the gravel dust down in widening rings. A searchlight snaps on, white and brutal, and starts to sweep.

Your earpiece and the helicopter's loudspeaker speak at the same time, half a second out of sync:

*"I said don't move."*

The voice is the helicopter. It has been the helicopter all along.

Mira's face changes. "That's the bird that brought me in," she shouts over the rising noise. "Same tail. No markings."

Behind you, the keypad on the roof door beeps — once, twice — and the lock disengages with a heavy clunk. The door swings inward an inch and the wind grabs it. A gloved hand comes through the gap, feeling for the frame.

The searchlight finds the HVAC housing thirty feet to your left and begins walking toward you, unhurried. The helicopter sideslips to cut the angle, and the rotor wash shoves at your back like an open hand.

Mira grips your sleeve. "Listen to me. On this roof, in that light, we're done. On *that* roof—" she jabs a finger across the gap "—they can't set down. Too many vents, no clearance. They'd have to come down through the building like everyone else."

The door opens wider. A shout from the stairwell, almost lost under the rotors. The light is twenty feet out and closing.

Mira plants her good leg at the ledge, hair whipping across her face, and holds up her hand — not for help. For a countdown.

"On three," she says. "Or don't. But decide now."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
There is no server room up here. The nearest thing is a concrete blockhouse between the HVAC units — ELEVATOR MACHINERY in flaking stencil — and it has a door, and a door is what you need.

You get Mira inside and set her down against the motor housing. The room is tight and loud with the building's pulse: cable drums, a control cabinet, breaker panels, a folded maintenance ladder bolted to the wall, a fire extinguisher. You shoulder the door shut and drag a spool of coax across it, then the tool cabinet, metal shrieking on concrete. It won't hold a breach. It will hold a minute.

Mira catches her breath. "A box," she says. "You picked a box."

The searchlight finds the blockhouse and holds. White light bleeds through the door seams. The rotor wash presses down on the roof like weather.

Your earpiece: *"I said don't move."* Dry. Almost amused. *"But fine."*

Then, across the gravel: the stairwell door bangs open. Boots — three pairs, spreading out in a sweep. You hear them checking behind the HVAC housings, one by one. Methodical. Getting closer.

The voice again, quieter now, like it's leaning in: *"There's a hatch in the floor. By your left foot."*

There is. A square steel panel with a recessed ring handle, half-hidden under a coil of cable. Mira follows your eyes. She limps over, crouches, hooks the ring — it rises on oiled hinges, and the smell that comes up is machine oil and cold moving air. The shaft. Cables drop away into black; far below, a sliver of light where the car sits at lobby level. Rungs descend the shaft wall into the dark.

Mira looks up at you. "Down into the building they're sweeping," she says. "Or we stay in the box."

A fist hits the door. Once. Testing. The tool cabinet shifts an inch.

"Well," Mira says. "You wanted time to think."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look at the hatch, then at the door. "This hatch. Where does it go?" *I try to remember the building schematics.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You close your eyes for half a second and pull up the schematics — the ones you memorized three days ago in a hotel room, the ones you hoped you wouldn't need.

This is a traction shaft, single car, serving all floors. Lobby at the bottom, where the car sits now, glowing. But shafts don't stop at the lowest landing — there's a pit beneath, four feet of clearance for the buffer springs. And this building's pit sits at garage level. The same garage where the hydraulic doors keep sighing open. The same garage the net is tightening around.

But between here and there: shaft doors on every floor. Including the service level — the tunnel level, three floors below where you started, the route you gave up when you ran up instead of down. Shaft doors aren't meant to open from inside, but they're meant to *be opened* — by technicians, by firefighters, by anyone who knows where the release sits. You know where the release sits.

"The shaft runs past every floor," you say. "Including the service tunnel level."

Mira's eyes narrow. "The tunnel they think we can't reach because they're sweeping the stairs." She almost smiles. It doesn't reach her eyes. "One problem. *He* told us about this hatch." She taps her ear. "Your friend in the helicopter. Why does the man with the searchlight want us off this roof?"

Fair question. No good answer.

The fist hits the door again — twice now, rhythmically, then a shoulder. The tool cabinet groans another inch across the concrete. Through the gap you can see the searchlight's glare and a slice of moving shadow. A voice outside, close, muffled by steel: "Blockhouse. Stack up."

Your earpiece crackles. The voice is patient. *"They're going to breach in about forty seconds. The rungs go down to the second floor, then they stop — shaft wall's smooth after that. You'll have to drop the last eight feet onto the car, or pry the second-floor doors from the rungs. Your call."* A pause. Static. *"I'd hurry."*

Mira hauls herself upright on her good leg and looks down into the dark, then at you. The rungs gleam faintly, descending out of sight. Somewhere far below, the elevator car hums at lobby level, oblivious.

"Down into the building," she says. "Past the sweep. Into the tunnel." She grips the hatch frame. "Or we open that door and take our chances with three of them and a helicopter."

The cabinet shifts again. A boot wedges into the gap.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I grab the fire extinguisher off the wall.* "Okay, here's the plan." I look at the hatch, then at Mira. "You go first. I'll cover you."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't argue. She never does.

She swings her good leg over the hatch rim, finds the first rung, and lowers herself into the dark. Her arms do the work. The bad leg hangs, toes brushing the rungs for balance, and she descends the way she does everything — controlled, quiet, jaw set. The shaft swallows her to the shoulders, then the crown of her head, then she's a shape below you, the rungs ticking softly under her grip.

Behind you, the breach comes.

The tool cabinet goes over with a crash. The door slams open to the width of the spool and the searchlight pours in — and you're already squeezing the trigger. The extinguisher answers with a horn-blast, a whiteout of chemical fog, and the light through the doorway goes diffuse and useless. Someone outside barks a word that dies in a cough. You hear a safety click off — and then nothing. They want her breathing. Nobody fires into a cloud they can't see through.

You go through the hatch backward, feet finding rungs, and the last thing you see above the fog line is the searchlight holding on the blockhouse like a fingertip. Then the floor passes over your head and the rotor noise dims, muffled by concrete. For the first time since the roof, the wind is gone.

The shaft breathes cold air up past you. Machine oil. The hum of the car somewhere below. You look down: Mira is a floor beneath you, one rung at a time, and far below her the dark narrows to a glowing seam — lobby light leaking around the edges of the car. Somewhere between you and that light: the second-floor doors, the end of the ladder, the drop.

Your earpiece crackles. The voice is fainter now, the building's steel eating the signal, but it's smiling. You can hear it.

*"Good. The car's at lobby — and the tunnel you want is underneath it. When you're ready for the car to move, say so."*

Static chews it down to nothing.

Above you, through the open hatch, a flashlight beam stabs into the shaft and sweeps the wall. A shout, muffled: "Shaft! They're in the shaft!"

Mira looks up at you from the rungs, her face pale in the seam-light rising from below.

"He hears everything we say," she says. "Doesn't he."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Seems that way." *I start descending, moving quickly now.* "Just keep going. We're almost to the second floor."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You go down fast.

The rungs blur under your hands — ten, twenty, thirty. Your forearms start to burn. The extinguisher bangs against your hip with every drop. Below you, Mira sets the pace she can: one rung, a controlled swing, her bad leg dangling, her breath coming in short pulls through her nose.

Your earpiece crackles. *"Eleven more,"* the voice says, conversational, like it's reading over your shoulder. *"Doors on your left."*

Mira is close enough to hear it. Her eyes flick up to yours in the dark. She mouths a single word. It looks like *later*.

Above, the rectangle of gray light at the hatch blots out. A flashlight stabs down the shaft, sweeping past you, and a shout comes down as pure noise. Then boots on the first rung. They're coming after you — and they're descending faster than Mira can move. You count the gap the way you counted the stairs: a floor and a half, closing.

"There," Mira says.

The rungs end. Just like he said they would. The last one sits beside a seam in the shaft wall, and below it the concrete drops away smooth and featureless. The second-floor doors — you can make out their outline from inside, the track, the interlock release you know how to trip. And below that, eight feet down, the roof of the car: a dim gray plane, humming, edged with lobby light. It sits there. Patient. Unaware.

Mira hangs from the last rung by both arms, bad leg tucked, and looks down at the drop, then up at you. Eight feet. On one leg, the landing folds her unless someone breaks it.

Then, from below: a chime. Soft. Cheerful. Obscene, in this place.

The car shudders. A relay clunks somewhere in the dark.

*"Lobby just called it,"* the voice says. *"Someone down there wants a ride. In about fifteen seconds it starts coming up — through where you're hanging, one way or another."* A pause. The static almost sounds like a smile. *"Doors or drop. Say so."*

Above, the flashlight beam bounces and steadies. The pursuer is descending one-handed, light in the other fist, and a second shape fills the hatch behind him. The beam finds your face and holds.

Mira's fingers are going white on the last rung.

"Whatever you're doing," she says quietly, "do it now."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I make a split-second decision.* "Mira, drop to the car! I'll pry the doors." *I kick out, trying to dislodge the pursuer above me.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't hesitate. She never does.

She lets go.

Eight feet, and she takes it the way she's taken everything tonight — good leg first, a fold, a roll across the car roof that kills the sound. The steel booms anyway, a deep drum-note in the dark, and the car hums on beneath her, oblivious. She comes up on one knee, hair across her face, and looks up at you.

You don't watch. You're already moving.

You hook an elbow through the rung and drive your boot upward, into the descending shape above you. It connects with something soft — a stomach, a chest — and the grunt it knocks loose is very human and very close. The flashlight goes first: it cartwheels past your face, strobing the shaft walls, and dies somewhere far below with a small, distant clatter.

Then the man follows it.

He doesn't scream. Training, maybe. He claws at the rungs on the way past, his fingers brush your sleeve, and then he's gone. A half-second later the car roof booms again — a different note, a wrong one — and Mira scrambles back on her palms as a body hits the steel three feet from her and folds around its own breath.

Above, at the hatch, the second shape shouts something. A weapon-light snaps on and its beam lances down the shaft, hunting.

The car chimes.

Soft. Cheerful. It shudders. A relay clunks somewhere beneath Mira's knees, and the whole gray plane she's kneeling on begins to rise.

*"Both,"* the voice says in your ear, through the static. Admiring. *"Ambitious."*

You find the interlock by touch — the roller, the latch, exactly where the schematics put it three days ago in a hotel room — and you trip it and set your shoulder into the doors and force them apart. A foot of gap. Then two. Beyond them: the second floor. A corridor of dark glass offices, empty, the alarm strobing red off the glass, an EXIT sign burning green at the far end. Carpet. Quiet. The sweep went up past this floor and the net is below it, and for one more minute this slice of the building belongs to nobody.

The car rises past you.

Mira comes up with it, standing now, balanced on her good leg on the roof of a moving elevator, rising through the shaft like a stage trick. Through the seams of the car's ceiling hatch leaks a ribbon of warm light and — absurd, obscene — the faint tinny sound of someone's music. The man you kicked loose is on his hands and knees beside her, shaking his head like a stunned animal, and his hand is crawling toward his hip.

The car roof draws level with your doors. A second. Maybe two. Then it carries her past, and up, toward the machinery and the narrowing dark.

Mira reaches for you.

The man on the roof reaches for her ankle.

And a shot from above cracks down the shaft and sparks off the wall a foot from your head.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I ignore the shot.* "Mira! Your left!" *I try to push the doors open wider to get out.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doors fight you — the interlock's spring, the grit in the track — but you get another foot, then another, and the gap is wide enough for a body.

Mira doesn't waste the warning.

The man's fingers close on her ankle — the bad one, which is its own mistake — and she drives her free heel down onto his wrist. Once. Twice. His hand opens, and the pistol he's half-drawn skids across the car roof, riding the vibration, and drops through the gap. It hits the carpet at your feet and slides to the wall.

Then the car roof draws level, and Mira comes through.

She doesn't jump. She steps — good leg first — and folds through the gap as the roof slides up past her, catching herself on the frame with both hands. For one second the car is still there: the man on all fours, riding it away, shaking his head. His eyes find yours through the gap as he rises. Then the car takes him.

A shot cracks down the shaft and spangs off the car's rising bulk — sparks, the scream of a ricochet — and then the car seals the shaft and the angle is gone. Through the narrowing seam above it: a shout from the hatch, dopplering up, and from the car's ceiling hatch, absurdly, that tinny thread of muzak, ascending with him like a joke nobody will admit to telling.

The doors spring shut. The tripped interlock doesn't quite re-seat. A sliver of shaft-light shows along the seam, thin as a blade.

Quiet. Relative quiet. The alarm strobes red off the glass offices. The EXIT sign burns green at the corridor's far end. Your ears ring. The extinguisher on your hip is lighter than it was.

Mira straightens against the frame, breathing hard, and looks at the pistol on the carpet. Then at you. Then — deliberately — at your earpiece. Two fingers to her own ear. She mouths the word again: *later.*

*"Doors,"* the voice says, pleased, static chewing the edges. *"Not what I'd have chosen. Noted."* A pause. *"The two on the roof are coming back down the stairwell — call it a minute. The lobby team is on the stairs coming up. And the car you just vacated is riding to the top, which means in ninety seconds someone sends it back down, and the shaft stops being a wall and starts being a door again."*

Outside the glass, the night goes white.

The helicopter has come around the building. The searchlight rakes the second-floor windows and the rotor thump presses through the glass like a hand on a drumhead. The light is three offices down and walking toward you, unhurried, throwing every desk and chair into hard-edged shadow as it comes.

*"Maintenance door,"* the voice says. *"Left side, twenty yards, red stencil. It opens on the service corridor, and the service corridor opens on the tunnel. Or take the pistol and make a stand in a glass box — your call. You're the one with the gift for improvisation."*

Mira limps a step closer, puts her back to the glass, and looks down the corridor — at the red-stenciled door, at the EXIT sign, at the sliver of light in the shaft seam.

The searchlight swings one office closer.

"Well?" she says.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Maintenance door," I say. *I grab Mira's arm and start moving, keeping low.* "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You go low and fast.

Twenty yards of corridor, glass on the right, the searchlight walking it like a patrol. You move in the gaps between sweeps — five yards, down behind a desk as the light pours through the glass and turns every chair leg into a black stripe on the carpet, then five more. The rotor thump comes through the windows as pure pressure. Your ears are still ringing from the shot in the shaft.

Mira moves better on that leg than she should. As you pass the shaft doors she dips without breaking stride and comes up with the pistol off the carpet. She checks the magazine one-handed, racks the slide against her hip, holds it low along her thigh. She catches you looking.

"Later," she mouths again — and this time she means the gun, too.

Halfway. The searchlight swings back for another pass — and behind you, a sound you now know in your spine: a chime. Soft. Cheerful. The car, coming back down.

And at the far end of the corridor, beneath the green EXIT sign, the stairwell door's handle turns.

"Go," Mira breathes.

You go. No more timing the light — you run it low, and the searchlight catches you for one white second as you cross the last office, and then the door is there: red stencil, MAINTENANCE — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL, a lever handle. You hit it with your shoulder and it gives — unlocked, thank God for fire code — and you're through, pulling Mira through, and the door swings shut on the alarm, the light, and the first shout from the stairwell end of the corridor.

Dark. Relative dark.

The service corridor is concrete and pipes — a utilitarian spine running the length of the building, caged emergency bulbs every thirty feet, everything painted institutional green gone gray with age. Ductwork sweats overhead. The floor slopes gently down. The air is cooler here, and it smells of damp concrete and, faintly, exhaust — the tunnel, breathing up at you from below.

Behind the door: muffled boots, muffled voices, the alarm's red pulse bleeding under the frame. They will check this door. In seconds, not minutes.

Mira leans against the wall, chest heaving, and looks at you — then, deliberately, at your ear. She holds out her hand.

"Now," she says. "Take it out, or give it to me. He hears everything. He knew about the hatch, the rungs, this door — he's not tracking us, he's *guiding* us, and I want to know why before we take one more step down his corridor."

Your earpiece crackles. Right on cue. Fainter down here, the building's bones eating the signal — but the smile in it comes through intact.

*"She's right. I am guiding you. Left at the junction ahead — the right fork's been locked since nine."* A pause. Static chews the edges. *"And while you're down there, ask her what she did before they put her on that helicopter. Go on. I'll wait."*

Mira can't hear it. She watches your face instead — and reads something there, because her own face changes. Closes. Like a door.

"What?" she says. "What did he say?"

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I pull the earpiece out and crush it under my heel.* "He wants me to ask about your past." I look down the dark corridor, then back at the door. "Doesn't matter. We're going left."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease the stairwell door open two inches and hold. The smell of concrete dust and old motor oil rises from the well. Fluorescent light buzzes on the landing below, steady and white, untouched by the red alarm bleeding through the corridor behind you.

You listen.

One floor down, a door slams — heavy, hydraulic, the fire door to the second-level offices. Boots follow. Two sets, maybe three, moving fast, moving *up*. They're sweeping from below. That cuts your options: garage is down four, and between you and it, someone is climbing.

But they're moving in a stack. Which means they're not on the landings yet. You have seconds, not minutes.

Mira's fingers tighten on your shoulder. She's listening too. Her breathing is controlled, measured — the breathing of someone trained to be carried and to hate it.

Above you, the stairwell continues. Eight floors up is the roof. The roof is nothing. The roof is a choice you make when you're out of choices.

Below, a voice barks something in a language that isn't English. A radio crackles an answer.

They're one flight down. Maybe less.

The door behind you begins to swing wide as the corridor's motion sensor catches your silhouette. Red light floods across your back like a warning hand.

You are out of time to be still.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I pull Mira through the stairwell door, easing it shut behind us*. "Up. We're going up." *I hiss, already moving, half-carrying her up the steps*. "Roof's better than getting boxed in down here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pull Mira through the door and ease it shut behind you. The latch catches with a click that sounds like a gunshot in the concrete throat of the stairwell. You don't wait to hear if anyone below noticed. You move.

"Up. We're going up," you hiss against her ear. "Roof's better than getting boxed in down here."

Mira doesn't argue. She just adjusts her grip on your shoulders and lets you haul her weight. Each step upward is a negotiation between speed and silence. Her left leg drags, catches the edge of each riser. Her jaw is clenched so tight you can hear her teeth grinding.

Two flights up. Three. Your calves burn. The air thins and warms — heat rising from the building's core. Below you, the voices get louder, then suddenly stop. The silence is worse. They've reached the door you closed. They know.

A metallic *bang* — someone tests the stairwell door from below. Then a second bang. Harder.

They'll have it open in seconds.

You round the landing to the seventh floor and see it: a heavy steel fire door marked **ROOF ACCESS — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY**. There's an electronic keypad on the wall beside it. The light on the lock glows red.

Locked. Of course it's locked.

Mira looks at the keypad. Then she looks at you. Her eyes are dark and very calm.

"I can get that open," she says. "But I need thirty seconds and both my hands. Which means you need to hold me up *and* hold that stairwell."

Below, the fire door explodes open. Boots flood the concrete. A flashlight beam sweeps upward, white and blinding, catching dust motes in the air like sparks.

The beam is two flights below. Moving fast.

Thirty seconds. You don't have thirty seconds. But you're going to give them to her anyway.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You spin on the landing, reversing your shoulders so your body turns to face down the stairwell while your arm keeps Mira moving up. You half-drag, half-fall against the roof door and pin her between the steel frame and your back. She understands instantly. Her hands leave your shoulders and go to the keypad.

Fingers fly. Fast. *Trained*-fast. The keypad beeps — once, twice — then stutters into rapid tones as she works.

Below, the flashlight beam bounces and climbs. It's on the fifth-floor landing now, sweeping the walls. A voice barks coordinates into a radio. Another answers. They're coordinating a funnel — one team pushing up the stairwell, another almost certainly cutting the elevator shaft or rappelling to cut you off above. Standard box drill. You've run it before. You know exactly how few seconds you have.

Mira's breathing is quick now. Not panicked — *focused*. The keypad gives a long tone, then silence.

Red light on the lock. Then—

Green.

The bolt inside the door retracts with a heavy metallic *chunk* that echoes down the concrete shaft like a heartbeat.

But the beam below has found the seventh-floor landing now. It swings up and hits you square in the chest, blinding. A voice shouts. Not a request this time.

Mira grabs the crash bar.

The door opens onto cold black air and the smell of rain on tar. Wind hits you like a wall — high, hard, carrying the sound of the city far below.

You have maybe two seconds before the first round comes up that stairwell.

Mira is already through the door, pulling herself along the frame, her bad leg barely touching ground. She looks back at you.

One second.

The flashlight beam leaps up the final flight. You hear a weapon's action cycle — the sharp mechanical *clack-clack* of a round chambered.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove her through the door, following close behind, already pulling my sidearm.* "Go! Go!" *I shout, turning and firing two quick shots down the stairwell at the flashlight beam*.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your sidearm is up before your feet clear the threshold. You twist, put the doorframe at your back, and fire twice down into the white glare of the flashlight. The shots are deafening in the concrete shaft — two flat cracks that stack on top of each other and roll. The beam snaps sideways and drops as whoever held it goes down or goes to ground. You don't wait to find out which.

The crash bar shrieks as you slam your weight against it. The roof door swings wide and you're through, hauling it shut behind you with a wrench of your shoulder. The bolt hasn't re-engaged. It won't. That door is a swinging promise that they'll be coming through it any second.

Rain needles your face. The roof is a flat black expanse of tar and puddled water — HVAC units squatting like sleeping animals, a forest of vent pipes, and beyond the parapet, the city, smeared with storm light and falling away into nothing. Wind tears at your jacket and steals the heat from your skin in seconds.

Mira is already moving. She drags herself along a ductwork run, using it like a railing, her left leg leaving a stuttering trail in the standing water. She's heading for the far edge of the roof. You follow because there's nothing else to follow.

"Helipad," she calls over the wind. "Service platform, east side. There's a — " A gust swallows the rest.

You hear the roof door handle turn behind you. Metal grinds. Shouts on the other side. They'll stack up, breach, and spread into a line — fifteen seconds, maybe less.

You reach her at the east parapet and look down. There is no helipad. There is a maintenance platform three meters below the roofline, a cable tray, and the dark mouth of an exterior service ladder bolted to the building's face. The drop from the platform to the street is thirty stories of rain and air.

Mira swings her good leg over the parapet before you can say a word. Her hands find the ladder's rails. She looks up at you, water streaming down her face, and for the first time you see something in her eyes that isn't calm.

Behind you, the roof door bursts open.

Three silhouettes pour through, spread-eagled against the gray sky. A spotlight lances across the rooftop, sweeping left to right. It will find you in one pass.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your hand closes around Mira's arm and you haul her back over the parapet before the spotlight sweeps this far. There's no time to argue, no time for the ladder. Instead you see it — a squat structure on the northwest corner of the roof, sheet-metal walls, a heavy door propped slightly open by years of bad maintenance. A telecom housing. Maybe an equipment room. You don't care what it is. You care that it has walls.

You shove Mira through the gap and follow, slamming the door behind you.

Inside, the world changes. The wind dies to a howl against thin metal. The rain becomes a drumming. Dark shapes resolve in the gloom — server racks, blinking green and amber, the hum of cooling fans, the smell of hot electronics and dust. A single utility bulb flickers overhead, casting everything in jaundiced half-light. Cables hang from a tray like vines.

Mira slides down the wall and finally lets her left leg give out. It buckles sideways and she catches it with both hands, jaw tight, breathing through her nose. For the first time you see the leg properly — the fabric of her trousers is dark and wet from mid-thigh down, and it isn't rain.

"You're hit," you say.

"I'm aware," she says.

You drag a server rack toward the door. It's heavy, dead weight, and it screams across the concrete floor. You tip a second one against it, then wedge the leg of a cable tray through the handles. It won't hold forever. It will hold for minutes.

Outside, boots hit the roof. Shouts. The spotlight beam rakes across the structure's exterior and bleeds through a seam in the metal wall, painting a thin white line across the floor. Someone tests the door. It groans against the barricade but holds.

Then the shouting changes. Coordinated. They're calling for breaching equipment — or worse, they're calling for the helicopter you heard earlier and chose to ignore.

Mira's fingers are busy. She's pulled a device from somewhere inside her jacket — small, matte black, no markings. She's typing on it one-handed, bracing it against her knee. Her face is lit by its faint glow, and she looks up at you.

"I can open a channel. Get us extraction," she says. "But the moment I transmit, they'll triangulate this room. Every gun on this roof converges right here." She holds your eyes. "So tell me. How much do you trust right now?"

The door shudders. A hydraulic spreader whines to life on the other side, a high mechanical keen that vibrates through the metal walls.

The rack begins to move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Trust?" *I scoff, looking at her leg, then the door, then back at her*. "Get us an exit. Now." *I pull my sidearm, checking the mag. Not much left*.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Trust is a luxury," you tell her, dropping the magazine, counting brass. Four rounds. You slam it home. "Get us an exit. Now."

Mira doesn't smile, but something in her mouth twitches. She turns back to the device and her thumb moves. A single keystroke. A low hum rises from the matte black shell — not a beep, not a tone, but a *presence*, like the room just got smaller.

"Channel's live," she says. "Thirty seconds for a handshake. Then we pray somebody's listening who isn't them."

The hydraulic spreader outside screams higher. The metal door bows inward at the center, a slow, obscene dent forming like a bruise. The server rack shudders, one caster lifting off the floor. You put your shoulder against it and shove back, boots sliding on dusty concrete. The cable tray wedged through the handles groans but holds.

Twenty seconds.

The spotlight outside snaps off. That's wrong. That's *wrong* — you realize it a half-beat before the reason lands. They don't need light anymore. They have thermals. They know exactly where you both are in this box.

"Wide open," you say through your teeth. "The moment that door comes, I'm wide open."

"Noted," Mira murmurs. Her device pulses once — a single blue light that lasts exactly one heartbeat. "Handshake. Someone's talking."

A voice crackles from the tiny speaker, tinny and distorted by distance and storm. Two words you can't make out. Then a third that sounds like a callsign.

Mira speaks into it. Fast. Code-words, coordinates, a string of numbers that must be her own authentication. Her voice has changed — the steadiness is still there but now it has an edge of command, the tone of someone used to being obeyed by people she's never met.

The door *shrieks*. The spreader bites deeper. Metal fatigues with a gunshot-loud *bang* as a weld splits along the frame. The barricade lurches forward an inch. Then another.

You feel the wall against your spine and the rack against your shoulder and the cold weight of four bullets in your hand and you do the math again. Four rounds, three silhouettes at least, probably six on the roof, a spreader team and a marksman somewhere on the neighboring high-rise whose crosshairs are almost certainly resting on this door right now.

"Tell me," you say, "that whoever's on the other end of that radio can get here before this door comes off its hinges."

Mira lowers the device. Rain hammers the roof like a thousand running feet. Somewhere above — high, high above the storm ceiling — a sound begins. Not the helicopter. Something else. A whine that drops in pitch, that grows teeth, that you feel in your sternum before you hear it with your ears.

Her eyes lift to the corrugated ceiling. For the first time since the corridor, since the alarm, since her name meant nothing to you — she looks *relieved*.

"They're close," she says. "Hold the door."

The roof door at the far side of the structure blows off its hinges with a single, concussive *boom*. The barricade doesn't hold. It doesn't even slow down.

You swing your sidearm toward the light and the rain and the shapes pouring through.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I brace, firing my last four rounds in quick succession at the shapes in the doorway, aiming for center mass.* "Get ready to move!" *I yell over the din, already looking for an alternate exit, a weakness in the walls*.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You fire four times. Four. Each one a flat, angry crack swallowed by wind and rain pouring through the ruined doorway. The shapes stagger — one drops, another spins into the frame of the door, a third falls back out of sight. You don't count casualties. You count triggers, and yours is dead.

Click.

The slide locks back. Empty. You don't holster it — you throw it. The pistol tumbles end over end and catches the nearest silhouette square in the helmet. It buys nothing. It buys a half-second. You take it.

Your eyes are already off the door and *on* the walls.

Sheet metal. Corrugated. Thin. You saw it when you came in — sweat-stained bolts, seams running floor to ceiling, a building material chosen for cost, not for defense. Your gaze snaps to the far wall where the utility bulb throws weak light across a section where two panels meet at a corner. The seam there is wide enough to slide a fingertip into. The bolts are rusted. Old installation. Bad maintenance.

That's your door.

"Move!" you roar, and you're already across the room, shoulder-first into the corner seam. Metal screams. The panel buckles but doesn't give. Your shoulder lights up with white-hot pain — you hit it again, and this time something *pops*, a bolt shearing, the seam splitting open into a jagged gap two feet wide with storm howling through it.

Behind you, boots on concrete. Shouts. Muzzle flash strobes the interior walls — muzzle flash and thunder that isn't the sky.

Something burns across your ribs. Hot. Sharp. A graze, or worse. You don't look. You grab the torn edge of metal and *wrench*, peeling it back far enough to fit a body through.

Mira is on her feet. Barely. She's shoved the device back inside her jacket and is dragging herself toward you, one hand on the racks, leaving a smear of dark on every surface she touches. Her face is grey. The leg is barely a leg now.

You grab her arm and pull her through the gap. The metal edge catches her jacket and tears it open from shoulder to wrist. Cold rain hits you both like a second gunshot.

You're on the roof again. The far edge. The northwest corner.

Below you, the maintenance ladder is nowhere — wrong side of the building. But the whine is *deafening* now, a descending shriek that vibrates the tar beneath your boots, and the rain overhead is being pushed outward in a spiral, and you understand.

Rotor wash. Not a helicopter.

Something much worse, and much better.

A shadow drops through the cloud ceiling — angular, matte black, running without lights. It hangs in the air over the east parapet like a wasp deciding where to sting. A cable unspools from its belly, and at the end of the cable, a figure in dark gear descends at a speed that makes your stomach drop just watching.

Behind you, the men in the telecom structure reach the gap in the wall. Flashlights converge on your back again. You hear the word "targets" shouted in two languages.

Mira's hand finds yours. Her grip is iron and ice.

"The cable," she says. Not a question.

You look at the cable. Twenty meters of free air and rain between you and it, across a rooftop that has just become a shooting gallery.

You look at the slide-locked pistol in your hand. Useless. You look at the roof door to the stairwell — open, the enemy's own breach now a highway pouring reinforcements up.

You look at Mira. She looks at you.

The cable swings closer. The figure riding it down raises one arm. You can't see a face behind the visor. You can see the weapon slung across their chest.

The first round cracks past your ear and punches a hole in the parapet beside Mira's head. Chunks of concrete spray your face.

You have one option left that isn't dying.

You run.

dialogue.name: Operative
