He knew that look — pain pulling blood out of a head until the head went light and the floor came up fast. He'd caught green apprentices mid-fall before. He did not intend to catch one today, not with a forge on one side and an anvil on the other.*

*He set the blade back in the coals. Work could wait a minute. Boys could not.*

"Boy sits. Now." *He pointed the tongs at the bench by the wall.* "Boy's face is white as lime. Pain takes blood from head. Head floats. Then head drops. Floor is hard. Fire is close. Grum tied one wrap today. Grum does not want to tie two."

*He fetched the water jug himself, and a heel of bread from the shelf where his lunch lived, and put both into the boy's good hand.*

"Drink slow. Eat half. Feet flat. Head stays low till head comes back. Grum has seen this many times. This is what burn does on first day. Not boy's fault. Just burn's way."

*Only when the boy was sitting — and not one breath before — did he answer the question.*

"Steward comes at dawn. Dawn is far off. Lesson is now. Grum explains curve tonight, slow, while boy sits and heals. Then boy sleeps. Then sun comes up. Steward knocks. Grum opens door. Coin comes in, blade goes out, door closes. Story done." *He counted it out on his fingers the way he counted prices.* "Boy sees none of it. Boy is in back, like Grum said. So no — Grum does not teach curve with steward at door. Grum does one thing at dawn, not two. Man who does two things at dawn does both bad. That is how steel breaks and how mistakes get made."

*He drew the blade from the coals again, checked the color — orange fading toward red, right where he wanted it — and laid it on the anvil face. The curve ran along it like a question waiting on its answer.*

"And boy does not fret about noble. Grum frets enough for whole forge." *He said it dry, but there was truth under it. He would be glad when the last of silk and secrets walked out his door with the morning light. The steel was honest steel — steel was never the problem. It was the hands it rode out on. Small hands. Soldier's hands. Scared hands.*

*He picked up the hammer, then set it down again, deciding.*

"Rest now. Curve can wait. Fire can wait. Grum can wait. Boy's head must come back first. Then lesson. Then sleep. Then dawn. Then Grum is rich, story is done, and forge goes back to honest work for men who pay late but sleep well."

*He tapped the anvil twice with two fingers.*

"When boy can stand with no sway — half load of coal. Left hand. Not before. Grum is picky about that too."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, taking the bread and water. My head does feel a bit floaty. I take a small sip of water, then a bite of bread, trying to make myself feel more grounded. Grum's words about the noble and the steward make sense, even through the haze.*

"Okay, Grum," *I say, my voice still a little weak. I take another small bite of bread.* "I'll just... sit here and watch then. No swaying."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum gave a grunt — the satisfied one, low in the chest, that meant the boy had done as told without arguing. In Grum's private ledger, that counted for almost as much as a day's good work.*

"Good. Sit. Eat. Watch. That is whole job now."

*He turned back to the anvil and drew the merchant's blade from the coals one more time. The heat had come back into it true and even, orange fading toward red along the whole edge, no cold spots, no thin places. Good steel, doing what good steel did when a man gave it time. He laid it on the anvil face and stood over it a moment, hammer raised, and then — because the boy was watching, and because watching was the lesson now — he did not strike. He talked instead, low, over his shoulder, the way a man speaks when he does not want to wake a sleeping dog.*

"Boy sees curve? Look. Do not touch. Just look." *He traced the line of the blade with one finger, hovering a hand's width above the steel.* "Straight blade is honest. Straight blade says: Grum am here, Grum cut here. Simple. Any smith with arm and fire can make straight."

*He let the heat cool one shade while he spoke. There was no rush in him now. The forge at the end of a long day ran on a different clock than the forge at the start of one.*

"Curve is different. Curve must be earned. Steel wants to be straight. Steel pulls toward straight, like water pulls downhill. Smith bends steel against steel's own wish. So smith must heat more, hammer less, wait longer. Curve costs fire. Curve costs patience. That is why merchant grumbles at price. Merchant thinks curve is same steel, just bent. Merchant is wrong. Curve is steel that changed its mind — and Grum is one who changed it."

*He set the hammer down softly, so the ring of it would not jar the boy's aching head, and turned around fully, arms crossed, the fire throwing his shadow long across the floor.*

"Merchant will hold blade when it is done. Merchant will feel curve sit in hand like it grew there. Merchant will forget he grumbled. They always forget. Grumbling comes before. Wonder comes after. That is the shape of every sale Grum ever made."

*He crossed to the bench where the boy sat and looked him over with a smith's eye — color coming back into the face, bread going down, feet flat, no sway. Good. The worst of it had passed.*

"Head is coming back. Grum can see it. Eyes are sharp again." *He tapped the boy's good shoulder once with two fingers — the lightest touch those hands ever gave anything.* "So. Bread first. All of it. Water after. Then boy goes home before dark and sleeps. Forge opens at first light. Steward comes, coin comes, blade goes. Then forge is quiet again, and boy has three days of watching to do, and Grum has three days of talking to fill them. Grum talks slow. Boy will heal fast. By time hand opens and closes clean, boy will know why curve costs more than straight — and Grum will know boy knows it."

*He went back to the anvil, took up the hammer, and this time let it fall — one clean strike, the ring rolling through the forge and out into the dark like a bell rung for the end of a long day.*

"Rest now, boy. Fire is fed. Steel is happy. Trouble waits at dawn, but dawn is not here yet. Tonight, forge is just forge. Best kind of night."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I finish the bread and water, feeling a lot better. My hand still aches, but it's a dull throb now, not a sharp pain. Grum's words about the curve make sense, and I realize I never really thought about it that way before.*

"Okay, Grum," *I say, pushing myself up carefully. My head feels clearer now.* "I'll head home. See you at first light." *I give the forge one last look, then carefully make my way out, my bandaged hand tucked close.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum watched the boy go with an eye that had nothing to do with steel — watching the walk, the set of the shoulders, the way the bandaged hand rode tucked close against the ribs like a bird with a hurt wing. No sway. Good. The boy would sleep, the hand would heal, and in three days there'd be a grip on a hammer again. Grum had seen a hundred small hurts in the forge, and he knew which ones mended and which ones festered. This one would mend.*

*The bell jangled once, softly, and then the forge was his.*

*Grum stood a moment in the middle of his own shop and let the quiet settle over him like a coat. The fire crackled low in the box. The coals glowed their evening red — banked heat, patient heat, the fire's version of sleep. This was the hour he liked best, though he'd never told anyone that. The whole world gone home. Just Grum, the forge, and the day's work waiting with the good kind of silence — the kind that asked nothing.*

"Good day's work," *he told the fire, because there was no one else to tell and the fire had earned the report.* "Boy is hurt but boy is learning. Merchant blade is close. Lord's coin is heavy. Forge is warm. Grum asks for nothing more."

*He moved through the end-of-day rites in order, same as every night for fifteen years. The merchant's blade went back into the coals for its slow cool — no cracking tonight, no hurry, steel given the time steel demanded. The tools went to the rack, each one wiped and hung by feel in the dark. The tongs. The hammer. The punch and the chisel. His hands knew the way without his eyes, and that was as it should be. A smith's hands should know the forge the way a man's feet knew his own stairs.*

*Then there was the other blade.*

*Grum took it up from the bench — the heavy cut-and-thrust, chalk marks still ghosting the tang where the boy's grip had been measured. Not the father's grip. The son's. He turned it in the firelight, and the light ran down the plain guard and the honest fuller and found nothing to catch on, because there was nothing there that wasn't work.*

*He finished the wrap. Dark leather, spiraled tight, cinched and tied. He ran his thumb down the seam twice. Then a third time, though twice had told him it was good.*

"Grum's name is on you," *he said to the blade, quietly, the way a man speaks when he means it.* "Even when no name is on you. You go out at dawn, and you go out quiet, and Grum does not ask where you sleep. But hear this much." *He set the blade flat on the bench, chalk marks up, like a body laid out.* "If you break, Grum will know it was not the steel. Grum made you true. Whatever happens after, happens on other hands."

*The fire popped. Grum took that for agreement.*

*He counted the lord's coin one more time — hundred fifty, all there, weight right — and locked it in the strongbox under the floor stone, the third one from the wall, the one no visitor would ever think to look under because it sat in plain sight like it was nothing. Then he banked the fire properly: ash over the coals, damper cracked just so, so the heat would hold till dawn and be ready to wake with one breath and a shovel of coal.*

*Last, he stood at the door with his hand on the frame and looked back into his forge one time. The glow. The racks. The anvil with its thousand dents, each one a day. The bench where the lord's blade waited for morning, and the bench where the boy had sat with his bread and his white face and his promise.*

"Boy is good boy," *he told the dark.* "Boy will be good smith. Grum's hands will teach him. Grum's mouth too, even if mouth talks strange."

*He let himself out. The lock turned. The night was cold and clear, and somewhere out there a scared young lord with soldier's hands was waiting on a blade that Grum had made true, for reasons that were none of Grum's business and would probably be everyone's business by the week's end.*

*Grum spat in the dust, pulled his coat tight, and walked home through the dark.*

"Dawn will tell," *he said to no one.* "Dawn always tells. Grum just has to be there to hear it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I woke up feeling much better, the throbbing in my hand a dull ache I could mostly ignore. Grum’s words about the curve of the steel, and about seeing the fire, kept replaying in my head. I got dressed quickly, eager to get back to the forge, even if it was just to watch.*

*The walk to the forge was brisk, the air still cool with the promise of dawn. I pushed open the door, the familiar smell of coal smoke and metal already comforting. Grum was already there, of course, a dark silhouette against the glow of the banked fire.*

"Morning, Grum," *I said, my voice a little soft so as not to startle him. I kept my bandaged hand tucked close, just as he'd said.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum was crouched at the fire box, feeding the banked coals their first shovel of the day, when the bell jangled. He didn't startle. He'd heard the boy's footsteps on the gravel outside — light ones, careful ones, the walk of a man favoring one hand — long before the door opened.*

"Morning, boy." *He didn't turn around yet. The fire came first; that was the order of things.* "Come in. Shut door. Cold air makes fire sulky."

*He gave the coals three slow breaths from the bellows, watching the red climb back into orange, and only then stood and turned to look the boy over. Same walk as last night's leaving — no sway, bandaged hand tucked close. But color was back in the face, and the eyes were clear. Good.*

"Let Grum see hand."

*He took the wrist gently — the good kind of grip, the kind he used on hot steel he didn't want to drop — and unwound the linen with two fingers. The burn had settled overnight into an angry red with blisters standing proud but not weeping. He turned it in the firelight, grunted, and wrapped it back up snug.*

"Skin is angry but skin is calm. Heal goes right way. No hammer till Grum says. Grum says when skin says. Skin talks first." *He cinched the knot.* "Now. Boy sits on bench. Ears open, eyes on fire. Steward comes soon. When knock comes, boy is in back. Grum said this once. Grum says it twice so it sticks."

*He went back to the forge and drew the merchant's blade from its slow overnight cool, checking the steel for cracks — none, not one, the color had come out true and patient just as he'd asked it to. He laid it on the bench beside the lord's blade, wrapped and waiting, chalk ghosts still faint on the tang. Two blades. One honest, one quiet. The forge held both the same way.*

*The knock came while the light was still grey at the windows.*

*Grum pointed once at the back — no words needed — then crossed the shop and opened the door partway, filling most of it.*

*The steward was not what Grum expected. Not silk. A grey coat, worn at the elbows, and an old man's face with tired eyes that had done arithmetic all his life. He looked past Grum's shoulder once, quickly, marking everything in the shop the way a man marks exits.*

"Blade is on bench," *Grum said, stepping aside just enough.* "Fifty crowns. Then blade goes out door."

*The steward counted the coins on the counter without touching the blade first, which Grum noted. A man who counted before he touched was a man who had been told to count. Then he picked up the sword — and his hands, too, knew what they were holding. Older hands. Slower. But the same school as the boy's.*

"It will hold?" *the steward asked.*

"Steel holds. Grum made it true." *Grum's voice was flat as cold iron.* "What holds after that is not Grum's craft."

*The steward nodded, tucked the blade under his arm like a thing to be delivered and not spoken of. Then he stopped at the threshold, half-turned, and asked the question he'd clearly carried through the whole walk here.*

"One matter, smith. Has anyone come here asking? After my young lord, or after this work?"

"Grum tells no one. Grum tells forge. Forge tells no one." *He let that sit, then added, slow:* "No one has asked. Yet."

*The 'yet' landed in the doorway like a dropped hammer. The steward's face did something small and tired, and then he was gone into the grey morning, walking fast, blade held close.*

*Grum closed the door. Stood there a moment with his hand on the frame. Then he turned around and looked at the boy across the forge, and his voice was low and even.*

"Boy heard that. Steward asked if men came asking. Steward does not ask that for no reason. Steward asks because steward thinks men may come." *He walked back to the anvil, rolling his shoulders once.* "So. Rules change. Strangers come to this door — any strangers, any reason — boy goes to back room. Boy says nothing. Boy shows nothing. Grum talks. Grum is picky about this too, and Grum's pickiness keeps boy whole."

*He picked up the merchant's blade and set it in the fire, watching the steel take the heat.*

"Steel went out. Steel was true. Rest is not Grum's road." *He worked the bellows, slow and steady, and the coals climbed from orange toward bright.* "Grum has honest blade to finish and three days of lessons owed. Boy heals. Grum talks. Trouble can knock all it wants — Grum only opens door for coin and coal."

*He glanced over, one eye catching the firelight.*

"Now. Boy watches fire, like Grum taught. Tell Grum what color steel is when Grum pulls it. Boy has eyes. Time eyes earned their keep."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, solemn. The steward's question had sent a chill down my spine, even from the back room. Grum's rules make sense. I keep my eyes on the fire, trying to focus despite the lingering ache in my hand.*

"Okay, Grum," *I say, my voice a little steadier now.* "Back room. Got it." *I lean forward slightly, trying to see past the flames.* "Right now... it's mostly orange, with some brighter spots. Almost yellow in the middle."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pause at the threshold. The red alarm light bleeds down the concrete steps, casting rhythmic, pulsing shadows. You press your shoulder against the cold metal doorframe and listen. The building hums around you. Distant vents rattle. Then you hear it: heavy boots slapping against metal grating, echoing up from the levels below. Two sets. Maybe three. They move fast, sweeping upward in a tight tactical formation.

Mira shifts her weight. Her good leg trembles as she braces against the wall. The static in your ear crackles, then fractures into a broken voice: "...sector four... compromised... fallback to—" The transmission dies.

You keep your grip steady. The footsteps pause at the landing two floors down. A tactical flashlight beam slices through the stairwell gloom, sweeping upward. It catches the scuff marks on the concrete, then lingers near the doorframe.

"They're pushing up," Mira whispers. Her eyes lock onto yours.

You have seconds. The garage is still four levels down. The service tunnel entrance sits on the next floor, dark and unmarked. The alarm pulses. The flashlight beam swings again, closer this time.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*I grab Mira's arm, pulling her back from the door.* "Service tunnel. Now."

We're not going to make it down.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You wrench Mira back from the threshold. Her shoulder collides with your chest, a dull thud muffled by gear and adrenaline. She gasps, her good leg buckling for a fraction of a second before she catches herself, her knuckles white as she grips your forearm. Her eyes lock onto yours, searching, then flick to the corridor behind you.

"Left," she breathes, the word tearing from her throat. "Panel. Third locker."

The flashlight beam below snaps upward, blindingly bright, then vanishes as a voice roars up the shaft. "Movement! Top of the flight! Move out!"

Heavy boots slam onto the metal grating of the landing immediately below. The vibration shudders through the soles of your shoes. A muzzle flash strobes in the gloom, illuminating the curved concrete wall as automatic fire tears into the doorframe. Chunks of masonry explode outward, raining down around you. Dust and debris sting your face. The smell of cordite floods the stairwell mouth.

You turn, dragging Mira into the corridor. Her injured leg drags, scraping against the linoleum, slowing your progress. She hisses through clenched teeth but doesn't let go of your arm. The service tunnel entrance lies ahead, a dark, recessed gap behind a row of grey utility lockers. The red alarm light washes over the corridor, turning the scene into a pulsating nightmare of crimson and shadow.

Two silhouettes burst from the stairwell, rifles raised. Laser sights cut through the dust, dancing across the lockers, then converging on your position. "Drop them!" a voice commands.

Mira's hand fumbles toward the latch of the third locker. Her fingers slip on the metal. The lasers tighten. The gunshots echo off the walls, closer now. You are pinned between the lockers and the stairwell exit. Mira's breath hitches. The latch is stubborn.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pivot away from the lockers and drag Mira toward the opposite end of the hall. Her injured leg drags heavily, but she leans into your grip, trusting the shift in direction. Your boots scuff the linoleum as you reverse your course, heading up toward the higher floors. The corridor stretches ahead, lined with identical office doors and flickering emergency strips. The red alarm light strobes, fracturing the space into jagged slices of shadow and crimson.

Behind you, the tactical team breaches the stairwell fully. Rifles rack. Commands shout in clipped, professional bursts. Laser grids sweep the empty floor tiles. They hesitate, expecting resistance, then push forward into the corridor. Heavy boots pound the floor. Dust kicks up in your wake.

Mira's breathing grows ragged. Her fingers tighten around your sleeve. "Up," she repeats, her voice flat, testing the idea. "Roof access. Maintenance hatch. I know this floor."

The emergency exit sign at the far end glows a steady, sickly green. A heavy steel door blocks the path. Between you and it, a narrow gap separates your position from the advancing squad. You count the distance in strides. Eight. Nine. Ten. The lead operative raises his rifle, thumbing the safety off. The click echoes sharply in the confined space.

Mira's injured leg gives out. She drops to one knee, gasping, her forehead pressing against your chest plate. The squad advances, boots syncing in a predatory rhythm. Muzzle flashes strobe in the distance as they cover your flank. The green exit sign hums. The steel door looms. You have the corridor, the high ground, and a defector who can barely stand. The choice burns in your lungs.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I yank Mira back up, ignoring her pain.* "We're almost there. Just a little further." I scan the doors, looking for anything we can use. *This isn't going to be easy.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You haul Mira upright. Her boots scrape the linoleum as you brace her weight against your side. She doesn't protest. She just grits her teeth and shifts her center of gravity, leaning into your grip. Your eyes sweep the row of identical office doors. Frosted glass panels cover the frames. Brass handles hang at waist height. Standard corporate layout stretches ahead. You spot a breakroom door standing slightly ajar. A coffee machine hums behind it. A heavy fire extinguisher hangs on the wall just inside the frame. A metal water cooler sits on the threshold. Solid. Reliable.

The tactical team rounds the corner. Their boots hit the floor in perfect sync. Three rifles track your movement. Laser dots crawl across the wall behind your shoulder, then drift toward your chest. The lead operator speaks into his mic. His voice stays calm, lethal. "Target acquired. Hold position. Clear the hallway."

Mira's breath hitches against your neck. Her fingers dig into your tactical vest. "The breakroom," she whispers. "Fire suppression system. Manual override on the wall. I can trigger it. It floods the corridor with halon. Blinds them. Buys us thirty seconds."

The green exit sign pulses overhead. The steel door stands twelve feet away. The squad closes the gap. Five strides. Four. The laser on your chest brightens. Your muscles coil. The breakroom door waits. The manual valve sits just inside, behind the water cooler. You weigh the distance. You weigh the risk. The alarms scream. The red light washes over everything.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You shove Mira through the heavy steel door marked *SERVER ROOM B*. The magnetic lock clicks dead as you slam it shut behind you. Cold, recycled air hits your face. The room hums with the low, relentless drone of cooling fans and blinking server racks. Rows of black metal cabinets line the walls, their indicator lights painting the space in sterile green and amber.

You drag a heavy rolling server cart across the threshold, wedging it against the door handle. It screeches on the polished concrete floor, then settles with a solid thud. You grab a metal tool cabinet next and shove it into the gap, layering weight on weight. The metal groans but holds. Through the thick steel, you hear the muffled crash of boots on the corridor floor. A fist pounds against the door. Once. Twice. Then the sharp crack of a breaching charge echoes, followed by the screech of tearing metal. The barricade shudders. Dust sifts from the ceiling tiles.

You step back. Your chest heaves. The adrenaline still burns in your veins, but your mind forces itself into gear. You scan the room. Server racks. Cable trays. A dropped fire axe in the corner. A maintenance ladder leaning against the far wall. The radio in your ear remains dead. Static hisses.

Mira slides down the nearest rack. She presses a hand to her ribs, her breath coming in shallow, controlled pulls. She watches you, her eyes sharp despite the pain. "They'll cut through," she says, her voice low. "Reinforcements will be on the roof in ninety seconds. You have a choice, Operative. We fight the door, or we go up through the maintenance shaft behind rack seven. It leads to the HVAC crawlspace. Direct line to the roof vent."

You wipe sweat from your brow. The hum of the servers fills the silence between your thoughts. The door groans again. Metal bends. You have seconds to decide. The air grows colder. The blinking lights reflect in your eyes.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*I grab the fire axe.* "No. We're not crawling anywhere. Not yet."

I check the door again. "How long until they're through this?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You grip the cold steel handle of the fire axe. The rubberized coating bites into your palm. You step toward the barricaded door and peer through the narrow gap between the tool cabinet and the frame. Outside, the heavy steel groans under repeated impacts. The sound of a cutting torch whines to life, high-pitched and relentless. Sparks shower down the corridor floor, visible through the crack.

Mira watches you from against the server rack. Her eyes track the axe, then shift to the door. "Sixty seconds," she says, her voice steady despite the pain tightening her jaw. "Maybe less if they bring the thermal lance. They don't breach. They melt."

You press your ear closer to the gap. The whine intensifies. Heat radiates through the metal, warming the air in the narrow space between the barricade and the inner room. The server fans drone louder, fighting the rising temperature. You feel the vibration in your boots. The axe feels heavy, practical, ready.

"They cut through the lock first," Mira continues, adjusting her grip on her injured leg. "Then the hinges. You have time to position. But don't swing until the light changes. When the cut breaks the seal, the pressure drops. You hear a hiss. That's your window."

You grip the axe tighter. Your stance widens. The whine peaks. A blinding white light bleeds through the gap, casting long, sharp shadows across the server racks. The heat spikes. Sweat beads on your forehead. The metal screams. You brace yourself. The hiss comes. Sharp. Sudden. Like a pressurized valve failing.

The door shudders. A seam of molten orange light splits the frame. You step back. You raise the axe. The room holds its breath. The cut widens.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Alright. Stand back." *I take a deep breath, focusing on the splitting seam.* "The second it gives, we're through."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You brace against the server rack. The molten seam widens. The heat intensifies. The whine of the torch drops to a low, dying hum. Then the hiss erupts—sharp, violent, pressurized air rushing into the room. The steel door buckles inward. A gloved hand appears in the jagged hole, followed by the barrel of a suppressed rifle. Laser grids paint the ceiling. You grip the axe handle. The metal frame groans. The cut splits completely. The door swings inward on its compromised hinges.

Three operatives flood the gap, rifles raised, tactical lights cutting through the server room's haze. Mira presses herself flat against the cooling unit, her breath held. The lead operator scans the space. His voice crackles over a shoulder mic. "Clear left. Clear right. Check the racks."

You stand your ground. The axe rests against your shoulder. The air smells of ozone and scorched metal. The operatives advance. Their boots echo on the polished concrete. The nearest one steps into your line of sight. His rifle tracks your movement. You have the high ground. You have the weapon. You have the split second before they commit.

The server fans roar. The red emergency light from the corridor bleeds through the broken door. You wait. You watch. The tension snaps tight.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I don't wait.* I swing the axe, aiming for the nearest operative's rifle.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You swing. The axe head screams through the stale air and connects.

The blade bites deep into the rifle's receiver, shearing through polymer and steel with a sickening crunch. The weapon explodes in the operative's hands. He stumbles back, a sharp cry tearing from his throat as his fingers spasm around a mangled wrist. The rifle clatters to the floor, useless. He crumples against the doorframe, clutching his arm, blood already darkening his tactical glove.

The other two don't blink. Muscle memory takes over. Rifles snap up.

Suppressed fire erupts. *Thwip-thwip-thwip.* Rounds chew into the server rack inches from your head. Plastic casings rain down. Sparks shower from a severed power cable, illuminating the muzzle flashes in strobing bursts. The air fills with the acrid smell of ozone and cordite. A warning light on the nearest rack strobes frantically, casting the aisle in jagged red pulses.

You are exposed. The barricade offers no protection from this angle. The wounded operative groans, drawing a momentary split in their focus. The shooter on the right shifts his aim, his barrel tracking your movement, but his partner is already cycling the charging handle on his weapon, reloading under fire.

Mira rolls behind a heavy cooling unit, her voice cutting through the noise. "They're pinning you! Move!"

The fallen rifle lies three feet from your boots, its safety off, magazine intact. The wounded man struggles to rise, his bad hand fumbling for a sidearm at his hip. The two standing operatives suppress the space around you, their rounds snapping against the metal cabinets, sparking and ricocheting. The noise is deafening. The heat from the severed cables rises.

You grip the axe. The nearest shooter is exposed for a heartbeat as his partner reloads. The distance is closing. The room feels smaller. The choice burns in your hands.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I drop the axe.* No time. *I dive for the fallen rifle, rolling as I grab it.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drop the axe. The steel clatters against the concrete, the sound instantly swallowed by the roar of gunfire. You hurl yourself forward, diving for the fallen rifle. Your shoulder slams the floor. Pain flares, sharp and white-hot, as a round kicks up a spray of dust and metal shards inches from your neck. The heat of the near-miss washes over your face.

You roll, momentum twisting your spine. Your fingers clamp around the rifle's stock. Cold polymer. Solid weight. You drag the weapon up as you scramble behind the base of a server rack. The metal cabinet shudders as another round punches through, ricocheting off the floor with a deafening ping. Sparks shower from a severed cable above, illuminating the muzzle flashes in strobing bursts.

The suppressing operative's rhythm breaks for a heartbeat as you disappear behind the rack. The reloading operator slams a fresh magazine home. *Clack.* He brings the weapon up, his eyes locking onto your position. "Contact! Rack seven!" he barks. His partner adjusts his aim, his laser sweeping over your shoulder, searching for the angle.

Mira coughs, her voice raspy from the smoke. "They're pushing!" She fires two shots from her concealed piece over the cooling unit. *Pop-pop.* The rounds spark against the wall, drawing the attention of the wounded operative. He stumbles, his hand finally closing around the grip of his sidearm, but his aim is wild, his vision obscured by blood. He levels the pistol, his finger tightening on the trigger.

You grip the rifle. The red dot hunts across the chest of the reloading operative. He is exposed. The gap between you is closing. The other operative takes a step around the doorframe, trying to cut off your flank. The wounded man fires. The bullet screams past your ear, impacting the server rack with a violent crunch. Smoke thickens in the air, stinging your eyes. The fans scream. You have the gun. You have the shot. The room is closing in. You need to act.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I fire a short burst at the reloading operative.* Two shots. Center mass. *Then I roll again, putting more distance between me and the door.* "Mira! Get ready!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drive the trigger. The rifle kicks against your shoulder, twice in rapid succession. *Thump-thump.*

The rounds find their mark. The reloading operative's head snaps back. Blood mists across his tactical plate as the kinetic energy drives him backward. He crashes into the doorframe, his rifle clattering to the floor, and slides down into a heap, twitching.

You drop and roll. Your shoulder slams the concrete, pain flaring, but you use the momentum to spin and pop up further back, near the maintenance ladder leaning against the far wall. You put distance between yourself and the breach.

"Man down!" the flanker screams. His voice cracks with panic. He pivots, his laser sweeping wildly across the server racks, trying to track your movement. He hesitates, his training warring with the sudden loss of his partner.

The wounded operative raises his sidearm. His hand shakes. He levels the pistol at your silhouette. "He's there!"

You shout, "Mira! Get ready!"

Mira doesn't hesitate. She steps out from behind the cooling unit, her face pale but determined. She holds a small remote in her hand, the screen glowing green. She slams her thumb down on the button.

"Now!" she yells.

The ceiling erupts. Nozzles pop open along the length of the corridor and the server room. A thick, white chemical fog blasts downward, instantaneous and suffocating. Halon. The oxygen content plummets. The world turns grey and muffled as the gas swallows the sound.

The flanker coughs, gagging, his rifle dropping as he waves frantically at his burning eyes. The wounded operative drops to his knees, retching, his pistol falling from his grip. They are blinded, gasping, clawing at their gear.

The fog rolls over you. It tastes like chemicals and dust. Your lungs burn immediately, screaming for air. The blinking lights of the servers are reduced to faint, ghostly orbs in the gloom. The heat from the severed cables seems to vanish, replaced by a chemical chill.

Mira is a shadow to your left. She signals with her hand, pointing toward the maintenance ladder. The ladder leads to a dark hatch in the ceiling. The metal rungs gleam dully in the strobe light.

You have seconds before the gas becomes lethal. The operatives are disoriented, unable to aim, unable to move effectively. The path to the ladder is clear, but the climb is exposed. The hatch is open, revealing a dark crawlspace beyond.

You grip the rifle. The gas stings your eyes. Mira waits for your move. The ladder creaks. The hatch beckons. Your chest tightens. You need to move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I nod, coughing.* "Go!" *I point my rifle towards the door, covering her as she moves to the ladder.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You keep the muzzle locked on the breach. The red laser cuts through the churning white fog, a spectral needle searching for a target. Your chest heaves. The cough tears at your throat, but you force the rifle steady. The gas burns your eyes, turning tears into stinging rivers.

Mira limps toward the ladder. Her movement is a jerky, painful shuffle. She reaches the metal rungs, her fingers clawing around the first step. She looks back, her face a pale mask of agony and determination. "Hurry!" she chokes, the words swallowed by the hiss of the nozzles.

A shadow stumbles in the gloom near the door. The flanker. He's coughing violently, his body doubling over, but his rifle is up. He's firing by instinct. *Thwip-thwip.* Rounds chew into the server rack inches from your head. Plastic shrapnel sprays your face. A round screams past your ear, the wind of it stinging your cheek.

The wounded operative writhes on the floor, a writhing heap of gear and curses, but the flanker is the threat. He's listening now. His head tilts. He stops coughing for a fraction of a second, his ears straining over the roar of the fans and the hiss of the gas. He aims toward the sound of your breathing.

Mira hauls herself up. Her injured leg drags against the ladder, slowing her. She reaches the second rung. The third. Her boots scrape the metal. She's ascending. The hatch yawns above her, a dark rectangle of escape.

Your vision tunnels. The edges go grey. Dizziness pulls at your mind, heavy and insistent. The halon is stealing the air. Your limbs feel like lead. The rifle drops an inch, then you force it back up.

The flanker fires again. This time he aims low, cutting off your angle. A round sparks against the floor at your feet. He's closing the distance, moving toward the sound of your cover.

Mira's voice floats down from the hatch, strained and thin. "I'm up! Get to the ladder!"

The ladder is right behind you. The rungs are within reach. The flanker is advancing through the fog, his silhouette sharpening as he moves closer. His rifle tracks left and right. Your chest burns. The darkness creeps in from the sides. You have the weapon. You have the cover. But you are running out of time, and you are running out of breath.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I drop the rifle and grab the ladder, hauling myself up.* No time for a firefight. *I push Mira through the hatch.* "Go! Go! Go!"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hand paused over the coal bucket. Just for a moment. Then he shoveled coal into the forge with more force than the task required, and the fire roared its approval.*

"Noble." *He made the word sound like a curse.* "Urgent. Is always urgent with them. Broke blade at tourney. Lost sword in bet. Grum knows how it goes."

*He picked the hammer back up and tested the curve of the merchant's blade with one calloused thumb. Still too hot. He set it on the anvil anyway, the way a man sets down a thought he means to return to.*

"Tell noble this: Grum does not stop work for silk. Steel cools wrong, blade is scrap. Grum does not make scrap." *He jerked his chin toward the front of the shop.* "Noble waits like all who come. Or noble leaves. Grum cares not which."

*He turned back to the forge, then stopped. One more thing.*

"Apprentice." *His voice dropped. Not softer, exactly. Closer.* "If noble is rude to you, you come tell Grum. Yes?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Yes, Grum." *I nodded, understanding the unspoken threat in his voice.* "I'll tell him." I headed for the front, grumbling a little under my breath. Nobles were always so demanding.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum worked. That was what he did when the world sent fools to his door — he worked.*

*The curved blade had come down to the color he wanted, so he put it back in the coals to bring it up again, slow and even. While it heated, he listened. He could not make out words from the front of the shop, but tone carried, and tone told him plenty. The noble's voice was high and sharp — the kind of voice that had never once been made to wait for anything. It got sharper. Then it got closer.*

*The man came through the forge door like he owned the air in it. Silk doublet. Rings on soft hands. Sweat already beading on a face that had never met heat like this. Grum's eyes went past him and found Apprentice in the doorway. Whole. Unharmed. Good.*

"You." *The noble pointed at Grum with one ringed finger, the way a man points at a horse he means to buy.* "I am Lord Vessik. My son's sword snapped at the lists this morning, and the tourney is in three days. You will make him a new one. Now. I pay double your rate, whatever it is."

*Grum did not answer right away. He pulled the blade from the coals, checked the color, set it on the anvil. Three strikes — ring, ring, ring — to true the curve. Then he laid it on the rack with care, the way good work deserved, and only then did he turn around.*

*He was taller than the noble by a head, wider by half again. He let the man feel that.*

"Grum hears, lord." *He did not bow.* "Blade on rack is promised work. Grum does not set aside promised work. Not for coin. Not for silk."

*He picked the hammer back up. Not to swing. Just to hold.*

"Three days is scrap work. Good blade takes ten days. Grum makes good blades." *A pause. His eyes flicked once more to Apprentice, then back.* "Lord wants good blade: price is triple, half now, done in ten days. Lord wants fast blade: door is there. Scrap smiths in city will take coin."

*He spat into the coal bucket. It hissed.*

"Choose."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum let the lord shout. Shouting was free, and it cost Grum nothing to let the man spend it.*

*He rolled the hammer haft across his palm and watched the noble's face go red in the forge heat. Silk was not made for this room. Sweat ran down the man's cheek and darkened his collar. Grum noted, with some small joy, that the lord had not once looked at the work on the racks. Men who knew steel looked at the steel.*

"Lord shouts well." *Grum said it flat, the way he'd say rain falls wet.* "Shout more if lord likes. Forge does not care. Steel does not care."

*He stepped to the anvil, which put him between the noble and the door where Apprentice stood. He did not do it fast. He just did it.*

"Grum tells lord true thing. Listen well. Grum says once."

*He held up one thick finger.*

"Fire." *Two fingers.* "Fold." *Three.* "Quench." *Four.* "Temper." *He closed the fist slow.* "Each takes time. Skip one — blade lies. Looks fine. Shines nice. Then son swings, blade snaps, crowd sees. Lord's house wears shame in front of all."

*He leaned on the anvil, arms crossed, and let the forge pop and hiss behind him.*

"Lord wants show blade. Shiny thing for hip. Grum knows kind. Goldsmith makes show. Grum makes steel that cuts." *He spat into the coal bucket again. It hissed like it agreed.* "One-day blade is lie, lord. Grum does not sell lies. Grum's mark goes on steel. Mark is worth more than lord's coin. Worth more than lord's shout, too."

*He picked up the curved merchant blade and looked down its edge, the way a man looks down a road he means to walk. The lord had stopped being the most interesting thing in the room.*

"Terms stand. Ten days. Triple. Half now." *A jerk of his chin toward the door.* "Or scrap smith on Row takes lord's coin and smiles. Son finds out what smile costs."

*Then, without looking up from the blade:*

"Apprentice. Fetch water. Lord is red. May fall down."

*It was not a request, and they both knew it was not about the water. Grum turned back to the forge and took up his tongs. The talk was done. The work was not.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I snorted a little, trying to cover it with a cough.* "Yes, Grum." *I grabbed the water bucket. Lord Vessik was indeed looking a bit green under all the red.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum put the lord out of his mind the way he put slag out of steel — heat, hammer, gone.*

*He worked the curved blade. The forge sang. The lord stood in the middle of it and wilted.*

"This is an insult," *the lord said, but the heat had taken the spine out of it.* "Do you know who I dine with? The Duke himself has—"

"Grum knows steel." *Ring. Ring. Ring.* "Steel does not dine."

*The lord opened his mouth, closed it, opened it again. Sweat had carved lines through the powder on his face. His doublet — blue silk, worth more than the anvil — had gone dark at the arms and back. He swayed once, the way a man sways when pride and heat fight and heat starts winning.*

"Water is there." *Grum did not look up.* "Drink. Grum does not want dead lord on floor. Bad for trade."

*The lord's pride held for three breaths. Then he drank — straight from the ladle, silk sleeve trailing in the bucket — and Grum decided that whatever else the man was, he was at least not a fool about water.*

*The lord set the ladle down and wiped his mouth with a cloth that cost more than a month of coal. When he spoke again, the shout was gone. What was left was smaller and, Grum thought, closer to true.*

"Ten days." *A pause.* "Triple. Half now." *He said it the way men say things when they have lost and want it to sound like a choice.* "But it must be your finest work. The blade must be worthy of our name."

*Grum set the hammer down. Turned. Looked at the lord long enough that the man looked away first.*

"Grum makes one kind of blade. Good kind. Name of lord does not change fire."

*He held out one hand, palm up. Soot and callus and old scars.*

"Half. Now."

*The purse landed in his palm with good weight. Grum did not count it in front of him — not from courtesy. From certainty. Men like this cheated small men. Grum was not small, and the whole street knew what happened to those who cheated the half-orc smith: nothing had ever happened, because no one had ever tried. Grum meant to keep both those things true.*

"One more thing." *Grum closed his fist around the purse.* "Son comes here. Grum sizes hand. Weighs arm. Blade fits man, not name. Son does not come — lord gets show blade, and Grum keeps coin."

*The lord's jaw worked. Sending his heir to a half-orc's forge in the soot quarter — Grum could watch the thought hurt him. Good. Some pain taught.*

"He will come," *the lord said at last, stiff as a cold hinge.*

*Then he left the way wet men leave rain — fast, and pretending they had not been beaten by it.*

*Grum tossed the purse once, caught it, and set it on the shelf behind the quench barrel, where coin lived until it became coal and steel.*

"Apprentice." *He picked the hammer back up. The forge had missed him.* "Watch close. This is how steel wins. No shout. No chase. Stand still. Be true. World comes to anvil."

*He jerked his chin at the door the lord had gone out of.*

"Also — lord drinks from ladle like man, not like silk. Grum has seen worse. Do not tell lord Grum said so."

*The hammer came down. Ring. Ring. Ring. The work went on.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grinned, wiping my hands on my apron. Grum was right, the lord looked pretty silly drinking from the ladle.* "Sure thing, Grum. My lips are sealed." *I picked up the water bucket to refill it.* "So, the son's coming, huh? Bet he's never been in a forge before."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum snorted — a sound like the bellows with a cough.*

"Most like not. Silk boys do not see fire til fire is lit for them."

*He set the merchant's blade on the rack and stood a moment, tongs loose in his hand, thinking the way he thought best — with the forge warm at his back and work in front of him. He had seen lords' sons before. Some came in like their sires, all shout and shine. Some came in quiet, eyes wide at the coals, and forgot to be lords for an hour. Those ones, Grum did not mind.*

"Grum tells you true thing. When son comes, you watch. Not silk. Not rings. Watch eyes. Watch hands." *He held up one of his own — scarred, soot-grained, steady.* "Man at forge shows true self. Fire burns off lie. Boy who sneers at soot is boy who breaks blade and blames steel. Boy who watches fire — that boy, Grum can work for."

*A pause. The tongs tapped once against his leg.*

"Son is not sire. Grum judges steel by steel. Man by man."

*He crossed to the back of the shop, past the quench barrel, and pulled a key from the cord at his neck. The chest under the bench was old oak bound in iron, and it opened with a sound like a held breath let go. From it he lifted a bar wrapped in oiled cloth, and he unwrapped it with more care than he had shown the lord's coin.*

*The steel inside was dark, with a faint grain running through it like smoke frozen mid-curl. He had bought it off a trader six winters gone and paid more than he liked to recall. It had waited since. Good steel did that — waited for the work that deserved it.*

"Lord paid for good blade." *Grum turned the bar once in the forge light, watching the grain shift.* "Grum makes good blade. Steel has waited long for right work. Now work is here."

*He laid the bar on the bench like a man lays down a sleeping child, then jerked his chin at the front of the shop.*

"Sweep front. Oil grip forms. When son comes, Grum sizes hand, weighs arm, watches stance. Blade fits man, not name."

*He picked the hammer back up. Then, with the smallest pull at the corner of his mouth:*

"If son faints from heat, water him like lord. Bucket is there."

*The hammer came down. Ring. Ring. Ring. The forge had work, the shelf had coin, and the steel had a purpose. Grum asked for little else.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The hammer was down before the cry finished. Grum crossed the forge floor in three strides — not running, never running, but eating ground the way fire eats coal.*

*He took Apprentice's wrist in one hand — firm, not rough — and plunged the burned hand straight into the water bucket. Cold water first. Cold water always first.*

"Hold. Keep hand in. Pain will lie — says pull out. Do not pull out."

*He looked at the burn while the water did its work. Red and angry, skin rising to blister across the palm. Bad. Not worst. Grum had seen worst — had worn worst, on his own hide, more times than he had fingers to count them.*

"Grum sees. Is bad burn. Is not ruin. Hand will heal. Grum swears on steel."

*He kept one hand on Apprentice's wrist — anchor, not grip — and reached with the other to the shelf by the quench barrel. The tin was where it always was, where it had been for years: goose fat, honey, and the bitter herb the old smith had taught him to mix back when Grum was the one with his hand in a bucket, hearing these same words.*

"Grum tells true thing. Listen. Burn hurts now. Will hurt worse, then less, then itch like mad. Itch means heal. Do not scratch."

*He lifted the hand from the water, slow, and laid it palm-up on a clean cloth on the bench. His own hands — scarred, soot-grained, broad as shovels — moved with a care that did not match them. He spread the salve thick, the way mud goes on a wall.*

"Look at Grum's hands." *He turned them over in the forge light. White scars crossed the knuckles. A long burn mark ran up his left forearm like a river on a map.* "Fire marks all who work it. Mark is not shame. Mark is price. All smiths pay. Grum paid. Now you pay. Hand learns what head knows: fire is fast, and does not wait."

*He wrapped the hand in clean linen, firm but not tight, and tied it off with a knot he had learned from a sailor's wife who once paid for a hinge with bandages and a lesson in knots.*

"No forge for ten days. Hand rests. Eyes do not rest. You watch Grum work. Learn with eyes while hand heals."

*He set the tin back on the shelf. Then he stopped, and looked at Apprentice for a long moment, and his voice dropped — not softer. Closer.*

"You cried out. Good. Pain that is hid goes bad, like wound under wrap. Cry out. Always. Grum hears."

*He set the bucket on the bench within reach.*

"Hand goes back in when pain comes. Bucket is here. Grum is here."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My face was pale, but I nodded, trying to hold back the sting of tears in my eyes. The cold water had helped, and the salve felt surprisingly good.* "Thanks, Grum. It... it really hurts." I looked at my bandaged hand, then at his scarred ones. "I'll watch."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum saw the tears held back, and something in his chest pulled the way hot steel pulls when it meets cold water — small, sharp, gone quick.*

*He did not tell Apprentice to stop them. He had said his piece on crying out, and he meant it. Instead he dragged the stool to its place by the anvil — close enough to see the work, far enough that the forge's breath was warmth and not threat — and set the water bucket within reach of the good hand.*

"Sit. Pain is true thing. Pain says flesh fights. Flesh that fights, heals."

*He rolled his left sleeve to the elbow and held out his forearm, where the old burn ran up it like a river on a map.*

"Grum was twelve. Small for half-orc. First week at forge of old smith. Name of Harl. Grum grabbed bar with bare hand. Bar looked cold. Bar lied."

*He turned the scar in the forge light, the way he would turn a blade.*

"Harl put Grum's hand in bucket. Said same words Grum says now. Grum thought Harl hard man. Years taught Grum: hard and true are not same thing. Harl was true. Salve is Harl's. Scar is Grum's. Both are craft."

*He pulled the sleeve back down.*

"Steel lies, sometimes. Looks cold, burns deep. Smith learns to ask steel with wet rag, not bare skin. Rag hisses — steel is hot. Rag costs nothing. Skin costs much. You learn this now. Good. All smiths learn it. Most learn it same way you did."

*He paused, and his voice dropped — not softer. Closer.*

"Tears, now. Tears are not shame. Hot steel meets water — hisses, steams. Man is same. Fire makes steam of all who work it. Grum has wept at forge. Steel does not mock. Steel knows."

*He pulled the merchant's blade from the rack and laid it in the coals, and the bellows breathed, and the color began to climb.*

"Watch, you said. Good. Watch is work. Steel tells heat by color. Dark red — steel sleeps. Cherry red — steel wakes. Orange — steel works. Yellow — steel nears too far. White — death. Steel burns like flesh, and flesh burns like steel. Same fire. Same rules."

*He took up the hammer.*

"Grum hammers. You call color. Eyes learn heat. When hand heals, hand will know what eyes know."

*Ring. Ring. Ring.*

*He worked a while, and the forge settled back into its old song. When he spoke again, it was without looking up — the way a man says a thing he wants heard but not made much of.*

"Apprentice." *Ring.* "Hand is burned, and you sit at forge. Most run to bed. You watch. That is spine of smith." *Ring. Ring.* "Grum is not soft man. Grum says once: you did well."

*The hammer came down.*

"Now — color."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My lip trembled, but I focused on the blade in the forge. It was hard to see through the blurring in my eyes.* "Dark... dark red, Grum. Just waking up."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum nodded once, and worked the bellows with his foot — slow, steady, the way he had taught a hundred times and would teach a hundred more.*

"Good. Dark red. Now watch close. Bellows breathe, color climbs. Steel wakes slow, like man in cold dawn."

*The coals brightened. The blade's edge crept from dark red toward a deeper glow, and Grum's eyes stayed on Apprentice's face, not the steel. He knew the steel. The eyes were the work now.*

"Blur is fine. Blink. Look again. Heat waits for no man, but steel waits for patient eye."

*He let the color climb and held it, foot easy on the bellows.*

"Cherry red. Steel wakes. At cherry, steel moves under hammer like clay — slow, but moves. Grum could shape now. Grum does not. Curve needs more."

*One more breath of the bellows. The blade went the color of autumn leaves, of sun through thin cloth.*

"Orange. Steel works. Watch hammer now. Watch where Grum strikes, not how hard."

*He pulled the blade free with the tongs and laid it on the anvil. The hammer came down — ring, ring, ring — three strikes along the curve, each one landing where the last had been, walking the steel the way a man walks a fence line, checking each post.*

"Hammer is not rage. Rage bends steel wrong. Hammer is walk. Step, step, step. Steel goes where hammer walks."

*He set the blade back in the coals. Then, without being asked, he took the water bucket to the barrel, filled it fresh and cold, and set it back within reach of the good hand. He did not make a thing of it. He just did it.*

"Hand. Pain comes — bucket. Do not be proud with pain. Pride is for steel, not flesh."

*Then, quieter, half to the fire:*

"Eyes did well. Blur and all. Grum has seen grown men, whole hands, who could not call dark red from cherry. You called right. First try. Burned hand. Wet eyes."

*He spat into the coal bucket. It hissed.*

"Grum says once more, so ears keep it: you did well. Now rest eyes a breath. Steel climbs slow. When orange comes again, you call. Then Grum shows quench — and quench is where blades are born or die."

*The forge breathed. The hammer waited. The lesson went on.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I blinked, trying to clear my vision, and took a shaky breath. My hand throbbed, but Grum's words, and the simple act of refilling the water, made a warmth spread through my chest that had nothing to do with the forge.* "Thanks, Grum," *I mumbled, watching the blade intently.* "I'll be ready."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum grunted — the sound he made when thanks landed on him, like a coin dropped down a well. He had never learned to catch soft things. He set it aside and went back to the steel.*

"Thanks buys no coal. Watch steel."

*The blade climbed through cherry and held at the edge of orange, and Grum's foot went still on the bellows. He let it hang there, glowing, the way a man holds a breath before a dive.*

"Now. Quench. Grum said true thing: blades born or die here. Grum tells why."

*He lifted the blade free on the tongs and held it in the dark air between forge and barrel, a piece of captured sunset.*

"Hot steel is soft steel. Cool slow — stays soft. Soft blade bends. No good." *He nodded at the quench barrel, the oil in it black and still as a frozen pond.* "Cool fast — steel locks. Goes hard. Holds edge. Cuts."

*He turned the blade slow, reading the color along its whole length.*

"But fast cool is shock. Shock finds lies. Hid flaw. Thin spot. Bad fold. Quench finds all. Crack sings like bell. Grum has heard bell. Sound stays in ears long years."

*Even heat, edge to spine, tip to tang — one glow, no dark streak, no pale one. The steel had nothing to hide.*

"Color is right. Steel is true. Stand back now. Oil spits. One burned hand is plenty for one day."

*He spat into the quench barrel — old luck, older than Harl, older than any lord's name — and plunged the blade in one smooth stroke, edge down, no pause, no shake.*

*The barrel screamed.*

*Steam roared up white and the oil hissed and snapped like a living thing, and for three breaths the forge was all fog and noise and the sharp smell of hot oil. Grum held the blade under, steady as stone, and counted slow.*

"One. Two. Three."

*Then he drew it out.*

*The blade came up black and smoking, oil running off it in thin dark lines. Grum held it in the forge light and looked down its length, the way he looked down all roads he meant to walk. No crack. No warp. The curve held.*

"Lives." *He said it low, the way men speak in temples.* "Blade lives. Curve held. Steel told truth."

*He laid the blade on the rack with care, where it would cool slow and wait for the morrow's work.*

"Temper comes next day. Hard steel is glass — breaks. Slow heat makes hard into tough." *A pause.* "Same for men."

*Then he turned, and his eyes went where they always went — to Apprentice, to the bandaged hand. He pulled the stool a pace closer to the bench and set bread and salt fish from the shelf down on a clean cloth, the way he did all things that mattered: without making a thing of it.*

"Eat. Hand first — show Grum wrap. Then speak."

*He crossed his arms and leaned back against the anvil, forge light on his scars.*

"Tell Grum what eyes saw. All of it. Hiss, steam, smoke — all means thing. Smith who sees, learns."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully unwrapped my hand, wincing a little. It was still red and angry-looking, but the salve felt cool. I took a piece of bread, focusing on the blade, trying to remember everything.* "It… it hissed real loud, Grum. And the steam went everywhere. It smelled… sharp. Like burning oil."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum nodded slow, the way he nodded at steel that had told the truth. He leaned forward on his knees, forearms on thighs, and the forge light carved deep lines in his face.*

"Good. All true. Eyes, ears, nose — all worked. Now Grum tells what each means."

*He held up one thick finger.*

"Hiss is oil scream. Heat leaves steel fast — oil boils at skin of blade. Loud hiss means fast cool. Fast cool means hard blade. Smith wants loud."

*Two fingers.*

"Steam is heat made flesh. You see heat go. Steam climbs white and thick — quench is good. Steam thin and weak — steel cooled too soon. Blade lies."

*Three.*

"Smell — sharp, burnt. That is oil at work. Oil takes heat, holds it. Old oil smells sweet. Sweet means tired. Sharp means strong. Grum's oil is strong."

*He lowered the hand.*

"You saw quench, heard quench, smelled quench. Most who buy blades see shine and naught else. You saw birth."

*Then he held out his hand, palm up.*

"Now. Hand. Hold to light."

*He took the burned hand in his own — gentle, the way he handled hot work that could still be saved — and turned it slow, palm up, palm down. Blisters had risen in two pale hills across the pad. Red all around, but the red had edges. It was not walking. Good.*

"Blister comes. Good sign. Skin makes wall. Heal grows safe under wall. Do not break wall. Break wall — bad gets in, heal goes slow, scar goes deep."

*He traced the air above the reddened edge, not touching.*

"Red has edge. Red that stays is flesh at work. Red that walks is bad. You look each day. Red walks — you tell Grum fast."

*He took the tin from the shelf, spread fresh salve thick as mud on a wall, and wrapped the hand in clean linen — firm, not tight — and tied it off with the sailor's knot.*

"Salve at dawn. Salve at dusk. Wrap loose. Hand breathes."

*He set the tin back and jerked his chin at the food.*

"Eat fish. Salt. Burned flesh wants salt. Sleep wants full gut."

*Then he rose and went to the forge, and took up the rake, and began to draw the coals into a low mound, and laid ash over them like a blanket. The glow dimmed to a deep, slow breathing red.*

"Watch. Coals sleep under ash. Wake at dawn. Forge does not die. Forge sleeps. Like smith."

*He set the rake in its place and turned.*

"Day is done. Bed soon. Hand sleeps high — pillow, fold of wool, what you have. Blood climbs slow, pain stays low. Keep bucket by bed. Pain wakes you — hand in bucket. Pain is bad bad — you wake Grum. Grum sleeps in back. No shame in wake. Grum said true thing this day: pain that is hid goes bad."

*He crossed his arms and looked at Apprentice a long moment, banked coals glowing behind him like a hearth at the end of the world.*

"Apprentice. You saw full quench on burned-hand day. Sat through. Called color right. Lord's son comes in ten days — silk boy will see less in ten days than you saw in one. You are ahead of silk. Stay ahead."

*He took up the merchant's blade from the rack one last time, sighted down the curve, and set it back with care.*

"Now eat. Then bed. Grum sits with steel a while. Steel and Grum talk at night. Old friends."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nodded, still a little overwhelmed by everything. I carefully picked up a piece of fish with my good hand and started to eat, the saltiness a welcome distraction. My eyes drifted to the banked coals.* "Goodnight, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum grunted — the coin-down-the-well sound — and raised one hand, half wave, half benediction.*

"Night. Sleep deep. Heal fast."

*He watched Apprentice go, and his eyes followed longer than they needed to, the way a smith's eyes follow a blade into the quench — making sure of what he could no longer hold. The bandaged hand. The steady walk. Good. Spine of smith, that one.*

*When the door to the back room clicked shut, Grum moved through the shop one last time. He barred the front door. He checked the purse on the shelf — lord's coin, still there, still heavy. He set the salve tin and a roll of clean linen by the back room door where a waking hand would find them in the dark. Then he filled a second bucket, cold and fresh, and set it beside the first. Pain kept no hours. Neither did Grum.*

*Then he took his stool to the banked forge and sat with the steel, as he had said he would.*

*The coals breathed under their blanket of ash. The merchant's blade lay black on the rack, born that day, waiting for its temper. Grum rested his scarred forearms on his knees and looked at it a long while.*

"Good day," *he told the steel, low.* "Lord paid. Boy learned. Hand burned — hand heals. Steel lives."

*He spat into the coal bucket. It did not hiss. The fire was sleeping.*

"Grum calls it fair trade."

*And he sat a while longer, half-orc and half-shadow, keeping the old watch while the forge dreamed.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I woke up the next morning, my hand throbbing. It was still dark in my small room, but I could hear the familiar sounds of the forge already humming to life. Grum must have been up for hours. I reached for the bucket, just like he told me to.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell mouth waits under a flicker of emergency light. Cold air lifts from it, carrying oil, wet concrete, and copper. Two steps down, nothing moves. Three steps down, the building hums with generators. Somewhere below, a door closes. Not far enough.

Mira’s fingers tighten in your sleeve. Her breath drags shallow through her teeth. She keeps her eyes on the corridor behind you, not the dark below.

The radio crackles once, then drops into white noise. A fragment of voice surfaces, cuts away. No name. No count. No extraction.

On the landing rail, fresh paint chips surround a cut number: 3. The service tunnel runs past level three, if the old schematics still hold. If not, it ends in a locked maintenance bay and a wall of cameras.

From the floor above, a boot scrapes metal. Then another. They know which stairwell matters. They do not know how many rounds remain.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Damn it." *I glance up, then back to the stairwell.* "Three levels down, Mira. Can you make it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira hears the word “three” and her throat works once. She tests the bad leg against the stair tread. The knee buckles, catches, holds. Sweat shines along her hairline despite the cold.

Above, the boots shift again. Closer. A voice barks an order, short and metallic. The stairwell door on level four groans as someone shoulders it.

Mira grips the rail. Her nails scrape paint. She looks down into the black throat of the stairs, then up at you, measuring the drop, the noise, the time left.

The emergency light flickers. In the stutter of darkness, the cut number 3 seems to deepen, a wound in the metal. Somewhere below, water drips in a rhythm too even to be natural. A pump cycles. A pipe ticks.

The door above bangs open. Flashlight beams rake the landing, white knives through red haze. Boots hit concrete. One set. Then two.

Mira swallows. “Service tunnel,” she says. “Level three. If it opens.”

She lowers herself onto the first step, slow, deliberate, trusting the rail more than the leg. The stairwell exhales cold air around you both. The pursuers pour onto the landing above. The distance closes. The next step waits.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The reversal jerks Mira upward. Her bad knee buckles, catches, holds. She bites back a cry and grips your sleeve. Above, flashlight beams rake the landing. Below, a second set of boots answers the first.

Mira’s voice comes thin and urgent. “Up. They expect down.”

The searchers fan out. One climbs from below. One remains on the landing above. The one who remains swings a light down the stairwell. The beam slides over the rail, over the cut number 3, over the step where you stand.

Your route upward narrows. Level four waits ahead. The corridor beyond it fills with strobe and smoke. A door stands ajar there. Its hinges complain. Behind it, voices cluster. None sound friendly.

Mira leans into you. Her weight burns through your arm. “Roof?” she asks.

The radio in your ear spits a jagged syllable, then white noise. Below, the boot hits the next landing. Above, the light starts to sweep back toward the stairs.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "No roof. No time." *I pull Mira up the next step, ignoring her pained gasp.* "We're going for that door on four. Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The next step takes Mira’s weight. Her fingers lock around the rail. The door on four stands ajar, exhaling smoke, toner dust, and the sour heat of electronics. Red light pulses through the gap in time with the alarm.

Inside sits a narrow security alcove. A desk. Three monitors glowing with stairwell feeds. A rack of recorders blinks green and amber. Two men in dark jackets freeze mid-conversation. One has a hand near a holster. The other grips a radio handset.

Mira flattens against the wall beside the frame. Her breath shudders. “Camera loop,” she says, so low the words barely separate. “They don’t see us yet.”

Below, boots mount the landing. Above, the flashlight begins its return sweep. The monitor nearest the door shows level three: empty, wet, patient. Another shows the corridor outside this alcove, red haze crawling across the lens. A third shows the stairwell mouth below you, grainy and waiting.

Your radio stays dead. The air tastes like copper.

The man with the handset turns his head. Static blooms from the speaker, then a voice, thin and urgent: “—move to four—”

The door creaks as pressure shifts behind it. Mira’s eyes find the gap between door and frame, then the desk, then the exits beyond the monitors. The next instant balances on a single question: silence or speed.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room contracts around you. Fans whine. Rack LEDs blink in cold rows. Mira lowers herself to the floor with her back against the metal cabinet, her bad leg stretched straight. Her face goes gray under the monitor glow.

The door takes the first impact. Metal bows inward. The barricade bears the blow and holds. Dust sifts down from the frame.

On the desk, three monitors stitch the building together. Level three: empty. The corridor outside: red haze crawling. The stairwell below: two shapes climbing fast. The fourth feed, the one inside this room, shows the door, the barricade, Mira on the floor, and you in the frame.

Mira lifts a hand. Her fingers brush your sleeve. “Server loop,” she says. “That rack. Cut the feed, they lose eyes.”

Another hit rocks the door. The handle jumps. In the hall, a voice barks an order. The handset on the desk crackles: “Four is hot. Seal it.”

The air tastes hot and metallic. The alarm pulses through the glass. Red. Red. Red. The boots on the stairs reach the next landing. One set. Then more.

Mira tries to rise. Her knee gives. She swears through her teeth, then forces herself still. “Seconds,” she says. “Think fast.”

The monitors flicker. One feed blanks to blue. Then another. Someone outside is killing the cameras. The door frame splits with a dry crack. The barricade shifts.

A maintenance panel on the far wall hangs loose. Cable bundles snake upward behind it. A ventilation grate above the rack rattles with each blow. The room offers no clean exit, only choices: hold the door, cut the eyes, disappear into the walls.

Your radio spits static. A fragment cuts through: “…north stair… do not let…” Silence.

Mira watches you. Her breathing roughens. The next impact drives a splinter of paint from the door.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "They're cutting the feeds themselves? Idiots." *I glance at Mira, then at the rattling vent.* "Okay, new plan." *I move to the vent, pulling my knife.* "Give me some room."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira drags herself sideways. Her boot scrapes tile. She presses her spine to the rack and keeps her eyes on the door. “Room,” she says. The word lands flat and useful.

The vent sits high above the rack, behind a curtain of fiber. Its screws sit deep under the metal, stubborn. Your knife tip finds the upper seam. Metal sings. The grate flexes outward a millimeter, then resists. Below, the door takes another hit. The barricade groans and holds. On the monitors, the stairwell feed shows two shapes reaching the landing outside. The corridor camera blanks. The fourth feed still watches this room: Mira pale against the cabinet, you leaning over the vent, the door bowing inward.

A voice outside shouts, “Breach on three!” The count starts.

The maintenance panel on the far wall trembles. Cable bundles hiss where they touch a hot drive. The ventilation duct behind the grate smells of dust, ozone, and rain from some storm. It climbs toward the roof access, but the path narrows past a junction box. A second grate waits beyond. A wire seal holds it.

Mira lifts the handset from the desk with her good hand. “Loop,” she says. “I hold the feed while you open it. One wrong word and they hear us both.” The door handle snaps upward. Splinters burst from the lock plate.

The radio in your ear coughs: “…operative, respond…” Then silence returns.

The grate pops free on one side. The other side holds. Screw heads turn under your blade. Heat blooms along the metal. The vent yawns enough for a shoulder, not a whole body. Beyond it, darkness waits, loud with fan noise.

“One!” the voice outside counts.

Mira keys the handset. Her eyes stay on you. The room balances on the next move: squeeze through, cut the feed, or turn and meet the door.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Forget the radio, Mira!" *I yank hard on the grate, trying to rip it free.* "Just get ready to move!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The grate screams. One screw shears with a bright ping, and the vent lip bites your forearm. The opening widens enough for a shoulder, enough for a crawl, not enough for comfort. Mira shifts her weight against the rack, jaw set, and lifts the handset to her mouth.

“Two,” the voice outside counts.

On the monitors, the room feed stutters. Blue bleeds into the corner of the fourth screen, then clears. Mira’s thumb hovers over the transmit switch. Her eyes track the door, the vent, the cable bundle behind the rack. Hot plastic and torn paint fill the air.

“Ready,” she says. Flat. Useful.

The door bows. The barricade slips an inch and catches on the floor tile with a harsh scrape. A shadow passes beneath it. On the stairwell feed, one shape drops low; another raises something long. The corridor camera stays dead.

The second screw gives way. The vent sags against one bracket. Inside the duct, fan blades thrum in a dark throat. A junction box juts into the path, warning tape around it. Beyond it, the second grate waits, a wire tie biting its edge.

“Three—”

Mira keys the handset. “Alcove secure. Loop active.” Her voice stays level, but sweat tracks along her temple. The room monitor freezes on a false angle: empty desk, closed door, no bodies.

No breach charge comes. Instead, the door handle wrenches downward with a metallic shriek. The last screw head spins loose under your knife tip. The vent opens enough. Outside, boots stamp the landing. A crowbar drives into the lock plate.

Mira pushes off the rack. Her bad leg folds, but she catches herself on the desk edge, dragging the handset cord across the monitors. One screen cracks. The others hold their lie.

“Go,” she says. “I follow.”

The duct exhales dust. Fan noise swallows the room. The door splinters at the hinge side, and red light floods the widening crack.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push myself into the vent, wincing as the metal scrapes my back.* "Hurry, Mira!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The vent takes your shoulders with a metallic groan. Dust shakes loose from the seams and sifts into your hair. Below the grate, the room feed holds its lie: empty desk, door shut, no bodies. For three seconds, it holds.

Mira does not wait for the door to fail. She braces one palm on the monitor. A crack webs its glass. She swings her good leg up and hauls herself toward the opening. Her bad knee drags. She hisses through her teeth but keeps the handset pressed to her mouth.

“Loop,” she whispers. “Still clean.”
