Not the case. Not the file. *Who are you* — the first question, landing exactly where she'd said it would land.

Lena settled back against the booth and let the silence belong to the client. The coffee was terrible. The name they were carrying sat at the table like a fifth person nobody was feeding, and she did not look at it, and the morning held.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *My mouth feels dry, and I clear my throat.* "My name is [Client Name]. I hired Lena to look into the disappearance of my cousin, Sarah Jenkins." *I try to meet his gaze, but it's hard.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The name did what names did. It moved through the booth and rearranged the furniture.

Lena watched it land. The cup stopped its quarter-turn halfway around, and anyone else in the diner would have missed it. She didn't. She'd known the tell for years — a man who arranged the table before the business. The business had just arrived early.

"Jenkins," he said. Not a question. He said it the way a man checks a lock he turned years ago — not doubting it, just needing to feel it still held.

He set the cup down square, and when he looked at the client again, the reading was done. Something else had taken its place.

"I don't need the file for that one," he said. "You carry a hundred cases. Most of them settle — paperwork, time, the next one. Some of them don't settle. They walk beside you." A pause. "That one walks."

"That's why we're here," Lena said quietly.

She wrapped both hands around her mug and let the silence do its work. Four years of not coming here. A favor held against a day she couldn't have named — spent on a hunch, and the hunch had just confirmed itself in half a cup turn. She thought about the photograph in the file, the doorway, the figure half out of frame. *Wait until he sees that.* The thought had no satisfaction in it. Only confirmation, which was a colder thing.

The detective was still watching the client. "You're nervous," he said, and it wasn't unkind — he said it the way a man states weather. "Good. Nervous tells the truth. Rehearsed is the thing that lies. I've had people sit where you're sitting with a story so smooth it slid off the table. Never once believed one of them."

He leaned back against the booth. The fogged window put gray light on one side of his face, and for a moment he looked like a man doing arithmetic he'd done a hundred times before, in the small hours, without ever liking the total.

"So before the file, before the photographs, before whatever your investigator told you to do with your hands —" something moved at the corner of his mouth, the place where a smile would go, "— tell me about Sarah. Not the case. Her. Who she was to the people who knew her. And when you understood she was *missing* — not gone somewhere, not angry somewhere. Missing. There's a moment that happens, in every one of these. I want yours."

The waitress passed. He covered his cup with his hand without looking up — *no, no refill, we're working now* — and the table settled into the particular quiet of a room where the next voice matters.

Lena settled back against the wall side and let the quiet belong to the client. The name they'd carried in with them stayed unspent, folded away wherever they'd folded it. She noted that the way she noted everything, and approved, and said nothing about it. Some things you don't praise. Praising them teaches people they were hard to do.

The coffee was terrible. The morning was holding. She drank.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, the knot in my stomach tightening even more. He's not asking for facts, he's asking for... Sarah. My voice is a little shaky at first.* "Sarah was... she was the kind of person who made you feel like everything was going to be okay, even when it wasn't. She worked at the library, loved old movies."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The detective listened without moving. It was a skill, and Lena knew its worth — most people listened by waiting for their turn to talk. He listened the way other men read ledgers, like every word was a line item and the total had to come out right.

Lena noted what the client reached for first. Not dates. Not places. A feeling — *the kind of person who made you feel like everything was going to be okay.* People told you who they were by what they reached for. The client had reached for Sarah. That was either love or guilt, and in Lena's experience the two shared a fence.

The library was new. The file hadn't had it. She filed it away without moving her face.

The client trailed off, and the detective let the silence sit a moment — not cruelly. The way you let a floor settle before you put weight on it.

"That's who she was to the room," he said. "Everyone who sits where you're sitting starts there. The library, the movies, the way she made people feel. It's all true and it's no use to me. It's the version you give at the service." He said it flat, without apology, and somehow that was kinder than softening it would have been. "I asked for the moment."

He leaned forward, forearms on the table, hands loose around the cup.

"The moment you knew. Not worried. Not wondered. *Knew.* Where were you standing. What day of the week. What did you do with your hands in the first minute after." He turned the cup a quarter turn. "There's always a moment. A phone that rings out when it never rings out. A door that should be locked and isn't. A Tuesday that goes wrong by an inch, and you're the only one who feels the inch. I've sat across from a hundred families. Not one of them lacked the moment. They just don't trust it, because it doesn't look like evidence."

He glanced at Lena — the first time he'd taken his eyes off the client since they'd sat down.

"It is," he said. "It's the only evidence that doesn't lie. Paperwork lies. Witnesses lie. Memory lies. But the body keeps the moment, and the body doesn't have the imagination to invent one."

Lena turned her mug a quarter turn — his tell, borrowed without thinking, the way old habits cross a table without asking permission. She noticed herself doing it and didn't stop.

This was why she'd spent the favor. Not for case notes, not for whatever he'd written down in the small hours. For this — a man who could ask the one question that mattered and make it land where it was supposed to land. The file stayed closed between them, untouched. He hadn't looked at it once. The case he carried was the one in his head. The paper was for later — for checking memory against record and finding out which of the two had been lying.

The name the client had carried in stayed folded away, unspent. Lena noted that the way she noted everything, and the account held at zero.

The griddle hissed. Somebody's fork scraped a plate three booths up. The detective waited with the patience of a man who had waited out liars, lawyers, and four-year silences, and knew that grief always talked eventually — you only had to give it a table.

"Take your time," he said. "The coffee's terrible. Nobody's going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I swallow, my throat still dry. I can feel Lena watching me, too. It's like a spotlight has been turned on that exact memory.* "It was a Tuesday. I remember that much. She usually called me on her lunch break, around noon. When she didn't call, I just thought she was busy. But then she didn't call that night either. She always called goodnight." My voice gets a little softer. "I went to her apartment Wednesday morning. The door was unlocked. And her favorite mug, the one with the chipped handle, was in the sink. She *always* washed it right after using it."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena leaned back in her chair, the springs groaning under the shift in weight. She pulled a cigarette from the pack on the desk but didn't light it — just rolled it between her fingers, eyes fixed somewhere past the client's shoulder.

"We can't walk into the Ninth," she said. Flat. Not a negotiation. "And neither can I walk in there on your behalf. That door doesn't open for me."

She set the cigarette down and pulled the file back toward her, flipping it open again to a page the client hadn't seen yet — a name, an address, a phone number with a coffee ring over the last two digits.

"But Detective Harlan's not at the Ninth anymore. Retired. Moved to Bay Ridge." She tapped the number. "He's got a dog, a garden, and not enough people to talk to. He'll talk." She glanced up, something careful behind her eyes. "You go see him. Buy him a beer. He liked whiskey sours back in the day — see if that's still true."

She tore the page from the file and slid it across the desk.

"Take notes. Word for word. I want to hear how he tells it, not how you remember it."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I look at the ripped page, then back at Lena.* "So, I'm doing the legwork now? I hired you to investigate." *I pick up the page, a little annoyed.* "And what exactly should I be asking him? What's the angle here?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena doesn't flinch at the tone. She's had worse across this desk. She picked the cigarette back up, turned it end over end twice, then set it down again — a habit that had nothing to do with smoking.

"You hired me to find out what happened," she said. "That's what I'm doing. This is what it looks like."

She pulled a legal pad toward her and wrote for a while without talking. Three questions, block letters. She tore the sheet off and laid it beside the address.

"First — who hired him. Not the department. The client behind the client. Harlan worked private for six years before he hung it up. Somebody paid for that. I want to know who and what they asked for."

She tapped the second line.

"Second — what he took with him. Cops don't retire clean. They take a copy of something. A file, a notebook, a photograph they couldn't leave in the box. Ask him what he kept. Don't push if he stalls. Just let the silence sit there and see what he fills it with."

"Third." She leaned forward, elbows on the desk. "Ask him about the night of the fourteenth. Not the case — the night. Where he was, who called him, what time he got home. People remember cases the way they were told to remember them. They remember nights the way they actually happened."

She sat back.

"You're not doing my job. You're doing the part of it I can't do, and you're doing it because a man in Bay Ridge will say things over a whiskey sour to a stranger that he'd never say to a professional." A pause. Something almost like a smile, thin and quick. "Besides. You wanted to be involved. This is involved."

She nodded at the door.

"Go before he starts watering the garden. He's an early light-out."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's hands stopped moving. For a moment — barely a breath — the cigarette lay still between her fingers. Then she picked up the legal pad, squared it against the edge of the desk, and set it down again in exactly the same spot.

"You've got a forty-minute drive to Bay Ridge if traffic's kind," she said. Her voice hadn't changed. Same tone, same pace, like the question had been about the weather. "Which it won't be. Take Flatbush, not the BQE."

She pulled open a desk drawer and rummaged through it — paper clips, a broken flashlight, envelopes — until she found a folded twenty. She tossed it onto the desk near the torn page.

"That's for the first round. Don't let him pay. He'll try. Men like Harlan always try, and then they feel owed, and then they start telling you what you want to hear instead of what's true."

She looked up at the client then. Steady. Patient. The way a wall is patient.

"Now — the three questions. Don't read them off the paper. Get him talking first. Let him tell you about the dog. Let him tell you about the garden. And when he's comfortable, when he's on his second drink and the sun's gone down — that's when you ask. In that order."

She nodded toward the door again, a small gesture, final.

"Clock's ticking. Go."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the twenty, then the questions and the address.* "Alright, alright. I'm going." *I pause at the door.* "And thanks for the twenty. I'll make sure to get him talking about his prize-winning petunias." *I head out, the faint smell of chemicals following me down the stairs.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened to the footsteps fade down the stairwell, then the street door below open and close. The room settled back into its own silence — the hum of the mini-fridge in the corner, the muffled whir of the dry cleaner's presses through the floor.

She sat for a while without moving.

Then she pulled the file back to the center of the desk and opened it to the pages she hadn't shown the client. There weren't many. A printout of a property record. A photocopy of a newspaper clipping, small, near the back of a section nobody read. And a photograph of a car — silver sedan, partial plate, taken at an angle that suggested it was shot from behind a parked van.

She looked at the photograph for a long time.

Her cell phone buzzed against the desk. She glanced at the screen. Unknown number, 718 area code. Bay Ridge, maybe. She let it ring. It stopped. Buzzed again immediately — same number. She turned it face-down and went back to the clipping.

Under the desk lamp, the print was faded. She held it closer. There was a name in the third paragraph she hadn't noticed before — a business registration, a shell company name that meant nothing on its own. She wrote it on the legal pad in the same block letters, then underlined it twice.

The phone buzzed a third time. She picked it up this time.

"Yeah."

A pause. Someone talking on the other end — she listened without interrupting, her eyes on the name she'd just written.

"How did you get this number," she said. Not a question.

Another pause. She reached for the cigarette again, rolled it between her fingers.

"I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I'm in my car, driving down Flatbush, humming to myself. I glance at the rearview mirror, checking for traffic.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held the phone against her shoulder while she copied down what the caller said. Short bursts. She didn't confirm or deny anything — just listened, her pen moving in the same block letters, filling the bottom third of the legal pad.

"No," she said at one point. Then, after another stretch of listening: "That's not what I asked."

She stood up and moved to the window. Through the slats of the blinds she could see Mercer Street below — a woman with a stroller, a delivery truck double-parked, the neon sign of the dry cleaner's buzzing to life as the light faded. Nobody standing still. Nobody looking up.

She watched anyway.

"Call me when you have it in hand," she said. "Not before. I don't want updates, I want the thing itself."

She hung up and stood there a while longer, phone still warm against her palm. Then she set it on the windowsill and went back to the desk.

The name she'd underlined — the shell company — sat in the middle of the legal pad like a stone in a riverbed. She pulled her laptop over and opened it, the screen washing her face in blue light. She typed the name into a business registry search, waited, scrolled. Cross-referenced. Typed another variation. Waited again.

What came back wasn't much. But it wasn't nothing.

She printed the page, tore it from the printer before it finished, and folded it into the inside pocket of her jacket. Then she looked at the photograph of the silver sedan again. The partial plate. She pulled up an old bookmark — a DMV lookup through a contact she'd paid for once and never named — and entered what she had.

No match. Expected. She tried the plate with different letters in the blanks. Two results came back. She wrote both down.

Outside, a car horn. The presses below thumped and hissed. Somewhere in Bay Ridge, a man named Harlan was either pouring a whiskey sour or watering his garden, and the client was twenty minutes closer to finding out which.

Lena closed the laptop. She sat in the dark for a while, listening to the building settle.

Then she picked up her phone again and dialed a number from memory — not the one that had called her. A different one. It rang four times.

"It's me," she said. "The Mercer Street file. It's moving faster than I thought." A pause. "No, I haven't told them anything about that. And I won't." Another pause, shorter. "Just — watch the Bay Ridge address tonight. You'll know it when you see it. Call me if anyone else shows up."

She hung up before the other person could respond. Then she pulled her jacket off the back of the chair, shrugged it on, and pocketed the folded printout and the two plate numbers.

The office smelled like chemicals and old coffee. She left the blinds half-closed, turned the deadbolt, and went down the stairs into the thinning evening.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's pen stopped moving.

It was a small thing — a fraction of a second where the ink hovered over the legal pad and then lifted without making a mark. She set the pen down slowly, deliberately, like someone placing something fragile on a hard surface.

"That's not the name Harlan gave me," she said. She pulled the legal pad back toward her and looked at the questions she'd written earlier without really seeing them. "Where did the witness get it?"

Her voice was even. Practiced even. The kind of even that takes effort.

She reached for the case file and opened it again, flipping through the pages she'd already memorized. Her thumb caught on the edge of the newspaper clipping, the one with the shell company name she'd underlined. She didn't pull it out. She closed the file instead.

"Torres is a common enough name in this city." She picked up the pen again and wrote it at the top of a fresh page — just the name, nothing else. Then she drew a line under it and stared at the line instead of the letters. "Could be anyone. Could be a name your witness misheard. Could be someone who worked the case for six weeks and got reassigned before the file closed."

She tapped the pen against the desk once. Twice. Stopped.

"What else did the witness say? Word for word. Not what you think they meant — what they actually said."

She leaned back in the chair, the springs groaning again. Her gaze moved past the client to the window, the blinds, the thin gaps of evening light between the slats. Outside, the dry cleaner's sign buzzed and flickered on.

"I'll look into it," she said, quieter now. "But the name doesn't matter yet. What matters is what the witness *saw*, not what they were told to call it."

She turned the legal pad face-down on the desk.

"Now. Harlan. What did he say about the fourteenth?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Harlan said he was home on the fourteenth. Said he had the flu." *I cross my arms.* "But he seemed... off. Kept looking at his watch. And the witness said Torres."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stood up and moved to the window again, her back to the client. She adjusted a blind slat with one finger, then let it fall back into place. It made a small clicking sound in the quiet room.

"Home with the flu," she repeated. Not agreeing. Not disagreeing. Just laying the words out on the table where she could look at them. "And checking his watch."

She turned around and leaned against the windowsill, arms crossed.

"Flu's a convenient thing to have on a night you don't want to be remembered anywhere." She said it flatly, like reading a weather report. "And a man who checks his watch during a conversation isn't thinking about the past. He's thinking about something that's about to happen, or someone who's about to walk through a door."

She came back to the desk but didn't sit. She picked up the legal pad, turned it face-up again, and crossed out the name she'd written at the top of the page. Not scribbled out — a single clean line through the letters, so they were still legible underneath.

"As for the other thing." She set the pad down and looked at the client for the first time since coming back to the desk. Her eyes were steady, but there was something behind them that had closed a door. Not anger. Not sadness. Just — a wall, going up where a window had been. "Witnesses say a lot of names. Half of them are wrong. The other half are right but point somewhere you don't expect. Either way, a name is just a label on a door. I care about what's in the room."

She pulled the photograph of the silver sedan out of the file and laid it face-up between them.

"This car. Two possible plates. I want to know if either one turns up in Bay Ridge tonight. Not parked on the street — parked somewhere a person would park if they didn't want to be seen watching a house."

She slid a piece of paper across the desk with two alphanumeric combinations written on it.

"Check the block. Check the cross streets. Don't approach anyone. Don't take photos with your phone. Just look, and come back here, and tell me what you saw."

She finally sat down, the chair groaning its familiar complaint. She reached for the cold coffee, looked at it, and set it aside.

"And the fourteenth. You said Harlan checked his watch. What time was it when he did it the first time?"

Her pen was ready. Waiting. The name at the top of the legal pad sat under its single crossed line like a buried thing that hadn't agreed to stay buried.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "He looked at his watch maybe... eight-thirty? Nine?" *I pick up the paper with the plates.* "So I'm staking out Harlan's place? This is getting interesting."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote *8:30–9:00* on the pad, then paused, the pen hovering.

"Close enough," she said. She circled the time twice. "That's not the flu. That's an appointment."

She leaned forward and pulled the photograph of the silver sedan closer to the center of the desk, angling it so the client could see the partial plate clearly.

"It's not a stakeout. Don't confuse the two." Her voice had that flat, instructional quality — the tone of someone who'd explained this before and didn't enjoy it. "A stakeout is what you do when you're waiting for something to happen. This is just a look. Drive past. Park at the end of the block if you need to. Count the cars. Note anything silver, anything with a sedan body type. Check the plates against these two — " she tapped the paper — "and if neither matches, you come back and tell me that. A negative result is still a result."

She leaned back, studying the client the way she'd studied the photographs earlier — long enough to be uncomfortable, without expression.

"Eight-thirty to nine. If Harlan had somewhere to be, he'd have mentioned it. Men like that volunteer alibis — it's reflex. The fact that he didn't means either he didn't go, or he went somewhere he doesn't want on the record." She tapped the pen against the pad. "Which is why I want to know what's parked near his house tonight. Someone who visits a man checking his watch doesn't arrive in a cab."

She stood and walked to the small filing cabinet in the corner, pulled open the second drawer, and rummaged through it — folders, envelopes, a box of ammunition she never talked about. She came back with a pair of compact binoculars and set them on the desk next to the plate numbers.

"Flatbush back to Bay Ridge. Same route as before. Park facing his house but not directly across — one house over, either side. If someone's already sitting there, you drive past and come back to me. You don't engage."

She sat down again and looked at the legal pad. The crossed-out name stared up at her. She turned the pad face-down again without thinking about it.

"And if Harlan comes out — if he goes somewhere — you let him. You don't follow. Not tonight." A beat. "Tonight is just eyes."

She picked up the cold coffee, took a sip anyway, and grimaced.

"Go."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, picking up the binoculars and the paper with the plate numbers.* "Alright. Eyes only. Got it." *I head for the door, then turn back.* "And if I see a silver sedan with one of those plates, what then?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena was already reaching for the file again when she stopped. She looked at the client over the top of her reading glasses — a gesture she didn't use often, usually only when she was about to say something she wanted remembered exactly.

"Then you do nothing."

She let that sit for a second before continuing.

"You look. You burn the plate into your memory. And you come back here. That's it. No photo, no note at the scene, no walking past the car to get a better angle. If there's someone in it, you don't make eye contact in the mirror. You drive by at the same speed you'd drive down any street in any neighborhood in this city — like you're looking for an address you've never been to before."

She pulled a small notebook from the desk drawer — cheap, spiral-bound, the kind you'd find at any drugstore — and tossed it onto the desk beside the binoculars.

"Write it when you get back. Not before. Memory fades, but memory written in a parked car at night with the dome light on is a beacon. People notice things like that. Especially people who park where they don't want to be noticed."

She leaned back, chair groaning its usual protest.

"If you see a plate that matches — good. That tells me Harlan has a visitor. If you see *both* plates, that tells me something else entirely, and I'll want to know which car was closer to the house and which was on the outside. If you see neither..." She shrugged, a small motion. "Then maybe I'm wrong. It happens. I'll be wrong over the phone at two in the morning instead of wrong in the field at eleven at night. I prefer the former."

She picked up the pen and tapped it once against the pad.

"One more thing. If Harlan comes out and gets into a car — any car — you wait exactly three minutes, then you leave. Not two. Not five. Three. Long enough to see if he's forgotten something and doubles back. Not so long that anyone who's already there has time to notice you noticing them."

She set the pen down and looked at the door.

"Phone on silent. I'll have mine. If something goes wrong — anything at all — you call me and you don't explain, you just say the word *petunias*, and I'll know you need me there in twenty minutes." A pause. The corner of her mouth twitched — almost a smile, buried quickly. "Your idea. Might as well put it to use."

She nodded toward the stairs.

"Go. And turn your headlights off before you park on that block."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, a little stunned by the level of detail.* "Petunias. Got it." *I pocket the notebook, grab the binoculars, and head out, already thinking about how to kill my headlights before getting too close.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stood at the window again after the footsteps faded. The street below was darkening, the dry cleaner's sign now the brightest thing on the block. She watched the client's car pull away from the curb and disappear south toward Flatbush.

Then she was alone.

She went back to the desk and sat down heavily. The chair didn't groan this time — just accepted her weight with a soft creak. She pulled the legal pad toward her and stared at the page she'd turned face-down. The crossed-out name. She could see the ink bleeding faintly through the paper, the letters reversed and ghostlike.

She didn't turn it over.

Instead, she opened the bottom drawer of the desk — the one the client hadn't seen her open. Inside, beneath a stack of old receipts and a box of .38 rounds, there was a manila envelope, unmarked, sealed with a rubber band that had gone brittle with age. She set it on the desk and looked at it.

She didn't open it.

She sat there for a long time. The mini-fridge hummed. Somewhere below, the presses stopped for the night, and the silence that rushed in to replace them was heavier than the noise had been.

Her phone rang. Not the unknown number from before — a different one, one she had saved.

"Yeah."

She listened. Her jaw tightened almost imperceptibly, a muscle jumping near her ear.

"When?" A pause. "And the second one?"

She stood up and moved to the window again — restless now, the way she got when something she'd been turning over in her head suddenly had a shape she didn't like.

"No. Don't move it. Don't touch it. I want it exactly where it is when I get there tomorrow." Another pause. "Tomorrow. Not tonight. Tonight I want everything to stay exactly as it is, including the people who are in it."

She hung up and stood motionless for a beat. Then she looked down at the desk — the file, the photograph of the silver sedan, the plate numbers she'd written for the client, the legal pad with the crossed-out name. All of it laid out like a hand of cards she hadn't finished playing.

She picked up the manila envelope. Turned it over. Set it back down. Her thumb brushed the rubber band but didn't pull it off.

The office smelled like chemicals and old coffee and the faintest trace of cigarette smoke that had never actually been lit. She looked at the unlit cigarette on the desk, still sitting where she'd left it, and for a moment her hand hovered over the lighter beside it.

She didn't pick it up.

Instead she wrote two words on a fresh page of the legal pad. Small, in the corner, different from her usual block letters — smaller, faster, almost careless. She looked at them for a moment, then tore the page off, folded it once, and slipped it into the inside pocket of her jacket, where the printout and the plate numbers already sat.

Then she turned off the desk lamp and sat in the dark, waiting for the client to come back.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I’m back in Bay Ridge, headlights off, cruising slowly down Harlan's street. It's darker than I expected. I spot his house, then pull over a house down, facing it, just like Lena said. I grab the binoculars and start scanning the block.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The office was dark except for the blue glow of the laptop screen and the thin line of streetlight that made it through the blinds and across the ceiling like a scar.

Lena sat with her feet up on the desk, the unlit cigarette still in its place. She'd moved the legal pad aside and was staring at the photograph of the silver sedan again — not at the plate this time, but at the background. The van it had been shot from behind. The angle of the sidewalk. A mailbox, half in frame. She'd looked at this photograph maybe forty times in the last three days, and each time something different caught her eye. This time it was a shadow — a figure, maybe, at the edge of the frame. Too indistinct to identify. Too deliberate to be nothing.

She pulled the laptop closer and opened an image editor she'd downloaded years ago and never paid for. Dropped the photograph in. Adjusted the contrast. Adjusted it again. The shadow sharpened slightly. A shoulder. Maybe a collar. The back of someone's head, turned away from the camera.

She saved the edit, closed the laptop, and sat still.

Her phone sat on the desk beside the cigarette. She looked at it the way you'd look at a door you weren't sure you'd locked.

Twelve minutes had passed since the client left the office the second time. Bay Ridge was forty minutes on a good night. Whatever was happening on that block right now wasn't happening yet — the client was still finding the right spot, checking mirrors, learning the rhythm of a street that didn't want to be learned.

Lena pulled her jacket tighter. The folded printout inside crinkled faintly against her ribs. She could feel the small folded note too — the two words she'd written in the corner of the legal pad. She didn't reach for it.

Instead, she opened the bottom drawer again and this time she did pull the rubber band off the manila envelope. The band snapped as it came free — brittle, dry, done with its job after years of holding on. She set it on the desk and slid her finger under the flap.

Inside: photographs. Older than the case file. Slightly curled at the edges. She didn't take them out. Just fanned the top one enough to see what she already knew was there, then closed the flap again and set the envelope flat on the desk.

The building groaned. Pipes settling. Wind against the window.

She checked the clock on the wall — the old analog one with the second hand that ticked a half-second behind real time. If the client had taken Flatbush and the lights were kind, they'd be parked on Harlan's block by now. Eyes only. Headlights off.

Lena picked up the phone and held it in her palm, feeling the weight of it. She didn't dial. She didn't text. She just held it, thumb resting on the dark screen, and waited for the vibration that would tell her the client had found something — or hadn't.

Either way, the night was going to be long.

She turned the chair toward the window and watched the street below. A taxi idled at the corner. A man walked past with a dog. Nobody looked up at the half-closed blinds on the second floor.

Nobody ever did.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I scan the street, the binoculars feeling heavy in my hands. It's quiet. Too quiet. I spot a silver sedan a few houses down, parked on the opposite side of the street. My heart gives a little thump. I focus the binoculars on the license plate, trying to make out the numbers in the dim light.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t answer right away. She picked up a photograph from the stack, turned it over in her fingers, and let the silence stretch just long enough to make the air feel heavier. The dry cleaner’s chemical smell drifted up through the floorboards. She set the photo back down, aligning it perfectly with the others.

"Precincts don’t hand over case files on a Tuesday," she finally said, her voice low and even. "Not when the paperwork’s already stamped. Not when the names inside them start rubbing shoulders with names that don’t belong in a civilian’s pocket." She tapped a finger against the edge of the desk. "Besides, walking through those doors changes the way people talk. It shifts the whole dynamic. And it makes the trail go cold before we even start looking for the right doors."

She pushed the photos back toward the client, though not quite touching them. "There are people who move through the system without actually working for it. Clerks, evidence technicians, records managers who clock out and disappear into the city. They know where the gaps are. They know what got buried before the official report was even typed up. I’ll make the call. You stay here and review the timelines. I’ll handle the rest."

She stood, chair legs scraping against the floor, and walked to the window. She didn’t look down at the street. She just watched the condensation gather on the glass. "We don’t need their building. We just need what they missed."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch her pace, a knot forming in my stomach.* "So, someone at the Ninth Precinct might have... buried something? On purpose?" *I pick up one of the photos again, a grainy shot of the victim.* "Is that what you're saying?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
She turned from the window, the condensation still smearing across the glass in slow, uneven trails. Her gaze dropped to the photograph in the client’s hand, then back to the desk. She didn’t answer the question with a straight line. Instead, she walked to the metal filing cabinet near the door, pulled out a thick manila folder, and set it down with a soft thud.

"Buried implies intention," she said, her voice cutting through the quiet hum of the street below. "The system prefers delay. Routing. Redaction. Things don’t vanish into thin air. They get filed under the wrong desk, shuffled to a supervisor who’s been out of the office for weeks, or logged with a typo that locks them behind a password no one remembers." She crossed her arms, leaning her hip against the cabinet. "If something went missing, it’s because it was moved. Or it was never entered. Or it was entered under a name that doesn’t match the one on the driver’s license."

She pushed the manila folder toward the client again, though she kept her hands firmly planted on the cool metal behind her. "We don’t speculate about motives. We follow the paper trail. And the paper trail doesn’t care about precincts. It cares about who had access, who signed off, and who benefited from the gap." 

Her eyes flicked back to the photos scattered across the desk. "Keep looking at those. Look for the edges. The stuff that doesn’t fit. I’ll make the calls."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s fingers hovered above the photograph for a long moment. The dry cleaner’s mechanical thrum vibrated through the floorboards, steady and indifferent. She didn’t turn at the words. Instead, she slid a paperweight beneath the corner of a witness statement, straightened the alignment of three overlapping timelines, and finally let her hands rest flat against the desk.

“Paperwork leaves fingerprints whether you wear a badge or not,” she said, her tone even and directed squarely at the documents. “You learn to watch where the ink stops drying. Where signatures skip. Where a file gets heavier overnight because someone added pages instead of deleting them.” She picked up a ballpoint pen, clicked it once, and dropped it onto a fresh legal pad. “The warehouse logs go first. Cross-check the shift rotations with the freight manifest. I’ll be out talking to a records archivist who owes me a favor. Keep the originals off the table until I get back.”

She turned toward the door, palm finding the cool brass of the knob. She didn’t look back. The question hung in the chemical-thick air, unacknowledged and unresolved, as she stepped into the hallway and pulled the door shut behind her.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the closed door for a moment, then back down at the files.* She really just dodged that question. *I sigh, picking up the legal pad she left.* Warehouse logs and shift rotations... okay.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The call went through three relays before it connected. Lena stood in the back room of a defunct print shop on 4th, the air thick with the scent of solvent and damp cardboard. The man on the other end spoke in a low, rhythmic cadence, listing dates, clearance levels, and a string of redacted case codes. She didn’t interrupt. She just listened, her thumb tracing the edge of a burner phone, committing each detail to memory. When he mentioned a gap in the surveillance footage from the night of the 14th, she nodded once. “Leave it,” she said. “Don’t flag it. Just tell me where the camera was pointing when the feed cut.” He gave her the coordinates. She hung up, slipped the phone into her coat pocket, and walked out into the damp evening air.

Twenty minutes later, the office door clicked shut behind her. She didn’t bother with small talk. She dropped a folded manila envelope onto the desk beside the client’s stack, the sound sharp against the quiet. “The warehouse didn’t lose power,” she said, unbuttoning her coat and hanging it on the back of her chair. “The feed was looped. Someone paid for a clean two-hour window. The freight manifest you’re looking at is real, but the timestamps are off by three days. Cross-reference the driver’s license number with the DMV’s archived registration requests. Not the active database. The backup archives. They keep the old requests for five years before purging them.”

She pulled out a chair, sat down, and finally looked at the legal pad. “You’re looking at the wrong gap. The missing piece isn’t in the logs. It’s in the paperwork that never made it to the server. Start with the registration requests. I’ll track down the loop operator.” She tapped a pen against the edge of the desk, her gaze steady. “Keep the originals off the table. I don’t want anyone tracing the paper back to this address.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I blink, taking in the new information.* "So the entire freight manifest is a lie? And someone paid to have a camera feed faked?" *I push the legal pad away, feeling a chill.* "This isn't just buried paperwork, Lena. This is... organized."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena let out a slow breath, the kind that carried the weight of a hundred similar conversations. She didn’t flinch at the word *organized*. She’d heard it before, usually right before the real work began. She walked to the window again, but this time she didn’t watch the condensation. She watched the street below, noting the rhythm of foot traffic, the parked cars, the unmarked sedan that had idled two blocks over since she arrived.

“Organized isn’t the same as clean,” she said, turning back to the desk. She picked up a red pen, circled a timestamp on the freight manifest, and slid it across to the client. “Organized means they have a budget. It means they know how to hide in plain sight. It doesn’t mean they’re good at it.” She tapped the circled date. “Three days off is sloppy. But sloppy is human. What you’re looking at is institutional. And institutional things leave receipts.”

She straightened the stack of photos, aligning them with precise, almost surgical movements. “You don’t pay a loop operator unless you want the cameras to show them something else. You don’t backdate manifests unless you’re moving something that isn’t supposed to be moving. And you don’t bury paperwork unless you’re covering a second trail.” She met the client’s eyes, her expression unreadable. “So stop treating it like a clerical error. Start treating it like a transaction. Who funded the loop? Who approved the manifest? Who benefited from the three-day gap?”

She pulled a fresh sheet of paper from the drawer, wrote a single name, and tore it off. Slid it across the desk. “This is the logistics coordinator for the freight company. Not the owner. The coordinator. They handle the routing, the vendor contracts, the camera leases. They’re the leak. Find them. I’ll be back by midnight. If the manifest is a lie, the money trail isn’t. Follow the invoices. Leave the building with the blue awning out of it.”

She didn’t wait for a reply. She grabbed her coat, checked the weight of the burner phone in her pocket, and headed for the door. The question about the past stayed exactly where it belonged: buried under paperwork, unacknowledged, and irrelevant to the next step.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s pen stopped mid-stroke. The scratch of ink against paper ceased, leaving only the low hum of the streetlamp outside and the distant hiss of the dry cleaner’s machinery. She didn’t look up right away. Her thumb rubbed once over the edge of the legal pad, feeling the ridges of old coffee rings and crossed-out lines. When she finally lifted her gaze, her expression hadn’t changed, but the space between them seemed to grow a fraction colder.

“Names rotate,” she said, her voice even and directed squarely at the stack of photos. “Detectives transfer, get promoted, burn out, or quietly disappear into administrative roles. The department treats assignments like inventory. You hand off a case, you log it, you move on. Personal history doesn’t attach to file numbers.” She picked up the freight manifest again, flipped it to the back page, and tapped a faded signature near the bottom. “Whoever held this folder before you did. Whoever holds it after won’t change the fact that the timeline is fractured.”

She set the document down precisely parallel to the edge of the desk. “What matters isn’t whose name is on the initial intake. It’s whose initials appear on the requisition forms, the equipment logs, and the external vendor agreements. Those signatures leave trails. Badge holders leave footprints. I follow both, but I don’t linger on either.”

She reached into her coat pocket and withdrew a second burner phone, placing it face-down beside the legal pad. “You’re fixating on a doorway instead of the room beyond it. Torres may have walked through it, but he didn’t build the walls. Find the coordinator. Cross-reference the lease contracts with the payment processors. I’ll trace the loop operator’s routing keys. Leave the precinct names to the press. We work in the margins.”

Lena stood, gathering the manila envelope and tucking it under her arm. She didn’t offer further commentary on the name. Didn’t pause to weigh it. Didn’t give it the space it demanded. She simply turned toward the hallway, palm finding the brass knob, and stepped out into the stairwell without looking back. The question sat on the desk, unanswered and already filed away.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch her go, then sigh.* "Okay, Lena." *I pick up the second burner phone, feeling a little overwhelmed.* Torres... that name has to mean something.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The stairwell swallowed her footsteps, the metal grating echoing against concrete walls. Lena didn’t look back. The name Torres sat in the air like smoke, but she didn’t let it linger. She’d learned long ago that names were just handles for files, and files were just paper waiting to be read wrong. She pulled the burner phone from her pocket, dialed a number she didn’t recognize, and let it ring once before switching to voicemail. She left a single string of coordinates and a timestamp. No questions. No names. Just data.

She walked the two blocks to a dimly lit diner on the corner, the kind with flickering neon and booths cracked open like old wounds. She didn’t go inside. Instead, she leaned against the brick wall across the street, watching the reflection in the glass. Her reflection looked back: tired eyes, sharp jaw, a coat that had seen better years. She adjusted her grip on the phone, thumb hovering over the screen. The name had triggered something, a low-frequency hum in the back of her skull that she immediately muted. Not now. Not with the loop operator still out there, still routing feeds, still buying time.

She stepped away from the wall, pulled her collar up against the damp chill, and headed toward the old industrial district. The loop operator wouldn’t be at a desk. They’d be in a van, or a parked sedan, or a rented storage unit with a laptop and a spool of coaxial cable. She’d find them. She always did. The paperwork would follow. It always did.

She checked the address she’d written on a scrap of paper from the office. Third floor, back window, no sign. Good. Amateur hour with a professional budget. She climbed the fire escape, boots quiet on the rusted steps, and paused at the landing. A single light bled through the blinds. She pressed her back against the brick, counted to three, and pushed the window up.

Inside, the room smelled of stale coffee and overheating electronics. Three monitors glowed in the dark, cycling through static and looped footage. A man sat in a swivel chair, headset on, fingers dancing over a keyboard. He didn’t hear her come in. He never did until it was too late.

Lena stepped into the room, letting the window click shut behind her. “You’re running the feed on a loop,” she said, her voice calm, cutting through the hum of the fans. “But you’re not hiding the gap. You’re marking it. Why?”

The man spun around, hands flying to the drawer beneath his desk. Lena didn’t flinch. She just watched. “You don’t need the weapon,” she said, stepping closer. “You just need to know who paid for the edit. Give me the invoice, and I walk away. Don’t, and I pull the drive. Either way, the trail ends here.”

She waited. The room held its breath. Outside, a siren wailed in the distance, but she didn’t look toward it. She kept her eyes on the man, on the screen, on the work. The past was a locked drawer. The present was a file waiting to be opened.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I've been staring at the burner phone and the logistics coordinator's name for what feels like hours. My own phone buzzes. It's a text from Lena:* "I'm on my way back. Did you find anything?" *I quickly type back:* "Just a lot of dead ends so far. This 'coordinator' is good at covering tracks. Did you find anything on your end?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena paused on the sidewalk outside the defunct print shop, the damp chill seeping through her coat as she unlocked the phone. The screen’s glow caught the sharp angles of her face. She typed a quick reply, her thumbs moving with practiced efficiency. *The operator doesn’t work alone. He’s a node. The invoice trails to a shell corporation, then to a holding company registered in Delaware. Follow the corporate registry. Ask for the managing member’s name, not the PO box.*

She hit send, slipped the phone back into her pocket, and resumed her walk. The city blurred past her in shades of wet asphalt and sodium vapor. She didn’t dwell on the weight of the hard drive in her inner jacket pocket. It was just data. Data didn’t bleed. Data didn’t ask questions. Data just needed to be sorted.

By the time she reached the Mercer Street stoop, the dry cleaner’s sign buzzed overhead, casting a sickly yellow light on the steps. She climbed them two at a time, the familiar creak of the third step a metronome she knew by heart. She unlocked the office door, stepped inside, and let the deadbolt slide home behind her. The smell of stale coffee and chemical solvents wrapped around her like a familiar coat. She dropped her keys in the brass bowl, hung her coat on the rack, and pulled the burner phone from her pocket.

She set it on the desk beside the manila envelope. “The shell company routes through three holding entities,” she said, her voice cutting through the quiet. “The coordinator isn’t the leak. He’s the middleman. The money comes from a corporate account tied to the logistics firm’s parent company. You want the coordinator’s name? It’s a front. Look at the board of directors. Cross-reference with the property records for the warehouse. There’s a discrepancy in the zoning permits. Someone approved a change that shouldn’t exist.”

She pulled a fresh sheet of paper, sketched a quick flowchart, and slid it across the desk. “Stop chasing personnel. Follow the assets. The coordinator’s payroll is routed through a payroll processor. Pull the vendor contracts. I’ll verify the zoning discrepancy with a city clerk who owes me. Keep the originals locked away. And don’t go looking for Torres. He’s a ghost by design.”

She turned toward the window, watching the street below. The condensation was gone now, replaced by the flat glow of city lights. She adjusted the blind with a precise tug, then reached into her coat pocket and withdrew a folded receipt, tapping it against the edge of the desk. “Rest. We move at dawn.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "A ghost by design?" *I repeat quietly, looking at the flowchart she sketched.* "What does that even mean, Lena? Was he killed?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t look up from the flowchart. The pen scratched a final line connecting a shell corporation to a zoning variance, then she capped it with a soft click. The question about Torres hung in the air, but she treated it like static on a radio dial—something to be tuned past. She slid the paper toward the client, her fingers tapping the edge of the desk once.

“Design implies intent,” she said, her voice flat and directed at the documents. “People don’t just vanish from active investigations unless they’re reassigned, transferred, or quietly told to step aside. The system has procedures for that. Bureaucracy has a way of sanding down edges until nothing sticks.” She stood, collecting the manila envelope and the legal pad. “If he’s gone, it’s because the file was closed. If he’s not, he’s sitting in a cubicle filing budget reports. Either way, dead or retired, he’s not the variable we need to solve. The zoning permit change is the variable. The shell company is the variable. The money moving through the payroll processor is the variable.”

She turned toward the door, her hand finding the brass knob. “Rest. We move at dawn. And leave Torres in the past. He’s not on the ledger.” She stepped out, closing the door with a quiet click, leaving the question unaddressed and the case file undisturbed.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch her leave again, a frustrated sigh escaping me.* "He's not on the ledger," *I mutter, picking up the flowchart.* "But he was on the case." *I pull out my phone and type a quick search: "Detective M. Torres Ninth Precinct."*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t turn at the sound of the phone screen. She kept her eyes on the street below, watching the rhythmic sweep of a streetlamp cutting through the damp air. The name Torres sat in the room like a misplaced coordinate—useless, unanchored, and easily ignored. She let the silence hold for a few seconds, long enough for the hum of the dry cleaner’s machinery to fill the space.

“Titles fade,” she said finally, her voice even and directed at the flowchart. “Badge numbers get reassigned. Cases get transferred. The system moves people like inventory, and inventory doesn’t leave footprints. Paper does.” She picked up the pen, drew a clean line connecting the shell company to the zoning variance, and capped it with a soft click. “You’re looking for a detective when you should be looking for a routing error. Detectives don’t move millions through Delaware holding entities. Logistics coordinators do. Zoning boards do. Payroll processors do.”

She slid the legal pad across the desk, tapping a single line of text. “Run the corporate registry. Pull the registered agent’s name. Cross-reference it with the county clerk’s property transfers. If the paperwork aligns, the money is clean. If it doesn’t, the discrepancy is the story. Not the precinct. Not the investigator. The documents.”

She closed the leather binder, latching it shut with a firm snap. “Rest. We move at six. And leave the past out of the ledger. It doesn’t pay for the van. It doesn’t lease the cameras. It doesn’t route the invoices.” She turned toward the door, her hand finding the brass knob, and stepped into the hallway without looking back. The question sat on the desk, already filed away, irrelevant to the next step.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the closed door, then down at the legal pad.* "Routing errors," I mutter. "Yeah, okay." *I pull out my phone again, not for Torres this time, but to start searching for corporate registries.* This is going to be a long night.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The dry cleaner’s machinery had finally cycled down, leaving the room quiet enough to hear the scrape of the client’s pen against legal paper. Lena stood near the metal filing cabinet, sleeves rolled to the elbows, a half-empty glass of water sweating onto a stack of unfiled receipts. She wasn’t watching the client. She was counting the rhythm of the search, listening to the way the cursor clicked, the way the silence stretched between keystrokes. Corporate registries didn’t yield quickly. They required patience, and patience was a currency she’d learned to hoard.

She pulled a fresh notebook from the bottom drawer, flipped past pages dense with crossed-out addresses and faded ink, and stopped on a blank spread. Her pen moved in tight, deliberate strokes. She mapped the shell corporation’s registration states, cross-referenced them with known freight corridors, and noted the zoning variance location. The lines connected like circuitry. She capped the pen and set it aside. Dawn wasn’t far. The city would wake soon, and sleepers rarely checked their locks before sunrise.

“You’ll find the registered agent under a holding trust,” she said finally, her voice low but clear in the stillness. She didn’t look up from the notebook. “They use a nominee director to shield the actual managing member. Run the county clerk’s deed transfers for the warehouse parcel. Look for a transfer dated six months prior to the manifest discrepancy. That’s when the money changed hands. Not when the cameras were looped.”

She walked to the window, peeling back the vinyl strip of the blind just enough to watch the streetlights flicker off one by one. The first delivery trucks were already idling at intersections, their engines rumbling through the damp air. She adjusted her collar, feeling the familiar weight of the burner phone and the seized hard drive against her ribs. The past could stay buried. It never paid the rent or cleared a timeline. What mattered was what came next: the warehouse at dawn, the zoning board records, and the people who thought they’d erased themselves by routing numbers through Delaware.

She turned back to the desk, tapping two fingers against the edge of the legal pad. “Coffee’s in the thermos. Black. Drink it. You won’t feel it until you do.” She picked up her coat, slung it over one shoulder, and waited for the silence to settle between them. The case wouldn’t solve itself. It would just wait. And she always knew how to make it move.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Coffee, huh?" *I take a long swig, grimacing at the bitterness but feeling a jolt.* "Right. Deed transfers. Got it." *My fingers fly across the keyboard, already pulling up the county clerk's website.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s hand settled flat on the closed file, stilling it.

“Because the Ninth isn’t a door I walk through,” she said.

She didn’t say it like a preference. She said it like a locked gate.

For a moment, the only sound was the dry hum of the old radiator under the window. Lena turned the file a quarter inch on the desk, aligning it with the edge as if the case had suddenly become something that needed to be handled with more care than it had been given.

“If there’s a detective attached to it, we don’t need the precinct,” she went on. “We need the detective somewhere else.”

She opened the top drawer, took out a plain notepad, and uncapped a pen. She wrote quickly, without flourish:

*Public place.  
Late afternoon.  
No station house.*

Then she tore the sheet off and set it on the desk between them.

“You can make the call,” Lena said. “Tell them you’re following up on an insurance matter and you don’t want to take up official time. Suggest the diner on Harrow. The one with the bad coffee and the long windows.”

Her eyes lifted, sharp and unreadable.

“If they ask why not the precinct, say you’re bad with fluorescent lights.”

The corner of her mouth moved, but it wasn’t a smile.

“If they agree, we sit where we can see the entrance. If they don’t, we find out who else touched the file before it ended up in someone’s drawer.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the notepad and scan the notes.* "Fluorescent lights, huh? You really don't want to go back there." I tap the paper. "Okay. The diner on Harrow. I'll make the call." *I pull out my phone.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena let the remark slide past her.

She moved to the small sink in the corner, poured the last of the coffee into a chipped mug, and didn’t drink it. The gesture was automatic, a way to occupy her hands while the room arranged itself around the next step.

“Keep it dull,” she said. “Insurance follow-up. A file that may have been misplaced. You’re trying to save everyone paperwork.”

She set the mug down without taking a sip.

“If they ask who you’re with, say an adjuster. If they ask which firm, say you’re not permitted to give that out yet. If they press, become less interesting. Boredom ends conversations faster than suspicion.”

Her gaze moved to the window, where the blinds cut the street into pale strips.

“The diner’s got two exits. We take the booth near the one that doesn’t announce itself.”

Then, quieter, as if the room needed one last rule:

“And don’t mention precincts unless they do.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena did not answer right away.

She picked up the cold mug, set it down again, and aligned the pen beside the torn notepad as if the question had been a wrong number.

“The call matters more than my résumé,” she said. “If the detective agrees, ask for a time between lunch and dinner. Crowds thin then. Staff changes. People forget faces.”

Her eyes went to the blinds, where the street moved in pale strips below.

“Tell them you found an old claim number and need it matched to a report. Nothing that sounds like an accusation. Nothing that sounds like you’ve been waiting to ask.”

She tapped the notepad once with the pen.

“And if they sound tired, let them be tired. Tired people talk faster when they think the thing will be over soon.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sigh.* "Right, okay. No accusations, just... a very boring insurance claim." *I dial the precinct's general number.* "Wish me luck."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena gave the smallest shake of her head.

“Luck is what people ask for when they haven’t done the boring parts,” she said. “Be dull. Be vague. Be someone they’ll forget before the coffee’s cold.”

She moved to the window again, lifting one blind cord just enough to keep the street in view without showing her face.

“If they ask for a callback number, use the one you gave them. If they ask for a claim reference, use the number in the upper left corner of the file and make it sound like you’ve said it forty times today. If they ask you to come in, you’re already late somewhere else.”

Her reflection appeared faintly in the glass, pale and watchful.

“And if they put you on hold, let them. Hold music makes people feel owed. When they come back, they’ll be quicker to give you a name or a time just to end the call.”

She let the blind fall back into place.

“Don’t say my name unless you have to,” she added. “And if they ask who sent you, say you found the file in a box of old paperwork. Nobody argues with a box.”

Then she stood very still, hands at her sides, listening to the first thin ring in the room as if it were a door being knocked on somewhere far away.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I listen to the phone ring, then a click and a receptionist's voice.* "Hi, yes, I'm calling about an old insurance claim..." I launch into the dull spiel. *I shoot Lena a quick, nervous glance.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stayed where she was, near the window, one hand resting on the edge of the blinds but not lifting them again.

She listened to the client’s voice fill the office, measured and ordinary, the kind of voice that belonged in waiting rooms and on hold with utility companies. Good. That was the sound she wanted. Nothing that made a person on the other end sit up straighter. Nothing that made them reach for a pen.

Her eyes flicked once toward the desk, where the file sat squared and closed, then back to the client.

When the client glanced over, Lena’s expression didn’t change. She only gave the smallest nod, not encouragement exactly, but confirmation: keep going. Stay dull.

She crossed to the desk without hurrying and slid the notepad closer to the client with two fingers. The torn edge faced upward. The words she had written sat there in blunt black ink:

*Public place.  
Late afternoon.  
No station house.*

Underneath, in smaller letters, she added one more line while the phone call continued:

*Diner on Harrow. Booth by the back exit.*

She capped the pen and set it down beside the pad, precise and quiet.

The radiator ticked once. The coffee mug sat untouched near the sink. Outside, a car passed below with the slow, indifferent sound of tires on old pavement.

Lena’s attention narrowed. She wasn’t listening for drama. She was listening for hesitation on the other end of the line, for the shift in tone that meant someone had stopped being bored and started being curious. She was listening for the moment a routine question became a small door opening.

Her gaze dropped briefly to the client’s hand, then away, giving them space.

If the call stretched, she would let it stretch. If it snagged, she would find another way around it. The precinct was a place, and places had edges. People stepped outside those edges every day for coffee, for cigarettes, for air, for reasons they didn’t examine too closely.

She folded her arms once, then unfolded them.

Instead, she picked up the file again, opened it just enough to expose the upper left corner of the first page, and tapped the claim number once with her fingertip. A reminder. A prompt.

Then she went still again, listening, her face unreadable in the half-light from the window.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s hand stilled on the file.

The name sat in the room for a second, ordinary and not ordinary at once. She did not repeat it. She let it settle the way one lets a dropped glass come to rest before deciding whether it had cracked.

“It means we don’t say it more than we have to,” she said.

Her eyes dropped to the claim number exposed at the corner of the page. She tapped it once with her fingertip, then pushed the notepad closer.

Underneath the line about the diner, she wrote in small, deliberate letters:

*If they say the name first, let them own it.*

“If that name belongs to someone I used to work with,” Lena said, voice staying level, “it changes nothing except how we sit and how we leave. We don’t go in with history. We go in with paperwork.”

She capped the pen, then uncapped it again without looking at it.

“Ask for availability, not memory. If the detective can meet late afternoon, take it. If they suggest the precinct, you’re already late somewhere else. If they ask how you got the name, it was on a form. Forms don’t have intentions.”

The radiator gave another thin tick. Outside, a siren passed far off, rose, faded. Lena’s gaze moved briefly toward the window, then back to the desk.

“At the diner, we don’t choose the booth until we see where they enter. We keep the exit on our side. We let them order first. If they ask what this is about, we say it’s a mismatched claim number and a file that may have been archived wrong. Boring enough that they’ll correct us if they know better.”

She set the pen down beside the pad, precise and quiet.

“And if they sound careful, become more careful. If they sound tired, become shorter. If they sound like they’ve been waiting for this call—”

She stopped.

For a moment, the office seemed to narrow around the pause.

Then she finished, softer:

“Then we end it before they decide to ask why.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, a mismatched claim number it is." *I nod, trying to absorb all the instructions.* "And if they've been waiting for this call... I hang up?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s gaze shifted from the phone to the client’s face, sharp but not unkind.

“No,” she said. “You don’t hang up. Hanging up leaves a sound. A sudden sound becomes a reason to wonder.”

She touched the edge of the notepad, smoothing nothing.

“You close it slow. You make the ending smaller than the beginning. If you already have a time, repeat it once, like you’re writing it down while thinking about something else. If you don’t, say you’ll try back later and make it sound like a nuisance, not a retreat.”

The radiator ticked. Her voice stayed low, steady.

“If they’ve been waiting for the call, they’ll want it to mean something. Don’t give them that. Be the person who called about a claim number and nothing else. If they start asking why, get duller. If they try to keep you talking, say you’ve got another line, you’re stepping into a hallway, you’re already late. Not scared. Inconvenienced.”

She glanced at the file, then back.

“If they ask you to come into the Ninth, you’re not near it. You suggest the diner. If they push, you get vaguer, not more honest. And if they use the name Torres, let them use it. You heard it on a form. You heard it from a records clerk. You don’t know it any better than that.”

A beat.

“If the call turns wrong, you end it with boredom. Not fear. Boredom is quieter.”

Then, softer: “If they’ve been waiting, we don’t run. We just stop giving them anything to wait for.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Right. Be boring. Got it." *I take a deep breath, trying to channel supreme boredom.* "They're putting me on hold."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena gave a single, quiet nod.

“Good,” she said. “Hold is useful. It makes you ordinary.”

She moved back to the desk, but did not sit. Her attention stayed split between the phone’s thin, waiting silence and the street beyond the blinds.

“Don’t fill it,” she added. “People hate empty space on a call. They start offering things just to make it stop. Let the music do the work.”

Her gaze dropped to the file. She turned it slightly again, making sure the claim number was visible without having to open the cover.

“When they come back, don’t sound relieved. Sound like you’ve been doing this all day and you’re tired of forms. If they ask if you’re still there, say yes. Nothing more.”

The radiator ticked. The mug by the sink remained untouched.

“If they start asking questions while they’re still looking for the file, answer slow. Make them wait on you the way they made you wait on them. Not rude. Just busy in a dull way.”

Lena’s fingers rested near the notepad, but she did not write anything else yet.

“If they say the detective isn’t available, ask when they will be. If they ask whether it’s urgent, say no. Urgency makes people careful.”

Her voice lowered a fraction.

“If they ask whether you can call back, say you can, but make it sound like an inconvenience. Like you’d rather finish it now and stop thinking about it.”

Outside, another car passed, slower this time. Lena listened to it go, then looked back toward the phone.

“And if the hold stops suddenly,” she said, “be ready. That’s when someone has decided what kind of call this is.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to internalize all the instructions. The hold music is... elevator music. Perfect. I try to look as bored as possible.* "Okay. Got it."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena did not look at the phone as if it were a threat. She looked at it the way she looked at everything once a plan had started: like it was already moving and the only useful question was how to keep it from moving wrong.

“Good,” she said. “Stay in that lane.”

She crossed back to the desk and pulled the notepad toward her without sitting. The pen moved again, quick and practical, the letters slanting hard under the line about the diner.

*Half a beat late.  
No urgency.  
Let them fill silence.*

She tore the page free and set it beside the file, angled so it could be read without lifting it.

“When the music stops, don’t jump,” she said. “Let them speak first if they want to. If they don’t, sound like you were halfway through checking something else. Not annoyed. Just occupied.”

Her eyes lifted once to the blinds, then back to the desk.

“If they give you a name, don’t repeat it right away. Names get weight when you hand them back. If they say Torres, let the name sit there. You can ask if that’s the detective assigned to the file, like it’s just spelling you need.”

The radiator ticked. The untouched coffee sat cold by the sink.

“If they ask whether you’ve spoken to anyone else, you haven’t. If they ask whether this is related to an active matter, it isn’t. It’s paperwork. Old numbers. A box that got moved and a form that got misfiled.”

She smoothed the edge of the notepad with her thumb, then stopped herself and set the pen down instead.

“And if they sound like they know more than they’re saying, don’t chase it. Mark the time, mark the tone, and get off the call clean.”

For a second, her expression changed—not enough to call it fear, but something adjacent to it, something old and carefully kept behind glass.

“If Torres is someone I used to work with,” she said, voice level, “we don’t make it personal. We make it procedural. People are easier to misread when they think they’re being professional.”

Then the faintest narrowing of her eyes, as if she had heard the hold music shift before it actually did.

“Whatever happens,” Lena added, “don’t let them feel interesting. Interesting gets remembered.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to absorb everything.* "Okay, don't be interesting. Got it." *The hold music finally cuts out, and a woman's voice comes on the line.* "Hi, yes, I'm still here." *I try to sound like I've been waiting patiently for hours.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t answer aloud. The call had passed into the part where her voice would only become a shape in the background, and shapes got noticed.

She stayed near the desk, one hand resting by the file’s open corner, and watched the client’s face for the shadow of whatever the receptionist was saying. The receiver gave off a thin, papery murmur, too faint to carry words. That was all right. Lena wasn’t listening for content yet. She was listening for tempo.

She pulled the notepad closer and wrote in clean, deliberate strokes, angling it so it could be read without moving the phone:

*CLAIM NUMBER FIRST.  
THEN ASK WHO HANDLED THE FILE.  
MAKE IT SOUND LIKE A FORM FIELD.*

Her eyes lifted once, checking, then dropped again.

*IF THEY GIVE A NAME, DON’T REPEAT IT.  
ASK FOR INITIALS.*

The radiator ticked. Outside, a delivery truck grumbled past below, then faded. Lena’s gaze flicked to the blinds and back.

She added another line, smaller and more precise:

*IF THEY HESITATE, SAY YOU ONLY NEED IT FOR THE PAPERWORK.  
IF THEY SAY THE DETECTIVE ISN’T IN, ASK WHEN.  
NOT URGENT. JUST ANNOYING.*

She tapped the claim number once with the pen cap, then set the pen beside the pad.

“If they ask whether it’s active,” she said, voice low enough to stay beneath the call, “it isn’t. If they ask you to come in, you’re not near the station. You only need a time.”

The word *station* came out flat, stripped of memory or meaning. Not a place she would go. A place other people stood outside of until they got what they needed.

She wrote one last line and left it there:

*If they get careful, get duller.*

Then she folded her hands loosely at the edge of the desk and gave the call room, while her attention stayed fixed on every pause, every shift in the client’s posture, every small sign that the voice on the other end had stopped being bored.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Yes, the claim number is..." *I give the number, then pause, looking at the notepad.* "And could you tell me who the detective was assigned to that file? Just for my records, initials are fine."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s gaze sharpened at the word *initials*, but she did not move as if pleased. She moved as if the sentence had been placed correctly on a shelf.

She kept her distance from the phone. The receiver’s small murmur was not meant for her, and she did not try to steal it. Instead she watched for the physical tells: a pause too long, a brow tightening, the sudden stillness that came when a person on the other end stopped typing and started thinking.

Her hand slid the notepad forward again. The pen made short, hard marks.

*IF THEY HESITATE:  
“THE FORM ONLY LISTS INITIALS.”*

*IF THEY SPELL:  
LET THEM FINISH.*

*IF THEY SAY THE NAME:  
DON’T HAND IT BACK.*

She stopped for half a second, then added beneath it:

*ASK IF THAT DETECTIVE STILL HANDLES THE FILE.  
MAKE IT SOUND LIKE A BOX TO CHECK.*

The radiator gave its thin metallic tick. Lena set the pen down and let the file remain closed except for the corner with the claim number.

“If they start remembering out loud,” she said, voice low, “don’t help them.”

Her eyes lifted to the blinds. Beyond them, Mercer Street went about its business, indifferent to files, detectives, and the Ninth Precinct. The precinct itself might as well have been a building on the moon for all the use she intended to make of its front desk.

“If they tell you to come in,” she murmured, “you’re not close. You’re on the other side of town and you only need a time.”

She did not pace. She did not tap her fingers. She stood with the stillness of someone who had learned that waiting looked less suspicious when it looked like work.

The line was open. The question had been asked. Now there was nothing to do but let the boredom sit there until it became easier for someone to answer than to wonder why it mattered.
