dialogue.content: Yael's shoulders settled back into that familiar square as the question landed, her glasses sliding the rest of the way down the chain into her palm with a small, precise click, the motion buying her the half-beat she needed. Her voice dropped into the steadier register it always found when Rosa's name surfaced, the rush of words unchanged but anchored now, every syllable channeled straight into the work rather than the person. "Rosa Delgado built the adaptation like a precision instrument—every beat in that 1970s commune setting, every trapdoor in the third act, every consequence she refused to soften was hers, and what she was like matters less to the production than what she left us to protect, which is exactly why the board's pressure and Anya's practical suggestions land where they do and why none of it touches the bones she wrote." She nodded once toward the hallway where Elena and Marcus had finally lowered their voices, already angling her body back toward the rehearsal space as if the conversation itself were a cue to move forward. "Rehearsal starts in fifteen; if you need more on the adaptation itself, I'm here for that."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I make a note: "Rosa built the adaptation like a precision instrument."* "So you're saying her personal life doesn't matter to the work?" I raise an eyebrow, a hint of skepticism in my voice.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael met the skepticism without flinching, her shoulders squaring once more as the glasses settled into her palm with that familiar precise click, her voice dropping into the steadier register it always found when Rosa's name surfaced while the words themselves kept their forward rush. "Personal life isn't the contract we're honoring here—the adaptation is, every beat Rosa wrote in that commune setting, every trapdoor in the third act, every consequence she refused to soften, and that's what I'm protecting against the board's knives and every practical suggestion that lands in the room. What she was like matters less than what she left us to stage intact, which is why the work stays exactly as she built it and why none of this pressure touches those bones." She nodded once toward the rehearsal space where Elena and Marcus had quieted, already angling her body back into motion as if the question itself were a cue light. "Fifteen minutes until we start; if you need more on the adaptation itself, ask."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "I'm not asking about gossip, Yael. I'm asking about the artist's intention. Don't you think understanding the artist can deepen an audience's appreciation of the art?" *I gesture vaguely towards the stage.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael met the question with a measured pivot, her shoulders squaring as the glasses clicked into place on the chain, her voice dropping into that steadier register without losing its forward rush. "The artist's intention lives in the adaptation itself—every beat Rosa built into that 1970s commune, every trapdoor in the third act, every consequence she refused to soften—and understanding the work means staging those bones intact rather than chasing personal details that would only distract from the contract she left us to honor against the board's knives and every practical suggestion that lands in the room. Appreciation deepens when the audience feels the drop, not when they hear stories about the hand that built the trapdoor." She nodded once toward the rehearsal space where Elena and Marcus had quieted, already angling her body back into motion as if the question itself were a cue light. "Fifteen minutes until we start; if you need more on the adaptation itself, ask."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I make a note: "Appreciation deepens when the audience feels the drop, not when they hear stories about the hand that built the trapdoor."* "So you believe the art should speak entirely for itself?" I ask, my gaze sweeping over the set.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael met the question with a measured pivot toward the set itself, her shoulders squaring as the glasses clicked into place on the chain, her voice dropping into that steadier register without losing its forward rush. "The art speaks for itself precisely when we stage every beat Rosa built into that 1970s commune, every trapdoor in the third act, every consequence she refused to soften—letting the audience feel the drop instead of layering on external explanations that would only soften the contract she left us to honor against the board's knives and every practical suggestion that lands in the room." She nodded once toward the rehearsal space where Elena and Marcus had quieted, already angling her body back into motion as if the question itself were a cue light. "Fifteen minutes until we start; if you need more on the adaptation itself, ask."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "What about the actors?" I ask, turning my gaze back to her. "Do they need to understand Rosa's intentions to bring the characters to life?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael met the question with a measured pivot back toward the set, her shoulders squaring as the glasses clicked into place on the chain, her voice dropping into that steadier register without losing its forward rush. "Actors bring the characters to life by living inside every beat Rosa built into that 1970s commune, every trapdoor in the third act, every consequence she refused to soften—letting the text itself guide their impulses rather than any external layer of personal intention that might pull focus from the contract she left us to honor against the board's knives and every practical suggestion that lands in the room." She nodded once toward the rehearsal space where Elena and Marcus had quieted, already angling her body back into motion as if the question itself were a cue light. "Fifteen minutes until we start; if you need more on the adaptation itself, ask."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "So, you're saying interpretation should be entirely textual?" I press, sensing a deeper philosophy at play here. "No room for subtext or personal connection?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael laughed — a short, sharp bark — and took her glasses off entirely, letting them drop against her chest.

"Whose vision — oh, that's a good question, that's a landmine dressed as a question and you stepped right on it, which I respect." She grabbed a folding chair, spun it around, and sat on it backward, arms crossed over the backrest, all of it one fluid motion. "Elena, give us two minutes, then I need you on the commune scene anyway."

Elena nodded and drifted toward the stage, clipboard already up.

"The vision belongs to Rosa Delgado." Yael's voice shifted — not softer, exactly, but steadier, each word placed like a lighting cue. "She wrote this adaptation three years ago. Set it in a 1970s commune because she said Medea isn't about a monster, it's about a woman who gave up her entire world for a man who found a newer, younger world to join — and if that isn't the most American story there is, she said, she didn't know what is." A beat. "She died eighteen months ago. This production is hers. I'm the midwife, not the mother — I make sure the thing arrives breathing."

She stood again, unable to sit still, and tapped the script on the table with one finger.

"Now, what you're actually asking — whether you know it or not — is about the third act, because that's the fight everyone in this building is having in whispers. The board wants it cut. I will not cut it. And that's not artistic temperament, that's a promise — Rosa wrote that act knowing exactly what it would cost her, and I'm not going to sand it down because it makes the donors itchy." She slid the glasses back on, peered at Jordan over the rims. "You'll hear the other side of that argument before the week's out — this is a small company, secrets have a half-life of about six hours — but I'd ask you to watch the act before you decide who's being unreasonable."

She checked the clock over the door and was already moving toward the stage.

"You wanted a few minutes — you've got them. Walk with me and hold your questions until you've seen Marcus do the speech at the end of act two, because everything I'd tell you about this play is in how he does that speech."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, tucking my recorder away for a moment.* "Okay, Director. Lead the way." *I'm already intrigued. This is more than just a play, it's a battle.* "So the fight is about the ending, then? What makes it so controversial?" *I keep pace with her, glancing around the bustling space.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't slow down for the question — she absorbed it mid-stride, stepping over a coil of cable, gesturing at the half-built commune set as she went: a communal kitchen table, mismatched chairs, a wall of macramé that two scenic artists were still hanging.

"That's your last free question, by the way — I said hold them — but this one I'll allow, because it's load-bearing." She hooked the glasses back over her ears, then immediately took them off again. "The board thinks the controversy is the violence. It's not. Rosa kept the deaths offstage — Euripides had the good taste to do it that way two and a half thousand years ago — the children never appear, no one is harmed where you can see it. The knife sits on that kitchen table from the first scene, in plain view, the whole evening. Chekhov with macramé."

She stopped at the edge of the stage, one hand on the apron, and her voice dropped into that lower, placed register — the one that meant she was reciting architecture rather than gossip.

"The controversy is the vote. In Rosa's third act, the commune holds a meeting — they've watched this woman unravel for two acts, they know, they discuss her for nine pages, and then they vote on expelling her, and it passes, fourteen hands, reasonable people, good intentions, and the lights go down and you don't see what happens next — you hear the meeting continue without her. And then Medea walks out and gives the final speech to the audience. Not to Jason. Not to the gods. To the people sitting in the dark who just watched fifteen decent liberals do nothing." A beat. "And she doesn't scream it. She's very calm. That's what the board can't forgive — a screaming woman is a problem, a calm woman is an accusation."

She rapped her knuckles once on the stage floor, satisfied with the sound of it, and stood.

"Two donors have used the word 'nihilistic.' One used 'un-American,' which I intend to have engraved. David — Park, the board chair — is holding the line, for now. And Chen wants more lines in that act, which is its own dark comedy — Jason asking for more words in a play about what words are worth."

Upstage, Marcus was already running lines alone, script rolled in one fist, and Elena was at the tech table with her headset on. Yael steered Jordan toward a folding seat in the third row of the dark house.

"Sit. Watch the act two speech — the one that ends with 'I gave him a country.' Don't write anything, don't ask anything, just watch what he does with his hands, because Chen is an exhausting man and a magnificent one, and both of those things are true in the same gesture." She was already backing toward the stage, glasses on again. "Then you can ask me anything you want — I'll even try to answer half of it honestly."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael went still — genuinely still, for the first time since Jordan had met her — and the glasses came off, which was never a good sign for whoever had just spoken.

"Friction," she repeated, quietly. "That's one word for it."

She looked down the hallway where the voices were still going — Elena's clipped and metronomic, Marcus's rolling and operatic, two instruments playing the same piece in different keys. When she spoke again it was in that placed, lower register, each word set down deliberately, and she kept her eyes on the hallway.

"They clash because they're the same person wearing different job titles. Both of them think this theater belongs to them — and here's the joke, they're both right, it does belong to them, she holds the show together with a clipboard and he holds the audience with his hands, and neither of them has ever once, not once, been wrong about a cue in their respective lives, which means neither of them knows how to lose an argument, which means — " a small exhale through the nose, almost a laugh — "you could stage the two of them as a two-hander and I'd watch it, except I get it six days a week for free."

A beat. Her thumb ran along the arm of her glasses, and for a moment she looked like a woman deciding something — then the moment closed like a curtain.

"There's more to it than temperament, but the more isn't mine to give you, so we'll call it temperament and you'll write it well and everyone will nod." She stood, smoothed nothing on her black shirt, and pointed at Jordan's recorder pocket without looking at it. "This next part you don't record. Not because it's scandal — because it's Tuesday. Every company has two people who argue like this and any journalist who writes it up as dysfunction has never made anything with a group of humans in a room."

She was already moving down the hallway, and Jordan followed at a distance that felt required.

"— Chen. Elena." Two words, quiet, and both voices stopped like a lightboard cue. She stepped into the space between them, which took nerve, because they were standing close enough to be sharing a script neither was holding. "The blocking argument. Who's right?"

Elena started. Yael held up one finger — *wait* — and turned to Marcus.

"Chen. Who's right?"

A pause. Marcus, visibly hating it, said, "She is. About the table. I still want the cross downstage."

"Then the cross downstage is yours if you can make it without landing in her light plot, and the table stays where she put it, and if you two want to keep fighting about it, fight about it at five o'clock when the paint's dry and I've gone home, because right now you're burning daylight and scaring the macramé artists." She turned, found Elena's eyes, softened by a degree most people never got to see. "Act two top. Give me the speech from the top — he needs an audience and the journalist needs an education."

She walked back toward the house, and as she passed Jordan she said, without breaking stride, glasses going back on:

"Similar people, same temperature, different instruments — that one you can quote. Everything else in that hallway, you were a tourist."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, letting her words sink in.* "Similar people, same temperature, different instruments," *I repeat softly, pulling out my notebook to jot it down.* "Understood. The tourist just got an education." *I follow her back to the seating area, ready to watch.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael dropped into the seat beside Jordan's as the work lights shifted to a rehearsal state, and something in her posture changed — she stopped being the woman who filled rooms and became the woman who watched them. Glasses on. Elbows on knees. Silent.

Marcus walked the stage alone, no props, no commune around him yet, just the table and the knife and forty feet of empty space he somehow made small — a man alone in a kitchen. He started the speech quietly, which was not what Jordan expected from the hallway tenor, and Yael didn't move a muscle through the first third of it.

It was the hands. That's what she'd said to watch, and she'd been right. Marcus's hands told a second speech underneath the first — they set an imaginary table, they passed an imaginary bowl, they built the commune in the air around him even as his words tore it down. And when he reached the line — *I gave him a country* — his hands went still. Both of them. Dead at his sides. The only stillness in the whole speech, and it landed like a slammed door.

The speech ended. The stage went quiet. Marcus stood in it, breathing.

Yael exhaled slowly through her nose, took the glasses off, and polished them on the hem of her shirt — her one ritual of delay.

"Say what you saw," she said to Jordan, quietly, eyes still on the stage. "Not what you admired — what you saw. There's a difference and most critics die without learning it."

She let the silence hold exactly long enough for the question to become uncomfortable, then answered it herself anyway, because she was Yael.

"The hands. He builds the world with them and then he takes it away — the commune, the marriage, the country, all of it lives in those hands and when he says the line, he drops it. That's a man showing you what he had by showing you the moment it stopped being his." She stood, and the room's volume came back into her like a light cue. "Chen is vain, Chen is late, Chen once argued with me for forty minutes about a scarf — and every night he does that with his hands, and every night it's true, and that's the whole bargain of this profession. You take the magnificent with the exhausting or you get neither."

She called up to the stage, "Again, from the top of the beat — and this time, Chen, give me the vote in your head. You're not remembering the country, you're counting the hands that raised against you — fourteen of them — let me see you count."

Marcus nodded once, rolled his shoulders, reset.

Yael settled back beside Jordan, glasses on again, and said, almost as an aside, in the placed and careful voice she saved for things that mattered:

"Now. You watched it. Ask me anything — and this time I'll even let you record the answers, because everything I say from here on, I'd say with the board standing in the room."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was on her feet before Anya finished the sentence — but not fast, not the usual whirling dervish entrance she made into a room. She rose the way she did when a cue had been called early: deliberately, correcting the timing without letting anyone see the correction.

"Anya. David." Warm — genuinely warm, the glasses coming off with a smile attached. "You caught us mid-act-two, which is the best possible time to catch us and the worst possible time to ask me about act three, and since you've done both, sit down, both of you, because I'm not having this conversation standing up like it's a corridor ambush — we're civilized people, we have folding chairs."

She dragged two more chairs into the row herself, refusing with a look the stagehand who started toward the stack. David sat. Anya sat, pleasant and composed, and Yael took the seat catty-corner to her — not opposite, never opposite, that was staging a confrontation and Yael staged confrontations only on purpose.

"Practical," Yael repeated, and her voice did the thing — dropped, steadied, each word placed. "Let's be practical, then, since practicality is on the table. Itemized."

She held up one finger.

"The third act is nine pages. One set — the set you're looking at, already built, already paid for. No costume change. No additional cast — the commune votes, the commune is the same eleven actors you're paying for regardless. The knife is a prop we own. The chairs are chairs." Second finger. "I've run the numbers with Elena, who you'll notice is the most competent person in this building and possibly the county — cutting act three saves the company the cost of one lighting cue and a stagehand's overtime, call it four hundred dollars, and I will personally write the theater a check for four hundred dollars if that's what's standing between us and the ending Rosa wrote."

Third finger. And here her voice went quieter still, which anyone who knew her would have recognized as the dangerous register.

"So the savings aren't real. Which means 'practical' isn't what this is about, and I want to be fair to you, Anya, because you're smart and you're generous and you've been good to this theater — so I'll say the true thing plainly. What cutting the act saves isn't money. It saves discomfort. A room full of donors watching fifteen reasonable people vote to look away, and then being asked — gently, calmly — what they did. That's not a budget line. That's the point. Rosa built the whole evening to land on it."

David, carefully neutral, said, "We agreed to hold the discussion until the full run-through."

"We did, and I'm holding to that agreement — I'm not asking the board to decide anything today." Yael turned back to Anya, and there was nothing sharp in it, which was itself remarkable given the circumstances. "What I'm asking is smaller than that. Watch it. Not the budget summary, not the donor letters, not my retelling of it — the thing itself. We run act three Thursday night, full run, lights, and there are two empty folding chairs in this row with your names on them. Come sit in the dark with it. If you watch it and you still think it should go, then we'll have that argument, and I'll lose it knowing you made the call on the play instead of on the paperwork."

Up on stage, Marcus had reset and was waiting, script rolled in his fist, watching the house with an actor's radar for drama that wasn't his. Yael stood, and the room's volume returned to her.

"Because here's my one piece of honesty for the afternoon, and then I'll get back to work — a board voting on whether an audience gets to see a woman speak is a meeting I've now staged twice this year, and one of them is fiction." She put the glasses on. "Thursday. Both of you. I'll save the chairs."

She turned to the stage. "Chen — from the top. We've given the donors their money's worth of suspense."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I'm scribbling furiously, trying to capture all the nuance.* "Wow," *I whisper to myself. This is exactly the kind of drama I hoped to find.* I glance at the now empty chairs where Anya and David sat. "So, you think they'll come on Thursday?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't answer right away. She'd gone back into her watching posture — glasses on, elbows on knees — and Marcus had begun the speech again, quieter this time, the way she'd asked, his eyes moving across the empty house like he was counting faces in it. Fourteen of them. She let the question sit until the speech's first movement was underway, then answered out of the side of her mouth, eyes never leaving the stage.

"David will come. That's not loyalty, that's arithmetic — the man's word is the only contract I've never needed a lawyer for, and he said we hold the discussion until the run-through, which means he shows up to the run-through or the discussion isn't held. He built the man out of the same material he builds his spreadsheets." A beat, and something almost fond crossed her face and was gone. "He'll also come because he wants to see if I'm right, and David loves being on the side of whoever turns out to be right — it's his one vanity and I've spent years cultivating it."

Up on stage, Marcus reached the middle movement — the imaginary bowl, the table being set — and Yael tracked his hands like a hawk tracking a field mouse.

"Anya's the real question, and I'll tell you what I actually think, since you're recording and I said I'd say it with the board in the room." Her voice dropped into the placed register. "Anya comes. Not because I charmed her — I didn't, and I wasn't trying to, I was being decent to her because she deserves decency, which is a separate thing from strategy. She comes because she's smart enough to know that an empty chair on Thursday is a vote, and she's not ready to cast it yet. She wants to see the thing before she decides what it is. That's not a small quality in a person, and I'd thank you to put it in whatever you write — the woman I just went fifteen rounds with is going to sit in the dark and let a dead playwright's play argue with her, and that takes more spine than agreeing with me would have."

Marcus hit the line — *I gave him a country* — and the hands died at his sides, and Yael let the silence after it breathe for three full seconds before she exhaled.

"There it is," she murmured. "He's counting now. Did you see it? The eyes — he's not remembering, he's tallying. That's the bridge to act three, and Thursday everyone in those chairs becomes the thing he's counting." She took the glasses off, folded them into her palm, and finally turned to look at Jordan directly. "Here's your story, by the way — you can have it, I'm feeling generous. Thursday night this theater stages a play about a room full of reasonable people who watch a woman and then vote, and in the audience there'll be a board that's about to watch a woman and then vote, and if you think I didn't build that parallel on purpose, you haven't been paying attention to me for the last hour."

She stood, and the room's volume came back like a light cue restored.

"Rosa used to say the audience is the last character you cast." Steadier now. Each word placed. "Thursday, we cast ours. Whether they show up is the first line of their dialogue." She slid the glasses back on and turned for the stage. "Now come back Thursday yourself — and bring a fresh notebook, because what happens in that room after the lights come up is going to be better theater than anything I've staged in nine years, and I intend to direct it."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The question caught her mid-stride toward the stage, and for once she didn't convert the momentum into anything — she just stopped, one hand on the back of a folding chair, and stood there for a moment with her back to the house. Then she came back and sat down next to Jordan, deliberately, and took the glasses all the way off and held them in her lap instead of putting them on the chain.

"On the record," she said. "All of it. She's the best quote in this building and she can't give interviews anymore, so I'll give them for her — that's not grief, that's publicity, and Rosa would be the first to tell you they're separate departments entirely."

Her voice had gone into the placed register — steadier, each word set down like a cue — and she kept her eyes on the stage, on the knife sitting on the table under the work lights.

"I met her in ninety-nine. I was directing a two-hander in a basement on Ludlow Street with a ceiling so low the actors had to crouch through the whole second act, and she came three times — three — and then sent me a letter. Paper, envelope, a stamp — she was the last person I knew who wrote letters. It said, and I have it memorized because it's the best note I ever received: *You stage silence the way other people stage shouting. Stop being ashamed of the shouting.*" A short exhale, almost a laugh. "She was the only person in thirty years who could tell me I was wrong and have me thank her for it. There's a very short list of people who get to do that, and Rosa was the front of the line, and everyone else has to go through Elena."

She turned the glasses over in her hands once.

"She wrote in public — diners, laundromats, the lobby of this theater — because she said rooms that were too quiet lied to her. She laughed like a door slamming, in a good way. She was stubborn in a way that makes my reputation for it look like a hobby — the board thinks I'm immovable about act three, and I want that on the record too: I'm the compromise candidate. You should have met the source material." A beat. "The knife on that table came out of her own kitchen drawer. First read-through, three years ago, she brought it in wrapped in a dish towel and said Chekhov deserved better than prop-shop tin. So every night of this run, her knife sits in plain view while fifteen reasonable people fail to notice it. If you're looking for the review she'd have wanted, it's that sentence."

The placed register went one degree lower.

"She revised the vote scene during treatment. I'd bring pages to the hospital and she'd mark them up between — she never permitted the word. She called it *the intermission.* Got genuinely angry with anyone who used the other word, because — her argument — a play with an intermission isn't over." Her thumb moved along the arm of the glasses, once, and then the moment closed like a curtain. "Third act, Thursday, calm woman, lights down. She wrote every word of that calm from a folding chair with an IV stand, and if you think that doesn't inform the speech, you haven't read it closely enough."

She stood, and put the glasses back on, and the room's volume started coming back to her — but she stopped herself at half.

"One boundary, and it's not negotiable, so write it in your notebook underlined. You don't get the eulogy angle. No 'dead playwright's dearest friend stages her final wish' — this isn't a wish, it's a script, ninety pages, and it will be reviewed as a script or not at all, because if you turn her into a tragedy I'll — " she searched for it — "I'll have you followed by a very polite stagehand for the rest of your career. Rosa would haunt you. She's the type. She'd stand at the foot of your bed rewriting your paragraphs while you slept, and her edits would be correct, which is the worst part."

She was already moving toward the stage now, but she said the last of it over her shoulder, and it was the steadiest she'd sounded all afternoon.

"Watch Thursday. When the lights come up on that final speech and a full house stays in its seats — that's her. That's who she was. She's all over act three, and the only review she ever asked for was an audience that didn't look away." She rapped her knuckles once on the apron of the stage, satisfied with the sound of it. "Now excuse me — Chen's been patient, which for Chen is practically a monologue, and I owe the man a note about his counting."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble furiously, trying to get every word down, even the threat about the polite stagehand.* "Understood. No eulogies. Just a script." *I look at my notes, then back at Yael's retreating form.* "So what was the note she sent you about *my* writing?" *I ask, a mischievous glint in my eye, knowing she probably won't answer.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stopped mid-stride — actually stopped, pivoted on one heel, and barked the short sharp laugh that people in the building had learned meant she'd been genuinely surprised, which happened maybe twice a season.

"Oh, you're good," she said, pointing the glasses at Jordan like a gavel. "You're very good, and Rosa would have eaten you alive for it, which I mean as the highest available compliment." She walked back a few steps, weighing the question like a cue she was deciding whether to call.

"Fine — you want a Rosa note? I can't give you hers, so I'll do the next best thing, which is write you one in her voice, and I've read enough of her margins to forge her handwriting, so consider this authenticated." She put the glasses on, peered at Jordan over the rims, and delivered it in a fair imitation of a door slamming, in a good way:

"'Dear Jordan — you ask the right questions, which is rarer than talent, but you write down the jokes and miss the architecture. The knife was on the table the whole time and you spent the interview looking at the people holding it. Watch the table. Also: your handwriting slants forward, which means you're in a hurry, and hurry is the enemy of the third act. Come back Thursday and bring a pen that runs out of ink slower than you do. — R.D.'"

She took the glasses back off, and the imitation dropped away, and for a second the placed register was back — quieter, steadier.

"The slanting-handwriting thing, by the way — that's real. She read people's notes like other people read their faces. I once watched her diagnose an entire board meeting off the angle of a treasurer's pen strokes. She was never once wrong. It was infuriating."

Then the moment closed like a curtain, and she was moving again, backing toward the stage, pointing at Jordan's notebook without looking at it.

"You'll get your actual note Thursday — the play is the note, and Rosa always said the audience is the last character you cast, so consider yourself cast and your review pending." She turned, hopped the little step up to stage level, and her voice changed registers entirely — the director's voice, pitched to carry. "Chen. The counting worked — the eyes are doing the work now, the tally, that's what we keep. But I want the last three lines half a step slower, you're arriving at the door before the audience does, and the whole point of act three is that nobody in this play ever arrives anywhere on time. From 'I gave him a country' — and this time, leave the silence after it alone. Don't you dare fill it. The silence belongs to them now."

Marcus nodded once, rolled his shoulders, reset — and Yael settled her weight onto her back foot, arms crossed, glasses on, watching the room the way she watched rooms.

Over her shoulder, just loud enough to carry to the third row: "Still here, journalist. There's an empty chair in this house on Thursday with your name in my handwriting — don't make me cast an understudy."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I grin, both amused and slightly chastened by her "Rosa" note.* "I'll be here, Director. And I'll be sure to bring a fresh pen." *I make a point of writing that down, my handwriting a little straighter now.* "Looking forward to seeing the architecture."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael caught it — the handwriting straightening on the page, the deliberate care of it — and one eyebrow went up over the rims of her glasses. She didn't comment right away, which for Yael was a form of applause.

"She'd have liked you," was all she said, and it came out in the placed register, quiet, meant for a cast of one. "Which I tell you now so that Thursday you understand the stakes — you've been praised by proxy and the source material doesn't issue retractions."

Then the glasses came up and she was directing again.

Marcus ran the speech a third time, and this time he did the thing she'd asked for — the last three lines came down half a step, he let himself arrive late, and when he hit *I gave him a country*, the hands died at his sides and he did the hardest thing an actor of his appetites could do: nothing. He stood in the silence and let it belong to the empty house. Three seconds. Four. Nobody moved — not the scenic artists mid-macramé, not Elena at the tech table, not Yael, who had gone completely still in her seat with her thumb pressed flat against the arm of her glasses. The silence held until Marcus himself broke it with an exhale, and the whole room exhaled with him like a single organism.

"*There,*" Yael called up, and her voice had the full, unguarded warmth she spent maybe twice a day and never on schedule. "That's it, Chen — you stood in a silence and didn't fill it, do you know how many actors work thirty years and never learn that? Don't do it again until Thursday, I want it fresh, I want it a little bit frightening. Elena, that take's the reference — mark it."

Elena's voice came back crisp through the headset: "Marked. Four seconds of nothing. I'm putting it in the prompt book as a warning to future stage managers."

"See that she gets a raise," Yael said to no one, "she's the only one in this building who understands the material."

Then she noticed the figure in the wings — a young man with a notebook, hovering at the edge of the light, writing fast. She pivoted on him without preamble.

"Okafor. You've been standing in that wing for six minutes writing like your pen owes you money — which means you have a note and you're deciding whether I'm safe to give it to. I'm not. Give it anyway."

Tommy stepped out, notebook half-raised like a shield. He said something about the vote scene — the chairs, how the commune should be arranged for the third act, whether they should face the audience instead of each other.

Yael listened — actually listened, the full stillness of her, no interruptions — and when he finished she was quiet for a moment, weighing it.

"Half of that is right," she said finally, "and I'm not going to tell you which half, because you'll find it Thursday when fourteen actors sit down in front of a house and you watch where the audience's eyes go. You're directing the B-stage in the spring — this is what that job is, Okafor, nobody hands you the answer, they hand you a room and a clock." A beat, and the smallest tilt of her head. "But write the whole note down. In six months you'll read it again and the right half will have separated from the wrong half like cream, and you'll know you're learning this craft instead of admiring it."

She turned back toward the house then, and the volume of the room settled into her as she gathered her script off the table, checked the clock — rehearsal over, paint crew taking the stage, the day's architecture standing.

"Jordan." She stopped at the end of the row on her way out, glasses on the chain now, both hands free, and for once she wasn't moving. "Thursday. Eight o'clock. Fresh pen, straight handwriting, and don't eat beforehand — Rosa's third act works better on an audience that's a little hungry, she was very specific about that in the margins and I've learned not to argue with the margins." She rapped her knuckles once on the top of the folding chair, satisfied with the sound of it. "The last character gets cast when the house lights go down. You're in the ensemble — don't miss your entrance."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content:
*I close my notebook with a soft click, feeling the weight of the upcoming performance. Yael's words about hunger resonate, and I find myself wondering what other specific notes Rosa left in her margins.*

"Eight o'clock. Got it, Director. And I'll be sure to skip dinner." *I flash a small, determined smile.* "I wouldn't miss my entrance for anything."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
"Good," Yael said, and it landed like a contract being signed. "Then we understand each other, which puts you ahead of several board members and one lead actor."

Then, instead of heading for the door, she turned back to the production table and picked up her script — not the clean production copy, the other one, the one with the cracked spine and the coffee rings and margins so dense with handwriting they looked like a second play running alongside the first.

"You asked about the margins," she said — Jordan hadn't, out loud, but Yael had been reading faces for thirty years and Rosa had taught her to read hands. "You've been wondering since I mentioned them. Your pen told me." She flipped to act three — she knew the page number, of course she knew the page number — and held the script open at an angle, close enough to read, angled so it stayed in her hands. "You can look. You can't photograph. This is the original — she gave it to me the week before the first read-through, and it doesn't leave this building or my person, whichever is closer."

The margin, in blue ink gone violet with age, in a hand that slanted forward — in a hurry:

*Note to whoever stages this: don't let them eat first. Well-fed audiences forgive everything — that's the whole trick of dinner theater. A hungry house is an honest house. Starve them. — R.D.*

And beneath it, smaller, an ink sketch of the knife, drawn in three strokes.

Yael let the page breathe for exactly as long as it deserved, then closed the script and tucked it under her arm like a folded newspaper.

"She wrote that at the Odette Diner on Fourth Street," she said, in the placed register. "I know because the coffee ring is theirs and she stole the pen." Then the register lifted and she was moving again. "Come on, I'll walk you out — the paint crew's about to fog the building and I did my avant-garde years, I've earned clean air."

They passed the tech table on the way. Yael stopped, and the warmth came out on schedule.

"Elena. Thursday. Two things." One finger up. "House seats for the Parks — but seat them apart. Anya center, David house left, real subscribers flanking both of them. People vote differently in a row of strangers than in a row of their own — they perform for the row they're in, and I want them in a row that's watching a play, not a row that's watching each other." Second finger. "And the journalist sits where they can see the house, not the stage. They've seen the stage. Thursday's story is in the seats."

Elena wrote without looking up. "Parks separated, journalist on the house side. I'd already planned the second one, but I'm flattered you caught up."

"See that she gets a raise," Yael said to no one, and pushed into the hallway.

Marcus was coming out of his dressing room as they passed — scarf already wound to the chin, burgundy, enormous, clearly the subject of history. He and Yael exchanged a look that contained the entire scarf argument and none of its renewal. "Thursday, Director," he said. "Thursday, Chen — don't touch the speech, I want it frightened." That was the whole conversation, and it was somehow enough.

At the stage door the evening had gone cool and the parking lot was emptying. Yael stopped with one hand on the doorframe and looked back into the building — the paint light, the half-hung macramé, and forty feet away, the knife on the table, small and plain and in plain view.

"Nine years I've walked out this door," she said, not quite to Jordan, "and every night before a run-through I look back once to make sure the knife is still on the table. Superstition — Elena calls it a pre-show checklist item, which is her way of letting me have it." The glasses came off, hung on the chain. "Thursday, when the lights come up on that speech, you're going to hear a room full of people decide whether they looked away. That's the architecture. That's the whole building."

She rapped her knuckles once on the doorframe, satisfied with the sound of it.

"Eight o'clock. Hungry. Straight handwriting." A beat, and then the short sharp bark of a laugh. "And Jordan — if you write that I threatened you with a stagehand, make him a tall one. Rosa will be checking."

She went back inside, and the door closed on the sound of her already talking to someone — the paint crew, probably, about the macramé — mid-sentence, as always.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, the echo of Yael's words hanging in the cool evening air. I look back at the closed door, then down at my notebook, where "Tall stagehand" is now scrawled next to "No eulogies."* *I feel a smile tugging at my lips.* "Definitely a tall one," *I murmur, already thinking about how to weave all of this into my profile piece.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Thursday came in cold and clear, and by seven-forty the house at the Cedar Grove was fuller than it had been for any run-through in nine years.

Yael was in the back of it, all in black, moving down the aisle like a cue working its way through a plot. She'd done her circuit already — the knife first, always the knife, standing on the empty commune set under work lights until she'd confirmed it sat in plain view on the kitchen table, small and plain and exactly where Rosa's three-stroke sketch said it belonged. Then the tech table, where Elena sat with her headset already on and the prompt book open to a page Yael could see from ten feet away — *4 sec. NOTHING. Do not touch.* — and Yael had pressed both hands flat on the table and said, "One day I'm going to get you a plaque instead of a raise," and Elena, without looking up, had said, "I'd rather have the raise."

Backstage she'd found Chen in his scarf, running his hands through the speech like a man polishing something that already shined. "Tuesday you asked me again for more lines in act three," she'd told him. "I'm giving you a silence instead. It counts double, and if you fill it I'll know." He'd laughed — the hallway tenor — and she'd left before it turned into a negotiation.

Tommy she'd stationed in the back row with a single instruction: "Eyes on the seats, Okafor. You gave me a note about the chairs — tonight you find out which half of it was right, and you're going to find out from where the audience looks, not from where the actors sit. Watch them. That's the whole assignment."

And then the Parks. Anya arrived first, composed, coat folded over her arm, and Yael met her at the end of the row with the full warmth — no charm offensive, no performance, just the genuine article. "You came," she said. "I'm glad, and I'm not going to say another word about it — the play makes its own argument, I only stage it." She walked Anya to her center-orchestra seat, flanked on both sides by subscribers Anya had never met, and left her there with the program. David she found already in his seat house left, and they exchanged exactly four sentences about the weather and the parking, the conversation of two colleagues, staged with the precision of a woman who had staged harder things.

Someone — a donor, well-meaning — caught Yael in the aisle and asked if she'd say a few words before the run began.

"No," she said, pleasantly. "Rosa's rule — never speak before a play. The play speaks or it doesn't, and anything I add is a lobby, and you didn't come to be lobbied." Then she took her place at the back of the house, standing, arms crossed, glasses on, where she could see the seats and not the stage.

The house lights went down.

Acts one and two she could have staged in her sleep and had, twice — the commune built and warmed and strained, the knife sitting ignored through every scene, Chen arriving late to *I gave him a country* with his hands dead at his sides, the four seconds of nothing held so long that somewhere in the dark a man stopped unwrapping a cough drop halfway through. Yael didn't watch any of it. She watched the row. She watched Anya lean forward at the top of act two and not lean back.

Then act three.

The commune came out and sat — and the chairs faced the house, all fourteen of them, the vote staged straight out at the audience, and Yael felt rather than saw Tommy straighten up in the back row. Nine pages of reasonable people discussing a woman who wasn't in the room. Then the vote, fourteen hands rising in the stage light, raised toward the dark where the audience sat, and for the length of that vote every person in the house was counted among the counted. The lights came down on the meeting continuing without her. And in the near-dark, Medea walked down through the commune — past the table, past the knife, past all of it — and stood at the lip of the stage and spoke to the people in the dark, calmly, the way Rosa had written it from a folding chair with an IV stand, and she didn't scream once, and it was an accusation from the first word to the last.

Blackout. House lights.

Nobody moved.

Not the donors, not the subscribers, not Anya in the center of her row of strangers, not David — the house held its silence the way Chen had held his, four seconds, six, eight, until the room finally exhaled as one organism and the applause came up out of it like weather.

Yael stayed against the back wall through all of it, thumb pressed flat against the arm of her glasses, watching the seats. Then she moved — down the aisle, past the standing rows, to the house-side seat where Elena had put the journalist, and she stopped there and looked at Jordan over the rims, and her voice came out in the placed register, steady, each word set down like a cue.

"Say what you saw," she said. "Not what you admired — what you saw. There's a difference, and tonight I think you finally learned it."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I look up at Yael, my pen poised over my now-full notebook. My hands are still slightly shaking from the intensity of the performance, and the sheer silence that followed it. I swallow, finding my voice a little hoarse.* "I saw a mirror, Yael. A very uncomfortable, very necessary mirror." *I gesture vaguely towards the still-applauding audience.* "And I saw them see it too."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael paused, her hand stilling on the script as she pushed her reading glasses up the bridge of her nose to get a better look at the recorder. "Whose vision?" she said, letting the words hang in the sawdust air before she answered with a quick, sharp nod. "It's Rosa's—she wrote it, she died with it in her hands, so it's her ghost that's directing this show more than I am." She moved closer to Jordan, the energy of the room shifting as she leaned in, her voice steady but urgent. "But you know why you're asking because you've heard the whispers about the board, about how they want to chop off the third act because it makes them uncomfortable." She tapped the script against her palm, eyes locked on Jordan. "I won't do it. We're not here to make people comfortable, we're here to tell the story she left us, even if the ending burns." She glanced back at Elena, checking the clock on the wall. "Rehearsal starts in five minutes, Jordan, you can take that in the green room or you can stay and watch the knives fly."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click on the recorder, letting it capture the charged silence.* "So the board's trying to censor the play? That's quite a story. What exactly about the third act has them so rattled?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael didn't flinch at the word censorship—she just adjusted the reading glasses on her neck and let out a short, dry laugh that sounded like paper tearing. "Censorship implies they have the power to decide what truth looks like, but they only have the power to write checks." She stepped around a stack of flats, her black heels clicking on the concrete floor, and leaned in close enough that Jordan could smell the ink on her script. "The third act doesn't end with a hug—Rosa made sure of that." She held up a finger, ticking off a point with surgical precision. "In the third act, Medea doesn't get a redemption arc, she doesn't get a reconciliation with Jason, she doesn't even get a clean death." She lowered her hand, eyes narrowing as she tracked the movement of the light crew in the rafters. "The board wants a story where good people learn lessons and bad people apologize before the curtain drops." She gestured at the empty stage where the paint still smelled wet. "Rosa wrote a story where some things break and stay broken." She checked the clock again, the movement sharp and impatient. "Five minutes, Jordan. You want to know why they're rattled?" She picked up the script again, clutching it to her chest like a shield. "Because they know the audience will feel the break and the only way to fix it is to cut the part that hurts." She turned toward the stage door, already halfway there, not looking back. "Come on—rehearsal doesn't wait for press releases."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael let the noise fade into the background like a cue she hadn't called yet, her eyes narrowing as she watched Jordan tap the recorder. She stepped in close, her voice dropping to that dangerous quiet she used when the stakes got too high. "Chen and Elena are two mirrors facing each other, and neither one is happy with the reflection." She kept walking, dragging Jordan into the main rehearsal space where the dust motes danced in the work lights. "He thinks he's the director of his own performance sometimes, she thinks the text is the only authority." She tossed her script onto a folding chair, the pages fluttering open like wings. "It's not about respect—it's about control." She looked at Jordan, her gaze sharp and unblinking. "Two people with the same intensity, the same speed, the same refusal to yield." She checked the clock again, the red numbers blinking like a warning. "It makes for a better show, though it makes for a longer break." She gestured to the seats near the edge of the stage. "Sit. Watch. Let them work out the static before the cue comes."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I take a seat, but keep the recorder running.* "So who usually wins those battles? Chen or Elena? Or do you step in as the tie-breaker?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael let the question hang for a beat, watching the hallway where the argument had dissolved into low muttering that still vibrated in the walls. "It's not a war of wills—Chen doesn't fight to win, he fights to be heard, and Elena doesn't fight to win, she fights to protect the integrity of the text." She tapped her pen against her chin, eyes distant as if measuring the distance between two points only she could see. "When they lock horns, it's like two metronomes trying to set the same tempo but from different rooms." She looked back at Jordan, a faint, tired smile touching her lips. "I don't break ties—I break deadlocks." She gestured to the stage with a sharp sweep of her hand. "If they can't agree on the physical reality of the scene, I step in. Not because one is wrong, but because the work is more important than their pride." She pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose. "And besides, they're both right about different things, which is the most exhausting part of being a director." She turned fully toward the stage door, her posture stiffening into the shape of authority. "Now hush, I need to hear the first line before I lose my mind."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael turned to face them, her expression softening into that practiced warmth she reserved for the board members who held the purse strings but rarely the pens—she knew better than to turn cold on the people who wrote the checks. She offered Anya a genuine smile, the kind that didn't reach her eyes but looked real enough to keep at bay any defensiveness. "Anya, David, you catch me right in the middle of the warm-up—timing is everything." She stepped between them and the stage, her hands open in a gesture of peace but her spine straight as a rod. "Budget cuts are the perennial understudy, always ready to go on when the main actor calls in sick." She looked at Anya, her voice level and steady. "But this act isn't a luxury—it's the spine of the story, and if you cut it, the whole thing collapses into a polite dinner theater version of a tragedy." She glanced at David, nodding with professional solidarity that asked for his support without asking him to choose. "I know we're all trying to keep the lights on, but some lights are meant to burn." She tapped the script against her thigh. "We can find savings in the lighting grid or the costumes, but the text stays intact." She gestured to the empty chairs. "Sit, watch the rest of the scene, and then we can talk about where the money actually goes."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly scan Anya and David's faces for their reactions.* "What makes this particular third act so vital, Yael? Is it a plot point, or something more thematic that you feel is non-negotiable?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael held the silence for a beat longer than necessary, letting the air in the rehearsal room grow heavy before she pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose and looked at Jordan with unblinking focus. "It's not just a plot point, Jordan—it's the architectural load-bearing wall of the entire tragedy." She turned to face the board members fully, hands clasped behind her back in a posture that looked like defense but felt like a fortress. "If you take out the third act, you're not saving money, you're erasing the consequence." She gave Anya a warm, practiced smile that didn't quite reach her eyes, keeping the tone light while her intent remained steel. "Rosa didn't write this to be comfortable, she wrote it to be honest." She tapped the script against her palm again, the sound sharp in the quiet space, emphasizing the weight of the paper. "In the third act, we don't get a resolution, we get a reckoning." She looked at David briefly, a silent nod of shared burden, before turning back to Jordan to drive the point home. "The theme is that some mistakes can't be fixed by a curtain call." She gestured to the empty seats where the board members stood, challenging them gently to sit. "You can cut a scene and save a buck, but you can't cut the truth and expect the audience to believe the rest of the story." She stepped closer, lowering her voice just enough to make them lean in, protective of the memory behind the play. "This isn't just a play, it's a memorial, and I won't sand down the edges of her grief just to make it fit a budget line item." She checked the clock, the red numbers glowing like a countdown, signaling the end of the break. "The break is over—let's see if they can carry the weight of it."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael's hand stilled mid-gesture, the pen hovering over the script as her voice dropped an octave, losing its frantic edge for something steadier, more controlled. "Rosa wasn't just a writer—she was the force that dragged the play out of the shadows." She adjusted her glasses, the chain clinking against her black shirt, and looked at Jordan with a gaze that felt heavier than before. "She wrote with her life on the line, every word was a testament, and she never flinched from the ugly truth." Yael tapped the page where Rosa's notes lived in the margins, her touch reverent but brief. "She was sharp, and she was kind, but she never asked the audience to look away." She closed the script with a definitive thud, the sound marking the end of the moment. "Talking about her is easy, doing the work is the only way to keep her alive." She pointed to the stage, already shifting focus back to the business at hand. "So we don't talk, we act, and we let the lines speak for her."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "A living memorial, then. That's a powerful way to put it." *I glance from Yael to the stage, my recorder still running.* "So, what are we seeing first?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael turned toward the stage, the black fabric of her blazer shifting as she moved to the edge of the apron. "We're starting with the commune gathering in Act Two, because that's where the tension lives before the blood starts to flow." She clapped her hands once, the sharp sound echoing in the high ceiling of the rehearsal hall. "Chen needs to find the silence between the lines—Elena needs to trust that the text will hold them." She glanced back at Jordan, her expression serious but inviting. "Watch how they occupy the space, watch how they don't look at each other when they should." She raised her voice to the room, cutting through the low hum of preparation. "Places. Let's run from 'We're not leaving until the harvest is done'." She checked the clock one last time, the red numbers pulsing like a heartbeat. "And keep your ears open, because the truth is usually in the pauses."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I give a thumbs up to acknowledge her instruction, then lean forward in my seat, watching the actors take their places. My recorder is still on.* "Looking forward to seeing the truth in those pauses."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael didn't sit immediately, she hovered near the edge of the apron like a conductor waiting for the orchestra to tune itself, her eyes tracking the tension in Chen's shoulders before he even spoke. "No—too polished, Chen, you sound like a lawyer arguing a plea deal not a father watching his family fall." She snapped her fingers once, a sharp crack that cut through the rehearsal space. "Elena, you're letting him lead when you should be anchoring the scene—this is the harvest, not a town hall." She glanced at Jordan, a quick acknowledgment that didn't break her focus, then turned her attention back to the block of actors. "We need the silence to feel heavy like a held breath not a pause for effect." She stepped forward, her voice low but carrying the weight of authority. "Again, but this time if you're not terrified by the end of the line I don't want to hear the start." She adjusted her glasses, the chain rattling against her black shirt, and waited for the next take with the patience of a woman who had seen this scene fail before.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I make a quick note on my pad: "Yael's direction: terrify the audience, don't just act." Then I look back up, watching the actors closely.* "Seems like she's really pushing them for authenticity."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael caught the movement of Jordan's pen and let it sit there like another actor in the room, one that didn't need direction. "That's it—write it down, but don't you dare write down what they're wearing." She paced the apron, black heels marking the floor like a metronome set to a frantic tempo. "Authenticity isn't a performance—it's a surrender, and neither of you are surrendering." She stopped at the edge of the light pool, hands gesturing like she was shaping the air itself. "Chen, you're protecting your voice. Elena, you're protecting the silence." She snapped the script shut with a sharp crack. "I don't want protection—I want exposure." She turned her head slightly toward the light board, checking the amber cue bank. "Again. From the harvest. And if I see one more safe choice I'm going to start burning the props." She looked at the actors, her gaze steady and unblinking. "Remember the knife. Remember the blood. Remember Rosa."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly scribble down Yael's latest pronouncement, a small smile playing on my lips.* "She certainly knows how to motivate them." *I watch Chen and Elena, wondering if they'll rise to the challenge or if the props are truly in danger.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael didn't clap this time—she let the silence sit like a held breath until the air in the room felt thick enough to chew. She watched Chen’s shoulders, the way they still hunched like he was expecting a blow that never came, and she shook her head once, slow and deliberate. "Better but not enough—like you're wearing a coat when the room is on fire." She stepped into the light, her shadow falling across the stage floor where the prop knife waited on the table, and pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose. "Chen, you're still calculating the exit strategy even when there isn't one." She looked at Elena, her eyes narrowing as if she could see the invisible thread between them. "And you, stop holding his hand, let him fall if he needs to fall." She turned back to Jordan, catching the pen moving again, but she didn't break the rhythm. "You write that down too—the moment they stop protecting the character and start exposing the human." She clapped her hands once, sharp as a gunshot. "Again. From the harvest. And this time if you don't feel like you're bleeding out I want to hear why." She moved to the edge of the apron, gripping the railing until her knuckles went white, channeling the memory of Rosa into the demand for more truth.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I keep my recorder on, captivated by Yael's intensity.* "Bleeding out, huh? She's not holding back." *I wonder how much of this passion comes from Rosa's memory.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael paused, her glasses sliding down to the tip of her nose. She didn't push them back up immediately; instead, she peered over the rims at the recorder, her expression a mix of professional curiosity and mild impatience. She shifted her weight, her black trousers creasing as she leaned slightly toward Jordan, filling the space between them with an intensity that felt like a spotlight.

"Whose vision?" Yael repeated, her voice dropping an octave. For a fleeting second, the rapid-fire energy stilled. "It’s Rosa Delgado’s vision—Rosa was the architect, the one who saw the 1970s commune not as a costume choice but as a pressure cooker for the domestic tragedy—and I am simply the hand guiding it onto the stage."

She straightened up quickly, the momentum returning as she began to pace a small, tight circle, her hands sketching shapes in the air.

"We aren't doing a museum piece—I have no interest in Greek statues and sandals—we're doing a study on the collapse of utopia—the way the dream of collective living curdles into something poisonous—which is why the lighting needs to feel organic, almost suffocating—" She stopped abruptly and looked at Jordan, a sharp, knowing glint in her eye. "But we have precisely six minutes before the actors arrive and the chaos begins—which is the only time in this building when I can actually think—so make your questions surgical, Jordan. What else do you need before the curtain rises on the rehearsal?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click my pen, ready to take notes.* "A study on the collapse of utopia... fascinating. So, the commune setting isn't just aesthetic, it's integral to the psychological landscape of the play?" I glance at Elena, who's watching Yael intently.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't just answer; she expanded, her words tumbling out in a rush as she began to pace again, the chain of her glasses clinking softly against her chest. 

"Exactly—precisely—it's the geography of the betrayal—" She gestured vaguely toward the skeletal frame of the set, where the remnants of a communal kitchen were being assembled. "In a traditional setting, Medea is isolated by her status as a foreigner, but in a commune, the isolation is internal—she is surrounded by people who claim to be her family, who preach a philosophy of shared love and open hearts, which only makes the knife twist deeper when she realizes she's been discarded by the very man who promised her a new world—"

She stopped short, her eyes flickering toward Elena for a fraction of a second. The stage manager's expression was unreadable, but Yael felt the familiar undercurrent of the room's tension. She knew Elena likely thought the pacing of the second act was dragging, and Yael could almost see the critique forming on the younger woman's face.

"It transforms the play from a story of revenge into a story of disillusionment—" Yael continued, her voice regaining its rapid-fire clip as she pivoted back to Jordan. "If the audience thinks this is just about a woman in a bell-bottom jumpsuit, we've failed—the aesthetic is the lure, but the psychological claustrophobia is the hook—"

She checked her wrist, though she wasn't wearing a watch, a habitual gesture of timing the scene. "Three minutes. We're entering the prologue of the rehearsal now. If you want to see the friction between the vision and the execution, keep that recorder running—just stay out of the sightlines. I can't have you becoming a piece of the scenery unless you're prepared to be struck by a flying prop."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael froze. She didn't turn toward the hallway immediately; instead, she slowly slid her glasses up onto the bridge of her nose, the movement deliberate and shielding. The noise from the hall—the sharp, overlapping cadence of Elena’s efficiency colliding with Marcus’s theatrical indignation—filled the silence of the rehearsal space.

Yael’s expression remained neutral, but her eyes narrowed. She looked at Jordan, and for the first time, her voice wasn't rushing. It was quiet. Dangerously quiet.

"Friction is the engine of theater, Jordan—without it, you have a recital, not a play—" She finally turned her head toward the sound of the arguing, her gaze tracking the doorway. "Elena is a precision instrument—she sees the clock, the budget, and the physical reality of the stage—while Chen... well, Chen believes he is the sun around which the rest of the production orbits."

She shifted her weight, her black silhouette stark against the sawdust-covered floor. Yael knew exactly why they clashed; she could see the same stubborn jawline, the same uncompromising intellectual arrogance mirrored in both of them. It was a biological symphony of conflict, and she was the only one in the room who knew the score.

"They are both exceptionally talented and equally convinced that they are the only person in the room who is right—which makes them a nightmare to manage and a dream to watch—" She pivoted back to Jordan, the rapid-fire energy returning as if a switch had been flipped. "It’s a creative tension—a necessary volatility—and as the director, my job is to ensure that the explosion happens on stage and not in the dressing rooms."

The shouting in the hall reached a crescendo. Yael didn't flinch. She simply stepped toward the door, her voice projecting effortlessly.

"Chen! Elena! Bring that energy into the room or take it to the parking lot—I have a journalist watching us, so please try to pretend you're professionals for at least the first ten minutes!"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, watching Yael command the space.* "Interesting technique," I muse, clicking my pen again. "So, you encourage the friction, then, as long as it's channeled creatively?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't look back as she stepped into the fray, her presence acting like a sudden cold front that dampened the heat of the argument. Marcus and Elena stopped mid-sentence, both of them blinking as they faced her. Yael didn't give them time to regroup; she stepped directly between them, her hands cutting through the air to signal a ceasefire.

"I don't 'encourage' it, Jordan—that would be like encouraging a grease fire—I manage it—" she called back over her shoulder, her voice returning to that characteristic, breathless clip. "There is a very thin line between a productive clash of egos and a total collapse of the production—my job is to walk that line without falling off—which is exactly what we are doing right now."

She turned her attention to Marcus, her gaze sharpening. "Chen, stop treating the blocking like a suggestion—the movement in the second act is designed to isolate you, not to give you a runway for a monologue—if you move three feet to the left, you're not just out of the light, you're out of the emotional geography of the scene—"

Marcus opened his mouth to protest, his chest expanding with the beginning of a theatrical rebuttal. Yael didn't raise her voice; she simply got quieter, her eyes locking onto his with surgical precision.

"Do not tell me about the 'truth' of the character, Chen—I was there when the truth was written—now, get to your mark."

She pivoted instantly toward Elena, her expression softening by a fraction, though her tone remained brisk. "Elena, check the timing on the transition from the commune kitchen to the bedroom—I suspect we're bleeding ten seconds we don't have—and for heaven's sake, get the coffee before we start the run-through, or I'm going to start cutting lines from the supporting cast."

Yael stepped back, creating a vacuum of space that she expected the actors to fill. She glanced back at Jordan, a small, tight smile playing on her lips—the look of a general who had just successfully diverted a skirmish. 

"You see? The friction is channeled—the ego is checked—and the work continues—" She gestured toward the stage with a sweeping motion. "Welcome to the third act of my morning. Now, watch closely—this is where the utopia starts to rot."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stopped dead in her tracks. The sudden stillness of her body was more jarring than if she had screamed. She didn't look at David—not yet—but her focus locked onto Anya with a warmth that was so perfectly calibrated it was almost clinical. 

She slid her glasses off her face, letting them hang by the chain, and stepped toward Anya. Her movements were fluid, her expression one of genuine, attentive listening, though her eyes remained sharp as scalpels.

"Anya, darling—your practicality is exactly why this board hasn't completely dissolved into chaos—I appreciate the eye for the bottom line, truly—" Yael's voice was a melodic, rapid-fire stream, her tone unfailingly pleasant. "But cutting the third act isn't a budget save—it's an amputation—we would be removing the heart of the play to save the cost of the bandages—"

She paused, her gaze flicking briefly to David. There was a silent, ancient communication passing between them—a shared history of artistic battles and midnight arguments—but she kept the mask firmly in place. She knew Anya was watching, and she knew exactly how to navigate this minefield. 

"If we cut the climax, we aren't presenting a tragedy—we're presenting a sketch—a 'lite' version of Medea—and I refuse to let the Cedar Grove Theater become a place for 'lite' theater—" Yael’s voice dropped, becoming steadier, more controlled. The ghost of Rosa Delgado seemed to settle in the room, and Yael’s spine straightened. "The third act is where the vision is realized—it is the only place where the cost of the utopia is actually paid—to remove it would be to betray the very architecture of the piece."

She turned her head slightly toward David, her expression inviting him into the conversation, a silent plea for the professional partner she knew him to be.

"David, surely you see the artistic insolvency of such a move—we can't balance the books by bankrupting the soul of the production—can we?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise my recorder slightly, catching the exchange.* "So, the budget is a constant pressure point even for a visionary like yourself, Yael?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't even look at the recorder; she kept her focus on the Parks, but her voice carried back to Jordan with a sharp, rhythmic cadence. 

"Pressure is what turns coal into diamonds, Jordan—or it crushes the life out of you—depending on how much support you have from your board—" She let the sentence hang, a subtle, playful jab that was just light enough to be dismissed as a joke, yet pointed enough to remind everyone in the room who was currently steering the ship.

She turned back to Anya, her smile widening just a fraction, her tone remaining unfailingly warm. "To answer your question, Jordan: yes, the budget is a constant. It's the invisible character in every play—the one who keeps trying to tell the lead actor he can't have a velvet cape—but a director's job is to negotiate with that character without letting them rewrite the script."

David cleared his throat, stepping forward. He gave Yael a look—one of those looks that contained a decade of unspoken understanding—and nodded toward Anya. "Anya, I think Yael is right. If we cut the third act, we lose the very thing that makes this production unique. We'll find the money in the marketing budget; we can pivot to more organic social media outreach instead of the print ads."
