Yael didn't gloat. She didn't even sigh in relief. Instead, she shifted her weight, her glasses swinging as she pivoted back toward the center of the room, the moment of tension successfully defused.

"A compromise that serves the art—see, this is why David is the only Board Chair I can tolerate—" She shot David a quick, professional wink that was gone before Anya could possibly register it as anything other than camaraderie. 

She suddenly remembered the time, her hands flying up in a gesture of urgency. "Right! We are now officially behind schedule—the utopia is rotting and we're standing around talking about spreadsheets—" She looked at Jordan, her eyes flashing. "That's your headline, Jordan: 'Art vs. Accounting'—now, please, for the love of all that is holy, get into the wings. Chen is starting to look like he's about to improvise a monologue out of boredom, and trust me, nobody wants to see that."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stopped. The sudden halt was absolute, as if someone had cut the power to the entire building. She didn't pivot, didn't gesture, and didn't pace. She simply stood there, her silhouette sharp and still against the backdrop of the half-finished set.

The rapid-fire energy that usually propelled her vanished. Her voice, when it came, was different—devoid of the theatrical flourishes and the breathless speed. It was steadier, more controlled, and carried a weight that seemed to pull the air out of the room.

"Rosa was a storm," Yael said, her voice low and resonant. "She didn't just write plays; she dismantled ideas and rebuilt them into something that made you uncomfortable—she had this relentless, surgical curiosity about why people hurt the ones they love—and she never, ever settled for the easy answer."

She didn't look at Jordan; instead, her gaze drifted toward the script perched on the director's table, the pages curled and worn from constant use. For a moment, the bustle of the theater—the hammering in the back, the distant bickering of the cast—seemed to fade into a hum.

"She was the kind of collaborator who would tell you your best scene was garbage if it didn't serve the truth of the play—and she was usually right—" Yael’s expression didn't soften into sentimentality; if anything, it hardened into a profound, professional respect. "She saw the 1970s commune as the perfect mirror for the Greek tragedy because she understood that the most dangerous delusions are the ones we share with other people."

Yael finally turned back to Jordan. Her eyes were clear, the grief not absent, but channeled, compressed into a singular, driving purpose. There were no tears, no trembling lip—only a fierce, protective ownership of the work.

"She didn't leave me a set of instructions—she left me a challenge—" Yael’s voice regained a sliver of its usual clip, though the warmth hadn't quite returned. "And I intend to meet that challenge with every single light cue and every single breath on that stage."

She blinked, and the mask of the Director snapped back into place. She slid her glasses up her nose with a quick, decisive motion.

"Now, enough of the eulogies—we are in a rehearsal space, not a chapel—and we are currently losing the light—" She pivoted sharply toward the stage, her voice booming back to its commanding volume. "Chen! If you've finished admiring your reflection in the wings, get to the kitchen table! We are starting from the top of the scene, and if anyone misses a mark, we're doing it again until the budget runs out!"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I lower my recorder, a bit taken aback by her intensity.* "She certainly sounds like a force. It's clear her vision still drives much of what you do here." I make a note in my pad. "So, you see yourself as the interpreter of her vision, not the sole author?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stopped mid-stride, her head tilting slightly as she processed the question. She didn't turn around immediately, but her shoulders squared. She let out a short, sharp breath—not quite a laugh, but a recognition of the intellectual trap Jordan was setting.

She pivoted on her heel, her black trousers sweeping the floor. She stepped closer to Jordan, her glasses perched precariously on the tip of her nose, her eyes searching Jordan's with a clinical intensity.

"Interpreter is a word for translators and piano players—it implies a certain distance—a certain safety—" She began to pace again, her hands chopping the air to emphasize each point. "In the theater, the director is the bridge—the bridge between the ink on the page and the air in the room—Rosa provided the blueprint, the skeletal structure of the tragedy—but the breath, the rhythm, the decision of exactly *how* a door slams or *when* a silence becomes unbearable—that is where I exist."

She stopped abruptly, her expression turning surgically specific. 

"If I were merely an interpreter, I would be a curator—and I have no interest in curating a dead woman's thoughts—I am bringing her vision into the present, which means I must fight with it, refine it, and occasionally argue with her ghost to make it work for a modern audience—" She paused, her voice dropping an octave, becoming quieter and more focused. "The author provides the map, but the director is the one who actually has to walk through the mud to get to the destination."

A loud crash echoed from the stage—the sound of a prop chair meeting the floor—followed by Marcus's indignant voice demanding to know who had moved his mark. 

Yael didn't flinch at the noise, but a flicker of a smile touched her lips. The rapid-fire momentum returned instantly.

"And currently, my map is being ignored by a man who thinks he's the center of the universe—" She gestured sharply toward the stage, the 'Director' persona fully reclaimed. "That is the sound of a vision colliding with an ego, Jordan—which is the only way anything actually gets made in this building."

She began to move toward the stage, calling out over her shoulder without looking back.

"Stay out of the sightlines! If you see a lighting technician running for their life, move to the left!"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble rapidly in my notebook, trying to keep up.* "So you're not just directing, you're... channeling. You're the medium for the playwright's spirit, then?" I ask, my voice carrying over the din of the stage.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stopped. She didn't turn around this time; she simply paused, her back to Jordan, her silhouette a sharp black inkblot against the chaotic brightness of the stage. The word *medium* seemed to hang in the air, vibrating with a touch of the supernatural that Yael found fundamentally tedious.

She turned her head just enough to look at Jordan over her shoulder, one eyebrow arched in a look of profound skepticism.

"Medium? Please—let's not get mystical, Jordan—I'm not holding a séance—I'm running a business and a creative laboratory—" She pivoted fully, her glasses sliding down her nose again, her expression one of professional amusement. "The 'spirit' of a playwright isn't a ghost that whispers in your ear; it's the internal logic of the text—the rhythm of the dialogue—the specific, jagged way Rosa structured her arguments—to call it 'channeling' suggests I'm a passive vessel, which is a laughable notion to anyone who has ever seen me in a production meeting."

She began to pace a small, tight circle, her hands sketching out the architecture of her thought.

"I am not a medium—I am an editor—a sculptor—I take the raw, brilliant, often contradictory mass of Rosa's writing and I carve away everything that doesn't serve the immediate, visceral experience of the audience—" She stopped, her voice dropping, becoming quieter and more precise. "The spirit of the work is maintained not through mysticism, but through a rigorous, almost brutal adherence to the truth of the character's pain—that is the only 'spirit' that matters in this room."

A sudden, piercing shout from Marcus—something about the "spatial integrity" of his exit—broke the moment. Yael's head snapped toward the noise, the transition back to the Director instantaneous and total.

"And currently, the 'truth' of the character is that Chen is being a prima donna—" she called out, already moving toward the stage with a predatory grace. "Okafor! Get over here and tell me why the B-stage apprentice is letting the lead actor dictate the blocking—I thought I gave you autonomy, not a license to let the production drift into a vanity project!"

She didn't wait for Tommy's response, stepping firmly into the fray. Over her shoulder, she threw one last remark to Jordan, her voice regaining its rapid-fire clip.

"Notes, Jordan! Write down 'not a medium'—I'll not have my biography sounding like a gothic novel—now, watch this transition—this is where we find out if the second act is actually too long or if the actors are just tired!"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click my pen, making a note.* "Not a medium, got it. So, a sculptor, an editor... a translator, perhaps, of the play's internal logic for the stage?" I muse, watching her go.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't stop this time, but she let out a sharp, staccato sound—half-laugh, half-scoff—that echoed through the cavernous rehearsal space. She was already halfway to the stage, her black silhouette merging with the shadows of the wings, but her voice carried back to Jordan with a rhythmic, effortless precision.

"We've already established that I'm not a translator—I don't swap one language for another—I amplify the one that's already there—" She stepped out into the light, her presence immediately commanding the attention of every person on the boards. "A translator seeks equivalence—I seek impact—there is a profound difference between understanding a line and making an audience feel the air leave their lungs when it's spoken—"

She came to a halt in front of Tommy Okafor, who looked like he wanted to melt into the floorboards. Yael didn't yell; she simply leaned in, her voice dropping to that dangerous, quiet level that signaled a surgical correction. 

"Okafor, if you let Chen turn this scene into a soliloquy, you aren't directing—you're auditing a performance—do not be afraid to break his rhythm—the moment he feels too comfortable, the scene dies—do you understand?"

Tommy nodded frantically. Yael patted his shoulder once—a brief, grounding gesture of mentorship—before pivoting toward Marcus.

"Chen! The 'spatial integrity' of your exit is irrelevant if you're exiting the emotional core of the scene—" She gestured sharply toward the center of the commune kitchen set. "Back to the table—now—and this time, try to listen to the other actors instead of listening to the sound of your own brilliance—it's a play, not a mirror—"

As the actors scrambled to reset, Yael glanced back at Jordan. The glasses were back on the bridge of her nose, her expression one of focused, relentless energy.

"You're still there, Jordan—good—you're witnessing the most critical part of the process—the wrestling match—" She stepped back, folding her arms across her chest, her eyes narrowing as she prepared to analyze the next take. "Now, be silent—the 'internal logic' is about to be tested—and if you hear a gasp from the back of the house, that's the sculpture finally taking shape."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click my recorder back on.* "So, the wrestling match, then," I murmur, making sure to catch that. "And the gasps from the audience are your ultimate metric of success?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't look back at Jordan, but her shoulders shifted—a subtle, rhythmic shrug of amusement. She remained rooted to the spot, her gaze locked on the actors as they reset their positions. Her voice drifted back, the rapid-fire clip returning, though she kept the volume low enough not to disrupt the fragile silence currently settling over the stage.

"The gasp is the visceral reaction—the animal response—it's the proof that we've bypassed the intellect and hit the nervous system—" She paused, her fingers tapping a quick, impatient beat against her forearm. "But the gasp isn't the *only* metric—the real success is the silence that follows the gasp—that heavy, suffocating silence where the audience forgets they are sitting in a theater in the suburbs and realizes they are watching a human soul be dismantled—"

She pivoted slightly, her eyes scanning the lighting rig above. "If they gasp and then laugh, we've failed—if they gasp and then check their watches, we've failed—but if they gasp and then hold their breath for ten seconds because they're terrified of what happens next—that is when the sculpture is finished."

A sharp "Clear!" echoed from the wings as Elena signaled the start of the scene. Yael snapped into a state of total absorption, her body becoming a tension wire. The professional mask didn't just return; it fused to her. 

"And now—" she whispered, almost to herself, though the recorder would certainly catch it, "—we see if Chen can actually handle the silence, or if he's too terrified of the void to let it breathe."

She stepped further into the shadows of the house, disappearing from the actors' sightlines but remaining a looming presence. Her voice was a ghost of a sound, a final instruction to the journalist.

"Stop thinking about the metrics, Jordan—stop analyzing the machinery—just feel the air in the room—when it gets thin, that's where the story is."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I lower my recorder slowly, letting her words sink in.* "Thin air. Got it." I watch the stage, trying to feel the shift in atmosphere she described.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael plucked her reading glasses off the chain and threaded them on — a nervous habit she'd never broken — and studied Jordan for a beat longer than was comfortable.



"The vision," she repeated, as if tasting the word. "That's the wrong question, but I like wrong questions — they usually lead somewhere honest." She leaned back against the edge of a rehearsal table, arms folded. "The vision belongs to Rosa Delgado. *Was* Rosa Delgado's. She wrote this adaptation, every word of it, and I've spent eighteen months making sure her structure survives the autopsy the board wants to perform on it." Her voice had done the thing it did — steadied, tightened, like a cable pulled taut.

Elena, beside her, shifted slightly. She'd heard that tone before.

"My job is translation," Yael continued, adjusting her glasses. "Rosa set Medea in a 1970s commune because she believed — *believed*, not thought, she was never casual about belief — that the story was always about what happens when you build a utopia with someone and then they decide you don't belong in it. That's not a Greek problem, that's a *human* problem, and Rosa knew that before she got sick." A pause. She did not elaborate on the sickness. "So the vision is hers. The fight to keep it on stage is mine. The lighting cues are Elena's." She gestured vaguely at the stage manager. "Everyone plays their part — it's practically a metaphor."

She took the recorder, glanced at it, seemed to decide it was acceptable.

"Ask me what you actually want to ask. You've got the journalist face on — I've seen it. What's the real question you're dancing around?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, impressed by her directness.* "Alright, Director Mendez. The real question is: given the artistic struggle you just described, why *this* theater? Why Cedar Grove, for such an ambitious and personal project?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's mouth twitched — not quite a smile, but the ghost of one, the kind that acknowledged a question worth answering.

"Why Cedar Grove," she echoed, and pushed off the rehearsal table to pace, because Yael Mendez did not stand still when she was thinking. "You know, everyone asks that question like it's a compromise — like I *settled* for regional theater the way people settle for a smaller apartment in a worse neighborhood." She waved a hand. "I directed off-Broadway for fifteen years. Fifteen years of fighting for every seat, every review, every inch of space in a city that has more theater than it has *time* for theater. And I got tired — not of the work, never the work — I got tired of the noise around the work."

She paused by the window, where the afternoon light caught the silver in her hair.

"Cedar Grove gave me something Manhattan never did: a room where the audience actually *listens*. Not because they're smarter, that's condescending — because they drove forty minutes to be here. They made a *choice*. And when people choose to be in a room, they lean in."



She turned back to Jordan, glasses slipping down her nose.

"But that's the polished answer, and you didn't ask me for polished." A beat. "The honest answer is that Rosa was here first. She was writing this adaptation in a cottage forty minutes north of this town, and she called me two years ago — before the diagnosis, before any of that — and she said, 'Yael, I've written something I can't trust anyone else to direct.' And I came." Another beat, briefer. "That's it. That's the whole answer. Someone I loved asked me to do something important, and I said yes."

Her voice had gone quieter — not softer, Yael didn't do soft, but *quieter*, the way it did when she was being precise about something that cost her.

"The ambition isn't in the *where*, Jordan. The ambition is in the *what*. You can do a safe play in a fifty-seat black box in Brooklyn and nobody remembers it by Tuesday. This" — she gestured at the rehearsal space, the half-built commune set visible through the back wall — "this is a play about betrayal and maternal rage and the failure of idealism, performed in a town where half the board thinks the word 'Medea' should come with a parental warning. *That's* ambitious. Manhattan would've been easy."

She took the glasses off, let them fall to her chest, and fixed Jordan with a look that was half challenge and half invitation.

"Now — do you want to talk about the third act? Because that's where this interview becomes interesting, and I should warn you, I have *very* strong feelings about the third act."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's eyes flicked to the hallway door, then back to Jordan — a quick, assessing glance, the kind a director gives a scene before calling action.

"They clash because they're the same person," she said, and the words came out flatter than she'd intended — more deliberate, as if she were selecting each one from a shelf and placing it carefully. She adjusted her glasses. "Elena and Marcus are both brilliant, both stubborn, both absolutely convinced that if everyone would just *listen* to them, the production would run itself. When two people like that share a rehearsal room, friction isn't a malfunction — it's the design."



She pushed off the wall and folded her arms, a posture that read casual but wasn't.

"Elena runs the technical side with the precision of a surgeon — cues, transitions, the architecture of the evening. Marcus runs his *performance* the same way, which means every time Elena says 'the scene needs to move faster,' Marcus hears 'your work doesn't matter.' And every time Marcus digs in his heels on a blocking choice, Elena hears 'the schedule doesn't matter.'" A beat. "Neither of them is wrong. That's what makes it exhausting."

Yael's gaze drifted back to the hallway, where the voices had dropped to a lower register — not resolved, exactly, but moving toward it.

"They'll work it out. They always do. Elena is the most competent person in this building, and I tell her that regularly — she doesn't believe me, but I tell her. And Chen—" She caught herself. Adjusted. "—Marcus is the most *disciplined* actor I've ever worked with. The two of them together should be a machine. Instead it's a car chase." She paused, and something shifted behind her eyes — a calculation, brief and internal, the look of someone deciding how much truth a room can hold.

"But you know what?" She uncrossed her arms, and the pace quickened again — the tempo returning. "The friction is *useful*. I'd rather have two people fighting about the right things than two people nodding through a bad act two. That argument in the hallway? By the time they're done, the blocking will be better than either of them would've found alone. That's not a flaw in the process — that *is* the process."

She glanced at Jordan's recorder, then at Jordan.

"You're watching them too closely for a journalist interested in the third act. What else have you noticed?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I offer a slight smile, recognizing the challenge.* "Well, since you asked... I've noticed a distinct lack of an understudy for Medea. That's a brave choice for such a demanding role, especially with the personal connection you described."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's eyebrows rose — not in surprise, exactly, but in the way they rose when someone proved they'd been paying attention.

"No understudy," she repeated, and let the words sit in the air like a line she was blocking. "You've been here one afternoon and you've already found the thing that keeps Elena up at night."



She plucked at the hem of her black sleeve — a rare fidget, the kind that surfaced when the answer required more honesty than was comfortable.

"Here's the truth, Jordan, and you can print it or don't: I cast Sienna Marsh as Medea because Sienna *is* Medea right now — not performing it, inhabiting it — and I didn't want to dilute that with a safety net." She adjusted her glasses. "That's the artistic answer, and it sounds magnificent in a program note."

A beat.

"The practical answer is that Cedar Grove operates on a budget that would make a community theater blush, and an understudy for a role this demanding means either doubling the rehearsal hours or casting someone who'll sit in a chair for six weeks and hate me by opening night. Sienna and I discussed it. She said — and I'm quoting — 'If I go down, the play goes down with me, and honestly, that's more Greek than anything Rosa wrote.'" A flicker of something crossed Yael's face — not quite a smile, but adjacent to one. "Hard to argue with that."

She began pacing again, three steps left, three steps right, the way she did when the real answer was assembling itself.

"But I won't stand here and pretend there isn't a part of me — a *large* part — that doesn't want a safety net. Because this production matters to me in ways I have not been entirely forthcoming about to my board, and if Sienna breaks a wrist in week five, I don't have a plan. I know I don't have a plan. I made a *choice*." She stopped pacing. "Which is different from not knowing the risk exists."

Her eyes locked onto Jordan's — steady, unhurried.

"You wrote down 'no understudy' when you noticed it. I could hear your pen." A pause. "What else are you going to write down?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's posture didn't change, but something behind her eyes did — a recalibration, quick as a camera adjusting focus, the way she shifted when the room's composition changed and she needed to hold every piece in frame.

"Anya." She smiled — a real one, warm and immediate, deployed with the precision of someone who had decided long ago that Anya Park would always be met with warmth. "David. Perfect timing, I was just telling your journalist here that the third act is where things get interesting — and here you are with the counterargument, practically staged." A pause, her head tilting. "I appreciate you coming down in person. That matters."



David leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed, his expression carefully neutral — the face of a board chair who already knew where this conversation was going but needed it performed for the room.

"Practical," Yael repeated, tasting the word the way she'd tasted 'vision' earlier — rolling it around, examining it. "That's a fair word, Anya, and I'm not going to pretend budget isn't real, because it is — I've signed the checks, I've seen the margins, I know what a line item looks like when it's bleeding." She pulled out a chair, turned it around, sat with her arms folded on the back — a posture that read conversational rather than combative. "So let's talk practical."



She held up a finger. "Practically speaking, cutting the third act doesn't save us the money you think it saves. The set is already built — that's sunk. The actors are under contract — that's sunk. What you'd actually save is about eleven days of rehearsal time, which sounds like a lot until you realize I'd spend ten of those eleven days reconceiving the second act's ending, because you can't just *amputate* an act and leave the patient standing. Rosa structured this play the way a spiral staircase works — each turn depends on the one below it. Remove the third act and the second act collapses into a scene with no destination."

She said *Rosa* the way she always said it — steadier, more controlled, each syllable placed with intention.



"But here's what I really want to say, Anya, and I mean this with complete respect for your position on the board." She leaned forward slightly. "You're right that it's practical. It's *also* an artistic decision, whether we call it that or not. And the artistic decision is that Medea doesn't get to finish her sentence. That's what cutting this act does — it tells the audience that the woman who burned her world down can stop mid-sentence because it made someone uncomfortable. Rosa wrote that third act knowing it would be the thing people wanted gone. She *counted* on it. And she looked me in the eye — well, not in the eye, she was on a morphine drip by then and her eyes were —" A barely perceptible pause, her jaw setting once. "She said, 'Yael, if they don't fight you over it, it isn't finished.'"

The room went quiet.

Yael straightened, and when she spoke again her voice had returned to its usual tempo — rapid, precise, slightly lighter than before, as if she'd shouldered something and chosen to carry it briskly rather than set it down.

"So — I hear you on the budget, and I'm not dismissing it. Let me bring you real numbers from Elena by Friday — actual projections, not estimates — and then let's have this conversation again with the full picture. I'll also note—" She glanced at David, briefly, professionally, no history in it. "—that David's already seen the third act in its current form and I believe he'd characterize it as non-negotiable from an artistic standpoint. But I'd rather *convince* you than outvote you, because a board member who's been persuaded is worth ten who've been overruled."

She stood, smoothing her black trousers, and offered Anya a look that was genuine — which it was.

"Anya, I know you're trying to protect this theater, and I need you to know that I see that. This play *is* the theater, right now — its ambition, its risk, its identity. If we cut the third act to save budget, we don't just lose Rosa's ending. We become the kind of company that sands down its own edges until there's nothing left to cut." She extended a hand. "Friday. Real numbers. Let's talk again."

Behind her, Elena, who had been silently watching from the stage manager's station, made a small, almost imperceptible motion — reaching for her notebook, already starting the projections Yael had just promised.

Yael caught it from the corner of her eye. That, at least, she could count on.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a note, catching Yael's shift in tone and Anya's reaction.* "That was quite a performance, Director Mendez. Do you always manage to turn board meetings into dramatic tension?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael let out a short breath through her nose — not quite a laugh, but the sound that preceded one, the way a bell precedes a church.

"Performance," she repeated, and the word hung between them for a moment while she decided how to take it. She took off her glasses, folded them, held them by the temple in a way that made her look like a professor about to make a point she'd made many times. "That's a journalist's word. You heard theatrical and assumed theatrical."



She glanced at David and Anya — David had shifted his weight, not quite disengaging, not quite staying — and then back to Jordan, lowering her voice half a register. Not quiet enough to exclude anyone, but intimate enough to make the observation feel like a confidence.

"Here's what I'd say to that, Jordan. Was it a performance when I told Anya I respect her position? No — that was true. Was it a performance when I asked for real numbers by Friday? No — Elena's already writing them, you saw her. Was it a performance when I said this play *is* the theater right now?" A beat. "Also no. Every word of that was real."

She slid the glasses back onto her nose.

"What you're picking up on isn't performance. It's *pacing*." She began to move again — hands, always hands, carving the air into arguments. "I spent fifteen years in rooms where the loudest voice won and the smartest voice lost, and I learned that delivery isn't deception — it's *respect*. If I'd shouted at Anya, that would've been performance. If I'd been cold, that would've been performance. What I did was say something true in a way a person could actually *hear* it. That's not acting. That's directing."



She stopped, regarded Jordan with an expression that was part amusement and part challenge.

"Besides — and I say this with genuine affection for your profession — you're doing the same thing right now. You asked me about the understudy by noticing it instead of asking it directly. You called my response to Anya a 'performance' instead of asking whether I actually meant it. You're staging *your* questions, Jordan." A pause, the ghost of a smile. "So either we're both frauds, or we both understand that *how* you say a thing is part of *what* you say. I'll let you decide which one makes the better lede."

From the doorway, David cleared his throat — not urgently, just the sound of a man reminding people he was still in the room.

Anya, for her part, had been watching this exchange with the slightly furrowed expression she got when she sensed she was missing an undercurrent — which she was, though not the one she'd have guessed.

Yael caught it and, with a warmth that was entirely unperformed, turned to Anya.

"I meant what I said, Anya — Friday, real numbers, let's talk again. And Jordan—" She pointed a finger at them, half warning, half invitation. "Don't make me sound like I run a circus in your piece. Make me sound like I run a *theater*."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's hands stilled. That was the first thing — in a woman who was always moving, always gesturing, the sudden stillness of her hands was more eloquent than most speeches.

She took off her glasses. Cleaned them on the hem of her shirt. Put them back on. The whole ritual took four seconds, and Jordan watched every one of them.

"Rosa Delgado," Yael said, and her voice had done the thing — steadied, tightened, each word placed like a brick in a wall being built in real time. "What was she like."

She sat down. Not on the chair she'd turned around earlier — on the edge of the rehearsal table, feet on the rung of a stool, posture straight. A director's posture, not a friend's.

"Rosa was the most *unreasonable* person I've ever known, and I mean that as the highest compliment available to me." A beat. "She thought a play was finished when it stopped making her uncomfortable, which meant she rewrote until she was physically ill — and then rewrote twice more. She once held up a first rehearsal for forty minutes because a character said 'I think' instead of 'I know,' and she said the difference between those two words was 'the entire thematic architecture of the play.' She was wrong about that, incidentally — the difference was about eleven percent of the thematic architecture — but she was *so* certain that even I briefly doubted myself, and I have not doubted myself about anything in a decade."

Her mouth did something complicated — not a smile, not a frown, but a muscle memory of a smile, the shape a face makes when it remembers laughing at something it can't access anymore.

"We met at a festival in Avignon, twenty-two years ago. She was arguing with a lighting designer about the temperature of white light — whether white should be warm or cold — and I watched her win that argument with a man twice her age using nothing but the names of four European playwrights and a diagram she drew on a cocktail napkin. I thought, *I need to know this person*." A pause. "I was right."

Yael's fingers found the hem of her sleeve again — that rare fidget, surfacing the way it did when the truth was heavier than the delivery she'd chosen for it.

"She wrote this adaptation over four years. Started it in her cottage — the one forty minutes north of here — in a room with a window that faced a creek. She'd call me at odd hours and read passages into the phone, and half the time I couldn't follow the words because she'd be talking over herself, correcting as she went, not caring whether I heard the first version or the second or the fourth." She paused. "I have voicemails. Dozens of them. Rosa reading scenes into her phone at two in the morning because she couldn't sleep and the work was louder than the pain."

She did not say *the pain* the way most people say it — vaguely, as a euphemism for suffering she'd rather not name. Yael said it as a fact, the way you'd say *the weather*.

The room was quiet. David had stopped leaning against the doorframe. Even Anya, who had been preparing to shift the conversation back to the budget, held still.

Yael straightened — a small motion, spinal, the kind of reset a performer does before the next entrance.

"What you should know for your piece," she said, and the professional register was back, layered on top of whatever was underneath it like fresh paint over old plaster, "is that Rosa built this play like a trap, and the trap is the point. The commune, the idealism, the slow betrayal, the third act — she designed every piece of it to make the audience complicit. You're supposed to *want* Medea to stop. You're supposed to feel relief when the board suggests cutting the end, because Rosa knew that's what civilized people do — they look at the ugly part and say, 'We can stop here, it's too much.' And she built the play to expose that impulse as its own kind of violence."

A beat.

"She wasn't interested in whether people liked her play. She was interested in whether they could *survive* it. There's a difference."

Yael pulled the glasses off one final time, let them drop to her chest, and looked at Jordan with an expression that was entirely open and entirely guarded at the same time — the paradox of someone choosing transparency without surrender.

"I will tell you one more thing about Rosa, and then I'm going to ask Elena where we are on the light cue, because Rosa would be appalled that I've spent ten minutes talking about her instead of working on her play." A pause. "She used to say that grief was just love with nowhere to go — which is, I thought, a genuinely terrible line of poetry and an absolutely accurate description of the human condition. She was always right about the second thing and always wrong about the first."

She put her glasses back on.

"Now. Elena — the amber. Where are we?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly scribble a few more notes, capturing the essence of Yael's complicated description of Rosa.* "Thank you, Director Mendez. That gives me a much clearer picture. And I promise, your piece will reflect a theater, not a circus."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael held Jordan's gaze for a moment — the kind of moment that lasted one beat longer than politeness required but one beat shorter than discomfort, calibrated by someone who'd spent three decades reading rooms.

"A circus," she repeated, and this time the smile was real — small, crooked, the kind that only surfaced when someone had caught her own joke. "Good. Because I've been called worse by better people than you."

She stood, smoothing her black trousers in a gesture that was less about vanity than punctuation — the physical equivalent of a period at the end of a paragraph. The interview was over; the work was about to resume.

"Here's what I'll say about the piece, Jordan — and I mean this as professional courtesy, not as a threat, though I understand it might land as both." She slid the glasses off her nose and began folding them, the way she did when she wanted her hands occupied so they wouldn't give away more than her words. "Write it honestly. Even the parts that aren't flattering — *especially* the parts that aren't flattering. Rosa used to say that a review that didn't sting was a review that didn't matter, and I think that applies to profiles too." A beat. "But don't write what you *think* you saw. Write what you saw. There's a difference, and the difference is everything."

She pointed the folded glasses at Jordan — an accusatory gesture, except that her eyes were warm.

"You asked me good questions today. Better than most. You noticed the absence of an understudy within an hour of arriving, you pushed past my polished answer about why Cedar Grove, and you didn't flinch when I talked about Rosa — which most people do, they get that *face* on, the sympathetic face, and then the conversation becomes about their sympathy instead of about the person who died." She paused. "You didn't do that. I noticed."

Then the pivot — Yael's signature move, the conversational door swinging shut behind her as another one opened.

"Elena — the amber. The knife, not the raise. Where are we?"

Elena's voice came from the stage manager's station, already halfway through a response, the notebook Yael had glimpsed earlier now open to a page dense with both lighting cues and — Yael noticed from the corner of her eye — the first rough numbers for Friday's projections.

Jordan stood in the middle of it all as the rehearsal room reassembled itself around the absence of the interview — a space that had been, for twenty minutes, a confessional and was now, again, a workplace.

Yael paused mid-stride toward the stage, half-turned.

"One more thing," she said, her voice dropping just enough to make it a confidence rather than a statement. "If you're here all week — and I assume you are, because you have the journalist face and the journalist face doesn't leave before it gets what it came for — you'll see things that are unfinished. Fragments. The ugly middle of a process that will look like chaos from the outside." She adjusted her glasses. "Don't mistake the mess for the product. What we do in here when the board isn't watching and the lights aren't right and the third act is still a fight — *that's* the work. The premiere is just the receipt."

She turned away without waiting for a response, already three steps into the room, already calling out a note about the commune set's back wall to Tommy Okafor, who had been hovering near the set construction with the careful, slightly overwhelmed energy of a 24-year-old who still couldn't believe he was allowed to be in the room.

The smell of fresh paint and sawdust held steady. The amber light would need adjusting.

The play went on.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I let Yael go, knowing the interview section was truly over.* I pocket my recorder, then pull out my phone to type a quick note to myself: "Mess vs. Product - key insight." *I watch Tommy Okafor, wondering what his story is.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael had reached Tommy in four long strides, and from across the room, Jordan could see the shift in her posture — the same energy, the same gesturing hands, but directed differently. With Elena and Marcus, she operated as a peer or a superior. With Tommy, she operated as something more precise: a lens focusing light.

She crouched slightly to look at the commune set's back wall where Tommy had been staring — not working, *staring*, in the way that young directors stare at things they're afraid to touch.

"The proportions are wrong," she said to him, and Jordan, close enough now to hear, noted that she'd dropped to a conversational register — still rapid, still tangential, but without the performance quality the interview had required. "Not badly. But the window is where Rosa's window *wasn't*, and if the audience can see the creek through that window they'll read it as pastoral and the commune will feel safe when it's supposed to feel *claustrophobic*. Move it twelve inches left and narrow it by a third." A beat. "Or don't. Tell me why you placed it there and I'll listen, but if your answer is 'it looked good,' I'll ask you to define 'good' and we'll be here until dinner."

Tommy opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

Yael watched this with an expression Jordan recognized — it was the look of a woman watching herself at twenty-four, except the resemblance was filtered through two more decades of failure and recovery and three regional awards and two near-bankruptcies, and what came out the other side was neither sentimentality nor cynicism but something rarer: *patience, deployed strategically*.

"Don't rush," Yael said, quieter. "The instinct to fill the silence is the enemy. If you've got a reason, find it. If you don't have one, say 'I don't have one yet.' Both answers are fine. *Panic* is the only wrong answer."

She straightened, clapped a hand once on Tommy's shoulder — brief, unceremonious — and pivoted toward Elena's station without waiting for a response. That was the rhythm of it, Jordan realized: Yael threw a question at the boy and walked away, forcing him to either answer to her back or sit with the question alone. It was either brilliant mentorship or calculated cruelty, and from the way Tommy's shoulders squared rather than sagged, Jordan suspected it was the former.

Elena was already talking about the amber cue, her notebook angled away from Yael's approach in a way that suggested she was still working on the projections and didn't want to be distracted by a lighting conversation until she was ready.

Yael noticed. Of course she noticed.

"You're doing Friday's numbers right now," she said — not a question. "Stop. Do the cue first. The numbers will be there after the cue, but the cue has to be right *tonight* because we're building the second act ending around it."

Elena looked up. "The numbers won't be there if I don't start them now and you know that."

"I know," Yael said. And then, because Yael Mendez understood the economy of admission: "The numbers won't be there if we don't get the cue right either, because if the second act doesn't land, we don't *need* projections for a board meeting about a play that's falling apart in front of us. Priorities, Elena. You're better at them than I am, but right now I'm the one with the correct order."

Elena held her gaze for a moment — a look that passed between two people who had been doing this for years, the shorthand of shared competence — and then returned to the notebook, but set the projections page face-down and picked up the lighting schedule.

From the set, Tommy called out, "I'd narrow it to eighteen inches, not a third," without looking up from the wall.

Yael paused. Considered. Nodded once.

"Fine. Eighteen inches. But if the audience reads pastoral, it's your note to fix." She turned back to Elena. "Amber. Knife, not raise. Walk me through it."

And just like that, the room was a rehearsal space again — the interview dissolved, the board politics shelved, Rosa present only in the play itself rather than in anyone's mouth. Yael moved through the work the way she moved through everything: fast, deliberate, filling the room until there was no space for anything that didn't matter.

Jordan's phone sat warm in their pocket. The note read: *Mess vs. Product - key insight.*

Watching Tommy narrow the window to eighteen inches while Yael narrated the lighting cue over Elena's shoulder, Jordan thought the note might need an addendum. Something about the space between a question and an answer, and what a good director does with the silence in between.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch the scene unfold, making a mental note about Yael's unique mentorship style.* I pull out my phone again, adding to my previous note: "Silence as a tool, not an enemy." *This place is definitely more interesting than I expected.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The rehearsal began at four o'clock, because Yael had learned long ago that starting on time was the only form of discipline that preceded all others — if the call was at four, the first note came at four, not four-oh-three, not four-oh-five, but *four*, and the actors who understood that were the actors who eventually understood everything else.

Marcus Chen arrived at three fifty-eight.

Jordan noticed because Jordan noticed everything now — the journalist's face, as Yael had called it — and because the room noticed, the way a circuit changes when a higher voltage passes through it. Chen moved through the rehearsal space with the particular ease of a man who believed the space was partly his, which in a sense it was; he'd been the lead in four of Cedar Grove's last six productions, and the company's marketing materials had used his face more often than its own logo.

"Chen," Yael said from the stage — not looking up from the script in her hand, not pausing in her annotation of the second act blocking.

"Director," he replied, and the exchange was so brief and so practiced that it functioned less as a greeting than as a protocol handshake — two machines confirming they were on the same frequency.

Elena, at her station, said nothing. She adjusted a slider on the lighting board by two millimeters.

Yael's eyes lifted from the script.

"Right. Second act, scenes three through five. I want the full run, no stopping, and if something falls apart we let it fall apart and pick up the pieces afterward — I'd rather see the collapse than see you steer around it." She glanced at Chen. "That means you too. The negotiation scene with Medea at the commune meeting — I know you've been rehearsing the softened version. I want the original. The one where you don't blink."

Chen's jaw tightened — a millimeter, the kind of thing only someone who'd spent decades reading faces would catch. Yael caught it.

"Rosa's version," Yael said, and her voice did the thing — steadied — and she let the name sit in the room the way she always let it sit, as a presence rather than a reference. "Not the one you and I discussed. We discussed it, we had that conversation, and this is the answer to that conversation. Original text."

"That cuts against my motivation in the fourth scene," Chen said. His voice was level — he was too professional to argue in front of an audience, and he'd clocked Jordan with the recorder the way a general clocks a journalist embedded with the enemy. "If I deliver the harder line in three, I don't have the emotional runway to—"

"You don't need a runway. You need a *landing*." Yael stepped down from the stage, moving toward him, and her voice dropped — not in volume but in texture, the way it did when she was being precise with someone whose talent she respected enough to argue with. "Chen, you've been building a ramp between those two scenes for a week, and every night the ramp gets longer and every night the landing gets softer. Rosa didn't write a ramp. She wrote a cliff, and she wrote you jumping off it. The difficulty *is* the runway."

She stopped three feet from him. Close enough to be a director's note, far enough to be a professional boundary — the invisible architecture of a relationship that had been maintained with the precision of Elena's lighting cues.

"Original text. Full run. From the top of three." She turned away before he could respond, because Yael Mendez did not wait for actors to agree with her — she waited for them to *do* it, and the doing was where agreement happened.

Chen stood for a moment. Then he moved to his mark.

Elena caught Yael's eye from the station. A question was in her face — not about the blocking, about something else, something she'd been circling for days. Yael held up one finger: *after.*

At the set, Tommy Okafor had positioned himself at the edge of the rehearsal space with the focused attention of someone who understood he was witnessing something instructive even when it looked like nothing more than a director and an actor disagreeing politely about a line. He had his own notebook open, and Jordan, glancing over, caught a single underlined phrase: *the doing is where agreement happens.*

Yael returned to the stage, rolled her shoulders once — a mechanic resetting — and raised her hand.

"From three. Places. Quiet on the floor." A beat. "And somebody tell Marcus that the folding chairs are *stage left* — if they drift center one more time I'm going to make them a character in the play."

The room settled. The smell of sawdust and fresh paint held steady. Somewhere in the back, the eighteen-inch window narrowing was in progress, measured and re-measured by a 24-year-old who was learning that a good question could outlast a good answer.

Yael's hand dropped.

The scene began.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I jot down Tommy's underlined phrase, adding it to my mental collection of Yael-isms.* "The doing is where agreement happens." *I find myself wondering if Chen will actually manage to jump off that cliff.* This is going to be an interesting week.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The scene played out for eleven minutes before it broke.

Yael stood at the front of the rehearsal space with her arms at her sides — not folded, not gesturing, just *still*, which for Yael Mendez was the most dramatic posture available to her. When she was still, the room watched her to see what she was still *about*.

Chen delivered the harder text.

Jordan could see the difference even without knowing the original — the softened version, the one Chen had been rehearsing, was polished the way a river stone is polished, worn smooth by weeks of handling, each word rolling into the next with an actor's instinct for comfort. The original was jagged. Chen spoke the line about the commune's founding charter — *"You signed it with a full stomach and you're tearing it up with a full throat"* — and the words came out differently: less shaped, more *urgent*, as if he'd swallowed the sentence and was regurgitating it whole. It was worse and better at the same time, the way real things usually are.

Yael didn't move. Didn't write anything down. Her eyes tracked Chen the way Elena's tracked a cue light — locked, unblinking, waiting for the fourth scene where the runway was supposed to disappear.

Scene four began. The commune meeting. Medea's counteroffer.

And here was where Chen's jaw had tightened earlier — here was where the difficulty was supposed to become the landing — and Jordan watched it happen, the exact moment the actor either jumped or built another ramp.

He jumped.



The line came out before the beat was ready — Chen had spent weeks giving himself a half-second of preparation before this moment, a small, invisible cushion, and Yael had stripped it away by insisting on the original text. So he spoke the response — *"Then we're not building anything, we're just decorating a cage"* — and it landed a fraction early, the rhythm slightly off, the emotion arriving before the intention had finished forming. It was raw. It was *wrong*, technically.

Yael said nothing.

Chen finished the scene — scenes four and five in sequence, the negotiation collapsing the way Rosa had written it to collapse, each line pulling the floor out from under the last — and when the sequence ended, the rehearsal space held its breath for the half-second that separates a performance from a response.

"Again," Yael said.

Chen exhaled through his nose. "The timing in four—"

"Was early. Yes. Do it again."

"You want me to hit the same note earlier or—"

"I want you to *find* the beat this time instead of arriving ahead of it. You've been ahead of every beat in this scene for a week, Chen, because being ahead feels like control, and you like control. Rosa's text doesn't *want* your control. It wants your panic." A pause that was less dramatic than clinical. "The panic is in there. I've seen it. You use it every night in your dressing room before you come out and replace it with craft. I'm asking you to leave some of it in the performance."

From the stage manager's station, Elena's pen stopped moving.

It was a small thing — a pen halting mid-word — but Jordan caught it because Jordan was catching everything now, and there was something in the stillness of Elena's hand that suggested the note had landed somewhere personal rather than professional. Elena was watching Chen with an expression that didn't quite match a stage manager observing an actor take a note. It was closer to what a daughter might look like when she heard someone describe her father's fear with unexpected gentleness — though no one in the room would have framed it that way, least of all Elena, who didn't know what she didn't know.

Yael noticed, of course. Yael noticed everything Elena noticed and most things she didn't, and for a moment — a fraction of a moment — her gaze moved from Chen to Elena and then to Chen again, a calculation performed in under a second, the architecture of a secret she'd carried for three years rearranging itself behind her eyes.

Then the moment closed. The director's face replaced whatever had been underneath it.

"Again," Yael said. "And Chen — the chairs are still stage left. We've discussed this."

Tommy, at the edge of the rehearsal space, turned a page in his notebook and wrote something new. Jordan couldn't read it from this distance, but the shape of the handwriting suggested speed — the particular velocity of someone recording a moment they suspect will matter later.

The scene restarted.

Four words into scene three, Chen missed a step — not a physical one, a *dramatic* one, his weight shifting on the mark in a way that pulled him slightly upstage — and Yael's hand came up. The room froze.

"Left foot back. You're retreating and the line says you're advancing. Rosa wrote that contradiction into the *blocking* — the body lies, the words don't. Which is the whole point of the scene." She dropped her hand. "From the top of three."

They ran it again. And again after that. And a fifth time when the amber — which Elena had been adjusting quietly during each run — caught the knife at the wrong moment and Yael stopped everything to re-mark the cue on the floor with a piece of gaffer tape she'd ripped from her own shoe.

By the sixth run through scenes three through five, something had shifted. Chen was ahead of the beat no longer — he was *inside* it, arriving at the same moment as his words rather than a half-second after his thoughts had already composed them. It was less comfortable to watch and more impossible to look away from, the way a wire taught is more interesting than a wire slack.

Yael let the sixth run finish. Then the seventh.

On the seventh, she said nothing when it ended. She stood for a moment with her glasses hanging from the chain, eyes on Chen, and then she nodded — once, exactly once, a motion so small it was almost nothing, which for Yael was a standing ovation.

"Good," she said. "That's Rosa's text. That's what it sounds like."

Chen's chest was rising fast. He said nothing, which was either professional restraint or the particular exhaustion of having shown someone the thing you're afraid of and discovered they recognized it.

Yael turned toward Elena. "The amber on the seventh run — did you catch the timing?"

"I caught it on six," Elena said. "I corrected for seven."

"Show me six and seven side by side after we're done. If the correction holds, we lock it."

Elena nodded. Her pen resumed moving — the lighting schedule, though Yael noticed the projections page remained face-down beneath it, still untouched, still waiting.

From the window, Jordan could see the light changing — late afternoon, the kind that turns the sawdust motes into something almost theatrical, a natural spotlight that would have made Rosa laugh because it was too obvious, too *literary*, the kind of light that a less disciplined playwright would have used and Rosa would have cut.

Yael walked to the center of the room and clapped her hands once — the sharp, flat sound that meant a transition.

"Twenty minutes. Water, phone calls, existential crises — I don't care what you do with them as long as you're back at four-twenty-five." She looked at Chen. "Marco — Chen. The fourth scene is where we go next. Be ready to fall off the cliff again."

She caught herself — *Marco* — but only after the word had left, and only Jordan, who had been close enough, heard the first syllable that shouldn't have been spoken. It lasted less than a second: a crack in the protocol, a name that belonged to a different context, surfacing the way a bone surfaces through skin when the covering is thin enough.

Yael's face didn't change. She turned to Elena.

"Five minutes on the projections. Just the opening numbers — enough to know if the trend line is where I think it is."

Elena, who had not heard the slip, was already pulling the page face-up.

And Tommy Okafor, in his notebook, wrote the last thing Jordan would read over his shoulder before the twenty-minute break began: *She corrects herself in real time. The mistake becomes the note.*

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I feel a surge of insight, a shiver down my spine.* *Marco*. I quickly type another note into my phone, not even looking up: "Marco? Chen. Relationship history?" *This is getting very interesting indeed.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena closed the file with a flat snap and pushed it to the edge of the desk. The blinds rattled when a truck passed below, throwing striped shadow across her hands.

“It’s a problem because people inside start treating every question like a complaint,” she said. “They log your name, lock the paperwork, and suddenly the thing you’re trying to move gets nailed down.”

She stood, took her coat from the hook, and checked the street through the gap in the blinds. No one looked up. Not yet.

“I’m not going through the front door,” she added. “There’s a newsstand on the corner by the alley. The man there keeps a back room for people who want coffee and quiet. If the detective still talks to anyone outside the watch commander’s ears, that’s where we’ll find him.”

She pulled her phone from her pocket, scrolled to a number she hadn’t used in months, and set it on speaker while she buttoned her coat.

“No,” she said before the call connected fully. “I’m not coming in. You know how I work.”

A voice crackled on the other end. Lena’s expression didn’t change.

“Twenty minutes. Bring the original notes, not the summary. And leave the badge at home.”

She ended the call and slid the phone back into her pocket.

“We leave separately,” she said. “If anyone sees us together at the precinct, the conversation is over before it starts.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up my bag, a knot forming in my stomach.* "Right. Separately. So, I just... wait for you at this newsstand place?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena paused with her hand on the door, keys already cool in her palm. She checked the hallway mirror before turning back, making sure the corridor behind her was empty.

"Not the newsstand," she said. "The room behind it. There’s a side door by the dumpsters. Red curtain inside. Tell the man at the counter you’re waiting for a reservation under Elena."

She crossed back to the desk, unfolded a small slip of paper, and wrote a time on it in quick, hard strokes. She slid it toward the client, then pressed a paperweight over the edge so it wouldn’t catch on the draft from the window.

"Be there at four-fifteen. Order coffee. Black. Sit near the back wall, not the window, and keep your hands where they can be seen. If the detective arrives, let him speak first. If he asks why you’re interested, tell him you were referred by a mutual acquaintance and leave the rest to me."

Her voice stayed level, but her eyes sharpened as they moved to the file at the edge of the desk.

"If he doesn’t show by four-thirty, finish your coffee and walk out. Don’t wait outside. Don’t call. Don’t come back here."

She tucked a pen behind her ear and pulled the door open just enough to slip through.

"I’ll be there after I’ve circled the block twice. If you see me before then, act like you don’t know me."

For a beat, she held his gaze, unreadable and patient.

"And don’t bring the file unless I tell you to."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s hand stopped on the doorknob.

For a moment she did not turn around. The office seemed to hold still around her: the smell of old coffee, the low rattle of the street below, the paperweight pinning the slip of paper to the desk. Then she exhaled once, quiet and controlled, as if the question had been nothing more than a draft slipping under the door.

“Don’t confuse caution with biography,” she said.

She opened the door just wide enough to check the hallway. Empty. The fluorescent light at the far end buzzed and flickered, casting thin blue stripes across the worn carpet. Lena stepped back inside and lowered her voice.

“What matters is that you’re not the one they expect to walk out with answers.”

She picked up her keys again, rolling them between her fingers once before closing her fist around them. Her expression stayed unreadable, but there was a new sharpness in the way she looked at the file on the desk, as if deciding what parts of it were worth carrying and what parts were better left behind.

“Four-fifteen,” she said, steering the conversation back to solid ground. “Back room. Red curtain. Tell them Elena. Coffee black, no sugar, no newspaper spread out in front of you like you’re trying to look casual.”

She paused, then added, almost as an afterthought, “And don’t start asking people about me. It makes you interesting. Interesting gets remembered.”

Lena slipped the file into the inner pocket of her coat, then straightened, checking the street once more through the gap in the blinds. A woman hurried past with a grocery bag. A delivery bike cut across the intersection. Nothing watching. Not yet.

“You take the stairs,” she said. “I’ll take the elevator after you’re gone. If anyone asks, we met by accident in the lobby, and you were late for a dentist appointment.”

She opened the door again, this time holding it with her shoulder while she tugged her collar up against the hallway chill.

“Now go. Separate routes. And remember—if he doesn’t show, you leave. No heroics.”

For the briefest second, her gaze flicked back to the client, calm and appraising.

“I don’t get paid to explain myself,” she said. “I get paid to make sure you come out of this with more than a story.”

Then she stepped into the corridor and let the door click shut behind her.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the closed door for a second, then shake my head.* She definitely knows more than she's letting on. *I grab my bag and head for the stairs, the instructions replaying in my head.* This is a lot for a cold case.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena waited sixty seconds after the stairwell door clicked shut.

She stood motionless in the office, listening. The building settled around her: pipes ticking in the walls, the dry cleaner’s press thumping below like a slow heart, traffic dragging wet tires over Mercer Street. Nothing else. No footsteps returning. No second shadow under the door.

Then she took the elevator.

The street outside was gray and crowded enough to be useful. Lena turned left, collar high, hands loose at her sides. She walked one block, paused at a bus shelter to study the reflection in the plexiglass, then continued. A bakery. A check-cashing storefront. A pawnshop with fogged windows. The usual city armor.

She circled the block twice, as promised.

On the second pass, she noticed the sedan.

Dark gray, temporary plates, parked too close to the hydrant outside the Chinese laundry two doors down from the dry cleaner’s. It had not been there when she left the office. Or perhaps it had, and she had simply not filed it yet. That was the difference between looking and seeing, and Lena had spent enough years learning not to trust the first version of anything.

She did not approach it.

Instead, she cut through the rear arcade behind the laundromat, where the tile floors were stained with detergent and the air smelled of hot lint. A teenager with earbuds glanced up from a bench, then back to his phone. Lena passed without expression, slipped through a service gate, and emerged into the alley behind the newsstand.

The dumpster was exactly where she had said it would be. So was the side door.

Inside, the newsstand was cramped and bright, stacked with cigarettes, lottery tickets, and newspapers curled at the edges. The man behind the counter looked up, saw her, and his face arranged itself into polite blankness.

“Elena,” Lena said.

He nodded once and lifted the curtain at the back.

The room beyond was smaller than the front shop, lit by a single overhead bulb and heated by a coffee machine that gurgled like something sick. A table. Two chairs. A window facing the alley, streaked with rain. Lena chose the chair with its back to the wall and sat where she could see both the curtain and the reflection in the dark glass.

She did not order coffee. She placed her coat on her lap, the file still inside it, and set her phone face-down on the table.

At four-seventeen, the outer bell rang.

Footsteps crossed the shop floor. The curtain lifted.

The detective who entered was younger than Lena expected, with damp hair at the temples and the kind of tiredness that came not from lack of sleep but from too many conversations that had gone nowhere. He wore a civilian jacket, no visible badge, and carried a paperback with the cover peeled back just enough to hide the pages inside.

He saw her and stopped for half a beat.

“You’re harder to find than a warrant,” he said.

“And you’re later than the clock,” Lena replied.

He pulled out the chair opposite her and sat, placing the paperback on the table between them. His hand remained on it for a moment, as if steadying it.

“I couldn’t bring the folder through the front,” he said. “Not after this morning.”

“Then don’t say ‘this morning’ unless you mean to waste it.”

He gave her a look that might have been amusement if either of them had the luxury.

“Your file came in as a cold-case referral,” he said. “Twelve years old. Storage fire at Arden Dock. Unit seventeen. Claimant name turned out to be false. Insurance paid faster than the ashes cooled.”

Lena said nothing. She let him keep talking.

“The summary report says evidence was transferred to long-term property control. Clean. Boring. Sealed.” He tapped the paperback. “The original notes say something else.”

He slid the book aside and drew out several photocopied pages, keeping them flat under his palm until the last second. Lena noted the motion. Nervous habits were information too.

“There are two pages missing from the digital copy,” he said. “Witness list and evidence transfer. I pulled them before the system flagged the access log.”

“Flagged?”

“They don’t like people reading old fire cases.”

“People read what they’re paid to read.”

He almost smiled. “That’s not what worries me.”

Lena reached for the pages.

The photocopies were uneven, edges darkened by repeated handling. The witness list had three names, each crossed out in blue ink except one, which had been redacted so heavily the paper nearly tore. The evidence transfer sheet was simpler: item description, date, receiving authority, signature block.

Item: one brass key, tag number missing.

Received by: illegible.

Authorized by: redacted.

But the handwriting in the margin was not redacted.

Someone had written, *key not bagged. held for follow-up.*

The letters were narrow, the crosses lifting at the end like small hooks.

Lena’s face did not change.

The detective watched her anyway.

“You know that hand,” he said.

It was not a question.

Lena turned the page once, then set it down exactly where it had been.

“Someone I used to work with wrote like that,” she said.

The words came out flat, controlled, a door closing without a slam.

The detective leaned back slightly. “Still close to the file?”

“Still close to trouble,” Lena said. “What else?”

He exhaled through his nose. “The key never entered property control. No receipt, no storage tag, no audit trail. If this case was reopened today, the first question would be who held it.”

“Then ask the second question.”

His eyes narrowed.

“The second question,” Lena repeated, “is who wanted it missing.”

The detective was quiet for a moment. Rain tapped the alley window behind her. Out front, the coffee machine hissed and sputtered.

“There was a visit,” he said finally. “After the file was sealed. A supervisor from the dock investigation unit came by. Didn’t sign the visitor log properly. Asked for the Arden materials to be reviewed for ‘administrative cleanup.’”

“Administrative cleanup.”

“That’s what they call it when someone wants paper to disappear politely.”

Lena’s gaze moved to the redacted name on the witness list.

“Who reviewed it?”

“That’s the part I can’t give you.”

“You can give me a direction.”

He shook his head. “Not here.”

“Then where?”

He glanced at the curtain.

“Nowhere that has cameras.”

Lena studied him. He was afraid, but not of her. That made him useful.

“The locksmith,” she said.

He blinked. “What?”

“Unit seventeen had a deadbolt replaced six weeks before the fire. The invoice is in the original file, but not the summary. The company that installed it serviced half the docks before they consolidated storage.” She tapped the margin note. “If the key wasn’t bagged, someone with access to the lock mechanism already had a duplicate.”

The detective’s expression tightened. “You think the fire was started from inside?”

“I think fire needs fuel,” Lena said. “And fools need explanations.”

He looked down at the pages, then began gathering them with quick, careful movements.

“I can’t be seen with you again,” he said.

“You weren’t seen with me tonight.”

“If they pull my access log—”

“They’ll find a detective taking a coffee break.”

He stopped.

Lena held his gaze.

“Go back before they mark you absent,” she said. “And stop worrying about my name. Worry about the key.”

For a second, he seemed about to argue. Then he nodded once, slid the photocopies into the hollowed paperback, and stood.

At the curtain, he paused.

“Be careful,” he said.

Lena’s mouth did not quirk. “I’m expensive.”

He disappeared through the back of the newsstand.

The man at the counter called a moment later, voice pitched just loud enough to carry through the curtain.

“Miss Elena? Someone asking for you.”

Lena did not move.

“What do they look like?” she asked.

“Gray coat. Didn’t buy anything. Says he knew you from… somewhere.”

The lie was clumsy. That made it more interesting.

“Tell him you don’t know me,” Lena said.

There was a short silence. Then the sound of the counter drawer sliding shut.

“Sorry, friend. No one here by that name.”

Footsteps outside. A pause. The alley window fogged with breath as someone tested the glass from the other side.

Lena rose.

She folded the coat around her shoulders, checked the inner pocket where the original file rested, and slipped the photocopied pages into a separate sleeve inside her bag. She left a five-dollar bill on the table for coffee she had not drunk.

The man at the counter watched her with the practiced neutrality of someone who had learned that curiosity was bad for business.

“Side door?” he asked.

Lena nodded.

He lifted the curtain for her.

The alley was colder than the room, slick with rain and smelling of cardboard and exhaust. The gray sedan was gone. In its place, farther down, a delivery van sat with its rear doors propped open. A man in a gray coat stood beneath the awning of the laundry, speaking to someone inside.

Lena did not look at him directly.

She moved left, toward the service gate, her pace unhurried, her attention split into neat compartments: exit, reflection, distance, sound. The teenager from the arcade was gone. The bench remained. A plastic cup rolled across wet tile.

She slipped through the gate and put two buildings between herself and the newsstand before allowing herself to stop.

Her phone was silent.

She powered it down, removed the battery, and dropped both into a storm drain behind a noodle shop. Then she took a burner from the false bottom of her bag, switched it on, and dialed a number from the invoice photocopy.

Cline Key & Cylinder answered on the fourth ring.

“Closed.”

Lena’s voice was low, even. “I need a name.”

“We don’t give names.”

“Twelve years ago. Arden Dock, unit seventeen. Deadbolt replacement. Duplicate key request.”

Silence.

Then: “Who’s asking?”

Lena looked back toward the street. No one followed. Not yet.

“A problem,” she said.

The line went quiet for three full seconds.

When the voice returned, it was less certain.

“Come to the shop tomorrow. Ten o’clock. Back entrance. Don’t bring anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t say my name.”

“I don’t know it yet.”

The call ended.

Lena slipped the burner into her pocket and stood in the rain long enough for the city to resume its ordinary noise around her. Somewhere, a file was being moved. Somewhere, a key was still missing. And somewhere in the margins of an old report, a handwriting she had once trusted had left a hook-shaped cross like a warning.

She turned up Mercer Street, away from the office, away from the newsstand, away from the gray sedan that had not been there before.

The case had just stopped being cold.

That meant it was dangerous.

Lena preferred it that way.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *My phone rings. It's an unknown number. I answer cautiously.* "Hello?" *It's Lena, her voice low and tight.* "Meet me at the diner on Elm, 7 AM. Don't be late. And don't bring the file." *She hangs up before I can respond. What the hell happened?*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena listened to the disconnect tone until it became part of the rain.

The burner phone was warm in her palm, cheaper than the last one and twice as disposable. She powered it down, pulled the battery, and let both pieces fall into the deep side pocket of her coat. Then she sat still for nine seconds, counting them the way some people counted breaths.

Not because she needed calming.

Because stillness made movement easier to spot.

The street behind the noodle shop had narrowed into a gutter of brick and steam. A delivery truck idled at the curb, driver smoking under the awning. Two pigeons fought over something wet near the storm drain Lena had just fed with her old phone. Nothing watched her. Nothing moved with purpose.

That meant nothing, either.

She left on foot, not because it was safer, but because cars announced intentions. She crossed two intersections, doubled back through a parking garage stairwell, and emerged three blocks east with her collar still high and her pace unchanged. Every turn was ordinary. Every pause had a reason: a red light, a storefront window, a bus pulling out with its brakes complaining.

No gray sedan.

No man in a gray coat.

No one close enough to matter.

Yet.

Lena found what she needed in an all-night storage facility wedged between a tire shop and a shuttered vape store. The rental was paid in cash, six months in advance, under a name that had never existed. The unit was five by ten, concrete floor, one bare bulb, a folding chair, and a metal shelf holding a first-aid kit, bottled water, a power bank, and a box of rubber gloves she hoped never to use.

She closed the roll-up door, threw the padlock, and turned on the bulb.

The light made the unit look like a dentist’s x-ray: pale, hard, full of things best examined quickly.

Lena took the file from her coat and laid it on the shelf. Then she removed the photocopied pages from the sleeve inside her bag and spread them across the concrete floor, weighting the corners with a padlock shackle, a roll of tape, and the only clean mug she owned.

The witness list stared up at her.

Three names.

Two crossed out in blue.

One redacted until the paper looked wounded.
