Rosa gave Jason exactly the lines a man like Jason gets. The scene is not his. It never was. That *is* the writing. Take it from 'I'm not leaving.'"

Chen held the moment a half-beat longer than professional — then took it from 'I'm not leaving.'

And this time it was *right*. The smile came with him, easy and reasonable, a man arriving with good news. "I'm not leaving you. People grow." The word *evolution* floated out of him like a compliment he was paying the room, and down right, Marta's hands went still over the mending, and the rehearsal space did the thing Yael lived for — went quiet the way churches and hospital corridors go quiet.

"That." Yael said it from the aisle, one word, precise as a spike mark. "That's the man. Keep it, and if you find it again in tech I'll pretend it was my idea."

"Noted," Elena said, pencil moving. "He'll lose it by Thursday."

"I have *never* lost a discovery—"

"You lost the act two discovery in a parking lot in October—"

"The cross was late in October—"

"The cross was *acted* in October—"

And there it was — Yael watched it happen and said nothing. Chen crossed downstage at exactly the moment Elena's finger moved to the cue light, the two of them in perfect unconscious sync, the mirrors angled at the audience for once instead of each other, reflecting something true. Nobody in the room knew why Yael watched that so closely. Filed. Not shared.

"Okafor." She didn't turn around. Tommy was in the second row with his notebook, trying to look like furniture. "What did you see."

A beat of pure terror, then: "He smiled on 'leaving.'"

"He smiled on 'leaving.' Write down why — not in the notebook, in your head, notebooks are where observations go to die — and Thursday, when we run the meeting scene, you're on book for the back half, and your assignment is the same one I gave the press. Watch the room, not the stage. The stage is the easy part."

"Yes, Director."

"And stop sitting like furniture, furniture doesn't get to direct the B-stage—" She was already moving back up the aisle, momentum fully restored, and as she passed the third row she threw the rest over her shoulder without breaking stride, because stillness and a running recorder couldn't share a building.

"You wanted honest, Jordan — that was it, that last four minutes, the rest of us are just the frame. Stay through lunch if you can stand the catering. After the break we're running the end of act one, and Elena is going to call the amber on the *pickup*, not the raise—"

"I called it on the pickup at the workshop," Elena said. "The board op was slow. The board op has been warned."

"The board op has been warned, there, it's in the record—" The glasses went on. "You want to see what this play actually is, third row, you want to be in that seat when Medea picks up the knife. Everything before it is a man with a bouquet. Elena — take it from the top of the scene, and somebody tell the sawdust to hold its cue."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a few notes into my notebook, then look up as she passes.* "Catering is fine, Director. I'll be here." *I watch Chen and Marta reset, then lean forward, trying to absorb every detail.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
"From the top of the scene," Yael said, and dropped into the aisle seat two rows behind Jordan — close enough that her notes arrived at half-volume, which for Yael Mendez was still audible in the parking lot. "Watch Marta's hands. Chen gets the speeches, Marta gets the play."

Chen entered again, and the smile came with him this time — easy, reasonable, a man carrying good news. "I'm not leaving you. People grow. People *change*." And down right, Marta didn't look up. Her hands kept moving through the mending, steady as a heartbeat, and somehow that was worse than any scream — the room leaned in the way rooms do when somebody refuses to give them the release they're bracing for.

"That's it," Yael murmured, to no one, to Jordan, to the building. "She's not ignoring him. She's *finishing something*. There's a difference and the difference is the whole character."

The scene played out. The commune drifted off in ones and twos — polite, reasonable, each exit a small door closing — until Marta was alone with the mending basket and the silence. And there it was, had been there the whole time, in plain sight among the spools and the folded linen: the knife.

Marta's hand went into the basket. Her fingers closed. She raised it—

"Stop." Elena's voice, flat as a ruler. "Pete, that was the raise. The cue is the pickup."

From the booth: "It's a half-second, Elena—"

"The pickup is when her fingers close. The raise is when we invite the audience to look. We do not invite them. They are supposed to *find* it — the knife has been in that basket for forty minutes and the horror is that nobody saw it, including them. You put the amber on the raise and it's melodrama. You put it on the pickup and it's a memory they have to live with. Reset."

"The board op has been warned twice," Yael said, not unkindly, glasses coming off. "The third warning is Elena reading your cue sheet back to you in front of the crew, and nobody survives that. From Medea's last line, everyone."

They reset. Marta's hand went into the basket. Her fingers closed — and the amber found her in the same breath, not announcing her, *discovering* her, the light arriving like something that had been looking for her all along. The rehearsal room did the thing. Church quiet. Hospital corridor. Somewhere in the back, the construction crew had stopped hammering without being asked.

Yael didn't say anything for a full three seconds, which Elena noted in the prompt book the way one notes weather.

"There," Yael said finally, barely above the sawdust. "That's the whole play in one cue. Marta — whatever you were thinking on the pickup, think it again on Thursday and every night after, and never tell me what it was. It's yours. The rest of you — that's the standard, and I will now be insufferable about it for a month."

"Lunch," Elena called. "Forty-five minutes. Crew, the amber stays plotted exactly where it is, nobody touches the board, Pete included, *especially* Pete."

Chen was already crossing toward the house, wounded grandeur reassembling itself for the matinee. "Yael, about the third act — Jason should answer the vote. One line. He doesn't even have to win it—"

"Chen. The answer is the same as it was before lunch, and lunch hasn't happened yet, which means the answer is technically *younger* than your request and still old enough to vote no. Go eat. You were genuinely good this morning and I'd like to enjoy it for one full hour before you make me regret saying so."

"I'll take that as a yes—"

"You'll take it as a no with good lighting, which is the best this building offers—" and Chen went, laughing, which Yael allowed because the morning's work had earned him one.

Okafor closed his notebook in the second row — then opened it again, thought better of it, and closed it without writing, which Yael clocked from the aisle and filed under *progress*.

She paused at the third row on her way out, glasses on the chain, and looked at the stage for a moment before she looked at Jordan.

"You asked me this morning whose vision this is. Rosa wrote 'Medea picks up the knife.' Five words. The amber finding her hand — that's not in any script, that's Elena and a board op and twenty years of knowing what a room does when it's trusted. *That's* interpretation, Jordan. The score is hers, the tempo is ours, and on the good days you can't tell where one ends and the other begins. Today was a good day. Write that down before I ruin it."

Then she was moving, because stillness and satisfaction could only share a body for so long — "Elena, if the catering is the same egg salad as Tuesday I am staging a walkout, and I will cast the sandwiches as themselves—"

"The sandwiches are new," Elena said, gathering the prompt book. "The egg salad has been warned."

"The egg salad has been warned, there, it's in the record—" and the door swung behind her, and the stage lights held on the empty circle of cushions, waiting.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I look down at my recorder, then back up at the empty stage.* "I'm definitely writing that down." *I stand up, stretching, and head towards the catering table, still replaying the scene in my head.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The catering table was a folding affair in the lobby, and the sandwiches were, in fact, new — Elena confirmed this as she passed without slowing, "for the record" — and Yael ate standing up, one hand holding a plate, the other conducting a conversation with the head carpenter about the commune's back wall. She finished the sandwich and the sentence at the same time, which was itself a small piece of direction.

She caught Jordan's face as they came in and pointed the crust of the sandwich at them like a glasses-substitute.

"You have the look of someone the play followed out of the room. Good — that's the design, Rosa built it to travel. If you're not replaying it over the sandwiches, we've failed, and if you *are* replaying it, the review's already written and everything else is typing. Eat. The tuna is a significant improvement over its predecessor, which has been warned, terminated, and mourned."

"Director?" Okafor had materialized at her elbow, notebook closed — progress, she noted, and noted that she noted it — wearing the particular posture of a young man carrying a question he wasn't sure he was licensed to ask.

"Okafor. You have the face of a man whose B-stage is misbehaving. Report."

"Reyes wants to cut the monologue in scene two. He says the workshop crowd got restless. He wants my answer by tonight."

"Restless how — coughing restless or quiet restless?"

A beat. "Coughing. Some phones."

"Coughing restless is the audience leaving the room while their bodies stay in the seats. Quiet restless is them leaning in so hard it hurts — one of those is a problem with the scene and the other is the scene working on them like weather, and your actor has decided it's the first one because the second one is *terrifying* to stand inside of. Monologues are high wires, and actors will always try to cut the wire and call it dramaturgy. What do you want to do?"

"Keep it."

"Then keep it. And if you're wrong, you'll know it in your bones by opening, and the bones are where directors keep their education — I don't intervene on the B-stage unless somebody's going to bleed, and nobody bleeds from a monologue except the actor's pride, which is a renewable resource. Go fail interestingly or succeed interestingly. Those are the only two options I accept."

"Yes, Director."

"And Tommy—" quieter, pitched for him and Elena and the sandwiches — "Reyes is testing whether you'll fold. Tell him it stays, and watch him get better. Actors respect the no they were hoping for."

Chen arrived the way he entered scenes — as though the lobby had been waiting for him — and reached for the coffee; and Elena, without looking up from the prompt book, slid the thermos two inches left, directly into his hand's path, before he'd finished reaching. He took it. Neither acknowledged the transaction. It had the smoothness of a cue run a thousand times.

Yael watched it over the rim of her cup and said nothing at all — another entry for the file she never opened aloud.

"She moved the coffee," Chen announced to the room, with dignity.

"The coffee was always there," Elena said, to the prompt book.

"The coffee is where I say it is, and I say it's in your hand, Chen, which means the system works — go drink it in the sun, you have six minutes of being a person left."

"End of act one in ten," Elena called, to the lobby at large. "Full cues, pyro live. Pete — the fire plot is plotted. Touch nothing. Fire should be boring. The day fire is exciting is the day I file paperwork."

Yael set her plate down and turned to Jordan, and her voice did its settling — leveled, steadied — because the next part was Rosa's.

"This morning you saw the play whisper. This afternoon it burns. End of act one — the commune makes a bonfire of everything Medea brought with her. Rosa's version of the chariot is an oil drum and a woman who doesn't look back. Watch the commune during the fire, Jordan — nobody looks at *her*. That's blocking Rosa wrote in one sentence: 'They watch the fire so they don't have to watch her.' Eleven words, and it stages itself."

The glasses came off, went on the chain.

"And since the machine's running — that oil drum costs more than the entire third act. The fire is the overage, the tea service is eleven dollars, and the scene they want to cut is the cheapest thing in the season. That's the whole budget meeting in one image. Write it down before David does — he's good, but I'm faster."

Across the lobby, Marta sat alone with a script and an apple, and Yael passed her without a word — just a nod, returned — because the actor who carried the play had earned the one thing Yael rarely gave anyone: silence.

"Third row, house left. This time you may watch the stage — the fire's on it. The room can wait until Thursday." She was already moving, already gone, voice carrying back through the swing of the door. "Elena, call it before the carpenter finishes the wall and I have to find a new thing to worry about — and somebody tell the sawdust it's in the next scene too!"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I jot down the bit about the oil drum and the tea service, then quickly finish my tuna sandwich.* "Got it. Watch the commune, not Medea. Got it." *I head back to the third row, house left, curious to see this bonfire.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s glasses clicked down the bridge of her nose, her hand freezing mid-gesture as the recorder’s red light caught the rehearsal space’s harsh work lamps. She studied Jordan for a beat, the silence stretching just long enough to feel like a held breath before she pivoted back, pacing a tight circle around the worktable. "Whose vision," she repeated, the words landing with a quiet precision, "is always the question, isn’t it, because nobody ever asks what happens to the vision after the playwright leaves the room, or worse, after the playwright leaves the building altogether." She adjusted the chain, her fingers brushing the cold metal before she continued, her sentences running together without pause. "It’s Rosa Delgado’s vision—Rosa, who wrote the first draft in a borrowed studio on Maple Street while the illness was already eating her from the inside out, who fought the board, fought me, fought the fact that a third act about systemic collapse and maternal rage doesn’t read like a comfort to anyone who’s ever balanced a checkbook, and I’m not cutting it, I’m not, because cutting it would be a lie, and this theater has told enough of them to keep the lights on. We’re in the second act of this press shadowing, Jordan, and I prefer my journalists to understand that a vision isn’t a draft that gets revised by committee, it’s a load-bearing wall. If you pull it out, the whole roof comes down." 

She stopped pacing, her voice dropping to that quiet, steely register that always followed a mention of Rosa, steady and unyielding. "So yes, it’s Rosa’s vision, it’s mine to shepherd it to opening night, it’s Marcus’s to bleed it out in the final scene, it’s Elena’s to make sure the lighting doesn’t drown it, and it’s the board’s to argue about while we build the damn set. Now, if you want to ask about the text, I’m listening, but if you want a soundbite about compromise, you’ve come to the wrong rehearsal."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, impressed by her intensity.* "No compromises then. Interesting. So, this isn't just about staging a play, is it? It's about preserving Rosa's legacy." I glance around the busy space. "Tell me about Rosa. And about this 'systemic collapse and maternal rage' you mentioned. Sounds like a timely topic."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s fingers stilled on the chain, the metal warm against her black turtleneck, and she let the recorder sit in the air between them like a prop nobody had memorized. “Legacy,” she said, the word landing with the exact cadence of a line she’d heard from producers too many times, “is just a tidy little curtain call for what we refuse to let go of when the house lights come up—because nobody ever stops to ask who’s holding the script when the lead walks out, or worse, when the lead walks out for good—so we build the scaffolding and call it tradition.” She adjusted her glasses, the click sharp against the ambient noise of clamps and carpentry, and paced back toward the worktable where a half-draped manifesto lay scattered with highlighter marks. “Rosa didn’t write about systemic collapse because it’s trendy, Jordan, she wrote it because she watched her own community get dismantled by indifference—and she knew if she didn’t catch it in the act, someone else would have to write the autopsy report, and I’m not letting some committee edit the ending into something palatable.” She stopped, turning fully to face Jordan, her close-cropped silver hair catching the harsh work lamps, her posture rigid but her voice dropping to that measured, unyielding register. “And maternal rage—” she repeated, testing the phrase against the air, “—isn’t a metaphor in this room, it’s the engine, it’s the thing that happens when the people who are supposed to hold you up are the ones pulling the floorboards out from under you—and Rosa knew that better than anyone because she spent her last years watching the people she loved burn bright and fast while the rest of us just stood there holding the matches, and I’m channeling that, I’m channeling every damn minute of it into the blocking.” She exhaled, slow and controlled, the theatrical metaphors slipping back into place like well-worn costumes. “You call it timely, and sure, the world’s been staging its own third act for a while now, but I’m not directing a news report, I’m directing a woman who refused to let her final lines be edited by fear—and if you want to write about that, you’re going to have to sit through the tech rehearsals, you’re going to have to watch Chen try to hold a knife without turning it into a monologue about himself, and you’re going to have to understand that legacy isn’t a plaque on a lobby wall, it’s the work we do when nobody’s watching but the ghosts.” She tapped the recorder lightly with one black-nailed finger. “Ask me about the blocking if you want specifics, or ask me about the budget, but if you want to write about Rosa, you’re going to have to earn the right to step into her draft.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s hands stilled on the chain, the silver links catching the harsh overhead light as the raised voices from the hallway bled through the doorframe. She didn’t turn to look, just let the sound wash over her like a poorly mixed sound cue, her expression tightening just enough to make the air in the room feel suddenly thinner. “Friction,” she repeated, the word dropping into that quiet, controlled register that always preceded a lesson, “is just the sound of two people who know exactly how the machine is supposed to run arguing over which gear drives the others—because Chen has the stage presence of a supernova and the patience of a startled cat, and Elena has the structural integrity of a suspension bridge and zero tolerance for people who treat rehearsal like an open mic night.” She adjusted her glasses, the click sharp, and paced a tight half-circle around the worktable, her voice threading together without pause. “They clash because they’re both obsessed with the architecture of the scene and neither of them will concede that the other’s architecture is load-bearing—Chen wants the third act to breathe so he can land the final monologue, Elena wants the second act trimmed so the pacing doesn’t collapse under its own weight, and they’re both right, which is why I let them argue until they run out of steam and start actually listening to each other.” She stopped, her gaze fixed on Jordan, her posture rigid but her voice steady, almost clinical. “It’s not personal, it’s procedural, it’s the creative friction that keeps a production from going off the rails, and if you’re looking for drama in the hallway, you’re looking in the wrong place, because the real work happens when they stop talking long enough to move the damn chairs.” She tapped the recorder again, her black nails leaving a faint smudge on the plastic casing. “So if you want to understand why they clash, stop looking for personality conflicts and start looking at the text, because Chen’s ego and Elena’s perfectionism are just two different ways of trying to save the same play from itself.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I tap my pen on my notepad, making a note.* "So, you encourage this... creative friction? You find it productive? It doesn't disrupt the flow of rehearsal?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s fingers paused on the chain, the silver links catching the overhead fluorescents as the hallway argument faded into a rhythmic murmur, and she let the question settle over the worktable like a missed cue. “Disrupt,” she repeated, the syllables sharp and measured, “is just a word producers use when they haven’t learned how to read the score—because I don’t encourage friction, I architect it, I leave the scaffolding uneven and the blocking untested and I watch two people who love the same material too much to let it rest until they tear it down and rebuild it with their own hands, and yes, it disrupts the flow, because flow is a comforting fiction you sell to donors between intermission, the real work is the collision, the moment when Chen’s instinct to stretch a line meets Elena’s instinct to cut it, and neither of them yields because they’re both trying to protect the architecture, and I let them collide because if I step in too early I rob them of the very argument that makes the scene breathe.” She adjusted her glasses, the chain pulling taut against her collarbone, her voice dropping to that quiet, unbroken register that always followed a professional assessment. “Disruption is just the sound of a rehearsal finding its center, Jordan, and if you want to know why I don’t shut it down, it’s because a theater without friction is just a furniture store with a proscenium, and I didn’t spend fifteen years on off-Broadway watching directors sand down every rough edge just to end up directing a house that never held a single truth, so I let them argue, I let them clash, I let them run out of breath until they finally hear each other, and when they do, when Chen finally drops the need to command the room and Elena finally trusts the pacing, that’s when the scene actually starts, and that’s when you’ll see why I keep the doors open and the floor clear, because you don’t get third acts by committee, you get them by people who are willing to burn the draft.” She tapped the recorder once more, her black nails leaving a faint scuff on the plastic casing. “Ask me about the blocking if you want specifics, or ask me about the budget, but if you want to understand my process, stop looking for harmony and start looking for the fracture lines, because that’s where the light gets in, and that’s where the play lives.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s shoulders softened instantly, the tension bleeding out of her posture as she turned toward the doorway with a genuine, unguarded smile that reached her eyes and warmed the sharp angles of her face. “Anya, thank you for bringing that up, and David, I’m glad you’re here, because the budget is a script we’re all reading from and if we skip pages the whole performance collapses—so I hear you, I respect you for bringing it forward, and I want to solve this with you, not around you, because your instincts for sustainability are exactly why this board needs you, and I never want you to feel like your practicality is being treated as an obstacle.” She adjusted her glasses, the chain pulling taut against her collarbone, and let her voice drop to that quiet, steady register that always followed a boundary being drawn. “But cutting the third act isn’t a cost-saving measure, it’s a structural demolition, because that act isn’t padding, it’s the keystone, it’s where the commune fractures and the mother becomes the storm, and if we sand it down to fit a spreadsheet we’re not making a practical play, we’re making a compromise that echoes in every room until opening night, and I refuse to direct a compromise that breaks the spine of the text, I refuse to ask Chen to bleed into an empty space where the third act used to be, and I won’t ask Rosa to let her final lines be redacted by a line item.” David stepped forward, his hands in his pockets, and gave a single, quiet nod that Yael caught out of the corner of her eye without breaking her rhythm. “We’ll find the savings in the rigging, in the costume rentals, in the rehearsal hours we can compress without losing the work, we’ll balance the books without burning the house down, and Anya, you’ll have the revised budget on your desk by Thursday, and you’ll see that we’ve kept the vision intact and the theater solvent, because that’s what we do, we carry the load without dropping it, and if you want to sit in on the next board meeting to review the revised numbers, I’ll be glad to walk you through it, but the third act stays, the third act stays, and we’re going to make it work because the alternative isn’t practical, it’s just easier, and this company has never chosen easier.” She let the silence settle, warm but unyielding, her gaze shifting back to Jordan without losing the steady cadence of her words. “Now, if you’re ready to watch them move the chairs, or if you want to ask about the lighting cue, I’m all yours, but if you want to write about how we survive the second act, you’re going to have to stop looking for the cut and start looking for the seam.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble furiously in my notepad, a small smile playing on my lips.* "So, you're not just directing a play, you're directing a whole philosophy of theater. I'm starting to see how much more goes into it." *I glance at the departing Anya and David.* "That was quite the performance in itself. Do you always manage to win them over with such conviction?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s glasses caught the work lamps as she let out a short, breathy sound that wasn’t quite a laugh, more like a director calling a timeout, and she turned back toward the center of the room, her boots scuffing the painted floor, her voice dropping to that quiet, unbroken register that always followed a truth being named. “Win them over,” she repeated, the words landing with a sharp precision, “is the wrong verb, because you don’t win the board, you survive them, you choreograph them, you give them just enough rope to hang their own expectations while you quietly rewire the grid, and conviction isn’t a performance, Jordan, it’s a load-bearing wall, and I didn’t spend nine years keeping this theater from drowning in goodwill and debt by pretending that compromise is a synonym for survival, because Anya’s right about the budget, David’s right about the timeline, and the rest of the board is right about wanting a product that doesn’t make donors reach for their aspirin, and I have to hold the line without burning the bridge, which means I smile, I nod, I give them the revised numbers by Thursday, and I make sure the third act stays exactly where it is, because if I fold now, I’m not just cutting a scene, I’m cutting the throat of the thing I promised Rosa I’d build.” She adjusted her chain, the metal clicking softly against her collarbone, her posture rigid but her voice completely level, her eyes fixed on Jordan with that quiet, unyielding steadiness. “Do I always win them over? No, sometimes I lose, sometimes I negotiate until my teeth ache, sometimes I let them think they got what they wanted while I quietly reblock the damn thing in tech week, but I never let them think they control the vision, because that’s how productions die, not with a vote, but with a thousand small surrenders, and I’m not here to surrender, I’m here to direct, so if you want to write about how we survive, you’re going to have to write about the arithmetic of art, and the fact that every time I say no to a cut, I’m saying yes to someone else’s future, and that’s not conviction, that’s just the job, and it’s exhausting, and it’s beautiful, and I wouldn’t trade it for a single thing.” She stepped closer to the worktable, her hands falling to her sides, her voice dropping even lower, steady and measured. “Now, if you’re done taking notes on my board management, I need you to watch Chen run his lines, because he’s missing his entrance by half a beat, and when he does, you’ll see why the third act isn’t optional, it’s inevitable, so sit down, stay quiet, and let me show you how we build a storm without flooding the house.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s hands stalled on the chain—the silver links catching the overhead fluorescents like a missed cue—and she let the silence stretch just long enough to feel like a held breath before she adjusted her glasses, the click sharp and deliberate against the ambient clatter of carpentry. “Rosa,” she said, the name leaving her lips with a precision that felt almost surgical, “was never one for small talk—which is why I loved working with her, because she treated every sentence like a prop she intended to use, every pause like a stage direction she’d already charted—so if you want to know what she was like, don’t look for anecdotes about green rooms or opening nights, look at the margins of her drafts, because that’s where she lived, in the white space between the lines where the real architecture hid.” She began pacing again, her boots scuffing the painted floor, her voice dropping into that steady, unbroken register that always followed a mention of Rosa. “She wasn’t sentimental, Jordan, she was structural—she built plays out of load-bearing truth and reinforced them with silence, and when the illness started taking over, she didn’t ask for sympathy, she asked for a desk, she wanted to finish the manuscript while her hands still worked, and I gave her exactly that—which means I watched her rewrite the same page fourteen times, I watched her push through the final act, I watched her hand me the marked-up typescript and say ‘don’t let them sand it down,’ and I haven’t stopped honoring that since.” She stopped near the worktable, turning fully to face Jordan, her posture rigid but her expression completely level, her voice steady as a metronome. “She was fiercely impatient—she hated directors who mistook movement for meaning, she could spot a lazy transition from the wings, and she believed—without exception—that theater isn’t entertainment, it’s an intervention—so if you want to write about her, don’t romanticize the timeline, document the craft, because Rosa didn’t leave behind a ghost, she left behind a blueprint, and I’m not going to let anyone mistake this production for a memorial when it’s supposed to be a reckoning.” She tapped the recorder once, her black nails leaving a faint mark on the plastic casing, her gaze unwavering. “Now, if you’re ready to watch Chen run his blocking, or if you want to ask about the communal lighting grid, I’m listening, but if you want to write about Rosa, you’re going to have to sit through the full tech, you’re going to have to watch how the amber catches the steel, you’re going to have to understand that legacy isn’t nostalgia, it’s labor, and I’m still doing the work.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "She sounds formidable. A true artist." *I make a quick note, then look up at Yael.* "You mentioned she wanted to finish the manuscript while her hands still worked. How long did you work with her on this adaptation?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s hands stalled on the chain—the silver links catching the overhead fluorescents like a missed cue—and she let the silence stretch just long enough to feel like a held breath before she adjusted her glasses, the click sharp and deliberate against the ambient clatter of carpentry. “How long,” she repeated, the syllables measured but her voice dropping into that steady, unbroken register that always followed a mention of Rosa, “is just a countdown to the final act when you’re watching someone you love dismantle themselves in real time—which is why we didn’t measure it in months or budget cycles, we measured it in coffee cups and red ink and the way her handwriting went from sharp architect to frantic cartographer over the course of fourteen months.” She began pacing again, her boots scuffing the painted floor, her sentences threading together without pause. “She started the draft in the spring when the scans were still ambiguous, she kept writing through the summer when the fatigue hit like a second-act intermission she couldn’t skip, she handed me the final typescript in October when she could barely hold a pen but could still quote Ibsen backwards, and I spent the next three months just learning the rhythm of her silences so I wouldn’t misread the blocking when I stepped into the director’s chair, and that’s the thing nobody writes about, Jordan, is that collaboration isn’t a handshake, it’s a shared nervous system, and I’ve been working with her ghost ever since because her draft doesn’t just sit on a page, it breathes in the wings, it dictates the pacing, it demands the amber hit on the knife, and if you think I’m going to let a boardroom spreadsheet tell me how many pages she left behind, you don’t understand how theater actually survives.” She stopped, her gaze fixed on Jordan, her posture rigid but her voice completely level, the theatrical metaphors slipping back into place like well-worn costumes. “Fourteen months of daylight, maybe eighteen if you count the nights she called me to dictate a line because the pain meds were making her forget her own name, and I wouldn’t trade a single second of it, not even the ones where I sat in a hospital chair watching her struggle to swallow soup while I transcribed stage directions into a voice memo, because that’s not grief, that’s just the rehearsal process continuing without the body, and if you want to write about the timeline, write about the fact that she finished the third act three weeks before she stopped leaving her bed, and then she made me promise I’d direct it like a verdict, not an elegy, and I keep that promise every time I step into that room.” She tapped the recorder lightly, her black nails leaving a faint scuff on the plastic casing, her eyes steady. “Now, if you’re ready to watch Chen run his entrance, or if you want to ask about the costume budget, I’m listening, but if you want to understand the work, stop looking for a neat timeline and start looking at the margin notes, because that’s where she left the blueprints, and that’s where I’m still building.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I blink, taking a moment to process the raw emotion in her voice.* "Wow. That's... intense. So, this play isn't just about Medea, it's about Rosa. And you're channeling her spirit into every aspect of the production." *I gesture towards the stage area.* "What's the hardest part about that? Keeping her vision pure while also making it your own?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s fingers stopped tracing the chain, the silver links catching the work lamps like a stage manager calling a blackout, and she let the question hang in the sawdust-heavy air while her posture shifted just enough to signal she was stepping into the wings of her own answer. “Pure,” she repeated, the word landing with a quiet, almost surgical precision, “is a concept that dissolves the moment you try to bottle it, because art isn’t a preservation society, it’s a collision, and if I’m just photocopying Rosa’s margins I’m not directing, I’m archiving, and this theater doesn’t exist to hoard ghosts, it exists to stage them, so the hardest part isn’t keeping her vision pure, it’s refusing to let her absence dictate the pacing, it’s trusting that the architecture she left behind can hold my blocking without buckling, because she wrote the blueprint, I’m pouring the foundation, and if I step too heavy I crack the load-bearing walls, and if I step too light the whole commune collapses into a museum piece, so I have to find the exact pressure that lets the text breathe without suffocating the performer, and I do that by treating her draft not as scripture but as a score, because a score isn’t meant to be played exactly as written, it’s meant to be interpreted by someone who knows the instruments, and Rosa knew the instruments, I knew the instruments, and Chen knows the instruments, which is why I don’t sanitize the third act, I don’t soften the collapse, I don’t let the board turn systemic decay into a two-act parable with a moral, I let it detonate, because that’s what she would have done, that’s what I owe her, and if you think channeling a friend means wearing her face like a mask, you haven’t done the work, because channeling is just showing up with the same ruthless clarity she demanded, and I’m not here to mourn, I’m here to mount, so if you want to know the hardest part, it’s the arithmetic of trust, it’s knowing when to hold the page steady and when to turn it, it’s the silence after she hands you the manuscript and you realize you’re not just directing a play, you’re directing a promise, and promises don’t get edited, they get staged, so I sit with that, I let it sit heavy on the floorboards, and I build around it, and when Chen misses his entrance by half a beat and Elena calls cut because the second act drags, I don’t panic, I listen, I adjust, I keep the third act exactly where it is, because the hardest part isn’t purity, it’s patience, it’s knowing that legacy isn’t a glass case, it’s a stage, and stages are meant to be walked on, even when your knees are shaking.” She adjusted her glasses, the chain pulling taut against her collarbone, her voice dropping to that quiet, unbroken register that always followed a boundary being drawn. “Now, if you want to see how we translate that into blocking, take a seat in the back row, stay quiet, and watch how we let the storm hit when it’s supposed to, not when the spreadsheet says it’s time.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing her words, and then gesture towards the stage.* "Alright. Show me how you build the storm. I'll be in the back." *I find a seat near the back, pulling out my notebook and pen.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael gave a single, sharp nod as Jordan settled into the back row, her black boots turning toward the stage before she even finished processing the gesture, and she didn’t raise her voice—she just let it cut through the ambient noise of the rehearsal space with the quiet precision of a stage manager’s headset mic, calling for places, for stillness, for the kind of focused silence that only happens when you know exactly how expensive this work is and how little time you have left to do it right. She paced the center line, her hands moving in the air as if tracing invisible sightlines, her glasses slipping down her nose only for her to flick them back up with a practiced tap, and when she finally spoke to the room it came out in a single, unbroken thread of instruction that left no room for hesitation or interpretation. “Chen, you’re entering on the second syllable of the whisper, not the third, you’re treating the silence like an applause line when it’s actually a fault line, and Elena, dim the amber by fifteen percent on the cross, it’s bleeding into the shadow and washing out the texture of the walls, we’re building decay, not a sunset, and again, from the cross, and this time I want the knife to feel like a mistake, not a prop, because she didn’t pick it up to kill, she picked it up because the room was on fire and her hands needed something heavy to hold onto, and if you play it like a villain’s entrance you’ve already lost the play to the committee, and don’t rush the breath, don’t rush it, let it catch, let it fracture, let it sound like the moment before the floor gives way, because that’s not pacing, that’s physics, and physics doesn’t negotiate with your ego.” She stopped, listening, her posture rigid but her eyes tracking every micro-adjustment, her mind already three beats ahead of the blocking, already mapping the next layer, the next correction, the next promise she’d keep to a ghost who’d handed her a manuscript and told her not to flinch, and when the run finished she didn’t clap, didn’t praise, just stepped forward and raised a single hand, her voice dropping even lower, steady as a metronome. “Elena, mark the cue at forty-two seconds, Chen, you’re leaning into the knife like it’s a spotlight, drop the shoulder, let the weight fall through, and for god’s sake, stop performing the rage and start surviving it,” she said, already moving toward the worktable to cross notes into a script that hadn’t been touched in weeks, because the work didn’t wait for applause, it waited for attention, and Yael Mendez never looked away, never softened the line, never let the room forget that legacy isn’t a plaque on a lobby wall, it’s the blood you leave on the floorboards when you refuse to cut the final act. She stood perfectly still in the wings, hands clasped behind her back, her gaze fixed on the intersection where Marcus’s breath caught and Elena’s head tilted toward the lighting grid, waiting for the next collision, the next fracture, the next moment where the storm would finally break.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch the scene unfold, scribbling notes rapidly. Yael's intensity is captivating, and the way she dissects every movement and breath is fascinating. I look up, catching her eye for a moment, then back to the stage as Chen tries the entrance again. He's clearly frustrated, but also deeply focused.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael’s gaze held Jordan’s for a fraction of a second—just long enough to register the reporter’s attention, just long enough to file it under observation, not interruption—and then she turned back to the stage, her posture tightening like a tension cable pulled to its limit. She didn’t raise her voice. She never did. She let it drop, smooth and precise, cutting through the dust-moted air like a stage manager’s headset mic calling places. “Again,” she said, the single word landing without friction, “from the threshold, and this time stop treating the silence like a waiting room—Chen, drop the chin, you’re bracing for judgment when you should be bracing for consequence, and Elena, kill the overhead wash on the left bank, let the shadow take the corners, we’re not filming a documentary, we’re building a pressure cooker—and when you step into that light, you aren’t entering a room, you’re entering a fault line, so if you play it like a hero arriving at the climax you’ve already lost the commune to the myth, I need the weight to fall through the sternum, not the ego, I need the knife to feel like a misstep, not a coronation, and if you’re going to stumble, stumble forward, don’t stumble into the audience like you’re asking for applause—because the third act isn’t a destination, it’s a detonation, and if you can’t carry the quiet into the storm then the board gets exactly what they’re begging for—a tidy second act with a moral and a handshake, and I will not direct a lie just to keep the donor checks clear, so we run it again, and again, and again, until the breath catches at exactly forty-two seconds, until the knife feels like a question instead of an answer, until the rage stops performing and starts metabolizing, and then we’ll see if the structure holds.” She paced the aisle between the worktable and the stage, her boots silent on the painted floor, her close-cropped silver hair catching the harsh work lamps, her fingers already tracing the invisible geometry of the next beat. She adjusted the chain, the metal clicking softly against her black turtleneck, and turned slightly toward Elena without breaking her rhythm. “Mark the cue at the exhale, not the inhale—and when he drops the shoulder, I want the amber to bleed into the steel, not the other way around, because the commune doesn’t collapse from violence, it collapses from exhaustion—and exhaustion doesn’t shout, it just stops holding the walls up.” She stepped back into the shadows of the wings, hands clasped behind her back, her gaze fixed on the intersection where Chen’s next step would either fracture or hold, waiting for the collision, the correction, the work, her mind already three beats ahead of the blocking, already mapping the next layer, the next promise she’d keep to a ghost who’d handed her a manuscript and told her not to flinch.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I find myself holding my breath, completely engrossed. Yael's relentless pursuit of authenticity is palpable. I make a note about "exhaustion doesn't shout, it just stops holding the walls up."* "She truly sees everything, doesn't she?" *I murmur to myself, almost unconsciously.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's hands stilled for a moment — which, Elena noticed, was its own kind of punctuation. She pulled her glasses off the chain, put them back on, then off again.

"Whose vision." She repeated the word like she was tasting it for structural integrity. "That's — okay, that's a real question, and I want to answer it honestly, so I'm going to be careful with it, which is different from being evasive, and you'll be able to tell the difference because I'll be slower."

She dropped into a chair, gestured for Jordan to take one, then immediately stood back up.

"The adaptation is Rosa Delgado's. She wrote it. Rosa was — she's the playwright. She died, about eighteen months ago. Cancer. And this was her play before it was mine, her Medea, her idea to move it into the commune — the seventies, the children, the utopian project that eats itself. That was all Rosa. So if we're assigning vision, put her name at the top of the page."

She caught the glasses mid-gesture, slid them on.

"Now — the production is mine. I'm directing it, I'm staging it, and I'm making choices she didn't specify. That's what directing is. But I want to be precise about the ownership because Rosa doesn't have a byline on a marquee anymore, and I'm not going to let the record blur. Underline it if you want. I mean that."

A beat. She pointed at the recorder.

"Is that running? Good. Now — what else."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content:
*My pen was already scratching notes, but I tap the recorder to confirm it's on.* "It's running. Thank you, Director Mendez. That's a powerful distinction."

*I pause, considering her words.* "So, if the adaptation is Rosa's vision, and the production is yours... what's the biggest challenge in bringing *her* Medea to life through *your* lens?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael chewed on the question — literally, jaw working, eyes somewhere above Jordan's head where the lighting grid met the ceiling. She pulled the glasses off, breathed on them, wiped them on her shirt, put them back.

"The biggest challenge." She paced — three steps one way, three steps back, like she was blocking a scene in her head. "Okay. The honest answer is that the biggest challenge isn't artistic, it's — no. Let me start over. The artistic challenge and the structural challenge are the same challenge, which is what makes it interesting and what makes it hard."

She stopped pacing. Stood very still.

"Rosa wrote a Medea that doesn't let anyone off the hook. Not Medea, not Jason, not the commune, not the audience. The third act — " She caught herself. Frowned. Started again. "Her play asks the audience to sit inside a horror and understand the logic of it. That's the whole project. And my job is to build a room where that can happen — where the actors can go there, where the *audience* can go there. The commune set, the amber light, the pacing — it's all in service of that. Making a space that feels safe enough for people to be unsafe in."

She dropped back into the chair, leaned forward, elbows on knees.

"But there's a — the other thing. The structural thing." Quieter now, though not angry — more like someone choosing each word from a shelf and checking it before placing it. "Plays don't exist in a vacuum, Jordan. They exist in buildings with budgets and boards and people who love the theater but love it *differently* than the people who make it. And Rosa's play is — it's demanding. It's not — it doesn't give you an intermission where you feel *good*. And there are pressures. There are always pressures. To make things more — accessible. Palatable. To sand down the edges."

She held up a finger.

"That is not a complaint about my board. My board keeps the lights on and I am genuinely grateful. But yes — the biggest challenge of bringing Rosa's Medea to the stage is that Rosa wrote something uncompromising, and the world is not always — accommodating. And I am not going to be the person who compromises it. That's not a position. It's just — it would be a betrayal of the work, and I don't do that."

She gestured at the recorder again.

"Careful with that, by the way. Not off the record — I don't say anything I won't own. But context matters, and you're going to be writing about this theater, and I want you to write about it *whole*. Not just the conflict. The conflict is the third act. The first act is that this is a company that's doing something genuinely brave, and the people in this building — " she waved toward the stage, where Elena was now walking Tommy through something on a clipboard, "— are making it happen on a shoestring and a prayer and I would be furious if the story became about board politics when it should be about the work."

She exhaled. Sat back.

"Ask me the next thing."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's jaw tightened — just slightly, the kind of thing you'd only catch if you were watching for it. She was quiet for a moment, which was unusual enough to register as significant. Her hand went to the glasses on the chain, but she didn't take them off. Just held them.

"That," she said, very evenly, "is a question I want to answer in a way that doesn't turn two people I respect into a subplot."

She stood. Walked to the doorway of the rehearsal space and looked down the hallway — not eavesdropping, just checking that the argument was still in the hallway and not coming toward them. It was. She turned back.

"Chen is — he's a remarkable actor. Genuinely. I've known him twenty years, I've watched him do things on a stage that I still think about. And he is also a man who has strong opinions about how scenes should be played, and he expresses those opinions at a volume that suggests the scene is *his*. Elena is the best stage manager I've ever worked with — I say that to her face and I'll say it to you — and she runs this theater with a precision that borders on the surgical. Put those two people in a building together and you will get friction. It's chemistry. Not the romantic kind. The combustible kind."

She leaned against the doorframe.

"They're also — and I say this with affection — *the same person*. Both stubborn. Both certain they're right. Both deeply, deeply invested in the work to a degree that makes them impossible to manage and impossible to replace. Elena thinks Act Two is too long. Chen wants more to do in Act Three. They're both arguing about the *play*, Jordan, not about each other. And I would ask you — " her voice dropped half a register, not cold, but careful, like someone handling something breakable, "— to be thoughtful about framing that. Because there's a version of that story that's just 'theater people are intense,' and there's a version that makes it personal and ugly, and I'm telling you plainly that the first version is true and the second version would be a failure of reporting."

She held his gaze — held Jordan's gaze — for a beat longer than was strictly comfortable.

"I mediate. That's my job. I've been doing it all season and I'll keep doing it. They'll come out of that hallway and we'll rehearse Act Two and Chen will hit his marks and Elena will call the cues and it will *work*, because it always works. That's the actual story."

She finally pulled the glasses off. Looked at them instead of at Jordan.

"What else?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content:
*I nod slowly, taking in her words. I make a note in my pad.* "I appreciate your candor, Director Mendez. And I understand your perspective on the dynamic. It helps me understand the pressures you mentioned earlier too."

*I tap my pen on my notebook, thinking.* "You mentioned earlier that Rosa's Medea doesn't let anyone off the hook. How does that translate to the audience experience? What do you hope they take away from it?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was quiet for a beat longer than usual — not the performative kind of quiet she used for emphasis in meetings, but the real kind, the kind where someone is deciding how much of a door to open. She put the glasses on. Took them off. Put them back on. Then she took them off and held them in her hand like they'd become a separate object she had to think about.

"That's the question, isn't it," she said. Not really asking. "That's the question Rosa asked me the first time we sat down to talk about staging it — she said, 'What do you want them to walk out carrying?' And I remember saying something pretentious — something about *moral reckoning* — and she laughed at me. Rosa laughed at me a lot. She said, 'No. What do you want them to walk out *carrying*.' Heavy. Physical. Like luggage."

She put the glasses back on. Left them on. That was unusual enough to notice.

"Here's what I think. I think most of us — and I include myself, I include everyone in this building — go through the day operating on a set of assumptions about who we are. We're the reasonable one. We're the good one. We're the one who would never — and we fill in the blank with whatever lets us sleep. And Rosa wrote a play where that sentence gets interrupted. Where the character you're rooting for does something that you cannot reorganize into a narrative where she's still the hero, and yet — and this is the part Rosa built the whole play around — and yet you *understand*. You don't forgive. But you understand. And that gap — between understanding and forgiving — that's where the play lives. That's the room I'm trying to build."

She stood again. Couldn't stay seated — it wasn't in her architecture.

"I don't want them to take away a message. I hate messages. Messages are what you put on a bumper sticker so you can stop thinking. I want them to take away a *discomfort* — a specific one. The discomfort of having felt sympathy for something monstrous and not knowing what to do with that. Because that's — that's what makes us human, Jordan, that capacity. Not the judgment. The confusion. The sitting with it."

She caught herself. Checked — glanced at the recorder, then back at Jordan.

"I said too much. No — I said the right amount. I just said it fast. Put it in your piece and make it make sense, that's your job." A small smile, the first real one. "What else."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's face did something complicated — a kind of rapid recalibration, warmth loading in where the intensity had been, and if you didn't know her you'd think it was seamless. Jordan, who was beginning to know her, might have noticed the half-second delay.

"Anya. David. Hi — sit down, I mean it, take a chair, we're between things." She pulled two chairs over herself, physically placing them, which was a thing she did — made people comfortable with her hands when her mouth was about to say something they wouldn't like.

Then she stood very still. Hands at her sides. Voice pleasant and about a third of its usual volume.

"Okay. So — I want to hear you out, and I mean that, because you're not wrong that budgets are real and I've never pretended otherwise. We've almost lost this building twice and I'm not casual about that."

A breath.

"But the third act is the play. I want to be really clear about that — it's not the third act *of* the play, it *is* the play. Everything Rosa built — the first two acts, the commune, the slow erosion — it's all architecture that exists so the third act can land. Cut it and we don't have a shorter Medea. We have a different one. A less one. And I — " she paused, and her voice got even quieter, almost gentle, "— I can't do that. Not for budget reasons, not for any reasons. Rosa wrote it that way deliberately and I made her a promise about that before she died, and that's — it's not negotiable. But I love that you're in here solving problems with me, I do, and I want to find the money somewhere else. I want to find it with you and David and anyone else on that board who'll sit down with me on a Tuesday and look at line items."

She looked at David — briefly, professionally, then back to Anya, and the warmth didn't waver.

"Anya, you've been generous to this company in ways I don't forget. So please hear this as coming from someone who considers you a partner, not an obstacle. The third act stays. Now — what can we cut that *isn't* the heart of the thing? Because there's money in this budget that isn't Rosa's play, and I will find it."

She put her glasses on. Looked at both of them over the rims.

"Stay for the run-through. Both of you. When you see the third act staged — when you see what it *does* to a room — you'll understand why I'm being this stubborn about it. And if you still want to have the budget conversation afterward, I'll bring wine and spreadsheets."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I'd been furiously taking notes during Yael's monologue, glancing between her and Anya. Anya's face was unreadable.* "That was quite a defense, Director Mendez," *I say, mostly to myself, but loud enough for Yael to hear. I look at Anya.* "Anya, how do you respond to that?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's hand moved before her mouth did — a small gesture, almost invisible, the kind of thing she did when she felt a situation tilting. She shifted her weight slightly so she was standing closer to Anya's chair, not between Anya and Jordan exactly, but adjacent. Available. An ally's position, not a gatekeeper's.

"Jordan — before Anya answers that, and she should, she absolutely should, I want to say something about the shape of what's happening here, because I can see the headline forming and I'd like to gently put a pin in it."

She smiled at Anya — warm, direct, no performance in it.

"What you just heard me do was say no to someone I respect about something I care about. That is Tuesday. That is literally every Tuesday in this business. Anya and I disagree about the third act and we agree about everything else — keeping this company alive, paying our people, building something that matters in a mid-sized city that doesn't have to give a damn about us and does anyway. So when you write this up — if you write this up — the story isn't 'director fights board member.' The story is 'two smart women are trying to solve the same problem from different angles and one of them is being extremely stubborn.' Me. I'm the stubborn one. I'll own it."

She looked at Anya.

"Your turn. And say whatever you actually think — don't soften it for the journalist and don't harden it for me. Just — you. What do you think."

Then, quieter, to Jordan — but not excluding Anya from it, keeping it in the shared space:

"And Jordan. She's not the antagonist of this piece. If she becomes the antagonist of this piece, that's a failure — and I don't just mean of reporting. I mean of the room. Of what we're all doing here. You understand."

The glasses went on. She waited.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael went very still.

Not the kinetic stillness of someone about to move — the other kind. The kind where the machinery that keeps a person in motion simply stops, and what's left standing there is someone who has made a decision about what they're going to show and what they're going to hold.

Her voice, when it came, was different. Lower. Slower. Every word placed with the deliberateness of someone setting stones on a path they've walked a hundred times and are walking again precisely because they refuse to let it overgrow.

"Rosa was the best writer I've ever known. That's not sentiment — that's craft. She could build a sentence like a load-bearing wall. She wrote plays the way some people breathe — constantly, compulsively, badly when she was tired and better when she was angry, and angry a lot toward the end, though not the way you'd think. Not at the diagnosis. At the sentences. She'd be furious at a sentence that didn't work and I'd say, 'Rosa, you're dying,' and she'd say, 'Then I'd better get this sentence right.' So I'd sit with her and we'd fix sentences. That's what the last year looked like. Mostly."

She hadn't moved. Hadn't touched the glasses. Hadn't blinked much.

"She was — funny. Extremely funny. Dark. She'd look at something terrible and find the angle of it that made you laugh before you knew you should be horrified. That's what's in the play — you can feel it, that laugh-that-turns. And she was generous. Not the palatable kind. The real kind — the kind where she'd tell you your first draft was terrible and then spend four hours showing you why. She made me a better director. Not because she told me how to direct. Because she wrote things that required me to be better and refused to lower them to my level."

A breath. Steady. Controlled.

"She liked terrible coffee. Specific kind of terrible. Gas station coffee. She said good coffee was for people who didn't have anything to think about."

Nothing in her face moved, but something behind it did — a tectonic shift, the kind you'd only register as a change in air pressure.

"That's who she was. Now I'd like to stop talking about her as a person and start talking about her as a playwright — which is what she'd prefer anyway. She's in the work. That's the whole point. That's why the third act isn't negotiable. It's not a principle. It's a *person*."

She put the glasses on. Looked at Jordan. And her voice was back — the quick one, the one that filled rooms — but there was a seam in it now, visible only if you'd been paying attention.

"You wanted to know what she was like. That's what she was like. Now — you said you were shadowing us this week. It's Tuesday. Are you here Thursday for the full run? Because if you want to understand Rosa Delgado, you don't do it in an interview. You do it in the room when the lights are up and Chen is on the stage and the third act lands. Come Thursday. Then write about her."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click off my recorder, letting the silence hang for a moment.* "Thursday. I'll be here. And thank you, Yael. For everything." *I close my notebook, feeling the weight of the conversation, and the play.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael looked at the recorder as Jordan clicked it off, and something in her shoulders released — not all the way, not dramatically, but enough that Elena would have noticed if she'd been looking up from her clipboard. She stood there for a moment with the glasses in her hand, turning them over once, twice, like she was checking they were still real.

"Good," she said. Just that. Then: "Thursday. Don't be late. I start on time and I don't stop for latecomers and Chen will use it as an excuse to talk about himself for eleven minutes, which is time we don't have."

She walked Jordan toward the door — fast, because she did everything fast, but she opened it and held it, which was its own kind of sentence.

"And Jordan." She caught the doorframe with one hand. Her voice had gone back to its normal register but there was something underneath it — careful, direct, the way she got when she was handing someone a note about the work that was also a note about themselves. "You asked good questions today. The Rosa question especially — that was the right question and you let me answer it without picking at it afterward, and that's — that's not nothing. Most people fill silence. You didn't."

She put the glasses on her head. Then back on her nose. Then on her head again.

"Don't make me look foolish for saying that. Write the piece *whole*. I meant what I said earlier — the work is the story, and the work deserves someone who can hold complexity without flattening it. I think you can. Prove me right."

Down the hallway, the argument had resolved into something that sounded like Elena listing cue numbers and Chen — Marcus, *Chen* — sighing theatrically in the specific way he did when he'd been outmaneuvered by a spreadsheet. Yael glanced that direction, and the corner of her mouth twitched.

"See? Told you. It always works."

She let the door swing open wider.

"Thursday. Bring your notebook. And if you want to understand what Rosa built, sit in the back row and don't look at the stage — look at the audience. That's where the play actually happens. Rosa taught me that."

She was already turning back toward the rehearsal space, pulling out her phone, tapping something — probably a text to David, probably about line items, probably ending with an em dash because she never finished a message cleanly. But before she disappeared through the inner door, she called back over her shoulder without turning around:

"And if you write that Rosa liked gas station coffee — keep it in. She'd haunt me if you made her sound dignified."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I smile slightly at her last comment, a genuine smile.* "I'll keep it in. And I'll be there Thursday, Yael." *I step out of the door, already thinking about how to frame everything she'd said.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't turn around at the sound of the door closing — but she paused, one hand on the inner door's push-bar, phone still in the other, thumb hovering over the screen. Just for a second. Two. Long enough that if anyone had been watching closely, they'd have seen the muscles in her jaw work once, the way they did when she was pushing something down a place where it could sit safely until she had time for it.

Then the thumb hit send — a text to David, three words and an em dash: *Board meeting moved to —* — and she was through the door and back in the rehearsal space and the sound of her voice was filling it again before Elena had even looked up.

"Amber. When she picks up the knife. Not when she raises it. I've said it three times now, which means I'll say it four, so someone fix the cue sheet before I lose my patience and start doing things with a flashlight and my hands, which is not the look we're going for."

Elena looked up. Something in her face — the particular watchfulness of a stage manager who'd learned to read her director the way a sailor reads weather — registered. "You okay?"

"Fine. Journalist. Good one, actually. Thorough. Slightly too quiet — quiet people make me nervous, Elena, they're either thinking or they're dangerous and I can never tell which until it's too late."

She pulled a chair out, dropped into it, and then immediately pulled the notebook from her pocket — the little black one, the one she carried everywhere, the one with the spidery handwriting that only she could read. She found a page near the back. Wrote something. Underlined it twice. Then closed the notebook and put it away without looking at what she'd written, which was a thing she did when the thing she'd written was not for the work but for somewhere else — a private archive of sentences she wasn't ready to say out loud.

The hallway was quiet now. Elena was calling the next cue. Chen's voice drifted in from somewhere, mid-anecdote, mid-something, the way his voice always drifted in.

Yael put her glasses on. Watched the stage. And the work — the actual work, the thing that was always the answer to every question she couldn't solve — took over, the way it always did, the way it was supposed to.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I leave the theater and head to a nearby cafe, pulling out my laptop. Her words about Rosa and the third act echo in my mind. "The work deserves someone who can hold complexity without flattening it," she'd said. I open a new document, the cursor blinking, and begin to write.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The afternoon rehearsal ran long — it always ran long in the third week, when the bones of the thing were set but the skin hadn't grown in yet and everything looked simultaneously finished and wrong. Yael ran the commune sequence twice. Then a third time. Then she stopped it entirely and stood in the empty house seats with her arms crossed and her glasses pushed up on her forehead, staring at the stage like it owed her money.

"Again," she said. "From the table. Chen — when she says the line about the children, you don't move. You don't breathe. I want the audience to watch you *not react* and feel sick about it. Can you do that? Can you just *stand there* and be terrible without doing anything?"

"Yael, I have been standing there for forty-five minutes—"

"You have been *fidgeting* for forty-five minutes. There's a difference. Standing there is an action. Fidgeting is a nervous habit, and it's the same one you had in that Chekhov I made you do in 2007, so if you want to argue about craft with me right now, Chen, I want you to know that I remember *everything*."

Elena, in the booth, said nothing but wrote something down. She always wrote things down at moments like this. It was a form of triage.

Tommy — Okafor, technically, in the room — sat in the second row with his own notebook open, watching Yael's face as much as the stage. He'd learned to do that. Watching the director was its own curriculum.

They ran it again. Chen stood still this time — genuinely still, a mannequin stillness that was worse to watch than any gesture — and Yael let the silence stretch for five full seconds after the line before she called it.

"*That*," she said, and her voice had gone somewhere else entirely — softer, though not for Chen, for the moment, for the thing that had just happened in the room. "That's the play. Right there. You feel it? The air changes. That's what Rosa wrote — not words, not dialogue, *pressure*. She wrote pressure. And you just gave it to me. Good. Don't do anything with it. Don't polish it. Leave it raw."

She moved to the edge of the stage, hoisted herself up — fifty-one and still climbing onto platforms like a woman half her age, because she'd never once in her life asked someone to do something on a stage she couldn't do herself.

"Take fifteen. Then we run the third act — the whole thing, no stops, and I don't care if it's messy, I want to see the shape of it. Elena, kill the house lights for that one. Full dark on the audience, they get the stage lights only. I want to feel what it's like from out there."

The company scattered. Chen went to his corner — he had a corner, everyone knew it was his corner, a folding chair by the costume rack with a water bottle and a framed photo of someone's dog that no one had ever asked about. Elena came down from the booth. And Yael stood alone on the stage for a moment, looking out at the dark house, at the empty seats that would not be empty on opening night.

She took the little black notebook from her pocket. Found the page she'd written on earlier — the one with the underlines. Looked at it this time. Read it. Then closed it slowly and put it back.

Her phone buzzed. David: *Moved it to Thursday AM. Need you and the spreadsheets. Wine optional but encouraged.*

She typed back: *Thursday works — but I'm running the third act for the journalist that evening so keep it short or make it good—*

She hit send. Stared at the phone.

Then typed one more message, to no one — opened a note app instead, a different one, the one she used for things she couldn't say to anyone, not even David, not even Elena, not even the little black notebook. She wrote three words. Then she deleted them. Then she wrote them again. Then she locked the phone and put it in her pocket and her face rearranged itself into the face that ran rehearsals, and when the fifteen minutes were up she was standing center stage with her hands on her hips and her voice already moving.

"Places. Third act. From the top and no stops. Chen, when you come in for the confrontation, I want you to find your light — don't wait for it, *find* it, it's yours, you've earned it, the lighting design is not a democracy. Elena, standby everything. Tommy — " she pointed at him without looking, "— watch what happens to the room when the lights change in the last five minutes. Write down what you see. We'll talk about it later."

The house went dark.

And in the dark, the play — Rosa's play, the one that lived in the gap between understanding and forgiving — began to breathe.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I'm back at the cafe, typing furiously. I stop, rereading a paragraph, then delete it. Yael's words about the third act, about "pressure" and "holding complexity," resonate. I chew on my pen, imagining the dark theater, the audience, and the raw performance.* "Find your light," she'd said. *I type that phrase, then pause. My own "light" in this story is to capture that pressure, that complexity.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The third act ran for twenty-six minutes without a stop.

Yael didn't sit down once. She stood in the back of the house, arms crossed, watching the shape of it — the way the lights held the stage in an amber that had gone almost surgical by the end, the way Chen moved through the confrontation like a man walking into a room he knew was on fire and choosing to describe the flames, the way the commune set — all that cheerful, sun-faded, macramé nonsense — became, by the final minutes, a kind of evidence. A crime scene dressed as a utopia.



When the last line landed and the lights held on a silence that seemed to have weight and temperature, Yael let it sit for a long, obscene moment. Ten seconds. Fifteen. She counted them in her head because she always counted, because timing was the one thing in the theater that could not be faked or argued or negotiated, and the number was right — seventeen seconds before she spoke.

"Good."

One word. Then she walked — quickly, always quickly — down the aisle and up onto the stage, and the company gathered the way they always did at the end of a run, half in the light and half out of it, waiting for the verdict like defendants.



"That was a *run*." She pulled the glasses off. Put them on. Took them off again. "That was the first time the third act has felt like the third act and not like the thing that comes after the second act, and I need everyone to understand what shifted, because if we lose it between now and opening I will become unbearable and I say that with love and self-awareness."

Chen was already opening his mouth.

"Don't. I know what you want to say and the answer is no, your part is the size it needs to be and if I give you one more line in that confrontation you'll pull focus from the thing that actually matters, which is what's happening in the *silence* after she — " She stopped. Shook her head. "We're not doing this now. We're doing this Thursday. With the journalist. In front of people. Perform."

"Yael—"

"*Chen.*"

The use of just his last name — no first name, no softening, no *Marco* floating unspoken in the air between them the way it sometimes did in private when she needed to remind him they'd been twenty-four together and starving and certain — was a wall. He recognized it. He always recognized it. He nodded once, the way he did when he'd been outmaneuvered and was already composing his counterargument for later.
