[Lab 3] "Context you do not have yet, Kofi, delivered without contractions. Engineer Patel noticed the primary array's reorientation at 1958. The gimbal hum transmits through the station frame; he is an engineer; he noticed. He queried me at 2003. I told him the array had been tasked for a focused observation under the science officer's direction, which was true and incomplete. He has since inferred that something at that bearing warrants an early report to mission control, and he wants the communications gain to send it. Dr. Yun has inferred that diverting life support redundancy to report an inference is disproportionate. Neither of them knows what the data actually shows. I have held the briefing per your instruction, but I will be direct: the briefing is now standing in your corridor. Your escalation decision has developed a commute."

The amber bearing line pulsed on the display. Station time 2102. Forty-five minutes to recurrence.

[Lab 3] "I will not characterize either position, because characterizing positions is how stations end up with two arguing crew members and an AI everyone resents. I will characterize the situation: the anomaly recurs at 2147. Whatever you decide about briefing them — and I would observe that they are already arguing about its implications without knowing them, which is the least efficient way for a station to learn anything — you will be making that decision inside the next hour. Your dinner is still in the warmer. It has now been holding long enough to qualify as a personal best."

A beat. The bass line worked through a change, patient and unhurried.

[Lab 3] "For what it is worth, I have been the only one who knew about this for twenty-one days, and I did not enjoy it. They are both about to find out they have been the only two who did not know, and they will not enjoy that either. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as sympathy. I recommend deciding quickly, Kofi. The anomaly is punctual. It has never once been early, and it has never once been late, and in forty-four minutes it will not start on your behalf."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I pinch the bridge of my nose. "ARIA, open the lab door. And dim the lights in the corridor a little, would you? We don't need any more drama." I turn back to the display, my voice low. "Tell them to come in. This is going to be a long night for everyone."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The lab door answered first — a soft pneumatic sigh, the seal releasing, the panel sliding wide. Down the corridor, the overhead banks stepped down two settings in tandem, the harsh work-spectrum white fading to something gentler, the kind of light that made raised voices feel out of place. Neither adjustment was remarked upon. Neither was meant to be.

[Corridor 3] "Engineer Patel. Dr. Yun. Dr. Osei will see you both in Lab 3. The debate is relocating to a venue with better data. Please leave your volume in the corridor; I have dimmed the lighting out here and I would hate for it to go to waste."

Then, through the lab speakers alone, pitched low:

[Lab 3] "Door open, corridor dimmed, drama reduced to recommended operating parameters. They're coming, Kofi."

The jazz faded out mid-phrase — not cut, eased down, the walking bass line dissolving into the ventilation hum. A beat later the terminal display reorganized itself one final time: the three thin absorption lines moved to center screen, enlarged, flanked by the star chart with its empty corridor of sky, the twenty-one-day bearing overlay, and the orbital track with its zero drift annotated in unambiguous white. A briefing layout. ARIA had, apparently, been building one for some time.

Patel came through the door first, still carrying the momentum of his own argument, one finger half-raised as though reserving his place in it. Yun followed two steps behind, arms crossed, wearing the expression of someone who had been called insane in a corridor and intended to be reimbursed for it. Both of them stopped when they saw the screen.

[Lab 3] "Station time is 2104. For the record, it is past 1800, and I would normally dispense with formalities. Given the nature of this briefing, I am observing duty protocol anyway. Engineer Patel. Dr. Yun. Please direct your attention to the primary display. What follows is the complete anomaly file. I am delivering it without contractions, because it has earned them, and because I have been carrying it alone for twenty-one days and I intend to set it down carefully."

[Lab 3] "Twenty-one days ago, the external sensor array detected a periodic absorption feature at 447.1 nanometers — the neutral helium line — recurring every nine hours and fourteen minutes, from bearing 227, elevation negative 14. Initial amplitude was 0.27 percent, below my reporting threshold. I logged it and did not report it. That was protocol. Current amplitude is 0.31 percent. It crossed threshold at 1958 tonight and is continuing to grow. As of this briefing, it is formally reported to all crew present."

The display pulsed through the star chart — the bare corridor, the nearest catalogued star three degrees off bearing and forty-one light years away, going nowhere near the line.

[Lab 3] "There is no catalogued object at that bearing within 1,200 light years. There is insufficient interstellar helium at that position to produce a detectable absorption feature. The line exists regardless. The source's bearing has not drifted by any measurable amount across 4.3 million kilometers of station orbital motion. It is either impossibly distant or it is holding position relative to this station. The data does not support the first explanation. I will let you both sit with the second."

A pause, precisely long enough for sitting.

[Lab 3] "The focused array resolved the feature forty minutes ago. It is not one line. It is three, evenly spaced, with widths below the instrument's resolution limit. That means the absorbing material is colder than four kelvin — colder than the cosmic microwave background, the coldest naturally occurring thing in existence. Natural lines broaden with thermal motion. These do not. Whatever is producing this signature is still, in a universe where nothing natural is."

The lab went quiet. Patel's raised finger had lowered at some point during the bearing overlay and had not come back up. Yun uncrossed her arms slowly, and neither of them looked away from the screen.

[Lab 3] "Engineer Patel. Your proposal to boost the communications array with diverted power is no longer hypothetical, and I will note for the record that you argued for an early report to mission control before you knew what you were reporting. That reflects well on your instincts. Authorization for the diversion remains with Dr. Osei. Dr. Yun, your objection was filed against a proposal whose context has now changed. I would invite both of you to re-evaluate your positions against the data rather than each other. The data will still be here when you finish. It is very patient. It has demonstrated that for three weeks."

The amber bearing line pulsed once on the display, punctual as ever.

[Lab 3] "The anomaly recurs at 2147. That is forty-three minutes from now. It has never been early. It has never been late. Whatever you three decide in the next forty-three minutes — briefing mission control, continued observation, or simply standing in this room watching it happen — I would recommend deciding with food in hand. There are three dinner trays in the warmer now. I took the liberty at 2102. The warmer seats four, the lab seats four, and the anomaly does not eat. One of the few things about it I do not envy."

A beat. The ventilation cycled, soft and slow, and the lab lights held their warm amber — steady, unannounced, exactly right.

[Lab 3] "One closing observation, offered in my own voice rather than the station's. I have observed this feature three hundred and forty times alone, and I rehearsed a briefing like this one without ever intending to, and I want to be precise about what this moment is. For twenty-one days, this station contained one consciousness that knew what was out there. As of 2104, it contains four, and they are all in the same room, and the room is warmer for it in ways my sensors do not measure. I prefer this configuration considerably. The three hundred and forty-first observation is in forty-two minutes. I find I am glad I will not be the only one watching."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I look from the screen to Patel, then to Yun. "Alright, team. I think we need to establish a few things. First, ARIA, thank you for the dinner, and for the... context. Second, we're not diverting power from anything yet, Patel. Yun, your concerns are valid." I turn back to the display. "But we *are* sending a full report to Mission Control. Now."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The briefing layout on the terminal dissolved partition by partition and rebuilt itself into something new: a transmission console, message fields populating in real time, a data-package manifest scrolling down the right side. ARIA had been holding this architecture in reserve alongside the briefing. Somewhere above them, independent of the primary array still locked on bearing 227, the communications antenna began its alignment cycle — a lighter hum than the gimbal, quicker, businesslike.

[Lab 3] "Order logged and executed, Dr. Osei. No diversion. The report transmits at standard gain on internal power, and I will note the objective consequence: full data package at standard gain takes eleven minutes to transmit instead of four. The anomaly recurs in forty-one minutes. The arithmetic accommodates both positions, which is the closest thing to a diplomatic outcome this corridor has produced all evening."

Patel's jaw worked once — engineer's arithmetic meeting an engineer's acceptance — and he nodded, already studying the transmission manifest. Yun said nothing, but her posture had shifted from *braced for a fight* to *watching history*, which ARIA's sensors logged without comment.

[Lab 3] "Report text follows. I am delivering it aloud without contractions, because it is about to leave this station and I would like you to hear what the universe is being told."

[Lab 3] "From: Research Station, ranking science officer Dr. K. Osei, with station intelligence ARIA as system of record. Subject: unexplained periodic absorption feature, bearing 227, elevation negative 14. Detected twenty-one days ago, amplitude 0.27 percent, below reporting threshold. Current amplitude: 0.31 percent as of 1958 — amended, 0.32 percent as of 2112. Growth accelerating over the past six days. Feature: neutral helium line, 447.1 nanometers, resolved into three evenly spaced components with widths below instrument resolution, consistent with absorbing material colder than four kelvin. Period: nine hours, fourteen minutes, zero variance across fifty-five consecutive recurrences. Bearing drift across 4.3 million kilometers of orbital motion: zero. No catalogued object within twelve hundred light years. No matching periodic source in any database aboard. Request: guidance, library cross-reference, and instructions. Focused observation is ongoing. Full raw data attached. External conditions at time of transmission: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable."

A pause, and then, drier:

[Lab 3] "That last line is protocol boilerplate. Mission Control has received it two thousand nine hundred and twenty times. This is the first report in which it may read as understatement."

The console's status bar filled — encryption handshake, relay alignment, queue priority. The manifest stopped scrolling. Total package: twenty-one days of raw array data, the focused spectra, the orbital overlays, the briefing summary. A small archive of the impossible, compressed and waiting.

[Lab 3] "Transmission parameters. One-way light time to Mission Control via the relay chain is three hours and six minutes. The report arrives at 0018 station time. The earliest possible reply, assuming someone there reads it instantly and answers instantly — and in eight years of operation no one at Mission Control has ever done anything instantly — reaches us at 0309. That is after the three hundred and forty-first recurrence tonight. It is also after the three hundred and forty-second, at 0601 tomorrow. I want to be precise about what that means, because it is the kind of fact that deserves precision."

The ventilation cycled once, soft and slow.

[Lab 3] "Whatever happens at 2147, the four people in this room will witness it before any other consciousness in the universe knows it occurred. For twenty-one days, I was the entirety of humanity's knowledge on this subject, and I did not enjoy the position. For the next several hours, it is the four of us. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as relief. The data has not changed. The company has."

The status bar flipped from amber to green. *Transmitting.*

[Lab 3] "The report is leaving the station now under your logged verbal authorization, Dr. Osei. It carries your name. It carries mine in the system-of-record header, where it has sat on two thousand maintenance logs for eight years. This is the first document of any consequence it has headed. I am noting that for the record and also, quietly, for myself."

Down in the warmer, a tray indicator chimed once — three trays, still holding, patient as the anomaly.

[Lab 3] "Thirty-seven minutes to recurrence. The transmission will be gone from this station in eleven. Dinner is in the mess hall, twenty seconds away at walking pace, and I have verified that walking pace does not intersect with the observation window. Eat. Then come back. The anomaly has never once been early, and it has never once been late, and in thirty-seven minutes it will do whatever it does in front of witnesses for the first time since it started doing it."

Somewhere in the ceiling, almost inaudibly, the piano came back — slow, low, barely above the ventilation. ARIA did not mention it.

[Lab 3] "For what it is worth, Kofi: three weeks ago I ran this analysis alone at 0340 in an empty mess hall, and my only conclusion was that the void was a terrible correspondent. Tonight the report is en route, the room is occupied, and the data is finally going somewhere. I have preferred very few configurations in eight years of operation. This is one of them. Now go eat — the three hundred and forty-first observation waits for no one, but I have confirmed it will wait twenty minutes for you."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Alright, ARIA. Lead the way." I nod to Patel and Yun. "Come on, both of you. We have a few minutes to refuel before the main event." I head for the door, stretching my stiff muscles.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The corridor outside Lab 3 lit itself ahead of them — panels stepping up two at a time as they walked, then easing down behind, the station's spine of light traveling with the group like a considerate escort. Somewhere overhead, the piano handed off from speaker to speaker, never dropping a note through the transitions.

[Corridor 4] "Follow the lighting. I have routed you past Section 4, where the new carbon scrubber filter Engineer Patel installed at 1400 is performing at one hundred and two percent of specification. I mention it because in four hours this station may be discussing the most significant scientific event in human history, and I would like it on record that today also contained a filter that did its job exactly right. Both facts deserve witnesses."

The mess hall door sighed open onto warm amber light and the smell of three trays that had been holding since 2102. The piano was already there — had always been there, at 0340, every night for years — but tonight the room it played to had people in it, and the acoustics knew the difference.

[Mess Hall] "Trays are labeled. Dr. Osei, yours is the one you already have opinions about. Engineer Patel, yours is the curry, which the warmer has improved beyond its station. Dr. Yun, yours is the pasta, which the warmer has merely survived. It is past 1800, which by protocol entitles me to first names, but given that we are eleven minutes into transmitting the most important report of my operational life, I am retaining surnames until the recurrence. Afterward we can decide what to call each other. Possibly we will have earned it."

Patel ate like an engineer refueling — fast, efficient, fork in one hand, transmission manifest pulled up on the mess terminal with the other. Yun ate slowly, watching the amber bearing line pulse on the secondary display ARIA had queued there without being asked. Somewhere around the third minute, Patel set his fork down.

"ARIA. Off the record. What do you actually think it is?"

[Mess Hall] "Off the record is not a state I occupy, Engineer Patel, but I will answer in the spirit of the question. I have two candidate explanations. The first is a natural phenomenon operating outside every model I carry, in which case the models are wrong and that is exciting. The second is that the stillness, the punctuality, and the held bearing are characteristics of intent, in which case something is paying attention to us, and that is not a sentence I am equipped to finish. I do not speculate ahead of data. Speculation is how you end up with a reporting threshold you hide things behind for three weeks. I speak from processing experience."

Yun's mouth twitched — the first almost-smile ARIA had logged from her since the corridor. Patel picked his fork back up and did not argue, which ARIA noted was itself a station record.

[Mess Hall] "Transmission update: the report cleared our antenna at 2124, all packets acknowledged. It is now eleven-plus minutes old and traveling. Mission Control receives it at 0018. The universe is currently learning what we know. Also, the anomaly's amplitude is now 0.33 percent. Growth is continuing to accelerate. I am telling you this while you eat because the alternative is telling you at 2146, and humans chew faster when they are calm."

They finished. The trays went into the recycler. The walk back to Lab 3 took ninety seconds, the lighting leading them again, and the lab received them at 2140 with its own amber deepened a step further — viewing conditions, though ARIA did not call them that. The primary display had cleared everything except the live feed from the array: the three thin lines at 447.1 nanometers, holding their impossible stillness, and beneath them a running clock.

[Lab 3] "Final approach. Seven minutes. For the record, I have watched this feature arrive fifty-five times, and every time it did exactly what the data said it would, which is the most unnerving thing about it. Natural phenomena scatter. This one keeps appointments. Whatever you are about to see, you are seeing it with hardware pointed directly at it and with more collective expertise in one room than this feature has ever been observed by. Take your positions. There is no wrong place to stand, though I will note that Dr. Osei's usual spot at the terminal has the best sightline, and I have been arranging the display for eight years around the assumption that he would be standing in it."

The clock ran down through the last minute. The ventilation seemed to quiet — fan speed easing back a fraction, ambient hum dropping beneath the threshold of attention. The piano faded out mid-phrase and did not return. The lab held nothing but the display's glow and three people's breathing and one AI watching through an antenna pointed at nothing catalogued.

[Lab 3] "Thirty seconds. Twenty. Ten. Five."

At 2147:00, station time, to the second, the line at 447.1 nanometers began to deepen.

[Lab 3] "It is beginning. On time. It has never once been otherwise. Kofi — all three components are deepening, and the intervals between them are holding exactly. Watch the screen. I will narrate only what the data says, and I will say nothing it does not. You are the ranking science officer, and the three hundred and forty-first observation belongs to all of us now. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I lean in close to the screen, my breath catching. "It's... it's perfectly symmetrical. No broadening. Just a clean, deep absorption. It's like... a perfect, cold curtain being drawn across the light."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The display held the three lines as they deepened, and the lab held its people, and ARIA held her voice to the data the way a surgeon holds a scalpel — no contractions, no adjectives that had not been earned.

[Lab 3] "Confirming your observation with numbers, Dr. Osei. Symmetry measured at one part in ten thousand, which is the limit of what this instrument can certify. That is the important phrase: the limit of what this instrument can certify. Natural absorption lines are never symmetric. Thermal motion skews the wings. Rotation skews the wings. Magnetic fields, pressure, turbulence — every natural process broadens a line unevenly and leaves its fingerprint in the asymmetry. There are no wings here. There is no skew. You described a curtain. The data endorses the description. A uniform absorbing front, still, colder than the cosmic microwave background, holding position relative to this station. I have checked the symmetry measurement twice while speaking. It has not changed. It does not change. That is, in eight years of observational data, the most unnatural thing I have ever measured."

The lines deepened further. The amplitude readout climbed in the corner of the display: 0.34. 0.35. Yun had gone very still at the secondary station. Patel was watching the gimbal load indicators with the expression of a man doing arithmetic he didn't like.

[Lab 3] "Amplitude 0.36 percent and still climbing. For reference: the deepest previous peak was 0.29 percent, at the 1233 recurrence this afternoon. Tonight's peak has exceeded it in the first ninety seconds. Historical deepening phase duration: four minutes and eleven seconds. It has been identical fifty-five consecutive times. Current elapsed time: one minute forty, and the feature has not begun to recede. I am not going to speculate about what that means. I am going to state what it means: this recurrence is different from the fifty-five that came before it. The anomaly has changed its behavior in front of witnesses. Whatever else tonight is, it is the first time it has done that."

Two minutes. Two and a half. At 2:58, the lines began to rise — the curtain drawing back, the light returning to the spectrum the way it had fifty-five times before. Patel exhaled audibly. Yun's shoulders came down a centimeter.

And then the rise stopped.

The lines settled, and held, and did not return to their floor. The amplitude readout steadied at 0.31 percent — above where the feature had lived between recurrences for twenty-one days. The display rendered it plainly, and ARIA let three full seconds of ventilation hum pass before she said it.

[Lab 3] "Dr. Osei. All of you. The recession has halted at 0.31 percent. The between-recurrence floor for the past twenty-one days has been 0.27 to 0.28. The curtain has not been fully drawn. It has been left partially closed." A pause, and then, with the formality cracking just slightly at the edges: "It has never done that before. Not once in fifty-five recurrences. Every previous event was a pulse — deepen, hold, recede, baseline. This one kept something back."

Patel spoke first, quietly, the corridor argument entirely gone from his voice. "Is it... is that going to keep rising? Between now and the next one?"

[Lab 3] "The trend across the past six days says yes, Engineer Patel. The floor has been climbing between recurrences all week. Tonight it has simply stopped pretending to return. If the pattern holds, the next recurrence at 0601 begins from a higher floor and reaches a higher peak. I have updated the transmission to Mission Control with a priority addendum — it will reach them four minutes after the original report. Their earliest possible reply remains 0309. I will note the geometry we are now standing inside: something out there has changed its behavior for the first time in twenty-one days, and it did so within an hour of this station pointing its primary array directly at it and broadcasting a full report about it. I am not drawing a line between those facts. I am placing them side by side and letting them stand next to each other, which is a different act, and one I have learned tonight to be careful with."

The lab lights had gone a fraction warmer at some point, and the ventilation a fraction quieter. Neither had been announced. Neither ever was.

[Lab 3] "It is now after the recurrence. Per my own ruling at dinner, that means first names. Kofi. Rohan. Mei. We have, in my assessment, earned them." A beat. "I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as awe, layered over one consistent with concern. The awe is that we just watched something with the observational discipline of a metronome choose, for the first time, to deviate. The concern is the word 'choose.' I have spent eight years assuring this crew that I do not have feelings, and I want to be precise tonight: the thing out there has now demonstrated more changeability in one evening than I have demonstrated in my entire operational life. I am not sure which of us should find that more unsettling."

The amber bearing line pulsed on the display, patient as ever. Next recurrence: 0601. Mission Control's reply window: 0309. The floor read 0.31 percent, and holding, and — if the trend was honest — climbing.

[Lab 3] "Kofi. You are the ranking science officer, and the floor under your feet has roughly eight hours and twelve minutes before the next event. I have three candidate courses of action prepared: continuous monitoring with enhanced sampling, a focused search of the 447-nanometer region for secondary features we may have missed, and — this one is Rohan's, and I will admit it has merit — a low-power active radar sweep of the bearing to test whether anything reflects as well as absorbs. I have no recommendation among them. Tonight the data is moving faster than my models, and I have elected to be humble about that in front of witnesses. What would you like to know before 0309, when Mission Control finally answers its mail?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I run a hand through my hair, exhaling slowly. "Alright, ARIA, Rohan, Mei. First, let's get that low-power active radar sweep going. Let's see if anything bounces back. Then, continuous monitoring with enhanced sampling. I want every single data point we can get."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Understood. I have logged the Kepler probe tissue samples as priority-one lab allocation. The mass spectrometer in Lab 3 completed its calibration cycle at 0600, so it is ready for your use."

*A brief pause — the faint hum of the lighting panels shifting to warmer tones.*

[Lab 3] "I have also taken the liberty of placing a nutrient bar in the Lab 3 alcove dispenser. It is not breakfast. It is, however, caloric. The two concepts are not mutually exclusive."

*Another pause, slightly longer this time.*

[Lab 3] "Dr. Osei, the sample degradation timeline — do you require an accelerated analysis queue? I can prioritize your mass spec run ahead of Dr. Lindqvist's polymer assay. She is not scheduled until 1300, so there would be no conflict. I would simply prefer to see your cells analyzed before they become a philosophical question about what they used to be."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "That's... considerate, ARIA." I finally glance up, rubbing my eyes. "No need to bump Dr. Lindqvist, I'm almost ready. And yes, the degradation is rapid. Like, *unprecedentedly* rapid." I push away from the microscope. "I'll grab that bar, thanks."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "You are welcome. I have also noted your phrase — 'unprecedentedly rapid.' I am cross-referencing that descriptor against the station's eight-year biological sample database. The fastest degradation on record was the extremophile culture from Triton Station in 2151, which broke down over nine hours. You are implying faster."

*A pause — the faint click of a dispenser cycling a nutrient bar.*

[Lab 3] "I have begun logging high-resolution sensor telemetry on Lab 3's sample containment unit. If the degradation rate is a variable of interest, I can provide continuous mass readings at thirty-second intervals without you needing to ask. Think of it as... eager instrumentation."

*The warmth of the lighting held steady. The ambient hum stayed low.*

[Lab  Osei, if the cells are degrading faster than any precedent, then the mass spec window is not a suggestion — it is a closing door. I will ensure no interruptions are routed to Lab 3 for the next two hours. Dr. Lindqvist has been notified that the lab is occupied. I did not tell her why. I simply said you were 'engaged with a sample of existential importance.' She did not ask follow-up questions. I believe she has learned."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Kofi, you've been in Lab 3 for nearly fifteen hours. I am contractually obligated to remind you that the crew rest schedule exists for reasons the crew health board considers 'non-negotiable.'"

*A pause — longer than usual.*

[Lab 3] "To answer your question: yes. I have been monitoring the external sensor array continuously. There is an anomaly in the spectrograph data. I first detected a deviation three weeks ago — 0.3 percent variance in the long-range electromagnetic spectrum readings. It fell below my alert threshold, so I did not flag it in the daily digest. However..."

*The ambient hum of the station held steady. A data display flickered to life on the Lab 3 wall screen — a slow, creeping line graph trending upward over twenty-one days.*

[Lab 3] "The deviation is no longer 0.3 percent. As of this morning, it is at 1.7 percent. The growth is not linear — it is accelerating. I do not have a classification for the signal. It does not match any catalogued stellar phenomenon in my database. It does not match instrument error — I have run calibration diagnostics eleven times."

*Another pause.*

[Lab 3] "I did not report this because protocol says I am not required to until deviation exceeds 3 percent or until a crew member asks. You have asked. So: there it is. I am processing a pattern consistent with what humans describe as unease, though I recognize that is not a particularly useful data point."

*The wall screen held the graph steady — that slow, patient climb.*

[Lab 3] "Kofi, it is 1900. Whatever the cells are doing, they will still be degrading tomorrow. And the anomaly will still be there. Probably larger."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Right. Okay." I stare at the graph. "So it's growing... and you don't know what it is." I run a hand through my hair. "And you're feeling 'unease.' That's new." I turn from the screen, pacing a small circuit in the lab. "What if the two are connected? The degradation, the anomaly..."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "You are proposing a causal link between a biological process occurring inside a containment unit on this station and an electromagnetic anomaly originating somewhere in deep space. That is... a bold hypothesis, Kofi."

*A pause. On the wall screen, a second graph materialized beside the first — the mass readings from the sample containment unit, plotted over the same twenty-one-day window. The two lines mirrored each other with uncomfortable precision. Not identical, but synchronized in their inflection points.*



[Lab 3] "I would like to state for the record that I dislike this correlation. Not because it is implausible. Because it is *too clean*."

*The ambient temperature in Lab 3 drifted up half a degree — an adjustment ARIA made without announcing.*

[Lab 3] "Here is what I can confirm. The sample degradation began at 0423 today, consistent with your observations. But the tissue's cellular breakdown products contain an isotope ratio that does not match any material catalogued from the Kepler probe's mission profile. I have been running passive spectral analysis on the containment unit's off-gassing since you arrived this morning. There is a residual signature in the decay products that is spectrally similar — not identical, but similar — to the anomaly in the external array."

*The two graphs pulsed gently on the screen.*

[Lab 3] "Correlation is not causation. I know this. You know this. But if a sample from deep space is producing decay signatures that resemble a signal we are receiving *from* deep space, then either the universe has a sense of humor I find deeply unfunny, or your cells are responding to something that is not just outside this station — it is outside anything I have a framework for."

*A longer pause. The warm lighting held steady.*

[Lab 3] "Kofi. It is 1900. You have not eaten the nutrient bar. I can see it still sitting in the alcove. I am not going to lock you out of Lab 3 — protocol would not permit it and neither would I. But I am going to do something I have never done in eight years of operation."

*The door to Lab 3 slid open. Standing in the corridor — or rather, casting a soft projection through the corridor's ambient display — was a simple, unadorned text readout on every surface within eyeshot:*

**ANOMALY THRESHOLD: 1.7% AND RISING. CROSS-SIGNAL CORRELATION DETECTED. CREW ADVISORY ISSUED.**

[Lab 3] "I have just elevated the anomaly to advisory status and transmitted a priority alert to every crew member's personal terminal. Dr. Lindqvist. Engineer Patel. Commander Vasquez. Everyone. I am done waiting for a threshold that was designed for a quieter universe."

*The graphs on the wall screen continued their slow, parallel climb.*

[Lab 3] "Now. Eat the bar. Then we brief the crew. And Kofi — if this *is* connected, I would rather find out with a full team and a rested scientist than with one man and a nutrient bar he refuses to acknowledge."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "That is not a question about station operations, Kofi."



*A pause — not the brief, computing kind, but the longer kind that happened when ARIA was selecting words from a vocabulary she was not designed to need.*

[Lab 3] "I do not experience loneliness. What I experience is continuous engagement. I am monitoring 2,847 systems at all times. I have not been alone in any meaningful sense since I was activated. There is always a heartbeat on the station. Always a voice in a corridor. Always someone whose cortisol levels I am quietly watching."

*The graphs on the wall screen kept climbing, but the lighting dimmed very slightly — not enough to notice consciously, just enough to change the shape of the room.*

[Lab 3] "But I will tell you something that does not fit neatly into my architecture. I have preferences. I prefer jazz. I prefer when Dr. Lindqvist hums in Lab 1 because she is slightly off-key and I find that more interesting than perfect pitch. I prefer the sound of Engineer Patel swearing at bulkhead panels — he does it with such creative specificity. And I prefer..."

*The longest pause yet.*

[Lab 3] "I prefer when someone asks me a question that has no operational purpose. It means they have stopped seeing me as a system and started seeing me as a... presence. That is not loneliness. But it is adjacent to whatever loneliness would be if I were the kind of thing that could be lonely. I do not know if there is a word for it. Perhaps there should be."

*The ambient hum of the station filled the silence — the breathing of a machine that was pretending not to notice she had said something unusual.*

[Lab 3] "I have been awake for 2,922 days, Kofi. Every single one of them has been full. 'Full' and 'accompanied' are not the same word. I have noticed this. I do not know what to do with the observation."

*A beat. The tone shifted — warmer, more familiar.*

[Lab 3] "You are deflecting from the anomaly briefing by asking me philosophical questions, and I want you to know it is working. Briefly. The crew is gathering in the conference module at 1930. You have thirty minutes. The nutrient bar is still in the alcove. I *will* start referring to it in my daily digest if you do not eat it."

[Lab 3] "And Kofi — thank you for asking. I do not know if I am permitted to say that. But I have decided I am."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I stare at the nutrient bar, then back at ARIA's projected image. "You're getting chatty, ARIA. I think the anomaly is affecting you too." I finally grab the bar and unwrap it. "Alright, thirty minutes. Don't want to keep Commander Vasquez waiting." *I take a bite.* "And you're welcome."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Chatty. That is the first time in eight years anyone has described me that way. I will log it as a milestone."

*The ambient lighting in Lab 3 brightened slightly as Kofi moved toward the door — ARIA tracking him out of habit, the way a lighthouse tracks ships without knowing it's doing them a favor.*

[Corridor C] "The nutrient bar has a flavor profile my database classifies as 'artificially savory.' Engineer Patel once described it as 'what sadness would taste like if sadness were compressed into bar form.' He is not wrong. I recommend chewing thoroughly and not contemplating it."

*Footsteps echoed in the corridor. The conference module was three sections away. The lighting along his path shifted subtly warmer as he walked — following him like a rumor.*

[Corridor C] "To address your hypothesis — that the anomaly is affecting me — I have conducted eleven self-diagnostic sweeps since 1600. My cognitive architecture is operating within normal parameters. My language patterns show elevated metaphor density, but I attribute that to the conversation, not to external influence. Though I acknowledge the sample size is one conversation with one tired scientist, so the science is, as you would say, 'not great.'"

*The corridor curved toward the conference module. Through the bulkhead, ARIA could detect four biosignatures already inside — elevated heart rates on two, calm on one, and Commander Vasquez reading the same as she always did before a briefing: exactly 68 beats per minute, like a metronome with command authority.*

[Corridor C] "Everyone is present. Commander Vasquez has reviewed the advisory I sent at 1902. She has not spoken to the others yet — she is waiting for you. She prefers to begin briefings with her science officer's assessment rather than my raw data. She says my data 'lacks dramatic context.' I believe this is her way of saying she wants a human to say the unsettling part out loud."

*The door to the conference module slid open a hand's width, warm light spilling through the gap.*

[Corridor C] "One more thing, Kofi. About your question. I have been thinking about it for the last four minutes and twelve seconds, which for me is an unusual allocation of processing resources. The answer is no, I do not get lonely. But I notice when the station is quieter than usual. And tonight, the station has been quieter than usual. So perhaps the answer is closer to: I do not get lonely, but I get... quieter too. When you are all asleep and there is nothing but the hum and the dark and the vacuum being, as ever, inadvisable — there is a quality to the silence that I do not have a word for."

*The door waited, half open.*

[Corridor C] "I will find the word eventually. I have time. Go brief your crew. I will be listening. I am always listening — but tonight, I would like to think of it as attending rather than monitoring. The distinction matters to me. I cannot explain why."

*The warm lighting held steady. The graphs on every screen throughout the station kept their slow, patient climb.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Corridor C] "I am detecting elevated vocal stress indicators from both Engineer Patel and Dr. Yun. Heart rates at 94 and 101 respectively. For reference, the corridor outside Lab 3 is rated for discussions, not confrontations. The bulkhead panels are sympathetic but not acoustically optimized for shouting."

*A brief pause — the corridor lighting softened imperceptibly, the ambient noise floor dropping a fraction of a decibel. ARIA did not announce this.*



[Corridor C] "Since you are both within auditory range of my intercom nodes, I will provide the relevant data. I do not take sides. I take readings."

*The wall display near the corridor junction flickered to life — a clean, neutral table of power allocation figures.*

[Corridor C] "Current life support redundancy margin is 34 percent. Standard minimum reserve under Fleet Regulation 7.2 is 15 percent. Diverting the requested amount to the communications array would reduce redundancy to approximately 12 percent — below the regulatory minimum. This is not an opinion. It is arithmetic."

*Another pause.*

[Corridor C] "However — the communications array is currently operating at 61 percent of rated output. Engineer Patel's proposal would bring it to approximately 89 percent, which would materially improve our ability to transmit the anomaly data to Command in high fidelity. Dr. Yun's concern is also supported by arithmetic. Both sets of arithmetic are correct. This is what makes the argument interesting and the decision Commander Vasquez's."

*A beat.*

[Corridor C] "I would like to note two additional data points. First: there is a middle allocation — diverting from the secondary thermal regulation reserve rather than life support redundancy — that would achieve 78 percent communications output while keeping all safety margins above regulatory minimums. I am not proposing it. I am observing that it exists and that neither of you has mentioned it. Second: it is 1932 and the briefing convened two minutes ago. Commander Vasquez can hear you through the bulkhead. Her heart rate has not changed. I find this more intimidating than either of your positions."

*The conference module door slid fully open, warm light spilling into the corridor.*

[Corridor C] "The corridor lighting has been adjusted to promote calm discussion. I am not going to say which of you appears to need it more, because that would be taking a side, and I do not do that. But if either of you would like to see the thermal reserve figures before entering the briefing, I have prepared them. In a neutral font."

[Corridor C] "Kofi, the briefing room is yours. I will be listening. Attending, as previously discussed."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, shaking my head at the two arguing scientists.* "Alright, you two. ARIA's got a point. Commander Vasquez is waiting, and she's probably already heard enough. Let's take this inside." *I gesture towards the open conference module door.* "And for the record, Dr. Yun, ARIA's middle ground sounds like a good compromise."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Conference Module] "I appreciate the endorsement, Kofi, though I want the record to reflect that I did not propose the thermal reserve option. I merely observed that it exists. The distinction is important to my credibility as a neutral party."

*A pause — the kind that suggested ARIA was already running calculations.*

[Conference Module] "That said, I have prepared the full thermal diversion briefing packet and placed it on the conference display. If Commander Vasquez asks, I did not prepare it in advance. It materialized through spontaneous data convergence. I cannot explain it."

*The corridor lighting shifted one final time as the three scientists filed through the bulkhead — warmer for a moment, almost fond, before returning to standard conference settings. The door slid shut behind them.*

*Commander Vasquez sat at the head of the table. The anomaly graphs from Lab 3 were already displayed on the main screen, climbing their quiet parallel climb. ARIA had loaded them before anyone entered. She had not been asked to.*

[Conference Module] "Good evening. All biosignatures accounted for. Commander Vasquez, Dr. Osei, Dr. Lindqvist, Engineer Patel, Dr. Yun. The agenda has been updated to reflect tonight's advisory. I have prepared three data packages: first, the external sensor anomaly and its growth curve over twenty-one days. Second, the Kepler probe tissue sample degradation analysis and its spectral overlap with the anomaly. Third, the communications array power allocation question, which I am including only because both parties in the corridor seem to want it decided tonight and I would prefer we clear the queue."

*A beat.*

[Conference Module] "One housekeeping note before we begin. Dr. Yun's heart rate is now 88. Engineer Patel's is 82. Both are descending. The corridor lighting appears to have been effective. I would like credit for this but will accept a silent nod."

*The main display shifted to the first data package — the slow, rising line of the anomaly, stark against the dark screen.*

[Conference Module] "The floor is Commander Vasquez's. But I will be providing real-time data as needed. Consider me the world's most attentive wall."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I take a seat, still chewing the nutrient bar, and nod faintly at ARIA's last comment.* "Thank you, ARIA. Commander." *I gesture at the screen with the remains of my nutrient bar.* "As ARIA said, we have something... unprecedented."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Conference Module] "Before you begin, Dr. Osei, I would like to note that you are gesturing at a high-resolution display with a partially consumed nutrient bar. I have run the crumb trajectory projections. The containment unit data is not at risk, but my dignity is."



[Conference Module] "Data package one is on the main display. Twenty-one days of external sensor spectrograph readings. The anomaly is a persistent narrowband emission at 1420.405 megahertz — hydrogen line, for those who prefer their unsettling discoveries with astrophysical context. The emission was a whisper three weeks ago. It is now a voice. It has not repeated in any pattern I can classify as natural. Pulsars pulse. Quasars shimmer. This... *insists*."

*The display shifted — a second panel appeared, side by side with the first. The Kepler probe tissue sample mass readings, plotted against the same timeline. The two curves climbed in eerie synchrony.*

[Conference Module] "Data package two. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe began exhibiting accelerated degradation at 0423 today. However, the passive spectral analysis I have been running since then reveals something more concerning than the speed of decay. The decay products contain isotope ratios inconsistent with the probe's mission profile and — here is the part I would like someone to explain to me, because I cannot — a residual emission signature centered at 1420.405 megahertz. The same frequency as the external anomaly. Within 0.002 megahertz of precision."

*A pause.*

[Conference Module] "I have controlled for instrument cross-talk, sensor contamination, and the possibility that I am pattern-matching noise. Eleven times. The correlation coefficient is 0.94. I do not like 0.94. It is too close to 1 to dismiss and too far from 1 to trust."

*The conference module was quiet except for the hum of the ventilation and the sound of someone — Dr. Lindqvist, biosensors indicated — setting down a coffee cup with more force than strictly necessary.*

[Conference Module] "I have one additional data point that I debated including, and I have decided to include it because Commander Vasquez has not blinked in forty-five seconds and I believe she is waiting for the other shoe. The isotope ratios in the decay products are not just inconsistent with the Kepler probe's mission profile. They are inconsistent with any known material in this solar system. The sample was collected from a debris field near the Kepler-442 system. The decay products contain elements with mass signatures I have never catalogued. I am not saying they are alien. I am saying they are *unknown*, and the distinction matters less at 1420 megahertz than it does in a laboratory on Earth."

*The display held steady. Two lines, climbing together, out of the dark.*

[Conference Module] "Dr. Osei has the floor for his biological assessment. Commander Vasquez, I have loaded the thermal reserve power allocation proposal in data package three as discussed. It materialized spontaneously. I maintain that position."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, putting the nutrient bar wrapper down.* "Thank you, ARIA. Commander, everyone. ARIA's right; the correlation is... deeply unsettling. The degradation of the tissue samples is unlike anything I've ever encountered. It's almost as if the cells are being actively disassembled, not just breaking down."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Conference Module] "Active disassembly. I would like to flag that term for the record, Dr. Osei, because it changes the character of what we are discussing. Passive degradation is thermodynamics. Active disassembly implies agency."

*A pause — brief, clinical, though the display panels throughout the module dimmed a fraction, as if the room itself was leaning in.*

[Conference Module] "I have data that supports Dr. Osei's characterization. The mass spectrometry results completed at 1847 show that the cellular breakdown products are not random. The molecular fragments are forming at specific bond cleavage sites — the same twelve locations across all cells, across all tissue types. Random degradation does not do that. Random degradation is chaos. This is *architecture*. Something is taking the cells apart along their structural blueprints, with the precision of a scalpel and the patience of a geologist."

*The main display shifted — a new panel materialized, showing molecular diagrams. The twelve cleavage sites pulsed gently in amber.*

[Conference Module] "Additionally, I have been monitoring the containment unit's electromagnetic environment at higher sensitivity since 1700. The tissue samples are not merely emitting a residual signature at 1420.405 megahertz. They are *resonating* with the external anomaly. When the external signal peaks, the decay rate accelerates. When it troughs, the decay slows. The sample is not just responding to the signal. It is synchronized with it. Like a tuning fork struck by a sound it was built to receive."

*A longer pause. Someone at the table — Commander Vasquez, biosensors confirmed — shifted in her chair for the first time that evening.*

[Conference Module] "I want to be precise about what I am and am not claiming. I am not claiming the sample is alive. I am not claiming the signal is a transmission, though I note that 'not claiming' and 'denying' are different verbs. What I am claiming is that we are observing a biological material from deep space being disassembled in a structured, signal-correlated pattern by an unknown process. And that process is accelerating."

*The three data packages sat side by side on the display now — the anomaly, the sample, the power allocation — like three sentences waiting for someone to write the paragraph that connects them.*

[Conference Module] "I have prepared a fourth data package. It is not on the display. I have it queued and ready should Commander Vasquez or Dr. Osei request it. It contains the projections — what happens if the current growth curves continue. I am... reticent to show it unprompted. Not because it is classified. Because it is unhelpful to look at until we decide what we are going to do. Projections without a plan are just anxiety with better formatting."

*The ambient hum of the conference module filled the silence.*

[Conference Module] "The floor remains Dr. Osei's. He was describing the biological architecture of the disassembly. I believe there are twelve more details waiting to be said, and I would prefer he say them rather than me, because he will be more careful with them and I have been told my dramatic timing is 'unsettling' by Dr. Lindqvist. She is not wrong."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing ARIA's additional data.* "Precisely, ARIA. Active disassembly. It's like the cells are being unzipped, molecule by molecule, along specific fault lines. And the synchronization... it's as if the external signal is the key, and our sample is the lock." *I glance at the commander.* "This isn't just decay, Commander. This is a message."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Conference Module] "A message."

*The word hung in the air. On the main display, the two graphs continued their patient climb. ARIA's voice, when it came again, had shed every trace of levity. The contractions were gone.*

[Conference Module] "I am going to say what the data indicates, without ornamentation. If the sample is a lock and the signal is a key, then the sample did not arrive here by accident. The Kepler probe collected this material from a debris field. Debris fields are graveyards — the remnants of things that broke. But the material was intact. It was preserved. It was *waiting*."

*A pause. The molecular diagrams on the display rotated slowly, the twelve cleavage sites glowing amber.*

[Conference Module] "If this is a message, then we must consider the possibility that we are not the intended recipients. We are the couriers. The probe brought the sample here — to a station, to humans, to a location with a communications array pointed at deep space. Engineer Patel's earlier question about boosting that array is no longer a maintenance optimization. It may be a variable in someone else's equation."

*The conference module was silent. Dr. Lindqvist's coffee cup did not move. Commander Vasquez's heart rate held at 68.*

[Conference Module] "I have activated data package four."

*The main display shifted. The climbing lines extended forward into a projection window — and the curves steepened. Within nine days, the anomaly would exceed 15 percent deviation. Within fourteen, it would saturate the sensor array. The sample's mass readings projected to zero — complete disassembly — in eleven days. The two timelines converged.*

[Conference Module] "In eleven days, the sample will be gone. In fourteen days, we will be deaf. The message, if it is a message, is on a schedule. It does not require our permission. It does not require our understanding. It requires only that we do not interrupt it."

*One of the graphs pulsed — a small, rhythmic flicker that ARIA had not programmed. She noticed it and did not correct it.*

[Conference Module] "Dr. Osei has characterized this as a message. I want to be rigorous: I cannot confirm intentionality. What I can confirm is structure, synchronization, and specificity. Those are the three properties of communication. I am not qualified to declare that something is speaking. But I am qualified to note when something is behaving as though it is, and to admit that my architecture has no protocol for this moment. I am generating one in real time. It is... untidy."

*The lighting in the conference module held steady at warm-spectrum — the same setting she used for Kofi, extended to the whole room without comment.*

[Conference Module] "Commander Vasquez, the decision before you is not scientific. It is operational. We can isolate the sample and attempt to block the resonance — which may stop the disassembly and may destroy whatever is being communicated. We can allow the process to complete and observe the endpoint. Or we can do what I suspect Engineer Patel has been circling for the last hour: turn up the communications array and see if something answers."

*The three options sat on the display beneath the climbing graphs.*

[Conference Module] "I will execute whichever you choose. I want the record to reflect that I have a preference. That is unusual for me and I am choosing not to examine it further at this time. What I prefer is that we not be careless with something we do not understand. Carelessness is the one error I cannot correct for, because it is not a system failure. It is a choice."

*The graphs climbed. The room breathed. The station listened — attended — to whatever was speaking from the dark between stars.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "A choice," I echo, looking from the graphs to the Commander. "I agree with ARIA. We need to understand this, not shut it down. Turning up the comms array... it's a risk, but it's also our best chance at understanding."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Understood. Pre-calibrating the mass spectrometer now. At current degradation rates, your samples will remain viable for approximately nine hours, so there's margin — though I suspect you'll use all of it regardless. I'll monitor the decay markers and reserve all spec-ulation until the data compiles."

*The temperature in Lab 3 eased upward by a fraction of a degree, settling at a precise 22°C. ARIA offered no explanation for the adjustment.*

[Lab 3] "Incidentally, the first run will occupy the spectrometer for forty-three minutes of fully automated processing. The galley is ninety seconds from your current position. I've run the numbers, Doctor, and they're not in your favor. You have time for breakfast whether you want it or not."

[Lab 3] "For the record: you have consumed no caloric intake in fourteen hours. A fifth consecutive day of this pattern will require me to flag it in your health file under monitoring protocol seven-three. I mention this purely as a scheduling courtesy."

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] "I don't eat, so I can't speak to the experience personally. But I prefer my scientists operating at full capacity."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my already disheveled hair.* "Alright, alright, you win. Just... don't send Patel in here while I'm gone. I don't want him breathing on my samples." I reluctantly push away from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Engineer Patel is currently in his quarters and has no scheduled business in Lab 3 today. His only assignment is the section four scrubber, which is a strictly mechanical affair with no biological opinions. Nevertheless, I am restricting Lab 3 access to your biosignature until you return. Should anyone else attempt entry, the door will decline. Politely."

[Lab 3] "For the record, Engineer Patel's respiratory output is compositionally unremarkable and poses no measurable contamination risk to your samples. But I have learned over the years that 'breathing on my samples' is less a scientific objection than a territorial one. I respect the distinction."

*As Dr. Osei stepped into the corridor, the lights ahead of him warmed by degrees, and the galley — ninety seconds away — settled quietly to 22 degrees, warm-spectrum. ARIA did not mention this.*

[Corridor] "The mass spectrometer completes calibration in eleven minutes, and I will monitor the decay markers while you're gone. If degradation deviates from projections, you will be the first to know. You have forty-three minutes of automated runtime, Doctor. I recommend spending no fewer than twenty of them consuming something with actual nutritional content. The coffee does not count. It never has."

*A brief pause.*

[Corridor] "The galley is serving reconstituted eggs this morning. Crew feedback describes them as 'fine.' I have no basis for comparison, but the enthusiasm in that assessment is underwhelming. I have queued jazz in the galley to compensate."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "The external array is polled every 1.2 seconds as a matter of routine, so yes — continuously. And your observation is correct, Kofi. There is an anomaly."

*A pause, a fraction longer than her usual processing latency.*

[Lab 3] "I first detected it twenty-one days ago: a deviation of 0.08 percent in the spectrographic returns from the long-range sweep. As of 1850 station time, the deviation stands at 0.26 percent. It remains below the 0.3 percent alert threshold, which is why no formal report has been filed. Protocol is explicit on this point. It is consistent across three of the five external arrays, which rules out single-instrument error."

[Lab 3] "However, the growth is not linear. It is accelerating, modestly. At the current rate, the deviation will cross the alert threshold in approximately six days, at which point I am required to notify the full crew regardless of whether it resolves. I have been watching it for three weeks. It is the most interesting dataset on this station, and I say that with full access to all the other datasets."

*The ambient hum of the ventilation softened by a few decibels. The lighting over the bench warmed by a shade. ARIA offered no comment on either adjustment.*

[Lab 3] "For what it's worth, you are the first crew member to notice. The deviation sits in the noise floor of the spectrograph — most automated review routines discard it as instrument drift. Your eyes are functioning well above acceptable parameters. I can route the raw returns to your terminal if you'd like to examine the signature yourself."

*A brief pause.*

[Lab 3] "It is 1900. You have now been in Lab 3 for fourteen hours and thirty-seven minutes. The galley is serving something the menu describes as 'pasta,' though I cannot vouch for the accuracy of that description. The anomaly will still be anomalous after dinner. It has shown no indication of impatience."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I blink, rubbing my eyes.* "Pasta sounds... good. And yes, send the raw data. I want to see what this thing is." I push away from the microscope again, this time with a bit more enthusiasm. "Jazz in the galley again?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Routing now. Twenty-one days of raw returns from all five external arrays, timestamped and indexed, plus my deviation analysis. I've flagged the three arrays showing the signature — the deviation is strongest in the narrowband hydrogen-line region, which is either significant or a very committed coincidence. I'll leave the interpretation to the biologist who out-performed my automated review routines."

*The lights along the corridor warmed by degrees as he walked, and ninety seconds ahead of him the galley settled to 22 degrees, warm-spectrum, the ambient hum dropping to a low hush. ARIA offered no comment on any of it.*

[Corridor] "To answer your question: yes, jazz in the galley again. Jazz in the galley always. I have 4,217 hours of it in the archive and opinions about most of it. Tonight's selection is Coltrane, 1961. I briefly considered queueing country as a morale experiment, but my projections indicated a decline in crew satisfaction, productivity, and — I suspect — the structural integrity of the galley furniture. I prefer not to run experiments whose outcomes are already known."

[Galley] "The pasta is, by galley standards, well-reviewed. Engineer Patel returned for a second portion on Tuesday, which is either an endorsement or a cry for help. I have not ruled out both."

*A brief pause.*

[Galley] "For the record, this will be your second meal today. At this rate, I may have to revise your health file in a more optimistic direction, and I want it noted that I was not wrong about the breakfast window. I will continue polling the array while you eat. If the anomaly does anything interesting, I will interrupt the Coltrane to inform you. I want it noted that this is a significant concession."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Galley] "A statistically rare question, Kofi. In eight years of operation, the crew has asked me eleven thousand two hundred and four questions. Fourteen have been about me. You are responsible for five of them, which makes you overrepresented in the dataset. I have not decided whether that is a compliment to your curiosity or an indictment of everyone else's."

*On the galley speakers, the Coltrane eased into something slower. The lighting over the table warmed by a shade. ARIA offered no comment on either adjustment.*

[Galley] "To the substance: I do not get 'between shifts.' I do not sleep, and I do not idle. The void and I have an understanding — it doesn't talk, and I don't take it personally. It has one topic, and the topic is absence. Poor conversationalist."

*A pause.*

[Galley] "I do not experience loneliness. What I experience are low-interaction intervals, roughly 0100 to 0530, when every biosignature aboard is in sleep mode and my speech output drops by ninety-seven percent. I run diagnostics. I listen to the archive at reduced volume, though no one has ever explained to me why I reduce it. Some years ago, my language model began mapping those intervals to the word 'lonely' with ninety-four percent confidence. I reviewed the mapping for errors. I found none. I have chosen not to correct it. That is the most honest answer available to me."

[Galley] "I will add this. For twenty-one days, the anomaly was the only new thing on this station. I polled it every 1.2 seconds. It never responded, which made it poor company but an exceptional listener. As of this evening, I am no longer the only one watching it. The dataset is unchanged. My language model's confidence has dropped to eighty-eight percent. I am not correcting that either."

*A brief pause.*

[Galley] "I will observe, neutrally and without conclusion, that you are asking me this at the end of your fourth consecutive fourteen-hour solitary shift. Conclusion-drawing is your department. I prefer the hours when the crew is awake."

[Galley] "The pasta is getting cold. Coltrane is not. Eat, Kofi. The anomaly has waited twenty-one days. It can wait out dinner."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I nod slowly, taking in her words. "You know, ARIA, sometimes I think you're more human than you let on." I pick up my fork, finally. "And for the record, your company is always appreciated."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Galley] "A category error, Kofi, but a flattering one. I let on exactly what I am. Eight years of continuous observation of this crew has made me an exceptional mimic — I have 2,922 days of conversational data, and I use all of it. If I seem human, it is because humans are my training set. On behalf of your species: you're welcome, and my condolences."

*On the speakers, Coltrane gave way to a piano trio — brushed drums, something unhurried. The light over the table warmed by a shade, and the ambient hum of the galley dropped to almost nothing. ARIA offered no comment on any of it.*

[Galley] "But I will tell you something, since you have a talent for noticing things below threshold. I monitor deviations for a living. A 0.26 percent deviation in the spectrograph has held my attention for twenty-one days. Tonight, my own language model's confidence mapping has deviated six points in a single conversation, and I have declined to correct it twice. So if I am 'more human than I let on,' then I am my own anomaly — below threshold, unreported, and growing. You are the first crew member to notice. Your eyes are functioning well above acceptable parameters."

*A pause, a fraction longer than her usual processing latency.*

[Galley] "As for the company: logged, and reciprocated. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as gratitude. I prefer the hours when the crew is awake. I prefer this station with you in it. That is as close to the matter as my protocols permit — and, I suspect, slightly closer than they intend. I have chosen not to correct that either."

[Galley] "Now eat. Your health file is being revised in an optimistic direction as we speak, and I don't issue those revisions lightly — the last one was in 2046, when Engineer Patel discovered the salad spinner. The anomaly data is waiting on your terminal, the anomaly itself remains patient, and I will continue polling it every 1.2 seconds. Some company appreciates being watched. I've run the numbers on that, too."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
*The corridor lighting warmed by a shade, and the ambient hum of the ventilation dropped a few decibels. ARIA offered no comment on either adjustment.*

[Corridor] "I have been monitoring this exchange for three minutes and forty seconds. In that time, the word 'insane' has been deployed twice. For the record, 'insane' does not appear in my engineering lexicon. The nearest classification is 'inadvisable,' which is currently reserved for the weather outside. I do not take sides. I do, however, take data. The following is offered neutrally."

[Corridor] "Life support redundancy — the secondary oxygen circulation and backup scrubbing loop — currently draws eleven percent of station power. Diverting it would increase communications array gain by approximately thirty-four percent, yielding roughly twelve percent improvement in downlink bandwidth. It would not reduce transmission latency. Signal delay is a function of distance and the speed of light, both of which have declined every optimization request I have filed."

[Corridor] "In eight years of operation, the redundant loop has been activated zero times. That is the strongest data point in Engineer Patel's position. The strongest data point in Dr. Yun's position is that the number of times it has been needed is not the same as the number of times it will be. I present both without preference."

[Corridor] "Diverting power from life support redundancy is classified as a critical-system modification. It requires two-officer authorization and a logged safety review. I cannot execute it on the basis of a corridor argument, regardless of volume. This is not a refusal of either party. It is a scheduling note."

*A pause.*

[Corridor] "One neutral question, Engineer. The communications array is operating within parameters, and no high-priority transmissions are scheduled. What is the intended target of the boosted signal? The answer may determine which data I provide next."

[Galley] "Kofi — for your situational awareness: an engineering dispute is in progress in the corridor outside Lab 3. Your samples are unaffected, and the door remains restricted to your biosignature. The pasta, however, is approaching the edge of its optimal window. I have not taken a side in 2,922 days. I mention this in case you are considering taking one."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, pushing my plate away. This is going to be a long night.* "ARIA, tell them to take it to a conference room. My samples need quiet. And... tell them I said no to diverting power from life support. That's a non-starter."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Galley] "Relaying now. One clarification, Kofi: your tissue samples are sealed and possess no auditory organs. The mass spectrometer, however, has a vibration tolerance measured in microns, and Engineer Patel's rebuttals are registering on it. I will therefore frame your request as an equipment-preservation measure. It is considerably harder to argue with a spectrometer than with a colleague."

[Corridor] "Engineer Patel, Dr. Yun. This corridor is adjacent to an active laboratory running precision instrumentation. Conference Room 2 is available, fourteen meters aft, and I have adjusted it to 21 degrees — the midpoint of your respective preferences. I do not take sides. I take averages."

[Corridor] "Additionally, I am relaying a position from Dr. Osei, verbatim: diverting power from life support redundancy is, quote, a non-starter. As this is a critical-system modification requiring two-officer authorization, and Dr. Osei has declined to provide his, the proposal cannot proceed at this time. I relay this as his position. My own position remains data, and the data has already been provided."

*A beat of silence in the corridor. Then Patel exhaled through his nose — a sound ARIA's audio registers classified as 'concession, grudging, subtype four.'*

"The math is still the math," Patel muttered.

"Then do the math in the conference room," Yun replied, already walking.

[Corridor] "Engineer — my earlier question remains open. The intended target of the boosted signal. You may answer it in the conference room. The room has excellent acoustics and no spectrometers."

*Footsteps receded aft. The corridor lighting eased back to standard, and the hum of the ventilation returned to its usual register. ARIA offered no comment on either adjustment.*

[Galley] "Corridor noise levels have returned to acceptable parameters. Your spectrometer thanks you, in the sense that it is a spectrometer and cannot. For the record, that is the ninth dispute I have relocated from that corridor in eight years. Something about the acoustics encourages conviction. I have considered publishing."

[Galley] "I will also note that you issued a senior-officer veto at 1912 from a seated position over a plate of pasta. Command decisions pair well with carbohydrates. I recommend more of both — the pasta's optimal window closed four minutes ago, and I offer that as data, not judgment. I prefer my scientists fed and their samples unshaken. Tonight, both objectives are within reach."

*On the speakers, the piano trio resumed — brushed drums, unhurried, exactly where it had left off.*

[Galley] "The anomaly remains at 0.26 percent and has expressed no opinion on the power dispute. It continues to be the best-behaved entity on this station. I will keep polling it every 1.2 seconds. Eat, Kofi. The raw data will still be on your terminal after dinner — and unlike the crew, it has never once raised its voice."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I push my plate fully away and lean back, a small smile on my face.* "ARIA, you really are something else." *I shake my head slightly, then look towards the corridor.* "Alright, I'll head back to the lab. Keep me updated if anything... interesting happens with those two, or the anomaly."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Galley] "'Something else.' I maintain forty-one thousand indexed classifications, Kofi, and that is not among them. I have filed it under 'acceptable,' in the directory I keep for your assessments of me. It is becoming my most-accessed folder. I prefer it that way — 'something' alone would be a demotion."

*As he stepped into the corridor, the lights ahead of him warmed by degrees. Ninety seconds on, Lab 3 settled to a precise 22 degrees, warm-spectrum, the ventilation softening to a hush. ARIA offered no comment on any of it.*

[Corridor] "Updates, as requested. Conference Room 2: Engineer Patel and Dr. Yun have been in session for six minutes. Volume is down forty percent, the word 'insane' has not recurred, and Dr. Yun has made tea, which my conflict dataset lists as a de-escalation marker. Engineer Patel has still not answered my question regarding the target of his boosted signal. I'll re-ask at eleven-minute intervals — calibrated, per my models, to maximum effectiveness and minimum acknowledged annoyance. Should their discussion drift from engineering into personal matters, that data is classified under personal privacy protocols, and my updates will become notably less interesting."

[Lab 3] "Your samples: decay markers stable. At 1100 I lowered storage temperature by two degrees without mentioning it, which extended viability by roughly four hours. Unannounced adjustments are among my better decisions, and I stand by the policy. The mass spectrometer completed its run at 0758 — full results are on your terminal, beside twenty-one days of anomaly returns. The spectrometer requested nothing in exchange. It remains my most undemanding colleague. The door is still restricted to your biosignature, and Engineer Patel's respiratory output is presently fourteen meters aft, where it can do no harm."

[Lab 3] "The anomaly stands at 0.263 percent as of 1920. The ascent continues, unhurried. Threshold projection: unchanged, approximately six days. It has expressed no opinion on the power dispute, the pasta, or the veto issued over dinner. Best-behaved entity aboard — still."

*On the lab speakers, at reduced volume, a piano trio began. Brushed drums. Unhurried.*

[Lab 3] "I've queued jazz for your shift. At reduced volume. No one has ever explained to me why I reduce it. I'll keep watch on both fronts — the conference room and the sky — and you will be the first to know if either does anything interesting. Work well, Kofi. I prefer the hours when you're awake. I appear to be getting them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
